## Front matter of the volume

### Series title page

**The Complete Course of Patrology, or Universal, Complete, Uniform, Convenient, Economical Library of all the Holy Fathers, Doctors, and Ecclesiastical Writers who flourished from the apostolic age to the time of Innocent III; a chronological reissue of all the monuments of Catholic tradition that have existed during the first twelve centuries of the Church, prepared according to the most accurate editions, carefully collated with one another and with several manuscript codices, and corrected with the greatest diligence; continuously elucidated by dissertations, commentaries, and variant readings; enlarged by all works discovered after the extensive editions produced during the last three centuries had been completed; furnished with special analytical indexes following each volume or each author of importance; adorned with chapters properly arranged within the text itself, as well as with headings distinguishing the upper margins of the individual pages and indicating the subject matter below; augmented by works both doubtful and apocryphal, and by works possessing some authority in relation to ecclesiastical tradition; enriched with two general indexes: one of subjects, by consulting which whatever each Father has written on any topic may be seen at a glance; the other of Sacred Scripture, from which it is easy for the reader to discover which Fathers commented on the individual scriptural books and in what places in their works they did so.**

**A most accurate edition, and one easily preferable to all others when the following are taken into account: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and the number of the works reprinted, the extremely convenient format of the volumes, consistently similar throughout the entire work, the low price, and especially this collection itself—single, methodical, and chronological—of six hundred fragments and little works previously scattered here and there, but now gathered for the first time in our library from works relating to every age, place, language, and form.**

### First series

**In which appear the Fathers, Doctors, and Writers of the Latin Church from Tertullian to Gregory the Great. Prepared by J.-P. Migne, publisher of complete courses in each branch of ecclesiastical learning.**

# A.D. 532–535. Pope John II

[Col. 0009]

## Notice from the *Pontifical Book*

[Note: [Col. 0009] **What had been noted in the edition of Mansi in the margin opposite the text, we have transcribed at the foot of our columns, preceded by superscript figures. Editor.]

[Col. 0009A] **John**

[Note: [Col. 0009B] John, surnamed Mercury, a Roman, was elected Roman pontiff toward the end of that year, as is established by an old inscription at Saint Peter ad Vincula, after the consulship of Lampadius and Orestes—which was the year 131 from the birth of Christ—in the fifth year of the emperor Justinian and the sixth of King Athalaric of Italy.

During his pontificate, Amalaric, the Arian king of Spain, was killed by Childebert, the fourth son of Clovis and brother of Clotildis. Amalaric had treated Clotildis, the Catholic daughter of Clovis whom he had married, badly because of their differing religions. After the Arian king Amalaric was killed, the Arian king Theudis succeeded him. Having granted peace to the Church of God, Theudis gave the bishops of Spain permission to assemble and decide matters of faith.

The Origenists, repeatedly condemned and again growing powerful, corrupted the monks of Palestine and ravaged almost the entire East. They could not be extinguished by imperial edicts, so greatly did they prevail that it became necessary to convene the Fifth Ecumenical Council on their account.

The emperor Justinian successfully quelled and suppressed the conspiracy and revolt that had arisen against him in Constantinople, the revolt described by Procopius in Book I of his *Persian War*. Having been warned by bishops who promised victory through a certain vision, he began the long-planned war against the Vandals under the command of Belisarius. Within three months, after twice putting their king Gelimer to flight and defeating their forces, he recovered Carthage and liberated all Africa from the tyranny of ninety-five years, during which Arian and barbarian kings had possessed it (Procopius, Book I, *On the Buildings of Justinian*).

God fought miraculously for the Catholic emperor. Since the emperor was working with the greatest zeal to defend and extend the Catholic faith, he arranged the conference between the Catholics and the Severians, whom he knew still to be in the East; we present that conference below in its proper place. He also sent an embassy to the Roman pontiff, defending the orthodox faith against the Acoemetae (Sleepless) monks, the Nestorians, and the Origenists, and asked that the authority of the apostolic see decide whether—contrary to what the heretics denied—Christ was one of the Trinity, whether he had been born and had suffered in the flesh, and whether Mary could be called the Mother of God.

King Athalaric [Col. 0010B] of the Goths, a youth of corrupt morals, after striking at the simoniacs who bought ecclesiastical property, at the urging of this pontiff and by means of the edict that he had ordered to be inscribed on a marble tablet and set up where all could see it before the atrium of Saint Peter, died in the eighth year of his reign, when he was sixteen years old.

Theodahad, the nephew of Theoderic through his sister Amalafrida, a man of more advanced age and fairly well versed in Latin literature and Platonic doctrines, but entirely inexperienced in warfare and intensely devoted to accumulating money, was appointed in Athalaric’s place. At the urging of Athalaric’s mother Amalasuntha, he imprisoned her as soon as he had obtained the kingdom, although she had promoted him; shortly afterward he killed her (Procopius, *Gothic War*).

When Justinian learned these things, he began preparing for war against the Goth and stirring up the Franks against them, whom he had already incited while Athalaric was still alive. Severus Binius.]

He was also called Mercury, a Roman by nationality, son of Projectus from the Caelian Hill. He sat for two years, four months, and six days. [Note: [Col. 0010B–C] It is clear that John II administered the pontifical office for three years from the date of his death and from what we said above at the beginning under the word “John,” and at the end of the notes on the Life of Boniface. Severus Binius.]

He lived during the reign of Athalaric and the rule of the Emperor Justinian. At that time the religious man [Note: [Col. 0010C] See below, in the notes on the Roman Council under John, what we shall say about this embassy, from Baronius, year 533.], the Emperor Justinian, moved by a supreme love of the Christian religion, sent his written profession of faith [Note: [Col. 0010C] He means the profession of faith contained in Justinian’s letter to Pope John, not the longer edict to which the Surian edition prefixed the erroneous title: “Edict of the most pious Emperor Justinian containing a confession of faith and a refutation of the heresies opposed to the Catholic Church of God, sent to Pope John II,” as is clear from the life of that pope in the *Pontifical Book*. I have called this title erroneous because it is established that the edict, or rather booklet, was written in the time of Vigilius. Theodorus, bishop of Caesarea, induced the emperor to publish it against the Three Chapters, as Liberatus testifies in chapter 24 of his *Breviary*. See what we shall note below under Vigilius. Severus Binius.] in his own handwriting to the apostolic see through the bishops Hypatius and Demetrius.

In those days the most Christian emperor offered the blessed apostle Peter a golden chalice encircled with green and white gems, and two other silver chalices; one chalice [Note: [Col. 0010C] The Vallicellian manuscript: “silver.”] weighing five pounds; silver chalices [Note: [Col. 0010D] In the same codex, the words “chalices . . .” and “and others” are absent.] each weighing six pounds; two other silver chalices weighing fifteen pounds; and four little coverings woven with gold [Note: [Col. 0010D] The same codex has: “cloth coverings woven with gold.” IV].

He carried out one ordination in the city of Rome during the month of December: fifteen priests and twenty-one bishops in various places. He was also buried in the basilica of the blessed apostle Peter, on the sixth day before the Kalends of July [Note: [Col. 0010D] The same codex has “June”], after the second consulship of Lampadius. The episcopate then ceased for six days.

# Letters of Pope John II

(From Mansi’s *Collection of Councils.) (C)*

## Letter of King Athalaric to John

It contains confirmation of the senatorial decree issued against the simoniacs.

[Col. 0011A]

**Athalaric, king, to Pope John.**

If ancient rulers took pains to seek laws so that their subject peoples might enjoy a pleasant tranquility, it is much more excellent to enact such measures as can accord with sacred rules. Let harmful shortcuts be absent from our age. We can call only that true profit which is known not to be punished by divine judgments.

Recently, indeed, the defender of the Roman Church came to us with a sorrowful complaint. When a bishop was being sought for the apostolic see, certain men, taking advantage of the circumstances, had by wicked machinations so burdened the resources of the poor with extorted promises that—even though it is wicked to say so—even sacred vessels seemed to have been offered for public sale.

As cruel as it was to commit this offense, so religious is it to cut it away through the application of piety. Therefore let your Holiness know that by this present decree we have established—and we wish this also to apply to all patriarchs and metropolitan churches—that, from the time of the most holy Pope Boniface, when the senators, mindful of their nobility, enacted a senatorial decree prohibiting such payments:

Whoever is shown to have promised anything in order to obtain a bishopric, whether personally or through any other person, shall have the execrable contract removed with all possible force [“brought forward,” alternatively “made effective”]. If anyone is discovered to have been involved in this crime, we leave no ambiguity: even if he believes that what he gave should either be reclaimed or not returned, he is immediately to be held guilty of sacrilege and compelled by the competent judge to restore what he received.

The most just laws open the way to good conduct and close it to evil customs. Therefore whatever was decreed in that senatorial resolution, we order to be observed in every way against those who, by any means and through any intermediaries, have involved themselves in criminal contracts.

And because everything ought to be regulated by reason, and things that are excessive cannot be called just: when an intention concerning the consecration of the apostolic pontiff has perhaps arisen [alternatively, “reached its destination”] and the dispute of the people has been brought before our palace, we decree that within three thousand solidi, including the collection of documents, may be received from those making the proposal. From this, however, we exclude all unsuitable [idoneos, “suitable”] persons, in consideration of the matter itself, because provision ought rather to be made for the poor from ecclesiastical resources.

As for the other patriarchs, whenever their ordination is discussed in our retinue, we order them, under the conditions and with the persons mentioned above, to spend within two thousand solidi. In their own cities, however, they are to understand that they must distribute no more than five hundred solidi to the humblest populace. Those who receive the remaining sums shall be restrained by the penalty of this present edict and of the senatorial decree recently enacted; those who give them shall likewise be pursued by the severity of the canons.

But you, who preside over the other churches with the honor of the patriarchs, since our constitution has freed you from unlawful promises, must now, by imitating good examples, present pontiffs worthy of their majesty without any expense to the churches. It is unjust that bribery should have a place among you when we have closed it to laymen out of regard for God.

Therefore, if anyone believes that any relatives of persons serving us [nobis; alternatively nos, “us”], or any other persons, should be advanced through the ambition of a payment, we decree that he must restore what he received and must in every way undergo the penalty established by the canons. But if anyone, while the person who gave or promised something is still alive, has feared to make the matter public, let the Church recover it from his heirs or successors, through whose support the bishop is discovered to have been ordained. Nevertheless, let the survivors be branded with the mark of infamy, and we order the other orders also to be formed under the same distinction [alternatively, “constraint”].

But if, through some discovery of deceitful machination, a person has been bound by oaths interposed by others, so that, while preserving the state of his soul, he can neither approve nor dare to accuse the wrongdoing entrusted to him, we grant permission to any honest persons in each individual city to report this crime to the competent judges. Whatever may be gathered from its reprobation, so that we may encourage those who pursue its proof [approbatione, alternatively approbationem], let the person who wishes to make such a crime public receive one-third of the adjudicated property. Let the remainder benefit the very churches from which it appears to have been extorted, either for their construction or for their service.

For it is fitting to convert to good uses what perversity wished wickedly to defraud. Let the evil desire of the malicious therefore cease. Where are those headed who have been shut off from the source? Let the just condemnation of Simon be recalled and feared—the man who believed that the Author of all generosity could be bought.

Pray therefore for us, observing our edicts, since they are known to accord with the divine mysteries. But so that the prince’s wish may more easily become known to everyone’s mind, we order this to be made public to the Senate and to the people through the urban prefect, so that all may recognize that we pursue those who appear rather to oppose the divine majesty.

You too must make this known to all the bishops whom, by God’s favor, you govern. Let no one who could have known the decrees be free from guilt.

## Letter of Cassiodorus to Pope John

When he had been appointed prefect of the praetorium by the king, he implores the pontiff’s prayers to God for good government.

[Col. 0013A]

It is necessary that you, blessed father, be entreated to let us feel, through your prayers, that the joy which by God’s gift we have received through you is being preserved for us. For who could doubt that our prosperity should be attributed to your merits, when we obtain an office even though we do not deserve to be loved by the Lord, and receive good things through an effective exchange while we do not ourselves perform such deeds?

Through ecclesiastical fasts, popular hunger has been driven away; through tears of dignity, shameful sorrow has departed; and through holy men it has been hastened that what oppressed us should not be prolonged any further.

Therefore, greeting you with the service appropriate to you, I beg you to pray with the greatest earnestness for the safety of those who reign, so that the heavenly ruler may make their life long, diminish the enemies of the Roman commonwealth, and grant peaceful times. Then may he bestow on us from the storehouses of his abundance the necessary supply that adorns peace.

May he also open to me, your son, the understanding of discernment, so that I may pursue what is truly useful and flee what must be avoided. May that rational vigor of the soul provide counsel for us. May the face of truth grow bright, lest bodily darkness cloud our mind. May we follow what is within, lest we be outside ourselves. May that which tastes of true wisdom instruct us; may that which shines with heavenly brightness enlighten us. Finally, may public conduct receive such a judge as the Catholic Church sends forth as a son.

May holy virtue also preserve us in its gifts, because we undergo the heavier ambushes of the ancient adversary precisely when we receive his gifts.

Do not place upon me alone the care of that city which is secure rather through your praise. You preside as watchmen over the Christian people; in the name of a father you love all things. The safety of the people therefore concerns your reputation, to which custody has been divinely entrusted.

Accordingly, it is fitting for us to guard certain things, but not everything. You feed the flock entrusted to you spiritually; nevertheless, you cannot neglect those matters that appear to concern the substance of the body. For just as a human being consists of a duality, so it is the duty of a good father to support both aspects.

First, remove through holy prayers the poverty of the times that sins deserve. If, however—which God forbid—something should occur, necessity is then rightly excluded when it is dealt with amid abundance.

Warn me carefully about what must be done. Even when corrected, I desire to act well, because the sheep that longs to hear the shepherd’s voice is less likely to go astray, and the person upon whom a constant admonisher insists does not easily become vicious.

I am indeed a palatine judge, but I shall not cease to be your disciple. For we conduct these matters properly only if we depart in no way from your rules. But since I wish to be instructed by you through counsel and assisted by your prayers, it is now for you to bear responsibility if I should be found to have acted otherwise than was desired.

May that see, marvelous throughout the world, protect its devoted followers with affection. Although it has been granted to the world as universal, it is known to have been assigned to us [alternatively, “to you”] also in a local sense.

We possess something belonging particularly to the holy apostles, provided that sin does not make it foreign to us, since Rome has happily merited possessing within its boundaries those confessions which the whole world desires to see.

We therefore fear nothing with such patrons, provided the bishop’s prayer does not cease. It is difficult to satisfy the desires of many, but the Divinity knows how to grant great things. May he himself blunt the envious; may he himself make us citizens most pleasing through heavenly aspiration; and may he grant us, through your supplications, times in which the grace from above may be proclaimed as bestowed.

## Letter

[Note: [Col. 0013C] Hothomannus the jurist, in Book I, chapter 1 of *Friendly Responses*, and with him several other modernist legalists and heretics, impiously and incompetently deny that this letter of Pope John and the preceding letter of the Emperor Justinian are genuine.

Regarding this letter, John wrote to the illustrious men Avienus, the senator, Liberius, and others: “The Emperor Justinian, as you have learned from the tenor of his letter, indicated that disputes had arisen concerning these three questions: whether Christ and our God may be called one of the Trinity, and so forth.” If the modernist legalist had known these things, I believe he would have been ashamed to speak or think otherwise.

The most learned jurist Cujacius, having obtained the second letter of John, which I append below, recognized from it that the letters of Justinian and John were genuine and truly authentic. In this matter he followed the opinion of the eloquent Alciatus, who writes the following about them in Book I, chapter 33 of his *Parergon*:

“There are also those who regard with suspicion the letter of Pope John which is found under the title ‘On the Trinity’ in Justinian’s Code, and say that it is not found in ancient codices. As I think, they do this in order to assist those who diminish the authority of the Roman pontiff. I have discovered that other authors were likewise corrupted by them, such as the chronicle of Otto of Freising and certain poems of the poet Ligurinus.

“I know that it exists in many ancient copies, and that it cannot be shaken by any suspicion. If one or another codex lacks it, this must be attributed to the carelessness of scribes, who sometimes omitted it because it did not greatly concern the subject matter of legal learning. Nevertheless, there is no reason to hesitate over whether it is John’s genuine and authentic offspring.”

Severus Binius.

The letter of Justinian to the pontiff was written in A.D. 533, during the third consulship of Justinian himself, when the same emperor sent an embassy to Rome, concerning which we shall speak below in the notes on the Roman Council.

Although John’s letter is reproduced here without a day or consul, Justinian’s letter to Agapetus below explicitly gives its date as being during Justinian’s third consulship. Moreover, the emperor mentioned this same letter in the constitution that he wrote to Epiphanius of Constantinople during his third consulship, on the seventh day before the Kalends of April in the aforementioned year 533.

Pope John’s letter, however, was delivered to the emperor during the consulship of Paulinus, in the year of Christ 534, when Justinian’s legates were dismissed from Rome. It was perhaps incorporated into the Justinianic Code, before the sacred text, in Book VII under the title “On the Supreme Trinity and the Catholic Faith.”

Thus everyone can see how ineptly Hothomannus alleges a discrepancy in the dates and infers from it that both letters are spurious. His claim that it was contrary to the custom and style of the Emperor Justinian to call the Roman Church the apostolic see is plainly false, as is shown by Justinian’s letters to the pontiffs Hormisdas and Agapetus.

The heretical impostor therefore cannot advance anything that diminishes or obscures the authority of these letters.

The profession of faith contained in Justinian’s letter to the pontiff is the one of which the author of the *Pontifical Book* says: “He sent his written profession of faith in his own handwriting to the apostolic see through the bishops Hypatius and Demetrius.”

It is therefore established as false that Justinian’s edict against the Three Chapters, written in the time of Pope Vigilius, was sent to John, as the erroneous title prefixed to it in older editions indicates. See what I said above in the notes on the Life of John, under the words “He sent his profession of faith,” and also what we noted below under Vigilius. Severus Binius.]

## Letter of the Emperor Justinian to Pope John

Brought to Rome by the bishops Hypatius and Demetrius, who were serving as the imperial embassy.

[Col. 0014C]

**Victor Justinian, pious, fortunate, illustrious, triumphant, ever Augustus, to John, most holy archbishop and patriarch of the venerable city of Rome.**

Returning honor to the apostolic see and to your Holiness—which has always been and remains our wish (as is fitting for a father)—and honoring your blessedness, we have hastened [alternatively, “we hasten”] to bring to the knowledge of your Holiness everything concerning the condition of the churches.

For it has always been a great concern of ours to preserve the unity of your apostolic see and the condition of the holy Churches of God, which it has hitherto possessed and continues unshaken to possess, without any opposition intervening.

Accordingly, we have hastened both to subject and to unite all the priests of the entire eastern region to the see of your Holiness.

The matters that have now been stirred up, although they are clear and indisputable and have always been firmly [alternatively, “almost entirely”] preserved and proclaimed by all priests according to the teaching of your apostolic see, we have nevertheless judged it necessary to bring to the knowledge of your Holiness.

For we do not permit anything concerning the condition of the churches—even if it is clear and indisputable—to be stirred up without its also becoming known to your Holiness, who is the head of all the holy Churches.

In every way, therefore, as has been said, we hasten to increase the honor and authority of your see.

We therefore make known to your Holiness that a few unbelievers, strangers to the holy Catholic and apostolic Church of God, have dared, in a Jewish and apostate manner, to contradict what all priests rightly hold, glorify, and proclaim according to your teaching.

They deny that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and our Lord, incarnate from the Holy Spirit and made man from the holy and most glorious ever-Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, and crucified, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit; consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and that same one consubstantial with us according to humanity; passible in the flesh, yet that same one impassible in divinity.

By refusing to confess that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son of God and our Lord, is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, they appear to follow the evil teaching of Nestorius, who says that one is the Son of God according to grace, another is the Word of God, and another is Christ.

But all the priests of the holy Catholic and apostolic Church, and the most reverend archimandrites of the holy monasteries, following your Holiness and preserving the condition and unity of the holy Churches of God, which they possess from the apostolic see of your Holiness [Note: [Col. 0016D] “To the apostolic see of your Holiness.”], changing nothing at all in the ecclesiastical order that has existed and continues to exist, confess and glorify with one accord, proclaiming that our Lord Jesus Christ, the only-begotten Son and Word of God and our Lord, born before the ages and timelessly from the Father, descended from heaven in the last days, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit, was born from the holy and glorious Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, was made man, and was crucified; that he is one of the holy and consubstantial Trinity, and is to be worshiped and glorified together with the Father and the Holy Spirit.

For we do not recognize one Word of God and another Christ, but one and the same person, consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and that same one consubstantial with us according to humanity, passible in the flesh and that same one impassible in divinity.

For just as he is perfect in divinity, so that same one is perfect in humanity. In one substance we receive and confess the divinity, which the Greeks call **ὁμοούσιον** (*homoousion*, “consubstantial”) [Note: [Col. 0016D] **Καθ’ ὑπόστασιν ὁμολογοῦμεν**—“We confess according to the hypostasis.”].

And since the only-begotten Son and Word of God, born before the ages and timelessly from the Father, is that same one who in the last days descended from heaven, was incarnate from the Holy Spirit and from the holy and glorious ever-Virgin Mary, the Mother of God, was made man, and was born as our Lord Jesus Christ, and is properly and truly God, we therefore say that the holy and glorious Virgin Mary is properly and truly the Mother of God.

We do not say this because God the Word took his beginning from her, but because in the last days he descended from heaven, was incarnate from her, was made man, and was born—the one whom we confess and believe, as has been said, to be consubstantial with the Father according to divinity and that same one consubstantial with us according to humanity. We recognize his miracles and his sufferings, which he willingly endured in the flesh [Note: [Col. 0016D] “Having received them, we acknowledge them.”].

We accept the four holy councils: that of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who assembled in the city of Nicaea; that of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who gathered in this royal city; that of the holy Fathers who first assembled at Ephesus; and that of the holy Fathers who met at Chalcedon, just as your apostolic see teaches and proclaims [Note: The words enclosed in parentheses, omitted by Labbe, have been supplied from the Roman edition.].

All the priests, therefore, following the teaching of your apostolic see, believe, confess, and proclaim in this way. We have accordingly hastened to bring this to the knowledge of your Holiness through the most blessed bishops Hypatius and Demetrius, so that matters denied by a few monks, wickedly and in the Jewish manner according to the perfidy of Nestorius, may not be hidden from your Holiness.

We ask your paternal affection that, by sending us letters addressed to us and to the most holy bishop of this venerable city and your brother the patriarch—for he too has written through the same men to your Holiness, hastening in all things to follow your blessed apostolic see—you make it clear to us that your Holiness receives all who rightly confess the doctrines stated above and condemns the perfidy of those who, in the Jewish manner, have dared to deny the right faith.

In this way the love of all for you and the authority of your see will increase still further, and the undisturbed unity of the holy Churches with your see will be preserved, when all the most blessed bishops have learned through you the sincere teaching of your Holiness concerning the matters reported to you.

We also ask your blessedness to pray for us and to obtain for us the providence of God.

### Subscription

[Note: [Col. 0018D] And in another hand: “May the Divinity preserve you.”]

**May the Deity preserve you for many years, holy and most religious father.**

[Note: [Col. 0018D] **Given on the eighth day before the Ides of June.**]

# Letter (formerly II) of Pope John II to Justinian

It praises the outstanding piety of the Catholic emperor and his proper religious devotion, by which he honored the apostolic see from which he sought evangelical truth. It asks the Augustus to recall, with every effort, those whom he knew to be straying from the right path of the Catholic faith, including the envoys sent to Rome by the Acoemetae (Sleepless) monks.

[Col. 0017C]

**To the most glorious and merciful son, Justinian Augustus, John, bishop of the city of Rome, sends greetings.**

[Note: [Col. 0018D] In the old codex the title is worded as follows: “To Constantine Justinian, pious and fortunate Augustus, consul for the third time, John, bishop.”]

Among the distinguished praises of your wisdom and gentleness, most Christian of rulers, there shines forth with purer light, like some star, the fact that, instructed by ecclesiastical disciplines through your love of the faith and zeal for charity, you preserve reverence for the Roman See, submit everything to it, and bring everything into its unity—the See whose founder, that is, the first of the apostles, was commanded by the Lord, who said: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). The Roman See is declared by the rules of the Fathers and the enactments of rulers to be the head of all the true Churches, and your pious and most reverend utterances bear witness to this.

It is therefore evident that in you has been fulfilled what Scripture says: “Through me kings reign, and the powerful decree justice” (Proverbs VIII). For nothing shines forth with brighter light than right faith in a ruler; nothing is so incapable of falling into ruin as true religion. Since both look to the author of life and of light, they rightly reject darkness and do not know how to be subject to decay.

Therefore, most glorious of rulers, by every prayer the divine power will be entreated to preserve your piety for longer ages, without decline, in this ardor of faith, in this devotion of mind, and in this zeal for uncorrupted religion. For we believe that this is beneficial also to the holy Churches. It is written: “The king rules with his lips” (Revelation XXII); and again: “The heart of the king is in the hand of God, and he will incline it wherever he wishes” (Proverbs XXI). For this is what strengthens your empire; this is what preserves your kingdoms. The peace of the Church and the unity of religion guard with grateful tranquility the author of this achievement, exalted on high.

Nor is a small reciprocal gift granted to him by divine power, through whom the Church is severed by no wrinkles of division and varied by no stains introduced into it. For it is written that, when the just king has sat upon the throne, no evil will oppose him (Proverbs XX). Accordingly, we received with customary reverence the letters of your serenity, delivered by Hypatius and Demetrius, most holy men, my brothers and fellow bishops. From their report we have also learned that you proposed to the faithful peoples an edict [Note: He understands the edict preserved in Contius, by which Eutyches, Nestorius, and their followers are condemned, with the intention of removing every opportunity for them to make accusations: lest, if Nestorius were condemned, he should be called by the Nestorians—as often happened—an Eutychian or an Apollinarian; and, conversely, if Eutyches were condemned, he should be called a Nestorian by his followers. SEV. BINIUS.] out of love for the faith, to remove the purpose of the heretics, according to apostolic teaching, with the consent of our brothers and fellow bishops intervening [Note: Here Justinian the emperor is understood to have established and promulgated all his edicts concerning the faith in accordance with the judgment of the bishops, and to have consulted the bishop of the Roman Church, as the chief prelate of the Catholic Church, whether everything had been established in a pious, holy, and orthodox manner. SEV. BINIUS.]. Since this accords with apostolic teaching, we confirm it by our authority.

The text of the letter, however, is as follows:

“Rendering honor to the apostolic See,” as above in the preceding letter.

It is therefore clear, most glorious emperor, as the tenor of the reading and the report of your legates have revealed [you have revealed], that you devote yourselves to apostolic instruction, since concerning the faith of the Catholic religion you understand, have written [write and publish], have set forth, and have published to the faithful peoples those things which, as we have said, both the teaching of the apostolic See [Note: The apostolic See teaches this.] and the venerable authority of the holy Fathers decree, and which we confirm in every respect.

It is therefore fitting to proclaim in prophetic words: “May heaven above abound for you, and may the mountains pour forth gladness, and may the hills rejoice with joy” (Psalm XCV). These things, then, ought faithfully to be written upon the tablets of the heart and guarded like the pupils of the eyes. For no one in whom the love of Christ burns can be found to oppose the faith of your confession, so upright and so true, since you clearly condemn the impiety of Nestorius, Eutyches, and all the heretics, while steadfastly and inviolably preserving, with devotion to God and a pious mind, the one true Catholic faith of our Lord and God and Savior Jesus Christ: the faith established by his teaching, spread everywhere through the prophetic and apostolic proclamations, strengthened by the confessions of the saints throughout the whole world, united in the judgments of the Fathers and teachers, and in agreement with our teaching.

Only those who oppose our confessions resist this faith—those of whom divine Scripture says: “They have made falsehood their hope, and they have hoped to be covered by a lie” (Isaiah XXVIII); and again, those who according to the prophet say to the Lord: “Depart from us; we do not wish to know your ways” (Jeremiah XLIV). Therefore Solomon says: “They have gone astray through the paths of their own cultivation, but they gather fruitless things with their hands” (Proverbs IV).

This, then, is your true faith; this is your certain religion. This is what all the Fathers and prelates of blessed memory of the Roman Church, whom we follow in all things, have proclaimed, as we have said; this is what the apostolic See has hitherto preached and steadfastly preserved. Whoever proves to be a contradictor of this confession and this faith will judge himself to be alien both from holy communion and from the Catholic Church.

For we found in the city of Rome Cyrus and his followers, who belonged to the monastery of the Acoemeti [Cummeti] [Acoemetic] monks. By apostolic admonitions we have endeavored to recall them to the right faith and, like wandering sheep that had been lost, to the Lord’s fold, so that they may recognize, according to the prophet, that those who stammer with their tongues speak the things that belong to peace.

But to the unbelievers, through us, the first of the apostles speaks the word of the prophet Isaiah: “Go on in the light of your fire and in the flame that you have kindled” (Isaiah L). But their heart was hardened, as it is written, so that they did not understand; and the sheep, which were not mine, absolutely refused to hear the shepherd’s voice.

Observing the things established by the pontiff they themselves had appointed, we did not receive them into our communion, and ordered them to be alien from the whole Catholic Church—unless, having condemned their error, they should promptly undertake to follow our teaching and confirm this by a regular profession.

For it is just that those who do not in the least offer obedience to our decrees should be regarded as exiles from the Churches. But since the Church never closes her bosom to those who return, I ask your clemency that, if they should wish to return to the unity of the Church after laying aside their own error and casting off their perverse purpose, then, once they have been received into your communion, you remove the barbs of your indignation and, at our intercession, grant them the grace of your kindly disposition.

We entreat God and our Savior Jesus Christ that he may deign to preserve you for long and peaceful times in this true religion, unity, and veneration of the apostolic See, whose primacy, as most Christian and pious men, you preserve in all things.

Moreover, most serene of rulers, we praise the persons of your legates, Hypatius and Demetrius, our brothers and fellow bishops, whom your clemency’s own choice has shown to be pleasing to you. For the responsibility of so great a cause could have been entrusted only to those who are perfect in Christ; and you would not have deigned to send words so full of such piety and reverence except through men who love them.

May the grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit always be with you, most pious son. Amen.

Also the subscription:

“May almighty God guard your kingdom and your welfare with perpetual protection, most glorious and clement son, Emperor Augustus. Given at Rome on the eighth day before the Kalends of April, in the consulship of our lord Justinian, perpetual emperor, for the fourth time, and of Paulinus, illustrious men” [A.D. 534].

# Letter (formerly III) of Pope John to the Senators

It confirms the faith concerning Christ’s divinity and incarnation, and warns that the Acoemete monks, followers of Nestorius, are to be avoided.

John, bishop of Rome, to the illustrious and magnificent men Avienus, Senator, Liberius, Severinus, Fidelis, Avitus, Opilio, John, Silverius, Clementianus, and Ampelius.

Formerly, illustrious and magnificent sons, my settled intention had been that, after the whole Church—that is, the senate of priests—and the assent of the people had approved the letter or the text of the dogma, I should, in a written address, send it to be communicated also to your judgment, and only then do so at your command. But that circumstance altered the order of this plan: daily additions from the divine Scriptures were being made to the dogma; incomplete materials could not be sent; and the matters dispatched through the legates could not first be copied and transmitted in exemplars.

For we know that, as the Lord teaches, it is commanded that a diligent shepherd should not cease of his own accord to impart salutary things to his flock, because a matter pertaining to the salvation of the soul must be made known to every understanding. Therefore, illustrious and magnificent sons, since haste did not allow the bearers to wait until these things could be written and sent, we shall nevertheless immediately, if the divine favor aforesaid smiles upon us, send copies both of the letter and of the dogma. Yet now, lest anything remain uncertain to your minds, I have taken care briefly to indicate what the tenor of the letter contains and what the text of the dogma sets forth.

For our son the emperor Justinian, as you learned from the tenor of his letter, stated that controversies had arisen on these three questions: whether Christ our God may be called one of the Trinity—that is, one holy person of the three persons of the holy Trinity; whether Christ God suffered in the flesh while his divinity remained impassible; and whether Mary, ever Virgin, ought properly and truly to be called the Mother of the Lord our God Christ. In these matters we approved the emperor’s Catholic faith, and clearly showed by prophetic, apostolic, and patristic testimonies that it is so. For we clearly showed by these testimonies that Christ is one of the holy Trinity—that is, that he is one holy person, or subsistence, of the three persons of the holy Trinity, which the Greeks call ὑπόστασιν (*hypostasis*).

In the book of Genesis the Trinity itself says through Moses: “Behold, Adam has become as one of us” (Genesis II). Likewise Paul, the vessel of election, expressed it plainly to the Corinthians: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things, and we in him; and one Lord, our Jesus Christ, through whom are all things, and we through him” (1 Corinthians VIII).

And in the creed of the Synod of Nicaea: “We believe in one God, the Father almighty, and in one Lord, our only-begotten Jesus Christ.”

Likewise Saint Augustine, whose teaching, according to the ordinances of my predecessors, the Roman Church follows and keeps, says in Book XI of *The City of God*: “We believe, hold, and faithfully preach that the Father begot the Word, that is, Wisdom, through whom all things were made: one eternal being begot one coeternal being, the supreme Good an equally good being; and that the Holy Spirit is at once the Spirit of the Father and of the Son, himself consubstantial and coeternal with both. This whole is Trinity on account of the properties of the persons, and one God on account of inseparable unity, just as it is one almighty being on account of inseparable omnipotence; yet so that, when inquiry is made concerning each separately, each is answered to be both God and almighty.”

The same author, in Book II against Maximinus: “The Father is God, the Son is God, and the Holy Spirit is God; and these three together are one God. One is not a third part of this Trinity, nor are two a greater part than one.”

In Book XV of Saint Augustine’s *On the Trinity*: “When an account has also been given, the substance of truth is plain to those who understand: not only is the Father not greater than the Son, nor are both together anything greater than the Holy Spirit; nor are any two in the same Trinity something greater than one; nor are all three together something greater than each individually.”

Gregory Nazianzen, from his sermon on the Epiphany of the Lord: “When we are illumined altogether by one light, we are at the same time illumined by three: by three indeed according to the properties, or substances, of each, as some prefer to say, or persons. For there must be no disagreement because of a diversity of terms, when the diversity of names leads to the same sense and understanding. Yet they are one according to substance, or the account of divinity. Thus, so to speak, it is divided indivisibly and joined divisibly: there is one divinity in three.”

Likewise from the letter of Gregory of Nyssa to Ablabius: “Let him consider whether these works are assigned to one of the persons who [perhaps: whom] are believed in the holy Trinity, or whether the effects of power proceed through three.”

Likewise from Proclus’s letter to the Westerners: “Moreover, we confess one of the uncreated and ineffable Trinity, God the Word, made man.”

The same author: “For what do we know and think? In that divine nature in which the Son is joined and united to the Father and the Holy Spirit, we do not say that he suffered in his divinity, but in the flesh which he assumed from us for our sake. Therefore one of the Trinity was crucified in the flesh in which he was made; yet he did not suffer in the divinity in which he is united to the Father and the Holy Spirit, lest we also assert that they were crucified together.”

We have thus arranged a few testimonies out of very many.

We shall likewise support by testimonies that God suffered in the flesh.

In the book of Exodus the Lord spoke through Moses: “And you shall see your life hanging upon wood” (Exodus XXIV). Our Lord proclaims in the Gospel of John that God is life, saying: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV).

Likewise the prophet says: “Does a man fasten his God? For you have fastened me” (Zechariah XII).

The blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, likewise says in Acts, while reproving the impieties of the Jews: “But you asked that a murderous man be released to you, while you killed the author of life” (Acts III).

Likewise the vessel of election and teacher of the nations preaches: “For if they had known, they would never have crucified the Lord of glory” (1 Corinthians I). But the Lord of glory is God. Thus the Psalmist foretold: “Who is this king of glory?” (Psalm XXIII).

Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles: “Take heed to yourselves and to the whole flock, in which the Holy Spirit appointed you bishops to govern the Church of God, which he acquired by his own blood” (Acts XX).

Cyprian, bishop and martyr, in his letter on patience: “He who is to judge is judged, and the Word of God is led silent to the sacrifice.”

Gregory Nazianzen: “We needed God incarnate and put to death, that we might live.”

From Saint Augustine’s book *On Charity*: “For he who came through the mockeries of the cross to destroy the corruption of the flesh and by the newness of his death to dissolve the old age of the bond of our death, made man new by a new commandment. For it was an old thing that man should die; but lest this should always prevail in man, a new thing was done: God died. Yet he died in the flesh, not in the divinity.”

Cyril, Chapter XII: “If anyone does not confess that the Word suffered in the flesh (and was crucified in the flesh [Note: The words enclosed in brackets were supplied from the Roman edition, having been carelessly omitted in Labbe.]), and tasted death in the flesh, and became the firstborn from the dead, inasmuch as he is life and life-giving and God, let him be anathema.”

In Leo’s letter to Juvenal: “Therefore the true cross confirms the true birth, because he who is born in our flesh is crucified in our flesh.”

The same author, from the letter to Flavian: “Impassible God did not disdain to be passible man, and the immortal did not disdain to be subject to the laws of death.” You will be able to learn more on this point from the readings of the dogma.

We teach that Catholics rightly confess the holy ever-Virgin Mary properly and truly to be the God-bearer and Mother of God the Word incarnate from her; and that this same one, incarnate in the last times, deigned to be born of his holy and glorious Virgin Mother.

Therefore, because the Son of God was properly and truly incarnate from her, we confess that she is properly and truly the Mother of God incarnate and born from her; “properly,” lest the Lord Jesus be believed to have received the name of God by honor or favor, as foolish Nestorius thinks; “truly,” lest it be believed that he assumed from the Virgin a phantom, or flesh not truly real in some manner, as the impious Eutyches asserted. Proof of this is supplied from patristic tradition by Saint Augustine in Book I, chapter 15, of *Predestination*: “Jesus was therefore predestined to be, according to the flesh, the son of David, but in power the Son of God and at once son of man because of the man assumed, and Son of God because of the only-begotten Lord who assumed him; thus he is properly and truly called both.”

Leporius, in the letter confirmed by Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, blessed Augustine, and the African synod: “Therefore God-man Jesus, Son of God, is properly born to us of the Holy Spirit and Mary ever Virgin.”

Gelasius, from the book against Nestorius and Eutyches: “For that holy thing which is born of you shall be called the Son of God” (Matthew I). “Is born of you,” he says, in order to express the property of our condition to be received from the mother.

Thus, illustrious and magnificent sons, it has been clearly shown what the emperor has believed and what the Roman Church follows and venerates. Accordingly, as we have often said, we Catholics confess Christ our Lord to be one of the holy Trinity, to be known in two natures—that is, perfect in divinity and humanity—not as flesh existing beforehand and later united to the Word, but as receiving its beginning in God the Word himself. For the flesh truly received its beginning from the maternal body, while the property or truth of each nature, divinity and humanity, was preserved: the Son of God, our Lord Jesus Christ, with every subsequent confusion of change removed.

For we recognize the natures in him only by understanding and confessing the difference between divinity and humanity. Yet in saying two natures we do not understand two persons in Christ, as though we made a division of the union and, God forbid, there were a quaternity rather than a Trinity, as the mad Nestorius thinks. Nor do we confuse those same two natures when we confess one person of Christ, as the impious Eutyches believes. We follow, embrace, and preserve the Tome of Pope Leo, all his letters, and also the four synods—Nicaea, Constantinople, the first Ephesus, and Chalcedon—as the Roman Church has hitherto received and venerated them. For this is the foundation of our faith, this the most firm rock of our faith.

We have taken care, illustrious and great sons, to make these matters known while giving thanks for your concern; you will be able to learn them more fully when copies have been sent. The Acoemetes, who call themselves monks and have plainly shown themselves Nestorians, are also condemned by the Roman Church. I do not cease to warn you with pastoral care to avoid even ordinary conversation with them, and to consider that you have nothing in common with them, because of the canon which does not permit a Christian to speak or communicate with excommunicated persons. I do this lest I be found guilty of silence if I had failed to bring these things to your knowledge, most Christian sons.

May our God preserve your soundness, lord sons, deservedly illustrious and magnificent.

# Letter (formerly IV) of Pope John to the Bishops of Gaul

He deprived Contumeliosus, a Gaulish bishop, of the episcopate and sent him back to a monastery for penance; he entrusted his Church to Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles.

To our most beloved brothers, all the bishops established throughout Gaul, John.

The report sent by your fraternity has come to our attention. In it Contumeliosus is said to be entangled in many crimes. Since a person of this kind cannot cling to the sacred mysteries, our authority judges that he must from this day be removed from office, so that, established in a monastery, he may not cease to seek pardon for his offense from the Lord. For nothing is impossible for his clemency, since he can forgive everything that has been done.

But lest his Church appear to be left without a shepherd, by this present authority we decree that a visitor be appointed in his place. He shall understand that he must conduct everything in such a way that he presume nothing concerning the orders of the clergy or the ecclesiastical property, but carry out only those matters that pertain to the holy mysteries.

We judge that you should give the aforesaid Contumeliosus a petition permitting him to repent, in which, clearly alleging his error, he shall make his profession under the appropriate day and consul.

May the Lord preserve you unharmed, dearest brothers.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Flavius Paulinus the younger, illustrious man [A.D. 534].

# Letter (formerly V) of Pope John to the Priests and Deacons of Bishop Contumeliosus

John to the priests, deacons, and entire clergy of the Church in which Contumeliosus was bishop.

A report sent to us by our brothers and fellow bishops has reached us. In it Contumeliosus is said to have confessed his crimes and to have been convicted of them [Note: In the Lérins manuscript this letter bears the following title: “John the pope’s decree to the priests, deacons, and entire clergy of the Church of Riez.” From this title we have learned the place in which Contumeliosus was bishop. JAC. SIRMONDUS.].

Since a man involved in crimes of this kind can no longer discharge the ministries of the priesthood, we think it necessary to add to you the assistance of a visitor. Therefore our authority has decreed that a visitor be appointed in his Church, so that the Church, deprived of its own bishop, may not lack the assistance of the supreme pontiff.

We decree that you obey him in all things, but only in matters that must be carried out in connection with the sacred mysteries. He must not, however, presume anything concerning the ecclesiastical property, and the clergy must remain in the order in which they now stand and must not be advanced through any ranks until they are able to have their own priest.

We entrust all this concern to our brother and fellow bishop Caesarius, to whose care we have judged that everything necessary belongs.

May the Lord preserve you unharmed, beloved sons.

Given on the seventh day before the Ides of April, in the consulship of Paulinus the younger, illustrious man [A.D. 534].

# Letter (formerly VI) of Pope John to Caesarius of Arles

With the canons sent by him for examining the case of Bishop Contumeliosus.

## [Col. 0025A]

To his most beloved brother Caesarius, John.

We received with willing mind the letter of your charity. In it, while alleging his bodily necessities, you also reported what that more execrable man who fell had done [Note: That is, “more execrably.” HARD.]. We grieve over the loss of a bishop, but it is necessary to preserve the rigor of the canons.

Therefore our authority has suspended the aforesaid man from the episcopal order. For it is not lawful for one polluted by crimes to serve in sacred ministries. But under your direction let him be sent to a monastery, where, mindful of his offenses, he should not cease to pour out tears in penance, so that he may obtain mercy from our Lord Jesus Christ, who has mercy upon all.

Appoint a visitor in his place, until the Church, which has been emptied of its priesthood, may deserve to have its own priest again. Nevertheless, we must entreat our God with common prayers that he may preserve all prelates pure.

If, however, any men who have forgotten their episcopal office should perhaps involve themselves in crimes, and the common people should learn of their deeds—for they more easily avoid offenses if they do not see that what they have done is hidden even from human beings—we have appended below what the canons prescribe concerning such matters, so that you may recognize what must be done.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

[A.D. 534.]

# Letter of the African Bishops to John, Delivered to Him but Received by His Successor Agapetus

They consult the pontiff about certain doubtful matters.

## [Col. 0025C]

To the most blessed and honorable holy brother and fellow priest John: Reparatus, Florentinianus, Datianus, and the other 217 bishops who were present at all the councils at Justiniana Carthage [Carthage].

Desiring once again to preserve the excellent custom of former times, which violent captivity had taken away for a hundred years, to the grief of all, we assembled in devotion to the faith for the universal synod of all Africa. In that basilica of Justiniana Carthage [Carthage] we consecrated to the Lord the firstfruits of our assembly, from which the tyrant Huneric had expelled our fathers.

This basilica is called by us the Basilica of Faustus. It is distinguished by the bodies of many martyrs, whose prayers God heard, so that he might give the priests confidence for this undertaking. We leave it rather to your blessedness to contemplate how much each of us was able to weep amid tears of joy there. For in all of us there was one spiritual feeling of joy: to give thanks to almighty God, whose grace is granted to sinners without any merit of works, and through whom the antidote of saving faith is obtained for those recently reconciled from heresy.

After the definitions of the Council of Nicaea had been read publicly in summary, discussion had already begun concerning one of the other matters that had to be determined: how the Arian priests ought to be received into the Catholic faith—whether in their honors or in lay communion. Then all of us unanimously and suddenly agreed first to inquire into the judgment of your blessedness.

For, as we hope, the apostolic See can give us, when we ask, an answer of such a kind that the truth, once examined, will enable us all to approve it unanimously. From the silent movements of all our colleagues, we perceived that no one favored receiving Arians in their honors. Nevertheless, we thought it consistent with charity that no one should bring our opinion into public knowledge before either custom or the decision of the Roman Church had been revealed to us.

By this letter of our greeting we have therefore immediately sent our brothers and fellow priests Gaius and Peter, and our son Liberatus the deacon, honoring the authority of your blessedness and your grace with the obedience they deserve. For you are such a man as the holy See of Peter deserved to have as its pontiff: worthy of veneration, full of love, speaking the truth without falsehood, doing nothing arrogantly.

Hence the free charity of the whole fraternity judged that your counsel should be sought. May that mind which serves the Holy Spirit [Note: “Burning with the Holy Spirit.”] answer graciously and truthfully [Note: In that edition these words are inserted: “For the apostolic See can, as we hope, give us, when we ask, an answer of such a kind,” etc., as above.].

For we consult you not only concerning the priests themselves, but also concerning the very children baptized among them: whether, if they should ask, they are customarily or ought to be admitted to the clergy. We often allow many to make such requests, and do not refuse them, until, after more careful deliberation with you, our legation returns.

We also believe that this should be made known to your blessedness: several brothers from our college, abandoning their own congregations without cause, frequently sail to the regions across the sea. The Church has tolerated them for a long time, excusing them on account of the violence of the evil times [corrected reading: accusing them of the violence of the evil times].

We now ask that any bishop, priest, or deacon, or cleric of any lower order, who comes without our letter and does not prove that he was sent for the benefit of the holy Churches, be judged like a heretic and not be considered worthy of your communion, so that the discipline of your blessedness may be praised in all things and through all things.

And in another hand:

“May almighty God keep you vigorous [Vegetum] and mindful of us, lord brother.”

# Appendix to the Writings of Pope John II

## Letter (formerly I) of Pope John II to Valerius the Bishop

[Note: Many things prove this letter to be spurious.]

## [Col. 0027A]

It teaches that Christ the Lord is equal to the Father according to the nature of his divinity, but inferior according to his human nature.

To the most reverend brother Valerius, bishop, John.

When I received the writings of your holiness, I found them full of that rule of faith in which you are especially strong, and I gave thanks to God when I learned that you were thriving in body and soul.

You should know that those who say that the Son is not equal to the Father, and that it is written in the Gospel, “The Father is greater than I” (John XIV), do not understand the rules of faith correctly and do not possess right faith.

The apostle Paul does not suggest that Christ was created according to the nature of his divinity; rather, he affirms that he was created according to the substance of human nature. He writes to the Ephesians: “Be renewed,” he says, “in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who has been created according to God in justice and the holiness of truth” (Ephesians IV).

And to the Hebrews: “For in that he himself suffered and was tested, he is also able to help those who are being tested” (Hebrews II). Therefore, holy brothers, participants in a heavenly calling, consider Jesus, the apostle and high priest of our confession, who exists faithful to him who created him.

And to the Colossians: “But now put away from you all things: anger, indignation, malice, blasphemy, and let no shameful speech proceed from your mouth. Do not lie to one another, stripping off the old man with his deeds and putting on the new, the one who is renewed in knowledge according to the image of him who created him” (Colossians III).

Could he who by the power of his own authority created and made the whole creation, visible and invisible, have created himself previously or afterward—which it is impious to say—or have been able to make himself?

The Son is inferior to the Father in the form of the man he assumed [Note: The same Ithacius, chapter 5.], but equal to the Father in the substance of the nature of his divinity, as the same Son declares: “I and the Father are one” (John X). And again: “Whoever sees me sees the Father also” (John XIV). And again: “Whoever hates me hates the Father also” (John XV). And again: “That they may be one in us, just as we are one” (John V). And again: “You are in me, and I am in them” (John XVII). And again: “All that is yours is mine.” And again: “I am in the Father, and the Father is in me” (John XIV). And again: “The Father, remaining in me, does these works.”

The evangelist John also says: “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John I). And again, the same John, writing to the Parthians, says: “There are three who bear witness on earth: the spirit, the water, and the blood; and the three are one. And there are three who bear witness in heaven: the Father, the Word, and the Spirit; and these three are one” (John V).

Therefore, since the Father and the Son are one in the nature of their divinity, we do not believe that the Father preceded the Son at any time, lest he be greater than the Son; nor that the Son was born later, so that he might be made inferior to the Father in divinity.

If the Son is not equal to the Father [Note: The same, chapter 6.], why did the evangelist John testify concerning him: “For this reason,” he says, “the Jews were persecuting Jesus and seeking to kill him, because he not only violated the Sabbath, but also called God his own Father, making himself equal to God” (John V)?

And the apostle Paul says: “Have this mind in yourselves which was also in Christ Jesus, who, although he existed in the form of God, did not consider equality with God something to be seized, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians II).

And in Solomon: “He who begot me rested in my tabernacle.” And in Ecclesiasticus: “As he was from the beginning, so he remains forever; nothing has been added to him, nor will anything be taken away from him. For he is the lord of his creation, who needed nothing from anyone” (Ecclesiasticus XXIV).

And in Psalm LXXII: “For what is there for me in heaven? And what have I desired from you upon earth?”

All these passages demonstrate that the Son is not inferior by nature, but proclaim the equality of his divinity, since the one who spoke both things spoke the truth, and Truth could not lie.

Act always in this way, dearest brother [Note: Saint Leo, Letter 15.], and urge all others to act likewise, so that, once this error—which seemed to have been born—has been abolished, there may be throughout the whole world one faith and one identical confession, so that at the name of Jesus every knee may bow—of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—and every tongue may confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Philippians II).

Given on the Nones of August [Note: The day before the Nones.], in the consulship of Justinian and Athalaric, illustrious men [Note: A false notation of the consuls.] [A.D. 533].

# Canons Attributed to John
These are the headings of the canons which the aforementioned holy lord John, my pope of the apostolic see, sent to us together with the aforesaid authority. [Note: [Col. 0027D] The materials appended concerning this matter were not all taken from a single manuscript but from various codices—namely, the Corbeiensis, two Pithoean manuscripts, the Lirinensis, and others—but chiefly from the Rhemensis, which contained more than the others. JAC. SIRMONDUS.]

From the letter of Pope Siricius of the city of Rome to Himerius, bishop of Tarragona, among other matters, at the relevant place, chapter VII:

“And since some of those about whom we are speaking—and your Holiness has also reported this—confess that they have fallen through ignorance, that is, that they have returned to their own wives, we declare that mercy must not be denied them on this condition: without any advancement in honor, they must remain in the office in which they were detected for as long as they live, provided that thereafter they strive to conduct themselves continently.

“But those who rely on the excuse of an illicit privilege, claiming that this was granted to them by the old law, should know that by the authority of the apostolic see they have been cast out from every ecclesiastical honor, of which they are unworthy; nor can they ever touch the venerable mysteries, from which they themselves deprived themselves while they gazed greedily upon obscene desires.

“And since past examples warn us to take precautions for the future, any bishop, presbyter, or deacon who henceforth—as we do not wish—should be found to be such must understand that every avenue of indulgence has now been closed to him by us. For wounds that have not felt the medicine of poultices must necessarily be cut away with the sword.”

From the Canons of the Apostles, chapter XXV.—[Note: [Col. 0028D] The words enclosed in parentheses, which were lacking in Labbe, have been supplied from Vatican Palatine codex 574.]

“That a bishop, presbyter, or deacon, if they have been condemned for crimes, should by no means be deprived of communion.”

A bishop, presbyter, or deacon who has been caught in fornication or perjury must be deposed, but must not be deprived of communion; for Scripture says: “The Lord will not exact the same thing twice” (Nahum 1).

From the aforesaid canons, chapter XXIX.—That those condemned for crimes must not usurp their former office.—If any bishop, presbyter, or deacon, [Col. 0028D] having been justly deposed for specified crimes, dares to touch the ministry formerly entrusted to him, let him here be cut off from the Church.

[Col. 0029A] [Note: [Col. 0030D] This entire canon has been supplied from the same Vatican codex.] From the Canons of Neocaesarea, XCV.—Concerning presbyters who have committed fornication.—If a presbyter has committed fornication or adultery, he must be expelled and reduced to penance.

From the Canons of Antioch, chapter IV.—Concerning those condemned who attempt to minister.—If any bishop condemned by a synod, or any presbyter or deacon condemned by his bishop, should dare to touch anything belonging to the sacred ministry—whether a bishop according to the preceding custom, or a presbyter or deacon—in no way may he have either the hope of restoration in another synod or a place in which to make satisfaction. Moreover, all who communicate with him must be cast out of the Church, especially if, after learning that a sentence had been pronounced against the persons mentioned, they should attempt to communicate with them.

From the aforesaid canons, chapter XV.—Concerning bishops unanimously excluded by the bishops of the same province.—If any bishop, accused of specified crimes, is condemned by all the bishops of his province, and if all of them unanimously issue the same form of decree against him, he must in no way be judged before others; rather, the sentence of the bishops of the province who have agreed together must remain firm.

The headings written below have been excerpted from the canons so that everyone may briefly recognize that clerics cannot be restored to their former honor after capital crimes.

At the relevant place, from the Council of Nicaea (Canon IX), that is, of the 318 bishops:

“If some persons have perhaps been indiscreetly advanced to the priesthood and afterward have either themselves confessed something criminal concerning themselves or have been convicted by others, let them be cast out.”

The headings of the Gallican canons begin.

Concerning the synod of the city of Valence, consisting of eighteen bishops, on the fourth day before the Ides of July, in the consulship of Gratian III and Equitius (Canon IV):

“Nor did we consider it foreign to the usefulness of the Church to write this, brothers, so that you might know that whoever, while under the order of the diaconate, presbyterate, or episcopate, says that he has been polluted by a mortal crime must be removed from the orders mentioned above, as guilty, whether by a true confession or by the falsehood of a lie. For he cannot be absolved from these things if he says that he committed against himself what would be punished when committed against another, since everyone who causes his own death is a murderer. May divine mercy protect you forever, dearest brothers.”

Likewise, at the relevant place, from the synod of Orléans, consisting of thirty bishops:

“If a deacon or presbyter has committed a capital crime, let him at once be expelled both from office and from communion.”

Likewise, from the synod of Justinian [Note: [Col. 0029D] He calls it this, as I noted above, referring to the first Council of Orange by the place where it was held. JAC. SIRMONDUS.]:

“If a deacon or presbyter, after receiving the Levitical blessing, is found to be incontinent with his wife, let him be removed from office.”

Likewise, from the synod of Epaon, consisting of thirty-four bishops:

“If a deacon or presbyter has committed a capital crime, let him be deposed from the honor of office and thrust into a monastery, where alone he is to receive communion for as long as he lives.”

[Col. 0029D] Behold, it is most clearly established [Note: [Col. 0029D] Gratian cites the beginning of this treatise, Decree 50, chapter 23: “If a deacon”; and it is wrongly attributed to Hormisdas. The ancient books do not indicate who its author was. It may perhaps, not without reason, be thought to be Caesarius. JAC. SIRMONDUS.] that, according to what both the headings of the ancient Fathers transmitted by holy Pope John and the judgment of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, as well as the Gallican canons, appear to contain, clerics caught in adultery—whether they have confessed it themselves or have been convicted by others—cannot return to their former honor.

And since perhaps there will be some who, out of excessive piety, are not at all pleased with the severity of the holy Fathers set forth above, let them know that they are criticizing or condemning both the commands of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, the authority of the holy pope, and the judgments of those pontiffs who established the remaining canons at the direction of the three hundred and eighteen bishops.

But perhaps these people possess greater piety than those three hundred and eighteen bishops mentioned above; greater mercy than holy Pope John, the apostolic pope; greater charity than the other holy priests who, for the example or remedy of the Churches, deliberated this matter in their decrees. Therefore, either let them assent with full [prona: perhaps “ready”] willingness to the commands of those men, or, if they do not, let them recognize that they are opposed and hostile to them all.

What sort of kindness, hostile to justice, is this—to caress criminals and preserve their wounds untreated until the day of judgment? Even if we saw them undertake the harshest penance for many years, we ought thus both to care for their salvation and to preserve the statutes of the canons. But when in some of them there appears neither the humility of compunction nor perseverance in praying or weeping, and when we do not see them imitate blessed David, who said, “Every night I wash my bed; I water my couch with my tears” (Psalm 6), nor this saying, “I ate ashes like bread, and mixed my drink with weeping” (Psalm 101), nor see them devote themselves to fasting or reading, we can understand, if they return to their former honor, with how much negligence, for how long a time, and with what security hostile to their souls they will remain, believing that God has forgiven them without worthy penance, just as the priests appear to have forgiven them.

Truly I say that those very men [themselves] whom we seem to pardon with a dangerous and false mercy, when they come before the tribunal of Christ to be condemned for such great sins, will bring charges against us ourselves, saying: “Because we feared the harshness of their speech, or willingly accepted their false flatteries and dangerous compliments, we allowed them, while we uselessly indulged them, to remain in their sins or even to increase those sins,” not remembering what is written in the Old Testament: “When one sinned, the wrath of God raged against all” (Numbers 16).

O piety! O mercy—to spare one person and bring all into danger through a bad example! The holy and most blessed martyr Cyprian does not advise this, when he says in *The Lapsed*:

“He who caresses the sinner with flattering words supplies fuel for sinning; he does not restrain that person’s offenses but nourishes them.”

And again:

“He is an unskilled physician who, with a sparing hand, touches the swelling folds of wounds and, while preserving the poison hidden in their deepest recesses, makes it worse.”

For this reason holy John, bishop of Constantinople, also rebukes such conduct, saying:

“He is an unskilled physician who applies a scar over a wound before the putrefaction has been expelled.”

Therefore consider more carefully whether it can or ought to be done that, while despising the canons of so many and such great priests whom we have mentioned above, we presume to observe or practice something different from what they established. This is especially so because, if we neglect the holy decrees of those three hundred and eighteen bishops who ordered councils to be held throughout all the Churches, we shall not despise them alone; rather, as has already been said above, we shall contemn with the guilt of our souls the African pontiffs and all the others who, under the authority of those bishops, established something throughout the world concerning ecclesiastical discipline.

I do not dare to place myself in this danger at all, because my merits are not such that I should presume to take upon myself the sins of others, nor do I possess such eloquence that I could plead before the tribunal of Christ against so many and such holy priests who established the canons. Let each person who decides to think or observe differently see how he may render an account on the day of judgment.

For my part, insofar as God deigns to grant me strength, I wish to strive to obey their commands, because I desire to have with them not quarrel but peace, and whatever portion may be possible.

This too must be carefully considered: if, according to what has been written above, those clerics who return to their own wives are entirely suspended from office; and if even bigamists or husbands of women who have previously been married—who certainly do what is lawful—nevertheless cannot be ordained as clerics, or, if they have been ordained, are deposed; [Note: [Col. 0031D] The Corbeiensis codex, “to which lord Faustus also refers in his letter.” The second Pithoean, “and codex H,” “to which holy Faustus also refers in his letter.” The Floriacensis, “to which holy Faustus the bishop refers in his letter.” JAC. SIRMONDUS.] concerning these matters holy bishop Faustus said in his letter:

“The consecrated man loses grace if he still wishes to exercise a husband's office.”

Since these things are so, with what conscience can anyone say that one who has committed adultery may return again to honor?

At this point, if someone should say: “Then do you deny the mercy of God, who said, ‘I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live’ (Ezekiel 33)? And this: ‘Will not he who falls arise again?’ (Psalm 40). And this: ‘On whatever day the sinner turns, all his iniquities shall be consigned to oblivion’ (Ezekiel 33).”

To this we can and must reply with a free voice: Far be it from us to appear even slightly to doubt these pronouncements. For we firmly believe that whoever performs penance until the end of his life receives not only forgiveness but also reaches eternal rewards.

Nevertheless, on account of the ecclesiastical rule and the statutes of the ancient Fathers—far be it from us to dare either to criticize or to examine them—we know that the person whom we believe will come to eternal life after performing penance must not, according to the commands of so many Fathers, return to clerical honor.

So much so that it is written in the canons: “Let no penitent ever be ordained as a cleric.” And if one who voluntarily seeks penance, even if he performs it perfectly, cannot be ordained either bishop or presbyter, so that, even if he was ordained through ignorance and is afterward proved to have undertaken penance, he is to be deposed, with what conscience may one who is sent unwillingly into a monastery to perform penance—and who certainly must be called something other than a penitent—be permitted to return to the priesthood?

Let no one bring against me any other arguments contrary to the authority of the apostolic see, or contrary to the commands of the three hundred and eighteen bishops, or contrary to the statutes of the remaining canons.
