For whatever is said against the definition of those men, in whom we believe the Holy Spirit spoke, I do not doubt that accepting it would be not only rash but also dangerous.

For I greatly fear and tremble at the condemnation which the priest Eli deserved because of foolish indulgence (1 Samuel 4). Because he chastised his sons negligently, refusing either to strike or to excommunicate them, the sons themselves were killed on one day, thirty thousand of the people were slain, the ark of the covenant was carried into captivity, and he himself, falling backward and breaking his neck, died; his name was also erased from the book of life.

By contrast, Phinehas, because he was moved by zeal for God and killed two adulterers together, delivered the whole people from God’s wrath (Numbers 25). I do not say this so that, as he did, the priests of the Lord should now avenge such matters through bodily death, but because it is better for each person to endure shame or disgrace for a short time, while he lives in this world, than afterward to reach eternal punishments. It is much more useful for him, for the example of others, to perform penance removed from honor for as long as he lives and to acquire a remedy for himself on the day of need.

Whoever wishes to burden my lowliness in this matter, I do not intend to give him any other answer than what the canons written above appear to contain.

[Note: [Col. 0032D] Up to this point the Corbeiensis codex and both Pithoean codices [together with codex H]; the rest is from the single Rhemensis codex.]

I say this because, when we quickly forgive those who commit capital crimes, many who neither fear God nor dread the discipline of ecclesiastical judgment deceive themselves without any shame or reverence through unworthy intimacies with foreign women, and even cause the reputation of the Christian religion to be blasphemed by people of another religion. Therefore it is just that, since the way back to honor is closed to them according to the statutes of all the canons, an appropriate end should at last be placed upon so great an evil.

For when, by the devil’s persuasion, some clerics have fallen into some sin, and especially into adultery, [Note: [Col. 0032D] The passage is corrupt in the manuscript.] how greatly they consider what the canons decree concerning souls! Through false pity they strive with all their strength either that such men not be sent into monasteries at all, or, if they are sent, that after no long time, through excessive pressure hostile to ecclesiastical discipline, they may extort their return to honor.

Whoever does not disdain this little document together with the headings of the canons written above, and does not despise it because of the rusticity of its language, will be able to use it greatly against the enemies of ecclesiastical rule, so that he may say with an untroubled face, as has already been written above, that he cannot in any way oppose such holy constitutions of the ancient Fathers.

In offering these things with complete humility, I discharge my conscience before God. But whoever is bent by pressure, flattery, or false compliments so that he does not uphold the severity of ecclesiastical discipline must consider how he will extricate himself before the tribunal of Christ, where all those who established the canons will undoubtedly bring charges against him.

If the priests, my lords, into whose hands this document has come should be unwilling not only to offer it to other priests for reading but also to press them to copy it, let them fear that they will have to render an account for this on the day of judgment.

Nor do we believe that this should be omitted: we declare that those who, because of their crime, have been killed by magistrates or governors of the people must not be denied burial in the cemetery of Christians or permission for offerings to be made on their behalf.

As for violators of tombs, although the sentence of the August emperors condemns this crime capitally, nevertheless, if any persons are found to have survived after committing this offense, let them be deprived of ecclesiastical communion. For it is impious that the fellowship of Christians should not be closed to those who, with the audacity of their recklessness, have presumed to disturb the ashes of the buried.

# In the Year of Our Lord 536. Pope Agapetus I.

[Col. 0031]

## Notice from the *Pontifical Book*

[Col. 0031D] Agapetus, [Note: [Col. 0031D] In the year of Christ 535, during that very winter, Agapetus, an exceptionally learned archdeacon, was substituted in the place of Pope John, as is established by the letters of Agapetus to the emperor Justinian and to Reparatus, bishop of Carthage, written in response during this year. The ninth *Novella*, which is an imperial constitution of Justinian issued in this year, during the consulship of Belisarius, to Pope John, is indeed said to have been dated on the sixth day before the Kalends of May, but this is erroneous, as we shall show more fully below.

“When the emperor Justinian learned of Agapetus’s ordination, he sent, according to the custom of his predecessors, a profession of the Catholic faith. Consulted by the African Church through a delegation sent to John, his predecessor, concerning the manner in which Arians wishing to return to the Church should be received, Agapetus replied that they were to be admitted to penance and communion only according to the canons and ecclesiastical constitutions observed from ancient times, as can be seen from the letters of Agapetus sent on this matter to the Council of Carthage, to Bishop Reparatus, and to the emperor Justinian.

“During his pontificate, through the crafty and secret counsel of the most impious woman Theodora, the empress and wife of Justinian, Anthimus, bishop of Trebizond, a secret adherent of the Eutychian heresy, a dreadful monster, was intruded into the see of Constantinople after the death of Epiphanius, the orthodox bishop. At Alexandria, after the death of Timothy, Theodosius was installed through the favor of the same woman.

“When that utterly wicked heresiarch Severus, expelled from his see and city of Antioch during Justin’s reign, recognized that these men were of his own kind and hoped that, through the power of the same Theodora, he would be restored to the Church of Antioch, he came out of hiding and hastened to Theodora herself and to Anthimus the patriarch, his associate in propagating heresy. There he confirmed Anthimus in the Eutychian heresy and impiety.

“When this became known to the emperor Justinian through rumor, Anthimus cleared himself before him and openly professed that he would assent in all things to whatever the apostolic see prescribed should be believed. He indicated that no clearer sign of Catholic and orthodox faith could be given than to promise that he would believe and do whatever the Roman Church proposed should be believed.

“He would have established a school of sacred theology at Rome, as Cassiodorus testifies in the preface to *Divine Readings*, had he not been prevented by the tumult of war.

“Provoked by the unjust death of Amalasuntha, whom the utterly ungrateful king Theodahad had killed by strangling or slaughtering, Justinian began the Gothic War, which he had already been considering, under the command of Belisarius, and brought Sicily under the Roman Empire. Theodahad was so terrified by this that, in order to obtain peace, he offered the emperor through Peter, Justinian’s envoy, the whole of Sicily or, if this could not otherwise be achieved, the kingdom of all Italy.

“We shall relate below what happened afterward. SEV. BINIUS.] A Roman by nationality, the son of the presbyter Gordianus, a cleric at Saints John and Paul, he held the see for eleven months and eighteen days. [Note: [Col. 0033D] Baronius proves from the letters written to Agapetus and from his replies that Agapetus held the see for more than a full year. SEV. BINIUS.]

At the beginning of his episcopate [Note: [Col. 0033D] See the notes on the life of Boniface and on the Second Roman Council held under that same Boniface II, above. SEV. BINIUS.] he burned in the middle of the church, with everyone assembled, the libels of anathema which Boniface had extorted by the deceit of envy from presbyters and bishops against the canons and against Dioscorus, and he absolved the whole Church from the envy of the treacherous.

He was sent by Theodahad, [Note: [Col. 0033D] When the barbarian king Theodahad had suffered losses in Dalmatia and Sicily and feared that, once winter had passed, Belisarius—who was wintering in Sicily—would invade Italy, he acted through Peter, Justinian’s envoy, to avert the danger threatening his life. He offered the emperor the whole of Sicily and, if that were insufficient, the kingdom of all Italy, provided that the lives of both king and queen were spared.

“After dismissing the envoy, the king, utterly unfit for warfare, severely threatened the senators and Pope Agapetus, as Liberatus testifies in *Breviary*, chapter 2, saying that he would kill them, their wives, and their sons and daughters unless they acted with the emperor to withdraw the army he had designated from Italy.

“For this and another reason concerning the whole Church, the pontiff undertook the embassy and departed for Constantinople. Since he lacked the expenses for the journey, he had to pawn sacred vessels to the royal treasurer; these he recovered through the good offices of Cassiodorus.

“While on the journey, he healed a man both mute and lame in the regions of Greece, to the great amazement of those present.

“Gregory, *Dialogues* 3.3: ‘On entering Constantinople, he first honorably received those sent to him by the emperor,’ says Liberatus; ‘he spurned Anthimus’s presence and refused to receive him for a greeting. Then, after seeing the sovereign, he pleaded the cause of the embassy he had undertaken.

“But the emperor, unwilling to withdraw the army dispatched against Italy at great expense from the treasury—perhaps because Theodahad, elated by a certain victory won by the Goths against the emperor in Dalmatia, had withdrawn his promise—refused to hear the pope’s supplications. Instead, he ordered Belisarius, who was already preparing to cross into Sicily, to complete the expedition he had begun. Arriving with an unexpected army in Campania, Belisarius besieged Naples, which, according to Procopius, was very strongly fortified.

“After these events, the pontiff carried out the embassy for which he had been sent by God. He first obtained from the emperor, who had incurred suspicion of heresy because of the ordination of the heretic Anthimus, a second profession of faith, which appears below among the letters.

“Then he summoned to judgment the leaders of the Acephali—Anthimus, Severus, Peter, and Zoaras—whom orthodox bishops and archimandrites had accused of heresy in libels presented to him, and he condemned them. He added this condition: if Anthimus wished to return to the Church after first professing the faith, renouncing his error, and performing penance for the offense committed, his former episcopate of the Church of Trebizond would be preserved for him intact.

“When Anthimus refused to do this at the urging of Severus, the head of the Acephali, the pontiff simply deposed him from the episcopate and substituted in his place Mennas, an orthodox man of great reputation, an Alexandrian by birth, superintendent of the great hospice, and a professed adherent of the Council of Chalcedon.

“To make these events known to all the bishops, he wrote encyclical letters to the Eastern bishops concerning Anthimus’s deposition and Mennas’s substitution.

“After completing these matters, Liberatus says in *Breviary*, chapter 22, ‘the pope appointed Pelagius, his deacon, as his representative to the emperor on behalf of his Church. While he was preparing to return to Italy, he died at Constantinople. Called from battle to the crown, he obtained the reward of eternal life, for the attainment of which he had conferred many benefits upon the Church during the short time he presided over it.’

“Accordingly, what Anastasius writes here about Anthimus being summoned to judgment, seen and heard, and condemned after an examination appears to be erroneous, because, in addition to Nicephorus, the synodal acts of the Council of Constantinople presented below testify that Anthimus was neither summoned nor seen, but was entirely rejected and condemned by Agapetus.

“These matters are drawn from Liberatus, Cassiodorus, Nicephorus, the synodal acts, and Baronius, year 536, no. 1 and following. SEV. BINIUS.] king of the Goths, on an embassy to the lord Justinian Augustus, because at that same time the emperor, the lord Justinian Augustus, was angry with King Theodahad because he had killed Queen Amalasuntha, [Note: [Col. 0034B] Codex Lucianus reads *Amalasuentam*.] the daughter of King Theodoric, who had been entrusted to his protection and had made him king.

Agapetus, proceeding to Constantinople, entered on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [Note: [Col. 0034D] Everyone agrees that he died in the year 536. But since his memory is celebrated in the Church on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October, what Anastasius reports here concerning the time of his death and the vacancy of the see is unreliable. You will find the account of Agapetus’s history given by Sophronius in *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 150, in Baronius under the aforementioned year, no. 60 and following. SEV. BINIUS.] and was received with honor.

First he began an argument concerning religion with the most devout sovereign, the emperor and lord Justinian Augustus. The most blessed Bishop Agapetus gave a most steadfast response of apostolic faith concerning the Lord Jesus Christ, God and man—that is, concerning the two natures in Christ.

While the dispute was continuing, the Lord was so present that Pope Agapetus discovered Anthimus, bishop of Constantinople, to be a heretic. When contention arose between the Augustus and Pope Agapetus, the emperor Justinian said to him: “Either agree with us, or I shall send you into exile.”

Then the most blessed Pope Agapetus replied joyfully, saying to the emperor: “I, a sinner, desired to come to Justinian, the most Christian emperor; but now I have found a Diocletian. Nevertheless, I do not fear your threats.”

Again the venerable Pope Agapetus said to him: “Yet, so that you may know that he is unfit for the Christian religion, let your bishop confess the two natures in Christ.”

Then, at the Augustus’s command, the bishop of Constantinople, Anthimus by name, was summoned. After an examination, he never wished to confess, in accordance with the teaching of the Catholic response, when questioned by the blessed Pope Agapetus, the two natures in the Lord Jesus Christ.

When holy Pope Agapetus had defeated him, Christ was glorified by all. [Note: [Col. 0036B] The same codex reads “by Christians.”]

Then the most devout Augustus Justinian, filled with joy, humbled himself before the apostolic see and worshiped the blessed Pope Agapetus.

At that same time he expelled Anthimus from communion and drove him into exile. Then the most devout Augustus Justinian asked the blessed Pope Agapetus to consecrate a Catholic bishop named Mennas in Anthimus’s place.

Pope Agapetus obtained everything for which he had been sent. After some days, however, he was seized by illness and died at Constantinople. His body was brought to Rome in a lead coffin, as far as the basilica of blessed Peter the apostle, where he was also buried on the twelfth day before the Kalends of October.

He held an ordination in the city of Rome: four deacons and eleven bishops in various places. The episcopate was vacant for one month and twenty-eight days.

## Taken from Gratian’s Decree

Pope Agapetus, a Catholic vessel, a trumpet of the Gospel, a herald of justice, erased by his Catholic prayers the veils of the altar and the see, infected by the sacrilegious tales of Anthimus.

[Col. 0035]

# Letters of Pope Agapetus I

## Letter of Justinian to Agapetus

Following the custom of his ancestors before the Roman pontiff, the emperor sets forth his profession of faith, the same profession that he had previously sent to Pope John II.

In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, God, the Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alamannic, Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Antic, Alan, Vandal, African, Pious, Fortunate, Illustrious, Victor, and Triumphant, ever Augustus, to Agapetus, most holy archbishop of the nourishing city of Rome and patriarch.

Previously, a diseased dispute over certain matters of the faith arose in this royal city of ours. Properly rejecting it, we suppressed it by an edict. Since it is our practice to refer such matters, when they arise, to the judgment of your apostolic see, we sent to your blessed predecessor John, through a legation entrusted to the venerable bishops Hypatius and Demetrius, our letter containing the substance of the faith which we had decided must be followed.

Your aforesaid predecessor, receiving it with willing joy because of the integrity of the faith, confirmed it by his own assent and that of the whole Roman Church. The substance of our letter was as follows:

Victor Justinian, Pious, Fortunate, Illustrious, Triumphant, ever Augustus, to John, most holy archbishop of the nourishing city of Rome and patriarch.

[Col. 0036B] In returning the honor due to the apostolic see and to your Holiness—which has always been and remains our desire—and in honoring your blessedness as is fitting for a father, [Col. 0036C] we hasten to bring to the knowledge of your Holiness everything that pertains to the condition of the Churches.

For it has always been a matter of great concern to us to preserve the unity of your apostolic see and the state of the holy Churches of God, which has hitherto been maintained and remains undisturbed, with no opposition intervening.

We therefore ask your paternal affection to make clear to us, by letters sent to us and to the most holy bishop of this nourishing city and your patriarchal brother—for he too has written to your Holiness through the same men, hastening in all things to follow the apostolic see of your blessedness—that your Holiness receives all who rightly confess the faith mentioned above and condemns the faithlessness of those who have dared, in a Jewish manner, to deny the true faith.

In this way the love of everyone for you and the authority of your see will increase, and the unity of the holy Churches with you will remain undisturbed, since all the most blessed bishops will learn through you the sincere teaching of your Holiness concerning the matters reported to you.

We ask your blessedness to pray for us and obtain for us the providence of God.

Form of the subscription:

May the Divinity preserve you for many years, holy and most religious father.

Given at Constantinople on the eighth day before the Ides of June, in the third consulship of our lord Justinian, perpetual Augustus. [Note: [Col. 0037D] These details do not agree, as we state in the notes.]

## First Letter of Pope Agapetus I to Justinian

He confirms Justinian’s profession of faith insofar as it conforms to the sacred canons.

[Col. 0037]

Agapetus, bishop, to Justinian Augustus.

We rejoice, venerable emperor, that you have been kindled with so great a zeal for the Catholic faith that throughout all the times of your most devout life you mercifully display pious concern for preserving and increasing the harmony of the Churches, and that you desire one faith, alike in its firmness in all respects, to be proclaimed among all Christian peoples.

Nor is it surprising that your clemency should persist in such a disposition, inspired by a thought pleasing to God, since no advancement of your empire is more blessed than the increase of religion. Therefore I shall gladly sing this also in the prophetic voice: “Our mouth was filled with joy, and our tongue with exultation” (Psalm 125), because we daily see your most flourishing principate adorned with divine benefits.

For you desire, venerable emperor, that we should confirm by our authority your pious letter concerning the exposition of your faith, recently sent through the bishops Hypatius and Demetrius to our predecessor John, of blessed memory, bishop of the Roman see, and confirmed by that prelate. We praise and embrace it—not because we grant laymen the authority of preaching, but because we confirm and strengthen your zeal for the faith, which accords with the rules of our fathers.

Through this, the unity of the Church has already been produced, and we trust that the remaining Catholic members of the Church will return with Christian steadfastness to its structure.

Appending below the substance of your profession, or letter, we confirm by our authority the devotion which you display toward God in its integrity. We proclaim that this faith agrees with all the rules of our fathers and accords with the doctrines of the apostolic see.

We decree that if anyone should attempt to oppose our Catholic faith—which by the present definition we confirm as consonant with the rules of our fathers for removing the suspicion of heresy—he shall become an outsider to holy communion.

Therefore, since Cyrus and his followers were previously suspended from communion with the Catholic Church because of this madness and have persisted until now in their own faithlessness, unless they should attain the apostolic teaching under canonical satisfaction, we in no way permit them to be restored to sacred communion. Rather, we subject them to anathema as heretics, so that whoever has scorned to obey our constitutions may not defile the ecclesiastical order and purity.

The text of the letter is as follows: “In the name of our Lord Jesus, etc.,” as above, cols. 35–36.

> **[Note: Col. 0037D]** The material enclosed in parentheses belongs to Justinian’s letter to Agapetus.

Therefore we ask your Holiness to confirm the aforementioned letter by your authority and to hold Cyrus and his followers excluded from communion until they obey the decrees of your Holiness.

**Copy of the subscription**

May the Divinity preserve you for many years, holy and most religious father. Given on the day before the Ides of March at Constantinople, during the consulship of Flavius Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank.

> **[Note: Col. 0037D]** It should read “after the consulship of Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank,” namely, in the year 536, as it is read in the Vatican manuscript, according to Em. Norisius in his *Dissertation on the One of the Trinity Who Suffered in the Flesh*, rather than “during the consulship of Flavius Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank,” that is, 535, as it is read here. For in that year, in the month of March, Agapetus was not yet pope, and his ordination, as Cardinal Norisius correctly argues, would have had to be placed toward the end of January, so that the emperor could have written to him from Thrace. Yet Agapetus replied to the first letter sent to him by Justinian on the Ides of October in the year of Christ 535, as is clear from Letter 4 of the same pope, at its beginning: “Although, concerning the first fruits of my priesthood,” etc., col. 0038D. It is therefore incorrectly stated here, in the title of this letter: “Letter sent by the Emperor Justinian, according to ancestral custom, to the newly elected Roman pontiff, with a profession of faith,” since Agapetus had already been seated as pontiff at Rome for a year, and the emperor had sent other letters to him. Pagius, on the year of Christ 535, no. 5.

Whoever has presumed to contradict this confession and this faith must know that he is excluded from Catholic communion. Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, during the consulship of Flavius Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank [in the year of Christ 535].

> **[Note: Col. 0038D]** “After the consulship of Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank.” This consular dating, read by Cardinal Norisius in the aforementioned Vatican manuscript, designates the year 536. In the editions of the Councils, through a serious error, it is written: “At Constantinople, during the consulship of Flavius Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank,” because the compilers had not observed that on 18 March of the current year, in which Belisarius held the consulship, he was by no means at Constantinople, whereas this letter of Agapetus is explicitly dated in that city. Pagius, on the year cited, no. 7.

## [NOTE]

The constitutions concerning the faith enacted by the Emperor Justin are confirmed by pontifical authority insofar as they rest upon the sacred canons. Accordingly, whenever Justin is read to have enacted anything concerning ecclesiastical matters and the cause of the faith, it should be believed that he did so at the prompting of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople, and of the Roman pontiffs. — **Severus Binius**

## LETTER IV, TO JUSTINIAN

He thanks Justinian for having congratulated him on his election to the pontificate; praising his faith, he exhorts him to defend the Catholic faith; he replies that fallen bishops cannot be received with their honors.

### Agapetus, bishop, to Justinian Augustus

Although, concerning the first fruits of my priesthood, I was bound by the gifts of divine goodness to offer manifold thanks, nevertheless, venerable emperor, when through Heraclius, the venerable presbyter and our son, I received the greetings of your Serenity, which you sent filled with the abundance of eternal fruit, the joys of my vows in the Lord were doubled. For, by joining the advances of your felicity, you subject earthly kingdoms to yourself with such a glorious purpose of mind that you may at the same time seek the heavenly kingdoms.

The proofs of this are not ambiguous, since the light of the Catholic confession shines so brightly through the oracles that you sent that it also gleams through blessed works. For this is the complete and firm belief in our God, commended at once by the abundance of spiritual fruits, as the Chosen Vessel announces when he says: “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but faith working through love” (Galatians 5).

What greater work of your faith could there be than that you have raised the apostolic see by such titles of love and generosity that you have surpassed even the desires of those who hope? Indeed, as I too have observed, this disposition has long flourished in you by the grace of God: the extent of what you have given has shown the excellence of your capacity, and you have advanced toward the heights of power you have attained so that the kindness innate in you might either anticipate or surpass the petitions of those who ask.

Hence it is that your tranquility, through prosperous successes, now rejoices up to the heights of the imperial crown and beyond, and will never be deprived of heavenly assistance, because it is written: “For those who love God, all things work together for good” (Romans 8).

Accordingly, as you commanded, I have caused the most pious words of your generosity to be written into the divine mysteries, together with the devotion of the rejoicing Church, so that they may always be presented before the gaze of the supreme Majesty in tireless prayers, and so that their remembrance may be everlasting in obtaining for you the rewards of your recompense.

Therefore, most merciful lord and son, respectfully offering you the service of the fullest greeting, I embrace you in the bosom of a special affection, hoping that, so far as lies within me, you will promise yourselves—concerning those matters which you command for the unity of ecclesiastical peace—what is Catholic, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “Thus, what depends on me is ready for you also” (Romans 1).

Nor should you believe that in any matter in which we may lawfully obey, we withdraw from the exhortations of your gentleness, since, as the Teacher of the Nations asserted: “I hope, as your faith increases, to be magnified among you according to our rule” (2 Corinthians 10). Therefore I offer immense thanks to our God, because you burn with such ardor of charity for the multiplication of the Catholic people that wherever your empire is extended, the eternal kingdom immediately begins to advance.

While pursuing this zeal and benevolence with even greater intensity, you also judge that we may depart from the strictness of our fathers’ tradition in acquiring those whom, as you indicate, you wish to prevent from following the Arian unbelief—namely, that they may remain in the honors they held among the heretics and be promoted to others.

Accordingly, it is indeed a good thing, and one deserving the highest praise, that you wish to gather everyone into the Lord’s sheepfold through the true faith. But we ought not to receive those who attempt to enter improperly, as the blessed Apostle Paul warns: “Giving no offense in anything, so that our ministry may not be blamed” (2 Corinthians 6).

But lest anything concerning the offense against the ancestral constitutions which they would incur if they were received in this way (which God forbid) remain hidden from your piety, I have thought it necessary to append the very rules which expressly decreed that no one reconciled in this manner should be advanced in ecclesiastical rank, so that he might further desire to possess honors which he ought no longer to doubt that he had culpably lost.

From these your Piety will be better able to judge whether it is in any way permissible to violate such clear and synodal decrees of the apostolic see, when the Apostle’s sentence cries out: “But if I rebuild the things that I destroyed, I prove myself a transgressor” (Galatians 2).

Therefore, with the Apostle’s voice, I confidently profess that “I trust in you, in the Lord, that you will think nothing otherwise” (Galatians 5). For, as the same teacher asserted: “I am confident about you, that you are full of goodness, filled with all knowledge, able also to instruct one another” (Romans 15).

If, then, those whom you have mentioned hasten lawfully to come to the right faith, let them not refuse to follow the rules of our faith, since the Lord says: “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself and follow me” (Matthew 16).

But if they are still stirred by ambitions for discreditable honor—or, according to the alternative reading, for recovered honor—and fear suffering the loss of human glory for the sake of the gain of holy faith, they themselves declare that they have not yet departed from their vices and error, and that they prefer to involve us in their offenses. Of such people the Apostle says: “They are zealous for you, but not well; they wish to exclude you, so that you may be zealous for them” (Galatians 4).

Since this is so, do not believe that anything is thereby diminished from your holy zeal, by which you desire the Catholic Church to be enlarged, if such persons are not received into the clergy. The Apostle gives warning: “But what if some did not believe? Will their unbelief nullify the faithfulness of God? Certainly not” (Romans 3).

For although the blessed Peter, keeper of the gate of the heavenly kingdom, might be drawn by a similar zeal of charity for the multiplication of the faithful, and, in order to acquire more Jews, had departed from the regular doctrine and path by refusing no form of Judaism, nevertheless the younger Paul, bound in the Lord, opposed him, saying: “But when I saw that they were not walking rightly according to the truth of the Gospel, I said to Peter before them all: If you, though a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to Judaize?” (Galatians 2).

Weighing all these matters with God presiding in your heart, you will be able to recognize that we are not seeking an occasion for excuse, but are humbly informing you of what, by reason of our office, we cannot overstep, as the Apostle says: “We can do nothing against the truth, but only for the truth” (2 Corinthians 13).

Accordingly, do not believe that, concerning the person and case of Bishop Stephen, we are being driven by any zeal for defense. Far be it from Christian minds to condemn innocence or absolve guilt in any person whatsoever. Rather, everything recently decreed by the apostolic see in this matter has always proceeded from the desire that you too wish the primacy of blessed Peter to be preserved in every respect—namely, so that among those who had sought a hearing from his see, the respect they hoped for from it would not be replaced by another person’s judgment.

Therefore, since your clemency has graciously offered that the entire case should be handled by our legates, we entrust this task, by God’s authority, to those whom we are sending immediately, with this proviso: the religious man Achilles should now rejoice in our communion in obedience to your command.

But concerning the enjoyment of the priesthood, when everything that our legates have learned has been reported to us in their fullest account, after the rules of the holy canons—which you command to be observed—have been considered, the course to be followed will be judged more firmly.

As for the fact that your clemency has deigned to excuse the person of our brother and fellow bishop Epiphanius, on the ground that in Achilles’ consecration your command had preceded his ordination, we believe that Epiphanius himself recognized that he was rightly at fault. For, apart from his other offenses, he will scarcely be able to excuse this: that he did not, either at an opportune or an inopportune moment, suggest to so pious and merciful a prince, who also defended the privileges of blessed Peter, what reverence was owed in this matter to the apostolic see.

Concerning this case, and also concerning the city of Justiniana, witness to your glorious birth, as well as concerning the tasks to be entrusted to the representatives of our see, we shall quickly inform you, God willing, through the legates whom we are sending to you, after fuller deliberation has taken place, while preserving the primacy of blessed Peter, which you love, and in accordance with the affection of your piety.

It remains for us, as we unceasingly ask of blessed Peter, always to rejoice in the safety and prosperity of your empire.

Given on the Ides of October [in the year of the Lord 531].

## FIRST COPY OF THE PRAYER OF THE EMPEROR JUSTINIAN TO POPE AGAPETUS

He professes the Catholic faith before the pontiff. (G)*

The first salvation is to guard the rule of the right faith and in no respect to depart from the decrees of the Fathers, since the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over, when he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

The truth of these words is proved by events, because in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved inviolate. Desiring in no way to be separated from this hope and faith, and following the decrees of the Fathers, we anathematize all who are opposed to the holy Roman and apostolic Church, etc., as above, after the letter of Pope Boniface II, volume 65, col. 45.

## [NOTE]

The Emperor, made wiser by the judgment of the preceding pontifical letter, no longer sent a private profession of faith issued by himself, but a public one: the profession which Pope Hormisdas had formerly sent through legates to Constantinople, to be signed by those who wished to obtain communion with the Catholic and apostolic Church. — **Severus Binius**

## OBSERVATION OF FATHER ANTONIUS PAGIUS, ON THE YEAR OF CHRIST 535, NO. 6

On the third day after the letter just mentioned, Justinian sent to Agapetus the profession of faith signed by himself. Cardinal Norisius observes that in the aforementioned Vatican manuscript, on page 45, it is written in larger letters: “Copy of our most pious lord Justinian, the emperor, which he gave to Agapetus at Constantinople concerning the faith,” and that it begins: “The first salvation is the right faith,” etc.

Labbeus, after quoting the first eleven verses of the *Libellus*, adds “etc.,” as above, after the letter of Boniface II, pages 735–736; there he says that the *Libellus* was fabricated by a cunning forger.

Baronius, however, no. 35, says that this profession of faith is precisely the one which Hormisdas delivered through the legates sent to Constantinople to those who sought communion with the apostolic see.

Cardinal Norisius corrects this error from the aforementioned manuscript, in which the *Libellus* quoted there is exactly the same as that reported by Labbeus on pages 857–858. The profession of faith obtained from Hormisdas is read appended to Hormisdas’s Letter 51 to the bishops of Spain, and previously in Letter 9 to John of Nicopolis.

The present profession is indeed similar in its opening words to the *Libellus* presented by Justinian, but afterward it is shorter than that text and consists entirely in anathematizing the heretics and their supporters. Justinian’s *Libellus*, however, fully expounds Catholic doctrine against Nestorius and Eutyches.

This *Libellus* of Justinian is dated in the Vatican manuscript: “Given on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, after the consulship of Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank.” In earlier editions it read: “During the consulship of Flavius Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank”; Binius and Labbeus removed this error. In their editions, “the eighteenth day before the Kalends” should be corrected to “the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April,” in the year of Christ 536.

## SECOND CONFESSION OF FAITH WHICH JUSTINIAN PRESENTED TO POPE AGAPETUS AT CONSTANTINOPLE, WHEN HE HAD FALLEN UNDER SUSPICION OF HERESY BECAUSE OF HIS APPROVAL OF ANTHIMUS’S ORDINATION

> **[Note: Col. 0041D]** After the death of Epiphanius, bishop of Constantinople, the heretic Anthimus, a secret Eutychian, was substituted in the dead bishop’s place through the efforts and favor of the Empress Theodora. Since the emperor, still unaware of Anthimus’s heresy, had consented to this ordination, he incurred suspicion of heresy in the eyes of the Church. When the pontiff therefore came to Constantinople by God’s providence for this reason, after the case of King Theodatus had been presented, he exacted this profession of faith from the emperor.

The consular note added at the end is erroneous and should be corrected as follows: “Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April, at Constantinople, after the consulship of Belisarius, a man of illustrious rank.” — **Severus Binius**

**CONFESSION OF FAITH WHICH JUSTINIAN PRESENTED TO POPE AGAPETUS AT CONSTANTINOPLE, WHEN HE HAD FALLEN UNDER SUSPICION OF HERESY BECAUSE OF HIS APPROVAL OF ANTHIMUS’S ORDINATION**

Copy of the *Libellus* of our most pious lord Justinian, the emperor, which he gave to Pope Agapetus at Constantinople concerning the faith. — He professes the Catholic faith and anathematizes the heretics.

In the name of our Lord God Jesus Christ, the Emperor Caesar Flavius Justinian, Alemannic, Gothic, Frankish, Germanic, Antic, Alanic, Vandalic, African, Pious, Fortunate, Illustrious, Victorious, and Triumphant, ever Augustus, to Agapetus, most holy and most blessed archbishop of the venerable city of Rome and patriarch.

The first salvation is to guard the rule of the right faith and in no respect to depart from the tradition of the Fathers, because the sentence of our Lord Jesus Christ cannot be passed over when he says: “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church” (Matthew 16).

The truth of these words is proved by events, because in the apostolic see the Catholic religion has always been preserved inviolate. Therefore, desiring not to fall away from this faith and following in all things the decrees of the Fathers—that is, of the three hundred and eighteen holy Fathers who assembled at Nicaea and expounded the holy anathema, or confession of faith; of the one hundred and fifty holy Fathers who assembled in the city of Constantinople and clarified and made manifest that same holy anathema; of the holy Fathers who assembled at the First Synod of Ephesus; and of the holy Fathers who met at Chalcedon—and following the doctrines contained concerning the faith in each of these councils, by which every heresy attacking the holy and apostolic Church is removed, and approving and embracing in every respect all the letters of blessed memory Leo which he wrote concerning the Christian faith, and confessing that one and the same Christ the Lord, the only-begotten Son, must be acknowledged in two natures, that is, in divinity and humanity, without confusion, without change, without separation, with the distinction of the natures nowhere removed because of the union, and with the proper character of each nature preserved, while the two converge into one person and substance, not divided or separated into two persons, but one and the same only-begotten Son, God the Word, the Lord Jesus Christ, as the prophets formerly taught concerning him, as Jesus Christ himself instructed us, and as the symbol of the holy Fathers handed down to us—

we anathematize all heretics who have held or hold opinions other than those stated above, and especially Nestorius the heretic, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, condemned at the Synod of Ephesus by blessed memory Celestine, pope of the city of Rome, and by holy Cyril, bishop of the city of Alexandria.

Together with him we anathematize Eutyches and Dioscorus, formerly bishop of the city of Alexandria, condemned by the Synod of Chalcedon, whose teaching we embrace and follow. With these we join Timothy the parricide, surnamed Aelurus, and his disciple and follower in all things, Peter of Alexandria, likewise condemned.

We oppose also Acacius, formerly bishop of the city of Constantinople, a fellow-heretic who became their follower and participant. For whoever embraces communion with them also receives a similar sentence of condemnation. In like manner we condemn Peter of Antioch together with his followers and all those named above.

Therefore, as we have stated, following in all things the apostolic see, we proclaim what it has decreed. We profess that these things must be observed without wavering, and we require that all bishops act according to the tenor of this *Libellus*: the most holy patriarchs are to act toward your Holiness; the metropolitans toward the patriarchs; and the others toward their metropolitans, so that in all things our holy Catholic Church may possess its stability.

*Written by another hand:* May the Divinity preserve you for many years, holy and religious father.

Given on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of April at Constantinople, during the consulship of Flavius Belisarius—

> **[Note: Col. 0043D]** It should read: “the seventeenth day before the Kalends of April, at Constantinople, after the consulship of Belisarius,” since the month of April has no more than seventeen days before the Kalends. Pagius, on the year of Christ 536, no. 4. Pagius’s correction is supported by the old Avellana collection in the Vatican manuscript, which likewise reads as Pagius does. See the Ballerini, in the preliminary dissertation to volume 3 of the works of Saint Leo the Great, page CLXIII.

> **[Col. 0043D]** a man of illustrious rank, consul.

> **[Note: Col. 0044D]** In the year of Christ 536, because no new consul was appointed in that year.

## LETTER II, TO THE AFRICAN BISHOPS

He congratulates them on escaping unharmed from the hands of the heretics and replies to the matters on which they had consulted John.

### Agapetus, bishop, to Reparatus, Florentinianus, Datianus, and the other bishops established throughout Africa

Long ago, indeed, our mouth was filled with joy over your prosperity, and our tongue with exultation (Psalm 125). But now also, when we received the letter of your charity addressed to our predecessor, we renew the joys formerly conceived, blessing the everlasting Lord, who delivered us from our enemies and from the hand of all who hated us (Luke 1).

With you, rightly, we say that we are those who have also suffered tribulation. For since the Church is everywhere one body, its principal members here also suffered together with the other members. Your sorrow was always our affliction, and, with charity ruling our inmost hearts, we often uttered sobs at the groaning of all your people.

Since this is so, now that our brothers and fellow bishops Caius and Peter have returned, together with Liberatus, our son and deacon—

> **[Note: Col. 0044D]** Liberatus mentions his earlier journey to Rome in chapter 20 of his *Brief Account*—

we express the most sincere affection of your counsel. For, as was fitting for wise and learned men, you did not forget the primacy of the apostolic see. Wishing to loosen the bonds of the question brought before you, you sought access from that see, as was proper, to which authority over the locks has been granted.

Accordingly, we gladly disclose what the Fathers established in the innermost chambers concerning such a case, and we append what has been conveyed in the present communications, so that you may recognize without doubt that it is not lawful to cross the boundaries established long ago.

Therefore, if we wish to avoid the offense announced by our elders, let us follow this. Those who, after being warned, happen to transgress have no excuse; and ignorance does not protect those whose transgressions are thereby made more grievous.

Hence, because Almighty God has raised up for us the horn of salvation in the house of David his servant (Luke 1), so that we may deal with the reconciliation of all those under whose wickedness we have suffered, we must apply remedies carefully, lest the restoration of their health become harmful to our own safety, or the medicine acquire a stain from the wound to which it wishes to bring healing.

We must therefore perform such an office—as has also seemed most cautiously right to us—in the discipline of shepherds, lest, while we wish to gather the lost, we perish, and, while we release them through excessive relaxation, we fall into guilt, which God forbid.

This is especially so since the judgment of our predecessors embraced with such great charity in the faith those returning to us from the Arians, in whatever manner or at whatever age they had been stained by that plague. Such justice rebuked them under the guise of love, and such reasoning excluded them from the pursuit of honor that they were ashamed to seek anything other than return.

Regarding what you asked with most pious compunction—whether they should be restored to their office, or whether they should not be promoted at all, or whether at least they should be assisted with the necessities of life—we praise, exhort, and embrace you, so that, by refusing them promotion or the office in which they had served, the reverence due to the canons may judge that all of you seek rather to suppress the ardor of ambition than to exercise it.

Let humanity nourish those who come to the most sincere faith; let mercy console them and be ready for all, for concerning its reward it is said: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matthew 5).

We also judge that your instruction that Catholics who preside over or serve the Church should not be received by us without letters from their priests is in accord with the canons and beneficial to discipline and to the faith. By remaining in the churches in which they serve, they will be able through the constant exercise of their ministry to grow fervent in the love of God our Savior and to avoid what is blameworthy in wandering about.

> **[Note: Col. 0045D]** In this letter and the following one, Pagius argues that “the fifth day before the Ides of November” should be read. Pagius, on the year of Christ 535, no. 4.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September.

## LETTER III, TO REPARATUS

He thanks him for having congratulated him by letter on his election to the pontificate, while also indicating that he has replied to his consultations and will do the same through legates. Meanwhile, he urges him to ensure that what he wrote for the Catholic faith is circulated.

### Agapetus to Reparatus, bishop of Carthage

In your letter you indicated that, after the letter had been sent to my predecessor, amid delays in undertaking the voyage—delays caused by the severity of the continuing winter—you had been informed, by the grace of Almighty God, of our ordination, and that you had congratulated me with brotherly affection because the Divinity had granted me the office of the pontificate. We were not surprised at this, given your sincerity.

For the affection expressed in the letter you sent presented you to us in such a way that, when I read your most beloved letter, I seemed to see you. Therefore, embracing you in the very mind with which I saw you, I ask the mercy of the Divinity that restored peace may bear fruit among you, and that Almighty God, who gave me the gift of priesthood, may also grant me its merit.

Moreover, concerning the matters which our brothers and fellow bishops Caius and Peter, and also Liberatus, our son and deacon, were sent by your fraternity to discuss with us, we thought it appropriate to give a reply by word, which we shall not delay to return through our legates, if it pleases the Lord.

Furthermore, restoring to your charity the metropolitan rights which the perversity of enemies had seized, we urge you to make known to everyone what we have written in your name or in the name of others, supported as it is by metropolitan authority, so that no one may plausibly claim ignorance of what the primacy of the apostolic see has written after consideration of the canons.

Given on the fifth day before the Ides of September, after the consulship of Paulinus, a man of illustrious rank.

## LETTER VI, TO CAESARIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

That estates belonging by right to the Church should not be alienated under any title.

### Agapetus to his most beloved brother Caesarius

So great, by God’s favor, is our devotion both toward granting most willingly whatever advances the sustenance of the poor and toward the affection we owe your fraternity, that we do not consider it burdensome to grant what you request of us.

But the venerable and most explicit decrees of the Fathers recall us; by them we are forbidden to transfer, under any title, estates belonging by right to the Church, over which Almighty God has appointed us to preside, into the rights of others.

In this matter, we believe that your wisdom will also be most grateful that we do not presume, for any reason or out of regard for any person, to act against the decrees or rules of the ancient definition.

Do not believe that we do this out of an inclination toward stinginess or for the sake of secular advantage. Rather, in consideration of divine judgment, we must inviolably observe whatever the holy synodal authority has decreed.

So that this may shine unmistakably before your charity, we have caused the relevant passage concerning this matter to be disclosed from the decrees of the Fathers, and we believe that it should be sent to you together with this letter.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger, a man of illustrious rank [in the year of Christ 535].

## LETTER VII, TO CAESARIUS, BISHOP OF ARLES

Concerning Contumeliosus, after he had appealed to the apostolic see.

### Agapetus to his most beloved brother Caesarius

We had wished, dearest brother, that, while the reputation of Bishop Contumeliosus remained unimpaired, neither you would earlier have been compelled to judge nor we to issue a sentence, especially since, in the accusation of the aforementioned man, the reverence due to our common honor seems in some way to have been assailed.

Therefore, since he wished to flee to the aid of an appeal, as he says, relying upon the presumption of his innocence, let us support this with continual prayers, so that the benefit of a renewed investigation may restore him, acquitted, to the gratitude of all.

For, with the help of our God, we are about to delegate the examination, so that, according to the decrees of the venerable canons and under consideration of justice, everything that has been done or recorded before your fraternity concerning this case may be demanded through the most careful investigation.

It is not fitting that the aforesaid man should be oppressed by the outcome of the earlier hearing, since he himself has sought judgment. Let the will of the mind not be turned away from the prayers of the weak when they are in need, lest, God forbid, what is read in Proverbs be said to us: “Whoever closes his ear to the cry of the poor will himself call and not be answered” (Proverbs 21).

For who is weaker than Bishop Contumeliosus, who, placed in tribulation, is confounded by the shame of the former judgment and disturbed by expectation of the investigation to come? For although purity of innocence, as is to be hoped, may perhaps support him, he cannot fail to be anxious about the judgment.

Although Emeritus the defender, whom we had censured, strengthened the aforementioned bishop’s return to his own church with your charity’s consent, we nevertheless wish Bishop Contumeliosus, until the conclusion of the judgment which we shall delegate, to remain suspended from administering the ecclesiastical patrimony and from celebrating Mass, with his own property restored to him for the time being. For if the truth supports him, he will receive by judgment, with greater glory, what he appeared to have lost by judgment, rather than seize it through acts of usurpation.

Your fraternity would have acted better if, after he had requested an investigation by lodging an appeal to the apostolic see, you had permitted nothing concerning his person to be diminished from the time of the sentence, so that the case to be examined upon the appeal might remain intact. For if the first sentence is put into execution, the second hearing has nothing left to investigate.

It should be added that, even if the aforesaid bishop had not resisted the judgment, he could, according to the canons, have sought a private withdrawal rather than encounter the severity of religious discipline.

> **[Note: Col. 0047B]** Since these words are read with a meaning foreign to the context, we correct them from the Reg. manuscript as follows: “Therefore, with Bishop Contumeliosus suspended, as we have stated, from only that celebration of Mass which he is said to have presumed to undertake,” etc. — **Hardouin**

The printed text, apparently corrupt, reads: “Therefore, with Bishop Contumeliosus suspended, as we have stated, let him have only the celebration of Mass which he is said to have presumed [to undertake].” Following the emendation cited above: Therefore, with Bishop Contumeliosus suspended, as we have stated, from only the celebration of Mass which he is said to have presumed to undertake, and with the church’s patrimony placed under the administration of the archdeacon of that same church, so that adequate support is not denied to the bishop, we order that a person be appointed in his place as visitor, and that he patiently await the judges whom, with the Lord inspiring us, we shall appoint to hear the case.

Furthermore, lest there be anything concerning which your charity might seem uninformed, out of a zeal for love we have caused the chapters of the decrees to be appended below, so that we may share knowledge of the canons just as we share affection.

May God preserve you unharmed, dearest brother.

Given on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of August, after the consulship of Paulinus the Younger, a man of illustrious rank [in the year of Christ 535].

## [INTERPRETATION OF THE SYNODAL LETTER]

> **[Note: Col. 0047]** The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.

**Interpretation of the synodal letter, written in Roman (Latin) letters, which they appended because of their unfamiliarity.**

### To the beloved brother Peter, Agapetus

We wished, beloved brothers, because of the bond of our love, to find all the priests of the Lord irreproachable according to the apostolic tradition, and no one departing from the ecclesiastical canons either through favor or through fear.

But since many things frequently follow which can produce repentance, and since the mercy of God conquers the offenses of sinners, punishment is therefore deferred so that correction may be able to find an opportunity. We judged it necessary to admonish you, so that what has been overlooked may henceforth be preserved inviolate.

For your charity, mindful of the traditions of the Fathers, ought not to have allowed anyone to do what is forbidden; rather, if anyone appeared bold enough to do so, you ought to have resisted with all your strength.

When, therefore, we arrived at the court of our most serene emperor, our son, we found that the see of the Church at Constantinople had been improperly usurped, contrary to all the dignity of the canons, by Anthimus, bishop of the Church of the Trapezuntines. We desired to recall his soul from perdition—not only in this respect, but, what is more important, in his confession of the true faith. But, persisting in the error of Eutyches, he scorned to return to the way of truth.

Therefore, since in accordance with apostolic charity we await his repentance in the faith, meanwhile we judge him worthy neither of the name of Catholic nor of priest, until he receives, with the proper instruction, everything handed down by the Fathers, through which the faith and knowledge of true religion are preserved.

Your charity should likewise turn away from the others who share his madness and have been condemned by the judgment of the apostolic see, from whose communion he made himself separate.

With God’s help, by apostolic authority and through the assistance of the most faithful emperors, we corrected the outrage against the see at Constantinople.

And we have been astonished, in a certain sense, that your fraternity not only neglected to bring to our knowledge this deed, so manifestly contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, but also confirmed it by blameworthy consent.

But we give thanks to God, by whose spirit evils are for the most part turned toward what is better, and small transgressions become occasions of benefit and of great joy.

I announce this in order to awaken the joy of your unanimity: the Church of Constantinople just mentioned has received as bishop our brother and fellow bishop Menas, a man adorned with many forms of praise.

Although the choice of the most serene emperors showed him special favor above the others, such great consent of the entire clergy and people was added that he may be believed to have been chosen by each one. For he was unknown to no one either in knowledge or in life. His reputation shone so brightly through the integrity of his faith, his zeal for the sacred Scriptures, and also his service in pious administration that he seemed to have come later than the dignity to which he had been appointed.

We also believe that this was added to his merit: since the time of the Apostle Peter, no other Eastern church had ever received as bishop anyone ordained by the hands of our see. Whether this was done to demonstrate his praise or to put an end to the opposition of his enemies, the election proceeded so far in this affair that he seemed to them like those whom, once in these regions, the choice of the first of the apostles ordained. [The Greek wording is grammatically irregular.]

Therefore, brothers, receive a common joy with devout rejoicing, and signify by your customary reply how much you accept the judgment of our apostolic see. You have a double cause for gladness: both that the evils have been corrected without delay and that excellent things have followed in their place.

For the future, be on guard, so that nothing contrary to the canonical decrees may again occur through you—God forbid—or be confirmed by your cherished consent. For just as a mistake arising from a single offense is worthy of pardon, so repeated transgression requires a movement of severity.

May God keep you strong, most honored brother.

> **Alternative reading:** “May God preserve you in strength, most honored brother.”

## INTERPRETATION OF THE SYNODAL LETTER, WRITTEN IN LATIN LETTERS [FROM THE GREEK], WHICH WERE OMITTED BECAUSE THEY WERE UNFAMILIAR

### To the beloved brother Peter, Agapetus.

We should indeed have wished, beloved brothers, on account of the bond of our charity, to find all the priests of the Lord irreproachable, according to the apostolic tradition (1 Tim. 3), and no one departing from the ecclesiastical canons either through favor or through fear. [Col. 0048C] But since many things often follow that can produce repentance, and God’s mercy overcomes the sins of sinners—and for this reason punishment is deferred, so that correction may find an opportunity—we judged it necessary to admonish you and to ensure that what has been received be henceforth kept inviolate.

For your charity ought, mindful of the traditions of the Fathers, to permit no one to do what is forbidden; but if anyone should appear audacious, to resist with all your strength. When, therefore, we arrived at the court of our most serene emperor, our son, we found that the see of the Church of Constantinople had been unlawfully usurped, contrary to all canonical propriety, by Anthimus, bishop of the Church of the Trapezuntines. We desired to bring his soul back from perdition—not only in this matter, but, what is more serious, in his confession of the true faith. [Col. 0048D] But, persisting in the error of Eutyches, he refused to come to the way of truth.

Therefore, while awaiting his repentance in the faith in this manner, we judged him worthy neither of the catholic nor of the sacred name, until he accepts, with appropriate satisfaction, everything handed down by the Fathers, through which the faith and discipline of true religion are preserved. Let your charity likewise turn away from the others condemned for similar obstinacy and by the judgment of the apostolic see, since he made himself their associate.

With the authority of the apostolic see assisting us, and with the aid of our most faithful emperors, we shall remedy the injury done to the see of Constantinople. We have also marveled at the manner in which your fraternity not only neglected to bring to our notice this work, so openly contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, [Col. 0050A] but confirmed it by a reprehensible consent.

Yet we give thanks to God, by whose Spirit evils are very often turned to better things, and small transgressions become an occasion and opportunity for great joy. I make this known to awaken the joy of your fellowship in the Spirit: the aforesaid Church of Constantinople has received our brother and fellow bishop Mennas, a man adorned with many forms of praise, as its bishop. Although the choice of our most serene emperors favored him above the others, the consent of the entire clergy and people likewise followed, so that he seemed to have been chosen by everyone.

Indeed, he was unknown to no one either in learning or in life; rather, through the integrity of his faith, his devotion to the sacred Scriptures, [Col. 0050B] and the duty of pious administration, the reputation of this man shone forth so brightly that he seemed to have arrived more slowly than the dignity for which he had been considered worthy. We believe that this was added to his dignity: since the time of the apostle Peter, the Eastern Church has never received another bishop ordained by the hands of our see.

Perhaps, whether to display his merit or to destroy his enemies, so great an event has come to pass that he seems like those whom, in these regions, the choice of the first of the apostles once ordained. Receive, therefore, brothers, our common joy with devout rejoicing, and signify by your customary reply the extent to which you approve the judgment of our apostolic see. You have a double cause for rejoicing: both that evils have been corrected without delay, [Col. 0050C] and that desired things have followed in their place. Henceforth take care lest anything contrary to the canonical decrees be done through you again—which I do not believe—or be approved with your consent. For just as the error of one who has sinned once is worthy of pardon, so repeated transgression demands a movement of severity.

May God preserve you in good health, most honored brother.

## Booklet of the Monks

[Note: [Col. 0049] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.]

### Booklet of the Monks against Anthimus and Severus

[Col. 0049C]

To our lord, the most holy and most blessed archbishop of elder Rome and ecumenical patriarch, Agapitus, from Marianus the presbyter, [Col. 0049D] exarch of the monasteries of the imperial city, and from the other archimandrites of that city, and from the Jerusalemite and Eastern archimandrites and monks residing there.

Considering the things that oppress the holy Churches of God, and seeing the enemies of God daily growing insolent against her, we appropriately make the lamentation of the divine Gregory our preface, addressing your blessedness:

It seems that God’s providential care, which in the times before us guarded the Churches, has entirely departed from the present life. [Col. 0051A] Indeed, every soul has been so immersed in calamities that the personal pains of our life, though so many and so great, are scarcely counted among our troubles; instead, we look only toward the common sufferings of the Churches. If there should not now be some earnest effort toward their correction, these sufferings will gradually lead to complete despair.

Although we have already related these matters in many ways, we shall now no less set forth the great and incalculable plots spread against the holy Churches of God. The schismatics and Acephali descended from the madness of Dioscorus and Eutyches—we do not know who stirred them to such insanity—as though possessed by some license, glory in their own disease, gathering unlawful assemblies and introducing novel rebaptisms, as though doing this by commission. [Col. 0051B] They arrogate to themselves the name of bishops in our regions and openly, fearlessly dare everything—not merely against the Churches, nor merely against the members of the Church, but now even against our most pious emperor and against your honored head, as your blessedness has learned. Such is the madness of these men.

For when they found in a certain house, shaped like a place of prayer, in which certain monks of their unlawful faction reside, an image of our God-loving emperor, they carried out, blinded by madness, the work of their father the devil, who, unable to display his madness against the Creator, displays it against the creature. One of them, the notorious evildoer Isaac the Persian [Latin parallel: Persa, a variant reading], who used a certain magical practice and deceived the hearts of those willing to be deceived by him, [Col. 0051C] and who was being cauterized at Verina’s residence for fifty days—[Note: The old translator read καυτηρικός, “cauterizing”; Hardouin. The Latin parallel calls this an obscure passage and proposes: “and with encaustic art he was branding [objects] in Verina’s house for fifty days.”—] struck the image on the head with a staff.

He uttered words against our orthodox emperor—or rather against God, for whose sake he struck the image—words that could neither be endured by the ear nor received by the mind. When the staff broke as he struck, as though at a loss what else he might do to the image of the man of God, he advanced to something still more dishonorable: he tore apart the painted linen and committed to the fire whatever he had torn from it.

What, then, would this violent and irrational man not have done against the orthodox emperor if he had him in his hands with authority, when he did not spare the lifeless image depicted on linen? It is fitting to say to God, to you, and to our most pious emperor, in the words of the prophet: “How long shall we cry out, and you will not hear? We shall call to you while suffering wrong, and you will not save us?” [The Latin parallel cites Heb. 1.]

For if those who think and do such things are permitted to live with us as equals at every time and in every manner, consider, most blessed ones, that if we do not agree with what they think and their drunken insolence is not restrained, to give them power to assemble, or to permit them to dare such things, is nothing other than to regard them as more truthful than our doctrine and to make them more unjust and violent against us.

[Col. 0053A] If they are permitted, as though piously minded, to teach what they think and openly proclaim their doctrine, it is clear that the Church’s teaching has been condemned, since truth is held to be with them. For nature does not allow two contrary statements about the same matter to be true, as the great Gregory says.

Since, therefore, for this reason they enter the houses of many persons of rank and commit outrageous deeds, taking captive certain little women laden with sins, driven by various desires, always learning and never able to come to knowledge of the truth, and since they also erect altars and baptisteries in private houses and suburbs, in opposition to the true altar and the holy font, they have despised everything together because of the protection granted to them by those in the imperial household and by others who exercise power in one way or another, do not endure this, most blessed ones; do not fail to use your customary boldness to correct so great an evil. [Col. 0053B]

Rather, just as formerly you rose up against Anthimus, stripped the wolf who tried to cover himself with a sheep’s skin, exposed him as one who had crossed the door of ecclesiastical institutions and canons and had entered the sheepfold like a robber, and drove him far from the fold, so now also keep watch. Teach our most pious emperor that, as the divine Gregory says, all his remaining zeal for the Churches will profit him nothing if such an evil prevails through their boldness to the destruction of the sound faith, and if these men are still permitted to lurk in imperial and private houses for the corruption of the Church and to perform their unlawful deeds there.

For the present we endure these things, although bent beneath terrible sufferings, even if they seem beyond endurance, placing our hopes in the humane God who at the proper time has shown us your presence. Just as he sent the great Peter, chief of the apostles, to those in Rome for the destruction of Simon’s sorcery, so, having sent you for the overthrow and expulsion of Severus, Peter, Zoara, and those who think like them and surround them with every kind of honor to the dishonor of God, blasphemy, and arrogance, he will grant you power—our most faithful and God-protected emperor also strengthening you—to expel them from every Church and city as conspirators and destroyers not only of the most holy Churches but also of this commonwealth.

For the enemy of goodness, having found them suitable instruments for his wickedness, has thrown the whole world into disorder, stained the earth with the blood of saints, and disturbed cities with slaughter and tumult. [Col. 0053D]

Expel them, therefore. We know well that, if you teach our most pious emperor and his Christ-loving rulers that those who keep the anathema in their midst share in the anathema—as ancient Scripture showed in the cases of Achan and Jonathan, who fell under it knowingly and unknowingly, and of those who, unaware that the anathema was in their midst, were in danger of perishing with them—they will do so.

Remind his God-loving authority to bring before God those whom these men have drawn away from the right faith, or, if this cannot be done, to drive away the conspirators against the Church. [Col. 0055A]

For it has not escaped your blessedness that, although our most pious emperor had ordered them neither to hold unlawful assemblies nor to rebaptize, Zoara nevertheless despised this command and rebaptized not a few on Easter Day, among them children of those who remain in the imperial household. This was reported by the man who, by God’s grace, was able to escape from them, return to the Church of God, and take refuge there. The same things, and others like them, have also been done in other places and in the houses of persons of rank.

If these men alone were disturbing and troubling the Church of God, we would have stopped our lament at this point. But since she is also being utterly ravaged by those who seem to be within her and to hold the rank of bishops, it is time to say of them the words of the psalm:

“If an enemy had reproached me, I would have endured it; and if one who hated me had spoken boastfully against me, I would have hidden myself from him. But you, a man of equal spirit, my leader and my acquaintance, who together with me sweetened the food, in the house of God we walked in harmony.” [Col. 0055B]

Such have some of those residing in the great, imperial, and foremost city appeared—bearing the name of shepherds, but entirely ravenous wolves. Chief among them is Anthimus of Trapezus, together with others from other cities.

For this man and those like him, being from the heretical Acephali and having pretended for a short time to be orthodox, infiltrated the Churches like Egyptian plagues. They were unwilling in any way to attend to their own Churches; and, although they thought rightly in this one respect—that they should not ravage the Churches assigned to them—they thought wrongly in another, choosing to live in such great numbers in the imperial city so that they might drag many down with them into their own abyss.

For the aforesaid Anthimus practiced not an evangelical but a fabricated way of life, as the outcome showed. He abandoned the Church of the Trapezuntines entrusted to him and came to this city, having for many years publicly displayed his feigned ascetic discipline and made piety a source of gain.

Having won people over by this means, he was also able to enter the imperial palace, seemingly expecting to increase the deceptive reputation of his way of life. He lived there for a long time with the heretics lurking there, doing and saying what pleased them, as one suffering from the same heretical madness. When he saw Epiphanius, of holy memory, lying at the point of death, he contrived something which plainly exposed his corrupt purpose. [Col. 0055D]

As though eager to reveal to everyone the deceit of his long residence there, and to bring into the open—against his will—what was uncertain to many and suspected only by the wiser, he was driven to make his intention manifest. Long beforehand he had planned the adulterous seizure of the imperial Church.

Through the support of those men he was thus able to seize the venerable throne of this city and to be advanced to so great a jurisdiction, while neglecting his own Church and leaving it widowed and without a husband until now. In this he made the deceitfulness of his fabricated way of life evident to all. For, disdaining to hold a small Church, he immediately offered himself to that incomparable Church, as though he were capable of caring for it.

Since, then, he has rightly been punished by you and expelled from the throne of this imperial city, and since our most faithful emperor has received your just indignation against him and supported you, together with the divine canons and the catholic faith, you do not desire his complete destruction, but rather his conversion.

For you imitate Christ our God, who came to call not the righteous but sinners to repentance. Therefore, with paternal compassion, receive him if he recognizes his own sin and turns back.

We adjure your blessedness—even if we do something bold—by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, by Peter, chief of the apostles, and by the salvation and victory of our most pious emperor: do not disregard the divine canons, which he tramples underfoot, nor the Church entrusted to him, which he despises. Rather, following all those who shone before your blessedness in your apostolic throne, act against him, who even now grows bold against the authority of the canons and has preferred association with the aforesaid heretics to his own Church.

Do to him what the holy Celestine plainly did against the impious Nestorius: set him a deadline, as Celestine did for Nestorius. If, before it expires, he does not present the aforesaid booklet to your apostolic see, to your blessedness and to the most holy archbishop of the imperial city, free himself from the heretical disease, and set out for the Church of the Trapezuntines entrusted to him, declare, most holy ones, that he is alienated and stripped of every episcopal dignity and function, that he has subjected himself to the condemnation of the aforesaid heretics and embraced their portion, and that another is to be appointed in his place to the Church of the Trapezuntines. [Col. 0057C]

Since not only he, but also many other bishops, clerics, and archimandrites, using plots against the Church of God and for that very reason remaining in this city, never cease to cause disturbances both here and throughout the Churches everywhere, we ask that all such persons be brought before you and made to undergo the penalties appropriate to the canons—both the aforesaid Anthimus and all the others—while the just judgment of the canons, which you rightly preserve, remains vigilant. Thus the Church of God may breathe a little, freed from them, and those who wish to enter the pastoral office and the clergy in this manner may learn that the Lord will not remain silent forever, but will keep watch over such shepherds, against whom, according to the prophet, his anger has been provoked. [Col. 0057D]

For these men—these men—feed not the sheep but themselves. They despise judgment, distort everything upright, and regard as nothing the plot against the Church and the blasphemy against the holy Fathers. In defending these matters, most blessed ones, receive our supplication; turn against them the authority given to you by God; cleanse the Church of God from the wolves, applying to them not your pastoral staff but your disciplinary rod.

Even if they promise to repent, their previous life, changing at one time in one way and at another time in another, not in accordance with truth, does not permit the flocks to be entrusted to them. Those who have denied the Church of God and have rightly been placed outside it as heretics—Severus, Peter, Zoara, and those who think like them—have already been condemned by your apostolic throne, by the other patriarchal thrones, and by the entire episcopate. Since they do not permit themselves to approach the Church of God canonically, expel them from every public and private house, with our most pious emperor agreeing with you for the peace of the Churches, for whom all his care and concern, day and night, is directed above all else to this matter.

Put an end to all the disturbance they cause in the Churches, and expose all their false teaching.
