At the same time, most blessed ones, see to it and urge our God-loving lord to decree that, just as the writings of the impious Nestorius were treated, so also the soul-destroying writings of the deranged Severus, which blaspheme the holy Council of Chalcedon and the Tome of our holy father Leo, archbishop, be committed to the fire. [Col. 0059B]

Through these writings he has sought to make the faith uncertain in the souls of the simple and has caused the great and revered name of Christianity to be mocked among the nations. For this reason we sent to Rome to you; and, having received word of your desired arrival, we welcomed it, having received such promises from our most pious emperor: that his piety would make every effort to carry out whatever we canonically decreed against them and thereafter free the whole world from their long-standing disturbance.

At the proper time we shall name the aforesaid bishops, clerics, and monks, showing how some of them, thinking the things of Nestorius and others those of Eutyches, attempt from opposite sides to tear the Church apart. [Col. 0059C]

# Independent Latin parallel

## LIBELLUS MONACHORUM AGAPETO OBLATUS CONTRA ANTHIMUM, SEVERUM, etc.

# Latin parallel: first pass

## Petition of the monks presented to Agapetus against Anthimus, Severus, and others

[Col. 0050C]

To our most holy and most blessed lord Agapetus, archbishop of ancient Rome
and ecumenical patriarch: Marianus, presbyter and chief of the monks of the
imperial city, and the other archimandrites of that city, together with the
archimandrites and monks of Jerusalem and the easterners assembled in the same
synod. [Col. 0050D] [Note: “Better, *city*.“]

Considering the things which oppress God's holy Churches, and seeing God's
enemies daily grow insolent against her, we make the lament of divine Gregory
the preface to this petition, saying fittingly to Your Blessedness:

It seems that the care of God has utterly abandoned this present life, which
in earlier times guarded the Churches. [Col. 0052A] Now every soul is so
overwhelmed by calamities that even the sufferings of our own life are not
thought evils among evils. So numerous and great are the common evils of the
Churches, when each is considered; unless some care for reform were taken now,
we should little by little reach the utter confusion of despair. Although we
have already set these things out in many ways, we shall now no less expose
the great and incredible snares laid against God's Church.

The schismatics and Acephali, descended from the madness of Dioscorus and
Eutyches—we do not know who drove them mad—trusting, as it were, in a certain
boldness, triumph in their own disease. They make synagogues and devise
counter-baptisms; acting as though in overthrow, [Col. 0052B] they proclaim
among our places the name of bishops for themselves. They openly press on and
dare everything freely: not only against the Churches or the Church's
children, but even against our most pious emperor himself and your honourable
head, as the great madness of the men named above has been made manifest to
Your Blessedness.

For they came to a certain house having the form of an oratory, where some
monks of their wicked association live, and, blinded by frenzy, did to the
image of the most pious emperor the deed of their father the devil, who, when
he cannot attack the Creator, displays his rage against the creature. One of
them, pre-eminent in evil, rushed in: Isaac the Persian [Note: “Alternatively,
*Persa*.“], who by a certain magical practice had deceived the hearts of those
willing to be deceived by him. [Note: “An obscure passage. It ought to be
translated: ‘and by encaustic art he branded [images] in Verina's house for
fifty days.’“] With the cauterizing art—καυτηρικὸς—[Col. 0052C] up to Verona
for fifty days [Note: “The old translator reads καυτηρικός. Harduin.“]—because
the adherents of the man who urge him to do these things spread [reports] for
the corruption and deception of the simpler people—he struck the image with a
stick. He spoke certain words against the head of our true and orthodox
emperor, indeed against God, for whose sake he struck the image: words neither
fit to be heard nor admitted by the mind. The stick was broken there in
striking it. Then, wishing as though with an overflow to do something else
more dishonourable to the image of the true God, he tore the inscribed garment
and committed to fire what he had torn from it.

What, then, would this violent and irrational man not at least have done
against the orthodox emperor, had he had him with power in his hands, when he
did not spare even the inscribed lifeless garment? [Col. 0052D] It is now
fitting to say to God, to you, and to our most pious emperor the prophet's
words: “How long shall we cry, and you will not hear? We shall cry to you,
being wronged, and you will not save” (Hab. 1).

For if men who think and do these things are allowed to live with us always
and in every manner, consider, most blessed fathers: unless we confront what
they think and diminish their drunkenness, to give them authority to assemble
or to permit them to dare such acts is nothing other than to judge them truer
than our doctrine and to make them more unjust and violent against us. If they
are allowed, as though piously minded, to teach what they think and boldly
preach their doctrine, it is clear that the Church's teaching has been rebuked
and truth is with them. Two contrary propositions about one thing cannot by
nature be true, as great Gregory says.

For this reason they enter many houses of persons in high station and do
unseemly things there, taking captive certain little women burdened with sins,
[Col. 0054A] led by various desires, always learning and never able to come
to knowledge of the truth. In their own houses and suburbs they also set up
altars and baptisteries in opposition to the true altar and holy font. They
have despised all things because of the patronage granted them by persons
powerful in the house of the Lord and in other ways. Do not allow, most blessed
fathers, the customary confidence to go unused in reforming so great an evil.

Rather, as you first rose against Anthimus, stripped the wolf who tried to be
covered by a sheep's skin and to pass the door of the Church's orders, laws,
and canons, displayed him, and drove him far from the sheepfold—he who had
leapt into the flock like a thief—so now again keep watch. Show our most pious
emperor that, as divine Gregory says, no profit will come from his remaining
care for the Churches if such an evil prevails, through their protection, to
destroy sound faith; and if they are still allowed to build nests in the homes
of lords and in their own homes for the corruption of the Church and to commit
wrong there.

We bring only these things, though incredible, [Col. 0054C] bowed by grievous
sorrows, while hoping in the most merciful God. At the fitting time he showed
us your arrival: just as he sent Peter, prince of the great apostles, to the
Romans to overthrow the sorceries of Simon Magus, so he sent you for the
overthrow and expulsion of Severus, Peter, Zoaras, and those who think like
them. Though they are surrounded by every honour, they bring dishonour to God,
blasphemies, and arrogance. With our most pious, God-protected emperor aiding
you, God will give you power to expel them from every Church as plotters and
violators not only of the holiest Churches but of this commonwealth.

For when the plotter against good found in them instruments suited to his
malice, [Col. 0054D] he disturbed the whole earth, stained the ground with the
blood of saints, and troubled cities with slaughter and tumults. Expel them,
therefore. We know well that, if you inform our most pious emperor and his
Christ-loving princes, they share an anathema in their midst, as ancient
Scripture shows in Achan and Jonathan (Joshua 7; 1 Samuel 14). Those who fell
into anathema knowingly or unknowingly were in danger of perishing with it,
because the anathema was in their midst. If you have reminded the God-loved and
beloved imperial power to bring back to God those led by them from the right
faith, or if it cannot do this, let the Church's plotters be driven away.

Nor is it hidden from Your Blessedness that, although our most pious emperor
ordered that there be no reassembly and no rebaptizing, Zoaras despised such
an order and counter-baptized not a few on Easter Day. Among them were the
children of those who remain in the master's household, as testified the man
who, by God's grace, was able to escape them and flee to God's Church. In
other places and houses of persons in high station these and like things were
done. Yet these alone have always disturbed and saddened God's Church, and we
have continued our lament until their time.

But since the Church is altogether attacked even by men who seem to be within
her and to stand in the order of bishops, it is time to say of them the Psalm's
words: [Col. 0056B] “If an enemy had cursed me, I should surely have endured
it; if one who hates me had magnified himself against me, I should surely have
hidden myself from him. But it was you, a man of one soul with me, my guide
and my familiar, who sweetened food together with me; we walked in God's house
with one accord” (Psalm 55:13–14).

Such were some of those living in the great and imperial city, first of
cities: they bear the name of shepherds but are wholly ravening wolves. Chief
among them is Anthimus of Trebizond, with others from other cities. These men,
being heretics and Acephali, and pretending a little piety of religion, forced
themselves into the Churches like Egyptian plagues. They would by no means
attend to their own Churches, and, though they knew well enough not to lay
waste those assigned to them, they perversely chose to live amid such a great
multitude in this imperial city so that they might draw many into their own
abyss.

**Pass boundary:** `ut multos sibi amplectantur proprio barathro.` The next
pass begins with `[Col. 0056C] Instituit enim praedictus Anthimus...`.


# Latin parallel: second pass

[Col. 0056C] The aforesaid Anthimus adopted not an evangelical but a counterfeit life, as the end proved. Leaving the Church of Trebizond entrusted to him, he crossed some years ago to another church in this city, displaying a feigned continence and acquiring from it a reputation for piety. By this deception he slipped in, even put on imperial garments there to enlarge the false opinion of his life, and for long lived with heretics nesting there, doing and saying what pleased them and sharing their heretical frenzy.

When he saw Epiphanius of holy memory [Col. 0056D] lying at the point of death, he devised the corrupt plan he had conceived against Epiphanius' intention. He tried to make certain, even against men's will, the thing uncertain to many and suspected only by the prudent: long before he had planned the adultery and seizure of this imperial Church. Through their association he seized the venerable see of this city and entered so great a diocese, though he had neglected his own Church, leaving it a widow without a husband and exposing to all his counterfeit manner of life.

Too proud to take up a small Church, [Col. 0058A] he immediately thrust himself into a Church great and incomparable to it, as though he were sufficient to care for it. You have justly punished him and driven him from this imperial city's see; our most faithful emperor accepted your just indignation, aiding the divine canons and the catholic faith. Yet you seek not his destruction but his conversion, imitating Christ our God, who came to call sinners to repentance (Matthew 9), and receiving him with paternal compassion if he acknowledges his sin. We therefore adjure Your Blessedness by the holy and consubstantial Trinity, Peter prince of the apostles, and the safety and [Col. 0058B] victory of our most pious emperor: do not despise the divine canons he tramples, or the Church entrusted to him which he scorns.

Following those who shone in your see before you, do against this man—who grows strong against canonical authority and preferred living with heretics to his own Church—what Saint Celestine did against Nestorius. Set him a term: unless within it he presents this petition to your apostolic see, to Your Blessedness and the most holy archbishop of the imperial city, frees himself of heresy, and goes to the Church of Trebizond entrusted to him, determine, [Col. 0058C] most holy fathers, that he is alien and stripped of all episcopal dignity and authority, has submitted to the condemnation and taken the part of the aforesaid heretics, and that another must be ordained in his place for Trebizond.

Many other bishops, clerics, and archimandrites likewise use snares against God's Church and live in this city only to cause disturbances to it and all Churches. We ask that all be brought before you and suffer canonical penalties, so that God's Church may find some relief when freed from them. Let those who seek pastoral care and clerical office in this manner know [Col. 0058D] that the Lord will not be silent forever but has awakened against such shepherds, against whom his anger is inflamed, as the prophet says (Ezekiel 34). They feed not sheep but themselves; hating judgment and perverting what is right, they have treated as nothing the Church's dangers and blasphemy against the holy Fathers.

Defend the Church, most blessed fathers; receive our plea and, wielding the authority God gave you, cleanse her and free her from wolves by applying not a pastoral but a disciplinary rod. Though they promise repentance, their former life—[Col. 0060A] changing from time to time and not truthfully—does not allow us to trust men who denied God's Church and joined Severus, Peter, Zoaras, and those like them, heretics rightly outside her. Since they have been condemned by your apostolic see, other patriarchal sees, and the whole episcopate, and cannot canonically return to God's Church, let them be expelled from every public and private house. Our pious emperor agrees with you for the peace of the Churches and labours night and day; stop every disturbance they have made and every alien teaching.

Urge our God-loved lord to decree that the corrupt writings of Severus, mad in mind, [Col. 0060B] issued against the holy Council of Chalcedon and blaspheming the Tome of our holy father Leo the archbishop, be committed to fire just as the writings of impious Nestorius are. By them Severus made faith doubtful to simple souls and exposed Christianity's great and venerable name to mockery among the nations. We sent to Rome, announced and received your desired arrival for this reason. Our pious emperor promises to carry out our canonical determinations and thereafter free the world of their temporal disturbance.

At a suitable time we shall name the aforesaid bishops, clerics, and monks, showing how some think Nestorian thoughts, others Eutychian, and both tear the Church apart.

# Letter or Libellus of the Orthodox Eastern Bishops against Anthimus, Severus, and the Other Acephali, Presented to Agapetus

[Note: The Latin and Greek versions of the following letter are printed in parallel in Migne.]

[Col. 0067]

[Col. 0067B] To our lord, in all things most holy and most blessed, father of fathers, archbishop of the Romans and patriarch, Agapetus, from the bishops of the Eastern diocese residing in this imperial city, and from those under the holy places of Christ our God, and from the apocrisiarii and the other clergy.

Since Christ our God, on account of the rewards owed to you, caused the confession published through him at every time with true boldness to rest upon your venerable head by his invisible and fearful power, entrusting to you, most blessed father, the throne of the chief of the apostles—“and he set your feet upon a rock, directed your steps, and filled your mouth with a new song, a hymn to our God; many hoped in the Lord”—according to the psalmic saying, we have been enlightened by your spiritual radiance. Through it, like a lamp shining upon a holy lampstand amid the darkness of those sitting in darkness, you have illuminated the eyes of their minds by opening them.

Therefore, taking courage and believing the divine word which declares, “At the proper time the heart established in understanding will not be afraid,” and having learned by experience that you are exact guardians of the apostolic treasures, we have just expelled Anthimus, who put on the appearance of piety but denied its power; who drove away the bride assigned to him and dared to take another contrary to the divine canons.

[Col. 0067C] We also know that our God-protected emperor, like a disciple of Christ, possesses a proven soul and became your partner in this good work. From the beginning of his reign until now he has diligently sought to preserve the entire body of the Church sound, wholly intact, and free from every heretical disease. For this reason he decreed that the four holy synods should be proclaimed aloud by the sacred heralds during every divine and sacred celebration whenever it is held—synods which fortify the hearts of the faithful and suffocate those of the heretics.

[Col. 0067D] He hopes, through his natural philanthropy, and supposes that, just as those who have been led astray through simplicity may reasonably be expected to return in time, so also the inventors of this error—or rather, the disciples of the devil, who have never recognized the truth—should have the expulsion of the original heretics postponed [variant: “deferred,” Hardouin].

We beg you, most blessed fathers, to remind our most mindful and God-protected emperor of that sacred utterance: “The Lord hates every abomination.” The first, middle, and last of these is the accursed Severus, who has always spoken iniquity against God. At one time he was initiated into the mysteries of the Greeks and honored them; at another he taught the doctrines of Eutyches and Mani; and throughout his entire life he declared that the faith of the Christians was worthless.

He devised the designation “Nestor­ius the man-worshiper” as a means of deception for those who, in their simplicity, have ears ready to receive it. He explicitly repeated their teachings and called the teachers of orthodox doctrines Nestorians. He spared neither the man who baptized him nor anyone else, filling the whole world with ineffectual anathemas. He himself dared to issue decrees, having secured powerful men who, together with those who assisted him, supplied him with the semblance of ordination against the aforesaid holy ecumenical Council of Chalcedon and against the sacred and God-beloved letters of Pope Leo of holy memory, who became an illuminator and pillar of the Church and strengthened the faithful to walk along the royal road.

Thus it remains for the saying of divine Scripture to be fulfilled against him: “He will fall into the pit that he made.”

[Col. 0069A] Therefore, since we are at a loss how properly to call him one in mind with the Greeks, of the same doctrine as Eutyches, and of the same character as Nestorius, we shall name him by the more authoritative and distinguished designation, calling him, in truth, the instrument of the devil.

Passing over the multitude of crimes committed by him, and the blood of holy men poured out in the East by the Jewish army then assembled, which he had stirred into factionalism along clan lines, as well as many other matters much more grievous than those mentioned, because of the length of the account, we beseech you, most holy father: since “now is the acceptable time, now is the day of salvation,” we cry out, “Help us,” and help the holy souls who were murdered. Consider them to stand before you spiritually and to show you that for Christ’s sake they were delivered to death by the many-headed beast.

[Col. 0069B] We ask that, lest once again, through the magic openly displayed by him before all and through Manichaean error—which this wretched man, relying upon it, dared to enter the pure imperial courts—he should possess any place, except that he should be overturned into the abyss as his dwelling. At the present time, since the peace secured with so many labors and exertions by you and by our Christ-loving emperor has been bestowed upon the churches of the faithful everywhere, hasten to drive him far away, even to the very boundary of the world, sparing the souls who associate with him and, through their petition, share in the anathemas pronounced against him.

[Col. 0069C] Drive away the impure and repudiated man, already condemned by written and perpetual anathemas from your apostolic throne, by so many high priests, and in heaven by his chosen angels, according to that evangelical and divine voice, together with the other wicked Peter—the disciple who has not blushed, even to this day, to falsify his own name and who has uttered words of apostasy every day.

Drive him away also together with Zoara, who is wholly uninitiated in divine Scripture and in every priestly ministry and order, and who, with an audacity whose source we do not know, tramples upon the prevailing ecclesiastical decorum and order through the daily gatherings and unauthorized baptisms which he dares to perform. His assembly is filled with women devoted to revels, drunkenness, wantonness, and licentiousness.

[Col. 0069D] We persuaded our most pious emperor not to permit bloodthirsty beasts to dwell together with lambs, since the statement spoken by the divine Apostle has been made perfectly clear: “What partnership has righteousness with lawlessness? Or what fellowship has light with darkness? Or what portion has the believer with the unbeliever?”

What has now been perpetrated by Isaac the Persian we cannot recount without tears, nor can we narrate without fear what he did not shrink from doing with his lawless hands.

For, in a certain lodging where an honored image of the most pious emperor who presently holds the scepter was displayed, the aforesaid wretched and accursed man, as though competing to blaspheme the divine in the manner soon to be described, raised the staff upon which he pretends to support his dishonored old age. Fulfilling his deluded assault, before those who were his followers he mercilessly struck the likeness of the Christ-loving emperor, calling him a heretic—him who was thus united to God and guarded by him, and who preserved the proclamation of the truth.

[Col. 0071A] He did not cease his rage until he tore the cloth bearing the illustrious image and broke off a portion of it, which he also committed to the fire. He was unable to destroy the whole of it, for it was preserved by the providence of the superior power as a precise proof of this murderous outrage and of the greatest accusation of all. Men stood as witnesses, as you know, most holy fathers, possessing clear truth as their advocate.

Since, contrary to expectation, the aforementioned heresiarchs have exchanged their expulsion—which ought to have occurred with disgrace long ago—for the privilege of dwelling in the imperial treasuries, and have granted audacity to those who deny God in another manner, with many people enrolled alongside them under the name of counterfeit orthodoxy; and since the faithful throughout the world are in danger of no longer walking in concord in the house of God, remove the wicked from us quickly.

Offer this sacrifice, as usual, to God and Savior, for the good defense that will be preserved for you at the fearful judgment to come. Preserve the prevailing ecclesiastical order, free from every fear and tempest of heresy, confirming its stability. Again submit to our most law-abiding emperor the lawful, just, and pious decisions previously issued against them by your apostolic throne, and enact that their impious writings be handed over to the fire and that those who possess them be subjected to confiscation, following the example of those who zealously possess the Manichaean writings, those of the impious Nestorius, of the reckless Eutyches, and of Dioscorus, their father and defender.

[Col. 0071B] Thus every expectation will be abolished for those who vainly hope in them.

We also request, most holy fathers, that you bring your divine and sacred judgment against Anthimus to a complete conclusion, in harmony with your ancestral canons, so that you may remove every stumbling block from the midst and hear from all of us, even from the little ones who believe in the Lord, the desired voice:

“May the Lord preserve your throne and that of our Christ-loving emperor as the days of heaven,” preserving the examples of Peter, saving us from those who afflict us, and putting to shame those who hate us.

After the reading of the libelli, the most God-fearing lector and secundicerius of the notaries of ancient Rome brought forward the record of the synodal letter written by Agapetus of holy memory and read it in Latin words. Christodorus, deacon and secretary-notary, read its interpretation, which was as follows.

[Col. 0068B] To our lord, in all things most holy and most blessed, father of fathers, archbishop of the Romans and patriarch, Agapetus, from the bishops of the Eastern diocese and from those who are under the holy places of Christ our God, as well as from the ambassadors and other clergy assembled in this imperial city.

Since Christ our God, on account of the rewards owed to you, caused the confession published through him at every time with true confidence to rest upon your venerable head by his invisible and fearful power, entrusting the apostolic throne to you, most blessed father, he established your feet upon a firm rock, directed your steps, and filled your mouth with a new song, a hymn to our God: “They hoped in the Lord” (Psalm 36). According to the psalmic utterance, having been made radiant by your spiritual splendor, through which, like a lamp shining upon a holy lampstand, you illuminated the darkness of those sitting in darkness, and the blind, and opened the eyes of their minds.

Therefore, trusting and believing the divine word which says, “At the proper time the heart that takes refuge in understanding will not fear,” and having learned through experience that you are zealous guardians of the apostolic treasures, we have now expelled (Latin *exossavimus*; perhaps *exsulavimus*, “we have banished”) Anthimus, who bore about the appearance of piety but denied its power (2 Timothy 3); who abandoned the bride suited to him and dared to take another contrary to the divine canons.

[Col. 0068C] We also know [Note: Thus in all manuscripts.] that our God-protected emperor, like a disciple of Christ, possesses a proven soul and became your participant in this good work. From the beginning of his reign until now he has labored to preserve the whole body of the Church sound, perfectly intact, and free from every heretical disease. For this reason he decreed that the four holy synods should be proclaimed aloud by the sacred preachers during the divine and sacred initiations whenever they are celebrated—synods which strengthen the hearts of the faithful and pierce those of the heretics.

[Col. 0068D] He himself hopes, out of his kindness according to his nature, and supposes that, just as those who have been led astray through simplicity ought in time to return, so also the inventors of this error—or rather, the disciples of the devil, who have never recognized the truth—should anticipate and prepare for the expulsion of the heretics from the beginning [Note: This means “expulsion.”].

We beg you, most blessed fathers, to remind our most mindful and God-protected emperor of that sacred saying: “The Lord hates every abomination” (Psalm 100). The first, middle, and last is the criminal Severus, who always spoke iniquity against God (Psalm 11). At one time he was instructed in the myths of the Greeks and honored them; at another he taught the madness of Eutyches and Mani, and throughout his life declared that the faith of the Christians was worthless.

[Col. 0070A] He devised the title “Nestorius the man-worshiper” to deceive those who, in their simplicity, have ears ready to receive it. He explicitly stated his doctrines and called the teachers of correct beliefs Nestorians. He spared even the man who baptized him, and filled the whole world with powerless anathemas. He himself arrogantly presumed to issue decrees, having obtained powerful men who, together with those who adhered to him, supplied him with the semblance of ordination against the aforesaid holy ecumenical Council of Chalcedon and against the sacred and God-beloved letters of Pope Leo of holy memory, who was an illuminator and pillar of the Church and who strengthened the faithful to walk on the straight path.

Thus the statement of divine Scripture will be fulfilled against him: “He fell into the pit which he made” (Psalm 7).

[Col. 0070B] Therefore, since we hesitate how properly to call him one who thinks with the Gentiles, of the same opinion as Eutyches and of the same character as Nestorius, we shall call him by his more proper and distinguished designation, naming him there, in truth, an instrument of the devil.

Passing over the multitude of things presumed by him, and the blood of holy men poured out in the East [Note: That is, in the Orient] by the Jewish army formed from factions and then serving under him [Note: That is, by a Jewish army assembled through associations, then serving under him, etc.], as well as many other matters more grievous than those mentioned, because of the length of the narrative, we beseech you, most holy father: since now is the acceptable time and now the day of salvation (2 Corinthians 6), we cry out, “Help us,” and help the holy souls who were killed (Revelation 11). Consider them wisely to stand before you and to show you that, for Christ’s sake, they were delivered to death by the many-headed beast.

[Col. 0070C] Lest once again, through his magic openly manifested to all and through Manichaean error, relying upon which this wicked man dared to enter the pure imperial courts, although he ought to have no place—or rather, unless it be the abyss [Note: For “except the abyss”]—as a place of residence and destruction, drive him away.

Since, at the present time, peace has been granted to all the churches of the faithful through so many labors and exertions of you and of our most Christ-loving emperor, spare the souls that hold meetings with him and that, through their intercession, share in the anathemas pronounced against him. Strive to drive far away [Col. 0070D] the polluted and repudiated man, already condemned by written anathemas and more openly by your apostolic see, by so many bishops, and in heaven by his chosen angels.

According to that evangelical and divine saying, drive him away together with the other wicked and criminal Peter, his disciple, who has not blushed to this day to falsify his own name and has uttered words of apostasy every day; and also together with Zoara, who is entirely ignorant of divine Scripture and of every sacred order and liturgy, but, with audacity—we do not know from where it was given to him—destroys the ecclesiastical order and decorum through the conventicles and unauthorized baptisms that he rashly performs every day. His synagogue is filled with little women devoted to feasting, drunkenness, luxury, and adulteries.

[Col. 0071A] We also persuaded our most pious emperor not to permit bloodthirsty beasts to be gathered together with lambs, since he clearly and openly recognizes the divine saying of the Apostle: “There is no participation of righteousness with lawlessness, no fellowship of light with darkness, and no share of the believer with the unbeliever” (2 Corinthians 6).

But what has now been perpetrated by Isaac the Persian we cannot describe without tears, nor can we rid ourselves of fear if we recount what he did not shrink from doing with his lawless hands.

For, in a certain lodging where an honored image of the most pious emperor who now holds the scepter had been placed, the aforesaid wicked and arrogant man, as though striving to blaspheme God in the newer manner of speech that will be described, raised the staff on which he pretends to support his dishonored old age. Completing his simulated assault, before those who were deceived by him he struck without mercy the likeness of the Christ-loving emperor, calling him a heretic—him who was thus united to God, guarded by him, and preserving the preaching of the truth.

[Col. 0071B] He did not cease his fury until he tore apart the tunic bearing the noble image and kept a piece for himself, which he also cast into the fire. He could not destroy the whole image, for it was preserved by the providence of the better power as an evident and recognizable refutation of this murderous outrage and of the greatest accusation of all. Men stood as witnesses, as you know, most holy fathers, possessing manifest truth as their advocate.

Since, contrary to expectation, the heresiarchs mentioned above exchanged the expulsion that ought to have occurred with disgrace for the privilege of dwelling in the royal chambers long beforehand, and gave license to those who deny God in another manner, many being registered alongside them under the name of counterfeit orthodoxy; and since the faithful throughout the world are in danger of never again walking in harmony in the house of God, quickly remove the wicked from us.

Offer this sacrifice, as usual, to God and Savior, for the defense that will be preserved for us at the fearful future judgment. Preserve and confirm the ecclesiastical order, armed against every fear and heretical turbulence. Again submit to our most law-abiding emperor the pious and just decisions previously issued against them by your apostolic see, decreeing that their impious writings be handed over to the fire and that those who possess them be forfeited to the public treasury, in imitation of those who zealously possess the Manichaean writings, those of impious Nestorius, of foolish Eutyches, and of Dioscorus, their father and protector.

[Col. 0071C] Thus every expectation will be emptied for those who vainly hope in them.

We also ask, most holy fathers, that you bring the divine judgment of your authority against Anthimus to a complete conclusion, one suitable to your ancestral decrees, so that every scandal may be removed from the little ones who believe in the Lord, and you may hear from all of us the desired voice:

“May the Lord preserve your throne and that of our most pious emperor like the days of heaven,” saving the examples of Peter, saving us from our tribulations [Note: Or “saves”; and shortly afterward, “putting to shame”], and putting to shame those who hate us.

After the reading of the libelli, Menas, the venerable lector and secundicerius of the notaries of ancient Rome, brought forward the record of the synodal letter written by Agapetus of holy memory and read it in Latin words. Christodorus, deacon and secretary-notary, read its interpretation, which was as follows.

[Col. 0077]

# Appendix. Letter V

[Note: This letter, in which Anthimus is refuted for the Eutychian heresy and which is attributed to Agapetus, suffers from suspicion of forgery. For when Anthimus was defamed for heresy through letters from Severus, with whom he had spent a long time in Constantinople, the crafty man cleared himself by oath and professed before the emperor himself that he would assent in all things to whatever the apostolic see proposed should be believed. Moreover, the forgery is exposed by the entirely false consular dating, which gives Justinian as consul for the fourth time with Theodatus [the *Codex Justinianus* reads Deodatus], or rather with his colleague Theodorus, since the letter is found to have been issued on the Kalends of May in the year 534, when John, the predecessor of Agapetus, was still alive [he died on 26 June 535]. Indeed, the style itself, being far different from Agapetus’s other letters, sufficiently indicates that this letter is the offspring of another author. See Baronius, year 535, no. 88 [The preceding letter, as neither Baronius nor Binius noticed, is wholly taken from chapters 1 and 2 of Letter 97 of Pope Leo I. “Rather, it should perhaps be said: by the royal compiler,” to whom this little observation belongs.] Sev. Binius.]

## To Anthimus, Bishop

[Note: Much proves this letter false; it does not merely suffer from suspicion of forgery.]

It demonstrates that there are two perfect natures in Christ and condemns Anthimus for asserting the contrary.

[Col. 0077A]

Agapetus to Bishop Anthimus, greetings.

I would have been filled with great joy [Note: Hormisdas, Letter 80] if I had found you such in regard to the peace of the Church and the doctrine of the most glorious emperor and people as I heard that you were at the beginning. But now, because we have learned from the most reverend brothers that you teach the emperor and the other peoples contrary to the decrees of the Fathers, so that, by denying the reality of human flesh [Note: St Leo, Letter 97; Baronius, Binius, and others should have noticed this, as R. C. observed] and soul, you assert that our Lord Jesus Christ is of one nature only, as though the divinity of the Word itself had changed into flesh and soul, and as though conception and birth, nourishment and growth, crucifixion and death, burial and resurrection, ascension into heaven, sitting at the right hand of the Father, and coming to judge the living and the dead had been matters of the divine will alone—which accepts none of these things in itself without the reality of flesh—

[Col. 0077B] and as though that nature, united to the nature of the Father, were the nature of the Holy Spirit, at once impassible and immutable, the undivided unity of the eternal Trinity and the equality of one will: therefore, if any man of evil will or any unbeliever withdraws lest he be convicted of thinking the divinity passible and mortal, and yet dares to declare that the incarnate Word—that is, the Word and the flesh—is of one nature, he plainly passes into madness open and hateful to God.

He believes that the mediator between God and human beings, the man Christ Jesus, acted everything merely in appearance, and that what appeared to the eyes of those who saw him was not a true body in him but a phantom likeness of his body.

[Col. 0077C] Since the Catholic faith long ago detests these impious lies, and since such sacrilegious assertions have long been condemned by the unanimous judgments of the blessed Fathers throughout the world, there is no doubt that we preach and defend the faith taught by the holy apostles. Following the teaching of those apostles and of their successors, this holy Roman and apostolic Church has held and continues to hold it; it has taught and continues to teach it.

For if some [Note: The same holy pontiff, in the same passage.] are so blinded and alienated from the light of truth that they deny the reality of the Word of God from the time of the incarnation, let them show how they can claim the Christian name and agree with the Gospel of truth if, through the Virgin’s birth, either flesh arose without divinity or divinity arose without flesh.

[Col. 0078A] For just as it cannot be denied, as the Evangelist says, that “the Word became flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), so it cannot be denied, as the blessed Apostle Paul proclaims, that “God was in Christ, reconciling the world to himself” (2 Corinthians 5).

What reconciliation could there be by which God would be reconciled to the human race if the mediator between God and human beings did not undertake the human cause? In what way could he fulfill the truth of the Mediator unless he who in the form of God is equal to the Father also became, in the form of a servant, a participant in our condition, so that the bond of death contracted through the transgression of one might be loosed by the death of one who alone owed nothing to death?

[Col. 0078B] The outpouring of Christ’s righteous blood was so rich as a price that, if the entire company of captives believed in its Redeemer, no bond of the devil would retain anyone. For, as the Apostle says, “where sin abounded, grace abounded all the more” (Romans 5). And although those born under the sentence of sin have received the power to be reborn into righteousness, the gift of freedom has become stronger than the debt of servitude.

What hope, then, do they leave themselves in the protection of this sacrament who deny the reality of a human body in our Savior? Let them say by what sacrifice they were reconciled and by what blood they were redeemed.

Who is it, as the Apostle says, “who gave himself for us as an offering and sacrifice to God for a fragrant aroma” (Ephesians 5)? Or what sacrifice was ever more sacred than that which the true and eternal high priest placed upon the altar of the cross through the offering of his flesh?

[Col. 0078C] “Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his saints” (Psalm 115); yet the killing of no innocent person was the redemption of the world. The righteous received crowns; they did not give them. From the courage of the faithful arose examples of endurance, not gifts of righteousness.

Their deaths were individual, each belonging to the individual who died; no one paid another’s debt by his own end. But the one Son of Man, our one Lord Jesus Christ, who truly was the spotless Lamb, is the one in whom all were crucified, all died, all were buried, and all were also raised. Of them he himself said: “When I am lifted up from the earth, I will draw all things to myself” (John 12).

[Col. 0079A] For faith, which justifies the impious and creates the righteous, having been drawn into participation in humility, obtains salvation in him in whom alone a human being finds himself innocent, possessing through the grace of God the freedom to glory in the power of him who, confronting the enemy of the human race in the humility of our flesh, won his victory and granted it to those in whose body he triumphed.

Although, therefore, in the one Lord Jesus Christ, the true Son of God and of humanity, there is one person of the Word and the flesh, possessing inseparably and indivisibly common actions, the qualities of those actions must nevertheless be understood. In contemplating the true faith, one must discern to what the humility of the flesh is exalted and to what the height of divinity descends; what the flesh does not do without the Word and what the Word does not accomplish without the flesh.

[Col. 0079B] Without the power of the Word, the Virgin would neither conceive nor give birth; and without the reality of flesh, infancy wrapped in swaddling clothes would not lie there (Luke 2). Without the power of the Word, the Magi would not worship the child revealed by the star (Matthew 2); and without the reality of flesh, the child would not be commanded to be taken into Egypt and withdrawn from Herod’s persecution.

Without the power of the Word, the voice of the Father sent from heaven would not say, “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; listen to him” (Matthew 3). Without the reality of flesh, John would not testify, “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1).

Without the power of the Word, the restoration of what was owed and the giving of life to the dead would not occur; and without the reality of flesh, food would not be necessary for one who was hungry, nor sleep for one who was weary.

Finally, without the power of the Word, the Lord would not declare himself equal to the Father (John 10); and without the reality of flesh, he would not say that the Father was greater than he (John 14). The Catholic faith accepts and defends both, believing, according to the confession of the blessed Apostle Peter, that the one Christ, Son of the living God, is both human and the Word.

[Col. 0080A] Our Christ and God appeared as mediator between God and humanity in such a way that, joining both natures in the unity of one person, he exalted the ordinary through the extraordinary and tempered the extraordinary with the ordinary.

What then? Since Christ is God and man [Note: Saint Augustine, Letter 3, cited by Saint Leo in Letter 97, by Theodoret at the Council of Chalcedon, and elsewhere], the man speaks, and you bring an accusation against God? He commends the human nature in himself, while you dare to distort the divine nature in him.

[Col. 0080B] Christ’s substance is therefore twofold: divine, by which he is equal to the Father, and human, by which he is less than the Father. Yet together they are not two Christs but one Christ, so that there may be no quaternity instead of the Trinity of God.

For just as a human being is one in rational soul and flesh, so Christ is one, God and human being; and therefore Christ is God, rational soul, and flesh. We confess Christ in all these elements, and we confess all these elements in Christ.

May God convert you to the good, brother, and grant you to hold and teach the rule of the right faith in all things. Amen.

Given on the Kalends of May, in the consulship of Justinian for the fourth time and Theodatus, men of illustrious rank.

[Note: A.D. 534, when the emperor held the consulship with Paulinus; no consular list places the name of Theodatus, the Gothic tyrant, before it.]

# In the Year of Our Lord 537. Pope Silverius

[Col. 0079]

## Notice (from the *Book of the Pontiffs*)

[Col. 0079C] **Silverius** [Note: [Col. 0079C] When, at the end of the year 536, the Romans learned that Pope Agapetus had died, King Theodahad, by force and fear, as Anastasius says, intruded Silverius, a Campanian. The Roman clergy, having previously rejected him, shortly afterward received and approved him, in order to avoid a schism. On what day and in what month he was created cannot be stated with sufficient certainty, as will become clear below. While these events were taking place at Rome, the following occurred at Constantinople between the empress and Vigilius, which Liberatus recounts in chapter 22 of his *Brief Account* in these words: “When the city of Rome heard of the death of Agapetus, it chose Silverius the subdeacon, formerly the son of Pope Hormisdas, to be ordained. But the empress, summoning Vigilius, Agapetus’s deacon, secretly demanded from him a promise that, if he became pope, he would abolish the synod and write to Theodosius, bishop of Alexandria, Anthimus, and Severus, and confirm their faith by his letter, promising to give him an order to Belisarius that he should be ordained pope, and to give him seven hundred pounds of gold. Vigilius therefore willingly accepted her promise, out of love for the episcopate and the gold, and, after making his undertaking, departed for Rome. When he arrived, he found Silverius already ordained pope.” Thus far Liberatus. [Col. 0080C] During Silverius’s time, Theodosius, bishop of Alexandria, after having occupied the see for one year and four months, was sent into exile because he refused to subscribe to the Council of Chalcedon. Paul, an orthodox bishop, was substituted for him; but when Paul was likewise accused of murder, he was expelled into exile, and Zoilus was appointed in his place. SEV. BINIUS.]

By birth a Campanian, the son of the Roman bishop Hormisdas [Note: [Col. 0080D] He was certainly born legitimately from his father’s preceding lawful marriage; otherwise he would plainly have been ineligible for so high a dignity. SEV. BINIUS.], he occupied the see for one year, five months, [Col. 0080C] and eleven days [Note: [Col. 0080D] That he occupied it for four years and entered upon a fifth will be established from the time of his death below. Those who assign fewer years to him calculate the duration of his pontificate only up to Vigilius’s intrusion; but they do so absurdly, since Silverius, after being driven from the papal see and sent into exile, remained the true and legitimate pontiff until his completed martyrdom, and performed such pontifical acts as he was able to perform. On what day or in what month of the year 536 Silverius was created cannot easily be determined, because the precise day of Agapetus’s death is unknown. See Baronius, year 536, no. 122. SEV. BINIUS.] He was raised to the pontificate by the tyrant Theodahad without any deliberation or decree. Theodahad, [Col. 0081A] having been corrupted by the payment of money, [Note: [Col. 0081C] That what Anastasius writes here about Silverius’s simoniacal entry is false may be inferred both because Liberatus, who lived at this time and is therefore more worthy of credence, makes no mention of the matter in the words quoted above, and especially because Silverius, in the written judgment that he composed concerning the condemnation of Vigilius, his usurper, forcefully charges Vigilius with the crime of simony. He certainly would not have acted so freely if he himself had been guilty of the same crime. SEV. BINIUS.] inspired such fear in the clergy that those who did not consent to his ordination were to be punished by the sword. Certain priests did not subscribe to him according to ancient custom, nor did they confirm the decree before the ordination. But after Silverius had been ordained under compulsion and fear, the presbyters later subscribed, for the sake of the unity of the Church and of religion.

After two months, Theodahad was extinguished by divine will [Note: [Col. 0081C] In the third year of King Theodahad, which was A.D. 537, after Naples, a most noble city, had been occupied, the Goths acclaimed Vitiges, a commander of the army summoned from Dalmatia, an energetic man everywhere distinguished by the exertions of war, as king. They did so because King Theodahad was extremely cowardly and suspected of betraying the entire kingdom, since he had neglected, to no purpose, the destruction of that most noble city and the strongest defense of all Italy. When Theodahad learned of this through the condemnation of a certain Jewish sorcerer, he fled from the city. As he was departing toward Ravenna, he was overtaken and killed by soldiers whom Vitiges had sent, after he had reigned for three years, as Procopius testifies. Vitiges advanced toward Rome and there threw Theodahad’s son, Theodegisclus, into prison. While writing letters to win everyone’s good will and admonishing Pope Silverius and the entire senate to remain loyal, he left a garrison of four thousand men at Rome so that he would not be cut off by Belisarius, who was preparing to besiege the city; then he himself went out of the city with his whole army and sought the assistance of the neighboring Goths. Meanwhile, Belisarius surrounded the city with a siege. The Romans, fearing that they might suffer what the Neapolitans had suffered, surrendered to Belisarius at the urging of Silverius the pontiff. Belisarius sent the keys of the gates and Leuderis, the Gothic commander, bound—since he preferred to be captured, however disgracefully, rather than flee—as trophies of victory to Constantinople. Thus the city of Rome was restored to the Roman emperors, after it had obeyed Odoacer of the Heruli for sixty years, and Theodoric and his successors, the Gothic kings. SEV. BINIUS.] The tyrant died, and Vitiges was raised to the kingship.

At the same time Vitiges went to Ravenna and forcibly took the daughter of Queen Amalasuntha as his wife. Angered by this, the lord Emperor Justinian Augustus [Note: [Col. 0082C] Above, on the authority of Procopius, we attributed the beginning of the Gothic war to the murder of Amalasuntha.]—because Theodahad had killed the queen entrusted to him—sent the patrician Belisarius with an army to free all Italy from the captivity of the Goths. Then the aforesaid patrician came to part of Sicily and remained there for some time. But when he heard that the Goths had made a king for themselves [Note: [Col. 0082C] Anastasius is mistaken. After Naples had been occupied, the Goths defected from Theodahad and chose Vitiges, as I have related above from Procopius. SEV. BINIUS.] against the will of the lord Justinian Augustus, he came into Campania, near the city of Naples, and began to besiege it with his army, because the citizens of Naples refused to open the city to him.

At that time, while fighting against the city, the patrician entered it. Driven by fury, he killed the Goths and all the citizens of Naples [Note: [Col. 0082C] Procopius, in Book I of *The Gothic War*, writes that Belisarius received Naples by surrender and therefore treated its citizens humanely. Yet we find it handed down by our predecessors that Belisarius, after taking possession of Rome, was severely reprimanded by Silverius, the Roman pontiff, for the excessive slaughter that he had perpetrated there and was compelled to do penance, as Paul the Deacon, the author of the *Miscellany*, testifies in Book XVI of his history. SEV. BINIUS.], and sent out the booty, sparing not even the churches in his plundering. Thus, while their wives were present, he killed their husbands with the sword, and drove out the captive sons and wives of the nobles, sparing no one—not priests, not servants of God, not consecrated virgins.

At the same time there was a great war when Vitiges came against the patrician Belisarius and against the city of Rome. When the patrician Belisarius entered the city of Rome on the fourth day before the Ides of December [Note: [Col. 0082C] On this matter Evagrius writes the following in Book IV, chapter 18: “The city was surrendered to Belisarius without a battle, and Rome was again subjected to the Romans after sixty years, during which it had been occupied by the Heruli and the Goths, on the ninth day of Apellaeus”—that is, on the fifth day before the Ides of December—“in the eleventh year of Justinian’s reign,” which is A.D. 537, sixty years after Augustulus was conquered by Odoacer, king of the Heruli. SEV. BINIUS.], he surrounded and fortified the Roman city with guards and defenses, with the construction and repair of the walls, and with the restoration of the ditch.

On the very night when the patrician Belisarius entered, the Goths who were in the city or outside the walls fled, left all the gates open, and fled to Ravenna. Later, gathering a multitude of Goths, King Vitiges returned against Rome on the ninth day before the Kalends of March [Note: [Col. 0082D] Namely, in A.D. 538. During this siege it is first remarkable that, throughout the entire year of the siege, they never attempted to storm the city at the place where the wall was divided from top to bottom and leaned downward as though it were already about to collapse. It is even more remarkable that the Arians, enemies of the Roman Church, inflicted no insult or damage on the basilicas of the apostles situated outside the city; they allowed sacred rites to be performed there freely according to the Catholic rite, as Procopius testifies—quite otherwise than the recent heretics of our own time, who have never thought of anything before destroying and removing by fire and plunder the sacred monuments of the saints dedicated to God. SEV. BINIUS.]. He fixed his camp at the Milvian Bridge, and they began to besiege the city of Rome.

Then the patrician Belisarius, who stood for the Roman name, shut himself inside Rome, within the city. During those days the city was besieged so that no one had the opportunity either to leave or to enter. [Col. 0082B] Then all private and ecclesiastical possessions [Note: [Col. 0082D] The Luc. manuscript reads “possessions.”] were consumed by fire, while people were killed by the sword. Those whom the sword struck, the sword killed; those whom hunger struck, hunger killed; those whom disease struck, disease killed. For even the churches and the bodies of the holy martyrs were devastated by the Goths.

Within the city there was a great famine, so that water was sold at a price, unless the remedy of the nymphs came to the aid of the people. There were also great battles against the city. During these days the patrician Belisarius, fighting against King Vitiges and the multitude of the Goths, protected the Romans, or by his defense freed the city and the Roman name. The city was then besieged for one year, as was the Roman port, by the Goths. But the patrician Belisarius defeated the Goths in battle. Afterward the Goths fled to Ravenna [Col. 0083A] after one year.

At the same time there was such a great famine throughout the world that Datius, bishop of the city of Milan, clearly related in his report that in the regions of Liguria women had eaten their own children because of the scarcity caused by famine; he reported that these women belonged to the household of his own church.

At the same time the patrician Belisarius went to Naples and put it in order. Afterward he came to Rome, where he was kindly received by the lord Silverius. The patrician Belisarius went to the Pincian Palace [Note: [Col. 0084D] The Luc. manuscript reads “V.”] on the sixth day before the Ides of May, in the fifteenth indiction.

At that time Vigilius the deacon was the *apocrisiarius* at Constantinople. The empress, grieving on behalf of Anthimus the patriarch because he had been deposed by the holy Pope Agapetus, who had found him to be a heretic and had appointed Menna, a servant of God, in his place, then, [Col. 0083B] having taken counsel with the deacon Vigilius, sent a letter to Rome to Pope Silverius, asking and imploring him: “Do not hesitate to come to us, or at least restore Anthimus to his place.”

When the blessed Silverius had read the letter, he groaned and said: “Now I know that this matter will bring about the end of my life.” But the most blessed Silverius, placing his confidence in God and in blessed Peter, replied, saying: “Lady Augusta, I shall never do this: restore to his place a heretical man condemned in his wickedness.”

Then the empress, enraged, sent her commands to the patrician Belisarius through the deacon Vigilius. They ran as follows: “Look for some pretext against Pope Silverius and depose him from the episcopate, or quickly send him to us. Behold, there you have our deacon Vigilius, archdeacon and *apocrisiarius*, our dearest man, who has promised us that he will restore Anthimus [Note: [Col. 0083C] Add the promise of two hundredweight of gold, if, after removing Silverius, he would arrange for Vigilius to be ordained. SEV. BINIUS.] the patriarch.”

Then the patrician Belisarius received the command and said: “I shall indeed carry out the command, but the one who is involved in the death of Pope Silverius will himself render an account of his deeds to the Lord [Col. 0084A] Jesus Christ.”

When the command was pressed, certain false witnesses came forward and said: “We have found Pope Silverius many times sending writings of this sort to the king of the Goths: ‘Come to the gate called the Asinarian Gate, near the Lateran; I surrender the city and the patrician Belisarius to you.’”

When Belisarius heard this, at first he did not believe it, for he knew that these things were being said about him out of envy. But when many persisted in the same accusation, he became afraid. Then the patrician Belisarius had the blessed Pope Silverius come to him at the Pincian Palace, and at the first and second curtains he held back the entire clergy.

When Silverius entered the mausoleum with Vigilius alone, the patrician Antonina was sitting on a bed, and the patrician Belisarius was sitting at her feet. When the patrician Antonina saw him, [Col. 0084B] she said to him: “Tell us, lord Pope Silverius, what have we and the Romans done to you, that you wanted to hand us over to the Goths?”

While she was still speaking, the regional subdeacon John, of the first region [Note: [Col. 0084D] Likewise, “of the first region.”], entered, took the pallium from his neck, and led him into a room. After stripping him, he clothed him in a monk’s habit and hid him.

Then Sixtus, the regional subdeacon of the sixth region, seeing that he was already a monk, went outside and announced to the clergy: “The lord pope has been deposed and has become a monk.” When they heard this, they all fled.

Vigilius the archdeacon received him, supposedly in good faith, and sent him into exile [Note: [Col. 0083C] What the heretical woman had requested, the ambitious deacon had arranged, and Belisarius, worse than Pilate, had wickedly completed. Belisarius did indeed repent of having laid sacrilegious hands upon Christ’s priest, when, to expiate his crime and appease the divine power, he arranged for a church to be built at Rome. But because, by his own testimony, he had declared that whoever cooperated in the death of the pontiff would have to render an account to Christ the Lord, it happened that, while carrying out the empress’s wicked commands so as not to incur the woman’s displeasure, he made the emperor intensely hostile to himself by executing the empress’s sacrilegious order. He deservedly fell from the highest glory into the deepest misery and poverty. What Silverius, the exiled pontiff, decreed against Vigilius, the false pontiff who usurped the duties and privileges of the true pontiff, will be evident below from Silverius’s letter to Vigilius. SEV. BINIUS.] to the Pontian Islands, and sustained him with the bread of affliction and the water of distress [Note: [Col. 0083D] Liberatus says that Silverius, handed over to two defenders and servants of Vigilius, wasted away from hunger under their guard. For this reason plague, famine, and wars arose, concerning which see Baronius, year 539. Severus Binius.]. [Note: [Col. 0084D] Likewise, “at Ponza.”]

As he grew weak, he died, having become a confessor. He was also buried [Col. 0084C] in the same place, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of June [Note: [Col. 0084C] In the year of Christ 540. For in June of A.D. 539 he sent a letter to Vigilius. Therefore, if what Anastasius says is true—that he died on a day in May—it is necessary to affirm that he died in no year other than A.D. 540. Hence what I said above is established: that, having occupied the papal see for four years and perhaps longer from the death of Agapetus until this point, he continued to be the legitimate pontiff until his completed martyrdom, and performed such pontifical duties as he could. This is established by the judgment that he pronounced from prison and chains against Vigilius. SEV. BINIUS.]. There a multitude of afflicted people came, and they were healed.

He conducted one ordination in the month of December: thirteen presbyters [Note: [Col. 0084D] Likewise, fourteen.], five deacons [Note: [Col. 0084D] In the same manuscript, “five deacons” is absent.], and nineteen bishops in various places [Note: [Col. 0084D] The same manuscript has eighteen.]. The episcopate then remained vacant for six days [Note: [Col. 0084D] In the same manuscript, “six days” is absent.] [Note: [Col. 0084C] Unless we say that Vigilius, after the death of the most holy [Col. 0084D] Silverius, restored himself to the proper order and abdicated the pontificate, which he had occupied by intrusion, I do not see how the apostolic see could have remained vacant for six days after Silverius’s death. It is therefore highly probable that, as soon as he heard that Silverius had died and was performing miracles, he abdicated the apostolic see, because of the crimes he had committed—simony, the expulsion and killing of Silverius, and contempt of the anathema—until he was once again legitimately elected by the consent of the entire clergy through Belisarius’s secret machination. Baronius, year 540, nos. 4, 5, and 6. SEV. BINIUS.]

[Col. 0085]

## LETTERS OF POPE SILVERIUS (G,S)*

[Note: [Col. 0086D] This letter is of doubtful authenticity; among other reasons, its barbarous style establishes this.]

### FIRST LETTER OF POPE SILVERIUS TO VIGILIUS, THE FALSE POPE

He reproaches Vigilius for his ambition for the apostolic see and for the crime of simony, and condemns him by a sentence of anathema [Note: [Col. 0086D] The condemnation of Vigilius is inscribed in Justellus’s canon. See the notes on the Second Roman Council under Boniface II.].

[Col. 0085A]

**Silverius, bishop, to Vigilius**

[Note: [Col. 0086D] On the spuriousness of this letter and the following one, see Pagi under A.D. 539, nos. 3 and 4.]

The entire priestly community has long known that you are entangled in many transgressions. Many of the faithful also know that, by your obstinacy, you have seized the ministries of the Levites, having robbed our predecessors with hands stained by human blood [Note: [Col. 0086D] Felix III, Letter 6 to Acacius of Constantinople.].

For when, contrary to canonical law, during the time of Pope Boniface of holy memory, while he was still alive, you attempted to have his successor designated, unless the justice of the most illustrious senate had opposed you, your abominable beginnings should then have been cut short by pastoral foresight and pontifical [Col. 0085B] authority [of yours from pontifical honor]. But because a small wound in you was previously neglected, it grew into an incurable abscess. Unless it is cut away by another’s knife, it cannot feel the medicine of poultices. For, conceiving in the audacity of the most wicked spirit a frenzy of ambition, you behave insultingly toward that apostolic physician to whom the power of binding and loosing souls has been entrusted and granted. You again strive to introduce a new crime of error into the apostolic see, and, in the manner of Simon—whose disciple you show yourself to be by your deeds—you endeavor, by money given and by rejecting me, who by the favor of the Lord have now continuously presided over it for three terms, to invade my term of office [the variant reads *niteris* for *nitaris*].

Therefore accept, together with those who agree with you, the sentence of perpetual condemnation, and acknowledge that the name and office of the priestly ministry have been taken from you, condemned by the judgment of the Holy Spirit and by apostolic authority on our part. For it is fitting that the faith of the holy Fathers be preserved in the Catholic Church, so that he who has taken up by reprehensible presumption what he did not receive should lose what he possessed.

Given on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, in the consulship of Basil [Note: [Col. 0085D] The appended consular notice appears to have been inserted later, because, as Binius says in the margin, neither Belisarius nor Basil held a consulship during Silverius’s time. But it seems to me that this instead indicates the audacious ignorance of a forger who placed Basil, the famous consul of A.D. 541, at least two years too early. We have already complained often enough about these chronological errors of Mercator. PHIL. LABBE.].

Caelius Silverius, pope of the city of Rome, consenting to all the provisions of this decree of anathema made against Vigilius the usurper [against Vigilius the usurper], have signed; four bishops likewise signed, namely the bishops of Terracina, Fundi, Firmum, and Minturnae. This document was delivered by Anastasius the subdeacon.

## LETTER OF AMATOR, BISHOP OF AUTUN, TO POPE SILVERIUS

[Note: [Col. 0086D] Learned men likewise consider this to be of doubtful authenticity, and not without reason, since it suffers from the same defects as the following letter.]

He sends the pontiff small gifts to alleviate the hardship of exile and asks to be informed of the condition of the exile.

**Amator, bishop, to the most blessed Silverius**

From certain people arriving from those regions, dearest father, we have heard that you were unjustly driven from the see of Saint Peter and condemned to exile. Taking this very grievously, we have sent small gifts—namely, thirty pounds of silver—for the support of you and your companions. We ask that you receive them with as grateful a disposition as the intention with which they are sent is grateful.

We also ask that you not disdain to inform us by letter how matters were handled with you, and how they are being handled now, so that I may know the truth about you and be able to report it to the brethren. For what do you think is happening to us, supreme father, when such things are done to the supreme shepherd and vicar of Saint Peter? Nevertheless, do not grieve excessively, but always take courage in the Lord, because the divinity [Note: [Col. 0086D] Ennodius, Letter 24, Book IV.] of immeasurable power is able to remove the uncertainties of a tremendous storm by the blessing of fair weather. Pray for us, most blessed pope.

## SECOND LETTER OF POPE SILVERIUS

[Note: [Col. 0086D] Baronius, Binius, and others condemn it.] **Forged in Silverius’s name, to Amator** [Note: [Col. 0085D] This letter, written in Silverius’s name to Amator, bishop of Autun—perhaps the Amator who was exceedingly famous for holiness at this time—appears to have been cobbled together by some idle person from the writings of Anastasius. The false consular notice attached to it is far removed from historical truth, as is clear from Liberatus the deacon, the most trustworthy writer of this period. Judging it therefore unworthy of publication under Silverius’s name, we have thought it appropriate to present it here in an unusual place and with this unconventional inscription. SEV. BINIUS. [Col. 0086D] It would likewise have been appropriate to apply the same criticism to many other inscriptions, so that precious wares might be separated from the scraps of a cheap ὑποβολιμαῖος—“substituted” or “counterfeit”—merchant. PHIL. LABBE.]

He praises Amator’s charity and explains what was done against him. On not accepting false witnesses against a bishop.

[Col. 0086C]

**Silverius to his beloved and most loving bishop Amator**

O how good is charity, which presents absent persons to one another through an image [Note: [Col. 0086D] Gregory, Letter 50, Book IV.], and makes those who are present mutually present through love. It touches what is divided [it joins what is divided], puts what is confused in order, unites what is unequal, and perfects what is incomplete.

How rightly the excellent preacher calls it “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3), because the other virtues indeed produce perfection, but charity binds them together so that they can no longer be dissolved from the mind of the one who loves.

Therefore, dearest brother, I find you filled with this virtue, since you not only take care to inquire about me and visit me, but also do not cease to strengthen and support me with your possessions. Yet I can neither recount nor write to you everything about the many evils inflicted upon me.

Above all, the patrician was hostile to me [Note: [Col. 0087C] At the command of the empress Theodora.], because I would not restore Anthimus, formerly patriarch of Constantinople, whom my predecessor Agapetus of holy memory had condemned as he deserved. At her command, moreover, certain false witnesses came forward, making accusations against me in which I had never shared.

But when many persisted in the same accusation, our patrician Belisarius was afraid [Note: [Col. 0087C] Anastasius, or some other author of the *Pontifical Book*.], and ordered me to come to him peacefully, allegedly for certain ecclesiastical arrangements, at the Pincian Palace [Note: [Col. 0087C] Elsewhere, “the palace of the prince,” as in Justellus’s canon.]. At the first and second curtains he held back all the clergy [Col. 0087B] and people who were coming with me, and permitted no one to enter except me and my deacon Vigilius.

After I had been forcibly detained and brought before the aforementioned patrician woman, they sent me into exile. There I am now sustained by the bread of affliction and the water of distress. Nevertheless, for that reason I neither abandoned nor do I abandon my office. Rather, with the bishops whom I was able to gather, I anathematized those who acted in this way against me [Note: [Col. 0087C] That sentence against Vigilius is rightly considered suspect, as we observed shortly before.], and together with them, by apostolic and synodal authority, I decreed that no one should ever again be deceived in such a manner as I was deceived; and if anyone should thereafter deceive any bishop in such a way, let him become *anathema maranatha*—anathema at the coming of the Lord—in the presence of God and the holy angels.

Likewise, strengthening the decrees of the holy Fathers, we determined—although it has already been determined very frequently—that neither false accusers, nor enemies, nor suspect witnesses should ever be admitted against bishops, nor should they be able to harm them in any way [Col. 0088A], because the holy Fathers judged that a false, suspect, hateful, or deadly accusation should rather be forbidden than heard.

Above all, dearest brother, such persons must be avoided [Note: [Col. 0088C] Isidore repeats this theme again and again in his forged letters.], turned away from, and rejected if they are found to be guilty. For not only the laws of the Church but also the laws of the world do not admit such people; they repel them.

Therefore it is written: “The mouth of the wicked devours iniquity” (Proverbs 19). And the Lord speaks through the prophet, saying: “With the holy man you will be holy, and with the innocent man you will act innocently. With the chosen man you will be chosen, and with the perverse man you will become perverse” (Psalm 17). And the Apostle says: “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Corinthians 15).

For this reason, as has already been said, the wicked must always be avoided, and one must cleave to the good and benevolent, so that, as far as we can, we may avoid the danger of negligence [Col. 0088B] [Note: [Col. 0088C] Saint Leo, Letters 2, 4, and 92.] and cut off this plague with whatever severity we can, lest it spread more widely. For there is no rashness of presumption where there is the diligence of piety.

Let each of you, supported by apostolic authority, always act according to this instruction [Note: [Col. 0088C] Saint Boniface of Mainz, Letter 17.], preserving his own conduct according to his strength, with brotherly love and holy religion; let each help the other in common, remain in charity, and continually strive to cling to the will of God, so that, praising the Lord together, we may always give him tireless thanks.

Farewell always in Christ, dearest one. With the Lord’s help, strive to fulfill the foregoing as well as you can and to instruct the remaining brethren by apostolic authority.

Given on the ninth day before the Kalends of December, in the consulship of Justinian five times [Note: [Col. 0088C] A false consular notice.], and Belisarius [Vuilisiarius] [Col. 0088C], men of illustrious rank.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 540. SAINT LAURENCE, BISHOP OF NOVARA

[Col. 0087]

**Notice by Margarino de la Bigne**

[Col. 0087D] I suspect that this was Laurence the elder, who, having been made bishop of Novara, became the twenty-fifth archbishop of Milan in A.D. 507. His praises appear to be celebrated by Ennodius [Note: [Col. 0087D] “Come,” he says, “most pious Lord,” and so forth, “summoned by the merit of holy priests, having been separately chosen by the conscience of this present father of ours, Laurence, who, so full of gifts, rose to the summit of the Church with as many qualities as would individually have made each of them a supreme pontiff. In him flourished the beginning of good works, modesty, the mother of honor, patience, the nurse of holy religion, and piety, ever intent on pleasing God; and he will bestow upon the members of the Church the institutions of life not by speech but by examples,” and so forth.] in the address sent to Honoratus, bishop of Novara, at the dedication of the Basilica of the Apostles.

Honoratus, after administering the bishopric of Novara for thirty-eight years—during which, after the elder Laurence, Saint Eustorgius occupied the Milanese throne for seven years, Saint Magnus for three, Saint Datius for twenty-two, Saint Vitalis for four, and Saint Auxanus for two—was likewise elevated to the archbishopric of Milan, not long before the Lombards came into Italy.

[Col. 0089]

# HOMILIES OF SAINT LAURENCE

(from the Library of the Fathers of Lyon) (C,S)*

## FIRST HOMILY: ON PENANCE

[Col. 0089A]

There are two times appointed by the Most High in which a twofold remission of sins is granted to human beings. For there is a public remission, and there is a private remission. The public has its own appointed time; the private exercises its own time. In the former there is the fountain of indulgence; in the latter, the fruit of repentance. In the former, God’s gift; in the latter, human labor. In the former, baptism; in the latter, repentance. These times must be recognized.

The first time extends from Adam to Christ. The second extends from Christ to the consummation of the age. These are the two times. What is found in the first? Adam’s sin, which Christ removed. And in the second? What? Personal sins, which human labor and vigilance extinguish [Col. 0089B]. The former is general; the latter particular.

Observe what is said: Adam’s sin, which remained in his children, divine mercy removed. The Savior took that burden upon himself and overturned it. When? In the first time. Where? In the baptismal font and in the river Jordan. There the Baptist was crying out and pointing with his finger to the heavenly Prince, saying: “Behold the Lamb of God; behold him who takes away the sins of the world” (John 1). What is “the sin of the world”? Adam’s offense, transmitted through the descent of seed to his children. Christ, therefore, is the Lamb of God. Baptized in the river, he took away the baneful burden passed down from the father to his children. That most evil crime, suggested by the serpent, he plunged into the font, abolished in the river, and burned away in the flesh. He took away the debt of one and bestowed forgiveness upon all. He healed the head, and all the members were made sound [Col. 0089C].

But from this font, or general indulgence, another time now arises: committed sins are not erased by water, but are forgiven by repentance. The psalmist David also marked both these times in the fiftieth Psalm. He set down the first time, speaking through Christ in the person of Adam. And what does he say? “Make manifest to me,” he says, “the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom.” And what are these? It was uncertain that Adam, fallen into death, would be saved; but his salvation was made manifest, and his redemption in the flesh and his remission in water. I saw in the spirit how your mercy, sent through your only-begotten Son, received the father from his crime and granted the son salvation. These are the uncertain things of your wisdom, which your graciousness revealed to me.

What, then, of Adam? He is the one who, through Christ, rejoices in David, saying: “You will sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Psalm 50 [51]). For my guilt overwhelmed me; indeed, the crime of transgression defiled me. But “you will sprinkle me with hyssop”—that is, with living water—and I shall be cleansed. Sprinkle me with water mingled with the sacred blood of your Son, and I shall be cleansed. “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” You will wash me in that future fountain and mystical river in which not only my crime will be extinguished, but also my whiteness, which I shall receive, will surpass even snow [Col. 0089D–0090A].
