It is destined, Father, that you will send your only-begotten Son, who will take away from the world the evil introduced through me, so that the children may not be cheated because of their father’s crime. He will open the way of salvation; he will unlock the remission of the font, and he will abolish my crime in water and Spirit. He will sprinkle me with drops of his grace, and I shall be cleansed. He will wash me with fiery light, and I shall be made whiter than snow.

This is the general remission of the first time. Let us see what belongs to the second. The Psalms likewise declare: “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” (ibid.). Behold the two times: the earlier, Adam; the later, David. There is a washing of water, where he says, “You will wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow.” Here there are tears of repentance, where David says, “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity, and cleanse me from my sin” [Col. 0090B].

The former is public; the latter private. The former is grace; the latter mercy. The former belongs to all; the latter is individual. The former is mystical; the latter moral. Adam is washed in the body of Christ, so that he may cast off the old man and put on the new. David is washed in a contrite heart, so that he may restore in himself the likeness which crime darkened. The former is renewed in the font; the latter repaired in weeping. Grace healed the former; groaning reformed the latter.

He who grieves over his offense with a bristling body, and, mourning his sin, paints its image before himself, thus declares: “Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity.” Why “thoroughly”? Because “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is always before me.” It is as though he said:

“You had healed me, Lord, earlier in my father Adam, when you took his members into yourself and baptized them in the font [Col. 0090C], washing them in the river. Through your beneficence I existed as a free man, yet I could not retain the grace granted to me. For I went astray again within myself. Freed from my father’s offense, I committed my own offense; rescued from the public snare, I fell into a private one. There is now no protection of the font or of water. What shall I do, or from where shall I obtain cleansing? Do I perhaps deserve once more to be drenched by the rain of your indulgence and washed in the river of the general bath? Far be it from me. I shall not seek again the gift of water by which I was washed. I shall ask once for what was granted once. I redeem myself from my own poverty; from my own labor I drench myself.

“There is in me a little moisture—not pouring over me like a torrent, but sprinkling me with a modest sweat. With the drops of my labor I seek to wash myself; with sparks of words I desire to burn away the poison conceived within me. ‘Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity’ [Col. 0090D]: wash me now not with water but with work; not with the baptismal font but with the dew of repentance. For my sin is always before me.

“I have seen myself; I have recognized my deed. The sin that disfigured me stands before me. ‘Wash me thoroughly from my iniquity,’ because I recognize what I have done. What I have recognized, graciously forgive. Look away from what I behold. This sight of it is enough for me. I have displeased you: ‘Turn your face away from my sins, and blot out all my iniquities.’ Why? Because my sin is always before me. It is written in my heart, engraved beneath my eyes, fixed in my conscience. Wash away what I have written; remove what I have depicted.”

These things were lamented figuratively. I have introduced them into the mirror of the fiftieth Psalm, in which, for our contemplation, the twofold image of the first and second times is reflected: the first in Adam, the second in David. Although both Adam and David may be enclosed within the span of the first time, it is the Holy Spirit who speaks through the prophets, distinguishes the time of each from the other, marks pardon for transgression in Adam, and lets the hand of repentance make satisfaction in David. For prophetic speech depicts in the Psalm both the earlier face of the time and the later one [Col. 0091A].

This discourse, therefore, is composed for you, beloved; this assertion is directed to you. This discussion is brought before you with the promise of clear progress, you in whom the warmth of faith has perhaps grown cold through the intervention of sin. The mind, having been lost, is stunned; corrupted hope melts away; and every expectation directed toward the future grows numb in perplexity, while each person weighs the matter with himself, reckons it up within himself, and speaks thus:

“What am I to do now? What more must I undertake, or what remains for me to hope? I was redeemed and have become a slave. I was free and have become a slave of sin. I have lost the grace of the giver and forfeited the beneficence of the redeemer. I came forth from the font with a radiant body, but have again soaked and defiled myself with filth and stained myself with mud. Pure through God’s grace, I have become ruined through my own excess.

“My error has made me from a son a servant, from an intimate an enemy, from an heir an outsider [Suppl. fecit: ‘made’]. I have violated my creed; I have corrupted the covenant written at the very entrance of the font. O how unhappy my condition! O how pitiable my deliberations! I had promised that I would renounce the works of the devil, but I could not fulfill it. I relapse into and am defiled by the evils from which I had been free. I have changed the evangelical tunic once again into a garment of skins. I have darkened with the stain of vices the robe of merit which I had woven clean. I have again clothed the new man in old age.

“What do I seek now, or what do I still expect? Where shall I seek the fountain, or where shall I find baptism? Is there perhaps still access to water? Will the water receive me again, so as to reform me in the womb of water and give birth to me innocent? Or should I perhaps still seek the priest’s right hand, to plunge me into the font [Col. 0091D] and purify me once again from it?”

These are the things you say to yourself; these are the matters you turn over within yourself, weighed down by the burden of your conscience. But what are these words of yours? O human being, recognize that you are the image of God. God made you wise, provident in spirit, mystical in mind, exalted in your senses, and he wishes not to destroy you but to save you; not to kill you but to protect you. Why, then, do you despair when he does not despise you?

You fear your conscience and do not hasten to the source of indulgence. What do you think the fountain was that conceived you, or what do you consider the water to be that gave birth to you? Is water the intermediary, or is the stream the cause? Far from it! Learn the mystery. Your prudence is the fountain, and your understanding within you is the overflowing water, possessing the sight of the heart so that you may see yourself.

You have received [Col. 0092A] a mind that seeks higher things. Stand in the height of your mind as the image of God, and from this mirror of divine workmanship you will search out profound things. You possess free choice and understanding granted by God. Consider within yourself: since you are the image of God, how could you be extinguished? If there is prudence in you, if you possess counsel and the proper freedom of mind, God is in you. He himself will be your repentance, your fountain and baptism, and your remission—he who never ceases or fails within you.

Why do you seethe in uncertainty? Why are you unsettled in mind and, exhausted by the futile weariness of your conscience, grow numb? You sinned after the font; you fell after baptism; you committed a crime after the general indulgence. What now? Is hope already lost? Has the reward perhaps been cut off? It is not so, human being! Why are you led astray?

You received a sign from the [Col. 0092B] font—not of despair but of compassion, not of defection but of remission, and not so that you should ever despair. The Jews received a sign. What kind? Circumcision. Christians also received a sign. What kind? Compassion. Behold the sign among the Jews: circumcision of the flesh; among Christians: circumcision of the heart. But the latter is by far the superior. In the former there is the blood of incision; in the latter, the water of remission. There, a wound of the flesh; here, the palm of mercy. There, strict observance; here, royal indulgence.

Christ, hanging on the cross, prefigured both these seals when he brought forth from his wound both water and blood (John 10). He did so to give the seal of blood to the Jews, but the sign of water to the gentile Christians. You therefore received a sign from the font—not a Jewish sign, but an evangelical one.

From that day and that hour when you came forth [Col. 0092C] from the washing, you yourself are for yourself an unfailing fountain and enduring remission. You do not need a teacher or the priest’s right hand. As soon as you rose from the sacred font, you were clothed in a white garment and anointed with mystical ointment. Invocation was made over you, and a threefold power came upon you, pouring this new vessel full through this new teaching.

From then on, he established you yourself as your own judge and arbiter, and gave you knowledge so that you might learn from yourself good and evil—that is, the difference between merit and sin. And because, while remaining in the members and structure of the body, you could not exist free from sin or immune from guilt, after baptism he established your remedy within you and placed remission in your own free choice, so that, when necessity demanded it, you would not seek a priest; rather, like a knowledgeable and perceptive teacher, you would correct your error [Col. 0092D] within yourself and wash away your sin through repentance.

Therefore let hardness cease; let despair end; let sloth cease. The fountain never fails. The water is within; cleansing lies in free choice; sanctification lies in skillfulness; remission lies in the dew of tears. Do not collapse into sluggishness. A fountain of perpetual repentance has been preserved in the human being.

There is repentance at the voice of the Baptist, who cries out in the wilderness and, with a penetrating shout, rouses the deserted minds of human beings, saying: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matthew 3).

No one can possess the summit or height of the heavenly empire unless he has been supported by the aid of repentance. No one reaches the innermost places of the heavenly kingdom [Col. 0093A] unless he has repented.

The Baptist repeats further: “I baptize you with water for repentance, but another is coming after me who will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire.” Do not now seek either John or the Jordan. Be your own Baptist.

Have you been polluted after the washing? Have your inward parts been corrupted? Has your soul been defiled? Dip yourself in the water of repentance; wash yourself with an abundance of tears; let the fountain of compunction overflow within your inmost parts; let living waters gush forth in your entrails.

Prepare yourself for the coming Lord, and he himself will baptize you in the Holy Spirit and fire, holding a winnowing fan in his hand (ibid.). This signifies the examination or weighing of repentance and sin. He weighs both burdens within you; he examines the mass and the mass within you: one of repentance and one of corruption. The fruit of repentance [Col. 0093B] he gathers, as though it were wheat, for your advancement; but your sins, like the chaff of corruption, he burns with unquenchable fire (Luke 2).

This is private remission, summoned from the innermost heart and acquired through repentance.

Much must be repeated, very much recounted. The human race is fragile and always walks with an unsteady step. Bodily nature is exposed to opposing forces, for it is subject to various passions and vices; it is guided not so much by its own purity as by divine mercy. And if someone today trusts in merit, strength of spirit, or vigor of his inward parts, tomorrow he is deceived and led astray. Thus the Apostle testifies, saying: “Let the one who thinks he stands beware lest he fall” (1 Corinthians 3).

There is indeed a prison that weighs down the soul’s strength and stains its brightness. There is always a snare hanging over us and continually lying in wait [Col. 0093C]; a snare stretched out along the road in a destructive fall. Hence the prophet cries: “Along this way on which I walked, they concealed a snare for me” (Psalm 39). And again: “Beside the path they placed a stumbling-block for me” (Psalm 139 [140]).

The soul is often entangled in this bodily snare, and, whether it wishes it or not, is not freed of its own accord before it supplicates divine assistance through repentance, as the prophet again says: “Blessed is the Lord, who did not give us as prey to their teeth. Our soul, like a sparrow, has been rescued from the snare of the hunters. The snare has been broken, and, with the Lord’s help, we have been freed” (Psalm 123 [124]).

The soul was caught in the snare; it was rescued not by its own strength but by divine protection. And what is this snare except the flesh, which always troubles the soul when it is running well toward its purpose [Col. 0093D], continually tears at it, and frequently captures it? For there is one goad lying in wait throughout the members.

I say: consider how grievous a snare lies in the eyes. Have you not understood how the soul is taken captive in the act of seeing—not merely often, but always? From where does greed lie in wait, from where is lust kindled, except from bodily sight? You have seen a strong snare. And not without reason is it written: “What has been made is more wicked than the eye in a human being” (Ecclesiasticus 31)—that is, “What is more wicked than the eye in a human being?” And again: “Death will enter through the windows” (Jeremiah 9).

Your tongue too is an incurable snare. For it scatters the poison of cursing, blasphemy, whispering, and detraction; and it wounds not only hearts but also the soul. Hence that leader of repentance entreats, saying: “Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” [Col. 0094A]. Another likewise inserts this prayer: “Who will give a scourge to my thoughts, or who will place a seal upon my lips?” Certainly, so that I may speak when silence is not permitted, and so that what the tongue brings forth may not bite but nourish the soul.

An adverse voice will sound in the ears, and the inner person will be goaded to anger and stirred to slaughter. Do you see that a snare also remains in the ears? Hence that admonition of Scripture resounds: “Hedge your ears with thorns; do not listen to an evil tongue” (Ecclesiasticus 28).

There is a snare in the hands, as it is said: “Your hands weave iniquity.” And again: “Why did you fast for me, when you wound those subject to you and strike the humble with your fists?” (Isaiah 58).

What shall I say about the harmful movement and blood-stained running of the feet, as in the words: “Their feet are swift to shed [Col. 0094B] blood” (Psalm 13 [14]; Romans 3)?

The Savior determines through his own sentences that these bodily ambushes, these snares of the individual members, must be torn out of the body: “If your right eye,” or “if your hand or foot, causes you to stumble” (Matthew 5; Mark 9)—that is, if they corrupt your soul, which desires divine things and thinks upon heavenly things. If they entangle you in their snares or seek through their deceit to tear out your sight, cut off not your hand or foot but the corruption and disease inflicted upon you through these members.

For this reason it is said: “If your right eye causes you to stumble,” or if your right hand or foot does so. Is it not because everything good is called right, just as evil is called left? There is a right side, and there is a left side. The right retains its approved ones; the left likewise retains its rejected ones.

What does Christ say to [Col. 0094C] those on the right? “Come, you blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world” (Matthew 25). And what to those on the left? “Depart from me, you accursed, into eternal fire.”

Do you see how great the separation between left and right is? What, then, if your right eye causes you to stumble? Learn what happens when you commit sin with the eye serving as its instrument, and the act appears sweet and right to you. This right side is then corrected into the left when, with the Lord seated and examining sins, you begin, among many others, to hear this also: “Depart from me, you accursed, unjust sinners, into eternal fire.”

Has the eye caused you to stumble, stolen you away, made you sin, and entangled you through sight? Tear it out. What does he command you to tear out—the eye or the sin? The eye that suggested the offense. Did the eye sin because it saw, or did the mind [Col. 0094D] rather sin because it desired? But if, throughout all sins and stumbling-blocks, it is not the mind’s desire that must be restrained, but the eye must be dug out because it saw, then no one will any longer have eyes.

There is no one, I think, whose eyes will remain, since among mortals there is no one who does not lust, or take offense, or sin. Man, would you condemn the eye granted to you by grace, by whose service you see the light? It is the adornment of the head, the mirror of the limbs, and the most cherished window of the whole body! Do not condemn it because it sees, but condemn what it sees; rather, condemn yourself, because you lusted! Tear out—not the eye from your head, but error from your heart; pluck out—not bodily sight, but the guilt of lust: it is not useful to destroy the eye, but to uproot the guilt. The eye was “right” when it brought scandal upon you—that is what it does when it defiled and polluted you. But tear it out with the opposing strength. Do not think of wounding yourself, but gird yourself for victory. Become the armed soldier of repentance, and immediately you will overthrow sin.

Vice was sweet when it delighted the soul; but now let repentance become sweeter to you, since it not only delights but also nourishes the soul. You lusted after evil, desire conquered you, and you committed a crime! Your mind will be your right eye—that is, the sweetness of sin. Tear out that eye, joined to left-handed sight, which does not illuminate you but darkens you, and transfers you from the right to the left.

But you say: “This evil which you claim must be uprooted from me—this wicked eye—is within! It is not visible in the breast, but is held fixed in the heart of the conscience. By what art shall I be able to tear it out, since it can neither be touched by hand nor removed or plucked out by a finger?” Do you want me to show you the hand, the finger, and the art by which it can be plucked out? When you struck a humble person with your fists, you brought the eye of sin into yourself; when you extended your hand to lift up the humble or satisfy the needy, you tore from your heart the eye of wickedness that had scandalized you. Do you see by what hand, finger, and art that harmful eye is torn out—the eye that directs you from the right to the left?

Vices are sweet while they are being committed, but immediately afterward they are bitter. “Honey,” he says, “drips from the lips of a prostitute” (Prov. V), and this is sweet. For a time it oils the throat and fattens the palate, but at last it is turned into the bitterness of gall; what was sweet for a time becomes bitter in the end. Hurry, therefore, and do not delay in correcting yourself from the left to the right.

You fell through the eye: did its sight contaminate you? Let its water wash you. Did it bring a snare upon you? Let it rescue you from the snare, for it possesses within itself the great help of tears. Did it drive you to defile yourself with obscene acts and cut off your head with a shameful sword—that is, with greed or lust? Come, then; exercise yourself against such an eye. Raise yourself against your own sight; stir the veins of your heart that extend toward the eye, and say to it:

“Eye, I turn back to you; I charge you with this! Remove what you entangled. You wounded me; heal me. You polluted me; purify me. Wash away what you stained; raise up what you struck down; correct what you overthrew; release what you bound through scandal. You saw, and I lusted; you looked, and I sinned. You saw gold, you saw the possessions and estates of others: ambition blinded me. I began to desire what was not mine; I began to seize or, under some pretext, invade what belonged to another. With such a scandal you blinded me.

“What shall I say about a woman’s beauty? How greatly the soul collapsed by gazing upon it, how the inner parts were made effeminate, and, as though struck by the arrow of desire, I fell headlong from a certain precipice! Give now your fluid, and erase my sin. Water me with your rains; let your waters rush upon me and overwhelm my crimes.”

Speak these things with the eye that scandalized you. Moreover, anticipate the judgment that awaits you. Pierce the vein of your heart with the goads of repentance, and draw forth from the depth of your heart and the innermost part of your mind living water flowing over your head.

Let your head become a fountain of remission and a river of indulgence; and from it let twin streams run forth—not only through the right eye but also through the left. Let both your eyes flow equally for you, with the dew of healing and the rain of indulgence. For the most indulgent Judge wills that weeping cleanse what sight polluted, and that compunction restore what desire defiled: that you may tear the poisonous eye from your heart, weeping and sighing and grieving, as the prophet Jeremiah grieved when he mourned the people carried away, saying: “Who will give water to my head, or a fountain of tears to my eyes?” (Jer. IX).

He indeed lamented the people held captive; but you must sigh for the soul that desire violated and the right eye made degenerate. Thus must the eye be torn out; thus must the hand, or the harmful members, be cut off. For where greed is, there is the right hand armed with poisonous teeth, to strike, to afflict, and to take away what belongs to others. Where lust is, there is the right eye armed with harmful sight, which gives little pleasure and causes much harm.

“He who looks upon a woman in order to lust after her,” he says, “has committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matt. V). The eye saw, the flesh lusted: did the soul sin? The eye wept again: the flesh was washed, the soul was released.

Greed is an unspeakable vice among human beings: it is a single root fixed in the innermost parts, from which all evils sprout. What is greed? “Desire is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. VI). From this root arise lies and perjuries. For whoever is a seller or buyer, whoever conducts business for the sake of profit out of desire—does he not often swear falsely and frequently lie? Without this vice, a merchant is either rare or nonexistent.

And why do I speak of a merchant, a trickster practiced in commerce? Let us see what makes robbers, or from where traitors burst forth. Was not King Ahab a robber because of greed, when through the conspiracy of a deceitful woman he falsely betrayed and killed a righteous man in order to seize his vineyard by force? Judas too was greedy when he betrayed Christ to the Jews (Matt. XXVI), receiving thirty pieces of silver from them.

Take away greed, and there is no discord; remove greed, and love alone reigns; let greed cease, and ambition comes to an end. Take away desire, and no one says, “This is mine,” or, “This is yours.” From it fraud germinates, from it deceit arises, from it conspiracy is contrived. Anger too, ambushes, murders, and wars themselves—whether public or civil—are the fruits of desire and greed. Thus, whenever one person overcomes or cuts down another by arms or by schemes, he plunders that person’s possessions as though they were his own and satisfies his greed.

This is also what the Apostle’s Scripture testifies, saying: “Greed is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. VI). Learn carefully what exists in a human being. He has within himself two fixed roots of two evils, by resisting which he is inwardly troubled and gnawed. And what are these roots? One is greed, and the other is lust. Where is the root of greed? In the desire of the mind. Where is lust? In the will of the members.

For the desire of the mind, burning with greed, arms the hands and feet and makes sin in them a public offense, a crime outside the body. But the root of lust, nourished by the juices of the members and watered by the fluids of the veins, compels the very inner parts to sin in obscene desire and to commit an inward sin.

Thus there is the sin of greed and there is the sin of lust in the members. There are two capital crimes in a human being: one inward and one outward; one in the members and one outside the members. There is the sin of lust in the members, and there is the sin of greed outside the members.

And so that you may believe that what is said is true, hear the same Apostle continuing: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body; but the one who commits fornication sins against his own body” (1 Cor. VI).

But you say: “If the feet run after plunder, and the hands seize it, how can the sin be outside the body?” There is no doubt that every sin is committed with the members serving it; but it is one thing to commit sin through a member, and another to sin against the members. In what is committed through the members, the mind takes delight; but the pleasure of the flesh neither perceives nor receives it. Therefore it was said: “Every sin that a person commits is outside the body.” But the flesh contains within itself the torches of lust and the burning furies that sprout from the root of sexual desire.

For, aroused or stimulated for a short time by sweet enticements, the fluid draws to itself from the deepest inner parts and the marrow of the veins the pleasure of the whole body. When the Apostle examined this with the greatest attention, he firmly established the sentence, saying: “The one who commits fornication sins against his own body.”

Woe to me! What shall I do, a frail human being? By what strength shall I be able to resist such savagery? By what means can I avoid the poisons of the two things that dwell within me? If the root of greed—a many-formed crime—ulcerates the soul; if the root of lust supplies fiery torches of desire, with which it burns the marrow of the inner parts, what shall I do? What strength is in me? What substance do I possess?

Two serpents live together within me, greed and lust. They always bite, continually ulcerate, and frequently clash; by my own strength I cannot stand against such beasts. If there is no longer the aid of water, if the Holy Spirit is absent, who will free me from this body of death? Who will tear me away from this mass of wickedness and this savage bite?

Human being, do not despair: the matter is ready at hand, life is in your hand, strength is in your will, victory is within your choice. If you wished it, you conquered; if you do not wish it, you will be left defeated. Whoever wishes to conquer strives in order to conquer; whoever despairs has lost the victory.

Why do you fear the crime of desire or the deed of greed? Do not fear! This root of all evils—that is, greed—has its own water. And what is this water, if not almsgiving? Have you not heard what is written? “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Eccl. XXIII).

A great sentence! Let complaint cease; let doubt cease. For where there is almsgiving, there is water; where there is water, there is the Spirit; and where there is the Spirit, there is remission. Let despair cease: water, washing, and remission are present in the almsgiving of the giver.

Do not delay in washing your polluted body and soul in the fountains of almsgiving, so that you may return again to the form of the baptism you previously received: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins.” It is as though it had also been said: “As water extinguishes blazing fire, so almsgiving tears greed apart; it breaks the deadly bonds of human crimes.”

You have seen the water of almsgiving! Do you wish to know that lust and desire too have their water? Sin defiles the body, but now it has a contrary water. Where? Is it not in the eyes—and rightly so, from the body? From the eyes flows water that dissolves the pollution contracted by the whole body and washes away its foulness.

For just as almsgiving strikes down and extinguishes the sin that is outside the body, so an abundance of tears uproots the vice of lust that defiles the members. Thus the sin outside the body has its own fountain in almsgiving, and the crime committed within the body has its own fountain flowing from the eyes. So you may know that almsgiving quenches the flames of greed, and that the inner parts darkened by lust become white again through abundant tears and recover their worth.

But how long shall I merely suggest these things in words? Receive evangelical instruction; receive two witnesses to two crimes. You have the tax collector, and you also have the prostitute: the tax collector in greed, the prostitute in lust. These leaders of crimes became witnesses to divine mercy.

Do you wish to know how these two conquered and escaped the contagion of their crimes? The tax collector was saved: by what hand? Was it not through almsgiving? The prostitute was received: by what protection? Was it not through tears?

But let us recount the matter. “The Lord Jesus,” it says, “was passing through Jericho; and behold, there was a man named Zacchaeus” (Luke XIX), a sinful, greedy man, rich through robberies. He sought to see the Lord Jesus, in order to know what sort of man he was; but he could not see him, being shut out by the obstruction of the crowds, for he was of small stature.

It happened that he found a sycamore tree. He climbed it quickly and saw him. What did he see? The Savior of the world. He hurried well; he climbed exceedingly well. In his eager desire to see the Savior, he found the salvation of which he was ignorant.

And what shall I say—he saw? He was seen before he saw. “The Lord Jesus passed by, saw him, and said to him: Zacchaeus, hurry and come down, for today I must remain in your house.”

“Lord, what is this that you say? Are there not believers? Why do you attach yourself to such a man? Zacchaeus is a tax collector—indeed, the chief of tax collectors; he is a sinner and a robber. He merely wished to see you. Should he already be saved by sight alone? He climbed a tree in order to see you; but if he has not yet seen you, if he has not yet lamented his deeds, has he confessed his stain or recounted his crimes? Has he wept before you, or given alms for his sins? He is still a profane man, and you say to him, ‘Today I must remain in your house’? He has scarcely yet deserved to see you, and already you visit his rooms and embrace his hospitality!”

But this is truly your office and your most indulgent care: you did not come to invite the righteous, but to correct sinners. You remain with tax collectors, eat with sinners, and join yourself to the unjust, so that by this association you may convert and correct them, as though by a certain art, for salvation.

“Zacchaeus,” he says, “come down, because today I must remain with you.”

And what did Zacchaeus do? He immediately came down from the tree, already made better by the Lord’s word. The sight corrected the robber, and a single word changed his mind. He came down, hastened swiftly, and joyfully prepared hospitality. He received the leader of life and became a son of Abraham.

Christ remained with him and breathed into him the fire of hidden things, the fire of faith, the secret ardor of the Holy Spirit, so that, burning with love of God and the warmth of faith, he might utter such words:

“Lord, behold, I give half of my possessions to the poor.”

Did you hear what he said? “Behold, I scatter half of my possessions among the poor.” It was as though he were saying:

“Now I have seen; now I have understood. Savior, my correction has come not from myself but from you. I have recognized my robberies and weighed the harmful deeds I committed in my greed. I beg and entreat you: help me, wretched and sinful as I am! Behold, I give back what I took; I restore to the needy whom I harmed; behold, I clothe those whom I stripped. And if I defrauded anyone of anything, I shall repay fourfold.”

Have you seen the generosity of the robber? He continues to say:

“Be present, Lord; I repay fourfold what I unjustly took. You care for the guilty; you receive my vow and heal my wounds. Let almsgiving tear out what greed buried.”

They were indignant and tried to blame the Lord because he had turned aside to a sinner and wished to remain in the tax collector’s house. But what did the Lord say to them?

“Are you like this? Do not think of me in this way. Do you not know that I am the Savior of tax collectors and sinners? Amen, I tell you: today salvation has come to the house of Zacchaeus, because he too is a son of Abraham.”

Salvation came to him because he both saw and recognized the Savior, received him, and fulfilled his command. Have you not heard what he said? “I give half of my possessions to the poor, and if I defrauded anyone of anything, I restore it fourfold!”

Why are you indignant at such a worker? Can I reject one converted so promptly, refuse to receive him gladly, and despise someone transferred so quickly from evil to good, from plunder to victory? Have you not seen that a tax collector became the leader of the needy, and that a public man deserved to become a son of Abraham?

Do you not remember that “the Son of Man came to seek what had gone astray and to save what had perished” (Matt. XVII)?

Look, tax collectors; behold, sinners; persist, greedy people, thieves, and robbers. See the example of Zacchaeus. Observe what vein of the fountain and what streams of water he found, with which he willingly drenched himself through almsgiving and destroyed all the filth he had contracted in his public office. In Zacchaeus that sentence was decisively fulfilled: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving cleanses sin” (Eccl. III).

Small in body, he became renowned in deed. Conceived in wickedness, he suddenly emerged fortunate through almsgiving. He climbed a tree, small as he was, so that he might be seen by Christ and become known throughout the world. A desirable tree, full of healing medicine, which by sight alone helped a sinner and sanctified a profane man!

That tree was not like the primordial tree of which it was said, “On the day you eat from it, you shall die” (Gen. III). In that tree the serpent deceived the simple; in this one the Savior came to the sinner’s aid.

Imitate Zacchaeus yourself: climb the tree of your soul. There is another tree within you—your faith—and a lofty watchtower. Stand at the summit of this tree and watchtower, so that you may be able to see God and Christ passing by, just as Zacchaeus saw him.

He climbed a tree because he could not see on account of the crowds. You are not held back by a crowd of people or excluded by a multitude, but you have among you a forest of vices and throngs of thoughts that overshadow your mind and obscure your sight. But tear this badly shadowing forest from your heart. Drive away harmful thoughts and the noise of your conscience.

Leave in your soul a single clear, fruitful tree bearing the marks of the cross. Climb it, so that you too may see Christ, just as Zacchaeus saw him, and so that he may say to you: “Amen, I tell you: today salvation has come to this man, because he too is a son of Abraham.”

Be immediately pierced by the feeling conveyed in his words, and conceive in your mind, with great eagerness, the intention to give alms. Offer a little, and earn much. Give earthly things, and demand eternal things, as Zacchaeus did. While scattering his earthly substance, he not only dissolved his accumulated wealth in the fountains of almsgiving, but also merited to be already an heir of the heavenly kingdom and a son of Abraham.

You have seen a most elegant lesson; you have seen Zacchaeus cleansing the crime of greed with the rains of almsgiving. O singular shortcut to salvation—to give to the poor and be washed from sins! Almsgiving suddenly converted a person from sins, not only purified him but also crowned him, and made a citizen of paradise from a tax collector.

If the account has been completed, if the measure of remission has been filled from the wages of the poor, the example of the tax collector is enough for you: through almsgiving, as through a river, he drew the pitiable deeds of his past life into indulgence and washed them clean, and by giving he rescued himself from the snare of greed.

Now receive another example of piety, set before you in the woman who was a prostitute, so that you may escape the crime of lust and the captivity of fornication. Hold fast what we stated earlier: there are two capital crimes in a human being, greed and lust. We have taught that the tax collector trampled underfoot the crime of greed. For you heard that he gave to the hungry and escaped; he fed the poor and merited to become what he had not been.

Now the discourse will concern the prostitute, in relation to lust. Woman, we demand from you what may benefit many. Prostitute, give us an example, so that we may know how your violated members were not despised by God but rather received. Tell us, criminal woman, how you became chaste! Do not be silent, tax collector, but reveal to us Christ’s benefit, and teach us by what manner you became a virgin from a prostitute.

Hear the matter; learn the care, for the prince of mercy has performed wonders. He received the prostitute, cleansed the tax collector, and glorified the corrupted woman.

A certain Pharisee named Simon invited Christ into his house and prepared a banquet for him, so that he might eat with him. “The Lord entered,” it says, “and graciously reclined.” This too is a marvelous act of humanity: that God should recline and eat in a Pharisee’s house! He remained with Zacchaeus; with the Pharisee he ate. And why was this, unless because he was both the friend and the Savior of tax collectors?

But while he was reclining and eating in the Pharisee’s house, what happened? Behold, a sinful woman who was in that city learned that Christ had entered and reclined in the Pharisee’s house. Suddenly, like a bold prostitute, she entered the house and offered to the Savior a brow worn down by public gazes.

She entered boldly—no longer as a prostitute, but as a modest woman; not to satisfy lust, but to see the light. She entered not to pursue the form of lust, but to reach the fountain of indulgence. She entered not to become still more defiled, but to lay down the filth she had contracted and, with the Lord’s mercy, cleanse her violated inner parts.

She passed beyond her former life and did not look toward the Pharisee, but directed herself along a straight path to the fountain, stripped of shame and armed with repentance. And what did she do? She approached the feet of Christ as he reclined there. She stood anxiously; and, though her body had been restored, she held the Lord’s feet as a guilty woman and drew forth a remedy.

She acted, she spoke in her heart, she was silent and groaned quietly; she persisted without restraint, driven by repentance. She raised her mind to heaven and fixed her gaze upon the earth. She saw only the one whose feet she held. To him she opened her sin; to him she disclosed her sins and unlocked her guilty conscience.

She poured out her heart, mingled with tears, over his feet. With her soft hair she wiped his feet, drenched with tears, as though with a linen cloth. Nor was it enough to wash them with tears and wipe them with her hair: in addition, she poured over them the ointment from the alabaster vessel she held in her hand, so that she might anoint with perfume the feet she had moistened.

In these three things—the tears, the hair, and the ointment—the unclean woman drew, as it were, the fountain of her baptism from Christ’s feet. For what else is there in the fountain of baptism but water, chrism, and a white garment? For this woman, tears took the place of water, ointment the place of chrism, and hair the place of the garment.

O sinful woman, what an ingenious device of yours! Who showed you or taught you to discover and propose such an art, by which you might overcome the crimes heaped up within you with momentary tears, shave them away with your hair, and uproot them with ointment?

What happened, then? “The sinful woman entered with an alabaster vessel of ointment and stood beside Christ’s feet.” And what did the Savior do? Was he unaware of her? Did he not know that she was a tax collector? It would be wicked to say so. But when he saw that she was pierced with compunction, he no longer rejected or despised her as a tax collector because of her persistence; rather, he received her in her grief and embraced her in her repentance.

He did not charge her with what ought to have been charged against her. The Lord did not say to her:

“Prostitute, adulteress, fornicator, wanton woman, you come to me? You have drawn near? You have dared to touch my feet with polluted hands? Do you not see the mass of your evils? Your crimes are still hot within you; your members breathe the heat of lust; your body is full of criminal stains. The deadly burden of your contamination presses upon your very soul within. And you, corrupted by such great crimes, have dared to come to me?”

Christ neither charged nor addressed her in this way. Even if he had spoken so, such a woman would doubtless have been ready to answer in opposition. If Christ had said to her, “Unclean woman, most foul and polluted, stop; depart from me. I have no dealings with prostitutes,” she could have replied and set this against him:

“Lord, heavenly King, Redeemer of the world, what are you saying? Did you come down from heaven only for the righteous? And how many are the righteous? Do you reject sinners in this way? Where is your people? Or did you, as a physician, come to heal the healthy? Far from it! The healthy have no need of a physician; prostitutes need medicine.

“Tax collectors press around you in order to receive care. You came to stretch out your hand to sinners, to raise up those who have been struck down, and to restore sight to the blind. Physician, do not reject me, wounded as I am. And if you reject me, I will not withdraw; rather, by right I shall demand healing from you, because you came to heal the injured, not to reject them.

“I hold your feet, and I will not depart before I receive care. Almighty, receive this persistent woman and do not despise one who knocks, even though she is a prostitute.

“Behold, I offer you the price of my redemption: turn your gaze toward me. And what is it that I offer? I am needy; I am destitute; I have nothing in my substance except tears—and this is enough for you. I know that this offering is pleasing to you.

“You do not seek money, but require repentance. You do not seek libations so much as you delight in tears. A contrite heart is a sacrifice to you, and a spirit pierced with compunction. Receive, therefore, the price of my repentance, and give me the reward of your indulgence.

“Good shepherd, tell me, I beg you: am I not one of your sheep? But I strayed from the flock and became like a lost sheep. Seek your handmaid and make me chaste from a prostitute!

“Do not despise me. I am not alone; I have many companions, and a very large part of your sheep is in me. Exalted shepherd, seek the sheep scattered and infected with mange. Gather them together and fill your sheepfold.

“For you yourself said: ‘I have other sheep that are not from this sheepfold; these too I must gather, so that there may be one flock and one shepherd.’ What are these sheep that are not from your fold? Are they not prostitutes and tax collectors? Are they not sinners, adulterers, and unjust people?

“Otherwise, if you reject or exclude these people, who will remain to fill your sheepfold? Prophets and apostles, martyrs, virgins, and the continent? How many are they in comparison with the whole people! If sinners are barred, then few will be inside and many outside.

“But since you are the universal Redeemer and common shepherd, who came not to destroy but to save, gather the sheep corrupted by mange and bring the scattered back to the heavenly folds. Make one flock from all, and be for all, as you promised, both Savior and Shepherd.

“I, a woman, beg you as one unworthy, and silently within myself I make my request, knowing that you are the physician of those who have gone astray. In words I lament my pain, and with secret sobs I press down my deed.

“Be my advocate: receive my case and release my chains. Great indeed is what I have deserved by touching your feet. I drench your feet with the tears of repentance. You are the light of indulgence: erase my crimes.

“I touch you, Savior—I, an unclean woman—and I kiss your feet, not to pollute what I touch, but to be washed by the one whom I touch.”

O prostitute, great is your faith, marvelous your way of life, glorious your confession! We no longer call you a prostitute, but the physician of all prostitutes, for many take from you an example of recovery.

But let me return to the order of the chapter with which we began. Meanwhile, the Pharisee who had invited the Lord, when he saw the woman as though unworthy, said within himself: “If this man were a prophet, he would not allow this woman to touch him, since he would know her reputation.”

While he was weighing these things within himself and trying to obscure the favorable deed, the Lord grasped and exposed his thought:

“Simon,” he said, “I have something to say to you.”

He replied: “Teacher, speak.”

“A moneylender had two debtors. One owed five hundred denarii, the other fifty. Since they had nothing with which to repay, he forgave both. Tell me, please: which of these two ought to love him more?”

Simon replied: “I suppose, the one to whom he forgave more.”

The Lord said to him: “You have judged correctly.”

Simon, Pharisee and host, apply this parable to yourself. Do you not know that I brought it forth on your account? Why are you indignant? Why do you turn poison over in your breast? Why do you raise the serpent’s head against a good deed?

You judge it unworthy for me to receive a fornicating woman, a woman overflowing with fountains of tears. But you do this like an unbelieving Pharisee, since you do not wish me either to be or to be believed to be God.

“Friend, you have done a good deed. You prepared a banquet for me and offered me a meal. But what does that amount to in comparison with this woman? Her soul is worth more than your hospitality; her love has surpassed your banquet.

“Did you not see what she did? I entered your house, and you gave me no water for my feet; but she moistened my feet with tears. You gave me no kiss; but she, from the moment she entered, has not ceased kissing my feet. You did not anoint my head with oil; but she has poured ointment over my feet.

“Therefore I tell you: her countless sins have been forgiven.”

Pharisee, you are indignant because of bad leaven. It troubles you that I saved a sinner and released her from sins. And what is that to you? Your intention is evil. Is it not lawful for me to do what I wish with what is mine? Or is your eye evil because I am good? (Matt. XX).

But, if you are willing, apply my parable to yourself. Open your eyes and see. You prepared a banquet, and the prostitute was crowned. Why? Because she loved much, wept much, and repented much. The prostitute’s tears had greater value with me than your dishes.

And for this reason the fornicating woman was preferred to you twice over: when you were compensated with fifty coins, she was compensated with five hundred. Nor was it without reason that it was foretold concerning you: “Prostitutes and tax collectors will go before you into the kingdom of God.”

And the Lord Jesus turned to the woman and said: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Matt. XXI).

Behold how the things proposed have been made clear in these two examples. Behold how crimes have been struck down by opposing weapons. Almsgiving repels the weapons of greed; tears restrain the crimes of lust. The tax collector lent at interest and became righteous; the fornicating woman wept and became holy.

What will you do in response to these things, lustful man, challenged by these examples? Perhaps, because you are divided against yourself, you despair. Stop despairing and learn what you must do.

When you wish to pray concerning the lust that is within you, or to give something for your sins, I know that your conscience resists you and rolls before you the infinite number of your sins. It silently clamors against you, saying:

“What is it that you are praying for, or what is it that you are giving? Ruin is within you; a heap of crimes weighs upon you. And how great are your prayers or your giving?”

When your conscience rebukes you in this way, do not be frightened. Set the tax collector against it; oppose the prostitute to it, and say:

“Be silent, conscience. Do not clamor against me; do not resist me. There is access to God and a place of return to Christ.”

The tax collector was impious, but he did not despair. The tax collector lent at interest and became intimate with God; the prostitute wept and became blessed.

“Why do you rebuke me, conscience? Why do you shame me and strive to corrupt me? If God receives, who is the one who rejects? If God justifies, who is the one who condemns?

“Christian, why do you delay? You see that the tax collector was received before he had even repented, and yet you hesitate. What do you fear? If, concerning the vice of lust by which the body is polluted and the members stained, you groan with your whole soul, you will be released.”

Human being, if you see your heart, you see it washed clean in a single moment by tears alone, and yet you doubt?

But you say: “Behold, I prayed in compunction, or wept for the things I did wrong; to some extent I deserved to be released from the Lord’s indulgence. After this, however, given the very condition of things, if I sin again, what shall I do? Must I weep again, or plead for indulgence? Or is there still a remedy to be repeated?”

I answer you: if the root of sin were to wither in your members, or depart from your minds, you would rightly say this. For if the goad of the flesh were to rest, you would be secure: you would neither commit sin nor seek repentance, but would always walk about like an undefiled angel.

But if natural desire presses and pricks you, and lust drives you, what will you do, frail human being? You are repeatedly conquered, frequently bent, and do something that God does not will.

You do what perhaps you yourself detest, as the Apostle says: “I do not do what I will, but what I hate, this I do” (Rom. VII, 19).

What now? Behold, you prayed, and the Lord gave assent. The merciful one helped you; the compassionate one forgave you; you escaped sin. But once you have been released from the goad of the flesh, behold, the condition of things again compels you to fall after obtaining forgiveness, to sin after indulgence, and after tears to fall once more into transgression.

Here indeed a great hatred and immeasurable difficulty intervene. You must strive with your whole soul and fight stubbornly against the goad of the flesh and the desire of the heart, so that you may conquer and not sin.

But if perhaps, contrary to your wish, the condition of the flesh prevails, and desire throws you down into sin, what will you do? Should you now despise or despair of salvation?

Do not think in this way. Rise again, human being; rise. Do not fear; do not lie prostrate. There is one who will receive you and will not despise you, if you rise.

As soon as you rise, as soon as you lift yourself up, God now regards not your error but your disposition; he does not reckon the sin, but weighs your repentance. He certainly hates you if he sees you negligent, lax, or slothful, if he sees you not laboring in repentance but remaining in sin. Such, indeed, is God toward human beings: he hates the sinner but embraces the penitent.

Have you fallen, then? Do not lose heart or delay, but rise. If you have gone astray each day, turn back each day and make amends; for this is what God expects and requires of you. Or have you not heard how his voice resounds through the prophet Jeremiah? “Surely, he who falls will rise again, will he not? Or will he who has turned away not return?” [Col. 0105A] He does not say this of a single fall, but bears witness to the lapses of an entire lifetime. For if it should happen that someone falls often and frequently commits offenses, he continually cries out and says: “Rise, human being.” What does he say? “Surely, he who falls will rise again, will he not? Rise, sinner, and turn back to me, for I do not desire the death of the sinner. However much, and however often, he has sinned, let him turn away from his evil way, and he shall live.”

He says this so that you may not waste away through your many falls, as though despised and hopeless, but may lift yourself up with greater vigilance and, after every fall, stand against sin. Set your tears against it; oppose almsgiving to it; insert into the struggle the vigils of prayer, so that you may overwhelm and overthrow the weight of sin with the weight of repentance. In this way divine mercy never abandons the one who perseveres.

Placed in this contest, a person does not walk along a broad road, but proceeds by a narrow path. The person who does not wish to rise from his ruins plainly keeps to the broad road; but the one who, whenever he has sinned, arms himself anew, mourns, and continually maintains repentance on the narrow way that leads to life—that person undoubtedly hears: “The one who perseveres to the end will be saved.”

## HOMILY II. On Almsgiving.

Dearest brothers, all divinely inspired and salutarily ordered Scripture (as the Apostle says [1 Tim. 3]) is useful for hearing, suitable for instruction, necessary for retention, and pleasing for enjoyment. But among the many useful and salutary commands written in the divine pages, there is none other [Col. 0105C] so effective, so powerful, and so swift a medicine for our wounds as the commandment of almsgiving. For almsgiving not only cleanses sins and heals the wounds of conscience, but also recalls the soul itself from death and makes it a participant in the heavenly kingdoms.

The author of this commandment and practice is the supremely just Tobias, blind in body but renowned for his deeds; tested for a time but not destroyed; deprived briefly of physical sight but filled forever with the light of good works. With such admonitions he instructed his son:

> My son, give alms from your substance, and do not turn your face away from any poor person; thus it will happen that the face of God will not be turned away from you (Tob. 4).

He also removed the scruple from the mind of one who gives anxiously or doubtfully, so that no one would cease giving, whether from much or from little:

> My son, act according to what you have: if your substance is abundant, give more abundantly; if it is small, offer a little. And do not hesitate while you give, nor despair, saying, “Perhaps it will not be enough for us”; but be cheerful while you give, because God loves a cheerful giver.

You are storing up a good reward for yourself, one that will raise you up on the day of necessity; for almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit one to enter into darkness: it is the reward of eternal life.

You have proved the effectiveness of almsgiving; you have seen its faithful and singular consolation. For if it is bestowed faithfully, it not only overturns sin but also extinguishes death. How powerful is fire when it burns! Yet water, which extinguishes fire, is still more powerful. What, then, is sin? Fire [Col. 0106A] has strength; almsgiving has the fluidity of water. Thus the comparison stands: matter against matter, water against fire, almsgiving against sin. Have you heard what is written? “As water extinguishes a burning fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sins” (Eccl. 3).

Since we human beings possess an unstable nature and frequently sin, let the water of justice overflowing in the soul never cease. What is the root of all evils? Avarice (1 Tim. 6). What is the root of all good things? Almsgiving. And you who are now wounded by avarice, heal yourself through almsgiving. Are you dead through avarice? Bring yourself to life through almsgiving. Is your soul ulcerated by sins? Anoint it with the work of piety and justice. Have you heard the admonition of the righteous man? “Almsgiving delivers from death and does not permit one to enter into darkness” (Tob. 12).

[Col. 0106B] Has greed entangled you, and do you have many offenses? Do you lie there possessed by avarice and deformed by lust? Have you reviled and blasphemed because you have often lied to many and frequently sworn falsely? If your mind is buried beneath these and similar parts of wickedness, if your conscience is shaken, what then? Is there no hope amid all this? The Lord does not command so. What does he command? “Give alms,” he says, “and behold, everything will be clean for you” (Luke 11). Do not despair of yourself in such matters; “turn away from evil and hasten to do good” (Ps. 36). God does not despise you—and you despair? Have you gone astray through avarice? Correct yourself through almsgiving. Has impurity polluted you? Let justice purify you.

For if you give from the heart, you will not only be cleansed from sin, but the prophet will also praise you and proclaim your justice, saying:

> Happy is the man who shows mercy and lends; for he will not be shaken for ever. Why? Because he has scattered and given to the poor; his justice endures forever and ever, and his horn will be exalted in glory (Ps. 111).

If the sinful person thus understands and is concerned for himself; if he nourishes the needy and helps the afflicted, the prophet adds even greater praise for him, saying:

> Blessed is the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor; on the evil day the Lord will deliver him (Ps. 40).

And he does not merely deliver him, but preserves, gives life to, and blesses the one delivered. If almsgiving finds a righteous person, it increases his merits; if a sinner, it absolves him from sins; if a sick person, it lifts him from sufferings. “May the Lord help him,” he says, “upon his bed of pain” (ibid.). Whom? Clearly, the one who understands concerning the needy and the poor.

These things we have said are David’s. Behold still stronger consolations from Solomon, which nourish the sick with the medicine of mercy and support those who stumble:

> Shut up almsgiving in the mouth of the poor, and it will itself plead for you on the evil day (Eccl. 29).

What does this mean? Let it be made clear. You have accumulated a great mass of many offenses and sins. Since you cannot drive it away from your soul by yourself, do not grow weary: help is at hand. If you wish, helpers are near. Open your eyes and look upon the poor, for they are helpers in such a work. Give as much as your hand is able; shut up almsgiving in the bosom of the poor, and it will rescue you.

Give alms, and that mass of crimes which you feared is diminished in a moment and slips away from your conscience.

[Col. 0107A] A diligent farmer often invites his neighbors to work, so that at the proper season he may apply suitable cultivation to his fields and vineyards. Otherwise, if he neglects them because he cannot prevail or succeed alone, either the field will become filthy with thorns or the vineyard grow wild with shoots. He brings in laborers as helpers, multiplies his efforts in earthly cultivation—and you, while wishing to cultivate the field of your heart and the vineyard of your soul alone, leave them deserted? Man, attend to what is being said. This is spiritual cultivation, not carnal.

Hire laborers for almsgiving. Whom? The blind, the lame, the weak, and others like them. These are laborers hired for a small wage; they cleanse the field of your heart and renew the vineyard, so that through the cultivation of almsgiving you may become both a fruitful field and a fruitful vineyard.

“Shut up almsgiving in the mouth of the poor,” and so forth. What is the evil day, or the day of evils, if not the day of judgment, the terrible day of the coming examination? Provide for yourself, man; set your vineyards in order; place yourself here in the mouth of the poor. Shut up your almsgiving in the food of the hungry, so that that fearful day may come to you not in terror but in expectation.

For that day comes swiftly and bitterly upon the strict, but it is desirable and gracious to the merciful. Shut up almsgiving in the mouth of the poor, and it will plead for you on the day of evils. You are silent, but the almsgiving you have performed pleads for you. What you have done in silence is proclaimed in the mouth of the poor. The good deed you performed secretly is praised on the tongues of the needy. The remission of your offenses resounds in their mouths.

Shut up almsgiving in the mouth of the poor, and it will itself appease God’s anger on your behalf. It appeases anger by washing away crimes. The mouth of the poor is corrected for you into baptism, and the belly of the hungry, once filled, pours out upon you the water of forgiveness. Little is what is given to them, but much is what arises from them.

The Lord himself exhorts us through the prophet: “Break your bread for the hungry” (Isa. 58). What will you receive for this? Hear the evangelical promise:

> Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world (Matt. 25).

Why? Not because you were proud or rich or powerful in the world through estates, but because “I was hungry and you gave me food.”

O exchange! You gave bread to the hungry and received a kingdom. How much money a person pours out in this world to purchase slaves or plunder! Christ sells you the kingdom above at so cheap a price, and you neglect to purchase it!

[Col. 0107C] Do not despair: break your bread for the hungry, nourish the needy, clothe the naked, shelter the stranger, and possess the kingdom—not an earthly one, but the heavenly.

The Father cries out from the earlier volume: “Break your bread for the hungry.” The Son responds from the Gospel page: “I was hungry, and you gave me food.” The two voices agree. What the Father foretold through the prophets, the Son fulfilled by taking it upon himself. He became poor, both to shelter the poor and to move the rich. He became poor so that he might correct the faults of the rich in the poor and expiate their vices through almsgiving.

For this reason he will say: “I was hungry, and you gave me food”; and because you refreshed me, receive in return the kingdom. What kingdom? The just kingdom that Christ gives, which is paradise. And what is in paradise? The tree of life. And what is in the tree of life? Hidden manna. The Lord himself promises this in another Scripture:

> To the one who conquers I will give the tree of life and the hidden manna that is in the paradise of God (Rev. 2).

Who are those who will live, except those to whom he said:

> Come, blessed of my Father; possess the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world. I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink; I was naked, and you gave me clothing.

Behold the palm and the rewards. For the little bread you gave, you received hidden manna; you offered drink and received paradise.

Therefore, if you see someone hungry, break your bread for him (Isa. 56); if you see someone naked, give him clothing. And when you do this, you are not giving a gift but paying a debt.

What does the Lord command? “If you see the naked,” he says, “clothe him,” and in doing this you act with interest. The one who commands you to do this wishes to heal you, and he who repays both gives you recompense.

For he sees bodily nakedness in the poor, but in you the foulness of the soul. Therefore, if you see the naked, clothe him. When you have covered him, you have adorned your soul, which sin had stripped and left naked. You covered him with a bodily tunic; he drove foulness away from you. As soon as you cover the inner parts of the needy with your garment, he restores in you the garment of baptism and reweaves the tunic you received from water and the Spirit.

For no human being can preserve the gifts of the bath undefiled or remain always pure, since a harmful nature weighs upon him. But when he walks in instability and repeatedly incurs offenses, works produce forgiveness, repentance restores [Col. 0108C] purity, and prayer provides access to the fountain of remission. Tears wash the darkened tunic; almsgiving restores its whiteness.

If you practice these things, there will be within you a daily offering and a daily remission. He is the fountain of refreshment; he is the forgiveness of your crimes, the one who said to you: “I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was naked, and you gave me clothing.”

Do not look at the beggar, stranger, captive, or naked person merely as such; contemplate Christ, who speaks through them. Have you not heard what he says? “As long as you did it for one of these least ones, you did it for me.”

But you say: Christ, the Son of God, who is fed in the poor—why does he not himself enrich the needy, exalt the humble, and raise up the indigent, since he is the provider and giver of all things?

Whoever raises this objection should hear the answer. Do you perhaps think, man, that anything is impossible for him? Do not think so, man, but hear the reason. If he had made all human beings equal, where would there be the exercise of faith, where the testing of virtue? If he had made all people rich, they would all sin freely. And if that were so, from where would a remedy come, or where would forgiveness remain? From where would indulgence be expected?

Therefore divine providence opened for us sinners the storehouse of medicine, so that he might make—as it is written—both rich and poor, humble and exalted. Since the rich, through an abundance of possessions, are inclined toward vices and frequently stumble through intemperance, they would have the needy joined to them like a fountain of cleansing—or, to say more, like the river Jordan, where Christ was baptized, and in which, through the generosity of almsgiving, daily offenses might be overcome.

In the Jordan he sanctified the waters by being baptized once; but in the poor he remains continually and constantly washes away the crimes of those who give.

Thus Christ gave us, as it were, agents of forgiveness. Whom? The blind, the lame, the weak, the paralytics; also orphans and widows, strangers, proselytes and newcomers, and people of every kind who need all assistance. Through them, all who are wealthier may display a devout affection; let them be readily moved toward weak and afflicted bodies and troubled souls; let them make such people their friends, according to evangelical teaching, from the unrighteous mammon—that is, from transient possessions—so that when they fail here, those friends may receive them into eternal dwellings (Luke 16).

Therefore, rich people, do not despise the poor or reject the needy, knowing that they are friends of souls and physicians of inward wounds. The field is beside you: sow at the proper time and be faithful, because this cultivation does not deceive you. Here you sow, elsewhere you will reap; you scatter a little and will gather much. Whatever you give is stored there in the heavenly storeroom; whatever you offer prospers in the future.

Can Christ not enrich a beggar? Can he not now give sight to the blind, heal the lame, strengthen the paralytic, and cleanse the leper? He certainly can, but he dissimulates in you, so that through these people he may remove the weaknesses of others and avert their illnesses.

For though they are weak, they nevertheless become physicians of those who sin—not they themselves, but the one who said: “As long as you did it for these, you did it for me.” Christ is the physician in them, healing through them the wounds of rich sinners, so that when the appointed time comes, he may exalt his poor in glory and receive the rich who are devoted to just works—as I said—into eternal lodgings.

Therefore, dearest brothers and desired friends, retain these things and learn still others in addition. My teaching has not yet been fully disclosed: the Gospel pattern must be repeated, so that from it we may unfold what is perfect. We have not yet shown the pattern of perfect almsgiving.

The Savior established the pattern of almsgiving by his commands: “Take heed,” he says, “that you do not perform your righteousness before people.” If you hope for a heavenly reward, you must avoid human sight. It is enough that the one who gives the reward for the deed sees it in secret. Why do you seek to have people know what you reserve for God? Or why must people see what God rewards? Your conscience is enough; you have a witness to your deed. What is hidden from human beings is open to him in you.

If you applaud yourself, you do not please him. If you wish to please people, you displease the one who taught this. If you displease him, you have diminished your righteousness, wounded grace, and violated your reward.

Finally, the same teacher adds: “If you wish to please people, you will have no reward with your heavenly Father.” In a similar matter the Apostle also declared: “If I were pleasing people, I would not be a servant of Christ.”

Therefore, when you give alms, do not sound a trumpet before you; be silent and suppress your deed within yourself. Do not play the flute, lest you wound your work; do not disclose what you have done. You have lost the reward of the deed if you wished to be praised by people. This is enough for you: you have your reward.

Divine speech called such people hypocrites. “Thus,” it says, “the hypocrites act in synagogues and in the streets.” They give publicly so that they may be publicly honored—not by God, but by people.

The Lord therefore gave a beautiful and modest pattern of conduct when he forbade us to imitate such people and commanded us to act in silence. And what do I mean by “in silence”? Can it be hidden when you give alms or perform some pleasing work? Certainly not. For while you are silent, the works themselves cry out and proclaim your deed. Without your knowledge, many people praise your righteousness and proclaim your almsgiving.

Your grace is doubled: you receive full praise from people because you were silent, and perfect reward from God because you did what he commanded. What did he command? That you should not sound a trumpet before you—that is, that you should not be the one to publicize yourself, but others should.

A fruitful tree does not speak, yet it is known by its fruit. Bees, when they weave their waxen cells, make honey, and fill their combs with sweet nectar, do not perform their work in public; enclosed beneath a humble covering, they labor, and afterward the sweetness of their product bursts forth publicly. Not without reason is it said that “the bee is small among flying creatures” (Eccl. 11), yet its fruit possesses the primacy of sweetness.

Retain, then, this small command: give alms and conceal them with yourself. Let your inner chamber be within you, so that what you conceal may be proclaimed by others and then rewarded by Christ, who says: “When you give alms, let your left hand not know what your right hand is doing” (Matt. 6).

The saying must be examined and its meaning sought. What does this mean? Is a person divided within himself in one body, so that one person is on the right and another on the left? Certainly not. It is the same person who has both a right and a left hand. How, then, can it happen that the left hand does not know what the right hand does?

Although there are two hands in the body, right and left, the human being has one mind, which covers both sides, right and left. It is therefore clear and not ambiguous that something deeper and more exalted is introduced in this commandment.

A person is plainly double within himself. Though he is one, he is nevertheless divided into right and left. Divided? How? Not in mind, but in conduct; not in thought, but in morals. He possesses good and evil: good on the right, evil on the left.

The Lord commands: “Let the left hand not know what the right hand is doing.” This is ordinarily understood by us as though it had been said: The left hand does evil; let the right hand not consent to it—that is, if your body compels you to sin, let your soul not agree with it.

What is the right hand in a human being? Is it not the part of the soul? What is the left? Is it not the part of the body? Learn what is being introduced: “Let the left hand not know what the right hand is doing.”

Does the flesh not know when good is being done, or does the soul not know when the flesh does evil? It is not so. Understand the left and right differently. What he says amounts to this: When the right hand—that is, the soul—attempts to do something good, let the left hand, which is the flesh, not hinder it. Rather, as though the left hand were asleep, let the right hand hasten secretly to do good and drive evil from the limbs, which is called the left. This is the meaning and understanding of the right and left hands.

Let the saying be explained more openly, and let it shine forth in action. Has your left hand—that is, your flesh—gone astray? Let your right hand, which is the soul, correct the error. Both sides could have been made right in a person; but for this reason he was made different in the two, so that he might retain in himself the leaven of both good and evil.

The leaven of good is on the right, that of evil on the left. This may be distinguished as follows: Has your left hand led you into sin? Let your right hand rescue you from sin. Has the left sinned through the eyes? Let the right make atonement in secret. Has the left committed robbery? Let the right give alms. What the former did thoughtlessly, let the latter correct silently.

Has the left stolen clothing? Let the right clothe the naked. Has the former struck cruelly? Let the latter humbly lift up and heal. Has the former accumulated impiety? Let the latter be full of piety. Has the former inflicted wounds? Let the latter apply medicine and provide care. Is guilt on the left? Let forgiveness be on the right.

Let the right repel the evil that the left has inflicted; let it extinguish the latter’s poison. And why say more? There is fire on the left and water on the right. When the fire of sin blazes on the left, let the water of justice rain down on the right, and then there is nothing that can harm you, while you fulfill what was said: “As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes crimes” (Eccl. 3).

Here it is clear that neither sin ceases in a person, nor does the fountain or forgiveness ever fail. The divided person, with a left and a right, is himself the arbiter of his own fate: he either loses or finds himself. What of these things concerns you? Are you perhaps afraid that the left will prevail? Do not fear: the right is stronger, if it wishes to be. And although the left is an enemy that condemns, the right is a friend that saves. Although the left pollutes, the right immediately sanctifies.

The water on the right is stronger than the fire on the left. For if the former overflows, it immediately subdues the latter’s harm. Know, then, that although the flame of sin is in the body, there is a divine fountain in the heart: the limbs supply the flames, but let the mind bring forth the fountain. Thus what the left has polluted, the right will sanctify.

The left has daily pollution, and the right has daily absolution, so that what is defiled on the left may be purified on the right. The wise person understands these things. Be provident; be profitable to the holy, because the heavenly judge will soon come to examine the acts of his servants and uncover their secrets.

The heavenly lender lends to the holy; he comes to demand with interest the money he distributed. What is this money of evangelical observance? It is the words of life that have been sown. That sower comes to gather the fruits of his seed and to demand the installments of his money.

If you have done what was commanded, he says to you: “Well done, good and faithful servant; because you were faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your Lord” (Matt. 25).

Do you wish to know what sort of being this one is who comes? He is equal to the threefold power; he is prince of the angels, commander of the heavenly host, Lord of the heavens, governor of the earth. He sits above the cherubim and searches the depths of the abyss.

Clothed in flesh, he indeed granted a general remission in baptism, through water and the Spirit; but now he will come to demand the debt—not what he previously forgave, but what each person contracted after the washing of water and did not erase through repentance.

This judge holds in his hand a balance in which he weighs two things against each other: one weight of merit and one of sin. Look to yourself beforehand, man; discern your weight before he comes and suspends you on his balance. Consider your condition and become a balance for yourself. Let your own body be enough for your balance. Your two hands are two weights hanging on either side of the balance.

Do you see how you yourself are your own balance? Weigh your heart and conscience. Weigh your soul and your very limbs in the balance before you encounter divine examination. Let your mind be the judge of your actions and the inspector of your weights. Carefully examine what the right hand holds and what the left hand does.

You have evil stored up on the left, and merit gathered on the right. See what is greater in your work, which side predominates in your actions—the left or the right—and it seeks to crush you down. Do not yield, because it is written for you: “Do not be overcome by evil, but overcome evil with good” (Rom. 12).

The left is troublesome to you and seeks to subdue you. It enters at an opportune moment, torments you violently, strikes you frequently, and continually captures you. With its perverse weight it presses upon the soul and inflicts savage bites; it sinks the teeth of carnal desire into you and furrows your inner sides with the claws of its vices.

When you see that this hostile part is growing strong in evil, and that the left, armed with hostile weapons, seeks to conquer you and tear down the camp of your breast, do not be frightened. Return to your senses, and there you will find God as your helper.

Yet if you fear him and dread his future judgment, then in this place, in this struggle, do not let the left be ignorant; rather, let it know more fully [Col. 0112C] what your right hand is doing.
