Let it know what it does not know. Pay close attention when the left makes a disturbance through evils—that is, when the flesh multiplies hostile forces against the virtue of the soul and piles up crimes.

Let your right hand stand against the forces of pestilence, against hostile weapons, against enervating vices, against sins and crimes. Let your right hand stand armed: that is, let it be strong faith, hope, and steadfastness joined with love. Let it cover itself with the shield of faith, put on the breastplate of hope, present the spear of justice, draw the bow of prayer, and raise the trophy of almsgiving. Immediately the adversary not only yields in defeat but falls, struck down. It lies wounded and succumbs to victory.

Let us repeat more clearly what we have said. Has the flesh provoked you in a hostile manner? Has your condition constrained you to sin? Have you sinned? Have you offended repeatedly? Has your mind been oppressed by horror? Is your soul sorrowful unto death? Has the measure of crimes overflowed on the left? Is your understanding lame, your balance wavering, and your right hand suspended from the scale, with the whole weight inclining to the left?

When you see this, say to your soul:

> Soul, where are you? What are you going to do amid these things? Why do you not cry out? You see evil threatening, and you are silent? Why do you not keep watch? You see death hanging over you, and you do not look? Where are you sitting, sluggish one? Where are you lying on your back? Your right hand is sleeping, and you do not awaken it? Do you allow the left to conquer you and join your portion with those who perish? What will you do, overcome by the flesh, when you begin to suffer punishments with it? Is the left to labor earnestly while the right must sleep? Is the measure full there, while here it must remain empty? Is the left powerful in vices, and does the right not thrive more powerfully in virtues? Why is sin not diminished there and merit increased here? Why does wickedness not melt away and justice grow?

You see the judgment of God drawing near, and you are stunned? The throne of the terrifying judge burns on fiery wheels, as Daniel says (Dan. 7), and you do not tremble? A fiery river runs, rolling balls of flame, and you lie there helpless? Do you not know that this river passes through sinners and does not murmur against the repentant?

Have you not heard what Isaiah announces: “Behold, the day of the Lord, incurable, comes—to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it” (Isa. 14)?

Weep over your crimes; correct yourself immediately and transfer yourself from the left to the right. There is no ambiguity: it has sounded openly that God destroys sinners.

I said “sinners”: if you have done penance, he no longer destroys you but protects you. If you have been pierced with remorse for your sins, he no longer condemns you.

The prophet indeed testifies in a threatening voice and with a terrible trumpet, saying: “Behold, the day of the Lord, incurable, comes—to make the world desolate and destroy sinners from it.” Yet God does not threaten in order to destroy; he testifies in order to correct, reproves in order to set right, rebukes in order to rescue. He rises up not with the fear of one who destroys but with the affection of one who shows mercy.

Otherwise, if he strikes the city and destroys sinners, where is the whole people whom he acquired for himself and redeemed with his blood and passion?

But you say: “Show me, please, by what method I can unload the left and heap up the right.” What you ask is not unknown. Is it hidden from your sight, or is it some art of which you are unaware?

When you see that the law of sin rules over you, that vices command, that crimes multiply, and that the entire burden inclines toward the left side, do not yield or rest; rouse yourself. Return to opposing weapons and gird yourself on the right, fulfilling what David the psalmist sang:

> “Gird yourself,” he says, “with your sword—you whom the left conquered, sloth overcame, and wickedness cast down—around your thigh, mighty one.”

What sword? “With your appearance and your beauty.”

This is said to you, who yield to crimes; he speaks to you, who are conquered by crimes. He admonishes and pierces you with remorse, sinner! The left side has conquered you; it will seize you in your deed. Weep in remorse, so that you may recover the appearance of your heart and the beauty of your body.

What does this mean? Have you gone astray in the loins? Have you offended in the thigh? It is clear that where there is the loins, there is lust, and where there is the thigh, there is fornication.

What, then? Have you defiled your thigh with carnal desire? Restore it through spiritual beauty. Have you polluted your loins through fornication? Do not despair, but wage war against the left and against bodily sin, against violation or adultery. Has the thigh defiled you? Let the thigh restore and recover you.

“Gird yourself,” he says, “with your sword around the thigh, mighty one.” The prophetic word rebukes you because you have sinned. Have you been wasteful in lust? Be most powerful in virtue. Have you loosened your limbs in wantonness? Tighten them through the vigor of your weapons. Arm the loins of your heart; adorn the thigh of your soul, so that you may remove the foulness from your bodily thigh and tear the wounds from your inward parts.

“Gird yourself with your sword around your thigh, mighty one.” What is this sword? He himself says: “With your appearance and your beauty.”

And what is this appearance except the virtue of the soul, and within it complete repentance? And what is this beauty except the tears of the eyes and the generosity of almsgiving?

And what follows? “Press onward,” he says, “prosper, and reign.”

The meaning is clear. Press onward, sinner, because you have sinned; prosper, because you have repented; proceed and reign, because you have triumphed. Proceed confidently because you have wept over sin; you have conquered guilt in order to reach the kingdom. Proceed and reign. Weep here, so that you may rejoice elsewhere.

“Proceed,” he says, “and reign.” Why? “Because of truth, meekness, and justice.”

When the left brings and thrusts upon you the burning goads of avarice, lust, arrogance, or desire, stand against your left, girded with truth, armed with meekness, adorned with justice. When you have conquered the left, then your right hand will lead you forth wonderfully.

Then the right wins and the left falls silent, when impiety flees and revived piety flourishes; crimes fall and merits grow. Whatever evil diminishes on the left, merit increases on the right.

When you act in this way, your right hand will lead you wonderfully, according to David’s word. Remove the weight from the opposing side; take away the wounds from the left, so that on the day of judgment your right hand may lead you forth wonderfully.

Fill up the measure of justice. How? By praying, keeping watch, weeping, giving, and fasting; also by striking at extravagance through frugality, neglecting delicacies, and nourishing discipline; by avoiding festive banquets and enduring moderation; by laying aside fatness and loving pallor.

When you practice established virtue, your right hand rejoices and the left lies hidden. For when the burden of wickedness on the left has diminished, the sanctification of your right hand outweighs it, and the right itself will lead you wonderfully to salvation.

Therefore, dearest brother, let weariness not overcome you, nor laziness draw you away. Let cold despair not drench you as you are tossed by alternating movements between hope and fear. Rather, let your heart grow warm while you doubt; let your spirit burn within you while you struggle uncertainly between the two—that is, let the fire of meditation blaze between hope and fear.

Raise yourself in the warmth of your heart; stirred by zeal in your breast, make full use of your right hand and emulate the left, saying to it:

> What have I to do with you, left hand? Stop, cease, be quiet. Do not persuade me to go astray; do not subdue me so that I may offend. Why do you keep me entangled and do not allow me to be released? Do not capture me with your flavors, which are sweet for a short time but afterward always bitter. Such are your flavors as the dreams of sleepers. They rise from sleep and have forgotten what they saw. Such is your flavor, such your delight: in sins your delight lightly anoints the throat, and afterward your pleasure burns the soul.

O left hand! You cause prolonged pains unless you are restrained. Your sweetness becomes bitter; your honeycomb is turned into gall.

Have you not heard the judgment of Solomon, who said: “The Lord knows the ways that are on the right, but those on the left are perverse” (Prov. 4:27)?

Do you not know that narrow is the way that leads to life? Why do you break and bend me toward the broad way? Why do you lead me to the spacious road that opens for me the jaws of hell, where pitchy flame burns and punitive darkness seethes?

Your left side repeats lamentation; your foresight possesses Tartarean darkness. Your storeroom contains corrupted forms; your treasures are full of liquid fires. An asp is in your work—that most ancient serpent, the hydra breathing many poisons. Thus the author of crimes, the armorer of wickedness, scatters pestilence.

In your left-hand portion are the causes of stumbling, to whom it was said: “Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire which my Father prepared for the devil and his angels.”

Fire will burn in your portion, devil, ancient asp, author of wickedness. Fire has been prepared for you and your angels; what does this have to do with human beings?

Your left hand is powerless. The left side is powerless: people correct themselves from sins and live. They cease to sin and are free from pains; they renounce you and reign with Christ. You have remained alone with your angels.

Devil, why do you rule the left side? I direct my word against you; I charge and rebuke you. Why do you glory in the left side? That flame of Gehenna burns for you, not for human beings; the furnaces of Tartarus have been prepared for you and your angels.

Why? Because you are God’s adversary: you always go astray and never amend; always impious and seductive, always wasteful and profane; savage in evil things and hostile to good things—and because you never repent, you are therefore destined to perish. What does this have to do with a person who repents and confesses his sins? Repentance is greater than your pestilence. Human tears are greater than your most treacherous snares. Almsgiving is greater than your defilements. Anxiety dissolves sins, vigilance conquers wickedness, and compunction uproots crimes.

Enemy devil, deceiver, why do you fabricate terror? It is little enough that I fear until I turn to Christ, who saved me. I see my sins and consider the few offenses I have committed; and I shudder until I turn to the Lord. My crimes stand before me like an iron tower and a bronze wall, until I see myself and, thirsting, embrace Christ, the fountain of forgiveness, and hold his feet—he who said: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but rather that he should turn from his evil way and live.” If I do this, the bronze wall collapses in a moment, and the iron tower, struck by lightning, is scattered. For the ram of repentance overturns sins and demolishes crimes. They will fall before the weeping of the penitent like fallen leaves shaken by the wind, or like feathers blown about by the wind.

The Lord is present to the one who prays; Christ, the exalted, generous, and liberal giver of pardon, stands ready beside the one who keeps vigil and distributes alms. And that entire burden of sins which you feared melts like wax, is dispersed like smoke, vanishes like vapor, or perishes like singed down.

After you have thus chastised the left-hand parts and with those same parts struck down the devil himself, turn to the right and speak to it, multiplying words of exhortation to it, saying:

“My right hand, consecrated to God, savior of my soul, strengthening of my heart, protection of my body, do not sleep, but keep watch. Your work is sweet; your action is honeyed; your vigilance gives life. Stretch yourself out to prayers together with the left hand; raise yourself toward heavenly aid. Stir your veins and seek remedies; confound the enemy and crush the minister of sin. How do you confound him, or by what path do you crush him, except in the work of God, in observance of the Gospel, in the ordering of discipline, and in the ordering of generosity?

“Right hand, do the work of justice: look upon the hungry, clothe the naked, visit the sick, receive strangers, release the fettered, cherish captives, console the penitent. If you do this, you will have rescued me from sorrow and freed me from the snare.

“O right hand, do you not see? The left is raging and piling up punishments? The left conquers you, and you sleep! The serpent bites you, and you do not see the opposing parts growing hard, thrown into confusion, and rising up like whirlwinds? Hostile winds blow; the sea rises over you; the sea of sin presses upon your soul; storms of iniquity shriek within your limbs—and you are not aroused, but neglectful! You are not goaded, but sluggish!

“Right-hand helmswoman, stand at the stern and guide the prow; spread the sails and arm the ship. Behold, dangers threaten; behold, reefs lie before you; behold, dreadful rocks; shipwrecks lie in hiding—and you do not keep watch! Be fully vigilant; be a lover of good works; be a warrior of repentance. For when you triumph, I live by the power of God and escape the harmful parts. Stretch yourself toward justice; fill your handful with heavenly seed. Sow the seed of repentance and gather the fruits of forgiveness.

“Do not sleep, right hand, but perform the works Christ expects from you. Correct my error; erase my grief; gather the merit that I scattered; restore what I lost, but make whole what I diminished. The furnace of crimes is blazing, and you are drying up the spring of your work? Sins prevail, and you withdraw the supports of mercy? Give your dew and cool in me what burns with heat. For I fear that, while the left hand sleeps, it may overcome me and carry me away.”

As the left hand tears me away toward death, Christ receives and embraces you as you thus awaken the right hand and rebuke the left. He breaks your bonds and leads forth your justice like light, illuminating your judgment with noonday brightness, so that, visited by his right hand, endowed with grace, and enriched with gifts, you may not depart sorrowful or useless, but may rejoice with the righteous who come to the right hand and remain in eternal rest.

# BOOK [Note: In the manuscript the title reads as follows: “Here begins the first book of Saint Laurence, bishop, on the Canaanite woman.” [Col. 0116D] Compare the annotation appended to the work, shortly after its beginning. EDITOR.] ON THE CANAANITE WOMAN

Many winds indeed are struggling and storms are raging; yet temptation has not dissolved your assembly, nor violated your zeal. The Church does not cease, for it always fights and always triumphs; it is tested but not overcome. The more it is struck and pressed, the more it prevails and grows: waves rage around it, but the rock is not moved.

While we were speaking, sleep withdrew from you; night poured itself into day. O assembly of the forum! For this too can be an assembly of the Church. Night made a church in the forum, and the tumult of your minds armed your diligence: all laziness ceased, and sloth grew quiet. Who would not turn this over in his mind, or who would not marvel that not only our own people remained with us, but even strangers gathered and came, and that temptation progresses toward an increase of benefit? For just as falling rain nourishes germinating seeds, so temptation, when it has tested the soul, saves it.

The word of the Lord is immovable, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it. The Church’s attacker wounds himself, but shows the faithful people to be more distinguished. Whoever envies the Church clashes with his own strength, but confers upon us the dignity of triumph. Job was righteous before; but afterward he emerged from the contest more righteous. The sick man, made sound and strong, became stronger than before: he became renowned in deed and more renowned still in reputation. Therefore never be afraid in temptation. For if you are founded upon your own strength, tribulation will never harm you; rather, it displays the virtue of patience. Just as a furnace, when it tests gold, increases its beauty, so temptation adds beauty to the soul. In what respect is flame harmful to the appearance of gold? Or in what respect does temptation humble patience, when it removes sadness, increases joy, and makes the human soul shine with the beauty revealed by testing?

He introduced temptations in order to drive out the adversaries who think me their enemy. The wicked gathered together; but what became of them in their confusion, and what became of our people in their compassion? Where are they? Do they appear? I look through the forum and go along the streets, but I see none. They were leaves, and they fell in the wind; lead was poured out, and melted; but these people shine with the appearance of gold. What drove them away except the criminality of their own conscience? They themselves know what they have done. For when Cain had begun to kill his own brother, after committing the crime he walked upon the earth in fear and trembling. So these men acted wickedly—not with their hands, but in their minds; and while those men carried out death, the Lord bestowed salvation.

I have said these things for your sake, so that your mind may rejoice in the Lord and never tremble in temptations. The rock is immovable. O man, why do you fear a breath of wind? “Upon this rock,” he says, “I will build my Church, and the gates of hell will not prevail against it” (Matthew 16:18). Whether the wars are foreign or internal, no one can shake the stability of the structure. As for the time I spend reproaching the wicked, I do so because it is not proper to insult enemies for too long and to despise children who understand.

Yesterday, then, the apostle Paul prepared a banquet for us; today, Matthew does so: yesterday, a leatherworker; today, a tax collector; yesterday, a blasphemer; today, a robber. But the blasphemer did not remain a blasphemer, nor did the robber remain in robbery. Paul became a true apostle and useful teacher; Matthew too became a preacher of the Gospel. I shall recall their former sins so that their later merits may shine forth, so that you may learn what it means to turn from evil to good and never at any time abandon your own life. Our teachers, then, first were stained by crimes, and afterward, converted, resounded with merits.

What did the blasphemer and the tax collector become? Were they not the head of robbery and the law of violence? What is a tax collector? A shameless plunderer, a physician of destruction. Is the tax collector not more savage than thieves? A thief steals, at least, out of fear; but this man commits wrongdoing boldly. Yet this tax collector suddenly became an apostle. How, and by what process? As the Lord passed by, he saw him sitting at the tax booth and said to him, “Follow me.” And he rose and followed him (Matthew 9:9).

O power of the word! The victory of the cross came and made a soldier out of a captive, immediately turning mud into gold. The victory of the cross came, and the tax collector rose and followed Christ; from the deep whirlpool of sorrow he was raised above every height of beauty. Therefore no one who despairs should enjoy salvation, for evil is not naturally implanted in your members: by free choice we acquire grace and liberty. The tax collector became an evangelist; the blasphemer became a teacher; the thief earned paradise; the deceiver became a most genuine worshiper. There is nothing among crimes that cannot be undone by repentance. And therefore the Lord destroyed the heights of that very crime, so that no one, even in the sixth age of life, should despair of his salvation.

Do not say within yourself, “I have sinned; what shall I do?” You have an imit—[Note: The manuscript reading is *inimitabilem*, “inimitable”; the printed text appears to have *imitabilem*, “imitable.”]—a physician who cuts away sickness and heals every disease; you have a physician who is present to groans and, by a sign, commands health. From such great material he unexpectedly fashioned and gave you life so that you might exist: now that he has made and nourished you, could he forget you? You were not previously a human being, and he fashioned you from clay. Perhaps you ask about the manner: I do not know; he himself knows his craft.

Were you not earth? Yet that powerful craftsman took a portion of earth and first made your body, in which he arranged and distinguished various limbs: hands and feet; also the head, in which are eyes and ears, mouth and sense of smell, forehead and cheeks, and the remaining lower limbs. Can that craftsman, who fashioned you in this way by his own will, not take away your sins? Do not search into his intentions; do not examine the knots of his power; do not ask how he did it, but marvel at what he has done.

But you say, “I have committed many great sins.” And who among human beings does not sin? Say this: “I have gone astray beyond all people.” This confession is sufficient for me as a sacrifice. First declare your iniquities, so that you may be justified; acknowledge that you are a sinner. Be sorrowful when you have turned; be as one despairing and mournful, and pour out tears in compunction. Was there anything else in the prostitute except the pouring out of tears? Through that outpouring she found protection, and, having gained confidence, approached the fountain, the Lord Jesus.

But let us come to the matter itself. What, then, does the Evangelist say? “And departing from there, Jesus came into the region of Tyre and Sidon; and behold, a Canaanite woman” (Matthew 15). The Evangelist relates a wondrous event. Behold a woman, the source of sin, the devil’s weapon, the expulsion from paradise, the mother of deceit, the corruption of the ancient law. Behold, a woman was coming to the Lord Jesus—a foreign woman from the nations, a new planting. A wondrous affair! The Canaanite follows; the Jews flee; the household members abandon him; the foreigner clings to him.

Behold, a woman came out from those borders, crying out and saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.” This woman becomes an evangelist. For she proved the mystery of the divine plan when she both implored divine power and confessed the nature of the flesh, saying, “Have mercy on me, Son of David.” Consider the woman’s beautiful mind; see what she says: “There is nothing in my deeds, no righteousness arising from my manner of life. I flee to your mercy, where there is no fixed or required place for saving.”

And how did a woman ignorant of the law, so wicked, dare to approach the fountain of salvation so abruptly? She did not ask for James; she did not appeal to John; she did not approach Peter. But, omitting all this, what does she say? “I do not need a guarantor. She takes upon herself the protection of repentance, and runs alone; she holds him with her voice and says: ‘Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.’”

For this reason you descended; for this reason you assumed flesh: so that I too might speak to you and ask with confidence. The cherubim tremble at his appearance in heaven, yet the woman does not fear on earth. Angels are afraid in the heights, yet the woman is not frightened. She persists shamelessly and intensifies her plea with her voice, saying, “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David. I do not need a sponsor: I approach through myself, I implore through myself; have mercy on me.”

“What do you need?”

“I seek mercy.”

“What do you suffer?”

“A pain I cannot endure.”

“What do you have?”

“My daughter is held captive.”

“What is wrong with her?”

“She is grievously tormented by a demon.”

“And what now?”

“Have mercy on me, Lord. My pledge is being consumed, and a part of my body is being violated. A report, I say, has gone out concerning my daughter. Do not regard me as sinful and wretched: you are God, who considers hidden things. My daughter is grievously tormented.”

“What do you desire?”

“That she be freed from her affliction.”

“Wretched lament has consumed my womb and disturbs my soul like a savage storm. I do not know what to do. The wretched girl suffers but does not perceive her torments; she does not know how to fear death or hope for life. Have mercy on me. She lies confused and does not know the cause of her torment. Look upon me, Lord; hear me; see my daily wounds. She suffers, and I waste away. Her condition strikes terror into everyone; I have become a spectacle to all. What shall I do, or where shall I go? I cannot be separated from her in any way, and she cannot be abandoned alone.

“For the attacker has not come from outside; he is within. She has the enemy and the sword within herself. She is a ship that raises a storm from within itself. I cannot find a name for her affliction. Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.

“Would that my daughter had died rather than lived in this condition! For if she had died and been buried, after some time I would have forgotten her and no longer remembered the wound or the pain. But now a corpse is always in the house; her grave is my own grief. My wound increases daily, and my disgrace grows.

“How so? I see it with my own eyes: her hands twisted, the ribbons of her hair undone and scattered, foam pouring from her mouth, a dreadful bellowing, an invisible enemy raging within, an unforeseen foe and an open battle. Have mercy on me, Lord, because she was my daughter and has become the devil’s food. I dare not approach her; I cannot touch her. Fear prevents me, and the dreadful affliction itself drives me away. Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.

“Those among you who have been fathers, let them help my words; those who have been mothers, let them weep with me.”

I am not able to explain the grief that this woman endured. “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David.”

O the woman’s prudence! She does not use human deceivers; she did not follow false prophets; she did not seek empty charms or flee to false remedies. Rather, abandoning all worship of the devil, she came to the Lord Jesus, the savior of all, and said, “Have mercy on me; my daughter is grievously tormented.”

You have seen the woman’s understanding, proving her wisdom; but see another new and unprecedented event. She asks and implores, extending her lament into a cry; yet God, the lover of all, did not answer her a word. The fountain of life is silent; the merciful physician has brought medicine and refuses treatment. What is this, Lord? I do not understand, unless you refuse to receive the woman who knocks!

O the wisdom of the physician! “The Lord,” it says, “did not answer her a word.” Why, then, except to reveal the power of her wisdom? Therefore the disciples say, “Send her away, because she cries out after us.” But the human-loving God was testing the woman’s life and strength. And what does he say? “I was not sent except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.”

They accomplish nothing—not even the apostles who intercede. The true physician delays treatment even more, aggravates the wound, and excuses his power by a certain artifice, in order to disclose hidden mysteries. “I was not sent,” he says, “except to the sheep that had perished from the house of Israel.”

Consider this speech and direct your understanding to my words, because I wish to unfold a profound comparison. “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of Israel.” What is this word? What is this excuse of yours? You have revealed many mysteries about yourself merely to free one corner and leave the entire world untouched? Would you abandon Pontus, Asia, Egypt, Cilicia, Cappadocia, and the remaining nations, and care only for Israel? Would you leave the earth deserted, disregard the nations, and become liberator only for the Jews?

Do you not see the injuries done to your Father through false images and the rites of demons? Have not the prophets also proclaimed these things? What does your kinsman David say? “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and your possession to the ends of the earth” (Psalm 2). What does Isaiah say, who looked upon the seraphim with his own eyes? “A branch will arise from the root of Jesse, who rules over all, and in him the ends of the earth will hope” (Isaiah 11). What does the patriarch Jacob say? “The ruler will not fail from Judah, nor a governor from his elders, until he comes to whom it has been appointed; and he is the expectation of the nations” (Genesis 49:10).

And what does the prophet Zechariah say? “For your sake the bronze gates will be closed, because from the rising of the sun to its setting the name of the Lord will be glorified; in every place they will pour out offerings before him” (Zechariah 1:10–11). What does David himself say again? “All nations, clap your hands, because God is exalted, awesome, and a great king over all the earth” (Psalm 46:1).

Finally, when you were born in the flesh, whom did you call? Was it not the Magi? Did you not come to call the prophets, who proclaimed that very salvation to the nations? And when you sent the apostles, what did you say to them? “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matthew 28:19).

And now, when this wretched woman, constrained by sharp pains and goads, asks and implores you on behalf of her daughter, so that you may free her from her deadly affliction, you say, “I was not sent except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel.” A centurion came to you, asking for his servant, and you said, “I will come and heal him.” You restored paradise to the thief hanging on the cross; you commanded the paralytic, saying, “Rise, take up your bed, and walk.” Lazarus, calling to you from the tomb, rose again; you healed various kinds of illnesses by a word; you freed thieves; you preferred prostitutes to virgins; yet you alone rejected this wretched Canaanite woman who was entreating you.

What is this unheard-of word of the miracle? Now pay attention, so that you may know what sort of concise explanation he is beginning to reveal.

When Israel had been freed from the plagues of the Egyptians and, brought out from Pharaoh, had passed through the wilderness, the Lord commanded the people in the law not to associate or mingle with the Canaanites, because they were without the law and worshiped unclean idols. Therefore God commanded the Jews in the law not to trade with them or mix their marriages with their offspring, lest through these things they be deprived of their lawful customs and joined to the profane worship of idols.

Look, consider, and attend to what I say, because the web is still being woven. This woman was a Canaanite, from an unclean people with whom association was forbidden. What then? The Lord came under the law in order to fulfill it, not abolish it. Therefore, if he had listened to the woman even for a moment, the Jews would have said, “For this reason we neither hear you nor follow you: because you abolish the law. For the law commands abstention from Canaanites.”

For this reason the Lord is silent; for this reason he did not answer the woman. See how he preserves the law in order to confound the Jews, saying, “Which of you convicts me of sin?” Behold, I do not regard the Canaanite woman; behold, she cries out without cause; behold, she implores and is not heard. Behold how I maintain the form of the law, so that you may not say that I have transgressed the law. “For this reason we do not believe in you.” The error does not come from me, but from you. Be silent, then, because of your observance of the law. Behold, the nations come to me; behold, a people whom I did not know hastens to serve me. Do not use crafty pretexts. Behold, I am known by those who did not know me and ignored by those who did know me. Behold, foreigners obey, while members of my household rage. This, then, was the first reason why the Lord delayed answering the woman.

Meanwhile the woman persisted in her cry, saying, “Help me, Lord.” And he answered only this: “It is not permitted to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.”

O the wisdom of the physician! He held the woman back through many difficulties so that at the end he might crown her with a double honor, saying, “It is not permitted to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.” Who are the children? You see them. He says this to confound them, because they were children and became dogs, concerning whom Paul says, “Beware of dogs; beware of evil workers; beware of mutilators.”

But we, who were like dogs, have become children from the nations in their root—those whom Paul exhorts as follows: “My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.” He therefore accuses the Jews when he says, “It is not permitted to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs.”

But what did the woman answer? “Yes, Lord; you can, if you wish.”

O violent woman! The Lord says, “It is not permitted,” and she says, “Yes, Lord; you can, if you wish.” She has forgotten modesty and, setting shame aside, tries to conquer the Lord. The Lord says, “It is not permitted to take the children’s bread and throw it to dogs,” and she replies, “Yes, Lord; I am what you say. You call me a dog; I am a dog. I recognize my name. You confound me, but I do not withdraw from you. I am a dog; I will follow you like a dog. Give me something. I do not ask for the children’s bread; give me even crumbs, because puppies too eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

O contest of devotion! O woman’s prudence! “You call me a dog, Lord; I am one. Then feed me as a dog. I cannot leave my master’s table. You call me a dog; give me crumbs. You have stated my condition; you have delayed my requests; you have revealed my status. Help me now, because puppies too eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

O woman! You have suddenly received praise and been found more elect than the elect. For this reason the Lord is silent; for this reason he delayed and prolonged matters, so that he might assess your mind and bring forth from you a living voice. For if you had received what you asked for as soon as you began to ask, you would have gone away, and no one would have tested your faith; no one would have known the secret of your mind.

But because you understand God’s power and know yourself so well that you say, “Even puppies eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table,” I praise you and say: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

Let the idle and wicked hear this—those who say, “We prayed, and we did not obtain what we asked.” What are you saying, man? Pray persistently; implore insistently, since “to the one who knocks it will be opened.”

But you say, “I have pleaded once, twice, three, four, seven, ten, and twenty times, and God has not heard me.” What a foolish invention! What now? Because you have not been heard, do you withdraw from the Lord and cease praying? Or do you not see the persistence of the Canaanite woman—how, the more she was perplexed, the more insistently she persisted, and, when rejected, implored more urgently, nor ceased until she found what she sought?

There are many who enter the church and make a disturbance in prayer, scattering their words in a confused and uncontrolled voice, and, once they go outside, have forgotten everything. These are the people who neigh with their lips but do not conceive in their hearts. If you yourself do not know what you have said or prayed, how will God hear you?

You say, “I bent my knees and prayed.” You bent your knees toward the ground, but your mind ran outside in different directions. Your body was inside, but your thought was outside; your tongue was counting money and interest. The evil and envious enemy, the devil, presses upon us especially when we pray and makes noise against us. He does not trouble us when we lie secure in our beds; we come to prayer, and he disturbs us with the goads of thoughts.

Considering his tricks, let us return to the Canaanite woman, who entreats in this way: “Have mercy on me, Lord, Son of David; my daughter is grievously tormented by a demon.” You too say, “Have mercy, Lord, because my soul is assaulted by a demon.” Sin is a great demon of the soul. For a demon is extinguished, but sin remains unless it is absolved through acts of satisfaction.

“Have mercy on me, God” is a great utterance—brief indeed, but full of power. Even if you are outside, cry out and say, “Have mercy on me, God.” Cry out not with your voice, but with your mind; for God hears even those who are silent, and he seeks not so much a place as an attitude.

Jeremiah is comforted in prison; Daniel rejoices among lions; the three boys dance for joy in the furnace; Job triumphs naked beneath the open sky; the thief finds paradise from the cross. What, then, if you are in a public forum? Pray within yourself; do not seek a place—the place is yourself. Wherever you are, pray.

If you are in a bathhouse, pray; there too is a temple. If you stand before a judge, pray; the judge rises against you—pray. The sea is before you, and Pharaoh follows behind you—pray. Moses says nothing, and the Lord says to him, “Why do you cry out to me?” His mouth is silent, but his inmost heart cries out.

And when you stand before a furious judge, where cruel officials are present, pray within yourself, and his storms will immediately be dissolved. The judge is against you; turn yourself toward the Lord. He approaches to afflict you with punishments; pray without fear, and his madness will be calmed.

Is God a human being, so that he must be sought through various places with labor? God is the one who is present everywhere. If you seek a human being, you are told, “He is not here,” or, “He is not free.” It is not so in God’s case. All that is required is that you say, “Have mercy on me, God,” and he himself is near to free you. And while you are still speaking, he says, “Behold, I am present.”

What, then, does the Canaanite woman say? “Yes indeed, Lord, for puppies too eat the crumbs that fall from their masters’ table.”

And what does God say? “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done for you as you wish.”

Where are the wicked disputers? Did he say, “Wait, woman, until I pray to my Father”? What did he say? “Let it be done for you as you wish.” The more excellent she was in faith, the more eminent Christ was in power, for he infused his grace into her understanding. “O woman, great is your faith.” How great? You did not see the dead rising; you did not see lepers cleansed; you did not know the law; you did not hear the prophets. But you heard insults and deserved rejection; I repudiated you, and you did not withdraw from me. “O woman, great is your faith.”

The woman has died, and her praise is more splendid than a crown woven with pearls. Wherever you go, you will hear Christ proclaiming, “O woman, great is your faith.” In the assembly of the Goths, in the gathering of the Sidonians or Persians, the Lord Jesus cries out today and says, “O woman, great is your faith.”

And what follows? “Let it be done for you as you wish.” He did not say, “I heal your daughter,” but, “Let it be done for you as you wish”—that is, “You yourself heal your daughter; I entrust her to you; I place her care and her medicine in your hands. Go in peace, lay your hands upon her, and let it be done for you as you wish, so that she may be cleansed from her affliction by your own will.”

He did not command or order the demon to depart, but said, “Let it be done for you as you wish.” For he wished the mother herself to heal her daughter and drive away the demon.

Where are those who say that she obtained everything not by power but by prayer? If he is lesser than the Father, how does he say, “Let it be done for you as you wish,” and her daughter was healed from that hour? The mother was coming from outside, but before she arrived, the daughter had been healed. She entered and found her daughter freed from the unclean demon. Her will was fulfilled, and healing took place. For all these things let us give thanks to the living God, to whom are honor and glory for ever and ever. Amen.

# ANNOTATION

Laurence, bishop, whose little book or homily I have just reported from a manuscript codex of Germani, is the man whom Sigebert of Gembloux, a monk, praises in chapter 120 of his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*. Laurence Mellifluus wrote a book *On the Two Ages*: the first extending from Adam to Christ, the second from Christ to the end of the age. He also delivered homilies with an almost honeyed mouth, whence he received the surname “Mellifluus,” or “Honey-flowing.”

Laurence’s book *On the Two Ages* was published in print in volume 6 of the *Bibliotheca Patrum*, prefaced by this title: “Homily of Saint Laurence, bishop of Novara, on Repentance.” In our copy this homily is appended to the preceding book or homily under the following inscription: “HERE BEGINS THE SECOND BOOK OF SAINT LAURENCE ON THE TWO AGES. There are two ages appointed by the Most High,” and so forth.

No one, therefore, should doubt that he is the Laurence whom Sigebert surnames Mellifluus and who is the author of both books or homilies. But which bishop Laurence was he? Margarinus Binius suspects that he was “Laurence the elder, who, having been made bishop from Novara, became the twenty-fifth bishop of Milan in the year of Christ 507. His praises may be seen celebrated by Ennodius, bishop of Ticinum, in the address delivered to Honoratus of Novara at the dedication of the Basilica of the Apostles.”

I readily agree with Binius, persuaded by certain conjectures drawn both from the book or sermon published here and from Ennodius’s first address on the birthday of Laurence, bishop of Milan. For in his sermon on the Canaanite woman, which he delivered at night in the forum, Laurence mentions certain adversaries of his, by whose wickedness not only he himself was troubled but also other supporters of his party.

Now Ennodius, in his first address, praises Laurence for his patience amid the evils that came upon him once and again through the faction of his adversaries: first, when the city had been captured by enemies and, amid the insults of both his own people and the populace, he stood unshaken; then when he was sent into exile and finally restored to his city; and afterward when, summoned to Rome for the synod in the year 502 for the absolution of Pope Symmachus, he endured the storms of his opponents.

That capture and plundering of the city of Milan, together with Laurence’s exile, occurred under Odoacer, as Sirmond believes, when Tufa, as commander, rebelled against Theodoric, king of the Ostrogoths. After Theodoric won the victory, Laurence returned to Milan and restored the city after its former sufferings.

It was then, I believe, that he delivered the preceding homily on the Canaanite woman. Ennodius celebrates his return in this way in his first address:

“When the heavenly Ruler looked down from on high with kindly eyes, the light of its own priest was restored to the city of Milan. Then, when there was a rare inhabitant; then, when confusion wandered through the houses and across the pleasant thresholds of the chambers; then, when everywhere fear and mourning prevailed, and God’s temples stood disgraced, assigned to the habitation of wild beasts; when neglect, withering away, had covered the splendid halls—recently so bright—with the decay of ancient dampness, you gave joy to the rest by your return; you returned amid tears,” and so forth.

Ennodius also indicates, to some extent, the name Mellifluus below, where he says that Laurence subdued the assaults of threatening men at the Roman synod with the honey of his blandishments.

Moreover, in his homilies Laurence is chiefly intent upon instilling in sinners confidence that they may obtain forgiveness from God; and he speaks of repentance as though he seemed to attribute it solely to the powers of human free choice.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 543. SAINT BENEDICT, HEAD AND SAVIOR OF ALL WESTERN MONKS

# PROLEGOMENA. The Life of Saint Benedict

*(Excerpted from Book 2 of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory the Great).* [Note: [Col. 0125] The Latin and Greek versions of the following work are printed in parallel in Migne.] (C, S)

[Col. 0125A] There was a certain man, most devout in his manner of life and adorned with the grace of God; his name was Benedict. From childhood he shone with purity of heart and was beautified by chastity of body, having not submitted his soul at all to any carnal desire. While still a youth, with a vigorous body—[Note: [Col. 0125C] Colb. “with a most vigorous body.”]—he voluntarily rejected what he could have done for the sake of sensual pleasure, and thereafter considered this world, together with its bloom, as something dry and withered. Like the morning star, he rose from the region of Nursia over the land of the Romans and had been handed over to the instruction of the liberal arts. But when he observed many people falling through corrupt passions, he drew back with devout reflection the foot which he had placed upon the path of learning, lest he should fall utterly into an irreparable abyss—[Note: [Col. 0125C] Reg. “an endless precipice.”]—[Note: [Col. 0125C] Colb. “fall headlong.”]

Therefore, detesting the instruction of letters, and abandoning both his household and his father’s property, desiring to please God alone, he longed for the habit of a holy and solitary life. Thus he withdrew from the education of letters, knowing as one who did not know and wise as one who was unlearned.

I have not seen with bodily eyes the God-pleasing achievements of this venerable father, but I shall relate what I have heard recounted by four of his disciples: Constantine, a most devout man who succeeded him in pastoral leadership; Valentinus, who for many years directed the most holy monastery at the Lateran—[Note: [Col. 0125C] Colb. “the Lateran monastery.”]—; Simplicius, who afterward governed his community in succession as the third—[Note: [Col. 0125C] Colb. “as third.” The Regius manuscript has *tertium*, “as the third,” whatever Gussanville may say in the marginal note.]—; and Honoratus, who now presides over his cell, in which he had previously lived.

[Col. 0126A] There was a man venerable in life, Benedict by grace and by name, bearing a mature heart from the very time of his childhood. [Note: [Col. 0125C] John uses a similar manner of speaking below, Book 4, chapter 47: “John … a young man who surpassed his age in understanding and humility, gentleness and gravity.” Also in Homily 14 on the Gospels: “children who here surpassed their years in conduct.”] For he surpassed his age in conduct and gave his mind to no pleasure; but while he was still in this world, in which he could have freely enjoyed temporal things, he already despised the world with its bloom as something dry and withered. He was born of a family of greater distinction in the province of Nursia—[Note: [Col. 0125C] Nursia was formerly an episcopal city in the Sabine territory, situated among the mountains and at the foot of the Apennines, under a cold sky. Hence Virgil sings of it in Book 7 of the *Aeneid*:]

“Whom cold Nursia sent.”

Nursia. ] sprung from …, he had been sent to Rome to study the liberal arts. But when he saw many in those studies proceeding along the steep paths of vice, he drew back the foot which he had, as it were, set upon the threshold of the world, lest, if he touched anything of that knowledge, he too should afterward fall altogether into an immense precipice. Thus, rejecting the study of letters, abandoning his home and his father’s possessions, and desiring to please God alone, he sought the habit of holy conduct. He therefore withdrew, knowingly ignorant and wisely unlearned.

I did not learn all his deeds, but I came to know the few that I relate from the testimony of four of his disciples: Constantine,

[Note: [Col. 0126C] Concerning the Constantine and Simplicius mentioned here, Paul the Deacon writes in *History of the Lombards*, Book IV, chapter 18: “After blessed Benedict, Constantine; after him, Simplicius; after him, Vitalis; and finally Bonitus ruled the congregation itself.” This confirms the succession of Saint Benedict’s abbots asserted here by Saint Gregory, contrary to Baronius, who, under the year 581, made Valentinian the first successor of Saint Benedict and at the same time abbot of the Lateran monastery, although four had preceded him. Valentinian, however, was the first to rule the Lateran monastery, which was built after the Cassinian monastery had been destroyed, under Abbot Bonitus, as Paul the Deacon testifies in the passage cited.]

that is, a most reverend man, who succeeded him in governing the monastery; Valentinian, who ruled the Lateran monastery for many years;

[Note: [Col. 0126C] *Germ.* has “Valentiano,” *Big.* “Valentino.” The Greek translator agrees.]

also Simplicius, who governed his congregation third after him; and Honoratus, who still presides over his cell, in which he had formerly lived.

[CAPUT PRIMUM.]

## Chapter One

### Concerning the broken winnowing-tray and its restoration through the saint’s prayer

ΚΕΦΑΛ. Α'. Concerning the broken winnowing-tray and its restoration through the saint’s prayer

[Col. 0127]

[Col. 0127A] This Father Benedict, therefore, who had shone forth abundantly in virtues,

[Note: [Col. 0127D] Both manuscripts, *Reg.* and *Colb.*, read *πολλοῖς ἐν ἀρεταῖς* (“in many virtues,” or “abounding in many virtues”).]

after he had already abandoned the vanity of life, received into his soul a God-pleasing desire to dwell in the wilderness. His nurse, who loved him very warmly,

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The same manuscripts read *πάνυ θερμῶς* (“very warmly”).]

alone followed this holy young man. When they reached a place locally called Enfide,

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The manuscripts read *Ἐφηδέ* (*Ephide*).]

many most devout men, drawn there by spiritual love for him, came and stayed with him in the church of Saint Peter.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] In the *Colb.* manuscript the title *περὶ τοῦ κλασθέντος* (“Concerning the broken [tray]”), and so forth, is placed here.] The nurse of this aforesaid and memorable Father Benedict asked some women living nearby to lend her a winnowing-tray for cleaning grain, using the *magidin* [*magidion*].

[Note: [Col. 0127D] *Reg.* has *μαγίδην* (“tray”), a form also frequent in *Colb.*; below *Reg.* has *μαγίδιον* (“little tray”).]

Having received it, she simply and carelessly placed it on the table. But, hurled down by the demon who hates goodness, it broke and was found divided into two parts. When the saint’s nurse returned and found the tray split in two, she began to weep bitterly, because she saw broken the vessel which she had borrowed for use.

But Benedict, that most earnest servant of God, when he saw his nurse weeping, shared in her grief and tears. Taking both pieces of the broken tray with him, he prostrated himself in prayer before God. When he rose from prayer, he found the vessel lying beside him whole, so that not even a trace of the break could be found in it. Immediately, having comforted his nurse with words of consolation and exhortation not to lose heart amid the misfortunes that occur,

[Col. 0127C]

[Note: [Col. 0127D] *Reg.* reads *σῶον … μαγίδιον* (“the tray whole”).]

he returned to her whole the tray which he had taken broken.

This extraordinary miracle became known to everyone in that same place. Therefore the inhabitants of the place hung the aforementioned tray at the entrance of the church there, so that it might be seen by all who entered and left, for the glory of God, for the praise of his genuine servant Benedict, and so that everyone might know the divine grace which had dwelt in him from his youth.

The vessel remained hanging for many years at the very entrance of the venerable church, so that it continued to be seen by everyone even until the coming of the Lombards.

[Note: [Col. 0127D] The manuscripts read *Λογγιβάρδων* (“of the Lombards”).]

But Benedict, a man who loved God and hated human glory, devoted himself more and more to bodily labors, judging it better to take delight in these than to be puffed up by human praise. Then, secretly leaving his nurse, he chose to withdraw into the places of the wilderness and live in solitude. He reached a place locally called the Lake,

[F. *reached*]

situated about forty miles from the city of Rome, where a multitude of waters customarily gush forth; from this lake the abundance of water is carried away into the channels of streams.

[Col. 0129A] As the man of God was traveling,

[Note: [Col. 0129D] *Reg.* reads *πορευθῆναι τόν* (“for the … to go”), continuing with “man of God.”] a monk named Romanus saw him on the road. Having learned where he was going and recognized his desire,

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The same manuscript reads *τόπῳ ἀπῄει* (“to what place he was going”).] Romanus kept the matter secret within himself but provided him with help and assistance whenever necessity required.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The manuscripts have *συνδρομὴν* (“assistance”); the printed editions have *καὶ συντροφήν* (“and companionship/support”).]

He clothed him in the holy habit of monks and, as far as he was able, ministered to him in bodily necessities.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Both manuscripts read *ἀμφιάσας αὐτῷ καὶ τό* (“having clothed him also with the …”), continuing into “holy habit of monks.”]

This God-minded man shut himself up in a very narrow cave in that same place and for three years remained completely unknown to human beings except for the monk Romanus. Romanus lived not far away in a monastery under the rule of Father Adeodatus.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] *Colb.* adds *ἁγιωτάτου* (“most holy”).]

But Romanus piously concealed from his own abbot the hours when he went away, and on appointed days brought bread to the man of God Benedict. There was no path from the monastery by which Romanus could reach the holy man’s cave,

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The manuscripts read *εἴσοδος* (“entrance”) instead of *ὁδὸς* (“path”).] because a very high cliff rose above it. Instead, Romanus had become accustomed to lower the bread to him from the same cliff by means of a very long rope. He attached a respectable little bell to the rope,

[Note: [Col. 0129D] *Reg.* reads *μικρόν κώδωνα* (“a small bell”).]

signaling by it to the saint his own arrival and the delivery of the bread.

But the demon, enemy of the devout and plotter and envier of virtue, opposed Romanus because of his compassionate kindness born of love, and envied the venerable Benedict because of his lack of necessities and his grateful disposition toward God. Wishing to blunt this gratitude

[Note: [Col. 0129D] The same manuscript reads *ἀπαλύναι* (“to soften it”).]

and lead him into negligence, one day, when Romanus was customarily delivering bread to the holy man by the aforesaid rope, the enemy of our souls threw a stone and shattered the bell.

Yet the most honorable Romanus did not abandon that God-pleasing service, but continued it by suitable means.

[Note: [Col. 0129D] Two manuscripts read *Εὐδόκησεν* (“He was pleased”); a little later they read *φιλοθέου ἐκείνης* (“of that God-loving [service]”).]

When almighty God was pleased to release Romanus from the labor of that service dear to God and to display the way of life of blessed Father Benedict for the benefit of many—he did not permit the divine grace, flashing forth from him in miracles, to remain hidden for long under a bushel—

[Note: [Col. 0129D] *Reg.* reads *τὸν δι’ αὐτοῦ* (“the one through him”); *Colb.* has *τὴν δὲ αὐτοῦ* (“but his own”).]

he placed him above the lampstand, so that he might shine for all who were in the house of God.

[Note: [Col. 0130D] The manuscripts write *ὑπεράνω* (“above”) as one word; the edition has *ὑπὲρ ἄνω*.]

For the Lord deigned to appear in a vision to a certain presbyter who lived some distance from the cave in which the memorable Benedict dwelt in solitude. The priest had prepared for himself an abundant meal for the feast of the holy Pascha. The Lord said:

> “You are preparing an elaborate meal for yourself, while my servant Benedict is being afflicted by hunger in that cave because of his love for me.”

[Note: [Col. 0130D] *Reg.* reads *ἐν ἐκείνῳ* (“in that [cave]”).]

The presbyter immediately rose and, on the very feast of holy Pascha, taking with him the food he had prepared for himself, went to the cave.

[Note: [Col. 0130D] *Reg.* reads *αὐτῇ τῇ ὥρᾳ καὶ ἑορτῇ τοῦ πάσχα μεθ’ ὦν παρ’ ἑαυτῷ ἦν* (“at that very hour and feast of Pascha, with what he had at hand”).] He searched for the man of God among the mountain cliffs, in the ravines of the valleys, and in the holes of the earth. Having found him in the cave, he greeted him.

After both had prayed, they blessed God and sat down, nourishing their souls with divine words. Then the presbyter rose and urged the saint, saying:

> “Come, Father; let us partake of food, for today is Pascha.”

The man of God replied:

> “I know that it is Pascha, because I have been deemed worthy to see you.”

The holy man did not know that it was truly the feast of the resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ.

The most devout presbyter said to the man of God:

> “In truth, Father, today is the day of the resurrection of our Lord, and it is in no way fitting for you to fast. Indeed, I have been sent by God for this purpose, so that together we may partake of his gifts.”

[Note: [Col. 0131D] *Reg.* reads *πρὸς σὲ ἀπεστάλην* (“I have been sent to you”).]

After giving thanks to God, they both partook of food. When the spiritual rejoicing and the beneficial conversation concerning the Scriptures had ended, the presbyter embraced him and departed, glorifying God for the righteous man’s poverty.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] *Reg.* reads *ὁ γέρων* (“the old man”).]

[Col. 0131A] At that same time some shepherds saw him hiding in the cave, clothed in garments of skin. They thought they were looking at some animal; but when they recognized that he was a servant of God, they abandoned their bestial opinion and were transformed into compassion. Thus the God-inspired report about him spread through the neighboring places. As a result, very many people came to him, bringing bodily necessities;

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The same manuscript reads *παρέβαλλον* (“they kept coming”).] but the holy Father nourished them more abundantly with spiritual teachings.

### Latin recension

**CAPUT PRIMUM.** Concerning the restoration of the broken winnowing-tray

[Col. 0128A]

When he had now decided, having abandoned the study of letters, to seek the wilderness, his nurse, who loved him very closely, alone followed him. When they came to a place called Enfide,

[Note: [Col. 0127D] *Germ.* has *Beccens.* and the second *Aud.* *Fide.* Others have *Enfidus* or *Effide.* Commonly it is *Afide* among the Aequi, two miles from Subiaco.]

and while many honorable men, detained there by affection, were staying in the church of the blessed apostle Peter, the aforesaid nurse asked neighboring women to lend her a winnowing-tray for cleaning wheat.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] *Ventilabrum*, “winnowing-tray,” from Greek καπύω, “I blow.” The French translator thought it was a sieve.]

She carelessly left it on the table, and by an accidental occurrence it was broken, so that it was found divided into two parts. When his nurse returned immediately afterward and found it so, she began to weep bitterly, because she saw broken the vessel which she had received on loan.

But Benedict, a religious and devout boy,

[Col. 0128B]

when he saw his nurse weeping, sympathized with her grief. Taking with him both parts of the broken winnowing-tray, he gave himself to prayer with tears. When he rose from prayer, he found the vessel beside him sound, so that no trace of the break could be found in it. He then gently comforted his nurse and returned sound to her the winnowing-tray which he had taken broken.

This event became known and was held in such great wonder by everyone in the same place that the inhabitants hung that very winnowing-tray at the entrance of the church, so that all present and future might recognize from how great a perfection Benedict the boy had begun the grace of his religious life.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Most printed editions are obscure and corrupt: “from how great a perfection Benedict the boy …” The note concerns the grace of his way of life and its perfection.]

It remained there for many years before everyone’s eyes and hung above the church doors down to the time of the Lombards.

But Benedict,

[Col. 0128C]

desiring more to endure the evils of the world

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Gussanville adds, against three German witnesses, *Reg.*, *Norm.*, and others, “to seek them from human beings.”]

than to seek praise, and more to be wearied by labors for God than to be exalted by the favors of this life, secretly fled from his nurse and sought the retreat of a deserted place called Subiaco,

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Now Subiaco, in the territory of the Aequi.]

about forty miles from the city of Rome. There cold and clear waters gush forth. This abundance of water is first gathered in an extensive lake and finally led off into a river.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Namely, the Anio.]

As he was traveling there in flight, a certain monk named Romanus found him on the way and asked where he was going.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Saint Romanus is commemorated on 22 May.]

When he learned his desire, he both kept his secret and supplied him with assistance; he gave him the habit of holy conduct and, as far as possible, ministered to him. The man of God, arriving at the same place, shut himself up in a very narrow cave and for three years remained unknown to human beings except for the monk Romanus. Romanus lived not far away in a monastery under the rule of Father Adeodatus.

[Note: [Col. 0128D] Elsewhere *Deodatus* or *Theodatus*.]

But he piously stole hours from the sight of that father, his own abbot, and on appointed days brought Benedict bread which he had been able to take away for him at mealtime. There was no path from Romanus’s cell to the same cave, because a lofty cliff rose above it. Instead, Romanus used to lower the bread from that cliff, tied to a very long rope. Into the rope he inserted a small bell,

[Note: [Col. 0130D] *Becc.* and the second *Aud.* have “in which also the rope.”]

so that by the sound of the bell the man of God might know when Romanus was offering him bread, which he would receive as he came out.

[Note: [Col. 0130D] The second *Carn.*, the first *Aud.*, *Big.*, and *Lyr.* read “which he would eat after receiving.”]

But the ancient enemy, envying the charity of one and the nourishment of the other, when he saw the bread being lowered one day, threw a stone and broke the bell. Romanus nevertheless did not cease to minister by suitable means.

[Note: [Col. 0130D] *Germ.*, *Gemet.*, and other Norman witnesses read *horis congruentibus* ("at suitable times") in place of *modis congruentibus* ("by suitable means").]

When almighty God now wished Romanus to rest from the labor and Benedict’s life to be displayed as an example to human beings, so that the lamp placed upon the lampstand might shine and give light to all who are in the house of God, a certain presbyter who lived some distance away and had prepared food for himself for the Paschal feast received a vision in which the Lord appeared to him and said:

> “You prepare delicacies for yourself, while my servant is being tortured by hunger in that place.”

The presbyter immediately rose and, on the very Paschal solemnity, set out for the place with the food he had prepared. He searched for the man of God among the mountain cliffs, through the hollows of the valleys, and in the excavations of the earth, and found him hidden in the cave. After they had prayed and blessed almighty God, they sat down and, after sweet conversations of life, the presbyter who had come said:

> “Rise; let us take food, because today is Pascha.”

The man of God replied:

> “I know that it is Pascha, because I have been deemed worthy to see you.”

Living far from human beings, he did not know that the Paschal solemnity fell on that day. But the venerable presbyter again declared:

> “Truly today is the Paschal day of the Lord’s Resurrection. It is not fitting for you to abstain, for I have also been sent for this purpose, that together we may partake of the gifts of almighty God.”

Blessing the Lord, they therefore took food. When the meal and conversation were completed, the presbyter returned to the church.

[Col. 0132A] At the same time shepherds also found him hiding in the cave. When they saw him clothed in skins among the thickets, they thought he was some wild animal. But, recognizing him as God’s servant, many of them were changed from a bestial mind to the grace of compassion. His name therefore became known to everyone throughout the neighboring places. From that time many began to visit him; when they brought him bodily food, they carried away from his mouth nourishment for life in their own hearts.

## Chapter Two

### Concerning the carnal adversary who rose up against him

[Col. 0131B]

One day, while the saint was living in solitude, behold, the tempter appeared in the form of a black bird, locally called a blackbird,

[Note: [Col. 0131D] *Reg.* reads *κώσσυφον* (“blackbird”).]

and began shamelessly to fly around his sanctified face, so that it could have been caught with the hands, if the saint had wished to do so. But, recognizing the enemy’s ambush and arming himself with the sign of the life-giving cross, this God-bearing man made invisible the demon who had appeared to him in the form of a bird.

After the departure of the dark-looking bird, such a temptation of the flesh was inflicted upon the saint as had never before befallen the holy man.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The same manuscript reads *οἷος οὐδεποτε* (“such as never [before]”).] For this chaste and honorable man had once seen a certain woman in the prime of his youth. The demon of fornication fashioned her image and set it before the righteous man’s inward eyes. It kindled in him so great a burning of the flesh that he was almost shaken from his spiritual apathy and driven to return to the world.

But the saving grace of God strengthened him and made him victorious over the passions. Regulating himself by the better and more temperate reasoning, he guarded himself against the enemy’s cunning.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] Both manuscripts read *πριεφρόνησεν* (apparently *περιεφρόνησεν*, “he despised it”).]

Looking up with his eyes and seeing nearby a mass of nettles and thorns, he stripped off his garment and threw himself naked upon the sharpest spines of the nettles and thorns. He rolled about in them for many hours, persevering, and saw his entire body drenched with blood. Bravely enduring their pains, and delivered from such a death-dealing thought, he remained giving great thanks to God.

[Note: [Col. 0131D] The manuscripts read *διέμεινεν* (“he remained”).]

From that time onward, throughout his entire life, the demon of fornication who had appeared to him in the form of a woman did not dare to trouble him in any way, as that father, unconquered in temptations, later related to his disciples.

Many people therefore abandoned the pleasures of the world and came to him for spiritual edification; and they learned from him to resist courageously the various powers of wickedness. Hence, through Moses, we are commanded to assign the Levites to service from the twenty-fifth year of their age, and from the fiftieth year to make them guardians of the vessels.

Peter. From the testimony just given, a marvelous understanding shines upon me; but I beg you to explain it clearly to me.

Gregory. It is clear to all, Peter, that in the youth of the flesh the body’s burning and the boiling of the passions ordinarily trouble human beings; but from the fiftieth year onward the heat naturally present in the body contracts.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The manuscripts read *προσοῦσα* (“present in”); the edition has *οὖσα* (“being”).]

The sacred vessels dedicated to God are the thoughts of the faithful. While the elect are tossed about in the storm of the passions, it is necessary for them to remain in services and bodily labors.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] *Reg.* reads *ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν αὐτοὺς διαμεῖναι* (“it is necessary for them to remain”); *Colb.* has *ἀναγκαῖόν ἐστιν αὐτοῖς διαβῆναι* (“it is necessary for them to pass through”).] But when the youth of the passions has grown old, reached the harbor of calm, and the body’s heat has departed, then they are appointed guardians of the vessels, because they become teachers of souls.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The words *τότε φύλακες τῶν σκευῶν καθίστανται* (“then they are appointed guardians of the vessels”), absent from the Vatican edition, were supplied by the manuscripts; the Latin text sufficiently proves that they had to be restored.]

Peter. I confess that I am pleased by what has been said. But I ask you to disclose what is difficult to interpret in the testimony just given and to narrate to us the life of this righteous man and the beginning of his way of life.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] The manuscripts read *προλεχθείσης … διήγησιν ποιήσῃς μοι* (“of the foregoing [testimony] … make the narration for me”).]

### Latin recension

**CAPUT II.** Concerning the temptation of the flesh overcome

[Col. 0132A]

One day, while he was alone, the tempter appeared. For a small black bird, commonly called a blackbird,

[Note: [Col. 0131D] *Primus Theoderic.* and *Bigot.* have “which is commonly called.”]

began to fly around his face and insolently hover before his countenance,

[Note: [Col. 0132D] *Compend.* omits “insolently.”]

so that it could have been caught by hand if the holy man had wished to hold it. But, when the sign of the cross was made, the bird withdrew. Such a temptation of the flesh followed its departure as the holy man had never before experienced. For he had once seen a certain woman, whom the evil spirit brought again before the eyes of his mind. He kindled the servant of God’s soul with such a fire in the woman’s likeness that he could scarcely contain himself beneath the flame of love in his breast, and, overcome by pleasure, was already almost deliberating about abandoning the wilderness.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] Thus the manuscripts of *Germ.*, *Norm.*, *Compend.*, and other better witnesses read. The printed editions have: “so that, while the flame of love was gaining force in his breast …”]

But suddenly the grace from above looked upon him, and he returned to himself.

[Note: [Col. 0132D] The first *Carnot.*, *Prat.*, and *Gemet.* read *subito supernae gratiae respectu* ("suddenly, through the regard of heavenly grace"). The first *Theod.* likewise has this reading, substituting *aspectu* for *respectu*; *Big.* reads *Tum subito sup. gratia repletus* ("Then suddenly filled with heavenly grace").] Seeing a dense growth of nettles and brambles nearby, he stripped off his clothing and threw himself naked among their sharp spines and the burning nettles. Rolling about there for a long time, he came out covered with wounds over his entire body and, through the wounds of his skin, drew from his body the wound of his mind, because he turned pleasure into pain. When he was burning outwardly in a fitting punishment, he extinguished what was burning unlawfully within. Thus he conquered sin, because he changed the fire.

From that time, as he himself later testified to his disciples, the temptation of pleasure was so subdued in him that he felt nothing of the kind. Thereafter many began to leave the world and hasten to his instruction. Once freed from the fault of temptation, he had rightly become a teacher of virtues. Hence Moses also commands (Num. VIII, 24–25) that the Levites from the age of twenty-five and upward should minister,

[Note: [Col. 0133D] This manner of expression occurs countless times in Gregory. See *Homily 17 on the Gospels*: “that they should lick from the same rock of salt,” that is, “let them lick.” *Book II, Letter 33*: “Your Fraternity should come to me before the summer season,” that is, “come.” The same usage recurs in that letter and twice in Letter 34. Gregory of Tours uses the same manner of expression: “He cast into him the thought that, having abandoned the wilderness, he should return to the world,” *Life of the Fathers*, chapter 9; and Bede, *Ecclesiastical History* I.23: “They send Augustine, who was to obtain from blessed Gregory that they should not undertake so dangerous a journey.” In the privilege granted by Pope Adeodatus to the monastery of Saint Martin of Tours: “He begged in a suppliant voice that we should grant him the privilege,” that is, “grant it.” See also *Councils of Gaul*, vol. I, p. 507. Similar examples are read in *Moral Commentary on Job* XXIII, formerly chapter 6, now chapter 11, no. 21, and are cited by Paterius, chapter 4 in the book of Numbers.]

but from the fiftieth year onward should become guardians of the vessels.

Peter. Some understanding of the testimony just brought forward now shines upon me, but I nevertheless ask that it be explained more fully.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The Clermont witness (*Val. cl.*) reads *planius* ("more plainly"); the two *Theod.* witnesses do likewise.]

Gregory. It is clear, Peter, that in the youth of the flesh temptation burns, while from the fiftieth year the body’s heat grows cold. The sacred vessels are the minds of the faithful. While the elect are still in temptation, they must remain subject, serve, and be wearied by duties and labors. But when, with the tranquility of mature age, the heat of temptation has departed, they are guardians of the vessels, because they become teachers of souls.

Peter. I confess that I approve what you say. But since you have unlocked the barriers of the testimony you brought forward, I ask you to run through the matters begun concerning the life of the righteous man.

## Chapter Three

### Concerning the glass vessel shattered by the sign of the cross

Περὶ τοῦ προσενεχθέντος αὐτῷ φαρμάκου ἐν ποτηρίῳ ὑελίνῳ. Concerning the poison brought to him in a glass cup

[Col. 0133C]

Gregory. Once the temptation mentioned above had been removed from the saint,

[Note: [Col. 0133D] *Colb.* reads *ἁγίου τὸ ῥηθὲν τοῦ πειρασμοῦ* (“the aforesaid temptation from the saint”); shortly afterward it has *ὑπὸ τοῦ ἁγίου πνεύματος καὶ χάριτος* (“by the Holy Spirit and grace”).]

the man of God, as though delivered from thorns, remained in an undisturbed state of mind. Thereafter, as his heart was cultivated by the grace of the Holy Spirit, he yielded the fruit of teaching more abundantly, so that from this time his admirable reputation became known to everyone.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] *Reg.* reads *μνήμην* (“memory”) rather than *φήμην* (“reputation”).]

There was a monastery not far from the cave of the holy Father Benedict, in which the superior of the community there had died. All the brothers who were there came together to the blessed man and earnestly begged him to become their guide and shepherd.

[Note: [Col. 0133D] Here the translator ranges more freely beyond the bounds of the Latin text, something not unusual for him.]

But he could not bear to abandon the Godlike humility that had grown together with him from childhood. He rejected their request, calling himself sinful and unworthy, and added:

> “My character does not agree with your characters.”

Overcome, however, by compassionate brotherly love, he reluctantly yielded to their entreaty.

While the blessed man was watchfully maintaining the order of the monastery and not permitting them to be carried along by their own desires, they saw that the holiness and most exacting discipline of the holy man did not accord with their own wickedness.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] *Reg.* reads *οἱ δὲ ὡς ἐθεάσαντο* (“but when they saw”).] They began to quarrel among themselves and to regret that they had sought for themselves so exacting and ascetic a man as their superior. Their crookedness therefore fought against the law of the blessed man; for the way of life of the righteous is hateful to crooked dispositions.

When those rebellious men realized that their disorderly purpose had not been accomplished according to their wishes, they mixed a deadly poison into wine, placed it in a glass, and dared to offer this deadly drink to the holy man as he reclined at the customary hour of the meal.

[Col. 0135B]

[Note: [Col. 0135D] The same manuscript reads *ποτήριον* (“cup”).]

But Benedict, the great father who worked signs, stretched out his hand and made the sign of the life-giving cross. Immediately the vessel burst apart and fell to the ground. It was shattered by the power of the precious and all-venerable cross

[Note: [Col. 0135D] *Colb.* adds *καὶ ζωοποιοῦ σταυροῦ* (“and of the life-giving cross”).]

so completely that those who saw it thought that the fatal cup had been crushed by a stone.

The man of God understood that the drink had been deadly, since it could not withstand the sign of our life made by the saint. He immediately rose, with cheerful face and tranquil mind, called the brothers, and said to them:

> “May almighty God have mercy on you, my children. Why did you wish to do this to me? Did I not tell you earlier that your ways do not agree with my character? Go, and seek for yourselves a father according to your ways; for I cannot remain with you.”

Then the saint returned with complete eagerness to the place where he had previously lived, embracing the solitude he had loved from the beginning. Guarded by God alone, who dwells on high and watches over the lowly, he lived attentive to himself—in solitude with himself.

Peter. A little of what has been said remains unclear to me: what does “he lived in solitude with himself” mean?

[Note: [Col. 0135D] *Colb.* reads *κατοικῆσαι* (“to dwell” or “to live”).]

[Col. 0135C]

Gregory. Because this holy man had not found among the brothers who were with him people of one mind and one spirit, but had seen that they were far from his way of life and unwilling to force themselves to walk along Christ’s humble path, and because he often saw them neglecting their own salvation, he felt deep compassion for them and hastened to shelter and shepherd them under his care.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] The manuscripts read *σκέπειν* (“to shelter”); the printed editions have *σκέπτειν*, using *σκέπτω* for *σκέπτομαι* (“to consider”).]

But whenever he labored daily for their correction and saw himself diminished in his ascent toward God, he more often left himself and did not find them.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] *Reg.* reads *εὕρισκεν* (“he was finding”).] For how often are we carried outside ourselves by the movement of improper thoughts? Then we exist, but are not with ourselves: not attending to what belongs to us, we are carried around toward other things.

[Note: [Col. 0137C] The same manuscript reads *περισκοπούμεθα* (“we look around”).]
