We call a man outside himself when he has gone into a distant country, consumed the portion of his substance, attached himself to one of its citizens, and fed pigs, which he saw eating pods while he himself was wasting away with hunger. He began to reason within himself about the good things he had lost. For it is written of him:

> “Coming to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house have more than enough bread?’”

If, then, he was with himself, how did he come back to himself?

[Note: [Col. 0137C] The same manuscript reads *ἐπανῆλθε* (“he returned”); a little later it has *ἐπώνυμον πατέρα* (“the father named accordingly”).] I have therefore said that this father, whose name signifies blessing, lived with himself because he always watched over himself with vigilant care, continually seeing himself before the eyes of the Creator, and examining himself.

[Note: [Col. 0137C] *Colb.* reads the corruptly printed form *τὸν … ἀκοίμητον ὀφθα` μόν*, meaning “the sleepless eye.”]

[Note: [Col. 0137C] The translator adds much of his own here, too much to indicate in detail. Certainly there is no trace in the Latin text of this verse, Psalm 15: “I kept the Lord always before me; because he is at my right hand, I shall not be moved,” which is quoted in Greek.]

He examined his own affairs according to the prophet David, the forefather of God, who says:

> “I foresaw the Lord always before me, because he is at my right hand, so that I may not be shaken.”

Peter. What, then, of what is written concerning the blessed Apostle Peter, that he was brought out of prison by an angel? For, coming to himself, he said:

> “Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people.”

Gregory. We are carried outside ourselves in two ways, Peter: either through dangerous and evil thoughts we fall beneath ourselves, or through the revelation of divine grace we are raised above ourselves.

[Note: [Col. 0137C] *Reg.* writes *ὑπεράνω* (“above”) as one word here and below.]

Thus the man who fed pigs fell beneath himself through the neglect and impurity of his own mind. But the man whom the angel released and brought out of prison, illumined in his intellectual eyes, was carried away in ecstasy: he was not outside himself, but above himself.

Both, therefore, returned to themselves. The one, rising from the error of evil deeds, gathered himself together in his own heart; the other, having entered into ecstasy through the angel’s vision, returned to the state in which he had previously existed through recognition of his natural condition.

Thus Father Benedict, predestined by God, lived in the calm and single-minded dignity of his character—in other words, he lived with himself—whenever he preserved himself under the God-pleasing governance of his thoughts. For whenever the greatness of a vision lifted him on high, he left himself, that is, he left himself beneath himself.

Peter. What you say has become clear to me. But I ask you to answer why he abandoned the brothers once entrusted to him, whose care he had undertaken.

Gregory. As I understand it, Peter, people who are joined there in one mind for their own destruction require great endurance if one is to bear the opposition of their evils, especially when no consolation is added by the discovery among them of a few good men.

[Note: [Col. 0138C] *Reg.* reads *πολλῆς χρεία ἐστί* (“there is need of much [endurance]”); a little later it has *προσγένηταί τις* (“someone may be added”).]

For where no fruit from labor can be expected at all, living together with the wicked nevertheless becomes a foolish expenditure of many struggles and sweats upon people who possess an evil and incorrigible disposition. Yet sometimes a helper is found.

It is a great thing if those so crookedly disposed can be brought to God as a better fruit. But why should that blessed man have remained with them when he saw them all united in one mind to persecute him?

[Note: [Col. 0139D] *Reg.* reads *χάριν εἶχε κατοικεῖν … ὁμοψύχως καταδιώκοντας* (“for what reason did he have to dwell … persecuting with one accord”), and so forth.] Certain things therefore take place in the souls of the righteous which cannot be passed over in silence.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The same manuscript reads *ἔστι σιωπῆσαι ἢ παραδραμεῖν* (“it is possible to keep silent or to pass over”).]

When they see that their labors are fruitless and foolish,

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The manuscripts read *καὶ ἀνόνητον* (“and unprofitable”).] they migrate to another place where they can bear fruit. So too the herald of truth, who desired to depart and be with Christ, saying, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain,”

the man who not only endured the contests of suffering himself but also taught others to endure them—when he once suffered persecution in Damascus, he sought a wall, a rope, and a basket, and wished to be lowered secretly.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Four *Colb.* copies read *ἐκέλευσεν* (“he ordered it”). *Reg.* reads *κατενεχθῆναι τοῦ τείχους ἐκέλευσε* (“he ordered himself to be lowered from the wall”), followed by *Μὴ τὸν … λέγωμεν δεδοικέναι ὡς ἑαυτὸν διὰ τὸν εἰς Χριστὸν πόθον μαρτυρίῳ ἀπέδωκεν* (“Are we to say that he feared death, since out of longing for Christ he surrendered himself to martyrdom?”).]

Are we to say that blessed Paul feared death, when he surrendered himself to martyrdom out of love for Jesus Christ? But while he was still in Damascus, he did not see himself bearing much fruit. Therefore he judged it necessary to migrate to other places, where he brought Christ an abundant harvest with much labor.

As a most excellent champion, he did not consent to remain within the walls of Damascus, but sought the arena of combat in which he conquered the enemy. In the same way, venerable Father Benedict—if you willingly listen to what will be said—you will soon recognize that, while still alive, he left many disciples in different places and strengthened and raised them up against the enemy’s error.

Peter. It is as you teach, and the testimony appropriately brought forward makes clear that these things are so. But I beg you to return to the profitable narrative of the earlier part of the righteous man’s way of life.

[Col. 0139C]

Gregory. While that blessed man continued to shine forth in the aforesaid cave through divine virtues, powers, and signs which God performed through him, and was raised to the height of angelic glory, many people came there to that very place, asking to be shepherded under his God-given grace.

The father Benedict, who loved both God and human beings, established twelve monasteries there by the power of Christ, appointing twelve monks in each monastery.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The manuscripts read *δὶς δέκα* (“twice ten,” that is, twenty).]

He kept only a few with himself, judging that they should be formed under his teaching and guidance.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] *Reg.* reads *διδασκαλίαν καὶ παιδαγωγίαν ἔκρινεν* (“he judged [them fit for] teaching and education”).]

Many people then began to come to him, including the most noble and devout men from the city of Rome,

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The same manuscript reads *σπουδαῖοι ἄνδρες* (“devout” or “earnest men”).] and to offer their sons to God through him.

Then Equitius and Maurus, children of good hope, were entrusted to him, and the patrician Tertullus also handed over Placidus.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] The same manuscript reads *Ἐβίζιος* (“Evizius”).]

Maurus, being the younger, began, as he grew in good character, to become his teacher’s assistant. Placidus, while still a boy, subdued his youth through ascetic labors.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] *Reg.* reads *Πλακίδας* (“Placidas”).]

### Latin recension

**CAPUT III.** Concerning the glass vessel shattered by the sign of the cross

[Col. 0134C]

Gregory. Once the temptation had departed, the man of God, as though earth freed from thorns, yielded more abundantly the fruit of virtues. His name therefore became famous through the proclamation of his outstanding way of life.

There was a monastery not far away,

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The remains of that monastery still survive at Vicus Varronis, commonly Vicovarro, on the left bank of the Anio between Subiaco and Tivoli, as several have noted, including D. Mabillon in his *Italian Itinerary*. More fully, D. Bernard de Montfaucon supplies, in *Italian Diary*, chapter 22, p. 340, a ground plan of the monastery and the place where it stands.]

whose abbot had died. The whole community therefore came to the same venerable Benedict and begged him earnestly to preside over them. He delayed for a long time by refusing and declared that his character could not agree with theirs.

[Note: [Col. 0134D] The first *Carn.* has “that his and their characters could not agree.” *Germ.*, *Norm.*, and others have “that his and their characters could not agree in morals.”]

At last, overcome by their entreaties, he consented. While he was maintaining the discipline of regular life in that monastery and allowing no one, as before, to turn to the right or left from the path of religious conduct through unlawful acts,

[Col. 0134D]

[Col. 0136A] the brothers whom he had received began insanely to accuse themselves for having asked him to preside over them. Their crookedness was offended by the rule of his uprightness.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Most printed editions have *fortitudo*, “strength,” an error which the Bollandists retained in the text but corrected in the notes. All the English, French, and other manuscripts have *tortitudo*, “crookedness.”]

When they saw that unlawful things were not permitted under him, regretted abandoning their accustomed ways, and found it hard to be compelled to think new thoughts with an old mind, some of them attempted to plot his death. For the life of the good is always burdensome to evil dispositions. They took counsel and mixed poison into wine.

[Note: [Col. 0135D] Two copies, *Germ.* and *Theod.*, and *Norm.* have a different sense, “something.” But the agreement of all the Benedictine witnesses makes it clear that they conspired below, where it says: “If the holy man had wished to endure those who were unanimously conspiring against him,” and near the end of the chapter: “For whom should the holy man remain as guardian, when he saw all unanimously persecuting him?” It is possible, however, that not all were aware that poison had been infused into the wine.]

When the glass vessel containing that deadly drink was offered to the reclining Father, according to the monastery’s custom,

[Note: [Col. 0136D] *Comp.* omits “according to custom.”]

for him to bless it, Benedict stretched out his hand and made the sign of the cross. By that same sign he broke the vessel, although it was being held some distance away. It was shattered as though, in that vessel of death, he had cast a stone in place of the cross.

[Col. 0136B]

The man of God immediately understood that the drink had been deadly, since it could not withstand the sign of life. He rose at once, with peaceful face and tranquil mind, summoned the brothers, and addressed them:

> “May almighty God have mercy on you, brothers. Why did you wish to do these things to me? Did I not tell you beforehand that your ways could in no way agree with mine? Go and seek for yourselves a father according to your ways, because from now on you cannot have me.”

Then he returned to the place of his beloved solitude and lived alone beneath the eyes of the heavenly Watcher.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] The first *Big.*, *Aud.*, and several copies of *Norm.* have “Inspector.”]

Peter. I understand less clearly what “he lived alone with himself” means.

[Col. 0136C]

Gregory. If the holy man had wished to keep for a long time under him those who were unanimously conspiring against him and were very unlike his way of life, he might have exceeded the use of his strength and the measure of his tranquility

[Note: [Col. 0136D] The second *Carn.* reads “to endure.”]

and turned the eye of his mind away from the light of contemplation.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] The manuscripts read this; the printed editions have “and cut off.”]

Being wearied daily by their incorrigibility, he might have cared less for his own affairs, left himself behind, and not found them. For whenever we are carried too far outside ourselves by the movement of thought, we exist, but are not with ourselves: because we do not see ourselves, we wander among other things.

[Note: [Col. 0136D] *Gilot.* has “and are not.” Gussanville has “and are with ourselves.” The reading in the Vatican manuscript is better and is supported by the German, Carnot, Norman, and most manuscripts: “and we exist.”]

Do we say that a man was with himself who went into a distant country, consumed the portion he had received, attached himself to one of its citizens, fed pigs, and saw them eating pods while he himself was starving? Yet afterward he began to consider the good things he had lost, and it is written of him:

> “Coming to himself, he said, ‘How many hired servants in my father’s house have an abundance of bread!’” (Luke 15:17)

If, then, he was with himself, how did he return to himself? I would therefore say that this venerable man lived with himself because, always watchful in his own custody, he continually saw himself before the eyes of the Creator and continually examined himself, never sending the eye of his mind outside himself.

[Note: [Col. 0138C] The first *Aud.* and *Lyr.* have “did not draw it away.”]

[Col. 0138B] Peter. What, then, of what is written concerning the Apostle Peter, when he had been led out of prison by an angel? “Coming to himself, he said: ‘Now I know truly that the Lord has sent his angel and delivered me from the hand of Herod and from all the expectation of the Jewish people’” (Acts 12:11).

Gregory. We are carried outside ourselves in two ways, Peter: either through a lapse of thought we fall beneath ourselves,

[Note: [Col. 0138C] *Germ.* has “we are carried outside ourselves, so that we are led beneath ourselves,” which represents the Greek especially well. *Gemet.* has “we are led beneath ourselves.” The first *Aud.*, *Big.*, *Lyr.*, and *Theod.* have “we withdraw.”]

or through the grace of contemplation we are raised above ourselves. The one who fed pigs fell beneath himself through wandering of mind and impurity; but the one whom the angel released and whose mind he carried into ecstasy was outside himself indeed, yet above himself.

Both, therefore, returned to themselves: the first, rising from the error of his actions, gathered himself back into his heart; the second, having entered into ecstasy through contemplation, returned from the summit of contemplation to the state in which he had previously existed through ordinary understanding.

Venerable Benedict therefore lived with himself in that solitude, insofar as he guarded himself within the enclosure of his thoughts. For whenever the ardor of contemplation carried him upward, he undoubtedly left himself beneath himself.

Peter. I approve what you say, but I ask you to answer whether he ought to have abandoned the brothers whom he had once received.

[Col. 0138C] Gregory. As I understand it, Peter, the wicked must be borne patiently where there are some good people who may be helped. But where there is absolutely no hope of fruit from the good, living together with the wicked sometimes becomes a useless expenditure of labor, with much struggle and sweat spent on people who possess an evil and incorrigible disposition. Yet it is sometimes possible for a helper to be found.

It is a great thing if those so perversely disposed can bring forth better fruit for God. But why should that blessed man have remained with them when he saw them all unanimously persecuting him? Certain things therefore take place in the souls of the righteous which cannot be passed over in silence.

When they see that their own labors are fruitless and foolish, they migrate to another place in which they will be able to bear fruit. So too the distinguished herald of truth, who longed to be released and to be with Christ, saying, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1:23), who not only endured the contests of sufferings himself but also taught others to endure them: when he suffered persecution in Damascus, he sought a wall, a rope, and a basket in order to escape, and wished to be lowered secretly.

[Note: [Col. 0139D] Four copies of *Colb.* have “he ordered it.” *Reg.* has “he ordered himself to be lowered from the wall.” The note adds: “Are we to say that the blessed Paul feared death, who surrendered himself to martyrdom because of his desire for Jesus Christ?”]

Are we then to say that blessed Paul feared death, when he gave himself to martyrdom because of his desire for Jesus Christ? But while he remained in Damascus, he did not see himself bearing much fruit. Therefore he judged it necessary to migrate to other places, in which he brought Christ an abundant harvest with much labor.

As a most excellent champion for Christ, he did not consent to remain within the gates of Damascus; he sought the arena of combat in which he conquered the enemy. Thus, venerable Father Benedict also—if you listen willingly to what follows—you will soon recognize that he did not abandon so many disobedient men as he raised from the death of the soul in other places.

[Col. 0140C] Peter. It is as you teach, and both clear reasoning and the fitting testimony brought forward show that these things are so. But I beg you to return to the order of the narrative concerning the life of so great a Father.

[Col. 0140C] Gregory. While the holy man continued for a long time to increase in virtues and signs in the same solitude, many gathered there through him for the service of almighty God. Thus, with the aid of almighty Jesus Christ the Lord, he built twelve monasteries there, assigning twelve monks to each under appointed superiors.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] Their names are supplied in *Acta Sanctorum Ordinis Sancti Patris Benedicti*, vol. I, p. 8, at the end.]

He kept only a few with himself, judging that they should still be more suitably instructed in his presence.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] *Val-cl.* reads “more deeply instructed.”]

Then noble and devout men from the city of Rome also began to come to him and entrust their sons to him for nourishment by almighty God. At that time Equitius and Maurus, sons of good hope, were given to him, and the patrician Tertullus handed over Placidus.

[Note: [Col. 0140D] The manuscript *Germ.* together with *Gemet.* and most copies of *Norm.* has *Evitius*; the first *Theod.* has *Euticius*.]

Maurus, being the younger, began, as he flourished in good character, to become his master’s assistant. Placidus, still a boy, subdued his youth through ascetic labors.

## Chapter Four

### Concerning a monk who left the monastery and occupied himself with earthly concerns

Περὶ τινὸς μοναχοῦ ἐῶντος τὴν μονὴν καὶ σχολάζοντος εἰς γηΐνας θεωρίας. Concerning a monk who left the monastery and occupied himself with earthly concerns

[Col. 0141A]

In one of the monasteries which the servant of God Benedict had established in the surrounding region, there was a monk troubled by negligence. He could not endure standing with the brothers at the time of prayer. Whenever all the brothers prostrated themselves before God in prayer, he went outside and gave himself over to idle talk and negligence.

His abbot admonished him repeatedly but accomplished nothing, and so brought him to the man of God. The latter solemnly and appropriately exposed his vanity, strengthened him by his admonition, and dismissed him. After returning to the monastery, the monk scarcely kept the man of God’s admonition for two days. On the third day, reverting to his devilish habit, he began to wander about at the time of prayer.

When his abbot saw that he had been overcome by the demon of spiritual weariness,

[Note: [Col. 0141D] *Reg.* reads *διαβόλου* (“of the devil”).]

he again went to the man of God and told him what had happened to the brother. The saint said to him:

> “I will come and correct him myself.”

[Note: [Col. 0141D] *Colb.* reads *δι’ ἑαυτόν* (“by himself”). A little farther on it has *ἐν τῇ μονῇ* (“in the monastery”), a reading also found in *Reg.*]

When he had come to the monastery, and at the appointed hour, after the hymn of psalmody had been completed and the brothers had knelt and devoted themselves to prayer, the saint saw that a certain Ethiopian youth had seized the hem of the garment of that brother who could not persevere in prayer and was dragging him outside the church.

Then the saint secretly said to the superior of that monastery, whose name was Pompeianus, and to Maurus, the servant of God:

> “Do you not see who is dragging this monk outside the church?”

They replied:

> “No, Father.”

The saint said to them:

> “Let us pray, so that you too may see whom this monk is following.”

After they had prayed for two days, the monk Maurus saw him, but Pompeianus, the father of that monastery, was unable to see him. On the following day, when the prayer had been completed, the man of God came out of the oratory and found the monk standing outside. Because of the blindness of his heart, he struck him with a staff.

From that very day the monk was freed from the demon of negligence that had held him. Thereafter he remained eagerly with the brothers in prayer until its completion. The enemy no longer dared to touch that brother, as though he had been scourged by the blow of the saint’s staff.

### Latin recension

**CAPUT IV.** Concerning the monk of wandering mind brought back to salvation

[Col. 0142A]

In one of the monasteries that he had built all around, there was a certain monk who could not stand for prayer. As soon as the brothers inclined themselves to the exercise of prayer, he would go outside and, with a wandering mind, occupy himself with earthly and transitory things. Since he had often been admonished by his abbot, he was brought to the man of God, who himself also severely rebuked his foolishness. After returning to the monastery, he kept the admonition of the man of God for scarcely two days; on the third day, reverting to his former habit, he began to wander about during the time of prayer.

When this had been reported to the servant of God by the father of that monastery whom he had appointed, he said: “I am coming, and I myself will correct him.” When the man of God had come to the same monastery and, at the appointed hour, after the psalmody had been completed, the brothers had given themselves to prayer [Gemetensis: “after the psalmody, the brothers had given themselves to the hour of prayer”], he saw that a certain black little boy was pulling the same monk, who could not remain at prayer, outside by the hem of his garment.

Then he said secretly to Pompeianus, the father of that monastery, and to Maurus, the servant of God: “Do you not see who it is that is pulling this monk outside?” They replied: “No.” He said to them: “Let us pray, so that you also may see whom this monk is following.” After prayer had been offered for two days, the monk Maurus saw him; Pompeianus, however, the father of that monastery, could not see him.

On the following day, after the prayer had been completed, the man of God left the oratory and found the monk standing outside. Because of the blindness of his heart, he struck him with a staff. From that day onward the monk suffered no further persuasion from the black little boy, but remained steadfast in the exercise of prayer. Thus the ancient enemy no longer dared to rule in his thoughts, as though he himself had been struck by the blow.

[The addition “any further” occurs in two manuscripts, Audomarus and Beccensis, and in Lyranus.]

[CAPUT V.]

## CHAPTER V  
### Concerning the water produced from a rock on the summit of the mountain through the prayer of the man of God

[Greek heading: “Concerning the stream that flowed forth from a living rock through his prayer.” Colb. reads: “Concerning the miracle of the spring.” In the Regius manuscript the heading is the same as in the printed editions.]

[Col. 0141C]

Of the monasteries mentioned above, which the holy father Benedict established in that very place [Colb. adds: “our holy father Benedict”; and later: “they were on the cliff of the mountain”], three of them were situated above the mountain’s cliffs. It was exceedingly laborious for the brothers continually to descend to the pool in order to obtain their supply of water [Regius reads “continually”; Colbensis, “of continually”]. For the route passed along the dangerous side of the mountain, so that they had to descend and climb again in great fear.

Then the monks living in those three monasteries gathered and came to the servant of God Benedict. They begged him, saying:

“Honored father, it is difficult for us, because of the steep passage over the mountain, to descend as far as the pool and obtain the water we need. It is therefore necessary to move the monasteries [Regius: *metoikisai*, “to relocate”], lest some of the brothers, slipping, should suffer a violent death.”

He dismissed them after soothing them with words of counsel and encouragement.

That very night he took with him a young man named Placidus, whom I mentioned earlier, climbed the same difficult cliff of the mountain, and there persevered for some time in prayer to God. Rising from prayer, he picked up three stones and placed them at intervals in that very spot. While everyone was unaware of what had happened, he returned to his own cell.

On the following day the brothers mentioned above came to him again because of their earlier request for water. The holy man said to them:

“Go up, children, to that cliff where you will find three stones lying one above another, and dig there. For God, the Almighty, is able to provide you with an abundant supply of water even at that height of the mountain, and to make easy the difficult labor of the road.”

[The Regius manuscript reads “to the place of the cliff.”]

They went and found the cliff of the mountain just as the Father had said. At that place the dry hardness of the mountain was sending up a certain moisture and drops of water. When they had made a large excavation, a great quantity of water immediately burst forth. It has continued to flow abundantly down to the present day, displaying forever to all the miracle-working power of the saint. The surplus water can be seen running down beneath the mountain.

[The manuscripts read “flows out abundantly.”]

## CHAPTER V  
### Concerning the water produced from a rock at the summit of the mountain by the prayer of the man of God

[Col. 0142C]

Of the monasteries that he had built in the same place, three were situated high up on the mountain’s crags. It was very laborious for the brothers always to descend to the lake in order to draw water [that is, “so that they might draw water”; compare the note above, col. 133], especially since the descent was along the precipitous side of the mountain and involved grave danger for those who went down in fear.

Then the brothers from those three monasteries gathered and came to Benedict, the servant of God, saying: “It is laborious for us to descend every day as far as the lake for water, and therefore the monasteries must be moved from this place.”

He comforted them gently [Gemetensis and most Norman manuscripts, together with the German manuscript, read “comforting them gently”; others read “having gently comforted them”] and dismissed them. That same night he climbed the crag of the same mountain with a little boy named Placidus, whom I mentioned earlier, and prayed there for a long time. When his prayer was finished, he placed three stones in the same spot as a sign, and returned to his monastery, while no one there knew what he had done [in most printed editions, “while they did not know”].

When the brothers mentioned above returned to him on the following day because of their need for water, he said: “Go, and dig a little into that crag in which you find three stones placed one above another. For Almighty God is able to produce water even on that summit of the mountain, and graciously to remove from you the labor of so long a journey.”

They went and found the mountain crag that Benedict had described already sweating. When they had hollowed out a place in it, it was immediately filled with water. It flowed forth so plentifully that it continues even now to run abundantly, descending from the summit of the mountain to the lower ground.

[Gemetensis reads: “and to graciously remove from you the labor …”]

[CAPUT VI.]

## CHAPTER VI  
### Concerning the iron tool that fell into the lake and returned to its handle

[Colb. reads: “Concerning the Goth and the wood-cutting tool.”]

[Col. 0143B]

At another time a certain man, a Goth by race but poor in spirit, came to the holy Benedict in conversion and repentance. The man of God received him willingly.

One day the saint ordered one of the brothers to give him an iron tool, locally called a *xylokopion* [Regius: *xylokopion*; Colb.: *xylokopē*], so that he might clear a thorny and brush-covered place and perhaps cultivate a garden there for the brothers. The place that the Goth had undertaken to clear was above the lake.

While the Goth, obedient to the father’s command, was cutting down the thickets of thorns with all his strength, the iron tool, by an accident, fell into the deep part of the lake, where there was no hope of recovering it.

The aforementioned Goth ran to the monk Maurus, reported what had happened, and asked repentance for his fault. The monk Maurus promptly reported the event to the man of God.

When this miracle-working man heard it, he went to the place where the iron had fallen. He took the handle from the Goth’s hands and lowered the part of it to which the tool had been fastened into the lake. Immediately the tool rose from the depths of the water and entered its own place on the handle.

The saint returned the thorn-cutting tool to the Goth, saying: “Here is the tool. Take it, work, and do not be saddened.”

[The two manuscripts read *manougrion* instead of *manouvrion*.]

## CHAPTER VI  
### Concerning the iron that returned from the depths of the water to its handle

[Col. 0144B]

At another time a certain Goth, poor in spirit, came to conversion. Benedict, the man of God, received him most willingly.

One day he ordered an iron implement to be given to him. It was called a *falcastrum*, because of its resemblance to a sickle [Gemetensis: “which is called a sickle-tool because of its resemblance to a sickle”], so that he might cut down the brambles in a certain place and make a garden there. The place that the Goth had undertaken to clear [the Second Theodulfian, Vallicellian, and several other manuscripts read “which he had undertaken to clear”] lay above the very bank of the lake.

As the Goth cut down the dense mass of brambles with all his strength, the iron sprang from its handle and fell into the lake. The water was so deep that there was no longer any hope of finding the implement. Thus, having lost the iron, the trembling Goth ran to the monk Maurus. He reported the damage he had caused and performed penance for his guilt. The monk Maurus immediately took care to report it also to Benedict, the servant of God.

The man of the Lord Benedict, hearing this, went to the lake [Gussanvillian: “to the place”]. He took the handle from the Goth’s hand and put it into the lake. Immediately the iron returned from the depths and entered the handle.

At once he gave the tool back to the Goth, saying: “Here it is. Work, and do not be saddened.”

[CAPUT VII.]

## CHAPTER VII  
### Concerning the monk Maurus, who walked on the waters

[Col. 0145A]

One day, while this miracle-working man Benedict was at rest in his cell, the monk Placidus, mentioned above, came to the lake to draw water. The vessel in which he wished to draw the water fell from his hand and was carried along by the force of the water. As the brother wished to snatch the jar from the water, he himself slipped and fell into the water. By the extremely violent movement of the water, the monk Placidus was carried inward into the lake, almost, so to speak, the distance of an arrow-shot.

Benedict, the faithful servant of God, was at leisure inside his cell when he perceived what had happened. He quickly called his disciple Maurus and said to him:

“Brother Maurus, hurry, for brother Placidus has fallen into the lake, and the movement of the water has carried him far away.”

A wondrous thing—and one that occurred after the Apostle Peter: an extraordinary commission, faithfully requested by the monk Maurus and granted by the blessed Benedict [the manuscripts add: “a wondrous thing, which also occurred after the Apostle Peter: a strange command, requested faithfully from the monk Maurus and granted by the blessed Benedict.” The editor remarks that the wording is seriously corrupt and suggests reading: “for, when the prayer had been requested … and granted …, he went quickly,” unless the manuscript reading is preferred].

Maurus went quickly at the Father’s command. When he reached the place where Placidus was being carried in the water, trusting in unwavering faith and in the Father’s prayers, he stepped onto the water and walked rapidly as though on dry land until he reached the place where Placidus was being carried by the force of the water. He seized him by the hair of his head and returned at great speed.

As soon as Placidus came onto dry land, he came to himself and realized that he had run across the water and that it had been impossible for him to walk on the water unless the prayer of the miracle-working Father had strengthened him. He marveled at what had happened and trembled. Returning to the Father, he reported the divine marvel that had taken place.

Benedict, the man of God, attributed the miracle not to his own holiness but to Maurus’s obedience. Maurus, on the other hand, said that it had been accomplished solely through the saint’s command; he declared that he himself had not possessed the power in which he had been when he stepped upon the water.

When the monk Placidus heard this godlike humility and most loving dispute between them [Colb. reads “theological dispute”], he said:

“While I was being dragged along by the force of the water, I saw my abba’s cloak above my head, and I perceived that he himself was drawing me out of the water.”

[The Latin note explains that *melotes* here means a cowl. Paul the Deacon, writing to Charlemagne on behalf of Abbot Theodemar, says that the garment called by the Gallic monks a *cuculla*, and by them a *cappa*, which properly designates the monastic habit, should be called a *melotes*, as it is still called by some in that province. Mabillon, in the cited work.]

Peter: “The things you relate are exceedingly great and provide great edification for souls. But the more I drink in the miracles of this holy man, the more I thirst.”

## CHAPTER VII  
### Concerning Maurus, his disciple, who walked on the waters

[Col. 0146A]

One day, while the same venerable Benedict was staying in his cell, the aforementioned Placidus, the holy man’s young monk, went out to draw water from the lake. Carelessly lowering into the water the vessel that he held, he himself followed it when he fell. The wave immediately seized him and dragged him inland from the shore almost the distance of an arrow’s flight.

The man of God, being inside his cell, immediately perceived this and hurriedly called Maurus, saying:

“Brother Maurus, run, because that boy who went to draw water has fallen into the lake, and the wave is already carrying him far away.”

This was a wondrous event, unparalleled after the Apostle Peter. After requesting and receiving a blessing, Maurus hastened at his Father’s command. He went as far as the place where the wave was carrying the boy, thinking that he was walking on land, but in fact he ran across the water. He seized him by the hair [in the early centuries of our Order, novices retained secular clothing; see chapter 58 of the Rule of Saint Benedict and the cited notes concerning the life of Lanfranc, and the life of Saint Maurus by Flodoard in Mabillon’s *Acta*, vol. I, p. 9].

He then returned at a rapid pace. As soon as he touched land, he came to himself, looked behind him, and realized that he had run across the water. Astonished that he had presumed to do what could not happen, he trembled at the event [Vallicellian: “he feared it”]. Returning to the Father, he reported what had happened.

The venerable Benedict began to attribute this not to his own merits but to the other’s obedience. Maurus, on the contrary, said that it had happened solely because of his command, and that he himself had not been conscious of possessing the power by which he had acted without knowing it.

During this friendly dispute of mutual humility [the Second Carnotensis reads “during this friendly and mutual dispute of humility”; the two Theodulfian manuscripts read “during this friendly dispute of mutual humility”], the boy who had been rescued became the arbiter. He said:

“When I was being dragged from the water, I saw my abba’s *melotes* above my head, and I perceived him himself drawing me out of the waters.”

Peter: “The things you relate are truly great and astonishing. For in the water that flowed like a river from the mountain through the prayer of the blessed man, I perceive Moses; in the iron tool that rose from the depths of the lake’s water, I see Elisha; in the course across the water, I understand Peter; in the obedience of the raven, I see Elijah. Thus, as I understand it, this man was filled with the spirit of all the righteous.”

## CHAPTER VIII  
### Concerning the bread in which poison was mixed

[Col. 0145C]

Gregory: “When the blessed man had begun to shine throughout those regions [the printed editions incorrectly read ‘throughout those labors’], many people came to him from far away through longing for our Lord Jesus Christ. Abandoning the vanity of the world, they submitted their necks to the good yoke of the Lord.

But the father of envy and the ancient enemy of the devout, unable to endure the flashes of miracles radiating from him and seeing himself defeated by the God-given power of the saint, entered into [the reading is conjecturally corrected from *enskēpsas* to *eneskēpse*, “came upon”] the soul-destroying thoughts of disorderly people, as it is customary for them to envy the achievements of others. For the praise of one who lives purely becomes a reproach to those stained by envy.

Accordingly, a certain presbyter of the neighboring church, named Florentius—the grandfather of our subdeacon Florentius—having received into himself the hatred and envy of the utterly wicked demon, began to mock and envy the virtues of the holy man, hoping thereby to draw many away from the saint’s soul-benefiting instruction.

When he failed in this deranged hope and saw many drawn by the saint’s reputation, visiting him and increasing through his teachings, Florentius, as though wounded by arrows, slandered the holy father’s way of life [the manuscripts read “the way of life of the holy man”]. Yet he did not choose to acquire for himself an honorable life through ascetic struggles.

Blinded by the devil, he advanced so far that he sought to kill the servant of God with poison. He mixed flour, then kneaded bread, concealed deadly poison in it, baked it, and sent it to the man of God as though for a blessing.

The visionary man received the bread gratefully, but the treachery hidden in it did not escape him [Regius: “the treachery hidden inside”]. At the hour when the saint was accustomed to take food, a bird commonly called a raven, which lived in the nearby forest, customarily came to him and received bread for food from his venerable hands.

The holy man took the deadly bread that the elder Florentius had sent him, placed it before the raven, and ordered it, saying:

‘In the name of Jesus Christ, the Son of the living God, take this bread and throw it in such a place that no human being may find it.’

Then the raven began to fly around the bread with its mouth open and its wings extended, crying out, and by its movements indicating the diabolical plot contained in it.

The man of God again began to say to it:

‘Take it, take it without fear, and put it there where it cannot be found.’”

Then the raven fulfilled the saint’s command. With great fear it took the bread in its mouth, departed, and threw it into a place completely inaccessible to human beings. After three hours it returned and received from the saint’s hands its customary food.

Benedict, that most simple and in every respect most gentle man [Regius: “father”], saw the murderous plot of Florentius and that he had not been able to correct his wickedness. He prayed to God for Florentius rather than for himself.

But the aforementioned Florentius, unable to kill the saint’s body, devised another evil and satanic scheme against the saint’s disciples. While they were working in the garden, Florentius, the devil’s agent, sent seven girls beautiful in appearance and entirely naked into the garden. He ordered them to behave wantonly and play before the monks, wishing by this means also to ruin the men’s chastity.

But in this too his utterly wicked folly failed. Benedict, the imitator of Christ, saw his diabolical plan and feared spiritual harm to the disciples. Considering that Florentius was doing these things solely out of envy against him, the servant of God judged it better to secure the salvation of his own disciples by withdrawing.

He therefore summoned the brothers and stewards of the monasteries [Regius: “monks”], established them in their places, entrusted them to God, and, taking a few monks with him, withdrew from his own cell, humbly avoiding Florentius’s hatred and hostility.

Florentius sinned unlawfully and in vain, but God rescued his own servant and preserved him for the salvation of many, striking down the wicked man.

For when the God-hating foreigner Florentius rejoiced at the blessed man’s departure and stood in the sunny upper room of the house in which he lived [the same manuscript reads “in the solarium”], he suddenly fell from the great height together with that sunny upper room, paying a penalty worthy of his wickedness and suffering a deadly death.

When Maurus, the saint’s disciple, mentioned above many times, saw this, he immediately sent a messenger to the saint, who was about ten miles away, saying:

‘Return, father, return, for the presbyter who pursued you in vain has died.’

When Benedict, the man of God, heard this, he melted in great grief over that pitiable death. He also grieved over his own disciple, as though the disciple had rejoiced in Florentius’s wretched downfall. He ordered him to repent of such a fault, since he had rejoiced at Florentius’s death [the manuscripts read: “as one who had, so to speak, rejoiced at Florentius’s death”].”

Peter: “The things you have said are truly marvelous and astonishing [the manuscripts read “and greatly astonishing,” which more faithfully represents the Latin text]. In the water that flowed like a river from the mountain through the blessed man’s prayer, I see Moses; in the iron tool that rose from the depths of the lake’s waters, I see Elisha; in the course across the water, I see Peter; in the raven’s obedience, I see Elijah. As I consider it, this man was filled with the spirit of all the righteous.”

Gregory: “Benedict, the man of God, possessed, Peter, the Spirit of the one God [Vallicellian, Lyranus, and the first Audomarus: “he possessed one spirit”; the two Theodulfian manuscripts, the Compendian, and most Norman manuscripts omit ‘of God’], who through the grace of the redemption granted to all filled the hearts of all the elect.

Concerning him John the Evangelist said:

‘He was the true light that enlightens every human being coming into this world’ (John 1:9).

And again it is written concerning him:

‘From his fullness we have all received’ (John 1:16).

For the holy men of God were deemed worthy by the Lord to receive powers of grace, but not also to hand them on to others. He himself gave signs of power to those subject to him. He promised his enemies that he would give them the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39), so that he might consent to die before the proud and rise again before the humble; thus the proud would see what they ought to have despised, and the humble what they ought to have loved while revering it.

From this mystery it came about that, while the proud looked upon the contempt of death, the humble received the glory of power over death [Beccensis reads “looked upon”; the Greek interpreter supports this reading].”

Peter: “After this, I beg you, tell us to what places that holy man moved and whether he later displayed any powers there.”

Gregory: “When this holy man moved to other places, he changed his dwelling, but not his enemy. For afterward he endured battles both greater and more severe, having found the author of evil openly fighting against him.

The fortress called Cassinum lies on the slope of a lofty mountain. The mountain, spreading out its side, encloses this fortress, while its summit rises three miles high, as though reaching toward the sky, so that to those who do not know the place it appears like a star.

There was there a very ancient pagan shrine built by the ancients. In it Apollo was worshiped by the foolish rustic population according to the custom of the pagans [Regius: “honored”]. Around that most polluted temple stood a great number of altars. Even then a great multitude of unbelievers went there, serving the statue of Apollo with sacrifices, libations, and sacrificial smoke.

Benedict, enlightened in mind and zealous for devotion, came to the place. Entering with courageous resolve [the manuscript has *tharsalaion*, perhaps for *tharsaleō*], he smashed the statue of Apollo, overturned the altars, and burned the groves. In the very temple of Apollo he made a consecrated oratory of Saint Martin.

Where the altar of Apollo had stood, he established a venerable consecrated oratory of Saint John [the manuscripts read “a consecrated oratory of Saint John”]. From then on the multitude of the people living there, guided by his teaching, was converted to God.

The crooked enemy of the faithful could no longer endure this. No longer secretly or through dreams, but openly, he displayed himself before the Father’s eyes and shouted with the loudest cries that he was being subjected to violence by the saint. The brothers heard his cries, although they did not see him with their bodily eyes.

The teacher of truth said to them:

‘Believe, children, that with my bodily eyes I see a terrifying figure who appears like a spark in his manifestations and sends flames of fire from both his mouth and his eyes.’

Whatever the deceiver uttered, they all heard.

At first he called the saint by name. When he saw that the man of God did not answer him at all, he immediately turned his filthy tongue to insults against him and assailed the friend of God with abuse. Then he called the saint again, saying:

‘Benedict, Benedict!’

When he did not answer, he immediately added:

‘Accursed one, not blessed one, what have you to do with me? Why do you persecute me?’

These new struggles of the ancient enemy against the servant of God are truly worthy of remembrance, since he brought such battles against him; but by the very course of the contest, the life of the saint served the purpose of victory [perhaps the reading is *violentia*, “violence,” rather than *vita*, “life”].”

## CHAPTER VIII
### Concerning bread poisoned and cast far away by a raven

[Col. 0146C]

Gregory. Since those same places were now everywhere aflame with love for our Lord God Jesus Christ [the printed Greek text wrongly reads “those labors”], and many were abandoning secular life and taming the neck of their hearts beneath the gentle yoke of the Redeemer, a priest of a neighboring church, named Florentius—the grandfather of our subdeacon Florentius—was struck by the malice of the ancient enemy [two German manuscripts, two Audomarus manuscripts, and most Norman manuscripts read “struck down”]. As wicked people commonly envy in others the good of virtue which they themselves do not seek to possess, he began to envy the holy man’s efforts and disparage his manner of life; he also tried to keep from visiting him all whom he could.

When he saw that he could not oppose Benedict’s progress and that the reputation of his way of life was increasing, while many were continually being called to a better state of life by the very renown of that reputation [Gilotian and Vatican manuscripts read “to call”; some, “to be free”], he became ever more inflamed by the fires of envy. He desired the praise of that way of life, but did not wish to possess a praiseworthy life.

Blinded by the darkness of this envy, he was carried so far as to send to the servant of Almighty God bread infected with poison, as though it were a blessing. The man of God received it with thanksgiving, but was not unaware what pestilence lay hidden in the bread.

At the hour of his meal a raven was accustomed to come from the neighboring wood and receive bread from his hand. When it came as usual, the man of God threw before it the bread sent by the priest and commanded it: “In the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, take this bread and cast it in such a place that no human being can find it.”

Then the raven, with open beak and outspread wings, began to move about and croak around the bread, as though plainly saying both that it wished to obey and that it could not carry out the command. The man of the Lord repeatedly commanded it: “Take it, take it without fear, and cast it where it cannot be found.” After lingering for a long while, the raven at last took it in its beak, lifted it, and departed. After three hours had passed, it returned, having cast away the bread, and received from the man of God the food to which it was accustomed.

The venerable Father, seeing the priest’s mind burn against his life, grieved more for him than for himself. But Florentius, since he could not kill the master’s body, set himself on destroying the souls of his disciples. In the garden of the cell occupied by Benedict, he sent seven naked girls before their eyes, so that, holding one another’s hands [the manuscripts, in strong agreement, read “stretching out their hands”], and playing for a long time before them, they might inflame the monks’ minds toward the perversity of lust.

The holy man saw this from his cell and feared a fall for his still more vulnerable disciples. Judging that this was being done because of persecution directed against himself alone [the manuscripts agree; editions altered it slightly to “because of himself alone”], he yielded place to envy. He arranged all the oratories that he had built, appointing superiors and assigning brothers to them [most Norman manuscripts read “under those appointed”], and, taking a few monks with him, changed his dwelling-place.

As soon as the man of God had humbly avoided Florentius’s hatred, Almighty God struck Florentius terribly. For when the priest learned that Benedict had departed and rejoiced while standing in a *solarium* [an elevated place where the ancients used to bask in the winter sun for their health; hence in Greek it is called *hēliakon*, “sunny place”], the very *solarium* on which he stood fell, though the entire fabric of the house remained otherwise immovable, and, crushing Benedict’s enemy, killed him.

Maurus, a disciple of the man of God [apparently not Saint Maurus, the son of Equitius, since that Maurus is said in the Acts of Saint Placidus, no. 11, always to have remained with Benedict when he moved; but those Acts are interpolated and scarcely deserve credence. The translator considered him to be the Maurus mentioned above by Saint Gregory], judged that this should immediately be reported to the venerable Father Benedict, who was still scarcely ten miles from that place. He said: “Return, for the priest who persecuted you has been killed.”

Hearing this, Benedict gave himself to deep lamentation: both because his enemy had died and because his disciple had rejoiced in his enemy’s death. Consequently he imposed penance on that disciple also, because, in reporting such news, he had presumed to rejoice at an enemy’s destruction.

[Col. 0150B]

Peter. “The things you say are wonderful and greatly astonishing. In water brought forth from a rock I see Moses (Numbers 20); in the iron that returned from the depths of the water, Elisha (4 Kings 6:7); in the journey over the water, Peter (Matthew 14:29); in the raven’s obedience, Elijah (3 Kings 17:6); and in grief over an enemy’s death, David (2 Kings 1:11; 18:33). As I judge it, this man was full of the spirit of all the righteous.”

Gregory. “Benedict, man of God, Peter, possessed the Spirit of the one God [Vallicellian, Lyranus, and the first Audomarus manuscript read ‘he possessed one spirit’; two Theodulfian manuscripts, the Compendian manuscript, and most Norman manuscripts read ‘of one spirit,’ omitting ‘God’]. Through the grace of the redemption granted, that Spirit filled the hearts of all the elect. Of him John says: ‘He was the true light which enlightens every human being coming into the world’ (John 1:9). And again it is written of him: ‘From his fullness we have all received’ (ibid., 1:16).

“For holy men of God could receive powers from the Lord, but could not also transmit them to others. But he gave signs of power to his subjects who promised his enemies that he would give the sign of Jonah (Matthew 12:39), so that he might deign to die before the proud and rise again before the humble: in order that the former might see what they despised and the latter what, in revering it, they ought to have loved. From this mystery it came about that, while the proud saw the contempt of death, the humble received the glory of power over death [Beccensis reads ‘saw’; the Greek translation supports that reading].”

Peter. “I ask you: to what places did the holy man move after this, and did he later perform any miracles in them? Tell us.”

Gregory. “The holy man, in moving elsewhere [the second Carnotensis, German, and Lyranus manuscripts read, with substantially the same sense, ‘moving to other places, he changed his dwelling, not his enemy’; Beccensis has ‘moving to other places, he changed his dwelling, not his enemy’], changed his dwelling-place, not his enemy. For afterward he endured battles all the graver because he found the master of wickedness himself openly fighting against him.

## CHAPTER IX  
### Concerning the enormous stone made light through his prayer

[Col. 0153A]

One day, while the brothers were building the dwelling of the cell where the saint was to live in solitude [Regius: “the building in which he was to remain in solitude”], a stone lay in the middle of the site. The brothers wished to place it in the building.

When three brothers came to move the stone, they could not lift it from the ground. Many more gathered, but accomplished nothing [Regius: “achieved nothing”; Colbensis: “benefited nothing”]. The stone remained immovable, so that it seemed to them to be rooted in the earth.

It became clear to everyone that the devil himself was sitting upon it, since the hands of so many men could not move it.

The brothers, therefore, finding themselves at a loss, sent to the man of God, asking him to drive away the enemy through his intercession with God, so that they might be able to lift the stone.

He came immediately, offered a prayer, and returned to the disciples, telling them to lift the stone. It was raised with such effortless speed that they thought it had previously possessed no weight at all, although earlier it had been immovable.

## CHAPTER IX  
### Concerning the huge stone lifted through the prayer of the man of God

[Col. 0154A]

One day, while the brothers were building the quarters of the same cell [the term “cell” is clearly used here for the monastery itself, as it frequently is throughout these Dialogues], a stone lay in the middle. They had decided to lift it into the building.

When two or three could not move it, more men joined them, but it remained so immovable that it seemed to be held in the earth by its roots. Thus it was plainly understood that the ancient enemy himself was sitting upon it, since the hands of so many men could not move him.

When the difficulty arose, someone was sent to the man of God to ask him to come and drive away the enemy by prayer, so that they might lift the stone. He came at once, prayed, and gave a blessing. The stone was lifted with such speed that it seemed to have had no weight before.

[CAPUT X.]

## CHAPTER X  
### Concerning the bronze figurine that was found and from which fire appeared in a vision

[Colbensis: “Concerning the bronze idol.” This manuscript’s chapter headings differ consistently from those of the printed editions and the Regius manuscript.]

[Col. 0153B]

The saint therefore decided to instruct his own disciples to dig the ground in the place where the stone had previously lain. In accordance with his command, they made a deep excavation and found there a bronze idol. When it was thrown into the kitchen, fire suddenly appeared to come out of it and, before the eyes of all the monks, showed through its appearances as though the entire structure of the kitchen had been consumed.

The brothers therefore began amid great confusion to pour water upon it, as though extinguishing the visionary flame that had appeared before their eyes through the enemy.

The man of God perceived that the brothers were in great turmoil and learned the cause from them. He came into the kitchen. While the brothers said that they saw fire, he declared that he saw nothing of the sort. Immediately, as was his custom, he bowed his head to God in prayer and prayed that the devil’s illusory mockery, which had appeared to the brothers, might depart from their eyes.

[Regius: “that the illusory mockery in their eyes might depart from the brothers”; Colbensis reads “might be forgotten” instead of “might depart.”]

Rising from prayer, through his supplication to God he restored the deceived eyes of the brothers to strength and natural sight. Thus they no longer saw the kitchen building burning in the devil’s flames [Regius: “burning before their eyes, but thereafter it was seen unharmed”]; instead, before their eyes it appeared unburned and undisturbed.

## CHAPTER X  
### Concerning the illusory fire in the kitchen

[Col. 0154B]

Then, in the presence of the man of God, it was decided that they should dig the ground in the same place. As they penetrated more deeply by digging, the brothers found a bronze idol there. When it happened to be thrown into the kitchen, fire suddenly appeared to come out of it and showed before the eyes of all the monks as though the entire structure of the kitchen were being consumed.

As they made a great commotion by throwing water and pretending to extinguish the fire, the man of God, disturbed by the tumult, arrived. He observed that the same fire appeared before the brothers’ eyes but not before his own. Immediately he bowed his head in prayer and recalled the brothers, who he found deceived by an illusory fire; he urged them to mark their eyes with the sign of the cross, so that they might see the kitchen building standing sound and unharmed and no longer see the flames fabricated by the ancient enemy.

[The Gussanvillian manuscript, supported by the first Theodulfian, the Gemetensis, and many Norman manuscripts, reads “so that the brothers might mark their eyes, and thus see it sound,” etc.]

[CAPUT XI.]

## CHAPTER XI  
### Concerning the young monk crushed when a wall collapsed and healed by his prayer

[Col. 0155A]

Again, while the brothers were building a wall and were hurrying to raise the structure higher, the servant of God remained in his cell, occupied in prayer. The utterly wicked enemy appeared to him, as if rejoicing, and indicated that he was going toward those working on the building [both manuscripts add “the brothers”].

When the God-bearing man learned this, he signaled it to the brothers through an exceedingly swift messenger, saying:

“Children, be careful, for at this hour the devil, the tempter, is coming toward you.”

The messenger who brought the announcement had not yet managed to deliver it when, behold, the evil spirit overthrew the wall being built and crushed beneath its collapse a young monk, the son of a certain *curialis* [Colbensis: *kyriakos*, “of a lord”].

When the holy man’s disciples saw this, they became deeply grieved—not so much because of the destruction of the wall as because of the brother’s danger—and came with tears to the venerable Father Benedict, reporting what had happened.

The most compassionate Father ordered the young man to be brought to him. They could not lift him with their hands, because the stones that had fallen from the wall had crushed not only his body but also his bones.

Unable to lift him with their hands, as has been said, they were compelled to lay him on a mat and bring him in this way to Benedict, the miracle-working man. Immediately he ordered him to be placed on his own *psiathion*, on which he was accustomed to pray. He sent the brothers outside, shut the door of the cell, and gave himself to prayer. Bending his knee, he begged God for the healing of the crushed brother.

At that moment it was possible to see a truly terrifying and astonishing miracle. When the prayer had been completed, the young man immediately rose up by himself, healthy in every part of his body.

The saint then sent him back to the brothers so that he might work with them in rebuilding the wall that had collapsed.

The enemy had expected, through the danger he had devised, to bring death upon the brother by his deceptive activity. Instead, he was put to shame through him, and brought upon himself the mockery that he had prepared for the blessed man. He became an object of reproach and contempt among the saint’s disciples [the manuscripts read “among the saint’s students”].

From that time onward the man of God received from God the gift of prophecy: to foretell future events and announce them as though they were already present.

## CHAPTER XI  
### Concerning the young monk crushed by the collapse of a wall and healed by his prayer

[Col. 0156A]

Again, while the brothers were building a wall somewhat higher, as circumstances required, the man of God remained inside the enclosure of his cell, devoted to prayer.

The ancient enemy appeared to him, mocking him, and announced that he was going toward the brothers who were laboring. The man of God immediately reported this to the brothers through a messenger, saying:

“Brothers, conduct yourselves carefully, because at this hour an evil spirit is coming toward you.”

The messenger had scarcely finished speaking when the evil spirit overturned the wall that was being built and crushed beneath its collapse a young monk, the son of a certain *curialis*.

Everyone was distressed and deeply afflicted. They hurried to report the matter with great mourning to the venerable Father Benedict—not because of the loss of the wall, but because the brother had been crushed.

The Father Benedict ordered the mangled boy to be brought to him. They could carry him only on a sheet [some Norman manuscripts read “in a sack,” as do many printed editions], because the fallen stones of the wall had crushed not only his limbs but also his bones.

The man of God immediately ordered him to be laid in his cell upon the *psiathion* [a *psiathion*, frequently mentioned by Jerome, Cassian, and others, is a mat or covering made from reeds. For monks it served as a bed, blanket, or seat, and they also spread one beneath themselves when praying; Jerome describes the monks of Tabennesis as possessing nothing in their cells apart from a *psiathion*], commonly called a mat [Mabillon thinks these words may be a lemma or marginal explanation inserted into the text. They do not occur in the Greek translation and are absent from many manuscripts. They are, however, found in very ancient manuscripts, including Gemetensis and others of the Norman group, the first Carnotensis, apparently written in the ninth century, the first Theodulfian, and the Compendian. In these manuscripts *matha* and *natta* sometimes occur instead of *matta*. In chapter 55 of the Rule of Saint Benedict, a *matta* is listed among the bedding materials].

He sent the brothers outside, shut the cell, and devoted himself to prayer more fervently than usual.

A wondrous thing occurred: at that very hour he sent the boy back unharmed and as strong as before to the same labor, so that he too might complete the wall with the brothers—the wall whose collapse the ancient enemy had believed would enable him to mock Benedict.

[CAPUT XII.]

## CHAPTER XII

[Greek heading: “Concerning the monks who partook of food contrary to the rule.”]

A canonical ordinance had been legislated by the saint in the monastery: whenever brothers were sent out on service, they were not to partake either of food or drink until they had returned to the monastery. Thus the rule was observed by them with strictness.

One day, then, some of the brothers were sent out on service by this venerable man. It happened that the monks who had been sent, after covering a considerable distance along the road, were unable to return to the monastery; evening had already come, and the hour was pressing. They stopped at the house of a most respectable virgin and partook of food in her cell.

They sent one of the brothers to the holy father Benedict to request a blessing, as was customary, so that they might partake of food. That prescient father asked him, saying:

> “Where did you eat?”

He replied:

> “Nowhere, Father.”

The saint said to them:

> “Why do you lie so? Did you not stop in this virgin’s cell and eat? Did you not taste these and those dishes? Did you not drink so many cups?”

[Note: [Col. 0157D] Colb. reads “lady” instead of “virgin.”]

[Note: [Col. 0157D] The Reg. manuscript reads: “saying, ‘Did you not partake of food?’” He replied, “Nowhere, Father.” To him the saint said: “Why do you lie so? Was it not in this virgin’s cell?” etc. The Colb. manuscript reads: “Why lie in this way?”]

The next day, when the monks had returned from the service assigned to them, they were wisely and accurately exposed by the father. They disclosed the woman’s house, the kinds of food, and the measure of the cups; recognizing their guilt, they fell at his venerable feet, confessing that they had sinned.

[Note: [Col. 0157D] The manuscripts read “brothers” instead of “monks.” But in the Guss. manuscript, after this word, there is corruptly inserted: “from the service assigned.” The best reading is that of the Colb. manuscript.]

[Note: [Col. 0157D] The Reg. manuscript reads “clearly” instead of “wisely.”]

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Perhaps the text should read *διελεγχθέντων* (“after they had been exposed”).]

[Note: [Col. 0158D] The Reg. manuscript reads “and the measure of the cups.” Shortly afterward, “having disclosed” seems to be required. EDIT.]

But the gentlest father immediately forgave them their fault, being assured that, since he had been absent, they would not henceforth transgress the command entrusted to them by the saint—whom they recognized as being present with them in spirit even when absent.

[Note: [Col. 0158D] The remainder of the dialogues is missing in the Colb. manuscript.]

## CHAPTER XII. On the monks who had eaten outside the cell

[Col. 0156C]

Meanwhile the man of God also began to possess the spirit of prophecy: he foretold future events and announced things absent to those who were present.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] Another reading: “to recount.”]

For it was the custom of the cell that whenever the brothers went out to attend to some matter, they were not to take food or drink outside the cell.

[Note: [Col. 0156D] That is, “to attend to some business.” See the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 51, where this is prescribed for brothers who go out for any matter whatsoever. See also note b at the beginning of the *Moralia*, column 1.]

And while this observance of the rule was being carefully maintained, one day some brothers went out on business and were compelled to remain there until a later hour. They knew a devout woman who lived nearby, and, entering her dwelling, they took food.

When they had returned to the cell rather late, they asked for the Father’s blessing, as was customary. He immediately questioned them, saying:

> “Where did you eat?”

They answered:

> “Nowhere.”

He said to them:

> “Why do you lie in this way? Did you not enter the dwelling of such-and-such a woman? Did you not take these and those foods? Did you not drink so many cups?”

When the venerable Father described to them the woman’s lodging, the kinds of food, and the number of drinks, they recognized everything they had done, fell trembling at his feet, and confessed that they had sinned.

But he immediately forgave the fault.

[Note: [Col. 0158D] Thus the manuscripts agree remarkably, or “he forgave the fault.” In the Gilot., Vatic., and Guss. manuscripts, the reading is: “he imposed penance for the fault.” The Greek translation corresponds excellently to the manuscript reading.]

He understood that, in his absence, they would do this no more, since they knew him to be present to them in spirit.

[CAPUT XIII.]

## CHAPTER XIII. On Valentinian the monk’s carnal brother

[Col. 0157B]

There was a certain man who was a layman in appearance but serious in conduct and very devoted to monastic life. He happened to be the brother of Valentinian the monk, whom I mentioned earlier.

[Col. 0157C]

Each year he visited the wonder-working father Benedict in order to enjoy his soul-profiting instruction and to visit Valentinian, his own brother.

This man had imposed upon himself the rule that whenever he left his own house, he would not partake of food in any way until he had been granted the holy man’s blessing; and he faithfully observed it.

One day, as he was traveling to the monastery, a traveling companion suddenly joined him—someone entirely unknown to him—who was carrying a variety of foods. After a very late hour had passed, the companion said to him:

> “Come, brother, let us eat, lest we grow weak on the road.”

He replied:

> “Away with that, brother. I will not do this, because I am accustomed to go to the venerable Father Benedict fasting.”

[Col. 0157D]

After receiving this answer, the companion was silent for a little while. But after they had traveled a short distance, the companion again urged him to partake of food. He would not consent, but continued the journey fasting.

Again they traveled a very considerable distance. As they were far from the monastery, they came to a pleasant place where there was a spring of exceptionally clear water and a flower-filled meadow.

[Note: [Col. 0158D] The Reg. manuscript reads “most transparent.”]

Then the companion, urging him once more, said:

> “Look, water; look, a meadow; look, a suitable place where we can partake of food and rest for a little, so that we may complete our journey without difficulty.”

[Col. 0159A]

Pleased by the pleasantness of the place and enticed by the companion’s third recommendation, he lay down and ate with him. Then he rose and continued along the road leading to the monastery.

When evening came, he reached the cell of the holy father. After he had been announced, he was received by the venerable man Benedict.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads: “by the venerable holy father.”]

He fell to the ground and asked to receive a blessing. But that prescient man reproached him for the offense that had occurred to him on the road, saying:

> “What is this, brother, that the enemy accomplished against you through your traveling companion? At first he could not lead you astray; the second time he was unable to entice you; the third time he conquered you and brought you to what he wanted.”

Then, recognizing the sin of his weak reasoning, he crawled to the saint’s feet and began to mourn and be ashamed of his fault all the more because he recognized that he had sinned in the father’s absence and understood clearly that the misfortune brought upon him by the enemy had been carried out before the father’s eyes.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads: “the misfortune that occurred along the road.”]

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads: “so much more.”]

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads: “when he recognized himself as having sinned.”]

[Col. 0159B]

**Peter.** As I hear of the deeds of this holy man—his foreseeing future events and bringing into the open things done in secret—I see that the spirit of Elisha was present in him, since, while the disciple was absent, he discerned what had happened as though he were present.

## CHAPTER XIII. On the brother of Valentinian the monk, whom the man of God knew to have eaten on the road

[Col. 0158B]

The brother of that monk Valentinian, whom I mentioned above, was a layman but a religious man.

[Col. 0158C]

To receive the servant of God’s prayer and to see his brother, he was accustomed each year to come fasting from his own place to the servant of God’s cell. One day, then, while he was traveling to the monastery, another traveler joined him, carrying food to eat on the road.

When the hour had grown late, the traveler said:

> “Come, brother, let us eat, lest we grow weary on the road.”

He replied:

> “By no means, brother. I will not do this, because I have always been accustomed to reach the venerable Father Benedict fasting.”

After hearing this answer, his fellow traveler was silent for a while. But after they had gone on for a short distance, he again urged him to eat. The man who had resolved to arrive fasting refused to agree. The one who had invited him to eat was silent, and for a little while consented to continue with him while he still fasted.

As they traveled farther and the late hour wearied them, they found a meadow and a spring along the road, together with whatever seemed pleasant for restoring the body. Then the fellow traveler said:

> “Look, water; look, a meadow; look, a pleasant place where we can refresh ourselves and rest for a little, so that afterward we may complete our journey safely.”

Since these words charmed his ears and the places charmed his eyes, he was persuaded by the third urging, consented, and ate. In the evening he reached the cell.

When he was presented to the venerable Father Benedict, he asked to be given a blessing. But the holy man immediately reproached him for what he had done on the road, saying:

> “What is this, brother? The malign enemy, who spoke to you through your traveling companion, could not persuade you the first time, nor the second time, but persuaded you the third time and overcame you, bringing you to what he wanted.”

[Note: [Col. 0159D] Two Gemet. manuscripts read “persuaded.”]

Then, recognizing the guilt of his weak mind, he fell at the father’s feet and began to mourn and blush over his fault all the more because he recognized that, even in Benedict’s absence, he had sinned before the father’s eyes.

[Col. 0160B]

**Peter.** I see that the spirit of Elisha was present in the heart of this holy man—Elisha who, when his disciple was absent, was present to him.

[Note: The reference is to 2 Kings 5.]

[CAPUT XIV.]

## CHAPTER XIV. On King Totila’s deception, which was detected

[Col. 0160B]

**Gregory.** It is necessary, Peter, for you to be silent for the moment, so that you may hear what is greater still.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads: “that you may hear what is fitting.”]

In the time of the Goths, their king Totila, having heard of the holy man’s achievements and that he was full of the prophetic gift, set out for the monastery. He stopped at some distance from the monastery and announced his intended arrival to the blessed man.

The saint sent word from the monastery that he should come to him. But Totila, reasoning within himself that it was impossible for a mortal man to share in prophetic grace, dared to put him to the test.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads “to share.”]

He dressed one of his spatharii, named Riggo, in his own royal clothing and put his shoes on him. He ordered him to go to the man of God in his name, as though he were testing him, and supplied him with several guards.

With them he also sent the counts—namely, Vulteric, Ruderic, and Brindinus—and ordered crowds of nobles and soldiers to walk on his right and left, thinking that through this fabricated and false display he would deceive the servant of God.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads “he permitted” instead of “he ordered.”]

When this man reached the monastery, escorted by a formation of soldiers and officials, it happened that the saint saw him approaching while seated in an elevated place. When he was still at a distance from which the saint’s voice could be heard by him, the saint cried out:

> “Take off, my son, take off what you are wearing, for it is not yours.”

[Col. 0161A]

When Riggo heard this, he fell before him upon the ground, repenting what he had done, because he had dared to mock such a holy and most discerning man. All who were with him prostrated themselves on the ground before the man of God.

When they rose, they did not dare approach the saint at all. Instead, trembling and reproaching themselves for their own folly, they returned to their king.

## CHAPTER XIV. On King Totila’s feigned identity being exposed

[Col. 0160B]

**Gregory.** It is right, Peter, that you should be silent for a while, so that you may learn still greater things. In the time of the Goths, when their king Totila had heard that the holy man possessed the spirit of prophecy, he went toward his monastery, stopped a little way off, and sent word that he was coming.

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The manuscript reads: “that you may hear what is fitting.”]

When an order was immediately sent from the monastery that he should come, Totila, true to his treacherous mind, attempted to test whether the man of God possessed the spirit of prophecy.

There was a certain spatharius of his named Riggo.

[Note: [Col. 0160D] It was the duty of a spatharius to carry the prince’s *spatha*, or sword, and guard his side. MABILL.]

Totila gave him his shoes.

[Note: [Col. 0160D] Shoes formerly varied according to each person’s rank and condition: commoners wore white shoes, senators red, and kings purple, as Haeften observed. MABILL.]

He had him dressed in royal garments and ordered him to go to the man of God as though in his own person. He sent with him three counts who were accustomed to cling to him more closely than the others—Vult, Ruderic, and Blidin—so that, pretending before the servant of God that he himself was King Totila, they might walk at his sides. He also supplied him with other attendants and spatharii.

[Note: [Col. 0160D] In old editions: “so that other attendants might render him service as spatharii.”]

Thus he intended the man to be thought the king both from the attendants accompanying him and from the purple garments.
