When Riggo, splendidly dressed and accompanied by a crowd of attendants, had entered the monastery, the man of God was sitting some distance away. Seeing him approach, and when he was already close enough to be heard, he cried out:

> “Put down, my son, put down what you are carrying; it is not yours.”

Riggo immediately fell to the ground and was terrified that he had presumed to mock such a great man. All who had come with him to the man of God were thrown down upon the ground.

[Col. 0162A]

When they arose, they did not dare approach him but returned to their king, trembling and reporting how swiftly they had been exposed.

[CAPUT XV.]

## CHAPTER XV. On the prophecy delivered to that same king Totila

[Col. 0161A]

Then Totila himself came to the man of God.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript reads “came.”]

When he saw him seated at a distance, he did not dare approach him; instead, he threw himself upon the ground and begged to receive forgiveness from the saint.

The servant of God addressed him twice and three times, telling him to rise. But when he saw him held fast by fear and not rising,

[Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript reads: “held fast, not rising … servant of Christ.”]

Benedict, servant of the Lord Jesus Christ, deigned to raise the said King Totila himself and reproved him for his deeds.

In a few words he foretold everything that was to happen to him.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript reads “to happen.”]

He said:

> “You have done and are doing many evil things. From now on, withdraw from iniquity and repent, even if late. For you are destined to enter Rome and to cross the sea; you will reign for nine years, but in the tenth year you will die.”

[Col. 0161B]

Hearing this, the king of the Goths was utterly terrified and astonished at the blessed man’s unexpected prophecy. He threw himself upon the ground, asked for a blessing, and departed from the monastery.

From that time onward he was changed from his former harshness and inhumanity through the holy man’s instruction and beneficial admonition. Not long afterward he entered Rome and came to Sicily. In the tenth year of his reign, divine judgment did not permit him to continue living; according to the saint’s prophecy, he lost both his kingdom and his life.

Afterward the bishop of the Church of Canusium came, as was customary, to the great Benedict;

[Note: [Col. 0161D] *Kathesthentōn* is the uncommon aorist participle of *kathesthēn*, from *kathizomai* (“to sit”). EDIT.]

the venerable Benedict loved him greatly because of the holiness of his conduct.

When they had sat down and conversation had begun concerning King Totila’s entry into the city and the destruction of the city of the Romans, the bishop said to the blessed man:

> “Because of this king, the city of Rome will be destroyed, so that it will never again be inhabited by human beings.”

The man of God replied:

> “The city of the Romans will not be destroyed by nations; rather, shaken by disasters, flashes of lightning, and earthquakes, it will be dissolved within itself.”

[Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript reads: “but by disasters and upheavals … against itself.”]

And behold, the mysteries of the venerable man’s prophecy now lie before everyone’s eyes, brighter than the sun. In that greatest city we no longer see its splendid adornment; instead, we observe houses buried, churches deserted because of the earthquakes that have followed, and its buildings grown old. For the variety of its structures has been defiled by disasters and continual earthquakes.

Honoratus, the holy man’s disciple, explained to me the meaning of this God-given prophecy. That same most devout Honoratus said that he had not heard these things from the saint himself; rather, he testified to them after receiving confirmation from truthful brothers.

## CHAPTER XV. On the prophecy made to the same King Totila and to the bishop of Canusium

[Col. 0162A]

Then Totila himself approached the man of God. When he saw him seated far away, he did not dare draw near but threw himself upon the ground.

Although the man of God twice or three times said to him, “Rise,” he did not dare rise from the ground before him. The servant of Christ Jesus, Benedict, deigned to approach the prostrate king himself, raised him from the ground, and reproved him for his deeds.

In a few words he foretold all that would happen to him.

[Note: [Col. 0161D] The manuscript reads “to happen.”]

He said:

> “You do many evil things; you have done many evil things. At last, cease from iniquity. You are destined to enter Rome, to cross the sea; you will reign for nine years, but in the tenth you will die.”

[Note: [Col. 0161D] Most printed editions read “rest.”]

[Note: [Col. 0161D] From this it appears that Totila’s encounter with Saint Benedict took place in the eighth year of the Gothic war, nearly completed—corresponding to the year 542—when Totila had already reigned a full year. For he held the principate of Italy for eleven years. Procopius supports this calculation in book 3 of *The Gothic War*: “After crossing the Tiber River, Totila turned toward Campania and Samnium.” Cassinum, which is near Campania, lies in Samnium.]

When the king heard these things, he was greatly terrified. Having asked for a prayer, he departed, and from that time he became less cruel.

Not long afterward he went to Rome and proceeded to Sicily.

[Note: [Col. 0162D] During this expedition, there is considerable reason to conjecture that Saint Placidus, a disciple of Saint Benedict, suffered martyrdom and that his monastery was destroyed by flames. I discussed this in book 2 of the *Life of Cassiodorus*, chapter 7, pp. 266 and following of the earlier edition, where I also treated what concerns Totila.]

In the tenth year of his reign, however, by the judgment of almighty God, he lost his kingdom together with his life.

Moreover, the bishop of the Church of Canusium used to visit the same servant of God, whom the man of God greatly loved because of the merit of his life. While conversing with him about King Totila’s entry and the destruction of the city of Rome, he said:

> “Through this king that city will be destroyed, so that it will no longer be inhabited.”

The man of the Lord replied:

> “Rome will not be exterminated by nations; rather, wearied by violent storms, whirlwinds, and earthquakes, it will decay within itself.”

The mysteries of this prophecy have now become clearer to us than daylight: in that city we see shattered walls, overturned houses, and churches destroyed by storms; we see its buildings worn out by long age, since they have been thrown down by continually recurring collapses.

Honoratus, his disciple, from whose report I learned this, says that he did not hear this from the saint’s own mouth. He testifies, however, that the saint said it because brothers had reported it to him.

[Note: [Col. 0162D] Canusium, commonly called Canosa, was a city of Apulia Peucetia on the Aufidus River, three miles from the ruins of Cannae. This bishop of Canusium is called Sabinus or Savinus in the Acts of Saint Placidus.]

[CAPUT XVI.]

## CHAPTER XVI. On the cleric possessed by a demon and healed through his prayer

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Perhaps read *daimoniōntos* (“demon-possessed”).]

[Col. 0163A]

At that same time, a certain cleric of the Church of Aquinum happened to be afflicted by an unclean demon. His most holy bishop, Constantius, repeatedly sent him to various cemeteries of the saints so that he might obtain healing. But the saints of God, the martyrs, were unwilling to grant him the gift of healing, wishing to demonstrate to all the divine grace of healings that abounded in the blessed Benedict.

The afflicted man was therefore brought to Benedict, the servant of God. After offering prayers to the Lord Jesus Christ, he drove the unclean spirit from him and restored him to health by the grace of God, saying to him:

> “Depart. Behold, you have become healthy—healthy indeed. Do not eat meat, and do not enter the priestly order. On whatever day you dare to accept priestly rank, you will immediately be delivered mercilessly into the power of the unclean demon.”

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads: “for on whatever day … you dare.”]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Aquinum, an episcopal city five miles this side of Cassinum, was the birthplace of Saint Thomas, the most celebrated doctor of the Church.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Saint Constantius is commemorated on September 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] That is, the burial places and memorials of the martyrs, or sacred buildings dedicated to preserving their relics or commemorating them.]

[Col. 0163B]

The man who had been healed returned to his own place and, as recently received punishment commonly frightens the mind, kept for a time the command given him by the holy man.

But after many years had passed, when all those who had been senior to him had departed this life and he saw his juniors promoted above him in the sacred orders, he set aside the words of the man of God, as though he had forgotten them over the long passage of time, and entered the priestly order. Immediately the demon who had left him seized him again and did not cease tormenting him until it tore his soul from him.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Nearly all printed editions read: “to presume to enter the sacred order,” contrary to all the manuscripts. The second Carn. manuscript reads: “to presume rashly to enter the sacred order.” Both the minor and major orders may be understood here. In the *Book of the Sacraments* we read: “Here begins the rite for blessing the sacred orders,” followed by the heading: “The higher grades are conferred before the Gospel, the lower after Communion,” and then: “The ordination of a doorkeeper,” followed by the other minor orders. These are followed by the ordinations of deacon, priest, and bishop.]

[Col. 0164C]

**Peter.** This man of God, as I see, also penetrated divine secrets, because he perceived that this cleric had been handed over to the devil for the purpose of preventing him from daring to enter the sacred order.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads: “that he might not defect again.”]

**Gregory.** How could one who kept the commands of Christ not know the secrets of divinity, when it is written:

> “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit.”

[Note: [Col. 0164D] The Vulgate manuscripts add “with him.” We do not count Mabillon’s edition among them, since it reproduces the manuscript codices with great fidelity. “With him” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek version.]

**Peter.** If the one who clings to God becomes one spirit with the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads: “why does he become one?”]

what does the same excellent preacher mean when he again says:

> “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”

It seems very inconsistent to me that one who has become one with the Lord should be ignorant of his mind.

[Note: [Col. 0164D] Printed editions read: “with whom one has become one.” The manuscripts vary here. Prat. reads: “with whom one has been.” Two Gemet. manuscripts agree. But the first Theod., Lyr., and Becc. manuscripts read: “with whom one has become one.”]

**Gregory.** Holy men, insofar as they are one with God, are not ignorant of the Lord’s mind.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads: “the Lord himself says through the Apostle.”]

For the same apostle also says:

> “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

[Col. 0166A]

To show that he knew the things of God, he added:

> “But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is from God.”

From this he says again:

> “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him—God has revealed to us through his Spirit.”

**Peter.** If, then, the things of God had been revealed to the same apostle through the Spirit of God, how could he have prefaced what I have proposed by saying:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!”

[Col. 0165B]

But as I say this, another question arises for me. For the prophet David addresses God, saying:

> “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

If knowing the judgments of God is less than also declaring them, how can blessed Paul declare God’s judgments unsearchable, while David testifies that he not only knew all these judgments but also declared them with his lips?

**Gregory.** I answered both your questions briefly above, saying that holy men, insofar as they are one with the Lord, are not ignorant of the Lord’s mind.

For all who follow the Lord with undistracted prayer are, clearly, in their prayer with the Lord.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads “it is clear.”]

But those who are weighed down by the passions through the burden of this earthly and transient body cannot be with the Lord.

Thus they know the hidden judgments of God insofar as they are united with him; insofar as they are separated from him, they do not know them. Because they do not yet perfectly penetrate his secrets, they testify that his judgments are unsearchable. But because they cling to him in mind, and by clinging to him recognize and understand as much as they receive either through the words of sacred Scripture or through hidden revelations, they know and proclaim these things.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads “revelations” and “they know these things and understand them.”]

[Col. 0165C]

They do not know, therefore, the judgments that God keeps silent about; they know those that God speaks. Hence the prophet David, after saying:

> “With my lips I have declared all the judgments,”

immediately added:

> “of your mouth,”

as though he were openly saying to God:

> “I was able both to know and to declare those judgments that I recognized you had spoken to me. For those things that you yourself do not speak, you undoubtedly keep hidden from our knowledge.”

Thus the prophetic and apostolic testimony agree: God’s judgments are unsearchable, and yet those that proceed from his mouth are uttered by human lips. Human beings can speak and know what God reveals; but those things that he has placed in obscurity by his inscrutable judgments remain hidden and unknowable to us.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The Gilot., Vatic., and old editions read: “what has been disclosed can be brought forth, and what is hidden cannot be hidden.”]

[Col. 0167A]

**Peter.** In the addition to my question, you have made clear the difficult meaning of the testimonies cited above—those of the prophet David and of the Apostle. But I beg you: if anything further remains concerning the blameless conduct of that holy man, tell us fully.

## CHAPTER XVI. On the cleric temporarily freed from a demon

[Col. 0164A]

At that same time, a certain cleric of the Church of Aquinum was being tormented by a demon. He had been sent by Constantius, the venerable bishop of that Church, to many places containing martyrs, so that he might be healed.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Aquinum was an episcopal city five miles beyond Cassinum, and the birthplace of Saint Thomas, the most celebrated doctor of the Church.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Saint Constantius is commemorated on September 1.]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] “Places containing martyrs” means their tombs and monuments, or sacred buildings preserving their relics or dedicated to their memory.]

But the holy martyrs of God were unwilling to give him the gift of health, so that they might demonstrate how great was the grace in Benedict.

He was therefore brought to Benedict, the servant of almighty God. Benedict poured out prayers to the Lord Jesus Christ and immediately expelled the ancient enemy from the possessed man.

To the man, once healed, he gave this command:

> “Go, and from now on do not eat meat. Do not presume ever to enter the sacred order. On whatever day you presume to violate the sacred order, you will immediately be delivered again into the devil’s jurisdiction.”

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads: “for on whatever day … you dare.”]

[Col. 0164B]

[Note: [Col. 0163D] Almost all printed editions read: “presume to enter the sacred order,” although all the manuscripts resist this reading. The second Carn. manuscript reads: “presume rashly to enter the sacred order.” Both the minor and major orders can be understood here. In the *Book of the Sacraments* we read: “Here begins the rite for blessing the sacred orders,” followed by the heading: “The higher grades are conferred before the Gospel, the lower after Communion,” and then: “The ordination of a doorkeeper,” followed by the other minor orders. These are followed by the ordinations of deacon, priest, and bishop.]

The cleric departed healthy. Since fresh punishment commonly terrifies the mind, he observed for a time what the man of God had commanded.

But after many years, when he saw all those who had previously been senior to him depart this life and his juniors advance in priestly rank, he forgot, as has been said, the admonitions given him by the holy man and entered the priestly order. Immediately the demon returned to him, as though a savage beast had taken up residence within him, and tore him mercilessly until death.

[Col. 0164C]

**Peter.** This man of God, as I see, penetrated even the secrets of divinity, because he understood that this cleric had been handed over to the devil for the very reason that he should not again dare to be entrusted with priestly office.

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads: “that he might not defect again.”]

**Gregory.** How could one who kept Christ’s commands be ignorant of the secrets of divinity, when it is written:

> “Whoever clings to the Lord is one spirit with him.”

[Note: [Col. 0164D] The Vulgate adds “with him.” Mabillon’s edition is not included among those editions, since it reproduces the manuscript codices with great fidelity. “With him” is absent from the manuscripts and from the Greek version.]

**Peter.** If the one who clings to God becomes one spirit with the Lord,

[Note: [Col. 0163D] The manuscript reads: “why does he become one?”]

what does the same excellent preacher mean when he says:

> “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?”

It seems very incongruous that one who has become one with the Lord should be ignorant of his mind.

**Gregory.** Holy men, insofar as they are one with God, are not ignorant of the Lord’s mind. For the same apostle says:

> “For who among human beings knows the things of a human being except the spirit of the human being that is in him? So also no one has known the things of God except the Spirit of God.”

To show that he knew the things of God, he added:

> “But we have not received the spirit of this world, but the Spirit that is from God.”

From this he says again:

> “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart—what God has prepared for those who love him—he has revealed to us through his Spirit.”

**Peter.** If, then, the things of God had been revealed to the same Apostle through the Spirit of God, how could he have said before what I proposed:

> “O the depth of the riches and wisdom and knowledge of God! How unsearchable are his judgments, and how inscrutable his ways!”

[Col. 0166B]

But as I say this, another question arises. The prophet David addresses God, saying:

> “With my lips I have declared all the judgments of your mouth.”

Since knowing God’s judgments is less than also declaring them, how is it that Paul asserts that God’s judgments are unsearchable, while David testifies that he not only knew all these judgments but also declared them with his lips?

**Gregory.** I gave you a brief answer to both questions above: holy men, insofar as they are one with the Lord, are not ignorant of the Lord’s mind.

All who devoutly follow the Lord are also, through their devotion, with God; but those who are still weighed down by the burden of corruptible flesh are not with God.

Thus they know the hidden judgments of God insofar as they are joined to him; insofar as they are separated from him, they do not know them. Since they do not yet perfectly penetrate his secrets, they testify that his judgments are unsearchable. But because they cling to him in mind, and through that attachment recognize as much as they receive either through the sacred utterances of Scripture or through hidden revelations, they know and proclaim these things.

[Note: [Col. 0165D] The manuscript reads “revelations” and “they know these things and understand them.”]

They therefore do not know the judgments that God keeps silent about; they know those that God speaks. Hence the prophet David, after saying:

> “With my lips I have declared all the judgments,”

immediately added:

> “of your mouth,”

as though he were saying plainly:

> “I was able both to know and to declare those judgments that I recognized you had spoken. For those things that you yourself do not speak, you keep hidden from our knowledge.”

Thus the prophetic and apostolic judgment agree: God’s judgments are unsearchable, and yet those that proceed from his mouth are uttered by human lips. What God reveals can be known and spoken by human beings; what he does not reveal cannot be known or spoken.

[Note: [Col. 0166D] The Gilot., Vatic., and old editions read: “what has been disclosed can be brought forth, and what is hidden cannot be hidden.”]

[Col. 0168A]

**Peter.** In the objection contained in my little question, the ground of the reasoning became clear.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The first Aud., Bigot., and Lyr. manuscripts read: “the ground of your reasoning.”]

But I beg you, if there are still further things concerning this man’s virtues, add them.

[CAPUT XVII.]

## CHAPTER XVII. On the prophecy concerning the destruction of his monastery

[Col. 0167A]

**Gregory.** There was a certain man of great nobility, a namesake of the blessed Benedict.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads “of Benedict.” The Greek translator does not at all reproduce the name Theoprobus and omits much that is plainly contained in the Latin. He was often not reluctant to depart from this text. He also added much of his own in place of what he omitted.]

Having been educated by Benedict’s divine wisdom, he abandoned the pleasures of worldly life and returned to God. Because of the great virtue of the holy man’s way of life, he acquired a secure confidence in spiritual frankness toward him.

[Col. 0167B]

When he came, as usual, to the man of God and entered his cell, he found the inspired father weeping and lamenting bitterly. He remained standing for a long time. Seeing the continual flow of his unrestrained tears, he became perplexed, for he had not seen him weep in silence at the hour of prayer, as was his custom, but saw him uttering cries and mournful sighs.

Frightened and trembling, he sought to learn from the saint the cause of such great lamentation. The divinely wise father replied:

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads “the God-bearing father.”]

> “This entire monastery, which I built through God, and everything I prepared for the brothers, have been handed over to the nations by the judgment of almighty God. Only with difficulty have I appeased God through prayer so that the souls of my brothers in the Lord who live in the monastery might be granted to me.”

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads: “the souls of my brothers in Christ who are in the monastery.”]

That Benedict, who had come to the saint and received from him this pledge concerning future events, departed from the monastery in wonder.

But we now see that his monastery has been destroyed by the people of the Lombards. While the brothers were resting at midnight, the Lombards suddenly burst into the monastery and plundered everything there. Yet they were not permitted to gain control over any of the brothers at all.

[Col. 0167C]

The prayer of the man of God guarded them, so that the grace of divine power dwelling in him might be shown to all. For God, faithful to his promises, fulfilled what he had promised his genuine servant Benedict: although, by God’s permission, they plundered the monastery’s possessions, the Lord nevertheless granted him the preservation of the souls.

Thus we recognize that the blessed Apostle Paul also entreated God for the multitude of his fellow travelers amid the stormy danger of the voyage and did not fail in his prayer. For although the loss of much of the cargo aboard the ship occurred, Christ granted him the profitable salvation of the souls.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] The manuscript reads “the nation of the Lombards.” I would not have noted this variant were it not for another error that entered the Guss. edition, namely *ἔθους* (“of custom”) instead of *ἔθνους* (“of the nation”).]

## CHAPTER XVII. On the destruction of the monastery of the man of God, foretold by him

[Col. 0168A]

**Gregory.** A certain noble man named Theoprobus had been converted through the admonition of that same Father Benedict. Because of the merit of his life, he possessed great confidence of intimacy with him.

One day, when he had entered Benedict’s cell, he found him weeping most bitterly. He remained there for a long time and saw that his tears did not cease. Yet the man of God was not weeping as he was accustomed to do while praying, but in grief. Theoprobus therefore asked what was the cause of such great sorrow.

The man of God immediately replied:

> “This entire monastery that I built, and everything that I prepared for the brothers, have been handed over to the nations by the judgment of almighty God. With difficulty I was able to obtain that the souls of those from this place be granted to me.”

Theoprobus heard these words at that time; we, however, see their fulfillment, for we know that his monastery has now been destroyed by the Lombard people.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] Prat. and the first Gemet. manuscript read “by the Lombard army.”]

At night, while the brothers were resting, the Lombards recently entered there.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] Most editions read “the Lombards entered there.” The Germ. and other manuscripts read “the Lombards entered there.”]

They plundered everything, but could not keep even one person there. Thus almighty God fulfilled what he had promised his faithful servant Benedict: if he handed over the possessions to the nations, he would guard the souls.

[Note: [Col. 0167D] These words seem to conflict with the prologue to this book, where Gregory says that Valentinian presided for many years over the Lateran monastery, which was built after the Cassinian monastery had been destroyed. It is therefore clear that the Cassinian monastery had been overthrown many years earlier, and hence not “recently.” But, as Mabillon observes here, “recently” is sometimes used of a more distant time, as Carolus Stephanus proves in his dictionary. Indeed, says Mabillon, Gregory himself frequently uses the word in this sense. See book 3, chapter 8, where he says: “The venerable man Constantius was bishop of the city of Aquinum, who recently, in the time of my predecessor Pope John of blessed memory, died.” This John was Pope John III, who died in 573. Thus Constantius had already been dead for about twenty years, yet Gregory calls it “recently.” On the date of the destruction of the Cassinian monastery, consult Mabillon’s note on this passage.]

In this matter I see Benedict occupying the role of Paul, for although Paul’s ship suffered the loss of all its goods, he himself received the lives of all who accompanied him as a consolation.

[CAPUT XVIII.]

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the flask hidden on the road and exposed by the saint’s foreknowledge

[Col. 0169A]

At another time, our Exhilaratus—whom you yourself know after his conversion—was sent by his master to the man of God, carrying two wooden vessels full of wine, which in the common language are called flasks.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscript says that they are called *flaski*. “Which person…”]

He brought one of them to the saint but hid the other along the road. That discerning man, from whom none of the other man’s actions was hidden,

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The negation is absent from the manuscript.]

received the one flask with thanksgiving. Then, dismissing him, he instructed him:

> “See, my son, do not drink any longer from that flask which you hid along the road. Instead, empty it carefully, and you will find what it contains.”

[Col. 0169B]

The man, greatly ashamed, made a prostration before the holy man and returned. When he reached the place where he had hidden the flask, wishing to test whether what the saint had said to him was true, he tilted the vessel to empty it. And behold, a serpent immediately came out together with the wine that was emptied.

When the aforementioned Exhilaratus saw the fault he had committed, he became fearful, was struck with remorse, and repented.

## CHAPTER XVIII. On the hidden flask, known by the man of God through the spirit

[Col. 0170A]

At another time, our Exhilaratus, whom you know to have been converted, had been sent by his master to bring the man of God in the monastery two wooden vessels full of wine, commonly called flasks.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] Two Theod. manuscripts and Val-cl. read: “which are called flasks by the common people.”]

He brought one and, as he proceeded along the road, hid the other. But the man of the Lord, from whom things done in his absence could not be concealed, accepted one with thanksgiving and, as the boy was leaving, admonished him:

> “See, my son, do not drink from that flask which you hid. Instead, tilt it carefully, and you will find what it contains.”

The man left the presence of the man of God in great confusion. Returning, he wished to test further what he had heard.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The first Theod. and second Carnot. manuscripts read: “wishing to test what he had heard.” The first Carn. reads: “wishing to test this.”]

When he tilted the flask, a serpent immediately came out of it.

[Col. 0170B]

Then the aforementioned boy Exhilaratus, by what he found in the wine, was terrified at the evil he had committed.

[CAPUT XIX.]

## CHAPTER XIX. On the handkerchiefs received from a nunnery and exposed by the saint

[Col. 0169B]

There was a market town not far from the monastery of the saint, in which there was a large number of men devoted to idols.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscript reads “idolaters.”]

Illuminated by the blessed man’s soul-profiting instruction, they returned to the saving faith of God.

In that same market town there was an ascetic community of devout and respectable virgins. Because of their surpassing holiness, he was accustomed to send his own disciples to them for their edification and instruction.

[Col. 0169C]

One day, as usual, the man of God sent a certain monk to the virgins’ ascetic community for their spiritual benefit. After the extensive admonition given by the venerable father, the monk who had been sent was prevailed upon by the virgins to accept handkerchiefs, which he hid in the fold of his garment.

When he came to the father, the saint exposed him concerning this and said to him sternly:

> “Brother, how did iniquity enter your bosom?”

The monk was terrified and, through his carelessness, had forgotten his own offense—the very matter concerning which his own father was exposing him. He did not understand what the father was saying to him.

[Note: [Col. 0169D] The manuscript reads “his own fault.”]

The saint said to him:

> “Surely I was not present there when you received the handkerchiefs from the holy virgins and hid them in your bosom?”

When he heard this, he crawled to the saint’s feet and declared that he had sinned. He took the handkerchiefs that he had received from the virgins out of his bosom, threw them down before the saint, and sincerely repented this offense.

## CHAPTER XIX. On the receipt of the handkerchiefs, known by the same man

[Col. 0170B]

Not far from the monastery there was a village in which a considerable number of people had been converted from the worship of idols to faith in God through Benedict’s exhortation.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] The first Theod. manuscript reads “not a great number.”]

There were also some holy women there, and Benedict, the servant of God, frequently arranged to send his brothers there to exhort their souls.

[Col. 0170C]

One day he sent a monk, as usual. But after the admonition had been given, the monk who had been sent, at the request of the holy women, accepted handkerchiefs and hid them in his bosom.

[Note: [Col. 0170D] These are not the handkerchiefs customarily used in the sacred ministry, which will be mentioned below in the letters. Rather, they are cloths and linens suitable for wiping the buttocks, cleaning mucus, and wiping away sweat.]

As soon as he returned, the man of God began to rebuke him with the greatest severity, saying:

> “How did iniquity enter your bosom?”

The monk was stunned and, having forgotten what he had done, did not know what he was being rebuked for. The saint said to him:

> “Surely I was not present there when you received the handkerchiefs from the handmaids of God and put them in your bosom?”

He immediately fell at the saint’s feet, repented of his foolish action, and threw away the handkerchiefs he had hidden in his bosom.

[CAPUT XX.]

## CHAPTER XX. On the monk who despised the saint in his thoughts

[Col. 0169D]

One day, at the hour when the saint was accustomed to partake of food, when evening had already grown deep, it happened that a certain monk, who was the son of a defensor, was holding a lamp before the saint’s table.

As the saint was eating, the demon of pride began to trouble the monk and cast thoughts of exaltation upon him.

[Note: The printed *epaphiein* stands for *epaphienai*.]

In his arrogance he said within himself:

> “Who is this whom I attend and serve while he eats, holding a lamp in my hands? Why do I serve him like a slave?”

While he was entertaining these thoughts in his mind, Father Benedict, adorned with the gift of foreknowledge,

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The manuscript reads “with the gift of prescience.”]

exposed him with paternal compassion and said:

> “Seal your heart, brother. Why are thoughts of arrogance arising within you? Pay attention to yourself.”

He then called the brothers and immediately ordered the lamp to be taken from the monk’s hands.

The monk went outside and sat there with tears.

[Col. 0171B]

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The manuscript has the single word *sýndakrys*, “with tears.”]

When the brothers asked him what he had done and what anger the saint had shown toward him, he laid bare to them the devilish delusion that had arisen in his thoughts: how he had been puffed up by the spirit of pride and what words against the man of God he had been turning over in his heart, thereby reaching the height of arrogance.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The manuscript reads: “and what words against the man.”]

Thus the poison hidden in his heart became evident to all, and they marveled at the holy father’s prescient purity, since the things planted in the monk’s mind by the common enemy could not escape him.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] The manuscript reads: “the poison hidden in his heart became manifest.”]

## CHAPTER XX. On the monk’s proud thought, known by the man of God

[Col. 0170D]

One day, while the venerable Father was receiving bodily nourishment in the late evening, a certain monk, who was the son of a defensor, was holding a lamp before him at table.

[Col. 0172A]

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Defensores formerly existed in two kinds, political and ecclesiastical. The latter attended to the affairs of churches, the poor, and widows; the former managed the causes and business of cities, places, and provinces. See Haeften on this passage and Angelus Nuce on chapter 37 of book 4 of the *Cassinian Chronicle*. We have already discussed defensores and will say more below; the relevant passages can be found through the indexes.]

While the man of God was eating and the monk was attending him with the lamp, the monk began silently to turn thoughts over in his mind through the spirit of pride and to say in his thoughts:

> “Who is this whom I attend while he eats, holding a lamp and rendering service? Who am I that I should serve this man?”

The man of God immediately turned to him and began to rebuke him severely, saying:

> “Seal your heart, brother. What is this that you are saying? Seal your heart.”

He immediately called the brothers and ordered the lamp to be taken from the monk’s hands. He commanded the monk to withdraw from the service and sit quietly at that very hour.

When the brothers questioned him about what he had harbored in his heart, he recounted in order how greatly he had been inflated by the spirit of pride and what words he had silently spoken in thought against the man of God.

[Col. 0172B]

Then it became evident to everyone that nothing could be hidden from venerable Benedict, since even the words of silent thought had sounded in his ears.

[Note: [Col. 0172D] The Carnot. manuscripts read: “in whose ear even the words of thought had sounded.”]

[CAPUT XXI.]

## CHAPTER XXI. On flour found before the saint’s cell in a time of famine

[Col. 0171B]

At another time, famine occurred in the regions of Campania, and there was a shortage of all the foods necessary for life. There was also a scarcity of grain in the saint’s monastery and a shortage of bread, so that at the time of the brothers’ meal no more than five loaves could be found.

[Col. 0171C]

Seeing them downcast, the venerable father corrected their faintheartedness with his gentlest admonition and dispelled it with a true promise, saying:

> “Why are you so sorrowful because of the shortage of bread? Today you have a shortage, but tomorrow you will have an abundance of necessities in plenty.”

On the following day, by God’s providence, they found two hundred *modii* of flour in sacks before the monastery gate.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Perhaps the reading should be *σακίοις*, “in sacks.” Cangius observes from Symeon the Logothete that *σακίον* means a small sack.]

Certain persons, moved by God, the supreme governor of all things, had brought and deposited the sacks before the monastery gate; they were wholly unknown to the brothers.

Rejoicing in the saint’s wondrous miracle, they gave glory to God. From then on they learned not to be distressed in famine, should such a circumstance ever occur, since they possessed as a pledge the saint’s boldness before God.

[Note: [Col. 0171D] Perhaps the reading should be *ἐνέχυρον*, “pledge.”]

[Col. 0173A] **Peter.** Tell me, I beg you: was the spirit of prophecy continually present in the man of God, or did the spirit of prophecy work within him at different times?

**Gregory.** Peter, the spirit of prophecy does not always illumine the minds of the prophets. For just as it is written concerning the Holy Spirit, “It blows where it wills” [Note: The manuscript reads “where he wills.”], so it is clear that it also blows when it wills. This is what happened when the prophet Nathan, asked by King David whether it was pleasing to God that he should build the Lord’s temple, first gave his approval and afterward forbade it. This is also what happened when the prophet Elisha saw the woman weeping but did not know the reason; to the servant who tried to restrain her he said: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not revealed it to me” (2 Kings 4:27).

This is arranged by the all-governing God out of His great compassion: sometimes granting the spirit of prophecy and sometimes wisely withdrawing it, He both raises the minds of those who prophesy to exaltation and keeps them again in humility, so that when they receive the spirit they may recognize the inspiration from God within them, and when it is likewise withdrawn they may learn, by God’s providential ordering, what they are of themselves.

**Peter.** I confess that this is so, and I am greatly convinced. But I beg you to complete what remains of the account of the achievements of the venerable Father Benedict, and to recount to me anything that comes to your holy mind.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning the two hundred measures of flour found before the man of God’s cell during a time of famine

[Col. 0172B]

At another time famine had settled upon the same region of Campania [Note: That is, in the year 538, according to Procopius, *The Gothic War*, book II, where he reports that famine spread throughout all Italy.], and great scarcity of every kind of food pressed hard upon everyone. By then wheat was lacking in Benedict’s monastery, and nearly all the bread had been consumed [Col. 0172C], so that at the hour of the brothers’ meal no more than five loaves could be found. When the venerable Father saw them grieving, he sought to correct their faintheartedness with a gentle rebuke and again to encourage them with a promise [Note: Bigot, the first Aud., and Prat add “a kindly promise.”], saying: “Why is your spirit grieved because of the shortage of bread? Today there is indeed little, but tomorrow you will have an abundance.”

On the following day two hundred measures of flour [Note: Here one may recall what Gregory of Tours narrates as having happened to Saint Paulinus (*On the Glory of the Confessors*, ch. 107): several ships loaded with wine and wheat arrived unexpectedly, as though brought by divine agency, to repay Paulinus for his generous almsgiving and to confirm the faith of his wife Terasia. See the cited passage.] were found in sacks before the door of the cell [Note: Compend. reads “before the door of the church-cell.”]. Who had sent them, and by whom the almighty God had conveyed them, remains unknown to this day. When the brothers saw this, they gave thanks to the Lord and learned henceforth not to doubt abundance even in poverty.

[Col. 0174A] **Peter.** Tell me, I beg you: should we not believe that the spirit of prophecy was always able to be present with this servant of God? Or did the spirit of prophecy fill his mind only at intervals?

**Gregory.** The spirit of prophecy does not always illumine the minds of the prophets, Peter. For, as it is written concerning the Holy Spirit, “It blows where it wills” [Note: Gemet. and most manuscripts read “it breathes upon.”], so it must be understood that it breathes when it wills. This is why Nathan, when the king asked him whether he might build the temple (2 Samuel 7:3), first consented [Note: Val-cl. reads “agreed”] and afterward forbade it. This is why Elisha, seeing a woman weeping but not knowing the reason, said to the man who tried to restrain her: “Let her alone, for her soul is in bitterness, and the Lord has hidden it from me and has not revealed it to me” (2 Kings 4:27).

This the almighty God arranges through a dispensation of great mercy: by sometimes granting and sometimes withdrawing the spirit of prophecy, He both elevates the mind of those who prophesy and preserves it in humility, so that those who receive the spirit may discover what they are from God, while those who again lack the spirit of prophecy may recognize what they are of themselves.

**Peter.** That this is so, as you assert, reason clearly declares. But I beg you, continue whatever about the venerable Father Benedict still occurs to your mind.

## [CHAPTER XXII]

### CHAPTER XXII. Concerning the direction, through a dream, of the building of the monastery at Tarracina

[Col. 0173C]

**Gregory.** At another time the enlightened Father Benedict was asked by a certain faithful and most devout man to establish a monastery on the man’s estate, situated nearby the city of Tarracina [Note: Tarracina, formerly called Anxur, was a colony and city of Latium at the mouth of the Ufens River. Almost no remains of the monastery at Tarracina survive. It was united to the monastery of Cassino by the authority of Agapetus II after having long been destroyed. The site still paid a certain rent to the monastery of Cassino, according to the later edition. See Mabillon, *Iter Italicum*, p. 100 and following.], by sending some of his disciples there [Note: The conjunction “so that” appears redundant. Editorial note.].

Yielding to his request, he summoned those whom he decided to send, appointed a father over them and a steward [Note: The translator understood this as “the one who was second to the abbot or Father,” namely the steward. For the grounds of this interpretation, see above, note 5 to chapter B, or chapter 2.], and dismissed them in peace. He also gave them this assurance, saying:

“Go, brothers. On this very day I shall come to you and show you in what place the oratory ought to be built, in what place the brothers’ refectory, in what place the guesthouse, and in what place all the other things required by necessity should be made.” [Note: The manuscript reads “ought to be built.”]

Having received the saint’s blessing, they immediately departed. They gathered all the things necessary for the building [Note: At this point the Greek differs substantially from Gregory’s Latin text. The Latin speaks of preparations for receiving Saint Benedict and his companions; the Greek speaks instead of procuring and supplying the materials needed for construction, as Gussanville has already observed.] and cleared the site, preparing everything so that, when the venerable Father arrived according to his promise, he might arrange the construction of the building.

During the night that preceded the day on which the saint had promised his arrival, he appeared in a vision to the superior whom he had appointed there and to his steward, showing them the places for the construction and, practically speaking, giving them precise instructions about everything that had to be done there.

When the abbot of the monastery and his steward arose, each with great fear and joy recounted to the other the vision that the saint had shown them. Having been convinced by the vision revealed to them by the man of God, the superior of the monastery and his steward awaited the bodily arrival of the Christ-bearing man [Col. 0175B].

But when the appointed day had passed—the day on which he was supposed to arrive among them visibly—and they had failed to receive him, they were exceedingly grieved. They went to him and asked to learn why he had not come to them, reproaching him in their sorrow and saying:

“Holy Father, we awaited your arrival, as you promised, so that you might show us the placement of the buildings.”

The friend of God [Note: The manuscript reads “the man of God.”] answered them: “Why, brothers, why do you say this to me? Have I not come to you as I promised?”

When they replied, “Father, you have not come to us bodily,” he answered: “Did I not appear to both of you while you were sleeping? Did I not show you how the monastery was to be laid out? Go, and build it just as you saw in the vision and as I showed you with my hand.”

When they heard this and were greatly astonished, they returned to the estate mentioned above and built all the monastery’s buildings exactly as they had been represented to them in the vision.

[Col. 0175C] **Peter.** I want to be taught by what manner this could happen, so that an answer might reach men sleeping from far away, which the saints heard and recognized through a vision.

**Gregory.** Why, Peter, do you hesitate while investigating the orderly course of what happened? Do you not know that the nature of the spirit is more mobile than the body? We have truly heard the testimony of Scripture: the prophet Habakkuk was suddenly lifted from Judea to the land of the Chaldeans, carrying the meal that he had prepared for himself, and after he had brought it to the prophet Daniel, he found himself again in Judea.

If, then, the prophet Habakkuk, transported by God across so great a distance and bodily arriving with a meal for the prophet Daniel in a single moment of time, carried it to him [Note: The manuscript reads “brought it.”], what is so astonishing if Father Benedict, transported in spirit through prayer, appeared to the two men—that is, to the superior and his steward—and gave them instructions about the monastery’s construction? In the same way that the prophet, carrying bodily food, arrived bodily before the prophet Daniel, so Father Benedict arrived in spirit before his disciples, bringing them immortal nourishment—that is, the establishment and construction of the monastery.

**Peter.** Wiping away with the right hand of your soul-benefiting and saving account the fear that was growing in my mind, you have brought my eagerness to ask questions to maturity. But I wanted to know what sort of man he was in ordinary intercourse.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning the nuns whom he excluded from communion

[Col. 0177A]

**Gregory.** Peter, even his ordinary speech rarely failed to carry the weight of divine power. For the blessed man’s voice, burdened with the working of signs, was effective and not empty. Since he had raised his heart to sublime things, none of the words proceeding from his mouth could be found vain or falling short. If he ever happened to speak with a threat, his word was extremely powerful, because he rebuked wisely not with timidity or hesitation, but by a decisive pronouncement.

Now, not far from his monastery, two virgins who practiced asceticism and belonged to a very noble family lived in their own house. A serious and devout man habitually attended to the service required for their needs and household management. But nobility of birth does not always lead to vigilance of mind, so that those who have remembered themselves as superior to others may despise themselves in this world and regard themselves as no better than anyone else.

Had the women mentioned above understood this and practiced it attentively, they would not have sharpened their tongues like a razor against that most devoted man who willingly supplied them with what was necessary for the body, nor would they have provoked him to anger with insults. That devout man, no longer able to endure the excessive dishonor inflicted upon him by the women [Note: The manuscript reads “the dishonor inflicted upon him.”], went to the man of God, exposed the virgins’ ungrateful disposition, and reported how many insults he had received from them [Col. 0177C].

When Father Benedict, the worker of signs, heard this about the virgins, he sent them a warning, saying: “Correct yourselves and discipline your tongues. For if you do not correct yourselves, I shall exclude you from communion.”

He did not pronounce this sentence of exclusion as though he wished to bind them with the chains of punishment, but wisely and fatherly sought to improve their ungrateful disposition. Yet they did not abandon their folly or pay heed to the saint’s admonition.

After a few days, the virgins mentioned above died and were buried in the church. Whenever the gatherings for the divine liturgy were held in that same church, and the deacon, as usual, cried out, “If anyone does not communicate, let him go out of the church,” the nurse of the aforementioned virgins—who habitually offered an oblation to the Lord on their behalf [Col. 0179A]—saw the two virgins themselves coming out from their tombs and leaving the church.

When she had seen this happen many times, observing them emerge from their tombs at the deacon’s proclamation and being unable to remain in the church, the woman remembered that the man of God had declared while they were still alive that he would deprive them of participation in the divine mysteries unless they corrected their behavior and their words [Note: The manuscript reads “unless they correct.”]

She went eagerly to Benedict, the servant of God [Note: The manuscript reads “friend of God.”], and, rolling at his feet amid much lamentation, reported to the Father the terrifying and fear-filled vision that she had seen with her own eyes.

When the saint heard this and was moved by the compassion dwelling within him, he took an oblation and placed it in her hand, saying to her: “Go, and have this oblation offered to the Lord on their behalf. From now on they shall no longer be excluded from communion.”

When the oblation had been offered to the Lord on their behalf and the deacon, as usual, proclaimed that those who did not partake should leave the church, their nurse no longer saw them going out of the church.

Therefore we believe beyond all doubt that when the oblation given by the saint on their behalf was sacrificed, they were immediately deemed worthy of forgiveness and received from the Lord, through the blessed Benedict, participation in holy communion.

[Col. 0179B] **Peter.** It is exceedingly astonishing if this venerable and most holy man, while still in this life and dwelling in corruptible flesh [Note: The manuscript reads: “this man, while still in this corruptible flesh, had the power…”], had the power to release souls already placed before the invisible tribunal.

**Gregory.** Was the one who heard from God, “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed also in heaven,” not still in this flesh, Peter? Those who adorn the throne of the holy Apostle and shepherd by their faith and conduct now exercise his office, binding and loosing.

Thus, in order that an earthly man might be deemed worthy of such glory, the Creator of heaven and earth descended from heaven to earth; and, so that flesh might be able to judge spirits, God, having become flesh for the sake of human beings, granted this power to it [Note: Some connection appears to be missing here. Editorial note.]. Our weakness lies outside Him; for the dominion of God was not weakened by it.

**Peter.** Along with the power of the signs, the explanation of the words has been fittingly given.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the young monk who went to his parents against the saint’s will and died there

[Col. 0179C]

**Gregory.** On another occasion, a certain monk, living as a young man and belonging to the monastery of the man of God, loved his parents according to the flesh beyond measure. He often went to their house without the permission of the holy Father [Note: The translator frequently has this younger monk leave to visit his parents, a detail not found in Gregory’s text.]. One day, as was his custom, he went to his parents; but as soon as he entered their house, he died.

After they had prepared him for burial and committed him to the grave, they found his body thrown outside on the following day [Col. 0179D]. They buried him again, but immediately saw it cast out of the earth once more, just as before.

When his parents according to the flesh saw this, they ran to the most compassionate Father Benedict with the greatest lamentation [Col. 0181A], begging him, through the divine grace dwelling in him, to pity the one who had died so miserably and command that the earth retain him.

When the blessed man saw their anguished hearts, he took a portion of the Lord’s body and placed it in their hands, saying: “Go, place this Lord’s body upon his breast and commit him to the proper burial.”

When the dead man’s parents had done this, the buried body was no longer cast out by the earth [Note: The manuscript reads: “They saw the buried body, thrown out by the earth, but…”]; rather, according to the saint’s command, it remained held by the earth.

Do you see, Peter, what condemnation that man received from Jesus Christ? His body was rejected by the earth because he had not possessed the favor of blessed Benedict [Note: The manuscript reads: “because that man experienced this judgment from Christ.”].

[Col. 0181B] **Peter.** I am truly amazed and exceedingly astonished.

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning the boy-monk whom the earth cast out after burial

**Gregory.** One day a certain little monk of his, loving his parents more than he ought and heading toward their dwelling, left the monastery without a blessing. As soon as he reached them that same day, he died.

When he had been buried, his body was found thrown outside on the following day. They again arranged to commit it to burial. But the next day they found it once more cast outside and unburied [Col. 0180D], as before.

Then they hurried to the feet of Father Benedict and, with much weeping, begged him to grant the dead man his favor. The man of God immediately gave them, with his own hand, communion of the Lord’s body [Note: Menardus demonstrates through many examples in his notes on the *Sacramentary*, pp. 267 and 258, now note 680, formerly, that the sacred body of Christ was sometimes placed upon the breast of certain dead persons in the tomb. This was a customary practice in burying bishops. Nor is it prohibited by the Councils of Carthage III, canon 6, or Auxerre, canon 12, when they forbid giving the Eucharist to the dead; this must be understood of communion, which ought not to be given to the dead, since God said, “Take and eat.” It is therefore clear that only those who can eat may receive it. Many have explained this passage, including Haeften, Mabillon, and Bultellus, in their studies on the Life of Saint Benedict. Gussanville admits that Saint Basil also practiced this, but argues that the examples of all the ancients should not indiscriminately be introduced into our customs. See the Life of Basil supposedly written by Amphilochius. Also consult the *Gregorian Confession* by Theodore Petreius of Campen, a Carthusian of Cologne, book III, chapter 6, no. 3, where he effectively argues against Peter Martyr, who wrote against Gardiner, objection 38, that the Eucharist was placed in a dead man’s mouth at Benedict’s command. The cited author judges instead that the Eucharist was placed upon the dead man’s breast but immediately removed afterward.], saying: “Go, and place this Lord’s body upon his breast with great reverence, and then commit him to burial.”

When this had been done, the earth retained the body it had received and did not cast it out again. You can judge, Peter, what merit this man had before the Lord Jesus Christ, that even the earth cast out his body because he did not possess Benedict’s favor.

[Col. 0182B] **Peter.** I judge it clearly, and I am exceedingly astonished.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the monk who left the monastery and encountered a dragon on the road

[Col. 0181B]

**Gregory.** There was one of the monks of the monastery of the holy Father Benedict who, overcome by wandering thoughts and mastered by the demon of accidie, was entirely unwilling to submit to the strict observance of the rule [Note: The manuscript reads “to submit.” Shortly afterward it reads: “he did not cease … he did not choose.”].

The man of God did not cease admonishing him and did not neglect to instruct him continually. But the monk refused to obey the Father’s admonition and, repeatedly throwing himself shamelessly at the saint’s feet, did not stop asking to be allowed by him to go to his parents.

One day the venerable Father, wearied by his importunity [Col. 0181C], ordered him angrily to leave the monastery. As soon as he had gone out, he found a dragon directly in front of him on the road, its mouth open and ready to swallow him [Note: The manuscript reads: “He found it with its mouth open, wishing to swallow him, and then he began…”].

He began to tremble and, feeling about with his hands, cried out in a loud voice: “Run, run, for this dragon wants to devour me!” Two brothers ran there together. They did not see the dragon, but found the monk trembling and feeling about with his hands, and brought him back to the monastery.

He immediately promised never again to leave or abandon the monastery. From that moment he remained faithful to his promise, and, fortified by the prayers of the holy man, he never again saw the dragon standing before him—the dragon whom he had previously followed without seeing.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning the monk who left the monastery and found a dragon on the road

**Gregory.** One of his monks had yielded his mind to restlessness [Note: Gussanville and nearly all later editions read: “was devoted to restlessness of mind.”] and did not wish to remain in the monastery. Although the man of God rebuked him constantly and frequently admonished him, the monk would not consent in any way to remain in the community, but pressed him with importunate prayers to release him.

One day the venerable Father, wearied by his excessive persistence, angrily ordered him to leave. As soon as he had departed from the monastery, he encountered a dragon standing opposite him on the road, with its mouth open. When the dragon that had appeared [Col. 0182C] wished to devour him, he began, trembling and palpating [Note: The Greek word means “feeling about,” not “palpitating,” as the Latin reads. The translator may have been misled here and shortly afterward by the similarity of the words, or may have used a corrupt manuscript in which *palpans* and *palpantem* had been read. See Gussanville.], to cry out in a loud voice: “Run, run, for this dragon wants to devour me!” [Note: The first Carn. reads “Come quickly”; the printed editions have “Come to my aid.”]

The brothers ran up, but did not see the dragon. They found the monk trembling and feeling about with his hands and brought him back to the monastery. He immediately promised never again to leave the monastery, and from that hour remained faithful to his promise, since through the prayers of the holy man he had seen standing before him the dragon whom previously, without seeing him, he had followed.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the boy healed of leprosy

[Col. 0183A]

I think that this too should not be passed over in silence. I heard it related by a man of senatorial rank named Antonius [Note: The printed editions read “Antoninus.”], who said that his father’s son had suffered an outbreak of elephantiasis. After the boy’s hair had fallen out, his skin swelled; then, as the disease progressed, he could no longer conceal it.

He was sent by his father to the man of God, and the boy was restored to his former health and returned with all haste to his own father.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning the boy cured of elephantine disease

[Col. 0184A]

Nor do I think that this should be left unmentioned: I learned it from the account of the illustrious man Antonius [Note: Germ. reads “Aptonius”; Compend. agrees.]. He said that his father’s boy had been afflicted with elephantine disease [Note: Gussanville reads “corrupted”], so that, after his hair had begun to fall out, his skin swelled and he could no longer conceal the increasing discharge [Note: Two Carn., the first Theod., and Val-cl. read “and, as the discharge increased, he could no longer conceal it.”]. He was sent by his father to the man of God and was restored to his former health with the greatest speed.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the thirteen coins found through the saint’s prayer

[Col. 0183A]

[Col. 0183B] Nor do I think it right to consign to silence what was told me concerning Peregrinus, the disciple of the blessed man Benedict. He himself told me that one day a faithful man, pressed by the necessity of a debt and being required by his creditor to repay the loan [Note: The manuscript reads “the lender”], but having no means by which to repay it, believed that he would receive the greatest benefit if he went to the man of God.

He therefore went and fell at the saint’s feet, reporting the necessity caused by his debt of twelve coins. The venerable Father compassionately said to him in a gentle voice: “Brother, forgive me, for I have no twelve coins at all. But go, and return to me after two days, for today I do not have what I ought to provide for you” [Note: The manuscript reads “what I owed.”].

During those two days the Father remained occupied in prayer. On the third day the man who was burdened by the necessity of his debt came to the man of God. There was a chest in the monastery filled with legumes; suddenly, through the prayer of the God-bearing Father, thirteen coins were found above it.

The worker of signs, Benedict, ordered them to be brought and given to the distressed man, saying to him: “Go, my child, and repay the creditor with the twelve coins [Note: The manuscript reads “the lender”]; keep the one coin for yourself to meet your necessary needs.”

But let us return again to the subject before us, recounting the divine wonders of the miracle-working Father that I have learned by hearsay from his disciples, mentioned earlier in this book.

There was a man who had another man jealous of him and hostile toward him. The evil-loving demon drove the latter to such madness that he devised a deadly poison against his enemy and induced the man, who did not know what it was, to drink it [Note: The manuscript reads “urged him.”], so that he might more quickly deprive him of this present life.

The man drank the poison but did not die. Instead, when the appearance of elephantiasis spread throughout his whole body [Note: The manuscript reads “when elephantiasis was poured over his body as a whole”], he was presented as a pitiful sight to everyone’s eyes. Then he was carried to the man of God and quickly recovered his former health. For when the saint touched his body with his wonder-working right hand, he drove the entire disease of elephantiasis from his skin.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning the coins miraculously restored to a debtor

[Col. 0184A]

Nor should I omit what his disciple named Peregrinus used to relate [Col. 0184B]: one day a faithful man, driven by the necessity of a debt, believed that he had one remedy—if he went to the man of God and disclosed the necessity of debt that oppressed him.

He came to the monastery, found the servant of almighty God, and explained that he was being severely harassed by his creditor for twelve solidi. The venerable Father replied that he certainly did not possess twelve solidi, but consoled his poverty with gentle words and said: “Go, and return after two days, because today I lack what I ought to give you.”

During those two days he remained occupied in prayer according to his custom. When the man oppressed by the necessity of the debt returned on the third day, thirteen solidi were suddenly found upon a chest in the monastery, which was full of grain. [Col. 0184C] The man of God ordered them to be brought and given to the distressed petitioner, telling him to repay twelve and keep one for his own expenses.

But let me now return to those matters that I learned from the reports of his disciples mentioned earlier at the beginning of this book. A certain man suffered greatly from the jealousy of an adversary, whose hatred against him grew so far that he gave him poison in his drink without his knowledge [Note: The first Aud. and Lyr. read “mixed poison for him.”].

Although it could not take away his life, it changed the color of his skin, so that the discoloration spread over his body and seemed to imitate the appearance of leprosy. But when he was brought to the man of God, he quickly regained his former health; for as soon as the saint touched him, he drove away all the discoloration from his skin.

## [CHAPTER XXVIII]

### CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the glass vessel containing oil that was thrown down at his command but was not broken

[Col. 0185A]

At the time when a most severe famine held Campania in its grip, the faithful and prudent steward of Christ did not cease distributing suitably and compassionately to all who were in need whatever was necessary for the body. Eventually everything was exhausted from the monastery, and nothing else remained in the storeroom except a small quantity of oil in a glass vessel.

A subdeacon named Agapitus came to the friend of God and earnestly begged that a little oil might be given to him. This wonderful man, who had already resolved in his mind to distribute and scatter everything on earth so that it might be kept in heaven, ordered that the little oil remaining in the monastery’s storeroom be given to the petitioner [Col. 0185B].

The monk entrusted with the storeroom obeyed the Father’s command but did not choose to carry it out. A little later the Father asked the steward whether he had given that small quantity of oil to the petitioner. He answered that he had not, saying: “If you order all that oil to be given to the man, absolutely no consolation at all will remain for the brothers.”

Then that most gentle man became angry and ordered the brothers to throw through the window the glass vessel in which the little oil remained, so that nothing belonging to disobedience might remain in the monastery.

It happened as the blessed man had commanded. Beneath that window was a heap of many large stones [Note: The printed editions read “a mountain.”]. When the glass vessel containing the oil was thrown onto them, it remained so intact that it seemed never to have been thrown. Though hurled from a height, it was not shattered, nor was the oil spilled.

The venerable Father ordered it to be brought back and given, intact as it was, to the petitioner. Then, after the brothers had assembled, he rebuked the disobedient monk before them all for his unbelief and disobedience.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the glass flask thrown upon the rocks and not broken

[Col. 0186A]

At the time when scarcity of food was grievously afflicting Campania, the man of God had given everything to the various needy people of his monastery, so that scarcely anything remained in the storeroom except a little oil in a glass vessel.

Then a subdeacon named Agapitus came, earnestly asking that a small amount of oil be given to him. The man of the Lord, who had resolved to distribute everything on earth so as to reserve everything in heaven, ordered that the small amount of oil remaining be given to the petitioner.

The monk in charge of the storeroom heard the command but delayed carrying it out. After a short while the Father asked whether what he had ordered had been given [Col. 0186B]. The monk replied that he had not given it, because if he distributed it, nothing at all would remain for the brothers.

Then the Father, angry, ordered others to throw through the window the very glass vessel in which a little oil seemed to remain, so that nothing might remain in the storeroom through disobedience. This was done.

Beneath the window there was a great precipice rough with masses of stone. The glass vessel fell among the rocks [Note: Optatus relates something similar concerning a flask of chrism, *On the Donatist Schism*, book II, chapter 19 of the new edition: “thrown down, it could not feel the impact … it settled unharmed among the rocks.”], yet remained unharmed, as though it had not been thrown at all. It could neither be broken nor have its oil spilled.

The man of the Lord ordered it to be lifted up and, since it was intact, gave it to the petitioner. Then, after gathering the brothers, he rebuked the disobedient monk before everyone for his lack of faith and pride.

## [CHAPTER XXIX]

### CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the empty jar filled with oil through his prayer

[Col. 0185C]

After this had happened, the venerable Father devoted himself to prayer together with the brothers. In the place where he stood praying with them there was an empty jar covered with a lid.

While the holy Father persevered in prayer, the lid of the jar began to rise as the oil inside increased. When it had been moved and lifted, the oil that had risen above the jar’s mouth overflowed and filled the entire floor where the saint was kneeling in prayer [Col. 0185D].

When the miracle-working Father Benedict saw this, he brought the prayer to an end. He then admonished the unbelieving and disobedient brother in a fatherly manner, saying: “My child, acquire unwavering faith and humility worthy of the monastic vocation.”

That brother, properly and beneficially instructed by the Father, was ashamed. For this famous Father displayed to everyone, through the divine miracles wrought by the grace of almighty God, the power of the admonition he taught. From then on no one in his company dared to fear or disbelieve the saint’s promises or what he said, especially after seeing the extraordinary visitation from God that had occurred in a single moment of time.

For, in place of a glass vessel containing a very small amount of oil, he provided a jar overflowing with oil.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning the empty vat filled with oil

When this rebuke was complete, he devoted himself to prayer with the same brothers. In the place where he prayed with them there was a vat empty of oil [Note: The first Carn. and first Gemet. read “an empty vat”] and covered.

While the holy man persisted in prayer, the lid of the vat began to rise as the oil increased. When it had been moved and lifted, the oil that had risen overflowed the mouth of the vat and flooded the floor [Col. 0186D] on which he had been kneeling [Note: The earlier Theod., Longip., and second Gemet. read “on which they had been kneeling,” referring to Saint Benedict and the brothers.].

When Benedict, the servant of God, saw this, he immediately completed the prayer, and the oil ceased to flow onto the floor. Then he more fully admonished the doubting and disobedient brother, so that he might learn to have faith and humility.

The brother was beneficially corrected and became ashamed, because the venerable Father demonstrated through miracles the power of almighty God that he had declared in his admonition. From then on no one could doubt his promises, since in one and the same moment, in place of an almost empty glass vessel, he had provided a vat full of oil.

## [CHAPTER XXX]

### CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the demon-possessed monk healed by the saint’s slap

[Col. 0187A]

One day, while the holy man was going to the oratory of Saint John, which had been built at the very summit of the mountain, the utterly wicked enemy came out to meet him in the form of a veterinary surgeon, carrying a horn and a three-footed hobble [Note: Manuscript: “a three-footed hobble.”].

The servant of God asked him: “Where are you going?” He answered: “Behold, I am going to the brothers to give them a potion” [Col. 0187B].

The miracle-working Benedict then proceeded and, as was his custom, stood in prayer. When he had completed it, he quickly returned.

The evil spirit found one of the saint’s older monks drawing water, immediately entered him, threw him down, and tormented him mercilessly. When the man of God returned from prayer and saw him being so pitiably tormented, he merely gave him a slap on the cheek. At once the unclean spirit came out of him and thereafter did not dare return to him.

**Peter.** I should like to know whether he always performed all these miracles through the power of prayer, or whether he accomplished them solely by the will of foreknowledge.

**Gregory.** Those who cling to God by deliberate will and longing perform miracles in various ways whenever the need of circumstances requires a display of wonders. Sometimes they occur through supplication, and sometimes by authority.

As the Evangelist John says: “To all who received him, he gave authority to become children of God.” If, then, those who are children of God through God’s authority can perform signs by that authority, what is astonishing about this?

That they perform wonders in both ways is attested by Peter, who raised the dead Tabitha through prayer, and exposed Ananias and Sapphira when they lied and delivered them over to death. For it is not written that he prayed when they expired, but only that he exposed the offense they had committed.

It happens, therefore, that they sometimes act by authority and sometimes through supplication. From these examples, by exposing the latter he took away their lives by authority, while through prayer he restored life to the former.

I therefore present the power of the true servant of God, Benedict, in these two modes of miracles, in which I show him more brilliantly: sometimes we know that he received authority from God and performed miracles, and sometimes that he prevailed through prayer to work them.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the monk freed from a demon

[Col. 0188A]

One day, as he was making his way to the oratory of blessed John, situated on the very summit of the mountain, the ancient enemy came to meet him in the guise of a mule-doctor [Note: [Col. 0187D] Longipontanus has “sitting on a mule in the guise of a physician.” Val-cl. agrees. We have restored this passage from the manuscripts and from the Greek Version, which has “veterinarian,” or horse-doctor. Indeed, the entire apparatus of a veterinarian is described here: the three-footed or triple fetter by which horses’ feet are hobbled, and the horn by which drink or medicine is poured into sick animals.] carrying a horn and a three-footed fetter [Note: [Col. 0188D] In Germ. and Longip., with which the edition of Gil. agrees, *trepidicam*. In the first Theod., *tripedicum*.]. When he asked him, saying, “Where are you going?” [Note: [Col. 0188D] Germ. and almost all the manuscripts: “Where are you going?”] he replied, “Look, I am going to the brothers to give them a potion.”

Accordingly, the venerable Father Benedict went to prayer; when it was completed, he returned quickly. But the evil spirit found an elderly monk drawing water, immediately entered him, threw him to the ground, and tormented him most violently. When the man of God, returning from prayer, saw him being tormented so cruelly, he merely struck him on the cheek, and at once drove the evil spirit from him, so that it no longer dared to return to him.

**Peter.** I should like to know whether he always obtained such great miracles through the power of prayer, or whether at times he also performed them by the mere command of his will.

**Gregory.** Those who cling to God with devoted minds, whenever the need of circumstances requires it, commonly display signs in both ways [Col. 0188C]: sometimes performing marvelous deeds through prayer, and sometimes through authority. For when John says, “But to all who received him he gave power to become children of God” (John 1:12), those who are children of God through authority—what wonder is it if they are able to perform signs through authority? That they display miracles in both ways is attested by Peter (Acts 9), who raised Tabitha, who had died, by praying, but rebuked Ananias and Sapphira when they lied (Acts 5) and delivered them over to death. For it is not written that he prayed at their destruction, but only that he rebuked the fault they had committed. It is therefore clear that at times they perform these things through authority, and at times through petition: he took life from the former by rebuking, and restored it to the latter by praying [Col. 0188D].

Now I shall relate two deeds of the faithful servant of God, Benedict, in which it may plainly appear that in one matter he was able to act through authority received from God, and in another through prayer.

**[CHAPTER XXXI]**

**CHAPTER XXXI. On the peasant who was bound and released by the mere glance of the man of God.**

[Col. 0189A]

There was a certain man who was a Goth by race and was called by the name Zalla [Note: [Col. 0189D] The manuscript has “called.”], being a follower of the godless unbelief of the Arians.
