In the days of Totila, king of the Goths, whom we mentioned earlier, he was inflamed with uncontrollable rage against distinguished men of the holy and catholic Church [Note: [Col. 0189D] The manuscript has “of the holy catholic and apostolic Church.”], and, habitually employing the cruelty that had grown up with him, whenever he saw anyone before him, whether cleric or monk, he immediately dealt with him, subjecting him to death by the sword.

One day, therefore, inflamed by the heat of his own cruelty and with his mind deranged by the confusion of events, he happened upon a certain peasant. He oppressed him with the most savage tortures and scourged him with various instruments of punishment [Note: [Col. 0189D] The manuscript has “he scourged him with rods.”]. Since the peasant could no longer endure the torments, and the grave barbarian was demanding from him the goods belonging to him, he said that he had entrusted them to the servant of God, Benedict. Perhaps he said this in order to escape punishment by torture and gain the preservation of his life [Note: [Col. 0189D] The manuscript: “having dealt with these matters.”].

Then Zalla ceased torturing him, but ordered his arms to be tightly bound with strong leather straps. He began driving him before his own horse in order to show him who Benedict was, the man who had received his property. The peasant, with his arms bound, ran ahead of him and led the arrogant Zalla to the monastery of the holy man. There he found the blessed man sitting alone opposite the entrance of his cell [Col. 0189C] and reading.

As Zalla followed him in a rage, the peasant said, “Behold, this is Father Benedict, about whom I told you.” That proud man, then, boiling with anger and looking at him with a distorted gaze, his mind having become deranged [Note: [Col. 0189D] The manuscript has “having fallen into a disordered state of mind.”], thought that by frightening the saint he would terrify him. Fixing his eyes intently upon him, he began shouting at the top of his voice and saying to the saint, “Rise, rise, and return the property of this peasant which you have taken.”

At his voice the man of God immediately raised his eyes from his reading. When he saw that puffed-up Zalla, and with him only the peasant standing there bound, he looked at the man’s arms, tied with the straps—and a mystery beyond all wonder followed [Col. 0189D]. For as soon as the blessed man extended his God-illumined eye toward the bound man, the straps were released with such speed as the efforts of many men could not have accomplished [Note: [Col. 0189D] This phrase is altogether corrupt and seems to require correction as follows: “For at once, when the blessed man extended his God-illumined eye toward the bound man, a release of the straps followed with such speed as …” EDIT.].

When Zalla saw that the peasant whom he himself had bound had been released without the use of hands through the authority of the holy man, he became terrified and fell to the ground [Col. 0191A]. He placed his neck—which had been raised by arrogance—at the revered feet of the man of God, entrusting himself to his prayers.

But the holy man did not rise from his reading at all. Instead, he called the brothers and ordered them to lift Zalla inside, so that he might partake of food. When he had come to himself, the sanctified father admonished him to cease from such great cruelty and inhumanity.

Zalla, crushed, returned from the monastery. He did not demand anything further from the peasant, whom the man of God had released not by touching him, but merely by looking at him.

This, Peter, is what I said: those who serve the almighty God with confidence are sometimes able to perform miracles through authority, and at other times they bring about a multitude of signs through prayer. For he who, while seated, subdued the Goth’s beastlike madness, and by the sight of his own eyes loosed the straps and knots of the bonds that had tightened the innocent man’s arms, makes clear through the swiftness of the miracle that he had received from authority the power to do what he did. I shall add to the narrative what sort and how great a miracle he was able to obtain through prayer.

**CHAPTER XXXI. On the peasant who was bound and released by the mere glance of the man of God.**

[Col. 0190A]

A certain Goth named Zalla [Note: [Col. 0190D] Germ., Longip., and Val-cl. have “Galla.” The Greek interpreter supports our reading.] was a follower of Arian perfidy. In the time of their king Totila, he burned with the most savage cruelty against the religious men of the Catholic Church, so that no cleric or monk who came before his face could in any way leave his hands alive.

One day, inflamed by the heat of his avarice and yearning to seize property, while he was afflicting a certain peasant with cruel tortures and mangling him with various punishments, the peasant, overcome by the torments, declared that he had entrusted his property to Benedict, the servant of God. He did this so that, while the torturer believed it, his cruelty might meanwhile be suspended and time be gained for preserving his life [Col. 0190B] [Note: [Col. 0190D] Here both the manuscripts and the editions disagree. In Becc. we read “that an hour might be restored.” In the first Aud. both readings occur, “might be restored” and “might be snatched away.” We follow Germ. and the better witnesses.].

Then that same Zalla stopped tormenting the peasant. But after tightly fastening his arms with strong leather straps, he began driving him before his horse, so that he might show him who Benedict was, the man who had received his property. The peasant, going before him with his arms bound, led him to the monastery of the holy man, and found him sitting alone before the entrance of his cell and reading.

As the peasant was followed by the savage Zalla, he said, “Behold Father Benedict, about whom I told you.” When Zalla, with a fiery spirit and the madness of a perverse mind, looked upon him, he thought that he would frighten him with the terror he ordinarily inspired. He began shouting in a loud voice, saying, “Rise, rise, and return the property of this peasant which you have taken.”

At his voice the man of God immediately raised his eyes from his reading. When he looked at him, he also at once noticed the peasant who was being held bound [Col. 0190C]. When he lowered his eyes to the man’s arms [Note: [Col. 0190D] Big. has “fixed his eyes upon them.”], the straps fastened around them began, in a wondrous manner, to unwind with such speed [Note: [Col. 0190D] Germ., Longip., and Norm. have “to dissolve.”] that no human haste could have loosened them so quickly.

When the man who had arrived bound suddenly stood free, Zalla, shaken by the force of such power, fell to the ground. Bending his stiff neck of cruelty before the saint’s feet, he commended himself to his prayers.

But the holy man did not rise from his reading. He called the brothers and ordered them to carry Zalla inside, so that he might receive a blessing [Note: [Col. 0190D] That is, food, as Zack. understood and expressed it. Mabillon explains it as the *eulogia*, or blessed food.]. When he had come to himself, Benedict admonished him to cease from the madness of such great cruelty. Broken, Zalla departed and did not thereafter dare to demand anything from the peasant, whom the Lord’s servant had released not by touching him, but by looking at him.

Behold, Peter, what I said: those who serve the almighty God more familiarly are sometimes able to perform miracles through authority. For he who, while seated, restrained the terrifying ferocity of the Goth, and by his eyes dissolved the straps and knots of the bonds that had tightened the innocent man’s arms, shows by the very speed of the miracle that he had received through authority the power to possess what he did. Again, I shall relate what sort and how great a miracle he wished to obtain by prayer.

**[CHAPTER XXXII]**

**CHAPTER XXXII. On the dead man raised through the prayer of the saint.**

[Col. 0191B]

One day, then, the blessed man went out with the brothers to work in the field. A certain farmer had a son who had died a short while earlier. Carrying the body in his arms and consumed by a flood of tears, he came to the monastery and sought the enlightened Father Benedict.

He was told that Benedict was working in the field with the brothers and would be delayed. Hearing this, he laid the body of his dead son before the monastery gate. Overcome by unspeakable grief, he then set out at a swift run in search of the venerable father [Note: [Col. 0191D] The manuscript has “at a swift pace.”].

And behold, at that very hour the man of God had ceased from his work and was returning to the monastery with the brothers [Col. 0191C] [Note: [Col. 0191D] The manuscript has “he returned, and this man …”]. When the father of the dead child saw him, he began to cry out to the saint with tears, saying, “Give me back my son; give me back my son.”

The man of God was astonished at this and stopped, saying, “Surely, man, I did not take your son?” The child’s father replied, “My son has died, venerable father; come, raise him.”

When that miracle-working father heard these words, he was deeply grieved and said, “Go away, brothers, go away. Such things do not belong to us; they belong to the holy apostles. Why do you wish to lay upon us burdens which we cannot bear?” [Note: [Col. 0191D] The manuscript has “to impose … to carry.”]

But the father of the dead child, struck by the most violent grief, persisted in his request, affirming and swearing, “I will not leave unless you raise my son.”

The man of God then asked him, “Where is the child’s body?” He replied, “It is lying by the monastery gate, venerable father” [Note: [Col. 0192D] The manuscript has “before the gate.”].

The man of God therefore went to the place with the brothers who were with him. He bent his knees in prayer, leaned his revered head over the child’s body, and, rising again, stretched out his hands toward heaven, saying, “Lord God, do not look upon my sins, but upon the faith of this man who asks that his son be raised, and restore to this body the soul which you took away.”

Before the saint had finished praying, the soul entered the body. The child’s whole body quivered and, trembling, felt with its hand, so that all who were present could see the fearsome miracle performed upon the child [Note: [Col. 0193D] The manuscript has “and the child’s whole body …”] [Note: [Col. 0193D] The manuscript has “performed upon the child.”]. Taking the child by the hand, the saint gave him back alive and whole to his father.

This miracle, Peter, he did not possess within his own authority. Rather, he prostrated himself in prayer and asked that he might be able to perform it.

**Peter.** I confess that everything is as you say. You have clearly confirmed through deeds the words you set forth. But I ask you to say whether holy men can do everything they wish, and whether they obtain everything they desire to receive.

**CHAPTER XXXII. On the dead man who was raised.**

[Col. 0192B]

One day he had gone out with the brothers for work in the fields. A certain peasant came to the monastery carrying in his arms the body of his dead son and burning with the grief of bereavement; he sought Father Benedict. When he was told that the father was staying in the field with the brothers, he immediately laid the body of his dead son before the monastery gate. Distraught with grief, he hastened at a run to find the venerable father.

At that same hour the man of God was returning from the work in the fields with the brothers. As soon as the bereaved peasant saw him, he began to shout, “Give me back my son; give me back my son.”

The man of God stopped at these words and said, “Did I take your son from you?” He replied, “He has died. Come, raise him.”

As soon as the servant of God heard this, he was greatly saddened and said, “Go away, brothers, go away. These things are not ours, but belong to the holy apostles. Why do you wish to impose upon us burdens which we cannot bear?” [Note: [Col. 0192D] Norm. and the second Carnot. have “Go away, brother … Why do you wish to impose burdens upon us …” The Greek interpreter does not support this reading, but the other reading, which we retain.]

But the man, compelled by excessive grief, persisted in his petition, swearing that he would not leave unless Benedict raised his son. The servant of God immediately asked him, “Where is he?” He replied, “Behold, his body is lying at the monastery gate.”

When the man of God arrived there with the brothers, he bent his knees and leaned over the child’s little body. Then he raised himself, stretched out his hands toward heaven, and said, “Lord, do not look upon my sins, but upon the faith of this man who asks that his son be raised, and restore to this little body the soul which you took away.”

He had scarcely completed the words of his prayer when the soul returned, and the child’s whole little body trembled so that, before the eyes of all who were present, it appeared to palpitate with a wondrous quivering. He immediately took the child’s hand and gave him alive and unharmed to his father. It is clear, Peter, that he did not possess this miracle within his own power: he prostrated himself and asked that he might be able to perform it.

[Col. 0194A] **Peter.** It is plainly established that everything is as you say, for you prove through deeds the words you put forward. But I ask you to tell me whether holy men can do everything they wish, and whether they obtain everything they desire.

**[CHAPTER XXXIII]**

**CHAPTER XXXIII. On the miracle concerning his sister Scholastica.**

**Gregory.** Who, Peter, was more exalted in this life than Paul, who three times asked the Lord concerning the thorn in his flesh (2 Cor. 12), and yet was unable to obtain what he wished? From this I must tell you about the venerable Father Benedict: there was something he wished to do, but was entirely unable to accomplish.

He had a sister by birth named Scholastica, who by the favor of almighty God had been sanctified from her youth [Note: [Col. 0193D] The manuscript has “who had been sanctified by grace.”]. Once each year she was accustomed to come to her blessed brother. For her sake the man of God would descend not far outside the gate, to a property belonging to the monastery.

One day, then [Note: [Col. 0193D] The manuscript has “one of the days.”], the man of God came to her as usual, together with his disciples. They spent the entire day in discussions of the sacred sayings and divinely inspired Scriptures. When evening came, and darkness still remained [Note: [Col. 0193D] The manuscript has “when evening came and darkness was already present,”] they reclined and partook of food.

While they were eating and lingering in conversation about the divinely inspired Scriptures, much of the night passed. Then that most holy and honored virgin, his sister by birth, asked him, saying, “I beg you, my brother, do not leave me this night, so that until morning we may speak together about the joy of heavenly life and eternal life.”

The blessed man replied, “What are you saying, sister? I cannot in any way remain outside my cell.”

The weather was so clear that no trace of a cloud appeared. But when that most holy virgin saw that her brother would not yield at all to her request, she intertwined her fingers, placed her hands upon the table, bowed her head over her hands, and implored almighty God.

When she raised her head from the table, there arose such a sound of flashes and thunder, and such an outpouring of rain followed, that neither the venerable man of God Benedict nor the brothers who had come with him could advance even a little beyond the threshold of the house.

That most holy woman kept her head bowed in her hands as it had been upon the table and poured out rivers of tears, through which she changed the clear weather into an abundance of rain [Col. 0195A], so that after the prayer the movement of the water followed [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript has “outpouring.”]. Such was the power of the prayer that the raising of her head from the table, accompanied by the sound of thunder, and the descent of the rain occurred in the same instant.

The blessed man, realizing that he could not return to the monastery because of the disturbance of the flashes and thunder and the overwhelming flood of rain, was grieved and said to his sister, “May almighty God forgive you, sister. What have you done?”

She replied, “Behold, I asked you, and you did not wish to obey me. I asked my Lord, and he heard me. Now, if you can, go out, leave me, and return to the monastery” [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript has “my God; now, if you can …”].

He was unable to step outside the house. Though he had not wished to remain there voluntarily, he stayed with her involuntarily. They spent the entire night awake, filling themselves with words concerning eternal life and with discussions of the divinely inspired Scriptures.

Behold, then, I have said that he wished to do something but was unable to do it. Yet if we consider the will of this venerable father, we do not find him hesitating. He wished the clear weather to remain as it had been when he came down from the monastery to his most devout sister [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript has “when he entered from the monastery.”]. But the opposite occurred: through the power of God, the miracle that took place in his most holy virgin and sister was contrary to what he had wished.

For it is truly marvelous that the virgin was able at that moment to do more than he, since she had greatly desired to see her brother. For, according to John’s saying, “God is love.” By a wholly just judgment, therefore, she was able to do more who loved more.

**Peter.** I confess it, and I am very pleased with what you say.

**CHAPTER XXXIII. On the miracle of Scholastica, his sister.**

[Col. 0194A]

**Gregory.** Who in this life, Peter, was more exalted than Paul, who three times entreated the Lord concerning the thorn in his flesh (2 Cor. 12), and yet was unable to obtain what he wished? For this reason I must tell you about the venerable Father Benedict, because there was something which he wished to do but could not accomplish.

His sister, named Scholastica, had been dedicated to the almighty Lord from infancy. She was accustomed to come to him once a year [Col. 0194B]. For her sake the man of God would descend not far outside the gate, to an estate belonging to the monastery [Note: [Col. 0193D] Observe from this passage that, at the very beginning of the Benedictine order, estates were assigned to monks for their sustenance, so that they were not forced to obtain the necessities of life by begging or by manual labor. We shall show this elsewhere from the letters of St. Gregory. It is clear from Letter 3, Book III, formerly Book II, indiction 11, that some lived from the offerings of the faithful, like the clergy themselves. Gregory himself endowed the monasteries he founded with revenues, as another Gregory, namely Gregory of Tours, testifies in Book X of his *History*.]

One day she came as usual, and her venerable brother descended to her with his disciples. They spent the whole day in the praises of God and sacred conversation. When night had already fallen, they took food together. While they were still sitting at table and the hour grew late amid sacred conversation, the nun, his sister, asked him, saying, “I beg you not to leave me this night, so that until morning we may speak about the joys of heavenly life.”

He replied, “What are you saying, sister? I cannot remain outside my cell.”

The sky was so clear that no cloud appeared in the air. But when the nun heard her brother’s refusal [Col. 0194C], she placed her hands, with fingers intertwined, upon the table and bowed her head over them to pray to almighty God.

When she lifted her head from the table, such a force of lightning and thunder broke forth, together with such an inundation of rain, that neither the venerable Benedict nor the brothers who were with him could move their feet beyond the threshold of the place where they sat.

The nun had poured rivers of tears upon the table with her head bowed in her hands, and through those tears she drew the clear weather toward rain. The inundation did not follow the prayer even a little later; rather, the prayer and the inundation corresponded so exactly that the raising of her head from the table and the falling of the rain occurred in one and the same moment.

Then the man of God, seeing that amid lightning, thunder, and the flood of the great rain he could not return to the monastery [Col. 0194D], began to complain in grief, saying, “May almighty God forgive you, sister; what have you done?”

She replied, “Behold, I asked you, and you did not wish to hear me. I asked my Lord, and he heard me. Now, if you can, go out, leave me, and return to the monastery.”

Unable to go out beyond the shelter, he who had not wished to remain voluntarily stayed there against his will. Thus it came about that they spent the whole night awake [Note: [Col. 0195D] Two Carnot., Bigot., and Becc. have “keeping vigil,” a reading supported by the Greek interpreter], satisfying one another through sacred conversations concerning spiritual life.

For this reason I said that he wished to do something but could not: for if we look into the mind of the venerable man, there is no doubt that he wished the same clear weather in which he had descended to remain. But contrary to what he wished, through the power of almighty God he found a miracle arising from the woman’s heart [Col. 0196B].

Nor is it surprising that the woman who had long desired to see her brother was able at that moment to do more than he. For, according to John’s saying, “God is love” (1 John 4:16); by a very just judgment, therefore, she was able to do more who loved more.

**Peter.** I confess: what you say pleases me greatly.

**[CHAPTER XXXIV]**

**CHAPTER XXXIV. How he saw the soul of his sister Scholastica depart, as a dove flying up to heaven.**

[Col. 0195C]

**Gregory.** On the following day the same venerable virgin withdrew to her own cell. The man of God likewise returned to his monastery. And behold, after three days, while standing in his cell and raising his eyes into the air, he saw the holy soul of his devout sister depart from her body in the form of a dove and be taken up into the mysteries of heaven [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript has “tabernacles.”]

Rejoicing with her in such glory, he rendered thanks to almighty God in hymns and praises, and announced her completion to the brothers. He immediately sent them to bring her revered and honorable body to the monastery and bury it in the tomb which he had prepared for himself [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript has “which he himself had prepared.”]. For since their minds had been united with one another in the Holy Spirit and were continually turned toward God [Note: [Col. 0195D] The manuscript has “continually stretched upward,”], burial could not separate their most holy bodies.

**CHAPTER XXXIV. How the soul of his sister was seen to depart from her body.**

[Col. 0196B]

[Col. 0196C] **Gregory.** On the following day, when the same venerable woman had withdrawn to her own cell, the man of God returned to the monastery. And behold, after three days [Note: [Col. 0196D] Scholastica is commemorated on February 10.], while standing in his cell and raising his eyes into the air, he saw the soul of that same sister depart from her body and penetrate the secrets of heaven in the form of a dove.

Rejoicing with her in such glory, he rendered thanks to almighty God in hymns and praises, and announced her death to the brothers. He immediately sent them to carry her body to the monastery and place it in the tomb which he himself had prepared. Thus it came about that, since their minds had always been one in God, burial likewise did not separate their bodies.

**[CHAPTER XXXV]**

**CHAPTER XXXV. On the soul of Germanus, bishop of the city of Capua.**

At another time Servandus, a deacon and abbot of the monastery located in the region of Campania and founded by Liberius, then a patrician, came to the blessed Father Benedict at the monastery for a customary visit [Col. 0197A]. He himself was also a man filled with heavenly instruction [Note: [Col. 0197D] The manuscript has “full.”].

Having watered themselves with the honey-sweet words of eternal life, they now enjoyed the sweetest nourishment, yearning with insatiable longing for their heavenly homeland. They continually saw themselves delighting in these things, admitting no satiety of such spiritual pleasure; but when the body’s need demanded physical food, they received it with sighs.

When the time required them to rest, the most devout Father Benedict went up into his tower. Likewise the deacon Servandus entered his lower chambers, where the lower rooms had been constructed beneath the upper ones [Note: [Col. 0197D] The manuscript has “in the lower rooms … in the upper rooms.”] so that the ascent might be made quickly [Col. 0197B]. Directly opposite the tower there was another dwelling where the disciples of both men rested.

While the man of God Benedict, with the brothers still resting, had anticipated the time of nocturnal prayer by keeping vigil, he stood at his window and implored almighty God. Suddenly, at an untimely hour of the night [Note: [Col. 0197D] The manuscript has “at the hour.”], he looked upward and saw that a great flood of light had appeared from heaven, so that all the darkness of night was driven away. That night was illumined by such light that it surpassed the brightness of day, because light shone down from heaven.

A mystery full of wonder followed at the time of that vision, as the same father later related. “I saw,” he said, “and behold, the whole world had been gathered together as if beneath a single ray of the sun.” While he gazed intently at the brilliance of that light, he saw the holy soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, being received into heaven by angels in a fiery sphere.

Then the venerable Father Benedict, wishing to make the deacon Servandus a participant in and witness of this fearful vision, called him twice and three times with a loud cry. Disturbed by his father’s unusual shout, Servandus went up, astonished and in haste. He did not see the whole vision, but only a small portion of that light.

When he was amazed at the miracle, the man of God narrated to him in order everything he had seen. Immediately he sent word to Theoprobus, a most devout man in the fortress of Cassinum, that he should send to the city of Capua [Note: [Col. 0197D] The manuscript has “Capua’s city.”], investigate what had happened concerning Bishop Germanus, and report it clearly to him.

When this had been done, the man who was sent found Germanus, the bishop, already perfected in the Lord among the saints. After investigating and learning the facts precisely, he discovered that Germanus had died at that very instant [Note: [Col. 0197D] The manuscript has “at that same hour and instant.”] at which the man of God had seen his ascent into heaven.

[Col. 0197D] **Peter.** A very wondrous and exceedingly astonishing thing [Note: [Col. 0197D] The manuscript has “we are astonished.” Perhaps “I am astonished.”]. But I ask about what was said: how could the whole world have been gathered before the eyes of the righteous man, as if beneath one ray of the sun, before the universal resurrection? [Col. 0199A] I cannot even understand in what manner it ought to have happened, so that the whole world could be seen by one man.

**Gregory.** Hold firmly to what I say, Peter. To a soul contemplating the Creator, all creation is narrow [Note: [Col. 0199D] The manuscript reads: “It is narrow for it; therefore, whoever saw even a little of the uncreated light …”]. Whoever has seen even a little of the light of the Creator becomes aware that every part of created things is small, because the very contemplation of the light expands inwardly in the act of understanding and stretches the mind so far toward God that it becomes higher than the whole world. The soul of the contemplator becomes, as it were, greater than itself.

When it begins to be seized in the light of God, it is expanded above itself in its inner regions. When it sees itself thus expanded, it recognizes how small is what, while in humility, it had been unable to comprehend [Note: [Col. 0199D] The printed editions corruptly read “small” as a masculine form; we have preferred the manuscript reading.].

This man, then, who saw the fiery sphere and the angels returning into heaven, clearly could not have seen these things unless he was in the light of God. What wonder, then, if he also saw the whole world gathered before him, since, raised up in intellectual light, he was outside the world?

When it is said that the whole world was gathered before his eyes, this does not mean that heaven and earth were physically brought together; rather, the soul of the one contemplating was expanded, and, seized up toward God, it was able without difficulty to contemplate everything that is beneath God.

Thus, within the light that flashed before his outward eyes, there was an interior light in the intellectual eyes of his soul. For the sight of the soul being seized up into the heights showed him how exceedingly narrow all lower things are [Note: [Col. 0199D] The manuscript has “it was shown to him how much …”].

[Col. 0199C] **Peter.** I see that I have not understood exactly what you said. Because of my slowness, your explanation increased so much. But since you have now poured these things clearly into my understanding, I ask you to return to the order of the narrative.

**CHAPTER XXXV. On the world gathered before his eyes, and on the soul of Germanus, bishop of the city of Capua.**

[Col. 0196D]

At another time Servandus, a deacon and abbot of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0196D] Servandus, the deacon and abbot mentioned here, presided over the monastery of St. Sebastian in the city of Alatri, which lies five miles from Veroli and thirty from Cassinum, according to the Acts of St. Placidus, no. 11. On the patrician Liberius, see Haeften’s note on this passage. MABILL.] which had once been built in the region of Campania by the patrician Liberius [Note: [Col. 0197D] The first Theod. has “established.”], came to him as usual for a visit.

He frequently visited Benedict’s monastery; for since that man too was overflowing with the grace of heavenly teaching, they poured into one another sweet words of life and, because they could not yet enjoy the sweetness of their heavenly homeland perfectly, at least tasted it through longing.

When the hour already demanded rest [Note: [Col. 0197D] In the edition of Gussanville, after “demanded,” there is a passage beginning “so that they ought to have given themselves to sleep …” and continuing with a tower standing in the same place. These words are absent from the manuscripts and from the other editions. They are also absent from the Greek version.], venerable Benedict placed himself in the upper part of the tower, and the deacon Servandus in its lower part; the lower rooms were connected with the upper by an accessible ascent. Before this tower there was a spacious dwelling in which the disciples of both men rested.

While the man of God Benedict, with the brothers still sleeping, had anticipated the time of nocturnal prayer by keeping vigil, he stood at the window and prayed to almighty God. Suddenly, at an untimely hour of the night, he looked upward and saw that light poured down from above and drove away all the darkness of night. The light that shone amid the darkness was so brilliant that it surpassed the day.

A very wondrous thing followed this vision [Note: [Col. 0198D] Compend. has “A very wondrous thing followed the same vision.”] For, as he later recounted, the whole world was brought before his eyes as if gathered beneath a single ray of the sun. While this venerable father fixed his gaze upon the brilliance of the flashing light, he saw the soul of Germanus, bishop of Capua, being carried by angels into heaven in a fiery sphere [Note: [Col. 0198D] Germ. has “in a sphere.” St. Germanus is commemorated on October 30.].

Then, wishing to provide himself with Servandus the deacon as a witness to so great a miracle, he called him twice and three times by name with a loud cry. Disturbed by the unusual shout of so great a man, Servandus went up and looked, seeing only a small portion of the light that remained.

As he stood astonished at this miracle, the man of God narrated to him in order what had happened. Immediately he sent word to the religious man Theoprobus in the fortress of Cassinum that he should send to the city of Capua that same night and discover and report what had happened concerning the bishop Germanus.

This was done. The man who had been sent found the most reverend Bishop Germanus already dead, and, investigating carefully, learned that his death had occurred at the very moment when the Lord’s servant had perceived his ascent [Note: [Col. 0198D] The first Aud., Lyr., Becc., Prat., and Bigot. have “departure.”].

**Peter.** A very wondrous and exceedingly astonishing thing. But regarding what was said—that the whole world was brought before his eyes as if gathered beneath a single ray of the sun—since I have never experienced such a thing, I do not know how to imagine the order by which it could happen that the whole world should be seen by one man.

**Gregory.** Keep firmly in mind what I say, Peter: to a soul that sees the Creator, all creation is narrow. For however little of the Creator’s light it may have seen, everything created becomes small to it. Through the light of inward vision the mind’s inner capacity is enlarged, and it is expanded in God to such an extent that it exists above the world. The soul of the one who sees also becomes greater than itself.

When it is seized above itself in God’s light, it is expanded in its inner regions. And when it sees itself exalted above itself, it understands how small is what, while humbled, it had been unable to comprehend [Note: [Col. 0200D] Prat. and the first Gemet. have “when the mind sees itself beneath itself.” We follow Germ. and the other better witnesses.].

The man of God, therefore, who saw the fiery globe and also saw the angels returning to heaven [Col. 0200B], could undoubtedly perceive these things only in the light of God. Why, then, is it surprising that he saw the world gathered before him, since, raised up in the light of his mind, he was outside the world?

When it is said that the gathered world was before his eyes, this does not mean that heaven and earth were contracted into one; rather, the mind of the one seeing was expanded. Seized up into God, it was able without difficulty to see everything that is beneath God.

Thus, within the light that shone before his outward eyes, there was an inner light in his mind. When that light seized the mind of the one seeing and carried it toward higher things [Note: [Col. 0200D] Most manuscripts, with Germ., have “because it carried it toward higher things.”], it showed him how narrow all lower things are.

[Col. 0200C] **Peter.** I see that I have profitably failed to understand what you had said, since because of my slowness your explanation grew so much. But since you have poured these things clearly into my understanding, I ask you to return to the order of the narrative.

**[CHAPTER XXXVI]**

**CHAPTER XXXVI. That he wrote a rule for monks.**

**Gregory.** I would gladly continue to relate many things about this venerable man, Peter, but I pass over some matters deliberately because I am hastening to unfold the deeds of others. I do not, however, want you to be unaware that, amid the miracles by which the man of God was renowned in the world, he also shone greatly through the teaching of his words.

For he composed the rule of the monks with exceptional discernment and luminous expression. If anyone wishes to learn his customs and manner of life more precisely, he can discover in that same written rule the entire course of his teaching; for that holy man was in no way able to teach or form others except as he himself had lived.

**CHAPTER XXXVI. That he wrote the rule of monks.**

**Gregory.** I am glad, Peter, to tell you still more about this venerable father, but I deliberately pass over some of his deeds because I am hastening to unfold those of others. This, however, I do not want you to miss: amid all the miracles by which the man of God became renowned in the world, he also shone greatly through the word of teaching.

For he wrote a rule for monks, distinguished for its discernment and lucid in its expression [Note: [Col. 0200D] Two Gemet., two Carnot., and Prat. have “lucid in its expression,” masculine.]. If anyone wishes to know his conduct and manner of life more subtly, he can find all the acts of his teaching in that same rule of formation: for the holy man could in no way teach otherwise than he lived.

**[CHAPTER XXXVII]**

**CHAPTER XXXVII. On the prophecy of his departure, which he announced to the brothers.**

[Col. 0201A]

At the time when this renowned man was about to depart from this temporary life [Note: [Col. 0201D] The manuscript adds “to God.”], he announced the day of his holy death to the disciples who were with him and to those living at a distance. To those present he solemnly charged that they should secretly keep within themselves what they had heard; to those absent he announced what sign would occur when his soul was about to leave his body.

Six days before his most honored death, he ordered his tomb to be opened. Immediately he was seized by a most severe fever, and, through the intensity of the burning, the powers of his soul gradually weakened.

Seeing himself each day, so to speak, wasting away under the fiercest fever, on the sixth day he caused himself to be carried by the disciples and brought into the oratory [Note: [Col. 0201D] The manuscript has “he ordered himself to be carried.”]. There he fortified his departure by receiving the Lord’s body and blood. Standing among the disciples, with his powerless limbs supported by their hands, he raised his hands toward heaven, faced east, and, with prayer, sent his sanctified and most pure soul up to heaven [Note: [Col. 0201D] The manuscript has “sent it upward. At that same hour …”].

On that same day, two brothers—one quietly remaining in his own cell, the other living some distance away—received one and the same comparable revelation. Each saw a road extending from Benedict’s cell all the way to heaven, entirely paved with silken garments, with countless lamps burning along it in orderly fashion toward the east.

And behold, a dignified man, radiant in appearance, standing above them, asked, “Whose is this road which you behold with wonder?” When they confessed that they did not know, he said to them, “This is the road by which Benedict, beloved of God, ascends into heaven.”

Then they understood the completion of the holy man. Just as the disciples who were present had seen it, so those who were absent recognized it from the sign that had been announced to them beforehand.

His sanctified body was buried in the oratory of blessed John the Baptist, where he had destroyed the altar of Apollo and established the oratory of the Forerunner.

In the cave beneath the reservoir, in which he had formerly lived, a great grace of miracles shines forth even to the present day whenever those who ask approach with faith.

**CHAPTER XXXVII. On the prophecy of his departure announced to the brothers.**

[Col. 0202A]

In the same year in which he was to depart from this life, he announced the day of his most holy death to some disciples who lived with him and to others who remained far away. He charged those present to conceal what they had heard in silence [Note: [Col. 0201D] Pratel. has “in place of silence.”]; to those absent he indicated what sign, and of what kind, would occur when his soul departed from his body.

Six days before his departure he ordered his burial place to be opened [Note: [Col. 0201D] Pratel. and the first Gemet. have “tomb.”]. He was immediately seized by fever and began to be exhausted by a fierce burning [Note: [Col. 0201D] The second Gemet. has “pain.”]. As his weakness grew worse day by day, on the sixth day he had himself carried by the disciples into the oratory. There he fortified his departure by receiving the Lord’s body and blood. Supporting his weak limbs among the hands of the disciples, he stood with his hands raised toward heaven and breathed out his final spirit amid the words of prayer.

On that day, two brothers—one living in his cell, the other situated farther away—were granted a revelation of one and the same vision. They saw a road stretching straight from his cell to heaven along the eastern path, spread with garments and shining with countless lamps [Note: [Col. 0202D] The second Carnot., Bigot., and Becc. have “They saw a road spread … which …”].

A man of venerable appearance, radiant and standing above it, asked whose road it was that they saw. They confessed that they did not know. He said to them, “This is the road by which Benedict, beloved of the Lord, has ascended to heaven.”

Thus the disciples who were present saw the holy man’s death, while those who were absent recognized it through the sign that had been foretold to them.

He was buried in the oratory of blessed John the Baptist, which he himself built after destroying the altar of Apollo [Col. 0202C]. He also shines with miracles even now in the cave in which he had formerly lived at Subiaco [Note: [Col. 0202D] So Germ., Val-cl., two Carnot., and both Theod. Other manuscripts differ. Compend., Bigot., Lyr., and the first Aud. read: “in which he formerly lived at Subiaco.” The first Gemet. has: “in which he formerly lived, whose name was Subiaco.” The second Gemet. has: “in which he formerly lived, which was called Subiaco.”], whenever the faith of those who ask requires it.

**[CHAPTER XXXVIII]**

**CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the woman healed through the prayer of the saint.**

The event I am now relating took place there. A certain woman, having departed from her natural reason, wandered night and day through mountains and valleys, forests and plains [Col. 0201D] [Note: [Col. 0201D] The manuscript has “and both by day and night.”]. She lay down only where exhaustion compelled her to sleep.

One day [Note: [Col. 0201D] The manuscript has “one of the days.”], while she was wandering through the wilderness, she was led to the cave of the blessed man Benedict. Entering it unknowingly, she remained there. When morning came, she emerged so sound in mind that she seemed never to have suffered any disorder of reason. She remained in the health granted to her throughout the whole of her life.

**Peter.** What are we to say about this, which we see happening at the relics of the holy martyrs? For, practically speaking, more miracles are performed in the oratories where relics are deposited in their name than in the places where their bodies themselves lie.

We fully believe that the grace of God is present there as well as in their holy bodies. Yet they display greater signs there where their bodies do not lie in their entirety.

### Gregory

Where the bodies of the holy martyrs lie, there is no doubt, Peter, that they are able to display many signs, as indeed they do. For to those who approach with a pure mind they display immeasurable miracles. But because those whose minds are weaker may doubt whether the saints are present to hear them where it is evident that their bodies do not lie there in their entirety, they must necessarily display greater signs precisely where the weak mind doubts their presence. But those whose mind is firmly established in God, possessing the dignity of faith, know that even if their bodies do not lie there, nevertheless they do not cease to hear prayers.

Therefore our Lord Jesus Christ himself, who is the Truth, wishing to add faith to the disciples, said: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you.” [Note: Here the reader should observe that the words Φανερὸν οὖν ὑπάρχει, ὅτι τὸ Παράκλητον Πνεῦμα ἐκ τοῦ Πατρὸς προέρχεται, καὶ ἐν τῷ Υἱῷ διαμένει—that is, “It is therefore evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son”—are read very differently in Gregory’s Latin, namely: “Since it is evident that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son.” From this it clearly appears that the Greeks later corrupted Pope Zacharias’s translation, as John the Deacon rightly noted in Book IV, chapter 75, of his Life of the same blessed Gregory, speaking of the Dialogues in these words: “These books Zacharias, bishop of the holy Roman Church, highly learned in the Greek and Latin languages, translated into Greek in the time of the emperor Constantine, about 175 years later, and circulated among the Eastern Churches; although the cunning perversity of the Greeks, in mentioning the Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, maliciously scraped away and removed the name of the Son.” Thus John the Deacon. The Roman editors under Sixtus V, and others afterward, took care to append this censure. See what we have already prefaced on this subject, no. 26.]

“It is therefore evident that the Paraclete Spirit proceeds from the Father and remains in the Son.” Why, then, does the Son say that he must depart so that the one who was never separated from him may come? The disciples, seeing the Lord in the flesh, desired always to behold him with bodily eyes. Therefore he rightly said to them: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come”—that is: “Unless I conceal my body, I do not show what the longing for the Spirit is; and unless you cease to behold me bodily, you will never learn to love me spiritually.”

### Peter

I approve what you say.

### Gregory

Let us cease speaking for a little while, so that, if we extend our discourse in narrating the remaining miracles, we may restore our strength for speaking through silence.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII  
### Concerning the mad woman healed in his cave

For the event I am relating happened only recently: a certain woman, having completely lost her reason, wandered through mountains and valleys, woods and fields, by day and by night; and she rested nowhere except where exhaustion compelled her to rest. One day, while she was wandering about in great disorder, she came to the cave of the blessed man Benedict; she entered it without knowing what she was doing and remained there. When morning came, she emerged with her reason so completely restored that one would have thought she had never been afflicted by any insanity of mind. She remained in the same health that she had received for the whole of her life.

### Peter

What are we to say about what we often see happening even at the shrines of the martyrs? For, as we understand it, they display not so many benefits through their bodies as they do through their relics, and they perform greater signs there where they themselves do not lie bodily. [Note: In the writings of the medieval sacred authors, the phrase “the patronages of the saints” often means relics; Cangius proves this with numerous examples. For the present, it is enough to cite the capitulary of Charlemagne in which he forbids the servants of God to go to war, except those who had been selected for this purpose on account of the divine ministry—namely, to fulfill the solemn rites of Mass and to carry the patronages of the saints. Volume II of the Councils of Gaul, p. 235, chapter 3, title 2, of the Selected Capitularies of Charlemagne. Zacharias understood “patronages” to mean relics: λειψάνους, λείψανα. The miracles of the saints are also signified by “patronages.” Dynamius the patrician writes in his Life of Saint Maximus of Riez: “The body of the blessed bishop was buried in the church of Saint Peter . . . which afterward was called by his name because of his frequent patronages.”]

### Gregory

Where the holy martyrs lie in their own bodies, there is no doubt, Peter, that they are able to display many signs, as indeed they do, and they show countless miracles to those who seek them with a pure mind. But because weak minds may doubt whether they are present to hear prayers where it is certain that they are not present in their own bodies, they must display greater signs there where the weak mind may doubt their presence.

But those whose minds are fixed in God have the greater merit of faith insofar as they know that, although the saints do not lie there bodily, they nevertheless are not absent from hearing prayers. Hence the Truth himself, wishing to increase the disciples’ faith, said: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come to you” (John 16:7). Since it is evident that the Paraclete Spirit always proceeds from the Father and the Son, why does the Son say that he will depart so that the one who never departs from the Son may come? But because the disciples, seeing the Lord in the flesh, longed always to behold him with bodily eyes, he rightly says to them: “Unless I go away, the Paraclete will not come”—as though he were plainly saying: “If I do not withdraw my body, I do not show what the love of the Spirit is; and unless you cease to behold me bodily, you will never learn to love me spiritually.”

### Peter

I approve what you say.

### Gregory

We must now cease speaking for a little while, so that, if we proceed to narrate the miracles of others, we may meanwhile restore our strength for speaking through silence.

[Col. 0205]

# PREFACE TO THE RULE OF SAINT BENEDICT

[Col. 0205A] I think that no one can be unaware of the esteem in which the Rule of Saint Benedict has until now been held by everyone. In itself, or merely because of the name of its author, it is greater than any commendation. It has not only been called a holy Rule in councils, and said to have been composed by the same Spirit by whom the sacred canons were composed, and promulgated in all the monasteries of monks; it has also been read with singular devotion by the very princes of the world, who profess that from the prescriptions of so prudent a holy Father they derive means highly suited to the peoples entrusted to their faith. Therefore I have no doubt that pious and religious readers will receive it, read it through, and commit it to memory with the reverence and devotion of mind that are proper to it.

But how and with what disposition they will receive the exposition of that same Rule which I present here is uncertain, especially since this kind of subject has already been treated so often that anyone who considers treating it again may be thought to be merely going over ground already covered. Yet the very great number of commentators, which ought to have dissuaded me from this manner of writing, instead moved me to undertake the work. For although many writers, both ancient and recent, men of the greatest authority and weight because of their learning and their way of life—among the ancients Smaragdus, Hildemar, and Bernard of Cassino; among the more recent Menard and Haeften, men distinguished for learning and wisdom—have carried out this task with great praise, nevertheless one thing seemed still to be lacking for a complete and thorough knowledge of the Rule.

The copies of the ancient commentators on the Rule are either extremely rare or almost unknown, hidden in the obscure corners of libraries, where they wage war with cockroaches and moths. Some of the more recent commentators, however, have handed down a doctrine so alien to the mind of Saint Benedict that they seem to have explained anything rather than his Rule. It therefore seemed worthwhile for certain men distinguished in piety and learning to draw the former out of darkness and, in some fashion, refute the latter.

Accordingly, when some years ago I had prepared such a commentary for my own use according to my limited ability, those same men persuaded me to publish it, so that both from the authority of the ancients—whose testimonies are reproduced here word for word—and from practice, which is the best interpreter of laws, it might become clear how far from the true and genuine meaning of Saint Benedict those have strayed who teach and approve more permissive opinions; and at the same time it might be possible to judge what should be thought of those whose stricter opinions are less in conformity with the Rule’s principal discretion.

Some readers may perhaps be disturbed by the frequent and abundant quotation of ancient authors in their own words, which often tends to weary readers who hurry on to what follows, or those already steeped in the reading of the authors themselves. But since my purpose was to support and explain the Rule of Saint Benedict by the authority and practice of the ancients, it was scarcely possible for me not to pile up their authorities and testimonies in great number. Although this manner of writing may afford less pleasure to the mind, it nevertheless seems much more effective for persuasion, which is the one thing I had before my eyes here. I have not written these things to entertain the reader but to edify him; and would that I might at least test this effect in some readers!

If, however, our discussions seem to anyone to present something too harsh, austere, or restrictive, let no one rightly be angry with me, since I am not reporting my own doctrine but simply setting forth the examples of the saints and the testimonies of the ancients. Nor do I do so with the intention of condemning and attacking those observances which, because of time and place and pressing necessity, have departed somewhat from the exact and literal understanding of the Rule. For although they do not keep it entirely, as the saying goes, to the last detail, and although they alter or omit something according to the custom of their own monastery, nevertheless they do not depart altogether from the regular profession, provided that they do not cease to live soberly, justly, and piously according to the character of their communities (Saint Bernard, *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 16). It may perhaps not be irrelevant to our purpose to say a little about those who have devoted their efforts to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

First among these appears Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, whom all the disciples of the monastic order ought to venerate in a special way and whom the ancients rightly called “the second Benedict”—indeed, second to no one after the holy legislator. According to the testimony of his disciple Ardo, he had directed all his desire toward observing the Rule, and this was especially his concern: that nothing should exceed his understanding . . . . . To show disputatious people that nothing frivolous or empty had been issued by Saint Benedict, but that his own Rule was supported by those of others, he composed one book by collecting the provisions of various rules and called it the *Concordia of Rules*, arranging it so that the provision of Saint Benedict came first, followed by those that reasonably corresponded to it.

Smaragdus, abbot of Saint Michael in the region of Verdun, made considerable use of this work in composing his commentary on the holy Rule. He wove it together not only from various provisions of ancient rules but also from different sayings of the holy Fathers, suppressing the names of the authors. It is a work worthy of so great a writer, although not everyone agrees in assigning it to its true and genuine parent. Some attribute it to Rabanus Maurus, archbishop of Mainz; but our Mabillon proves how wrongly in volume II of the *Analecta of the Ancients*. To his proofs one may add this: Gratian cites it under the name of Smaragdus, its true author.

Menard attributes the same book to Smaragdus Ardo, a disciple of Benedict of Aniane. The name, age, and period of the author, as well as his use of the *Concordia of Rules*, do indeed agree; but the abbacy attributed by the manuscript copies to the writer of the commentary is an obstacle, and Smaragdus of Aniane did not attain it. Finally, others recognize Smaragdus, abbot of Lüneburg, as the author of this commentary, which is also preserved in the library of Saint-Germain in Paris under the name of Saint Dunstan. But those men lived later—namely, in the tenth century—than is possible for them to have produced a work whose composition is known to have occurred long before.

Smaragdus is followed by Hildemar, a Frankish monk who flourished in the time of the emperor Louis the Pious. Summoned to Italy by Angilbert, archbishop of Milan, and sent to Rampert, bishop of Brescia, he restored the stricter form of life at the monastery of Saints Faustinus and Jovita. There he composed, if I judge correctly, the best of all commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict. Leo of Marsica and Peter the Deacon attributed it, six hundred years ago, to Paul the Deacon, with Bernard of Cassino and Peter Boherius supporting them.

That it is more recent than Paul the Deacon is evident from the fact that the famous Council of Aachen under Louis the Pious is cited in it, whereas Paul ceased to live in the eighth century. Trithemius attributes the same work to Ruthard, a monk of Hirsau and a pupil of Rabanus and Strabo; Menard attributes it to Ruthard of the monastery of the Blessed Mary of the Hermitage in Switzerland. But the author was neither German nor Swiss, since he mentions his monastery in France more than once.

Our Mabillon also found it in the monastery of Reichenau with this inscription: “Here begins the exposition of Basil, abbot, on the Rule of Saint Benedict, abbot, at first.” But many Gallican manuscript copies prove it to be the genuine work of Hildemar, especially the very ancient copy from the library of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, written about eight hundred years ago, which bears this inscription at its head: “Here begins the tradition concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict, which Master Hildemar the monk handed down and taught to his disciples.”

The letter of Hildemar himself supports this attribution; it is reproduced in full in chapter 38. Add that, in chapter 14, when discussing the feasts of the saints, he gives as examples the feasts of Saints Ambrose, Protasius and Gervasius, Nabor, Nazarius and Celsus—the saints of the diocese of Milan, over which Angilbert presided and who had summoned Hildemar from France. Finally, this commentary is praised under the name of Hildemar in the *Customs of the Roman Monastery of Saint Paul*, written six hundred years ago. No doubt should therefore remain that the commentary circulated under the name of Paul the Deacon ought to be restored to Hildemar, its genuine author.

Not long afterward, toward the end of the ninth century, Hugbold, a monk of Elnone who had been placed by Archbishop Fulco in charge of the schools at Rheims, composed an exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict by collecting into one work various sayings of the holy Fathers. The manuscript is preserved in the famous monastery of Saint-Amand in Belgium.

During the following two centuries, the tenth and eleventh, scarcely any interpreter of the Benedictine Rule can be found. For Saint Dunstan and Saint Æthelwold, who are listed, should be said to have revised and corrected the Rule, or translated it into the English language, rather than expounded it. At the end of the eleventh century, however, Blessed Theuzo, a disciple of John Gualbert and abbot of Saint Paul of Razzolo, wrote a commentary on the same Rule, which is preserved in manuscript in the rich library of the grand duke of Tuscany.

The twelfth century was somewhat more productive. In it four expositors of our Rule, distinguished alike in piety and learning, present themselves to us: Rupert, abbot of the monastery of Deutz near Cologne, a man instructed in the divine Scriptures by the Holy Spirit through a vision; Peter the Deacon, a Cassinese monk and librarian; Saint Hildegard, the first abbess of Mount Saint Rupert at Bingen in the diocese of Mainz, well known to Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, whose writings were read before Pope Eugene III, Saint Bernard, the bishops, and the cardinals, and confirmed at the assembly of Trier; and finally Master Stephen of Paris.

The first two, Rupert and Peter, wrote four books on this subject. Saint Hildegard wrote one brief book, and Stephen of Paris likewise one, which he dedicated to Roffredo of Insula, cardinal priest of Saints Marcellinus and Peter, abbot of the Cassinese monastery, and to his brothers. This work, written by hand, is preserved in the Ursinian monastery of Germany near Augsburg.

We might add Edmund Stoutton, a monk of Glastonbury, and William Peraldus of the Order of Preachers and bishop of Lyon, who are said in Possevin’s *Sacred Apparatus* to have written expositions of the Rule of Saint Benedict. But William’s work is nothing other than an excellent treatise on the profession of monks, divided into three parts, which was published at Paris in 1512 together with John Nider’s treatise *On the Reform of Religious*. It exists in manuscript in the library of Saint-Germain-des-Prés under the name of William of Poitiers; in the libraries of Jumièges and Lyre it is without an author’s name.

I now come to the Cassinese writers Bernard, Nicholas, and Richard of Saint Angelo, to whom we may add Peter Boherius, bishop of Orvieto, since he had at one time lived at Cassino and Subiaco.

Bernard, a Frenchman by birth, learned and devoted to the study of the sacred Scriptures, a zealous lover of regular discipline, subtle in intellect, ready in counsel, sound in judgment, and clear and orderly in speech, as Trithemius says, was first a monk and abbot of the monastery of Saint-Honorat at Lérins in Gaul. Later, by order of Pope Urban IV, he was appointed, in place of a certain Theodinus, a Cassinese monk elected bishop of Acerra, and by command of Manfred, prince of Taranto, he became the fifty-ninth abbot of the Cassinese monastery in the year 1263, as Arnold Wion writes. Later, having become a cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, and at the request of Thomas, dean, and the Cassinese brothers, he wrote an excellent commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict. His successors valued it so highly that Peter Boherius transcribed it almost word for word in his first commentary, and John de Précis, abbot of Saint-Germain in Paris, rendered it into French. We too have made use of that translation on several occasions.

Nicholas of Fractura, called by Arnold Wion Nicholas of Saint-Germain, a doctor of both laws and first a Cassinese monk and afterward abbot of the monastery of Saint Vincent near the Volturno, wrote in the year of the Lord 1299 a sufficiently clear and learned exposition of the Rule of our holy father Benedict according to canon and civil law, as the same Arnold testifies. The manuscript we used ends as follows:

“Here ends the exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict according to Nicholas, abbot of Saint Vincent, doctor of decrees, which he expounded in the Cassinese monastery in the year of the Lord 1299, under Abbot Gallard, who at that time governed the Cassinese monastery.

“This book has been written; blessed be its expounder:

“As the rose is the flower of flowers, so this book is the book of books.”

I find three commentators on our Rule named Richard of Saint Angelo. One was a Cassinese abbot, according to Placid of Cassino, a Cassinese monk, in the supplement to his *Illustrious Men of His Monastery*; he was made a cardinal by Gregory IX in the year 1240. Another was a Cassinese monk and later, during the time of Pope Celestine V, abbot of Saint Justina of Padua; his work was at times praised by Paul Augustine of Genoa. The third was likewise a Cassinese monk and provost of Vallis Lucis, as well as chaplain to Landulf of Saint Angelo, cardinal deacon, to whom he also dedicated his book. I was unable to examine the works of the first two, but only that of the third. In his commentary I found several chapters left untouched, as though they were known to everyone or were to be explained by more learned men, as he himself says—namely, chapters 8 through 19.

Peter Boherius, doctor of decrees, first abbot of the monastery of Saint-Agnan in the diocese of Saint-Pons-de-Thomières and afterward bishop of Orvieto, published two expositions of the Rule of Saint Benedict after the middle of the fourteenth century. One was written at the request of his brothers, which he offered to the abbots presiding at the provincial chapter for correction and emendation. Trithemius writes of it as follows: “Peter Boherius wrote on the Rule of our holy father Benedict a work certainly laborious and commendable, in which he shows that the Rule itself agrees with the law and the canons in almost every word.”

But since in this work he had somewhat neglected the teachings of the holy Fathers, after becoming bishop he composed another from various sayings of Saints Pachomius, Basil, Jerome, Cassian, and from the Lives of the Fathers. He began to subscribe this work in the sacred cave of Saint Benedict, with his body placed there and the light of a candle supplied, trembling as he wrote. He dedicated this second commentary to Charles, king of France. In the prefatory letter to that same Charles are these words:

“I therefore ask you, our hero and illustrious prince, to receive this same Rule of the monks, newly commented upon through the saving sayings of the holy Fathers by me, the most humble ambassador of your majesty, in the cave where Benedict himself is said to have issued it and in which he is said to have long remained for the sake of penance. And although you have no need of it, I beg you to extend your sacred right hand with it to the venerable abbot of Saint-Denis and to his sacred community, my fathers in Christ and brothers especially dear to me through true charity and equal profession.”

The verses placed at the beginning of the book itself show that Peter also sent the same work to the monks of Subiaco.

The Cassinese are followed immediately by several most learned and eminent writers from Germany who applied themselves to expounding the Rule of Saint Benedict. Among them was John of Castell, a monk in the Upper Palatinate near Amberg, of whom Trithemius writes: “John, a monk of Castell in the diocese of Eichstätt, a man very devoted to the divine Scriptures and not unfamiliar with secular literature, subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech, published several considerable volumes worthy of reading. Among them are said to be these: Two books on the Rule of Saint Benedict,” and so forth. According to Wion, this was in the year 1390. His exposition is preserved in manuscript in the monastery of Saint Peter at Salzburg. At its end there is a gloss on the Rule by the same author, which perhaps ought to be regarded as his second book.

John Keck of Tegernsee, a monk in Bavaria and a particularly learned man who also took part in the Council of Basel, where he delivered an address before the supreme pontiff, likewise composed a learned commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict. He dedicated it to Gaspar of Granden, abbot; it is preserved in manuscript in the library of Tegernsee.

John Ulitpacher, a monk of Melk in Austria, also contributed a work. His composition is preserved in manuscript in the library at Weingarten with this inscription: “Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, by John Ulitpacher, a monk of Melk, after the reform of his monastery—that is, after the year 1420, when the monastery of Melk was reformed.”

There is also in the library of Tegernsee a commentary by another John, likewise a monk of Melk, called Schlippacher, whose title runs as follows: “A traveling manual on the Rule of our holy father Benedict, published by the venerable Father and Master John Schlippacher, a professed monk of the monastery of Melk. Do this and you will live.”

Chrysostom, abbot of Upper Altach, used this work in the exposition which, as he himself says, he collected from various distinguished men who had written on the same Rule: Bernard, abbot of Cassino; Stephen of Paris; Abbot Hildemar; the most reverend Lord John, cardinal called of Torquemada; Master John Keck of Tegernsee; John of Castell; and John Schlippacher of Melk, professors of the said Rule. This work is also held in the monastery of Scheyern, written in the year 1491 on the day of Saint Mark the Evangelist.

John Trithemius, abbot of Sponheim, a man of no ordinary piety and learning, published his commentary shortly after the year 1484, when he was first made abbot. This work displays the man’s profound learning and his wide reading of the holy Fathers. Unfortunately, it is abridged—a matter that cannot be sufficiently regretted—and contains only seven chapters with a prologue. Yet in them one can scarcely desire anything better or stronger for kindling and nourishing devotion to religious discipline.

We might add quite a few Spanish authors who likewise applied their pen to this subject. Besides the aforementioned Cardinal of Torquemada, if we believe Manrique, at the general chapter of the reformed congregation of the Cistercian Order in the year 1557, Ludovicus de Estrada, a distinguished preacher of the word of God, was charged to publish commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict for abbots to use in explaining it at private chapters. When he presented them in Spanish at the general assembly of 1560, he was ordered to translate them into Latin, “worthy to be read throughout the whole world,” as Manrique says.

From the same congregation, Ludovicus Bernardus de Quiros, the twenty-first general reformer, also wrote twelve books of *The Monastic Republic*, or *Commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict*. Nevertheless, Nicholas Bravus, abbot of the monastery of Oliva in the same congregation, asserts in his literal notes—which he printed at Oliva in 1648 for the genuine understanding of the Rule and the obligation of conscience, together with a *Lacinia* against the opinions of John Caramuel—that these books do not exist.

From the congregation of Valladolid we have two superior generals, one of whom wrote on the Rule of Saint Benedict in Latin and the other in Spanish. The first was Antonius Perezius, later bishop of Urgell and afterward archbishop of Tarragona; the second was Alphonsus de San-Vitorez, a man of no small merit.

Finally, to finish briefly, it is not useful to mention Theobald Artaldus, Peter Crespetius of the Celestines, and Matthias Lambert, prior of the monastery of Alne, who published three French expositions of the Rule; nor John Berthelius, John Craesbreck, Columbanus Urancus, and several others, whose catalogue Benedict Haeften compiled in his *Monastic Inquiries*. As for John Caramuel, although we have quoted his words on several occasions, far from recommending him, we think that he deserves complete oblivion.

The case of Gerard, a Belgian monk, is different. Gabriel Bucelin published his pious and devout little commentary, with notes, in the monastery of Saint Gall. Nor, I think, should Julian Warner, general of the Cistercian Order of Strict Observance, be deprived of his due praise. Besides his French book *On the Ancient Practice of the Rule of Saint Benedict*, printed at Paris in 1645, Julian of Paris, abbot of Mont-Faucon, cites a further commentary on the same Rule by him.

Nor does the work of Paul Augustine of Genoa, a monk of the Cassinese congregation who revised the same Rule according to Cassinese manuscripts and adorned it with most learned notes, seem wholly contemptible.

To all these I add two men who ought to be preferred by far to the others: Hugh Menard and Benedict Haeften, men worthy of eternal memory. The former, originally a monk of Saint-Denis in France, gave his name to the congregation of Saint-Maur out of zeal for stricter observance. He united learning with piety so completely that he ought to be numbered not only among the most perfect practitioners of the monastic life but also among the most learned writers of our age; he was richly supplied with ecclesiastical, monastic, and secular learning.

Among the many works he published, he made the *Concordia of Rules* of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, available to the public. He collated it with several manuscript copies and illuminated it with the most exacting notes. All who afterward wrote anything of importance on the Benedictine Rule drew from this source, especially Charles Cointius, a priest of the Oratory of the Lord Jesus, in his observations on the same Rule, which he inserted in full in volume I of the *Ecclesiastical Annals of France*.

Benedict Haeften, provost of the monastery of Affligem, was deeply experienced in monastic matters, as his twelve books of *Monastic Inquiries* prove. It is a work especially worthy of praise and useful; if one were to remove or correct certain things in it, I do not know whether one could seek anything more excellent on the Rule of Saint Benedict.

He also published a commentary on the life of Saint Benedict and several other works, all equally breathing sincere piety and uncommon learning. Charles Stengelius, abbot of Anhausen, had his *Monastic Inquiries* reduced to an abridgment and printed at Augsburg. His epitome could especially suffice for those who have no leisure at all to read Haeften’s lengthy works attentively.

I have chosen to pass over in silence commentators on the Rule who are still alive, lest anyone should perhaps think that I had not shown sufficient consideration for their reputation or modesty. Nor do I claim that I have mentioned all the deceased. I freely admit that the care and diligence of many of them, especially those preserved in manuscript, have escaped me.

Some years ago our Mabillon had intended to print six commentaries that had not yet been published and to make from them a continuous, almost chainlike commentary on the Rule. But when he learned that I was meditating on something concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict, he, being occupied with greater and more useful matters, urged me at least to attempt to publish their agreement. I have tried to accomplish this with the greatest possible thoroughness, drawing both on those works and on many more already published, as well as countless other approved authors, so that nearly everything of any importance contained in them might be included in this single commentary of ours.

To all this I added the practice that I was able to discover in ancient monastic rules, in the oldest and more recent statutes, customs, and ordinances of monasteries, whether handwritten or printed, and in various acts and histories of the saints. If I have erred in this matter—as is human—or if something has perhaps slipped from me through carelessness, I beg candid readers, in their kindness, to forgive my faults and correct and amend my errors. They will always find me ready immediately and sincerely to agree with those who teach what is more certain.

Finally, so that nothing belonging to me might be lacking in this work, I took care to correct the text of the holy Rule against numerous manuscript copies, especially against the oldest of all, written a thousand years ago in uncial letters. Its variant readings were sent from the Bodleian Library at Oxford in England to our distinguished Mabillon by Edward Bernard. I also consulted the copy written at Narbonne nine hundred years ago, whose variant readings, as well as those of another six-hundred-year-old copy from the monastery of Saint-Savin at Tarbes, were recorded by our Claude Estiennot.

I consulted five others as well: two from Saint-Germain-des-Prés in Paris; a third from Saint-Corneille at Compiègne; a fourth from Saint-Pierre at Conques; and a fifth from Blessed Mary of Lyre. Assistance was also provided by the text of the holy Rule quoted by the ancient commentators, especially Hildemar and Smaragdus of the monastery of Fleury, whose manuscripts approach at least eight hundred years of age. The *Concordia of Rules* of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, ought to have preceded them.

Nor did it seem right to disregard the old editions—the Venetian edition of 1489 and the Parisian edition—as well as the more recent editions of Baldwin Moreau, Hugh Menard, Benedict Haeften, and Paul Augustine of Genoa, a Cassinese monk, since they themselves corrected the Rule most diligently against several manuscript copies. Both their editions and their variant readings brought considerable light and assistance to my efforts. I have thought it useful to give readers this brief preliminary notice.

[Col. 0213]

# TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING THE RULE OF OUR HOLY FATHER BENEDICT

### From Book II of the *Dialogues* of Pope Saint Gregory, chapter 36

[Col. 0213B]

But I do not want you to be unaware that the man of God Benedict, amid all the miracles by which he shone forth in the world, also shone forth no less through the word of his teaching. For he wrote a Rule for monks distinguished above all by discretion and brilliant in expression. If anyone wishes to know more precisely his character and way of life, he can find all the actions of his teaching in that same institution of the Rule, because the holy man could in no way teach otherwise than he lived.

### From the Council of Autun, held under Saint Leodegarius in the year 670, canon 15

Concerning abbots and monks, it is fitting that they observe the following: whatever the canonical order or the Rule of Saint Benedict teaches, they must fulfill and preserve in every respect. For if all these things are lawfully maintained by the abbots and monasteries, then, with God’s favor, the number of monks will increase, and the whole world will be free from harmful contagions through their continual prayers.

### From the book of Saint Ambrose Autpertus, *On the Conflict of the Vices*, at the end of volume VI of the new edition of the works of Saint Augustine

[Col. 0213C]

Always strive to live according to the rule of the Fathers, but especially according to that of the holy confessor Benedict. Do not deviate from it in anything, nor add anything to it; for it contains everything that is sufficient. Its words and commands lead its followers to the palaces of heaven.

### From the exhortation of the emperor Louis the Pious to Eigil, elected abbot of Fulda, in his Life by Candidus, book I, in the fourth century of the Benedictine era

Saint Benedict, filled with the Holy Spirit, composed the Rule of monks with great discretion.

### Likewise from the same work, in the same place

The man of God Benedict composed the Rule in brilliant language. It contains nothing of hidden doctrine, nothing obscure; therefore it does not require exposition but admonition. For this is the narrow gate and the constricted way that leads those who follow it to God. Indeed, it teaches you to possess discretion, moderation, and charity to such a degree that, even while exhorting with charity, you may prevail in cutting out the vices themselves; that you may do everything with moderation for the sake of the fainthearted; that you may keep before your mind the discretion of Saint James; and that in all these matters you may always recall your own frailty to yourself.

### From the Second Council of Douzy, held in the year 874
