Blessed in grace and name, Benedict, inspired by the Holy Spirit, says in his Rule things consonant with the sacred Scriptures and with the preaching of other orthodox Fathers.

### Likewise from the same Council

The Holy Spirit, through blessed Benedict, issued the Rule of monks by the same Spirit by whom the sacred canons were issued.

### From a letter of Leo, archbishop of Ravenna, to Durandus the monk
Saint Benedict, taught by that same Holy Spirit, knowing by God’s revelation that he was soon to pass from this light, wrote out this Rule with his blessed hands at the request of his disciple Maurus and handed it to him, so that he might know perfectly how to instruct himself and his disciples.

Also in the same place

But you, dearest brother, do not follow a rejected interpretation; imitate instead the chosen Rule, issued by the chosen holy Benedict, dictated by the holy and devout Spirit, praised by the illustrious teacher and supreme pontiff, and imitated by perfect men. It leads its followers to the kingdom of heaven.

From John the monk, in the Life of Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny

He explained to the monks the treasures hidden in observance of the Rule, and taught by his own example and that of many others that no part of it is imprudent for the wise, useless for the diligent, difficult for the believer, or harsh for the penitent.

From the exhortation of Saint Benedict, abbot of Chusa, reported in chapter 4 of his Life

Therefore I exhort your brotherhood, laying aside certain superstitions and human institutions that are irrelevant to the matter and contrary to true religion, to direct your minds purely toward the study of the Rule of our holy father Benedict, in which all evangelical and apostolic perfection consists.

From book 13, chapter 7, of Peter Damian’s Opusculum

The holy Rule has become like a broad, capacious, and beautiful house, able to receive every kind of person: children and old men, the strong and the weak, the delicate, and those differing greatly from one another in the manifold variety of their character.

From a sermon of Gaufridus, abbot of Vendôme, on Saint Benedict

[Col. 0215A]

There were abbots and institutions of abbots before Saint Benedict, just as Moses existed as a legislator before Christ. Moses indeed brought a good and holy law to the Jewish people; but just as Christ conferred a better law upon the Christian people, so the holy men of that age established monastic laws according to the grace given them by God. But our father and lawgiver Benedict, just as he received greater grace from God, so instituted a better law. For whatever those men prescribed to be done, whether less or more, or permitted to be done, he corrected after them.

From book VI, chapter 2, sermon 4, of the Sentences of Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni

What shall I say of blessed Benedict, who made for us so remarkable a well—for by the well he means the Rule—whose most healthful and sweetest water benefits the refreshment and salvation of all who thirst and desire to drink? No well has been made after the Apostles and Evangelists that has satisfied so many people and freed them from the danger of death and from every affliction of the soul.

A saying of Richard, prior of Fontaines in the diocese of York, reported in a letter of Thurstan, archbishop of York, to William, bishop of Canterbury

Whatever blessed Benedict instituted was so entirely arranged by the providence of the Holy Spirit that nothing more useful, nothing holier, and nothing more felicitous could have been devised.

From sermon 4 of Guerric, abbot, on Saint Benedict

Moses, because of the hardness of the Jews’ hearts, gave them ordinances that were not good, apart from a few moral precepts. Saint Benedict handed down only evangelical purity and a simple discipline of conduct. Moses writes so many things difficult to understand, impossible or useless to perform; Benedict writes the most upright Rule of life, lucid in expression and outstanding in discernment.

From a homily on the Gospel “Behold, we” by Gauffridus, notary of Saint Bernard and later abbot of Clairvaux

What the Rule of our blessed Father taught, the reading of the Gospel commends to us; and the herald of truth proclaimed nothing other than what Truth itself had taught beforehand.

From a letter of Odo, a monk of Canterbury, to his brother Adam, a novice at Igny, in *Veterum Analecta*, vol. I, p. 349

[Col. 0216A]

O marvelous mystery, and marvelous sacrament! God first gave a testament in the hearts of human beings, which was called the natural law; if they had kept it, they would not have needed a second. But because human beings are lovers of novelties, when the first testament had grown old through neglect, he gave a second in circumcision, which some embraced somewhat more willingly because of its novelty. But when this too had grown old and been neglected, he gave a third in baptism, predestined to remain forever. But because, after growing old through long custom, it began gradually to be led by human beings into neglect, he gave a fourth in the monastic cowl, toward whose novelty almost the whole world, now a lover of novelties, is flocking. After this there will be no fifth, because in this new and marvelous form are contained the blessings of all nations. For whatever religion and holiness are contained in the three preceding testaments is all gathered together in the testament of Benedict.

From Saint Hildegard’s *Life of Saint Disibod*

For Saint Benedict, the holy Father, had composed the Rule suited to spiritual people from the Lives of the Saints, with the Holy Spirit teaching and revealing it.

From her commentary on the Rule of our holy father Benedict

Saint Benedict himself wrote his teaching in fear and piety, in charity and chastity. Nothing should be added to or taken away from this teaching, because it lacks nothing, since it was made and completed by the Holy Spirit.

The Rule of Saint Basil is sufficiently intricate. The Rule of Saint Augustine is very general and descends little into particulars. [Col. 0215]

## The Rule of Our Holy Father Benedict, with Commentaries (C, S)

### Prologue

[Col. 0215D] **1. “Listen,”** [Note: [Col. 0215D] Older manuscripts read *obsculta*.] **O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart. Receive willingly the admonition of a loving Father and fulfill it effectively, so that through the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom through the laziness of disobedience you had withdrawn.**

“Therefore my word is now addressed to you,” [Note: [Col. 0215D] Oxford manuscript: *dirigetur*, “will be addressed.”] whoever renounces your own wills [Col. 0216D] [Note: [Col. 0215D] Another reading: *voluptatibus*, “pleasures.”] and, intending to serve Christ the Lord, the true King, take up the strongest and most splendid weapons of obedience [Note: [Col. 0216D] *Obedientiae* is absent in the Oxford manuscript]. Above all, whenever you begin any good work that must be done, ask him with the most urgent prayer to bring it to completion, so that he who has already deigned to count us among his children may never have cause to be saddened by our evil deeds. [Col. 0217A] For we must at all times obey him concerning his good gifts in us, so that he may not only, as an angry father, ever disinherit his children [Note: [Col. 0217D] Another reading: *iratus*, “angry.”], but also, as a master to be feared, become provoked by our evil deeds and hand us over, as utterly wicked servants, to everlasting punishment because we would not follow him to glory. [Note: [Col. 0217D] Oxford manuscript: “provoked by our evils.”]

Let us rise, then, at last, since Scripture rouses [Note: [Col. 0217D] Another reading: *exhortante*, “exhorting.”] us and says: “It is now the hour for us to rise from sleep” (Romans XV). And with our eyes opened to the deifying light, let us listen with astonished ears to what the divine voice cries out daily to admonish us, saying: “Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts” (Psalm XCIV). And again: “Whoever has ears to hear, let him hear what the Spirit says to the churches” (Apocalypse II). And what does it say? “Come, children, hear me; I will teach you the fear of the Lord” (Psalm XXXIII). “Run while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you” (John XI).

And the Lord, seeking among the multitude of the people the worker to whom he cries [Note: [Col. 0217D] Oxford manuscript: *exclamat*, “cries out.”] these things, says again: “Who is the man who desires life and longs to see good days?” (Psalm XXXIII). If you, hearing this, answer, “I do,” God says to you: “If you wish to have life, restrain your tongue from evil and your lips from speaking deceit. Turn away from evil and do good; seek peace and pursue [Note: [Col. 0217D] Another reading: *persequere*, “pursue earnestly.”] it. And when you have done these things, my eyes will be upon you and my ears attentive to your prayers” (Isaiah LXV); “and before you call upon me, I will say to you, ‘Behold, I am here.’” What could be sweeter to us than this voice of the Lord inviting us, dearest brothers? Behold, in his mercy the Lord shows us [Col. 0217C] the way of life.

Therefore, with the loins of our faith or observance [Note: [Col. 0217D] Oxford manuscript: “the loins of faith or observance.”] girded and our feet shod [Note: [Col. 0217D] Another reading: “our feet shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace”; another: “shod in readiness for the Gospel of peace.”] (Ephesians VI), let us proceed along his paths under the guidance of the Gospel [Note: [Col. 0217D] *Per ducatum Evangelii* is absent in Hildem.], so that we may deserve to see him who has called us in his kingdom. If we wish to dwell in the tent of that kingdom, we shall certainly not arrive there unless we run there by good works [Note: [Col. 0218D] Another reading: *curratur*, “one must run.”]. But let us ask the Lord with the prophet, saying to him: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tent, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Psalm CXXXVI). After this question, brothers [Note: [Col. 0218D] Oxford manuscript: “dearest brothers.”], let us hear the Lord answering and showing us the way to his tent, saying: “He who enters without blemish and practices justice, who speaks truth in his heart, who has not acted deceitfully with his tongue, who has done no evil to his neighbor, who has not accepted reproach against his neighbor” (Psalm XIV). He is the one who, rejecting from the sight of his heart the wicked devil when he suggests something to him, together with the suggestion itself, has reduced it to nothing; he has taken hold of the devil’s little thoughts and dashed them [Col. 0218A] against Christ. He is the one who, fearing the Lord, does not become elated because of his good observance, but, believing that the good within him is accomplished not by himself but by the Lord, magnifies the Lord who works within him, saying with the prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory” (Psalm CXIII). Thus the Apostle Paul did not attribute anything of his preaching to himself, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am” (I Corinthians XV). And again he says: “Let whoever glories, glory in the Lord” (II Corinthians X).

Therefore the Lord also says in the Gospel: “Everyone who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man who built his house upon a rock. The rivers came, the winds blew, and they struck that house, and it did not fall, for it had been founded upon a rock” (Matthew VII). [Col. 0218B] The Lord, bringing these things to completion, waits every day for us to answer his holy admonitions with our deeds. Therefore, for the correction of our evil ways, the days of this life are prolonged for us as a respite, as the Apostle says: “Do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?” (Romans II). For the merciful Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should turn and live” (Ezekiel XVIII).

When, therefore, brothers, we had asked the Lord about the inhabitant of his tent, we heard the precept concerning dwelling there [Note: [Col. 0218D] Oxford manuscript: *habitantis*, “of the one dwelling there.”]. If we fulfill the duty of an inhabitant, we shall be heirs of the kingdom of heaven. [Note: [Col. 0218D] From here to the end, these words are lacking in the Oxford manuscript.] Therefore our hearts and bodies must be prepared to serve in the holy obedience of the precepts [Note: [Col. 0218D] Another reading: “which must be served.”]; and whatever our nature finds less possible in us, let us ask the Lord to command the assistance of his grace to be provided for us [Note: [Col. 0218D] Lyranus: “to be provided by assistance.”]. And if, fleeing the punishments of hell, we wish to reach everlasting life, while there is still time and we are in this body, while there is opportunity to fulfill all these things during this life of light [Note: [Col. 0218D] Another reading: “this way of light.”], we must run and act now in the manner that will benefit us forever.

We must therefore establish a school of the Lord’s service, in which we hope to establish nothing harsh, nothing burdensome. Yet if, in accordance with the demands of equity, something a little more restrictive should arise for the correction of faults or the preservation [Note: [Col. 0218D] Another reading: “the conduct.”] of charity, do not immediately, terrified by fear, flee the way of salvation, which cannot be begun except by a narrow beginning (Matthew VII). As our way of life and faith progress, with the heart enlarged, we run along the way of God’s commandments with the indescribable sweetness of love. Thus, never departing from his instruction, but persevering in the monastery in his teaching until death, we may share in the sufferings of Christ through patience [Note: [Col. 0218D] Another reading: “that we may share.”], and may deserve to be companions in his kingdom.

## Commentary

[Col. 0219]

### “Listen, O son”

Here Saint Benedict, our holy Father, addresses all who observe his holy Rule. He calls them by the gentle name of “son” chiefly for four reasons, saying: “Listen, O son.”

First, because he became the spiritual father of as many sons as he brought forth for God as monks through his holy institution. For, as Saint Dorotheus says (*Doctrine* 4, no. 6), “Holy men call those whom they have converted from wickedness and evil to virtue and good fruit by their word and preaching ‘sons,’ as the Apostle says: ‘My little children, for whom I am again in labor until Christ is formed in you.’” Hence Saint Basil also wants those who have begotten us for God in this manner to be acknowledged as true parents: “He will recognize as true parents,” he says, “those from whom one who is such—that is, a monk—has been born in Christ Jesus through the Gospel” (*Long Rules*, chapter 8).

Second, because those who follow his Rule also follow his life; and according to the universally accepted rule of the holy Fathers, those should be considered true sons of the saints who imitate their examples. “These are sons of the saints,” says Jerome, “who perform their works” (*Letter to Heliodorus*). And Augustine says: “Every person is the son of the one whose works he does. Therefore, if we do the works of God, we are sons of God” (*Sermon 286). Thus Christ also rebuked the Jews who loudly proclaimed themselves sons of Abraham, although they did not follow Abraham’s faith and life, saying: “If you are Abraham’s sons, do the works of Abraham” (John VIII). Augustine—or whoever else wrote the passage—says again: “Let the actions of offspring reveal the likeness of their father; let the likeness of the work reveal the likeness of their descent” (*Appendix to Sermon 312*).

Third, in order to demonstrate toward all a singular and truly paternal affection, and so that, if some have perhaps become childish in understanding—for he is not addressing only those who have already reached the summit of monastic perfection, but especially those who are beginning to climb it, indeed those who propose it to themselves—if such people should be so deterred by the rigor of discipline that they flee its yoke as too harsh and burdensome, he may kindle them to undertake it bravely by so gentle and mild an address. Thus, following a familiar human custom, people are accustomed to call little ones, and all whom they wish to draw toward what they desire, “sons.” The ancient monks also sometimes used this name, perhaps as a sign of that childlike simplicity which true imitators of monastic perfection profess; this is evident throughout the *Lives of the Fathers*.

Fourth and finally, Saint Benedict calls his people sons because he wished not to exercise supreme authority over them as a master, but to govern them like a devoted father and lead them to the eternal joys of heaven.

### “The precepts of the master”

By “precepts” he means those things contained throughout the Rule, such as voluntary poverty, abstinence from meat, almost perpetual silence, and other things of this kind. For secular people these are admonitions, but for us monks they have become precepts. “All the institutions of Saint Benedict,” says Saint Bernard (*On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 1), “except, of course, certain spiritual matters—for example, charity, humility, and gentleness—which are not so much instituted by him as by God and therefore must not be changed at all—are otherwise to be regarded by those who have not professed them as mere admonitions or counsels, whereas for those who have professed them they become precepts, and for those who transgress them, crimes. Or, to give you your own terms, they are rightly regarded by the former as voluntary or self-imposed, and by the latter as necessary and, so to speak, natural.”

### “And incline the ear of your heart”

That is, understand what I am now about to say. The ear of the heart is understanding. “The ear,” says Smaragdus, “is called from hearing or drawing in; the bodily ear of a human being receives voices, but the ear of the heart draws in the meaning of speech.” Indeed, the bodily ear is struck in vain unless the external sound of words reaches the inner understanding of the heart. Or the ear of the heart is affection, desire, and readiness to hear, so that to incline the ear of the heart means nothing other than to hear the teacher’s precepts with the whole eagerness of the mind, with complete desire, and with the greatest attention of the soul.

### “And willingly receive the admonition of a loving Father”

“Willingly” means voluntarily and wholeheartedly, with great joy. Receive the admonitions of a loving Father in such a way that no forgetfulness can ever erase them.

Some ask who that master is whose precepts the holy legislator commands us to hear, and who that loving Father is whose counsels he commands us to receive willingly. Some answer that it is none other than the Holy Spirit himself, under whose inspiration and dictation Saint Benedict wrote his holy Rule. And indeed, who could believe that a man of such humility as Saint Benedict undoubtedly was wished to claim for himself the title of loving Father and master? This is especially so since Christ in the Gospel forbade his disciples to call anyone on earth their father or to be called masters, since we have one Father in heaven and one master.

On this matter we should hear Peter Damian speaking of Saint Benedict in these words (*Opusculum* 13, chapter 6): “This is clearly gathered at the beginning of the book if one carefully considers to whom the Holy Spirit directs his words. I say, to the Holy Spirit; for surely a holy man and such a devoted practitioner of humility would not suddenly burst into these words and arrogate to himself the chair of teaching and, above all, the privilege of a loving Father, saying: ‘Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master, and incline the ear of your heart, and willingly receive the admonition of a loving Father.’ Rather, he made himself the servant and instrument of another’s voice—of him who likewise, at the beginning of the prophetic utterance, began to cry out through Isaiah: ‘I have nourished and exalted sons.’”

Although Saint Benedict, because of the supreme humility that shone in him, rejected the title both of loving father and of master, everyone nevertheless readily grants it to him because of his supreme holiness and his experience and learning in monastic matters. Among these is Pope Saint Gregory [*Book IV, chapter 4*], or whoever else wrote the commentary on the Books of Kings, where he calls Benedict “the excellent master of the strictest way of life.”

[Col. 0220C]

### “And fulfill it effectively”

This means: overcome whatever difficulty you encounter; once you have heard the Lord’s precepts, carry them out. The excellent master and teacher of the strictest way of life therefore requires three things from his disciples. For just as the principal duties of a teacher are three—to teach, to delight, and to move—so the duties of disciples and hearers are also three: to listen to the teacher, to receive willingly what delights them, and to fulfill effectively what the speaker moves them to do. Saint Augustine seems to have had these three in mind in the passage cited when he says of the teacher: “When he says these things, let him act so that he may be heard intelligently, willingly, and obediently.”

But just as teaching and delighting are insufficient unless the speaker also moves his hearers, so understanding and retaining in memory what has once been heard are useless unless it is fulfilled in action. For it is not the hearers of the law but the doers who will be justified. It would have been far better never to have known the way of life than not to walk in it, for then every excuse ceases and our own conscience makes us guilty. “If I had not come,” Christ says, “and spoken to them, they would not have sin.”

Let us plainly hear the Apostle’s terrifying judgment: “It would have been better for them not to have known the way of righteousness than, after knowing it, to turn back from the holy commandment handed down to them” (II Peter II). God himself says through the prophet that his word shall not return to him empty, but shall prosper and accomplish that for which he sent it (Isaiah LV). Therefore, so that the word of the Lord may not return to him empty, let us strive to fulfill it in good works.

“It shall not return to me empty,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 71 on the Song of Songs*, no. 13), “or fasting, but, acting prosperously in all things, it shall be filled with the good works of those who rest in love of it. Finally, according to common usage, speech is said to be fulfilled when it has been committed to action; until then it is empty, lean, and in a certain sense hungry, until it is filled by the burden of accomplishment.”

Saint Jerome therefore rightly says (*Letter 14 to Celantia*): “Do not think it sufficient for you to retain the commandments of God in memory while forgetting them in your actions. Rather, know them for this purpose: that you may do whatever you have learned must be done. For it is not the hearers of the law who will be righteous, but the doers of the law who will be justified.” And Saint Benedict says: “Fulfill it effectively.”

Someone might perhaps be troubled by the fact that Saint Benedict, addressing all who have professed the holy Rule, nevertheless appears to direct his speech to one person alone when he says: “Listen, O son, to the precepts of the master,” and so forth. By this manner of speaking he commendably signifies the indivisible unity of holy monks: they have one heart and one soul; although they have many bodies, they do not have many hearts. Of them, as Saint Augustine says (*On Psalm CXXXII*), the royal Psalmist sang magnificently: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together as one!” Saint Basil likewise says (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 19): “People moved from various groups and places have been joined together in such perfection of likeness that one soul may be seen in many bodies, and many bodies may be displayed as the instruments of a single soul.”

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, supplies this interpretation for us in these words (*Sermon on Saint Benedict*): “Addressing the flock of monks—as though it were one person because of its single heart, voluntarily obedient through the hearing of the ear—he calls it ‘son.’”

Or it may be because, just as all the faithful of Christ throughout the world constitute only one mystical body, namely the Church, so all monks, although numerous in number and widely diverse in nation, constitute only one body. Some represent the head, others the feet, and others the hands, as Saint Dorotheus teaches (*Doctrine* 6): “What do monasteries seem to you to be? Do they not seem to be one body and mutually members? Those who administer and govern are regarded as occupying the place of the head. Those who watch and correct hold the place of the eyes. Those who benefit others by speech perform the function of the mouth. Those who obey are considered to occupy the place of the ears. Those who perform the work are compared to the hands. Those who give answers and are sent here and there for services fulfill the role of the feet.”

### “So that through the labor of obedience you may return to him from whom through the laziness of disobedience you had withdrawn”

What could be sweeter than this voice, dearest brothers? Behold, here our excellent leader “sets before us the contest, the manner of contending, and the reward of the victor,” as Trithemius says. In the word “labor” he signifies the contest; in “obedience,” the manner; in “return,” the reward.

What could be proposed to us that is sweeter or more useful than a return to God? Indeed, what could be more desirable to God himself? “What does the Lord seek from you,” Saint Augustine says, “except yourself? Since among all earthly creatures he made nothing better than you, he seeks you from yourself, because you had lost yourself.”

By what path shall we return to him? Clearly by no other than the one which the holy legislator indicates here and elsewhere when he says: “Knowing that by this way of obedience they will go to God.” This is the way; let us walk in it.

Thus Peter Damian says (*Sermon on the Exaltation of the Holy Cross*): “Man was driven from that blessed inheritance; he received exile in place of his homeland, death in place of life, and disgrace in place of glory. If, therefore, you wish to return to your inheritance, deny your own will. The denial of the will is therefore the recovery of the inheritance.”

And Saint Bernard says (*Sermon 64 on Various Matters*): “This is the virtue that makes the soul perfectly subject to God live securely beneath the shadow of his wings.”

When Benedict says not simply “obedience” but “the labor of obedience,” he shows that obedience is not an easy matter but a very laborious one. Pope Gregory confirms this in Homily 32 on the Gospel, writing: “Perhaps it is not difficult to leave one’s possessions, but it is very difficult to leave oneself. It is a lesser thing to renounce what one has, but a very great thing to renounce what one is.”

Hence that heavenly saying: “Obedience is better than sacrifices” (I Samuel XV). For, as Saint Gregory says, “Through sacrifices another’s flesh is slain; through obedience one’s own will is slain.”

But lest such great labor frighten us, let us look upon the reward promised for the labor, and every difficulty will easily appear slight. The return to God is promised: “So that through the labor of obedience you may return to him.” O recompense! O reward!

### “From whom through the laziness of disobedience you had withdrawn”

We withdrew from God when, through transgressing the divine commandment, we all sinned in Adam, or when through our own guilt and disobedience we surrendered ourselves to the prince of darkness. He significantly says “the laziness of disobedience.” By these words he teaches that those should truly be considered lazy and sluggish who, transgressing God’s commandments, labor neither for God nor for their own salvation.

Although many people perform many deeds, if they do not refer these deeds to God with a pure and sincere affection of mind, you would more rightly regard them not as works but as the destruction of works. William, abbot of the monastery of Saint-Thierry, writes most aptly to the Carthusian monks (*On the Solitary Life, to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*, chapter 8): “It is not idleness to be free for God; indeed, this is the business of all businesses. Whoever in his cell does not faithfully and fervently do this—whatever else he does, which he does not do for this purpose, namely that God may be served—idles in what he does.”

### “Therefore my word is now addressed to you, whoever renounces your own wills”

Just as no believer is admitted into the Church without first renouncing the devil, his pomp, and his works, so Saint Benedict, our holy Father, did not wish any monk to be introduced into the cloister who had not renounced his own wills, as Bernard of Cassino correctly noted after Hildegarus.

From this it is clear what aim the holy legislator set for himself in the Rule, and what end he proposed: obedience, namely the renunciation of one’s own will. Saint Peter Damian teaches this above all when he says (*Opusculum* 13, chapter 6):

“Let us see, when he begins to write, to whom Saint Benedict directs his words and toward what kind of people he directs the entire force of his coming discourse. For he says: ‘Therefore my word is now addressed to you,’ and so forth.”

Here he reports the entire text of the Rule and then adds:

“From the words of the holy man, therefore, we can gather that the school of this Rule was established more for learning obedience than for performing penance. It does not exclude either sinners or the righteous, nor does it reject any one kind of person; rather, it directs all its force and intention toward teaching the precepts of obedience.”

Since the holy Father had proposed to organize the strongest kind of monks, namely coenobites, he could not have intended any other goal than the very end of coenobitic life. Abbot John, in Cassian, teaches what that end is in these words (*Conferences* 19, chapter 8): “The end of the coenobite is to mortify and crucify all his own wills.”

Severus Sulpicius says (*Dialogues*, book I, chapter 5): “Their first virtue is to obey another’s authority.”

Finally, Jerome, writing about coenobites, says (*Letter 22*): “Their first bond, he says, is to obey their superiors and to do whatever they command.”

The same teaching is found in the Rule of Saint Posthumius, delivered by an angel, no. 1, as it appears in his Life, chapter 8.

Hence scarcely any chapter exists in the entire Rule of our holy father Benedict in which he does not commend obedience in some way. We could demonstrate this easily, unless the most learned Benedict Haeften had already undertaken the task before us in his *Monastic Investigations*, book II, *Monastic Catechism*, part 2, investigation 12.

Thus Christ the Lord also says to Saint Bridget (*Revelations*, book IV, chapter 127): “He is Benedict’s monk who obeys the Rule more than the flesh.”

From all this it is perfectly clear how appropriately John Trithemius said concerning this passage:

“Before all else, as the title of the hearer, he places the renunciation of one’s own will, because no one who still serves his own wills has any part in this Rule. A monk who has not abandoned his own will is not what he is called; indeed, he is one who frustrates God. The first instrument of a monk is the renunciation of his own will, without which no one is a monk. Therefore abandon your own will if you wish to become a monk.”

### “Intending to serve Christ the Lord, the true King”

Are we therefore soldiers, or is our profession a military service? Certainly it is, for “the life of man upon earth is warfare,” and this can be affirmed with even greater right of the life of monks, whose entire life is spent amid conflict and temptation.

Therefore Scripture says: “My son, when you approach the service of God, stand in righteousness and prepare your soul for temptation.” This is so true that Peter of Blois said (*Letter 134*): “I know that scarcely half an hour passes in the cloistered life without temptations.”

Thus we must continually fight: on one side, against the superfluous desires of the world by voluntary poverty; on another, against the pleasures of the flesh by inviolate chastity; on yet another, against the proud suggestions of demons by humble obedience; against the fickleness of an unstable spirit by stability; and finally against every vice by conversion of life. We may plainly say of our monasteries: “These are the camps of God.”

What indeed prevents us from saying this with Peter the Venerable? “The common dwelling of those who live together in the cloister,” he says (*Book I, Letter 20*), “may be compared to the multitude of troops arranged for battle. There each person fights the adversary with greater security the closer an assistance he hopes to receive from the hand of a fellow soldier.”

And elsewhere, writing to Saint Bernard (*Book I, Letter 28*), he says: “You promise that, according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, you will serve as soldiers in the heavenly camps.”

Now in these camps there are two kinds of soldiers, as Haeften observes (*Monastic Catechetical Investigations*, book II, part 2, investigation 3): some who fight in the battle line, and others who enter single combat. The coenobites who serve under a Rule or an abbot belong to the first kind; the anchorites, who, well instructed from the fraternal battle line, descend into the solitary combat of the desert, belong to the second.

### “You take up the strongest and most splendid weapons of obedience”

Saint Benedict calls the weapons of obedience “the strongest,” because in truth nothing is stronger than obedience. With its protection the monk speaks of victories, “since through the good of obedience he triumphs over the devil, the world, and himself in Christ,” as Peter of Blois says (*Letter 134*).

Hence Saint Gregory—or whoever else wrote the passage—says: “When we subject ourselves to human beings for God’s sake, we overcome proud spirits. We attack demons through the other virtues, but through obedience we conquer them. Those who obey are therefore victors, because when they perfectly subject their will to others, they themselves rule over the angels who fell through disobedience.”

Saint John Climacus therefore rightly says (*The Ladder*, step 4): “Just as trees shaken by the winds send their roots deeper, so those who contend under obedience become strong and invincible.”

The weapons of obedience are called not only “strongest” but also “splendid,” because through the victories won over so many and such great enemies they make us splendid and illustrious, turning us into a spectacle wondrous to God, angels, and human beings. Or they are called splendid because nothing is more beautiful than virtue. “Whatever things are virtuous,” says Boherius, “may be called splendid.” He cites Jerome writing to Celantia: “The highest nobility before God is to be splendid in virtues.”

### “Above all”

That is, before and above everything else; or, as Smaragdus explains it, “first,” meaning at the beginning of one’s way of life and of the commencement of a good work. Nevertheless, this manner of speaking by no means excludes the remainder of the life or of the work itself.

### “Whenever you begin any good work that must be done, ask him with the most urgent prayer to bring it to completion”

Saint Benedict does not say this as though he thought that something good could be begun by us independently, as the Semi-Pelagians once wished. For he also commands the disciples, whenever they see some good in themselves, to attribute it to God and not to themselves; and below he introduces God himself as saying: “And before you call upon me, I will say, ‘Behold, I am here.’”

So that he who has deigned already to number us among his children may not at some time be saddened by our evil deeds. Here he gives the reason why, when beginning some good work, we ought to ask God to bring it to completion by earnest prayer: namely, lest God, most justly withdrawing his grace when we do not pray, we should do evil and thus sadden by our evil deeds him who has already deigned to count us among his children. Here he impels us to pray by a twofold motive, one of love, the other of gratitude: of love, so that, as true children, we may fear to offend and sadden God by evil deeds; and of gratitude toward him who has deigned to count us among his children. By these words he also commends both God’s immense goodness toward us and man’s supreme dignity: God’s goodness, since he has deigned to count us among his children. Concerning this the Apostle John says: “See what kind of love God has given us, that we should be called and should be the children of God”; and Smaragdus, on this passage, writes: “Great is the condescension of God the Father! We do not deserve to be numbered among servants, yet he does not disdain to count us among his children. Great, I say, is this condescension: although by nature we are children of wrath and sinners from infancy, we are mercifully called children of God.” He commends also man’s supreme dignity, since although by nature we are children of wrath, by grace we become partakers of the divine nature. Both realities were recognized by the venerable Gerard of Clairvaux, monk and brother of Saint Bernard the abbot. As he himself relates, when Gerard was about to breathe forth his last spirit, he exclaimed (*Sermon 26 on the Song of Songs*, no. 11): “How great is God’s condescension, that he should be Father of men! How great is the glory of men, that they should be children and heirs of God! For if children, then heirs also.”

What is said here about God’s being saddened must not be understood as though the immutable God by nature, in whom there is no change or shadow of alteration, were subject to passions. Rather, because here he addresses human beings, he also speaks in a human manner. And since saddened people commonly withdraw from those who have injured them and deprive them of their customary benefits, so, when God abandons sinners and withdraws the graces that he is accustomed to pour forth, he is said to be saddened, just as he is said to be angry when he punishes.

[Col. 0224C] Thus we must obey him at all times by means of his good things within us.] “To obey” means to serve—to serve him, namely God—and indeed by means of his good things, and to do so at all times. “By means of his good things,” he says; for whatever good we possess, we hold from him whose mercy we are. Hence the familiar saying: “When God crowns our merits, he crowns his own gifts”; and Saint Bernard (*Sermon 23 on the Song of Songs*): “The righteousness of man is God’s indulgence”; and, from Peter Damian (*Sermon 12*): “The works of the righteous are called the Lord’s righteousness, and therefore the righteous themselves are so called, because every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, from the Father of lights. For what do you have that you did not receive?” Therefore let us serve him by the Lord’s good things and gifts. Let us serve him with the body that he has kindly granted us, mortifying its members that are upon the earth, cutting away its superfluous desires, and subjecting the flesh to the spirit, so that we may courageously take upon ourselves Christ’s gentle yoke and his light burden. Let us serve him with the soul, which he created by his will alone, so that, contemplating his supreme perfections in continual meditation, retaining his benefits in our memory, and embracing him with a sincere and intimate gaze of the heart, we may cling continually to the divine Majesty. Let us serve him by his precepts, by his counsels, and by those interior illuminations and impulses that he mercifully inspires in the soul, faithfully carrying out his will so that we may offer the service of our servitude that is owed. 12

And this, as Saint Father Benedict says, is to be done at all times. Smaragdus and the other interpreters commonly understand this after him to mean both in prosperity and in adversity—that is, throughout the whole of life. Here you may rebuke those who believe for a time and withdraw in the time of temptation; who, after spending some period under Christ’s gentle yoke in monasteries, or after being appointed to some office or dignity, then suppose that they have made their own bargain and need not bind themselves to the common exercises of the brethren—a situation that, to our great sorrow, we see in certain monasteries. But Saint Benedict plainly does not speak so, not so; rather, he says, “at all times we must obey the Lord by means of his good things within us.” Therefore, “freed from the hand of our enemies, let us serve him without fear in holiness and righteousness before him all our days,” so that, to speak with Saint Bernard, the term of obedience may be the term of life. Particularly noteworthy in this connection are the words of Hildemar: “It is an excellent admonition when it is said, ‘At all times,’ because where the service of God is mentioned, we are warned that it must be rendered at all times. Human servitude cannot exist at all times, but only for a period of time.”

So that the angry Father may not at some time disinherit his children.] God is said to be angry when he punishes; and he punishes when, as a devoted father, he disinherits wicked children—a most serious punishment, since those who through adoption as children have become heirs of God and fellow heirs with Christ are deprived of the heavenly inheritance as punishment for the offense committed against the Father.

But neither so that the Lord, when provoked by our evil deeds, may, as one to be feared, hand over his most wicked servants to everlasting punishment—those who have been unwilling to follow him into glory.] Similarly, God is here said to be provoked when he hands his most wicked servants over to everlasting punishment—not merely because of sin, but because of sin committed maliciously. “For being provoked is more than being angry,” says Hildemar; “for one who provokes— that is, challenges—causes another to become angry through deliberate evil intention. Anyone who simply sins can cause anger, but the one who acts from an evil will provokes.”

Let us therefore rise at last.] This is a just and legitimate inference from what has preceded. If God is saddened by our evil deeds; if the angry Father disinherits his children; if the Lord, who is to be feared, hands his most wicked servants over to everlasting punishment—what conclusion can be drawn except that these things must be seriously avoided? Therefore, he says, “let us rise at last.” By this manner of speaking he indicates that no time is excluded from repentance. Although it is good for a man to bear the Lord’s yoke from his youth, nevertheless all hope is not therefore entirely to be abandoned if someone postpones his conversion until mature age or even old age. For the master of the household hires workers to be sent into the vineyard even at the eleventh hour and makes them equal in the distribution of rewards to those who have borne the burden and heat of the day. Yet it is altogether dangerous to delay conversion to the Lord for too long, as Saint Augustine teaches (*Sermon 87, on the Scriptures*), and as Saint Father Benedict suggests here. He does not simply say that we should rise, but that we should rise up— that is, rise without delay, as Hildemar explains, or, as Bernard of Cassino and Peter Boherius say, rise with effect.

The Scripture arousing us and saying: “It is now the hour to rise from sleep.” “Now,” that is, at the very time in which I am speaking, without any delay whatsoever. For, as Abbot Germanus says in Cassian (*Conference 17, chapter 5*), “for those striving toward spiritual progress and virtue, even a brief delay is dangerous and harmful”; and, as Saint Ambrose says (*On Luke, book I*), “the grace of the Holy Spirit knows no slow efforts.”

To rise from sleep.] Here “sleep” signifies the torpor of negligence, as Saint Gregory the pope explains (*Book V of the Moralia*, chapter 22).

And with open eyes toward the deifying light.] The deifying light is the Savior Christ himself, who enlightens every person coming into this world and who says of himself: “I am the light of the world.” The deifying light is sacred Scripture itself, concerning which the royal Psalmist says: “Your word is a lamp for my feet.” The deifying light is the teaching of our superiors and teachers, for “those who are learned will shine like the brightness of the firmament, and those who instruct many in righteousness like the stars for everlasting eternities” (*Daniel 12*). Finally, the deifying light is the interior inspiration of the Holy Spirit.

With our eyes therefore opened toward the deifying light—that is, toward Christ, whose example and life show the way of salvation; toward sacred Scripture, whose truth teaches us; toward the admonitions of our superiors, whose exhortations enlighten us; and toward the inspiration of the Holy Spirit himself, whose inward illuminations dispel the darkness of our minds—with our eyes opened, I say, that is, having abandoned our former way of life, shaken off the torpor of the mind, and entirely destroyed vices and sins. “Someone is said to open his eyes when he is freed from sin, because through sin a person is separated from the light, namely Christ,” says Richard of Saint Angelo. Rightly, after saying, “It is the hour to rise from sleep,” he adds, “and with open eyes,” and so forth, because the first action of a person awakened from sleep is to open his eyes.

With attentive ears.] That is, the ears of the mind. “Attentive,” that is, heedful, “as though attentive or astonished at the words of one who thunders, or attentive to the tone,” says Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius after him. Or rather, “astonished” means terrified and, in amazement, marveling at the great kindness of God who calls us.

Let us hear what the divine voice, crying out daily, admonishes us.] We can understand “divine” in two ways: first, as neuter, as though he were saying “divine things,” or things that make God known, so that the meaning would be: “Let us hear what the voice, crying out daily, admonishes us concerning divine things”; second, as feminine, referring “divine” to “voice,” as though it said: “Let us hear what the divine voice, crying out daily, admonishes us.”

The divine voice cries out through the Word of the Father, namely Christ, whose words are found in the Gospel. It cries out through the mouths of the prophets, whose oracles are in the sacred pages. It cries out through the mouths of the apostles, whose teaching is read daily in the Church in their Epistles. 14 It cries out through the life and examples of the saints, whose deeds are recited at the gathering before Compline. It cries out through the exhortations of the holy doctors, according to the saying: “Whoever hears you hears me.” It cries out through creatures, by whose benefit divine things, indeed God himself, become known to us. Finally, it cries out through the mouth of David, saying:

“Today, if you hear his voice, do not harden your hearts.”] Nothing is worse than a hardened heart. Saint Bernard presents us with a faithful likeness of it in these words (*Book I of On Consideration*, chapter 2): “What is a hard heart? It is one that is neither broken by compunction, softened by compassion, nor moved by prayers; it does not yield to threats but grows hard under blows. It is ungrateful toward benefits, faithless toward counsels, savage toward judgments, shameless toward disgraceful things, fearless toward dangers, inhuman toward human beings, reckless toward divine matters; forgetful of the past, neglectful of the present, and unconcerned for the future. It is one for which, of the past, nothing at all passes except injuries; of the present, nothing is lost; and of the future, there is no foresight or preparation except, perhaps, for vengeance. And, to embrace briefly all the evils of this horrible evil, it is one that neither fears God nor reverences man.”

Truly this is a foul image, yet a genuine and vivid one, of the hardened heart, which the sinner displays in himself through a perverse habit of sinning, once heavenly grace has been extinguished. As a result, like the mountains of Gilboa, he receives neither the dew of divine grace nor its rain, nor any illumination from the Sun of righteousness. Or, if some divine ray should happen to shine upon him, it does not soften him but rather hardens his muddy heart, just as Pharaoh’s heart was hardened after the miracles performed by Moses. Therefore, lest so deep an abyss of such misery swallow us up, “today, if you hear the voice of the Lord, do not harden your hearts.”

“For what great recklessness and madness it is,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 23 on Various Matters*), “if, while the Lord of majesty is addressing us, we foolishly turn away our ear and turn our minds to I know not what silly matters! What an injury this is, and how severely it must be avenged, when a most worthless worm disdains to hear the Creator of the universe calling to it! And how great and ineffable is the divine condescension of goodness, which sees us wretched people daily turning away our ears and hardening our hearts, and nevertheless cries out to us!”

And again: “Let anyone who has ears for hearing hear what the Spirit says to the churches.”] “Ears for hearing” are the desire to hear the truth, together with a sincere will to follow it. What the Spirit—that is, the Holy Spirit—says to the churches, means to all Christ’s faithful, from whom, like living stones, the one Church is built. Rabanus notes (*On Matthew*) that “whenever this little admonition—‘Let anyone who has ears for hearing hear’—is inserted, whether in the Gospel or in the Apocalypse of John, what is said is mystical, and something salutary for hearing and learning is being intimated.”

And what does he say? “Come, children, hear me.”] “Come,” namely, with the steps of charity. “Your feet,” says Saint Augustine (*On Psalm 33*), “are your charity; have two feet—do not be lame. What are the two feet? The two commandments of charity, toward God and toward neighbor. With these feet run to God; draw near to him, who himself exhorted you to run.”

“I will teach you the fear of the Lord.”] Entirely rightly, because, as Saint Ambrose says (*Book I on the Hexameron*), “whoever fears the Lord avoids error and directs his steps toward the path of virtue. Unless someone fears God, he cannot renounce sin.” And Saint Bernard (*Sermon 54 on the Song of Songs*): “In truth I have learned that nothing is equally effective for winning, retaining, and recovering grace as being found at all times before God not thinking highly of oneself, but fearing.”

Run.] Very appropriately, after he has introduced the Holy Spirit as calling us to himself, he urges us to run to him who called us. We ought not to approach God with a slow step, but, like giants rejoicing to run their course, since he is impatient of every delay.

While you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you.] These words can bear two interpretations, mystical and literal.

According to the mystical sense, the light of life is grace itself, through which the true way of life is made known to us. Or the light of life is the Lord Christ himself, the true light of the world and the true life of our soul. We possess this light when, through grace, we possess him within our soul and follow his footsteps through a sincere manner of life, just as he himself says: “Whoever follows me will not walk in darkness, but will have the light of life.”

The darkness of death is the blindness of the heart itself, through which miserable people fall into the unhappy pit of sin and consequently into eternal death; for this reason it is called the darkness of death. Or the darkness of death is sin itself, the death of the soul, so called because it drives us wretched people into the outer darkness, where there will be weeping and gnashing of teeth, and separates us from the true light, Christ. Or finally, the darkness of death is the devil. For, as Saint Augustine says (*On Psalm 48, sermon 2*), “The devil is death, not because he himself is death, but because death comes through him.” It is called “the darkness of death” because he is wholly dark and inhabits the darkness of hell.

Thus, in this sense, when Saint Father Benedict says, “Run while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you,” it is the same as if he were saying: While divine grace is available to you, while Christ dwells in your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you, run by means of good works, making your calling sure, lest through your own fault grace, neglected, be withdrawn and Christ depart from you altogether. Thus may blindness of heart plunge you into the depths of vices, and may the devil, and sin itself, overtaking you, cast you as faithless servants into eternal darkness—which may God avert.

According to the literal sense, however, the light of life is the present time, or the very life by which we live; the darkness of death is natural death, which occurs through the separation of the soul from the body. Thus, “run while you have the light of life, lest the darkness of death overtake you,” agrees with the saying: “While we have time, let us do good,” lest, suddenly overtaken by premature death, we seek in vain for an opportunity for repentance.

16 And the Lord, seeking his laborer among the multitude of the people to whom he cries these things.] Here Saint Father Benedict commends the distinguished benefit of the monastic vocation. In these words he especially intimates three things: first, that the Lord himself deigns to call and seek us, worthless servants and servants of sin—“the Lord seeking”; second, that in this matter he has preferred us to so many others, perhaps better than we are—“among the multitude of the people”; and third, that he has done this so that we may labor in the vineyard of so great a master of a household and serve him whose service is to reign—“his laborer.”

The most merciful Lord ordinarily seeks and calls us in three principal ways, which Cassian expresses in these words (*Conference 3, chapter 4*): “The first is from God, the second through a human being, the third from necessity. The first is from God whenever some inspiration sent into our heart awakens us, sometimes even while we are asleep, to desire eternal life and salvation, and urges us through salutary compunction to follow God and cling to his commandments. The second manner of vocation is the one that we said occurs through a human being: when, stirred either by the examples of certain saints or by admonitions, we are kindled with a desire for salvation. The third manner of vocation is that which arises from necessity: when, bound by the riches or pleasures of this world, we are suddenly beset by temptations that threaten the dangers of death, strike us through the loss and confiscation of possessions, or pierce us through the death of loved ones, and are compelled, at least unwillingly, to hasten to the Lord whom, amid prosperity, we scorned to follow.”

Whatever the manner in which God calls us, the condescension of the one who calls is certainly great. Yet nothing so commends the grace of the monastic vocation as what Saint Benedict intimates in these words: “His laborer among the multitude of the people.” He says “his laborer” in the singular, as though he had chosen us not as a few from among the few, but as one from the entire multitude of the people that fills the whole world. Contemplating the greatness of this benefit, Peter Damian exclaims (*Opuscle 52, chapter 2*): “When almighty God withdrew you from the world and established you to serve him under monastic discipline, what else does he appear to have done than, as once in the Flood, to choose you, a few from among the many perishing, and bring you into the hiding place of a pitch-covered ark so that you might live?”

Great indeed is your mercy, good God, that you deigned to save eight souls from the whole multitude of mankind that was perishing; great that you rescued the one Lot together with his two daughters from the flames of burning Sodom; great that you brought two men from the entire nation of Israel into the promised land, while the others perished in the wilderness. Yet, I dare say, greater—far greater—is the mercy by which you chose us from the great number of others and brought us into the enclosure of sacred religion.

For those others were righteous and, if it is lawful to say so, had always deserved well of you: hitherto faithful in all things and promising greater things in the future. We, however, are sinners, unjust, and faithless, promising nothing but sin and misery. What shall we repay the Lord for all that he has bestowed upon us? Let us serve sin no longer, 17 but serve him in newness of life who sought, called, and chose us for this purpose: that, cultivating the garden of sacred religion, we might produce flowers of every kind of virtue and, at last, good fruits to be stored in the heavenly granary.

Again he says: “What man is there who desires life?”] Certainly a blessed life, and an eternal one. For, as Saint Augustine says (*Sermon 84*), “There is no life except blessed life; and blessed life cannot exist unless it is eternal, where the days are good—not many, but one.” Or he may also mean “life,” that is, the Lord Christ, who is the way, the truth, and the life. Concerning him Saint Bernard devoutly says (*Sermon 75 on the Song of Songs*): “And what is so truly the life of hearts as my Lord Jesus Christ, of whom the one who lived by him said: ‘When Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory’?”

“And desires to see good days.”] The good days are blessed eternity. Concerning it Saint Augustine says (*Sermon 84*): “That day knows neither rising nor setting; tomorrow does not follow that day, because yesterday does not precede it.” For the Apostle calls the days of the present age evil, saying: “Redeeming the time, because the days are evil” (*Ephesians 5*). And certainly, as Saint Augustine says, “Are the days we spend in the corruption of this flesh, under and amid so great a burden of a corruptible body, amid so many temptations and difficulties, where there is a false will, no security of joy, tormenting fear, greedy desire, and arid sorrow, not evil?” Hence shortly afterward he adds: “What is living long except adding evil days to evil days?”

But if, hearing this, you answer: “I,”] Who would not answer so? “Give me,” says Saint Augustine (*Sermon 231*), “a thief, a criminal, a fornicator, a sorcerer, a sacrilegious person, one stained by every vice and overwhelmed by every disgrace or crime—who would not wish to live a blessed life? I know that you all wish to live happily, but you do not wish to live in the way by which a person lives happily.”

God says to you: “Keep your tongue from evil.”] [Col. 0229B] Entirely rightly, he commands one who desires life and good days to keep his tongue from evil, because if anyone thinks himself religious while not restraining his tongue, his religion is worthless; and whoever does not offend in speech is a perfect man.

“And let not your lips speak deceit.”] “For God will destroy all deceitful lips,” says the prophet; and Solomon: “Deceitful souls go astray in sins” (*Proverbs 13*). Deceit, as Saint Augustine says (*On Psalm 5*), occurs “when one thing is done and another is pretended.” Hence, “what is it,” he says (*Book 50 of Homilies, homily 1*), “to speak deceit, except to bring forth one thing with the lips while something else is shut up in the breast?”

“Turn away from evil and do good.”] This is the brief summary of our salvation, as Boherius says. Concerning it Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, used often to say, as his disciple Ardo writes in his Life of him (*Fourth Century of Benedictine Writers*, part I, no. 30): “He was accustomed to impress this upon certain people: If you recognize that many commandments are impossible for you, keep this small commandment: ‘Turn away from evil and do good.’ This saying became so familiar to him that, at the time of his death, after collecting the sayings of all the Fathers, he wished to compose from it a single book.”

18 Seek peace and pursue it.] Saint Father adds this as a unique and singular good: “Seek peace.” For true and sincere peace is a great good, by whose aid we become children of God, as he himself says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God.” And “rightly,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 1 on All Saints*), “they shall be called children who have fulfilled the work of children.”

“And pursue it.”] For it is not enough to seek it unless you also pursue it once it has been found—indeed, pursue it even when it flees. Or understand “pursue it” in the future tense, that is, “you shall pursue” or “you shall attain it,” as the fruit and reward of the labor expended in seeking it. Saint Augustine seems to have understood the prophet’s words in this sense when he said (*Book 50 of Homilies, homily 1*): “We are commanded to seek peace, but we are promised that we shall pursue it.”

“And when you have done these things, my eyes are upon you.”] These words must not be understood as though God, incorporeal by nature, possessed bodily members, as the Anthropomorphites once maintained. Rather, they are spoken figuratively and according to our manner of speaking. “Whenever, however, members of God are named that are visible and bodily in us, the powers of his operations ought to be understood,” says Augustine (*On Psalm 9*). Thus “the eyes of the Lord” sometimes signify his knowledge, as when Saint Benedict says that the eyes of the Lord watch the good and the wicked in every place; sometimes his just judgment upon the wicked, as when it is said in the Psalm: “But the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to cut off their memory from the earth”; and sometimes his gracious mercy toward the good, as when the prophet says: “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous,” and so forth. It is in this sense that the eyes of the Lord must be understood here—may he look upon us, miserable sinners, in this way!

“And my ears are toward your prayers.”] Likewise, “we should regularly understand the ear of God not as a bodily member, but as the power by which he hears,” says the aforementioned Augustine (*On Psalm 9*). Thus “my ears are toward your prayers” means the same as “I will hear your prayers.”

“And before you call upon me, I will say to you: Behold, here I am.”] “What does ‘Behold, here I am’ mean?” Saint Augustine again says (*On Psalm 33*). “Behold, I am present; what do you want? What do you ask of me? Whatever I give you is less than I am. Have me myself; enjoy me; embrace me.”

What is sweeter to us than this voice of the Lord inviting us, dearly beloved brothers? Hildemar aptly says here: “It is customary for holy preachers, after instruction, exhortation, or prayer, to add something of this kind, as the Apostle Paul is very frequently read to have done. But Saint Benedict, since he was not far removed from the merit of the saints, likewise did not wish to be far removed from their teaching. Therefore, after instruction, he added an exhortation,” namely: “What is sweeter to us than this voice, dearly beloved brothers,” and so forth.

[Col. 0230B] Dearly beloved brothers.] Here he calls them dearly beloved brothers whom earlier he had called children, showing that he wished to be regarded as one of them, in accordance with the saying of Saint Gregory the pope (*Book I, Letter 24*): A prelate “should, setting aside his honor, consider himself equal to his well-living subjects.”

19 Behold, in his kindness the Lord shows us the way of life.] “In his kindness,” that is, in his mercy. And rightly so, “because he is not obliged by necessity to show us the way of life,” says Richard of Saint Victor; and because, as Hildemar says, “no one is saved by his own merit, but is saved by the kindness and mercy of God.” Or “behold, in his kindness” may refer to the kindness that he shows by calling us so gently to life, teaching us the means that lead to it, and promising us himself. The demonstrative word “behold” makes clear that this is to be referred to the preceding words.

The way of life.] God is life; charity is the way to life. May we never depart from it!

[Col. 0230C] Therefore, with our loins girded by faith or by the observance of good works.] Once the way of life has been shown, why do we still linger motionless, or what remains except that we walk along it eagerly? To enable us to do this with freedom, Saint Benedict rightly says: “With the loins of your faith or of the observance of good works girded,” alluding to the Apostle’s words to the Ephesians: “Stand therefore, having girded your loins with truth,” and so forth.

But because here he invites us to a spiritual race, he also invites us to a spiritual girding of the loins. And because carnal pleasures proceed from the loins, the holy Fathers very frequently use “loins” to signify lust; accordingly, by the girding of the loins they commonly understand the mortification of carnal pleasures, and virginity itself, in accordance with the saying of Saint Gregory (*Homily 13 on the Gospels*): “We gird our loins when we restrain the lust of the flesh through continence.”

But because, as the same holy pontiff says (*Book XXVIII of the Moralia*, chapter 4), “one kind of lust is of the flesh, by which we corrupt chastity; another kind of lust is of the heart, by which we glory in chastity,” Saint Benedict therefore wished us to be girded with a twofold belt: namely, faith and the observance of good works. With faith we acknowledge God as the author of every good thing and therefore also as the author of chastity; through the observance of good works we restrain the wanton movements of the flesh. Perhaps he was alluding to Isaiah: “Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the belt of his kidneys” (*Isaiah 11*). By the observance of good works he signifies righteousness, which is exercised only through good works. The Lord also commands the same thing in other words in the Gospel, saying: “Let your loins be girded and your lamps burning in your hands.” “For virginity is signified by girded loins, and good works by burning lamps,” says Saint Augustine.

He appropriately placed faith before good works and joined the observance of good works to faith. For nothing can please our Redeemer without the other. Hence the bride says in the Song of Songs: “Sustain me with flowers; surround me with apples.” Concerning these words Saint Bernard writes (*Sermon 51 on the Song of Songs*): “Understand the flower as faith and the fruit as action. Nor, I think, will this seem inappropriate to you if you observe how, just as a flower necessarily precedes fruit, a good work must also be preceded by faith. Otherwise, it is impossible to please God without faith, as Paul testifies, and even more explicitly teaches: ‘Whatever is not from faith is sin.’ Thus there is neither fruit without a flower nor a good work without faith. But faith without works is also dead, just as a flower appears useless when no fruit follows.”

Likewise Scripture says elsewhere: “If you offer rightly but do not divide rightly, you have sinned.” To these words Saint Bernard again adds, after first saying that works must be joined to faith (*Sermon 24 on the Song of Songs*): “Whatever of these you offer, you offer rightly; but you do not rightly divide them from one another. Do not be a right offerer and a wrong divider. Why do you divide action from faith? You divide unjustly, destroying your faith. For faith without works is dead; you offer God a dead gift. If the very devotion of faith is the soul, what is faith that does not work through love except a lifeless corpse? Do you honor God well with a foul-smelling gift? Do you appease the slayer of faith well? Do you believe in Christ? Do Christ’s works. Let love give life to your faith, and let action prove it, so that your faith may live. But even works, however right, are not sufficient to make the heart right without faith. For who would call a person right who does not please God? Without faith it is impossible to please God. Whoever does not please God cannot make God pleased with him; for one who pleases God cannot displease God.”

Saint Gregory the pope confirms the same by this comparison (*Book III of the Register*, chapter 33): “As branches wither without the strength of the root, so works, however good they may seem, are nothing if they are separated from the solidity of faith.”

And with your feet shod.] The feet of the soul commonly signify its affections. We are said to shoe them when we adorn them with various virtues. And rightly are the feet shod, lest, while running along the way of life, you strike your foot against a stone by succumbing to temptation.

Under the guidance of the Gospel.] That is, following the Gospel as our guide.

Let us proceed along his paths.] Namely, those of the Lord Christ, who calls us so mercifully. His paths are voluntary poverty, because, although he was rich, for our sake he became poor; the denial of one’s own will, because for our sake he became obedient unto death; and humble patience amid tribulations and distress, because he suffered, leaving us an example so that we might follow his footsteps. These paths are narrow and harsh for human beings, but all the safer because accessible to fewer, and all the more direct toward the heavenly kingdom.

Or “let us proceed along his paths” may refer to the Gospel, which he mentions. Concerning its paths Boherius writes: “Under the guidance of the Gospel there are four paths, all leading toward the kingdom of God: precepts, commandments, testimonies, and examples. In the precepts righteousness is found; in the commandments, charity; in the testimonies, faith; and in the examples, perfection.”

[Col. 0231D] So that we may deserve to see him who called us in his kingdom,] whose vision makes the whole blessedness of man. Hence Saint Philip also said to Christ: “Lord, show us the Father, and it is enough for us.”

If we wish to dwell in the tabernacle of that kingdom, unless one runs there by good works, one does not arrive there at all.] Here he establishes the necessity of good works, without which one does not in the least reach the tabernacle of the heavenly kingdom. Significantly, however, he added “running,” thereby censuring the sluggishness and laziness of those who, content with the common life, quickly grow weary on the way of life. For them it is considered a great achievement if they do not actually turn back, and scarcely having entered upon the road, they think of rest as though they were excessively fatigued. But Saint Benedict plainly does not speak in this way, not at all; rather, he says, “unless one runs there, one does not arrive.” Certainly a great road still lies before us: the distance from earth to heaven is immense, and only the very brief days of this life are granted to us for completing so great a stretch of the journey, so that we may exult “like giants to run the course” [Col. 0232A]. Let us therefore imitate the examples of the saints, who, as Peter the Venerable writes (*Book I of the Miracles*, chap. 20), “regarding the good things they do as nothing, always strive with their whole desire to rise to greater things.” Concerning them Saint Bernard likewise says: “The just person never thinks that he has attained, never says, ‘It is enough’; but always hungers and thirsts for righteousness, so that, if he were to live forever, he would always strive, insofar as he could, to become more righteous, and would always endeavor with all his strength to advance from good to better.” Let us also hear that most devout exhortation of Abbot William of Saint-Thierry to the brothers of Mont-Dieu (*chap. 2*):

> “Do not neglect, do not delay; for a great road still lies before you. Your profession is most exalted: it passes beyond the heavens, is equal to that of the angels, and resembles angelic purity. For you have vowed not merely all holiness, but the perfection of all holiness and the end of every consummation. It is not for you to languish over the common precepts, nor merely to attend to what God commands, but to what he wills, approving what the will of God is: good, well-pleasing, [Col. 0232B] and perfect. It belongs to others to serve God; it belongs to you to cling to him. It belongs to others to believe, know, love, and revere God; it belongs to you to taste, understand, know, and enjoy him.”

Furthermore, so that we may not fail on the way but run in such a manner as to attain, we must know that some things advance and assist our running, while others delay and hinder it. “There are three things that make one run,” says Saint Bernard in *The Book on the Love of God*, which our Mabillon appended to his sermons on the *Song of Songs*: “namely fear, desire, and love: fear by fleeing, desire by pursuing, love by loving one’s neighbor. There are also four things that impede this running: cold, heat, a difficult road, and excessive running; which, under other names, are distrust, lust, impatience with hardship, and excessive self-confidence.”

But let us ask the Lord with the prophet, saying to him: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?”] “When ‘tabernacle’ is taken in its proper sense, it is a military object; hence soldiers who share a tent are called *contubernales*, as though they had tabernacles together,” [Col. 0232C] says Saint Augustine (*On Psalm XIV*). But here Saint Benedict uses “tabernacle” for the heavenly homeland.

“Or who shall rest upon his holy mountain?”] What he had earlier called a tabernacle he now calls a holy mountain, perhaps because of the labor and difficulty of climbing toward heaven, for “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it.”

After this question, brothers, let us hear the Lord answering and showing us the way to that tabernacle itself, saying: “He who enters without blemish.”] For the kingdom of heaven is promised to the pure in heart: “Blessed are the pure in heart,” says Christ, “for they shall see God.”

“And practices righteousness.”] According to Saint Anselm (*Cur Deus Homo*), “righteousness is the freedom of the soul, assigning to each person according to his proper dignity: reverence to the greater, harmony to one’s equal, discipline to the lesser, obedience to God, holiness to oneself, [Col. 0232D] patience to an enemy, and active mercy to the needy.”

“He who speaks truth in his heart.”] For, as Saint Augustine says (*On Psalm XIV*), “Some have truth on their lips but do not have it in their heart, as if someone were to point out a road, knowing that robbers were on it, and say: ‘If you go by this road, you will be safe from robbers,’ and it happened that no robbers were actually found there. That man spoke truly, but not in his heart; for he thought something else and, unknowingly, spoke the truth. Therefore it is not enough to speak truth unless it is also so in the heart.”

“He who has not practiced deceit with his tongue.”] Saint Augustine again explains these words: “Deceit is practiced with the tongue when one thing is uttered with the mouth and another is concealed in the breast.”

“Nor has done evil to his neighbor.”] Every human being is one’s neighbor; since we are bound to love him, we must refrain from inflicting any evil upon him.

“He who has not accepted reproach against his neighbor.”] That is, he “has not willingly or rashly believed [Col. 0233A] the accuser,” as Saint Augustine says (*On Psalm XIV*). Hildemar transmits another interpretation of this verse from Saint Jerome:

> “He does not accept reproach against his neighbor who has injured no one, harmed no one, and scandalized no one, so that he ought to have received reproach from him.”

“He who, rejecting the wicked devil when he suggests something to him, together with the suggestion itself, has reduced it to nothing before the sight of his heart.”] Up to this point Saint Benedict has shown the way to the heavenly tabernacle. But because he knew that the devil, armed for our destruction, continually lays ambushes for our journey—for this reason the devil is so called, since in Greek he is interpreted as “accuser” and in Hebrew as “one flowing downward,” as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius note with Smaragdus: he provokes us to crimes and causes those who wish to climb the holy mountain of God to flow downward—he consequently adds that we should reject the wicked one from the sight of our heart and reduce his perverse solicitations to nothing by contemptuously refusing consent. [Col. 0233B] He shows that it lies within human power to resist the tempting devil and that the devil overcomes no one except one who wills it, in accordance with the words of Saint Caesarius (*Sermon 37 in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*):

> “He is bound, as though fastened by chains like a dog, and he cannot bite anyone except one who has joined himself to him with deadly security. He can bark; he can solicit; he absolutely cannot bite unless one wills it. For he harms not by force but by persuasion; he does not extort consent from us but asks for it.”

“And he has taken the little thoughts of the devil and dashed them against Christ.”] “Little thoughts” means the enemy’s suggestions as they arise: he suppressed them lest, growing stronger, they themselves be suppressed only with difficulty and eventually prevail, in accordance with the poet’s saying: “Resist beginnings; the remedy is prepared too late.” Hence Saint Jerome (*Letter 22*) says:

> “I do not want you to allow a thought to grow. While the enemy is small, kill it; let wickedness be struck down in the seed, lest the weeds grow.”

Peter Damian treats this subject at length in the little work he wrote on the institutions of his congregation (*chap. 19*), where [Col. 0233C] among other things, he says:

> “First of all, my son, whoever you are who prepare to join hands in combat with the invisible enemy, strive to fortify your mind with vigilant watchfulness against every assault of creeping suggestions. Just as you immediately throw into the fire the refuse and every scrap that falls from the work of your hands, so likewise cast the movements of your thoughts upon God. And since fire consumes, hand over to it the superfluous things of your heart to be consumed, remembering the apostolic word: ‘Casting all your care upon him’; and that of the prophet: ‘Cast your thought upon the Lord, and he himself will nourish you’ . . . . Regard temptation as a serpent. If it is immediately repelled at the moment of hearing it, everything remains sound; nothing at all is corrupted, and none of the things within is polluted. But if it has once been admitted, even though it may later be driven out by every possible effort, it will nevertheless be necessary for something, however small, of its poison or scales to remain.
