Therefore be watchful, so that at the beginning, when temptation is being born, you may meet it armed and undaunted, and dash the little movements of emerging thoughts against the rock, which is Christ” [Col. 0233D]—meditating very frequently upon his immense love for you and recalling the benefits he has bestowed upon human beings. In this way you will utterly crush all the enemy’s hosts. “But if a sudden wolf should rise up against you,” Peter Damian says again (*Opusculum 52*, chap. 6), “seize the rock, and immediately it flees. And what is the rock except Christ?” See Saint Ambrose, *Hexameron*, book VI, chap. 4, and Cassian, *Institutes*, book VI, chap. 13.

“Those who fear the Lord do not make themselves arrogant because of their good observance; rather, believing that the good things within them are accomplished not by themselves but by the Lord, they magnify the Lord who works within them.”] Since the adversary neither sleeps nor slumbers, and, as Saint Bernard aptly observes (*Sermon 54 on the Song of Songs*), “If he cannot hinder the action, he tests the intention, persuading you to claim for yourself the effect of grace,” therefore, after commanding the person who wishes to enter God’s tabernacle to turn away from evil, [Col. 0234A] do good, pursue righteousness, and reject the devil’s suggestions, he cautiously adds: “Those who do not make themselves arrogant because of their good observance, but believe that the good things within them,” and so forth. In these words he teaches three things: first, to flee pride arising from good observance; second, to acknowledge God, not oneself, as the author of the good work; third, consequently, to magnify God working within oneself.

“Those who fear the Lord do not make themselves arrogant because of their good observance,”] imagining themselves to be something great, although they are nothing; rather, they abase themselves beneath everyone, as Saint Bernard did. Although his life possessed such holiness as the Catholic world still admires in him, he nevertheless wrote of himself in this way to another Bernard, prior of Portes (*Letter 250*):

> “My monstrous life cries out to you, as does my wretched conscience. For I am a kind of chimera of my age: I am neither cleric nor layman. I discarded the monastic way of life long ago, though not the habit.”

Pope Saint Gregory likewise wrote of himself to [Col. 0234B] Anastasius, bishop of Antioch (*Book I, Letter 7*):

> “The fact that you call me the mouth of the Lord, that you call me a lamp, that you say I benefit many, adds also to the accumulation of my iniquities, so that when iniquity ought to have been punished in me, I receive praises in place of punishment.”

“But believing that the good things within them are accomplished not by themselves but by the Lord.”] For, as Saint Bernard says most excellently (*Sermon 54 on the Song of Songs*): “What is more hateful than that utterance: ‘Our hand is exalted, and the Lord has not done all these things’?” John Cassian thought quite differently, although he attributed very much to human free choice, when he said (*Book XII, chap. 16*):

> “For we must believe not only that we cannot possess perfection itself by our own industry or labor, but also that we cannot accomplish even those things which we undertake with a view to it—that is, our labors, efforts, and studies—without the help of divine protection, the inspiration of God, and the grace of his correction and exhortation. This grace he is accustomed to pour mercifully into [Col. 0234C] our hearts, either through another person or by visiting us himself.”

Here Cassian recognizes four kinds of grace: protection, by which God guards us from the plots of our enemies; inspiration, by which he inwardly awakens a mind that is, as it were, asleep to goodness; correction, by which he turns our soul away from all earthly things; and exhortation, by which he kindles us to perform good through holy teachers. If you add to these the benefits of creation, redemption, and preservation, as well as God’s cooperation in all our natural acts, how could we then presume to claim for ourselves the glory of good observance and deny it to God? Otherwise the Apostle would rightly say to us: “What do you have that you have not received? But if you have received it, why do you boast as though you had not received it?”

Saint Bernard likewise says (*Sermon 13 on the Song of Songs*):

> “Whatever favor you seek here which you do not refer back to God, you steal from him. From where, then, do you have glory, foul dust? From where do you have it? From the holiness of life? It is the Spirit who sanctifies—the Spirit, I say, not yours but God’s. And if you shine with wonders and signs, they are performed by your hand, [Col. 0234D] but by the power of God. Does popular approval flatter you because you have uttered a good and perhaps a forceful word well? But Christ gave you mouth and wisdom; for what is your tongue except the pen of a scribe? And this too you received on loan.”

Earlier he also says:

> “Who would believe a wall if it claimed to give birth to the ray of light that it receives through a window? Or if clouds boasted that they had produced the rains, who would not laugh? It is plainly clear to me that streams of water do not arise from channels, nor words of wisdom from lips or teeth, even if bodily sense cannot reach beyond this. Nor is a painting or writing to be praised because of the pen, nor is a good speech the glory of the tongue or lips. It is time for the prophet also to speak: ‘Will the axe boast against him who hews with it, or will the saw exalt itself against him by whom it is drawn?’ Just as a rod would be lifted against the one lifting it, and a staff, which is merely wood, would be exalted, so is everyone who boasts against the Lord, unless he boasts in the Lord.”

[Col. 0235A] “They magnify the Lord who works within them.”] That is, with thanksgiving they return all praise and glory for every good work to God, lest the flow of thanksgiving cease if there is no return-flow. To use Saint Bernard’s words (*Sermon on the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin Mary*), “Let the streams of grace be returned to their source, so that they may flow more abundantly; otherwise, unless they return to the fountain, they dry up.”

Saying this with the prophet: “Not to us, Lord, not to us, but to your name give glory.”] Here Saint Benedict teaches from the prophet’s words how we ought to magnify the Lord working within us: namely, by ascribing to God all the glory of good works, so that the one who has worked all our works within us may receive all the praise and honor arising from them. “God alone created all things,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 13 on the Song of Songs*); “he alone triumphed over the enemy; he alone freed the captives—and shall he have a companion in glory? ‘My arm,’ he says, ‘helped me’; ‘I have trodden the winepress alone, and of the nations there was no man with me.’ What, then, have I to do with victory [Col. 0235B] if I was not in the battle? I most shamelessly claim either glory without victory or victory without a struggle.”

Nor did the Apostle Paul attribute anything of his preaching to himself, saying: “By the grace of God I am what I am.”] He confirms by the Apostle’s example what he had stated above. The assertion that the Apostle attributed nothing to himself concerning his preaching can be understood in three ways: first, with respect to the dignity of the preacher, to which he was raised from being a blasphemer and persecutor; second, with respect to the exercise of his preaching, as he proclaimed the Gospel throughout so many regions of the earth; third, with respect to the fruit of his preaching, by which so many faithful were won for Christ. Thus, in every sense, Paul attributed nothing of his preaching to himself. For although he says, “I am an apostle,” he is “an apostle by the will of God” (I Cor. I); or, as he says elsewhere, “an apostle not from men nor through man, but through Jesus Christ and God the Father.” And if he “labored more abundantly than all,” he adds, “yet not I, but the grace of God with me” (Gal. I). Finally, if he seems to have acquired so great a people for the Lord, he says: “[Col. 0235C] I planted, Apollo watered, but God gave the growth” (I Cor. XV). Thus, “by the grace of God I am what I am.”

And again he himself says: “Let him who boasts, boast in the Lord.”] To boast in the Lord is to attribute to him all the glory of a good work, so that, when people marvel at our good deeds and exalt us with praise because of them, we may say with Abbot Paphnutius in Cassian (*Conference III, chap. 15*):

> “It is not free choice, but the Lord who releases those in fetters; it is not our strength, but the Lord who raises up those who are crushed; it is not diligence in reading, but the Lord who enlightens the blind”—in Greek, **Κύριος σοφοῖ τυφλούς** (“The Lord makes the blind wise”), that is, “The Lord makes the wise blind”—“it is not our vigilance, but the Lord who guards the strangers; it is not our strength, but the Lord who lifts up, or supports, all who fall, and so forth.”

In this way we may appropriate Saint Bernard’s words (*Sermon 13 on the Song of Songs*):

> “I boast securely if, with my conscience as witness, I claim nothing for myself from the glory of the Creator; securely indeed, because I am no longer boasting against the Lord, but in the Lord.”

[Col. 0235D] Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: “He who hears these words of mine and does them, I will compare him to a wise man.”] Saint Benedict adapts to his purpose words taken from the Gospel of the Lord Christ, saying: “Hence the Lord also says in the Gospel: ‘He who hears these words of mine,’ namely, he who enters without blemish, and so forth, ‘I will compare him to a wise man,’ namely Christ, who is the Wisdom of the Father and who built his house. Of this Scripture says: ‘Wisdom built herself a house; she hewed out seven pillars.’ He built himself a house, I say, namely the Church, upon the rock—that is, upon himself—for ‘the rock was Christ.’ The rivers came and the winds blew,” namely the persecutions inflicted by tyrants, heretics, and false brothers, or the prosperity enjoyed under Christian rulers. “They beat against that house,” because the Church is shaken no less by prosperity than by adversity, “and it did not fall,” for it perseveres until the consummation of the age. It was founded upon the rock, namely [Col. 0236A] Christ, concerning whom the Apostle says: “No one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid.”

“The Lord, fulfilling these things.”] That is, having so mercifully and gently gone before us, inviting us to life and showing us the way to the tabernacle.

“He waits for us each day to respond to these holy admonitions of his by our deeds,”] namely by obeying the admonitions and eagerly carrying out what he urges, lest he rebuke us with the prophet, saying: “I called, and there was none who answered; I spoke, and they did not hear, but they did evil in my sight and chose what I did not will” (Isa. LXVI).

“Therefore.”] Namely, so that we may respond by our deeds to the Lord’s holy admonitions.

“For the correction of our evils, the days of this life are prolonged for us as a respite.”] We who have hitherto disfigured our life with vices and sins must henceforth enter without blemish. We who presented our members to serve iniquity unto iniquity must present those same members to serve righteousness unto righteousness.

[Col. 0236B] The Apostle saying: “Or do you not know that the patience of God leads you to repentance?”] He confirms by the Apostle’s words what he had said above: that the days of this life are prolonged as a respite for the correction of our evils. For, as Hildemar says, “what Blessed Benedict calls a respite, Paul calls patience; what Blessed Benedict calls correction, Paul calls repentance; and what he calls ‘are prolonged,’ Paul calls ‘leads.’” Therefore the patience of God is the respite which the just, strong, and patient Judge most graciously grants us for the correction of our evils. As Saint Caesarius says (*Sermon 29 in the Appendix to Saint Augustine*), “When we have sinned for a long time and suffer no evil from the Lord, it is patience, not negligence. He has not lost his power; rather, he has preserved us for repentance.”

Summoned by such great kindness, let us hasten to do penance; otherwise, when placed at the final judgment, what shall we answer God if we have neglected it? “There is no excuse,” says Saint Augustine (*Sermon 22 on Scripture*), “that can be offered [Col. 0236C] to the Lord at the end: ‘You did not allow me to live well,’ or ‘You did not grant me time to correct myself,’ or ‘You did not show me what I should seek and what I should avoid.’ See how he is silent; see how he delays; see how he shows kindness, exhorts, and threatens.”

For the merciful Lord says: “I do not desire the death of the sinner, but that he should be converted and live,”] or, as the Apostle Peter says: “He deals patiently for your sake, not wishing any to perish but all to return to repentance”; and Paul says: “God wills all human beings to be saved”; and the Lord himself says through the Prophet: “On whatever day the sinner groans, I will not remember any of his iniquities.”

Therefore, when we had asked the Lord, brothers, about the inhabitant of his tabernacle,] namely, when we said with the prophet: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle?”

“We heard the command concerning dwelling.”] That is, we heard what is commanded to those who desire to dwell there, when the answer was given after the question: “He who enters without blemish,” and so forth.

“But if we fulfill the duty of an inhabitant, we shall be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.”] The duty of an inhabitant may be understood in two [Col. 0236D] ways: first, as the duty of those who already dwell there, whose task is continually to cling to God, praise him, bless him, and love him; second, as the duty of those who do not yet dwell there but ardently desire to do so, whose task is to enter without blemish, practice righteousness, and so forth. Thus, if we fulfill the duty of an inhabitant, we shall be heirs of the kingdom of heaven; if we do otherwise, we shall not. Hence Saint Basil says excellently (*Preface to the Longer Rules*):

> “We say of ourselves that we await the kingdom of heaven, but we do not concern ourselves with the things by which it is acquired . . . . Yet who, having remained at home or slept during the time of sowing, filled his lap with sheaves at harvest? Who harvested a vineyard that he did not plant? The fruits belong to those whose are the labors; honors and crowns belong to those who have conquered by striving. Who will crown one who has not even begun to engage the adversary?”

“Therefore.”] So that we may be heirs of the kingdom of heaven.

[Col. 0237A] “Our hearts and bodies must be prepared.”] Namely, hearts through good will and bodies through holy discipline, as Bernard of Cassino explains; or hearts for understanding well and humbly, and bodies for enduring with patience, as Richard of Saint Angelo has it. Or “hearts” on account of God, who searches hearts, and “bodies” on account of human beings, so that they may be edified; thus we may provide what is good not only before God but also before human beings, as may be gathered from Hildemar. Or, finally, “hearts and bodies” means that we should consecrate our entire selves to God, who consecrated himself wholly to us: “He was given wholly to me and wholly expended for my use,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 3 on the Circumcision*, no. 4). We should therefore give everything to him who has made his kingdom our inheritance. For, as Venerable Bede says (*Sermon 18 on the Saints*): “This thing, O human being—that is, the kingdom of heaven—seeks no other price except yourself. It is worth as much as you are: give yourself, and you will have it.”

“Of holy obedience to the commandments.”] [Col. 0237B] He calls obedience holy because it makes us holy, like the saints and participants in the saints’ holiness.

“For military service.”] He says “for military service” in order to express the labor of obedience.

“And what human nature has less ability to accomplish in us.”] The word “less” may here be taken adverbially, so that the sense is: for obtaining the heavenly kingdom and preparing our hearts and bodies for the holy obedience of the commandments, which is to serve as a military undertaking, human nature, corrupted and depraved by sin, has less ability in itself—that is, it can do nothing of itself. For, as our Menard observes on this passage, *minus* frequently means “not” in Cicero.

“Let us ask the Lord to command that the help of his grace be supplied.”] That is, let us ask him to be willing, as Menard explains, to provide assistance. We cannot possess this assistance from ourselves, but it is granted to those who ask, in accordance with the saying: “Ask, and you shall receive.”

“And if, fleeing the punishments of Gehenna, we wish to reach eternal life swiftly.”] [Col. 0237C] Here he urges us to pursue the good by a twofold motive: the fear of Gehenna and the hope of attaining eternal life. Indeed, what hardship would a Christian—much less a monk—refuse if he seriously meditated upon those everlasting punishments of the damned? In them, as Peter Damian says (*Opusculum 50*, chap. 12), “there is death without death, an end without end, exhaustion without exhaustion, because death lives, the end always begins, and exhaustion does not know how to cease.” Or, as Peter of Blois says (*Letter 131*), in them “the end will always begin, death will not die, and exhaustion will not be exhausted, so that the condition of the condemned person may continually return as material for pain and fuel for eternal death.”

Finally, Saint Bernard cries out concerning them (*Sermon 42 on Various Matters*):

> “O harsh and grievous region, fearful region, region to be fled, land of forgetfulness, land of affliction, land of miseries, in which there is no order but eternal horror dwells; a deadly place, in which there is burning fire, freezing cold, an immortal worm, intolerable stench, [Col. 0237D] striking hammers, darkness that can be felt, confusion of sinners, the binding of chains, and the terrifying faces of demons! I tremble wholly and shudder at the memory of this region, and all my bones are shaken.”

On the other hand, who would not rise up toward the promised reward of eternal happiness, in which, as Saint Bernard says (*Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs*), “nothing is feared, nothing is found distasteful, nothing fails; paradise is a secure dwelling, the Word is sweet food, eternity is exceedingly great abundance”? Concerning it the same holy Doctor says elsewhere (*Declamation on the Gospel*):

> “Eye has not seen, nor ear heard, O God, what you have prepared for those who love you. For it is peace that surpasses all understanding, peace upon peace, unfailing exultation, a torrent of infinite delight, a river of joy, complete gladness. Think whatever you wish, desire whatever you can; that happiness, that eternity, that blessedness exceed every thought and surpass every desire.”

And elsewhere (*Sermon 31 on the Song of Songs*):

> “Those to whom God appears desire to see nothing more desirable, nor can they desire anything more [Col. 0238A] delightful. When, then, will that eagerness grow weary, or that sweetness withdraw, or that truth deceive, or eternity fail? If both the opportunity and the will to see are extended forever, how could there not be complete happiness?”

See Peter Damian, *Opusculum 50*, chap. 15.

“While it is still possible, and while we are in this body.”] That is, while we are healthy, possess reason, and are able to turn away from evil and do good. For, as Saint Basil rightly says (*Preface to the Longer Rules*), “Now is the acceptable time, says the Apostle; now is the day of salvation. This age is the age of repentance, but the future is the age of recompense; this is the age of action and effort, that of reward; this is the age of patience, that of consolation. Now God helps those who withdraw from the evil way; then he will be a terrible and infallible judge of human actions.”

Therefore, so that God may recompense us in the age to come and release us from the punishments we deserve, while we have time let us do good. “O human being who desire to possess the kingdom of God,” Saint Augustine—[Col. 0238B] or whoever else the author may be—cries out (*Sermon 251 in the Appendix to the Sermons*), “why did you do evil? While you can, correct yourself; while you have time, cry out to almighty God. While opportunity is granted, mourn; while permission remains, repent. Hasten while you can, while the soul is still in the body. While you are still alive, seek future healing for yourself, before the deep sea swallows you, before the wicked hell snatches you away—where no pardon is granted and no one returns to forgiveness.”

“And it is possible to fulfill all these things throughout this life of light.”] The life of light is the monastic life, which here, I readily persuade myself, Saint Benedict understands in this way, since here too he is addressing monks. Opposed to this life is the secular life, sheer night, concerning which Saint Bernard says when addressing his own people (*Sermon 5 at the Vigil of the Nativity of the Lord*):

> “Was not the night also dark for each of us when we lived in this world as though without God, when we walked after our desires, pursued the allurements of the flesh, obeyed [Col. 0238C] secular longings, presented our members as weapons of iniquity to sin, and served iniquity unto iniquity—things of which we now rightly blush as works of darkness?”

“We must now run and do what is advantageous for us forever.”] “We must run and act now,” he says—that is, at the present time—so that, if you are young, you do not postpone repentance until the final limit of life, when because of the weakness of extreme old age there is scarcely any opportunity to run. And “now” means that, if you are old, you should at least devote even the last moments of your life to the good and supreme God, who rewards even the smallest things.

Peter the Venerable says this entirely splendidly (*Book V of the Letters*):

> “Leave earthly things before they themselves leave you. And if you were unwilling to offer God the first portions of the victim—that is, of your life—at least offer him devoutly the tail, that is, the end of your days.”

Therefore “now,” if you are old; but “now” also if you are young, so that you do not delay your running any longer. Otherwise, if death overtakes you, when you wish to fulfill what is now permitted and possible, you may no longer have the opportunity.

“Thus the day must be anticipated,” says [Col. 0238D] Saint Augustine—or whoever else the author may be (*Sermon 154 in the Appendix*)—“which is accustomed to anticipate us. A person deceives himself and toys with his own death when he thinks: ‘The indulgence of time may come to my aid.’ This is not so. First, because security promised for the final day is exceedingly dangerous; and second, because it is utterly foolish to entrust a matter concerning eternal necessities to the final useless moments of a failing life. It is hateful to God when a person sins more freely under the confidence of repentance reserved for old age. Believe me, dearest ones: it is difficult for the clever concealment involved in arranging one’s end to be considered worthy of receiving the opportunity. Before him who interprets the heart, artifice is not admitted to salvation.”

Saint Augustine—or whoever else the author may be—also attacks the person who postpones conversion until the final course of life (*Sermon 293 in the Appendix*):

> “Someone says: ‘I am young; I do what pleases me, and afterward I will repent.’ This is to strike myself with a cruel sword and afterward go to the physician, without knowing that a wound is received in a single moment, while one is scarcely restored to former health after a long time, and so forth.”

[Col. 0239A] “Therefore we must establish for ourselves the school of the Lord’s service.”] In the proper sense of the name, a school is a place in which young people customarily devote themselves to liberal literary studies. “School” also, as our Menard observes, is a room in which monks do something, read, and sleep. He proves this from the Second Council of Tours, canon 15 (*Notes on the Council’s Rule*, chap. 15, § 2):

> “Monks may not have common cells, but a school shall be built through common labor, where all shall lie down, under the governance either of the abbot or of the prior.”

He also cites a certain Rule, chap. 12:

> “If there are penitents in the school, let two of them make the fires each week.”

And the Rule of Saint Caesarius, chap. 3:

> “As for changing the habit itself or having a bed in the school, this shall be in the power of the prior.”

Here, however, Saint Benedict uses and applies “school” to signify the Rule; hence he immediately calls it an institution. [Col. 0239B] Nor is it at all unusual among the ancients to call sacred writings and the institutions of the saints “schools.” Saint Jerome, as Boherius reports, calls the Book of Exodus the physician’s school in a letter to Evagrius, where the laws given by God to the people of Israel are set down. And when Abbot John was asked by Cassian why, having abandoned the eremitical life, he had embraced the institutions of the coenobitic life, he replied that he had returned to the schools of the beginners, considering himself unequal to the eremitical discipline and unworthy of the lofty perfection of such a life, if indeed he could fulfill even their institutions according to the merit of his profession.

Furthermore, this school is called “the school of the Lord’s service” because it consists entirely in learning the obedience owed to supreme Majesty. Hence, addressing the disciples, he says: “Under one Lord we carry an equal military service of servitude.”

“In this institution we hope to establish nothing harsh and nothing burdensome.”] Here I seem to hear Saint Father Benedict being challenged in this way: “Is this so, holy Father? You call nothing harsh and nothing burdensome [Col. 0239C] the chastisement of the body, refusal to embrace pleasures, love of fasting, hatred of one’s own will, and obedience even to impossible commands? Where is what you said in chapter 58, concerning the discipline of receiving brothers: ‘Let him be tested in all patience’; and, ‘Let all hard and difficult things be proclaimed to them’? And what agreement is there between ‘we hope to establish nothing harsh’ and ‘let all hard and difficult things—not merely some or many—be proclaimed to them’?” Do you perhaps also call your Rule a yoke?

Saint Father Benedict would answer: “The Rule I propose is indeed a yoke, but it is Christ’s yoke, which he himself declares to be light and sweet. As Saint Caesarius says (*Appendix to Saint Augustine, Sermon 28*), it is accustomed to lift up rather than press down, and it carries us more than it is carried by us.”

Saint Bernard likewise says of it (*Letter 72*):

> “Is that not truly light which does not burden the one who carries it but lifts him up? What burden is lighter than that which not only does not weigh one down but also carries everyone upon whom it is laid?”

And indeed, to speak here with Saint Bernard—or whoever else the author may be (*Treatise on Charity*, chap. 12):

> “[Col. 0239D] What is sweeter for a human being, what is more delightful, than to despise the world, to consider oneself higher than the world, to stand upon the summit of a good conscience, and to have the world beneath one’s feet, seeing nothing in it that one desires; to trample underfoot deceitful riches, pernicious honors, and damnable pleasures? What, I ask, is more tranquil than to establish one’s soul in such a way that it is agitated by no movements of carnal desire, and to compel the flesh, warmed by the dew of chastity, to serve, so that one may have in it a most willing helper for the exercise of spiritual warfare? And so forth.”

It is worthwhile to insert here several reasons why Saint Benedict declares that he will establish nothing harsh or burdensome in the Rule. The first is that God fills the mind of the person who obeys him with such numerous and such great inward delights that there is nothing hard which they do not soften, nothing bitter which they do not transform into sweetness. Thus, even if the Rule is a yoke, “the yoke plainly rots away [Col. 0240A] before the face of oil,” to speak with the prophet—oil, indeed, of exultation and joy, by which God refreshes the faithful soul.

The second is that it is given not to servants but to sons, who are moved not by fear but by love; they consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ. Moreover, where there is love, there is no harshness of life. “Once you have been imbued with this,” Peter the Venerable once wrote to the hermit Gislebert (Book I, letter 20), “your cell will be wider to you than the whole world, fasting a refreshment, vigils sleep, work leisure, labor rest”; and Abbot William of Saint-Thierry, writing to the brothers of Mont-Dieu (Chapter 8, no. 23), says: “Bran bread, plain water, vegetables, and simple pulses are by no means pleasant things; but in the love of Christ and the desire for inward delight, to be able to satisfy a well-disciplined stomach gladly with these things is exceedingly delightful.” Finally, Saint Bernard (Sermon 85 on the Song of Songs): “Where love is, there is no labor, but savor.”

The third is that even for servants constrained by fear, if they truly desire salvation and eternal life and seriously meditate on man's last things, even the bitterest things become sweet. Saint Bernard once taught his nephew Robert that the harshness of monastic life could be mitigated, writing to him as follows (Letter 1): “You fear vigils, fasts, and the labor of your hands; but these are light to one who meditates on everlasting punishments. Moreover, remembrance of the outer darkness makes solitude not seem dreadful. If you consider the future examination concerning idle words, silence will not greatly displease you; eternal weeping and that gnashing of teeth, brought before the eyes of your heart, will make a mat and a pallet equal to you.” In almost the same way John Trithemius writes: “If the harshnesses of the cloister frighten anyone, let him think of the torments of hell; if you consider the morning vigils burdensome, know that there they never sleep or rest; if you shrink from the hardness of the beds, consider that their bed is a fire that will not be extinguished; if you fear the restriction of food and drink, think that their food is the immortal worm, and mourning, and woe; if you dread the custody of the cloister, remember the confinement of hell, for they will not come out from there forever, etc.” (32)

The fourth is that everything becomes cheapened through habit. Thus something Saint Bernard once wrote in a negative sense (Book I, On Consideration, chapter 2) could aptly be turned here to our purpose: “What does habit not overturn? What does continual practice not harden? What does use not make familiar? How many things that at first they shuddered to encounter because of their bitterness have, through use itself, been wrongly transformed into sweetness! Hear what the righteous man laments concerning such things: ‘What my soul formerly refused to touch, now, because of my distress, is my food.’ At first, something will seem unbearable to you; as time goes on, if you become accustomed to it, you will judge it not so burdensome; a little later you will feel it to be light; a little later you will not feel it at all; and a little later it will even give you pleasure.”

The fifth is that the holy legislator so tempered and adapted everything that there is something for the strong to desire and something from which the weak will not shrink. He arranged everything in such a way that no one would be unable, with reasonable ease, to observe the Rule. Hence Peter Damian (Opusculum 13, chapter 17): “The holy Rule,” he says, “has been made like a broad, capacious, and spacious house, capable of receiving every kind of person: children and old men, the strong and the weak, the delicate, and those differing in many ways through the inequality of their characters.”

But even if something somewhat more restrictive should proceed, at the prompting of equity, for the correction of faults and the preservation of charity, do not immediately, terrified by fear, flee the way of salvation. For whoever puts his hand to the plow and looks back is not fit for the kingdom of heaven; and the fearful are not admitted to battle under the Law, lest they themselves become afraid and make others afraid. He calls his Rule the way of salvation because, for those who practice it, the eternal kingdoms will be opened, in accordance with what Saint Fulgentius says (Book on Faith, chapter 3): “To everyone who makes a vow and fulfills what he has vowed, God himself also gives the rewards of the heavenly kingdom that he promised”; or, if you prefer, he calls monastic life itself the way of salvation, since it is a shortened road to heaven.

Which must be begun only from a narrow beginning. After Saint Benedict had promised that he would establish nothing harsh in the Rule, lest the severity of an unfamiliar life deter delicate novices from their holy purpose, should the rigor of monastic discipline, contrary to their expectation, present some difficulty, he guards them against the customary temptations of novices by asserting that they will experience some trouble at the beginning of their conversion. Perhaps moved by this example, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, prescribed the following among his instructions for forming a novice (To the Brothers of Mont-Dieu, chapter 7): “He must be continually fortified against the temptations that rage most fiercely against the solitary novice, when vices never cease to assail the servant of God, who serves God freely, with the reward of the offered pleasure: the devil suggesting, the flesh desiring, and the world presenting things to be desired.” (33)

We likewise think it worthwhile, for the benefit of novices, to set before their eyes the causes of the difficulties and temptations that they ordinarily experience at the beginning of their conversion, so that they may fortify themselves against them if they should ever arise. These causes may be considered either from the side of religion, or from the side of the devil, or from the side of the world.

From the side of religion, the austerity of the regular life terrifies novices accustomed to the delights of the world. For, as Saint Augustine—or whoever else may be the author—says (Sermon 196 in the Appendix): “It cannot happen without violence that someone passes from abundance and delights to hunger and thirst, to abstinence and the cross; that he brings flesh formerly a friend to sleep and leisure to ruin through discipline and vigils. I repeat, it cannot happen without violence that each person exchanges anger for patience, pride for humility, overcomes the abundance of riches and sufficiency through love of poverty, condemns drunkenness by sobriety and lust by chastity, and is suddenly transformed into a perfect man, so that in a certain sense one person is believed to have become another.” Yet all these things are commanded and required by the laws of sacred religion.

Hence Saint Bernard (Sermon 33 on the Song of Songs): “The beginnings of our conversion, according to the common experience of things, are first shaken by fear, when, immediately upon entering, the horror of a stricter life and the austerity of an unfamiliar discipline confront us”; and elsewhere (Sermon 93 on Various Subjects): “When some simple people come to conversion, they are frightened by the severity of the Rule. If they are told of contempt for the world, of the conflict between virtues and vices; if anxiety about keeping vigil, constant perseverance in prayer, and moderation in fasting are required of them, they say among themselves in complaint: ‘What is this? Who is sufficient for so many and such great demands?’” Finally, Peter of Blois, writing to R., a cleric who had vowed to enter religious life, says: “Because you have hitherto immersed yourself in the pleasures of the world, the change of food, the roughness of clothing, the yoke of obedience, the discipline of silence, regularity of conduct, and austerity of discipline seem unbearable to you.”

From the side of the devil, a far more strenuous battle must be endured. “For just as robbers,” to use the words of Chrysostom (Homily 1 to the People of Antioch), “do not dig where there is hay, straw, or reeds, but where there is gold and silver, and there they keep constant watch, so the devil presses most intensely upon those who engage in spiritual affairs; where virtue is, there are ambushes.”

Although demonic cunning attacks all monks without exception, it rages much more fiercely against recent converts, whom it grieves to see—delicate young people—have defected from its allegiance. “Although the wicked enemies,” says Peter the Venerable, speaking of the novices of the monastery of Cluny (Book I of the Miracles, chapter 15), “lay in wait for everyone generally, nevertheless they pressed much more hostilely upon recent converts. They were indeed grieved, envying the progress of the veterans; but when the novices’ conversion was added, as though from a newly received wound, they were enraged more fiercely. As if in despair of recovering their former prey, they set aside the spoils of the earlier capture and burned far more vehemently against what was being snatched from their eyes. Thus they stirred up powerful wars against the novices; armed with various weapons of temptation, they assailed them with all their strength.” In this way Pharaoh, the true figure of the devil, pursued the people of God as they departed from Egypt, becoming more violently inflamed; and Satan himself, as he departed from the man whom he had possessed from childhood, tore him apart by afflicting him more grievously.

It is worthwhile to set before our eyes all the stratagems of the crafty enemy. In this matter Saint John Climacus must be heard above all, for he vividly represents them to us in these words (Step 2): “After we have renounced human affairs, the demons suggest to us that we should call blessed those who are kind to the needy, and declare ourselves miserable because we lack every virtue. The counsel of the enemies, however, is to draw us back, under the appearance of humility, either to the profane life of the world or, if we persevere in religion, to drive us into the snare of despair.”

And elsewhere (Step 3): “Let neither the deceit nor the cunning of those robbers escape you; for they suggest to us that we should not withdraw from the crowds of men, on the grounds that we will receive a great reward of glory if, after looking upon a woman, we nevertheless abstain from her.”

And near the end of the same step: “Through dreams the evil demons try to disturb us, presenting to us the images of our family members and displaying them either lamenting, or dying, or afflicted and tormented by troubles on our account.”

Thus, according to the account of Saint Athanasius (Life of Saint Antony, chapter 4), Saint Antony was tempted: “To see whether he could somehow draw him away from the undertaking he had begun, the devil brought before him the memory of his possessions, the protection of his sister, the nobility of his family, his love of possessions, the fleeting glory of the world, the various pleasures of food, and the other attractions of a more relaxed life. Finally he suggested the arduous end of virtue and the immense labor of attaining it, as well as the frailty of the body and the long span of life, etc.”

See the Anonymous author of Regensburg, volume IV of the *Analecta*, and the book *On the Teaching of Saint Stephen of Grandmont*.

The struggle that proceeds from the side of the world yields to none of these. From one side friends, from another relatives, and from another brothers and parents assail the novice, still weak in his good purpose, and try in every way to recall him. Saint Jerome describes their attacks most excellently and, as is his custom, eloquently, in writing to Heliodorus (Letter 1):

“I do not fail to understand by what bonds you say you are now hindered. We do not have a breast of iron or hard inward parts; Hyrcanian tigers did not nurse us, born from flint—and we too have passed through these things. Now your widowed sister clings to you with coaxing arms; now the household servants with whom you grew up say: ‘To whom are you leaving us to serve?’ Now your former nurse, already an old woman, and your foster father, second only to your natural father in affection, cry out: ‘Wait a little for us who are dying, and bury us.’ Perhaps your mother too, with the loose skin of her breasts and her forehead furrowed with wrinkles, recalling the ancient lullaby at the breast, may repeat her lament: and let the grammarians say if they wish, ‘In you the whole household leans and reclines.’ The love of God and fear of Gehenna easily break these bonds.”

Such were formerly the struggles of Saint Blathmac, prince and later abbot of Iona and martyr, when he fled to the monastery. For, as Walafrid Strabo writes, recounting his life in verse:

> When the flying report by chance reached the father’s ears,  
> Amazement and grief then encircled the parent’s mind.  
> He grieves that his heir has been taken away, and sends the senate,  
> The troops, the magistrates, the people, commands, and companies;  
> Duke and count went, and the bishop hurried to be present,  
> Along with a cohort of abbots and neighboring relatives by blood;  
> Their sole purpose was this: by whatever means they might,  
> To make his mind return and face the dangers it had avoided  
> With a different heart. O how blind such a will!

Such were, and will in the future be, the struggles of many others. But, as the aforementioned Saint Jerome said to his Heliodorus:

“Even if a little nephew hangs upon your neck; even if your mother displays the breasts that nourished you, with disheveled hair and torn clothing; even if your father lies across the threshold, go on over your prostrate father, and with dry eyes fly to the banner of the cross. In this matter, the only kind of piety is to be cruel.”

Saint Columbanus was moved by this kind of cruelty (Jonas, *Life of Saint Columbanus*, no. 8, *Acta Sanctorum*, Benedictine series, second century), when, despite his mother’s opposition and her clinging to the doorway, he asked that she allow him to go to the monastery, while she wailed and threw herself upon the floor, declaring that she would not permit it:

“For he, stepping over the threshold and his mother, asked his mother not to be overcome with grief, saying that she would never again see him in this life.”

The prophet also urges us to this kind of cruelty when he says: “Forget your people and your father’s house, and the King will desire your beauty.” Attending to this, Saint Jerome exclaims (Letter 10, to Furia): “Great is the reward for one who has forgotten his parent: ‘And the King will desire your beauty.’”

As the course of one’s conversion and faith proceeds, and the heart is enlarged, one runs along the way of God’s commandments with the indescribable sweetness of love, in accordance with what the Holy Spirit says in Proverbs (chapter 4): “I will lead you along the paths of equity; when you have entered them, your steps will not be cramped, and when you run you will not stumble”; and Ecclesiasticus 6: “You will labor little in his work [that is, Wisdom’s], and soon you will eat of his fruits”; and in the Apostle: “All discipline for the present seems not to be of joy but of sorrow; afterward, however, it yields the most peaceful fruit of justice to those exercised by it” (Hebrews 12).

Here, however, it is worthwhile to examine Saint Benedict’s text. “As the course of conversion and faith proceeds,” he says. These words may bear a double meaning. First, “as the course of conversion proceeds” may be understood as though he were saying: with the passage of time, through use and practice, and through a good habit of regular observance, you will find easy what previously seemed difficult, and very broad what previously seemed narrow.

“Bare feet,” says Peter Damian (Opusculum 15, chapter 21), “scant clothing, the hardness of the bed, the harshness of food, drinking water, and other things of this kind we beginners do indeed shrink from with a certain fear; but as we persevere and apply ourselves patiently, we consider them easier and more tolerable. Frequency mitigates harshness, and habit commends rigor.”

And Peter of Blois, writing to the novice Alexander (Letter 137), says: “Let not the beginnings of your conversion, the new yoke of obedience, the unfamiliar rigor of the order, and the austerity of discipline terrify you. Whatever now seems harsh, obedience will turn to profit for you; what is now bitter will grow sweet through use. For those who proceed from darkness to light, light is at first troublesome, until their eyes become accustomed to the light.”

For the same reason Saint Bernard encouraged his nephew Robert (Letter 1): “When someone suddenly proceeds from shade to sunlight and from leisure to labor, everything he begins seems burdensome. But after he has begun to abandon the former and gradually grow accustomed to the latter, use removes the difficulty, and he finds that what he previously thought impossible is easy. Even the bravest soldiers commonly tremble when they hear the trumpet before the engagement; but once they have come to battle, the hope of victory makes those who feared being defeated fearless.”

Finally, the Ordinary Gloss teaches the same thing when it gives a moral explanation of Elisha’s miracle, in which a stew made bitter by colocynth is said to have been sweetened by the addition of a little flour: “By this,” it says, “is signified that to people delicately nourished in the world, religious life seems bitter at the beginning. But just as the stew became flavorful through the addition of flour, so through God’s grace and good habituation, religious life, which previously seemed harsh, will not only be endured but will also become sweet.”

Hence Saint Bernard, writing to the novice Hugh, says (Letter 351): “Let not the harshness of the order terrify your tender age. Remember that the rougher thistle makes cloth smoother; conversion makes the conscience [smoother]; the sweetness of Christ will be present, and the prophet’s flour will season the uneatable stew.”

In another sense, “as the course of conversion proceeds” means as the course of virtue proceeds, that is, when you have made some progress in virtue. Thus Smaragdus explains it: “By ‘progress,’ he says, he means the increase of virtues and the progress of the soul, in which the monk must increase and grow daily.”

And this is certainly correct. For mere practice of regular exercises, if virtue is lacking, will not remove the difficulty of religious life; rather, languor and tepidity will increase it. Therefore, as virtue progresses, you will feel no difficulty; everything will seem light, and you will disperse all the schemes of the evil demons, who will flee from you in terror. Saint Bernard teaches this with an excellent comparison (Sermon 60 on the Song of Songs):

“They say that when vines are flowering, every poisonous reptile gives way and cannot in any way endure the fragrance of the new flowers. I want our novices to attend to this and act confidently, considering what kind of spirit they have received, whose first fruits the demons cannot endure.”

These first fruits are indeed the flowers of virtues, which the ancient enemy dreads and shuns in the novice.

With the heart enlarged. That is, when righteousness itself becomes delightful; for, as Saint Augustine says (On Psalm 118), enlargement of the heart is delight in righteousness. The monk’s heart is enlarged in this way when, clinging wholly to God, he becomes one spirit with him and possesses the Creator dwelling within him through grace. Why would the heart of one whom the great, infinite, immeasurable God inhabits not be enlarged?

With the indescribable sweetness of love. He says “the sweetness of love” because where love is, there is not labor but savor, as Saint Bernard says. And it is indescribable because it may be experienced but cannot be expressed by anyone. Refreshed by this sweetness, the prophet sang in complete astonishment: “How great is the multitude of your sweetness, Lord, which you have hidden for those who fear you!”

With this sweetness—“with this new wine they are inflamed, and by this excellent cup the hearts of the faithful and the souls of converts are daily made drunk,” Saint Augustine, or whoever else may be the author, once said (Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine, sermon 182)—as we frequently see when, out of desire for salvation, parents and country are abandoned; when people leave their land and their kindred without compulsion; and, dead to this world, seek other parents spiritually for their souls; when the free come under the yoke; when those who shortly before were proud and exalted pursue humility and despise arrogance; when they desire to be what they formerly disdained and begin to hate what they once were; when, guests in the present and seekers of the future, they sigh for that eternal homeland, having despised the falsity of temporal things.

Thus, intoxicated and thoroughly changed by this spiritual wine, souls prefer abstinence to delicacies, vigils to sweet sleep, poverty to riches; they count the arduous labor against vices as the most delightful pleasure; vices become sweet to them, while the things that had formerly been precious become worthless; they love their enemies and do good to those who hate them; they are not overcome by the anger of those who are angry, are not provoked by insults, and are not broken by injuries. In a word, they feel none of these things because of the fervor of the Holy Spirit.

Such is the sweetness, force, and power of divine love, from which there also follows this:

Never departing from his instruction, persevering in his teaching within the monastery until death. For it is of no benefit to have begun well unless we persevere in what is good until death. Hence, in Cassian, Abbot Pinufius, instructing a young man whom he had received into the monastery, says (Book IV of the *Institutes*, chapter 37): “To have begun well will be of no benefit, nor will it avail that one seized the beginnings of renunciation with full fervor, if a suitable end does not likewise commend and complete them; and if the humility and poverty of Christ, which you have now professed before him, are not guarded by you to the end of life in the same manner in which you undertook them.”

That we may share in Christ’s sufferings through patience. That is, that we may suffer together with Christ. Here the holy Father shows that it is proper to monks to suffer and bear the cross. For if the whole life of a Christian, when lived according to the Gospel, is a cross and martyrdom, how much more so the life of a monk, whose particular aim is to deny himself and put to death all the desires of his heart?

That we may also deserve to share in his kingdom. For “if we suffer with him, we shall also reign with him,” and if we are companions in his sufferings, we shall likewise be companions in his consolation. O consolation! “Many suffer many things for perishable money, and you do not wish to suffer for enduring life!” Saint Augustine once said. “Thus you refuse to labor for God’s promises, as though you did not labor for your own desires! How much do robbers suffer for their wickedness! How much do the depraved suffer for their crimes, the lustful for their depravity, and merchants crossing the sea for their greed, entrusting body and soul to winds and storms, leaving what they know and seeking what is unknown!” (38) And shall we not suffer for eternal happiness, so that we may reign with Christ forever? Let us therefore follow Christ, so that at last we may attain to him. Amen.

# CHAPTER ONE  
## On the kinds, or life, of monks

[Col. 0245]

[Col. 0245A] It is clear that there are four kinds of monks. The first is that of cenobites: this is the monastic kind, serving under a rule or an abbot. The second kind is that of anchorites, that is, hermits—those who, not through the novice’s fervor of conversion [Note: Oxford, “of conduct” (*conversationis*)], but through long testing in the monastery, have learned, already trained by the support of many, to fight against the devil; and, well instructed and coming from the brotherly battle line to the solitary combat of the desert, now secure without another’s consolation, they are sufficient, with God’s help, to fight alone or single-handed against the vices of the flesh or of thoughts.

The third and most detestable kind of monks is that of the Sarabaites. Tested by no rule, as gold is tested in a furnace, nor by the experience of a teacher [Note: Another reading: “of a female teacher” (*magistra*)], but softened into the nature of lead, they are still faithful to the world in their works and are known to lie to God through their tonsure. In pairs, or threes, or certainly singly, without a shepherd, shut up not in the Lord’s but in their own sheepfolds, they regard the pleasure of their desires as law. Whatever they think or choose, they call holy; and whatever they do not wish, they consider forbidden.

The fourth kind of monks is called gyrovagues. They spend their whole life [Note: Another reading: “their whole lifetime”] lodging for three or four days in the cells of different people throughout various provinces, always wandering and never stable, serving their own pleasures [Note: Oxford: “their own wishes”] and the allurements of the belly, and in every respect worse than the Sarabaites. Concerning the wretched way of life of all these, it is better to remain silent than to speak. Passing them over, then, let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to arrange the strongest kind of monks, the cenobites. (39)

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0245]

[Col. 0245C] Monks. A monk is one who, separated from all human company, devotes himself in solitude to the tears of repentance; clinging wholly to God, he becomes one spirit with him, as even the etymology of his name indicates. For *monk* derives from the Greek word μόνος (*monos*), that is, “one.” Hence that canon of the Council of Nicaea cited by Gratian:

“It pleased all those present at the holy synod of Nicaea that the conduct and life of monks should, according to the etymology of the name, differ from everyone else—for *monk* in Greek is rendered in Latin as *singularis*, ‘solitary’; therefore the monk ought to act in every respect as one who is solitary.”

And Saint Jerome, writing to Heliodorus (Letter 1): “Interpret the word *monk*—that is your name. What are you doing in a crowd, you who are alone?” And to the monk Rusticus (Letter 4): “Why do we desire the crowds of cities, we who are reckoned by our solitude?” And to Paulinus (Letter 13): “If you desire to be what you are called—that is, alone—what are you doing in cities, which certainly are not dwelling places of the solitary but of the many?”

According to Pope Eugenius as well, cited by the aforementioned Gratian, a monk is the same as “one who is sad”:

“Let him acknowledge his name. For μόνος in Greek means *unus* in Latin, ‘one’; ἄχος in Greek sounds in Latin as *tristis*, ‘sad.’ Hence he is called ‘one who is sad.’ Let him therefore sit sadly and devote himself to his duty.”

Saint Jerome alludes to this interpretation when he writes against Vigilantius: “The monk has not the office of a teacher but of one who mourns—one who mourns either himself or the world and anxiously awaits the coming of the Lord.”

The author of the book *On the Ecclesiastical Hierarchy* derives the etymology of *monk* differently (chapter 6), namely from the Greek word μονάς (*monas*), that is, “unity”: “because, through pure service to God and the renunciation of the diversity of temporal things, he ought to become one with that which is one and be gathered into sacred unity.”

In a similar way Saint Augustine explains it in his commentary on Psalm 132, where, rebuking the Donatists, he says: “It is rightly displeasing to them that the name of monks is given, because they do not wish to dwell together with their brothers; but, following Donatus, they have abandoned Christ.”

For other etymologies and designations of monks, see Menardus in his notes on the *Council of Regulæ*, chapter 3, § 1, and Haeftenus, *Monastic Investigations*, Book III, entire treatise 1.

It is clear that there are four kinds. Namely: cenobites, anchorites, Sarabaites, and gyrovagues. Saint Jerome recognizes the first three in his letter to Eustochium (Letter 22), for the fourth had not yet arisen in his time.

Saint John Climacus also seems to have indicated the same three when he said (Step 1): “There are altogether three forms of every religious life: either you live alone and in solitude, contending by yourself; or with one or another companion; or, in a cenobium, you rest through patience among many.” By the first he denotes anchorites, who live alone; by the second, Sarabaites, who live in pairs or threes; by the third, cenobites, who live among many.

Abbot Piamun likewise testifies in Cassian that these same three kinds of monks existed in Egypt (Collation 18, chapter 4): “Two of them,” he says, “are excellent, but the third is lukewarm and must be avoided in every way.”

In chapter 8 of the same Collation he adds a fourth, which had arisen in his own time: those “who, at the beginning, in a certain brief fervor, seem to seek the perfection of the cenobium, but, immediately growing lukewarm, refuse to cut away their former habits and vices, and are unwilling to endure longer the yoke of humility and patience. They disdain to be subject to the command of their elders, seek separate cells, and desire to sit alone, so that, being harassed by no one, they may appear patient, gentle, and humble to men.”

Alardus Gazaeus wrongly confuses these with gyrovagues in explaining this passage of Cassian. For gyrovagues are always wandering and never stable; these, however, seek cells and desire to sit in solitude. You might say that they come closer to the Sarabaites, from whom they seem to differ only in this: the Sarabaites, it is said, have never been approved by any rule or possessed the experience of a teacher; these, however, previously lived in a monastery whose yoke they have shaken off.

Saint Isidore, distinguishing hermits from anchorites, lists six kinds of monks: cenobites, hermits, anchorites, those who flatter themselves under the appearance of anchorites—the people Cassian has just described—circumcellions (these are the gyrovagues), and Sarabaites.

Saint Valerius, cited by Saint Benedict of Aniane in the *Concordia of the Rules* (chapter 3, § 7), adds a seventh kind: those who, from the household service and servitude of the monastery, were forcibly tonsured by abbots, since at that time few people were coming forward for conversion. In this category could be placed those whom a certain abbot of the monastery of Mediana, “going around the cities, brought back with him whomever he could find who wished to become monks, and made them monks by tonsuring them not in heart but only in outward habit,” as Richerus writes in chapter 18 of the *Life of Saint Hidulphus*.

We could add here an eighth kind: those who, as Saint Fructuosus says in chapter 1 of the *Common Monastic Rule*, “are accustomed, through fear of Gehenna, to establish monasteries for themselves in their own homes, and, together with their wives, children, servants, and neighbors, to join themselves together under oath, and, in their own villages, as we have said, to consecrate churches in the name of martyrs and falsely call them monasteries. We, however, do not call these monasteries but the destruction of souls and the subversion of the Church.”

Of all these, if cenobites and anchorites are excepted, it is better to remain silent than to speak. For the rest might more truly be called not monks but masks and monsters of monks. Hence Saint Augustine assigns only two kinds of monks.

The first, that of cenobites, so called from the common life that they profess. In Greek, κοινός (*koinos*) means “common,” and βίος (*bios*) means “life.”

Among the kinds of monks, the cenobitic kind is called first either by reason of its institution, its usefulness, or the natural order of things.

First, by reason of its institution, since it is said to have taken its origin from the earliest times of the Church. For, as Abbot Piamun reports in Cassian (Collation 18, chapter 5):

“Such was then the whole Church as it is now difficult to find even a very few in the cenobia. But when, after the departure of the apostles, the multitude of believers began to grow lukewarm, … those who still possessed apostolic fervor, remembering that former perfection, withdrew from their cities and from the society of those whose laxity of life they believed unlawful for themselves and for the Church of God, and began to remain in suburban and more secluded places and to practice privately what they remembered had been established generally by the apostles throughout the whole body of the Church.

“Thus there grew up the discipline of those disciples whom we have mentioned, who had separated themselves from the contagion of the others. Gradually, as time proceeded, they were separated from the crowds of believers because they abstained from marriage and distinguished themselves from the company of their parents and from the conduct of this world. They were called monks or *monazontes*, after the strictness of a singular and solitary life. Consequently, because of their common association, they were called cenobites, and their cells and dwellings cenobia.

“This, therefore, was the most ancient kind of monks. It was first not only in time but also in grace, and for many years it alone remained inviolate, until the age of Abbot Paul or Antony.”

Those who make Saint Pachomius the first father of the cenobites do not, however, accept Cassian’s view. But Turrecremata, tracing the origins of the cenobites further back in his *Treatise 8 on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, asserts that the cradle of cenobites began with the assemblies of the prophets, and proves it by this authority of Saint Jerome: “The sons of the prophets, whom we read to have been monks,” etc.

Second, the cenobites are first in usefulness, for common life, as we shall demonstrate later, is preferable to the anchoritic life, which, the more sublime it is, is the more dangerous.

Third, the cenobitic kind is first in the natural order of things, because the desert receives no one unless he has first been tested in the cenobium.

This is the monastic kind. Saint Benedict the Father seems here to confuse monasteries with cenobia. Yet Abbot Piamun, in Cassian (Collation 18, chapter 10), makes some distinction between them:

“Although some people customarily call monasteries cenobia indiscriminately, there is nevertheless this difference between them: *monastery* is the name of a dwelling, signifying nothing more than the place—that is, the habitation—of monks; but *cenobium* also designates the quality and discipline of the profession itself. A monastery may even be the habitation of one monk; but it cannot be called a cenobium unless it is a place where the united fellowship of many who dwell together exists.”

Indeed, it is clear from the Lives of the Holy Fathers that the word *monastery* is frequently used to designate the habitation of a single monk. Thus Saint Athanasius, in the *Life of Saint Antony* (chapter 21), says: “There were monasteries on the mountain like tents.” Rufinus also reports (*Lives of the Fathers*, Book II, chapter 23) that the brothers who had gathered together “built a monastery in a single day.” Who could believe that this refers to a cenobium?

In the same place, when someone wished to renounce the world and asked Abbot Ammonius for an empty cell, he says: “Then he replied: ‘I will look for one; but until I find it, remain here in this monastery …’ And, leaving him everything together with the monastery, he himself found a very small cell some distance away and settled in it. To the brother who had recently arrived and did not understand, he yielded the monastery in its entirety, with all that had been in it.”

Saint Nilus uses the word *monastery* in the same sense in the *History of the Massacre of the Holy Fathers on Sinai*, chapter 9, in Bollandus, January 13.

### “Serving under a rule or an abbot.”

The particle *vel* (“or”) may here be taken in two ways, disjunctively and copulatively. Disjunctively, because, as Bernard of Cassino says: “When monks do not have abbots over them, but provosts, deans, and priors, they nevertheless serve under a rule; but they follow the rule according to the commands of their provosts.” And Hildemar says: “Perhaps Blessed Benedict was filled with the spirit of prophecy and saw, by that prophetic spirit, the time in which there would be many monasteries without regular abbots; therefore he wrote: ‘Serving under a rule or an abbot.’” Nevertheless, both admit that *vel* may here be taken copulatively, in the sense of “and”; and in this sense the other interpreters generally understand it as well. Thus, by “abbot” is understood any superior, whatever title he may bear—whether provost, dean, or prior.

### “The second kind consists of anchorites.”

Anchorites—whose leaders Saint Jerome and Cassian made Paul and Antony, and whose Old Testament shadows were represented for us by Elijah and Elisha, while in the New Testament John the Baptist offered another such example—“are those who dwell in the deserts,” says Saint Jerome (Epistle 22). Or, as Abbot Piamon says in Cassian (Conference 18, chapter 4), they are those “who, having first been trained in coenobia and having attained perfection through active conduct, chose the seclusion of solitude”; those who, “not at all content with the victory by which they have trampled underfoot the Devil’s hidden ambushes among human beings, desire to engage the demons in open battle and manifest conflict, and therefore do not fear to penetrate the vast recesses of the wilderness.” Hence they also received the name “anchorites,” “for they are so called because they have withdrawn far from human beings,” as Saint Jerome says [Col. 0249A] (Epistle 22). For the Greek verb ἀναχωρεῖν (*anachōrein*) is rendered in Latin as *secedere*, “to withdraw,” although Boherius and Trithemius derive a different etymology for this word.

They, for their part, maintain that the men were called *anchorites* from ἀνά (*ana*), “upward,” and χόρος (*choros*), “choir,” because they are especially devoted to the contemplation of heavenly things and “ought to breathe toward the choir of the celestial spirits,” as Trithemius puts it. Hence Abbot John says in Cassian: “The perfection of the hermit is to have a mind stripped of earthly cares and, insofar as human frailty permits, to live with Christ.”

Boherius adds that they were called anchorites as though “pressing their hearts toward the Lord” through fasts and abstinence. This interpretation agrees sufficiently with what Severus Sulpicius writes about anchorites (Book I of the Dialogues, chapter 9): “Most of them dwell in the desert without any shelters; they are called anchorites. They live on the roots of plants, never remain in any fixed place, lest they be visited by human beings; wherever night compels them, there they have their dwelling.”

### “That is, of hermits.”

Saint Benedict confounds anchorites with hermits, yet Saint Isidore establishes some distinction between them (Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15). He wishes hermits to be those “who are said to withdraw far from human beings, to seek out and inhabit deserted places and vast solitudes, and so forth.” Anchorites, however, are those “who, having already been perfected in coenobitic conduct, shut themselves away, removed far from human sight.”

More truly, however, one might say that both constitute only a single kind of monk. For those whom Saint Isidore here describes as hermits are called anchorites by Saint Jerome, Severus Sulpicius, and Cassian. Nevertheless, I will not deny that this kind of monk can be divided into two or three species. For, as Blessed Peter Damian says (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 52):

> “The order of hermits is divided in two. Some of them inhabit cells; others, wandering everywhere through the deserts of the wilderness, refuse to have fixed dwellings. Those who roam through the desert are called anchorites; those who are content with cells are called hermits by the customary name, which has become a particular designation from a common one.”

The latter, too, existed in a twofold distinction. For, as Menardus observes (in his note on the Council of Regulæ, chapter 3, §6):

> “Some were enclosed in cells within the bounds of a monastery, as is clear from Justinian’s Novella 5: ‘Unless some of them, living in contemplation and perfection, maintain a secluded life in a lodging—those whom they customarily call anchorites, that is, those who depart, and hesychasts, that is, those who rest.’ Here ‘lodging’ is understood as a cell, for the discussion concerns those who are enclosed within monasteries. This is also clear from canon 41 of the Sixth Synod, which says that such enclosed persons are to exercise an ἀναχωρητικὴ παιδοτριβεῖσθαι διαγωγήν—that is, to practice an anchoritic way of life. Others were enclosed outside the bounds of monasteries; Saint Isidore treats of these in this chapter.”

Women themselves were not excluded from the first kind of enclosure. We often find in the authors that women lived enclosed within men’s monasteries. Such was, among the Meldi, Gibelina, sister of Otger, duke of Carmentriacum [Col. 0249D], who in the eleventh century was enclosed for the love of God in the monastery of Faro, according to the *Notice* concerning the aforementioned Otger by Abbot Fulco (Fourth Century of Benedictine History, part I, p. 659).

Likewise, at Verdun there was Blessed Adelwiif, mother of Saint Poppo (Bollandists, 25 January). After first professing the coenobitic life by receiving the veil, “she later began to live as a solitary at Saint Vitonus; there, after triumphing over the Devil with all the forces at his disposal, she completed the course of her life in peace,” as Everhelmus writes about her in the *Life of Saint Poppo*, no. 18.

Finally, at Saint Gall there was Saint Wiborada (Fifth Century of Benedictine History). At first she was enclosed for four years beside the church of Saint George; afterward, summoned to Saint Gall by the bishop, she remained there until the end of her life, which she completed by martyrdom. “The bishop, accompanied by a few men, followed her and, after blessing her, sealed the enclosure,” as Hartmann, monk of Saint Gall, testifies in her *Life*, II.15.

Such enclosed women lived under the governance and discipline of the monastery’s abbot, as our Mabillon proves in his preliminary observations on the *Life of Saint Wiborada*. The same law bound men and women alike. Whether enclosed within or outside the monastery, or otherwise living in solitude, they nevertheless remained subject to the abbot of the monastery from which they had departed. This may be inferred, among other examples, from the *Life of Saint Aybert*, monk of Crespin, no. 1 (Bollandists, 7 April). Having received permission from Abbot Lambert, he “entered into enclosure, and as long as he lived served the Lord under the authority of the abbot of Crespin.”

Those who were not committed to perpetual enclosure customarily came to their monastery at appointed times. We have a clear example of this in Adhegrin, a monk of Cluny, described by John the monk in the *Life of Saint Odo* (Book I, no. 22, Fifth Century of Benedictine History). Having lived in the desert for more than thirty years with the abbot’s permission, he “was accustomed to descend only on Sundays or on the principal feast days to the monastery of Saint Peter, called Cluny, because it was situated nearly two miles away” [Col. 0250B]. Finally, Grimlaicus wrote a rule for those perpetually enclosed; in chapter 15 he discusses the manner and order of enclosing a solitary.

### “Those [who do not go forth] in the fervor of a recent conversion.”

As Hildemar says, this “means that they do not go to the desert whenever the thought of going to the desert happens to occur to them.” For one must not believe every wind, nor is every spirit from God; Satan, too, sometimes transforms himself into an angel of light and tries, under the appearance of piety, to persuade us to undertake many things for which we are unequal.

Nor should they be sent “by the fervor of a recent conversion”—that is, not at the beginning of their conversion, when monks are accustomed to burn with zeal. Such fervor is highly suspect and liable to change, and beginners are generally not suited to the anchoritic life. Thus we read in the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book V, booklet 10, no. 110):

> “A certain brother renounced the world and received the monastic habit; immediately he enclosed himself, saying: ‘I wish to be a solitary.’ When the neighboring elders heard this, they came and expelled him. They made him go around to the cells of the brethren, do penance before each one, and say: ‘Forgive me, for I am not a solitary, but have only recently taken up the beginning of monastic life.’”

### “But only after prolonged testing in the monastery.”

This was demanded by the discipline of the ancient monks: no one was admitted to the desert unless he had first been tested for a long time in a coenobium. “From the training ground of monasteries we wish such soldiers to depart as will not be frightened by the harsh beginnings of the desert,” says Saint Jerome in a letter to the monk Rusticus (Epistle 4). The same is taught by the aforementioned Abbot Piamon in Cassian. The same rule is found in canon 7 of the Council of Vannes in 465; in canon 5 of the Seventh Council of Toledo; and in canon 41 of the Sixth Synod. It may also be seen in the *Life of Saint Euthymius*, abbot, no. 89, volume II of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, and in the *Life of Saint Theodosius the Coenobiarch*, chapter 2, in the Bollandists, 11 January. Certainly, as someone aptly said, just as the flower precedes the fruit, so the coenobitic life ought to precede the anchoritic life.

Someone may ask how extensive and of what character this testing in the coenobium was, since Saint Benedict prescribes only its duration, and that indefinitely. Saint Isidore determines the matter in his book *On Ecclesiastical Offices* in these words:

> “But these men, tested in the examination of the coenobia in all the disciplines of the monastery, are chosen through obedience for this contemplation after thirty years.”

Francis George, however, speaking in his *Harmony of the World* about Rachel and Leah, the wives of Jacob, limits the period of testing to eighteen years, or twenty at most:

> “Jacob sighs for Rachel and serves her, yet he is first joined to Leah, because the spiritual man sighs for repose and vision, which belong to contemplation, and for this he has undertaken the yoke of service to God. Nevertheless, in order that he may be joined to Leah and to the active life, it is first necessary that he pass through this before he reaches contemplative perfection. Therefore those ancient Fathers decreed that no one should be admitted to the solitary and contemplative life unless he had been exercised for eighteen or twenty years in works of charity and the services of the monastery.”

From this passage one might suspect that, through the carelessness of copyists, an error entered Isidore’s text and that “thirty” was written in place of “twenty.” Possevinus, too, in Book V of the *Bibliotheca*, chapter 57, citing this passage of Isidore, reads “twenty” without qualification.

The Sixth Synod reduces that long period to four years, issuing the following canon:

> “Those who wish to live in solitude within enclosures, whether in cities or villages, must first enter a monastery and thoroughly learn what is required for this anchoritic way of life. For three complete years they must remain subject to the superior of the coenobium in the fear of God. After they have fulfilled obedience in all things, as is proper, they are to be examined by the bishop to determine whether they freely and wholeheartedly desire to embrace this purpose. They are then to make profession of this institution; yet even then they are not immediately to be enclosed, but must remain outside the enclosure for another year, so that their intention may become more certain” (canon 41).

Saint John Climacus gives the rationale for this institution by a familiar but appropriate comparison (*The Ladder*, Step 4):

> “Just as it is dangerous for an inexperienced novice and an ordinary soldier to commit himself to single combat, so for a religious man to withdraw into solitude before acquiring experience and much practice in subduing the passions of the soul is a perilous venture. For just as the former risks his life, so the latter risks eternal salvation.”

Saint Theodosius the Coenobiarch used the same argument (*Life*, chapter 2; Bollandists, 11 January). Add that anchoritic life consists in continual contemplation of heavenly realities, which cannot be reached without a preceding active life in coenobia, as Abbot Nesteros teaches, among others, in Cassian (*Conference* 14, chapter 2), and as Grimlaicus says in the *Rule of Solitaries*:

> “Whoever attempts to climb to the summit of the contemplative life must first test himself through many trials in the active life.”

Since not all who live in coenobia, even for a long time, therefore become better or are judged suitable for the anchoritic life, we must now see who and what sort of persons are to be transferred from coenobia to it. Saint Benedict indicates this when he adds:

### “Already trained to fight against the Devil with the support of many.”

This is equivalent to saying: those who, having overcome all vices and been imbued with every virtue insofar as human frailty permits, no longer fear the Devil. Such men have learned to fight against the Devil, and the desert truly requires men of this kind.

“We wish such soldiers to enter from the training ground of the monasteries as will not be frightened by the harsh beginnings of the desert,” says Saint Jerome (Epistle 4)—“men who have given proof of their conduct for a long time; who have been least of all, so that they might become first of all; whom neither hunger nor satiety has ever overcome; who rejoice in poverty; whose habit, speech, countenance, walk, and teaching are lessons in virtue.”

Cassian says likewise (*Institutes*, Book V, chapter 36):
