> “Those who first remain for a very long time in coenobia, carefully instructed in every rule of patience and discernment, possessing equally the virtue of humility and nakedness, and having been thoroughly purged of every vice, enter the deepest recesses of the desert in order to engage in the fiercest battles with the demons.”

And elsewhere (*Institutes*, Book VIII, chapter 17):

> “Only the perfected and those cleansed of every vice ought to seek the desert. They should enter it not as a refuge from faintheartedness, but for the sake of divine contemplation and the desire for a higher vision, after their vices have been thoroughly burned out in the community of the brethren; for this vision can be attained in solitude only by the perfected.”

Saint John Climacus states the matter most clearly (*The Ladder*, Step 27):

> “The signs and proofs, or exercises, of those who pursue solitude not without cause are these: a mind disturbed by no waves of agitation; vain thoughts absent; rapture toward God; the ever-present memory of eternal punishments; consideration of imminent death; an inexpressible eagerness for prayer; an impregnable custody of oneself; the extinguishing of lust; ignorance of cravings; death to the world; no desire for food; a fountain of discernment; the gift of tears; the destruction of talkativeness; and whatever else belongs to this kind, which is hateful and hostile to crowds.”

Before this he says:

> “Let no one subject to anger, pride of spirit, dissimulation, hypocrisy, or other such vices dare set foot in solitude.”

And again, explaining the reason:

> “He who suffers from illnesses of the soul and nevertheless dares to undertake the solitary life acts like one who leaps from a ship into the waves of the deep sea and imagines that he can reach the harbor safely on a plank.”

For, as Cassian says, solitude “customarily preserves and even magnifies the vices of those who are less reformed.” But enough on this.

Saint Benedict’s words deserve notice: “with the support of many.” He does not say, “with the assistance of some outstanding Father” or “of one particular companion,” but “with the support of many,” already trained. For, as Saint Antony said in Cassian (*Institutes*, Book V, chapter 4):

> “He who, after the coenobitic profession, strives to attain the heights of a higher perfection, and who, having grasped the test of discernment, is already capable of standing by his own judgment and reaching the citadel of anchoritic life, ought by no means to seek every kind of virtue from one person, however eminent. One is adorned with the flowers of knowledge; another’s path is strengthened more firmly by reason; another is grounded in the weight of patience; another in humility, and so forth.”

From this he inferred that “the monk who desires to store up spiritual honey, like a most prudent bee, ought to gather each virtue from those who possess it most intimately and deposit it in the vessel of his own heart.”

### “Well instructed and coming from the fraternal battle line to the solitary combat of the desert, and so forth.”

From this passage it is therefore clear what we said in the prologue: both the coenobitic and the anchoritic life are a perpetual military service, with this distinction, however, that the latter is more dangerous, while the former is easier and safer. Peter the Venerable elegantly describes this distinction in a letter to the hermit Gislebert (Book I, Epistle 20):

> “The common dwelling of those who live together in the cloister may be compared with the multitude of an army arranged for battle. There each man fights his adversary more securely insofar as he hopes for assistance nearer to him from the hand of a fellow soldier. In that battle, each combatant relies not only on his own valor but sometimes even more on the strength of those fighting at his right and left than on his own. There each man labors both to destroy those lying in wait for his salvation and to defend his companions by every means. They understand no less the danger in the death of their comrades than they perceive the harm caused by the life of their enemies.

> “But the solitary combat is conducted with so much greater danger as the combatant waits longer for another’s help. And what increases the danger is that, unlike what occurs in a battle line, where many fight against many, and unlike a duel, where one fights against one, he contends in an unfamiliar manner of combat alone against many, superior both in number and in strength, under an uncertain fate.”

From this testimony of the Holy Rule Blessed Peter Damian also infers that Saint Benedict not only permitted anchoritic life to his monks but even urged it. After quoting the aforementioned words of the Holy Rule, he concludes as follows (*Book VI, Epistle 12):

> “From these words it is plainly gathered that the blessed teacher not only did not forbid a brother to ascend from the monastery to the desert, but even urged, taught, and encouraged him to do so by certain exhortations. He grants authority so that, after a prolonged period of testing in the monastery, the brother may learn how to struggle in the desert against the stratagems of the cunning tempter. … In those words of the Holy Rule which we set forth above, it is clearly declared that Saint Benedict, while placing a man in the monastery, directs him toward the desert. Here he establishes him, but invites and exhorts him to go there.”

He develops this at length.

Indeed, the Camaldolese order, itself serving under the Rule of Saint Benedict, has its hermits. Even today, many cells of anchorites can be seen on Mount Serrat, inhabited by Benedictines. We also infer that in former times many of our own monks lived as anchorites on Mount Vosges from the *Life of Saint Paul*, bishop of Verdun, II.2, where we read (Second Century of Benedictine History):

> “At last, with the Lord leading him, the servant of Christ enters the desert called Vosges. Many anchorites are said to have inhabited the solitude of this desert, divided among cells and separated from one another except on Saturdays and Sundays, when they met and spoke with one another, unless bodily weakness or concern for the salvation of a soul compelled them to visit one another. Paul eagerly sought to attain their desirable way of life.”

No one, however, withdrew to the desert without the prior permission of the abbot and the consent of the brethren; both were required, as could be demonstrated by many examples.

The *Life of Saint Bavo the Confessor* offers us a clear instance (Second Century of Benedictine History). Coming to Abbot Frorbert, he “humbly asked him to grant him a little cell in which he might familiarly entreat the Lord’s mercy for his crimes. When the pious father of the monastery heard his request, he received him with joy and, in accordance with the command of the pious Father Benedict, summoned the whole community of the monastery and disclosed his petition to the brethren”; and the brethren assented to his wishes.

Similarly, Saint Baronius “began earnestly to ask the father of his coenobium in repeated prayers that, with his permission, he might be allowed to leave his native land of Gaul and thus finally lead an anchoritic life. After a very long and uninterrupted persistence in his request, his pastor, together with the entire flock, though unwillingly, satisfied his desire.”

So too Saint Cuthbert, according to Bede (*Life*, chapter 17):

> “After he had completed many years in the monastery, at last, with the favor of both the aforementioned abbot and the brethren accompanying him, he went with great joy to the long-desired, sought-after, and requested solitude.”

And Saint Madalgisilus, “desiring to undertake a stricter and more secluded form of life, humbly asked that he be allowed to seek a remote and quiet place. … What he devoutly requested, the free kindness of the brethren granted him with great sweetness,” as Hariulf writes in his *Life*, II.5.

Finally, when Saint Wilfrid, bishop of York, and abbot of Ripon, was about to grant Celino, the provost, permission to seek the desert, he first referred the matter to the brethren, as Eddius records in his *Life*, no. 60.

It certainly seems equitable that those who are accustomed to be admitted to the monastery with the consent of the brethren should not depart from it without the benevolent consent of the entire community. Among the ancients, however, it could be shown that the abbot’s consent alone was sufficient, from Severus Sulpicius, whose words are these (*Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 5):

> “Not far from the desert adjoining the Nile there are many monasteries. Most of their inhabitants live together in one place. If any of them conceives in his mind a desire for greater virtue, so that he may go to the desert to lead a solitary life, he does not depart unless the abbot permits it.”

One of our own, Saint Tillo, a monk of Solignac, left the monastery secretly and went to the desert without the consent either of the abbot or of the brethren.

### “But the third, and most detestable, kind of monks.”

Saint Benedict paints the third kind of monks in the darkest colors and therefore calls it *teterrimum*, that is, “blackest, darkest, most horrifying, uncivilized, or savage,” as Smaragdus explains.

Saint Jerome uses the same expression (Epistle 22):

> “The third kind is what they call Remoboth, most detestable and neglected.”

And Abbot Piamon says in Cassian (*Conference* 18, chapter 7):

> “After these there emerged that most detestable and faithless kind of monks—or rather, that harmful planting revived—which in the beginning of the Church was cut down by the severity of the Apostle Peter through Ananias and Sapphira.”

That this kind originated with Ananias and Sapphira is likewise asserted by Saint Isidore (Book II, *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15) and by the Venerable Bede in his commentary on Acts, chapter 5.

### “It consists of Sarabaites.”

“They were called Sarabaites, according to the characteristic usage of the Egyptian language, because they separated themselves from the communities of the coenobia and individually took care of their own needs,” says Cassian (*Conference* 18, chapter 7).

This seems to agree with the reading cited by Menardus from the *Apology of the Emperor Henry IV*, where this passage is quoted: “Sarabaites, that is, those who live for themselves.” Smaragdus says: “Sarabaites are interpreted as ‘refusers,’ because they refuse to follow the examples and virtues of their elders.”

Hence Abbot Odo of Cluny says (*Conference* 3, no. 22):

> “We wretched men,” he said, “are not monks, as we are falsely called, but Sarabaites—that is, refusers—because we refuse the yoke of regular discipline.”

Bernard of Cassino likewise says: “They are called Sarabaites, as though ‘refusers,’ because, rejecting holy glory, they refuse to serve under a shepherd.”

### “Approved by no rule.”

They are so called because they approve no rule; rather, they avoid it lest they be reproved, as Boherius reports.

### “Without the experience of a master.”

For they themselves live without a shepherd, and in this they are known to reject the entire discipline of the coenobites, who serve under a rule and an abbot. Thus Cassian describes their conduct very aptly:

> “They seek the discipline of the coenobia in no way; they do not submit to the judgment of the elders, nor, trained by their traditions, do they learn to conquer their own wills; nor do they receive any rule of sound discernment through legitimate instruction.”

### “Like gold in a furnace.”

That is, like gold in the furnace of the monastery, where coenobites are tested in the fire of regular observance so that they may emerge purer.

### “But softened according to the nature of lead.”

He compares the Sarabaites to lead, which, when applied to fire, not only becomes soft but completely flows away. For as soon as they feel even the fire of a minor difficulty, they entirely dissolve and flow away into empty pleasures. Hence pleasure according to their desires is their rule.

### “Still serving the world by their works.”

Smaragdus explains this passage as follows:

> “What does it mean still to serve the world by one’s works, unless it means doing what a man did in the world while he was still in secular dress? He serves the world because he does not cease to fulfill its will; he serves the world because he separates himself from it neither in desire nor in deed, but merely pretends to be a son of God through the tonsure and the religious habit. Outwardly, in habit and religious profession, he appears to ignorant observers to belong to the Lord.”

These words apply excellently to the Sarabaites, who live no differently than they did in the world.

### “They are known to deceive God by the tonsure.”

For, as Abbot Piamon says in Cassian, they “renounce only publicly—that is, before the eyes of human beings—or, under the privilege of this name, namely ‘monk,’ continue to be bound by the same occupations in their own dwellings; or, building cells for themselves and calling them monasteries, they remain in them according to their own right and freedom, in no way submitting to the commands of the Gospel, so that they may not be occupied by any concern for daily sustenance or distracted by any affairs of household property.”

### “Those who live two or three together, or certainly singly.”

Saint Jerome says similarly (Epistle 22):

> “They live together in twos or threes, and not many more.”

And Abbot Piamon says in Cassian:

> “Those who, as we have said, avoid strictness, remain two or three together in cells.”

In this they present some appearance of both the anchoritic and coenobitic life, while in reality they possess neither: not the first, because of the companionship rejected by anchoritic life; not the second, because of the lack of numbers required by coenobitic life if it is to be practiced truly and religiously.

Not very different from these hiding places of the Sarabaites are the cells outside coenobia—priories or provostships—in which two or three brothers live without order and without discipline. Saint Bernard therefore calls them “synagogues of Satan” in his letter to Abbot Guarinus (Epistle 254), and he greatly commends anyone who destroys them.

And rightly so. For, as John of Torquemada says (*Treatise 13 on the Rule of Saint Benedict*):

> “In small priories religion is destroyed. There one approaches the vice of ownership, the merit of obedience is diminished, and continence is easily endangered. He who is alone in a priory, or with one companion, as often happens, is almost always an owner, possessing most things for himself. His obedience has less merit when no one commands him anything, and therefore he does what he wishes. Continence too is easily endangered, because the opportunity for sin is available.”

Hence the salutary warning of a certain deacon to Saint Leobinus, monk and afterward bishop of Chartres (*Life*, First Century of Benedictine History):

> “I warn you beforehand not to associate yourself with a small cell, because when individuals desire to place themselves over one another, obedience is rendered to no one.”

To prevent this danger, the abbots assembled at the Council of Aachen decreed (canon 44) that in such cells “the abbot must take care not to permit fewer than six monks to live there.”

Peter the Venerable seems to have extended this canon when he decreed:

> “Wherever the capacity of the place permits, twelve brothers are to be established, apart from the deans, with a thirteenth added as prior; and they are to maintain the full order.”

The Cistercians likewise decreed in statute 41 that “twelve monks, with an abbot as the thirteenth, are to be sent to new coenobia.” The same is found in their *Institutes*, chapter 12, and in the *Institutions*, distinction 1, chapter 6. They confirm it in the *Book of Ancient Definitions*, distinction 3, chapter 3, where they prescribe:

> “The Fathers are to join and unite smaller monasteries, of both monks and nuns, to others, with the advice of the founders and the general chapter, whenever such monasteries cannot suitably support at least thirteen monks or nuns living there continuously and thus observe the common statutes of the order in all things.”

The Feuillants likewise state in their constitutions (chapter 1):

> “To avoid in this congregation that most detestable kind of monks called Sarabaites, we decree that henceforth no monastery offered to or constructed for the congregation is to be received unless it possesses, or can reasonably be expected to possess, revenues sufficient to support at least thirteen or twelve brothers.”

The Carthusians made a similar provision in their new collection of statutes (Part II, chapter 21, no. 3):

> “Because we know that many scandals and reproaches have come upon our order from the careless and indiscriminate acceptance of new houses insufficiently endowed, and because we reasonably fear worse things in the future unless a salutary remedy is applied, we decree that no house is henceforth to be accepted unless it has first been endowed with sufficient revenues or assigned properties for the support of the prior and twelve monks and for bearing the other burdens.”

The statutes of Guigo assign this number, which they here determine as a minimum, as a maximum:

> “The number of inhabitants of this desert consists of thirteen monks—not because we are always so many, for at present we are not, but because, if God provides them, we intend to receive that number. If, however, some individual should ask for mercy who seems, because of his usefulness and uprightness, scarcely recoverable, a fourteenth may be added, provided that the house is thought able to bear it” (chapter 78).

The ancient statutes of the Carthusians say the same (chapter 25). Hildemar certainly writes that twelve monks are sufficient in the desert, though not at all in cities. Torquemada, however, says that a community is not to be called a congregation if fewer than twelve monks live there (*On chapter 17 of the Rule of Saint Benedict*).

Moreover, the Council of Epaon forbids “new cells or small communities of monks to be established without the bishop’s knowledge” (chapter 10).

If there is such danger where only three or four monks live together, how much greater is it where someone lives alone, without a companion, without a witness, without a prior, abandoned to his own desires? It can scarcely be imagined. Therefore, to provide some remedy for this evil, Pope Gregory IX decreed in a bull to the Benedictine monks, preserved by Matthew Paris, and specifically in another addressed to the Cluniacs, later renewed by Nicholas IV:

> “No single monk is to reside alone in any priory. Rather, one or more companions are to be joined to the monk who is alone, if the resources of the place permit; otherwise the monk is to be recalled to the cloister, with provision being made that divine worship be celebrated there properly.”

After them, Benedict XII issued the same provision in his Constitution:

> “We also order and wish the decree of the Lateran Council concerning the non-placement of individual monks throughout villages, towns, and parish churches, as well as the constitution of our predecessor Clement, issued at the Council of Vienne, to be firmly observed: namely, that individual monks presume not to live alone in the administrations or priories entrusted to them.”

The Council of London in the year 1200 contains the same provision. So do the constitutions of Richard, bishop of Salisbury, in 1217, and the constitutions of Richard, bishop of Durham, in 1220, preserved by Spelman in volume II of the *Councils of England*.

### “Without a shepherd.”

Certainly without him who says, “I am the good shepherd,” from whom they separate themselves by living according to the flesh. Or, “without a shepherd, that is, without an abbot, who appears to act in the monastery in Christ’s place, who says, ‘I am the good shepherd,’” as Smaragdus explains. For they reject his commands and authority, living according to their own judgment and power, as Saint Jerome says (Epistle 22).

### “Enclosed not in the Lord’s sheepfolds, but in their own.”

Smaragdus explains this passage:

> “The Lord’s sheepfolds are the monasteries of the holy monks, who are rightly ruled by Christ, the supreme Shepherd, and placed in a pasture.”

But these folds are far too narrow for the immense instability of the Sarabaites’ minds. Therefore they do not allow themselves to be enclosed in the Lord’s sheepfolds, but, as Saint Jerome says, “they live for the most part in cities and fortified towns.”

What the author of the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert* says—that they lived in caves or holes in the rocks—seems to have been invented without basis (Sermon 21):

> “Such were those Sarabaites of whom Father Jerome wrote to us in the third place, a kind that must be avoided with every affection. They were in Egypt, living in holes in the rocks, dressed in the skins of pigs and oxen, girded only with ropes, carrying the spines of palms as spurs fastened to their belts, barefoot and bloodied. Leaving their caves, they went to Jerusalem for the festival of the Coenopægia; entering the Holy of Holies, they preached poverty and abstinence, which they professed to preserve with devotion of spirit. Later they hastened to pluck out their beards before the eyes of men without compensation, and thus, having acquired fame and profit, they returned to their own places, rejoicing in solitude and feasting beyond anything we can describe.”

At that time, however, there was no Jewish temple in Jerusalem, nor is any of this found in Jerome or Cassian, who described the conduct of the Sarabaites with considerable accuracy. Nevertheless, almost the same account, word for word, can be found in the ancient *Readings* of Caelius Rhodiginus, Book XXVII, chapter 6.

For them the pleasure of their desires takes the place of a rule.] For this reason they refuse to have a shepherd, so that they may more freely accomplish whatever they please: “not content,” says Abbot Piamon in Cassian, “to be governed by the care and command of an abbot, but chiefly seeking this: that, released from the yoke of their elders, they may have the freedom to exercise their own wills, to go forth or wander wherever they please, and to do whatever they desire.” Hence follows what St. Jerome says: “Among these there are often quarrels, because, living on their own food, they do not endure being subject to anyone. Indeed, they commonly compete in fasts and make a secret matter of victory. Everything among them is affected: loose sleeves, leggings that wrinkle and puff out, coarser clothing, frequent sighs, visits to virgins, disparagement of clergy; and whenever a feast day comes, they gorge themselves until they vomit.”

Whatever they have thought or chosen, they consider holy; and whatever they have not wanted, they consider impermissible. St. Benedict notably says “whatever they have chosen,” not “whatever is commanded them”; in this too they differ from coenobites, whose way is to obey another’s authority, not to choose what pleases them. But the wretched men do not notice what Abbot Piamon says in Cassian: “The sluggishness of their own will plunges these men alive into hell.”

The fourth kind of monks is that called the gyrovagus, or “wandering monk.”] These are the men whom the Sixth Council, canon 42, ordered to be confined in monasteries or driven into solitude—men who, under the falsely assumed name of hermits, dressed in black garments, wearing their hair long, go about the cities and associate with secular persons and women. St. Isidore calls them *Circilliones* (*Ecclesiastical Offices*, II.15); St. Augustine calls them *Circelliones* and *Circumcelliones*; Bernard of Cassino calls them *Circumcellariones*, because they continually wandered around cells and were never stationary. Of them Bishop Synesius writes: “Some among us wander about without occupation. They wish to have no fixed rule, having abandoned the one they previously possessed; and they wander wherever there is greater profit.”

Who throughout their whole life pass through various provinces,] that is, through various regions and different kingdoms. The extremely narrow prisons of monasteries cannot contain them; indeed, even the spacious places of solitude are too confined for them. Nor are they content with one province for their wandering: they run through many, so that one could most truly say with Bernard of Cassino that they have made the whole world their cloister. But who could set out their practices as they wander and run about in this way? It is useful here to cite Augustine, who depicts them with complete vividness (*On the Work of Monks*, 28):

“He has scattered everywhere so many hypocrites under the appearance of monks—the enemy, of course, of the human race—going around the provinces, sent nowhere, fixed nowhere, standing nowhere, sitting nowhere. Some sell the limbs of martyrs, if indeed they are martyrs; others magnify their fringes and phylacteries; others falsely claim that they have heard that their parents or relatives are living in this or that region, and that they are going to them. And all of them ask, all of them demand, either the expenses of profitable poverty or the price of feigned holiness.”

Through the cells of various persons.] The word “cell” can be understood in various ways:

1. It may mean any place in which something is stored and concealed; for *cella* is said to derive from *celare*, “to conceal.”

2. It may mean some more secluded part of a temple, into which it was not lawful for everyone to enter, such as the place where the seat of a god existed. Thus Varro says (*On the Latin Language*, IV): “For this reason, in sacred buildings, before the cell where the seats of the gods are, the Greeks say *πρόδομον*”—that is, “forecourt” or “vestibule.”

3. It may mean the place where monks customarily sleep, as in the Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 22: “Let a lamp burn in that same cell until morning.”

4. It may mean the monks’ sleeping chambers, which, as is also clear from ancient sources, were assigned individually to individuals, as appears from Justinian’s Novel 5, *On Monks*. Hence the Second Council of Tours says: “Nor shall they be permitted to have common cells in which two may stay, but let them lie in separate ones.”

5. It may mean the small dwellings of anchorites, because there they lie hidden, removed from all intercourse with human beings, so that they may reveal their ways to God.

6. It may mean a monastery or coenobium. Thus St. Benedict, addressing his sister Scholastica, says: “I cannot remain outside the cell at all”; and St. Gregory says (*Register*, I.54): “The oratory of Blessed Mary, which has recently been built in the cell of the brothers, where Abbot Marinianus is known to preside.”

7. Finally, it may mean a small monastery subject to a larger one, commonly called a priory or provostship. Of these is canon 44 of the Council of Aachen: “Let abbots be permitted to have cells in which there may be either monks or canons, and let the abbot take care not to allow fewer than six monks to reside there.”

Here, however, the word “cells” may be understood in the last three senses. For it is certain that those gyrovagi visited anchorites and coenobites, whether the latter lived in larger or smaller monasteries; and it is also clear from canon 42 of the Sixth Council that they went around the cities.

They lodge for three or four days,] that is, for as long as they are treated lavishly as guests, as Boherius explains. They know, of course, that it is the custom of monasteries for guests, for some days after their arrival, to be received more humanely and more generously than usual. When those days have passed, they are reduced to the common manner of life of the brothers. Palladius relates that among the Nitrian monks “near the church there is a guesthouse, in which they receive a visiting guest for the entire period—even if he wishes to remain for two or three years—until he chooses of his own accord to depart. They allow him to remain at leisure for one week; on the following days they occupy him with work, either in the garden, the bakery, or the kitchen.” Thus, for as long as they are permitted to remain at leisure, and for as long as they are received with more sumptuous food, they lodge as guests. But when they must be compelled to follow the common discipline of the coenobium, they take their leave, “and immediately inquire about the neighboring monks or the location of the monastery; when they have lifted themselves from there, they settle or attach themselves somewhere else like weary men,” as the Master says in chapter 1 of his Rule.

Always wandering and never stable,] or, as St. Basil says (*Longer Rules*, 9), “unstable, continually changing their place, going now to these brothers, now to those, and driven by an unresting impulse, continually occupying themselves in touring monasteries.” Their mind is no more stable or firm than their body, but, as St. Basil again says in the same place: “Their winged mind is continually beaten as though by certain gusts of wind; their plans resemble the flights of bats, since they never move straight ahead, but, with crooked and uncertain flight, aimlessly wander and circle here and there.”

These words of St. Hildegard on the Rule of St. Benedict seem especially applicable to them: “Before the time of Blessed Father Benedict, monks were established under no definite rule; in diverse uncertainty and instability they wandered here and there, lacking a sure discipline and a fixed dwelling. Therefore, in describing the vices of their instability, so that their way of life might be avoided by faithful monks, he admonishes them.”

And serving their own pleasures and the allurements of gluttony.] Their own pleasures, since “under the pretense of charity they gratify the lusts of the flesh,” as St. Basil says (*Longer Rules*, 9). And the allurements of gluttony: for this is why they are always running about and do not lodge in monasteries for more than three or four days. Thus, “on the occasion of the arrival of guests,” says the Master’s Rule (1), “they want to be newly received every day by different hosts, and for the joy of those arriving they arrange for elaborate dishes to be prepared for themselves; and they take care that living creatures, young chickens, should be killed for them every day by different hosts with a knife on the occasion of their arrival. . . . On the pretext of the journey they desire their intestines, soiled by a more generous dinner or lunch, to be refreshed by innumerable cups rather than their feet; and after the table has been emptied by the hungry guest, and even the crumbs of bread wiped up after the journey, they shamelessly impose their thirst upon the host. If a cup should happen to be lacking, the guest is asked, even in the very dish, to mix the drink. And after they have been crushed on both sides by excess of food and drink, even to vomiting, they attribute everything to the hardship of the journey that their gluttony has won. . . . Therefore they prefer to travel, and to move newly from one host to another and through various meals, so that on the pretext of the thirst of the road they may drink cups poured out again. They do this so that their gluttony may appear each day to be making them travelers rather than their souls.”

Thus far the Master. St. Isidore of Pelusium reproaches a certain gyrovagus named Philip in these words (*Letters*, I.41): “Changing places continually and seeking, as it seems, a fatter table rather than sounder and more substantial instruction.”

With regard to the text of the holy Rule, it should incidentally be noted that the Holy Father does not simply say that gyrovagi serve gluttony, but that they serve “the allurements of gluttony.” “It is called an allurement,” says Hildemar, “because it lures one into another sin. For example, satiety arises from gluttony, and from excessive satiety fornication sometimes arises.” By this manner of speaking, therefore, St. Benedict indicates that we cannot serve gluttony alone unless we are also subject to other vices. Hence St. Gregory says: “From the greed of the belly arise foolish merriment, buffoonery, impurity, excessive talk, and dullness of understanding.”

And in every respect worse than the sarabaites,] because, as Hildemar says: “The sarabaites build cells for themselves; the gyrovagi do not build cells, but run through various places. The sarabaites, although badly, nevertheless live by the labor of their own hands; the gyrovagi live by the labor of others. The former do not give others a bad example; the latter, because they run through different places, give bad examples. The former, because they remain in one place, do not see good examples; the latter, because they travel, see good examples and refuse to imitate them. The sarabaites act in ignorance of many things; the gyrovagi, knowing that it is evil to run through places for the sake of gluttony, nevertheless do not amend their ways.”

Of all of whom,] namely, the gyrovagi, about whom the present discussion is concerned.

Their most wretched manner of life.] He calls the manner of life of the gyrovagi most wretched, since, as St. Basil says (*Monastic Constitutions*, 9), “there is in their minds no firmness, no solidity, nothing that accords with the order of discipline, and finally no prudence or seriousness. Instead, the greatest curiosity, perversity of character, frivolity, inconsiderateness, deceit, hypocrisy, and an ostentatious display full of lying and crafty speech abound in them. For they are crude in speech and intemperate in the belly.”

It is better to be silent than to speak,] lest it perhaps become an example to others. If, then, the most wretched manner of life of the gyrovagi must be covered in silence, how much more must it be avoided! Indeed, St. Basil strongly urges, in the passage we have cited so often, that they be avoided above all. St. John Climacus even advises that they be driven out and expelled when they come to us, in *The Ladder*, step 27, where he says:

“I have observed demons often arouse wandering solitaries, and those who entered solitude without counsel, to go more frequently to true and righteous anchorites, and through those wanderers to hinder the soldiers of Christ even slightly from their exercises of piety. You, good man, watch these wanderers, and do not refuse piously to grieve these idle men; perhaps, indeed, through this grief they will cease to run about and wander.”

Having omitted these,] namely, the sarabaites, the gyrovagi, and even the anchorites.

Let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to arrange the strongest kind of coenobites.] He therefore places the coenobitic life above all others. And indeed, all the teachers and masters who have written about ascetic matters proclaim it safer and more useful than all other forms of life. As for sarabaites and gyrovagi, no one fails to see that coenobites are far preferable to them. The case of anchorites appears more difficult. For since St. Benedict not only permits but also recommends the transition from coenobitic to eremitic life, as we saw above from St. Peter Damian, it seems to follow that the anchoritic life is superior to the coenobitic: who would persuade someone to pass from a perfect life to a less perfect one?

Bernard of Cassino replies that St. Benedict did not recommend the transition, but merely permitted migration from the coenobium to the desert. Moreover, although anchoritic life may appear more perfect by its very nature, since it is wholly occupied in continual contemplation of God, nevertheless, generally speaking, because it is more dangerous, less secure, and less useful, it should be placed after the common life practiced in a monastery. All the holy teachers customarily teach this, supported by many arguments, which it may not be useless to set forth here for the benefit of coenobites.

First. Because the Lord’s command not to think about tomorrow is very easily fulfilled in a coenobium, but never in solitude. Indeed, an anchorite scarcely suffices for himself even in procuring and preparing the necessities of the body: “No one,” says St. Basil (*Longer Rules*, 7), “is self-sufficient with regard to the needs of the body; rather, for the provision of necessities, each requires the work of others.”

Second. The coenobite does not follow his own will, but, after the example of Him who became obedient for us unto death, humbly subjects himself to the abbot and obeys him in everything. The hermit, however, having no one above him to whom he may be subject and no one commanding whom he may obey, is deprived of the merit of obedience. Abbot John considered these two reasons so important that he preferred them to all the advantages of the desert, as he himself testifies in Cassian (*Conferences*, 19.6), saying:

“If, while established in a coenobium, something is taken away from that purity of heart, I shall be content with the compensation of the evangelical commandment. It is certain that this cannot be placed below all the fruits of the desert: namely, that I should think of nothing concerning tomorrow, and, subject to an abbot until the end, should seem in some measure to imitate Him of whom it is said: ‘He humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death.’ May I deserve humbly to say His word: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of Him who sent me, the Father.’”

St. Cuthbert, although himself leading an anchoritic life, also used to tell the brothers, as the Venerable Bede testifies in his *Life* (second Benedictine century, chapter 22), that they should not marvel at his way of life as though it were uniquely exalted, because he preferred to live securely after abandoning secular concerns. “But,” he said, “the life of coenobites is rightly to be admired: they submit in everything to the commands of the abbot, and at his discretion regulate all the times of their watching, praying, fasting, and working. I know many of them who surpass my littleness by far both in purity of mind and in the height of prophetic grace.”

Third. “The principle of Christ’s love,” says St. Basil (*Longer Rules*, 7), “does not permit anyone to seek what is his own. For love, he says, does not seek its own; but the solitary life has this single aim: that each person should seek what is his own.”

Fourth. A monk falls more easily in the desert than in a coenobium. For the tempter approaches the solitary more willingly with the entire host of demons, and, finding him deprived of every external aid, easily overcomes him. For this reason above all St. Bernard deters a certain nun from the desert, responding to her objection as follows (*Letter* 115):

“Will my chastity not be safer in the desert, where, living peacefully with a few companions—or alone—I may please the One to whom I have commended myself? By no means. For anyone wishing to act wrongly finds abundance in the desert, shade in the forest, and concealment in solitude. Evil that no one sees is reproved by no one; but where a reprover is not feared, the tempter approaches more securely and iniquity is committed more freely. In a community, however, if you do something good, no one prevents you; but if you wish to do evil, you are not permitted. For it is quickly discovered by many, reproved, and corrected.”

Moreover, as Peter the Venerable has already noted (*Book I, Letter 20*): “It is not, as usually happens in battle, many against many; nor, as in a duel, one against one. Rather, in an unusual manner of combat, the anchorite contends alone against many who surpass him both in number and strength.”

For this reason Abbot Victorianus of Assan, in Spain (*Life of Victorianus*, 19; *Bollandists*, 12 January), when he saw certain monks who “were leading a solitary life outside in various oratories and cells,” recalled them to the coenobium and prescribed for them a definite rule and standard of life. He proclaimed it good and joyful for brothers to dwell together, where there is one heart and one soul; it is necessary to fight the ancient and crafty enemy with united strength, and it greatly benefits spiritual athletes if they stimulate one another through mutual exhortations and examples to fight bravely. The enemy’s forces are great, but they are greatly weakened by the strength of many resisting together; the camp of the faithful, fortified by charity, is not easily conquered.

58 Fifth. The hermit rises more slowly from sin: first, because, being subject to many vices, he does not recognize them; second, because, even if he did recognize them, he would not easily correct them, since he has no one by whom he might be reproved:

“In solitude,” St. Basil says again (*Longer Rules*, 7), “there is also this difficulty: one who is alone does not easily recognize his own fault and error, since he has no one to reprove and correct him with gentleness and merciful affection. For even reproof, when it comes from an enemy, often produces in a good man a desire for amendment.”

But “the one who sins among many is easily led away from sin by the condemnation imposed unanimously by many. He is more afraid, so that what Paul says may apply to him: ‘The punishment inflicted by the majority is sufficient for such a one.’”

Sixth. “The commandments of God are more easily fulfilled by many united together than by one person alone. For while the solitary carries out one commandment, another is obstructed; while he visits the sick, he is prevented from receiving guests” (St. Basil, same place).

Seventh. “The one who is alone cannot receive spiritual gifts. Rather, according to the proportion of faith that is in each person and of the Spirit’s distribution, which exists in the sharing of life, each person’s particular gift becomes common to those who live together. To one is given the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge, to another faith, and so forth. Each of these gifts is possessed by the recipient not more for his own sake than for the sake of others. Thus in the common life the operation of the Holy Spirit, which is in each person, must reach all. Therefore, whoever lives apart has some one gift, and through idleness renders it useless by burying it in himself. . . . But whoever lives in the fellowship of many and enjoys his own gift multiplies it by sharing it; he also makes the gifts of others his own gain” (same place).

Eighth. “The common life is more useful for preserving the gifts bestowed by God,” says St. Basil again (same place). In solitude, however, one easily loses not only gratuitous gifts but also the virtues acquired with great labor in the coenobium. St. Bernard had experienced the danger of this when he said (*Sermon* 64 on the *Song of Songs*):

“How many fervent in spirit have been received from monasteries by the solitude of the desert, and either expelled lukewarm or kept contrary to the law of the desert—not merely relaxed but even dissolute! Thus it became evident that a little fox had been present where such devastation of the vineyard had occurred, that is, where the man’s life and conscience had suffered harm. He had thought that if he lived alone he would receive much more abundant fruits of the Spirit, since in the common life he had experienced so much spiritual grace. His thought seemed good to him, but the outcome showed that the same thought had rather been a fox destroying him.”

Before him, St. John Climacus likewise says (*Ladder*, 4):

“I have observed others who, through the discipline of obedience, had become perfect, and through the care of their superior had been brought to an immediate awareness of their lamentable sins, to extraordinary gentleness, self-control, diligence, unconquerable steadfastness, and spiritual fervor. The evil demons, lying in wait for them, strive to persuade them that they are now fit for solitude, by which they may strive toward the highest degree of virtue and dispassion. These wretched men, thus deceived, abandon the secure station of the religious harbor and are carried out into the deep sea of solitude. When the storm breaks, deprived of the help of their helmsmen, they finally perish miserably, overwhelmed by the waves of the foul and salt sea.”

Ninth. Among other things, the solitary is especially liable to pride: “In solitude,” says St. Jerome (*Letter* 4), “pride easily creeps in. If he has fasted for a little while and has not seen a human being, he thinks himself important; forgetting whence he came and whither he is going, he wanders inwardly in heart and outwardly in speech.” And St. Basil says (*Longer Rules*, 7): “The solitary life is dangerous, because the solitary is pleased with himself. Since he has no one who can approve his work, he thinks that he has reached the perfection of the divine commandment.”

Tenth. The hermit can scarcely ever ascend to the highest summit of perfection, because, as St. Basil says in the same place, “the solitary does not understand how much he is progressing in good works, since all opportunity for practicing God’s commandments has been removed from him. For where will he display humility of spirit, when he has no one before whom he can show himself humbler? And so forth.”

Eleventh. There is no exercise of solitude that you cannot fulfill in a coenobium. Thus Peter of Blois writes in his book *Against the Corrupter*:

“You had in the cloister the secrecy of solitude, a place for repentance, peace of soul, the mystery of contemplation, joy in the Holy Spirit, counsel in uncertainty, a remedy in temptation, and in all things the effective benefit of medicine. There is the school of virtues; there is the highest practice of moderation, regularity of conduct, freedom to read, affection for the brotherhood, sharing in all things, strength of discipline, the law of obedience, the bond of charity, and mutual service.”

Twelfth. Finally, a more abundant reward in heaven is reserved for the coenobite, as we learn from a vision of a certain Father, which Rufinus reports in these words (*Lives of the Fathers*, III.141):

“One of the Fathers, having fallen into ecstasy, saw four orders before God. The first was that of men who were sick and gave thanks to God; the second was that of those who practice hospitality, persevere in it, and serve; the third was that of those who pursue solitude and do not see human beings; the fourth was that of those who, for God’s sake and because of obedience, are solicitous and subject to the Fathers.

This fourth order was superior to the other three: it displayed a golden collar and possessed greater glory than the others. The elder who had shown him this in ecstasy said to him: ‘Why does this fourth order possess greater glory than the others?’ He answered: ‘Because all the others have some rest, fulfilling their own wills in good works. But the obedient person, abandoning his own will, hangs upon the will of the Father who commands him; therefore he has received greater glory than the others.’”

Convinced by these and similar arguments, the teachers of the ascetic life have proclaimed the coenobitic life not merely equal to anchoritic life but much more useful. Thus Abbot John, after spending twenty years in solitude, gladly and joyfully returned to the coenobium, as Cassian relates (*Conferences*, 19.3). St. Benedict himself and many others began in anchoritic life but ended their lives in a coenobium. St. John Climacus strongly commends those who act in this way, as these words of his testify (*Ladder*, 4):

“Whoever, having lived in solitude, begins to recognize his own weakness, and then moves into a coenobium and willingly subjects and dedicates himself to obedience—this man, previously blind, suddenly begins without labor to behold Christ.”

Therefore, when the holy Fathers permit or recommend a transition from the coenobium to the desert, this should not be understood of everyone indiscriminately, even of those who appear to have made some progress in the way of virtue. It must be maintained that it is permitted only to those who have ascended to such a degree of perfection that there is no, or scarcely any, shadow of fear concerning their fall. Otherwise, if persons subject to vices sought the secrecy of solitude, they ought not merely not to be permitted to go there; if they had already sought it, they ought to be recalled to the monastery.

Thus St. John Climacus relates that when he once visited certain anchorites and found some of them subject to anger, “I piously urged them,” he says, “to move from solitude to monasteries, lest they be changed from human beings into demons.” And St. Isidore, who, as we saw above in Book II of *On Divine Offices*, chapter 15, does not permit anyone to pass into the desert before spending at least twenty years in a monastery with the brothers, entirely excludes reclusion in his Rule:

“No one,” he says (chapter 5), “should seek a separate cell, withdrawn from the community, in which, under the pretext of reclusion, he may serve either a hidden vice—especially vainglory—or the reputation and fame of worldly opinion. For many wish to be recluses and remain hidden so that they may become known; those who were worthless or unknown while outside wish to be recognized and honored once enclosed. Indeed, everyone who withdraws from the crowds for the sake of life, the more he separates himself from public view, the less he remains hidden.”

## CHAPTER II. What the Abbot Should Be Like

[Col. 0263]

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery must always remember what he is called and fulfill by his deeds the name of “superior.” For he is believed to act in the monastery in the place of Christ when he is called by Christ’s title [Note: Oxford manuscript, “by the pronoun”], as the Apostle says: “You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry, ‘Abba, Father’” (Romans I [citation as printed]). Therefore the abbot must not—God forbid—teach, establish, or command anything outside the Lord’s commandment. Rather, his command or teaching must be sprinkled like leaven of divine justice into the minds of the disciples [Note: Oxford manuscript, *fermento*, “with leaven,” instead of *fermentum*, “leaven”].

61 Let the abbot always remember that an examination will be made before the dreadful judgment of God concerning both his teaching and the obedience of the disciples [Note: Another manuscript omits *sit*, “let him be”]. Let the abbot know that whatever usefulness the head of the household is unable to find in the sheep will be charged to the shepherd’s fault. Yet he will then be free if all diligence has been devoted to a restless or disobedient flock, and every care has been given to their diseased behavior; at the Lord’s judgment their shepherd, acquitted, will say with the Prophet to the Lord: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation” (Psalm 39). “But they themselves, despising me, rejected me.” And then, finally, for the disobedient sheep entrusted to his care, their very death shall be a prevailing punishment.

Therefore, when someone receives the name of abbot, he must preside over his disciples by a twofold teaching. That is, he must display all that is good and holy more by his deeds than by his words; to disciples capable of understanding he must set forth the Lord’s commandments in words [Note: Another manuscript, *proponere*, “to set forth,” instead of *proponat*, “let him set forth”]; but to those hard of heart and simpler in understanding he must demonstrate the divine commandments by his actions [Note: Another manuscript, *monstrare*, “to demonstrate,” instead of *demonstret*, “let him demonstrate”]. Whatever he teaches his disciples to be contrary, he must indicate by his own deeds is not to be done, lest, while preaching to others, he himself be found reprobate (1 Corinthians IX), and lest God should at some time say to him in his sin: “Why do you recount my ordinances and take up my covenant in your mouth? You hate discipline and cast my words behind you” (Psalm 49). And you saw the speck in your brother’s eye but did not see the beam in your own (Matthew VII).

No distinction of persons is to be made by him in the monastery. One is not to be loved more than another, unless he is found better in good works or obedience. A freeborn man is not to be preferred to one who has entered from servitude, unless there is another reasonable cause. If the abbot, guided by justice, judges that this should be done, let him do so with regard to anyone’s rank; otherwise, let them retain their proper places. For whether slave or free (1 Corinthians XII), we are all one in Christ, and under one Lord we bear an equal service in the army. For there is no partiality with God (Acts X). We are distinguished before him in this respect alone: if we are found better than others in good works and humble. Therefore let his charity be equal toward all; let discipline be applied to all [Note: Another manuscript reads *omnibus*, “to all,” in a different position], according to merit [Note: Oxford manuscript, *disciplinae*, “of discipline”].

In his teaching, the abbot must always preserve that apostolic pattern in which it says: “Reprove, entreat, rebuke” (1 Timothy IV)—that is, blending occasions with occasions and encouragements with terrors. Let him display the severe affection of a teacher and the loving affection of a father [Note: Another manuscript reads “of a severe teacher, of a loving father”]. The undisciplined and restless he must reprove more harshly; the obedient, gentle, and patient he must entreat, so that they may advance toward better things; but the negligent and contemptuous, we instruct him to admonish and rebuke.

Nor should he conceal [Note: Hildemar adds, “above all, let him not conceal”] the sins of those who offend. As soon as they begin to arise, let him cut them out by the roots, as far as he can, remembering the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh (1 Samuel II). Let him reprove the more honorable and perceptive minds by words at the first or second admonition [Note: Another manuscript reads “more perceptive”]. But let him restrain the wicked, hard-hearted, proud, or disobedient at the very beginning of their sin by blows or bodily correction, knowing what is written: “A fool is not corrected by words.” And again: “Strike your son with a rod, and you will deliver his soul from death” (Proverbs XXIII).

The abbot must always remember what he is and remember what he is called, and know that from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required. Let him know how difficult and arduous a task he has undertaken: to govern souls and serve the character of many. Let him adapt and conform himself to everyone—one by kindness, another by reproof, another by persuasion, and according to the quality or understanding of each person—so that he not only suffers no loss to the flock entrusted to him, but rejoices in the increase of the good flock.

Above all, let him not, by concealing or undervaluing the salvation of the souls entrusted to him, show greater concern for transitory, earthly, and perishable things. Rather, let him always consider that he has undertaken to govern souls, concerning which he will also have to render an account. And lest he complain of perhaps lesser resources, let him remember what is written: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his justice, and all these things will be added to you” (Matthew VI). And again: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him” (Psalm XXXIII).

Let him know that whoever undertakes to govern souls must prepare himself to render an account [Note: Another manuscript reads: “Let him know that whoever undertakes to govern souls must prepare himself to render an account”]. And according as he knows the number of brothers under his care, let him recognize with certainty that on the day of judgment he will render an account to the Lord for all their souls, without doubt together with an account of his own soul. And thus, always fearing the future examination of the shepherd concerning the sheep entrusted to him, while he guards against being called to account for others, he becomes concerned about his own account; and while he supplies correction to others through his admonitions [Note: Another manuscript reads “instructions”], he himself is corrected from his vices.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0265]

The abbot who is worthy to preside over a monastery.] By the name “abbot,” St. Benedict calls the one placed in charge of the brothers in a monastery. By this name, as Boherius notes, “priests are sometimes called, and sometimes superiors.” Indeed, even the elders of coenobiums or inhabitants of solitude are so called, although they preside over no monks, as can be seen frequently in the *Lives of the Fathers*. Thus St. Paul, the first hermit, is called Abbot Paul. The word *abbot* is Hebrew and means “father” in Latin: “If you ask what *abba* means,” says St. Augustine (*Sermon* 156 on Scripture), “the answer is given to you: ‘Father’; for *abba* means ‘father’ in Hebrew.”

He must always remember what he is called.] His life must correspond to the meaning of the name; and just as he is called “Father,” he must truly show himself a father toward those under him. “In a fatherly manner he must nourish his sons, that is, his monks; in a fatherly manner he must love them; and when necessary, in a fatherly manner he must chastise, reprove, and entreat them,” as Smaragdus says.

And fulfill the name of “superior” by his deeds.] For, as St. Gregory says, “the action of the ruler ought to surpass the action of the people by as much as the life of the shepherd differs from that of the flock. He must carefully strive to measure the severity of the obligation to maintain uprightness by which he is bound, since the people are called a flock under his judgment. He must therefore be pure in thought, outstanding in action, discerning in silence, useful in speech, near to each person through compassion, raised above all in contemplation, and through humility a companion to those who act well, and so forth.” He develops these matters more fully in the following chapters, and repeats the final words in almost the same terms in Book I of the *Register*, chapter 24.

Christ is believed to be represented by the abbot in the monastery.] That is, he represents Christ’s person, or possesses and exercises his authority over his subjects; “because,” says Richard of Saint Angelo, “when they are elected abbots, they are called by God, like Aaron; and after they have been called, they receive the power and office of Christ from the pope, who stands in the place of the true God.””

When they are called by his title.] That is, by the same name by which Christ is called—namely, abbot and father. He did not say simply “by his name,” but “by his title,” which signifies the burden of the name, or its dignity, as Bernard of Cassino explains.

64 Saying through the Apostle.] Namely, Paul, who is always understood whenever only “the Apostle,” or “the Great Apostle,” occurs without further qualification in the text: “Who is speaking?” asks Peter the Venerable (Book VI, Letter 24). “The Great Apostle. If you ask who the great one is, I reply that there is no need to ask. Where ‘the Great Apostle’ is added, Paul is understood.”

You have received the Spirit of adoption as sons, in whom we cry out, “Abba, Father.”] Since father and abbot share the same meaning of the name, one may ask why the Apostle used both, when either one alone would undoubtedly have sufficed. Hildemar replies: “Abba in Hebrew and Syriac means ‘father’ in Greek and Latin. Because blessed Paul knew that the Gentiles would read his letters, he says, ‘Abba, Father,’ so that each nation might have this name, which is ‘Father.’” Perhaps also because Christ had used both expressions in his Passion, when, praying to the Father, he said, “Abba, Father”; evidently he spoke in Greek and Hebrew, since with him there is no distinction between Jew and Greek.

[Col. 0266A] Therefore.] If the abbot is believed to exercise the Lord’s office in the monastery.

Nothing beyond the commandment of the Lord.] That is, against, beyond, or apart from the commandment of the Lord, which is contained in the divine Scriptures, in the Rule, and in the lives and writings of the holy Fathers.

He ought either to teach.] By word or example, since he must preside over his disciples with a twofold instruction.

[Col. 0266B] Or to establish.] That is, to enact statutes or decrees.

Or to command.] That is, to order. Saint Benedict included these three because, as Bernard of Cassino says, “the abbot’s entire authority, as it were, depends upon these three things: that he teach what is sound, establish what is just, and command what is lawful, possible, and honorable.”

But his command or teaching should be mingled like the leaven of divine justice into the minds of the disciples.] “Leaven” is sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one; for although it corrupts the mass of flour, it nevertheless makes it flavorful by corrupting it. The leaven of divine justice is therefore mingled into the minds of the disciples when the abbot’s teaching makes divine justice flavorful, sweet, and pleasing to them. Or, if “leaven” is understood as charity and love of God, as some prefer, the abbot’s teaching and command become the leaven of divine justice when, although it commands hard things, it makes divine justice lovable.

[Col. 0266C] Let the abbot always remember that an account will be required before God’s judgment both of his teaching and of the disciples’ obedience.] So that the abbot may not presume to do anything against the Lord’s commandment, Saint Benedict wisely admonished him to remember always that, at the dread judgment of God, an account would be required both of his teaching and of the disciples’ obedience. As Smaragdus says, these words need no interpretation; rather, they inspire abbots and monks with the greatest fear. Nevertheless, Hildemar investigates three matters here.

First, since an account will be required both of the abbot’s teaching and of the disciples’ obedience, why did he admonish only the abbot, and not the disciples as well, to remember the future accounting? For he said, “Let the abbot always remember,” and did not add, “and the monks.” Hildemar himself replies: “He mentioned only that the abbot should remember, so that he might be concerned about his own teaching and make the disciples concerned about their obedience. He said the abbot alone should remember for another reason also: because he will render an account to God on the day of judgment both for his teaching and for the obedience of his disciples. Therefore he said that the disciples’ obedience would be examined, whether it was perfect or imperfect, just as the whole of the abbot’s teaching would be examined, whether it exceeded or fell short of the teaching he ought to provide.”

The second question is why he says “always.” He replies: “Because Saint Benedict wished this accounting never to depart from the abbot’s heart.” Hence Saint Benedict’s great concern to recall the last judgment to the abbot’s memory: scarcely ever does he speak of it in the Rule without impressing it upon his mind. Indeed, nothing can restrain the abbot’s presumption and keep him within the limits of his office so effectively as the constant memory of the future accounting. The philosopher Xistus, cited by Boherius in his first commentary, says splendidly in his Book of Moral Sentences: “Since you preside over everyone, remember that God presides over you as well; and know that you judge human beings, because you too will be judged [Col. 0267A] by God. The judge is in greater danger than the one judged.”

The third question is why he said “dreadful”; for it would have been enough to say, “on the day of judgment.” He replies: “He said ‘dreadful’ in order to instill fear in those reading this law.” And because that judgment will truly be dreadful and terrible: “What,” asks Saint Bernard (Sermon 8 on Psalm 90), “can be imagined so fearful, so full of anxiety and the most intense concern, as to stand for judgment before that terrifying tribunal and still await an uncertain sentence from a strict judge?” Saint Jerome likewise says (Book II Against the Pelagians): “Who goes without fear to the judgment of God while conscious of sins?” Indeed, speaking of himself, the holy doctor says (on Matthew): “Whenever I consider that day, I tremble throughout my body.” If, then, a holy and just man will tremble, where will the impious and sinful appear?

And let the abbot know that whatever useful benefit the master of the household is unable to find in the sheep will be charged to the shepherd’s fault.] Hildemar comments on this passage: “It is as though he were saying: Just as the master of a household carefully investigates the shepherd of his sheep concerning their neglect—asking, ‘Why has my sheep died? Why has the wolf carried it off?’—so, if the shepherd is able to give him an account concerning the sick or dead sheep, he will be released; but if he cannot, he will be subject to punishment. So also will the Lord deal with the abbot. The master of the household is the Lord; the shepherd is the abbot; the sheep are understood to be the monks; and the time when the abbot will render his account signifies the future life, in which the abbot must give an account of the neglect of his monks.”

66 As for what he says, “whatever is found in the sheep,” and so forth, “that is, he will have to render an account not only of their spiritual negligence but also of their temporal needs,” Hildemar again says. And indeed, when he says “whatever,” he omits nothing at all; nor is the abbot less bound to provide temporal necessities for his monks than spiritual ones, since they can scarcely practice the latter without the former.

[Col. 0267C] Whatever useful benefit he is unable to find.] A thoroughly terrifying sentence. For if whatever useful benefit the master of the household finds lacking in the sheep is charged to the shepherd’s fault, what if he finds them sick, dead, or torn apart by the voracious teeth of the wolf? Without doubt, he will have to give skin for skin. It is written that a son will not bear the iniquity of his father; but certainly a father will bear the iniquity of his son.

“Thus,” says Peter Damian (Book IV, Letter 15), “when that Israelite people had been initiated into the worship of Beelphegor in the desert and had shamefully fallen into the prostitution of Moab, the Lord, angry with Israel, said to Moses: ‘Take all the leaders of the people and hang them on gallows before the sun, so that my anger may be turned away from Israel.’ What does it mean that the people plunge into the abyss of lust, while vengeance is taken upon their superiors? Subjects sin, and rulers are hanged on gallows; one person sins, while another is punished. Why is this, unless because the guilt of subjects rebounds upon the reproach of their superiors, and what is done wrongly by the sheep is attributed to the shepherd’s negligence? And see how fearful is the condition of those who preside: they are punished not only for their own offenses but also for those of their subjects.”

Let all shepherds and all who govern souls therefore heed the salutary admonition that Gregory the Great wrote to Bishop Columbus (Book II of the Register, chapter 33): “Let us strive to inflame our hearts by the example of earthly shepherds, who often spend the winter nights sleepless, constrained by rain and frost, lest even one sheep—and perhaps not even a useful one—should perish. If a predator has bitten one with its greedy mouth, how they labor! With what anguish of heart they pant! With what cries they rush forth, driven by anxiety, to rescue the captured animal, lest the master of the flock demand from them whatever they have lost through negligence. Let us therefore watch, lest anything perish; and if something should happen to be captured, let us restore it to the Lord’s flock by the words of the divine utterances, so that he who is the Shepherd of shepherds may deign by his judgment to show that we have watched over his flock.”

Only then will he again be free, and so forth.] The one whom he has just terrified with the danger of the future accounting and of having to render an account for the offenses of his subjects, he now consoles, lest he lose heart, saying: “Only then will he again be free”—that is, if every diligence of the shepherd has been devoted to the restless and disobedient flock, and every care has been shown toward their diseased actions. He alludes to the prophet’s words: “But if, when you announce to the wicked that he should turn from his ways, he is not converted from his way, he will die in his iniquity; but you will have delivered your soul” (Ezekiel 33).

He will therefore be free—that is, blameless—if the flock is restless, meaning wicked, ungrateful, and impatient, as Boherius explains, or if it does not remain in a good resolution. For, as Bernard of Cassino says, “peace of mind is that firmness of a good resolution in which the monk perseveres and finds rest.” Or “restless” may mean one who seeks to wander and run here and there outside the cloister. [Col. 0268B] For, as the commentators Smaragdus, Hildemar, and Bernard of Cassino observe, there are two kinds of restlessness: one of the mind, which Bernard of Cassino locates in instability and failure to persevere in a good resolution; the other of the body, which may be placed in perpetual wandering within or outside the monastery.

If every diligence of the shepherd has been devoted to the restless and disobedient flock, he uses the universal word “every” “to indicate fully both spiritual and bodily diligence,” says Bernard of Cassino, and before him Hildemar. For the abbot is bound to show both kinds of care toward his brothers: spiritual care, by doing all he can through exhortations, rebukes, and good examples to make them advance from virtue to virtue; bodily care, by providing adequate and respectable food and clothing, selecting places suitable for the solitary life and the construction of the monastery, regularly constructing the monastery’s workshops, and arranging everything in such a way that the brothers have no cause for murmuring.

Peter Boherius follows this interpretation in his first commentary, although he rejects it in his second in these words: “Some explain ‘diligence’ here as spiritual and temporal care, because of the universal word ‘every.’ This is not pleasing, since the chapter speaks of the spiritual care of souls. Note clearly that these two universal signs, namely ‘every’ and ‘all,’ stir the mind of the one who presides to diligence.”

And toward their diseased actions.] That is, negligent actions, for “diseased actions are works performed negligently and other vices,” as Hildemar says. Or, as Bernard of Cassino says, “diseased actions are those that proceed from an infirm mind.”

All care has been shown.] These words have the same meaning as the preceding ones, “every diligence has been devoted.” Yet Saint Benedict repeated them “to intensify the wording,” says Hildemar. He rightly said “all care,” not “all treatment,” because, as Bernard of Cassino aptly observes, “the power to cure a sick person is not always in the physician, so that the sick person may be restored; therefore he said ‘all care,’ not ‘all treatment.’ For God, who entrusted the care to the abbot, reserved the cure for himself, and so forth.”

The shepherd of them, acquitted at God’s judgment.] Namely, acquitted from the sentence owed to the condemned, or freed from the negligence of the monks, as Bernard of Cassino explains. He will say—that is, he will say with the prophet to the Lord: “I have not hidden your justice in my heart; I have declared your truth and your salvation.”

According to Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino, “justice” here means the general virtue that concerns all virtues, although the latter asserts that it may also be taken as a particular virtue. Moreover, Saint Benedict, according to the same Bernard, says three things here: not to hide justice, to proclaim truth, and to declare salvation.

“He hides justice who does not show his subjects, by preaching, the terrors and threats of sacred Scripture. He declares truth who preaches and teaches that the promised heavenly kingdoms will certainly be attained by the virtuous and those who act well. He also declares salvation who teaches how to attain the promised salvation. Understand ‘salvation’ here as including the Savior himself, the Lord Jesus Christ, concerning whom the Psalmist says, ‘Grant us your salvation,’ and so forth.”

But they, despising me, rejected me.] That is, my teaching.

And then, at last, for the sheep entrusted to his care that are disobedient.] These words can be understood in two ways: first, “for the sheep entrusted to his care that are disobedient,” that is, sheep whose actions do not correspond to the care he provides; second, “for the sheep entrusted to his care,” that is, for the sheep who are under his care.

Let it be punishment for them.] That is, “it will be punishment for them.” This is a Hebrew expression in which the pronoun is often redundant, as in the phrase, “whose participation is in the same thing.”

Prevailing death itself.] That is, divine vengeance, as Richard of Saint Angelo explains. It is perpetual death, which is called “prevailing,” that is, exceeding their iniquities in punishment, says Bernard of Cassino.

Boherius alone thinks that in both interpretations this passage should be understood not of eternal death but of temporal death. Thus, commenting on Saint Benedict’s foregoing words, he says in his first commentary: “I believe that the master means that temporal death prevails over the disobedient more than eternal punishment, so that the phrase ‘let it be punishment for them’ follows the preceding word.”

This interpretation should not be entirely rejected, because, as Boherius himself says, “the longer this life is prolonged for them, the more eternal punishment increases; and it is better for them to die quickly than to persist against the good of obedience.” Nevertheless, interpreters generally understand “death” here as eternal death.

Certainly Saint Benedict appears here to be speaking of the punishment to be repaid at the future judgment, which presupposes temporal death and is followed by eternal death. Whatever the case may be, it is certain that disobedient monks deserve both temporal and eternal death, since by despising the abbot and his teaching they disdain not a human being but God himself.

He himself says to teachers, “Whoever despises you despises me”; and through the prophet: “They refuse to hear you because they refuse to hear me.” On these words Saint Bernard says (Sermon 42 on the Song of Songs): “Do you see what majesty is being despised? Do not suppose that you alone have been rejected. The Lord has spoken, and he said to the prophet, and he said to the Apostles: ‘Whoever despises you,’ he says, ‘despises me.’ I am not an Apostle; I am not a prophet. Yet I exercise the office of prophets and Apostles, and although I do not equal them in merits, I am involved in their concerns—though to my shame and to my great danger. I sit upon the chair of Moses, although I do not claim his life for myself or experience his grace.”

Therefore, when someone assumes the name of abbot, he ought to preside over his disciples with a twofold teaching.] That is, he should shine by word and example, for Saint Isidore expressly requires both in an abbot and in every prelate (Book III of the Highest Good): “An ecclesiastical teacher must shine both in teaching and in life, for teaching without life makes one arrogant, while life without teaching makes one useless.””

Thus, in Exodus 28, the priest is commanded to wear the shoulder-piece and the breastpiece, connected and joined to each other. Explaining this, Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, says (Commentary on Exodus): “Let us say what it signifies that they are joined to each other in such a way that they cannot be separated. The breastpiece and shoulder-piece are joined when the bishop’s preaching and conduct harmonize well together. Just as the breastpiece signifies teaching and preaching, so the shoulder-piece signifies burden and action. If a bishop teaches well but acts badly, or conversely acts well but teaches badly, his shoulder-piece and breastpiece are not joined.”

What he says of the bishop must therefore be asserted of the abbot and every other prelate. Hence Saint Bernard, writing to Abbot Baldwin (Letter 201), says: “Understand that in these two commandments—namely, word and example—the whole security of your office and conscience depends.”

And certainly, as Saint Jerome argues most aptly: “Holy rusticity benefits only itself; and insofar as it builds up the Church of Christ by example and the merit of its life, it harms it if it does not resist those who destroy it. An innocent life without speech benefits by example as much as it harms by silence; for the madness of wolves must be driven away by the barking of dogs and the staff of shepherds.”

Conversely, “nothing is more disgraceful than for someone to neglect in practice the good that he preaches,” says Saint Isidore (Book III of the Highest Good, chapter 36). Therefore Abba Poemen said to Rufinus (Book III of the Lives of the Fathers, no. 183): “A man who teaches others but does not do what he teaches is like a lofty spring, which washes everyone’s things and satisfies everyone with drink, but cannot wash itself; rather, it contains filth and mud.”

From these examples it is clear how deservedly the Council of Orléans, celebrated in the seventh century, decreed “that if any abbot is not prudent in governance, humble, chaste, sober, merciful, and discerning, and does not display the divine commandments in words and examples, he is to be deprived of his honor by the bishop in whose territory he resides, by neighboring abbots, and by all others who fear the Lord—even if the whole congregation, assenting to his vices, wishes to have him as abbot.””

That is, he should show all good and holy things more fully by deeds than by words.] Hildemar explains this as follows: “Saint Benedict wishes both things, namely teaching by words and by deeds. But because there are many who cannot accomplish both—that is, teaching by words and by deeds—he therefore said, ‘more by deeds,’ as though he were saying: He ought to accomplish both; but although he ought to preside in both ways, nevertheless more by deeds, and so forth.”

The Wise Man is entirely right: “The journey through precepts is long; it is short and effective through examples.” Saint Gregory likewise says (Book II of the Pastoral Rule, chapter 3): “Let the ruler be outstanding in reason, and let him announce the way of life to his subjects by living it; and let the flock, which follows the shepherd’s voice and conduct, advance by examples better than by words.”

Elsewhere he says (Book I of the Register, chapter 24): “Whoever is compelled by the necessity of his position to say the highest things is compelled by that same necessity to display the highest things.
