For that voice penetrates the hearts of hearers more willingly which the speaker’s life commends; what he commands by speaking, he assists by showing, so that it may be done. Hence it is said through the prophet: ‘Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion.’”

Saint Basil, speaking of the head of a monastery, says (Longer Rules, chapter 43): “He ought to preserve humility of spirit through the charity of Christ in such a way that, even if he remains silent, the example of his works may be displayed for the instruction of the brothers, more powerful than any speech.”

Christ the Lord showed himself to be such a man, for we read that he began to do and to teach. The Apostle likewise showed himself to be such, saying: “Be imitators of me.” He sought such prelates when he wrote to Timothy: “In all things, present yourself as an example of good works—in teaching, in integrity, and in seriousness.”

To disciples who are capable.] That is, “those who are mindful, receptive, and intelligent, who quickly grasp what they hear from their teachers, retain it in memory, and fulfill it in their works,” says Smaragdus.

Let him set forth the Lord’s commandments in words.] For words are sufficient for such people, who are naturally borne toward God.

But to those hard of heart.] That is, “the stubborn, rigid, and incorrigible,” as Smaragdus again explains.

And to the simpler ones.] That is, “the uneducated, who possess scarcely any memory or understanding of the divine Scriptures,” as the same Smaragdus continues.

Let him demonstrate the divine commandments by his own deeds.] Here “commandments” means instructions or counsels, “because a commandment does not always have here, or in the Gospel, the force of necessity,” says Boherius. For those hard of heart, words alone are therefore insufficient; they must also be compelled by works, according to Peter Damian (Opusculum 15): “Precepts move one toward the summit of perfection, but examples compel.”

But let him indicate by his own deeds that everything he has taught the disciples to be contrary is not to be done.] By a bad example he would confirm the perverse and negligent in evil and easily corrupt the good; indeed, to speak more accurately, he would truly kill both groups.

“There are very few healthy and fat sheep,” says Saint Augustine (Book on Pastors, chapter 4)—that is, those who feed on the pastures of God’s gift and use the solid food of truth. “But those bad shepherds do not spare such sheep. It is little that they do not care for the sick, weak, wandering, and lost; they also kill, insofar as they can, the strong and fat. These live by God’s mercy, yet, insofar as bad shepherds are concerned, they are killed. How, you ask, do they kill them? By living badly and providing a bad example. For when even a strong sheep watches its superior living badly, if it turns its eyes away from the Lord’s rules and fixes them upon a human being, it begins to say in its heart: ‘If my superior lives this way, who am I that I should not do what he does?’” Saint Augustine develops this at length, showing that even if a bad shepherd does not turn a sheep away from the good work it has begun, he must nevertheless truly be considered a murderer.

Lest, while preaching to others, he himself be found rejected.] These words admit of two interpretations. First: “lest he perhaps be found rejected,” that is, blameworthy and estranged from God, and consequently excluded from his eternal glory and happiness. Second: “lest he perhaps be found rejected,” that is, lest his teaching be rejected by the disciples.

For, as Saint Augustine says (Book IV of On Christian Teaching, chapter 27): “There are many who seek a defense of their bad life from their own superiors and teachers, answering in their hearts—or even bursting forth in speech and saying: ‘Why do you command me to do what you yourself do not do?’ Thus they do not obediently hear the one who does not hear himself, and they despise the word of God preached to them together with the preacher himself.”

Hence Saint Jerome, writing to Nepotian, says: “Let your works not confound your speech, lest, when you speak in church, someone silently answer: ‘Why do you yourself not do what you say?’”

Cassian agrees in his Book on the Spirit of Anger (Book VIII of the Institutes, chapter 5), where he says: “He who wishes to heal another’s wound ought to remain healthy and free from every disease of sickness, lest the Gospel saying be addressed to him: ‘Physician, first heal yourself,’ and, seeing the speck in his brother’s eye, he fail to see the beam in his own.”

Saint Caesarius likewise says in his Rule for Nuns (chapter 7): “Let the abstinence preached by the tongue be felt by the throat or stomach nearby, lest perhaps the subjects who hear it say in silent thought: ‘How beautifully he preaches abstinence with his belly full!’”

Finally, Saint Bernard, writing to Abbot Baldwin (Letter 201), after exhorting him to carry first himself the burden he imposes upon others, gives this reason: “Otherwise the wise man will mock you, as a lazy man to whom it is labor to bring his hand to his mouth. The Apostle too will rebuke you, saying: ‘You who teach others, do you not teach yourself?’ And you will also be marked with the fault of the Pharisees, who bind heavy and unbearable burdens and place them on people’s shoulders, but are unwilling to move them with their finger. A living and effective speech is an example of action: it readily makes what is said persuasive while showing that what is urged can be done.”

To all this we may add what Peter Damian writes (Opusculum 15, chapter 27): “He preaches vigils most excellently who, after a long course of psalmody, strikes the signal to awaken the brothers. While we are silent, we commend silence most eloquently. He speaks fruitfully about the edges of garments who disfigures himself by tearing his clothes. But one conspicuous for the splendor of his garments, like the rich man, vainly preaches the hairs of camels with John. He who avenges an injury does not urge patience. He who burns with the desire to amass monetary gains does not extinguish the fire of greed in another’s breast. He who is carried away by frequent wandering is a frivolous disputant when he censures lingering. But he who continually inhabits his cell makes his whole body a tongue in praise of stability; and although his mouth is silent, his mute limbs cry out more effectively and more sincerely.”

For this very reason, all who have written laws of the coenobitic life have required an irreproachable abbot to be the first to fulfill the rule he is to impose upon others. For this reason the Eastern Rule begins as follows (Eastern Rule, chapter 1): “So that the elders may not labor uselessly in governing the brothers, nor the discipline of the juniors waver, but remain stable and firm through the abbot’s conduct, the abbot must be irreproachable, strict, patient, fasting, pious, and humble, so that he may fulfill the place of teacher and Father, presenting himself as a pattern of good works.”

For this reason Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, counts among the abbot’s other qualities the following: “There must be such harmony between speech and life,” he says (chapter 20), “that what he teaches in words he confirms by diligent works; and, advancing before others with a two-edged sword, whatever he teaches others by word he himself practices zealously, so that neither action destroys speech nor, conversely, unsuitable speech weakens good action.” See also Saint Caesarius’ letter to the abbess Oratoria.

If, however, Saint Benedict’s words—“lest, while preaching to others, he himself be found rejected”—are taken in the first sense, as though he were saying, “lest he lead others, converted by his preaching, to eternal happiness while himself being rejected from it,” they seem to allude to Christ the Lord’s saying: “Whoever loosens one of these least commandments and teaches people so will be called least in the kingdom of heaven”—that is, no one, according to the interpretation of the holy Fathers.

Lest God ever say to him while he sins.] That is, while he speaks but does not act, as the commentators explain; for knowing the good and not doing it is sin for him.

Why do you recount my ordinances?] That is, why do you display and preach virtue and the way of life?

And take my covenant upon your lips.] God’s covenant consists of the words of sacred Scripture, which is divided into the Old and New Testaments. It is called a covenant because it is a witness of the divine mind or will.

But you hate discipline.] That is, regular observance, because, as Smaragdus says, “a prelate hates holy discipline when he refuses to live according to the precepts of the Rule.”

Or “you hate discipline” means Christ’s teaching, as Boherius explains, in agreement with Hildemar: “Discipline is the keeping of all God’s commandments.”

Or “discipline” means correction inflicted by God, according to Trithemius, who explains this passage of the Rule as follows: “He corrects his subjects for their transgressions and nevertheless wants them to be patient; but as soon as it happens that he himself is rebuked by God for his sins, he is not merely impatient but even murmurs against God. Such a man undoubtedly hates discipline and casts Christ’s words behind him, because he does not wish to see his life as evil but considers himself righteous.” Trithemius adds: “Second, a prelate hates discipline when he disdains being advised by his subjects.”

And you cast my words behind you.] “A prelate casts the Lord’s words behind him when he neglects to fulfill what he preaches to his subjects from the divine Scriptures,” says Smaragdus.

Or again, “you cast my words behind you” is the same as “you hated discipline,” as Trithemius explained above: “For what we love,” says Bernard of Cassino, “we frequently keep before the eyes of the mind, according to the saying, ‘Where there is love, there is sight’; but what we hate we willingly cast away from us.”

And when you saw the speck in your brother’s eye, you did not see the beam in your own.] That is, when you saw and rebuked the smallest sins in your brother, you not only failed to punish crimes in yourself but did not even allow others to see them, whereas you ought to have been gentle toward others and strict toward yourself.

Hear the salutary admonition of Saint John Chrysostom (Homily 43 on Matthew): “Be severe concerning your own life and kind concerning others. Let people hear you command small things and do great ones.”

Let no distinction of persons be made by him in the monastery.] Namely, “whether someone is old or young, slave or free,” says Boherius in his commentary; or, as he has it in his second commentary, “whether someone is small or great, old or young, a neighbor or a newcomer, cleric or layman.”

For the abbot is believed to exercise Christ’s office in the monastery, and with Christ there is no partiality, but in every nation whoever fears him is acceptable to him. Hence the Apostle Saint James says in his Epistle (chapter 2): “Brothers, do not hold the faith of our glorious Lord Jesus Christ with partiality. For if a man wearing a golden ring and white clothing enters your assembly, and a poor man in shabby clothing also enters, and you look upon the one wearing the splendid clothing and say to him, ‘You sit here comfortably,’ while you say to the poor man, ‘You stand there,’ or, ‘Sit under my footstool,’ are you not judging among yourselves and becoming judges with evil thoughts?”

Saint Ambrose, writing on Malachi, indicates how great an evil this is in these words: “Among all the sins of priests, the greatest is that they consider not causes but persons, and, despising the just poor, honor the unjust rich.” From this it is clear how deservedly and justly Saint Benedict forbade the abbot to distinguish or favor persons in the monastery.

According to Hugh of Saint Victor, partiality is “a foolish reverence shown to someone without a due reason, but because of fear or advantage.” We may explain this definition from Saint Thomas (II–II, question 63, article 1, body of the article) as follows:

“Partiality is opposed to distributive justice. The equality of distributive justice consists in assigning different things to different persons according to proportions corresponding to the dignity of the persons. If, therefore, someone considers that property of a person by reason of which what is conferred upon that person is owed to him, this is not partiality toward the person but consideration of the cause. Thus the Gloss on Ephesians 6, ‘There is no partiality with God,’ says that God, the just judge, distinguishes causes, not persons. For example, if someone promotes a person to a teaching office because of adequate knowledge, the due cause is being considered, not the person.

“But if someone considers, in the person to whom something is being given, not that for which what is given would be proportionate or due to him, but merely that he is this particular man—for example, Peter or Martin—this is partiality. For something is not assigned to him because of a cause that makes him worthy, but simply because of the person. Any condition that does not contribute to the cause by which he is worthy of the position is referred to the person. Thus, if someone promotes a person to a prelacy or teaching office because he is rich or because he is a relative, this is partiality, and so forth.”

Partiality has its principal place in three areas. First, in affection—for example, when someone is loved more than others because he is handsome or cheerful, not because he is holy. Saint Benedict prohibits this when he says, “Let one not be loved more than another.”

Second, in the conferring of both spiritual and temporal honors, as Saint Thomas proves in articles 2 and 3 of the same question. Saint Benedict excludes this when he decrees that a freeborn person should not be preferred to one converted from slavery.

Third, in judgments, as can be seen in article 4 of the aforementioned question. Saint Benedict opposes this by decreeing that discipline should be administered to everyone according to merit. These matters, however, must be explained somewhat more fully.

**“Let no one be loved more than another.”**] This sentence, like those that follow, explains the preceding statement, as the commentators observe. For what he had first said in general terms—“Let no distinction of persons be made in the monastery”—he now explains more particularly, saying: “Let no one be loved more than another.” He thus excludes altogether from monasteries special friendships, which, as St. Teresa says (*The Way of Perfection*, chapter 4), are rightly condemned among superiors as a kind of plague. For this is the source and origin of nearly countless evils: the doorway to envy, and fuel for quarrels among the brethren. Some, unable to endure being repeatedly placed by the abbot below another who is often unworthy, enter into agreements with one another and spread quarrels and dissensions against the abbot [Col. 0274A] and his associates. Others, trusting themselves excessively to the abbot’s friendship, despise their brothers. Everyone can see how great an evil this is; therefore St. Ferreolus rightly prescribed (*Rule*, chapter 37) that no one should be so familiar with the abbot as to presume to have anything more than the others.

The chief reason is that, since the abbot is obliged to love all equally, while his love is limited, whatever additional love he gives to one he undoubtedly takes away from another. Here, then, that famous saying of St. Bernard applies (*Sermon 13 on the Song of Songs*): “Love is accustomed to efface love.”

Moreover, what this holy Father forbids in the abbot must be considered even more strictly forbidden among all monks. He sufficiently indicates this when, in chapter 69 of the Rule, he forbids anyone to presume to defend another monk in the monastery—a characteristic effect of special friendship—for, he says, from this a very grave occasion for scandals may arise. Certainly nothing was more important to all the teachers of the ascetic life than to cut off such friendships. To comply with their admonitions, it will not be out of place to quote here some of their statements on this subject.

Among others, St. Basil, instructing monks, speaks as follows (*Sermon 1, On the Institution of Monastic Life*):

> “In a common household, the law of charity does not permit partial friendships and factions. For it is entirely necessary that divided affections disturb common harmony in many ways. Therefore all ought to love one another equally, and the same measure of charity must be maintained toward the whole brotherhood. If anyone is found to love a brother monk, a relative, or anyone else with greater inclination for any reason whatever, he must be corrected.”

And elsewhere (*Sermon 2, On the Institution of Monastic Life*):

> “All ought to love one another with an equal measure of affection. For it is unjust that private alliances and factions should be found in the community. Whoever loves one person more than the others shows by this that he does not possess perfect charity toward the others. … From particular friendship and faction arise suspicions [Col. 0274C] and envies. Everywhere, the deprivation of equality is the beginning and occasion of hatred and envy for those who are deprived of it. Therefore we receive from the Lord the command to imitate the goodness of him who makes the sun rise equally upon the just and the unjust. Just as God communicates light equally to all, so those who imitate God offer to all alike and in common the ray of their affection.”

St. Dorotheus agrees with Basil (*Teaching 21*):

> “It is good for a monk who desires to advance not to become excessively attached to his contemporary. Such association and prolonged intimacy with friends and contemporaries commonly extinguish both tears and the fervent purpose of the soul.”

And St. Caesarius, in his exhortation to his sister Caesaria:

> “Take heed, holy soul, and carefully understand how many evils arise from disordered association. For the familiarity of anyone, if it begins to become frequent, sows nothing but corruption, makes vices sprout, covets desire, produces disgrace, stirs up rage, extends fury, nourishes lust, feeds insolence, raises up falls, builds ruins, erects banks, opens precipices, sails amid dangers, spreads its sails toward shipwrecks, rejoices in destruction, fosters ruin, and deserves confusion,”

and so he continues at length. I add Peter of Blois (*Book on Friendship*, chapter 4):

> “Friendship, following the impulse of wandering affection, is indiscriminately carried away toward unlawful things. It observes no measure and does not serve honesty, but is led by a spirit of giddiness.”

See Cassian, *Conferences* 16, chapter 28; St. Laurence Justinian, *Book on Discipline*, chapter 22; St. Teresa, *The Way of Perfection*, chapter 4; and the treatise of Julius Nigronus, tract 13.

**“Unless he finds someone better in good works or in obedience.”**] Here St. Benedict distinguishes obedience from good works.

First, because an act of obedience is not always followed by a good deed: for example, when something impossible is commanded, an obedient monk undertakes it but does not accomplish it; consequently no good work follows from it. Second, because obedience can be exercised not only by carrying out a command but also by refraining from what has been forbidden. Third, even if every act of obedience were a good act, it would not follow that every good act is obedience, as with all those acts we perform by our own choice without any command from our superiors—tears, compunction, prayer, and the like.

Therefore, although all are to be loved equally by the abbot, the holy Father permits those who are better in obedience and good works to be loved more than the others. Thus St. Wandregesilus began to love his monk St. Ausbertus more dearly, “as the monastic norm teaches that one flourishing in every way in the splendor of religion should be loved,” says Aigradus (*Life of St. Ausbertus*, no. 10, Benedictine century II). St. Peter the Venerable seems to have had the same thing in mind when he wrote to Pope Innocent (*Book II, Letter 3*):

> “All indeed are to be loved according to the Lord’s command, but, as life and conduct require, some are to be preferred to others in the affection of love.”

And certainly, as Smaragdus very ably explains this passage:

> “That person will rightly be loved by a human being who is honored by God for good works and holy obedience. I say that the person whom the immortal God loves must necessarily be loved with such love.”

Boherius, however, understands this passage as though St. Benedict permitted only good acts, and not the brothers who perform them, to be loved more:

> “He makes an exception with respect to acts, not persons. For although better acts are to be loved more, I nevertheless think that every neighbor is to be loved equally as a neighbor, namely, to the extent that one loves oneself. Hence, conversely, it is commonly said that sins are hated, not human beings.”

Yet since a good act is nothing other than the person performing it, and does not appear to be distinct from that person, an act cannot be loved without the person being loved. Moreover, if the motive cause of love is goodness, wherever there is more goodness, there must also be found something more of love. A sinner is indeed to be loved according to the good that exists in him—for example, because he is God’s creature, made in his image, redeemed by his precious blood [Col. 0275C], and capable of grace and blessedness. But the just person seems to be loved more, since, in addition to these things, he also performs many good works, adorned with God’s grace and singularly loved by him.

In conferring honor and favor, however, the abbot must conduct himself in such a way that he seems to have regarded not the person so much as the virtue, thereby removing every occasion of envy from the negligent.

**“Let him not be preferred.”**] That is, let him not be placed in a higher position than the one in which he entered, nor be put in charge of a more distinguished office or ministry; or, as Smaragdus says, let him not be preferred in rank or ministry.

**“A freeborn man.”**] Namely, one who was free from the beginning, says Richard of St. Angelo, or a nobleman.

**“From servitude.”**] That is, “born of servile condition and coming from slavery into religious life,” as Boherius says. For, as the Richard cited above observes, “nobility is lost through becoming a monk.” Boherius gathers this from the passage and adds:

> “From this paragraph it is gathered that, through entering religious life, slavery and worldly nobility vanish, because in position, affection, or office no one is honored except according to the merits of his life.”

Indeed, true and sincere freedom consists not so much in nobility of birth as in the eradication of vices. Cassian says well (*Book V, chapter 13*):

> “We too must first show our freedom by the subjection of the flesh.”

For this reason Diogenes was accustomed to say that between bad slaves and bad masters there is no difference except in their names: slaves serve their masters, while masters serve their desires.

**“Coming to conversion.”**] That is, coming to enter religious conversion. It is as though he said: If a slave and an ignoble man comes to conversion at the first hour and enters the monastery, a noble and freeborn man who arrives at the second hour must not be preferred to him.

**“Unless some other reasonable cause exists.”**] This reasonable cause can be understood under two headings: first, the merit of one’s life; second, some natural ability or skill in an art or office by which one excels another [Col. 0276A]. For example, if a younger brother who is ignoble according to worldly status is skilled in singing, he ought to be preferred in singing in the church to an older and freeborn brother less skilled in singing. Or, to use Hildemar’s example, if in a monastery inhabited by Greek monks there is a junior monk who knows the Latin language exceptionally well, and a Latin guest arrives, the junior monk should speak with the guest, even though he is the youngest of all.

In external offices and ministries, aptitude and skill for carrying out such duties are required; in spiritual matters, the merit of life is additionally required.

**“Otherwise, let them retain their proper places.”**] For, as the devout Belgian monk Girardus piously and truly says:

> “An idol in the temple of God is anyone who is honored in the monastery under a title other than that by which each person is commanded to honor another, or who is worthily received before others on account of holiness of life.”

**“And if, justice so directing, it seems right to the abbot.”**] Here “justice,” as Hildemar observes, is understood as the particular virtue that gives each person what belongs to him; or, as Boherius says, “justice directing” means reason—or even God, who is true justice.

**“And let him do this with respect to everyone’s rank.”**] Hildemar notes that there are various ranks in the monastery: first, those who come as laymen to conversion; second, clerics and priests; third, foreign monks. From each of these ranks he may prefer some to others; thus clerics may even be preferred to priests and foreign monks.

**“Otherwise, let them retain their proper places.”**] Namely, according to the order in which they enter conversion.

**“For whether slave or free, we are all one in Christ.”**] Here St. Benedict alludes to the Apostle’s words:

> “All of you who were baptized in Christ have put on Christ. There is neither Jew nor Greek; there is neither slave nor free; there is neither male nor female, but you are all one in Christ Jesus.”

Therefore we are all one in Christ—that is, one body—as Hildemar and Smaragdus explain. The latter confirms this from the Apostle’s words (*1 Corinthians 12*):

> “In one Spirit we were all baptized into one body, whether Jews or Gentiles, whether slaves or free,”

and so forth. Christ himself is the head of this body, under whom we are members of one another.

Or “we are one in Christ” means that we are one in condition, creation, redemption, calling, and the promise of heavenly glory. St. Caesarius says splendidly (*Sermon 116 in the appendix to St. Augustine’s sermons*):

> “We and all peoples are servants of one Lord. We were redeemed at one price; we entered this world on equal terms, and we shall depart by a similar exit. If we act well, we shall likewise come to one blessedness.”

**“Only in this respect are we distinguished in his sight.”**] Namely, with respect to attaining grace or glory.

**“If we are found better than others in good works and humble.”**] In accordance with the saying attributed to St. Augustine—or to someone else (*Sermon 117 in the appendix to the sermons*):

> “With God there is no distinction except that of merits. … In God’s sight each person’s soul is not to be distinguished by nobility but by work, not by lineage but by action.”

And St. Gregory says (*Book I, Rule, chapter 72*):

> “In God’s sight it is not a more distinguished rank but the action of a better life that is approved.”

Hence Aristotle also said (*Politics I*):

> “Virtue and vice determine slaves and free persons, nobles and ignobles.”

Moreover, St. Benedict joins humility to good works because, as St. Gregory writes with great precision:

> “Whoever gathers virtues without humility carries dust into the wind.”

And Smaragdus says:

> “By these two things the elect are always distinguished from the reprobate: true humility of heart and the performance of a good work.”

Here they ask why St. Benedict earlier said, “Let no one be loved more than another, unless he is found better in obedience and good works,” whereas here he says that we are distinguished by God only if we are found better than others in good works and humble—substituting humility for obedience. The answer is that obedience is not distinct from humility, since it constitutes its first degree according to chapter 5 of the Rule; or, if they are distinguished, they are so closely connected that neither can tolerate the absence of the other.

**“Therefore let him have equal charity toward all.”**] Similar is the statement of St. Orsiesius, a disciple of St. Pachomius, in his exhortation to monks:

> “Show equality to all, lest perhaps God hate the one whom you love, and love the one whom you hate.”

Here a difficulty is raised: the one who earlier permitted the good to be loved more than others now wishes equal charity to be shown to all. The difficulty is easily resolved, with Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius, by distinguishing two kinds of charity: one of the heart alone, and the other of heart together with action.

The abbot must have equal charity of heart toward everyone, because he ought to desire and, as far as possible, procure the salvation of all. But he is not obliged to extend charity of heart together with action equally to everyone. For, as Boherius says:

> “Charity in action treats the good in one way and the evil according to their merits in another; the strong in one way and the weak in another; the prosperous in one way and the needy in another.”

Hildemar offers another solution to this difficulty: charity should be equal toward all—by “all,” he means all who are equally good. Nicholas of Fractura agrees, explaining the passage as follows:

> “He means that if all are equal in holy conduct, he should show equal charity to all; otherwise, according to what each one requires.”

**“Let discipline be administered to all according to their merits.”**] That is, correction or punishment, when the fault is the same, in accordance with St. Jerome’s saying:

> “Show partiality to no one—not to wealth, not to power. However powerful or noble he may be, if he has sinned, rebuke him, and you have eaten the unleavened bread of sincerity in bitterness.”

So detested was partiality by the ancient Fathers in administering correction and judgment that St. Pachomius commands a superior who is negligent in this matter, and who judges not according to the truth of the case but according to persons, to be removed from his seat until he is corrected (*Rule*, article 94).

**“For in his teaching.”**] Here “teaching” is understood as correction.

**“He must always preserve that apostolic form in which he says: Rebuke, entreat, reprove.”**] St. Jerome, cited by Smaragdus, explains these words as follows: “Rebuke those who sin; solemnly warn them not to sin; reprove those who resist.” St. Prosper says: “Rebuke equals, entreat elders, reprove the younger.” Richard of St. Angelo says: “Rebuke by admonishing, entreat by threatening, reprove by proceeding to punishment.” But, in Smaragdus’s judgment, St. Benedict gives the best exposition of the apostolic sentence when he adds:

**“That is, mingling times with times, encouragements with threats.”**] “As though he were saying,” Smaragdus remarks, “mingle times of entreaty with times of rebuke.” Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino, however, explain the passage differently: the abbot mingles times with times when, because of the fury or some other passion of a brother, he postpones the rebuke until another time, since the angry or disturbed brother could not bear it then; at that moment it might not only fail to help but even do great harm.

St. Gregory, cited by Hildemar, says excellently:

> “The disturbed do not know what they should hear; but when they have returned to themselves, they receive words of exhortation all the more willingly because they are ashamed that they have been borne with so calmly. To a mind drunk with fury, everything right that is said appears perverse. Thus Abigail laudably kept silent about Nabal’s fault while he was drunk, and laudably spoke of it after he had sobered up.”

Therefore, whenever superiors seem to remain silent and spare someone, their silence should not always be attributed to negligence, but sometimes to prudence, in accordance with St. Odo, abbot of Cluny (*Book III of the Conferences*, no. 44):

> “Certainly, when someone does not rebuke because he is waiting for a more suitable time, or fears that those rebuked may become worse and injure the weak more seriously, this is not negligence or an occasion of self-interest but a counsel of charity. For, as it is said in Book XX of the *Moralia*: When holy men see certain people despising their words, and understand that those people are being abandoned by God, they fall silent with groans. Hence the saying: ‘How shall we sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land?’ It is written: ‘Do not rebuke a scoffer, lest he hate you.’ Holy men therefore remain silent, not because they fear the hatred of such people, but lest those people become worse through hatred.”

St. Bernard, or whoever authored the treatise *On the Passion of the Lord*, agrees with this in chapter 19:

> “The vices of the wicked must sometimes be rebuked and sometimes silently tolerated, according as it seems useful for each person of that kind; for not all sick people are cured by the same kind of medicine.”

Yet if prelates must mingle times with times by postponing correction until their subjects are able to bear it fruitfully, they themselves are no less obliged to wait for a time when they can administer it profitably. They should never punish sinners while their own minds are still disturbed, lest they seem to give more weight to vengeance than to reason and justice:

> “Certainly, because as soon as an injury is inflicted the mind is disturbed” [the excellent warning of Blessed Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 18, dissertation 3, chapter 4], “it can scarcely pronounce a right judgment immediately. Just as water permits the sight of the observer to penetrate when it is still, but blunts it when disturbed, so the human mind, at the very moment of disturbance, does not attend to the unimpeded rule and line of right judgment. Therefore the sentence must be postponed, so that, the balance of justice having been restored, a calm mind may suspend the judgment that a disturbed mind could not.”

And rightly so. For St. Basil says (*Long Rules*, chapter 50):

> “Whoever rebukes a brother with an agitated and angry mind does not free him from sin but involves himself in sins.”

Boherius gives another interpretation of this passage: “mingling times with times” means taking account of the seasons in which faults are committed. The abbot should correct differently in summer and during Lent; for negligence committed during Lent ought to be corrected more severely.

**“Encouragements with threats.”**] Blessed Peter Damian says rightly (*Opusculum* 51, chapter 14):

> “If your breast is the ark of God, as it certainly ought to be, let it contain not only the rod that strikes but also the manna that is sweet upon the palate of a brother’s mind. Let it contain not the zeal of bitterness that terrifies but rather the zeal of charity that corrects for salvation. Let the sharp wound of correction pierce the guilty in such a way that the oil of gentleness may sweeten it with a milder soothing.”

Certainly abbots should present themselves toward their subjects in precisely the manner in which God himself, whose place they occupy, conducts himself toward human beings. For God himself, as St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, says (*Book I of the Conferences*, no. 3),

> “sometimes terrifies us with harsh goads, and sometimes refreshes us with gentle consolations; he mingles terror with soothing and soothing with terror, so that he may incline the hearts of sinners to humility through the terrors he declares, and raise humble sorrow through the consolations he proclaims, so that, while both are tempered toward us by a marvelous art of instruction, those who are terrified may not despair, nor those who are secure be careless.”

See Pope St. Gregory, *Pastoral Book* II, chapter 6.

**“Let him show the sternness of a master and the loving affection of a father.”**] In accordance with St. Gregory’s saying (*Book IX, Letter 8*):

> “Let the good feel you as gentle, and the wicked as a corrector.”

**“That is, he must rebuke the undisciplined and restless more severely, and so forth.”**] This is an entirely clear and evident exposition of the apostolic sentence, and therefore seems to require no addition. I will only note in passing that Hildemar—whom Bernard of Cassino cites under the name of Peter the Deacon, and Boherius under the name of Paul the Deacon—observes that the undisciplined are of three kinds:

1. Some neither understand discipline nor feel shame, and fall into sin.
2. Others understand and fear excommunication, but commit the sin through habit and desire for sin.
3. Others, whether they understand or not, say that they do not wish to accept discipline.

It is as though he were saying: some are undisciplined through ignorance, others through negligence, and others through contempt.

**“Nor should he conceal the sins of those who offend.”**] Sometimes the abbot conceals the sins of offenders so that he may not appear less gentle or kind to his own people; but in this he shows himself especially cruel. “He is cruel,” says St. Basil (*Short Rules*, question 4), “who is silent and does not rebuke, just as someone would be who allowed poison to remain in a person bitten by a poisonous animal and did not remove it.” And St. Augustine says (*Sermon 13, On Scripture*):

> “It is written: ‘Whoever rejects discipline is wretched.’ One may rightly add to this sentence: Just as the person who rejects discipline is wretched, so the person who withholds discipline is cruel.”

See St. Basil, *Long Rules*, questions 24 and 25.

**“But as soon as they begin to arise, let him cut them out by the roots as far as he can.”**] St. John Climacus applies this aptly (*The Ladder*, step 5):

> “While a wound is recent and still hot, it is easily cured. But when it has grown old with time and has been neglected and corrupted, it is difficult to cure, and requires much labor, fire, iron, medicine, and cautery.”

One of the ancient Fathers taught the same thing to his disciples with marvelous skill (St. Dorotheus, *Teaching* 11, no. 5). Once, while he was sitting with them in a place planted with many cypresses of various sizes, he ordered one of them to pull up a very small cypress with his hand. The disciple did so without difficulty, using only one hand. Then the elder pointed out a somewhat larger one, which the disciple pulled up with both hands. After that he showed a third, which the disciple extracted only with great labor. He then ordered him to pull up a fourth, larger than the others; after applying every effort and labor, the disciple could scarcely accomplish it. Finally, he showed him a fifth, which he himself could not uproot. He then ordered another disciple to help his brother, and the two of them could scarcely pull it out.

Then the elder turned to all his disciples and said:

> “So it is with our passions and affections. While they are small and recent, we can cut them off and uproot them with the greatest ease and calm. But if we neglect them as though they were insignificant, they will gradually grow strong; and the stronger they become, the greater the labor that will be required.”

**“Remembering the danger of Eli the priest of Shiloh.”**] To remove from the abbot all sluggishness in rebuking and punishing faults, St. Benedict proposes the example of Eli the priest, who did indeed rebuke his offending sons; but because he did not punish them in the manner he ought to have done, the ark of the Lord was captured, and he fell backward and died. From this St. Peter Damian draws the following conclusion (*Opusculum* 17, chapter 2):

> “If Eli therefore perished with his two sons, whom he rebuked without the severity they deserved, and with so great a multitude of people, what sentence do we think those deserve who sit in the ecclesiastical court and on the judges’ seats, and remain silent about crimes of the wicked that are not unknown to them?”

**“Let him rebuke the more honorable and understanding souls with words at the first and second admonition.”**] Following Smaragdus, later commentators understand “more honorable” to mean more worthy of honor, since *honestus* is so called as though referring to a status of honor. Hildemar, however, calls those more honorable who lead an exemplary life. This is the correct interpretation. Here St. Benedict contrasts the more honorable and understanding souls with the wicked, hard-hearted, proud, and disobedient, whose life is not merely unworthy of imitation but utterly detestable.

**“But the wicked.”**] According to Smaragdus, the wicked are “imprudent and lacking integrity of mind.” According to Hildemar, they are those who have ascended through six stages: first, two private admonitions; second, public correction; third, excommunication; fourth, severe fasting; fifth, flogging; and sixth, the prayer of the brothers. Those whom these six measures do not amend may rightly be called wicked.

According to Menard, “a wicked monk is one who is shameless and obstinate in evil.” He adds:

> “St. Fructuosus, as recorded by Canisius, writes that St. Benedict calls a contumacious person wicked; sometimes, however, someone is called wicked who, although often rebuked, does not contradict the discipline of the Rule.”

**“And the hard-hearted.”**] The hard-hearted and the wicked differ little, if at all. Hildemar says (*Commentary on chapter 23 of the Rule*):

> “The hard-hearted are those who, whether admonished or excommunicated, are not corrected and do not even feel shame. With obstinate minds, fearing neither shame nor excommunication, they follow the impulse of their hearts.”

Smaragdus calls the hard-hearted “stubborn, contumacious, and incorrigible”; Boherius calls them untamed.

**“And let him restrain the proud and disobedient with blows and bodily punishment at the very beginning of their sin.”**] In accordance with St. Aurelian’s saying:

> “The proud, the disobedient, and those who prolong their anger must never be spared until they are corrected.”

We discussed the infliction of blows in *Book II, On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 11. Bodily punishment means excessive fasting, imprisonment, and similar measures, although Smaragdus places bodily punishment in excommunication, verbal rebukes, and blows.

**“Knowing that it is written: ‘A fool is not corrected by words.’”**] Namely, Proverbs 18, where it says:

> “A fool does not accept the words of wisdom unless you say what is in his heart.”

Therefore, let those whom words do not correct at least be corrected by blows.

**“And again: ‘Strike your son with the rod, and you will free his soul from death.’”**] Namely, eternal death, in accordance with Proverbs 23:

> “Do not withdraw discipline from a child. If you strike him with the rod, he will not die. You will strike him with the rod and deliver his soul from hell.”

Blessed is the blow that frees from so many blows.

From this distinction between the good and the wicked in correction, you will gather that people are not sanctified by places, but places by people; and that no congregation is so holy that it does not contain some wicked people within its midst. Abbot Piamon teaches this splendidly in Cassian (*Conference* 18, chapter 16):

> “Let us not be surprised that perverse and detestable people are found hidden among the number of holy men. For while we are trampled and crushed in the threshing floor of this world, it is necessary that the chaff destined for everlasting fire also be mixed among the choicest grain. Finally, if we remember Satan among the angels, Judas among the apostles, and Nicolas, the inventor of a most wicked heresy, among the chosen deacons, it cannot be surprising that the worst people are found inserted into the order of the saints.”

St. Augustine teaches the same in *Sermon 15 on Scripture*, where, when asked why God permits the wicked to be mixed among the good and religious, he answers:

> “Answer me: what does chaff do in the goldsmith’s furnace? I think the chaff is not there without cause where gold is purified. Let us see what is there: there is a furnace, chaff, gold, fire, and an artisan. But the three—gold, chaff, and fire—are in the furnace; the artisan is beside the furnace. Consider this world also: the world is the furnace, wicked people are the chaff, good people are the gold, tribulation is the fire, and God is the artisan. Consider and see: gold is not purified unless the chaff is burned.”

**“The abbot must always remember what he is and remember what he is called.”**] Here he says two things. The abbot must remember what he is—namely, a human being, mortal, fragile, sinful, and so forth. Then he must remember what he is called—that is, abbot, father, and superior. First, he must remember what he is, so that, humbled by the recollection of his own frailty and misery, he may not exalt himself on account of his dignity. Then he must remember that he is called abbot and represents Christ, from whom he ought to expect special and particular graces, with whose help he may carry out the office entrusted to him and not lose heart.

**“And know that from the one to whom more is entrusted, more is required.”**] For when gifts increase, an account of those gifts also increases.

**“And let him know how difficult and arduous a task he has undertaken: to govern souls.”**] For, as St. Gregory says, the government of souls is an art among arts. Indeed, if someone can scarcely govern his own soul, how will he govern another’s? If bodily or temporal matters require so many cares and labors, who will be sufficient for caring for souls?

**“And to serve the dispositions of many.”**] These words, according to the commentators, explain the preceding ones: to govern souls is the same as to serve the dispositions of many. That is, he must adapt himself and make himself suitable to the dispositions of his subjects, so that he may encourage the good, rebuke the wicked, humble the proud, strengthen the weak, guide the strong, and lead those who have strayed back into the way of truth and justice, as Trithemius says. He must have as many dispositions as he has sons under his governance, as the *Rule for Virgins*, chapter 1, says.

From this passage of St. Benedict’s Rule it may rightly be inferred that abbots and all other superiors should truly be called servants of those whose care has been entrusted to them, since they are commanded to serve their dispositions. Indeed, if spiritual superiors are physicians of souls, they must remember that it is characteristic of physicians not to rule over the sick but to serve them. Hence St. Basil (*Long Rules*, chapter 30):

> “Let the dignity of office not exalt the superior, lest he fall from the blessedness of humility and modesty and, puffed up, fall into the devil’s snare. Rather, let him know this for certain: because he has undertaken the care of many, he is thereby required to serve many.”

**“And according to the quality or understanding of each person, let him conform and adapt himself to everyone.”**] He will certainly do this “when he becomes great with the great and small with the small; when he becomes weak with the weak, so that he may save the weak; when he becomes a pattern for the flock and shows the humble the form of humility, gives the obedient examples of obedience, and likewise provides those who fast, keep vigil, pray, and practice every good virtue with a model of salvation,” as Smaragdus says.

**“So that he may not merely suffer the losses of the flock entrusted to him, but may rejoice in the increase of the good flock.”**] Here the increase of the flock means not so much an increase in number as in virtue and good conduct. For what benefit is there in a multitude of monks where the number of virtues is lacking and a multitude of vices is multiplying? “You have increased the nation,” the prophet says to the Lord, “but you have not increased joy.”

Certainly it would be much better to have a few good monks than very many bad ones, whose example corrupts the good and utterly undermines all regular discipline. Thus our Mabillon rightly counted among the causes of relaxation in our Order the negligence of certain abbots who cared not which monks, or what kind of monks, they had, but only how many. Charlemagne censured this error in a short published capitulary in the eleventh year of his reign, in these words (*Preface to the fourth Benedictine century, part I, no. 140*):

> “What benefit does it bring to the Church of Christ that the person who ought to be pastor or teacher of any venerable place takes greater care to have many rather than good people in his community, and delights not so much in the worthy as in the multitude?”

It is not a multitude of people but a multitude of people living well that sanctifies monasteries. Indeed, just as a small number of monks makes it difficult for the discipline of the Rule to be strictly observed, so a large monastic population is no less harmful to monastic observance. In so great a multitude it is scarcely possible that some wicked people will not be found, whose perverse conduct corrupts the good and religious.

Furthermore, wherever there are many, there are some to whom, for legitimate reasons, certain exemptions must be granted; through these the rigor of regular observance is gradually and imperceptibly weakened. The author of the *Life of St. Stephen of Obazine*, book I, no. 16 (Volume IV of the *Miscellanea* of Baluze), seems to have foreseen this, writing:

> “While we make excuses for the smallest matters, we neglect the greater. Exhausted by the long duration of time and weighed down by the multitude of those living with us, we have declined from our former vigor and conduct ourselves with greater laxity and negligence. While we wish to accommodate the weak, we hasten rather to follow their negligence than to draw them toward perfection.”

Add to this that in so great a multitude of brothers the abbot can scarcely be sufficient for the spiritual needs of all, especially since he has no time to learn those needs personally.

St. Benedict significantly said, “the flock entrusted to him,” because, as Hildemar says:

> “That flock is not his but the Lord’s and is entrusted to him. Therefore, because it is not his but entrusted to him, he ought to care for it with diligent attention.”

**“Above all, not concealing.”**] That is, not neglecting. For, as Boherius says, in many places “concealment” is used to mean negligence.

[Or treating it as insignificant.] That is, despising it. You should recognize that what follows is important; for, as Smaragdus and Hildemarus say, *parvipendere* means the same as to look down upon something great with a proud mind, or to value it little.

[The salvation of the souls entrusted to him.] The salvation of the souls is indeed a great matter, for Christ died for them.

[Should show greater concern for earthly, transitory, and perishable things.] Supply: than for souls. The holy Father does not remove from the abbot every concern for temporal matters, but only excessive and superfluous concern. Concerning this, Augustine says (*Sermon* 101, on Scripture): “What is worse than the anxiety of this life, which does not permit one to attain life? What is more wretched than to lose life while caring for life?”

He condemns such anxieties in the abbot, confronting the greed of certain perverse men, about whom Peter of Blois writes vividly (*Letter* 134):

“There are abbots,” he says, “who seek rather what is theirs than what belongs to Jesus Christ; you will know them by their fruits. Having set aside the care of souls, they consider the height of their office to consist in magnificently increasing and extending, by right and wrong, the possessions of their church through cultivation and buildings, to the ruin of themselves and their dependents. But the care of souls—which, conceived through the spirit of fear, had brought forth the fruit of salvation—they wickedly cause to miscarry, so that the prophet’s word may rightly be applied to them: ‘They have cut open the pregnant women of Gilead, so that they might enlarge their borders’ (Amos 1). These are the men driven by the spirit of this world, the spirit of dizziness and error. It is better to enlarge your house by moral character than by possessions; it is better to fill heaven than a granary.”

Yet I would not have this understood as though an abbot might neglect temporal matters, without whose assistance spiritual and eternal things can scarcely be obtained. Hence Saint Teresa also said (*On the Manner of Visiting Monasteries*, no. 2): “For spiritual things to advance continually from good to better, it is of the greatest importance, even in monasteries that are needy and without income, to exercise great care over temporal affairs.”

Saint Gregory rightly says (*Book I of the Register*, chapter 24):

“Whoever presides over the governance of brothers cannot be entirely free from external cares; nevertheless, one must take the greatest care that he not be excessively weighed down by them. Hence it is rightly said through Ezekiel: ‘The priests shall neither shave their heads nor let their hair grow long, but they shall cut their heads by trimming them.’ What do the hairs on the head signify except more abundant thoughts in the mind? While they imperceptibly arise above the brain, they express the cares of the present life; because they emerge from a neglected and sluggish understanding, they come forth inopportunely, as though proceeding without our awareness.

“Therefore, since all who preside must indeed have external concerns, but must not devote themselves excessively to them, priests are rightly forbidden both to shave their heads and to let their hair grow long. In this way they neither cut off entirely from themselves the carnal thoughts arising from the life of their subjects, nor again allow them to grow excessively. Hence it is well said: ‘Let them trim their heads by cutting them,’ so that the care of temporal affairs may emerge as far as necessity requires, yet be cut back quickly lest it grow beyond measure, and so forth.”

Saint Gertrude, abbess of Nivelles, had rejected such immoderate cares (*Second Benedictine Century*, p. 465). As the Anonymous author writes in her *Life*, chapter 3, she “entrusted the external household administration to good and faithful stewards from among the brothers, while within the monastery enclosure she entrusted the household care of the spiritual sisters, so that day and night she might be able to fight against spiritual wickedness in holy combat through vigils and prayers, sacred readings, and fasts.”

Moreover, since the abbot is not required to devote himself to every kind of temporal care, but—as we have said—only to what is necessary and not superfluous, the question arises whether he may and ought to extend that care even to undertaking lawsuits for the preservation of the monastery’s goods. Certainly, just as I do not think that, in matters of greater importance, one should yield to plunderers of the monastery’s goods, so I do not approve of servants of God contending in judgment over trifles.

Saint Augustine seems to condemn lawsuits altogether in many places. Saint Bernard particularly disapproves of them among monks (*Homily* 4, *On “He Was Sent”*, no. 10):

“I see others,” he says—“and this ought not to be seen without sorrow—who, after entering Christ’s warfare, again become entangled in worldly business and again plunge into earthly desires. With great care they raise walls while neglecting morals; under the pretext of common utility they sell words to the rich and greetings to noblewomen; and, contrary to the command of their emperor, they covet what belongs to others and reclaim their own through litigation. They do not hear the Apostle, sounding the trumpet by command of the King: ‘This is itself a fault among you, that you have lawsuits: why do you not rather suffer wrong?’ Have they so crucified the world to themselves, and themselves to the world, that those who formerly were scarcely known in their own village or town now travel through provinces, frequent courts, and obtain acquaintance with kings and familiarity with princes?”

Again, writing to Odo, abbot, and the brothers of the Greater Monastery (*Letter* 387), he says:

“We say that it is safer for every Christian, and especially for a monk, to possess something less without litigation than something more with litigation.”

A little earlier he had written:

“But perhaps you say: ‘We injure no one; we hold what is ours, prepared, if anyone opposes us, to submit to judgment.’ Quite right. But what if another replies and says: ‘This is itself a fault among you, that you have lawsuits. Why do you not rather suffer wrong?’ What if someone else reads: ‘If anyone takes away what is yours, do not demand it back; rather, offer the other cheek to one who strikes you on the right, and give your cloak to one who takes your tunic’?”

Peter of Blois held the same view when he wrote to H., abbot of Reading (*Letter* 102):

“Against the decree of the heavenly Emperor it is not only wrong to covet or seize what belongs to others, but also to reclaim one’s own through litigation. The Apostle says to Timothy: ‘The servant of God must not quarrel’; and again: ‘This is itself a fault among you, that you have lawsuits, and do not rather suffer wrong.’”

Elsewhere he wrote to G., abbot of the Greater Monastery (*Letter* 117), who had summoned the prior of Saint Cosmas to court:

“If you carefully considered the vow of your profession, to which you are bound, and sought with greater zeal the things that are above, not the things that are on earth, in accordance with the Apostle’s teaching—‘The servant of God must not quarrel’—since he says elsewhere, ‘This is itself a fault among you, that you have lawsuits, and do not rather suffer wrong.’”

Concluding the letter, he adds:

“Therefore cease—or rather, let all religious cease—from such practices, by which the consciences of holy men are wounded, the good reputation of religious is blackened, the order is scandalized, and souls are strangled. For those who litigate for land or pasture are unworthy to be placed in the land of the living or in the place of pasture.”

To these may be added the ancient monastic rules. The *Rule of Saint Posthumius, Delivered by an Angel*, no. 18, says:

“Do not permit a married man to contend with you in judgment; for it is better for a monk to endure wrong and injury than for the voice of a soldier of Christ to be heard amid an outcry.”

The rules more fully discussed by Saint Basil (*chapter* 9) say:

“One ought to admonish foolish relatives—those who unjustly retain the goods of persons who have renounced the world—lest they commit the sin of sacrilege, in accordance with the Lord’s command, in which he said: ‘If your brother sins against you, go and rebuke him,’ and so forth. But to contend against them in judgment before secular tribunals was forbidden by the teaching of piety, where the Lord says: ‘To the one who wishes to go to judgment with you and take your tunic, leave him your cloak also’; and the Apostle says: ‘Does any one of you, having a matter against another, dare to go to judgment before the unjust and not before the saints?’”

He adds:

“And before those saints we may summon them to judgment, but in such a way that the brother’s salvation is preferred to an abundance of money. For after the Lord said, ‘If he hears you,’ he added: ‘You have gained your brother,’ not money. It can sometimes happen that, for the sake of making the truth known, when the person who first began to act unjustly against us summons us to the prescribed hearing, we consent; but we do so as obeying a summons, not as yielding to our own anger or spirit of contention, and as making the truth clear. In this way we shall both rescue our adversary from evil, even against his will, and ourselves shall not transgress God’s commands.”

The *Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks* (no. 39) says:

“You shall have no lawsuits, obeying the Apostle’s command, where he says: ‘The servant of God must not quarrel, but must be gentle.’”

The *Rule of Saint Stephen, Founder of the Order of Grandmont* (chapter 24) says:

“We command you never to draw up a document concerning things given or to be given to you for the purpose of litigating, nor even presume to litigate.”

And below (chapter 31):

“We most firmly command you never to presume to litigate or contend in judgment with anyone on account of your own or another’s possessions, nor to take into your hands the cases or controversies of others. What more is there to say? Whether you are present or absent, lawsuits and such secular conflicts shall in no way be conducted in your places.”

Not long after the death of the holy Father, his most holy disciples obeyed this command as a vow. When “the monks of the village of Ambazac, belonging to the abbey of Saint Augustine of Limoges, began to bring a claim against the site of Muret, where faithful servants of God lived and had long served together with their most holy Father, they—preferring to leave their cloak to one who took their tunic rather than be dragged from there into hearings and the practice of litigation—carefully sought another place where they could suitably establish the center of their religious life.”

Finally, in the third compilation of their statutes, the Carthusian monks list among the matters they consider worthy of reproach (chapter 3, no. 6):

“Some are excessively eager in acquiring, others imprudent in alienating, and still others inclined to lawsuits, to no small detriment of themselves and their houses.”

Accordingly, not much later they issue this statute (no. 14):

“As far as we can, let us avoid lawsuits and legal proceedings; for it is not permitted for servants of God to litigate. If necessity sometimes drives us to this, let us seek peace with our adversaries by an amicable or arbitral route, if this can be done, or let us embrace peace when it is offered, in order to avoid various journeys, the uncertain outcomes of lawsuits, and expenses. From these things many disadvantages have arisen for the houses and persons of the order.”

I had almost omitted Saint Fructuosus, who in the *Common Monastic Rule* (chapter 3) wishes such a man to be elected abbot who “rootedly drives every practice of litigation from his heart and, if it is lawful, under no circumstance contends with men in judgment. But if someone provokes him and takes his tunic, let him contend in accordance with the Lord’s command by immediately leaving his cloak. If, indeed, some persecutor of the monastery approaches, attempts to take something, and wishes to seize it by force, let him entrust the case to one of the laymen, to a most faithful Christian commended by a good life and not discredited by a bad reputation, who may judge and pursue the monastery’s affairs without sin. If it is customary to swear, let him do this without an oath or penalty, not merely for the gain of the property, but to bring the humble and gentle persecutor back to ask forgiveness. If the persecutor persists in his obstinacy and loves gain more than his soul, let the litigant immediately cease contending with him. But let the abbot, without any practice of litigation and with the resentment of his stomach erased, live simply in his monastery with his monks, and have no license to litigate with secular persons.”

[Note: [Col. 0283] See the Second Life of Saint Oswald, bishop of York, no. 56, *Fifth Benedictine Century*, p. 752.]

To all these may be added the following definition of the Council of Mainz, celebrated in 813 (Canon 12):

“We altogether wish this: that monks in no way come to secular hearings, nor that the abbot himself go without the consent of his bishop when necessity requires it. Then he shall go at the bishop’s command and with his counsel. Nevertheless, he shall presume to initiate no contentions or lawsuits, but whatever must be sought or answered, he shall conduct through his advocates.”

Happy indeed are the monks of this age when they find such advocates to whom the monastery’s affairs may safely be entrusted, and when miserable necessity does not compel them to groan beneath the burden of temporal matters that they must manage themselves, although they ought rather to groan over their own and others’ sins.

Saint Anselm, however, relieves us of this scruple. Once, when consulted by a certain brother who said:

“Having left the world, I came to the monastic order, hoping that there I could devote myself entirely to eternal life and to God. But now, by command of my abbot, I attend to secular business; and while I desire to defend and protect the Church’s possessions against secular persons, I plead, litigate, and so forth,”

he replied, among other things:

“A monk should devote himself to the obedience imposed upon him, so that he may both defend and protect the Church’s possessions courageously and justly against everyone, and not strive to bring anything belonging to another under the Church’s authority by injustice. If he conducts himself and lives in this way, although on account of such matters he loses Masses, sometimes speaks while the brothers are silent in the cloister, and does or omits certain similar things that neither make nor unmake him, the virtue of obedience that he exercises consumes all these things. Preserving his vessel intact, it gathers and stores up, whole and pure, the flour flowing from his mill, which will feed him eternally, and so forth.”

This applies to one who is drawn into secular business unwillingly and with a reluctant spirit. He adds:

“And what should be thought of one who voluntarily offers himself for the administration of estates and secretly calls helpers to himself, promises gifts, and pledges favor so that what he desires may be brought to fulfillment?”

Anselm reports the answer:

“None of this belongs to the purpose of a monk.”

When the questioner asked:

“Is it not the case that such a man, although he desires what I have described, nevertheless attempts to do nothing without the permission of his superior?”

he replied:

“Permission has deceived many. Obedience and disobedience are contraries; permission lies between them. Therefore, the person whom obedience does not compel to leave the monastery enclosure nevertheless wishes to leave and to evade the strictness of the rule under the cover of permission. Although he is unwilling to presume to do this without permission, and therefore may defend his action by the permission on which he relies, he nevertheless incurs sin through his unlawful intention. For after he had died to the world and entered the cloister, he ought not in any way, even by intention, to return to the business of the world.

“Yet because he wished to fulfill his intention in action only after being permitted, the obedience that he embraced in this matter will excuse the action. But the intention he held against obedience will be dangerous for him unless he repents. Many, failing to pay sufficient attention to this, are often deceived by the permission they seek in order to fulfill their intention.”

Thus far Anselm. Would that everyone understood and followed his mind! If you wish to see how he conducted himself in lawsuits and legal proceedings, consult Book I of his *Life*, p. 792, in Surius.

[But let him always consider that he has undertaken the governance of souls, for which he will have to render an account.] Similar is the statement of Orsiesius in his exhortation to monks:

“Let us learn that we must stand before the tribunal of Christ, and that we shall be judged concerning each thing—not only our works but also our thoughts—and that after rendering an account of our own life, we shall likewise render an account for others who have been entrusted to us.”

This is a sentence truly to be feared by all superiors; it has shaken even the pillars of monastic life and terrified men distinguished by every holiness.

Struck by this fear, Peter the Venerable wrote to Guigo, prior of the Carthusian monastery (*Book I, Letter* 24):

“Fearing this more than I can say, and knowing that it is a dreadful thing to fall into the hands of the living God, I am hemmed in by a double danger as I consider myself and those entrusted to me. For, as blessed Gregory says: ‘In that fearful examination of judgment, one person’s testimony will scarcely suffice for himself alone; how much less for himself and his neighbor?’ How, then, shall I stand before Christ, the just judge of the living and the dead, on behalf of so many thousands scattered throughout the world, whom I am rarely or never permitted to see? How shall I be able, according to blessed Father Benedict, to render an account of the number entrusted to me, when, questioned about the care of my own life, I may perhaps appear speechless?” And so forth.

Saint Bernard indicates that he was even more deeply moved by this in these words (*Sermon* 3, *On the Advent*):

“Those who will have to render an account for many souls are bound by a debt far heavier and more dangerous. What shall I, wretched man, do, where shall I turn, if this great treasure, this precious deposit—which Christ judged more precious to himself than his own blood—should happen to be guarded negligently? If I had collected the blood dripping from the Lord’s cross, and it had been stored with me in a glass vessel that would often have to be carried, what state of mind would I have in so great a danger? Certainly I have received for safekeeping that for which a merchant who was not foolish—Wisdom itself—gave that blood. Yet I have this treasure in earthen vessels, which seem exposed to far more dangers than glass vessels.”

[And that he should not make an excuse on account of perhaps lesser resources.] As our Menard observes, *causari* sometimes means to excuse and defend. Thus, “that he should not make an excuse on account of perhaps lesser resources” means: he should not excuse or defend his negligence toward the souls whose governance he has undertaken, or his excessive concern for temporal matters, on the pretext of poverty or limited resources.

[Let him remember what Scripture says: “Seek first the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be added to you.”] Saint Basil therefore rightly says (*On the Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 35):

“For if, where two or three are gathered in Christ’s name, Christ is in their midst, much more is this so where there are more people and a congregation of many. Either, then, in Christ’s presence we shall lack none of the necessities of life, since even the Israelites in the wilderness lacked nothing necessary; or, if something is lacking for our testing, it is better to be needy and be with Christ than to abound in all the goods of this life without his companionship.”

These words of Saint Basil also wonderfully illuminate the following sentence.

[And again: “Nothing is lacking to those who fear him.”] For, as Smaragdus says, “whoever possesses God, through whom all created things came into being and in whom all things remain and endure, cannot possess less of either spiritual or earthly substance.”

Saint Hugh of Autun, a monk, had tested this matter in practice. As we read in his *Life*, no. 16, he “asserted, in the public declaration of the common and true faith, that if the tenor of the aforesaid Father Benedict’s rule of discipline were observed in any place whatever, those who lived there would suffer no want. This is recognized as having been proved even today in many places where it is preserved; while in those places where it has grown cold through neglect, poverty and unrest have made their dwelling.”

The anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Stephen, Abbot of Obazine*, his disciple, lamented the same thing when he wrote:

“But now, while we are more concerned than is fitting with earthly and perishable things and do not think about heavenly ones, it comes about that we abound in neither the one nor the other, because we were commanded to seek heavenly goods first—that is, above all—and ought to have entrusted the care of the remaining things to divine providence.”

Perhaps for this reason Saint William, abbot of Dijon, as Glaber writes in his *Life*, according to Rodulfus, chapter 15 (*apud Bollandistas*, 1 January), “when placed in charge of the interests of three monasteries, frequently impressed upon them that they should be prudent in collecting what had been entrusted to them, lest those who were too poor in relation to the income from their taxes be oppressed. For he said that he preferred to give something to a needy person rather than demand anything from one who was without means.”

This is an excellent admonition for those who manage temporal affairs, and we earnestly urge them to follow it.

[And let him know that whoever undertakes the governance of souls, and so forth.] A thoroughly terrifying sentence, requiring more fear than exposition.

[Col. 0288A] [And thus always fearing the future examination of the Shepherd concerning the sheep entrusted to him, while he is wary of the accounts of others, he becomes concerned about his own, and so forth.] Thus it comes about that, as Saint Gregory says, cited by Peter of Blois (*Letter* 132; *Pastoral Rule*, Part III, admonition 5), he multiplies as many crowns for himself as he wins souls for God.

## CHAPTER III. On Calling the Brothers to Counsel

[Col. 0287]

[Col. 0287A] Whenever anything especially important is to be done in the monastery, let the abbot summon the entire congregation and himself state what the matter concerns. After hearing the brothers’ counsel, let him deliberate within himself and do what he judges more useful. We have therefore said that all are to be called to counsel [Note: [Col. 0287B] Florence manuscript: “to call.”], because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger brother [Note: [Col. 0287B] Florence manuscript: “to the younger.”]. Let the brothers give counsel with complete humility and submission, so that they do not presumptuously and boldly defend what seems right to them; rather, let the matter depend upon the abbot’s judgment, so that all may obey whatever he judges more salutary [Note: [Col. 0287B] Florence manuscript: “and whatever.”]. But just as it is fitting for disciples to obey their master [Note: [Col. 0287B] Another reading: *discipulos* (“disciples”), rather than *discipulis* (“for disciples”).], so it is fitting for the master himself to arrange everything prudently and justly.

[Col. 0288A] In all things, therefore, let everyone follow the rule as a teacher; let no one rashly depart from it [Note: [Col. 0288B] Another reading: “deviate from it.”]. Let no one in the monastery follow the desire of his own heart, nor let anyone presume to contend insolently with his abbot, whether within or outside the monastery [Note: [Col. 0288B] Another reading: *proterve intus vel foris monasterium* (“insolently, within or outside the monastery”); another reading: *monasterio*, rather than *monasterium*.]. If anyone presumes to do so, let him submit to regular discipline.

Nevertheless, let the abbot himself do everything with fear of God and observance of the rule, knowing without doubt that he will render an account to God, the most just judge, for all his judgments. But if there are smaller matters to be undertaken for the monastery’s welfare, let him use only the counsel of the elders, as it is written: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it” [Note: [Col. 0288B] Another reading: “you will not be sorry.”] (Ecclesiasticus 32).

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0287]

[Col. 0287C] Whenever anything especially important is to be done in the monastery, let the abbot summon the entire congregation and himself state what the matter concerns; after hearing the brothers’ counsel, let him deliberate within himself, and let all obey whatever he judges to be more useful.] In these words, as Boherius notes, Saint Benedict chiefly includes five points:

1. That in doubtful matters of greater importance the abbot should gather all the monks: “let the abbot summon the entire congregation.”
2. That he himself should explain the matters to be considered: “and himself state what the matter concerns.”
3. That he should solicit the brothers’ opinion concerning the matter proposed: “after hearing the brothers’ counsel.”
4. That, after hearing the brothers’ counsel, he should deliberate with himself: “let him deliberate within himself.”
5. That he should carry out in practice what he has judged best.

All these points must be considered individually.

[Whenever anything especially important is to be done in the monastery.] Matters of special importance are those that are of greater consequence and concern the entire congregation. Hildemarus chiefly lists five such matters:

1. The reception of novices.
2. Expulsion from the monastery.
3. The imposition of penance or excommunication for a grave fault, including the question of its character and duration.
4. The gift of any object of some value.
5. A serious alteration of some matter.

To these may be added the conferral of benefices, the sale of monastery property, the leasing or renting of immovable goods, and many other matters of this kind.

[Let the abbot summon the entire congregation.] By “congregation” is understood the assembly of monks living under an abbot or superior. Novices are not counted among them, since they have not yet been joined to the body of the congregation and may freely return to the world. Nor are lay brothers included—whether they are called converts, assistants, servants, or by any other name—who have been received only for the monks’ external services.

Although Saint Benedict excludes no one from the consideration of such matters—for he commands the entire congregation to be summoned—those under interdict, suspended persons, excommunicated persons, prisoners, and those deprived of active and passive voice as punishment for some serious offense or in any other way are not ordinarily called to these proceedings and should not be called.

There is greater difficulty concerning the absent. Boherius discusses them as follows in his first commentary:

“By law, the absent are not summoned for the making of contracts. In elections of superiors, in the reception or creation of monks, and in the conferral of benefices, the absent are to be summoned, provided that they can conveniently be called without danger. If it is not known where they are staying, they must be cited by a public notice in the church or in the place where they are accustomed to stay—unless the custom is that they are not called to the chapter. Understand, however, that they are to be called in this way when the aforesaid receptions, creations, or conferrals concern both the abbot and the convent.”

They were summoned by the sound of some instrument, such as a rattle or small bell. Among the monks of Bursfeld this was rung with the following distinction (*Bursfeld Ceremonial*, distinction 1, chapter 15): “For a chapter of deliberation, two signals are made; for the ordinary daily chapter, only one.” On the meaning of the chapter in which such summonses were made, see Benedict Haeften, Book VIII, treatise 1, discussion 1.
