[And let him himself state what the matter concerns.] After the brothers have been summoned, the abbot explains the matter for which he gathered them. As Plato says (*Phaedrus*), “In every matter requiring counsel, the beginning is to know the matter about which the counsel has been established; otherwise one must go astray along the entire route.”

Before explaining the matter to be discussed, Hildemarus says that, “with his bodily eyes fixed upon the earth and the eye of his heart upon God, he ought to beseech God, saying: ‘Lord, I ask your mercy: through whomever you wish to reveal it, deign to make it known.’”

After invoking divine help, he should explain the matter, presenting arguments on both sides, but in such a way that he does not disclose his own opinion. Thus every opportunity for flattery or sycophancy is removed; even the more timid are given free and unrestricted permission to state what they think; and a badly disposed person, driven by the evil spirit of discord, cannot—after learning the abbot’s desire—adopt the opposing view merely to cause him annoyance.

The Constitutions of the Congregation of Monte Oliveto directly guard against this danger. They decree (Part II, chapter 3) that “both the general and the particular abbot must take care, when proposing matters in chapter, not to indicate by a gesture, words, or any other means what outcome he would prefer. Let them merely propose the matter, listen to everyone, and prudently discuss and establish everything by common counsel, adopting what the greater part judges more useful. If he acts otherwise, he is to be publicly rebuked the first time and suspended for six months the second.”

[And after hearing the brothers’ counsel.] In accordance with Scripture: “The wise person listens to counsels” (Proverbs 12). He should not tolerate others interrupting the speeches of those who have begun to speak before they have fully expressed their counsel; nor should he resent those who put forward an opinion contrary to his own.

[Let him deliberate within himself.] Although Saint Benedict seems to require nothing more of the abbot than that he seek and hear the brothers’ counsels, granting him afterward the free power to carry out whatever he wishes—and although the nature of counsel itself seems to demand this—the ancient custom of the Benedictine order became established: after hearing the brothers’ opinions, the abbot was to consider them not alone but with certain elder or prudent brothers, discern which was sounder, and finally judge what ought to be done. This is clear from the ancient commentators on the rule, Smaragdus and Hildemarus.

“Let him willingly hear whatever counsel each person gives,” says Smaragdus, “and afterward, in private and only with the elder brothers, let him carefully and acutely discern who gave the more useful and who the less useful counsel.”

Hildemarus explains the matter at greater length. First, he teaches that after hearing the brothers’ opinions, the abbot should deliberate with three or four elders for several days and weigh the brothers’ counsels with them. Then, after balancing everyone’s advice, he should summon the brothers again in chapter and say:

“We have considered your counsels and have been unable to find anything better than this; therefore I wish it to be done.”

All should obey him. Or, if he cannot find anything suitable in any of the brothers’ counsels, he should present his own. If the brothers do not agree with it, he should finally examine both his own counsel and theirs, weighing the arguments on each side, and only then do what he has seen to be better.

In such an examination the abbot should consider “what is permitted according to equity, what is fitting according to honesty, and what is expedient according to usefulness,” as Innocent III says.

[And let him do what he has judged more useful.] Thus he should prefer the best to the good, and the better to the merely good.

Saint Benedict therefore commands that the brothers’ counsel be sought in doubtful matters, not their consent. This was indeed the practice in the time of Smaragdus and Hildemarus, who merely wished the abbot, together with the elders, to weigh and examine the brothers’ counsels, without awaiting either their consent or that of the elders.

Saint Bernard teaches the same thing in writing to the monks of the Greater Monastery (*Letter* 387):

“What if the abbot has decided to stand by the counsel of the elders? Must he not do so if you have not all consented? Do you then either fail to heed or despise the clear statement on this matter in your rule? For it commands that when the brothers are called to counsel, each should answer what he thinks, in such a way that they do not presume to defend what they have answered. But after hearing each person’s opinion, all should assent without contradiction to whichever the abbot has chiefly chosen,” and so forth.

Later, however, it seemed appropriate to place certain limits upon the abbot’s wide authority. Thus there are now certain cases in which he cannot arrange anything according to his own wishes without the brothers’ consent. John Trithemius lists eight principal cases in which his authority is null without their consent:

1. He cannot sell the monastery’s immovable property—such as fields, meadows, and similar goods—unless the convent consents.
2. He cannot grant monastery property to anyone by hereditary and perpetual right without the will and consent of the convent.
3. He cannot receive a monk into profession without the convent’s consent.
4. He cannot burden the monastery with pledges or other securities, at least by accepting a large sum of money against any monastery property, without evident necessity and the consent of his brothers, just as he cannot alienate immovable property from the monastery.
5. Some wish to add a fifth case: that the abbot may not dismiss a monk to another monastery of the same order, where he is to establish himself permanently, without the convent’s consent. They say that just as he cannot increase the congregation without their will, so he cannot diminish it.
6. He cannot impose upon them statutes extending beyond the rule unless they consent to them.
7. He cannot spiritually admit anyone to the confraternity of the entire monastery.
8. He cannot receive perpetual prebendaries into the monastery without the will of the convent.

Thus far Trithemius. There are perhaps many other cases, concerning which the constitutions of each congregation should be consulted.

[We have therefore said that all are to be called to counsel, because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger brother.] Saint Cyprian testifies that he learned this by experience in these words (*Letter* 10):

“For among us, through nightly visions and also by day, the innocent age of children is filled by the Holy Spirit; in ecstasy it sees with its eyes, hears, and speaks those things by which the Lord deigns to admonish and instruct us.”

Thus the Lord revealed to Daniel, when he was only twelve years old, the fraud and deceit of the elders. Hence the Apostle Paul says: “If something is revealed to the younger, let the elder be silent” (1 Corinthians 14).

Therefore, because the Lord often reveals what is better to the younger, Saint Benedict also wished even the youngest of the younger brothers to be called to counsel. For the same reason the ancient monks admitted them to their conferences, as Cassian testifies (*Conferences* 16, chapter 12), although in some monastic congregations only those initiated into sacred orders—at least subdeacons—take part in chapter deliberations.

This is also the practice among the Carthusians according to the new collection of statutes, Part II, chapter 4. Yet this is a recent practice among them, for the Statutes of Guigo, chapter 37, and the Ancient Statutes, Part II, chapter 7, wish all monks to be summoned without exception.

[Thus let the brothers give counsel with complete humility and submission.] Up to this point the holy Father has taught the abbot how he ought to use the brothers in counsel; now he explains how the brothers ought to express their own judgment, saying: “Thus let the brothers give counsel”—namely, in the form given by Hildemarus in his explanation of the rule’s text, “Let him state what the matter concerns”:

“Then the monks ought to answer in this way: ‘It is your authority to ask, and permission has been given to us to answer. We now ask that you not take what we are about to say as having been said insolently; what we shall answer, we say with your permission.’”

The abbot should answer them:

“You have our permission to speak.”

Then each person should set forth what he thinks.

With all humble submissiveness.] That is, modestly and humbly. Whoever comes only when summoned, speaks when questioned, does not mock others who are speaking with contempt, and does not interrupt their words arrogantly and noisily will certainly fulfill this requirement. “For the proud man,” says Saint Bernard (*On the Degrees of Humility*, chap. 16), “sits first in assemblies, answers first in councils, approaches without being summoned, intrudes without being ordered, rearranges what has been arranged, and remakes what has been done.”

Or submission in humility, as Haeftenus observes (*Book III, treatise 5, disputation 7*), is chiefly evident in this: when questioned, a brother should not speak absolutely and authoritatively, as though pronouncing a definitive judgment—“This must be done; this ought to happen; this is my conclusion”—but rather: “This is how it seems to me”; “I believe it could be done in this way,” and so forth, adding the expression familiar even to the most learned theologians and jurists: “Without prejudice to a better judgment.”

Let them not presume to defend arrogantly what they have judged.] This is contrary to the humility with which he ordered counsel to be given. “What greater pride can there be,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 2, On the Resurrection*), “than for one person to place his own judgment above that of the entire congregation, as though he alone possessed the Spirit of God?”

Nor should Saint Benedict’s words be understood as though he altogether forbade anyone to maintain his opinion. Rather, it is permissible to answer objections and to support what seems sounder with the strongest arguments possible, provided that all obstinacy and stubbornness are absent. But what if someone rises in opposition to the speaker? Hear Hildemar:

“But if another rises at his side, saying, ‘What you say is neither good nor true,’ the first speaker must carefully be on guard lest he fall into arrogance. That is, he should say to the abbot: ‘If it pleases you, I shall set forth the reasoning that I have concerning this matter,’ and he should not say anything contrary to that brother who has spoken against him. If the abbot grants permission, he should humbly state his reasoning about the matter in this way: ‘It has this many points in its favor, and this many objections.’ But if the abbot does not grant permission to state his reasoning, he should remain silent.”

But let the decision rest more fully with the abbot, so that all obey what he has judged more beneficial.] Even if they themselves have thought otherwise. Nor should they take it badly whenever they see their own judgment set aside; rather, they should rejoice that the judgment of others has prevailed. Thus each person may silently appropriate to himself what Saint Bernard wrote to Oger (*Letter 87*):

“Recognizing the barrenness of my wisdom—or rather, always suspecting the rashness of my folly—when what I praise as the course to be followed is not done, I neither dare nor ought to be indignant, desiring that each person act with greater prudence. But whenever my opinion is chosen and followed, I confess that I feel myself weighed down by a heavy burden, always awaiting the outcome of the matter anxiously and never securely.”

There is no doubt that Abba Poemen held the same view. Of him it is reported (*Sayings of the Fathers*, vol. I of *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, p. 618) “that he never wished to give his own counsel after another elder’s response, but rather extolled that response to the skies with praises.”

But just as it belongs to disciples to obey their master, so it is fitting for the master himself to arrange everything prudently and justly.] He adds this lest the abbot, using his authority as though it were unrestricted, should disregard the brothers’ counsel and arrange something unjustly. Certainly, just as he does not bind the abbot to adhere to the brothers’ opinion, so it is not fitting for him readily to depart from their judgment, especially when they have come to agreement.

Therefore, in all things, let all follow the Rule as their mistress.] Until now he has admonished the abbot and the brothers separately; now he admonishes both together, so that in all things they may all follow the Rule as their mistress—not merely in giving counsel, which is his particular subject here, but in all other monastic observances as well.

Moreover, when he says “all,” he excludes no one; therefore he excludes neither abbots. Peter of Blois is entirely correct (*Letter 131*): “No superior or subject is permitted to follow his own will. For the legislator of monks, as though by a general edict, commands that all follow the Rule as their mistress, and neither abbot nor prior is exempt from this law.” Saint Bernard likewise says (*On the Precept and Dispensation*, chap. 4): “‘Let all follow the Rule as their mistress’; therefore, let no one follow his own will. I think that the abbot too is not excepted here.”

For this reason the abbots assembled at the Council of Aachen decreed (canon 1) “that abbots should examine the Rule word by word and read it through completely, and, understanding it with the Lord’s help, should strive effectively to fulfill it with their monks.”

Nor does Saint Benedict here rebuke only lazy and self-indulgent abbots who, disregarding the common life of the brothers, indulge themselves in private rooms. He also rebukes those who imagine themselves exempt from the Rules by reason of seniority or of some office that they exercise—as though age or rank released them from obligation, rather than binding monks more strictly. If younger monks are commanded to do what the example of their elders urges, and the elders are thereby entirely released from observing the Rule, all rules will become useless, since neither the older nor the younger will be bound to observe them.

When the holy legislator says “in all things,” this must be understood to include not only great matters but also small ones. Whoever says “in all things” excludes absolutely nothing. Here he silently reproves those who despise certain observances as insignificant—as though anything could be insignificant before God: something by which God is honored, something by which an eternal weight of glory can be acquired.

Saint Augustine says admirably (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book IV, chap. 18): “What is least is least; but to be faithful in what is least is great. For just as the principle of roundness is that all lines drawn from the center should be equal at the circumference, so the same principle is present in a great disk and in a tiny coin. Thus, when small things are rightly done, the greatness of justice is not diminished.”

Let those who despise the observances of the Rule as insignificant listen; let them listen to Saint Bernard writing to the emperor Lothar (*Letter 139*): “We must fear lest neglect of the smallest things become an obstacle to the greatest.” Let them also listen to Scripture: “He who despises small things will gradually fall.” Therefore let no one say: “This rule is nothing; this observance is small; this commandment is a mere straw.” A straw indeed at the beginning—but one that, with the passage of time, becomes a beam! “A straw, once nourished, becomes a beam,” says Saint Augustine (*Sermon 19, On Scripture*).

Bernard certainly frightens me when he says (*Sermon 1, On the Conversion of Saint Paul*): “Beware lest anyone regard anything as small, however small a transgression he may knowingly commit. Let no one say in his heart: ‘These things are trivial; I do not care to correct them. It is no great matter if I remain in these venial and very small sins.’ For this, beloved, is impenitence; this is blasphemy against the Holy Spirit, the unforgivable blasphemy.”

But even if we grant that these sins are small, are they for that reason to be despised? “Do not despise your sins because they are small,” says Saint Augustine—or whoever else may be the author (*Sermon 292, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*). “For raindrops too fill rivers, drag down massive structures, and uproot trees with their roots. You who say, ‘It is a small sin,’ I should like to know whether, if you admitted such a sin so often, you would wish to have so many small wounds on your body, or so many stains and tears in your clothing. Since you do not consent to wounds on your body or tears and stains on your garment, with what conscience do you not fear doing this to your soul? Whoever does so loves his clothing or his flesh more than his soul.”

A little later he adds: “And because, as I said, we have been made in our soul in the image of God, if you made your image on a wooden or stone tablet, and some shameless man wished either to break that image with stones or to defile it with filth, I should like to know whether your spirit would not be stirred against him,” and so forth.

Finally, to bring this matter to a brief conclusion, I add one word of Saint Bernard (*Sermon on the Lord’s Supper*): “Let no one despise or undervalue these things. For it is impossible to be saved while clinging to them; it is impossible for them to be washed away except through Christ Jesus and by Christ. Let no one, I say, sleep in destructive security, turning to words of wickedness in order to make excuses for sins; for unless Christ washes them away, we shall have no part with him.”

Anyone who desires more on this subject may consult Julius Nigronus, treatise 10 among the ascetical works; Benedict Haeftenus, Book II, treatise 8, disputation 8; Dionysius the Carthusian, *On the Monastic Refectory*, chap. 6; and Dacrianus, *Mirror of the Monk*, toward the end.

Nor let anyone rashly depart from it.] “Rashly,” that is, without legitimate cause. But is the abbot’s dispensation alone sufficient as a legitimate reason for departing from the Rule? I answer that it is legitimate, provided necessity or usefulness is present. Otherwise that dispensation will be nothing other than a disguised transgression.

Saint Bernard teaches this (*On Consideration*, Book III, chap. 4): “Where necessity presses, dispensation is excusable; where usefulness calls for it, dispensation is praiseworthy. I mean common usefulness, not private advantage. For when none of these is present, it is not faithful dispensation but cruel destruction.”

Peter of Blois writes similarly to E., prior of a little monastery (*Letter 131*): “If you claim that your abbot has relaxed for you the observance of the monastic law, know that although dispensation has been entrusted to the abbot, he is nevertheless not permitted to establish or tolerate anything that hinders the profit of charity.”

Let no one in the monastery follow the will of his own heart.] For this is what created hell. “Take away self-will,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 3, On the Resurrection*), “and hell will not exist.”

The phrase “in the monastery” should not be understood as though outside the monastery one were permitted to fulfill one’s own will. Here “monastery” is taken for its inhabitants, according to the figure by which the container is understood for the thing contained.

Nor let anyone presume insolently to contend with his abbot, or to contend outside the monastery.] In some more recent manuscripts one reads, “insolently, whether inside or outside.” But “inside” is not found in the Cassinese manuscripts, nor in the Oxford manuscript, nor in Hildemar, nor in Smaragdus. Indeed, it is not even found in the manuscript written by Saint Benedict’s own hands, as the same Smaragdus teaches; nor is it required.

Accordingly, according to our reading, the meaning is that Saint Benedict did not forbid every dispute within the monastery, but only one that was insolent, proud, and defiant; outside the monastery he forbade both insolent and friendly disputation. Smaragdus says:

“It must be understood that when he prohibited disputation with the addition ‘insolently,’ he permitted friendly and peaceful disputation. For there is a friendly and profitable dispute that frequently arises between two people according to the nature of the matter at issue, as is once said to have occurred between Blessed Benedict and his disciple Maurus concerning the boy Placidus. Outside the monastery he permitted neither insolent nor friendly disputation, because even if a friendly dispute occurs in public, it gives rise to contempt harmful to the master and to a deadly arrogance in the disciple.”

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, may perhaps be understood in this sense when he says (*Book I of the Conferences*, no. 20):

“That masters ought not to be reproved by their subjects was well represented by the ark of the covenant, which signifies rulers, when it was tilted by the oxen kicking. Because Uzzah, believing that it was about to fall, wished to steady it, he immediately received a sentence of death and was struck on the shoulder—the very shoulder by which, according to the command of the Law, he ought to have carried it. For when subjects lay a hand of submission against superiors whose commands they ought to bear, they are rejected from the company of the living.”

Gaufridus of Vendôme teaches the same in Book IV, Letter 22.

But if anyone presumes to do so, let him be subject to regular discipline.] A similar statement occurs in the Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 118): “If one of the brothers is found doing something contentiously or contradicting the command of a superior, he shall be rebuked according to the measure of his sin.”

They define regular discipline as follows: the one who has offended is admonished once and again in private; then, if he has not amended, he is rebuked publicly; afterward, if he still has not corrected himself, he is punished by excommunication; finally, if he remains uncorrected, he is subjected to bodily excommunication and punishment; if the scourging does not correct him, the prayers of the brothers are applied; and at last, when all remedies have been attempted in vain, he is expelled from the monastery.

This is more or less the account given by Smaragdus, Hildemar, and Bernard of Cassino. Their view seems to be confirmed by the *Customaries of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, published in volume IV of the *Analecta*. They called this “passing through the stages.”

In the Rule of Saint Donatus for virgins, to be subjected to regular discipline is the same as being committed to prison. For in chapter 2, which is taken entirely from chapter 3 of Saint Benedict’s Rule—with the masculine gender changed to the feminine—after saying, “If she presumes to do so, let her be subject to regular discipline,” it adds, as though explaining what this means: “That is, let her be thrust into a cell until she is humbled by repentance.”

Perhaps someone will understand “regular discipline” here as a stroke of the whip. Thus the abbot of Venosa says in the *Life of Saint Peter, abbot of Cava*, no. 28 (*Bollandists, 4 March*): “Leading him before the altar, he subjected him to regular discipline and began to beat him so severely that he cried out amid the pain.”

Certainly, it is clear that in Saint Benedict’s Rule “discipline” can mean some bodily punishment, from chapter 65 of the same Rule, where he commands that a defective provost be admonished verbally up to four times; and if he does not amend, he adds: “Let regular disciplinary correction be applied to him.”

But the abbot himself should do everything with fear of God and observance of the Rule.] First, with fear of God, because, as Cassiodorus—cited by Boherius—says, “everything is always done well when heavenly fear is added to human conduct.” Second, with observance of the Rule, so that he might show that the abbot is no less subject to the Rule than the monks.

Knowing without doubt that he will render an account to God, the most just Judge, for all his judgments.] The holy Father frequently impresses this upon the abbot, especially when granting him some authority, so that he may not be elated by the honor he has received and been granted, but, always considering what a burden he has undertaken, may remain in the fear of God.

If some matters of lesser importance are to be handled for the monastery’s needs.] Or, “for its disadvantage.” He calls “lesser” those matters that arise almost daily and do not concern the whole congregation, but only particular persons and their offices—or, as they called them, obediences. Examples include choosing a provost, as in chapter 65 of the Rule, where the abbot, with the counsel of the brothers, is to appoint for himself a provost, dean, cellarer, and so forth; purchasing this or that to adorn the church; and other matters of this kind.

“Lesser” may also refer to matters that the abbot can now execute by right without any consent of the brothers.

Let him use only the counsel of the elders.] Here “elders” does not mean those who are altogether decrepit, or those first in the monastery’s order, but prudent, discerning, and experienced brothers, in whose selection maturity rather than age should chiefly be considered. Nevertheless, old age is not to be despised in them, especially when joined with judgment and discretion. For, as the commonly cited Saint Ambrose says (*On 1 Timothy 5*): “Among all peoples old age is honored; hence both the Synagogue and afterward the Church had elders, without whose counsel nothing was done in the Church.”

Where maturity of character, discernment, and prudence are equal in an old man and a young man, the older should be preferred to the younger. If you ask what virtues in particular should be sought in elders, Hildemar replies:

“Three things must be sought in these elders: faith, hope, and charity. Faith, by which they conceal everything in silence; hope of eternal rewards, by which, strengthened, they endure everything in defense of the truth; and charity, by which they all think alike.”

To these add knowledge of good and evil, so that they may pursue the one and oppose the other; also the highest prudence and the highest discernment.

As for the number of elders, Boherius thinks that two are sufficient, and I would not deny that they are indeed enough in a smaller congregation. In a larger one, however, I would judge that three or four should be consulted. This appears to have been the practice among the monks of old, as may be gathered from these words of Hildemar:

“When three or four have spoken, another may approach among them without being summoned and without embarrassment.”

Among the Cassinese, the elders are the claustral prior, the deans, the master of novices, and the cellarer. In the congregation of Monte Oliveto they are the vicar, the cellarer, the master of novices, the procurator, and the senior according to profession.

The Fulda monks establish the following in their Constitutions (chap. 3):

“By the designation ‘elders’ we understand, besides the subprior of each monastery, two priests where there are ten voting members, or one priest where the number is smaller—those whom the superior has chosen from his community as superior in virtue, judgment, and experience, so that he may be assisted by their counsel. Whenever temporal matters are under discussion, the cellarer shall join them.”

As it is written: “Do everything with counsel, and afterward you will not regret it.”] Thus Saint Basil says (*Shorter Rules*, question 104): “In every matter generally, the superior must necessarily remember the Scripture that says: ‘Do everything with counsel.’”

Hence Saint Vitalis, abbot of the same order of Saint Basil, among other exhortations to his successor, says: “Whatever must be done, whether spiritual or bodily, should be done not according to one’s own judgment and will, but with awareness, with the counsel of superiors, and with those worthy of reverence.”

Peter of Blois writes similarly to the abbot of Saint Launomarus: “Do everything with counsel. For Wisdom, the mother of chaste counsels, says in the book bearing her name: ‘I dwell in counsel and am present in learned thoughts.’ Keep with you in counsel, service, and fellowship those who are proven in religion, guardians of your honor and witnesses to it.”

In this regard they especially praise Saint Fulgentius, who, as his anonymous disciple says in his *Life*, chap. 29 (*Bollandists, 1 January*), “was always the first consulted in Byzacena on major matters; in his own monastery he simply consulted Abbot Felix even about the smallest matters.”

They also praise the venerable Eigil, abbot of Fulda, who, according to Candidus in his *Life*, no. 22 (*Benedictine Century IV, part I*), “gladly listened to the counsel of the brothers and very frequently enjoyed their conversations. For he knew that it was written: ‘Do everything with counsel.’ Therefore he did not consider himself more exalted or wiser than the others, nor did he treat with empty pride the idea that he did not need another’s consolation.”

But among the others, Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, is especially worthy of attention. It is read in Book II of his *Life*, no. 14 (*Volume IV of Baluze’s Miscellany*), that “he was unwilling to do anything, however small, without another’s counsel. If the matter was urgent and admitted no delay, and he happened at that moment to have no one present except some simple brother or perhaps a member of the household, he nevertheless did not hesitate to seek counsel even from him.”

To conclude this chapter briefly: Saint Benedict submits matters of greater importance to the counsel of all the brothers; lesser matters to the elders alone; and the smallest matters, which occur almost every moment, to the abbot’s sole prudence.

## CHAPTER IV. What the Instruments of Good Works Are

[Column 295]

1. First of all, to love the Lord God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength (Luke 10).

2. Then, one’s neighbor as oneself.

3. Then, not to kill (Matthew 5).  
   [Note: Hildemar: “not kill.”]

4. Not *adulterari* (“to be adulterated” [reading uncertain]).  
   [Note: Another reading: *adulterare* (“to commit adultery”).] (Leviticus 19).

5. Not to steal (Exodus 20).

6. Not to covet (Deuteronomy 5).

7. Not to bear false witness (2 Peter 2).

8. To honor all people (Luke 9).

9. Not to do to another what one does not wish done to oneself (Tobit 4).  
   [Note: The readings are *alii* (“to another”) and *alio* (“to another person”); the distinction is one of Latin form.]

10. To renounce oneself in order to follow Christ (Matthew 7).

11. To chastise the body (1 Corinthians 9).

12. Not to embrace luxuries (2 Peter 2).

13. To love fasting (Daniel 1).

14. To refresh the poor (Tobit 4).

15. To clothe the naked (Isaiah 58).

16. To visit the sick (Matthew 25).

17. To bury the dead (Tobit 1).

18. To assist the afflicted (Ecclesiasticus 6).

19. To comfort the sorrowful (Ecclesiasticus 7).

20. To make oneself a stranger to the practices of the world (2 Timothy 2).

21. To prefer nothing to the love of Christ (Matthew 14).

22. Not to carry anger through to completion (Matthew 5).

23. Not to reserve time for wrath (Ephesians 4).

24. Not to harbor deceit in one’s heart (Proverbs 12).

25. Not to offer false peace (Psalm 27).

26. Not to abandon charity (1 Peter 4).

27. Not to swear, lest one perhaps swear falsely (Matthew 5).  
   [Note: Hildemar omits “lest one perhaps swear falsely.”]

28. To speak the truth from the heart and mouth (Psalm 14).

29. Not to repay evil for evil (1 Thessalonians 5).

30. Not to do injury, but also to bear patiently the injury done (1 Corinthians 6).

31. To love one’s enemies (Matthew 5).

32. Not to curse those who curse one, but rather to bless them (1 Peter 2).  
   [Note: Hildemar omits “but rather to bless them.”]

33. To endure persecutions for the sake of justice (Matthew 5).

34. Not to be proud (Tobit 4).

35. Not to be drunken (1 Timothy 3).  
   [Note: The Narbonne manuscript reads “not violent.”]

36. Not to be excessively gluttonous (Ecclesiasticus 37).

37. Not to be sleepy (Proverbs 20).

38. Not to be lazy (Proverbs 24).

39. Not to be a grumbler (Wisdom 1).

40. Not to be a slanderer (Proverbs 4).

41. To place one’s hope in God (Psalm 30).

42. Whenever one sees some good in oneself, to attribute it to God, not to oneself (James 1).

43. To know that whatever evil there is has been done by oneself, and to impute it to oneself (Hosea 13).

44. To fear the day of judgment (Job 31).

45. To dread Gehenna (Luke 12).

46. To desire eternal life with all spiritual longing (Psalm 83).

47. To keep death daily before one’s eyes (Matthew 24).

48. To guard the actions of one’s life at every hour (Deuteronomy 4).

49. To know with certainty that God looks upon one in every place (Proverbs 5).

50. Immediately to dash evil thoughts that arise in one’s heart against Christ (Psalm 36).

51. And to disclose them to one’s spiritual elder (Ecclesiasticus 9).

52. To guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech (Psalm 35).

53. Not to love much speaking (Proverbs 10).

54. Not to speak empty words or words suited to laughter (Matthew 12).

55. Not to love excessive or boisterous laughter (Ecclesiastes 7).

56. To hear holy readings willingly (Luke 4).

57. To devote oneself frequently to prayer (Luke 18).

58. To confess one’s past sins to God daily in prayer, with tears or groaning, and thereafter to amend those sins (Psalm 6).

59. Not to fulfill the desires of the flesh; to hate one’s own will (Galatians 5).  
   [Note: This instrument is absent from Hildemar’s text.]

60. To obey the abbot’s commands in all things (Hebrews 13), even if he himself should act otherwise—which God forbid—remembering the Lord’s command: “Do what they say, but do not do what they do” (Matthew 3).

61. Not to wish to be called holy before one is holy, but first to be what one may more truly be called (Matthew 3).  
   [Note: Florence manuscript: “so that one may be more truly called”; Narbonne manuscript: “who is also more truly called.”]

62. To fulfill God’s commandments daily by one’s deeds (Ecclesiasticus 6).

63. To love chastity (1 Timothy 5).

64. To hate no one (Luke 19).

65. Not to be zealous in the sense of envious rivalry, and not to practice envy (Galatians 5).

66. Not to love contention (2 Timothy 2).

67. To flee self-exaltation (Psalm 130).

68. To honor elders (Leviticus 19).

69. To love the younger (1 Timothy 5).

70. To pray for one’s enemies in the love of Christ (Matthew 5).

71. To be reconciled in peace with one who is at odds with one before sunset (Ephesians 4).

72. And never to despair of God’s mercy (Ezekiel 18).

Behold, these are the instruments of the spiritual craft. When we have fulfilled them unceasingly day and night and presented them again on the day of judgment, the reward that the Lord himself promised will be repaid to us: “What eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart, what God has prepared for those who love him.” The workshop in which we diligently practice all these things is the monastery’s enclosure and stability in the community.

## COMMENTARY

Before we examine the individual instruments of this chapter, it seems appropriate to offer several general observations. First, it is worth noting that this chapter on the instruments of good works is, as it were, a brief summary and compendium of the Rule itself and of the whole of perfection. I think nothing will be lacking to the person who has faithfully observed this chapter. Hence it contains as many instruments as the Rule has chapters, so that those who fulfill it in practice may seem to have fulfilled everything at once.

Next, it should be observed that this chapter was held in such esteem by the monks of old that Saint Donatus, bishop of Besançon, inserted it word for word into chapter 3 of his Rule for Virgins. The Master of the Rule did the same in chapter 3, under this title: “What is the holy art that the abbot ought to teach his disciples in the monastery?” He nevertheless altered some of the wording and omitted certain instruments.

Similarly, Grimlaicus included it in chapter 25 of his *Rule for Solitaries*, with this preface:

“Since the pages of all the holy Scriptures are filled with the instruments of good works, and throughout the fields of those same holy Scriptures weapons can be found by which vices may be restrained and virtues nourished, it is nevertheless necessary to insert into this Rule the teaching of a certain Father concerning the instruments of good works. In it, with great brevity, is contained what solitaries ought to do and what they ought to avoid. For they ought first of all to love God, and so forth.”

Theodulf, bishop of Orléans, reproduces these same instruments word for word in his *Capitularies*, chapter 21, borrowed from Saint Benedict, although he suppresses Benedict’s name and retains the preface just mentioned. They are also included in the ancient Roman Ordinal, from a canon of Theodore, bishop of the English, concerning the ordination of an abbess, as our Menard observes.

Third. Peter Boherius, Menard, and, after both of them, Haeftenus thought that all these instruments of good works had been transferred by Saint Benedict into his Rule from the First Letter of Saint Clement. Amalarius once held the same view in his supplement to the four books *On the Divine Offices* (vol. II of the *Analecta*, p. 142).

In fact, however, it was not Saint Benedict who took this entire chapter from Saint Clement; rather, Isidore Mercator, the forger of the Clementine material, took it from Saint Benedict’s Rule, as our Mabillon proves in his observations on the aforementioned supplement of Amalarius.

Fourth. The title of this chapter gives rise to the following difficulty: since the things contained here are themselves good works, how can they be called the instruments of good works? For nothing is the instrument of itself.

Several solutions may be offered. First, as Menard observes, by “good works” here we may understand a certain method of acquiring perfection, or, as Saint Benedict calls it, a spiritual art. All the things mentioned here prepare the way toward that art and may therefore rightly be called its instruments.

Second, virtues and good works may also be called the instruments of good works because they mutually require and assist one another. Thus, as Saint Gregory says (*Moral Works*, Book VII, chap. 10), “through love of God, love of neighbor is generated, and through love of neighbor, love of God is nourished.” In the same way, prayer assists fasting, and fasting assists prayer. Thus one is the instrument of the other. Although something cannot be called the instrument of good works with respect to itself, it can be so called with respect to other works.

Third, everything contained in this chapter can be considered either as commandments or as counsels. If we consider the definition of an instrument—“that which the principal agent uses”—all these counsels or commandments can be called moral instruments, which, when read or heard, God or Saint Benedict himself uses to move us to practice good works. Perhaps this is also the sense in which he called the Rules and Conferences of the Fathers “instruments of virtue” in the final chapter of the Rule.

Fourth, if we examine the etymology of *instrumentum*, an instrument is so called because it instructs. In this sense all these things may be called instruments of good works, since they teach us good works.

Fifth and finally, Hildemar observes that the title of this chapter can be understood in two ways. First, as a simple statement, as though Saint Benedict were saying: “In this chapter we shall discuss what the instruments of good works are.” Second, interrogatively: “What are the instruments of good works?” To this question the answer is: “First of all, to love God,” and so forth.

First of all, to love the Lord God with all one’s heart, all one’s soul, and all one’s strength.] The first instrument, he says, is to love God. For this is the first and greatest commandment of the Law: first in dignity, first in usefulness, and first in necessity.

It is first in dignity because, as Abbot Chaeremon says in Cassian (*Conference 11, chap. 12*), “nothing is more precious, nothing more perfect, nothing more sublime, nothing more enduring than charity.” Saint Caesarius likewise says (*Sermon 107, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*): “Charity is compared with oil. For just as we know that oil is superior to all liquids, so charity is considered higher than all virtues.”

It is first in usefulness because all things work together for good for those who love God—the good, namely, of possessing God. As Saint Augustine says (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book I, chap. 29): “God wishes to be loved, not so that anything may be given to him, but so that an eternal reward may be bestowed upon those who love him—that is, he himself, whom they love.”

Hence Saint Ambrose also says (*Hexameron*, Book I, chap. 12): “It is charity that binds us to the things above and grafts us into heaven.”

Finally, it is first in necessity, and indeed in the necessity of eternal salvation, which cannot be attained without love of God. The Apostle writes to the Corinthians:

“Even if I have prophecy and know all mysteries and all knowledge; even if I have all faith, so as to move mountains; but do not have charity, I am nothing. Even if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor; even if I hand over my body so that I may burn; but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Corinthians 13).

No one is exempt from this law of love, and no one can excuse himself by any pretext. “Someone may say to me,” says Saint Caesarius (*Sermon 225, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*): “‘I cannot fast; I cannot keep vigil.’ Can he say, ‘I cannot love’? He may say, ‘I cannot give all my possessions to the poor and serve God in a monastery.’ Can he say, ‘I cannot love’?”

And certainly, as Saint Thomas observes most aptly (*Summa Theologiae* I–II, question 109, article 3), “to love God above all things is connatural to man, and to every creature—not only to rational creatures, but also to irrational and even inanimate creatures—according to the mode of love that can belong to each creature.”

Saint Basil therefore says appropriately (*Longer Rules*, chap. 2):

“The love of God cannot be taught. We did not learn from anyone to rejoice in the light or to desire life; nor did anyone teach us to love our parents or those who nourished us. In the same way—or rather, much more—the divine desire cannot be learned from elsewhere through external teaching. Instead, the constitution of human nature has been endowed with a kind of seed-bearing principle that contains within itself the causes and impulses of familiar love.”

Yet because nothing is or ought to be done by a rational creature without a reason, it must be briefly explained by what arguments we may be moved to divine love.

Saint Bernard states the first reason briefly when he says (*On Loving God*, chap. 1): “The reason for loving God is God”—that is, supreme goodness, supreme love, supremely worthy of love, whom it is connatural for every creature to love.

The second is the greatness of his love toward us. For, as Gilbert of Holland says (*Sermon 19, On the Song of Songs*), “Love is an insolent challenger of itself: no price, no reward can repay it; it is repaid by love alone.” God asks nothing else from us, since he loved us for this one purpose: that we should love him.

“For when God loves,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 83, On the Song of Songs*), “he wishes nothing other than to be loved; indeed, he loves for no other reason than to be loved, knowing that those who have loved him are blessed by that very love.”

Since he himself first loved us, “he is plainly worthy of being loved in return, especially when one considers who has loved, whom he has loved, and how greatly he has loved,” as the same holy doctor says again (*On Loving God*, chap. 1).

The third reason for loving God proceeds from his greatest benefits toward us. Saint Bernard thus stirred up his love by contemplating them (*On Loving God*, chap. 5):

“What, then, shall I say of myself, who recognize my God not only as the free giver and most generous provider of my life, its merciful consoler and watchful governor, but also as its most abundant redeemer, eternal preserver, enrich­er, and glorifier?”

### Fourth

The fourth among the other causes that urge us on with powerful goads is the grace of redemption, purchased with Christ’s precious blood. “But there is something that moves me more,” says the same Saint Bernard (Sermon 20 on the Song of Songs), “urges me more, inflames me more, and, above all, makes you lovable to me, good Jesus: the chalice which you drank, the work of our redemption. This wholly claims our love for itself with ease; this, I say, both more gently attracts our devotion, more justly demands it, and binds it more tightly, etc.”

The fifth cause is that whoever loves God becomes one with him. Saint Bernard again says admirably (Sermon 59 on the Song of Songs): “Love looks up to no one, but neither does it look down on anyone; it regards all equally who love one another perfectly, and in itself blends the lofty and the humble—not merely making them equal, but making them one. Do you perhaps think that God is exempt from this rule of love? But whoever clings to God is one spirit. Why are you surprised? He himself was made like one of us” [Col. 0300B].

The sixth cause is that the proper work of monks is to love God. Hence Gilbert of Holland, addressing his monks, says (Sermon 19 on the Song of Songs): “Others have other duties; your special task is love.”

By these and other goads of this kind, which are found everywhere among the authors, the love of God must be stirred up in us. Of one who is not stirred by them, you would rightly say that he is not asleep but altogether dead. For “he is truly worthy of death who refuses to live for you, Lord Jesus, and is dead; whoever does not have good sense because of you is senseless; and whoever cares to exist for anything except you is nothing and is worth nothing,” says Saint Bernard.

Although the manner of loving God is to love him without measure, as the same doctor says (On Loving God, chapter 1), Saint Benedict nevertheless seems to have prescribed some measure for us when he said that God must be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength. Saint Augustine explains this measure as follows (Book I of On Christian Doctrine, chapter 22):

> “This is the rule of love divinely established: ‘You shall love your neighbor as yourself’; but God, with your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole mind, so that you may direct all your thoughts, your whole life, and your whole understanding toward him, from whom you have those very things that you direct toward him. When he says, ‘With your whole heart, your whole soul, and your whole mind,’ he leaves no part of our life that ought to be vacant and, as it were, provide room for us to wish to enjoy another thing; but whatever else comes into the mind to be loved must be carried away to that place toward which the entire force of love runs.”

Saint Bernard explains this passage differently (Sermon 20 on the Song of Songs):

> “It seems to me, if no more appropriate meaning presents itself in this threefold distinction, that love of the heart refers to a certain ardor of affection; love of the soul to diligence or the judgment of reason; and love of strength to the steadfastness or vigor of the spirit. Therefore love the Lord your God with the whole and complete affection of your heart; love him with all the vigilance and prudence of reason; love him with your whole strength, so that you do not fear even to die for his love, etc.”

And further:

> “Therefore, to love with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole strength means neither to be led away by flatteries, nor deceived by falsehoods, nor broken by insults.”

Nor, certainly, is God to be loved any less. For, as Gilbert of Holland says (Sermon 19 on the Song of Songs):

> “If love restrains and contracts itself below your strength, it is unjust; and if it remains merely within your strength, it is paltry. What, then? Let each one of us say again with the same Gilbert: ‘I will love you, good Jesus; I will love you, my strength, whom I cannot love without cause, yet cannot love enough. Let my efforts be directed wholly toward you, and let them not be led away and scattered by any alien affection. But how small are even our efforts toward you when they are whole! How, then, shall I diminish what, even when whole, is so slight? May I be carried wholly toward you, good God, by desire.’”

### Then: “Your neighbor as yourself”

To deal briefly with this instrument, I propose three matters for consideration [Col. 0301A]: first, who is to be called our neighbor; second, what our affection toward him ought to be; third, what the necessity or usefulness of this instrument is.

Saint Augustine—or whoever else he may be—explains the first in these words (Sermon 108 in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine):

> “If anyone should happen to ask who one’s neighbor is, let him know that every Christian is rightly called a neighbor, because in baptism we are all sanctified as children of God, so that we may be spiritually children in perfect charity.”

Elsewhere the holy doctor extends the narrow notion of neighbor somewhat more fully:

> “Every human being is a neighbor. Your neighbor is one who was born with you from Adam and Eve. We are all neighbors by reason of birth, and each is a brother to the other. By that hope of heavenly inheritance, you ought to regard every human being as your neighbor, even before he is a Christian.”

Nor does he remain content with these limits of love; in his books On Christian Doctrine he extends the notion of neighbor even to the angels (Book I, chapter 30). After establishing that the neighbor is one to whom a work of mercy ought to be offered, or from whom such a work ought to be offered to us, he proceeds:

> “It is evident that this commandment, by which we are ordered to love our neighbor, includes even the holy angels, by whom such great works of mercy are performed” [Col. 0301B].

Now the same Saint Augustine teaches what our love for our neighbor ought to be in these words (On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 28):

> “Therefore whoever loves his neighbor acts, as far as he can, so that he may be healthy in body and healthy in soul; but care of the body must be referred to the health of the soul.”

And elsewhere (On Christian Doctrine, chapter 22):

> “Whoever, therefore, rightly loves his neighbor ought to act toward him in such a way that he too may love God with his whole heart, his whole soul, and his whole mind.”

But since human weakness is so great that, although we are bound to love all people, we cannot nevertheless assist everyone, Saint Augustine describes what we ought especially to do when placed in such necessity (ibid., chapter 28):

> “All people are to be loved equally; but since you cannot benefit everyone, you ought especially to care for those who, by the opportunities of places and times or of any other circumstances, are joined to you more closely, as though by lot. For if you possessed something that ought to be given to one who did not have it, but it could not be given to two, and two people came before you, neither of whom surpassed the other either in need or in some necessity toward you, you could do nothing more justly than choose by lot to whom what could not be given to both should be given. So, among people whom you cannot assist all at once, you should regard it as a matter of lot, according to how closely each may happen temporally to be attached to you.”

The necessity of this instrument follows from the necessity of loving God and keeping his law; for we will never be able to love God and observe his law unless we love one another. Hence Saint Bernard says (Sermon 33 on Various Matters):

> “This is the profession of Christian faith: that whoever lives should no longer live for himself, but for him who died for all. Let no one say to me, ‘I will live for him, but not for you,’ since he not only lived for all, but also died for all. How does one live for him who neglects those whom he loved in this way? How does one live for him who does not fulfill his law or keep his commandment? Do you ask what law, what commandment? ‘This is my commandment,’ he says, ‘that you love one another as I have loved you’; and the Apostle says: ‘Bear one another’s burdens, and thus you will fulfill the law of Christ.’ Therefore do not think that the good you display toward your neighbor is a free gift, so that you may disregard him if you wish. You are a debtor; you are bound by the security of your sacrament and by your own profession.”

Add that love of neighbor may be called the distinctive mark of Christ’s disciples, just as he himself says: “By this all will know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another.” From this Saint Basil argues as follows (Longer Rules, chapter 3):

> “As the sign by which we may be recognized as his disciples, he does not demand miracles or the power to perform wonders—although he also granted the working of these through the Holy Spirit—but what? ‘By this,’ he says, ‘all will know that you are my disciples, if you have mutual charity among yourselves’” [Col. 0302A].

### Then: “Do not kill”

Menardus aptly comments on these words:

> “Someone may wonder why such dreadful crimes are forbidden to monks, whose profession is the pursuit of perfection. But although such things are rare in monasteries, it was not without reason that they were forbidden, so that monks might remember their own weakness and not imagine that, merely because of their religious state, they had already attained perfection and passed beyond the boundaries of sin.”

Indeed, the holy abbots Ermenoldus, Bercharius, and Gerard were impiously murdered by monk-parricides, men worthy of the sack and the ape; and Saint Gregory testifies that wine mixed with poison was offered to Saint Benedict by his treacherous sons. Hence, not without reason, among the canons issued under King Edgar concerning the imposition of penance, the following is found in Spelman (number 28):

> “If a mass-priest or monk kills a man, let him lose the dignity of his order and fast for ten years: namely, five years on bread and water, and for the other five years, three days each week. During the remaining time he may enjoy other food, but for as long as he lives let him diligently mourn his crime” (*Councils of the English Church*, volume I, p. 465) [Col. 0302B].

Yet it is not only the killing inflicted by the sword, nor is only he to be considered a murderer who kills bodies; much more so is he a murderer who kills souls. “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer,” says John; and Wisdom says: “The mouth that lies kills the soul.” He too must rightly be considered a murderer who slanders his brother. Hence Grimlaicus, in his *Rule for Solitaries*, as though explaining this instrument, says (chapter 25):

> “Then, ‘Do not kill,’ that is, do not slander; for, as the Apostle says, whoever slanders his brother is a murderer.”

Saint Bernard likewise says (Sermon 17 on Various Matters):

> “Life flees from those whom it hates, and those whom life flees must die. Does he not also die who drinks the poison that the malicious tongue of a slanderer administers to him? For the life of love is secretly taken away from him.”

Finally, he too is a murderer who urges others to sin, whether by word or example. For “whoever lives badly in the sight of the people, so far as lies in him, kills the one who watches him,” as Saint Augustine says (*Book on Pastoral Care*, chapter 4) [Col. 0302C].

### “Do not commit adultery”

Under the name of adultery he forbids every kind of fornication, not only carnal but also spiritual. Cassian (Conference 14, chapter 11) has Abbot Nesteros enumerate five forms of the latter:

1. Idolatry, concerning which Jerusalem is reproached through Jeremiah because she fornicated on every high hill and under every leafy tree.

2. Every superstition of the gentiles in auguries and observances of days and seasons.

3. Jewish superstitions in legal ceremonies.

4. Heresy.

5. “That which consists in wandering thoughts, because every thought—not only a disgraceful one, but even an idle thought, and one that departs from God by however little—is judged by the perfect man to be the most impure fornication.”

Concerning this Saint Augustine addresses God as follows (Book II of the *Confessions*, chapter 6):

> “The soul commits fornication when it turns away from you and seeks from you what it does not find pure and clear except when it returns to you.”

And elsewhere (Against Adimantus, chapter 7):

> “The fornication of the soul is its turning away from the fruitfulness of wisdom and its corruption and conversion toward the conception of temporal allurements.”

Saint Ferreolus adds a sixth form (Rule, chapter 25), placing it in obscene speech:

> “I ask you, brothers: what less than adultery does the man do whose tongue shares in sin? What less has the man practiced lust who has violated his chaste mouth by corrupt speech? And so that fear of condemnation may impose upon everyone the avoidance of this filth, we decree that the guilty person may receive neither Communion nor the kiss of the brothers for six months” [Col. 0302D].

If this is what he decrees for an obscene word, what does he prescribe for a carnal fall? Plainly, that the offender be subjected to the scourge, according to the final chapter of the Rule.

The *Rule of a Certain Person for Monks* establishes another punishment (chapter 18):

> “If one of the brothers should fall through a more grievous lapse—that is, fornication—he must be expelled from the community of the brothers and do penance in another region until the day of his death.”

The Council of Agde, cited in the excerpts of Egbert, bishop of York, chapter 68 (in Spelman, volume I of the *Councils of the English Church*), says:

> “If a monk commits adultery or theft—which may more properly be called sacrilege—we have decreed that the following order be observed: after being beaten with rods, the guilty man shall never exercise a clerical office. But if someone already a cleric is caught in this crime, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his office.”

And the German synod confirmed at Liptina, chapter 6:

> “Whoever among the servants of God or handmaids of Christ falls into the crime of fornication shall do penance in prison on bread and water. If he is an ordained priest, he shall remain in prison for two years, after first being flogged. But if a cleric or monk falls into this sin, after a third beating he shall be sent to prison and do penance there for one year. Likewise, veiled nuns shall be held to the same penance, and all the hair of her head shall be shaved.”

Finally, the canons issued under King Edgar of England concerning the imposition of penance, number 30 (in Spelman, volume I of the *Councils of the English Church*, under the year 967), say:

> “If a mass-priest or monk desires lustful intercourse or violates marriage, let him fast for ten years and always mourn.”

And number 31:

> “If a mass-priest, monk, or deacon had a lawful wife before he entered the order, and, having left her, entered the sacred orders, but afterward, inflamed by lust, secretly takes her again, let each of them fast as for homicide and mourn even more intensely.”

And number 32:

> “If a mass-priest, monk, deacon, layman, or cleric fornicates with a nun, let each fast according to what is appropriate to his order, as for homicide, and abstain from meat for as long as he lives. But the nun shall do penance for ten years, as shall the mass-priest, and shall always mourn what she has done.”

Concerning nuns Saint Gregory the pope establishes the following special rule in a letter to Bishop Januarius (Book III of the *Registrum*, chapter 9):

> “If any one of them has been led into the fall of adultery, whether by a prior license or by a perverse habit of impunity, or has been brought into the abyss of fornication, after the appropriate severity of punishment we wish her to be sent into another, stricter monastery of virgins for penance, so that there she may devote herself to prayers and fasts, advance through repentance, and provide the others with an example of the stricter discipline to be feared” [Col. 0303C].

Finally, I cannot pass over the deed of Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme. When a certain monk of the cell of Saint Clement at Credon had fallen into carnal sin, Geoffrey wrote back to the prior of that cell as follows (Book IV, letter 4):

> “By this letter we command you to destroy completely and without delay that little room in which that filthy and defiled man practiced his wicked deed, and to expel him from the cloister and from the estate of Saint Clement.”

For the rest, we ought not to be surprised at these things, since Gazaeus, commenting on Cassian’s Conference 13, chapter 5, observes that adultery was punished by death among the gentiles, the Jews, and even the Christians [Col. 0303D].

### “Do not steal”

Because thieves will not possess the kingdom of God, as the Apostle says, the ancient Fathers of monks always condemned theft with very severe punishments.

The brief penalties in Saint Basil prescribe as follows (number 9):

> “If anyone takes something from a brother and conceals it, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

The Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 121) says:

> “If anyone takes something that is not his, it shall be placed upon his shoulders, and he shall do public penance at the assembly and stand in the place where food is eaten. But if he is caught in the act of theft, they shall strike him thirty-nine times, send him outside, and give him only bread and water to eat; clothed in a hair shirt and ashes, they shall compel him to do penance at each of the hours of prayer.”

The Eastern Rule copies its first period.

Likewise the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers subjects those caught in theft to the scourge (chapter 13):

> “If a monk commits theft—which may more properly be called sacrilege—we have decreed that the following order be observed: the younger man [Note: The reading appears to be *junior* rather than *jejunior*. EDIT.] shall be beaten with rods and, as guilty of so great a crime, shall never exercise a clerical office. But if someone already a cleric is caught in this deed, he shall be deprived of the dignity of his office. For the lightness of his act, Communion may suffice him once the satisfaction of penance has been completed.”

This is cited in almost the same words from the Council of Agde in the excerpts of Egbert, bishop of York, chapter 68, in Spelman.

The Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins says (chapter 24):

> “If perchance, as human weakness has it, some of the sisters should dare, at the instigation of the devil, to rush into so great a wickedness as to commit theft or lay hands upon one another, it is just that they receive the proper discipline, since the institutions of the Rule have been violated. For it is necessary that what the Holy Spirit foretold through Solomon concerning undisciplined children be fulfilled in them: ‘Whoever loves his son applies the scourge to him’; and again: ‘If you strike him with the rod, you will deliver his soul from hell.’ Let them receive this discipline in the presence of the congregation, according to the Apostle’s command: ‘Rebuke sinners before everyone’” [Col. 0304B].

Saint Caesarius’s decree appears to be explained by the Rule of Saint Ferreolus in this statute (chapter 39):

> “We order that the accomplice of theft—if we may still call him a monk—be subjected to the scourge as a second adulterer and be regarded as deserving great affliction, assigning him the same sentence as for fornication, because he too has indulged himself when he stole.”

Finally, other holy Fathers judged that thieves should be expelled altogether from the community, as may be seen in Book V of the *Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 10, number 18, and in the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, number 58, in Bollandus, 14 May.

To all these add the constitution of the monks of Saint Andrew of Vienne, issued in the year 1000. They decree:

> “If henceforth any cenobite dares to commit sacrilege by taking from the refectory a cup, a knife, a tablecloth, or any utensil of the refectory, let him remain everywhere last, like a thief and sacrilegious person, until the sacrilege has been repaired; and let such satisfaction be imposed that the others may be afraid. Likewise, whoever steals from the dormitory, without regular permission, a cloak, a blanket, a pillow, or any piece of furniture, let him be deprived in every place of the fellowship of the brothers, like a thief and sacrilegious person, until the sacrilege has been restored; and especially let such satisfaction be imposed that the others may be afraid. But if this constitution is violated, let the bishop and a gathering of men of good reputation be summoned, the audacity of fools be broken, and the house of God be reformed for obedience to the sacred Rule” [Col. 0304C].

Since theft is the handling of another’s property against its owner’s will, it is not only the person who steals money or temporal goods who commits theft. “As Bernard of Cassino says, the person also commits theft who either withdraws himself, who has been dedicated to God, from his service, or draws another away by word or example and leads him into the service of the devil; by handling another’s property against its owner’s will, he undoubtedly commits theft.”

Likewise, as Boherius says in his first commentary:

> “In monasteries the steward commits theft if he appropriates for himself what he ought to distribute to the brothers; or if he reserves for the monastery surplus goods by taking them away from the poor.”

Finally, as Hildemarus says:

> “He commits theft who gives to others, without permission, something entrusted to him by the abbot—that is, assigned or given.”

### “Do not covet”

Covetousness is sometimes taken in a good sense and sometimes in a bad one. In the good sense, as when David sings: “My soul has desired to long for your judgments”; in the bad sense, as when it is said: “When desire has conceived, it gives birth to sin.” It is in this latter sense that Saint Benedict forbids it here. By the term, however, we must understand not the first movements of desire, which remain in us even with grace for the sake of struggle, but only consent to them.

### “Do not give false testimony”

This instrument is violated not only by one who says something contrary to the truth, but also by one who, having heard something false to another’s detriment, remains silent. Likewise by one who interprets what he hears or sees otherwise than it is. Again by one who publicly professes a holy life but acts wickedly in secret. Finally by one who neglects to fulfill in deeds what he has promised in words.

They make the false witness liable to three persons: to God, whose presence he scorns; to the judge, whom he deceives by lying; and to the innocent person whom he harms by false testimony. “For this reason,” says Richard of Saint Angelo, “a threefold penance is owed him: for the first contempt, penance of seven years, as in VI, question 1, ‘Whoever’; for the second evasion, he shall be punished with blows (V, question 5, ‘Those who’); for the third injury, he ought to be punished according to the measure of the injury. Argument: III, question 9, ‘We decree.’”

I think these provisions are to be understood of false testimony publicly given before a judge.

### “Honor all people”

In accordance with the Apostle Peter’s saying: “Honor everyone.” But since honor is properly the reward of virtue, how are we commanded to honor everyone, when so many wicked and depraved people exist throughout the world?

Hildemarus resolves this difficulty by taking Saint Benedict’s words in an appropriate supposition: namely, that we should honor all people who ought to be honored.

Moreover, it may be observed with Saint Thomas (II–II, question 63, article 3) that people may be honored for four reasons:

1. On account of their own virtue.

2. On account of another’s virtue, namely God’s or that of the community.

3. On account of a sign of virtue, such as old age.

4. On account of participation in divine goodness.

Thus we ought to honor all people, because there is no one in whom some participation in divine goodness is not present, at least in some respect.

If someone asks what honor is, or in what it consists, Saint Thomas answers (I–II, question 2, article 2) that it is a sign and testimony of the excellence present in the person honored.

In place of Saint Benedict’s wording, “Honor all people,” the Master reads, “Honor father and mother.” Saint Benedict, who elsewhere listed the other commandments of the Decalogue, deliberately omitted this one here, as though teaching that monks ought to be dead to their parents to such an extent that they should not even think about them.

He knew, of course, that disordered love of parents was a stumbling block to all monks, and that it would undoubtedly crush those upon whom it fell. For this reason nearly all the founders of monastic life diligently sought to keep parents away from their monasteries, permitting monks never—or scarcely ever—to visit them, as is shown by the notable laws they established on this matter, which we do not think it burdensome to report here.

Thus Saint Antony says (Rule, chapter 7):

> “You shall not return to visit your blood relatives, nor present your face for them to see, nor go to them.”

The Third Rule of the Holy Fathers says (chapter 12):

> “For the preservation of reputation we specifically decree that no monk who has fallen ill, after leaving the monastery, be entrusted to the care of his parents; for we judge that he is more likely to be polluted by the sight or hearing of secular spectacles than to be cleansed of his sickness.”

Similarly Abbot Poemen says in the *Apophthegmata of the Fathers* (volume I of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 637):

> “Do not go to your father’s house because of necessities.”

Evagrius likewise says in the *Monastic Writings*, number 5:

> “Do not be seized by concerns for your parents or by friendships with relatives; indeed, avoid constant meetings with them, lest they take you away from the quiet of your cell and lead you back to their affairs.”

But Saint Basil is much more emphatic in several places, especially in the *Monastic Constitutions* (chapter 21), where among other things he says:

> “It is fitting to be separated in affection from relatives, friends, and parents to the same extent that we see the dead to have no intercourse with the living.”

And elsewhere (Longer Rules, chapter 32):

> “Once a place has been given to anyone in the fellowship of the brothers, the superior ought not to permit him to turn his mind toward other things, or, under the pretext of visiting relatives, to withdraw from the brothers and live without the knowledge of witnesses, or to assume responsibility for relatives according to the flesh.”

And to the question (Shorter Rules, question 188), “How are we to regard household members or parents who come to us?” he responds:

> “As the Lord showed and taught when it was announced and said to him: ‘Behold, your mother and your brothers are standing outside, wishing to see you.’ To them he replied, as though sharply rebuking them: ‘Who is my mother, and who are my brothers?’”

And to the following question—“If holy parents ask that we go home to them, should we listen to them?”—he responds:

> “If they ask this for the building up of the faith, and if someone is such that he can go with them for this purpose, let him be sent with approval. But if he hears the Lord speaking of some human service to be performed to the one who had said, ‘Let me go and take leave of those at home’: ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.’ If such a judgment is given concerning one who merely wished to take leave, what must be said of the judgment concerning this man?”

Much more severe is the censure of Saint Stephen of the Order of Grandmont (On the Rule, chapter 34):

> “If perchance your father, or any secular friend of yours, is gravely ill near your cell and desires to confess his sins and arrange his affairs in your presence, and he orders you to visit him, do not go to his presence under any circumstances, provided that clerics sufficient for his need are with him. But if you presume to go there and die on the way, we shall in no way render an account of you to God” [Col. 0306B].

To all these I add the statutes of the Carthusian monks:

> “For devotion, piety, recreation, or visitation of parents, or for any other reason, monks shall under no circumstances leave their boundaries.”

And elsewhere:

> “All members of the order shall avoid and flee visits to parents and carnal affections; otherwise let them be punished according to the measure of their fault.”

And again elsewhere:

> “We entirely forbid our brothers—that is, the lay brothers—to undertake the concerns of any of their relatives, or to hire workers for them without the permission of the procurator or prior.”

From all this it is clear how strongly the holy Fathers wished monks to shrink from the sight of their parents [Col. 0306C]. Saint Basil gives the reason in these words (Longer Rules, chapter 32):

> “For besides the fact that we shall bring them no benefit, we shall also fill our own life with disturbance and disorder, and find occasions of sin.”

The holy doctor explains this more clearly and fully elsewhere:

> “Whoever carefully embraces friendship with secular people and desires to associate with them continually will, through constant intercourse, make their affections familiar to his soul. Filling his mind again with worldly understanding, he will fall away from a good beginning; abandoning spiritual understanding, he will send back into his mind the vomit of his former life, and will be wounded by the enemy, who disturbs spiritual fellowship through carnal kinship. … For when the devil sees that we have cast off all concern for this world and are steadfastly hastening toward heaven, he diligently seeks, by means of the thought implanted in us concerning our relatives, to make us assume responsibility for them and keep our minds anxious about worldly matters: what their property is, whether it is sufficient or insufficient, what profit they receive from their contracts, how far they have increased their wealth, what losses they have suffered through the calamities of this life, and how much has been taken away from their substance and possessions. In this way he causes us to rejoice in their successes and grieve if they suffer some misfortune; and, moreover, to be hostile in spirit toward their enemies, although we are commanded to have no enemy. We rejoice with their friends, who are often unworthy of spiritual intimacy, and take pleasure in their unjust and wicked gains. … It very often happens that, because of thoughts devoted to caring for relatives, the religious man dares even to commit sacrilege in order to relieve their poverty. For what is stored up for the support of the saints who have consecrated themselves to God is regarded as sacred and truly accursed to profane use. Therefore whoever steals anything from it belongs to the number of those who do not hesitate to commit sacrilege.”

Thus far Saint Basil. Although the text is lengthy, we have judged it thoroughly worthy of quotation, so that it might be evident how foreign careless association with parents is to the purpose of monastic life [Col. 0307A].

Paschasius Radbertus recognized this danger when, praising Saint Adalard because he had fled from his parents and homeland, he adds:

> “Let our fellow citizens, the monks, hear this kind of man—those who rest sluggishly, covered with the soot of shadows; let those who drag behind them herds of secular people hear him. Let them hear, I say, that it is not sufficiently safe to be wrapped in affection for one’s parents. Christ therefore does not know or acknowledge mother and brothers, so that he may show us the true fraternity of the mind: ‘Whoever,’ he says, ‘does the will of my Father who is in heaven is my brother, sister, and mother.’ Then he recalls the disciple from the duty of burial, so that he may not be permitted to bury his father according to the obligation of the flesh.”

The Emperor Louis the Pious, though a secular man, also knew this when he said in his exhortation to Eigil, abbot of Fulda (in the *Life of Eigil*, number 12):

> “Many monks, entangled in secular activities and legal business, according to the saying of a certain Father, have lost their souls while wishing to benefit their relatives” [Col. 0307B].

These words, which Saint Isidore also cites in chapter 5 of his Rule, ought to cover with the blush of shame certain monks who care more for the property of their parents than the parents themselves; who, although separated from the world, wish to become more entangled in the concerns of their relatives than they would have been or could have been while living in the world; and who, finally, love their blood relatives more than they are loved by them.

Entirely different was the intention of those outstanding monks who had so completely erased every memory of their parents from their minds that they did not even think about them.

Such was that exceptional monk of whom Evagrius writes that, when his father’s death was announced to him, he said to the messenger:

> “Stop blaspheming; the Father is immortal.”

For he meant God.

Such also was the man who, invited to receive the inheritance of his dying father, replied:

> “I died to the world before him; one who is dead cannot be heir to the living.”

Such was the distinguished Theodore, the disciple of Saint Pachomius. When his mother, supported by letters from a bishop, came to the monastery in order to see her son, he steadfastly refused to allow her to see him.

Such, finally, was Mark, the disciple of Abbot Silvanus. On one occasion he was ordered to go out to his mother:

> “He was wearing a garment sewn together from various scraps of cloth and stained with kitchen soot. Therefore, going out in obedience, he closed his eyes and said: ‘I wish you salvation.’ He saw no one, and his mother did not recognize him.”
