See chapter 28 of the *Life of Saint Pachomius*; Rufinus, Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, numbers 32 and 154; Cassian, Conference 5, chapter 3; and the *Life of Saint Vulmarus*, abbot, number 7, in the third century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*, where similar examples are reported.

But since some people conceal, under the attractive veil of piety, their itching desire to visit their relatives, it will not be inappropriate to place before them the most disastrous case of a certain monk. Saint Bernard, an eyewitness, relates the matter in these words (Sermon 64 on the Song of Songs):

> “I myself saw a man running well. And behold, a thought—why should it not have been a little fox?—said: ‘To how many people I could certainly impart the good that I alone enjoy, if I were in my homeland—to my brothers, relatives, acquaintances, and friends!” They love me, and they will easily comply with one who persuades them. Why this waste? I shall go there and save many of them, and myself as well. Nor need I fear a change of place; indeed, while I do good, what does it matter where I am, except that there, beyond doubt, I shall live better, where I shall be more fruitful?’ What more is there to say? He goes, and the wretch perishes—not so much an exile returning to his homeland as a dog returning to its vomit. The unhappy man destroyed himself and gained none of his own.”

See Saint Jerome, *Life of Malchus the Monk*.

Now, if someone objects that the Apostle says, “If anyone does not care for his own, and especially for members of his household, he has denied the faith and is worse than an unbeliever,” Saint Basil responds (Monastic Constitutions, chapter 21):

> “The Apostle spoke to secular people, to those who possess external and substantial wealth and are able to relieve the poverty of their relatives. … These things apply to the living, not to the dead; for the dead are free from this entire obligation. But you are dead and crucified to the whole world. By renouncing earthly wealth, you embraced poverty, and by offering yourself to God, you became his possession. As a dead man, therefore, you are free from every contribution to relatives; as a poor man, you have nothing to supply them. Even the body that you gained from all these things is not in your own power, and, having been offered to God, it may not lawfully be transferred to human uses” [Col. 0308A].

What, then, shall we give our parents? The same Saint Basil answers (ibid.): “We shall pray for our relatives for the best things—for justice, piety, and the same things that we have judged precious; for it is fitting that we pray these things for them, and it is useful for them to acquire them through us.”

Finally, to bring this instrument to a conclusion, Peter of Blois adds (Epistle 20): “Although I owe my parents natural affection, I do not owe them this: that I should destroy myself for their sake, or turn back from my purpose of uprightness on their account. For the cows that carried the ark of the Lord at Beth-shemesh, although a certain natural affection for their calves drew them toward them, nevertheless did not turn their necks toward them.” See Saint Jerome, Letter 1 to Heliodorus.

## And whatever one does not wish to be done to oneself, let one not do to another.

And, conversely, whatever one wishes to be done to oneself, let one do to another. Both principles are contained in this instrument, which therefore may be called both affirmative and negative, as Bernard of Cassino says (*Life of the Fathers*, Book III, no. 153). Observing this alone may be sufficient for salvation, as a certain Father teaches in Rufinus—since it embraces all the commandments of love, as Pope Saint Gregory teaches at length in *Moralia*, Book X, chapter 4, cited here by Hildemar.

Moreover, this saying was held in such esteem not only among Christians but also among pagans that they ordered it to be engraved on their houses and public buildings; Lampridius reports this of Alexander Severus in his *Life*.

## To deny oneself to oneself, in order to follow Christ.

We learn what it means to deny oneself from Saint Basil (*Longer Rules*, chapter 6): “The denial of ourselves,” he says, “is complete forgetfulness of what lies behind and withdrawal from our own desires.” Grimlaicus expresses the same in these words in chapter 2 of his *Rule for Solitaries*:

“To attain perfection, it is not enough for anyone to abandon his possessions unless he also denies himself. But what is it to deny oneself except to renounce one’s own wills? To deny oneself is for the proud person to become humble, for the angry person to strive to become gentle, for the lustful person to become chaste, for the formerly drunken person to become sober, and for the envious and malicious person to become kind and well-disposed. For if someone renounces everything he possesses but does not renounce his own habits, he is certainly not a disciple of Christ. Whoever renounces his possessions denies what is his; but whoever renounces his evil habits denies himself.”

Or again, to deny oneself [Col. 0308D] means not only to abandon what is unlawful and to put off evil habits, but also to abstain from what is lawful, discipline the body, and carry the cross. Peter Damian is to be understood in this sense when, after quoting the Gospel words, “If anyone wishes to come after me, let him deny himself,” and so forth, he says (*Sermon* 47):

“Listen to a counsel, not a commandment. For if it were a commandment, all who did not put it into practice could expect everlasting torments. But when he says, ‘If anyone wishes,’ he has left it to our will whether we hasten to run alongside him on equal terms. The labor is certainly great, but the reward is incomparable.”

For it is always commanded that we put off evil habits, flee what is unlawful, and abandon vices; it is never permissible to do the opposite.

Yet Blessed Benedict did not merely say, “deny oneself”; he adds *to oneself* (*sibi*), which Menardus explains as “within oneself, in one’s conscience, not before human beings.” He adds:

“This phrase is familiar to Saint Benedict, as in chapter 7 of the Rule: ‘saying to oneself with the prophet’; and in chapter 52: ‘as a brother who perhaps wishes to pray privately for himself,’ and so forth.”

The word *sibi* may also be understood in this way: it is never permissible to deny oneself to others, whereas with respect to oneself, insofar as the laws of discretion allow, it is always fitting. One must give one’s whole self to God and one’s whole self to one’s neighbor; but one may and must deny oneself to oneself if one desires to live perfectly.

Finally, *sibi* may mean “for oneself,” that is, for one’s own advantage, because whatever reward or recompense follows from this self-denial accrues to oneself, not to others.

Saint Benedict adds: “In order to follow Christ,” that is, in order to imitate him. Here what Saint Bernard says comes to mind (*Sermon 62 on Various Subjects*):

“Some do not follow Christ but flee from him; others do not follow him but go before him; some follow but do not attain him; others both follow and attain him. They do not follow but flee who have not yet ceased to sin. They do not follow but go before him who prefer their own opinions to those of their teachers. They follow but do not attain who act sluggishly and negligently and, not persevering to the end, turn back halfway along the road. They follow and attain who steadfastly imitate his way of humility with devoted affection of mind. Such people truly follow the Lord.

“‘Whoever serves me, let him follow me’—that is, let him imitate me. With what result? ‘So that where I am,’ he says, ‘there my servant may be also.’ The fruit of this imitation, therefore, is residence in eternal blessedness.”

## To discipline the body. Not to embrace pleasures.

With these two instruments the holy Father embraces the whole perfection of mortification, which consists entirely in enduring hardships and abstaining from pleasures. Saint Augustine says of these (*Sermon 38 on Scripture*):

“There are two things which, as laborious practices, are commanded by the Lord in this life: restraint and endurance. We are commanded to restrain ourselves from those things which are called good in the world, and to endure those evils which abound in this world. These two virtues—restraint and endurance—cleanse the soul and make it capable of divinity.”

First, then, we are commanded to discipline the body, after the example of the Apostle, who, as he himself said, disciplined his body and brought it into subjection. Blessed Raingardis, mother of Blessed Peter the Venerable, imitated this example perfectly. He reports the following about her (*Book II, Letter 17*):

“By vigils and fasts she declared a savage persecution against her body, and through these and other labors so exhausted her strength and flesh that, her flesh wasted away and her skin clinging to her bones, when I came to Marcigny after several years, she secretly said to me, playfully addressing me as her son: ‘Thanks be to God, because I have lost the world’s excesses; I have lost the old flesh with which I had served the world. Now I shall put on new flesh with which I may render new service to God.’”

The commentators rightly note here that Saint Father Benedict commands the body to be disciplined, not killed, because it must be afflicted with discretion so that it may be capable of sustaining the other exercises of monastic life. But this discretion must proceed not from the prudence of the flesh but from the charity of one’s superior. Otherwise, everyone might claim what the aged Dorotheus the Theban replied when Palladius asked why he wore down his body through such mortification: “That kills me, and I shall kill it in turn” (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 2).

Next comes “not to embrace pleasures.” For, as Saint Odo says (*First Book of Conferences*, no. 34), “the Christian soldier walks by a different road if he seeks joys and pleasures, when his commander has shown him the ways of bitterness.”

There are also various considerations by which the servant of God may be turned away from embracing pleasures. Grimlaicus’s statement should be sufficient for him (*Rule for Solitaries*, chapter 4):

“Those who serve God must flee pleasures. Those who wish to possess them do not seek them without pain, do not find them without difficulty, do not preserve them without care, do not possess them without anxious delight, and do not lose them without deep sorrow.”

The pleasures of the body, however, should not be understood, as Abbot John said (Rufinus, *Life of the Fathers*, Book II, chapter 1), as only those enjoyed by worldly people. For an ascetic must regard as pleasure anything he takes with desire, even if it is something humble and ordinarily used by those who practice abstinence. Finally, even water or bread, if taken with desire—that is, not to satisfy the body’s necessity but the soul’s longing—is counted, in one who practices abstinence, as the vice of pleasure.

[Col. 0310A] Yet, as Hildemar very aptly observes, Saint Benedict does not here forbid pleasures altogether, but only commands that we not embrace them. Sometimes they must be used for reasons of necessity or propriety, as when someone eats with an important person at a guesthouse. But to embrace them—that is, to love them—is never permitted. We ought to use them, but not enjoy them; indeed, we should use them as though we were not using them, imitating those perfected persons of whom Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, writes (*First Book of Conferences*, no. 39):

“They use temporal support as a traveler uses shade or a bed: he rests in body, but with his mind directed elsewhere he hastens to depart. So these people refuse to fix the step of their heart upon transitory things, lest the pleasure of the journey separate them from the station of their eternal dwelling. They desire to rejoice in what is their own, and therefore refuse to be happy in the place of their pilgrimage.”

## To love fasting.

He did not simply say “to fast,” because many people, for the sake of charity—for example, on account of a guest—or because of illness, neither can nor ought to fast. Others fast without profit because they do so unwillingly and with murmuring. But what is perfect is to love fasting, and not merely of the flesh but, what is greater, of the heart.

“For,” as Cassian says, “when the outer person fasts, the inner person too must similarly abstain from harmful foods.”

But since we truly fast when we give to the nourishment of the poor what we withdraw from the body, Saint Benedict very appropriately adds:

## To refresh the poor.

In accordance with the saying of Scripture: “Stretch out your hand to the poor, so that your propitiation and blessing may be brought to perfection” (*Ecclesiasticus* 7).

How lavish the ancient monks were in refreshing the poor can neither be expressed by speech nor grasped by understanding. We are especially able to read, not without a certain astonishment of mind, what Rufinus reports concerning those outstanding men who served Christ under Abbot Serapion (Book II of *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 18; Palladius likewise writes this in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 76):

“This was their custom, and not theirs alone but that of nearly all the monks of Egypt: at harvest time they would hire out their labor for reaping, and from that payment each of them would acquire approximately eighty modii of grain. Of this they offered the greater part for the use of the poor, so that not only the needy of that region might be fed, but ships laden with grain might also be sent to Alexandria, to be distributed to those confined in prison and to other foreigners and needy people. For the poor within Egypt are not sufficient to consume the fruits and generosity of their mercy.”

Whether Saint Isidore had these men, or all monks generally, in mind when he wrote about monks as follows is uncertain (*Book II on the Divine Offices*, chapter 15):

“Whatever remains beyond necessary nourishment from the work of their hands and the restriction of banquets is distributed to the needy with such care that nothing remains in excess.”

[Col. 0310D] How earnestly Saint Benedict wished the poor to be cared for is clear not only from this chapter and many other passages of the holy Rule—for example, when in chapter 31 he commands the cellarer to care for the poor with every concern; in chapter 53, to show careful concern for receiving the poor and pilgrims; and in chapter 55, to store old clothing in the wardrobe for the poor; and in chapter 58, for the person about to make profession to distribute his possessions to the poor or to the monks—but also from his *Life*, chapter 28.

The later sons of the holy Father piously imitated his mercy toward the poor, as their statutes on this matter repeatedly testify. Among them is the celebrated canon of the Council of Aachen (canon 49):

“Of everything given as alms, whether to the church or to the brothers, a tenth is to be given to the poor.”

Hildemar explains the meaning of this canon in his commentary on chapter 53 of the Rule:

“But since we have spoken about guests, we must now say from what source poor guests, and from what source rich guests, are to be fed. Everything—that is, whatever enters the monastery, whether gold, silver, bronze, iron, trees, wine, fruit, animals, and the rest, or anything produced by labor in the monastery—from all these things a tenth must be given solely to the hospital of the poor; that is, not so that others, namely servants or nobles, but solely the poor may be fed.”

Peter Damian confirms this in these words:

“So that more abundant supplies may be devoted to the nourishment of the poor, tithes of every kind of income are given in monasteries and hermitages—not only of livestock but likewise of birds and eggs.”

The manuscript *Customary of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon* concerning the office of the almoner says (chapter 45):

“For he receives a tithe of all the grain brought into the granary, both from nearby and from far away, and also of that which is left to the deans, whether for seed or for the things they need. For it is tithed when the whole quantity is assembled, both what is brought in and what remains. In the same way he receives a tithe of all the wine; the same rule applies to wine as to grain.”

Finally, an old manuscript concerning the observance of the Rule according to the custom of the Cluniacs, part III, chapter 24, cited by Haeften, says:

“The almoner also receives, in addition to what properly belongs to the almonry, a tenth loaf of all the loaves baked in the monastery oven; a tenth measure of wine produced in the church’s vineyards; and likewise a tenth of the lambs and other livestock, as well as of the cheeses made on the estates. He himself collects the tenth.”

Yet we should not attribute the original beginning of this pious custom to the Council of Aachen; rather, it should be believed that the council confirmed it rather than instituted it. For long before that time Saint Filibert, abbot of Jumièges (*Second Section of Benedictine History*, p. 822), “endeavored to tithe all goods.” He assigned that tithe to the redemption of captives and the nourishment of the poor, “to such an extent that he sent his monks with heavily laden ships to overseas regions for this purpose, and the crowds of captives redeemed through him praised the power of Christ,” as the anonymous author of his *Life* says, no. 21.

Nor did the overflowing pious mercy of our people toward the poor and needy stop here. Anyone who wishes to glance even briefly at the ancient statutes of Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, the customs collected by Ulrich of the monastery of Cluny, and many others will readily recognize that they distributed many other and still more generous alms daily for the benefit of the poor.

Antonius Yepez also writes that in some monasteries of our order in Spain not only a tenth but even a fifth of their goods was devoted to the use of the poor. Among other examples, he praises the monasteries of Galicia and Asturias, which, when famine and plague were raging, became true and reliable granaries for the needy.

Certainly, in the aforementioned statutes of Saint Adalard I read, among much else, the following (*Book I*, chapter 6):

“Furthermore, we have decided to give to the aforementioned hospitaler, from all the silver that comes to the gate, a fifth part, delivered through the hands of the senior porter.”

Saint Isidore showed still greater depths of mercy toward the poor when he assigned a third part of the monastery’s goods to the use of the needy (*Rule*, chapter 18):

“Everything that enters the monastery in the form of money is to be received in the presence of the elders. That money is to be divided into three parts. One will be for the sick and the elderly and for purchasing something more choice for the brothers’ food on holy days; another will be for the needy; the third will be for the clothing of the brothers and boys, or for anything necessary to be purchased for the monastery.”

In the following chapter and in chapter 10 he further prescribes that whatever remains from the table is to be reserved for the use of the poor.

This custom came to prevail in almost all the monasteries of our order. Certainly, according to the manuscript *Customary* of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, chapter 45, and according to Ulrich’s Book II, chapter 23, the monks of Cluny distributed whatever bread and wine remained from the table, as well as half of the other foods, to the poor.

Peter the Venerable later extended his piety to absolutely all food, issuing this statute:

“Whatever remains from the brothers’ daily table is to be received by the common alms fund” (Statute 33).

The same statute was renewed in the year 1200 under Abbot Hugh V and enacted in 1444 in the provincial chapter of the English monks held at Northampton. We find the same rule under the gravest penalties in the Council of Oxford in 1222, as recorded by Spelman (*Councils of England*, vol. II, p. 189):

“All provisions to be set before religious persons are to be set before them without any withholding, both in the refectory and elsewhere, wherever they take their meals. Of everything set before them, the entire remainder, without diminution, is to be assigned to alms and faithfully distributed to the needy by the almoner. Neither the abbot, nor the prior, nor the almoner may dispense contrary to this. Whoever refuses to admit or observe this statute, or the statute concerning clothing, shall, if he is a priest, be suspended from the celebration of divine offices; if he is in a minor order or a nun, from communion of the Lord’s Body until full satisfaction has been made.”

Pope Benedict XII likewise says in his Constitution, chapter 18:

“Whatever remains from the provisions administered is to be assigned to alms by the person appointed for this purpose. No one else, either personally or through another, is to presume to remove anything from the refectory, infirmary, or any other place where the monks eat, or to carry it elsewhere, or to apply it to another use. If anyone does so, he is to undergo, for each occasion, a penance of bread and water alone for two days.”

But what shall I say about the abundant almsgiving of our Cluniacs, who are remembered to have distributed assistance to seventeen thousand needy people in a single day? What shall I say about the other monasteries of Germany? It is better in this matter to hear an outsider than a member of our own household:

“There are in Germany alone,” says Dominicus Gravina of the Order of Saint Dominic, “monasteries of monks that distribute eight or ten thousand gold pieces among the poor. Hospitals are found everywhere, whose sick are continually cared for at their expense. Three times each year general alms are distributed to six hundred and more people; greater sums are poured out at the time of anniversaries, in accordance with the founders’ intention. At certain times of the year five or six thousand people, and often even four thousand, are supported. Who could count the secret gifts given privately to those who are ashamed to beg—especially noble maidens, afflicted widows, and very poor but noble men? There is also a more generous affection of charity toward those whose fortunes have been consumed by ruin, fire, or countless other disasters.”

Thus he speaks in praise of our people. There is no room here to enumerate the alms of all monasteries, still less those of individual abbots toward the poor. Yet I cannot omit certain acts of particular men, whose example may serve to edify later generations—and, would that it might also lead them to imitation!

Among these, Saint Ansbert, abbot of Fontenelle, stands out above all. Aigradus writes in his *Life*, no. 21 (*Second Section of Benedictine History*, p. 1054):

“In the aforesaid venerable monastery of Fontenelle, amid the happy works of his goodness, he also established a hospital for the weak and aged poor, after the pattern of the apostolic number twelve, assigning to them resources sufficient to provide nourishment. He established two further dwellings in the same monastery for the poor and infirm of Christ, and had eight of them live separately in each dwelling, from the sacred number eighty. He determined that they should be supplied perpetually with their daily food, without want. They had no other occupation than to remain at the appointed hours, by day and by night, in the house of God, to devote themselves faithfully to prayer and divine leisure, and at the time of the holy sacrifice to offer the saving victim for the welfare and salvation of the Christian people and of the Catholic Church spread throughout the world.”

Saint Peter, abbot of Cava, should apparently be counted among these men. Venusinus testifies in his *Life*, no. 7 (*Bollandists*, 4 March), that he “was accustomed to feed and clothe the needy in crowds, and to seek them out with such zeal for clothing and feeding them that he even explored cities in order to find them.”

Nor is the following account of his people at Centula by Hariulf of lesser value (*Chronicle*, Book II, chapter 2):

“They led a life rich in moral wealth, though not very wealthy in worldly goods—not because they lacked an abundance of estates, revenues, or villages bestowed on them by Saint Richarius, but because they devoted all the expenses of their revenues more to the needs of the poor than to their own uses.”

We consider entirely worthy of praise the act of William, abbot of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, who, in order to relieve the poor during a time of famine, dismantled the tomb of the holy martyr, which was covered everywhere with gold and silver. He sold the golden reliquary magnificently adorned with gems, together with three panels, two silver censers, crosses, and every ornament made of gold and silver.

Matthew of Paris tells a similar story about Leofric, the tenth abbot of Saint Albans in England (*Lives of Twenty-Three Abbots of Saint Albans*):

“This man, when a pitiful famine was growing severe throughout all parts of England, spent for the support of the poor the treasure that had long before been reserved for the construction of the church, together with the columnar panels found in the ground, as has been said, and also the materials and golden and silver vessels assigned both to his own table and to the church. For he used to say that the faithful of Christ, especially the poor of God, are the church and the temple, and that they themselves in particular ought to be built and preserved.”

With similar piety Geoffrey, the sixteenth abbot of the same monastery, “uncovered the bier of Blessed Alban the martyr, which he himself had covered with gold, silver, and precious stones, so that by stripping it of those costly ornaments he might alleviate the misery of the poor” (ibid.).

To these examples I add that of Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny. Jotsald the monk reports in his *Life*, chapter 7 (*Bollandists*, 1 January), that he “broke up many ecclesiastical vessels and distinguished ornaments for the use of the poor, among them even the imperial crown of Emperor Henry” [Note: Henry had sent him this crown as a memorial of himself, as Peter Damian writes.] “For he judged it unworthy to deny such things to the poor of Christ, for whom Christ’s blood was poured out.”

The same disposition and inclination toward the poor belonged to Saint Hugh, also abbot of Cluny, when he said that gold and silver “shine more brightly when spent than when stored,” and, according to the testimony of Ambrose, that a chalice of the church is truly a chalice when it redeems from hunger or from the enemy those whom the blood of the chalice has freed from death.

See the *Acts of Saint Eusebia*, no. 12, *Second Section of Benedictine History*, p. 988; and the *Life of Saint Athelwold*, chapter 29, *Fifth Section*, where similar deeds are reported.

It remains to conclude this discussion of our people’s charity toward the needy with a singular custom of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, which was also common among the Cluniacs and displayed not only their widespread care for the poor but also their careful precautions regarding women. The manuscript *Customary of Saint-Bénigne* says in chapter 45:

“This also belongs to the almoner: once each week he is to go throughout the entire town, taking his servants with him, visiting those who are lying sick and poor somewhere. If the sick person is a male, he himself enters to visit him; if a female, he remains at the door and sends his servant to her. Having given them whatever he can give best, he consoles them. If she desires anything beyond what he has given, and if it is in any way possible, he inquires about it for her and afterward sends it through his servants.

“It is also the custom that, when the women who are in the houses where the sick are lying see him coming, they all leave immediately. For as long as any woman remains inside the house, he never enters.”

Finally, no words can adequately express how brightly the charity of our ancestors shone in relieving the needy, receiving pilgrims, redeeming captives, and comforting the sick, so long as they possessed free administration of their goods—that is, until the age of secular abbots, who appropriated all these things for themselves. From this it is clear how destructive to the public good is the institution of such secular abbots, who convert to private advantage what ought to benefit an infinite multitude of wretched people.

[Col. 0314A] Moreover, when Saint Father Benedict here commands that the poor be refreshed, this chiefly concerns those to whom that responsibility has been entrusted. The others, who do not even have authority over their own bodies, can do nothing except pray.

In distributing alms, I would especially approve what Saint Caesarius prescribes in his *Rule for Nuns* (chapter 39):

“I also give this warning: because of excessive disturbance, daily or continual almsgiving is not to be carried out at the monastery gate. Rather, what God has given, so that it may remain for the monastery’s needs, is to be arranged by the abbess through the steward and distributed to the poor.”

Saint Aurelian seems to have enacted the same provision in chapter 44 of his Rule.

Furthermore, as Smaragdus observes, there is another twofold kind of almsgiving by which monks ought especially to refresh the poor. One kind is to be offered to the sick and afflicted; the other to the foolish and ignorant. For whoever shares compassion with a sick person and supplies consolation and counsel to one who is afflicted undoubtedly refreshes the poor. Likewise, whoever supplies instruction to the foolish and the word of knowledge to the ignorant deserves to be praised with the acclamations due to an almoner.

Richard of Saint Angelo gives another interpretation:

“To refresh the poor is one kind of almsgiving; the second is to forgive the person by whom one has been injured; the third is to correct those who do wrong and lead those who have gone astray back to the way of truth.”

The same teaching appears in chapter 55 of the *Rule for Solitaries*.

## To clothe the naked.

This instrument, like the preceding one, does not concern everyone, but only the abbot and those to whom he has entrusted this duty. Nevertheless, in monasteries where new garments are distributed to the brothers at fixed times, whoever carefully preserves the old garments so that they may afterward be given to the poor is, insofar as he is able, to be considered one who clothes the naked.

Yet, as Smaragdus very aptly observes, there is not only one kind of bodily nakedness; there is another, much more dangerous and worse—namely, that of the soul, whose garments are the virtues. Concerning these Isaiah says: “He clothed me with the garment of salvation.” Thus, says Bernard of Cassino, a person clothes the naked spiritually when, out of charity, he admonishes someone stripped of virtues and naked through vice, so that he may put off vices and put on virtues.

## To visit the sick.

This instrument is chiefly to be understood of the sick who are inside the monastery. For, as Hildemar observes, the workshop in which all these things are to be carried out is the monastery enclosure and stability in the community. Nor does this duty belong to everyone, but to the infirmarian, to whom care of the sick has been specially entrusted; to the cellarer, upon whom these works of charity are imposed by chapter 31 of the Rule; and to the abbot, who according to the same Rule must exercise the greatest care that the sick are not neglected by the servants.

The others, however, since they have all the hours of the day assigned to particular exercises, ought not to visit the sick without the superior’s permission. This was the ancient practice of the early monks, expressed in the Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 24):

“No one shall dare to visit a sick person without the permission of his superior.”

The abbot, however, as Hildemar says, when he is informed that a brother is seriously ill, should say in chapter: “Whoever wishes to visit the sick man may go today and visit him”—perhaps speaking according to the custom of his own time.

The visitor [Note: Read *visitans* (“visiting”), as the syntax requires. Editor.] ought especially to observe what Saint Ephraem teaches:

“If you visit a sick person, take care that the enemy does not introduce idle chatter or detraction between you, lest you suffer the loss of your reward. For it is the devil’s practice to harm one person through hearing and another through the tongue. Rather, the afflicted person ought to be consoled from the sacred Scriptures and through the Passion of our Savior Jesus Christ.”

This was also the pious practice of our monks of Farfa. It may not be useless to set it out here, from their manuscript customs, as an example for others:

“If a brother from the cloister wishes to visit a sick person, he is to ask permission from the prior; no one may enter without it. Once he has obtained permission, he is to begin the psalm ‘Lord, rebuke me not in your fury,’ and recite it on the way. After the psalm he is to say: ‘Our Father’; ‘Save your servant’; ‘Send him help, O Lord.’ Prayer: ‘Almighty and everlasting God, salvation eternal.’

“When he has reached the sick person, he says: ‘Bless.’ Then he is to ask him about his illness—how he is suffering and what patience he possesses—and offer him good spiritual exercise; but he is not to ask about bodily matters.

“If the sick brother complains of some need, the visitor, coming to the prior, is to say: ‘With your permission I went to that sick brother, but I heard a complaint about such matters.’ It belongs to the prior, if he thinks fit, to make provision concerning such things.”

Smaragdus teaches that the sick should chiefly be visited for four reasons:

“We ought to visit the sick because in them we visit the Lord. For among the other works of mercy he will say to us: ‘I was sick, and you visited me.’ Let us also visit the sick for the sake of compunction, so that with Paul we may be able to say: ‘Who is weak, and I am not weak?’ Let us visit them also for the sake of reciprocity, so that when we are sick we may be visited by the healthy. Let us visit them also for the sake of love, because it is written: ‘Do not be reluctant to visit the sick.’”

Finally, Grimlaicus explains in these words how someone who cannot visit bodily may visit the sick spiritually (*Rule for Solitaries*, chapter 25):

“Without doubt, the person visits the sick or one confined in prison who sees someone lying on a bed, or in the darkness of vices, suffering from the disease of his iniquity, and strengthens him by the example of his own conduct and by the healing antidote of exhortation, because he had seen him faltering and growing weak in good action.”

## To bury the dead.

This instrument commands not only those works of charity that specifically concern the burial of a deceased brother, but also the prayers and pious works of assistance that ordinarily precede or follow it. Thus Grimlaicus, explaining this instrument in his *Rule for Solitaries*, says (chapter 25):

“He buries the dead who pours forth devoted and diligent prayers to the Lord on his behalf.”

Then, showing how we can also bury the spiritually dead, he adds:

“He not only buries the dead but, so to speak, also raises him from death in a certain way when he sees someone bound by the cords of his sins and, as it were, buried in the darkness of his iniquity, and through diligent sacred admonition summons him to confession and the lamentation of repentance and healthfully urges him to return to the way of salvation.”

A monk also buries the dead spiritually when, not wandering outside, he confines himself within the boundaries of his cell. For he may be counted among those of whom the Apostle says: “You have died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.”

Peter the Venerable teaches that the cell is a tomb in a letter to the monk Gilbert (*Book I, Letter 20*):

“But you, in order to show yourself truly dead to the world, entered the tomb while still alive.”

All monks ought to pay the greatest attention to this. If, being too tightly confined by the narrowness of the cell, they presume to burst outside, they drag the dead man from the tomb and emit a stench no less intolerable to everyone than that of a decaying corpse outside its grave.

## To assist in tribulation.

Tribulation is sometimes aroused externally by a human being, sometimes by a demon, and sometimes by one’s own body, as Smaragdus says. Whatever its cause, however, the afflicted person must be helped as quickly as possible.

## To console the sorrowful.

Some people grieve and are afflicted because of past sins; others because of sins to be avoided in the future; others so that, once freed from affliction, they may sing the praises of the Redeemer; and others grieve both in this age and in the age to come, as Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, demonstrates fully and learnedly in Book I of his *Conferences*, chapter 5.

From that same book, chapter 4, we can gather the words with which we may approach and console an afflicted person. There he also teaches that God afflicts us justly, mercifully, and beneficially.

### To make himself alien to the acts of the world

For, as Saint Pachomius said (*In his Life*, chapter 46): “That soul is proved to be exceedingly wretched, and worthy to be mourned with every fountain of tears, which, after renouncing the world, again becomes entangled in the acts of the world, and, having been stripped of its former useless cares, returns once more to the service of harsh slavery.” Hence Saint Augustine (*Book I, On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 20): “The soul of one who does not die to this world, nor begin to be conformed to the truth, is dragged into a more grievous death by the death of the body; and it will revive not for communion with heavenly blessedness, but to suffer punishments.” And Peter of Blois (*Letter 137*): “Consider the conduct of those as damnable who abandon the world for the cloister, yet carry the ways of the world into the cloister.” And elsewhere (*Sermon 42*): “Certainly Achan, son of Charmi, was stoned because he took something from the accursed things of Jericho; and those who renounce worldly things, yet immerse themselves in worldly matters not in deed but in affection [Col. 0316B] and desire, bear his exact likeness.” And shortly afterward: “However religious you may become, you lose everything in the cloister if you have retained anything from the world.”

Hence Saint Bernard, writing to the monks of Saint Bertin, says: “You have done well by alienating yourselves more and more from the acts of this world, which is pure and undefiled religion: for a little leaven, brothers, corrupts the whole mass, and dying flies ruin the oil of sweetness. What benefit is there in making the fruit of so much bodily and spiritual labor and discipline less acceptable—or indeed placing it in danger—by some utterly worthless consolation, or rather desolation? etc.” And indeed, as Saint John Climacus said most aptly (*Step 3*): “It is impossible for us to look toward heaven with one eye and toward earth with the other.”

The reason for this instrument is as follows:

1. Because anyone who practices worldly activities easily slips into the wicked ways, dispositions, and vices of worldly people. [128]  
2. Because worldly people are given greater opportunity, not to say audacity, to commit the same acts when they see monks doing without hesitation what they formerly did not even dare to touch. [Col. 0316C]  
3. Because worldly activities generate contempt for virtue in upright men living in the world in a religious habit, and draw them away from their right purpose. On this matter see Peter Damian, *Book VI, Letter 32*.  
4. Because a monk entangled in worldly activities exposes himself to the contempt of the world. For, as Saint Ambrose says (*Letter 6*): “How can a person be respected by the people who has nothing distinctive from the people, nothing unlike the crowd? For what will they admire in you if they recognize their own traits in you? If they see nothing in you that they cannot find in themselves? If what they are ashamed of in themselves they encounter in you, whom they regard as worthy of reverence?”  
5. Because, as Saint John Climacus says (*Step 3*), “By fleeing our homeland we have sold ourselves for the pursuit of heavenly things.” It is therefore unfitting that those who have sold themselves for heavenly activities should be enslaved to worldly activities. See Cassian, *Book IV, On the Institutes of Renunciation*, chapter 34 and following chapters, and the *Life of Saint Teresa*, chapter 37.

[Col. 0316D] ### To prefer nothing to the love of Christ

This instrument is necessarily connected with the first. For whoever loves God with all his heart, all his soul, and all his strength will be able to prefer nothing to the love of Christ.

### Not to carry anger through to completion

By saying “not to carry anger through to completion,” he shows that anger has various degrees, which Cassian lists in *Conference 5*, chapter 11, and John Climacus in *Step 8*. Cassian also discusses anger at greater length in *Book VIII, On the Spirit of Anger*; consult it if you wish. Saint Basil teaches how a monk can avoid becoming angry in the *Short Rules*, question 2. We shall say no more about anger, since you will rarely see monks in the school of humility subject to this vice.

“If an irascible man frequently becomes angry without cause,” says Saint Pachomius, “and on account of some empty and worthless matter, he shall be admonished six times; on the seventh they shall make him rise from his place in the order of sitting [Col. 0317A] and he shall be placed among the last. They shall teach him to cleanse himself of this disturbance of mind; and when he has brought three trustworthy witnesses, who will promise on his behalf that he will never again do anything similar, he shall receive his place of sitting. Otherwise, if he persists in the vice, he shall remain among the last, having lost his former place.”

### Not to reserve a time for anger

Irascibility is distinguished from anger as a disposition is distinguished from an act. For someone who becomes angry once cannot thereby be called irascible, although he truly has been angry. An irascible person is one who is always becoming angry and is moved by the slightest breath of a reply, like a leaf by the wind.

A person reserves time for anger when he determines in his mind some fixed period during which he may take revenge, retaining in his mind the memory of the injury inflicted.

### Not to harbor deceit in the heart

Because, as Saint Augustine says (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 16), where there is deceit, there is no charity. We explained above in the prologue what deceit is.

[Col. 0317B] ### Not to offer a false peace [129]

But a true peace; for false peace is not peace. And if the true peacemakers are called sons of God, false peacemakers ought rightly to be called sons of the devil.

### Not to abandon charity

Saint Augustine teaches what charity is when he says (*Book III, On Christian Doctrine*, chapter 10): “I call charity the movement of the soul toward enjoying God for his own sake, and oneself and one’s neighbor for God’s sake.” Whoever abandons charity therefore loses God himself, because God is charity; and whoever remains in charity remains in God, and God in him.

### Not to swear, lest one happen to commit perjury

Halynardus, formerly a monk and abbot of Saint Benignus of Dijon and later bishop of Lyon, once cited this passage of the Rule when he refused to swear the oath of allegiance owed to Emperor Henry, preferring to refuse the episcopate rather than utter an oath.

What Saint Benedict here forbids was also forbidden by other Fathers of monks. Thus Saint Antony says: [Col. 0317C] “Do not swear at all, whether to what is true or to what is doubtful.” Saint Caesarius says: “Let them not swear, because the Lord said: ‘Do not swear at all,’ but let your speech be ‘yes, yes; no, no.’” Saint Aurelian says: “Do not swear, because the Lord said: ‘Do not swear’; and another Scripture says: ‘A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and punishment will not depart from his house.’”

Oaths are also prohibited by Saint Ferreolus in the *Rule*, chapter 23; the Rule of Tarnant, chapter 19; the *Rule of a Certain Man for Monks*, chapter 8; Saint Caesarius again in the *Rule for Virgins*, chapter 2; Saint Leander in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 19; and the Council of Aachen, chapter 43.

Moreover, Book II of the Lombard law, title 47, forbids bishops, priests, clerics, monks, and nuns to swear even when summoned to court, as our Menard observes in his notes on the Council of Regensburg, chapter 7, section 13. Indeed, Saint Fructuosus (*Monastic Rule, Commentary*, chapter 3) does not permit laymen who are defenders and patrons of his monastery’s property to swear when summoned to court. See the second *Life of Saint Oswald*, no. 56; *Benedictine Century V*, p. 752.

[Col. 0317D] Saint Benedict himself indicates why he wished monks to avoid oaths, saying, “lest he happen to commit perjury.” For the same reason Saint Augustine, according to Possidius (*Life of Saint Augustine*, chapter 25), “so that no one might fall into perjury through easy swearing, preached in the church to the people and instructed his own followers that no one should swear, not even on a minor occasion. If anyone slipped into this fault, he forfeited one of the portions prescribed by the rule; for a fixed number of cups had been established for those living and dining with him.”

When someone objected to the holy Doctor that the Lord, who had sworn, nevertheless forbade oaths, he replied as follows (*Sermon 307*): “It is not a sin to swear truly, but since it is a great sin to swear falsely, the person who does not swear at all is far from the sin of false swearing; the person who even swears truly approaches false swearing. Therefore, when the Lord forbade you to swear, he did not wish you to walk along the edge of a river, lest your foot slip in a narrow place and you fall. ‘But the Lord swore,’ you say. [Col. 0318A] He swears safely who does not know how to lie. Do not be moved by the fact that the Lord swore, because perhaps no one ought to swear except the Lord. But when you swear, what are you doing? You call upon God as a witness; he called upon himself, whereas a human being, because he is often deceived, generally calls upon the Truth as witness to his own falsehood.”

What follows from this? [130] “No one should utter any oath other than ‘Believe me,’ which we read in the Gospel that the Lord affirmed to the Samaritan woman; or, at any rate, some other expression that is customary among monks when swearing,” says the *Order of Monastic Conduct*. See Saint Augustine, *Sermon 182 on the Scriptures*, and Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, question 89.

### To speak truth from heart and mouth

What the holy Father says here should not be understood as though it were never permissible to remain silent about the truth. Sometimes this is not only expedient but even judged necessary for the good and benefit of others.

[Col. 0318B] Nevertheless, this instrument especially prohibits lying, which was never and will never be lawful, although Plato (*Book III of the Republic*), who in this matter was plainly not divine; Origen (*Book VI of the Stromata*); and Abbot Joseph, in Cassian (*Conference 17*, chapter 17), judged otherwise. Their teaching is opposed by Saint Augustine in *On Lying* and *Against Lying*; Saint Thomas, *Summa theologiae* II–II, question 110, article 3; and many others.

Indeed, Abbot Joseph’s opinion was so detested that, on account of it and other errors of Cassian, the theological faculty of Paris once censured *Conference 17*, as Adalard Gazaeus observes from an old manuscript in his commentary on chapter 22 of that conference.

The most serious legislators of monastic law also wished lying among monks to be punished with the harshest penalties. Thus Saint Pachomius (*Rule, article 119*): “Whoever lies, and is found to hate anyone . . . the Father of the monastery shall hear the matter and punish him according to the measure and nature of the sin.”

Saint Caesarius, in the *Rule for Monks* (chapter 5): “Whoever is found to have lied shall receive the prescribed discipline.”

Saint Columbanus (*Penitential*, no. 22): “If someone, in disputing, tells a lie and affirms a distinction [reading uncertain], he shall have one paximatium and water for two days.” [Col. 0318C] And below (no. 26): “If someone tells a lie unknowingly, fifty lashes; if knowingly and boldly, bread and water; if his lie is denied and he persists in it, seven days on bread and water.”

Saint Fructuosus (*First Rule*, chapter 16): “A liar, thief, striker, and perjurer—things unbecoming a servant of God—must first be rebuked by the elders in words, so that he may withdraw from the vice. After this, if he still delays correcting himself, he shall be admonished a third time before the brothers, so that he may cease from such error. If he does not amend even then, he shall be severely scourged and, receiving the punishment of excommunication for three months, shall be confined alone in a cell under strict penance, sustained from evening to evening by six ounces of barley bread and a small measure of water.”

[Col. 0318D] Finally, the *Rule of a Certain Man for Monks* (chapter 8): “Lying and swearing, or an idle word, must be condemned throughout the whole body of the brotherhood. If any brother is found with any of these things, he shall be sent to prison and do penance until he is corrected from the vice, because ‘the mouth that lies kills the soul’ . . . . If any brother, after examination in prison, cannot rid himself of these vices, he shall be expelled from the brothers and condemned.”

If you ask what a lie is, Saint Augustine replies (*Against Lying*, chapter 12): “a false signification accompanied by the intention to deceive.” From this you will infer that not everyone who does not speak the truth or deceives is lying, but only those who possess the intention to deceive.

### [131] Not to repay evil with evil

Because, as Origen, cited by Hildemar, says: “The person who repays evil is worse than the person who first commits the evil.”

Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, perfectly fulfilled this instrument. He not only spared the murderer of his own brother but also received him into the monastery when he was being sought for execution [Col. 0319A], and clothed him in the habit of holy conversion.

### Not to inflict injury, but also patiently to endure injury when inflicted

There are two kinds of injury: one intended for testing, the other for insult and damage to reputation. Saint Benedict forbids the latter as evil; he commands the former as good, useful, and necessary, since he orders that a person coming to conversion be subjected to injuries and that one admitted for testing be tested in all patience. Yet not everyone is authorized to inflict such injuries; the authority belongs to the abbot or to one to whom he has entrusted this responsibility. They themselves must use the utmost prudence and discretion in inflicting injuries, taking account of times, places, and persons.

Nevertheless, whether either kind comes from wherever it may, it must be patiently endured, as Saint Benedict commands here and in chapter 7, ordering the monk to embrace patience with a silent conscience in response to every injury inflicted upon him.

Such was that excellent monk who, as Rufinus relates [Col. 0319B] (*Book III, Lives of the Fathers*, no. 80), “the more someone insulted or mocked him, the more he rejoiced, saying: ‘These are the people who provide us with an occasion for our progress; but those who bless us disturb our souls. It is written: “Those who bless you deceive you.”’”

So too Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane (*His Life*, no. 31, *Benedictine Century IV*), used to send gifts to those who injured him.

Indeed, among the Athenians, those who could not endure injuries with equanimity were not considered fit for the pursuit of wisdom. Therefore, at the city gate there sat an old man devoted to wisdom who afflicted everyone entering with insults, in order to test them. With greater right, therefore, monks devoted to true—and therefore divine—wisdom ought patiently to endure injuries inflicted upon them, if they genuinely desire to be in reality what they profess to be.

For this reason Abbot Zacharias, about to say something before the brothers for the instruction of their morals, threw a cloak onto the ground and trampled it, saying: “Unless someone has been trampled in this way, he cannot be a monk.” See Rufinus, *Book III, Lives of the Fathers*, no. 77 and following.

[Col. 0319C] ### To love one’s enemies

For a full explanation of this instrument, it is necessary to inquire: first, who should be considered our enemy; second, what the love of enemies requires of us; third, by what considerations we can be led to love them; and fourth, how certain objections against the love of enemies should be answered.

We learn who is to be called our enemy from Saint Basil (*Short Rules*, question 176): “It is proper to an enemy to harm and plot against someone. Whoever, therefore, harms anyone in any way may properly be called an enemy; properly speaking, the one who sins, for insofar as it lies within his power, he harms and plots against a person connected with him as well as against one with whom he has any dealings.”

The same Basil teaches what we owe even to an enemy, adding in the same place: [132] “Since a human being is composed of body and soul, let us love such people according to the soul, reproving them, admonishing them, and leading them by every means toward conversion; but according to the body, let us do good to them if they are suffering from a lack of necessities.” [Col. 0319D]

The chief and strongest reason for this instrument is drawn from Christ’s command and from the reward promised to the love of enemies. For he says: “Love your enemies, so that you may be sons of your Father who is in heaven.” Saint Caesarius, explaining this (*Sermon 225, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*), says: “Choose now whatever pleases you: if you love your enemies, you will deserve to be not only a friend but also a son of God.”

A second reason proceeds from the threats against those who do not love their enemies. For Christ again says: “If you do not forgive people, neither will your Father forgive you your sins.” “In the face of so great a thunderclap, the person who does not awaken is not asleep but dead,” says Saint Augustine (*Enchiridion*, chapter 74).

If someone objects that this command is impossible, Saint Basil replies [Col. 0320A] (*Short Rules*, question 176): “The good and just Lord would not have commanded this of us unless he had also given us the strength to accomplish it. He has also shown that this strength is necessarily implanted in nature: even beasts naturally love those who do good to them. But what does a friend possess that can bring as much benefit as enemies do? For enemies gain for us that blessedness of which the Lord says: ‘Blessed are you when they persecute you, insult you, and falsely say every evil thing against you because of me. Rejoice and exult, for your reward is great in heaven.’”

If someone further objects that the souls of those who were killed in Revelation, chapter 6, cry out to God for vengeance for their shed blood, Saint Augustine—or whoever else is the author—replies (*Sermon 221, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*): “It must be understood that those saints, already standing in the sight of their Creator, see his will. Therefore they receive from him what they know he wills, and they drink from him what they thirst for from him. They ask for vengeance in two ways, and this out of charity: namely, that those predestined to eternal life may be converted from evil to good; but that those whom God, in his foreknowledge, knows will be condemned may die and cease from sinning, and thereby undergo a lesser punishment in hell.”

[Col. 0320B] ### Not to curse those who curse one, but rather to bless them

In accordance with the words of the Apostle Peter: “Not repaying evil for evil, nor insult for insult, but, on the contrary, blessing” (1 Peter 3); and Paul testifies that he himself did this, saying: “We are cursed, and we bless.”

Indeed, since a monk’s mouth has been consecrated to divine praises and blessings, nothing is more disgraceful than to hear from it a word of cursing. For, as the Master rightly reasons (*On the Rule*, chapter 11): “Just as a fountain cannot bring forth from one opening both bitter and sweet water, so neither can the mouth. When we bless the Lord with our tongue, how can we curse human beings with that same tongue?”

Moreover, as Saint Dorotheus says (*Teaching 17*, no. 6): “You ought to believe that whatever dishonor, disgrace, reproach, insult, or injury has happened to you [Col. 0320C] is a kind of antidote and medicinal remedy against the pride of your soul; and you should pray for those who revile and injure you just as you would for physicians, fully persuaded that the person who hates insult and disgrace also hates humility.”

### To endure persecutions for righteousness

He does not simply say “to endure persecution,” for many criminals—such as murderers and thieves—suffer persecution without receiving a reward. He adds “for righteousness,” which is characteristic of the righteous, to whom Christ therefore promises the kingdom of heaven in the Gospel.

Indeed, if we are members of him who suffered unjustly, for the unjust, and through the unjust, let us also willingly endure the same. Otherwise, as Saint Caesarius says (*Sermon 224, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*), “the person who does not wish to endure hatred with the head refuses to be in the body.”

[Col. 0320D] ### Not to be proud

Because God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble. Saint Bernard therefore aptly compares the proud (*Sermon 54, on the Song of Songs*) to the mountains of Gilboa, upon which neither dew nor rain falls, and to the hills over which the heavenly bridegroom leaps.

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny (*Book II of the Conferences*, no. 14), also says that the proud are represented by a reed that shines outwardly but is empty within. And Saint John Climacus says (*Step 23*) that a proud monk has no need of another demon, for he is already a demon and an enemy to himself.

From this it is evident how aptly Peter of Blois said that “although pride is detestable everywhere, it is more detestable in one who professes humility. What rust is in iron, what the moth is in clothing, what gall is in milk, and what poison is in honey—that is pride in the monastic habit.”

Pride, however, is “the desire for perverse elevation; and perverse elevation occurs when, having abandoned that to which the soul ought to cling, it makes itself somehow its own beginning and becomes its own principle,” says Saint Augustine [Col. 0321A] (*Book XIV, City of God*, chapter 13). He adds: “This happens when a person takes excessive pleasure in himself, when he falls away from that unchangeable good which ought to please him more than he pleases himself.”

### Not given to wine

According to Bernard of Monte Cassino, one given to wine is “one who, through excessive eagerness, excessive frequency, or excessive quantity, not content with the frugality of moderation, drinks wine as an intoxicated person.”

Or, as Smaragdus says, “one is called *vinolentus* who drinks enough and is slow to become intoxicated.” Saint Benedict absolutely forbids this, because, as the prophet says, “fornication, wine, and drunkenness take away the heart”; and Solomon says in Proverbs that “wine is a luxurious thing.” Hence the Apostle rightly said: “Do not become drunk with wine”—unless perhaps it be with the wine of divine love, for blessed is the person whom he introduces into the wine cellar and in whom he orders charity.

Moreover, from excerpt 10 of Book II of the *Penitential of Bishop Egbert of York* (*in Spelman, volume I, Councils of England*): “If any cleric or monk is a drunkard, let him do penance on bread and water for three months.” [Col. 0321B]

### Not a great eater

By this instrument Saint Benedict prohibits not only excess in food but every superfluous consumption of nourishment. He does not say, “Not excessively voracious,” but “not a great eater,” allowing what nature requires and cutting away what is superfluous.

Indeed, he condemns here all the vices of gluttony, which Saint Gregory lists as five in these words (*Book XXX of the Morals*, chapter 13): “The vice of gluttony tempts us in five ways. Sometimes it anticipates the proper time of need; sometimes it does not anticipate the time but seeks more sumptuous foods; sometimes, whatever foods are to be eaten, it demands that they be prepared with excessive care; sometimes it is suitable both to the quality of the food and to the time, but in the very quantity consumed it exceeds the measure of moderate nourishment; and sometimes it sins more gravely in the very heat of its immeasurable desire.”

Saint Benedict confronts all these tendencies in the Rule. First, he forbids anyone to anticipate the canonical hour of eating in chapter 43. Second, he prohibits more sumptuous foods [134] by wishing everyone to abstain from meat, chapters 36 and 39. [Col. 0321C] Third, he guards against carefully prepared foods when he decrees in chapter 35 that all, even those ignorant of the refinements of cooks, should perform kitchen service by turns. Fourth, he condemns excess in quantity in chapters 39 and 40. Fifth and finally, he cuts off excessive desire by asserting in chapter 40 that, when necessary things are lacking, God must be blessed rather than complained against.

See William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, *On the Solitary Life, to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*, chapter 11, no. 32; Cassian, the whole of Book V of the *Institutes*; and John Climacus, *Step 14*.

### Not sleepy

He calls those people sleepy who indulge in sleep beyond measure. This is blameworthy not only in monks but in every human being, because, as Saint John Climacus says (*Step 20*), “much sleep is a wicked companion, which withdraws and steals half of life—or more—from the idle and sluggish.” Saint Arsenius therefore called sleep an evil [Col. 0321D] servant (*Rufinus, Book III, Lives of the Fathers*, no. 211), and the aforementioned John Climacus taught that one must fight against it “at the very beginning of religious life and training” (*Step 19*).

Sleepiness has both physical or natural causes and moral causes. The same saint lists the physical causes in these words: “There is one cause of sleep, but it has, as it were, many causes of desire: from nature, from foods, from demons, or perhaps even from the great and excessive privation of fasting, by which the weakened body afterward tries through sleep to restore and refresh itself. Just as frequent and abundant drinking arises from habit, so does much and prolonged sleep.”

Saint Basil describes the moral causes (*Short Rules*, question 32). [Col. 0322A] To the question, “What is the cause of untimely and immoderate sleeping, and by what means can we drive it away from ourselves?” he replies: “Such drowsiness arises whenever we allow our mind to grow sluggish in contemplating divine things and despise the judgments of God.”

Then he gives the remedy: “We drive it away whenever we conceive, as is fitting, such a thought concerning the majesty of God, together with a desire to fulfill his will.”

And Saint John Climacus (*Step 7*): “When you go to bed, let your very lying down in your bed be for you an image of the posture of a body lying in a tomb, and you will sleep less . . . . Let the memory of the eternal fire of hell depart with you to bed in the evening and rise with you in the morning, and sleepiness will never seize you during the time of prayers and psalms.”

[Col. 0322B] ### Not lazy [135]

Although a lazy person is called *piger*, as though sick in the feet, since he is slow to walk, as Smaragdus observes, laziness is considered not so much in the body’s idleness and torpor as in the soul’s sluggishness and neglect of salvation.

Hence Smaragdus says: “The word ‘lazy’ rightly designates the person who wishes to reign with Christ but does not wish to work for him.” Certainly Christ calls not the quiet and idle but the laboring and burdened to himself for refreshment. And if monks, as Gerard the Belgian says, are Christ’s beasts of burden, what use is a lazy beast of burden that deserves neither fodder nor a stall?

### Not a murmurer

The Rule of Saint Ferreolus likewise decrees in chapter 7 “that no murmur or detraction be heard within the congregation against the abbot or any other of the brothers, although this is a practice monks are very familiar with; lest the anger of God, which has often condemned a pitiable people for this fault, be similarly stirred against the destructive crowd of murmurers, and lest their own murmuring cause them to lose the promised land, which we rightly understand as the place of future blessedness promised to us by divine pledge.”

For the same reason Saint Isidore forbids murmuring in the Rule, chapter 6, and Saint Fructuosus in the common monastic Rule, chapter 5.

Other monastic rules also prohibit it under the gravest penalties. The Rule of Saint Macarius, chapter 12: [Col. 0322C] “If anyone murmurs . . . after being duly corrected according to the judgment of the elder or the measure of his fault, let him abstain for as long as the nature of the fault requires, or until he has humbled and corrected himself through repentance, so that, once corrected, he may not dare to fall into it again.”

The Rule of Saint Pachomius (*Rule, article 164, in the Codex of Rules*): “Whoever has the habit of murmuring and complains that he is oppressed as though by a heavy task shall be instructed five times that he murmurs without cause, and the evident truth shall be shown to him. If after this he is disobedient and is of mature age, they shall treat him as one of the sick, and he shall be placed in the infirmary and fed there in idleness until he returns to the truth.”

Finally, the *Rule of a Certain Man for Monks* (chapter 6): “If any brother is found murmuring, he himself shall be sent to prison and his work shall be set aside. He shall do penance according to the judgment of the elder; if permitted, he shall make satisfaction to him. But if he does this frequently, he shall be expelled from the monastery.”

They considered murmuring such a grave sin. Certainly, if we weighed the punishments due to our sins, there would at no time be any reason for us to complain.

[Col. 0322D] “Who, then, would murmur any longer?” Saint Bernard once said (*Sermon 22, Various Sermons*), adding: “‘We labor too much, we fast too much, we keep vigil too much,’ when no one can answer even a thousandth—or even the smallest—part of what he owes.”

And Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny (*Book III of the Conferences*, no. 37): “If the equity of judgment is considered, murmuring will cease, because it is profoundly unjust for the accused to accuse the judge when he has received an equal return worthy of his deeds.”

And Grimlaicus (*Rule for Solitaries*, chapter 65): “Let the person who suffers evil learn not to murmur, even if he does not know why he suffers evil; and let him consider that he suffers justly because he is judged by one whose judgments are never unjust.”

### Not a detractor [136]

Not without cause does Saint Bernard compare detractors [Col. 0323A] to foxes, which destroy vineyards, and Peter Damian to locusts, which gnaw away others’ crops. For detraction is nothing other than a biting report against another intended to diminish that person’s glory. Cassian therefore calls it the destructive devouring of the brothers.

We can disclose how great a vice and sin this is neither more clearly nor more eloquently than in the words of Saint Bernard (*Sermon 63, on the Song of Songs*): “Is this tongue not a viper? It is plainly most ferocious, infecting three people so lethally with one breath. Is this tongue not a spear? It is indeed exceedingly sharp, piercing three people with one stroke. ‘Their tongue is a sharp sword’; truly, the sword is double-edged, indeed the detractor’s tongue is three-edged.

“You should not hesitate to call such a tongue more cruel even than the blade by which the Lord’s side was pierced. For this tongue too digs into Christ’s body, member from member; and it does not dig into a body already lifeless, but by digging makes it lifeless.

“It is more harmful even than the thorns that military fury placed upon that sublime head, and than the iron nails that the consummate iniquity of the Jewish people drove into those most holy hands and feet. For unless he had preferred the life of this body, which is now pricked and pierced, to the life of his own body, he would never have surrendered that body, on behalf of this one, to the injury of death and the disgrace of the cross.” [Col. 0323B]

These words seem to agree with those of Gilbert of Holland: “Christ fears the harshness of conduct and the stings of the tongue more than the prickles of thorns—especially in those who have been called to the simplicity of silence, to the work of charity and the repose of leisure, to the school of humility, and to the vow of submission and the bond of unity.”

No one, therefore, should wonder if the ancient Fathers of monks formerly condemned detractors to such severe penalties as those we read in their rules.

For example, Saint Pachomius decrees (*Rule, article 84*) that “one who is quick to detract and says what is untrue, if he is caught in this sin, shall be admonished twice. If he disdains to listen, they shall separate him outside the assembly for seven days, and he shall receive only bread and water until he promises and affirms that he will withdraw from this vice; and then he shall be released.”

When Saint Basil was asked (*Short Rules*, question 26) [Col. 0323C], “What punishment does one deserve who detracts from his brother or listens to someone detracting?” he replied: “Both must be expelled from the company of the others.”

A passage of almost uncertain authorship found with the same Basil says: “If anyone is found detracting from others, or listening to a detractor without rebuking them or reporting them to the archimandrite, let him be excommunicated.”

Saint Columbanus has this in his *Penitential*: “If anyone detracts from his abbot, seven days with one paximatium” (that is, he shall have it as his food, whereas they ordinarily had two paximatia per day, as our Menard observes); “if from his brother, twenty-four psalms; if from a layman, twelve psalms.”

Finally, the *Rule of a Certain Man for Monks* (chapter 26): “If anyone detracts from his elder, he does not detract from the elder but from the Lord, for whom the elder performs his work. If he does this frequently, let him be cut off from the brotherhood and from the care of the fraternal body; but if he repents, his sins are to be forgiven.”

Since they subjected not only detractors but also those who willingly listened to them to penance [137], [Col. 0323D] and since this poison can infiltrate even among servants of God, it may not be out of place to present here the most salutary advice of Saint Bernard (*Sermon 17, Various Sermons*): “The tongue slips easily, and what it says slips no less easily into the heart, so that for many people it has been less beneficial to forbid their own tongue because they did not guard against another’s.

“The brother who speaks to you is useful, wise, religious, and God-fearing; more than that, he is an angel, and an angel of light. Even so, be on your guard lest you hear something by which you are harmed. I do not wish you to suspect the person, but the tongue, especially in ordinary conversation. The person’s simplicity may indeed be good, but in this matter do not lose the serpent’s prudence.”

[Col. 0324A] Nevertheless, someone is not always to be called a detractor merely because he reports something bad about another. Cases sometimes arise in which this is both permitted and necessary. Saint Basil identifies two in particular (*Short Rules*, question 25): “I think, then, that there are two occasions on which it is permissible to say something bad about another. The first is when someone needs to consult with others who have been judged suitable for this purpose, concerning how the person who committed the sin should be corrected. The second is when necessity requires that provision be made for the danger of certain people who, very often through ignorance, might become involved with evil as though it were good, since the Apostle commands that no one associate with such a person, lest someone fall into the snares of his soul, etc.”

### To commit one’s hope to God

For it is good to hope in the Lord rather than to trust in a human being. But what should one hope for from the Lord?

“There is hope for forgiveness, grace, and glory,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 46, Various Sermons*).

For what reason? “I entrust myself confidently to the one who wishes, knows, and is able to save me,” adds the same holy Doctor (*Sermon 20, on the Song of Songs*).

With what result? [Col. 0324B] “Wherever your foot treads, it will be yours. Your foot is certainly your hope; however far it advances, it will take possession—provided that it is fixed entirely upon God, so that it may be firm and not stumble,” Saint Bernard replies again (*Sermon 15 on Psalm 90, and Sermon 32 on the Song of Songs*).

### When he sees some good in himself, let him ascribe it to God, not to himself.

Here belong what I said above in the Prologue. Yet, lest I seem to have left this instrument untouched, I shall explain it in the distinguished words of St. Bernard (Sermon 84 on the *Song of Songs*):

> “From great goods, no small evils commonly arise, when, having been made eminent through the Lord’s goods, we use his gifts as though they had not been given, and do not give glory to God. Thus, certainly, those who seemed greatest on account of the grace they had received are reckoned smallest before God because they have not returned it. But I spare you: I have used the more moderate words ‘greatest’ and ‘smallest,’ but I have not expressed what I feel. I have concealed the distinction; I shall now uncover it. I ought to have said ‘best’ and ‘worst’; for truly and without doubt each person is worst precisely when he is best, if he ascribes to himself that by which he is best—for this is indeed the worst thing of all.  
>
> “But if someone says, ‘Far be it from me; I acknowledge that I am what I am by the grace of God,’ yet strives to seize a little glory for the grace he has received, is he not a thief and a robber? Let such a person hear: ‘By your own mouth I judge you, wicked servant.’ What is more wicked than a servant appropriating the glory of his master?”

St. Gregory the Pope teaches the same doctrine, and illustrates it with this excellent comparison:

> “Those who overcome vices perish when they grow proud over their victory, as the enemy itself falls upon them and destroys them. Eleazar, when he struck down an elephant in battle, felled it, but died beneath the very creature he had destroyed. What, then, does this signify except those who overcome vices but, by growing proud beneath the very things they have subdued, succumb to them? For he dies, as it were, beneath the enemy he has overthrown, who is lifted up by the fault he has overcome.”

### But let him know that every evil has been committed by himself, and reckon it to himself.

Thus Peter Damian, writing to Desiderius, abbot of Monte Cassino:

> “Do not do what many do,” he said (*Book II, Letter 11), “by considering only whatever virtue there may be in you, and neglecting to judge your vices as though they were placed behind your back. Imitate the natural example of the peacock’s diversity: it always keeps its little, seemingly ignoble feet before its eyes, while displaying behind itself the remarkable beauty of its tail, visible to all. In its feet it sees something rustic to despise; behind itself it carries what enables it to be proud, as though it surpassed the other birds.  
>
> “Let whatever virtue there is in you likewise be hidden, in a certain sense. But if there is anything vicious and deserving correction, let it never withdraw from the judgment of your sight.”

### To fear the day of judgment.

Whoever does not fear the day of judgment must rightly be said to lack judgment and to be rejected:

> “For it is an irremediable danger,” says St. Augustine—or whoever the author may be (*Sermon 154 in the Appendix to the Sermons)—“to loosen the reins to vices and desires in such a way that one does not remember that one will have to render an account to God. I think that it is already a great punishment of sin to have lost the fear and memory of the future judgment.”

### To dread Gehenna.

And who would not dread it, when even the greatest of the saints trembled utterly at the mere thought of Gehenna? Who among us was holier than St. Bernard? Yet who could hear him trembling without trembling himself?

> “I tremble,” he says (*Sermon 16 on the Song of Songs), “at the teeth of the infernal beast, at the belly of hell, at the roaring creatures prepared for food. I shudder at the gnawing worm and the consuming fire, at smoke and vapor, sulfur, and the spirit of storms. I shudder at the outer darkness. Who will give water to my head and a fountain of tears to my eyes, so that by my weeping I may anticipate the weeping, the gnashing of teeth, the harsh bonds of hands and feet, and the weight of chains that press, constrict, and burn without consuming?”

St. Pachomius likewise drove away evil thoughts with a similar terror, as we read in chapter 29 of his *Life*.

### To desire eternal life with every spiritual longing.

For, as St. Bernard says (*Sermon on the Feast of St. Martin*), God

> “therefore made man upright even in body, and gave man a lofty face, whereas the other animals look down toward the earth, so that, raising his countenance toward the stars, he might sigh for the place where he sees so blessed and everlasting a dwelling. For is not the sight of so luminous a dwelling, to those who contemplate it devoutly and faithfully, a most powerful incentive to love and an incitement to the most ardent desire?”

See also his Sermons 12 and 19 *On Various Subjects*, and Sermon 33 on the *Song of Songs*.

### To keep death daily before one’s eyes as something to be feared.

[139] St. John Climacus calls the frequent daily meditation on death “daily death” (*Ladder*, step 6), and describes its usefulness in these elegant words:

> “Just as bread is most necessary among all kinds of food, so among all actions the meditation on death is most necessary. The remembrance of death produces labors and pious exercises in those who live among a community of brothers; indeed, it produces a desire for contempt and sweetness.
