But to those who live in solitude, away from the crowds, it brings neglect of every care, suggests perpetual prayers, and promotes watchfulness of mind. . . . True and effective meditation on death utterly kills gluttony; and when gluttony has been overcome, all the vices likewise lie defeated.”

At the end of the same step he adds:

> “It is impossible,” someone has said, “it is impossible for us to pass the present day sufficiently piously and religiously unless we regard that very day as the final and last day of our whole life. And it is truly remarkable that even pagan writers—Plato and Seneca—have uttered something of this kind, saying that the pursuit of wisdom is nothing other than meditation on death.”

Evagrius appears to have held the same view when he said:

> “The monk should always be ready as though he were going to die the next day; and he should likewise use his body as though he were going to live with it for many years.”

The same is found in St. Anthony’s Rule, no. 41:

> “Consider within yourself and say: ‘Certainly I shall not remain in this world beyond the present day,’ and you will not sin against God.”

The same is read in the Rule of Abbot Isaiah, no. 12. St. Pachomius also frequently commended remembrance of death, saying (*Life*, chapter 46):

> “Whoever always considers these things obtains purity of mind, acquires humility of heart, rejects vain glory, and strives to be free from every worldly prudence.”

Our ancient Fathers considered the remembrance of death so necessary that, in order that it might adhere more firmly to the monks’ minds, they wanted an open tomb always to be kept in the church or cloister. Haeftenus testifies that this was once customary in the Benedictine Order (*Commentary on the Life of St. Benedict*, chapter 37). See John Climacus, step 7, and Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 15, chapter 23.

### To guard the acts of one’s life at every hour.

This instrument follows from the preceding one; for it is impossible, when thinking of death, not to guard one’s life. St. Bernard teaches most beautifully how necessary this self-watchfulness is when, explaining the words of the *Song of Songs*, “As a lily among thorns, so is my beloved among daughters,” he says (*Sermon 48 on the Song of Songs*):

> “If the soul itself is the lily, according to the Bridegroom’s word, let it see how watchful and solicitous it ought to be concerning its own keeping, surrounded on every side by thorns that thrust out their prickles here and there. . . . The world is full of thorns. They are on the earth, they are in the air, they are in your flesh. See, therefore, how cautiously you must walk among thorns.”

And elsewhere (*Sermon 82 on Various Subjects*):

> “People of this world are accustomed to say: ‘He guards a good fortress who guards his body.’ But not so with us: he guards a vile dungheap who guards his body. . . . The fortress of the soul must be guarded more carefully, since from it eternal life proceeds. But a fortress situated in the land of enemies is attacked on every side, and therefore must be fortified with every kind of protection—that is, with vigilant care on every side: below, above, before and behind, on the right and on the left.  
>
> “Below, the desire of the flesh attacks, which wages war against the soul, because the flesh desires against the spirit. Above, the terrible judgment of God hangs over us; for it is terrible to fall into the hands of the living God. Behind is the deadly pleasure arising from the recollection of past sins. Before us are the temptations that press upon us. On the left is the unrest caused by the murmuring of arrogant brothers. On the right is the devotion of obedient brothers. These too, unless care is taken, can harm us in two ways: either by making us envious of their good works, or by making us imitate their singular grace,” and so forth.

### To know for certain that God sees one everywhere.

Nothing is more effective for guarding all the acts of life than to know for certain that God sees one everywhere.

> “For when can he become negligent who never ceases to behold God beholding him, who sees God intent upon him in such a way that God never ceases to consider all his inward and outward things at every hour, and examines and judges not only all his actions but even the most subtle movements of his soul?”

Thus says St. Bernard (*Sermon 2 on Psalm 90*). Hence St. Basil also says (*Short Rules*, question 21):

> “Whoever does this—that is, thinks that he is seen by God—or anything similar, will never wander about, nor will he have leisure to indulge in vain thoughts or to think anything that does not pertain to the edification of faith and the benefit of the soul. How much less will he dare to think anything opposed to God or displeasing to him!”

This passage of the Rule may nevertheless be understood in another way: that “God sees us” means that he cares for us and directs his attention to our salvation, so that we may direct our attention solely to him who directs his attention toward us with such love, according to the words of the Apostle Peter:

> “Casting all your care upon him, for he cares for you” (1 Peter 5).

How great that care is, the author of the treatise *On Charity* explains excellently in chapter 23, in St. Bernard’s fifth volume.

### To dash evil thoughts coming to one’s heart against Christ, and to disclose them to a spiritual elder.

To dash the evil thoughts that come to our hearts against Christ means, according to Smaragdus,

> “to implore Christ’s help against their allurements, so that one may emerge victorious; to entrust one’s hope to Christ, to believe faithfully and hope firmly in him, and not to take pleasure in the victory of the triumph for oneself, but to give thanks to Christ.”

Or, as Bernard of Monte Cassino says, to dash them against Christ means to do so through remembrance of his Passion and through devout prayer; for Christ himself is the bronze serpent, and whoever looks upon him will by no means perish from the deadly bite of the infernal serpent.

What St. Benedict adds—“to disclose them to a spiritual elder”—we shall explain in chapter 7. Here it is enough to note that, with Boherius, the spiritual elder is to be understood as the superior of each monastery. Though he may sometimes be younger in age, he is rightly called greater and senior by reason of his jurisdiction. Richard of St. Angelo, however, interprets “spiritual elder” as a priest-confessor.

### To guard one’s mouth from evil or corrupt speech.

For the mouth of the just ought to meditate on righteousness. Moreover,

> “evil speech is speech that is not good; corrupt speech is speech that is more harmful than evil,”

says Hildemar.

### Not to love speaking much.

For in much speaking you will not escape sin. Yet this does not altogether prohibit speaking much. Some are compelled to it, willingly or unwillingly, either by the law of charity or by the requirements of their office, such as abbots and cellarers. But “not to love speaking much” condemns that destructive eagerness to speak which Abbot Agatho compared to a great fire (*in St. Dorotheus, Teaching 4, no. 9*), which, when it blazes up, forces everyone to withdraw far from its sight.

### Not to speak vain or laughter-provoking words.

As Gerard the Belgian monk piously, devoutly, and truthfully said:

> “Never are even the most amusing jokes more tasteless than in the mouth of a monk; nor is anything more unworthy or detestable than mimic gestures and simian behavior in such a mournful garment.”

Hence the Rule of Tarnant, chapter 18:

> “Whoever dares to utter anything jocular or suitable for laughter in the assembly of the brothers, or whoever wishes to tell idle words to the younger brothers or to maintain friendships with those of immature age, shall, as he deserves, be subjected to correction.”

### Not to love excessive or uncontrolled laughter.

[142] Tears suit monks much more than laughter. Hence the Master says in his Rule:

> “If he sees a brother very quick to laughter, let the superior present admonish him, saying: ‘What are you doing, brother? Do with seriousness what you are doing, because the time of conversion is not a time of joy for laughter, but of penance for mourning over sins.’”

Similarly, before him, St. Basil says (*Short Rules*, question 31):

> “Since the Lord condemns those who laugh in this life, it is entirely clear that no place at all is given to the faithful in which to laugh, especially amid so great a number of those who dishonor God by transgressing the law and die in sin. Over these one ought to mourn and groan.”

After them Smaragdus says on this passage:

> “We are in a valley of tears, and therefore we ought not to laugh but to mourn. We ought to have tears for our sins, tears for the dissolution of the body, tears from desire for the Redeemer and for the fellowship of all the angels and all the saints, tears so that we may be freed from the punishments of hell and from the snares of the devil.”

St. Benedict, however, does not here prohibit every kind of laughter, but excessive or uncontrolled laughter, as an indication of a negligent mind and a dissolute spirit, in the words of St. Bernard (*On the Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 8). For, says St. Basil (*Long Rules*, chapter 17), to smile gently and to express inward joy is not unbecoming; this is shown by the Scripture that says, “When the heart is cheerful, the face flourishes.”

What, then, should the laughter of monks be like? Certainly it should be like that which St. Bernard describes in St. Malachy (*Sermon on St. Malachy*):

> “Laughter either indicating charity or provoking it; yet even then rare—sometimes drawn forth, never uncontrolled—so that it might announce the joy of the heart without diminishing the grace of the mouth, but rather increasing it; so modest that it could not be suspected of levity; yet so slight that it would suffice to preserve a cheerful face from every blemish or cloud of sadness.”

Add what St. Dorotheus says (*Teaching 19, no. 24*):

> “When it is necessary to laugh, take care not to expose your teeth in your laughter.”

St. Benedict therefore permits this kind of laughter and prohibits every other kind. Along with him, it is prohibited not only by St. Basil and the Master cited above, but also by the Rule of Paul and Stephen, chapter 37, as an occasion of dissension and scandal; by St. John Climacus, step 7, no. 6, and step 26, no. 35; and by St. Leander in his book or Rule *On the Instruction of Virgins*, in which he devotes an entire chapter, chapter 11, to the title “That it is a sin for a virgin to laugh” (*Analecta*, volume 4, p. 462).

In former times, moreover, in our Order,

> “the Circators observed this: if they saw anyone laughing or whispering something, he was immediately noted on the tablets and corrected most kindly at the proper time,”

as is read in the *Customs of St. Benedict of Aniane*.

Trithemius notes here that laughter is especially unbecoming to four classes of people: to virgins, because of modesty; to women, because of propriety; to the sick, because of their weakness, since loud laughter disturbs them; and to monks, because of the eminence of their state.

### To hear holy readings willingly.

He did not say “to read willingly,” but “to hear willingly,” because, as Bernard of Monte Cassino notes, some are unable to read because of impaired sight or another infirmity. Or, as Trithemius says, because in the time of St. Benedict some were admitted to the habit who were entirely ignorant of letters. So that none of them might be deprived of the fruit of sacred reading, they were at least commanded to hear it read by others.

Or “to hear willingly” means to offer free and voluntary assent of heart to what is read and to carry it out in practice. For what benefit is there in reading much and learning much, unless we do much? “For whoever knows the good and does not do it, to him it is sin.”

Here St. Benedict does not permit just any readings to monks, but holy ones: sacred Scripture; the passions of the holy martyrs; the lives and conferences of the Fathers; and the writings of the holy doctors that contribute to the formation of morals. Reading all these is of the greatest benefit to monks, especially the young, to whom William, abbot of St. Thierry, commends it in writing to the brothers of Mont-Dieu:

> “The outward deeds of our Redeemer are proposed for reading and meditation more safely, and in them an example of humility, an incentive to charity, and an expression of piety are displayed. From the holy Scriptures and the holy treatises of the Fathers, moral and clearer matters should be proposed. The deeds and passions of the saints should be placed before him, where there is no labor over the plainness of the historical narrative, and where something will always arise to stir the novice’s soul to love of God and contempt of himself.  
>
> “Other histories, to be sure, give pleasure while they are read, but they do not edify. Rather, they infect the mind and, at the time of prayer or spiritual meditation, cause all kinds of useless or harmful things to well up from the memory.”

[143] Let the books of the pagans therefore be far from our hands, and far from us the deceptions of poets and philosophers, since they turn the mind away from true blessedness—unless perhaps they are used to refute their absurdities and to confirm the mysteries of our faith, according to St. Augustine:

> “As for the philosophers who are so called, if by chance they have said anything true and suited to our faith—especially the Platonists—not only should they not be feared, but what they possess should also be claimed for our use from them as from unjust possessors.”

Peter Damian agrees in these words:

> “He takes treasure from the Egyptians, from which to build a tabernacle for God, who reads poets and philosophers, through whom he may grow more capable of penetrating the mysteries of heavenly speech.”

But this is not for everyone; it is for learned men alone, and not even for all of them, but only for those to whom the abbot assigns it. As for the simple monk who devotes himself to such trifles, we could rightly say to him, with Peter the Venerable writing to Peter of Poitiers:

> “Why, in empty study, do you recite with comedians, mourn with tragedians, play with writers of verse, deceive with poets, and allow yourself to be deceived by philosophers? Why do you devote yourself not merely to philosophy—but, if I may say so without offending you—to such great folly? Folly, I say, for this too is the saying of the true Philosopher: ‘Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?’  
>
> “Run, therefore, my son, toward the one fruit of all philosophy appointed for you by the heavenly Teacher: the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven. You will not attain it except through true poverty of spirit. For if, according to the Apostle, you wish to be wise, become foolish so that you may be wise. Do not glory in knowing the chatter of logic, the curiosity of physics, or anything else, except Christ—and him crucified.”

Or, with Paschasius Radbertus writing to Odilmannus:

> “It is not our work, brother and fellow elder, to turn over again the false tales of poets or the Milesian stories, since our discipline demands other morals; nor is it our work to scrutinize the books of philosophers, since in the one there is play and amusement, while in the other there is difficulty and labor mixed with sweat. Rather, it is more fitting for us to persist continually in laments and mourning.”

Indeed, concerning Blessed Alcuin it is reported (*Life*, no. 19):

> “As a young man he had read the books of the ancient philosophers and the lies of Virgil, which he no longer wished either to hear or to have his disciples read. ‘The divine Poets are sufficient for you,’ he said, ‘and you have no need to pollute yourselves with the luxurious eloquence of Virgil.’”

Syrus writes the same words about St. Majolus in *Life*, book I, chapter 14. See the *Life of St. Odo*, fifth century of the Benedictine period; the *Life of St. Hugh, Abbot of Cluny*, by Hildebert of Le Mans, no. 18, in Bollandus, April 29; and the Rule of St. Isidore, chapter 9.

### To devote oneself frequently to prayer.

Following the example of St. Martin, concerning whom Sulpicius Severus writes (*Life*, book I):

> “Never did an hour or moment pass in which he was not either engaged in prayers or devoted to reading. Even while reading, or if he happened to be doing something else, he never relaxed his mind from prayer. Indeed, just as it is the custom of blacksmiths, who, while working, strike their anvil to relieve their labor, so Martin, even while he seemed to be doing something else, was always praying.”

And certainly, as Evagrius said most admirably (*Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, volume 3, p. 95):

> “We were not commanded always to work, keep vigil, and fast; but the law ordained that we pray without interruption.”

Since prayer is the monks’ proper occupation, it may perhaps not be displeasing to demonstrate briefly here what prayer is, what its power and efficacy are, what its necessity is, what dispositions are required for it, and in what manner it should be made.

St. Augustine—or whoever the author may be—teaches what prayer is in these words (*Sermon 73 in the Appendix to the Sermons*):

> “Prayer is the ascent of the soul from earthly things to heavenly things, the seeking of what is above, the desire for invisible things.”

St. John Climacus says (*Ladder*, step 28):

> “If you consider its nature or quality, prayer is familiar conversation and union between man and God.”

Similarly, William of St. Thierry says (*On the Solitary Life*, chapter 14):

> “Prayer is the affection of a person clinging to God, a certain familiar and devout conversation, and the standing of an enlightened mind in order to enjoy him for as long as this is permitted.”

Finally, the author of the treatise *On the Inner House*, quoted by St. Bernard, says:

> “Prayer is devotion of mind—that is, conversion toward God through a devout and humble affection: humble because of awareness of one’s own weakness, devout because of consideration of divine clemency.”

We cannot describe the efficacy of prayer more elegantly than in the words of St. John Climacus (*Ladder*, step 28):

> “If you consider its power and efficacy, prayer is the preservation of the world, reconciliation with God, mother of tears and again daughter of tears, propitiation for sins, a bulwark against the assault of afflictions, the suppression and extinguishing of wars, the office of angels, nourishment for all spirits, future joy, eternal action, a fountain of virtues, mediator of divine graces, spiritual progress, nourishment of the soul, illumination of the mind, an axe against despair, a declaration of hope, the dissolution of sadness, the riches of monks, the treasure of solitaries, the diminution of anger, and the mirror of religious progress,” and so forth.

John Trithemius demonstrates its necessity, especially for a monk (*Spiritual Exercises of the Monk*, consideration 6), when he says:

> “Just as breath is always necessary for the life of the flesh, so continuous prayer is altogether necessary for the health of the mind.”

Hence John Baptist de Lezana says (*On Monastic Discipline*, chapter 3):

> “I would more easily believe that a man could exist without a soul than that a perfect religious life could exist without prayer. Nor is it less improper to call a corpse a man than to call a religious without prayer a perfect religious.”

As for dispositions, some are remote and others immediate. The remote dispositions are purity of heart, flight from worldly affairs, and the mortification of passions and affections. The immediate dispositions are place, time, attention, and so forth. These should be established by the testimony of a few of the Fathers.

[Col. 0330A] First, therefore, sincere purity of heart is required for praying well. For although prayer is a gift of God, and, as Gilbert of Holland says (*Sermon 17 on the Song of Songs*), “it is not ours to confine the generosity of the divine gift within a rule,” nevertheless,

> “if human effort can contribute anything to this, observe this first: ‘Wash yourselves; be clean.’”

Indeed, if prayer is familiar union with God, how will one who is turned away from him by sin be able to pray? [145] Peter Damian, writing to Pope Alexander, says rightly (*Book I, Letter 15):

> “If some stranger breaks into the king’s chamber and stands before him as though he were a familiar friend, he nevertheless does not enjoy the king’s conversation, because he is not dear to him through the grace of an earlier acquaintance. So we too, unhappy and wretched—as I speak of those like myself—often stand alone in the seclusion of a narrow cell. Trembling, we stand before the gaze of the divine majesty, yet, because our sins obstruct us, we do not deserve either the spark of inward splendor or the grace of compunction. Thus we seem to stand before the presence of the King; but because we are not known to him through uprightness of life, we do not taste the sweetness of inward conversation.”

Second, renunciation of worldly affairs disposes one to pray well, so that, as the aforementioned Gilbert says, we may acquire wisdom in a time of leisure, “for whoever diminishes activity will receive it.” Hence Peter Damian says in the passage cited above:

> “A mind darkened by earthly affairs strives in vain to raise itself to the height of contemplation, while it is weighed down by the gathered rubble of worldly actions. For just as leather, after passing through muddy streams of clay, does not admit grease, so the human mind, unless it has been stripped of the moisture of worldly care, does not receive the grace of heavenly richness.”

And Gilbert of Holland, writing on the words of the *Song of Songs*, “On my bed by night I sought him whom my soul loves,” says:

> “In the crowd, in public, Jesus is scarcely touched. Therefore the bride, who desires not merely to touch but to embrace and handle him, avoiding the public place, chose secrecy, the bed, and the night.”

Third, there must be sincere mortification of the passions and of the flesh, as Peter Damian demonstrates by this familiar comparison:

> “A dry string gives a clear sound of harmony; when moist, it gives a dull one. A drum also sounds deaf if any moisture dampens it. So the human mind must be dry of the pleasure of the flesh, so that its prayer may be sharp in the ears of almighty God.”

Fourth, a suitable place for prayer must be sought: remote and secluded from every disturbance. For Christ commands one who wishes to pray to enter his room and close the door.

Fifth, says St. Bernard (*Sermon 86 on the Song of Songs*):

> “The person who wishes to pray must observe not only the place but also the time. A time free from other business is more convenient and suitable; especially when the deep sleep of night imposes silence, for then prayer will be freer and purer:
>
> “‘Arise at night, at the beginning of your watches, and pour out your heart like water before the sight of the Lord your God.’
>
> “How securely prayer rises at night, with God alone as witness, together with the holy angel who receives it to present it upon the heavenly altar! How pleasing and luminous it is, colored with a modest blush! How serene and peaceful, disturbed by no shouting or noise!”

Sixth, the greatest attention is required. For, as St. Cyprian says (*On the Lord’s Prayer*):

> “What kind of sluggishness is it to be distracted and carried away by foolish and profane thoughts while you are entreating the Lord, as though there were something else you ought to consider more than what you are saying while speaking with God? How do you ask to be heard when you do not hear yourself? Do you wish God to remember you when you pray, while you yourself are not mindful of yourself? This is to fail entirely to guard against the enemy; this is, when you pray to God, to offend God’s majesty through negligence in prayer.”

[Col. 0331A] Finally—and this is proper to this instrument—in order to pray well, prayer must be frequent and continual, as Scripture teaches us in many places. Certainly,

> “whoever is accustomed to pray only at the time when his knees are bent prays very little,”

says Abbot Isaac in Cassian (*Conference 10, chapter 14*).

### To confess one’s past sins to God daily in prayer with tears or groaning, and thereafter to amend oneself with regard to those evils.

St. Anthony prescribes something similar (*Rule*, no. 23):

> “Be sorrowful,” he says, “day and night for your sin; light your lamp with the oil of your eyes, namely, with tears.”

And again (no. 30):

> “Do not boast, and do not laugh at all. Take care to mourn over your sin, as one mourns when someone has died.”

And likewise (no. 44):

> “Force yourself to pray continually with tears, so that perhaps God may have mercy on you and strip you of the old man.”

But let us examine St. Benedict’s text.

Here the Holy Father chiefly commands five things. First, confession of sins, which, as St. Bernard says (*Letter 113*),

> “is the life of the sinner, the glory of the just, necessary to the sinner, and nevertheless fitting for the just.”

Second, he wants that confession to concern past sins, for he desires them not to be present. He calls “past” those sins committed in the world before conversion. Once conversion has taken place, he did not wish any such sin to be committed by the person whose life ought to have become wholly angelic, as Hildemar observes.

Or this may be because, as Bernard of Monte Cassino says:

> “The remembrance of past sins is useful, because presumption is removed through it, humility is preserved, and the virtue of good action is acquired, just as the addition of manure makes the earth more fertile and fruitful.”

Candidus uses the same comparison in the *Life of Eigil, Abbot of Fulda*, no. 26.

Third, this is to be done with tears or groaning: because one has offended God of supreme goodness and infinite clemency; because through sin one has made oneself a servant of the devil; because through a brief and momentary pleasure one has lost the eternal joys of heaven; and because one has deserved the fires of Gehenna that never end.

And rightly with tears, because,

> “just as fire consumes straw, so sincere tears wash away and erase whatever filth is apparent or hidden,”

as St. John Climacus says (*Ladder*, step 7).

St. Benedict did not simply say “with tears,” but appropriately added “or groaning,” because there are many whom God does not grant the grace of tears, yet who can nevertheless groan salutarily. Thus Blessed Alcuin (*Life*, no. 14, fourth century of the Benedictine period, part I)

> “offered secret prayer every day . . . with the prolonged extension of his hands in the form of a cross . . . and with many groans, for he was rarely able to have tears.”

By contrast, St. Benedict, abbot of Aniane, concerning whom Smaragdus writes (*Life*, no. 56, in the same work):

> “Who ever found him alone except weeping? Who, entering upon him suddenly, found his cheeks dry? Who did not find him either completely prostrate on the ground, or standing with his hands raised toward heaven? Who did not find him receiving his tears in his fists, lest the pages of the sacred volume be excessively moistened by his weeping?”

See the *Life of St. Philibert*, nos. 6 and 12; the *Life of St. Ansbert*, no. 9; the *Life of St. Cuthbert*, chapter 16, second century of the Benedictine period; the *Life of St. Adalard*, by Paschasius, no. 25; and the *Life of his brother Wala*, book I, chapter 10, where similar things are reported.

Fourth, St. Benedict commands this to be done daily, because

> “there should be no joy for criminals in prison, nor gladness on earth for true monks” (St. John Climacus, step 7).

Yet some discretion must be used in this. Thus St. Bernard, addressing his own people, said (*Sermon 11 on the Song of Songs*):

> “I advise you, my friends, sometimes to turn your foot away from the burdensome and anxious recollection of your ways, and to escape onto the smoother paths of a more serene remembrance of God’s benefits, so that, while you are confounded in yourselves, you may breathe again by looking upon him. I want you to experience what the prophet counsels when he says: ‘Delight in the Lord, and he will give you the desires of your heart.’  
>
> “Sorrow for sins is certainly necessary; but if it is not continuous, let it be interrupted by a happier remembrance of divine goodness, lest perhaps the heart be hardened by excessive sadness and perish through despair. Let us mix honey with wormwood, so that its salutary bitterness may be able to give health when it can be drunk tempered with the sweetness mingled into it.”

Fifth and finally, one must thereafter amend oneself with regard to those very evils, because,

> “this is true repentance: when a person is converted in such a way that he does not return, when he repents in such a way that he does not repeat the sin,”

says St. Augustine—or whoever the author may be (*Sermon 117 in the Appendix*).

And certainly, as Smaragdus says on this passage:

> “Whoever bewails sin and commits sin again is like someone who washes an unbaked brick: the more he washes it, the more mud he makes.”

Peter Damian puts it most aptly (*Opusculum* 52, chapter 22; see also book II, letter 13, and St. Bernard, Sermon 3 on the *Song of Songs*):

> “When the serpent desires to drink, it first vomits out its venom. But after drinking enough water, it returns to the place where it vomited and takes up its vomit again. So we too, when we desire to drink in the streams of heavenly speech, must vomit out through the effort of pure confession all the poisons of our vices and falls. But far be it from us to return to our vomit!”

### Not to fulfill the desires of the flesh.

According to the words of the Apostle Peter:

> “Beloved, I beseech you, as strangers and pilgrims, to abstain from fleshly desires, which wage war against the soul.”

### To hate one’s own will

“Own will,” says Smaragdus, as do Petrus the Deacon, cited by Bernard of Cassino and by Boherius, is that which is private and exclusively one’s own—something which no one else approves and which no one declares to be just. Or, according to Saint Bernard (*Sermon 2 for Eastertide*):

> “I call ‘own will’ that which is not shared with God and human beings, but is ours alone: when we do what we want not for God’s honor, not for the benefit of our brothers, but for our own sake, paying no attention to pleasing God and benefiting our brothers, but only to satisfying the inclinations of our own minds.”

It is this kind of will that we are here [Col. 0332C] commanded to hate, and rightly so. For, as Saint Peter Damian—or whoever else may be the author—says (*Sermon on Saint Benedict*):

> “No burden is heavier for a human being than the human being himself. What tyrant is more cruel, what power more savage toward a person, than that person’s own will? One may never rest from it, never sit down; and the more it realizes that you are worn out obeying it, the more it presses, goads, and burdens you, forgetful of compassion and ignorant of mercy. For this is peculiar to own will: the more obedient someone has become to it, the more cruelly it binds him in its chains.”

Nor does own will exercise its tyranny over us only in the present age; it does so much more fully in the future, since it procures our eternal damnation. Hence Saint Bernard (*Sermon 11 on Various Matters*) says:

> “Let us beware of own will as of the worst and most wicked viper, which alone can henceforth condemn our souls.”

And elsewhere (*Sermon 2 for Eastertide*):

> “Let own will cease, and hell will not exist.”

In Cassian (*Conference 24, chapter 23*), Abbot [Col. 0332D] Abraham says:

> “Our ruin is the delight of the present life, or, to put it more explicitly, the carrying out of our own desires and wishes.”

### To obey the abbot’s commands in everything

This accords with the saying of Scripture:

> “You shall do whatever those who preside over the place that the Lord will choose tell you, and whatever they teach you according to his law; you shall follow their judgment and shall not turn aside to the right or to the left. But the person who acts arrogantly and refuses to obey the command of the priest who at that time ministers to the Lord your God, and the decree of the judge—that person shall die, and you shall remove the evil from Israel” (*Deuteronomy 17*).

And indeed, as Saint Basil reasons (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 20):

> “If someone entrusts himself to some manual craftsman, one of those whose skills are useful to us in this present life, he obeys him in every way, contradicts none of his orders in anything, does not abandon him even slightly, but remains continually before his instructor’s eyes, and expects food, drink, and the rest of his regimen [Col. 0333A] only in accordance with the prescription laid down by him—how much more will those who approach the discipline of piety and holiness, having once persuaded themselves that they can acquire such knowledge from this instructor, show their superiors complete compliance and the most exact obedience. They will not demand an account from their instructors, but will carry out their work—unless, perhaps, they ought to ask and be instructed with proper and fitting reverence concerning whatever they do not know to be conducive to their salvation.”

What Saint Benedict says about obeying in everything must, however, be understood cautiously.

First, with regard to sins, no obedience is owed to superiors who command them. Among others, this is taught by Saint Basil (*Brief Rules*, question 114), Saint Bernard (*Sermon 41 on Various Matters* and Letter 7), Peter of Blois (*Letter 131*), and Saint Teresa (*Foundations of Her Monasteries*, chapter 17).

Second, the abbot cannot command the monks anything that is not in the Rule, or at least not in accordance with the Rule [Col. 0333B]; nor are the brothers bound to obey him in such a case. Peter the Venerable teaches this in a letter to Saint Bernard, in these words (*Book I, Letter 28, toward the end*):

> “Just as we know that those who flee the pleasures of the world and embrace its hardships with discretion for the sake of greater merit are altogether worthy of praise, so we say that those who wish to force others violently into what they have not undertaken and what is not expedient are not to be heeded at all.”

And Saint Bernard, in his letter to Simon, abbot of Saint Nicholas (*Letter 84*):

> “They should be invited to a stricter life, not compelled, since you once consented to preside over them in the Cluniac order.”

Elsewhere the holy Doctor gives this reason (*On the Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 4):

> “The will of the superior is prescribed a considerable limit by the fact that the person who professes does indeed promise obedience, but not unlimited obedience—rather, obedience specifically according to the Rule, and no other Rule than that of Saint Benedict. Thus the one who presides must not loosen the reins of his own will over his subjects, but must know the measure fixed for him by the Rule [Col. 0333C], and so regulate his commands only with respect to what has been established as right—not every kind of right, but only what the aforesaid Father instituted, or at least what is in accordance with what he instituted. For the profession is expressed in this way: ‘I promise—not the Rule itself, but obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, not according to the will of the superior,’” and so forth.

Third, just as the abbot may command nothing beyond the Rule, so he may command nothing against or short of the Rule—for example, that a healthy monk eat meat, abstain from the nocturnal vigils, or do anything of that sort; nor are the brothers bound to obey such a command. “Therefore,” Saint Bernard again says (*On the Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 5), “neither the command nor the prohibition of the superior should pass beyond the limits of the profession. It may extend no farther, nor contract to less: let the superior prohibit me from none of the things I promised, and demand no more than I promised. Let him neither increase my vows without my consent nor diminish them without certain necessity.” The reason is that “without necessity, relaxation of a vow is not dispensation [Col. 0333D] but transgression,” as the same holy Doctor puts it.

### Even if he himself, God forbid, acts otherwise

Obeying the command of the Apostle Peter:

> “Servants, be subject with all fear to your masters, not only to the good and gentle, but also to the harsh; for authority and the power to command reside in them. They do not forfeit these through bad character, and, no less than the good, they exercise Christ’s role toward us.”

Accordingly, Peter Damian aptly applies the following to this passage (*Opuscle 13, chapter 20*):

> “Do not, he says, debate the merits of your priors, who may perhaps be living wickedly; consider not the path by which they walk, but whose place they occupy, and obey them humbly in Christ.”

Remembering the Lord’s command:

> “Do what they say, but do not do what they do.”

Peter of Blois appears to have had this in mind when he said (*Letter 131*):

> “If the abbot is of a worse way of life, nevertheless one ought to obey him out of charity; for it is written: ‘Do what they say, but do not do what they do.’”

### [Col. 0334A] Not wishing to be called holy before one is holy, but first to be what one is more truly called

We must all desire holiness and practice good works, since God commanded this above all:

> “Be holy, for I am holy.”

But wishing to be called holy is not characteristic of Christians, much less of monks, but of pagans—unless it is done with regard to fraternal charity. “For there are occasions,” says Saint Bernard (*Sermon 83 on Various Matters*), “when we receive human praise beneficially, solely out of regard for fraternal charity and for the salvation of those who therefore more readily heed us,” as the Apostle did when he himself proclaimed his preaching and revelations. Outside circumstances of this kind, however, anyone who desires human praise resembles a naked person who seeks to find some torn and worn garment—or anything else at all—with which to cover his nakedness and disgrace, says Saint Dorotheus.

What is added—“but first to be what one is more truly called”—must not be understood as though, after acquiring holiness, it were lawful to desire human praise. Rather, he wanted us first to be holy, so that if we should ever be proclaimed holy against our will, [Col. 0334B] the statement might then be true.

### To fulfill God’s commandments daily by one’s deeds

Peter the Venerable elegantly explains what we should understand here by “God’s commandments” in a letter to Saint Bernard (*Book I, Letter 28*):

> “By divine commandments we mean not only those which the Divinity, appearing in the flesh, personally delivered to human beings, or those which he established through the Apostles as matters to be held, or those which he commanded through patriarchs or prophets before assuming flesh; we also mean those which, after the Apostles, apostolic men following in the Apostles’ footsteps commanded to be observed by the unanimous agreement of many. For the same divine Spirit who, infusing himself into the hearts of the earlier Fathers, gave through them commandments suited to human salvation has not ceased, through those who appear more recent, to work human salvation by commanding salutary things.”

### To love chastity

This is because of its supreme excellence, which “makes us familiar with God and, insofar as human nature permits, makes us like him,” as Saint John Climacus says (*Ladder 15*), or at least makes us like the angels themselves, according to the common judgment of the Fathers, especially Saint Bernard, abbot, who writes to Henry, bishop of Sens, concerning chastity (*Letter 42*):

> “What is more beautiful than chastity? It makes one pure from seed conceived in uncleanness, a member of the household from an enemy, and finally an angel from a human being. [Col. 0334C] A chaste human being and an angel do differ from one another, but in happiness, not in virtue. And although the chastity of the angel is happier, that of the human being is nevertheless recognized as stronger.”

Peter the Venerable held the same view. In a letter to his nieces Margaret and Pontia he writes (*Book VI, Letter 39*):

> “It is not patience, nor humility, nor charity, nor any other virtue that is called the sister of the angels, but virginity. Hence blessed Jerome says: ‘The angel is rightly sent to the virgin, because virginity is always akin to the angels.’ Certainly, to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not earthly life but heavenly life. Thus, to acquire angelic glory in the flesh is a greater merit than to possess it; to be an angel is a matter of happiness, but to be a virgin is a matter of virtue.”

And below:

> “Why should I pursue the praise of chastity at greater length? Chastity made an angel, and whoever preserves it is an angel.”

It should be noted that Saint Benedict did not precisely say “to love virginity,” but “to love chastity,” because virginity is a virtue belonging to few, and is understood to consist in the incorruption not only of the body but also of the heart. [Col. 0334D] Indeed, the following saying is attributed to Saint Basil, whose chastity Saint Gregory of Nazianzus so highly commends in his funeral oration in his praise:

> “I know no woman, yet I am not a virgin.”

And in a letter to his disciple Chilo he himself says:

> “I avoided the disgrace of fornication, but by the secret thought of my heart I defiled the flower of virginal purity.”

Yet everyone can be chaste even after losing virginity.

Moreover, since we are commanded to love chastity, we are therefore commanded to guard it with the greatest zeal. Here the error of certain people must plainly be reproved. [Col. 0335A] Boherius writes that, because they read nothing about chastity anywhere in the Rule, they claimed that a monk did not vow chastity—as though the monastic profession did not include the vow of chastity just as it includes the vows of poverty and obedience. And should we not be ashamed, while serving in Christ’s army, to live unchastely, when chastity was maintained in the camps of ancient soldiers, especially the Romans, as Bernard of Cassino writes? Indeed, this is said to be the origin of the word *castrum*—a camp—because the soldiers living there appeared to be castrated.

Many things contribute to preserving the precious treasure of chastity, and it may not be entirely pointless to gather them here as well. These include, above all, fasting, avoidance of idleness, remembrance of the last things, frequent reception of the Eucharist, prayer, humility, awareness of God’s presence, patience, solitude, and avoidance of women. I shall say a little about these.

First, whoever desires to preserve chastity uncorrupted must, above all, afflict the body by fasting. [Col. 0335B] The common proverb says:

> “Without Ceres and Bacchus, Venus grows cold,”

and conversely. Hence Saint Ambrose (*Book I on Penance*) says:

> “Lust is a heavy fire, and therefore we must not provide it with fuel. Lust is fed by banquets, nourished by delicacies, kindled by wine, and set ablaze by drunkenness.”

And Saint John Climacus (*Ladder 14*):

> “Whoever serves his belly while at the same time attempting to conquer the spirit of lust acts like someone who wishes to overcome a fire with oil.”

Therefore, “the most holy founders of the monasteries, wishing to cut off the causes of lust, prescribed for us a frugal and scanty diet in a fixed measure, so that the body might be sustained for necessity and not fattened for lust,” writes Trithemius (*Homily 21*).

By the name “fasting,” people commonly understand every kind of bodily mortification, which the saints are often read to have employed in order to extinguish the foul heats of lust. Thus, a certain monk is said to have burned all his fingers in the flame of a lamp so that he would not allow the flame of lust to burn in his heart [Col. 0335C] (*Book V on the Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 5, no. 37). Thus Saint Benedict, afflicted by the temptation of the flesh, rolled his naked body into thorns and briars (*Saint Gregory, Book II of the Dialogues*, chapter 2). Thus Saint Bernard, because he had looked too curiously at a woman, immersed himself up to the neck in a pond bound by ice (*His Life*, Book I, chapter 3). Others attacked and overcame the temptations of the flesh with scourges, hair shirts, vigils, [*chameunis*—an uncertain term in the source], and iron chains. See the Rule of Blessed Aelred for Virgins, chapters 26 and 27.

Second, since idleness is no less hostile to chastity than to the soul itself, Trithemius says (*Homily 21*):

> “You who carry a great treasure in a fragile body, flee idleness; always do something good, so that whenever the tempting devil approaches, he may find you profitably occupied. Indeed, the idle person lies open to the ambushes of the tempter, while the person occupied in good work has closed every entrance to such ambushes.”

Certainly, what Saint John Climacus writes should terrify us (*Ladder 2*):

> “We have seen many people in the world escape the mad tyranny of their bodies through cares, anxieties, trifles, and vigils [Col. 0335D]; but after they withdrew into the silence of religious repose and a secluded life, they were miserably defiled and polluted by the refractory movements of the body.”

Third, meditation on the last things, especially hell, is extremely effective for protecting and preserving chastity. An old man taught this by the following comparison to a certain brother who was being attacked by an impure thought (*Book V on the Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 5, no. 30):

> “When a woman wishes to wean her child, she smears something bitter upon her breasts. When the infant comes, as usual, to suck milk and feels the bitterness, it recoils. So you too should put bitterness into your thought.”

When the brother asked what bitterness he should introduce, he replied: thoughts of death and of the torments reserved for sinners in the age to come.

Fourth, among the other means of preserving chastity, they recommend frequent reception of the most holy Eucharist [Col. 0336A], since it is “the grain of the elect, the wine that makes virgins flourish.” “For when Christ remains in us, he calms the law of the members that rages against us, strengthens devotion, and extinguishes disturbances of the soul,” says Saint Cyril (*Book IV on John*, chapter 17). Hence Saint Bernard, addressing his own people, says (*Sermon on the Lord’s Supper*):

> “If any of you no longer feels such frequent bitter movements of anger, envy, lust, or other things of this kind, let him give thanks to the body and blood of the Lord, because the power of the sacrament is working in him.”

See Cassian’s *Conferences*, conference 22, chapter 6.

Wisdom teaches a fifth means of preserving chastity by her own example when she said:

> “I knew that I could not be continent unless God gave it; I approached the Lord and entreated him” (*Wisdom 8*).

Therefore, whenever you feel an unruly movement of the flesh, whenever you perceive that the invisible enemy is present to harm you, flee at once to the Son of God hanging upon the cross. Aelred also urges us (*On the Rule*, chapter 25) to have recourse above all to Blessed Mary the Virgin.

Sixth, chastity: “The elders say that it cannot be grasped unless the foundations of humility have first been laid in the heart,” [Col. 0336B] says Cassian (*Book VI of the Institutes*, chapter 18). And Saint Gregory says (*Book VI of the Morals*, chapter 23) that “there is no chastity which humility of mind does not commend.” Saint Bernard’s saying agrees with this (*Book on the Love of God*, no. 30, volume III):

> “Proud chastity is not chastity, but a brothel adorned by the devil.”

Seventh, according to Cassian, we shall be able to maintain the state of perfect chastity perpetually (*Book VI of the Institutes*, chapter 21):

> “If we consider God to be not only the daily and nightly observer and knower of our secret actions, but also of all our thoughts, and if we believe that we shall render an account to him for everything that moves within our heart, just as we shall for our deeds and works.”

Eighth:

> “To the degree that a person advances in gentleness and patience of heart, to that degree he will progress in bodily purity; and the farther he drives away the passion of anger, the more tenaciously [Col. 0336C] he will possess chastity. For no one will avoid the body’s heat unless he has first restrained the movements of the soul. This is most plainly declared by the blessedness praised from the mouth of our Savior: ‘Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth.’ We shall therefore possess our own earth in no other way—that is, the earth of this rebellious body will be subjected to our authority in no other way—unless our mind has first been established upon the gentleness of patience; nor will it be able to suppress the battles of lust against its own flesh unless it has first been armed with the weapons of meekness.”

Finally, the lovers of chastity are lovers of solitude. The holy Fathers considered no remedy against all the assaults of the flesh more effective or more immediately present than avoidance of women, so that we might conquer the enemy, as it were, by fleeing. They did not believe chastity to be secure while the enemy was present.

Thus Saint Caesarius (*Sermon 293 in the Appendix to Saint Augustine’s Sermons*) says that, against the assault of lust [Col. 0336D]:

> “Take flight if you wish to gain victory. Do not be ashamed to flee if you desire to obtain the palm of chastity. Therefore, dearest brothers, every Christian—and especially clerics and monks—must flee disgraceful and dishonorable familiarity, because without any doubt the person who does not wish to avoid suspicious familiarity quickly falls into ruin.”

A little later he adds:

> “The Apostle Paul clearly shows that lust must be fled. Although he preached that one must resist all vices, when he spoke against lust he did not say, ‘Resist,’ but, ‘Flee fornication.’ Thus, with God’s help, we must resist the other vices in the present life, but overcome lust by fleeing it, although elsewhere in the divine Scriptures we read: ‘Do not fix your gaze upon the face of a virgin, lest her appearance cause you to stumble.’”

Saint Jerome teaches the same in writing against Vigilantius toward the end, as does Cassian (*Book VI of the Institutes*, chapter 3). The following saying of Goffrid, abbot of Vendôme, agrees with them (*Book IV, Letter 44*):

> “Where there is the disorderly and continual presence of worldly society, one cannot believe that great iniquity will be absent for long, especially in a place where the female sex is permitted to dwell, through which even religious persons are regarded with suspicion.”

Even the stronger-minded should be frightened by these words of Saint Bernard [Col. 0337A] (*Sermon 65 on the Song of Songs*):

> “To be always with a woman and not know a woman—is that not more than to raise the dead?”

I am no less moved by what one of the ancient monks used to say (*John Moschus, Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 227):

> “Little children, salt comes from water, and if it approaches water it immediately dissolves and disappears. A monk likewise comes from a woman; therefore, if he approaches a woman, he too dissolves and finally becomes such that he is no longer a monk.”

And Peter Damian says (*Opuscle 52, chapter 5*):

> “On a certain mountain in the East there are fire-bearing stones called male and female, and they are called *pyroboli*. When they are far from one another, they do not ignite. But if the female approaches the male, fire immediately issues from them, so that everything around the mountain is consumed by their smoking flames. From these stones, therefore, we learn that if we do not wish to be consumed by the fire of lust, we must turn our faces away from the sight of women, lest from the form we have seen a flame leap forth and spread within us through the thickets—not of the mountain, but of the mind.”

No one, then, should rightly wonder at the great care taken by the ancient monks to avoid women [Col. 0337B], so that they permitted them neither to enter their monasteries nor to enter the oratory; indeed, they did not readily allow them even to be seen or approached.

Certainly, the ancient monastic rules commonly testify that women were forbidden access to men’s monasteries. The Third Rule of the Holy Fathers says (*chapter 4*):

> “For the preservation of life and the avoidance of the devil’s snares, we decree that the familiarity of all women, both relatives and strangers, be prohibited from all monasteries or establishments of monks, and likewise that monks not frequent monasteries of maidens, as the Rule teaches. No woman should dare to enter the inner court of a monastery. If, with the counsel or consent of the abbot, any woman should enter the monastery [Col. 0337C] or the monks’ cells, that abbot shall rightly lay down both the title of abbot and recognize himself as inferior to all priests. For one such person ought to be placed over the holy flock as will strive to offer them spotless to God, not hasten to join them to the devil through any sort of familiarity.”

Saint Basil says (*Sermon 1 on the Institution of Monasticism*):

> “Women must be entirely barred from entering monasteries.”

Saint Caesarius says in his Rule for Monks (*chapter 11*):

> “Women shall never enter the monastery.”

The Rule of Saint Ferreolus says (*chapter 4*):

> “No woman at all is to approach the monastery, even if she appears to seek admission out of affection. Likewise, we remove from religious women and maidens the permission to approach, lest some opportunity be left for those who understand less clearly; for a dwelling cannot remain secure for long when the enemy is near and the foe is close at hand.”

Finally, the Rule of the Monastery of Tarnat says (*chapter 20*):

> “Women shall not frequent your dwelling. But when, out of devotion or love for your religious life, they seek the monastery [Col. 0337D], they shall not be permitted to enter the inner doors of the monastery; rather, honor and kindness shall be shown them in the oratory or in the guesthouse.”

The Council of Tours I confirms this ancient discipline in these words (*chapter 17*):

> “A woman shall in no way be permitted to enter within the enclosures of a monastery. If the abbot or superior appears negligent in this matter—if he sees her and does not immediately expel her—he shall be excommunicated.”

The Council of Auxerre says (*canon 26*):

> “If an abbot permits a woman to enter his monastery, or orders her to attend any festivities there, he shall be confined for three months in another monastery, content with bread and water.”

Likewise, the Roman council under Saint Gregory takes precautions (*Baronius, under the year 601):

> “That no opportunity be provided for popular gatherings in the retreats and shelters of the servants of God, and that no new entrance be made by women, since this is altogether harmful to their souls.”

The holy pontiff gives the same command in writing to Castorius, bishop of Rimini (*Book IV of the Register*, chapter 43), and to Valentinus, the abbot who had admitted women into his monastery (*ibid.*, Book III, chapter 40):

> “By the tenor of this command we admonish you that henceforth you permit no women to enter your monastery [Col. 0338A] on any occasion, nor allow your monks to make them their ‘co-mothers’ [*commatres*]. For if this should again come to our ears, know that you will be subjected to such a most severe punishment that, by the manner of your correction, the others will unquestionably be corrected.”

An ancient formula for establishing a privilege also stipulates (*It appears in the fourth-century Benedictine collection, Part I, p. 744*) that:

> “The approach of women within the gates of the monastery shall in no way take place.”

To all these are added the civil laws of the emperors. Justinian’s Novel 133 states:

> “No woman shall at all enter a monastery of men, nor a man a monastery of women, whether on the pretext of commemorating a deceased person buried there or for any other reason; and especially if someone should happen to claim that he has a brother, sister, or anyone related to him by blood in the monastery [Col. 0338B]. For monks have no kinship on earth, since they aspire to the heavenly life.”

This law also extends to the dead, decreeing:

> “A man shall not be buried in the tombs of women’s monasteries, nor shall women be buried in men’s monasteries or asceteries.”

What has been said thus far is confirmed by the ancient practice of the monks, who are known never to have introduced women into their monasteries. This could be demonstrated by almost innumerable examples. Indeed, some went so far as not to tolerate animals of the female sex—such as cows, goats, and others of this kind—being kept in their monasteries. Such was Saint Plato, hegumen of the monastery of Saccudion, as Theodore the Studite witnesses in his *Life*, no. 23; and such was Theodore the Studite himself, as may be seen in his Testament, which Baronius reports under the year 826.

Later orders of monks and other religious congregations voluntarily embraced the same discipline. Guigo of Chartreuse, their prior, prescribes it for his own community [Col. 0338C] in these words (*Statutes*, chapter 21):

> “We absolutely do not permit women to enter our boundaries, knowing that neither the Wise Man, nor the Prophet, nor the Judge, nor the guest of God, nor sons, nor even the first man formed by God’s hands was able to escape women’s blandishments and frauds . . . . Nor can a person hide fire in his bosom without burning his garments, walk upon live coals without injuring his feet, or touch pitch without being defiled.”

The New Statutes of the Carthusians likewise state (*Part II, chapter 6, no. 22*):

> “We forbid all persons of the order to permit women to enter within the enclosures of our houses, or within the boundaries of the enclosures marked by ditches or by any signs whatsoever. Rather, they should oppose them as far as they can and, insofar as it lies within them, prevent them from entering. Those who are found guilty or negligent in the matters stated above—if they are priors—shall remain outside their seats everywhere in the convent until the next general chapter, in which they shall also publicly confess their faults. Others in the order shall remain under general discipline until that same chapter and shall lose any obediences they possess.”

They renew the same provision [Col. 0338D] in the new collection of statutes printed at Paris in 1582 (*Part II, chapter 20, no. 3), and prohibit it by the authority of the supreme pontiffs Julius II and Pius V:

> “Under penalties of deprivation of the offices they presently hold, perpetual ineligibility for those and all other offices in the future, and suspension from divine services, incurred automatically without any further declaration.”

The Cistercians appear no less severe when they write in their ancient definitions (*Distinction 3, chapter 5*):

> “The entrance of women within the enclosures of our abbeys is altogether forbidden, unless they possess a special privilege of the lord pope. The exception is that, when the major church is newly dedicated, they may visit the church for nine days out of devotion; but neither then nor on any other occasion may they spend the night within the monastery’s enclosures. If this should anywhere be presumed contrary to the prohibition, the altars shall be uncovered and divine office shall not be celebrated in [Col. 0339A] the church for as long as the women remain there. Whoever does this, consents to it, or arranges it by apostolic letters or in any other way—if he is an abbot—shall spend every Friday on bread and water until the next general chapter, where he must ask pardon and shall be severely punished. If he is a prior, subprior, or cellarer, he shall be deposed from office and shall perform a light penance for three days, one of them on bread and water. Other monks and lay brothers shall receive a similar penalty and shall be last of all for a year.”

The practice of this decree can be seen, at least in part, in the general chapter of the Cistercian order in 1205, where the following is recorded (*It appears in the Cistercian Nomasticon, p. 500*):

> “The abbot of Pontigny, who, contrary to the form of the order, introduced the queen of France, along with not a few others of the same sex, into his monastery to hear a sermon in the chapter house, to join the procession in the cloister, to take refreshment, and to spend two nights in the infirmary—taking as his pretext that, by a rescript of the lord pope and by permission of the lord of Cîteaux, access to that monastery was open to the lady, although neither the lord pope nor the abbot of Cîteaux had granted or even contemplated permission to proceed so far [Col. 0339B]—and because he tolerated so enormous an act to the injury of the entire Cistercian order, although he deserved immediate deposition without any possibility of revocation, is nevertheless spared for the present at the request of the lord of Reims, to whom we neither wish nor ought to refuse anything, and also at the request of other bishops. Yet, so that such great presumption may not remain altogether unpunished, he shall remain outside the abbot’s stall until Easter, and shall not celebrate except as required by his office. He shall spend six days under light penance—three days at Cîteaux and three at Pontigny, one of them on bread and water in each place.”

The Cassinese monks also prohibit, under the penalty of automatic excommunication, the bringing or admitting of women—whether lay or religious—within the regular enclosures of the monastery [Col. 0339C] (*Cassinese Declaration on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 53). The Celestines prohibit it under penalty of deprivation of offices, perpetual ineligibility to obtain those and other offices in the future, and other penalties expressed in canonical enactments and the bulls of the Roman pontiffs (*Constitutions*, chapter 11, § 3). Finally, the Constitutions of the Congregation of Monte Oliveto contain this brief provision (*Part II, chapter 53*):

> “Women shall never be admitted into the monastery by the abbot, the bull of Pius V issued on this subject being inviolably observed.”

Moreover, what we have said above concerning the prohibition against women entering men’s monasteries must likewise be asserted in reverse concerning men entering convents of virgins: all access was forbidden to them. This is clear from the Justinianic Novel cited above, from Saint Isidore (*Book II on Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15), and from the *Life of Saint Lioba*, chapter 1, which relates that in a place in England called Wimborne there were two convents, one for men and the other for women:

> “From the beginning of their foundation, both were organized under this rule of discipline: neither was to be entered by the opposite sex. For a woman was never permitted to enter the congregation of men, nor any man the community of virgins [Col. 0339D], except only priests, who used to enter their churches solely to perform the offices of the Mass and, once the prayer was completed, immediately return to their own place.”

And in chapter 2, Saint Tetta, abbess of the same monastery, is said to have denied entry “not only to laymen or clerics, but even to bishops themselves” into their community, except, naturally, for the service of the altar.

The same may be seen in the privilege of Pope John IV for the nuns of a certain monastery of Blessed Mary in Gaul. Among other provisions, the supreme pontiff wishes that:

> “The bishop whom the spiritual mother, the father of the monastery, or the entire community shall choose to celebrate the solemn Mass in the community of the abbess or even of the other younger women, and also to consecrate the altar boards on which Masses are to be celebrated, shall have the power [Note: [Col. 0339] *Facundiam* is used here for *copiam*, “opportunity” or “authority,” unless one prefers to accuse the printers. —Ed.] to enter that monastery for the office of priestly [Col. 0340A] ministry for the office of priestly ministry, and that the pontiff himself introduce with him such persons as are commended by life and holy religious practice. When the office has been completed, he must hasten to return to his own place, without touching or seeking anything through the spur of lust or the schemes of predatory wickedness, but acting freely in every respect.”

What he says—“that the pontiff himself introduce with him such persons”—seems to be understood of other ministers of the altar, as we gather from the Rules of Saint Caesarius for Virgins, chapter 33, and of Saint Donatus, chapter 55. There I read:

> “No man shall enter the secluded part of the monastery or the oratories, except bishops, the steward, and the priest, deacon, subdeacon, and one or two readers whose age and life commend them, and who are to celebrate Mass from time to time. But when roofs must be repaired, or doors or windows put in order, or anything of this kind restored, only craftsmen and servants, to carry out the work if necessity requires it, may enter with the steward; nor may they enter without the permission or authorization of the mother.”

Saint Caesarius adds, in chapter 34 [Col. 0340B]:

> “Secular matrons or maidens, or other women, and likewise men still wearing lay clothing, shall also be prohibited from entering.”

What is more, Saint Gregory the Pope does not permit even physicians to enter monasteries of virgins. See the First Council of Mâcon, chapter 2; the Council of Fréjus of 791, chapter 12; and, most recently, the Council of Trent, session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 5.

What we have just adduced from the Rules of St. Caesarius and St. Donatus, from the privilege of Pope John IV, and from the Life of St. Lioba proves not only that men were altogether denied access to convents of virgins, but also—what is more significant—that they were denied access to their oratories or churches. This is confirmed by the Council of Epaon in 517, canon 38; the Council of Arles in 813, canon 7; and the Third Council of Tours, held in the same year, canon 29.

The same must conversely be asserted concerning the churches of monks: no women whatsoever, not even religious women, were allowed to enter them. This may be gathered from the Rule of St. Aurelian for monks, chapter 15, which does not permit women—whether relatives, acquaintances, or others—to enter for prayer [Col. 0340C], indeed not even laymen, as chapter 14 makes clear; from canon 26 of the Council of Auxerre, which takes precautions that the abbot admit no woman into the monastery or arrange for her to attend any festivities there; from the Roman Council, at which Pope St. Gregory forbade a bishop to celebrate Mass in a monastery of monks, lest “in the retreats of the servants of God and their dwellings any opportunity for a popular gathering be afforded, or a new entrance be made for women, which is altogether neither expedient for their souls”; from the previously cited Novel of Justinian, which does not even permit women to enter men’s monasteries in order to celebrate the third, ninth, fortieth, or annual day after the death of the departed; and from Gregory of Tours, who reports that St. Romanus, abbot of Condat, wishing women to have access to his tomb—which, as he knew by divine revelation, would shine with miracles—wanted to be buried outside his own church. “It cannot be,” he said, “that I should have a tomb in the monastery from which the access of women is barred” [Col. 0340D].

This was the common practice of the Benedictine Order and, almost universally, the custom of our monasteries. Lest anyone suppose that we have fabricated this freely, as though we wished to present the practice of certain monasteries—and those, moreover, only a few—as a universal custom, it may perhaps not be unwelcome, and would that it might at some time prove useful, to demonstrate the matter by the most certain testimonies, if not concerning all monasteries, at least concerning the principal and most distinguished ones.

To begin with the monasteries founded by St. Benedict himself: although we do not read that the holy Father excluded women from entering the churches, nevertheless, since neither in his Life nor in his Rule is it stated that he permitted them to do so, there is no slight ground for conjecturing that his churches were entirely inaccessible to women. At least the Cistercians of old seem to have been persuaded of this, when, following the example of the holy legislator, they denied women access to their oratory, as they themselves testify in the *Exordium Parvum Cisterciense*, chapter 12 [Col. 0341A].

Our conjecture is strengthened by the decree of St. Gregory cited above, which forbids bishops to celebrate Mass in the churches of monks, lest on that occasion a new entrance for women should be made into them. These words indicate something previously unheard of; otherwise it would not be called “new.” Certainly, the Roman church of St. Anastasius at Aquae Salviae was inaccessible to women in the time of Pope Constantine—that is, at the beginning of the eighth century—as is clear from the acts reported by Baronius under the year 613. There it is said that the relics of the holy martyr were carried outside the monastery to another church of St. John in order to free a possessed woman, because “a woman does not enter that monastery,” that is, the basilica of the monastery.

But whatever the case may be concerning the monasteries founded by St. Benedict, there can be no controversy concerning the monastery which he deigned to enrich after his death with the precious treasure of his body, namely, Fleury. This is clear from Adrevald’s testimony in Book I of the *Miracles of St. Benedict*, chapter 28. Speaking of the relics of Saints Denis and Sebastian granted to the monastery of Fleury, he says as follows (*Saeculum II Benedictinum*, p. 384):

“Furthermore, because it had been established by ancient authority that women should by no means pass inward beyond the outer gates of the monastery, those who had followed the memorials of the saints from distant places turned to prayer, asking that they might be permitted, for the sake of prayer, to enter the church in which the relics of the saints had been deposited and to fulfill their vows. But because this was contrary to monastic discipline, they were wholly unable to obtain their request by any means. While they persisted in prayer, even the more distinguished persons, stirred by the fame of so great a report, began to flock from every direction to so venerable a spectacle; and, joining their prayers, they could scarcely prevail upon the abbot and brothers by any means to order a tent to be spread outside the monastery gate, on the western side, in a wooded place, so that at the appointed time—that is, on the vigil of the Lord’s Day—the relics of the saints might be carried there.” [Col. 0341C]

These words—“from ancient custom” and “because it was contrary to monastic discipline”—must not be passed over casually.

We learn from Aimoinus, Book II of *The Translation of St. Vincent*, chapter 4 (*Saeculum IV Benedictinum*, part I), that the same custom prevailed at the monastery of St. Benedict of Castres in Narbonnese Gaul. He reports that the body of the holy martyr, after being transferred there, was not immediately placed in the basilica of St. Benedict, but that “they placed it for safekeeping and veneration in the church of the blessed Mother of God before the gate of that monastery, chiefly because of the devout crowds of women, who, according to the ancient custom of the Fathers of that place, were denied access to the monastery itself.” He adds:

“Nevertheless, they resolved to construct a new basilica in his honor near the monastery, to which devoted persons of both sexes would have free access.”

See also chapter 17 of the same book.

St. Benedict, abbot of Aniane, who bore the same name as our holy legislator and was animated by the same spirit, propagated the same institution in the monasteries he founded. This may be gathered from a sermon by an anonymous author, included in the appendix to the *Life of St. Benedict, Abbot of Aniane* (*Saeculum IV Benedictinum*, part I). Speaking of the basilica of the monastery of Aniane, he says:

“This place was held in such great reverence by the ancients that access to it was barred to women, lest any occasion should corrupt the morals of those observing the holy rule.”

We cite this passage because, since many monasteries were subject to the monastery of Aniane, we do not doubt that a similar discipline prevailed in all of them.

The same judgment must be made concerning all the monasteries founded by St. Columbanus, and others to which he sent colonies of monks. Theodoric, acting at the instigation of Brunhild, expelled him from Luxeuil because he refused to admit secular persons into the inner parts of the monastery, as Jonas testifies in his *Life of St. Columbanus*, no. 33; or, as the anonymous author of the *Life of St. Aile*, abbot of Rebais, says in chapter 7, “because he drove away the access of women from the aforesaid monastery” [Col. 0342A]. Later, however, out of regard for St. Aile, both Theodoric and Brunhild “nevertheless composed royal charters concerning the aforesaid monastery with munificent generosity, by which thereafter the servants of God might remain peacefully through the passing ages in perseverance of divine worship, with the access of women removed.”

This discipline was preserved afterward until the middle of the ninth century, when “Hucbert, a cleric, son of Boso, entered in a hostile manner the monastery established at Luxeuil in memory of Blessed Peter, whose cloister had never been open to women, and did not hesitate to remain there for several days with illicit women.” For this conduct Pope Benedict III rebuked him in a letter to the bishops established in the kingdom of Charles.

St. John of Réomay had preceded St. Columbanus. As we read in his Life, no. 10, he did not even allow secular men to take part in the sacred mysteries, much less women. This practice continued, at least with respect to women, until the second translation of St. John, carried out in the time of Charlemagne. Then, “because of the novelty of the event itself, persons of both sexes were indiscriminately permitted to enter the church,” as the anonymous author of the history of that translation writes, no. 8 (*Saeculum I Benedictinum*, p. 635). “But in the course of time,” the same writer adds, “the brothers of that place, by a devout decision, decreed that the monastery courtyard should be permanently restrained from the attendance of women, judging it inconsistent with the regular profession frequently either to accustom oneself to the sight of women or to become involved in conversation with them.”

Not far from Réomay stood the monastery of St. Peter at Bèze. In the time of King Pippin, it had been entrusted to the wife of a certain Theodard, not so much for safekeeping as for plunder. She refrained for a while from entering the sacrosanct basilica of the Apostles because the monks forbade it; later, becoming bolder, she paid a divine penalty for her rashness. The author is John the Monk in the *Chronicle of Bèze*.

A similar religious observance existed at the monastery of Cramailhac, chiefly under St. Theofred, abbot, as an anonymous author relates in his Life, no. 9 (*Saeculum III Benedictinum*, part I):

“He guarded the oratory with such careful regard for propriety that … women were kept at a distance around the temple door.”

Likewise, “the church of the monastery of Garactum contains the sarcophagus with the ashes of the venerable Pardulf, and, as a testimony to his most chaste life, admits no woman,” as Geoffrey, prior of Vosius, wrote in 1183.

These examples recall what is reported concerning St. Fiacre (*Life of St. Fiacre*, no. 6, *Saeculum II Benedictinum*): “From the time when a woman accused the man of God before the bishop, women did not enter his monastery”—that is, the church of the monastery. This practice is still observed at least in part, since no woman dares cross the grille of the chapel of the holy confessor with impunity.

What shall I say of the Greater Monastery? Its basilica was entirely inaccessible to women, as the history of the translation of St. Gorgonius, no. 8 (*Saeculum IV Benedictinum*, part I), shows. There it is described how the holy relics were “temporarily brought to an open place outside the walls of the monastery for the gathering of both sexes” [Col. 0342D].

The same must be said of the church of St. Martin at Tours. There the canons retained for some time the discipline they had received from the monks, even after abandoning the monastic institutions, as appears from a letter of Pope Leo VII to Hugh, prince and abbot (*Spicilegium*, vol. II, p. 375).

The steadfastness of St. Carilef in this matter seems altogether astonishing and worthy of the highest admiration. When Queen Ultrogoda had desired at some time to enjoy his presence, and had sent messengers to the holy man for that purpose, he returned this answer:

“Go, excellent young men, and report these words of mine to your lady. If I have any power, I shall pray for her; but let her know for certain that, as long as I remain in the body, I shall never see the face of a woman. Nor shall this monastery, which I built at the Lord’s command, ever be open to the entrance of a woman” [Col. 0343A].

That this must be understood of the church is clear from Book of the *Miracles*, no. 12.

The same prohibition against women prevailed at the monastery of Landevennec, as the third Life of St. Winwaloe, cited by Bollandus, testifies. In no. 4 we read (*Bollandists*, 3 March):

“This was the privilege of this place: from the time when it was first held by the saints under the law established by St. Guingaloeus, no female entrance ever profaned it.”

The same is evident concerning the monastery of Déas from Ermentarius’s history of the translation of St. Philibert to that monastery, which took place around the middle of the ninth century (*Saeculum IV Benedictinum*, part I). In it, “it was debated whether the female sex ought to be admitted with the other faithful or not, since, after the monks had begun to live there, no attendance of women had ever existed at all. It was decided by the sounder counsel that common access should be granted to them until the completion of one year,” as Ermentarius says in no. 30. See also no. 72.

If we now turn to our monasteries in Normandy and Picardy, it will be no less clear that the same institution was received in the principal ones, such as Fontenelle of St. Wandrille, Madrie of St. Leufred, and Flavigny of St. Geremar.
