In the case of Fontenelle, although the matter does not appear with complete clarity, it may nevertheless be gathered without difficulty from Book I of the *Miracles of St. Wandrille*. There a woman from the district of Caux, divinely punished for violating the religious observance of St. Wandrille’s feast day, “asked, with tearful voice, to be taken to the basilica of St. Mary, which was near the monastery of Fontenelle and under its jurisdiction.” When she had looked upon the church of the holy confessor, she was healed. Why, when seeking the patronage of St. Wandrille, would she ask to be taken not to his church but to the neighboring church of Blessed Mary, unless his church was inaccessible to women?

Concerning Madrie there should be no dispute, as is clear from chapter 4 of the *Miracles of St. Leufred* (*Saeculum III*, part I, p. 593), where “a blind woman, arriving near the monastery and learning that no access was open there for women to enter, sent a candle to the memorial of the man of God by means of a certain man.” In his Life, no. 6, it is also said that, while still a layman, he established an oratory on his own property “where no entrance or access was granted to women.”

The same is true of Flavigny, where St. Geremar built a church at an angel’s command, on the condition that, as the author of his Life says in no. 24, “no access to it would ever be open to women.” The anonymous author of Book I of the *Miracles of St. Richarius*, no. 4, and Hariulf in Book III, chapter 4, of the *Chronicle of Centula*, testify that Abbot Elizachar established a similar discipline in his monastery.

But now it is time to pass to Belgium. There the notable monasteries must undoubtedly be counted as those of St. Amand at Elnone, St. Bertin at Sithiu, and Laubium. In all of them the churches were formerly not at all open to women (*Spicilegium*, vol. IV).

Concerning Elnone, we have clear testimony in Milo’s Supplement to the *Life of St. Amand*, chapter 6. It says that the body of the holy bishop was transferred from the basilica of St. Peter (*Saeculum II Benedictinum*, p. 726):

“Because this basilica, on account of its small size, seemed unsuitable for the tomb of so great a bishop, and was also inaccessible to the female sex because of the monks’ dwellings, a large gathering of religious men decided that another basilica of greater size ought to be built, one that could accommodate the multitude of people flocking together from both sexes—namely, outside the monastery precinct.”

Concerning Sithiu, the matter is nevertheless clear from Book II of the *Miracles of St. Bertin*, chapter 12, covering the period from the time of the holy abbot until the year 938 (*Saeculum III Benedictinum*, part I). Adela, countess of Flanders, “being very often afflicted by severe illnesses, began to desire that the monks grant her permission to enter this monastery, so that she might be allowed to prostrate herself before the altar of St. Bertin and pray for her health.”

After the monks granted this permission, “on Easter Monday the bishops introduced her into the same monastery, not without great trembling, because she had been the first to dare do what none of the queens before her had even desired” [Col. 0344A]. Nor was this permitted thereafter until the fourteenth century.

Finally, Folcuin testifies concerning Laubium in his *Book of the Deeds of the Abbots of Laubium*, chapter 4 (*Spicilegium*, vol. VI), that access to the principal basilica of St. Peter was forbidden to women except at a fixed time. This custom still prevailed in Folcuin’s time—he died in 990—and therefore St. Ursmar built another church on the summit of the mountain, to which the people could flock.

The same custom prevailed in England, as is shown especially by the distinguished testimony of Turgot in Book II, chapter 17, of the *History of Durham*, concerning St. Cuthbert:

“In almost none of the churches which the blessed confessor, St. Cuthbert, either before, during, or after his flight, illuminated by the presence of his sacred body, is any permission for women to enter known to exist to this day.”

He then gives the reason and adds:

“Therefore, with all men and women agreeing, he forbade all female association with his own people, both for the present and for future times, and entirely removed women’s entrance from his church. Hence, when a church had been built on the island of his episcopal see, he ordered women to gather there to hear Mass and the word of God, so that they might never approach more closely to the church in which he lived with the monks. This custom is carefully observed to this day, to such an extent that, unless fear of an enemy or the burning of the place compels it, women are not even permitted to enter the cemeteries of those churches where his body had rested for a time.”

Turgot wrote this toward the end of the eleventh century.

But remarkable also are the things William of Malmesbury reports concerning the monastery of Thorney (*Book IV of the Bishops of England*, near the end):

“There a vast solitude was given to the monks for quiet, so that they might cling to heavenly things more firmly the more chastely they look upon mortals. If a woman is seen there, she is regarded as a monster; when men arrive, they are applauded as though they were angels. Besides, no one remains there except briefly.”

The discipline which St. Boniface had absorbed in England he carried into Germany, reproducing it in the monasteries he built there. Women were entirely forbidden access to the churches, especially at the most distinguished of all, Fulda. Its basilica was open only to St. Lioba, out of reverence for the holy martyr, as the monk Rudolf testifies in chapter 22 of the *Life of St. Lioba* (*Saeculum III Benedictinum*, part II, p. 256):

“From time to time she also used to come to the monastery of the monks of Fulda for the sake of prayer. Permission to do this could never be granted to any woman, either before or afterward, because from the time when monks first began to live in that place, female entrance was forbidden there. This woman alone was granted such permission because St. Boniface the martyr had commended her to the elders and had decreed that her body should be buried there.”

Brouwer writes (*Book I of the Antiquities of Fulda*, chapter 8) that this rule was observed by the elders with such sanctity “that it was expressly inserted in the privileges subsequently granted by Pope Marinus to Abbot Hadamar in the ninth century, by Sylvester to Erkembald in the tenth century, and later by John Richard and by other pontiffs, and was religiously observed by posterity” [Col. 0344D].

This is demonstrated both by the wife of King Lothair, who was not permitted to attend the sacred rites in the principal church of the monastery on the day of Pentecost, and by the wife of Emperor Frederick, “who, because she was a queen in his entourage, was not permitted to enter the city of Fulda.”

Brouwer adds that, after that discipline had once been relaxed by Pope Boniface IX at the request of John Merlavius, abbot, “in the year 1398 the church of Fulda was struck by lightning from heaven and burned on June 7,” which posterity believed had occurred as a punishment for violating the discipline.

Nevertheless, this concession of the supreme pontiff concerned only the feast of St. Boniface and certain other feast days. Otherwise, even in Trithemius’s time, access to the church of Fulda was still not open to women, as he himself testifies in the *Life of Rabanus*.

St. Boniface introduced this observance concerning the churches of monks wherever he could. Thus, when Blessed Alto asked him to consecrate the church of his monastery (*Saeculum III*, part II, p. 218), “when he arrived with him and wished, according to his usual custom, to consecrate it in such a way that no woman should enter it, Blessed Alto asked him not to consecrate his oratory on that condition. He particularly pointed out that men, being frequently away at various tasks, needed their wives to remain at home and pray for themselves and their husbands. St. Boniface agreed to this request and, in consecrating the church, made it common to both women and men; but he blessed a certain fountain located in the same place beside the church in such a way that no woman was permitted to approach it or draw water from it.”

I shall add two examples to all these: one concerning the monastery of Stavelot, from chapter 20 of the *Miracles of St. Remaclus, Bishop of Maastricht*. There it is said that a crippled woman was brought to the relics of the saint (*Saeculum II*, p. 501), but “because women are not easily admitted among us except for a definite reason, she was laid down before the monastery gate,” as the anonymous author writes.

The other is drawn from the monastery of Andage, from chapter 6 of the *Miracles of St. Hucbert* (*Saeculum IV*, part I, p. 298):

“At that time, under the venerable Sevoldus, such reverence for religion prevailed in the place that permission to gather there was difficult for any secular person to obtain, and no access for entering was granted to women except on the annual feast of that bishop.”

Sevoldus governed the monastery of Andage for nineteen years, beginning in 836.

From what has been said thus far, I believe it has been sufficiently demonstrated that it was not the practice of a few monasteries but almost the general custom of all monasteries to keep women away from the churches of monks. The Carthusians and Cistercians adopted this custom at the very beginning of their orders, and the Carthusians still retain it everywhere with the highest praise. In the Cistercian monastery itself, and perhaps in some others, the Cistercians also retain it; for now their churches are generally open to women, whereas at Pontigny they formerly opened them only to English women, out of reverence for St. Edmund, as Matthew Paris testifies under the year 1250.

The Camaldolese not only close their church to women, but do not even permit them access to the forest in which it stood. “Around the said hermitage of Camaldoli,” says Jerome, a Camaldolese monk, in his sermon on St. Romuald, no. 63, “there is a most beautiful firwood extending for one Italian mile. No woman may enter that firwood under penalty of excommunication pronounced by the lord pope.”

But the ancient monks formerly denied women not only entrance into the monastery or oratory; they also judged that women should not be admitted even to conversation. Thus, when someone once asked St. Pachomius to free a possessed daughter, he is said to have replied (*Life*, chapter 36):

“It is not our custom to speak with women.”

And St. Carilef, to the messengers of Queen Ultrogoda, who desired to enjoy his presence, said:

“Let her know for certain that, as long as I remain in the body, I shall never see the face of a woman” (*Life*, no. 28, *Saeculum I*).

Cassian likewise says (*Book II*, chapter 17):

“This has been the enduring judgment of the Fathers from ancient times until now: that a monk must flee women in every way, and bishops, and so forth.”

Bishops, indeed, because of the laying on of hands; women, because of the danger. But since necessity sometimes dictates otherwise, St. Basil permits a monk to speak with women only briefly and rarely, and only in the presence of a companion, in his monastic constitutions, chapter 4:

“For one alone to approach one alone is permitted by no principle of religion; for it is better to be two than one. Thus the matter is conducted both more faithfully and more safely.”

The Rule of St. Ferreolus likewise decrees in chapter 4:

“If an evident cause compels any brother to have a conversation with respectable women, let him obtain permission to converse, with the abbot’s knowledge or consent and with witnesses present—that is, with two brothers accompanying him. Yet the abbot must not be unaware of the matter about which the conversation has arisen.”

St. Columbanus imposes the same rule under very severe penalties in his *Penitential*, no. 31:

“Whoever speaks familiarly alone with a woman alone, without trustworthy persons present, shall remain without food, or for two days on bread and water, or receive two hundred blows.”

St. Fructuosus says likewise in his *Common Monastic Rule*, chapter 15:

“If any one of those mentioned above is discovered talking alone with a woman alone, he shall be publicly stretched out and beaten with one hundred blows. Whoever presumes to do such things shall be admonished with caution. If he behaves abusively toward the precepts of the monks and repeats this fault a second time, he shall be beaten again and committed to prison; or, if he refuses to repent, he shall be cast out.”

The same custom also prevailed among our Cluniacs, as may be gathered from John the Monk, Book I of the *Life of St. Odo*, no. 36.

Finally, to all these examples must be added what we read among the *Apophthegmata of the Fathers* (*Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. I, p. 517):

“This custom had become established at Scetis: if a woman came to speak with a brother, or with another person necessary to her, they would converse while sitting far apart from one another” [Col. 0346B].

See also what we cited above from the manuscripts of the Customs of St. Benignus of Dijon, concerning the office of the almoner, p. 124, and in Book V of *The Ancient Rites of the Monks*, concerning brothers sent on a journey. All these things show how deeply our Fathers dreaded even the slightest association with women of any kind, and how much we ought to fear their conversation, which can indeed do no good but can do very great harm.

Would that we recoiled from it as much as St. John, abbot of Gorze, who, while still a layman, possessed such a profound virtue of chastity that, if he happened to see a woman sitting in some place, he would by no means, once she had departed, take her place there himself, even if he were exhausted (*Life*, no. 16, *Saeculum V Benedictinum*).

But enough concerning these matters—if enough can ever be said on this subject. See St. Basil’s Rule, in Rufinus’s translation, Questions 197 and 198; the *Life of St. Paternus, Bishop*, no. 9 (*Saeculum II Benedictinum*, p. 1102); and the *Life of St. Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, no. 15, in the Bollandists, 1 April.

## To hate no one

St. Basil rightly says (*Sermon 2, On the Institution of Monastic Life*):

“If God, as John says, is love, then the devil must necessarily be hatred. Therefore, just as the one who possesses love possesses God, so the one who possesses hatred nourishes the devil within himself.”

Accordingly, John Climacus relates concerning the monks of the monastery of Alexandria (*The Ladder*, step 4) that, “if anyone from their community were discovered to be a hater of others, the shepherd would send him into a coenobium separated from the others, as a guilty person into exile. And when a certain brother had once insulted another, he ordered the insulter to be expelled from the church, saying that there ought not to be two demons in the monastery, one visible and the other invisible.”

## Not to harbor zeal or practice envy

This means the evil zeal of bitterness, which separates one from God and leads to hell; it is discussed in chapter 72. And envy, through which death entered the world. See Cassian, *Conferences* 18, chapter 17, and the Rule of St. Ferreolus, chapter 9.

## Not to love contention

“Contention,” according to St. Basil (*Shorter Rules*, Question 66), “is whenever someone strives to do something lest he appear inferior to another.”

The same holy doctor orders that contention be expelled from monasteries as a meditation upon and a path toward rebellion. Thus, among the penalties preserved under his name in his works, no. 21 (*Sermon 2, On the Institution of Monastic Life*), we find:

“If anyone argues contentiously about the Scriptures, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

And in the Rule of St. Pachomius, article 118, I read:

“If one of the brothers is found doing something contentiously or contradicting the command of a superior, he shall be rebuked according to the measure of his sin.”

The same words occur in the Eastern Rule, chapter 14 (*Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, vol. I, p. 561).

What, then? “If someone speaks about any matter,” Abba Matoes used to say, “do not contend with him. If he speaks correctly, say, ‘Yes.’ If he speaks wrongly, say, ‘You know how you speak.’ Do not quarrel with him about the matters he has mentioned; this is humility.”

Hence St. Columbanus says in his *Penitential*:

“Whoever replies to a brother making a judgment, ‘It is not as you say,’ unless elders are speaking simply to juniors, shall be punished by an imposed silence or fifty blows. The only exception is that an equal brother may say to his fellow, if he knows something to be more accurate than what the other has said: ‘If you remember correctly, brother.’ The other, hearing this, must not affirm his own statement, but humbly say: ‘I hope that you remember better; I exceeded in speech through forgetfulness, and I regret that I spoke wrongly. These are the words of the children of God.’

“But whoever excuses himself shall be judged not a spiritual son of God but a carnal Adam. If he does not quickly flee to the harbor of the rest afforded by the Lord’s humility, opening the way to excessive contradictions for others and persisting in pride, he shall be separated from the freedom of the holy Church and confined to a cell to perform penance.”

## To flee exaltation

Pope St. Gregory enumerates four kinds of it (*Morals*, Book XXVIII, chapter 7):

1. Those who think they possess goodness from themselves.
2. Those who acknowledge that goodness has been given to them, but believe that it was given on account of themselves and received for their merits.
3. Those who boast of possessing what they do not possess.
4. Those who, despising others, desire to appear uniquely to possess what they do possess.

## To venerate elders

By “elders” he means not only the aged, but also those who are senior in order, dignity, office, merits, and virtue; all such persons he commands to be venerated.

According to Smaragdus:

“The veneration of elders ought to appear in words and deeds. In words, the junior should speak few and reasonable words to them, humbly and with reverence. In deeds, when the elder passes, the junior should rise; when the elder again commands, the junior should sit; when the elder speaks, the junior should listen in silence; when asked, he should answer humbly; when commanded, he should obey; with bowed head, he should ask for a blessing; and in all matters where reason requires it, the junior monk should obey the elder.”

This accords with chapter 3 of the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen:

“Let juniors obey their elders with sincere submission. Let them not answer in any matter with a proud neck, nor refuse with a disdainful spirit and negligent ear to obey those in command. Rather, with one mind and in harmony, let all faithfully devote themselves both to spiritual work and to earthly labor.”

## To love juniors

Here Smaragdus teaches that love must be shown to juniors for two reasons: first, because they are brothers; second, because they obey their elders and serve them humbly. For it is written:

“Let a prudent servant be dear to you as your own soul; treat him as a brother.”

Hence the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, chapter 2:

“Let elders show paternal affection to juniors. When it is necessary to command them, let them impose what is required for the common good not with swelling anger and shouting voices, but confidently, with tranquil simplicity and the authority of a good life.”

## To rejoice in Christ’s love for one’s enemies

Something similar is found in the Rule of Abbot Isaiah, chapter 49:

“If, while sitting in your cell, you remember that someone has done you harm, rise immediately and pray for him in your heart, that God may forgive him. In this way the suffering you endure on his account disappears.”

## To return to peace with one who is at odds before sunset

Here the holy Father alludes to the Apostle’s words in Ephesians 4: “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

This passage may be interpreted in three ways.

First, literally: we should return to peace with those with whom we are at odds before the physical setting of the sun, lest, when night intervenes, the devil find a suitable opportunity and inflame more and more what has occurred. St. Ambrose explains the Apostle’s passage in this way in his commentary on Psalm 4; so does St. Isidore of Pelusium, Book II, letter 189; and Evagrius in volume III of the *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 72.

Second, allegorically: the sun may be understood as Christ the Lord, the true Sun of justice, who is said to set for us when, as a punishment for discord, he withdraws the rays of his grace. Cassianus interprets it thus in Book VIII *On Anger*, chapter 9 [Col. 0348A].

Third, tropologically: the sun may be understood as reason, “which is rightly called the sun because it examines all the thoughts and discernments of the heart,” as Cassian says in the passage cited. Therefore, it must not be extinguished by the fault of anger, lest, when it has set, the darkness of disturbances, together with its author the devil, occupy the whole sense of our heart.

Whichever meaning is adopted, nothing is certainly more unworthy of a servant of God than discord. For, to use the words of St. Bernard (*Sermon 3, On the Dedication of a Church*), “just as the Lord’s dwelling has been established in peace, so it is manifest that in discord a dwelling is made for the devil.”

Hence those who have given laws to monks seem to have considered nothing more important than eliminating dissensions from the cloisters, even under the gravest penalties.

Thus St. Caesarius says in his Rule for Monks, chapter 24:

“If, as human weakness entails, any of the brothers should dare, at the devil’s instigation, to break out into such great wickedness that … they hurl insults at one another, it is just that they receive the prescribed discipline, since they have violated the institutions of the Rule.”

By “discipline” he means flogging.

St. Ferreolus says in his Rule, chapter 39:

“We therefore decree that those monks whom even the end of a single day finds at odds—those who prolong quarrels until evening and do not exclude hatred before the sun perceives its setting, contradicting the Apostle’s command through disobedience—shall be worn down by abstinence until they voluntarily turn to true concord through satisfaction.”

St. Columbanus says in his *Penitential*:

“If anyone holds anger, sadness, or envy against his brother, for as long as he has held it—that is, for as long as he has preserved his anger—his penance shall be on bread and water. But if he confesses on the first day, it shall be twenty-four psalms.”

St. John Climacus also writes concerning the monks of the Alexandrian monastery (*The Ladder*, step 4) that those who refused to be reconciled “were excluded from the table until, having laid aside their hatred, they restored friendship; or else they were altogether expelled from the fellowship of the community.”

The Cassinese monks, in their commentary on chapter 70, suspend from the divine offices those who maintain quarrels among themselves and refuse to be reconciled; they deprive them of office and rank; and finally, if they persist stubbornly in their hostility, they commit them to prison.

“And never despair of God’s mercy.”] Saint Benedict is entirely apposite when, after prescribing prayer for enemies and reconciliation with those at odds, he says never to despair of God’s mercy. For there is no doubt that those who have shown mercy to others will obtain it: “Blessed are the merciful,” says Mercy itself, the Truth, “for they shall obtain mercy.” Many considerations can move us not to despair of God’s mercy; they may be found at length in Saint Bernard, Letter 385 and Sermon 38 on the Song of Songs.

“Behold, these are the instruments of the spiritual art.”] Thus far the holy Father has explained the instruments of the spiritual art. [Col. 0348D] But since it is not enough for a craftsman to discover the best instruments unless he eventually uses them for the work he has undertaken—for, as Cassian says (Conferences I, chapter 7), “one hastens to fashion and prepare for oneself the tools of any craft, not in order to possess them idle, nor to place the hoped-for profit from them in the mere possession of the instruments, but in order effectively to attain, through their service, the skill and purpose of that discipline whose aids they are”—therefore Saint Benedict urges us by this concluding statement to carry out the work entrusted to us with the aforesaid instruments, saying: “Behold, these are the instruments of the spiritual art which I have set before you and, so to speak, placed in your own hands.”

“When these have been fulfilled by us unceasingly day and night.”] “Day and night,” that is, always; or, as Trithemius explains it, in prosperity and adversity.

[Col. 0349A] “That reward will be repaid to us by the Lord which he himself has promised, what eye has not seen, and so forth.”] O reward! Who would grant me to enjoy it at once? Certainly, if in view of it we do not strive with all our strength to advance in the spiritual art, these words of Saint Odo may rightly be turned against us (Conference 3, no. 18):

“All who practice any crafts for the use of this life conduct them just as they learned them from their teachers, and they use those tools which suit the activity to which they are devoted, as do sailors, shoemakers, and smiths. Yet we monks alone cast away the instruments of good works which Saint Benedict constructed for attaining heavenly life; we alone, deserters from our profession, transgress now to the right, now to the left, the lines which he showed us through our teachers; nor do we deem it worthy to use the instruments of good works as they were handed down by our teachers.”

“The workshop in which we are to work diligently at all these things.”] Concerning this workshop Saint John Climacus writes (Ladder 26): “We call a religious coenobium a fuller’s workshop, because it cuts away and removes the soul’s filth, coarseness, and deformity.”

“The enclosure is the monastery.”] So that the monks will not need to wander outside under a pretext of piety in order to work diligently at all these things, since this is not beneficial to their souls.

“And stability in the community.”] That is, perseverance in the coenobium. By these words he censures the fickleness of those who pass from place to place, from monastery to monastery, or even from the common life to the solitary life, in which many of these instruments cannot effectively be practiced.

## CHAPTER V. On Obedience

[Note: Other copies: “on the obedience of disciples”; other copies: “what the obedience of disciples is like.”]

[Col. 0349]

[Col. 0349B] The first degree of humility is obedience without delay. This is appropriate to those who consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ, because of the holy service which they have professed [Lyons: “and because of”], or because of fear of hell, or because of the glory of eternal life. As soon as anything has been commanded by a superior [Cassian and Florence: “as soon as anything”], they know no delay in carrying it out [Cassian and Florence: “may they know”], as though it had been commanded by God himself. Concerning such people the Lord said: “At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me” (Psalm XXVII). And again he says to teachers: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matthew X).

Therefore such people immediately abandon what is theirs and forsake their own will; at once, with their hands freed from what they were doing, and leaving unfinished the task on which they were engaged, they follow the superior’s voice by the swift foot of obedience and by their deeds. Thus, as though in a single moment, the master’s command and the disciple’s completed work are both swiftly brought to fulfillment in the speed born of the fear of God; and these are the people upon whom love of advancing toward eternal life rests.

For this reason they seize the narrow way, of which the Lord says: “Narrow is the way which leads to life” (Matthew VII). They do not live according to their own judgment or obey their own desires and pleasures [Oxford: “wills”], but, living in monasteries, they walk according to another’s judgment and command and desire to have an abbot over them. Without doubt such people imitate that saying of the Lord in which he says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John V).

But this very obedience will then be acceptable to God and pleasing to human beings if what is commanded is carried out neither hesitantly, nor slowly, nor lukewarmly, nor with murmuring [other copies: *murmurio*, “murmuring”], nor with a reply expressing unwillingness; for the obedience offered to superiors is offered to God. He himself said: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Matthew X). [Cassian, with certain manuscripts, reads *obedit* (“obeys”) in place of *audit* (“hears”).] And it must be offered by the disciples with a good disposition, because “God loves a cheerful giver” (II Corinthians IX).

For if a disciple obeys with a bad disposition and murmurs not only with his mouth but also in his heart, then, even if he fulfills the command, it will no longer be acceptable to God, who sees the heart of the one who murmurs. [Oxford and Florence manuscripts: “who sees the one who murmurs.”] For such an action he receives no grace; rather, he incurs the punishment of those who murmur, unless he corrects it through satisfaction.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0349]

[Col. 0349D] “The first degree of humility is obedience without delay.” These words contain no slight difficulty. For in chapter seven he placed obedience in the third degree of humility, whereas here he establishes it in the first. Peter Boherius untangles the knot of this difficulty in two ways.

First, obedience may rightly be called the first degree of humility, not in order but in excellence and dignity. Bernard of Cassino also employs this solution. And indeed the virtue of obedience is so great that it is preferred even to sacrifices.

Second, obedience may be the first external degree of humility, while fear is the internal degree. He derived this answer from Smaragdus, who responds to the question as follows: “Fear is first in the heart; obedience is first in action.”

Our Menardus devised a third solution: “Obedience,” he says, “is not first in the order of humility, but is superior in usefulness.” Certainly, as Saint Gregory testifies, “Obedience alone is the virtue which implants the other virtues in the mind and preserves them once implanted.”

John Craesbeeck supplies a fourth solution when he says that obedience is the first degree of humility, not absolutely, but the first among those degrees which a religious person begins to practice and ascend while living in a monastery. For he ought to have ascended the first two before his conversion, that is, before he was joined to the body of the community. He proves this by the authority of Saint Bernard in his treatise On the Degrees of Humility, degree 10.

I add a fifth solution: by the word “humility,” the holy Father understands nothing other than obedience itself, which he calls by the name of humility, because these two virtues are so mutually connected and interwoven that neither can exist without the other. Hildemar seems to have understood Saint Benedict in this way, writing concerning this passage:

“It must be considered why he says ‘of humility,’ when, as the key to the chapter, he speaks of obedience. For he could have said, ‘The first degree of obedience is.’ But he said ‘of humility’ for this reason: these three virtues—charity, humility, and obedience—are so closely joined that one cannot exist without the other. For where obedience is, there are humility and charity.”

In this sense, “the first degree of humility” means the same as “one degree of obedience.” This interpretation seems to be the most ancient, since Hildemar testifies that “first” is understood here by some to mean “only.”

Indeed, Saint Benedict does not subsequently assign a second or third degree of obedience. Nor do the holy Fathers appear to have admitted any other obedience except that which tolerates no delay. Hence they defined it as conviction without examination (Saint Antiochus, Homily 39), and judged him guilty of disobedience who caused even the slightest delay in carrying out a command:

“If anyone,” says Saint Columbanus (Rule, chapter 2), “does not rise immediately upon hearing the word, he is to be judged disobedient.”

Something similar is read in A Certain Rule for Monks (chapter 29):

“If anyone, at the voice of one who calls or invites him to anything whatever, does not rise immediately, he is guilty of disobedience. Let him ask pardon and presume not to repeat it, because each person ought to rise at the voice of his own inviter as though a burning coal had fallen upon him. If this is not the obedience we have described, it is dead and unacceptable before God.”

Saint Basil demonstrates how ready and swift the monks’ obedience ought to be by a more pleasing comparison. When asked, “With what disposition ought one to obey the person who urges and presses us to carry out a command?” he replied:

“With as much as a little child obeys its nurse when she calls it to a meal, and as anyone whose life is dear obeys the person who supplies him with the necessities of life—indeed, with much more, since eternal life is nobler than the present life.”

“This”—namely, obedience without delay—“is appropriate to those who consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ.”] For who, unless inflamed by divine love, would obey a superior at his command so that he obeyed without any intervening delay?

“Because of the holy service which they have professed, and so forth.”] [Col. 0351C] Here he proposes three reasons, like so many spurs, by which a monk is urged to obey without delay.

The first is the holy service which they have professed—that is, their profession, by which before the altar they have devoted themselves as perpetual servants to the supreme Lord of all. Saint Bernard used the same spur to encourage his followers to repel unlawful thoughts:

“Are you, who are a priest, who are a cleric, who are a monk, then obliged to think of such things?” he asks (Sermon 33, On Various Matters). “Should a worshiper of justice admit anything unjust into himself? Is it fitting for a servant of Christ, a lover of God, even briefly to contemplate such a thing?”

With the same exhortation Peter the Venerable encouraged the hermit Gilbert toward perfection (Book I, Letter 20):

“I set a cell before you, so that, in accordance with the saying of an ancient Father, by its silence alone it may teach you more eloquently than all teachers. Certainly you will not be able not to listen to it, when you have it as your daily admonisher of salvation.”

Saint Benedict calls monastic profession not simply “service” but “holy service,” both because it makes the monk holy, and because through it he is consecrated to the service of the Lord of hosts, and also “because it was begun from the Holy Spirit with a holy purpose,” as Trithemius says.

The second reason is fear of hell. By this expression Hildemar understands not only eternal punishment but also temporal punishment, although Bernard of Cassino and Boherius hold that Saint Benedict’s words should be understood of eternal hell alone.

The third reason is the glory of eternal life, which can add so many spurs to human beings for right living and to monks for obedience that no one fails to see it.

“As soon as anything has been commanded by a superior.”] He says “by a superior” because they must obey not only the abbot or provost but also the priors or elders—provided that the command of the abbot or provost has been given first, as Boherius notes. Nevertheless, I would think that here “superior” should properly be understood as the abbot.

[Col. 0352A] “As though it had been commanded by God, they know no delay in carrying it out.”] This is like the Egyptian and Tabennesiote monks, of whom Cassian writes (Institutes IV, chapter 10):

“They hasten to fulfill everything that has been commanded by him as though it had been issued from heaven by God, without any examination. Sometimes they even accept commands which are impossible for them with such faith and devotion that they strive with all their strength and without any hesitation of heart to carry them out and complete them.”

The Rules of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius likewise teach that one must obey a superior as the Lord, with complete joy.

“Concerning such people the Lord says: ‘At the hearing of the ear he obeyed me.’”] That is, as soon as he heard, he obeyed.

“And again he says to teachers: ‘Whoever hears you hears me.’”] He says “to teachers,” lest anyone think that these words were spoken only to the apostles or disciples.

“Therefore such people.”] Those who consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ.

“They immediately abandon what is theirs.”] That is, what has been granted to them by the abbot and the Rule for their own use, as Hildemar explains. For monks possess nothing of their own, since neither their bodies nor their wills are in their own power. Or “what is theirs” may mean what belongs to them by work or custody, as Boherius says in his second commentary—that is, what they were doing and what had been entrusted to their care. Finally, “what is theirs” may mean what they prefer and like best, according to Bernard of Cassino and Boherius in his first commentary.

“And forsake their own will.”] By “their own will” Hildemar understands the delight and pleasure which we experience in working. Hence Bernard of Cassino asserts that these words explain the preceding ones, so that “to forsake one’s own will” and “to abandon what is one’s own” mean the same thing.

“At once, with their hands freed from what they were doing, and leaving unfinished the task on which they were engaged.”] Thus Marcus the monk, in order to obey the command of the one giving orders, left the letter O unfinished; and many examples of this kind occur throughout the lives of the saints. Yet no work is ever completed more perfectly than when it is left unfinished for the sake of obedience.

“They follow the superior’s voice by the swift foot of obedience,” and so forth.] These words require no exposition but practice.

From what has so far been said about obedience without delay, the conduct of certain monks remains sufficiently condemned: they wish to examine the commands of their superiors before carrying them out. Concerning such people Saint Bernard writes (Sermon 41, On Various Matters):

“We see many people, after the command of the one giving orders, raise many questions: asking again and again, ‘Why? For what reason? On what account?’; repeatedly making complaints; asking why he gave this command, where it came from, and who devised this plan. From this comes murmuring, words expressing and smelling of murmuring and indignation, words redolent of bitterness; from this frequent excuses, the pretense of impossibility, the calling in of friends.”

Yet, as Abbot William of Saint-Thierry says (On the Contemplative Life, no. 14), “perfect obedience, especially in a beginner, is undiscriminating—that is, not to distinguish why or for what reason a command is given, but to strive only to carry out faithfully and humbly what is commanded by the superior.”

Hence Peter of Blois writes (Letter 134):

“Without any selection, without any exception, let the professor of the Rule do what is enjoined upon him. Let him not distinguish what, of what kind, or how great the thing enjoined is. Otherwise he presumes to eat from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. For the judgment of discernment belongs to the spiritual father, who judges everything and is judged by no one. Let him therefore distinguish nothing; let him be undiscerning in order to understand, foolish in order to become wise.”

For, as he says elsewhere (Letter 131):

“It is a form of contumacy to inquire about the manner of a command, to hesitate, to distinguish, or to delay. In the covenant of obedience there is no place for argument or disputation. For if you subject what has been commanded to you to examination or suspicion, you stretch out the hand of transgression toward the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. This obedience is excessively delicate, passing over into the deliberative kind of case. This is not to obey at the hearing of the ear; this is not regular obedience without delay, but evasive cunning and open pride.”

Abbot Pynuphius thought very differently when, instructing a young brother, he said (in Cassian, Institutes IV, chapter 41):

“Make yourself foolish in this world, according to the Apostle’s saying, so that you may be wise: discerning and judging nothing of those things which are commanded you, but always offering obedience with complete simplicity and faith; judging only that to be holy, useful, and wise which either the law of God or the judgment of the elder has enjoined upon you. Established on such an instruction, under this discipline you will be able to persevere forever, and you will not be cast out of the coenobium by any temptations of the enemy or by any factions.”

“Upon whom rests the love of advancing toward eternal life.”] Smaragdus and Hildemar refer these words not to the preceding period but to the following one.

[Col. 0353B] “For this reason they seize the narrow way.”] Saint John Climacus demonstrates its signs and indications in these words (Ladder 2):

“The marks of the narrow way will be disclosed to you by affliction of the belly, all-night standing, moderation even in drinking water, frugality of bread or table, the cup of disgrace which purifies the soul, endurance of sarcasm, mockery, and ridicule, renunciation of one’s own wills, patience under offenses, no murmuring against our contempt, the assault of insults endured. If you bear firmly with the one who injures you, if you endure with an even spirit the one who slanders you, if you do not become angry when despised, if you humble yourself when condemned.”

Saint Benedict indicates the narrow way more briefly when he adds:

“So that they do not live according to their own judgment, or obey their own desires and pleasures, but, living in monasteries, walk according to another’s judgment and command.”] In these words, as Boherius observes, he kindles the three vows of our profession. In saying that they do not obey their own desires or pleasures, he indicates conversion of conduct. The following words, “walking according to another’s judgment and command,” signify obedience. “Living in monasteries” signifies stability.

“They desire to have an abbot over them.”] They do not doubt that those who rely on themselves and think they need no guide along the way are greatly deceived. Saint John Climacus speaks in this way (Ladder 1). Saint Dorotheus likewise said (Teaching 5, no. 1):

“Nothing is more pitiable, and nothing can be more easily deceived and overcome, than those who have no guide and seek no governor or instructor on the way of God. For what does divine Scripture say? ‘Those who have no guidance fall like leaves.’”

Saint Bernard held the same view, writing to Ogerius (Letter 87):

“He who makes himself his own teacher submits himself as a disciple to a fool. I do not know what others may think; I have learned from my own experience what I say: I can command more easily and preside more securely over many others than over myself alone.”

See the notes on this passage of Bernard in Mabillon’s edition.

[Col. 0353D] “But this very obedience will then be acceptable to God,” and so forth.] The holy Father now describes the conditions of perfect obedience. The first is that a monk obey neither hesitantly nor fearfully. Smaragdus writes:

“To hesitate is to fear and doubt.”

From this he concludes:

“He hesitates to obey who does not firmly hope in the Lord’s help”—that is, who fears and doubts concerning the future or the outcome of the matter.

Abraham certainly did not act in this way; nor did the one who, commanded to sacrifice his own son, believing in hope against hope, boldly undertook to fulfill the divine command. Following his example, let nothing terrify or disturb us. To use the words of Saint Bernard (Sermon 41, On Various Matters):

“If tribulation thunders, if persecution erupts, if sinners set a snare for you, if the wicked obstruct your way, do not abandon the way of obedience. Rather say: ‘I am ready and am not disturbed, that I may keep your commandments.’ For what benefit do the things listed above produce if strength is lacking—the strength which places the virtues in the stronghold of steadfastness and fortifies them with a rampart which the assault of raging forces cannot reach? Have you put your hand to a difficult task? It must be undertaken promptly, and obedience must be steadfast.”

The second condition of perfect obedience is to obey without delay, because, as Saint Bernard says in the same sermon:

“The word of God runs swiftly and desires to have a swift follower. Do you see with what speed the one who says, ‘I ran in the way of your commandments,’ runs? The faithful obedient person knows no delays, flees tomorrow, ignores slowness, anticipates the one giving orders, prepares his eyes for sight, his ears for hearing, his tongue for speech, his hands for work, his feet for the journey; he gathers his whole self together in order to gather the will of the one commanding.”

The third condition is not to obey lukewarmly, for God spews the lukewarm from his mouth. Hence Gilbert of Hoyland writes (Sermon 17 on the Song of Songs):

“He is dead who is overwhelmed by the weight either of weariness or of despair, in whom there is nothing of living devotion or fervent spirit. Even if he does not abandon the precepts of the law and confines himself within the embrace of the Rule, he nevertheless languishes with a cold and dying affection, sensing nothing pleasant in the holy work.”

The fourth condition is not to obey with murmuring, for whoever murmurs loses the reward of the good work.

The fifth is that obedience must not be carried out with a reply expressing unwillingness. Hence Saint Macarius says (Rule, chapter 4): “Do not use a reply against the command.” Saint Basil likewise says (Monastic Constitutions, chapter 23):

“Just as a smith or builder uses each instrument of his craft according to his own judgment, and the instrument does not say that it is unwilling to fulfill the use for which it is employed by the craftsman, but obeys the hand guiding it, so it is fitting for a religious person, like an instrument of his craftsman, to obey in all things for the completion of the spiritual building whatever the one giving the command judges can properly be administered by him.”

And elsewhere (Longer Rule, chapter 28):

“To reject and contradict displays many evils, such as sickly faith, hesitant hope, arrogance, and proud conduct.”

“For the obedience offered to superiors is offered to God,” and so forth.] “Therefore whatever a human being commands in the place of God, provided it is not certainly displeasing to God, is to be received no differently than if God himself had commanded it. For what difference does it make whether God makes his will known to human beings directly or through his ministers, whether human or angelic?” (These are Bernard’s words, On the Precept and Dispensation, chapter 9.)

“And it must be offered by the disciples with a good disposition, because God loves a cheerful giver.”] Hence Saint Bernard writes (Sermon 41, On Various Matters):

“Serenity in the face and sweetness in speech greatly enhance the obedience of the one who obeys. Thus that pagan poet also says: ‘Above all, good looks were added.’ For what place is there for obedience where the sickness of sadness is visible? External signs usually reveal the will of the mind, and it is difficult for those who change their will not to change their face. The cloudy arrangement of the body and the face darkened by shadows show that devotion has departed from the mind.”

Gerard of Cluny displayed himself as a thoroughly cheerful giver. Peter the Venerable writes of him (Book I of Miracles, chapter 8):

“I myself experienced his great constancy in this virtue. Although I often imposed upon him burdensome tasks which I would scarcely have dared to enjoin upon others, he received what was enjoined with great eagerness and fulfilled it with still greater eagerness.”

“For if a disciple obeys with a bad disposition.”] That is, with sadness, unwillingness, or murmuring.

“If a disciple obeys,” and so forth.] These words are clear.

“For such an action he receives no grace.”] From this one may infer how great a sin murmuring is, since by its cause even the best works of obedience are deprived of reward and recompense.

“Rather, he incurs the punishment of those who murmur,” and so forth.] Scripture records five punishments with which God punished murmuring:

1. Leprosy, as in the case of Miriam, the sister of Moses.
2. Heavenly fire, which consumed the tents of those who murmured.
3. The opening of the earth, which swallowed Korah, Dathan, and Abiram.
4. Fiery serpents, which killed the murmuring children of Israel.
5. Exclusion from the Promised Land.

“Saint Benedict,” says Bernard of Cassino, “brings the terror of these punishments, together with the loss of the reward of obedience, upon those who murmur.”

Boherius, however, seems to reject this interpretation, discussing the passage as follows:

“Some explain this of the fivefold punishment which certain murmurers endured severely in the Old Testament, such as the onset of leprosy, and so forth. But far be it from us to think that the Master, who assigned us a gentle Rule, invoked the ancient rigor rather than grace in this age of grace,” and so forth.

Richard of Saint Angelo seems to support Boherius’s opinion, writing:

“Their punishment will be at the abbot’s discretion, since no punishment is established here; or you may say that he will proceed against them according to the procedure set out below concerning excommunication for faults.”

Similarly, Nicholas of Fractura writes:

“The punishment will be this: according to the command of our Lord, he must be admonished once and again, and a second time secretly by his elders. If he does not amend, he is to be rebuked publicly before all. If he still does not correct himself, then, if he understands what kind of punishment is involved, he is to undergo excommunication; but if he is shameless, he is to be subjected to corporal punishment. Thus the Master defines below in the section on excommunication for faults.”

Nevertheless, Saint Benedict seems here to speak of a punishment inflicted by God, just as he speaks of a reward bestowed by him, of which the murmurers are deprived. Therefore Bernard’s opinion is preferable; Saint Benedict may have received it from Hildemar and Smaragdus.

Certainly, the holy Father here treats of the punishment due to those who murmur not only with their mouths but also in their hearts. Yet God alone knows the secrets of the heart, not the abbot or any other human being. Therefore this passage is not to be understood of a regular punishment imposed at the superior’s discretion, but of the just vengeance of God, who judges what is more hidden and from whose eyes nothing is concealed.

I do not mean by this, however, that God punishes every act of murmuring with leprosy, heavenly fire, the opening of the earth, and so forth. Rather, as Bernard of Cassino says, Saint Benedict instills the terror of these punishments.

Nor will I deny that murmuring should receive a regular punishment when it breaks out publicly. Saint Benedict strikes it with excommunication below, in chapter 23, and the ancient Fathers of monks inflicted various punishments upon it, as is clear from what was said above concerning chapter 4, and also from Cassian, Saint Basil, and Saint Columbanus.

Cassian’s words are these (Institutes IV, chapter 6):

“But if they discover that some fault of murmuring or some form of wicked disobedience has proceeded from him, they strip him of the monastery garments with which he had been clothed, dress him again in the ancient garments that had been set aside, and drive him away.”

Saint Basil (Longer Rule, chapter 29) commands in very severe words that the work of those who murmur be separated from the labors of the others, and forbids it to be converted to the common use of the brethren.

Likewise Saint Columbanus says (Rule, chapter 3):

“If anyone murmurs, he is to be considered disobedient, as one who does not obey willingly. Therefore his work is to be rejected until his good will is recognized.”

Boherius also cites the Eighth Council:

“Let the one who has murmured be separated from the unity of the brothers; and let the work of the one who has murmured be rejected, lest he incur the punishment of those who murmur, concerning whom the Apostle says: ‘Neither murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer.’”

Saint John Chrysostom agrees with these words (Homily 8 on the Epistle to the Philippians):

“It would be better to do nothing than to work with murmuring. We often prefer to be deprived of service than to endure one who murmurs. For the murmurer is grievous—very grievous, I say—and near to blasphemy.”

## CHAPTER VI. On Silence

[Col. 0355]

[Col. 0355C] Let us do what the prophet says: “I said, I will guard my ways, that I may not sin with my tongue; I have placed a guard over my mouth; I was silent and was humbled, and I kept silence from good things” (Psalm XXXVIII). [Other copies: “from this the prophet shows.”] Here the prophet shows that if at times one must keep silence from good speech because of the strictness of silence, how much more must one abstain from evil words because of the punishment of sin! [Other copy: “should be abstained from.”]

Therefore, although permission to speak concerning good, holy, and edifying matters [Narbonne: “of holy edification”; Hildemar: “holy matters for edification”] is granted only rarely to perfect disciples because of the seriousness of silence—for it is written [these words are absent in Hildemar], “In much speaking you will not escape sin” [Narbonne: “sin will not be escaped”] (Proverbs X), and elsewhere, “Death and life are in the power of the tongue” (Proverbs XIV)—speaking and teaching befit the teacher, whereas silence and listening befit the disciple. [Other copy: “befit the disciple.”]

And therefore, if anything must be asked of the prior, let it be asked with complete humility and submissive reverence, lest he appear to speak more than is fitting. [Oxford copy: “with the utmost reverence”; Conches manuscript: “with all humility and submission”; Lyons and Faro manuscripts: “with all humility and reverence”; several manuscripts: “with all humility, submission, and reverence”; Narbonne copy: “with restraint and the utmost reverence.” The words “lest he appear to speak more than is fitting,” which occur in the Oxford copy, are missing from nearly all the manuscripts. Hildemar, explaining this passage, also says: “It is not in the Rule, but is implied.”]

But we condemn forever, in every place, buffoonery, idle words, and words that provoke laughter; and we do not permit the disciple to open his mouth for such speech.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0355]

[Col. 0355D] “Let us do what the prophet says.”] Hildemar makes an acute observation here, followed by Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura: Saint Benedict, addressing his disciples, did not simply say, “Do this,” but “Let us do this.” In other words, he joins himself to his brothers and requires from them nothing that he himself is not prepared to carry out first, before the others.

“I said, I will guard my ways.”] That is, all the acts of life, concerning the guarding of which we spoke in chapter 4.

[Col. 0356D] “That I may not sin with my tongue.”] The tongue is therefore a difficult member of the human body, since it requires such guarding lest it sin—truly difficult. To use Saint Bernard’s words (Sermon 17, On Various Matters):

“For who could count the stains contracted by this small member, the tongue, or the manifold impurity that coagulates upon uncircumcised lips? How great is the danger of an unrestrained mouth! There is a tongue loose in idle speech; there is an immodest tongue; there is also a grandiloquent tongue. The first serves lust, the next arrogance. There is also a deceitful tongue and a slanderous tongue. The former is subdivided into false and flattering speech; the latter sometimes inflicts insult openly and sometimes secretly detracts.”

Peter Damian likewise writes (Opusculum 9, chapter 27):

“The Apostle says: ‘Every kind of beast is found in the tongue.’ For there is the lightness of birds, the fierceness of beasts, and the poisonous deceit of serpents. Those who set their mouths against heaven and whose mouth speaks vanity are birds, as it were in the lightness of birds. Those who sharpen their tongues like a sword are fierce beasts. Finally, serpents are those of whom it is said: ‘The poison of asps is under their lips.’”

“I have placed a guard over my mouth.”] Not a wall, but a guard, or a door or gate, which “is sometimes closed and sometimes opened . . . so that it may be silent at the proper time and at the proper time say what must be said,” as Hildemar says.

Or, as Bernard of Cassino says, “guard” can mean the enclosure of silence, or the door in which the virtue of silence is a kind of key for guarding. Hence our predecessors commonly used to say that silence is the key of religion.

“I was silent and was humbled.”] Hildemar notes that he joined these two expressions together as though he were saying: “I was not silent arrogantly.” For some remain silent either through pride or through anger. Saint Gregory writes of them (Moralia XXXIV, chapter 20):

“Sometimes the proud do not at all reveal the obstinate things they feel. Those whose talkativeness can scarcely be restrained sometimes become silent solely from the bitterness of inward resentment. By withdrawing the words of their insolence through mental pain, although they are accustomed to speak wickedly, they are silent still more wickedly. For when sinners hear something about correction, they angrily suspend even their words of reply.”

“And I kept silence from good things.”] From this Saint Benedict infers:

“Here the prophet shows that if at times he ought to refrain from good and edifying speech because of the strictness of silence, how much more ought he to abstain from evil words because of the punishment of sin!”] The holy Father adapts the prophet’s words to commend silence, although in their proper and genuine sense they seem to be understood of preachers who remain silent when they are unable to restrain the vices of sinners.

Nevertheless, as Saint Gregory says (Register II, chapter 101):

“Nothing in the interpretation of Sacred Scripture should be rejected that does not resist sound faith. Just as from one quantity of gold some make necklaces, others rings, and others bracelets for adornment, so the various interpreters compose from the one knowledge of Scripture, through countless interpretations, ornaments of many kinds; yet all of them contribute to the beauty of the heavenly bride.”

Saint Benedict draws two conclusions from the prophet’s words. First, one must be silent from good speech because of silence—that is, because of the dignity of silence, which is itself a service of righteousness. Second, one must be silent from evil words because of the punishment of sin. For if we are to give an account on the day of judgment for every idle word, how much more for an evil one?

Therefore, although it concerns good, holy, and edifying speech [Col. 0357D].—We may learn something of what sort of speech this is from what Peter the Venerable writes to Peter of Poitiers in these words (Book II, Letter 22):

> “How often, with the doors shut and no mortal admitted among us, with only that witness present who is never absent from those thinking or conferring about him, a fearful conversation was held concerning the blindness and hardness of the human heart; the various snares of sins; the manifold ambushes of demons; the abyss of God’s judgments—how terrible he is in his counsels toward the children of men; that he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills; that a human being does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred; our uncertain and fearful calling; the dispensation of human salvation accomplished through the incarnation and passion of the Son of God; the dreadful day of the last judgment; the incomprehensible severity of the divine examination, by which he punishes the wicked forever; and the ineffable mercy by which he repays the good with eternal rewards. The discussion of these and similar matters, removed from worldly bustle, brought before me, in a certain sense, the desert in the midst of human society and represented the Lord’s tabernacle, to which I fled from the tumults of the world as Moses fled from the stones of the Jews.” [Col. 0358A]

And to his brother Pontius (Book I, Letter 16):

> “You had lived with me for nearly ten years. How much we discussed among ourselves concerning divine things during that time; how fervent was our conversation about spiritual matters; how frequent our discussions concerning contempt for present things; how vigorous our exhortation toward the desire for eternal things—you yourself know, and I have not wholly forgotten. The fervor of charity had grown so hot between us that I, who had begun to love you solely through the impulse of nature, no longer knew how to love you except from God and in God.”

These and similar matters are called good, holy, and edifying speech. Such conversations befit the servants of God. To use the words of Gerard, a Belgian monk (Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 42):

> “This alone is a recreation worthy of monks, according to the examples of the Fathers; but whoever finds nothing equally delightful except to hear about the rumors of the world is plainly shown still to be a child of earth and of the world.”

Gilbert of Holland puts it very aptly (Sermon 18 on the Song of Songs):

> “Remember,” he said, “that your mouth has been consecrated to heavenly kisses and oracles; consider it sacrilege if anything not sweet, not divine, and not sounding forth from the divine page proceeds from it.”

With perfect disciples.—“Perfect,” he says. Therefore no permission to speak should ever be granted to the imperfect and foolish, except in matters that are necessary, whether spiritual or bodily, as Hildemar explains. Boherius, however, declares who are to be considered perfect disciples in these words:

> “Those are called perfect who renounce all their possessions and follow the life of Christ, as cenobites ought to be. … They are also called perfect who have already escaped the dangers of temptations, among whom there is nothing but thanksgiving and a voice of praise. Those, moreover, are proved perfect who do not even make use of what the law permits.”

By “disciples,” Nicholas Bravus understands “especially the juniors, and those who, whether because of their gray hair or because of the authority of their office, still appear not to have passed beyond discipleship.” [Col. 0358C] But far be it from us, while restraining the juniors under silence, to permit free speech to the elderly or to those elevated to some office; for they themselves ought rather to display to the younger monks examples of silence and of the other virtues. Saint Benedict himself decisively refutes so inept an explanation at the end of this chapter, where, while prohibiting buffoonery, he says: “We do not permit a disciple to open his mouth for such speech.” Here, as also in chapter 3, under the name “disciple” he includes all monks without exception, whom he calls perfect disciples because they have vowed not merely perfection but the perfection of perfection.

Because of the gravity of silence.—That is, its eminence, dignity, and usefulness.

Let permission to speak be granted rarely.—Concerning this passage Saint Hildegard writes:

> “That is, when something must be done jointly in councils, in business, or in matters of greater necessity, permission should not be given for people to speak individually, but they should say moderately and briefly what is required; then, after a signal has been given, all should remain silent according to the customary practice. Since Benedict had not fixed this permission at a definite hour on each day, but kept it in his own power as was fitting—for he did not grant it without being compelled by some just necessity or pious usefulness—nevertheless, because it is inhuman for a person always to remain silent and not speak, the same Father leaves the matter to the authority and discretion of the abbot, just as he grants him many other things, so that he may provide his disciples with a suitable hour in which they may speak with one another about what is honest and necessary, and may not become weary through indiscreet silence. After such permission to speak with one another, they can more suitably and strictly be admonished and restrained to silence.”

Thus far Saint Hildegard, from whose words we can gather three points.

**181. First**, the Rule assigns no fixed or established time for mutual conversation; rather, silence is imposed on monks almost perpetually. Hence Gilbert of Holland writes (Sermon 7 on the Song of Songs):

> “It belongs to monks not to converse but to be silent.”

Saint Benedict certainly adhered as closely as he could to the example of the Egyptian monks, who, as Cassian testifies, were perpetually silent. For Cassian says (Book II, chapter 15):

> “When the psalms had been completed and the daily gathering, as we mentioned above, had ended, none of them dared remain even briefly or converse with another. Indeed, no one presumed to leave his cell or abandon the work he was accustomed to perform there for the entire span of the day. They carried this out after entering through the doors, so that no conversation at all was heard among them.”

Palladius also reports of Abbot Theonas (Lausiac History, chapters 50 and 85) that he remained silent for thirty-five years; and of a certain virgin that she had spoken with no one for twenty-five years. “They also said” (Volume I of *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, p. 377) “that Abbot Agatho carried a stone in his mouth for three years, until he had learned to be silent.”

But all these were surpassed by John, surnamed the Silent, who, having become a monk from being a bishop, spent forty-seven entire years in silence. What shall I say of the Virgin Mother of God, who, as the Mellifluous Doctor notes (Sermon on the Sunday within the Octave of the Assumption), is recorded as having spoken only four times throughout the entire course of the Gospels?

There is no doubt that the holy Father wished examples of this kind to be proposed to his disciples for imitation when he prescribed no time for speaking in the Rule. In order to comply with his wishes, his beloved sons strove to maintain almost continual silence in the monasteries. Among these, the monks of Cluny excelled above all. They seemed to have exchanged their hands for tongues, with their mouths almost permanently closed, having devised signs [Note: These signs are found in Book V of *On Ancient Monastic Rites*, chapter 18] by which, while the tongue was silent, they expressed to one another whatever necessarily had to be requested. [Col. 0359C]

Yet we can read with no little astonishment what William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, writes about the silence of the Cistercians in Book I of *The Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 7:

> “Finally, in that valley full of people, where no one was permitted to be idle, while everyone was laboring and each person was occupied with his assigned tasks, those arriving at midday found the silence of midnight, except for the sounds of their labors—or if the brothers were occupied in the praises of God. Moreover, the order and reputation of that silence inspired such reverence even among the secular people who arrived that they themselves feared to speak there not only of anything wicked or idle, but even of anything irrelevant to the matter at hand.”

Saint Bernard himself confirms this when he urges his monks to give one another good counsel. When the following objection is raised:

> “What counsel shall I give a brother, when I am not permitted to say even one word to him without permission?”

he replies that they should counsel their brother “not by word or tongue, but by deed and truth”—that is, by a good example. [Col. 0359D]

At nearly the beginning of the present century, the nuns of the Cistercian order in Spain who followed the stricter observance likewise bound themselves to an almost equally severe silence. But what William of Malmesbury writes about the nuns of Font-Evraud seems to surpass every human conception (Book V of *The Kings of England*):

> “Apart from renouncing all other enticements, how small a matter it is that they speak nowhere except in the chapter house, under the rule of perpetual silence laid down by their master, since once silence has been relaxed women are prone to whispering frivolities!”

Later, however—that is, in the year 1450—the strictness of this silence was moderated by the authority of the supreme pontiff:

> “so that they might speak after the prayers called Prime, and then after the signal given for work,”

as John Picard observes in his notes on chapter 15 of Book I of the *History of Newburgh*. See the *Life of Saint Stephen of Obaz*, Book I, no. 9.

**Second**, although the Rule designates no definite time at which the brothers should meet with one another, it is nevertheless more suitable that they should sometimes be granted permission for mutual conversation in order to relax their minds. “For it is inhuman for a person always to remain silent and not speak,” says Saint Hildegard. Saint Anthony and Saint Basil, both distinguished observers of the monastic life, held the same opinion. “It will be useful to speak if virtue is discussed at an appropriate time,” says Saint Basil.

And Saint Anthony, according to Saint Athanasius (in his Life, chapter 15), “said that Scripture could suffice for the whole discipline of the commandments, but that it would also be very good if the brothers consoled one another through mutual conversation.”

That this was Saint Benedict’s intention is clear both from this chapter, in which he grants some speech, although rarely, and wishes a guard or door to be placed upon the mouth according to the example of the prophet—something which is opened at one time and closed at another, as Hildemar says—and from chapter 48, in which he mentions unsuitable hours, during which a brother may by no means approach another brother. This presupposes suitable hours during which the brothers may speak. [Col. 0360B]

Indeed, in chapter 31 he orders that at suitable hours what ought to be given should be given, and what ought to be requested should be requested. Our ancient Fathers understood this to refer to the hours of mutual conversation. Thus the cellarer and chamberlain were required to be present when the brothers spoke together in the cloister, so that if anyone needed anything, they would have them at hand and could freely request and receive it from them.

That this is the genuine meaning of the Rule is clear from Saint Adalard, both in Book II of the *Statutes*, chapter 6, where he says (Volume IV of *Spicilegium*):

> “When the unsuitable hours have passed, and the time for speaking and joining together has arrived, etc.”

and from his chapters on admonitions in the assembly, where number 43 concerns “unsuitable hours, that is, silence.” Therefore, speaking was permitted at suitable hours.

Nor should anyone argue that, because Saint Benedict prohibits a brother from joining himself to another brother at unsuitable hours, it cannot at all be inferred that there were suitable hours when the brothers could lawfully join one another and converse—as though “joining” and “speaking” were the same thing—since the holy Father distinguishes the two below in chapter 26. There, concerning those who associate with excommunicated persons, he says:

> “If any brother should presume, without the abbot’s command, to join himself in any way to an excommunicated brother, or to speak with him, or to send him a message, let him undergo a similar punishment of excommunication.”

No, I say, this does not stand in the way. For if there is any distinction, it is only that “joining oneself” refers to prolonged and extended conversation, whereas “speaking” may refer to something passing and brief, as well as to prolonged speech. Indeed, Saint Benedict, who in that chapter prohibits every conversation with excommunicated persons, gives the chapter this title: “Concerning those who without the abbot’s command join themselves to excommunicated persons.” He does not say “who join themselves or speak,” because both are understood under the word “join themselves.”

Someone might add the passage in chapter 49 on the observance of Lent, in which Saint Benedict commands that something be subtracted from the talkativeness of other times. This is also confirmed by the perpetual practice of the order, an example of which can be seen in the *Life of Saint Frodobert, Abbot of Celle* (Second Century of the Benedictines, p. 630), where he is said sometimes to have held familiar conversation with his disciples.

The result is that monks are not wearied and that silence may afterward be observed more strictly, as Saint Hildegard teaches. We must fear that if the mind is occupied too long either with silence or with prayer, it may eventually fail, like a bow which, when stretched too far or for too long, is either weakened or broken.

Nor does it matter that chapter 42 of the Rule commands monks to strive for silence at all times. “Always to be silent” and “to strive for silence at all times” differ greatly. To be always silent is never to speak; but someone can strive for silence even while speaking—for example, by saying only what is necessary, briefly and in a subdued voice. Nevertheless, we praise and proclaim blessed those who can and are able to remain perpetually silent in such a way that they need no human companionship; and we earnestly pray that God may at some time grant us this gift.

**Third**, the assignment of the days, hours, time or duration, place, and manner of conversation depends upon the abbot’s judgment. A common practice of the order nevertheless became established: the abbot permitted conversation only on ordinary days, while Sundays and feast days were consecrated to continual silence with the twelve lessons.

Among the five chapters that the Centuriators added to the received capitularies of the Council of Aachen (Volume II of Baluze’s *Capitularies*, p. 1092), the fourth reads:

> “That during Easter week they shall not speak in the cloister, but all shall attend to sacred reading; likewise during Pentecost week, and on all Sundays, and on Christmas Day, and on all the principal feasts of the saints.”

Similarly, the ancient *Customs of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon* (chapter 64) state:

> “For the eight days of Easter, Pentecost, and Christmas, and during Rogationtide, and on every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday of Lent, and during all twelve lessons, there is no speaking in the cloister.”

The same words appear in the old Corbie manuscript *Ordinary*, and the *Book of the Uses of Bec* agrees with it, allowing speech in the cloister only on ordinary days. By contrast, Guigo’s Statutes (chapter 7, no. 9) permit conversation on Sundays after None; the ancient Carthusian statutes add chapter feasts. In the new collection of statutes, however, Christmas, Maundy Thursday, Easter, and Pentecost are excepted, together with the feasts occurring during the week in Lent; they also grant a walk each week.

From Udalric we learn that the Cluniacs designated two hours each day for conversation: in summer, after chapter and after None; in winter, after chapter and after Sext. The same practice can be seen throughout the ancient Customs of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon and the Corbie *Ordinary*. [Col. 0361C]

Later, however, Peter the Venerable removed the second of these times by issuing a statute:

> “Of the two customary periods of speech in the cloister, let the second be withdrawn throughout the entire year.”

The *Uses of Bec*, taking the seasons into account, prescribe:

> “On all ordinary days on which Terce is said after chapter, they shall speak in the cloister only once, that is, after chapter, except from the octave of Easter until the Ides of September, during which period they speak in the cloister after None on ordinary days. When Terce is said before chapter, they speak twice in the cloister, after chapter and after Sext.”

In some monasteries in England the appointed hour for conversation was after dinner. But, “since some people after dinner are more inclined to say what is unprofitable than what edifies those who hear, in order to increase the cultivation of righteousness, which is found in silence, it has been decreed that the parlamento which is accustomed to take place after dinner in certain cloisters should be entirely prohibited, and that the time be devoted more abundantly to meditation and the repetition of readings,” as the abbots of our order state in statutes issued in 1249.

The monks of Casale spoke after Vespers on fast days and after supper on days when they ate. Many had neither a designated day nor a designated hour; all their affairs depended upon a single nod from the abbot.

The length of time for which the period of mutual conversation was extended was not the same in all monasteries. Concerning the Cluniacs, who had two periods of speech each day, we should first hear Udalric. Of the first, which took place after chapter, he writes (Book I, chapter 18):

> “At the time when I first came to the monastery, a priest who wished to celebrate a private Mass could finish it during that interval. This now rarely happens, however, because the number of brothers has increased. While offerings are made at both Masses, while the peace is given and received, while one thing or another is called out in chapter, and while so many are served in the refectory, no small portion of the day is consumed. Yet none of these things can be omitted without compromising and disrupting our order. For this reason the hour for speaking must necessarily be shorter; and if we speak somewhat less, no one in the order has perceived any harm in it.”

Since no one is unable to celebrate a private Mass in less than half an hour, the first period of conversation did not extend beyond that length of time; later it was shortened still further.

The second period was also much shorter, according to the same Udalric:
