> “The hour of None, at which they are to rise, will be so late that after they have drunk in the refectory and again received permission to speak, I should rightly call that same period of speech, and the interval before Vespers, not small but nonexistent. More often, before everyone has sat down in the cloister and any brother has said even a single word, the signal for Vespers is sounded—and behold, the end of speaking.”

Elsewhere (Book I, chapter 40), concerning the same period when it took place after Sext, he writes:

> “We have permission to speak not only after chapter but also after Sext, although that interval is usually extremely brief. It will last no longer than the time needed for the priest and the others who are to serve at the principal Mass to wash their hands and prepare themselves to vest.”

**185.** The Cistercians spent an entire hour in conversation, according to James of Vitry:

> “Observing silence for almost the whole day, they reserve one hour for mutual conversations and conferences, consoling and instructing one another” (Book II of the *History of the West*, chapter 14).

Julian Varnier explains this not as though they reserved one hour every day for mutual conversation, but as meaning that whenever the abbot granted the brothers permission to speak, they devoted a full hour to this activity. Saint Bernard should be understood as referring to this hour when, describing a proud monk, he writes (Treatise on the Degrees of Humility, chapter 14):

> “When the signal is sounded and the conversation must be interrupted, he complains that a long hour has been cut short by a brief interval.”

In these conversations, as I may observe in passing, discussion sometimes concerned books. “If discussion arises about books,” says Saint Bernard, “old works and new are brought forth; opinions fly about, and inflated words resound.” Sometimes it concerned religion: “But if the subject is religion, visions and dreams are immediately produced; then he praises fasts,” and so forth. Sometimes it concerned amusing matters: “If the conversation turns to entertainments, the more accustomed he is to these, the more talkative he is found to be.”

From this you may conclude that such conversations were not communal—that is, they did not take place with everyone gathered together at once—but occurred among individuals divided according to their own wishes or according to the abbot’s command. Otherwise Saint Bernard, who would have been present if they had been communal, would by no means have tolerated frivolous amusements.

How often this hour occurred is unknown to us. The nuns of the Cistercian order in Spain who followed the stricter observance (Constitutions, chapters 2 and 11, in Henriquez’s *Lilies of Citeaux*, p. 26) had recreation once a week outside Advent and Lent, meeting before or after Vespers at the command of the abbess, provided that the day was not one on which Communion was received.

Similarly, in the ancient Constitutions of Fuliens, chapter 6:

> “Only once a week, on a feast day, the brothers are permitted to spend some of the intervals during which they are absent from choir in pious and religious conversation.”

[Note: In the editions of 1631, this is assigned by the superior each day for approximately one hour.]

Much the same practice prevailed among those distinguished hermits with whom Saint Dominic Loricatus lived. According to Peter Damian (Life of Saint Dominic, chapter 6):

> “They maintained strict silence throughout the entire week; on Sunday, however, after they had ended Vespers and taken their food, they had permission to speak with one another until the office of Compline.”

[Col. 0363A] The Cassinese do not seem to have granted their monks so much indulgence. Their Declarations on chapter 6 of the Rule state:

> “To avoid enervation, the superiors and other leaders should grant consolations or recreations only every other week, except during Lent and Advent, when it is unlawful even to think of such things, much less to permit them.”

In the Declarations printed in 1642, however, “every week” appears instead of “every other week.” Moreover, both the new and the old Declarations on chapter 48 exhort superiors to be kind in granting recreations to the brothers, especially on double solemnities that do not occur during Advent or Lent.

The Camaldolese (Book I of the *Camaldolese Constitutions*), when they dispense from silence, permit conversation for only half an hour in the garden or some other part of the monastery where perpetual silence is not in force.

The monks of Casale conversed daily from supper until Compline, or on fast days from Vespers until Compline, but in such a way that during that period they could withdraw to their cells and devote themselves to reading and prayer. After dinner, however, they walked in the garden in silence for half an hour.

The Bursfeld monks do not appear to have had a fixed day, hour, or period for conversation. In their *Ceremonial* they decree only the following (Distinction 3, chapter 10):

> “Permission to speak in the monastery or outside it shall be granted only by the abbot and prior, or by the subprior in the prior’s absence, unless perhaps the abbot and prior have granted someone else authority for some special occasion. The person granting the brothers permission to speak shall say: ‘Bless,’ and they shall answer: ‘God.’ From that moment it shall be lawful to discuss with one another the matters permitted, until silence is imposed again with these words: ‘Our help is in the name of the Lord.’ Therefore no one may speak without permission; but once permission or the faculty of speaking has been granted, no one shall speak without first saying ‘Bless’ and receiving the response ‘The Lord.’”

There were various monastic customs concerning the place of conversation. Saint Adalard assigns the dormitory in Book II of his *Statutes*, chapter 6. The Cluniacs, monks of Dijon, Parisians, monks of Bec, and others commonly spoke with the Carthusians in the cloister; the Camaldolese spoke in the garden. It is rare, however, to find the ancient monks walking outside the monastery for the sake of recreation.

As for the manner or order to be observed in conversation, first, they did not begin it without saying “Bless.” The manuscript *Ordinary of Saint Peter above the Dives* says:

> “After chapter, let everyone sit in the cloister for conversation. When the drum has been heard, let them proceed to Sext; after it has been sung, let them return to the conversation, and let the last novice in order say: ‘Bless.’ Thus let them speak about customs and about good and edifying speech.”

Among the Bursfeld monks and Carthusians, it was not the last person but the one presiding over the conversation who said “Bless.” They also read something before beginning to speak. “When on chapter days we meet in the cloister after None has been said in the church,” they state in the new *Collection of Statutes*, “before we sit down, the person presiding over the assembly says: ‘Bless.’ Then a reading from the Statutes or the Gospels follows. When it has ended, we converse; no one should consult secretly, whisper, or say anything that he does not want everyone to understand or hear.”

The nuns of the Cistercian order in Spain who followed the stricter observance appear to have maintained the same discipline. Their Constitutions require (chapter 11):

> “When the abbess has granted permission for recreation or conversation, the conversations shall be religious; for this purpose some pious book may be used.”

Once permission to speak had been granted, two, three, or more persons were joined together by the superior. With these, and not with others, they exchanged conversation about honest and pious matters. The ancient Statutes of Saint Adalard prescribe this (Book II, chapter 6, Volume IV of *Spicilegium*):

> “When speaking is permitted—for speech must always be regulated there [in the dormitory]—let two, three, or even more be joined together, as normally happens when they rise from chapter.”

Alternatively, each person spoke promiscuously with whomever he wished, as his inclination directed. This seems to have been the custom of the Cluniacs, Carthusians, and even Cistercians, as we gathered above from Saint Bernard.

At that time, those who needed something especially requested it, as Udalric writes concerning the Cluniacs, and as Guido prescribes for his Carthusians in these words:

> “After None we meet in the cloister to speak about useful matters. During this interval we request and receive from the sacristan ink, parchment, pens, chalk, and books either to be read or copied; from the cook, legumes, salt, and other things of this kind.”

Finally, all might sit together in one place and listen to one another speaking, as Saint Hildegard seems to intend.

Saint Basil’s distinguished admonition applies especially to such people (Sermon 2 on the Monastic Institution):

> “Let useless speech and the immoderate exaltation that arises from mutual conversations not be uttered. If anything useful for the building up of souls is needed, let that alone be spoken; and let even useful things be said in an orderly manner, at a suitable time, and by those by whom they ought to be said. If someone is of lower rank, let him wait until he is invited to speak by his superior. Let whispering, speech into another’s ear, and signs made by nods be removed, because whispering carries the suspicion of detraction, and a sign made by a nod indicates that some deceit lies hidden. From such things hatred and suspicion arise in a brother. Whenever it is necessary to converse with one another, necessity should determine the volume of the voice: one should speak in a gentler voice to someone nearby, but call someone who is far away in a louder voice. Thus, whoever gives another counsel or offers exhortation about something should use a stronger and harsher voice, so that nothing insulting may be found in the assembly.”

Whether the following passage from the *Life of Saint Pachomius* should be understood as referring to this kind of conversation is uncertain:

> “It was their custom from the beginning, toward evening, after completing manual labor and supper, to sit down together in one place to examine the Scriptures, free at that time from every other concern except the concern that affected their salvation.”

Whether these conversations may be called recreations or by another name matters little, since they were granted not so much for pleasure as for the consolation of the weak. Just as we say that the body is refreshed when, after a long fast, we eat the poorest foods, so nothing prevents us from calling the exhausted spirit refreshed when, after prolonged silence, we speak about good and edifying matters—provided that all conversation about the world, kings, princes, prelates, and similar matters is absent. Such topics are commonly prohibited by all monastic constitutions, both ancient and recent.

The manuscript *Book on the Instruction of Novices* states quite rightly (chapter 14):

> “Never speak about the world or about wars; nor listen to those who report such things, since that is deadly poison to souls.”

See Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 49, chapter 10.

Apart from these conversations, which we have discussed at length and which were rare, the monks observed perpetual silence, subjecting those who rashly violated it to very severe punishments. Concerning these penalties for violators of silence, the *Rule of a Certain Person for Monks* decrees (chapter 16):

> “Nothing is to be said in any matter except what necessity demands. If anyone, contrary to this discipline, answers with a shout and in harsh speech, let him be noted until he is corrected. If he cannot be cured of this fault, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the brothers.”

The penalties of an unknown author preserved by Saint Basil state (no. 15):

> “If anyone is found conversing after Vespers and the Lord’s Prayer, let him be excommunicated.”

The *Book of Ancient Definitions of the Cistercian Order* states (Distinction 7, chapter 5):

> “Whoever knowingly acknowledges that he has broken silence within or outside the abbey, and is found guilty, shall spend one day on bread and water and be scourged in chapter. But those who break it indiscriminately and habitually, if they do not amend after being corrected repeatedly, shall remain on bread and water every Friday until suitable amendment has been made, and shall be regarded, at the discretion of their own abbot, as the last of all.”

Similarly, the Constitutions of the nuns of the same order who follow the stricter observance in Spain state (chapter 12):

> “The penance to be imposed on one who has broken silence is discipline, together with bread and water on the ground, from which the abbess should rarely dispense.”

The very ancient French statutes for the nuns of Blessed Mary of Sopwell in England, renewed three hundred years ago by Michael, abbot of Saint Albans, state:

> “Because you are bound by the Rule of Saint Benedict to keep silence in the church, in the cloister, in the refectory, and in the dormitory, we command you to keep silence in the aforesaid places. If any woman breaks silence, let her make her venia in chapter and receive regular discipline, acknowledging her fault. If one who breaks silence is unwilling of her own accord to make her venia, let her be reported to the guardian of the order and subjected to a harsher penance. And if it happens that one quarrels or behaves disorderly with another, let that woman be placed under silence as penance and observe the penance for three days.”

Finally, the Carthusians state in the *New Collection of Statutes* (Part II, chapter 14, no. 7):

> “Whoever breaks silence without permission shall acknowledge his fault and receive discipline with rods on the following Sunday. … If he is accustomed to breaking it, he shall be deprived of wine, or eat on the ground, or be punished with another penalty at the prior’s discretion.”

And elsewhere (chapter 8, no. 5):

> “Those declaring their faults concerning the breaking of silence must specify the place, the occasions, and the qualities of the persons involved; and they are required to receive discipline with rods from the presiding officer. … Let all priors observe and cause this statute concerning the discipline to be given for breaking silence to be observed; otherwise the visitors shall provide for the matter.”

[Col. 0365C] For it is written: “In much speaking you will not escape sin.”

“Much speaking,” says Saint John Climacus (Step 11), “is the seat of vainglory, through which a person habitually displays himself and brings himself onto the stage and into the theater. Much speaking is evidence of ignorance, a window of detraction, a teacher of buffoonish trifles, a servant of falsehood, the wiping away of compunction, the author and procurer of idleness, the herald of sleep, the distraction of meditation, the destruction of custody of the heart, the cooling place of divine fervor, and the languor—or rather extinction—of prayer.”

Saint Augustine explains what much speaking is in these words (Book III against Cresconius, chapter 1):

> “Much speaking is superfluous speech, a fault contracted through a love of speaking. Often even those who do not know what they are saying or how they should say it love to speak.”

And elsewhere (Book I of the *Retractations*, Preface):

> “Far be it from me to count as much speaking whatever is said when it is necessary, however lengthy the speech may be.”

He shows that only someone who says much without necessity is afflicted with the vice of much speaking, not someone who says much for a just reason, by virtue of his office, or because of some other necessity.

And elsewhere: “Death and life are in the power of the tongue.”—For the tongue can kill or give life, both to the one who speaks and to the one spoken to, and to the one about whom the speech is made.

For it is fitting that a master should speak and teach.—The prophet says to him:

> “Cry out, do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes and to the house of Jacob their sins” (Isaiah 58).

Saint Benedict appropriately says “speak and teach”:

> “That is, he ought to speak for the purpose of teaching,” says Bernard of Cassino. “For the words of a master ought to be nothing other than instruction. Whoever admonishes others to silence ought to have edifying speech, composed with reason and uttered at its proper time and with suitable appropriateness. Therefore blessed Benedict did not say merely, ‘It is fitting for a master to speak,’ but ‘to speak and teach,’ so that his speech may be the disciple’s instruction and his teaching the disciple’s edification.”

“To be silent and to listen is fitting for a disciple.” Hence Scripture says: “Listen in silence, and good favor will come to you because of your reverence” (Sirach 32). Clearly Pythagoras, the first to be called and acknowledged a philosopher, taught his approaching disciples nothing before teaching them to be silent; and the first exercise prescribed for the future wise man was to restrain his entire tongue. Hence he imposed five years of silence upon his disciples; they gladly endured it, though they were thereby learning profane philosophy. With far greater right, then, it is fitting for us, disciples as we are of heavenly philosophy, to be silent—unless, perhaps, we intend to cast off the conduct and profession of monks. “For the life of a monk,” says John the Monk (*Life of St. Odo*, Book II, no. 11, fifth century), “continues to be something only so long as he strives to remain under silence; once that is removed, whatever he may think he does well and honorably will, according to the teaching of the Fathers, amount to nothing.”

“And therefore, if anything needs to be requested.” Whether bodily or spiritual [Col. 0366B] necessity.

“From the prior.” That is, from the superior, says Nicholas of Fractura, meaning the abbot, who is understood by the name “prior” in all the places of the Rule where the word *prior* is used in the singular and absolutely, not relatively, as Menard proves. Here, however, Boherius judges that the term *prior* is used not only for the abbot but also “for any elder, or one earlier in time.” John Craesbreeck understands it as referring to one who is prior in rank, place, age, learning, or skill in any art—in short, any elder, wiser, or more learned man. Nicholas Bravus takes it to mean one who presides over the community, whether he is an abbot, provost, or anyone else senior by profession. It might also be understood of the provost, in accordance with the following passage from a Certain Rule for Virgins (chapter 22): “Let no nun, by herself, bring her personal need before the abbess; rather, let them all take care, through the provost, to make known to the abbess whatever necessities there may be.”

[Col. 0366C] “Let them ask with all humility and submissive reverence.” On this passage Bernard of Cassino writes: “He places three things in these useful words that must be observed: humility, submission, and reverence. Humility disposes the monk inwardly; submission shows, orders, and regulates his subordination in outward actions; and reverence composes his speech with its proper seasoning.” Or the phrase may mean “with humility and submissive reverence,” that is, so that whatever he has answered is held valid and firm, with absolutely no objection raised. In a manuscript Rule by an unknown author, chapter 8, we read: “During the hours assigned to you for carrying out your work, whatever may be necessary for you and your servants should be settled by mutual brief discussion . . . But when necessity compels you to speak, the authority of a certain holy Father commands you first to say three times: ‘O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.’ Once this has been said, immediately, with all speed, hastily, and with the warmth of charity, give your answer lightly [Col. 0366D] and without laughter; speak humbly, using few and reasonable words.”

“But coarse joking.” We learn what *scurrilitas*—coarse joking or buffoonery—is from St. Jerome, who explains the distinction between foolish speech and coarse joking as follows: “The difference, according to Paul (in his Letter to the Ephesians, chapter 5), between foolish speech and coarse joking is that foolish speech contains nothing wise or worthy of a human heart. Coarse joking proceeds from a prudent mind and deliberately seeks certain words that are either refined, shameful, rustic, or witty; we may call this by another word ‘playfulness,’ since it provokes laughter in those who hear it.” From this we learn that *scurrilitas* may be understood in either a good or a bad sense, since it may pour itself out both in refined and in shameful speech. Here, however, it is clearly taken by St. Benedict in the bad sense, according to the common and universal judgment of all. Thus Bernard of Cassino, describing *scurrilitas*, says: “Coarse joking is a shameful word, a shameful joke, something disgraceful or worthy of ridicule.”

St. Benedict condemns such coarse joking to perpetual confinement, as did before him St. Basil, St. Jerome, St. Nicetius, and others. St. Basil says (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 13): “All joking in speech and all coarse wit must be avoided; for it commonly happens that those who occupy themselves with such things abandon sound reason. The result is that the mind is spread out toward what is ridiculous and, in its silent inward reflection, strikes down all the sinews of gravity and seriousness.” St. Jerome, writing to Nepotianus (*Letter 2*), says: “All the pleasures, witticisms, urbane sayings worthy of laughter, and other absurdities of lovers, we blush at in comedians and detest in worldly people; how much more in monks and clerics, whose priesthood is adorned by their purpose of life, and whose purpose is adorned by their priesthood!” St. Nicetius, abbot and later bishop, says (*in Gregory of Tours, Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17): “Coarse joking must be avoided, beloved, and every idle word, so that just as we must present the whole body pure to God, so also the mouth must be used for nothing other than the praise of God.”

To these may be added the very grave judgment of St. Bernard (*On Consideration*, Book II, chapter 13): “Among worldly people trifles are trifles; in the mouth of a priest—and no less of a monk—they are blasphemies. If they happen to arise, they may perhaps be endured, but never repeated. One must intervene more carefully and prudently against frivolity. Certainly one should break into something serious, which they will hear not only profitably but gladly, and thus cease from idle matters. You have consecrated your mouth to the Gospel; to open it now for such things is forbidden, and to grow accustomed to them is sacrilege,” and so forth.

It is therefore not surprising that we read of coarse joking being condemned with very severe penalties among both monks and clerics. For example, the Fourth Council of Carthage (canon 60) decrees that “a cleric who is coarse and playful in obscene words is to be removed from office.” Among the excerpts from Book II of the *Penitential of Bishop Egbert*, the twenty-seventh reads: “If any priest, deacon, or monk has taken pleasure in idleness, foolish speech, coarse joking, loquacity, sleep, laziness, torpor, or similar things, let him do penance for three days.” To these are added the ancient rules of monks. Among them, the Rule of SS. Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius decrees as follows (chapter 15): “If anyone is caught laughing or engaging in coarse joking in speech, as the Apostle says, in something that does not pertain to the matter, we command that such a person be restrained for two weeks, in the name of the Lord, by every lash of correction.” The Rule of Tarnat (chapter 13) says: “Whoever dares to say something playful or suited to laughter in the assembly of the brothers, or whoever wishes to tell idle stories to the younger men, or to maintain friendships with those of immature age, shall be subject to the reprimand he deserves.” The Rule of St. Ferreolus, after prohibiting jokes, applause, and bursts of laughter, especially in the oratory and at table, adds (chapter 24): “If anyone fails to observe this, then, having been warned by the present admonition, let the punishment of a three-day fast chastise him.” Finally, the Rule of St. Donatus for Virgins [Col. 0367D] says (chapter 28): “If one tells idle stories to another and immediately reproves herself, simple pardon is sufficient. But if she does not reprove herself, let those who discuss such stories do penance by an imposition of silence or fifty blows.”

We could add the very severe punishments with which the just Judge, the Lord, has sometimes chastised coarse joking. Among these Durandus offers us a truly mournful example. Durandus, a monk of Cluny who became bishop of Toulouse, is discussed in the *Life of St. Hugh* by Raynaldus, no. 18, in Bollandus, 29 April.

Moreover, to avoid every occasion of coarse joking, the Cassinese forbid keeping birds or animals that encourage playfulness and frivolity; they also prohibit every kind of game. “They prohibit games of every kind, jokes, stories, obscene words, and dances,” say the Celestines (*Constitutions*, chapter 12, §3), “so strictly that if anyone acts otherwise, he is to be detained in prison for a month and otherwise corrected at the superior’s discretion according to the seriousness of his offense.” The Feuillants (*Constitutions*, chapter 6) punish those who keep birds, dogs, or any other animal acquired for pleasure by fasting on bread and water; the Cassinese likewise punish by this penalty acts of disorder, laying hands on others, pushing, and similar forms of joking.

Yet honorable jokes are not prohibited under the name of coarse joking. We sometimes read that devout men made use of them, such as those of Peter the Venerable, whom St. Bernard praises in a letter to him as follows: “I admit that I like a joke; it is pleasing both for its charm and for the gravity of serious matters. I do not know how you arrange your words in judgment while joking, so that the joke does not smell of frivolity and the preservation of authority does not diminish the gracefulness of your cheerfulness.”

“And idle words.” For St. Basil (*Shorter Rules*, chapter 23), an idle word is “every word that does not serve a useful purpose in the Lord.” For St. Jerome (*On Matthew* 12), it is “what is said without benefit to either the speaker or the hearer; when, leaving serious matters aside, we speak about frivolous things and tell old stories.” For St. Gregory (*Pastoral Rule*, Part III, chapter 15), it is “what lacks the justification of a legitimate necessity or the intention of pious usefulness.”

St. Benedict condemns such words together with coarse joking to the same perpetual confinement. The terrifying saying of Christ ought by itself to deter us sufficiently: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account of it on the day of judgment.” Reflecting on this saying, Peter Damian writes (*Book V, Letter 2*): “When I consider these words of the Gospel, what else do I perceive than that a kind of exchange has been proposed to us? For by a momentary laugh eternal weeping is brought forth, and by temporal weeping eternal joy is obtained.”

This saying deterred the Pachomians, among whom, according to Rufinus (*Lives of the Fathers*, Book III, chapter 35), it was impossible for anyone to speak an idle word. It deterred SS. Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius, whose Rule contains the following (chapter 15): “If any of the brothers utters an idle word in the assembly, so that he may not be liable to the judgment of the community, we command him to be excluded for three days from the assembly and conversation of the brothers, so that no one may associate with him.” The Rule of a Certain Author for Monks is much stricter (chapter 8): “Lying, an oath, and an idle word must be condemned throughout the entire brotherhood. If one of the brothers is found to have committed any of these things, he must be sent to prison and do penance until he is corrected of the vice . . . If, after examination in prison, one of the brothers is unable to avoid these vices, he must be expelled from the brotherhood and condemned.”

“And things that provoke laughter.” Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino distinguish these from coarse joking as follows: coarse joking pertains to wantonness, whereas words that provoke laughter may sometimes also be appropriate to the wise. We discussed these matters above, at chapter 4.

“We condemn under perpetual enclosure in every place, and so forth.” Here again, Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, together with Hildemar, observe that St. Benedict placed a safeguard around useful words, but a wall—as it were, a perpetual barrier—around coarse, idle, and laughter-provoking words. The addition “in every place” shows that useful and necessary words are not condemned everywhere, although they are not permitted everywhere either. It may therefore be worthwhile, as a conclusion to this chapter, to discuss briefly the places in which monks were especially forbidden to speak.

Among the monks of former times, two places in particular were so sacred that no one was permitted to break silence in them: the oratory and the refectory. Thus St. Euthymius, according to Cyril (*his Life*, no. 17, volume II of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*), “urged the brothers to embrace honorable silence in the temple of the Lord and forbade anyone to speak in the assembly of the brothers while the sacred mysteries were being celebrated; nor were they to loosen their tongues in the refectory when the brothers had gathered for dinner, but in both places they were to remain in the same silence.”

Likewise, the Rule of a Certain Author for Monks says (chapter 16): “Silence must be pursued everywhere, and the discipline of keeping silent must be practiced in all things, but especially near the Mass and at table.” St. Benedict likewise prescribes the strictest silence at table in chapter 38 and in the oratory in chapter 52. Under the name “oratory,” the sacristy must also be understood; hence among the chapters of St. Adalard there is a third entitled “On Silence in the Sacristy, or in the Churches.”

Benedict Haeften also believes that St. Benedict instituted silence in the dormitory. He infers this from the fact that the holy Father permits no one to speak after Compline and that the brothers scarcely used to inhabit the dormitory at any other time. The contrary, however, seems to appear in the Statutes of St. Adalard, Book II, chapter 6. Nor does it appear from the Customs of St. Benedict of Aniane (*Analecta*, volume IV), in which the following rules are laid down: “the strictest silence in the oratory . . . great silence in the sacristy . . . the strictest silence in the refectory . . . the strictest silence in the cloisters during the hour of reading,” with no mention of the dormitory.

Nevertheless, concerning certain monasteries, the same work adds: “We also saw this noteworthy practice: if anyone wished to attain perfection in silence, no brother dared to say anything in any place except in the two places appointed for that purpose.” What those two places assigned to speech were is not stated there. Yet I consider the following especially worthy of observation: “In the church, nothing is permitted except the divine office and words of prayer. If anyone had a necessity to speak, he touched the abbot’s garment, or that of any brother, and indicated the places assigned for speaking; after stating the very few words that were necessary and reasonable, they immediately withdrew, fearing that because of necessary words they might fall into harmful and useless ones.”

If I remember correctly, the practice of this observance may be seen in the *Life of Notker the Stammerer* [“of Balbulus,” fifth century]. It may perhaps also be referred to by a passage from the *Book of the Miracles of St. Dunstan*, no. 20: “Knowing that it was not the custom for monks to speak in the oratory, he indicated with his fingers that the man ought by no means to speak there,” and so forth. These matters may be passed over in passing.

I come now to the Cluniacs. Describing their ancient customs, Udalricus writes (Book II, chapter 3): “There are such workshops in the cloister as our fathers transmitted and established, in which perpetual silence is to be maintained: in the church, dormitory, refectory, and regular kitchen. In these places, by day and by night, if anyone speaks even one word within the hearing of anyone else, he does not easily obtain pardon without judgment.” The same is read in the manuscripts of the Customs of Benignus of Dijon, chapter 31.

It is clear, however, from the following statute of Peter the Venerable that many more places were devoted to silence (Statute 19): “In the Cluniac infirmary, which is divided into five chambers under one roof, silence is to be maintained with such discrimination that in the part where the brothers lie dying, which is the middle section, and in the upper section on the southern side, silence and conversation are to be observed according to the ancient custom; in the other three sections, the silence of the regular cloister is to be maintained.

“Likewise, in the novices’ cell and the adjoining cloister or workshops, the only exceptions are the novices and their master, who may speak where and when they customarily speak; and visiting bishops and abbots, the major prior, and the subpriors who are custodians of the order, who may speak in the parts of the novices’ cell, and in whose presence alone may others speak. In all the workshops continuous silence is to be maintained, except for one master of each workshop; and except in the workshops of the new church and their own workshops. The silence of the cloister is also to be maintained in the cemetery, the cloister of the cemetery, all the sacristies, and the road leading to the upper houses beside the greater church, and in the adjacent places. The abbots and priors mentioned above are excepted; in those places they may speak in the manner stated above.”

Peter the Venerable did not, however, demand such strict silence in the small cells or priories, as they are called. For in Statute 42 he decrees “that where twelve brothers cannot be present, silence must nevertheless always be maintained in the refectory and dormitory; in the cloister, perfect silence must be maintained from Vespers until the third hour of the following day. For it is certain that silence must always and everywhere be maintained universally in all churches.”

In the English monastery of St. Albans, after the middle of the eleventh century, Paul, abbot of that place, “established that complete silence be inviolably observed in the church, cloister, refectory, and especially the dormitory,” as Matthew Paris writes (*Lives of the Twenty-Three Abbots of St. Albans*). Shortly afterward he adds: “He established that silence be maintained in the infirmary, especially in the chapel, and everywhere after Compline.”

The supreme pontiffs Innocent III and Gregory IX likewise assign these same places—except the infirmary—to perpetual silence in the constitutions they published for the Benedictines. Similarly, St. Stephen, founder of the order of Grandmont, prescribes in chapter 47 of his Rule—something Clement V renewed after Innocent IV—with the following penalty:

“Whoever is found guilty of a deliberate violation of the said silence shall, for each transgression, without mercy or dispensation, spend one day on bread and water and be beaten in the chapter. Nevertheless, if, before completing the penance, after drinking water and abstaining from other food, he demonstrates by true humility as a penitent and by a firm intention to amend, the prior or his representative may judge it appropriate to dispense him from the remainder of the penance. If, after being corrected in this way more than once, he does not amend, then for each transgression he shall for two days sit on the floor of the refectory while the others are eating, content with the household’s coarse bread and water, and during those two days he shall be beaten in chapter. The prior or another presiding officer may not dispense him from this; the prior shall punish him further with a greater penalty if the insolence of the stubborn man deserves it.”

To the four places mentioned above as dedicated to silence, the Cistercians add the scriptoria (*Book of Ancient Definitions*, distinction 7, chapter 5), wherever monks customarily write. The common hearth must also be added, where, according to the ancient custom of our order, inviolable silence was maintained. This is clear from Hildemar, the most ancient commentator on the Rule, who writes concerning this chapter: “If it is winter and all have gathered together because of the cold to warm themselves, there must be silence there, and no one may speak there.” The *Concordia of St. Dunstan* likewise says: “From the Kalends of November, the brothers may approach the fire whenever necessity compels and excessive cold presses upon them, but this is to be done in silence.”

As for more recent congregations, the Cassinese prescribe (*Cassinese Declaration on the Rule*, chapter 52): “Silence is always to be maintained in the choir, dormitory, and refectory, even outside the hour of meals, and in a certain part of the cloister around the chapter house, except when it may be necessary to speak briefly and quietly in those places. The same silence is also to be maintained at the common fire of the brothers.”

The Calasinians renew the Constitution of Pope Innocent III, which prescribes “that silence be observed in the four regular places, namely, the church, cloister, refectory, and dormitory.” The same is found in the reforming statutes published in 1536 for the monastery of St. Porcianus and in 1549 for the monastery of St. Columba. The Constitutions of the Feuillants, chapter 42, add: “In the chapter house.” Finally, in the new collection of Carthusian Statutes it is decreed (Part II, chapter 14, no. 9) that “silence is to be more strictly maintained everywhere, but especially in the church, chapter house, refectory, cloister, and shaving room.”

# CHAPTER VII. On Humility

[Col. 0371]

[Col. 0371A] Divine Scripture cries out to us, brothers, saying: “Everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14). By saying this, it shows us that every kind of exaltation is a form of pride, which the Prophet indicates must be avoided when he says: “Lord, my heart has not been exalted, nor have my eyes been lifted up; I have not walked in great matters, nor in things too wonderful for me” (Psalm 130). But what if I did not think humbly, but exalted my soul, “like a child weaned from his mother” [Note: [Col. 0371C] Others: “like one weaned from his mother.”], “so may you requite my soul” [Note: [Col. 0371C] Others: “his mother.”].

Therefore, brothers, if we wish to reach the summit of perfect humility and wish to arrive swiftly at that heavenly exaltation to which one ascends through the humility of the present life, we must erect, by our ascending deeds [Note: [Col. 0371C] “Ascending” is absent in Hildemar.], that ladder which appeared in Jacob’s dream [Note: [Col. 0371C] Others: “in sleep.”] (Genesis 28), on which descending and ascending angels were shown to him. There is no doubt that we understand that descent and ascent to mean descending through exaltation and ascending through humility.

The ladder itself, once erected, is our life in this world, raised by the Lord toward heaven through a humbled heart. We say that the sides of this ladder are our body and soul. In these sides [Note: [Col. 0371C] Others: “in which sides”; others: “between which sides”; others: “in which”; others: “on which sides.”] the divine summons has inserted various steps of humility or discipline to be climbed [Note: [Col. 0371C] So all manuscripts; but Hildemar, with the printed editions, has “calling” instead of “summons.”].

The first degree of humility is that, always placing the fear of God before his eyes, a man should entirely avoid forgetfulness [Note: [Col. 0371D] Hildemar: “fleeing entirely from forgetfulness of God’s commandments.” Afflighem: “let the monk entirely flee exaltation.”], and always remember all that God has commanded; and consider how those who despise God fall into hell because of their sins [Note: [Col. 0371D] Oxford: “go into hell because of sins.” Florence: “fall in hell because of sins.” Cassinese, Conc, and a manuscript of the Rule of the Master: “may hell burn because of sins”; Menard prefers this reading. Boherius nevertheless writes: “Smaragdus and the Italians have: ‘They kindle hell because of sins.’ The first reading is more straightforward and requires less explanation.” Nevertheless, the Italian reading presents no difficulty, and Menardus rejects the common reading without sufficient grounds as the work of an unskilled corrector.], and always turn over in his mind the eternal life prepared for those who fear God [Note: [Col. 0372C] More recent witnesses: “turn over again.”].

Guarding himself every hour from sins and vices—of thought, tongue, eyes [Note: [Col. 0372C] “Of the eyes” is absent in Conc, Florence, and the Cassinese manuscripts.], hands, feet, and self-will—he must also hasten to cut off the desires of the flesh [Note: [Col. 0372C] Menardus thinks the words “hasten to cut off” should be “which must be cut off”; nevertheless, they occur in the Oxford manuscript.].

Let a man always believe that he is every hour seen by God from heaven, that his deeds are seen in every place [Note: [Col. 0372C] Others: “in every place,” omitting “in.”] by the gaze of the Divinity, and that they are every hour reported by the angels. The Prophet demonstrates this to us when he shows God as always present in our thoughts, saying: “God searches hearts and reins” (Psalm 7). And again: “The Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, that they are vain” [Note: [Col. 0372C] These words, “that they are vain,” are absent from Oxford, Cassinese, Conc, Hildemar, Lyra, the Compendium, and others; Hildemar nevertheless explains them.] (Psalm 93). Again he says: “You have understood my thoughts from afar” (Psalm 138), and: “For human thought will give thanks to you” (Psalm 138).

Thus, so that a useful brother may be watchful concerning his perverse thoughts, let him always say in his heart: “Then I shall be blameless before him, if I guard myself from my iniquity” (Psalm 17).

We are forbidden to do our own will when Scripture says to us: “Turn away from your own desires” [Note: [Col. 0372D] Oxford: “Turn away.”] (Sirach 18). And again, in prayer we ask God [Note: [Col. 0372D] “God” is absent in Conc and Florence] that his will be done in us (Matthew 6). We are therefore rightly taught not to do our own will when we avoid what Holy Scripture says: “There are ways that seem right to human beings” [Note: [Col. 0372D] Others: “seem right to human beings”; Hildemar, Sabinus, Conches, and Lyra: “are thought right by human beings”; Oxford: “are thought right by human beings.”], “but their end plunges down to the depths of hell” (Proverbs 16).

Likewise, we avoid [Note: [Col. 0372D] Cassinese: “we fear”; Florence: “let us fear.”] what is said about the negligent: “They have been corrupted and have become abominable in their desires” [Note: [Col. 0372D] Five manuscripts, with certain printed editions: “in their pleasures.”] (Psalm 52).

As for the desires of the flesh, let us believe that God is always present to us when the Prophet says to the Lord: “All my desire is before you” (Psalm 37). A wicked desire must therefore be avoided, because death lies beside the entrance of pleasure. Hence Scripture commands, saying: “Do not follow your lusts” (Sirach 18).

Therefore, if the eyes of the Lord watch over the good and the wicked, and the Lord always looks down from heaven upon the children of human beings (Psalm 33), to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God; and if our works are reported each day and night by the angels assigned to us to the Lord, our Creator [Note: [Col. 0372D] Cassinese: “of our deeds”], then we must beware every hour, brothers, as the Prophet says in the Psalm, lest God see us turning aside to evil and becoming useless (Psalm 52). Though he spares us at this time because he is merciful and waits [Note: [Col. 0372D] Smaragdus: “waiting”; Lyra and Ebrul: “by waiting.”] for us to turn toward better things, lest in the future he say to us: “You have done these things” [Note: [Col. 0372D] Conches: “You have done these things” in the plural], “and I was silent” (Psalm 49).

The second degree of humility is that one, not loving his own will, should take no pleasure in fulfilling his desires, but imitate in his actions the voice of the Lord, who says: “I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6). Scripture likewise says: “The will has punishment, and necessity brings forth a crown” [Note: [Col. 0373C] Cassinese, the Rule of the Master, Florence, Conc, Conches, the Compendium, and Dunstan: “Pleasure has punishment, and necessity brings forth a crown.”].

The third degree of humility is that, for the love of God, one submit himself in all obedience to his superior, imitating the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: “He became obedient unto death” (Philippians 2) [Note: [Col. 0373C] Oxford and other manuscripts add: “to the Father.”].

The fourth degree of humility is that, in the very act of obedience, amid harsh and contrary circumstances or even whatever injuries may be inflicted, one embrace patience with a silent conscience [Note: [Col. 0373C] Oxford: “embrace his conscience silently.” Narbonne: “let him silently embrace his conscience.” Florence: “let him embrace the patience of a silent conscience.” Sabinus: “let him embrace patience with a silent conscience.” Some manuscripts, with the Paris edition and Guido Juvenal, read “let him embrace the silent conscience,” omitting “patience.” Hildemar also rejects this, asserting that the verb *amplector* may take either the dative or accusative, and that one may correctly say either “to embrace injuries” or “to embrace patience”; therefore, he says, the word “patience” is not being embraced here.], and, enduring, neither grow weary nor depart, as Scripture says: “Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved” (Matthew 24). Likewise: “Let your heart be strengthened, and wait for the Lord” (Psalm 26).

To show that the faithful person must endure every adversity for the Lord, it says even in the person of those who suffer: “For your sake we are put to death all day long; we are regarded as sheep for slaughter” (Psalm 43).

And secure in the hope of divine recompense, they continue joyfully, saying: “But in all these things we conquer, because of him who loved us” (Romans 8). Scripture likewise says elsewhere: “You tested us, O God; you examined us by fire, as silver is examined by fire; you brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our back” (Psalm 65) [Note: [Col. 0373C] “By fire” is absent in certain witnesses.].

To show that we ought to remain under a superior, it continues: “You placed men over our heads.” And fulfilling the Lord’s command in adversity and injury through patience, those who are struck on one cheek offer the other also [Note: [Col. 0374C] Cassinese: “on the cheek”] (Matthew 5); those who are deprived of their tunic give their cloak as well; when compelled to go one mile, they go two (Luke 6) [Note: [Col. 0374C] Florence: “to the one who compels.”]; with the Apostle Paul they endure false brothers and persecution [Note: [Col. 0374C] In some witnesses, “and persecution” is absent]; and they bless those who curse them (2 Corinthians 11).

The fifth degree of humility is that a monk not conceal from his abbot, through humble confession, all the evil thoughts that enter his heart or the evil acts secretly committed by him [Note: [Col. 0374C] Florence: “from his abbot . . . his own.”]. Scripture exhorts us concerning this, saying [Note: [Col. 0374C] Others: “says.”]: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him” (Psalm 36). It also says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy is forever” (Psalm 105). And again the Prophet says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not cover my iniquities” [Note: [Col. 0374C] Others: “I did not hide them.”]. I said: “I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord”; and you forgave the wickedness of my heart [Note: [Col. 0374C] Others: “of my sin.”] (Psalm 31).

The sixth degree of humility is that a monk be content with every kind of lowliness or abasement and, regarding all that is imposed upon him, judge himself like a bad and unworthy laborer, saying to himself with the Prophet: “I have been reduced to nothing and did not know; I became like a beast before you, and I am always with you” (Psalm 72).

The seventh degree of humility is that he not merely declare with his tongue that he is inferior and more worthless than everyone else, but also believe it in the deepest feeling of his heart, humbling himself and saying with the Prophet: “But I am a worm and not a man, the reproach of men and the outcast of the people” (Psalm 21); “I was exalted, and I was humbled and confounded” (Psalm 87). And again: “It is good for me that you humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments” (Psalm 118).

[Col. 0374B] The eighth degree of humility is that the monk do nothing except what the common rule of the monastery and the examples of his elders exhort him to do.

The ninth degree of humility is that the monk restrain his tongue from speaking and, maintaining silence, not speak until questioned, as Scripture shows: “By much speaking sin is not avoided” [Note: [Col. 0374C] The printed edition: “sin will be avoided”; “you will avoid sin.”] (Proverbs 10). And: “The talkative man is not directed upon the earth” (Psalm 139).

The tenth degree of humility is that he not be quick or ready to laugh, because it is written: “The fool raises his voice in laughter” [Note: [Col. 0374C] Oxford: “into laughter.”] (Sirach 22) [Note: [Col. 0374C] Narbonne: “raised his voice.”].

The eleventh degree of humility is that, when a monk speaks, he speak gently and without laughter, humbly and with seriousness, using either few words [Note: [Col. 0374C] “Words” is absent in Oxford] and reasonable ones; and that he not be loud in his voice, as it is written: “The wise man is recognized by few words.”

The twelfth degree of humility is that a monk not only indicate humility in his heart but also always display it to those who see him through his very body—that is, in his work [Note: [Col. 0374C] Cassinese, Florence, Conc, and some others: “in the work of God”], in the oratory, in the monastery, in the garden, on the road, in the field, or wherever he may be sitting, walking, or standing, he should always have his head bowed and his gaze fixed on the ground, considering himself every hour guilty of his sins and believing that he is already being brought before the fearful judgment of God [Note: [Col. 0374C] Sabinus: “the day of judgment.” Cassinese and Florence: “judgment,” omitting “of God.”]. Let him always say in his heart what that publican in the Gospel said, with his eyes fixed upon the ground: “Lord, I am not worthy, a sinner that I am, to lift my eyes to heaven” (Luke 18). And again the Prophet says of him: “I have been bowed down and humbled completely” (Psalm 118).

[Col. 0375A] Therefore, after ascending all these degrees of humility, the monk will soon arrive at that love of God [Note: [Col. 0375A] “Of God” is absent in Hildemar] which casts out fear [Note: [Col. 0375A] Others: “outside,” or “outward.”]. Through this love he will begin to observe without any labor, as though naturally and by force of habit, all those things that he formerly observed not without fear [Note: [Col. 0376A] Conc and Florence: “and by habit.”]—no longer out of fear of hell, but out of love for Christ, through the very habit of good conduct, and through delight in virtue [Note: [Col. 0376A] Hildemar: “through love”] which the Lord will deign to reveal by the Holy Spirit in his laborer once cleansed of vices and sins.

# COMMENTARY

[Col. 0375]

[Col. 0375A] This chapter, which Saint Benedict adds concerning silence, following the example of the Prophet who says, “I was silent and was humbled,” was evidently held in high esteem among the ancients: Saint Donatus and the Master inserted it whole in their Rules; the venerable Benedict of Cluny, abbot of Saint Michael’s monastery in the eleventh century, inserted it so that “he might persuade everyone to commit it to memory, saying there that the sum of the virtues was contained in it, from which one could easily ascend to heavenly heights,” as his disciple William testifies; it was read at the full Council of Quierzy in the year 838, in the presence of the monks of Saint Carilef, so that they might be [Col. 0375B] restored to better fruitfulness; finally, after Grimlaicus had discussed humility at length in his Rule for Solitaries, he concluded as follows: “If anyone wishes to investigate humility more deeply, let him turn to the Rule of Saint Benedict; there he will find the twelve degrees of humility set forth with sufficient clarity.” Humility, moreover, is the virtue by which a person, through the truest knowledge of himself, becomes contemptible in his own eyes; or, as Saint Augustine, cited by Boherius, says: “The virtue by which the mind, exalting itself in nothing and attributing no good to itself, even outwardly prefers the appearance of one who has been cast down.”

“Divine Scripture cries out to us, brothers.”] It cries out, rather than simply admonishing; for it knew human beings to be deaf to the preaching of humility and abasement, whom it knew well always to be carried toward lofty things.

“Whoever exalts himself will be humbled.”] Saint Augustine explains this excellent comparison as follows (Sermon 22, *On Scripture*): “As smoke fails, so may they fail. Who are those who fail like smoke, except the proud who do not confess their sins [Col. 0375C] but defend them? Why are they compared with smoke? Because smoke raises and lifts itself up as though toward heaven; but the higher it rises, the more easily it vanishes and disappears. Consider again what I said: smoke is denser when it is near the fire and near the earth; it does not yet vanish so completely, nor is it yet so scattered by the winds. But when it becomes thin, when does it vanish and disappear? When it has lifted itself very high. Since, therefore, the proud person raises himself against God as smoke against heaven, it remains that he should fail in such a way that, scattered by the winds of his own vanity and arrogance, he perishes, just as smoke disappears when, inflated by a swollen and insubstantial greatness, it has risen aloft. Such indeed is smoke: you see a great mass, you have something apparently visible, but you do not have anything you can grasp.”

How those who exalt themselves are humbled, and conversely how those who humble themselves are exalted, Hildemarus—and Bernard of Cassino after him—understand in this way: those who exalt themselves in this world are humbled in the next, and conversely. Yet God humbles the proud not only in the future but also in the present, permitting them to fall into some grave sin, “just as a wise physician permits a sick person to fall into a lesser illness as a remedy for a greater one,” to use the example of the Angelic Doctor (*Summa theologiae* II-II, q. 162, a. 6, ad 3), and more frequently into lust. Conversely, he also exalts the humble in this world. Hence Peter the Venerable says piously (*Book I of the Miracles*, chapter 20): “The saints,” he says, “always strive to hide their works in the secret recesses of their retreats; but if human beings keep silent about them, the stones cry out.”

“When he says this, therefore, he shows that every kind of exaltation is a form of pride.”] Saint Benedict here assumes that there are several kinds [Col. 0376A] of pride, and the honey-tongued Doctor indeed seems to identify four in these words (*Sermon 47, On Various Matters*): “There is pride of heart, pride of speech, pride of action, and pride of appearance. Pride of heart occurs when a person is great in his own eyes; against this the Wise Man prays, saying: ‘Do not give me haughtiness of eyes’; and elsewhere: ‘Woe to you who are wise in your own eyes.’ Pride of speech, or of the tongue, which is also called boasting, occurs when a person not only thinks great things of himself but also speaks them; hence the Psalmist says: ‘May the Lord destroy all deceitful lips and the tongue that speaks great things.’ Pride of action occurs when a person acts with a certain outward arrogance in order to appear great; concerning this the same Psalmist says: ‘He who practices pride shall not dwell in the midst of my house.’ Pride of appearance occurs when a person adorns himself with costly clothing in order to appear glorious; hence Paul says: ‘Not in costly clothing’; and the Lord says: ‘Those who wear soft clothing are in the houses of kings,’ where pride abounds.”

Pride, however, which for Cassian is “the most savage beast, more monstrous than all the preceding vices of which he had spoken, attacking the perfect above all and, with a more dreadful bite, devouring those who are almost already established in the consummation of the virtues,” derives its name from the verb *supereo*, so that *superbire* means to go above oneself, above others, or beyond the proper measure. Hence Saint Isidore says (*On the Highest Good*, chapter 38): “He is called proud who wishes to appear greater than he is; for whoever wishes to go beyond what he is, is proud.”

“Which the Prophet indicates that he avoids, saying, etc.”] To persuade us to follow the traces of humility and flee pride, he adds to Christ’s warning the example of the Prophet, who says of himself: “Lord, my heart is not exalted,” etc. In these words, as Bernard of Cassino observes, he declares that he possesses a twofold humility: an inward humility when he says, “My heart is not exalted,” and an outward humility when he adds, “Nor have my eyes been lifted up,” etc. Smaragdus expresses this as follows: “I attributed nothing to my merits, I contributed nothing from my own knowledge; but if I possessed any good, I gave all the glory to God. I did not wish to become known to human beings as though I were remarkable, nor did I seek anything beyond my powers with which I might boast before the uninstructed. Alternatively: ‘To walk in great things’ means for each person to think great things about himself. ‘In wondrous things’ means to consider something about oneself wondrous.”

“But what if I did not think humbly, etc.”] What he says—“Like a weaned child,” etc.—Hildemarus understands in two ways.

1. Just as a weaned child, unable to eat solid food, is exposed to the danger of death, so I too, if I do not think humbly, will incur the danger of bitter death because of the sweetness of your blessedness. Bernard of Cassino follows this interpretation.

2. Just as a mother who is about to wean an infant puts something bitter on her breasts, so that, having tasted it, the child refuses to nurse, so you may give me bitterness in place of the sweetness of blessedness.

“Therefore, brothers.”] Boherius says that he calls not only monks “brothers,” but also all the faithful, whom he greatly desires to come to their heavenly homeland.

“If we wish to reach the summit of the highest humility.”] He says “of the highest humility,” thereby showing that the virtue of humility is something great. Indeed, humility undertaken for Christ possesses royal dignity, as Gilbert of Holland says (*Sermon 18, On the Song of Songs*). Its greatness may also be gathered from Christ’s own example and from love of this virtue, so that Saint Bernard rightly said (*Sermon 43, On the Song of Songs*): “Great is the virtue of humility, to which even the majesty of the Godhead so readily bows.” And again (*Letter 42*): “I do not know by what disposition of things the Godhead has always been accustomed to draw more familiarly near to humility. In the end, it clothed itself in humility so that it might appear to human beings; it bore a humble substance, form, and appearance, commending to us the excellence of that virtue which it chose to honor by its special presence.”

For Bernard of Cassino, the summit of humility is perfect charity, which casts out fear; he discusses it at the twelfth degree. For Boherius, it is either charity, the heavenly homeland, or God himself, who is both the example and the teaching of all humility.

“And to that heavenly exaltation.”] These words may explain the preceding ones, for “heavenly exaltation” and “the summit of the highest humility” have the same meaning—namely, the heavenly homeland—as Boherius immediately explains.

“To which one arrives through the humility of the present life, etc.”] This is the way to it, both the only way and the safest. Hence John Climacus says (*Ladder*, degree 25): “If pride made certain demons out of angels, undoubtedly humility can also make angels out of demons.”

“That ladder must be erected by our ascending actions, etc.”] On this ladder the angels are said to ascend or descend, never remaining or sitting still. “Thus,” Saint Bernard says in a letter to Garinus (*Letter 254*), “it would clearly be understood that between perfection and failure in the condition of this mortal life there is no middle state; but just as it is evident that our very body is continually either growing or diminishing, so the spirit must necessarily always either advance or decline.”

“We understand that this descent and ascent can mean nothing other than descending through exaltation and ascending through humility.”] To this the saying of Saint Cyprian corresponds (*On Jealousy and Envy*): “Through humility we grow to the highest things”; and that of Saint Jerome in his letter to Desiderius (*Letter 154*): “You know that our teaching holds aloft the banner of humility and that, walking through the lowest places, we climb to the highest.” Finally, Saint Augustine—or whoever else is the author—says (*Sermon 297 in the Appendix to the Sermons*): “By the steps of humility one climbs to the heights of heaven; for the exalted God is reached not through pride but through humility, of whom it is written: ‘God resists the proud but gives grace to the humble.’ Hence it is also said in the Psalms: ‘The Lord is exalted, and he regards the lowly, but the lofty he knows from afar.’ He placed ‘the lofty’ for the proud; he regards the lowly in order to raise them up; he knows the lofty—that is, the proud—in order to cast them down.”

“But we call the sides of that same ladder our body and soul.”] Smaragdus comments on this passage: “Wisely he says that our body and soul are the two sides of this ladder, because every human being is composed of both, and, for the love of Christ and eternal life, insofar as he is able, does good through both substances; and so that in the glory of the resurrection he may receive the rewards of his labor in both substances, he diligently strives to keep the Lord’s commandments in both substances.” For these two sides to fit together, they must be planed. The soul is planed, Boherius says after Bernard of Cassino, when, sympathizing with its body, it removes from its own will whatever is spent on the body’s needs and support. The body too is planed when it takes away from itself in drink, food, sleep, and necessity.

“In which sides are the various degrees of humility.”] Various people have assigned various degrees of humility; if you wish, see Haeften, book VI, treatise 4, disputation 64. But in enumerating or assigning them, no one wrote more successfully or better than Saint Benedict, who took his teaching on humility from Cassian, book IV, chapter 39, adorned it with a preface, arranged it in proper order, and illustrated each degree, adding an eleventh and twelfth degree. Later writers valued this ladder so highly that they illuminated it with various commentaries.

“The divine summons has inserted [the degrees] for ascent.”] More recent writers read “Divine calling,” and so does Bernard of Cassino, for whom “divine calling is the election by which God chooses through grace those whom, through the fruit of good works, he mercifully brings to glory”; or, as Boherius puts it, “predestination, because those whom he called, he also predestined; for only the predestined ascend to the heights by these degrees.” Perhaps for this reason Saint John Climacus says (*Ladder*, degree 25) that humility is the only virtue which none of the demons can imitate.

Our reading, however, is found in all the ancient witnesses, with the possible exception of Hildemarus. Smaragdus explains what “summons” means as follows: “A summons is said to occur when not only soldiers but also the others are called to the supreme battle. Hence *evocare* is understood to mean ‘to lead out’ or ‘to summon forth.’ The word is very suitably placed here, because we are summoned, led out, and called forth daily by the Lord so that, armed with the twelve degrees of humility, we may rise courageously to battle against the devil,” etc.

Thus far Saint Benedict has interpreted Jacob’s vision mystically and adapted it to humility; others are also found to have done the same. You will encounter other interpretations of the same vision among other authors. Saint Gregory gives this one (*Moral Exposition*, book V, chapter 22): “To sleep on the journey,” he says, “is in the passage of the present life to rest from the love of temporal things . . . . To see angels descending and ascending is to contemplate the citizens of the heavenly homeland: either with what love they cleave to their Creator by transcending themselves, or with what compassionate charity they condescend to our infirmities. It is also especially noteworthy that the sleeping man sees angels who rests his head on a stone . . . . For to place one’s head upon a stone is to cling in mind to Christ,” etc.

Hildemarus gives another interpretation: “The divine Scripture is understood by the ladder; by the ascending and descending angels are understood the holy preachers. The saints ascend when they preach about the Godhead, as John does when he says: ‘In the beginning was the Word’; and they descend when they preach about the humanity, as the same John does when he says: ‘And the Word became flesh and dwelt among us,’” etc.

Peter Boherius, in his first commentary, gives yet another: “This ladder may be understood as the monastic life . . . . Its sides are the enclosure of the monastery and the stability of the community; its steps are the life, institutions, and teachings of the holy Fathers. The ascending angels are good monks who, through observance of the rule’s commandments, proceed by a direct course to the height of perfection. The descending angels, on the other hand, are bad monks who, through transgressing the things mentioned above, descend to the lowest places of the world—and, if only not to hell.”

## On the First Degree of Humility

“Therefore, the first degree of humility is this: if, keeping the fear of God always before his eyes, etc.”] The first degree of humility, to which Saint Bernard opposes the habit of sinning, is the fear of God according to Saint Benedict. “The first in order,” says Smaragdus, “because it is first in thought, in the heart, and in the will.” It is first because the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom and of every virtue, as the Prophet says; and finally because, as Cassian says (*Book IV*, chapter 39), “the beginning of our salvation, and its preservation, is the fear of the Lord. Through it the beginning of conversion, the cleansing of vices, and the preservation of virtues are acquired by those who are being initiated into the way of perfection. When it has penetrated the human mind, it produces contempt for all things, forgetfulness of one’s parents, and horror of the world itself.”

People commonly distinguish this fear as servile, mercenary, and filial. “For Saint Bernard” (*Sermon 2 for the Sunday after the Octave of Epiphany*), “the first is fear lest we be tormented in hell; the second, lest, excluded from the vision of God, we be deprived of that ineffable glory; the third fills the soul with every anxious concern, fearful lest it be abandoned by grace.” Saint Benedict indicates all three here: the first when he says that those who despise God fall into hell for their sins; the second when he adds, “and eternal life, which is prepared for those who fear God”; the third when he has already said, “Let him always be mindful of all that God commands.” Here Saint Benedict especially prescribes the third, assigning as the first degree of usefulness not fear simply, but fear of God. Hildemarus says that he specified this because there is also fear of other things: fear of fire, fear of illness, fear of death, and so forth. Although the fear of God is divided into servile, mercenary, and filial fear, strictly speaking only filial fear is truly fear of God; for servile and mercenary fear can more properly be reduced to fear of other things, since they seem to fear not God so much as hell or the loss of glory.

“Let him altogether avoid forgetfulness.”] “This means that he should flee the sin which is forgetfulness,” says Hildemarus, “the remedy for which is continual meditation . . . . It is as though he were saying in other words: ‘Let him not be forgetful’”—that is, of all the things he ought to commit to continual memory: fear of eternal punishment, joy in the heavenly homeland, the labor of the present life, and so forth.

“And let him always be mindful of all that God commands.”] Mindful, I say, with an effective remembrance, which is proper to filial fear; for those who fear the Lord keep his commandments.

“And how those who despise God fall into hell for their sins.”] God is despised either in himself or in his own. He is despised in himself when gratitude is not returned to him for his benefits; when he is not feared as Lord; when he is not loved as Father; when he is not worshiped as God and Creator; when the service owed to him is not rendered; when sin is continually committed against him. He is despised in his own when obedience is not given to the superior, because he said, “Whoever despises you despises me,” and in other ways, when works of charity are omitted without mercy, as Bernard of Cassino says.

“And eternal life, which is prepared for those who fear God, etc.”] Concerning this the Psalmist says: “How great is the abundance of your sweetness, which you have hidden for those who fear you!”

“And guarding himself at every hour from sins and vices, etc.”] Although “sin” and “vice” are commonly used interchangeably, those who speak more precisely know how to distinguish something between them. Thus Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius refer sin to the omission of good and vice to the commission of evil. Boherius also gives this distinction: both omitted good and committed evil pertain to sin, whereas vice is the habit of sinning. More briefly and better, one might say that acts are sins and habits are vices.

But Smaragdus, explaining this passage, says: “When he says that he must guard himself from sins at every hour, this is understood to mean from evil works, which are carried out in thought, speech, and deed . . . . But when he says that he must guard himself from vices, this is understood to mean from the seven principal vices: gluttony, fornication, avarice, anger, sadness, acedia, and vainglory, together with pride, the eighth and their mother, and from all their harmful offshoots,” etc.

[Col. 0379D] “But let him hasten to cut off the desires of the flesh.”] For, as Saint Odo says (*Book II of the Conferences*, no. 6), “it seems utterly more detestable if professors of religion, to whom, as the Apostle says, the words of God have been entrusted, should happen to become slaves to carnal desires: abandoning heavenly things, to yearn for earthly things; despising God, to serve mammon.”

“Let a person always consider that he is continually observed by God from heaven, etc.”] To instill divine fear in us, he also instills in us the divine presence at every hour and in every place; for to be seen in this way, by such a one, always and everywhere, is a great terror, says Bernard of Cassino. He proves this with the words of the Prophet: “God searches hearts and kidneys.” Hildemarus wishes “hearts” to be understood as thoughts and “kidneys” as the recesses of thoughts, or their beginning and intention, from which the thoughts themselves arise. But it is more correctly interpreted, with Smaragdus, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Trithemius, as “hearts” meaning thoughts and “kidneys” meaning bodily pleasures; for sensual pleasures are especially active in the kidneys.

Boherius gives another interpretation: “‘Searching hearts and kidneys’ means the faithful and the Jews. Let the Jews be called ‘kidneys,’ because Christ descended from them according to the flesh. Hence in the Psalm: ‘Even by night my kidneys reproved me’—that is, the Jews, from whom I descended according to the flesh, persecuted me unto death.”

“And again, the Lord knows the thoughts of human beings, because they are vain.”] Hildemarus comments on this passage: “Does a human being have only evil thoughts and not good ones? When he meditates on something good, when he thinks about pleasing God, is that not a good thought? Indeed, that thought is good; but the Prophet said, ‘of human beings, because they are vain,’ as though he were saying: ‘Insofar as they belong to human beings, they are vain, because they are human; but insofar as they belong to God, they are good, because they are from God.’ For a human being has no good from himself; if he has anything good, he has it from God.”

“And again he says: ‘You have understood my thoughts from afar.’”] That is, before they come into being; for the issue here is not distance in space but in time.

“And because the thought of a human being will confess to you.”] That is, it will be known by you. “Because the thought is known to God,” says Hildemarus, “that very knowledge is called its confession to God.” Bernard of Cassino follows this interpretation, and Guido Juvenalis confirms it by rendering this text of the Rule in French: “The thought of a human being will reveal itself to you and pay homage to you, for it cannot escape your knowledge.”

Smaragdus, however, interprets it differently: “The thought of a human being then confesses to God when past sins are condemned by him with humble satisfaction; for when each person is anticipated by divine illumination, he is immediately assaulted by the distress of shameful thoughts, but he is not ashamed humbly to confess them to the Lord.”

[207] “For, being concerned about his perverse thoughts.”] That is, so that they do not proceed into deliberate consent, as Hildemarus says.

“Let the useful brother always say in his heart.”] For Trithemius, the useful brother “is the one who desires to benefit everyone and harm no one, who regards nothing as wise except what he knows to please God, who places all his hope in the Lord, without whose help he most certainly believes that he can do nothing.” For Nicholas of Fractura, he is “the one who repents of his perverse thoughts; he is called the useful brother.”

“Then I shall be blameless before him if I have kept myself from my iniquity.”] Although “iniquity” is commonly taken to mean sin, Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino believe that here it must be understood specifically as an evil thought; the meaning of Saint Benedict’s words seems to require this. For he wants the useful brother to be concerned about his evil thoughts and always to say: “Then I shall be blameless before him if I have kept myself from my iniquity,” as though, Smaragdus says, he were saying: “Then I shall be able to lead a blameless life if an evil thought does not stain me. No one whose iniquitous thought pollutes his mind can live without stain; only the one who guards himself from the iniquity of an evil thought lives blamelessly.”

“But we are forbidden to do our own will in this way, when Scripture says to us: ‘And turn away from your own wills.’”] Hildemarus and Bernard of Cassino understand “will” here to mean both a good and an evil will. Certainly a good will itself ceases to be good when it becomes one’s own will, even if it appears to desire good things. Hence the Lord also rejects those fasts in which our own will is found.

“And again we ask God in prayer that his will be done in us.”] That is, in our will, says Hildemarus. Entirely in keeping with the mind of Saint Benedict is the saying of Saint Augustine, or whoever else is the author (*Sermon 65 in the Appendix to the Sermons*): “Certainly, when we say, ‘Your will be done,’ we are taught always to look to God’s will, not our own, because in our will there are sometimes things contrary to one another; but in the Lord’s will there is always life and goodness.”

“There are ways that seem right to human beings, etc.”] Abbot Moses, cited by Boherius, explains this passage of Scripture as follows: “The writings of the Jews or the pagans may produce in a monk a certain complacency greater than that produced by the books of the Christian faith. Their interpretations of sacred Scripture, appearing to give a new understanding, seem right to him. He judges multiplied fasts and prayers beyond the common practice of the monastery to be right; he considers it right and holy to pursue outside the monastery pious causes—such as those of monasteries, monks, the desolate, and nuns—which is nevertheless often brought about by diabolical deception. Therefore those ways that seem right plunge a person down to hell.”

Smaragdus thinks that the passage may be understood of those “who now seem to be elect but, because they are not from the Lord, are rejected.” He adds: “It may also appropriately be understood of those whom vices deceive under the appearance of virtues . . . . It is also understood of heretics, whose doctrine seems right to them but is discerned by Catholic men and judged to be perverse, because it leads its followers to hell.”

Hildemarus, however, interprets the passage as referring to vice under the appearance of a broad virtue, or when something good is accepted in place of something better, and something better in place of what is best. He also applies it to those good works that are performed without the blessing of a spiritual father, such as fasting and keeping vigil—works that Saint Benedict attributes to presumption and vainglory rather than to reward.

“But in the desires of the flesh, let us believe that God is present to us in the way the Prophet says to the Lord: ‘Before you is all my desire.’”] Saint Augustine understands this verse of the Prophet as referring to good desire, whereas Saint Benedict understands it here of evil desire—namely, desire of the flesh. Since this desire opposes the spirit and right reason, it cannot be good except perhaps accidentally, insofar as it procures the good of the person who resists it.
