Hildemarus and Bernard of Cassino interpret it as referring both to good and to evil desire; they are supported by the universal word “all”: “Before you is all my desire”—that is, it is known to you. Or: “Before you is all my desire”—that is, it is subject to your will, and I desire nothing except what you command me to desire.

“Therefore, if the eyes of the Lord—”] For Smaragdus, the eyes of the Lord are “the divine regard by which he always looks upon the good, so that he may defend them from the enemy’s snares, guard them from sins, and make them persist continually in good works.” Or, according to Cassian (*Book VIII*, chapter 4), by the eyes of God “we may understand the immensity of his perception, by which he surveys and sees everything, and the fact that nothing among the things done or to be done by us, or thought by us, is hidden from him.”

For it would be wrong to imagine anything bodily in God, as the Anthropomorphites once did; Theodoret refutes their error (*Questions on Genesis*, question 20). Sozomenus discusses them in book VIII, chapter 11; Cassian in *Conference* 10, chapter 2 and following; Gennadius in *On Illustrious Men*, chapter 33; and Nicephorus in book II, chapter 14.

“They watch over the good and the evil.”] Therefore the eyes of the Lord watch over the good and the evil so that he may repay the good with good and the evil with evil, granting the former rewards for good works and the latter everlasting punishment for wicked actions; so that he may hear and save the former, but destroy and condemn the latter. “The eyes of the Lord are upon the righteous, and his ears are turned to their prayers; but the face of the Lord is against those who do evil, to destroy their memory from the earth,” says Smaragdus.

“And the Lord always looks down from heaven upon the children of human beings, to see whether there is anyone understanding or seeking God.”] Here Hildemarus takes the particle “or” jointly, in the sense of “and,” so that the person is one who both understands God and seeks him.

“And if our works are reported daily, by day and by night, to the Lord our Maker by the angels assigned to us.”] Those heavenly spirits therefore report our works to God; hence they are called angels, that is, messengers—not as though he were ignorant, but “so that they may fulfill their office and ministry, because they are messengers,” says Haimo of Halberstadt.

Or, as Origen says: “The holy angels offer [Col. 0382A] these things to God, not as though the one who knows all things before they happen were ignorant, but so that they may become witnesses to the holiness and devotion of the righteous. Again, as though mourning the impieties and injustices of the wicked, and even those of the devil, the Lord, demonstrating and signifying these things, says of those good servants, that is, the angels: ‘They came and reported to their lord everything that had happened.’”

Or, as our Menardus adds: “They report our evil works so that they may receive from God knowledge of how and when they are to be chastised for correction. Therefore that angelic report must be feared, and their correction must be anticipated by suitable amendment.”

Hildemarus explains the manner of reporting in these words: “When each angel, whether good or evil, rejoices in our good deeds or is saddened by our evil deeds, that very joy—because it is known to God—or that very sadness—because it is known to God—is said by the angels to report our deeds to God through the knowledge of that joy or sadness.”

Moreover, because Saint Benedict here speaks in the plural of the angels assigned to us, he appears to have held the opinion that two angels were assigned to each human being: one good angel for protection and one evil angel for exercise. There is plainly no controversy among Catholics concerning the good angel; for many testimonies of Scripture establish that each human being has a guardian. The matter of the evil angel, however, is not held with equal certainty: first, because this opinion seems to have little solid foundation in Scripture; second, because the *Book of the Shepherd*, on whose authority ancient writers accepted the opinion, is listed among the apocrypha by Gelasius; and third, because if God had assigned evil angels to human beings, he might in some way be regarded as the author of sin.

Nevertheless, some of the ancient Fathers did teach this. Origen does so in *Homily 10 on Luke*, Gregory of Nyssa in the *Life of Moses*, Cassian in *Conference* 8, chapter 17, and *Conference* 13, chapter 12; Bede in his commentary on chapter 12 of the *Acts of the Apostles*; Hildemarus and Bernard of Cassino in their treatment of this passage; and many theologians of no small reputation, among them Peter Lombard (*Sentences*, book II, distinction 11). Indeed, the Apostle testifies that an angel of Satan was given to him to buffet him. See Maldonatus on chapter 18 of Matthew.

As to when these angels are assigned to us, Hildemarus says that various opinions have existed: “Each human being has a good and an evil angel assigned to him. The evil angel is assigned from the day of birth; according to the opinion of some, the good angel also from the day of birth; others say from the day of baptism; still others say that each human being receives a good angel when he begins to distinguish good and evil.” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius say the same.

Of these three opinions, the first seems more probable. Smaragdus defends it in words taken from Saint Jerome (*Commentary on Matthew* chapter 18): “Great is the dignity of souls, that each soul should have an angel assigned to it for its protection from the moment of its birth.”

“Therefore, brothers, we must beware at every hour, etc.”] All these things are clear and require no explanation, but meditation.

## On the Second Degree of Humility

“The second degree of humility is this: if a person does not love his own will.”] The second degree of humility, to which Saint Bernard opposes the freedom to sin, is that a person should not love his own will. Why should he love it, when, having renounced it, he has taken up the powerful and splendid weapons of obedience in order to serve the Lord Christ, the true King; when he is forbidden to follow his own will in the monastery; when he is commanded to hate it; and when he recognizes that he has no power over it?

Hatred of one’s own will is rightly placed among the degrees of humility because, as Saint John Climacus says (*Ladder*, degree 25), “the humble in heart always curses his own will as a deceiver.” And later: “It is a cross and a heavy burden for the humble person when he is forced to trust himself, just as it is for the proud person when he is ordered to abide by another’s judgment.” Hence the excellent saying of a certain elder, reported by Boherius in his second commentary: “My sorrow is this: if I have done my own will.”

“Let him not take pleasure in fulfilling his desires.”] It follows naturally that one who does not love his own will should not take pleasure in fulfilling his desires. Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, rightly compares the person who fulfills his desires with a wild ass, explaining this passage of Scripture (*Book I of the Conferences*, no. 33): “He considers himself free like a young wild ass.” “The wild ass,” he says, “is a wild donkey; wild animals love freedom, going wherever they wish and resting whenever they wish. Therefore, whoever seeks through unrestrained freedom to fulfill the evil things he desires wishes to resemble a young wild ass. Such a person, since he is reserved for nothing else, is not restrained by discipline, like a wild beast.”

Saint Benedict therefore urges us toward hatred of our own will with a threefold goad: Christ’s example, the threat of punishment for one who follows his own will, and the crown that blessed necessity produces when one denies that will.

“But let him imitate by his deeds the Lord’s saying: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me.’”] “For this reason,” says Abbot Abraham in Cassian (*Conference* 24, final chapter), “our Lord and Savior gave us the pattern for cutting off our own wills: ‘I have not come,’ he says, ‘to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’; and again: ‘Not as I will, but as you will.’ Those who live in monasteries and are governed by the authority of a superior practice this virtue especially: they do nothing at all according to their own judgment, but their will depends upon the will of the abbot.”

Therefore, to use Hildemarus’s words here, “when something difficult or contrary to his wishes has been commanded, the monk should say: ‘I have not come to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’—that is: ‘I have not come to fulfill the will of the flesh, but the will of God, by whose prompting I was sent here.’ Or likewise: ‘I have not come to do my own will’—that is, the will of the flesh, meaning what is easy and pleasant for me—but the will of my abbot, who sent me into this obedience.”

And likewise Scripture says: “The will has punishment, and necessity produces a crown.”] This passage is found nowhere in the Old or New Testament; but writers sometimes use the word “Scripture” to signify writings other than the sacred Scriptures as well. Thus Saint Valerius says: “For Scripture testifies that every sin which a negligent and undisciplined brother has committed immediately reverts to the negligent elder.” Peter the Venerable says: “Let the sinner Theophilus also come forward, who, as Scripture—already widely known among many—relates, after forty days of penance, received Christ’s body, and his face shone like the sun.” Bishop Milo of Minden, writing to the monks of Gorze, says: “For although it is read in the divine page that the performance of a work is proof of true love.” These words are from Saint Gregory, not from Holy Scripture. Accordingly, Saint Benedict uses the word “Scripture” here in the same sense, although what he presents is implicitly [Col. 0383D] found in various passages of Holy Scripture. But whether it is found there or not, it is certainly a splendid saying, and one that ought to be deeply engraved in the minds of all monks: The will has punishment, and necessity produces a crown.

“The will has punishment.”] This can be understood in two ways from Hildemar. First, the renounced will has punishment both on the part of nature, since great labor must be overcome in cutting off one’s desires, and on the part of false brothers, who do not cease to harass the obedient monk. Second, one’s own will, not subject to a superior, has punishment—and indeed perpetual punishment: for it is an iron wall that separates and tears a person away from God, as Abbot Pastor said in Saint Dorotheus (Teaching 5, no. 4). Or it may have temporal punishment: first from the person who delights in fulfilling it, whom his own conscience tortures by God’s just judgment. For, as Saint Bernard says (Letter 11), “This belonged to God’s eternal [Col. 0384A] and just law: that whoever did not wish to be ruled gently by God should be ruled punitively by himself; and whoever willingly cast off the gentle yoke and light burden of charity should unwillingly suffer the unbearable burden of his own will.” Second, punishment comes from the superior, who chastises the subordinate’s own will. In this sense Richard of Saint Angelo seems to have understood this passage of the Rule, writing as follows: “In this it has punishment, because we renounce our own will when we undertake the religious life; afterward we promise obedience, and we must keep our renunciation or promise. But if we do the opposite, it has punishment, and the punishment will be discretionary, since no penalty is established here.”

“And necessity produces a crown.”] The necessity of cutting off one’s own will—both in evil matters, so that we do not sin, and in good matters, which we are forbidden to undertake without the blessing of our spiritual father—produces the crown that the just Judge will one day give us.

212. Moreover, those who extort permission [Col. 0384B] from their superior, either by importunity or by faintheartedness, to do even the good things they desire do not climb this degree of humility. For permission extorted or forced is not permission but violence, says Saint Bernard (Letter 87); and those who ought to have attended not so much to the superior’s words as to his will flatter themselves in vain about the abbot’s permission. See Peter the Venerable’s letter to the hermit Gilbert, Book I, Letter 20.

## On the third degree of humility

“The third degree of humility is that a person, for the love of God, submit himself to his superior in all obedience.”] It follows rightly that the person who does not love his own will and does not take pleasure in fulfilling his desires should submit himself to his superior in all obedience. This can be understood in two ways from Hildemar.

First, by referring the universal word “all” to “obedience,” so that the meaning is: whatever the abbot commands, whether it is contained in the Rule or not, the monk should carry it out eagerly. Saint Bernard understood this passage of Saint Benedict in this way (On Precept and Dispensation, [Col. 0384C] chapter 6): “In the same Rule,” he says, “the third degree of humility is prescribed, that the monk submit himself to his superior in all obedience. By saying ‘all,’ he does not wish us to be content with a measure of obedience according to our profession, to disregard the obligation of what we have promised, or to derive our measure from the agreement; rather, he wishes us to pass beyond our vow with eagerness and obey in everything.” Likewise Peter Boherius, in his second Commentary: “In all obedience—that is, he should entrust everything to his judgment, leaving nothing to his own discretion, and should gladly and thirstily listen to his instructions.” Menardus understands it in the same way.

Second, by referring the term “all” to “superior,” as though he were saying, “Let him submit and obey every superior.” By “superior” would be understood not only the abbot, who is called the “greater” of the monastery in the Council of Carthage IV, canon 13, but also anyone else placed above him: a provost, dean, or prefect of some obedience or office—for example, the sacristan, cellarer, or master of some craft—or even one senior to him in the order of profession; indeed, even an inferior whom, out of humility, he considers his superior. [Col. 0384D] That this is Hildemar’s meaning, followed by Bernard of Cassino and Boherius in the First Commentary, is sufficiently indicated by these words: “In another way it is understood, namely, that in all obedience he should desire or have a superior—that is, a teacher.”

“Imitating the Lord, of whom the Apostle says: He became obedient unto death.”] Saint Basil likewise prescribes this form of obedience to monks (Brief Rule, Question 116). When asked, “To what extent ought one to obey who wishes to fulfill the rule of pleasing God?” he answers: “The Apostle shows this when he sets before us the obedience of the Lord, who became obedient unto death, and death on a cross, having first said: ‘Let this mind be in you which was also in Christ Jesus.’”

The humble monk, therefore, must have the same mind as Christ Jesus and, following his example, obey 213 even unto death. This too can be understood in two ways with Hildemar. [Col. 0385A]

First, “unto death” means for the whole span of life. In this sense Saint Bernard says (On the Precept and Dispensation, chapter 6): “There is indeed a certain limit of obedience according to time, namely, the very end of time, so that the end of obedience is also the end of life. The example of God’s Only-Begotten One especially commends this to us: he became obedient to the Father unto death.”

Second, “unto death” means that, if it is necessary to undergo death for the sake of obedience, one should not shrink from it. Both meanings are excellent and especially fitting for a monk. But the latter applies only to those who consider nothing dearer to themselves than Christ and, for love of him, submit themselves to their superior in all obedience. In the love of Christ, no limit or measure is imposed, as Boherius says in the First Commentary. Saint Bernard opposes to this degree of humility the tenth degree of pride, namely rebellion.

## On the fourth degree of humility

“The fourth degree of humility is that, in obedience itself [Col. 0385B], amid hard and contrary things, or even amid whatever injuries are inflicted, he should embrace patience with a silent conscience.”] In this fourth degree of humility Saint Benedict establishes the supreme perfection of obedience. In the second degree, by commanding hatred of one’s own will, he had prepared the monk for obedience; in the third, by teaching him to submit himself entirely to his superior, he had made him obedient; here, by commanding him to embrace hard and contrary things and inflicted injuries with an even spirit, he perfects him in obedience in every respect.

Although “hard things,” “contrary things,” and “inflicted injuries” are sometimes used indiscriminately to signify the same thing, the ancient commentators on the Rule nevertheless distinguish something between them here. According to Hildemar, “hard things are those that concern the material difficulty of a task—for example, lifting a stone, or carrying or moving something of immense size.” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius teach the same. Turrecremata, however, understands “hard things” as matters that are weighty and difficult to carry out. Thus laws [Col. 0385C] and commands are called hard when greater difficulty is involved. Hence the people asked Rehoboam to lessen something of his father’s exceedingly harsh rule. Hard things also occur in the imposition of penances, such as lying on the ground, afflicting the body with fasts, striking it with scourges, and so forth.

According to the aforementioned Hildemar, “contrary things are those that concern the will, when what is commanded does not please the person.” Or, as Bernard of Cassino says, and Boherius after him (Book VI, treatise 5, disputation 7), “contrary things are those that disagree with the will of the person performing them.” Benedict Haeften explains more fully: “I understand ‘contrary things’ in two ways. First, things that seem to oppose reason: for example, if you are ordered to sew a garment and then immediately to undo the sewing; to plant herbs, graft trees, and then uproot them again; to go to bed and immediately rise from the bed; to draw water and pour it out in the sun. Second, things that oppose the obedient person’s inclination: for example, if a lover of solitude and the cell is assigned responsibility for guests or the office of cellarer; or, conversely, 214 if someone inclined to roam about the house [Col. 0385D] and chatter with guests is ordered to remain in his cell, keep silent, and study.”

Injuries, for their part, are insults, mockery, abusive words, and similar things.

Almost the whole—indeed, the whole—of monastic life is spent amid these three things, as anyone with even the smallest knowledge of ascetic matters knows. Peter Damian should be heard on this subject: “Often,” he says, “a brother is ordered to leave his cell and live in another cell, and is not permitted to take away any of the utensils he had acquired even through his own labor. Often those who desire to rest in retirement are compelled to go out to perform a task. Sometimes the keys of their cells are removed from the doors and are not returned for a long time, except on individual Sundays. Sometimes those who have imposed strict restraint on themselves in food are forced to live more indulgently, while those who wish to restore their strength are compelled, on the contrary, to fast. Often a brother is ordered to travel far behind pack animals; [Col. 0386A] often he is sent to the markets to sell or buy.”

For this reason Abbot Zacharias, trampling beneath his feet a discarded cowl, said: “Unless a man has been trampled in this way, he cannot be a monk.” For this reason Saint Benedict himself wished a person coming for conversion to be assailed with injuries, and not to be admitted into the monastery cloister until he had appeared to bear patiently the injuries inflicted upon him. Once admitted, he was to be told that everything was hard and rough, and he was to be tested in complete patience.

Even the sick and dying were sometimes not released from this rule. We have a notable example of this in the Life of Saint Bernard (Book VII, chapter 26). A certain lay brother of Clairvaux, a man of remarkable simplicity and innocence, was lying at the point of death and confidently boasting before everyone of the glory that would soon be granted him. Saint Bernard is said to have addressed him as follows:

“Mark your heart, brother, mark your heart! What is this that you have said? From where could such bold presumption have crept into you? Were you not that poor and pitiable [Col. 0386B] man who, possessing nothing or almost nothing in the world, driven perhaps more by necessity than by fear of God, fled to us and, only after many prayers, obtained admission? We, for God’s sake, gathered you in your poverty, and made you equal in food, clothing, and the other necessities of life to the wise and noble men who are with us; and you became as one of them. What, then, have you given to the Lord in return for all this? And behold, it is not enough for your ingratitude that you received so many benefits freely from the hand of the Lord, unless you also claim for yourself by hereditary right his kingdom, which no king or prince has ever been able to purchase with however great a mass of gold and silver.”

If the holy abbot attacked a dying man in this way, what do you suppose he did with the healthy and strong? He certainly reveals his mind and practice clearly when, congratulating his brothers that their virtues were concealed beneath the veil of rebuke, he says (Sermon 4 on Psalm 90): “If you wish to know how much we gain from this concealment, I believe that there is no one here who, if he practiced in the world a fourth part of what he does here, would not be worshiped [Col. 0386C] as a saint and regarded as an angel. But now he is 215 daily accused and rebuked as negligent.”

His opinion, therefore, was far removed from that of those who assert that pious and holy men cannot be rebuked by a superior without pretense or falsehood. If that were true, all irony, allegory, and metaphor would have to be called lies. For someone who, by way of rebuke, calls a brother reading unusually loudly in the refectory “a declaimer,” “proud,” and “a reader lacking proper decorum” should no more be considered a liar than someone who ironically calls a very wicked man “excellent.” None of these statements is made assertively but rebukingly. We mention this only in passing; whoever wishes to know more may consult the book On the Duties and Perfection of Monks, chapter 12.

I return to Saint Benedict’s text. As Hildemar notes, he does not simply command us to endure hard and contrary things and injuries patiently; rather, which is more demanding, he commands us to embrace them—that is, to receive them with joy and love. “For,” he says, “we embrace what we love, because a monk [Col. 0386D] must not merely suffer or tolerate adversity, but suffer it with joy.””

Such was that distinguished holy woman of the monastery of the Tabennesiots who, according to Palladius (Lausiac History, chapter 41), “did not murmur, did not say anything, whether small or great, even though she was insulted, beaten with fists, attacked with curses, and hated by very many.” Such was Saint William, founder and monk of the monastery of Gellone, who, “though sometimes beaten and wounded by injuries, neither resisted nor threatened; indeed, he rejoiced in subjection.” Such was Benedict, a monk of Cluny, of whom Peter the Venerable writes (Book I of the Miracles, chapter 20):

“He tolerated many verbal injuries from certain persons who did not dare to inflict blows. I myself often remember that, in the common assembly of the brothers, he was attacked by such men with countless accusations, or almost no accusations at all, and, as though he were guilty, thrown to the ground, although he had done absolutely nothing wrong; [Col. 0387A] yet he merely replied that he was guilty. For he had this custom: whenever he was blamed, he almost never denied the blame.”

“And while enduring, let him not grow weary.”] That is, let him not lose heart. “For,” says Hildemar, “it is necessary that this ‘grow weary’ be referred to the soul, not the body. For although the perfect monk may be wearied in body because of frailty, nevertheless in mind he always desires to fulfill [his obedience].”

“Or withdraw.”] But according to Bernard of Cassino, this “withdraw” pertains to both body and mind. “For if, because of the things mentioned above, he leaves the monastery or abandons the work assigned to him, that is to withdraw bodily. Likewise, if, murmuring in his heart, he resolves not to fulfill his obedience, that is to withdraw mentally.” Boherius puts it more briefly: he must not withdraw from God or from patience.

“Scripture saying: Whoever perseveres to the end will be saved. And again: Let your heart be strengthened, and endure the Lord.”] Bernard of Cassino explains this passage as follows: [Col. 0387B] “‘Endure the Lord,’ as though he were saying: You are not carrying some other burden; in obeying, you endure and carry the Lord himself. But he is a sweet burden, because his burden is light and his yoke 216 is gentle. Therefore endure him; carry him patiently. For you are supported by him, and you are saved by him.”

“And showing themselves faithful for the Lord, and so forth.”] To encourage us more strongly to climb this fourth degree of humility and to endure all contrary things with eagerness, the holy Father adds to the testimony of Scripture examples and the words of the holy martyrs, whose utterances Scripture presents to us in their name, saying: “For your sake we are put to death.” Guido Juvenalis renders this in French: “Nous pensons en la mort, et mortifions nos membres” (“We think upon death, and mortify our members”).

“All day long”—that is, throughout the whole period of life, as Hildemar explains—“we are reckoned as sheep for slaughter.” The holy martyrs compare themselves to sheep especially for three reasons.

First, just as a sheep does not resist the one who kills it, so they do not resist or repay evil with evil. [Col. 0387C] Second, just as a sheep gives its wool even to those who strike it, so the holy martyrs assist their adversaries with benefits whenever an opportunity presents itself. Third, just as a sheep gives milk from its innermost parts, so they display to their enemies the inward organs of mercy and compassion.

Saint Benedict sets this example before us so that we may imitate it in adversity and, like sheep before the shearer, remain silent. Hence Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius after him, aptly explain this passage: “Just as a sheep destined for slaughter is raised, fed, and preserved for this purpose, namely, to be killed later, so the monk is regarded by others—and ought to regard himself—as being fed in the refectory, served in the infirmary, and preserved in the cloister for no other purpose than to be Christ’s offering and Christ’s victim, and to die beneath the sword of obedience.”

“And secure in the hope of divine reward, they follow, rejoicing, and so forth.”] The holy Father continues the words of the holy martyrs, in which we observe a new stimulus to patience [Col. 0387D] in their immediate hope of divine reward. Encouraged by this, they follow, rejoicing. “For the disgrace of the cross is pleasing to the person who is not ungrateful to the Crucified One,” as Saint Bernard says (Sermon 25 on the Song of Songs).

“And saying: But in all these things”—that is, hard and contrary things and inflicted injuries—“we overcome,” that is, according to Hildemar and Boherius, we persevere unto death, “because of him who loved us when we were still his enemies.” Here too recognize a new stimulus to patience: if we love, even for a little while, the one who pursued us with such great love, what adversity will we not endure for his sake?

“And again in another place Scripture says: You have tested us, O God.”] These too are still the words of the holy martyrs. “You have tested us, O God,” they say; we were not tested simply or by chance, since no testing comes to human beings except from God, whether he wills or permits it. “You have tested us by fire, as silver is tested by fire.” O piety! O [Col. 0388A] mercy! You have tested us by fire, but you have not consumed us. For God sends the fire of tribulation for this purpose—not that we should perish, but that we should emerge purer, and, cleansed of every stain, become worthy to come to the diadem of the eternal King, as Smaragdus says.

217. “You brought us into a snare; you placed tribulations upon our backs.”] Smaragdus explains this passage: “He says ‘you brought us into a snare’ to intensify the tribulation, so that you may understand that every kind of tribulation comes upon the elect in this age, because they hope to receive every kind of glory from the Lord in the future.”

This snare of the holy martyrs is the prison and the chains by which they are bound. Monks too may rightly claim for themselves these words of those who suffer and say to Christ: “You brought us into a snare.” According to Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, their snare is the monastery cloister, in which the monk is bound by stability and monastic profession no less than a captured animal is bound by a snare. “Yet this kind of bond produces freedom of soul and closes the gate of hell [Col. 0388B],” says Boherius. Christ the Lord has caught us—thanks be to God—in this snare, when he freed us from the inextricable snare of the world.

“And to show that we ought to be under the prior.”] “Under the prior,” that is, under the abbot, according to Smaragdus, Hildemar, and Bernard of Cassino. The latter adds: “Or under the prior—that is, under the provosts, dean, and others who hold the place of a prior.”

He continues, saying: “You placed men over our heads.”] These too are again the words of the saints who were martyrs. Bernard of Cassino explains them here according to the subject:

“Notice that he does not say merely, ‘You placed men over us,’ but ‘over our heads.’ You placed men, not angels—men just by nature, pure, steadfast, and confirmed by God—but men formed from the clay of the earth, conceived from base seed, fragile, sinful, teaching one thing and doing another. ‘Over our heads’: in the head are rational and memorial faculties, so that everything may likewise be taken captive under his command. [Col. 0388C] Also in the head are the five bodily senses, which are taken captive through true obedience and the command of the superior. This is what it means to place a man over our heads, namely, that man who is the captain of monks.”

“But also fulfilling the Lord’s command in adversity and injuries through patience, those who are struck on one cheek offer the other as well.”] Smaragdus writes: “The person who does not repay injury with evil offers the other cheek to the one who strikes one cheek.”

In Cassian (Conference 16, chapter 22), Abbot Joseph understands “the other” not as the left cheek but as another right cheek, namely the interior one. Thus, “if your external right cheek receives the blow of the striker, let the inner person also offer his right cheek to be struck through humble assent, sympathizing with the suffering of the outer person and, in a certain way, yielding and subjecting his body to the striker’s injury, so that the inner person is not inwardly stirred, even in silence, by the wounding of the outer person.”

Hildemar likewise explains this passage as referring to the preparation of the soul [Col. 0388D] to endure the striker and, if it should so please him, to receive his blows a second time. He also adduces other mystical interpretations of the passage, as does Boherius, which we 218 deliberately omit. Nevertheless, it may also be taken in the literal sense, and it indicates great perfection, provided that it is practiced not from a proud mind, as though for insulting and provoking others, like those mentioned by Cassian (Conference 16, chapter 20), but from a humble heart thirsting for its own abasement.

“They give their tunic to the one who takes it, and leave him their cloak.”] Smaragdus explains this as follows: “The person who does not return a curse for a curse gives his cloak to the one who takes his tunic.”

Bernard of Cassino explains it differently: “This means that, to the person who takes away some of his useful or superfluous possessions, he also gives up some of what is necessary for him. ‘He leaves it,’ I say—that is, he is ready to leave it.”

But Hildemar takes the passage literally: “If some adversary and tester of our patience or impatience wishes to take something of ours from us [Col. 0389A] and transfer it from our right to his own, we ought not merely to leave him what he unjustly demanded, but also to give up what he himself had not demanded.” See the Life of Saint Macarius of Egypt, abbot, chapter 4, in the Bollandists, January 15.

“They compel them to go one mile, and they go two.”] “Compelled to go one mile,” that is, forced to travel a mile, or one thousand paces; for a mile marks one thousand paces, and a pace contains five feet, as Hildemar notes. “They go two,” so that they travel three miles in all. He says three because the number three is used in Scripture to signify perfection, in honor of the Holy Trinity, to show that the perfection of monks ought to be perfect, says Hildemar.

According to Smaragdus, however, “the person who is not overcome by evil but overcomes evil with good willingly goes two miles with the one who compels him to go one.”

“They endure false brothers and persecution with the Apostle Paul.”] According to Bernard of Cassino, false brothers “are those who do evil deeds and, through their suggestions [Col. 0389B] and the corruption of their example, lead the simpler or younger into sin; they are murmurers, detractors, conspirators, and so forth.” Nevertheless, they must be borne, and the weaknesses of their bodies or morals must be endured with the greatest patience.

“And they bless those who curse them.”] By responding kindly, praying to God for their conversion, and setting them a good example.

To this fourth degree of humility Saint Bernard opposes the ninth degree of pride, namely, false confession, by which someone confesses himself guilty not out of humility, so that he may be punished, but so that he may be regarded as a saint or may not be rebuked by others.

## On the fifth degree of humility

“The fifth degree of humility is that he should not conceal from his abbot, through humble confession, any evil thoughts that enter his heart or any evil deeds secretly committed by him.”] Hence Abbot Moses says in Cassian (Conference 2, chapter 10): “This will be the first test of humility: that each person submit to the examination of the elders [Col. 0389C] not only what must be done but also what is being thought.”

Saint Benedict quite rightly places humble confession in the fifth degree after establishing patience amid hard and contrary things and inflicted injuries in the fourth degree. For it is difficult for someone who suffers an injury not to be moved by some feeling of indignation or murmuring against the person who inflicted it; and humble confession contributes greatly to overcoming this.

But a serious difficulty arises here concerning what kind of confession Saint Benedict means: sacramental confession, or that customary and commendable confession practiced by teachers of the spiritual life, which monks use for the sake of counsel. On this matter I find the commentators’ opinions quite divided. Bernard of Cassino, Richard of Saint Angelo, Boherius, John of Turrecremata, Matthias Lambertus, and Columbanus Uranx seem to interpret Saint Benedict as speaking of sacramental confession. Some [Col. 0389D] think that he spoke of both kinds. Theobald Artaldus Coelestinus, in his French exposition of the Benedictine Rule, John Craesbeeck, and Antonius Perez hold this view; Benedict Haeften inclines toward it, though in such a way that he leans more toward understanding the Rule’s text as referring solely to the confession made for consolation or direction.

Menardus embraces this latter and sounder opinion alone: “For in sacramental confession,” he says, “not only hidden sins but also open ones must be revealed.” Certainly Saint Benedict commands that this confession be made only to abbots—for he names no others. In his time, and even long afterward, many abbots were not priests and therefore could not receive sacramental confession. Add to this what Nicolaus Bravus observes: all the testimonies from Scripture that the holy Father adduces here to confirm this confession are taken from the Old Testament [Col. 0390A], and cannot literally be understood of sacramental confession.

Moreover, the same practice that Saint Benedict establishes here concerning the humble disclosure of one’s conscience to the abbot is prescribed in the Rule of Saint Antony, no. 25, and in his Life, chapter 29; in the Rule of Abbot Isaiah, chapter 6; in the more extensive Rules of Saint Basil, chapter 26; in Cassian, Book IV of the Institutes, chapter 9, and Conference 2, chapter 10; in Saint Dorotheus, Teaching 5; in the Rule for Monks prescribed by Saint David, in Bollandus, March 1; in the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 14; in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 13; in the Rule of the Master, chapter 15; in the Rule of Saint Donatus, chapter 23; and in the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, chapter 6.

Indeed, this Rule prescribes that it be done three times each day: after the second hour, after the ninth hour, and before Compline. Saint Benedict of Aniane’s account, in the Concordia of Rules, chapter 15, section 12, testifies that this was once customary in the monastery of virgins called Evoriacum, commonly the monastery of Fara. See the Life of Saint Pachomius, no. [Col. 0390B] 85, in the Bollandists, May 14.

The same practice is frequently praised and commended among our own people, especially in the 220 Life of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, no. 33 (Saeculum IV, part 1); in the Life of Blessed Alcuin, no. 8; and in the Life of Saint Adalard, by Saint Gerard, no. 41. There one finds something worthy of the greatest admiration written about him:

“He, namely Saint Adalard, held such a remembrance of his sons in his paternal heart that he not only observed their conduct but always kept their number and names recorded in his hands, so that he would not forget for whom he would have to render an account to God, or for how many. Therefore, taking the greatest care of them, he did not leave a single one of them without a conversation during the week, lest the enemy, finding them unoccupied, should sow weeds over their hearts.”

There were more than three hundred and no more than four hundred monks at Corbie under Saint Adalard.

Scripture exhorts us concerning this matter, saying: “Reveal your way to the Lord, and hope in him.”] By this authority of Scripture [Col. 0390C] the holy Father Benedict indicates four conditions of this confession.

First, it should be clear and open, without any obscurity of words, as indicated by “Reveal”; for something is said to be revealed when it is declared openly.

Second, it should be made to the abbot not as to a human being but as to God or his representative; for the abbot is believed to act in the monastery in Christ’s place, as is indicated by the addition “to the Lord.”

Third, it should concern one’s own faults, temptations, and evil thoughts, with no mention made of other people, as indicated by “your way.”

Fourth, it should be made with a firm hope of obtaining forgiveness: “And hope in him.”

And again he says: “Confess to the Lord, for he is good, for his mercy endures forever.”] In him, therefore, one must place firm hope.

And again the Prophet says: “I made my sin known to you, and I did not conceal my iniquities. I said: I will declare my iniquities against myself to the Lord, and you forgave the wickedness of my heart.”] In these words he again indicates four things to be observed in this confession.

First, [Col. 0390D] one should conceal absolutely nothing from the superior, because a physician can scarcely provide suitable treatment to a sick person unless he has full knowledge of the disease: “I did not conceal.”

Second, before approaching the superior, one should consider the character of one’s illness and investigate its causes, nature, and effects, so as to provide the abbot with fuller knowledge of it. This is gathered from the word “I said,” that is, “I resolved within myself.”

Third, one should do this with the will and intention of accusing oneself: “I will declare against myself.”

Fourth, one should do so with humility, as indicated by the word “iniquities.”

Saint Benedict has dealt here with what is required on the part of the person who reveals his conscience to the superior. What he requires on the part of the superior himself, to whom evil thoughts and secretly committed deeds are revealed, he has omitted, because here he intends only to make the disciple humble. But it may perhaps not be unwelcome to readers if we retrieve that matter from elsewhere.

Therefore St Fructuosus chiefly requires four things of the abbot [Col. 0391A] (On the Rule, chap. 13), namely, that he remedy a brother who is tempted or otherwise afflicted by “consolation, prayer, correction, or even the exercise of a suitable work”: almost the same provisions can be found in the Rule of the Master, where it is prescribed (chap. 15) that “when the superiors have reported something concerning a brother to the abbot, the abbot shall immediately summon the whole congregation and say to all: Come, brothers, let us help one another through love before the Lord . . . . . Therefore, let us pray unanimously to the Lord for this brother of ours, that he may deign, by the sign of his cross or by the command of his power, to restrain the devil’s temptations in him.”

[Note: [Col. 0391] For they did not disclose the evil thought to the abbot personally, but through the superiors.]

Behold the prayer of the abbot and the whole congregation for the tempted brother. We have an outstanding example of this practice in the Life of St Anastasius the Persian monk. Once, when he was tempted by the recollection of the magical art that he had practiced in the world, he disclosed the matter to the abbot, who “admonished and strengthened him in the Lord, according to the grace that had been given to him in the Lord; and, making a prayer for him before all the brothers in the church, drove the diabolical struggle away from him” (Bollandists, 22 January).

The Master adds:

“When, therefore, everyone has prayed for him at great length, the abbot shall rise with all the others and conclude the prayer. Then, as they go out, each shall resume the work he had been doing. The abbot shall retain with himself only that brother who is suffering from the evil thought, bring out the books, and have a similar divine remedy read against the need of his wound. For on the days when that brother, being questioned by the abbot, perhaps answers that the thought has not passed away, during the hours appointed for reading—whether in winter or in summer—the appropriate passages from the books concerning that very need of thought shall be read, namely, the section dealing with the particular brother. For example, if he has been persuaded to fornication, passages shall be read to him from various books in which God loves chastity; if he is frequently persuaded to lie, passages shall be read to him in various places where truth is commanded . . . . . Therefore the abbot must be thoroughly instructed in the law, either so that he may teach everything by testimonies, or so that he may mark down the passages relevant to the matter for reading.”

[Col. 0391C] Here we have consolation. For this is why he ordered that, after all the other brothers had been dismissed, the tempted brother alone should be kept with him; this is why he prescribed readings suited to his illness; and this is why he required an abbot instructed in divine law, who could teach everything by testimonies from Scripture—that is, console him.

A little later he continues:

“On the following morning the abbot shall ask whether the hostile thought has ceased or not. If he answers that it has not ceased, a fast shall be imposed upon everyone. If, when questioned again on another day, he answers that it has not passed, wine shall be withheld from the table when everyone takes nourishment . . . . . If, when questioned again on the third day, he answers that it has not passed, oil shall likewise be withheld from the table together with wine, so that no one may perish through the labor of many and the torment of abstinence, but all may escape.”

Here we have bodily affliction, which all writers who have treated spiritual life and the direction of conduct have assigned among the other remedies for temptation. We possess an excellent example of it in the Life of St Eupraxia the virgin, who died at the beginning of the fifth century in the monastery of virgins in the Lower Thebaid (Bollandists, 13 March):

“This was the custom in the monastery,” says the anonymous author, no. 14, “if it happened that a sister was tempted by the devil during sleep: she immediately disclosed it to the deaconess—that is, the abbess. The latter, with tears, begged God that the devil’s temptation might depart from her, and ordered her to carry stones, place them beneath her bed, scatter ashes over her hair shirt, and sleep in this manner until the tenth day.”

Finally, the Master concludes:

“And the brother must be admonished that, whenever some thought comes to him, he should immediately fly to the Lord, with his knees fixed on the ground and his neck bowed, or with the sign of the cross traced upon his forehead, so that he may deign to defend his soldiers from the devil.”

The ancient monks were accustomed to dispel the devil’s tricks by the sign of the cross, as frequently appears in their histories.

To all this must be added what the Rule of the Monastery of Tarnat prescribes (chap. 8):

“He who confesses more privately, for the sake of his consolation, the assaults of thoughts must not be despised or made known to others; rather, insofar as lies within him, he should be supported by gentle exhortation.”

And the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins says:

“Let the abbess or superior in no way disclose lesser or greater crimes, except to the one just judge who washes away the crimes of all who confess. For she who has confessed her wounds modestly has confessed not in order to receive disgrace, but in order to be restored to salvation, having God as her just witness, from whom she also expects healing. Let the elder woman who receives the confession keep it most honorably with gravity and moderation, concealing it within herself, lest, while she pours medicine into another’s wound, she corrupt the brightness of her own mind.”

Abbots should pay especially close attention to these matters, so that, if they desire any confidence in themselves from their inferiors, they may cover forever with silence whatever has been revealed to them.

## On the sixth degree of humility

[Col. 0392B] “The sixth degree of humility is for a monk to be content with every kind of lowliness and extremity.”

If a monk is to derive benefit from the humble confession to the abbot discussed in the preceding degree, he must be prepared for everything. Consequently, St Benedict requires in the sixth degree of humility that he be content with every kind of lowliness and extremity. In these words three matters require investigation: first, what lowliness is; second, what extremity is; third, why the holy Father did not simply say that he must be content with lowliness or extremity, but prefixed the word *every*.

Although *lowliness* and *extremity* are often used indiscriminately—as St Gregory the pope appears to have understood them in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chap. 55—the more eminent commentators on the Rule, Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, and Turrecremata, nevertheless introduce some distinction between them. For, according to Bernard of Cassino, “lowliness concerns every useful or necessary use, whereas extremity concerns every condition, rank, work, and place.”

Lowliness, therefore, is considered in every useful or necessary use; or, as Hildemar says more distinctly, it “concerns food and drink, clothing, footwear, the bed, and even one’s dwelling.” Here he reduces lowliness chiefly to three matters: food, clothing, and habitation—things that are everywhere praised by ascetic authors.

We shall speak below, in connection with chapter 35 or 39, of lowliness in food, and in connection with chapter 55, of lowliness in clothing. Meanwhile, see St Gregory, Homily 40 on the Gospel, and St Bernard, Homily 4 on *Missus est*, no. 10.

I am compelled to speak here of the lowliness of habitation with no small pain of spirit, considering how far removed we are from those times when monks inhabited no houses other than those they had prepared for themselves with their own hands (Rufinus, Book II, *Lives of the Fathers*, chap. 23), and had sometimes built them in a single day; reflecting upon the example of that great father of so many monks, namely St Martin, who, as Sulpicius Severus relates (Book I, *Life of St Martin*), “had a little cell woven from branches, while many of the brothers had made shelters for themselves in the same manner, and most had hollowed out recesses in the rock of the overhanging mountain”; recalling those happy days when St Ebrulfus, abbot of Utica, together with his companions (*Life*, no. 8, First Century of the Benedictine Era), “invoking the name of the Lord, constructed, according to the number of the inhabitants, a hut from branches and leaves, surrounding it with a small enclosure made of the same material, and remained there”; when St Sigirannus, abbot of Longoretum (*Life*, no. 10, Second Century), is said to have built a little dwelling of wood; when our monks of Fleury covered the monastery roofs with straw.

But, O times! O morals! On seeing the buildings of some monasteries today, who would believe them to be the dwellings of monks—that is, of poor men who have renounced the vanities of the world—and not the palaces of princes?

[Col. 0393A] Yet this poison did not first creep into the hearts of monks in our own age. Among the principal causes by which the monastic order formerly perished and observance of the regular discipline was weakened, excessive magnificence of buildings is listed (Mabillon, preface to the Fourth Century). Wishing to remedy this disease, the monks of Fulda petitioned the Emperor Charlemagne in a humble booklet (no. 12):

“Let immense and superfluous buildings, and the other useless works by which the brothers are wearied beyond measure and the servants outside perish, be omitted; but let everything be done according to measure and discretion.”

Accordingly, the Emperor Louis the Pious, son and successor of Charlemagne, wrote in his exhortation to Eigil, the elected abbot of the monastery of Fulda (*Life of Eigil*, no. 12, Fourth Benedictine Century):

“Dismiss from this time onward, Father, immense buildings and unnecessary works, by which the servants outside and the congregation of the brothers within are wearied, and reduce them completely to measure. Remember how often the complaint of this excess disturbed my father’s ears and our own.”

Much more modest in constructing the buildings of monks was the great Benedict, abbot of Aniane (Fourth Benedictine Century, part I):

“For he had resolved to cover or construct houses not with ornamented walls and red tiles, nor with painted ceilings, but with straw and humble material. Although the number of brothers increased greatly, he always sought what was poorer and humbler,” says Ardo in his *Life*, no. 14.

I know, nevertheless, that certain most holy men once built costly monasteries for themselves. But these were more often built at the expense of great lords or princes; and in this, as Abbot William of St Thierry writes to the brothers of Mont-Dieu (*On the Solitary Life*, chap. 12), animals were treated compassionately. There he says many excellent and truly worthy things, which we omit lest we appear to have prolonged the subject too far.

It is enough for now to have recalled the ancient simplicity and humility that our fathers displayed in their buildings and that we are bound to imitate. Yet we do not wish these remarks to be applied to those who, reviving the nearly lifeless regular discipline in monasteries, restore fallen buildings so that they may restore solid buildings—monuments of piety, destined, if possible, to last forever—and dwellings suited to the dignity and renown of their places—suited, I say, to the dignity of the places. For it would not be seemly to surround the most august basilicas, which the devotion of kings and other faithful people erected for monks, or the most magnificent princely mausoleums, with crude huts. Nevertheless, vain and empty ostentation of ornaments must remain far from even these places. Otherwise, Jerome’s words to Heliodorus (Letter 1) will rightly rebound upon us:

“The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head, and you measure out spacious porticoes and immense expanses of buildings.”

Certainly, no forgetfulness should ever erase from us what the aforementioned Abbot William of St Thierry writes:

“Believe me, brothers—and may you never have occasion to discover it by experience—that these beauties and worldly distinctions quickly weaken a manly purpose and make a masculine spirit effeminate. For although their pleasures are often dulled by habitual use, and although there are some who use such things as though they did not use them, nevertheless such affections are eradicated and conquered better by contempt than by use.”

It can scarcely be said how much vanity magnificent buildings inspire in those who profess humility.

St Pachomius once experienced this to some degree. When he had caused an oratory to be built (*Paralipomena concerning St Pachomius*, in the Bollandists, 14 May), “beautifully adorned with porticoes and columns arranged upon bases, he loved that building greatly and congratulated himself that he had brought such an outstanding work to completion. But when he perceived that this affection of his mind had arisen from a diabolical deception, so that he was elated with joy because of the beauty of the constructed oratory, he ordered ropes to be prepared and fastened to the columns; then, after first beginning a prayer and with the assistance of the brothers, he commanded all the columns to be brought down to the ground and to remain bent in that condition. Then, turning to the brothers, he said: ‘I beg you, fathers, never to desire that the works of your hands be exceedingly beautiful for the sake of display.’”

There is no doubt that St Wulstan, bishop of Worcester, feared a similar danger. For, as we read in his *Life* (Bollandists, 19 February), “when he had completed a new church of the monastery of Worcester and saw the old church, which St Oswald had built, being demolished, he is said to have spoken these words amid tears: ‘Wretched men that we are! We destroy the works of the saints in order to win praise for ourselves. That age of blessed men did not know how to build ostentatious houses, but rather to offer themselves to God beneath whatever roof they had and to draw their subjects to follow their example. We, on the contrary, strive, while neglecting the care of souls, to pile up stones.’”

See Peter Damian, Book VIII, Letter 2; the *Life of St Robert, abbot of Molesme*, no. 8; and Jerome of Camaldoli, Sermon on St Romuald, no. 12, in the Bollandists, 7 February.

Extremity, according to Bernard of Cassino, concerns four things: condition, rank, work, and place.

As regards condition [Col. 0394B], the monk should be content with the most extreme condition of all—that is, with his own, which, if properly considered, is the humblest of all. Persevering in his profession, he should not seek ecclesiastical dignities or offices; indeed, anyone who has attained even the lowest degree of humility ought not merely to withdraw from them but, if one may speak so, to abhor them.

Everyone knows the ancient saying of the early monks (Cassian, Book XI, chap. 17; see chap. 14; and Book VII, *Lives of the Fathers*, chap. 35): “A monk must flee women and bishops in every way, lest, being taken up by them into the clergy, they should be advanced to ecclesiastical duties.”

As regards rank, he should not seek the dignities and offices of the monastery, in accordance with the saying of St Basil (*Monastic Constitutions*, chap. 25):

“It is plainly not fitting for a religious person to desire dignities. For if he seeks in this life the rewards of labors and virtues, let him know that the payment is wretched, since he exchanges eternal things for temporal and loses them. But if he prefers to strive here and receive crowns in heaven, he must not only refrain from desiring dignities but also refuse and scorn those offered to him, lest the dignity of this life diminish the future one, and so forth.”

This teaching is not pleasing to the proud monk who, as St Bernard says (*On the Degrees of Humility*, chap. 16), “when the time comes and he is not promoted to the priorship, judges his abbot either envious or deceived.”

St Bernard laments such men elsewhere in these words (Homily 4 on *Missus est*):

“I see something that grieves me greatly: after despising the pomp of the world, some learn pride more thoroughly in the school of humility, and under the wings of a meek and humble master become more gravely insolent, becoming more impatient in the cloister than they would have been in the world. What is even more perverse, many in the house of God cannot endure being despised, although in their own house they could be nothing but contemptible. Since they were not worthy to have a place where many sought honors, they at least wish to appear honorable where all despise honors.”

[Col. 0394D] As regards work, he should not merely refuse to shun the most despised tasks and obediences—for example, serving the kitchen assistants, washing filthy cloths, or cleaning the latrine—but should willingly embrace them, bearing in mind St Basil’s judgment (*Monastic Constitutions*, chap. 24):

“It is fitting for a religious person to undertake even the humbler works with great diligence and readiness of spirit, knowing that whatever is done for God is not insignificant but of great importance, spiritual, worthy of heaven, and brings us a heavenly reward. Therefore, even if he must follow pack animals serving the common need, he ought not to object, if he reflects how readily the apostles obeyed the Lord when he commanded them to bring a colt; and he should consider that the brothers are the Lord’s, for whose sake we undertake care of the animals . . . provided that such service does not become an occasion for negligence. Rather, he should guard himself with all diligence, so that he may benefit both himself and those with whom he deals. Whenever some humbler work must be done, he should know that the Savior himself served his disciples and did not disdain humble tasks. Finally, it is a work of great importance if a person becomes an imitator of God and ascends through those humble things to the sublimity of humility. Who, then, would say that something is humble when God himself made use of it?”

St Radegundis certainly thought in this way. Having been a most powerful queen of France, she professed the monastic life in the monastery of virgins at Poitiers (Venantius Fortunatus, *Life*, no. 23, First Benedictine Century):

“Taking her turns, she swept the streets and corners of the monastery and cleaned whatever was filthy. She did not shrink from carrying loads that others dreaded even to see, and she did not delay to clean the latrine but hastened to undertake the work. Bearing the stench of dung, she believed herself inferior to herself if she did not ennoble herself by the lowliness of service. She carried wood in her arms, tended the fire with breath and tongs, grew hot without withdrawing when injured, served the sick outside her assigned week, and so forth.”

Bede relates nearly identical things (Second Benedictine Century) concerning Easterwine, abbot of Wearmouth, formerly a servant of King Ecgfrith, in Book I of *The Life of St Benedict Biscop*, no. 8.

But the proud man cannot endure such things. “If some ordinary obedience is imposed upon him, he becomes indignant and scorns it, thinking that he should not be occupied with lesser matters, since he feels himself suited to greater ones” (St Bernard, *On the Degrees of Humility*, chap. 16).

Finally, as regards place, if the abbot orders an older monk to sit in the last rank and place of the congregation, he should willingly consent. For it will sometimes happen that the last shall be first and the first last. This is something the proud man must fear above all, since, as St Bernard says in the same place, he “sits first in assemblies, answers first in councils, approaches without being invited, and intrudes without being ordered.”

Why, then, did he say that a monk must be content not simply with lowliness or extremity, but with every lowliness and extremity? Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Turrecremata explain it in this way: some are content with lowliness in food but not in clothing; some with lowliness in clothing but not in food; some with both, but not with lowliness of habitation. Likewise, some endure lowliness but cannot bear extremity.

Or, as Hildemar says: “He said ‘with every lowliness and extremity’ because he includes both body and mind. That is, just as he is lowly and extreme in body, so he must also be so in mind. For if he appears lowly and extreme in body but not in mind, he is no longer a monk but a hypocrite.”

The word *content* clearly indicates this, since it signifies an inward inclination of the mind and the assent of the will. Thus Hildemar says:

“If the abbot orders the superior to sit in the last place, and he goes there with sadness, he is a transgressor of that command; and because he is a transgressor of that command, he is not a perfect monk.”

For not to rejoice or glory in one’s own abasement is something less than perfection, as St Bernard says (Letter 250).

Moreover, to preserve lowliness, another Bernard, namely Bernard of Cassino, proposes these four verses:

> To despise the world, to despise no one, to despise oneself,  
> To despise being despised—these four things bring blessedness.

“And in everything that is enjoined upon him, let him judge himself to be a bad and unworthy laborer.”

St Benedict does not merely wish the monk to be content with lowliness and extremity; he also wishes him to regard himself as unworthy of lowliness and extremity. Thus, whatever lowly things are supplied to him in food, clothing, and so forth, he should think that even lower things are owed to him; wherever he is placed, however humble the place may be, he should consider himself placed in a higher position than he deserves; and whatever obedience is enjoined upon him, however abject, he should nevertheless acknowledge himself worthy of it by his merits.

For just as a man who has been rescued from the gallows—this is Hildemar’s example—would not dare, if the master who had ransomed him assigned him some humble task, to answer that he did not wish to undertake work so lowly, since he was worthy of greater things, but would accept the command with complete submission of spirit, so the monk, rescued by divine kindness from the bonds of the world, should receive whatever the abbot, who acts in the Lord’s place, commands in the Lord’s name, and whatever humble work he assigns, as though it were a great favor.

Saying with the prophet: “I have been reduced to nothing and did not know.”

“That is,” says Smaragdus, “I recognized that I was ignorant, reckoned myself foolish and small, and despised myself as senseless.”

Or, as Turrecremata explains, “I did not know” means “I concealed [it], because true humility conceals its goods from itself.”

“I became like a beast of burden before you.”

That is, receiving and carrying whatever burdens, however lowly.

The comparison between a beast of burden and a monk is indeed beautiful. “You too are the Lord’s beast of burden,” Peter the Venerable once wrote to Gilbert the Recluse (Book I, Letter 20); “but you lie enclosed in his stable and chew his fodder. Those monks are strong horses prepared for the day of battle; upon them the heavenly rider sits, courageously attacking and destroying the prince of the world. They are driven by the bridle of obedience, urged on by the goads of discipline, and, panting and often with their flanks bloodied, they run along the path of God’s commandments; nor do they rest unless, having completed the course, they seize the prize. They endure the burden of the day and the heat; they support the yoke of obedience with a strong neck; and they repel with the shield of patience the darts of anger hurled by enemies and neighbors.”

Our abbot Nesteros knew this very well. In the *Lives of the Fathers* (Book V, tract 15, no. 30), he says of himself:

“When at the beginning I entered the congregation, I said to my mind: ‘You and the donkey must be one.’ For just as a donkey is beaten and does not speak, suffers injury and does not answer, so must you be, as it is written in the psalm: ‘I became like a beast of burden before you, and I am always with you.’”

“And I am always with you.”

That is, “in your works,” says Richard of St Angelo; or, “I am always with you through conformity of will and through tireless constancy,” as Turrecremata explains together with Bernard of Cassino and Boherius.

To ascend to this degree of humility, against which St Bernard places the seventh degree of pride, namely presumption, the seventh degree of humility—which we must now discuss—provides no small assistance.

## On the seventh degree of humility

“The seventh degree of humility is for a person not only to declare with his tongue that he is lower and more contemptible than everyone else, but also to believe it with the deepest affection of his heart.”

In this degree above all, the holy Fathers place the virtue of humility. Thus St Basil says:

“Humility is to consider everyone superior to oneself.”

And elsewhere (*Shorter Rules*, question 198):

“The humble person, rejecting all earthly honors, judges himself the last.”

St Ambrose says:

“For this is humility: that no one claim anything for himself, but consider himself inferior.”

St John Chrysostom (Homily 33 on Genesis) says:

“Let us not show honor only to those who are older than we are in age, or even to those who are our equals. For it is not humility to do what necessity requires you to do. True humility exists when we yield to those who seem to be lesser than ourselves and revere those who seem more unworthy than we are. If we think rightly, we shall consider no one inferior to us; rather, we shall say that we are surpassed by all human beings.”

Finally, St Bernard (*Sermon on the Octave of Epiphany*) says:

“For just as it is great and weighty pride to prefer oneself to an equal or to make oneself equal to a superior, so it is a great humility to show oneself inferior even to one who is inferior. For just as it is the highest and most intolerable pride to place oneself above a superior, so it is the highest and complete justice to submit oneself to an inferior.”

From these words of St Bernard we learn that not only the true virtue of humility, but also the highest virtue—so to speak, the virtue of virtues—the perfection of the saints, and the highest and complete justice, are established in this degree.

Thus the same holy doctor says elsewhere (*Sermon 13 on the Song of Songs*):

“Great and rare indeed is the virtue by which, although performing great works, you do not know yourself to be great; by which your holiness, manifest to all, remains hidden to you alone; by which you appear marvelous and consider yourself contemptible. I judge this more marvelous than the virtues themselves.”

And elsewhere, writing to the monks of the Alps (Letter 143):

“To do what is right and consider oneself useless is found among few; therefore many admire it. This, I say, this very thing makes the illustrious more illustrious and the holy more holy . . . . In my judgment, this virtue is preferred to prolonged fasts, vigils begun before their time, and every bodily discipline, as true devotion, which is useful for all things.”

At this point someone may perhaps be astonished and ask whether, without violating the truth, a person can think and proclaim such things about himself, and by what reasoning it can come about that a monk beloved by God, always intent upon God and adorned with the grace of virtues, should judge himself lower and more contemptible than a murderer, adulterer, blasphemer, or apostate.

St Basil answers him (*Monastic Constitutions*, chap. 2):

“You will not speak falsely if you say that you are a sinner. For, if you understand correctly, you will sin by that very assertion if you say that you are without sin.”

And St John Chrysostom (Homily 33 on Genesis):

“If we think rightly, we shall consider no one inferior to us; rather, we shall say that we are surpassed by all human beings. And I say this not merely of ourselves, who are submerged in countless sins, but even if someone is conscious of having performed many good deeds: unless he feels within himself that he is the last of all, he will derive no benefit from all his good works.”

How this can occur without violating the truth is explained in two ways by the commentators on the Rule, Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius.

First, it is because evils are hidden within us and good things are hidden in others. St Thomas agrees with this in these words (II–II, question 161, article 6, reply to objection 1):

“A person may, without falsehood, believe and declare himself more contemptible than everyone else on account of hidden defects that he knows in himself and the gifts of God that are hidden in others. Hence Augustine says in his book *On Virginity*: ‘Judge others superior in what is hidden, although you are better than they are in what is manifest.’”

Certainly, as the same Augustine cited here says elsewhere (*Eighty-Three Questions*, question 71):

“We must consider that there is no human being who cannot possess some good, even if it is hidden, in which he may be superior. This thought is useful for crushing and subduing pride. Do not suppose that, because your good qualities are prominent and visible, the other person possesses none that are hidden and perhaps of greater weight, by which he surpasses you without your knowing it.”

Perhaps for this reason St Bernard, addressing his own people, says among other things (*Sermon 36, On Various Matters*):

“Do not think too much, then, about what you seem to possess, except perhaps occasionally, so that you may give thanks and recognize yourself as indebted to the one who gave it; or for the sake of consolation, when this is necessary, lest you become sad for some reason. For the rest, always pay greater attention to what another possesses and you do not. Let this thought preserve you in humility, keep you from descending into tepidity, and kindle you more strongly with the desire to make progress.

“Consider, however, how many evils that contrary thought produces—the thought by which you continually turn over in your mind what you seem to possess and judge someone else not to possess. From this you are lifted up into pride, when you place yourself above another; from this you neglect to make progress, when you consider yourself great; and from this, finally, you begin to decline, when, by comparison with another, you think that you have done more than enough.”

With the same attitude, perhaps, Abbot Poemen answered a brother who asked him (Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 131):

“How can I consider myself inferior to a man who is a murderer?”

He replied:

“If, when you see a man who perhaps has killed another, you say within yourself: ‘This man has committed only this one sin, whereas I commit murder every hour, killing myself.’”

When the brother asked how this could be, he answered:

“This alone is the justice of man: that he should condemn himself. For then he is just when he condemns his own sins.”

Second, this may be explained by the incomprehensible judgments of God.

[Col. 0398A] “Terrible is God in his counsels concerning the sons of men,” since those whom we often consider holier may be known by God’s infallible knowledge to have been rejected, while those who are worse may be known to have been predestined.

For who, seeing Saul chosen by God and consecrated king by his command, but then seeing Paul breathing threats and bent upon death, would have believed that the former was to be erased from the book of life and that the latter was made by God a vessel of election?

Since no human being knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, let no one prefer himself to another. Rather, let him imitate the virtue of that Alexandrian leatherworker by which he surpassed the famous Antony, abbot throughout the world.

Once, when the holy man was praying in his cell, a heavenly voice came to him and said (Rufinus, Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 130):

“Antony, you have not yet attained the measure of that leatherworker who is in Alexandria.”

When he heard this, the venerable old man hurried to Alexandria, went to the leatherworker, and asked him to tell him about his works. He replied:

“I do not know of having ever done anything good. Therefore, when I rise in the morning from my bed, before sitting down to my work, I say that this entire city, from the least to the greatest, will enter the kingdom of God because of its righteousness, while I alone, because of my sins, will enter everlasting punishment. I repeat this saying with sincerity of heart before I lie down in the evening.”

When St Antony heard this, he added:

“In truth, son, like a good craftsman sitting in your house, you have attained the kingdom of God in repose; whereas I, living all my time in solitude without discernment, have not yet reached the measure of your saying.”

St Bernard elegantly illustrates this second explanation in these words (*Sermon 37 on the Song of Songs*):

“What if he should depart from the truth in judging and believing himself lower and more inferior than the truth would have him? His ignorance would undoubtedly excuse him, and he would scarcely be judged proud; his error would not be found so deserving of hatred as his humility might perhaps be deserving of grace.

“For if we clearly knew the condition in which God holds each one of us, we ought neither to withdraw above nor below it, but to acquiesce in the truth in all things. Now, however, since he has made darkness his hiding place for this counsel, and the hidden word has been concealed from us, so that no one knows whether he is worthy of love or hatred, it is plainly more just and safer, in accordance with the counsel of Truth himself, to choose for ourselves the lowest place, from which we may afterward be led upward with honor, than to presume upon a higher place, from which we would soon have to withdraw in shame.

“Therefore there is no danger, however much you humble yourself or however much you consider yourself lower than you are—that is, lower than the truth considers you. But it is a great evil and a dreadful danger if you exalt yourself even slightly above the truth; if, in your thought, you prefer yourself even to one person whom the truth perhaps judges your equal or even your superior.

“For just as, if you pass through a door whose lintel is—speaking for the sake of understanding—too low, it does not harm you however much you bend yourself, but it does harm you if you raise yourself even by the width of a finger beyond the door’s measure, so that you strike against it and are dashed with your head shaken; so in the soul there is plainly no need to fear any degree of humiliation, however great, but the slightest rash elevation is to be dreaded and feared exceedingly.

“Therefore, man, do not compare yourself with those who are greater, or with those who are lesser, or with anyone, or with a single person. For what do you know, man, whether that one whom you perhaps regard as the most contemptible and miserable of all, whose utterly criminal and singularly disgraceful life you shudder at and therefore think deserving of scorn—not merely in comparison with yourself, who perhaps confidently believe that you are now living soberly, justly, and piously, but even in comparison with all other criminals, as though he were the greatest criminal of all—what do you know, I say, whether he may be destined to become better than both you and them through the transformation wrought by the right hand of the Most High, and whether he may already be so in God?

“For this reason he did not wish us to choose merely an ordinary place, or even the second-to-last place, or simply a place among the last; rather, he says: ‘Recline in the last place,’ so that you may sit as the last of all, and presume not merely to place yourself above anyone, but not even to compare yourself with anyone.”

Three other reasons are added by Benedict Haeften (Book VI, treatise 6, discussion 5), on account of which we ought to judge ourselves inferior even to the most wicked. The first is drawn from the graces and benefits bestowed upon us: if another person had been endowed with them, he would have become far holier than we; whereas we would be much worse than he if we had been afflicted with the same temptations by which he was tried. The second arises from consideration of men distinguished by the highest holiness and virtue: if, setting aside the faults of the wicked, we attend only to the outstanding virtues of the good, and see by how great a distance they surpass us in holiness and how many virtues are lacking in us, then, no longer daring to lift our eyes, we shall easily judge ourselves inferior to everyone. Peter the Venerable chiefly uses this reason to exhort the hermit Gilbert to humility in Book I, Letter 20. The third arises from the account that must be rendered for benefits received: as gifts increase, so too do the accounts owed for those gifts. If, therefore, we consider how much we are bound to repay for benefits received from God, and how little we actually repay, how shall we not consider ourselves even the least of all? [Col. 0399B]

Having treated these matters concerning this seventh degree of humility at sufficient length, it would be proper to hasten on to the other degrees, were we not compelled to pause here by certain matters that remain to be examined concerning the text of the Holy Rule.
