For it does not simply say that one should declare oneself inferior and viler than all; it also says that one should believe this to be so. You may see many who proclaim themselves the greatest of all sinners and thrust themselves down even to hell; yet if you touch them with so much as the smallest word, they flare up and complain that they have been insulted. You would call such men not so much humble as masks of humility. Such was that monk described by Cassian (Collation 18, chapter 11): after abasing himself at great length in words, even declaring that he was unworthy to breathe the common air, he could not endure, nor conceal his distress, when Serapion admonished him not to wander about idly but to remain in his cell. [Col. 0399C] Saint Bernard further notes (Sermon 16, on the Song of Songs) that some confess their vices and evil deeds boastfully and shamelessly; others mention them deceitfully and as though in repentance, while seeking glory by their intention; and still others declare their sins to others not because they are humble, but so that they may appear humble. The holy doctor reproves and condemns them all.

Moreover, the holy Father Benedict did not merely say that a monk should believe himself inferior and viler than all; he said that he should believe it “with the inmost affection of his heart.” That is, he should display outwardly the person he considers himself inwardly to be; he should gladly be treated by others as he proclaims himself to be. For this is true humility of heart, which Christ so greatly commended when he said: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart.” He said “of heart,” not in word or tongue; he said “of heart,” not merely in judgment or knowledge. He said “of heart,” such as he himself was, of whom, as Saint Bernard says (Sermon 42, on the Song of Songs), it pleased him to be regarded as least, although he knew himself to be supreme.

And indeed, what benefit is there in proclaiming oneself a sinner? What benefit is there in believing oneself inferior and viler than all? [Col. 0399D] The demons themselves can possess such humility as our very knowledge requires and truth compels us to have—namely, humility of mouth and understanding, not humility of heart; humility of truth, not humility of love. What, then? “The true humility of heart must be retained,” says Abbot Piammon in Cassian (Collation 18, chapter 11), “which does not descend from an affected abasement of body and words, but from the innermost humiliation of the mind. It then shines forth with the clearest signs of its patience, when a person does not himself boast of crimes that others would not believe, but bears with a gentle equanimity of heart the insults arrogantly inflicted and the injuries committed by others.” Saint Jerome required this kind of humility from Caelantia when he wrote (Letter 50):

“Pursue humility—not that which is displayed or pretended by bodily gesture or a broken tone of voice, but that which is expressed by a pure affection of the heart. For it is one thing to possess virtue and another to possess the likeness of virtue; one thing to follow the shadow of things and another to follow the truth. Pride is much more deformed when it hides beneath certain signs of humility; for I do not know how vices are more shameful when they are concealed under the appearance of virtues.”

See also Saint Dorotheus, Instruction 2.

**Humbling himself.** Not only with the tongue, but also with the affection of the heart.

**And saying with the prophet: “But I am a worm.”** For just as a worm is the vilest of all animals, born from decay and in decay, moving without noise, despised and trampled underfoot, so I, the vilest of all, born from sin and in sin, living from sin and in sin, desire to be despised and trampled underfoot by everyone.

**And not a man.** For who would call him a man who, staining himself with so many sins, demonstrates that he has been deprived of reason?

**The reproach of men.** Since he is wholly from sin and wholly in sin. Or “the reproach of men” may mean: because I am a worm and not a man, I desire to be the reproach of men [Col. 0400B] and the outcast of the people, like Saint Arsenius. When Bishop Theophilus, together with a magistrate, questioned him, wishing to hear him speak, Arsenius remained silent for a while. Then he said: “If I speak, will you keep what I say?” When they had promised this, he continued: “Wherever you hear that Arsenius is, do not approach.”

**I was exalted.** That is, in the world, where I lived honored, as Hildemar and Bernard of Monte Cassino explain. Or, as Richard of Saint Angelo says, “exalted in pride”; or exalted through the remission of sins received in baptism.

**And humbled and confounded.** Having come to know my own vileness and the sins that afterward, in my wretchedness, I committed.

**And again: “It is good for me that you have humbled me, so that I may learn your commandments.”** Although I am humbled and confounded, nevertheless I give thanks to you, good Jesus, because when you humbled me, I learned your commandments, which formerly, when exalted, I despised.

## On the eighth degree of humility

[Col. 0400C] **The eighth degree of humility is if a monk does nothing except what the common rule of the monastery prescribes.**

This passage can receive several interpretations. First, Hildemar argues that the word “common” refers to the word “monastery.” According to Bernard of Monte Cassino, a common monastery is a cenobium, in which many live together in common. In this sense, the eighth degree of humility commands that a monk, content with his own state, should not rashly desire the manner of life of hermits:

“For the proud man,” says Cassian (Book XII, chapter 30), “abhors the discipline of the cenobium itself and, as though he were being held back from perfection by the fellowship of the brethren and recalled from the good of patience and humility by the fault and hindrance of others, desires the habitation of a solitary cell.” The humble man, recognizing that such a life is beyond his strength, venerates it in others but does not presume to desire it for himself.

Second, if the word “common” is joined to “rule,” as it is commonly understood, and the common rules in a cenobium—which are proposed to the entire congregation—are distinguished [Col. 0400D] from particular rules, which are written only for certain persons, as in chapter 21, concerning the deans; chapter 31, concerning the cellarer; chapter 65, concerning the provost; and chapter 66, concerning the porter, then the meaning of this passage may be that a monk, adhering to the common rules, should not meddle in particular matters. For example, a private brother to whom the abbot has entrusted no obedience should not go to the monastery gate to receive or deliver the replies of those who come, which is the porter’s duty; he should not concern himself with the monastery’s goods and necessities, which belongs to the cellarer; he should not prepare the beds in the guesthouse, and so forth. Such matters sometimes generate no slight quarrels in monasteries.

Third, if by “the rule of the monastery” we understand not only what was written by the Holy Legislator, but, with Boherius in his second commentary, the common statute or custom of the cenobium—for, taking account of the regions and places in which monasteries are situated, it is necessary to observe many things [Col. 0401A] that are not contained in this Rule, as the holy Father Benedict sufficiently indicates in chapters 40, 48, and 55—then the meaning of this passage will be that a monk, following the customs and established practices of his own monastery, should not desire the statutes of other cenobia. For example, where beer is served because wine is lacking, he should not demand that wine be given to him; or where wine is served, he should not require beer to be served to him. Saint Bernard appears to adapt this interpretation to the passage in his book *On Precept and Dispensation*, chapter 16.

Fourth and finally, this passage may mean that a monk should not merely avoid following the rites and customs of other monasteries, but should adhere so closely to his own rule that, content with the common exercises of the brethren, he does nothing against or beyond it, avoiding every form of singularity. Nicholas of Fractura understood Saint Benedict in this sense:

“This letter wishes to say that a monk placed in a congregation should not live a poor life, or even a splendid one in food or clothing, in a manner different from that of the other brothers; rather, he should conform himself to their conduct in everything, provided that they do not depart from the paths of the Rule. For that part is shameful which does not correspond to its whole.”

And since nothing is more pernicious in cenobia than singularity, and nothing has been so detested by all who have been true lovers of monastic life, it may not be useless briefly to add some reasons by which we may be deterred from it.

The first reason is taken from that celebrated saying of Saint Pope Leo (Sermon 3, on the fast of the seventh month):

“That which is celebrated by public law is more sacred than that which depends upon private arrangement. Nothing in such a people is disordered, nothing divergent, when all the members of the entire body agree with one another in a single vigor of devotion.” 234

The second reason is that whatever is presumed against the common rule of the monastery is recognized as coming from the evil spirit, as Cassian teaches among others (Collation 18, chapter 3), and Saint Bernard elegantly describes in these words (Sermon 33, on the Song of Songs):

“How often, for example, did he suggest anticipating the vigils, so that he might mock the solemn observances of the brethren while they slept? How often did he urge the prolongation of fasts, so that he might make a man useless for divine services by rendering him weak? How often, envying those who were making good progress in the cenobia, did he persuade them, under the pretext of greater purity, to seek the desert? Those wretched men learned at last how true was the saying they had read in vain: ‘Woe to the one who is alone, for if he falls he has no one to lift him up.’ How often did he incite someone to manual labor beyond what was necessary and, having broken his strength, render him incapable of the other regular exercises? And so forth.”

The third reason is indicated by Cassian in these words (Book V, chapter 23):

“Whatever is presumed beyond customary practice and common usage, the most ancient tradition of the Fathers has marked as polluted by the disease of vanity, glory, and ostentation. Nor have we ever known any of those whom we have rightly seen to excel in knowledge and discernment, or whom the grace of Christ has set before all as exceedingly splendid lamps for imitation, to have abstained from eating bread, which among them is considered cheap and readily available; nor have we ever seen any of those who, turning aside from this rule and abandoning the use of bread, pursued nourishment from legumes, vegetables, or fruits, counted among the most approved, or even regarded as having attained the grace of discernment or knowledge.”

He brings forward the same reason in Book I, chapter 3, and Book II, chapter 18; also Saint Basil, *Shorter Rules*, question 138; and Saint Bernard, *On the Degrees of Humility*, chapter 14.

According to Boherius, the fourth reason is that the singular monk claims again for himself the personal will that he renounced in his profession, contrary to what he promised. On this matter Saint Bernard complains against his own monks (Sermon 19, on the Song of Songs):

“You do not wish to be content with the common life; the regular fast is not sufficient for you, nor the solemn vigils, nor the discipline imposed, nor the measure of clothing and food that we distribute to you. You prefer private things to common ones. You who entrusted your care to us, why do you again meddle in your own affairs? For that which so often offended God, with your consciences as witnesses—your own will, namely—you now once again have as your mistress, not me. It teaches you not to spare nature, not to submit to reason, not to obey the counsel or example of your elders, and not to obey us.”

Saint Euthymius likewise condemned singularity among his monks, according to his Life, no. 17, volume II of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*; so did Saint Basil in the *Shorter Rules*, questions 137 and 138; and again Saint Bernard, Sermon 71, on the Song of Songs.

The fifth reason is that singularity disturbs the whole congregation. Thus, when the brothers complained to the abbot about Blessed Simeon Stylites because he had fasted for seven consecutive days, the abbot rebuked him, saying (in the *Life of Saint Simeon Stylites*, chapter 3): “Where has this man come from, wishing to destroy the rule of the monastery? My son, what do the brothers say about you? Is it not enough for you to fast as we do?” And so forth. 235 See Saint Bernard’s sermon on the death of the monk Humbert, and Peter of Blois, Sermon 50.

[Col. 0402B] Sixth and finally, Peter Damian, using Christ’s example, exhorts us (Opusculum 47) “not to presume to impose upon ourselves some novelty of foreign invention. For even he who is the Master of the angels in heaven observed on earth the custom he found; nor did he disdain to preserve an earthly practice, although he had come to display a heavenly one. For, to pass over innumerable examples, why did he allow his head and feet to be sprinkled with ointment by a woman’s service, unless it was because it was the custom of the Palestinian and Jewish region for its inhabitants to be anointed frequently?”

**“Or let them be encouraged by the examples of their elders.”** By “elders,” Smaragdus understands the Fathers of both the Old and the New Testament, so that a monk “may receive from Christ an example of humility, from Peter of devotion, from John of charity, from Abraham of obedience, from Isaac of patience, from Jacob and Job of endurance,” and so forth. Peter the Deacon adopts the same interpretation. Hildemar, however, understands “elders” as those whose lives Holy Scripture records.

[Col. 0402C] Second, Hildemar says that the examples of the elders are “those of whom he speaks in the final chapter,” namely, the Rule of Basil, the conferences of the Fathers, and the institutes of the monks. In these, there is found somewhat more concerning the external mortification of man than in the Rule of the holy Father Benedict.

Third, some, as the aforementioned Hildemar notes—and he does not depart from their opinion—interpret “elders” as hermits. Following their examples, withdrawing into solitude and exercising themselves there in various works of devotion and different works of penance, after sufficient probation in a cenobium and the abbot’s blessing, is not considered singularity. Only those should be judged singular in this matter who, although they have never properly fulfilled the observances of the monasteries, rashly undertake tasks greater than their strength and proceed to solitary combat even while the abbot resists.

Fourth, Boherius says: “Here, however, I understand ‘elders’ to mean the abbots and other seniors who are living, or even those who sleep in Christ.” It is indeed well established that among the ancients abbots and superiors of monasteries were frequently called “elders.” Richard of Saint Angelo and Turrecremata also appear to follow this interpretation.

Fifth, Menardus understands “elders” to mean the seniors and older monks of the same congregation:

“For, through long use of the regular life, seniors are more firmly established in it; and, as Saint Jerome says, a tired ox plants its foot more firmly. In them there is gravity and maturity of conduct, calmer movements of the soul, and the fire of the flesh and of the other senses almost extinguished—not a premature wisdom, as in the young, but wisdom matured through experience. Moreover, they are more tenacious of the ancient discipline, regular observance, and the things established by the ancient Fathers—which is the highest good in the religious life,” and so forth.

Sixth, those in whom greater examples of virtue shine forth may also be called “elders”: their old age is venerable, not merely prolonged or counted by the number of years; their understanding is gray with wisdom, and their life is unstained. Bernard of Monte Cassino appears to hold this view. After teaching that a monk may abstain from half a pound of bread, dilute wine with much water, pray silently before bed when rising for the nocturnal offices, confess frequently, and pour out prayers to God with tears, he concludes:

“This man does nothing either against the Rule or outside the Rule, and in these things he is greater than the one who does not do them.”

Although he thinks it safer to suggest such practices to a superior, Boherius judges that they cannot be undertaken without presumption unless the superior’s blessing has been granted. In matters, however, that are of lesser importance and are not performed in the sight of the brethren, the superior’s permission is presumed. Finally, Peter Damian, who will soon be cited, and John Caramuel appear to have taken the word “elder” in this sense.

In addition, Hildemar teaches that these later words of Saint Benedict, in which he proposes the examples of the holy Fathers for imitation, are stated in two ways: first, for the sake of humility, as in the final chapter, where he proposes to one striving for perfection [Col. 0403B] the teaching of the holy Catholic Fathers, the Rule of Saint Basil, and the lives and institutes of the Fathers, although nothing at all is lacking in Saint Benedict’s Rule for anyone wishing to live perfectly; second, because although the Rule prescribes the complete inner mortification of man, something more of the external mortification shines forth in the examples of the saints.

These are the principal matters concerning this eighth degree of humility, to which Saint Bernard opposes singularity as the fifth degree of pride. It must certainly be noted here that those who live in cenobia where the stricter observance of the Rule has been relaxed to some extent are not to be blamed under the charge of singularity if, with generous steadfastness, they preserve the statutes of the Rule beyond the common manner of life of the other brothers. Rather, all the others ought rightly to be called singular, since they act outside the common Rule.

Nor should we condemn those who, with the abbot’s blessing, attempt to do something beyond the Rule, since the holy Father Benedict himself advises this, and the examples and sayings of the saints exhort us to it. “But if anyone,” says Saint Basil (*Shorter Rules*, question 138), “thinks that he needs more, whether in fasting, keeping vigils, or in any other matter, let him disclose his reason to those entrusted with the common care of the brothers, and let him observe what they decree.” Peter Damian likewise writes:

“I especially warn you, and under the strictest admonition, not to be offended by the private fasts of any brothers; for I know the faults of some who resemble me. Some are so tormented by the gall of jealousy and envy when others fast that they turn the salvation of those others into their own ruin and, so to speak, fall headlong down the ladder of another’s progress. ‘It is not lawful,’ they say, ‘to do anything except what the common rule of the monastery or the examples of the elders encourage.’ They can easily be answered: if the Rule is so called from ruling, it seems to pertain rather to the strictness of fasting than to the relaxation or dissolution of the belly through gluttony. Therefore, those among them who are known to live under the laws of sobriety and the discipline of the stricter cross of Christ, walking through the narrow gate, ought not unjustly to be judged their elders, and their examples ought to be followed.”

Thus far Peter Damian. Would that it were not sometimes necessary to experience these things in cenobia. For now we have reached the point at which those who strive to rise to greater works of devotion and penance are branded with the mark of singularity; while, on the contrary, those who transgress the Rule and depart from the institutes of the Fathers—although they sometimes wrest dispensations from their superior—are quite certainly singular, yet are tolerated with the utmost patience, excused charitably, or rather without mercy, and sometimes even praised, when it would have been more fitting to cry out against them.

As for those whom God calls to undertake greater things beyond the Rule, Menardus gives them two admonitions: first, that they observe the whole Rule exactly. For that man is not to be tolerated who “keeps vigil in bed and sleeps in the choir; while the others sing the vigils, he sleeps throughout the night; and after the vigils, while the others rest in the cloister, he alone remains in the oratory” (Saint Bernard, *On the Degrees of Humility*, chapter 14); second, that, as far as possible, they perform what is permitted to them secretly, avoiding the eyes of others.

## On the ninth degree of humility

**The ninth degree of humility is if a monk restrains his tongue from speaking.** After the holy Father Benedict restrained the actions of monks in the preceding degree of humility, he consequently restrains their words in the present one. It is certain that silence belongs to the virtue of humility. For since it is characteristic of pride to excuse one’s sins, boast of one’s deeds—whether good or bad—and proclaim the talents granted by God, humility, on the contrary, consists in recognizing one’s own sins, perceiving no good in oneself, always desiring to remain hidden, and restraining the tongue from speaking. Thus Grimlaicus writes (*On the Solitary Rule*, chapter 61):

“Silence is a virtue of humility and an indication of gravity, the nurse of virtues and guardian of souls.” [Col. 0404B]

**And, maintaining silence, let him not speak until questioned.** Saint Basil says similarly (*Sermon on Renunciation of Possessions*):

“When questioned, answer in a fitting and humble voice; when not questioned, be silent. If another person is being questioned, restrain your mouth, lest your tongue, driven by an impudent heart, attack one of those who practices devotion and bind you with the chains of guilt.”

In the monastery called Hermopolis, there was likewise “such silence, together with abstinence, that no one dared to utter a word except in response to a proper question or with a suitable answer,” as Paphnutius testifies in the *Life of Saint Onuphrius*, chapter 3 (Book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*). This law was common among nearly all the ancient monks, as may be seen in the Rule of Saint Ferreolus, chapter 29; 238 in the First Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 12, and in the Second, chapter 5; in the Rule of the Master, chapter 8; in the Rule of Solitaries, chapter 61; in Rufinus, Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 186; and in Book V of the *Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 10, no. 58. [Col. 0404C]

Hildemar, however, opposes to this decree of Saint Benedict two other passages of the Rule: one from chapter 6, where the holy Father permits a monk to request what is necessary from his prior without being questioned; the other from the fifth degree of humility, where we are commanded to reveal to the abbot, through humble confession, perverse thoughts and evil deeds committed in secret, even without being questioned.

The same Hildemar, together with Bernard of Monte Cassino and Boherius, resolves the difficulty by distinguishing four kinds of questioning. There is questioning of the mind, in the reproach of conscience, which belongs to the fifth degree of humility. There is questioning of necessity, which occurs in matters of bodily provision, and belongs to chapter 6. There is questioning of usefulness, which occurs in instruction concerning conduct or conscience. Finally, there is questioning by a superior, either for the obedience of a subject or for an inquiry into some matter. Therefore, when conscience reproves, when some necessity arises, or when a serious matter of usefulness presents itself, the monk is considered to have been questioned and may lawfully speak.

[Col. 0404D] Boherius offers two further solutions to this objection: first, that a monk should not speak in the assembly or in the presence of seniors gathered for spiritual conference. This is especially fitting for young men, and, he says, he saw it observed by many regulars; second, that one who has not been questioned—that is, commanded—should not speak publicly by preaching the word of God. A monk is not permitted to do this, as we learn from the following decree of the Council of Constantinople, reported by Gratian:

“The life of monks has the word of submission and discipleship, not of teaching, presiding, or feeding others.”

And from this canon of Pope Alexander II:

“According to the tenor of the excellent Council of Chalcedon, we command monks, however religious, to remain within the cloister according to the norm of Saint Benedict; we forbid them to travel through villages, castles, and cities, and we have judged that they must abstain entirely from preaching to the people.”

Finally, the Council of Trent says (Session 5, decree on reform, chapter 2):

“Regulars of whatever order may not preach even in the churches of their own orders unless they have been examined and approved by their superiors concerning their life, conduct, and learning. With this permission they must personally present themselves before the bishops and ask their blessing before beginning to preach. In churches that do not belong to their orders, they must obtain, in addition to the permission of their superiors, the permission of the bishop; without it they may in no way preach in those churches that do not belong to their orders.”

To this may be added the authority of Saint Bernard (Sermon 64, on the Song of Songs):

“Public preaching is fitting neither for a monk, nor advantageous for a novice, nor permitted to one who has not been sent.”

Gilbert of Holland likewise says (Sermon 18, on the Song of Songs):

“Let no one assume the office of preaching; let no one take the honor for himself unless he has been called by God.”

The author of the *Sermons to the Brothers in the Desert* argues correctly when he says (Sermon 23):

“Your duty is not only to afflict the flesh with fasts and abstinence from food and drink, insofar as the health of nature permits, but also to despise the world. We must not seek the teacher’s chair, but persevere in the desert wearing sackcloth and ashes.”

See also Peter of Blois, Letter 13. The explanation of this passage of the Rule given here by Peter Boherius is also followed by Julian Warnier in the book he wrote on the ancient and true practice of the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 35.

**“Scripture showing that sin is not avoided in much speaking.”** We have explained this statement above.

**“And because the talkative man.”** According to Saint Augustine (*On Psalm 139*), the talkative man is one who speaks without a just necessity:

“Let there be necessity in your speech, and you will not be a talkative man, lest you fail to prosper,” says the holy doctor.

**“Is not directed.”** That is, he will not prosper.

**“Upon the earth.”** Namely, the earth of the living, for upon the earth of the dying the wicked often prosper.

## On the tenth degree of humility

[Col. 0405C] **The tenth degree of humility is if a monk is not easily and readily inclined to laughter.**

Since levity is clearly a sign of pride, and Saint John Climacus teaches that laughter arises from empty glory (*Ladder*, step 26), the holy Father Benedict rightly places among the degrees of humility the requirement that a monk not be easily and readily inclined to laughter. Hildemar observes that, although “easy” and “ready” have nearly the same meaning, a distinction may nevertheless be made between them: “easy” describes one who is quickly moved, while “ready” describes one who is intent upon or prepared for laughter—that is, one who applies his whole mind to laughter. Such are buffoons, who think of nothing except laughing or provoking laughter.

Nicholas of Fractura further notes that Saint Benedict does not here simply forbid laughter, since man is by nature capable of laughter; rather, he forbids being easily and readily inclined to it. As Saint Ferreolus says (chapter 24 of the Rule), this quality “changes a publican” [Note: Menardus considers *publicanum* incorrect and thinks *planum*, that is, “buffoon,” should be read.] from a monk, and for this reason imposes a three-day fast upon him. [Col. 0405D]

Certainly, what Saint Leander writes in Book I of *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 11, ought to make us fearful:

“What the heart of a virgin is like is generally shown by her laughter. For she would not laugh immodestly if she had a chaste heart; the face of a person is the mirror of the heart. No woman laughs lasciviously unless she is lascivious in heart.”

We have already said much about laughter, which we do not repeat here; and more could be added that we do not believe necessary for men who are penitent and crucified to the world.

**“Because it is written: ‘The fool raises his voice in laughter.’”** Hence Socrates, cited here by Boherius, also used to say: “Do not laugh or become angry excessively, because these are two works of folly.” Saint Ephraem likewise says: “Do not bring forth laughter with loosened lips; for to laugh noisily is madness.”

## On the eleventh degree of humility

240 [Col. 0406A]

**The eleventh degree of humility is if, when a monk speaks—** that is, when he has been questioned, in the manner explained above—

**Gently.** That is, sweetly, says Nicholas of Fractura; or, as Smaragdus says, “temperately or calmly. For gentleness proceeds equally from the fountain of sweetness and peace. Hence Solomon says: ‘A sweet word multiplies friends and appeases enemies.’” For Richard, to speak gently means to speak plainly or briefly, because prolixity produces confusion. For Hildemar, it means speaking in such a way that only the person being addressed can hear.

**Without laughter.** For “if nothing is so fitting to humility as sorrow of spirit, it is certain that nothing is so opposed to it as laughter” (Saint John Climacus, step 7).

**Humbly.** Avoiding grand, inflated, and bombastic words: “For the expansiveness of words is restrained by humility,” as Bernard of Monte Cassino puts it. Boherius has *ampullositas*—“bombast”—in place of this reading.

[Col. 0406B] **With gravity.** Or honestly, “for honesty is contained in gravity,” says the aforementioned Bernard. Or “with gravity,” that is, so that weight may be present in one’s words, according to Ecclesiasticus 28: “Make a balance for your words.”

**Or with few words.** For “the one who uses many words will injure his soul.” Saint Ferreolus gives the same command in chapter 29 of his Rule.

**And let him speak rationally.** For the person who is inconsiderate in speaking will experience evils. One is considered inconsiderate who speaks without necessity or just usefulness.

**And let him not be loud in voice.** According to Saint Ambrose (Book I of *On Duties*, chapter 17):

“Let moderation weigh the very sound of the voice, lest a louder voice offend anyone’s ear.”

Saint Benedict rightly included among the degrees of humility the requirement that a monk not be loud in voice, for the holy Fathers also count shouting among the signs of pride. Thus Cassian describes the proud man (Book XII, chapter 27):

“He is also more fiercely provoked by the goads of anger; then come a lofty voice, harsh speech, a bitter and turbulent reply, and so forth.”

And again (the same book, chapter 29):

“First of all, shouting is present in his speech.”

Saint Gregory likewise says (Book XXXIV of the *Moralia*, chapter 20):

“In all whose thoughts are swollen with pride there is shouting in their speech.”

Saint Basil elegantly explains what shouting is in these words (*Shorter Rules*, question 151):

“The necessity of those listening itself determines the level of the voice. If it is too subdued, so that, as though sluggish, it approaches a whisper, it is to be condemned. If, however, it is louder than necessity requires—louder than one who hears a person speaking softly could hear—then it becomes shouting, which is condemned, except when the slowness of hearing is so great that we are necessarily compelled to use a shout.”

He does not state there what penalties are attached to it. But Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, says (On the Rule, chapter 15):

“If one of this sort, although often chastised, is not corrected, he must be treated with lashes and blows [Col. 0406D] 241 and corrected severely.”

And the *Rule of a Certain Person for Monks* says (chapter 16):

“If anyone, contrary to this discipline, answers with shouting and harsher speech, let him be marked until he is corrected. If this vice cannot be cured, let him be expelled from the fellowship of the brothers.”

**“As it is written.”** Not indeed in Holy Scripture, unless perhaps with respect to the sense; but, as Menardus observes, it is found in the *Sentences of Sixtus*, sentence 134.

**“The wise man is known by few words.”** John Caramuel sometimes explained this, not without wit, in the following way: “The wise man is known from his words alone by few people; but from his deeds he is known by everyone.” This is contrary to the evident meaning of the Rule, which here commands us to speak few words, so that we may be swift to hear and slow to speak. Nature itself, which granted human beings two ears but only one tongue, [Col. 0407A] thereby intended it to be understood that we should hear twice as much as we speak, as Saint Basil observes in *On True Virginity*.

## On the twelfth degree of humility

**The twelfth degree of humility is if a monk not only in heart but also in body always manifests humility to those who see him.**

At the twelfth degree the holy Father finally completes the ladder of humility: he commands that humility be manifested not only in the heart but also in the body. In the heart, indeed, humility is for God; in the body, it is for one’s neighbor, who judges from the outward movement of the body—which he cannot see inwardly—whether a person is humble or proud: humble when he observes all the bodily actions composed with modesty, proud when he sees them disordered. See Julian Pomerius, Book III of *On the Contemplative Life*, chapter 8, and Cassian, Book XII, chapter 27.

Id is, “in work, in the oratory, etc.”] Here he expresses more distinctly what he had prefaced in general terms: that he should always manifest humility in his body to those who see him—namely, in work, whether human or divine; in the oratory, even outside the official course of the divine office; in the monastery, etc., or wherever he may be—in every place, that is; whether sitting, walking, or standing—in every bodily action, that is; always, and not merely sometimes; with his head bowed and his eyes fixed on the ground. For he demonstrates a fixed pride in his mind who disdains to walk with his eyes fixed on the ground.

Bernard of Cassino understands “the ground” here mystically as our body, “in which,” he says, “we ought to attend to the lowliness of the flesh, our frailty, and our inclination to sin. For this is to fix one’s gaze upon the ground: to consider the foregoing with the eyes of faith.” Nicholas of Fractura understands the passage mystically and literally. Mystically, according to him, “we ought to fix our gaze upon the ground because from the ground—that is, from Blessed Mary, the Truth, namely Christ—[he] arose . . .; or we ought always to fasten our eyes upon the ground so that we may consider the matter from which we were taken, [Col. 0407C] and into which we must ultimately be dissolved.” Literally, however, we should do so so that, with head bowed, we may always look upon this ground that we tread with our feet.

This seems to be the genuine meaning of the Holy Rule, so strongly commended by the holy Fathers and so often put into practice by perfect monks: “A monk ought to have his eyes cast down to the earth and his mind raised toward heaven,” says Saint Basil (Sermon on Asceticism). And Saint Dorotheus (Teaching 19): “The monk’s proper and modest bearing, pleasing both to God and to men, is this: first, restrain your eyes, so that they do not wander here and there, but desire to look upon and observe only what is before you.”

The monk Silvanus observed this so religiously (Book V of the Lives of the Fathers, little book 11, no. 28) that, when he was going to water the garden, he covered his head with his cowl, attending only to his feet so that he would not look at the trees. Many examples of this kind occur in the authors. Such is the story of Abbot Isidore, who went to Alexandria to visit Archbishop Theophilus; when he returned and the brothers asked him how the city was, he replied: “I saw no man’s face except that of the archbishop.” Likewise, there is the story of the monk Elladius, who, after spending twenty years in his cell, never lifted his eyes upward to see its roof (Volume I of Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments).

Everyone knows what is related of Saint Bernard in his Life, Book III, chapter 2 (Book V of the Lives of the Fathers, little book 4, no. 16). But what is reported of the virgin Sarah seems utterly astonishing: namely, that she lived for sixty years above a riverbed and never once bent down to look at the river itself (Book V of the Lives of the Fathers, little book 7, no. 19).

“Considering himself guilty at every hour, etc.”] Since it makes no sense for a monk to keep his eyes fixed upon the ground like statues or animals, he now describes with what disposition of mind we ought to observe this precept of the Rule, inserting several reasons by which, like so many goads, we may be stirred to practice it.

He gives the first reason in these words: “Considering himself guilty at every hour because of his sins.” For how, asks Saint Bernard [Col. 0408A] (Sermon 36 on the Song of Songs), “will the soul not truly humble itself when it realizes that it is weighed down by sins, entangled in cares, infected with the filth of carnal desires, bent down, weakened, and so forth? Whence this lifting of the eyes? Whence the raising of the head?” Hence that devout prayer of King Manasseh: “Lord, my iniquities have multiplied, and because of the multitude of my iniquities I am not worthy to look upon the height of heaven.”

The second reason is contained in these words: “Let him already judge himself to be presented before the dread judgment of God.” For who would appear before a strict judge with neck held erect to be judged? Certainly, “If men perceived in their minds what judgment hangs over the world, the human sense would not scatter itself in vanity,” says Saint Jerome.

The third reason is drawn from the example of the Publican, in whom the Pharisee’s humiliation is also included because of his pride. Therefore, if we do not wish to be humbled with the Pharisee, let us say with the Publican, our eyes fixed upon the ground: “Lord, I, a sinner, am not worthy to lift my eyes to heaven.” Hildemarus understands this in two ways: first, to lift one’s eyes into heaven, that is, the ethereal or starry heaven; second, into heaven—that is, toward the saints, who are very often called “heaven,” and toward the contemplation of whom he did not consider himself worthy.

Fourth, Saint Benedict adds to the example of the Publican that of the Royal Prophet, who bears witness concerning himself: “For I was bowed down and humbled exceedingly.” I was bowed down in body and humbled in mind, because the bowing down of the outward person accomplishes nothing unless the inward humbling of the mind accompanies it. Or, as Nicholas of Fractura says: “I was bowed down through the accumulation of sins; I was humbled through the confession of sins.”

Many other reasons could be added to these, by which we might be recalled from careless looking about; on these see Benedict Haeften, Book VI, treatise 7, disputation 4. I note in passing that in the manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon one reads, in chapter 3, where instruction is given concerning a novice: “Wherever he goes, he always walks with head bowed; and if he should at any time be seen with neck held erect, he is not left unmarked.” Uldaric has the same in Book II, chapter 11.

Although, as Saint Bernard says (On the Degrees of Humility, chapter 10): “For two reasons you may raise your eyes without blame: either to ask for help or to give it. David raised his eyes to the mountains in order to ask; the Lord also raised his eyes over the crowds in order to give. The one did so in distress, the other in mercy; both did so without blame. You too, if, considering the place, time, and cause, you raise your eyes because of your own or your brother’s need, I not only do not blame you but praise you greatly: misery excuses the one act, mercy commends the other. Otherwise, I would call you an imitator not of the prophet or of the Lord, but of Dinah or Eve—or even of Satan himself.”

“Therefore, after ascending all these degrees of humility, the monk will immediately arrive at that love of God.”] Thus humility is the way to love: truly the true and only way. Hence Saint Augustine: “Do you plan to construct a great edifice of exaltation? First think about the foundation of humility . . . dig this foundation of humility within yourself, and you will reach the summit of love.” Saint Bernard (Letter 42): “That chastity or love may be given, humility merits it, and so forth.” And one of the ancient Fathers (Rufinus, Book III of the Lives of the Fathers, no. 126): “Humility is the forerunner of love. Just as John was the forerunner of Jesus, drawing all people to him, so humility draws one toward love, that is, toward God himself, because God is love.”

“Which perfect love casts out fear.”] “For love disdains the commerce of fear, unable to be compelled, since it does not know how to be restrained,” says Gilbert of Hoyland (Sermon 19 on the Song of Songs). “Therefore perfect love casts out fear as useless and superfluous; but not that fear which remains forever and ever. For there is a fear which love casts out; there is a fear which truth casts out; and there is a fear which both love and truth admit. The first is cautious; the second is chaste, but does not remain forever and ever; the third is both chaste and enduring. The first fears punishment, the second offense, while the third is an entirely free and secure reverence, and so forth.”

“Through which he will begin to observe without any labor, and as though naturally through habit, all those things which previously he observed not without fear.”] 244 Here he describes the effects of that perfect love which casts out fear: through it, all the things that one formerly observed not without fear of punishment or toil, one now begins to keep without any labor. For “he who loves either does not labor, or loves the labor itself,” says Saint Augustine (On Holy Widowhood). And again: “The labors of lovers are in no way burdensome; rather, they themselves delight, as do the labors of hunters, bird-catchers, and fishermen.”

“Not now through fear of hell.”] This is what love has expelled.

“But through love of Christ, through the good habit itself, and through delight in virtue,”] which love itself admits.

“Which the Lord will deign to reveal in the laborer.”] He sought him out from among the multitude of the people so that, equipped with the instruments of good works, he might practice spiritual art in the monastery’s workshop; cleansed from vices and sins by the fire of love, whose summit he has reached; with the Holy Spirit going before and assisting him, the Lord will deign to reveal him and afterward repay him with eternal glory. May God grant it.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the Divine Offices at Night

[Col. 0409]

During winter, that is, from the Kalends of November [Note: [Col. 0409B] Cass., Flor.: *novembribus*] until Easter [Note: [Col. 0409B] Cass., Flor., Hild., Conch., Comp.: *in Pascha*], one ought to rise at the eighth hour of the night, so that they may rest a little longer after midnight [Note: [Col. 0409B] Comp.: *ut in ea modice*; Al.: *dimidia*] and rise when digestion is complete [Note: [Col. 0410B] Flor., Conch.: *pausentur*]. [Col. 0409B] Whatever remains after the vigils should be devoted to meditation by those brothers who need some work on the Psalter or on the readings. [Col. 0410A] From Easter, however, until the aforementioned Kalends of November [Note: [Col. 0410B] Cass., Flor.: *Novembres*], the hour at which the vigils are to be held should be so arranged that, after a very brief interval has been allowed for the brothers to go out for the necessities of nature, the morning office may immediately follow; it is to be performed at the beginning of daylight.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0409]

“During winter, etc.”] Although it is customary to divide the year into four equal parts or seasons—winter, which according to Saint Isidore begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of December; according to the Greeks and Romans, “whose authority,” says Hildemarus, “he has usually preferred to follow in matters of this kind rather than that of the Spaniards,” [Col. 0409C] on the seventh day before the Ides of November; spring, which according to the aforementioned Isidore begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of March, but according to the Greeks and Romans on the seventh day before the Ides of February; summer, which according to Isidore begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of June, but according to the Greeks and Romans on the seventh day before the Ides of May; and autumn, which according to Isidore begins on the eighth day before the Kalends of September, but according to the Greeks and Romans on the seventh day before the Ides of August—nevertheless, Saint Benedict, the Holy Father, judged that, on the basis of a proper consideration of reason, it was more suitable to divide the year into only two parts when arranging the divine offices: namely, from the Kalends of November until Easter, and from Easter until the aforementioned Kalends.

He calls the first part winter—“during winter”—although it contains something of autumn and spring, either because it contains only parts of the other seasons, whereas winter is contained in it whole and entire, and the whole is named from the greater part; or because it begins at the Kalends of November, the month in which winter begins.

“That is, from the Kalends of November.”] Strictly speaking, the Kalends are the first day of each month. But since the Kalends begin to be counted from the fourteenth or sixteenth day of the preceding month, one might rightly ask in what sense this passage is to be understood as referring to the Kalends of November: whether from 16 October, when the Kalends of November begin to be counted—in the manner in which chapter 48 uses “the Kalends of October” for 14 September—or instead from the first day of November, on which the Kalends themselves fall.

Hildemarus, perhaps having regard to the usage of his own time, thinks that “the Kalends of November” should be understood as the Sunday nearest the first day of November, whether it falls on the first of November, before it, or after it. Thus, if the first of November falls on Monday, Tuesday, or Wednesday, the order instituted by Saint Benedict should begin on the preceding Sunday; but if it falls on Thursday, Friday, or Saturday, it should begin on the following Sunday. An excellent explanation, provided that in the time of Saint Benedict there existed in the Church the same practice of reciting the divine office that has continued from the age of Hildemarus down to our own. But since this is not known to us, and there is no other indication that Saint Benedict meant 16 October here, we think that, taking “the Kalends of November” in its natural and genuine sense, the first day of that month should be understood.

“Until Easter.”] “In ancient times,” says Hildemarus, “the Church celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, no matter on what day it occurred. The holy Fathers prohibited this practice at the Council of Nicaea, establishing that it was necessary not only to determine the paschal moon and month, but also to observe the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, and so forth.”

If this passage is taken strictly, Hildemarus is seriously mistaken in saying that the ancient Church celebrated Easter on the fourteenth day of the moon, no matter on what day it fell. In the very beginnings of the nascent Church, Jews converted to the faith were permitted to follow the ancient custom of celebrating Easter on the fourteenth lunar day of March. But, out of honor for the Lord’s Resurrection, the paschal festival was always celebrated in the Church on the Sunday following the fourteenth lunar day of March.

Certainly, before the Council of Nicaea it had been decreed at the Council of Arles, canon 1, that the feast of the Lord’s Easter should be celebrated throughout the world on the same day, namely Sunday. Long before this, Pope Victor, having summoned a council at Rome, had ordered the same under penalty of excommunication, although the Asians objected, especially Polycrates, bishop of Ephesus. This decree concerning the celebration of Easter on Sunday was renewed at the Council of Antioch in the year 341, canon 1; yet it did not prevent the many disturbances that occurred in Ireland in later centuries for this very reason. On these matters see the preface to the Third Century of the Benedictines, Part I.

“According to a consideration of reason, one ought to rise at the eighth hour of the night.”] The commentators do not agree about what this eighth hour of the night is. Bernard of Cassino, having regard to the practice of his own time, when the natural day was divided into twenty-four hours, explains his meaning as follows:

“This statement of the Father, namely, that one ought to rise according to a consideration of reason, seems to have taken account of the time of the equinox, which is known to occur after the middle of September; and so, after that September equinox, November has fourteen hours of night. Considering, therefore, that November has fourteen hours of night, as I have said, divide the night in half, and seven hours remain in each part of the night. When the eighth hour has begun, it will be a little after midnight when the timekeeper who is responsible for guarding the clock rises at its signal, goes to the oratory, lights the lamps of the church, which may have been darkened because of the length of the night, and rings the bells to awaken the sleeping brothers. Half an hour, or somewhat more, may pass before the brothers rise. According to this interpretation, what he says can be understood: ‘One ought to rise at the eighth hour of the night according to a consideration of reason.’ Therefore he adds, to explain more fully what he had said: ‘so that they may rest a little longer after midnight.’ A little longer means half an hour, or slightly more.”

Thus far Bernard of Cassino. According to his view, the hour at which they should rise would be after our midnight. For he wants the clockkeeper to rise when the eighth hour of the night has begun—or, in November, as soon as the hour after midnight begins—to proceed to the oratory, light lamps that have perhaps gone out or at least become very dim, and finally ring the signal to awaken the sleeping brothers, spending half an hour on this; then the awakened brothers should rise, half an hour after our midnight has elapsed. This is confirmed by his exposition of the words “so that they may rest a little longer after midnight,” where he says: “A little longer means half an hour, or slightly more.”

Guido Juvenalis reaches the same conclusion in his French translation of the Rule of Saint Benedict, placing the eighth hour of the night during winter approximately between midnight and one o’clock.

Nor does John de Turrecremata seem to depart far from this view. He too thinks that the eighth hour of the night should be calculated proportionally to the time of the Kalends of November. At that time, as Bernard of Cassino had just said, the eighth hour of the night begins at our midnight and ends at our first hour. In this alone he differs from Bernard: he does not specify at what point within the eighth hour one ought to rise—at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end. Bernard, however, asserts that they should rise immediately after the middle of the eighth hour.

Neither of these men, however, seems to have grasped Saint Benedict’s meaning. It escaped the Spanish congregation of Valladolid even more completely. According to Antonio Perez, they fixed the eighth hour of the night at midnight because, from the Kalends of November, eight hours intervene between four in the afternoon and midnight. He does not disapprove of the practice of those who rise only two hours later.

All of them were misled by the practice of their own time, which divided the natural day into twenty-four equal hours. The ancients, however—especially the Jews, Romans, and Italians, as the historical and mathematical books testify—divided the artificial day, that is, the entire period extending from sunrise to sunset, and the night, that is, the period extending from sunset to sunrise, into twelve equal hours or portions. These hours were sometimes shorter and sometimes longer according to the shorter or longer duration of the night or day: in summer, when the nights are shorter, the daytime hours are longest and the nighttime hours shortest, and the reverse is true in winter.

They therefore called these hours unequal, not because they were unequal among themselves, but because, in relation to the preceding or following day—or because daytime hours were unequal in relation to nighttime hours, except at the equinox—they differed in length. Paul Lefort, a Cistercian monk, writes that this practice continued in the Church for twelve centuries, in the little book he composed on ancient and modern hours, chapter 2, section 3 (On the First Manner of Cistercian Life, Part III, chapter 1, section 1).

Indeed, Julian of Paris states that the Cistercians used unequal hours until the year 1429, when, in a general chapter, they decreed that in each monastery of the order the sacristan should ring vigils, on weekdays at the second hour after midnight and on solemn feasts and Sundays at the first.

Since this was the case, the eighth hour of the night began earlier or later according to the differing length of the nights. In November, when, according to our present system of hours, the night has fourteen hours, the eighth hour of the night according to the ancient custom began shortly before a quarter past our first hour and ended shortly after a quarter past our following second hour. In December, when the longer nights have sixteen hours, the eighth hour began shortly after a quarter past our first hour and ended shortly before three quarters past our second hour.

Now, since, as Hildemarus says, “it is uncertain whether one ought to rise at the beginning of the eighth hour, in the middle, or near the end of that eighth hour,” some fixed time must be assigned at which they should rise regularly each day—for this, we must suppose, was the intention of Saint Benedict, the Holy Father. It therefore seems necessary to agree with Hildemarus that “the shorter the nights, the nearer the end of the hour the signal should be struck,” 248 and conversely, the longer the nights, the nearer the beginning. Thus, around March, when the eighth hour of the night begins approximately when our first hour has elapsed and ends when our second has elapsed, they should rise at the middle of the eighth hour at the first signal for vigils; the second signal should be struck after a quarter of an hour; and when the entire eighth hour has elapsed, the third and final signal should be struck.

Smaragdus wants half an hour to be understood between the signals. John Bona says of him (On Divine Psalmody, chapter 4, section 3, no. 2) that he had drunk at the very fountain the purest streams of the monastic spirit.

In December, when the nights are longer and the eighth hour begins later, they should rise shortly after it has begun; the first signal for vigils should be struck then, and the last at the middle of the eighth hour—that is, around our second hour, at which nocturns are commonly celebrated in all the monasteries of our order.

I think this is how Saint Benedict’s statement, “according to a consideration of reason,” should be understood: one rises earlier when the hours of the night are longer and later when they are shorter. Thus, when Smaragdus says that one should sleep “through the entire seventh hour of the night and half of the eighth; then, when the signal has been struck, all should rise together, and the remaining half of the eighth hour should be distributed between the signals, so that from this ninth hour of the night the nocturnal praise of the psalm may begin,” it must be understood as referring to the time when the hours of the night are shorter—for example, in March.

When the nights are longer, as in December, they should rise when the eighth hour begins, or at least shortly afterward; once its middle has elapsed, which falls at our second hour, the final signal having been given, the nocturnal praise should begin. This is so if Saint Benedict wished the brothers to rise at the middle of the hour before the final signal for vigils. He orders them to sleep clothed so that they may be ready, and, once the signal has been given, may rise without delay and hasten to anticipate the Work of God [Col. 0412D].

I would not deny this, both because of Smaragdus’s authority and because it may be gathered from the ancient Order of Monastic Conduct, wrongly attributed to Saint Benedict but nevertheless ancient, and because the Rule itself seems to suggest it clearly in chapter 48, where it prescribes several signals for the hours of the divine office.

Indeed, monks ought to rest only “a little longer after midnight.” That “little” would no longer seem little but very great if it extended beyond a full hour and a half, since Bernard of Cassino asserts that half an hour is sufficient. This opinion concerning the hour of rising assigned by Saint Benedict, the Holy Father, seems to us the more certain. Hildemarus confirms it once again when, objecting that in December and January the night has eighteen hours, he replies that the Holy Father had the equinox in view, when the days and nights are equal.

“So that they may rest a little longer after midnight.”] From this passage it is evident that those depart from the hour prescribed by the Rule who rise at midnight, as do the Bursfeldians in Germany and the Vallisole­tans in Spain. For, as Antonio Perez says, “a little” is to be counted as nothing; it is little, and ought to be counted as nothing.

“And let them rise when digestion is complete.”] Some interpret “when digestion is complete” as meaning after the food has been digested, in accordance with Jerome’s statement to Eustochium: “When you rise at night for prayer, let indigestion not produce belching for you, but emptiness.” But since Saint Benedict is speaking here of winter, when the brothers receive only one meal at the ninth hour, this precaution does not seem to have been necessary. Accordingly, “when digestion is complete” seems here to mean that, refreshed by sufficient sleep, they should rise cheerful and alert.

“Whatever remains after the vigils should be devoted to meditation by those brothers who need some work on the Psalter or on the readings.”] This passage is not without difficulty, and therefore it is understood in various ways by different interpreters. Bernard of Cassino explains the words “let it be devoted to meditation” in three ways:

“First, for study and treatment of the Scriptures; second, for silently chanting the psalms to oneself; third, if God grants it, for attentive contemplation of hell, in order to fear it; of glory, in order to desire it; of God, in order to love him; of the saints, in order to imitate them; and of sins, in order to flee them.”

Saint Hildegard seems to have admitted the first and third of these interpretations, writing as follows concerning this passage: “After the night vigils, that is, after the nocturnal psalms have been completed, he designated an interval for meditation on prayers or readings.”

John Craesbeeck explains the passage differently, namely: “If someone, through inadvertence or negligence, has missed something from the psalms or another part of the divine office during the common synaxis, let him make it up privately.” This is certainly a new interpretation, and because of its novelty it deserves to be rejected. He adds, however: “Or if someone wishes to learn a reading that is to be recited publicly, whether to grasp it through thought or memory, or to study Sacred Scripture, or in some other way to exercise his spirit in piety, let him do this by meditating alone, not by discussing it with others, because it is a time of silence.”

Nicholas Bravus, however, interprets “meditation” here not as contemplation of the spirit but “as exercise concerning the psalms and readings and the learning of other such things.” He is evidently attending to the practice and custom of his own congregation, which John Caramuel describes more fully in these words:

“During the time between Lauds and Prime, the seniors are permitted to return to their cells. The novices and younger brothers, however—by ‘younger’ are meant those who have not completed five years of profession—because they are believed to need instruction in the Psalter, assemble in a room prepared near the calefactory, which in Spanish they call La Lamparilla; there they meditate on the psalms and commit them to memory. This gathering of the younger brothers is an act of the community, presided over by the hebdomadary of the principal Mass, without whose permission no one may leave that place. When the preparatory signal before Prime is heard, the novice master arrives, receives their lessons, and sees how much each has committed to memory. Behold, the text of the Rule is literally put into practice.” [Col. 0413D]

Menardus likewise explains “meditation” here as study of the Psalter and readings, “so that the less educated may learn to read and pronounce the readings and the Psalter correctly, and also to interpret them; indeed, so that they may commit the Psalter itself to memory, if they can.” He confirms this from the Life of Saint Goswin, abbot of Aquicinctum, 250 who instituted that after the vigils the boys should learn psalms, readings, and similar things by lamplight, and from the Concord of Dunstan, chapter 2.

It could also be supported from the ancient manuscript Customs of Germany, where no. 30 contains the following: “Whatever remains after the vigils should be devoted to meditation by the brothers who need something from the Psalter and readings, or from chant, as the Rule prescribes, until some sign of daylight appears.” It could likewise be supported from the Statutes of Lanfranc, which decree (chapter 1) that after nocturns “the boys, with lights, should be carefully guarded by the masters in the chapter house, singing whatever will be necessary” [Col. 0414A]; from the Customs of the Monastery of Cluny, in which Udalric, expressing what was done during the interval, says: “The boys sit in the chapter house and learn the chant from a precentor”; and finally from the Life of Saint Gildas, abbot of Rhuys, no. 42 (First Century of the Benedictines, p. 150): “One night, while the boy-monks were sitting at table and practicing the psalms, the adversary appeared.”

Finally, Guido Juvenalis understands Saint Benedict in his French translation to mean that those who need to read, prepare, and investigate something should carry it out; the others should devote themselves to contemplation, or meditation on divine things. Against the testimony of all the manuscripts, however, he corrupts the text of the Rule as follows: “Whatever remains after the vigils should be devoted to meditation by the brothers, except those who need something from the Psalter or from reading.”

To make clear what I myself think amid such a variety of opinions:

First, I think Saint Benedict did not prescribe meditation consisting in contemplation of divine things, which is commonly understood by the term mental prayer. For it does not seem credible that he would have applied the minds of his disciples to this for such a long interval, since he commands prayer to be greatly shortened when performed in common. Nor, if this were his meaning, would he have assigned another time for meditation to those who need the Psalter and reading; yet he does not do so. Finally, in the ancient rules of the monks we do not read that any hour was appointed for mental prayer, since they meditated continually on heavenly things in every place and at every time.

Second, I think the meaning of Saint Benedict, the Holy Father, is not that anyone who through his own negligence has omitted something in the psalms or readings during the common synaxis should repeat the omission after the vigils, although such repetition ought not to be omitted. This interpretation is destroyed by its novelty.

Third, I do not think that the Holy Father commanded those ignorant of chant to learn it at that time, because of the religious observance of nocturnal silence, which it would have been impossible not to violate in that way—unless, with Bernard of Cassino, we understand the passage as referring to silently chanting the psalms to oneself. It is nevertheless certain that this was a common and almost general custom of our order throughout the tenth, eleventh, and twelfth centuries.

Fourth, I say that Saint Benedict touched upon two matters here: readings and psalms. I strongly incline toward the opinion that the Holy Father prescribed that those less educated should privately prepare readings to be sung or recited publicly and should learn the Psalter itself by heart, 251 especially since the art of printing had not yet been invented and manuscript codices, filled with many errors, would lead younger and inexperienced readers into countless mistakes while reading. It was also customary among ancient monks to learn the Psalter by heart.

For among the ancients “to meditate” often means simply to read, as in the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers, chapter 5, or to study. Hence the ancient French manuscript version of the Rule from the monastery of Conches translates this passage of the Rule as follows: “Let the time that remains after the vigil be occupied in reciting the Psalter or in studying.”

[Col. 0414D] Fifth, I think that not only the Psalter but also other books of Scripture are, according to Saint Benedict’s intention, to be committed to memory, especially since he wished some readings to be recited by heart in the Work of God, and since the practice of committing Scripture to memory was common among ancient monks. I add that its hidden and various meanings were also to be investigated, for it is clear that the study of Sacred Scripture was of primary importance among them.

Thus Hildemarus says that when a brother was unwilling to keep vigil and claimed that, with the Lord’s help, he needed nothing, “the abbot ought to propose such a question that the brother cannot solve it, so that he may be humbled”—namely, some extremely difficult passage of Scripture whose meaning that negligent and proud brother does not know.

Sixth and finally, I do not think that Saint Benedict prescribed the study of Scripture and the other things we have mentioned in such a way that someone able to devote himself to prayer would not be permitted to do what God grants him the ability to do. This is especially so since he permits someone who wishes to pray at greater length to remain in the oratory.

Accordingly, the monk Oddo of Autun is said to have practiced this custom (in the Life of Saint Hugh, no. 11, Fifth Century of the Benedictines): “After the morning synaxis had been completed, as Blessed Benedict permits, he remained in the oratory for the sake of private prayer.”

Menardus understands Saint Benedict’s statement about “the brothers who need something from the Psalter or from the readings” to mean that the brothers who do not need the Psalter or the readings have these hours free during the interval. For Saint Benedict did not pursue every moment in minute detail, nor did he prescribe what should be done between Lauds and Prime, or during the time of fasting, what should be done from Vespers until the reading at Collation.

But Hildemarus, as we said above, thinks that, for anyone who believes he needs nothing, the abbot should propose a question from Scripture that he will find difficult to solve. Since, however, we have explained the text of the Rule as referring not only to preparing readings and learning the Psalter by heart, but also to studying and searching out the more difficult passages of Scripture [Col. 0415B], and since there is no one who does not need these things, this passage of the Rule must be said to concern everyone equally.

It could therefore be understood as follows: “Let all the brothers who need the Psalter and reading devote themselves to meditation,” since the words “who need” indicate the reason for this precept.

But did Nicholas of Fractura understand it in this way when, faced with the objection, “If someone does not need to apply himself to psalms or reading, should he then lie down in bed to rest?” he responds: “You should say no, because even if they do not need psalms, readings, or prayers for their instruction, they nevertheless need them for the salvation of their souls; and for this reason Jerome says to the monk Rusticus: ‘Let the Psalter never fall from your hand’”? [252]

Furthermore, I cannot pass over what Ekkehard the Younger writes concerning the devout monks of the monastery of Saint Gall—Notker, Ratpert, and Tutilo (in the Life of Notker, no. 4, Fifth Century of the Benedictines): “It was customary for those three inseparable men, with the permission of the prior, during the interval of the nocturnal Lauds, to meet in the scriptorium and hold conferences on Scripture especially suited to that hour.”

From what has been said thus far it is clear that the perfect disciple of Saint Benedict cannot return to bed after the nocturnal vigils. We see that this was enjoined under strict discipline both upon ancient and upon more recent monks. Thus Saint Chrysostom, describing the life of the monks of his own time, says (Homily 59, to the people of Antioch): “When they have celebrated the morning prayers and hymns, they turn to the reading of Scripture.” Cassian likewise asserts this of the Egyptian monks in Book II, chapter 12. Ruffinus also reports (Book III, *On the Lives of the Fathers*, no. 199) that certain brothers devoted four hours of the night to sleep, four to psalms, and four to manual labor. Saint Caesarius, in his Rule for Virgins, as it appears in Bollandus under January 12, prescribes that “the vigils themselves should be so regulated that those who are well are not overwhelmed by sleep after the vigils”; and Saint Aurelian (Rule, chapter 28) says: “After the morning prayers, it is not permitted to return to sleep.” In the ancient *Order of Monastic Conduct* we likewise read (chapter 2):

> “After the completion of the nocturnal praise, let the deepest silence be maintained in that interval, both in voice and in walking, and in the sound of any object, so that each person may be permitted, without disturbing another, to confess his sins to the Lord and, weeping, to ask God for pardon and remission of them.”

And in the *Customs of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane* (*Annals*, vol. IV):

> “After the morning hours, no one is to return to his bed, except when the full office is being celebrated, or when someone happened to rise before the appointed hour; excepted are the sick and those unable to continue because of weariness, whose weakness the prior must take into account.”

Crodegang, bishop of Metz (*Speculum*, vol. I), likewise forbids anyone in the Rule of the Canons, chapter 15, under penalty of excommunication, to sleep after the nocturnal vigils, unless perhaps he is ill, and even then only with permission. Saint Romuald so detested sleep after the nocturnal vigils that, according to Peter Damian (in the *Life of Saint Romuald*),

> “if anyone confessed to him that after the vigil of the twelve psalms, especially near dawn, he had fallen asleep, he could by no means celebrate the solemnity of Mass that day with Romuald’s permission.”

The same Peter Damian had prescribed this law for his own community (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 17):

> “Let it be entirely forbidden for us then to return to bed after the nocturnal office. Therefore, so that this regular observance might be kept more easily, we established that each day the signal should first sound for the vigils; then, after the Psalter had been completed according to custom, or as much of it as the consideration of the time permits, when the signal sounds again, the nocturnal office should be performed, so that near dawn—at precisely the hour when sloth presses most heavily—it may find us standing and occupied with canonical offices.”

The Statutes of Lanfranc (chapter 1, § 1) decree that after the nocturnal vigils the brothers should sit in the choir, while the boys should learn the chant in the chapterhouse with their teachers. Meanwhile the prior, with a lamp lit, should see whether all are sitting in an orderly fashion; and, inspecting all the parts of the monastery, if he finds anyone sleeping, he is to awaken him by a signal and order him to return to the choir. [Column 0416B]

Nearly the same discipline prevailed among the Cluniacs. Their ancient Customs, preserved by Udalricus, prescribe (Book I, chapter 41) that on ordinary days, if there are no octaves, once they have risen they are not to return to bed. When the question was then asked how long this interval lasted, the answer was that it was regulated so that during it the cloister prior could go through all the workshops of the monastery. Then the brothers, leaving the church of the Blessed Mary together, were to return to the choir after attending, if necessary, to the bodily requirements of nature. There they were to sit with their heads covered, and in that place they might do whatever they wished or were able to do; for no particular task was prescribed for the brothers at that time. If they wished, however, they could rise, go around the altars, and pray there privately.

Here Haeften is rightly corrected. Because Peter the Venerable complains that deep into the night the hymns of praise were still being sung—“The dawn of light gleams,” “Now dawn scatters the sky,” and similar pieces—Haeften thinks that the Cluniacs had already ceased to observe that interval. Peter the Venerable does not complain that no interval was observed, but that it was not prolonged as far as dawn. Udalricus says that at one time a monk would pray with greater concentration, at another would ruminate on psalms, and at another, overcome by sleep, would doze whether he wished to or not. He adds that not many at Cluny were unlike this.

These accounts recall the means by which Saint John of Gorze drove away sleep during this interval (in his *Life*, no. 80, *Benedictine Century* V), namely:

> “By continually turning over the psalms in a quiet murmur, like a bee, now going around the altars, now sitting for a little while and soon rising again and standing for some time; then going out of his cell to observe the time of night; afterward attending to the lamps, either trimming or repairing them; then also revisiting the schools of the singers; and sometimes spending what remained of the night weaving nets.”

The Cistercians likewise clearly did not return to bed after the nocturnal vigils, as appears from the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 74, which establishes:

> “After the vigils, or after the office for the dead, if it is to be said, once the church servant has lit a lamp before the bookcase and in the chapterhouse, let the brothers sit in the chapterhouse itself, and let those who wish read. Let them not sit in corners except while reading. Let them wear their hoods on their heads in such a way that it can be recognized whether they are sleeping or not.”

This was the practice in winter. In summer they withdrew into the cloister, as appears from chapter 84. Thus Saint Bernard, describing an exceptional monk (*On the Degrees of Humility*), says that while the others are resting in the cloister, he alone remains in the oratory. What he calls “resting,” however, is to be understood not as bodily repose but as spiritual quiet, as is clear from Aelred the abbot’s sermon on the two disciples going to Emmaus and from Gilbert of Hoyland, Sermon 23 on the *Song of Songs*.

Finally, among the first disciples of Blessed Stephen, abbot of Obazine (vol. IV of the *Miscellany* of Baluze), “the interval that remained after the vigils was not assigned to rest or sleep, but was devoted to private prayers or manual works,” as we read in his *Life*, no. 7. [Column 0417A]

This institution of the ancient monks, as we have seen, is commended by John Cassian for two reasons: first, lest the envious enemy contaminate through the illusion of sleep the purification acquired through nocturnal prayers; second, lest that sleep produce sluggishness in the monk, blunt his vigor throughout the day, drain the richness of his heart, and render him weak against the enemy’s snares.

Add what Smaragdus says:

> “It is written: ‘On my bed I sought him whom my soul loves; I sought him, but I did not find him.’ For Christ the beloved is not found in the bed of carnal pleasures, but in holy labors, sacred vigils, and frequent prayers; he is not found in the torpor of sleep, but in the prayer of watchfulness and in the compunction of prayer.”

And there is also the saying of Peter Damian (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 17):

> “Far be it from us at that hour to yield to sleep or idleness, at which, as is certain, our Redeemer rose after destroying the power of death. If we sleep at the time when, as the physical sun rises, our inner person ought also to await the unfailing light, may it never be that the saying applies mockingly to us: ‘His disciples came by night and stole him while we were sleeping.’”

Nevertheless, among the ancient monks there were some, though few, who permitted sleep after the nocturnal office: for example, Saint Isidore in chapter 6 of his Rule, and likewise the Master in chapter 44 of his Rule. We infer that this had become customary near the end of the sixth century in the monastery of Saint John at Réomé from the *Book on the Translation and Miracles of Saint John*, no. 1. Walafrid also states in the *Life of Saint Gall*, chapter 26 (*Benedictine Century* II), that the disciples of Abbot Saint Gall returned to bed after the labor of the morning office in order to rest.
