Similarly, when Abbot Saint Geremar of Flaviacum had completed the office, he was accustomed to return to the dormitory and place himself in his bed, as his acts state, no. 14. We learn that the same practice prevailed in the monastery of Longoretum from the *Vision of Barontus*, no. 7, *Benedictine Century* II; in the monastery of nuns at Pauillac from the *Life of Saint Austroberta*, no. 15, *Benedictine Century* III, part I; at Lindisfarne from the poem of the monk Æthelwulf, chapters 10, 21, and 22; in the monastery of Saint Corbinian from his *Life* by Aribo, no. 3; and finally at the monastery of the Blessed Virgin Mary at Soissons, where, while some women persisted in vigils and prayers in the church, others were permitted to sleep after the nocturnal office, according to the *Life of Saint Drausius*, bishop, no. 17, in Bollandus under March 5.

But these were merely concessions and were contrary to the Rule of Saint Benedict, which grants no sleep after the vigils.

There may be some difficulty concerning the time inserted between Lauds and Prime, since the Holy Father prescribed no activity for that period. The same question arises concerning Sundays, on which he ordered the monks to rise earlier for the vigils and immediately joined Lauds to the vigils: whether, at least on ordinary days, during that brief interval between Lauds and Prime, and on Sundays after the nocturnal office, we may return to bed according to the mind of Saint Benedict. [Column 0417D]

But since the reasons and causes for which our Fathers forbade sleep after the vigils clearly apply equally to anyone who might fall asleep after Lauds, it must be asserted that sleep was forbidden at both times. Indeed, since morning Lauds ought to be celebrated only at dawn and can be completed in no more than half an hour, so little time intervenes between the end of Lauds and Prime—which begins after the sun has risen—that one can scarcely find an opportunity to sleep.

Therefore Abbot Saint Benedict of Aniane says (in his *Life*, no. 52):

> “In summer, after the morning office had been completed, he immediately ordered them to leave the church because of sleepiness, put on their shoes, wash their faces, and hasten back to the church; and, according to the order mentioned above”—the order he had instituted before the vigils in chapter 31—“let them reverently go around the altars, sprinkle themselves with holy water, and then proceed to the appointed places to complete the day’s office properly.”

The chapters of the monks of Saint Gall, issued in the year 817, likewise prescribe (chapter 31):

> “Let the interval after Matins and before Prime, in winter or summer, be extended for the length of time necessary for the brothers to prepare themselves suitably and properly go around the altars in prayer, so that, in full daylight or after sunrise, when they leave Prime, they may either devote themselves to reading or undertake the obedience assigned to them.”

In the ancient *Order of Monastic Conduct* it is stated that “from this morning praise the deepest and chiefest silence should be maintained in praying and reading.”

Dunstan’s Concordia, chapter 2, joins Prime to Lauds from the Kalends of October until Easter, with no vacant interval, Lauds being completed at the dawn of light. Chapter 5 decrees that from Easter throughout the summer, after Matins have been completed,

> “the brothers leaving the church should put on their shoes, wash, and, after the three prayers have been completed in the church, sit in the cloister and devote themselves to reading until the signal for Prime is heard,”

although it permits them, if day has not yet dawned, to return to bed with the prior’s permission.

The Statutes of Lanfranc likewise join Prime to Lauds and the commemorations of the saints from the Kalends of November until Easter, so that everything is completed as the day grows light. If any part of the night remains, no one except those who have been bled is to return to bed; instead, they are to conduct themselves as during the first interval between the vigils and Lauds.

The same discipline probably prevailed among the Cluniacs. Their ancient Customs, concerning winter, are given by Udalricus as follows (Book I, chapter 41):

> “On ordinary days, and when there are no octaves, once we have risen we do not return to bed.”

Finally, the *Book of Cistercian Usages* decrees (chapter 74) that in winter,

> “if by chance after Matins it is not yet daylight, the brothers should light a lamp and let there be an interval; the brothers who wish may sit in the cloister, but they are not to read.”

In summer, however (chapter 84):

> “After Matins they shall say Lauds for the dead. When these have been said, and an interval has been made as on feast days, they shall put on their daytime shoes and take their knives, as they customarily do whenever they put on their daytime shoes. Then, sprinkled with water and having said a prayer, they shall say Prime according to the time.”

On the other hand, the Rule of Blessed Aelred for Virgins prescribes that from the Kalends of November until the beginning of Lent, Lauds should be performed as dawn grows bright, followed immediately by the hymns of Prime (chapters 14 and 15). From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends, however, after Matins have been completed and until full sunrise, they are to devote themselves to prayers and psalms, and only then is Prime to be said.

I will not deny, however, that some had a different custom and practice. Among others, the Master ordered that in summer Lauds should be joined to the vigils, so that after they had been celebrated those who wished might rest until Prime. The Statutes of Lanfranc decree for the period from the Kalends of October until the Kalends of November (chapter 1, § 1):

> “On ordinary days, after Matins they shall return to their beds.”

It is also clear that this was customary throughout the summer from the concession that “on the days of Rogations, after Matins for the dead have been said, the brothers may return to bed, and those who wish may sleep longer than usual.” Thus they did customarily sleep in summer, since we have seen above that this was forbidden in winter.

We find the same practice in Udalricus’s ancient Cluniac Customs (Book I, chapter 22), in which the same provision is made for the Rogation days, and additionally that sleep be permitted during the octaves of Saint Martin, the Nativity of the Lord, and the Epiphany. Saint Bernard perhaps had this in mind when he reproached his nephew Robert, who had transferred to the Cluniacs, saying (*Letter 1*):

> “Now, having thrown down your arms, you safely take your morning sleep, at the very hour when Christ rose.”

Yet, apart from the fact that this was a special arrangement for those congregations, and only for summer and, for the most part, at discretion, it is evident that the common rule was dispensed with in this matter. They nevertheless compensated for that dispensation by the great number of psalms that they added to the office prescribed by Saint Benedict.

[Column 0419A]

The difficulty seems greater concerning Sundays. Why rise earlier and carry the morning Lauds forward together with the vigils in one continuous course, unless some rest is afterward granted to bodies wearied by the labor? Moreover, according to Cassian, the ancient monks, whom Saint Benedict imitated in many matters, slept for approximately two hours after the nocturnal vigils on Saturday. And in the Rule of Paul and Stephen (Book I, chapter 8) we read:

> “After Prime has been said in the morning, no one is to lie down in bed, except on Sunday or feast days, when those of you who wish, being more fatigued than usual by the labor of the vigils and of the preceding day, may lay your limbs down in your little beds for a short while after Prime. This is not permitted at all times, but only during the summer months.”

Saint Hildegard’s testimony also supports this view. In commenting on the words of the Rule, “After the blessing has been given, let them begin Matins,” she says:

> “Here he does not indicate an interval for meditation, prayer, or reading; nor on these days does he prohibit the brothers, once Matins have been completed, from returning to their beds to rest. Rather, if the time permits it, since they have risen earlier and have been wearied by the length of the nocturnal and divine service, he leaves it to their discretion to return silently to their beds.”

Nevertheless, since the same reasons we have brought forward above apply equally to all days, it must be asserted, according to the mind of Saint Benedict, that Sundays too are included under the same law and that sleep after the vigils is not to be permitted on them.

Hence canon 5 of the Council of Aachen states:

> “At no time whatsoever are they to return to their beds for the sake of sleeping after the vigils, unless it happens that they have risen before the appointed hour.”

Browerus also relates (*Antiquities of Fulda*, Book II, chapter 16) that Emperor Louis the Pious obtained from Pope Gregory that monks in cities, and those residing in the matricular churches, who throughout the whole year performed the divine service with great labor and devotion, might refresh their bodies with sleep after the vigils of summer nights and on feasts having twelve lessons. If this had been permitted by the Rule, there would have been no need to seek a dispensation from the supreme pontiff.

Therefore, when Saint Benedict joins Matins to the nocturnal vigils on Sundays without any interval, this should not be understood as though he wished Lauds to be hurried and their customary hour altered. Rather, he should be understood to have prolonged the nocturnal office until dawn. For Matins, which we call Lauds, are always to be said at dawn, or, in the words of the Holy Father Saint Benedict, “when the light is beginning.” Thus they are called *matutini* from *matuta*, that is, dawn, because they ought to be celebrated at dawn.

For this reason Hildemar, commenting on the text of the Rule that they are to be performed “when the light is beginning,” writes:

> “In this passage Blessed Benedict makes clear, when he says ‘Matins, which are to be performed when the light is beginning,’ that Matins are to be performed when the light is beginning at all times—that is, on weekdays as well as on Sundays and feast days.”

Bernard of Cassino teaches the same in his commentary on chapter 11, as does Nicholas of Fractura in his commentary on the same chapter. Their opinion is confirmed by the practice found in the anonymous writer of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, who described during the reign of Charlemagne the translation of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris. In section 7 he reports (*Benedictine Century* III, part II) that a certain man who had fallen ill was cured “when morning had come, while the clerics”—that is, the monks—“were completing the office of Matins according to the custom of Sunday.”

The same is found in Aimonius, *Miracles of Saint Germanus*, Book II, chapter 10, where the Normans are said to have arrived while the brothers were celebrating “the office of the holy Paschal feast at Matins, after dawn had already risen.”

Hildegarius, in the *Life of Saint Faro*, chapter 113 (*Benedictine Century* II), writes:

> “One night, when the new dawn was already brightening with its clear twilight, and the singing monks were making the church resound with the verse, ‘May God have mercy on us and bless us,’ etc.”

That verse is said at Matins. This passage, however, does not establish the point entirely for Sunday. A clearer one is taken from Book I of the *Deeds of the Saints of Redon*, chapter 6 (*Benedictine Century* IV, part II):

> “When the dawn of day grew bright, and the monks were singing Matins and praising the Lord with one voice, they came to the psalm called ‘O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the light,’ etc.”

That psalm is sung only at the Lauds of Sunday or on feasts with twelve lessons.

Nothing more decisive can be offered on this matter than the passage from the *Life of Saint Ado*, formerly abbot and later bishop of Vienne, which our Mabillon published from an ancient Viennese breviary. In section 8 we read (*Benedictine Century* IV, part II):

> “He compelled the brothers to rise early for the nocturnal vigils. He himself was present according to custom and caused the lessons and responsories to be sung by prolonging them until, as the light of day approached, Lauds could be performed.”

In the same way, Venerable Benedict, abbot of the monastery of Clusium, as his disciple William writes in his *Life*, chapter 5,

> “observed the lessons by bringing them to an end and prolonged the processions, so that the divine work might continue until day, lest the envious enemy’s fraud steal anything from those returning to bed after Matins that might consume the sweet-smelling flowers of chastity and, by defiling their solemn joy, drive them away from holy communion.”

To all this must be added the excellent testimony of John the monk in Book I, no. 10 of the *Life of Saint Odo*:

> “For, behold, no more than six years have passed since, before the body of Saint Martin, a different order of the church was celebrating the vigils. It happened that he himself was present there. But because the antiphons of that office, as everyone knows, are short, while the nights at that time are longer, those who wished to prolong the office until daylight sang each antiphon by repeating it after each verse of the psalms,” etc.

All these testimonies confirm the ancient manuscript Customs of Germany, in which section 24 decrees that on Maundy Thursday “the nocturns should be so regulated that they are completed in darkness.” From this one may infer that at other times they were not completed in darkness but prolonged until daylight; otherwise it would be pointless to say that the nocturns were to be completed in darkness.

The *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 68, also states:

> “When the sacristan sees that he has risen earlier than he should, he customarily warns the cantor by a signal to prolong the twelfth lesson. Then the person who reads it is not to finish it until the sacristan gives the signal or the clock sounds.”

I do not see why the twelfth lesson would be prolonged unless the customary hour of Matins had not yet arrived.

Nor does it matter that Saint Benedict orders them to rise earlier for the vigils on Sundays and feast days, while the nights of winter are extremely long. First, according to Hildemar, the instruction to rise earlier concerns only the summer nights. In winter, he asserts, they should not rise earlier than usual:

> “It must be considered,” he says (in his commentary on chapter 11), “in winter, that they rise according to the number of the brothers and the length of the lessons, so that Matins may be performed when the light is beginning.”

Bernard of Cassino likewise writes (on chapter 11):

> “What he says about rising earlier on Sundays properly concerns the summer season. If they rose as late then as when the nights are long, there would be great negligence, and Lauds would not begin when the light was beginning, because dawn would appear during the lessons of the second watch. In winter, however, it is sufficient to rise at the eighth hour, because then the twelve lessons, with the twelve responsories, the psalmody of twelve psalms, the three canticles, the hymn ‘Te Deum laudamus,’ and the Gospel read with its proper modulation, will allow Lauds to begin when the light is beginning.”

Moreover, even if they rose half an hour earlier than usual, since on solemn days the divine office was celebrated with greater solemnity and modulation, they could easily fill the entire interval, even though it was long in winter. This is especially clear if we consider how lengthy the lessons were among our predecessors.

For example, Saint Caesarius, in his Rule for Monks, chapter 20, prescribes that three folios be read for each lesson. Similarly, Saint Aurelian, in the order of psalmody, says:

> “Let one brother read three or four pages, according to the size of the book. If it is written in small letters or in a larger format, let him read three pages; if it is smaller, four.”

Therefore, lest sleep creep in during such lengthy readings, he prescribes in the Rule, chapter 29, that some work with esparto grass or hemp, or some similar manual labor, be performed, and that on Sundays and feast days they stand. The Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins, chapter 13, and the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 6, prescribe the same. It is therefore clear that their lessons were not especially short; otherwise it would have been pointless to take up work at that time only to abandon it continually.

To say something also about our own communities: among the Cluniacs the readings at the vigils in winter were so long that during one week of Septuagesima they went through the entire book of Genesis in choir and, according to Udalricus, the whole prophecy of Isaiah within six ordinary vigils. The same author tells us that the brother who ended the readings was rebuked in chapter because he had had only one reading from the Epistle to the Romans made over two ordinary vigils, and had thus made the readings too short.

But what John of Metz writes about Saint John of Gorze would exceed all belief unless it were reported by an eyewitness and a trustworthy witness: namely, that “during one lesson, when the third reader had risen, he once completed the whole of Daniel.” Boherius also seems to support all these observations in his first commentary on chapter 11, writing:

> “During the longer nights, longer lessons are customarily read, and the psalms and responsories are sung more slowly.”

Menardus further teaches that Saint Benedict inserted prayers between individual psalms, following the custom of the Egyptian monks. Saint Isidore also prescribes this in Rule 7, Saint Fructuosus in chapter 3, and the Master in chapter 33.

Add to this that the Holy Father prescribes that the psalms be sung with antiphons. Someone could interpret this, not without foundation, as referring to antiphons inserted after each individual verse of the psalms, as we saw above in the church of Tours.

Since these things are so, everyone can now see how they could prolong the vigils until dawn even during the longer night. Otherwise, if they had performed Lauds together with the middle nocturns while it was still dark, they would have praised God not seven times, following the example of the prophet, but six times, as Hildemar again notes in his commentary on chapter 11.

Nor does Saint Hildegard say absolutely that Saint Benedict granted sleep after Matins on Sundays. She says only, “if the time permits it, since they have risen earlier.” In that case, as Hildemar says, “if it is not yet day, the prior ought to give the signal so that they may sleep.” At that point, I think, Lauds were separated from the nocturnal office, since according to the Rule they are to be said only when the light is beginning.

From all that has been said it is evident that on Sundays the longer vigils, with the nocturnal synaxis prolonged until daylight, do not allow sleep in the morning. This is what Stephen of Tournai wrote to the novice of Pontigny who was considering abandoning the Cistercian institution.

No one should find these vigils harsh or excessively austere if he considers the ancient fervor of the old monks. Cassian teaches that they spent almost the whole nights of Saturday and Sunday without sleep, except perhaps for the final two hours, during which they refreshed their bodies with whatever rest they could obtain. Saint Arsenius, however, did not think even those hours should be granted to a monk (vol. I of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*), saying that one hour of sleep was sufficient for him, provided that he deserved the name of “fighter.”

We once observed some trace of this practice in the Cluniac monastery, where on the feast of Saints Peter and Paul the nocturnal vigils began on the preceding day while it was still fully light and were not completed until the following day, after the sun had already risen (Udalricus, Book I, chapter 41). [Column 0422A]

From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends of November, the hour for celebrating the vigils should be regulated as follows: after preserving the shortest possible interval for the brothers to go out for the necessary functions of nature, Matins, which are to be performed when the light is beginning, should immediately follow.

In winter Saint Benedict assigns the eighth hour of the night for rising. As for summer, he fixes no specific time; rather, he commands that the hour be regulated so that, after the shortest possible interval has been observed, Matins immediately begin. Since the summer vigils are shorter and only a brief interval is prescribed, they generally fell at approximately the same hour throughout the year.

Saint Benedict does not say how long that interval ought to be; he requires only that it be very short. The sixth chapter of the statutes of the monks of Saint Gall decrees that “the interval after the nocturnal office in summer should be prolonged for as long as five psalms can be said.” In the manuscript Customs of Germany, section 28, we read:

> “From the octaves of Easter until the Kalends of November, let Matins for the dead be completed with the shortest possible interval between the nocturnal office and regular Matins, unless daylight should come first; in that case they are to be postponed until the office for all the saints has been completed.”

According to the Rule, it should be sufficient for the brothers to be able to go out for the necessary functions of nature—that is, to empty their bowels. Here Boherius, in his first commentary, says:

> “Note that those entering the necessary-house should hide their faces with their hoods as much as they can; nor is it proper to enter the dormitory without having one’s hood on one’s head, as our Fathers asserted and as the order of the Premonstratensians observes.”

Finally, the reason why Matins are to be performed when the light is beginning is taught by a manuscript Rule of uncertain authorship, which our Mabillon extracted from a codex of the Queen of Sweden’s library. In chapter 3 it reads:

> “The solemnity of Matins is to be celebrated when the light is beginning, because, when the morning light was shining, our Lord and Savior rose from the underworld.”

## CHAPTER IX. How Many Psalms Are to Be Said at the Night Hours

[Column 0421]

[Column 0421D]

In winter, after the opening verse has first been said, “O God, attend to my help; O Lord, hasten to help me” (Psalm 69). [Note: [Column 0421D] Oxford and Florence: “In winter, after the verse written above.”] [Note: [Column 0421D] Oxford: “First let the verse be said; secondly, let it be said,” with the words of Psalm 69 omitted. Florence: “First the verse,” that is, “O God, attend to my help,” etc., with the *Gloria*. In many manuscripts *Domine, ad adjuvandum me festina* (“O Lord, hasten to help me”) is absent.]

Secondly, it is to be said three times: “O Lord, you will open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise” (Psalm 50). [Note: [Column 0422D] Another manuscript: “third”; another: “for the third time.”] The third psalm is then to be added, followed by the *Gloria*. After this, Psalm 94, with its antiphon, is to be said. [Note: [Column 0422D] Oxford, with seven manuscripts, adds *venite exsultemus* (“come, let us rejoice”).] Or at least it is to be sung. [Note: [Column 0422D] Cassian: “by singing”; Haeften: “it is to be sung indirectly.”]

Next follows the Ambrosian hymn. [Note: [Column 0422D] Sabinus and Dionysius: “the Ambrosian hymn.”] Then six psalms with antiphons. After these have been said, the verse having been recited, let the abbot give the blessing. While everyone is seated on benches, let three lessons be read in turn by the brothers from a book placed on the lectern, and between them three responsories are sung. [Column 0423A] [Note: [Column 0423A] Other manuscripts: “are to be sung”; absent in Oxford.] Let two responsories be said without the *Gloria*. [Note: [Column 0423A] The words “Let two responsories be said without the *Gloria*” are absent from many manuscripts.] After the third lesson, the cantor is to say the *Gloria*. [Note: [Column 0423A] Another manuscript: “the glory.”] As soon as the cantor begins to say it, let everyone rise from his seat at once in honor and reverence of the Holy Trinity.

Books are to be read at the vigils, both of the Old Testament and of the New, from the divine authority; also explanations of them made by the most renowned orthodox and Catholic teachers and Fathers. [Column 0424A] [Note: [Column 0423A] Oxford: “by named doctors, and orthodox and Catholic Fathers.” Florence: “by named and orthodox and Catholic Fathers.” Cassian: “by the most renowned, orthodox, and Catholic Fathers.” The same reading occurs in the Saint-Germain manuscript, Ebrul, Faron, and the Victor manuscript, but with *Patribus* (“Fathers”) omitted. Compendium: “by the most renowned orthodox teachers.”]

After these three lessons with their responsories, let the remaining six psalms be sung with *Alleluia*. [Note: [Column 0424A] Ebrul: “with white garments.”] Then let a reading from the Apostle follow, to be recited from memory, together with a verse and the supplication of the litany—that is, “Kyrie eleison” (“Lord, have mercy”). [Note: [Column 0424A] The Victor manuscript: “and the litany.”] Thus let the nocturnal vigils be concluded.

## Commentary

[Column 0423]

[Column 0423B]

“In winter, after the opening verse, ‘O God, attend to my help,’ etc.” This is that verse so celebrated by the ancient monks, which they used in every undertaking they began. Cassian describes its force and efficacy in Conference 10, chapter 10.

Saint Benedict the Holy Father was the first to establish that this verse should precede all the offices of the divine course. Saint Gregory the Great later confirmed the custom by papal authority and caused it to be received by the universal Church, as Pamelius teaches in annotation 15 on Cyprian’s *Book on the Lord’s Prayer*, and Polydore Vergil in Book VI, chapter 2 of *On the Invention of Things*. Navarra, however, makes Damasus the author of this custom, at the urging of Saint Jerome (*On Prayer*, chapter 3, no. 64). But the letter of Saint Jerome from which he derives this claim, found in volume I of the Councils, is rightly rejected as fictitious and adulterated.

Saint Benedict rightly wished this verse, which we customarily use to implore divine help, to precede the nocturnal vigils, because it is especially at this time that, agitated by various assaults of evil demons, we need it most.

> “For when the signal of the spiritual trumpet sounds, calling us to prayer, the enemies assemble invisibly. Some of them, when we have awakened, urge us to lie down again: ‘Wait,’ they say, ‘until the principal hymns have been completed; then you may depart.’ Others, when we have begun to attend prayer, plunge us into sleep. Others persuade us to converse in the church. Others, contrary to custom, stimulate the belly excessively. Others drag our minds into shameful thoughts. Others advise us, as though we were weak, to lean against the wall; sometimes they even make us yawn excessively. Some provoke laughter in us, so that through it God may be stirred to anger against us. Others, through utter laziness, drive us to hurry in pronouncing the verses. Others encourage us, for the sake of pleasure, to prolong the psalmody. Sometimes they even sit upon our mouth and close it so tightly that it seems scarcely able to be opened” (Saint John Climacus, *Ladder*, step 18).

In the second place, it must be said three times: “O Lord, open my lips,” etc. Because, as St. Augustine says (*Book II against Two Letters of the Pelagians*, chapter 8), no one can praise God unless God opens his lips. But since prayer belongs more to the heart than to the lips, why do we ask that the lips, and not the heart, be opened? John Bona answers (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 4) that the use of the lips is not only for speech but also for kissing. Hence, “when the Church says, ‘O Lord, open my lips,’ she seems not so much to be asking divine assistance to proclaim his praises worthily as to be asking for a mystical purification of the lips, so that they may receive the most chaste kiss of the beloved.”

St. Benedict ordained that this verse be repeated three times, either because of the greater majesty and solemnity of the night office [Col. 0424B], or in memory of that threefold prayer which Christ prayed in the garden for the third time; or to awaken an affection of piety and intensity and perseverance in prayer; or in honor of the Holy Trinity and in imitation of that heavenly *trisagion* by which the heavenly beings adore the triune and one God. Haeften treats all these points at length in book VII, treatise 6, discussion 2. It may also have been because of the necessity of divine assistance for singing God’s praises properly; or finally to demonstrate how strictly we ought to close our lips in silence, since they must not be opened except after the thrice-repeated invocation of the divine majesty, and then only for praising God.

Moreover, when pronouncing this verse, we form the sign of the cross with a finger over the mouth, so that it may be opened with the same key by which it had previously been locked. Beletus relates (*Explanation of the Divine Office*, chapter 24) that in the earliest times of the Church priests fortified themselves with the sign of the cross, restraining their voices until matins, when they burst forth in praise of God. Hence Honorius of Autun [Col. 0424C] (*Gem of the Soul*, book II, chapter 1) says: “Signals are given to soldiers by trumpets; signals are given to Christians by bells. Like soldiers assembling, they greet their emperor when, through the verse ‘O Lord, open my lips,’ they begin the praises of Christ. For when they go to sleep at night, they fortify themselves with the sign of the cross as with a seal; and now they open what they had closed during the night, releasing their mouths for the praise of God.”

To this the third psalm and the *Gloria* are to be joined. St. Benedict also wished this psalm to precede the nocturnal office, either because it speaks of rising from sleep, as Hildemar and Durandus say; or because, since it concerns the Lord’s resurrection, the monk, hearing it, keeps himself wakeful and devout for the vigils, as Bernard of Cassino and Turrecremata teach; or because through it “divine assistance is invoked against the opposing demons, namely the world and the flesh,” as the same Bernard adds. He also wished it to precede the office so that it might give the more negligent time to arrive for the invitatory, just as he placed Psalm 66 [Col. 0424D] before lauds so that everyone might arrive for the fiftieth psalm.

And the *Gloria*. This is rightly joined to the third psalm, in which Christ’s resurrection is treated, because in it the glory of God is especially proclaimed, says Bernard of Cassino. Concerning this hymn of glorification, three matters must be observed: first, by whom it was composed; second, the manner in which it is to be pronounced; third, its use.

As to the first, “This is most certain: the hymn of glorification was composed by the apostles, enlarged by the Fathers of Nicaea, received by the universal Church, and is to be sung with all reverence,” says Cardinal Bona (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 6). It has therefore come down to us by apostolic tradition. Those were mistaken who, on the authority of Theodoret (*Ecclesiastical History*, book II, chapter 24); Sozomen (*Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 19); the *Tripartite History* (book IV, chapter 35); and more clearly Nicephorus (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IX, chapter 24), make the Antiochene monk Flavian the author of this hymn [Col. 0425A].

For when the Catholics, under Constantius, celebrated the Father and the Son with equal glory, while the Arians attempted through ambiguous expressions to show the Son to be inferior to the Father, Flavian, they say, gathered a company of monks and was the first of all to sing aloud: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” But the authorities of Saints Athanasius and Basil prove that this hymn is older than Flavian.

St. Athanasius says in his book *On Virginity*: “When you have risen from the table, give thanks again by saying three times: ‘The merciful and compassionate Lord has given food to those who fear him. Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit’; and again, after completing the glorification, conclude your prayers.”

St. Basil, in his book *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 7, says: “Therefore we offer the hymn of glorification to the Father together with the Son. But is it not enough for us that this is the tradition of the Fathers?” He teaches the same in chapters 27 and 29 of that book, where he treats apostolic traditions [Col. 0425B].

The same hymn is also mentioned in the *Life of St. Eugenia*, who flourished under the emperor Commodus: “And as the angels passed by, they sang a hymn to God. This alone was understood: that the name of Jesus Christ and of the Holy Spirit resounded in those praises: ‘Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now and always, and through ages of ages. Amen.’”

[264] Therefore, what Walafrid asserts in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25—that it was composed by the great Council of Nicaea—must be understood of the addition “As it was in the beginning,” etc. Cardinal Bona teaches that this was indeed added at that council, to stop the sacrilegious mouths of the Arians, who blasphemed and asserted that there had been a time when the Son was not with the Father. This seems to be attested by the Council of Vasense, or Vasatense—or, more correctly, Vasionense I (Vaison I)—in Gaul, held shortly after Nicaea, under the emperor Constantius and Pope Julius, although its canons are preserved together with those of Vaison II, under Leo the Great, in the following decree [Col. 0425C]:

“Because not only in the Apostolic See but also throughout the whole East and throughout Africa and Italy, on account of the craftiness of the heretics who blaspheme that the Son of God was not always with the Father but began to exist at a particular time, in all clauses after ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,’ ‘As it was in the beginning, and now, and always, and through ages of ages. Amen,’ is said, we too decree that this is to be said in all our churches.”

Menardus, however, thinks that the words “throughout the whole East” are an interpolation, since nowhere among the Greeks does one find “As it was in the beginning” to have been in use. Walafrid also says, in chapter 25, that the Greeks do not say “As it was in the beginning,” but instead: “And now, and always, and through ages of ages. Amen.”

The manner of expressing it was varied and manifold.

1. “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.”

2. According to St. Basil, *On the Holy Spirit*, chapter 27: “Glory to the Father, and to the Son, with the Holy Spirit.”

3. “Glory and honor to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.” This form appears in the *Life of St. Eugenia* cited above [Col. 0425D] and is prescribed by the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 14, in these words: “At the end of the psalms, let it not be said, as by some up to now, ‘Glory to the Father,’ but ‘Glory and honor to the Father,’ in accordance with the prophet David’s words: ‘Give to the Lord glory and honor.’”

4. The Arians, abusing the Apostle’s words in support of their heresy, expressed it thus: “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit.” This is clear from Theodoret, book I of his *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 24, where Leontius, patriarch of Antioch, wishing to conceal his heresy, would quietly say these words of the same hymn, “Glory to the Father through the Son in the Holy Spirit,” while saying the remainder, “through ages of ages,” clearly and distinctly.

5. Pope Vigilius, in his first letter, also censures the error of certain people who, by removing one connecting syllable, attempted to diminish the complete title of the Holy Trinity, saying: “Glory to the Father and to the Son, Holy Spirit.”

As for the addition, John Bona asserts (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 5) that “As it was in the beginning, and now, and always, and through ages of ages. Amen” was added by the Council of Nicaea; we have likewise seen it prescribed at the Council of Vaison. Yet in the *Life of St. Eugenia*, in the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom, and in John Moschus’s *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 119, only this conclusion is found: “Now, and always, and through ages of ages. Amen.” Walafrid states that this alone was in use among the Greeks, chapter 25. Some added only these words: “Through ages of ages. Amen,” as may be seen in the Fourth Council of Toledo.

[265] Now something must be said about the use of this verse. We customarily sing it at the end of every psalm, and some wrongly attribute this practice to St. Jerome, since the letter from which they derive it is rightly rejected by learned men as spurious. For in that letter it is said that this was sung in the East, whereas the testimony of Cassian proves that to be false (*Book II*, chapter 8):

“But what we saw in this province, namely Massilia—that when one person sings at the conclusion of a psalm [Col. 0426B], all those standing by join in with a shout, ‘Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit’—we nowhere heard throughout the entire East. Instead, in complete silence, after the one who sings has finished the psalm, a prayer follows.”

Sometimes longer psalms were divided, as St. Benedict prescribes, and at the end of each division “Glory to the Father” was added. The Council of Narbonne decrees this in the following words (canon 2): “In the ordered singing of the psalms, ‘Glory’ is to be said to almighty God after each psalm; but with longer psalms, according to their length, pauses are to be made, and at each pause the glory of the Trinity is to be sung to the Lord.”

Sometimes two psalms were said under a single *Gloria*, as the Rule of St. Benedict prescribes; but the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 33, forbids this. In the East they customarily ended only the antiphons with this glorification of the Trinity, as Cassian writes. Finally, St. Benedict decrees that it be said at the end of the last responsory of every nocturn, and Walafrid, chapter 25, asserts that the Romans used it frequently in responsories [Col. 0426C]. John Gerson composed an anagogical treatise on this verse; consult it, if you wish, in volume III, *On the Hymn of Glory*.

After this, the ninety-fourth psalm. This is customarily called the invitatory; the *Rule of the Master* calls it the “Responsory of Exhortation,” and St. Isidore, in the Mozarabic office, calls it the “Sound.” It is clear that this was recited at the very beginning of the divine office before St. Benedict’s time, since St. Athanasius testifies (*Sermon on the Mother of God*) that Christians, inviting and exhorting one another to begin their prayers, used to cry out the words of this psalm.

Concerning its use, Cardinal Bona writes (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 8):

“Mark the Deacon of Gaza, who lived in the year of Our Lord 430, describes a procession of Christ’s faithful singing the psalm ‘Come, let us rejoice,’ and, at the divisions between the verses of the psalm, saying ‘Alleluia.’ This melody represents something like the form of an invitatory. Amalarius also writes that he heard this psalm sung at Constantinople in the church of Hagia Sophia at the beginning of Mass.

“The Roman Church [Col. 0426D] customarily omits the invitatory only in the office of the Epiphany. This is a very ancient practice, as Alcuin and Hugh testify: first, because the entire office concerns the calling of the nations, as Bonaventure teaches, and the words ‘Come, let us adore him’ are repeated more frequently; and second, because the same psalm is sung at the third nocturn, whereas it would be inappropriate to recite the same psalm twice in the same office. But we, who according to the prescription of our Rule sing three canticles from the Old Testament at the third nocturn, also sing the invitatory in the customary manner on the day of the Epiphany.”

Thus far Cardinal Bona. Nevertheless, it is clear from Amalarius’s *Supplement* (*Analecta*, volume II) that formerly, among the Benedictines as well, this psalm was omitted on Epiphany [266] and sung at the second nocturn.

With the antiphon. Here he calls the invitatory normally placed before this psalm an antiphon—for example, “Come, let us adore the King, the Lord of confessors.” Amalarius (*On the Order of Antiphons*, chapters 69 and 70) calls this an “invitatory antiphon.” The Roman Order confirms this, where, for the Easter vigil, we read: “During the white-robed days of Easter, an antiphon is said over ‘Come’: ‘The Lord has truly risen’” [Col. 0427A]. It is then repeated either in full or in part after each verse of the psalm; and this has been done since the time of St. Benedict, as Boherius writes in his second commentary.

Or certainly, it is to be sung. The particle *aut* (“or”) seems here to be taken conjunctively for *et* (“and”), as if he were saying: “with the antiphon, and certainly it is to be sung.” For according to chapter 43 of the Rule, this psalm must be pronounced very slowly, and it has always been sung in the Church with great solemnity.

Bernard of Cassino, however, thinks that it should be understood as referring to direct singing. He writes concerning this passage: “Or certainly, by singing—supply, ‘directly’—and without an antiphon, like the third psalm. This is what they do in the Gallic regions during summer.” Likewise, the text of Peter the Deacon reads: “Or certainly, by singing directly without an antiphon.” Amalarius confirms this in his supplement to book IV of *On the Divine Offices* [Col. 0427B]: “On weekdays during the summer, the invitatory is customarily said without the melody of an antiphon.” Paul Augustine of Janua also observes, in his commentary on chapter 12 of the Rule, that the particle *de* is sometimes negative, so that *decantare* (“to sing”) has the same meaning as “not to sing,” but simply to recite without modulation of the voice.

Then let the Ambrosian follow. That is, the hymn which the Holy Father calls “Ambrosian,” as something genuinely Ambrosian, or divine and heavenly, and divinely inspired, as Smaragdus explains, followed by Peter the Deacon, whom Bernard of Cassino cites. Or it may be so called from Ambrose the bishop, master of hymns, as the same Smaragdus also explains, because the hymns composed by St. Ambrose began to be sung more frequently in his time, as Ambrose himself testifies at the end of his sermon *On Not Handing Over the Basilicas to the Heretics*.

Amalarius illustrates the latter explanation in the aforementioned *Supplement*, writing: “It is established, in a certain sense, that St. Benedict selected the customary practice of St. Ambrose in some ecclesiastical matters—for example, in the hymns which he calls Ambrosian” [Col. 0427C]. Walafrid likewise says in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25: “When St. Benedict calls them Ambrosian hymns, he either intends those composed by Ambrose or others composed in imitation of the Ambrosian hymns.”

Hence Cardinal Bona, speaking of his Cistercians (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 18, § 4), says: “Because the Lord Benedict calls them Ambrosian hymns, we have received all our hymns from the Ambrosians, and at all times precisely the same hymns as they use. The curious reader may find their catalogue in Ralph of Tongeren.” You will find more about hymns in the same cardinal’s *On the Divine Psalms*, book 16, § 9.

Then six psalms with antiphons. William Durandus thinks that an antiphon is so called with reference to the psalm, that is, because it sounds before the psalm (*Rationale*, book V, chapter 2). Properly, however, an antiphon is reciprocal singing, from the Greek word ἀντιφωνεῖν (*antiphōnein*), meaning “to call back,” or “to respond mutually and from opposite sides.” Moreover, “the difference between responsories and antiphons is that in responsories one person says the verse, whereas in antiphons the singers alternate in the verses” (St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book VI, chapter 19). Someone might explain this as follows: “They sing antiphons at each verse of the psalms,” because the learned Joseph Thomasius shows that this really was the ancient practice [Col. 0427D].

But did Hildemar understand it in this way when he writes: “The Greeks first composed antiphons, with two choirs singing alternately, like two cherubim. . . . Among the Latins, however, the same blessed Ambrose was the first to institute antiphons, imitating the example of the Greeks; from that point their use spread throughout all the western regions”?

When these things have been said, after the verse has been said. The word *versus* (“verse”) derives from *vertere* (“to turn”), either because we turn from the office of psalms to the readings, or because “when we hear the verse, we immediately turn our face toward the altar, so that every thought which has gone outside through distraction may return to God through devout inward turning [Col. 0428A],” as Cardinal Bona says (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 13).

In the ninth chapter of the monks of Saint Gall it is prescribed “that the verse at each assembly be said honorably in a higher, clearer, and more prolonged voice.” “It is said in a clear and high voice,” says the aforementioned cardinal, “so that, when they hear it, the sluggish may be awakened and return to their hearts. It is said at night before the readings, so that the person who has labored in psalmody may now sit and rest, and may be raised up to listen attentively to the teaching of the readings, lest inconvenient sleepiness creep over him while seated, etc.”

Let the abbot give the blessing. Boherius says that this is not by the sign of the cross but by a word of blessing. Smaragdus explains what those words of blessing are in the following terms: “That is, after the singer has said the verse, let the abbot say: ‘May the Lord save and bless us through the prayers of all his saints,’ or some blessing of that kind.”

This is the brief prayer which we call the absolution. It precedes the Lord’s Prayer [Col. 0428B], and is followed by the reader’s request for a blessing. Bernard of Cassino seems to include all these things under the name of “blessing,” writing concerning this passage:

“For before the readings are read, the abbot recites the Lord’s Prayer. Afterward he recites another prayer, namely, ‘From the bonds of our sins,’ etc. Then, when the reader asks for a blessing by saying, ‘Command, lord, that you bless,’ the abbot gives the blessing.”

St. Benedict did not explain all these details because he thought they were sufficiently known from custom. If it was customary in St. Benedict’s time to precede the readings with the Lord’s Prayer, Boherius judged that this prayer, like the absolution, was an addition beyond the prescription of the Rule. The Cistercians certainly omit both, as John Bona writes in *On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 18, § 4. Yet the practice appears to be very ancient; perhaps it is to this that chapter 5 of the monks of Saint Gall refers when it prescribes “that after the first six psalms at the nocturn they should not bend their knees, but should pray standing.”

The reader, asking for a blessing, says: “Command, lord, that you bless.” Gretser proves the antiquity of this rite in volume II of *On the Cross*, in the discussion *On Prayer*. Concerning this formula for requesting a blessing, Peter Damian writes in his book *The Lord Be with You*, chapter 2:

“The reader, out of profound humility, asks to be blessed not by the priest but by the person whom the priest has ordered to bless him, saying: ‘Command, lord, that you bless.’ The priest, however, in returning such great humility, neither delegates the office of blessing to any subordinate nor presumes to give the blessing himself; rather, he first asks that it be conferred by God, who is blessed above all.”

When everyone is seated on benches. Note how plain and humble he wants the furnishings of the oratory to be: he allows those who are seated not proud benches but only simple stools. Thus Cassian describes the monks of old sitting on very humble seats at the voice of the psalm-singer (*Book II*, chapter 12). We read the same of our own monks in book II of *The Deeds of the Saints of Roton*, chapter 5.

Although Peter Boherius [Col. 0428D], explaining this passage, says that the Rule does not explicitly state whether one should stand or sit when the psalms are sung, Menardus nevertheless rightly inferred from these words of St. Benedict that the monks of our institution are to stand while singing the psalms. For those who are ordered to sit while the readings are being read must previously have stood while singing the psalms. He confirms this from chapter 60 of the Rule: “Let him be permitted to stand and give the blessing after the abbot”; and from chapter 63: “Thus let him approach for the kiss of peace, for Communion, for the imposition of the psalm, and let him stand in the choir.”

Although *stare* (“to stand”) is not always taken for bodily uprightness but may sometimes signify presence—as when it is said, “those who are standing here”—nothing prevents it from being understood in that sense here. If they had been sitting, ordinary speech would have said: “Let him be permitted to sit after the abbot,” and “thus let them approach for the kiss of peace . . . let them sit in the choir,” etc.

This was also the practice of the monks of old [Col. 0429A], as may be seen in St. Athanasius’s book *On Virginity*: “Rise at midnight and say the psalms, standing as much as you can”; and in St. John Chrysostom, who writes concerning the monks of his own time (*Homily 14 on the First Epistle to Timothy*): “When the cock cries before dawn, all rise reverently, shaking off sleep, awakened by their superior; and they stand before the sacred choir, immediately singing the holy hymns with outstretched hands.”

Cassian likewise reports (*Book II*, chapter 12) that the person who sang the psalms while the others listened and sat, sang them standing. The *Rule of the Master*, chapter 47, says: “The one who sings the psalms ought to stand with an immobile body and bowed head, and sing praises to the Lord in a measured manner.” St. Vincent Ferrer says: “When matins has been rung, and prostrations and bows have been made, stand on your feet while singing the psalms, not leaning against anything.”

Boherius also testifies concerning this passage that at the monasteries of Subiaco and the Sacred Grotto, where St. Benedict first performed his penance, the brothers did not sit at all during the psalms; he says that he saw this many times [Col. 0429B]. He adds, however, that in the great monasteries of Gaul he observed the brothers sitting while the psalms were being completed; sometimes half of the brothers sat during one psalm and the other half during the next, alternately.

What Boherius says of Subiaco, Bernard of Cassino says of Monte Cassino: “To this day, the brothers on Monte Cassino do not sit while the psalms are being sung, although elsewhere I see them sitting alternately by turns. I do not condemn that practice; nevertheless, I praise this one as more consonant with the intention of our holy Father Benedict.”

[269] Among those great monasteries of Gaul in which Boherius says he saw the brothers sitting in the choir, the monastery of Cluny may rightly be included. There, if someone “wishes to sit during the psalmody,” says Udalric, “he takes care not to sit beside another who is sitting, but in such a way that one stands while the other sits; and they are to provide each other with the opportunity to sit.”

The monastery of Saint Benignus at Dijon likewise has ancient written customs prescribing the same arrangement as Udalric, with this sole addition [Col. 0429C]: one sits for two psalms while the other stands. The Cistercian monastery’s book of usages prescribes (chapter 68) that “no one should sit from the moment ‘O God, come to my assistance’ begins until after the hymn. Then, with hands folded over their knees, they should sit together for the first psalm, while they stand for the second, and so proceed through the remaining psalms.”

The monks of Bursfeld also sit alternately during the psalms. We, however, always stand at all the daytime hours, which is more consonant with the intention of St. Benedict, says Bernard of Cassino. Peter Damian composed an entire short work, opusculum 39, *On Not Sitting during the Work of God*; consult it, if you wish.

Let three readings be read in turn by the brothers from a book on the lectern. Since the holy Father Benedict commands that the readings be read from a book, Haeften rightly infers from this passage that, according to the legislator’s intention, the psalms are to be sung from memory without a book. He very properly distinguished between these two forms of expression: “let them be read” and “let them be said.” The holy Father uses the former when speaking of the readings and the latter when speaking of the psalms.

Indeed, this is demonstrated by the ancient custom [Col. 0429D] of the monks of old, who committed the Psalter and other books of sacred Scripture to memory. “Whoever wishes to renounce the world,” says St. Pachomius (*Rule*, article 26), “. . . shall remain outside before the door for a few days and shall be taught the Lord’s Prayer and as many psalms as he is able to learn.” Elsewhere he says (article 80): “There shall certainly be no one in the monastery who does not learn letters and retain something from the Scriptures, at least as far as the New Testament and the Psalter.”

St. Basil says (*Admonitions*, no. 1): “If anyone in sound bodily health neglects to pray or to commit the psalms to memory, making excuses in sins, let him be separated from the company of the others or fast for one week.”

St. Ferreolus says: “Anyone who wishes to claim the name of monk must not be permitted to remain ignorant of letters; indeed, he must know the entire Psalter by heart and must not defend himself with any excuse against being seized by this holy discipline.”

St. Jerome, instructing the monk Rusticus [Col. 0430A], writes (*Letter 4*): “Let a book never leave your hand and eyes; learn the Psalter word for word.” Elsewhere, speaking of the Egyptian monks, he says (*Letter 22*): “Every day something from the Scriptures is learned.” And again (*On Psalm 133*): “The monks commonly have this contest among themselves: that they learn more of the Scriptures by heart, and think themselves better in proportion as they have learned more.”

In the fourth century, moreover, when a woman asked to be admitted to the convent of St. Eupraxia, the abbess answered (*Life of St. Eupraxia*, Bollandists, 13 March): “Daughter, if you wish to remain here, you must learn letters and the Psalter.” St. Apollinaris, who died in the fifth century, desired to be consecrated as a nun and asked her parents “to bring a nun who would teach her the Psalter and reading”; they “a few days later brought her nuns who taught her the Psalter and the reading of the Scriptures.”

St. Sabas, admitted to the monastery of Flaviana (*Life*, no. 4, volume III of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*), “in a short time learned the Psalter and the other constitutions of the coenobitic rule” [Col. 0430B]. The Persian monk Anastasius, coming to conversion (*Life*, no. 12, Bollandists, 22 January), is said to have been entrusted to a certain brother “who taught him letters, together with the approved teaching of God and the Psalter.”

The same is evident concerning our own monks from what was said in the preceding chapter and in book I of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 6. But what of the fact that even priests and bishops were required to learn the Psalter? St. Gregory (*Register*, book XII, letter 6) certainly refused to ordain Rusticus, a deacon elected bishop, because he did not know the psalms, unless it had first been carefully investigated how many psalms he failed to know. The same holy doctor writes to Andrew the Scholastic (*Book IV*, letter 45): “Nor did we presume to ordain John the priest, who did not know the psalms; for this showed that he possessed too little zeal for his own progress.”

It is therefore surprising that Walafrid Strabo writes [Col. 0430C] (*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25) that before his own time the practice of exercising oneself in psalmody by heart had been rarer: “Thus, concerning almost the last of the Roman bishops, and those who preceded our time by scarcely two hundred years, it is written as something memorable and extraordinary if any of them appeared more eminent than the rest in these matters. . . . Of Gregory III, however, something seemingly unheard-of and new is reported: that he knew all the psalms by heart.”

To return to the subject: since all the monks of old learned the Psalter by heart, as has been demonstrated, and since at that time handwritten books were otherwise comparatively rare—for example, in the monastery of Centula, where there were at least three hundred monks together with one hundred boys, there were only seven psalters, as is clear from the catalogue of that monastery made in the year 831—it is evident that our monks sang the psalms by heart. Hence the ancient written customs of Germany prescribe (no. 13) that the reader be provided with a candle by the custodian of the oratory, and the abbot with one by the keeper of the books, because previously the psalms were sung in darkness without light [Col. 0430D] and therefore without a book.

St. Benedict wished the readings to be recited in turn by the brothers, “that is, by turns, alternately, or mutually: now this one, now that one; now from here, now from there,” says Smaragdus. Or, as Bernard of Cassino says, “succeeding one another alternately,” so that one and the same person would never read two readings. Hence a blessing is requested before each reading, which would not need to be repeated if one and the same person were to read several readings consecutively.

This was certainly required by the holy Father’s profound discretion, lest they become excessively tired from reading, especially since the readings at that time were longer and it was not so easy to read from manuscript books. See book II of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 1.

On the lectern. Boherius describes what a lectern is in his first exposition, in these words: “Here the lectern is called the elevated place above the choir where the books of sacred preaching stand, such as the legendary books or lectionaries, which contain the sermons of the holy doctors” [Col. 0431A].

This is entirely appropriate if we consider the etymology of the word: ἀνά (*ana*) means “up” in Greek, while λόγος (*logos*) means “speech.” Thus St. Isidore also says (*Etymologies*, book XV, chapter 4): “It is called an *analogium* because speech is proclaimed from it; for λόγος in Greek means ‘speech,’ and the lectern itself is placed higher.”

For others, however, an *analogium* is a pulpit placed beneath the book. Isidore’s Glosses say: “A lectern, an *analogium*, above which one reads.” And again: “A pulpit, an *analogium*, a lectern.” Hence Gregory of Tours, describing the *analogium* of the basilica of St. Cyprian the martyr (*On the Glory of the Martyrs*, book I, chapter 94), writes: “An *analogium*, on which a book is placed and from which one sings or reads.”

In an ancient drawing of the monastery of Saint Gall, there were three lecterns in the choir: two on either side for reading at night, and a third somewhat lower in the middle of the choir for the Gospel.

And among them let three responsories be sung. St. Isidore writes of responsories (*On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 8):

“Responsories were discovered by the Italians long ago [Col. 0431B] and were given this name because, when one person sings, the choir responds in harmony. Formerly each person performed alone; now one, sometimes two or three, sing together while the choir responds in many places.”

Rupert says that responsories are so called either because they respond to the readings—sad things to sad things, joyful things to joyful things—or because they are sung with the choir responding. Nicholas of Fractura explains it in nearly the same way.

Although St. Isidore says (*Book VIII*, chapter 8) that responsories were invented by the Italians, Sozomen nevertheless reports that St. John Chrysostom instituted responsorial songs in rivalry with the Arians, who, divided into groups, sang alternately in the manner of responsories and added refrains composed in favor of their sect.

Let two responsories be said without the *Gloria*. But after the third reading, let the singer say the *Gloria*. “In ancient times the *Gloria* was not sung after the verse, but the responsory was repeated,” says Amalarius (*On the Order of Antiphons*, chapter 2) [Col. 0431C]. But Blessed Benedict at least wished it to be sung in the third responsory. Walafrid reports (*On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25) that it was used more frequently by the Romans in responsories.

The Fourth Council of Toledo also rebukes those who did not use “Glory to the Father” in responsories, and decrees that it be sung with this distinction (canon 15): “In joyful matters, let the *Gloria* follow; in more sorrowful matters, let the beginning be repeated.” This remains the practice. Thus it is not said in the office of the dead, according to the Council of Aachen, chapter 66, nor from Passion Sunday until Easter, because at that time the reproach and insults directed against the Trinity are recited in the person of the Son, says Boherius. Hildemar, however, asserts that this is contrary to the Rule and says that in his monastery the *Gloria* was always said at the end of the responsory, except during the three days before Easter, when, according to the decree of the council held in France, they celebrated the Roman office.

Let books of both the Old Testament and the New, of divine authority, be read at the vigils. Here the holy Father explains from what source the readings at the nocturns are to be taken: namely, from books of the Old and New Testaments possessing divine authority [Col. 0431D]. “Of divine authority,” he says, meaning those which the Church recognizes as truly canonical, such as those whose catalogue the Council of Trent drew up in Session 4 [272].

It is said that Pope Gelasius distributed the order in which these books were to be read throughout the year at a Roman council with seventy bishops. They prove this from Gratian’s *Decree*, distinction 15, chapter “The Holy Roman Church.” Yet the material concerning this matter found in the said decree of Gratian does not appear in his manuscripts; and Theodemar writes that before Pope Gregory’s time the Scriptures were not read in the Roman Church.

And also expositions of them composed by the most renowned orthodox and Catholic Fathers. “He did not say ‘by renowned men,’” says Hildemar, “but ‘by the most renowned,’ because there were many who were renowned, and yet error was found in their books [Col. 0432A]. Therefore he said ‘by the most renowned,’ as if he were saying: let them read the expositions of those doctors in whose books no error is found, such as Augustine, Gregory, Ambrose, and the other Catholic Fathers.”

For Nicholas of Fractura, the most renowned doctors are Gregory, Augustine, Jerome, and Ambrose. He adds: “Other doctors, such as Hilary, Basil, John Chrysostom, Gregory of Nazianzus, and Bede the priest, may likewise be called most renowned, because their teachings have been approved by the Church, etc.”

These kinds of expositions may be read in church, provided a sincere and excellent selection is made from them: St. Gregory approves this as sufficiently pious and useful. Thus he writes to John, subdeacon of the Church of Ravenna (Book X, Letter 22):

> “I did not receive with pleasure what was reported to me by certain persons: that my most reverend brother and fellow bishop, Marianus, publicly has the commentaries on blessed Job read at the vigils. For that work is not suited to the people, and for uneducated hearers it produces more hindrance [Col. 0432B] than advancement. But tell him to have the commentaries on the Psalms read at the vigils, since these especially form the minds of secular people toward good morals.”

From these words it may be observed that lectionaries, as they are called, compiled from the homilies of the holy Fathers, had not yet been organized in the Church; rather, it was left to the discretion of bishops and prelates to assign the books from which the readings were to be taken. The first person who seems to have undertaken this successfully was the emperor Charlemagne, who, through Paul the Deacon of Cassino, prepared two volumes to be read throughout the year, drawn from the homilies and sermons of the holy Fathers, under this title:

*The distinguished work of all the homilies and postils of the venerable and eminent doctors Gregory, Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, Bede, Hericus, Leo, Maximus, John the bishop, and Origen, complete for the seasons and the saints throughout the entire year, with certain of their sermons inserted here and there, collected from their proper places and fitted to the appropriate times, divided into the winter and summer sections.*

This work, prepared by Alcuin, was revised by Paul the Deacon at Charlemagne’s command. There exists concerning it a letter of Charlemagne to all the religious readers under his authority (Volume I of the *Analecta*), which our Mabillon made publicly available. In it Charlemagne states that “certain readings for the nocturnal office had been compiled through the fruitless labor of some men, although with proper intention, yet less suitably” [273]. Before Paul arranged the aforementioned lectionary, however, the names of the authors whose homilies were recited in the divine offices were not announced, as Charlemagne testifies in the aforementioned letter.

St. Benedict does not even mention the passions of the holy martyrs. Nevertheless, the practice of reading them publicly in church had already become established in some churches before his time. We have a distinguished testimony to this in St. Augustine’s second sermon on St. Stephen, where he says (Sermon 315):

> “Although we scarcely find accounts of the other martyrs that we can recite on their solemnities, this martyrdom is found in the canonical [Col. 0432D] book.”

Certainly, at the Third Council of Carthage, held toward the end of the fourth century, permission had been given for the passions of the martyrs to be read when their anniversaries were celebrated. Likewise, in St. Caesarius’s *Rule for Virgins*, cited by Bollandus no. 69 (January 12), it is decreed that “when the feasts of the martyrs are celebrated, the first Mass is to be read from the Gospels, and the remaining ones from the passions of the martyrs.” The same provision occurs in St. Aurelian’s *Rule*, in the order of psalmody, and in chapter 18 of St. Ferreolus’s *Rule*.

Agobard, bishop of Lyon, therefore commits a serious error when, in his short work on the ancient practice of singing psalms and on the correction of the antiphonary, he argues that nothing divine should be heard in the offices except sacred Scripture, lest, as he says, “we offer strange fire to God.” The occasion for this error may have been provided by canon 59 of the Council of Laodicea, which forbids the reading of any books other than the sacred and canonical books that it lists individually.

After these three readings, with their responsories, let the remaining six psalms be sung with Alleluia [Col. 0433A]. This was modeled on that holy angel who, after chanting eleven psalms in an assembly of Egyptian monks, completed the twelfth with an Alleluia response and was suddenly withdrawn from the sight of them all (Cassian, Book II, chapter 5).

After these, a reading from the Apostle. That is, from Paul, who is always to be understood when the word “Apostle” is heard without qualification.

To be recited from the heart. That is, from memory and without a book. “By this,” says St. Hildegard, “he shows that when the brothers devote themselves to readings and meditations, they should commit to memory whatever they find necessary in divine Scripture, so that when a suitable time arrives, or when necessity intrudes, they may bring it forth without anything materially written down. In the same way they will recite the aforementioned readings—that is, those prescribed in chapters 9 and 10—from the heart and from memory, that is, without a book, because they are brief, so that their brevity may not cause them difficulty if they should not have a codex from which to read or a light available for seeing, and so forth.”

This interpretation is confirmed by the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 44:

> “As for the brother who has been ordered to recite a reading from memory, let him not read it from a codex, except only at the vigils. This is what we establish: that the brothers should meditate on certain things more frequently and retain the Scriptures in memory, so that, wherever it may be necessary, what is lacking from the text of the reading or page may be recited from memory” [“ex deesse”: evidently corrupt; the sense is uncertain] [Col. 0434A].

It is therefore clear how wrongly some explain “from the heart” as “with a great feeling of devotion,” especially since the contrary is made evident by the following chapter.

The supplication of the litany. Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, in both of their expositions, understand “supplication” to mean a bowing or genuflection, perhaps because formerly they bent the knees during the litany, as prescribed in chapter 7 of the monks of Saint Gall:

> “When the offices have been completed, as they are about to begin Kyrie eleison, let them bend their knees, and let them not rise before the priest has said, after all the names of the Holy Trinity have been pronounced, ‘For ever and ever. Amen.’”

What the litany is, St. Benedict himself explains when he adds, “that is, Kyrie eleison.” The term is understood in this sense in the Greek liturgies of Saints James, Basil, and Chrysostom. Concerning this expression, the Council of Vaison under Leo the Great defines it as follows (canon 2):

> “Since both in the Apostolic See and throughout the eastern provinces and those of Italy a sweet and salutary custom has been introduced, namely, that Kyrie eleison should be said more frequently with great devotion and compunction, it has pleased us also that, by God’s favor, this holy custom should be introduced into all our churches, both at matins, at Masses, and at vespers.”

See John Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 14, § 4.

And thus let the night vigils be ended. This was done by the collect, or prayer, which always brought the divine office to an end.

## CHAPTER X. How the Night Office Is to Be Conducted in Summer

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433B] From Easter until the Kalends of November [Note: [Col. 0433C] Cassino manuscript: *novembres*], the entire quantity of psalmody is to be maintained, as was said above, except that the readings are not to be read from a codex, because of the brevity of the nights [Note: [Col. 0433C] Sabina manuscript: “except that the readings are to be read without a codex”]. Instead of those three readings, one reading from the Old Testament is to be recited from memory [Col. 0434B] [Note: [Col. 0433C] Oxford manuscript: “is to be read from memory”], followed by a short responsory. Everything else is to be carried out as stated: namely, that never fewer than twelve psalms are to be said at the night vigils [Note: [Col. 0433C] Oxford manuscript: “of the night”] [Note: [Col. 0434C] So the Oxford manuscript; but nearly all the other manuscripts read “are to be said”], except Psalms 3 and 94 [Note: [Col. 0434C] Another reading: “psalms”].

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0433]

[Col. 0433C] From Easter until the Kalends of November, and so forth. By Easter, he says, he means the Resurrection, to distinguish it from the other solemnities of our Lord Jesus Christ, which certain provinces also call *Paschata*, says Boherius. Thus, in the ancient manuscript customs of Germany, Maundy Thursday is called Easter.

Instead of those three readings, one reading from the Old Testament is to be recited from memory [Col. 0433D]. This appears to correspond to a statute of Guigo, prior of the Carthusians (chapter 5):

> “From Pentecost until the Kalends of November, unless a feast intervenes, we are content with one reading, like the other monks.”

His saying “from Pentecost” shows that more readings were recited throughout the whole Paschal season. Indeed, formerly three readings were read in all monasteries everywhere, as we observed in Book III of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 18. It is also clear from the letter of Theodemar, abbot, to Charlemagne that the monks of Cassino followed the practice of the Roman Church throughout the whole summer. Amalarius likewise writes in the *Supplement* that:

> “In certain monasteries of monks, because of the Roman custom, so that they may not depart from it entirely and may read the history of the Old Testament more fully in the churches, three readings are given during the summer only on Monday, Tuesday, and Wednesday; and on the other three days, unless there is a commemoration of a saint, they are content with one, in observance of the Rule of St. Benedict.”

The Cistercians, however, adhered so rigidly to the laws of the holy Rule that throughout the entire summer they had no feast at all with three readings, as Cardinal Bona writes (*On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 18, § 4).

This reading, which the boys read among the Cluniacs, according to Udalricus Book III, chapter 8, and which the weekly cantor reads among the Carthusians, according to the *New Collection of Statutes*, Part I, chapter 16, must, as prescribed by the Rule, be recited from memory—that is, from the heart and without a book. It must therefore be brief, though shorter or longer according to the brevity or length of the nights.

“If anyone is troubled,” says Theodemar (*Letter to Charlemagne*), “by the question of why blessed Benedict ordered that, during the summer, only one reading from the Old Testament should be read on weekdays at the nocturnal office, let him know that at that time it was not yet customary in the Roman Church for the sacred Scriptures to be read as they are read now. Rather, this institution was established after some time, either by Pope Gregory or, as others affirm, by Honorius.”

Hildemar, and after him Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata, raise one question here: why, namely, did the holy Father prescribe only one reading for September and October, even though those months have nights equal in length to March and April, for which he established three readings? They say that this was done chiefly to relieve the brothers from the great labors they are compelled to undertake in gathering the crops and harvesting the grapes [Col. 0435A] [276]. Add to this that the Lenten season, into which March and April ordinarily fall, required something to be added to the usual allotment. Nevertheless, if St. Benedict’s intention is considered, the brothers of good will who recite three readings from a codex in September and October have done nothing contrary to the Rule, as the aforementioned commentators judge.

A short responsory is to follow. It is indeed short, usually composed from a single verse of one of the psalms, as Boherius notes.

So that never fewer than twelve psalms are said at the night vigils [Col. 0436A]. The holy Father Benedict retained the same number of psalms on Sunday as sacred and received from heaven. The Second Council of Tours prescribes the same number in canon 18. The Egyptian monks recited the same number at the vigils and at the evening synaxis, according to Cassian, Book II, chapters 5 and 6. Palladius reports in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 38, that the same number had been imposed by an angel on St. Pachomius for his monks. Other monks also observed the same number according to the *Rule of Solitaries*. Subsequently, as Hildemar teaches, the custom also prevailed throughout the African and Western Churches that twelve psalms should be chanted at the night vigils.

## CHAPTER XI. How Vigils Are to Be Conducted on Sundays

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0435A] On Sunday [Note: [Col. 0435C] Oxford manuscript: “On Sundays”] the brothers are to rise earlier [Note: [Col. 0435C] Thus in the Oxford and Narbonne manuscripts, the manuscript of Saint-Germain, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius. But most others read *temperius*, “more moderately”; this word is also occasionally used by certain writers of respectable Latin]. At these vigils let moderation be observed: namely, six psalms, sung in measured tones as we arranged above, with a verse, while everyone sits in orderly fashion and in rows on the benches. Then, as we said above, four readings from a codex are to be read with their responsories. Only in the fourth responsory is “Glory” to be said by the cantor. As soon as he begins it, let everyone immediately rise reverently.

After these readings, let six other psalms follow in order [Note: [Col. 0435C] The Oxford manuscript omits “six”], with antiphons, as before, and a verse [Note: [Col. 0435C] Another reading: “with the verse”]. After these, let another four readings be read [Note: [Col. 0435C] Oxford manuscript: “let three canticles be said, with the intervening material omitted”], with their responsories, in the order given above. After these, let three canticles from the prophets be said [Note: [Col. 0435C] Another reading: “of the prophets”], which the abbot shall choose; let these canticles be sung with Alleluia [Note: [Col. 0436C] Ebrul manuscript: “with white garments”]. After the verse has been said and the abbot has given the blessing, let another four readings from the New Testament be read [Note: [Col. 0436C] Florence manuscript: “from the Old Testament”], in the order given above.

After the fourth responsory, let the abbot begin the hymn *Te Deum laudamus*.

When it has been completed [Note: [Col. 0436C] Another reading: “when it has been said”], let the abbot read a Gospel reading, with honor and trembling [Note: [Col. 0436C] Cassino, Florence, and Afflighem manuscripts: “with fear”], while everyone stands. When it has been read, let everyone respond, “Amen.” Immediately afterward, let the abbot sing the hymn *Te decet laus*. After the blessing has been given, let them begin [Note: [Col. 0436C] Florence, Ebrul, Faron, Lyon, Afflighem, and the Venetian edition read “let him begin,” a reading approved by Menardus. In the Narbonne manuscript this sentence reads: “And immediately afterward let the abbot sing the hymn: ‘You are worthy of praise, you are worthy of a hymn.’ And after the blessing let them begin,” and so forth] matins.
