This order of vigils is to be observed equally on Sunday throughout the whole year, in summer as in winter. Unless, God forbid, they rise late [Note: [Col. 0436C] Another reading: “unless one rises late”], in which case something must be shortened from the readings or the responsories; but every precaution must be taken to prevent this from happening. If it should occur, the person through whose negligence it happened must fittingly make satisfaction to God in the oratory.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0435]

[Col. 0435C] St. Benedict devoted a special chapter to the sacred vigils of Sunday. This was appropriate for those most reverend nights, as St. Columbanus calls them; it was demanded by the special solemnity and prerogative of this day above all others. For this is the day that the Lord has made, on which David invites all the faithful of Christ to rejoice and exult.

“On this day,” says Boherius in his first commentary, “the world received its beginning; on this day, through the Resurrection, death received its destruction and life its beginning. This is the consecrated day, called the Lord’s day; a day full of grace, a happy day, a beloved day, a sweet day, not a bitter one.” More is said about it in sermons 167 and 280, in the appendix to St. Augustine, where it is fully shown how many benefits were bestowed on human beings on this day and, consequently, with what reverence it ought to be celebrated.

On Sunday the brothers are to rise earlier for the vigils. Because the office of Sunday vigils is more solemn and longer, the holy Father Benedict commands the brothers to rise earlier than usual, especially because of the brevity of the summer nights. If they celebrated the vigils at the customary hour, they would sing matins not at the beginning of daylight, as the Rule prescribes, but when the day was already bright. Nor does the whole of St. Benedict’s provision concerning rising earlier refer to every season; if we believe Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and John of Turrecremata, it refers only to summer. Hence, after treating of the summer vigils in the preceding chapter, the holy Father immediately issued this decree, in which he adds that matins is to be begun at the coming of daylight. In winter it is sufficient for the brothers to rise at the eighth hour of the night [Col. 0436C] [278].

The holy Father does not state by how much earlier than usual the brothers should rise. But if his mind and intention are considered, the hour of rising must be adjusted and advanced according to the brevity or length of the nights, so that matins may be joined to the night vigils without any intervening interval and celebrated as daylight begins.

In the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris, however, we infer that the brothers formerly rose before midnight from Aimo, a monk of that place, in Book II of the *Miracles of Saint Germanus*, chapter 1. There a certain woman is said to have been “allowed to spend that night resting in the atrium of the same church; but before the interval of midnight had passed, she awoke, as if touched by some medicine, and made her way into the church by herself, while the brothers were already celebrating the solemn vigils according to custom” [Col. 0437A]. These words must necessarily be understood of a Sunday or feast day, since on other days they would not rise so early.

Nearly the same may be inferred concerning Floriacum from Adalerius, in the *Book of the Miracles of the Holy Father Benedict*. At Centula, likewise, in the time of Gervinus, a most devout abbot, a certain prior named Revenardus, previously ill, “entered the choir with the brothers at the twelfth hour of the night, healthy and cheerful,” on the feast of St. Vigor the Confessor, as John of Capella writes in the *Life of St. Gervinus*, no. 7 (Bollandus, March 3).

We learn from Amalarius’s *Supplement* that this was formerly the common custom of monasteries. He writes:

> “For on all the Sundays of the Resurrection the monks rightly rise around midnight.”

Earlier he had said that the holy Father Benedict received this practice from St. Ambrose, “who,” he says, “always had the custom of rising before midnight on Sundays, as his hymn shows:  
> ‘Let us all rise more swiftly,  
> and seek the Holy One by night.’”

In the Cistercian general chapter of the year 1429, it was decreed that on Sundays and feast days the brothers should rise one hour earlier than usual. The monks of Bursfeld, who rise at the twelfth hour—that is, at midnight—on ordinary days, do so on Sundays and feast days with twelve readings at the eleventh hour or even earlier, according to chapter 3 of their *Ceremonial*. Similarly, the monks of Casale rise on Sundays and simpler feast days about half an hour before midnight, but on greater and highest feasts precisely at the eleventh hour, according to chapter 3 of the manuscript *Ceremonial*.

At these vigils let moderation be observed. “This,” says Nicholas of Fractura, “is to be maintained in all things, without which no one lives rightly. Hence there are certain instructional verses carved on the crown of the king of France:

> As it profits to set a measure in everything that exists,  
> so without measure royal governance will not stand.

And *mensura*—‘measure’—is so called as if from *mentis cura*, ‘care of the mind.’”

What “let moderation be observed” means, he explains by adding:

Six psalms, sung in measured tones as we arranged above [Col. 0437C] [279]. “In measured tones,” that is, sweetly chanted. For, as Smaragdus says, “*modulatio* means the sweetness or pleasantness of song, which occurs in measured, melodious [Note: [Col. 0437D] I do not see how this phrase can be explained unless it should perhaps read *in modulato canore vocis*, ‘in the measured singing of the voice.’ EDIT.] voice.” Or *modulatis* may mean, according to Bernard of Cassino, “chanted according to the tone of the antiphon”:

> “This measured singing is a kind of application of a mode, which must be carried out according to the appropriate tone of the antiphon.”

Therefore St. Benedict wished song to be used in the work of God not for the pleasure of the ears but to awaken devotion in his monks. There would be much to say here about ecclesiastical song; but it is enough to note what Rabanus reports (Book II, *On the Instruction of Clerics*, chapter 48):

> “The primitive Church sang psalms in such a way that, through a slight inflection of the voice, it made the singer’s voice resound, so that it was closer to ordinary speech than to singing. The custom of singing was instituted for the sake of the carnal, not the spiritual: because they are not pierced by words, they may be moved by the sweetness of melody.”

For the usefulness of ecclesiastical song, see John Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 17.

While everyone sits in orderly fashion and in rows on the benches [Col. 0437D]. “That is, on low seats, which are also called benches,” says Boherius. Smaragdus, however, seems here to make some distinction among *sedes*, *cathedrae*, and *subsellia*: *sedes* are the seats of kings, *cathedrae* those of teachers, and *subsellia* those of ordinary people.

“Glory” is to be said in the fourth responsory. In the ancient manuscript customs of Germany it is prescribed that “the fourth responsory of each nocturn, after ‘Glory,’ is to be repeated from the beginning and sung in a higher register.”

As soon as he begins it, let everyone rise reverently. Hildemar explains what it means to rise reverently in these words [Col. 0438A]:

> “They should not rise hastily, but honorably; with bowed heads they should remain bent until the cantor says, ‘To the Holy Spirit.’”

Bernard of Cassino explains the reverence in the same way, as a supplication and bowing, which should be such that the hands can be placed upon the knees. “Whoever does more or less,” says Hildemar, “must be led by degrees.” We have explained elsewhere what “to be led by degrees” means.

After these readings, let six other psalms follow in order, and so forth. “Blessed Benedict, aspiring to the summit of the more perfect life,” says John Belethus (*Explanation of the Divine Office*, chapter 23), “instituted that six psalms should be sung in the first nocturn, together with four readings and four responsories, and the same number in the second, so that through this he might clearly indicate to us the twofold life, contemplative and active. For the number six in the psalms signifies for us the active life, in which it is fitting to practice the six works of mercy if we wish successfully to reach the perfection of the contemplative life, which is likewise expressed here by the four readings, just as it is by the four Gospels” [Col. 0438B].

Three canticles from the prophets, which the abbot shall choose. Nicholas of Fractura adds: “with the counsel of his chapter.” These canticles ought to correspond to the season or feast being celebrated. Nevertheless, we sometimes find that psalms were sung in place of canticles. Thus, in the manuscript customs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, on the feast of the Dedication, the psalms *I Rejoiced*, *Unless the Lord*, and *Praise the Lord, Jerusalem* are assigned in place of canticles.

St. Isidore explains the difference between a canticle and a psalm in these words (Book I, *On the Offices of the Church*, chapter 4):

> “A canticle is a human voice; a psalm, however, is what is sung to the psalter.”

See John Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 16, § 12.

After the verse has been said and the abbot has given the blessing, let another four readings from the New Testament be read in the order given above. They are not, however, to be from the Gospel, since otherwise the brothers would be commanded to stand.

Let the abbot begin the hymn *Te Deum laudamus* [Col. 0438C]. The common opinion makes Ambrose and Augustine its authors, saying that it was composed while Augustine was being baptized by Ambrose, as is noted at the beginning of Dacius’s *Chronicle*, Book I, chapter 10. But since that chronicle does not bear the stamp of Dacius’s style and in any case contains many false statements, learned scholars generally regard it as not being his work. Consequently, the accounts concerning a hymn *Te Deum laudamus* composed by Ambrose and Augustine are altogether doubtful, if not entirely without credibility.

Who its author was remains unknown. Only Ambrose is believed to have been its author by Smaragdus and certain others. But in an unpublished letter of Abbo, abbot of Floriacum, it is attributed to St. Hilary, as I was informed by one of our own scholars who is engaged in preparing a new edition of this saint’s works.

Besides St. Benedict, St. Caesarius mentions this hymn in his *Rule for Monks*, chapter 21, and St. Aurelian in his *Order of Psalms*; both prescribe that it be sung at the morning praises. Alcuin, in his *Book on the Office*, calls it the Sunday hymn, perhaps because St. Benedict and all the ancient monks sang it on every Sunday without exception, including Advent and Lent, contrary to the general custom of the Church.

When the bishops assembled in councils in Gaul and Italy strongly disapproved of this and asked certain abbots and monks why they sang *Te Deum laudamus* at the vigils on Sundays of Advent and Lent, “they replied that they did this for no other reason than the command of the most distinguished and excellent Father, blessed Benedict, whose deeds and sayings had also been recorded and laudably confirmed by the supreme Roman pontiff, namely Gregory. When the bishops had learned these things, the monks’ custom prevailed as authoritative” [Note: [Col. 0438D] The phrase is evidently corrupt. Perhaps it should read: “When these things had been learned, the custom prevailed,” with *episcopi*—“the bishops”—removed from the sentence. EDIT.] Thus writes Rodulfus Glaber (*History*, Book III, chapter 3).

This practice was not peculiar to St. Benedict’s monks alone, for Amalarius shows in his *Supplement to Book IV on the Divine Offices* (Volume II of the *Analecta*) that it was observed by certain collegiate churches. Yet in his *Book on the Order of the Antiphonary*, chapter 2, he says that he asked a master of the Roman Church “whether they sang *Te Deum laudamus* on Sunday nights,” and that the answer given to him was: “We sing *Te Deum laudamus* only on the birthdays of pontiffs.”

When it has been completed, let the abbot read a Gospel reading [Col. 0439A] [281]. According to Hildemar and Rupert (Book II on the Rule of St. Benedict, chapter 7), this was done wearing a chasuble and stole, with two candlesticks and a thurible. We have described this rite in Book II of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 1.

The Master, in chapter 46 of his *Rule*, also entrusts the reading of the holy Gospel to the abbot, or, in his absence, to the provosts in rotation. Hariulf praises Gervinus, abbot of Centula, for observing this practice in Book IV, chapter 26 of his *Chronicle*.

For many centuries, however, the custom had become established that the weekly priest, not the abbot, should read the Gospel. Smaragdus explains the reason in these words:

> “For he says: ‘Let the abbot begin the hymn and read the Gospel.’ Yet not all abbots ought or are able to do these things. Some ought not to do so because of an impediment caused by guilt; others are unable because of a harmful incapacity. There are therefore abbots who perform neither the ministry of priest nor that of deacon and consequently cannot read the most holy Gospel. They do not hold the office of cantor and therefore cannot begin the Ambrosian hymn with a loud voice. Nevertheless, with heavenly assistance they can govern the flock entrusted to them, and for this reason they are chosen to carry out the office of abbot.”

Whether this was in fact the practice among the first fathers of monastic life or in the time of St. Benedict is unknown to us. It is nevertheless certain that they frequently read the Gospel in the synaxis, since on weekdays they had one reading from the New Testament and on Sundays and Saturdays two, while priests and deacons were not so common among them.

Whether ordination is absolutely necessary in order to read the Gospel at the vigils could also be questioned. Boherius resolves the issue by saying:

> “This reading, which takes place at the vigils, may be performed not only by someone who is not ordained, but even by a woman.”

He cites the *Extra*, title *On Penance and Remission*, chapter *Nova*; and *Sanctimoniales*, Causa 20, question 1. See Causa 16, question 1.

Why the holy Father ordered the holy Gospel to be read at the vigils, St. Hildegard explains in these words:

> “By commanding the Gospel to be read after the nocturns on Sundays and on other solemnities, he wishes it to be understood that at all times—both by night and by day—the message of God must be heard, fulfilled, and used in serving God. He also wishes the monks, after hearing the Gospel, to remember that Gospel passage: ‘Behold, we have left everything and followed you.’ He further intends that if, because of the scarcity of priests or because some impediment has intervened, anyone cannot have a Mass or attend Mass on that day, the Gospel that has been read and heard should be sufficient for him.”

With honor and trembling, while everyone stands. The words “with honor and trembling” may be referred either to the preceding words, “let the abbot read a Gospel reading,” or to the following words, “while everyone stands.” Hildemar and Boherius, in their first commentary, refer them to what precedes. Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura refer them to what follows.

“With honor,” says Nicholas, “because everyone must stand upright, with their hoods removed from their heads, while the Gospel reading is being read; with trembling, because we must understand and hear with great trembling the punishments and rewards promised to us through the Gospel.”

Boherius, by contrast, says:

> “With honor, because he is dressed in priestly vestments, because his head is uncovered, because he stands upright at the lectern facing the altar, and because there are light and incense.”

Hildemar likewise says: “With the chasuble, stole, two candlesticks, and thurible.”

While everyone stands. This follows the ancient custom handed down by the apostles, which is mentioned in the Liturgy of St. Mark: “Let us stand and hear the holy Gospel” [Note: [Col. 0439] “Let us stand and hear” seems to be the reading required; or at least the punctuation should be: “Stand; let us hear,” and so forth. EDIT.].

The Liturgy of St. Basil says: “The Gospel is read while everyone stands in fear and reverence.” The Apostolic Constitutions attributed to Clement (Book II, chapter 57) say: “When the Gospel is read, let the priests and deacons, and the whole people, stand in great silence.” St. Germanus, in his *Mystical Explanation*, says: “It is the word of God; let us hear the holy Gospel standing upright.”

Rodulfus, in the *Life of Rabanus*, no. 42 (*Saeculum* IV, Part II), writes:

> “When the solemn rites of Mass were being celebrated publicly in the church, and the Gospel reading was being read, everyone stood according to custom, in silence and reverence.”

Anastasius the Librarian writes that the same practice was confirmed by Pope Anastasius with apostolic authority, and the *Micrologus*, in his *Book on the Observance of the Church*, chapter 9, says the same.

There is a constitution of his on this subject in Gratian’s *Decree* (*On Consecration*, distinction 1, canon *Apostolica*) expressed in these words:

> “By apostolic authority we command that, while the holy Gospels are being recited in church, priests and all the other persons present are not to remain seated, but are to stand reverently, bowed before the sight of the holy Gospel, and are to hear the Lord’s words attentively and adore them faithfully.”

The reasons for this rite may be:

1. The honor and reverence due to the holy Gospel.
2. The fact that it is not fitting for others to sit while the reader of the holy Gospel is standing, “for whether he is the abbot himself or any other priest, he represents the person of our Lord Jesus Christ,” as Rupert says (Book II on the Rule of St. Benedict).
3. So that by this posture of our body we may demonstrate that, as true servants of God, we are always ready to carry out the commands that are proclaimed.

When it has been read, let everyone respond, “Amen.” This word is Hebrew and has two meanings. One is optative, namely, “let it be done”; in this sense it is used by the Church at the end of collects [Col. 0440C]. The other is affirmative, namely, “it is true.” It is in this sense that the holy Father Benedict uses it.

“For,” says Boherius, “everyone ought to attend to the words of God and, through the Amen, affirm that they are true, so that the mind of the hearer may agree with the voice of the teacher.”

Thus, with Smaragdus, one may rightly rebuke those who, with shameless recklessness, have dared to accuse the holy Father of having foolishly and improperly ordered that Amen be said at the end of the Gospel. Certainly, in the Mass of the Mozarabs, Amen is answered at the end of the Epistle, the prophecies, and the Gospel.

Alexander of Hales writes of the same practice as follows (*On the Office of the Mass*, in Part IV of the *Summa*):

> “After the Gospel has been read, those assisting say ‘Amen’: ‘May God cause us to persevere in the teaching of the Gospel.’ Others say ‘Thanks be to God,’ in thanksgiving for the benefit of such great and salutary teaching.”

John Belethus, a doctor of Paris who lived approximately five hundred years ago, says likewise (*Explanation of the Divine Office*, chapter 39):

> “Once the Gospel has been read, everyone ought to say ‘Amen’; or, as others wish, immediately after the Gospel has been recited, we ought to say ‘Thanks be to God,’ as after every reading or chapter. But it is better that ‘Amen’ be said.”

Incidentally, it is worth reporting what Boherius notes in his second commentary: that St. Isidore, bishop of Seville, instituted in the office of the Mass that, after each petition of the Lord’s Prayer, the clergy should answer “Amen”; but to the petition “Give us this day our daily bread” they should answer, “You are God.”

And immediately afterward let the abbot sing the hymn *Te decet laus* [Col. 0441A]. This is believed to be the same hymn that is expressed in these words in the *Apostolic Constitutions* attributed to Clement of Rome (Book VII, chapter 49):

> “To you is due praise, to you is due a hymn, to you is due glory, O God the Father, through the Son, in the Holy Spirit, for ever and ever. Amen.”

Nevertheless, it is called an Ambrosian hymn in Book I of the *Miracles of St. Richarius*, abbot, chapter 6, copied from an ancient author (*Saeculum* II of the Benedictine edition).

And after the blessing has been given, let them begin Matins.] What that blessing is, interpreters do not agree. First, Columbanus Uranx thinks that it signifies the blessing given when, at the beginning of Matins, “O God, come to my assistance” is said—that is, when the sign of the cross is made, through which a blessing is customarily given. Afterwards, however, he says that this blessing designates Psalm 66, at whose beginning and end it is said, “May God bless us.” This is put forward without foundation.

Second, “Some people indeed,” says Boherius in his second commentary, “and Gratianus as well in the canon, have wanted this blessing to be understood as the one given to those entering and leaving the kitchen duty; but that blessing is given, of course, when Matins has ended, as is clear below concerning the weekly kitchen servants.”

Third, “Perhaps,” the same Boherius adds, “the blessing was then given which today is specially reserved by particular right to bishops or privileged abbots; for at that time it was even more common.” But Bernard of Cassino contradicts this opinion in these words: “The blessing is not that which prelates solemnly give, because it is not proper for every abbot to say or give it; rather, that blessing is called the prayer customarily said after the Gospel.”

Nevertheless, Amalarius seems to indicate that the blessing is something other than the collect, writing in the Supplement as follows (Vol. II of the *Analecta*): “The blessing, however, which is said after the collect, while the abbot is reciting the Gospel, and with which they thus begin Matins, shows our prayers, etc.” But I fear that the reading should be *per collectam*, “through the collect,” rather than *post collectam*, “after the collect.” For Saint Hildegard, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius in his first commentary, John de Turrecremata, Antonius Perez, Theobaldus Artaldus, Nicholas Bravus, Benedict Haeften, and finally Cardinal John Bona all maintain that by the name “blessing” a prayer, or collect, is to be understood. Bona expresses his view as follows (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 16, § 17):

“I confess that I have often wondered what the blessed Father meant by the blessing which he wishes to be given before Lauds begins. For all the monks recite the collect of the current office, and Lauds follows immediately afterward. But at last I found Amalarius Fortunatus, who solved the difficulty. ‘The bishop,’ he says (Book II, chapter 9), ‘or the priest says, “Let us pray,” and then the blessing follows.’ The priest’s prayer is called by both names, blessing and prayer. Concerning the blessing the Apostle says: ‘If you bless in the spirit, how will the one who fills the place of the unlearned say “Amen” over your blessing, since he does not know what you are saying?’ Ambrose calls this blessing a prayer, saying: ‘The unlearned hearer, not understanding what he hears, does not know the end of the prayer and does not answer “Amen,” that is, “true,” so that the blessing may be confirmed.’”

The same point he confirms shortly afterward by the authority of Saint Augustine, who uses “blessing” for “prayer” (*On the Gift of Perseverance*, chapter 23): “Or would anyone dare to criticize, whether by voice or at least in thought, a priest invoking the Lord over the faithful when he has said, ‘Grant him, Lord, to persevere in you to the end,’ rather than responding to such a blessing of his with believing heart and confessing mouth, ‘Amen’?”

Certainly Saint Benedict himself calls the prayers and petitions to be said over the weekly kitchen servants, below in chapter 35, and over the reader at table, in chapter 38, a blessing (*Constitutions of Monte Oliveto*, Part I, chapter 11). But Saint Benedict does not state whether this blessing is to be said by the abbot; for this reason, in the congregation of Monte Oliveto it is said by the weekly officer.

Let this order of Vigils be observed equally on Sunday throughout the whole year, in summer as in winter.] What he says by “equally” must be understood with respect to the number of readings, psalms, responsories, and so forth, but not with respect to the length or drawn-out manner of the things being said, as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius explain. For although twelve readings must be said both in summer and in winter, they are not to be equally extended in summer and winter.

[Col. 0442A] Unless, perhaps—which God forbid—they rise later, something must be shortened from the readings or the responsories.] Nearly the same provision is made in the Rule of Saint Caesarius for virgins, cited by Bollandus (January 12): “But if it should happen that they rise later for Vigils, let them read single pages, or as much as seems good to the abbess; it will be in her power that, when she gives the signal, the one who is reading should rise without delay, so that the canonical number of Masses may be completed.” Almost the same words also occur in the Rule of Saint Aurelian in the order of psalmody.

But just as the readings were shortened if they had risen late, so conversely, when they rose earlier, the readings were lengthened. Hence the *Book of Cistercian Usages*: “When the sacristan sees that they have risen earlier than they ought, he customarily warns the cantor by a signal to prolong the twelfth reading.” From this one may readily conclude that formerly the readings were not divided as they now exist in our breviaries, nor was their length or brevity fixed. Rather, a book of Sacred Scripture or of some holy Father was brought forward, and they read continuously from it, so that when one person stopped, another began to read.

Thus the ancient customs of Germany, in manuscripts, state: “From the Kalends of November, on ordinary days, it is customary at Nocturns to perform three continuous readings from the prophets and the other books of the library; if the feast days of the saints occur, let them do nothing else on that account.” They therefore read Scripture and the other books of the library continuously—that is, without any division or distinction of readings—which they ended at the abbot’s discretion, as we have just read in the Rules of Saint Caesarius and Saint Aurelian: “Let as much be read as seems good to the abbot; when he gives the signal, let the one who is reading rise without delay.” What that signal was, he does not explain.

The ancient monks in Egypt, who interrupted the longer psalms, brought the singing to an end by striking their hands against their seats. “If any of the younger monks,” says Cassian (*Book II*, chapter 11), “either through spiritual fervor or because he has not yet been trained, begins to exceed the proper measure of the singing, the progress of the elder who is chanting is interrupted by a clap; he strikes his hand against the seat on which he is sitting and makes everyone rise for prayer.” I have no doubt that they ended the readings in precisely the same way.

In the royal basilica of Charlemagne, readings were ended by the sound made in the emperor’s throat, as can be seen in *Book I on the Ecclesiastical Care of Charlemagne*, where chapter 7 reads as follows: “He [the emperor Charles] indicated the end of the reading by a sound from his throat. To this all were so attentively responsive that, whether he gave the signal after a sentence had been completed, in the middle of a distinction, or under a subdivision, no one who followed began above or below, however unsuitable the beginning or end might seem.”

In very many monasteries, however, the practice had prevailed that the readings for the following day were ended by someone entrusted with this responsibility, who indicated to each reader what and how much he ought to read. This person was usually the cantor or armarius: “The readings are to be ended and corrected by the armarius on the preceding day,” state the manuscripts of the *Customs of Germany*. And the *Book of Cistercian Usages* (chapter 11) says: “On the first Sunday of Septuagesima … let the reading of Genesis, or of the other books mentioned, be begun at the place where the cantor has foreseen that the readings of the Vigils must be ended up to Lent.” And below (chapter 16): “On these days let the cantor divide the book of the prophet Jeremiah both in the church and in the refectory.” See Udalricus, Book I, chapter 1.

They marked the end of the readings either by placing wax there or by pressing a fingernail into the codex: “No one placed wax at the stopping point, or at least impressed even the slightest mark with his fingernail; rather, all took care to make themselves familiar with everything that had to be read, so that whenever they were unexpectedly ordered to read, they would be found blameless before him,” says the aforementioned book *On the Ecclesiastical Care of Charlemagne*. These words indicate that others followed the opposite custom.

I return to the text of Saint Benedict, who ordered not only the readings but also the responsories to be shortened. How this could be done is not easy to explain. Bernard of Cassino thinks that they could be shortened by drawing them out less and using a less elaborate melody, or even by reciting them straight through without singing, adding nevertheless: “Let the one who sees better say it better.” Nicholas of Fractura holds the same view.

Boherius nevertheless thinks that no inconvenience would result if, in such cases, the number of readings or responsories were reduced. Hildemar, however, contradicts him in these words: “The number of readings is not to be shortened, but the length of the readings, so that, although there are twelve, they may nevertheless be shorter than they should be.” Saint Benedict therefore wished the sacred number of twelve readings to be retained; the Gallican churches also formerly observed it, as is clear from the Gallican liturgy, Book II, p. 106.

But if it should happen, let the person through whose negligence it occurred make worthy satisfaction to God in the oratory.] Saint Benedict does not say what that satisfaction should be, but the commentators explain it to some extent. “After Matins has been completed,” says Hildemar, “and after the weekly kitchen servants have gone out or entered, the person through whose negligence it occurred must stand bent over before the altar for as long as it takes the brothers to go outside.”

And Boherius: “He will remain prostrate there on the ground until the abbot judges that satisfaction has been made; or he will certainly not intone a psalm and antiphon in the choir until then, etc.; or perhaps this will be the punishment in the oratory: he will not stand in his place in the choir, but in a place where he can be seen by everyone in disgrace.”

In a manuscript book of the *Usages of the Monastery of Bec* it is decreed: “If it should happen that they rise so late for Vigils that the collect of Lauds can be said in daylight, all the sacristans must make satisfaction there in the oratory where blessed Benedict commands. When ‘Kyrie eleison’ is said at Lauds, let them prostrate themselves in the choir and lie there until the priest says after the collect, ‘Through the Lord.’ After this satisfaction, let them make no other; whoever wishes to do so must make amends in the chapter.”

Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura think that this was left to the abbot’s discretion. Whatever the case, Saint Benedict certainly says two things here.

First, the satisfaction must be worthy: “let him make worthy satisfaction,” that is, according to the seriousness or lightness of the negligence. For according to Hildemar, the one whose negligence is greater must make satisfaction not only at Matins but also at Prime or Terce; the one whose negligence is lesser must do so only at Matins. The seriousness of the negligence, according to the same Hildemar, is inferred either from the length of time by which they rose late or from the attitude and intention of the negligent brother.

Second, the satisfaction must be made in the oratory, “so that,” says Smaragdus, “because he sinned by acting negligently in the presence of all the brothers, he may be seen by all making satisfaction, and mercy may be entreated from the Almighty for his offense.”

## CHAPTER XII. How the solemnity of Matins is to be conducted

[Col. 0443]

[Col. 0443B] On Sundays at Matins, first let Psalm 66 be said without an antiphon, straight through. After it, let Psalm 50 be said with “Alleluia.” After it, let Psalm 117 and Psalm 62 be said. Then the Blessings and Lauds, one reading from the Apocalypse recited from memory, and a responsory, and [Note: [Col. 0443B] The conjunction *et* is lacking in Flor. and in two manuscripts.] the Ambrosian hymn, a verse [Note: [Col. 0443B] Oxon., *versum*.], a canticle from the Gospel, a litany [Note: [Col. 0443B] Oxon., *litaniae*. Narb., *letaniae*. Cass., Flor., and certain others, *letania*. Some editors give the remainder of the chapter, beginning with this word, in the accusative.]: and it is complete.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0443]

[Col. 0443C] At Matins.] That is, at Lauds, which the ancients called *matutini* (“Matins”) from *matuta*, meaning dawn, because they began at its rising. Today, however, by the name *matutini* we understand the nighttime Vigils, which were also formerly called by this name, as our Menardus proves from the Second Council of Tours, canon 18, and Mabillon in Book II of *The Ancient Gallican Liturgy*. Thus Bede says in the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 45 (*Benedictine Century II*): “He completed the entire period of the nocturnal or matutinal psalmody standing.” The anonymous author of the *Life of Saint Austreberta*, no. 15 (*Benedictine Century III, Part I*), says: “One day, when Matins had been completed, and the sisters, their bodies weary after their labor, had placed themselves in their beds.”

On Sunday, first let Psalm 66 be said.] There is no mention here of the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” which Menardus and Haeften, Book VII, tract 7, disputation 2, therefore think should be omitted in accordance with the Rule, moved especially by this expression of Saint Benedict, “first.” I would nevertheless agree with Boherius that it should be said beforehand. For although Saint Benedict is silent about it, since he placed it before all the hours, I cannot persuade myself that he omitted it only at Matins, especially since no reason supports this; for the argument that it is implicitly contained in the first two verses of Psalm 66 could equally be made concerning the other hours.

Psalm 66.] He wished this psalm—in which we ask God that his face may shine upon us—to be said first, so that just as we then begin to be illuminated by the bodily sun, our mind may likewise be illuminated by God, the true Sun of Justice, for recognizing and following the way of truth and justice.

And because the chief light of our soul rests especially in faith in the Most Holy Trinity, we invoke it in its three persons, saying: “May God bless us,” namely, the Father; “our God,” namely, the Son; “may God bless us,” namely, the Holy Spirit. Here it may incidentally be noted that the Son is called “our” God among the others because, although the Father and the Holy Spirit are truly our God, the Son is most properly ours through the assumption of our nature, by which he deigned to become our flesh and our brother, as Bernard of Cassino observes.

Without an antiphon, straight through.] What it means to be said “without an antiphon” he explains by adding “straight through”: there is to be no modulation in a fixed tone, say the aforementioned Bernard and Boherius.

After it, let Psalm 50 be said with Alleluia.] He commands Psalm 50 to be sung with “Alleluia,” and Hildemar judges that the following psalms are likewise to be said in the same manner, although Saint Benedict is silent about this, since almost all of them are sung with Alleluia.

Nor is there no mystery in his wishing Psalm 50, which pertains to penitence and mourning, to be sung with “Alleluia,” the voice of exultation and joy. For this indicates that the lament of penitence always has attached to it the jubilation of inner joy, as Bernard of Cassino teaches. Or he may also have had regard for the following psalms, almost all of which are sung with Alleluia, and did not wish Psalm 50 to differ from them. Bernard likewise says that this was the view of Paul the Deacon, although Hildemar, whom he regularly cites under the name of Paul the Deacon, says nothing whatever about it.

After it, let Psalm 117 be said.] This psalm speaks of Christ’s resurrection, which we celebrate on Sunday; consequently, just as Saint Benedict prescribes it, Saints Caesarius and Aurelian prescribe that it be said at Sunday Matins.

And Psalm 62.] As Bernard of Cassino observes, this psalm contains two things especially appropriate to this hour: “O God, my God, to you I keep watch from the dawn,” and “in the morning I will meditate on you.” Perhaps for this reason Saint Athanasius prescribes that it be recited by holy virgins in the morning in his book *On Virginity*, as do Clement in the *Constitutions*, Book II, chapter 59, and Saint Aurelian in the *Order of Psalmody*. Cassian, Book III, chapter 3, testifies that the ancient monks likewise customarily sang it in the morning.

Then the Blessings.] Saint Caesarius in the Rule, chapter 21, Saint Aurelian in the *Order of Psalmody*, and the Master in the Rule, chapter 39, also decree that the Blessings be said at Matins. Mention is likewise made of the Blessings to be said at Matins in Gregory of Tours, *Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6.

Bernard of Cassino explains what the Blessings are in these words: “The Blessings are the song of the three boys in Daniel.” This is the song which Saint Athanasius established for virgins to sing as day was dawning, and which Alcuin calls the “Hymn of hymns” in his book *On the Use of the Psalms*.

And Lauds.] What “Lauds” means here can be gathered to some extent from Saint Aurelian’s *Order of Psalmody*, where it is prescribed: “After the blessing: ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens’; ‘Sing to the Lord a new song’; ‘Praise the Lord in his holy places.’”

Indeed, the commentators teach that Saint Benedict understands these three psalms, to be said under one “Glory,” by the term “Lauds.” He calls them “Lauds” in the plural either because there are several psalms, as Boherius says in his first commentary, or because we are invited several times to praise the Creator. The Egyptian monks recited these psalms in the morning, as Cassian testifies in Book III, chapter 6. Saint Caesarius also prescribes in the Rule for Monks, chapter 2, that at Matins they say “the Blessing” and “Praise the Lord from the heavens.”

Concerning this institution of Saint Benedict, Peter Damian writes as follows (*Opusculum* 10, chapter 2):

“Matins consists of five praises, namely four psalms and one canticle. Appropriately, when the daylight breaks forth, we offer praises to God, because beneath the appearance of external light we await the Sun of Justice shining upon our hearts. And just as the Church, full of joy and exultation, goes out to meet the bridegroom who is coming, so she is adorned with five praises, as though with an equal number of lamps received; and as though the cry of her final exultation had already been conceived in the ear of her heart—‘Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him’—the words are fulfilled in outward form: ‘Then all those virgins arose and trimmed their lamps.’

“That a canticle is daily joined to the psalms in this office of morning praise seems to breathe the mystery of both lives, namely the contemplative and the active. The Psalter, indeed, formed like a vessel in the shape of the letter delta, is played by a plectrum upon ten strings; but the canticle is expressed solely by the instrument of the voice. Therefore the former, because it requires the hands, signifies work and thus the active life; the latter, because it pertains to jubilation, signifies the contemplative life.

“And because we can scarcely persist in contemplation, briefly and hurriedly, even for a moment, while we are continually occupied in the administration of active conduct, we rightly insert one canticle among several psalms. Just as we ascend from the exercise of pious action to the summit of contemplation, and after the briefest instant of inner vision immediately descend again to the ministry of the same active life—so that our contemplation may begin from the active life and necessarily end in it—we neither place the canticle before the psalms nor put it altogether after them. Rather, positioned among them, we always place it second to last.

“Moreover, because throughout the four seasons of the entire year we weary our body, likewise composed of four elements, through the exercise of action, we therefore sing four psalms in the celebration of this morning office. But because in the ecstasy of contemplation we seek only one thing, which is certainly God, we sing one canticle likewise.”

One reading from the Apocalypse recited from memory.] That is, to be recited by heart, without a codex. Hildemar teaches that this reading must always be from the Apocalypse on all Sundays, whatever solemnity may fall on them, even Christmas or Easter. If someone objects that the reading ought to correspond to the solemnity of the day and season, he admits that this is indeed so, but nevertheless maintains that readings appropriate to any feast can easily be drawn from the Apocalypse. The same is to be understood when Saint Benedict instituted that a reading be recited from the Apostle.

And a responsory.] Saint Benedict did not make clear whether it should be said with the “Glory.” Consequently, different communities followed different practices in this matter. John Bona speaks as follows of his Cistercians (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 18, § 4): “For the responsories after the chapter we do not add ‘Glory be to the Father,’ since the Rule makes no mention of them.”

Although the Rule is silent, Hildemar nevertheless asserts that it should be said in accordance with the mind of Saint Benedict, because Saint Benedict always wished “Glory” to be said at the end of the final responsory. Since this is the sole and only responsory, it is considered both first and last and therefore is to be sung with “Glory.” Hildemar reasons in almost this way in his commentary on chapter 14.

A canticle from the Gospel.] Saint Benedict does not state which canticle this is, that of Zechariah or that of Mary. Although the common practice of the universal Church has now become established that the canticle *Benedictus* be said at Matins, and I do not think we should depart from it, I nevertheless find that the ancient monks also sang the *Magnificat*.

Thus Saint Aurelian, in the *Order of Psalmody*, prescribes that at Matins, along with many other things, they say: “After the Blessing, ‘Praise the Lord from the heavens’; ‘Sing to the Lord a new song’; ‘Praise the Lord in his holy places,’ with Alleluia; ‘My soul magnifies the Lord,’ either with an antiphon or with Alleluia; the hymn ‘Glory to God in the highest’; and the little chapter.”

Here it may incidentally be noted that Saint Caesarius also prescribes the angelic hymn “Glory to God in the highest” in the Rule for Monks, chapter 21, and Athanasius earlier in his book *On Virginity*. Similarly, Abbot Alexander the Sleepless is said to have instituted that “after the sequence of the office had been completed, the readings observed, and the ministries performed, they should sing the hymn of the holy angels seventy-seven times by night and by day. It is this: ‘Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, goodwill among men.’”

And it is complete.] “That is, with the blessing, namely ‘Let us bless’; otherwise, according to the Council of Agde, the people or assembly of monks ought not to be dismissed from the church,” says Boherius in his second exposition.

## CHAPTER XIII. How Matins is to be conducted on ordinary days

[Col. 0445]

[Col. 0445D] On ordinary days, the solemnity of Matins is to be conducted as follows: that is, so that [Note: [Col. 0445D] *ut* is lacking in Flor., Hild., and Comp.] Psalm 66 is said [Note: [Col. 0447A] *dicatur* is lacking in Hild.] without an antiphon, with a slight shortening, as on Sunday [Note: [Col. 0447A] Oxon., “on Sunday”]. so that everyone may arrive for Psalm 50, which is to be said with an antiphon.

After it, let two other psalms be said according to custom: that is, on Monday, Psalms 5 and 35; on Tuesday, Psalms 42 and 56; on Wednesday, Psalms 63 and 64; on Thursday, Psalms 87 and 89; on Friday, Psalms 75 and 91; but on Saturday, Psalm 142 and the Canticle from Deuteronomy, which is to be divided into two “Glories.” On the other days, let each canticle be said on its appointed day from the prophets, as the Roman Church sings it. [Note: [Col. 0447A] Flor., *unumquemque*, “each one,” instead of *unumquodque*, “each.”]

After these, let Lauds follow; then one reading from the Apostle [Note: [Col. 0447A] Sabin., “from the Apocalypse.”] to be recited from memory, a responsory, the Ambrosian hymn, a verse, a canticle from the Gospel, a litany [Note: [Col. 0447A] Oxon., *litaniae*; others, *letania*.]: and it is complete.

Plainly, the morning or evening office is never to pass away [Note: [Col. 0448A] Oxon., *transeant*.] without the Lord’s Prayer being said at the end, in due order, by the prior, with everyone listening, because of the thorns of scandals that commonly arise, so that those who have been summoned [Note: [Col. 0448A] Five manuscripts, “so that the converted”; Bernard of Cassino, “so that those who have been convicted”; Sabinus, “so that when they have come to him,” etc.] may cleanse themselves of such a vice through the pledge of that prayer, in which they say, “Forgive us as we also forgive” [Note: [Col. 0448A] Flor., Conch., Dion., and Boherius add “our debts.”]. In the other offices, let the final part of that prayer be said, so that all may answer, “But deliver us from evil.”

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0447]

[Col. 0447B] But on ordinary days, the solemnity of Matins is to be conducted as follows, that is, so that Psalm 66 is said without an antiphon, with a slight shortening, as on Sunday.] “With a slight shortening” means not singing so rapidly, or even singing somewhat less loudly, says Bernard of Cassino. Just as he wished Psalm 94 at Vigils to be prolonged and sung slowly, so at Matins he wished Psalm 66 to be sung in this manner.

So that everyone may arrive for Psalm 50.] Not one already begun, but one that is about to begin—so that, when the “Glory” of Psalm 66 has ended, everyone has already arrived, while those who come later make satisfaction, as Bernard of Cassino explains after Hildemar.

Which is to be said with an antiphon.] Saint Benedict says nothing about antiphons for the remaining psalms. Hence John Bona, speaking of his Cistercians (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 18, § 4), says: “At Lauds we say only one antiphon, according to whose melody we sing all the psalms.”

After it, let two other psalms be said according to custom.] The custom which he himself instituted, or, as Bernard of Cassino puts it, “according to the custom of the monks who were then in that monastery of Cassino,” not according to that of other churches.

That is, on Monday, etc.] Among the ancients, *feriae* were feast days, so called from the victims that they sacrificed on those days. But here Blessed Benedict understands by *feriae* ordinary days, just as we read that Pope Sylvester decreed in the readings recited at the Vigil of his feast:

“While retaining the names of Saturday and Sunday, he wished the remaining days of the week to be distinguished and called by the name of weekdays, as they had already begun to be called in the Church, so that it might be signified that every day the clergy ought, having cast aside care for other things, devote themselves entirely to God alone.”

Psalms 5 and 35, etc.] Here they ask why, disrupting the order of the psalms, Saint Benedict chose these psalms from different places. Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius following him, answer:

First, the authority of the one who established the rule is sufficient, since a man filled with the spirit of all the righteous did not choose these psalms for Matins without a reasonable cause and mystery.

Second, with Hildemar, something is contained in each of these psalms, either expressly or mystically, that pertains to the hour of Matins. Hildemar demonstrates this at greater length.

For on the other days let each canticle be said on its appointed day, as the Roman Church sings it.] That is, let the same canticles that the Roman Church sings be said; or, just as the Roman Church sings a particular canticle every day, so should we, whether the same canticles or others.

[Col. 0448B] A reading from the Apostle to be recited from memory.] You will learn how meritorious it is to obey this provision of the Rule from Book III of the *Revelations of Saint Gertrude*, chapter 82.

Plainly, the morning or evening office, etc.] Boherius explains what *agenda* means in these words: “*Agenda* is a substantive noun; for in certain regions the canonical hours are so called.” Menardus says: “*Agenda* is the office of a particular hour, the divine office, the course of the divine office, an annual celebration, the work of God, as below in this chapter: ‘in the other offices.’ Gregory’s Antiphoner says: ‘In the office of the dead, the antiphon “Eternal rest”’; and Anastasius the Librarian, in his account of Leo II, says: ‘And lest the anniversary or office of the Moorish bishop should be celebrated.’”

Let it never pass without the Lord’s Prayer being said at the end, in due order, with everyone listening, etc.] Saint Benedict prescribes here many things of the greatest importance.

First, that the Lord’s Prayer be said at the end of all the canonical hours. This is undoubtedly because of the excellence of that prayer, which Boherius commends chiefly for three reasons:

First, its dignity, because the Master of masters composed it.

Second, its brevity—and, he says, for many reasons: it is brief so that it may be better known, more easily retained, more fervently said, less burdensome to the one saying it, so that no one may excuse himself through ignorance, so that it may indicate that the Lord hears quickly, and so that it may signify that prayer ought to be made more through devotion than through the voice.

Third, its fruitfulness, because it contains all petitions within itself.

Saint Augustine, or whoever else the author may be, explains this last point as follows (*Sermon 64*, in the appendix): “This prayer, in concise words—that is, in seven petitions—contains all the kinds of prayer by which we appeal to God, whether for things to be desired, for evils to be avoided, or for offenses to be removed.” Alardus Gazaeus explains these three points fully and appropriately from the holy Fathers in his commentary on Cassian’s *Conference* 9, chapter 18.

Perhaps because of these prerogatives, “it was the custom of the apostles,” says Saint Gregory, “to consecrate the sacrificial offering only for this prayer”—the Lord’s Prayer. Saint Clement, in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, Book VII, chapter 25 (Epistle 63), warns Christians to recite it three times a day. At the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 9, priests and the other clergy are commanded to say the Lord’s Prayer daily, because it is a daily prayer. Finally, at the Council of Rheims, canon 2, we read: “No Christian is permitted either not to know the Lord’s Prayer by heart, or not to understand it, or not to practice it frequently.”

Second, Saint Benedict prescribes that the Lord’s Prayer be said aloud at Lauds and Vespers. This is recorded as having been decreed at the Council of Gerunda, held in the year 517 (canon 10), in these words: “It has always pleased us likewise to observe that every day, after Matins and Vespers, the Lord’s Prayer be pronounced by the priest.”

Durandus says (*Book V of the Rationale*, chapter 2) that in the primitive Church it was pronounced aloud after every hour, without any other prayer; and, he says, the Lateran Church is still said to observe this. Abbot Isaac, in Cassian (*Conference* 9, chapter 22), implies that it was likewise sung aloud in church when, explaining the words “And forgive us our debts,” and so forth, he says:

“We are forgiven only as much as we forgive those who have harmed us by whatever wickedness. Fearing this, some people, when this prayer is sung in church by the whole people, silently omit this passage, lest by their profession they seem to bind themselves rather than excuse themselves.”

When he says that the prayer is sung by the whole people, he seems to refer to the statement of Saint Gregory (*Book VII*, letter 63): “Among the Greeks the Lord’s Prayer is said by the whole people, but among us by the priest alone”—namely, at Mass.

Third, that it be said by the prior. “That is, by the abbot,” says Boherius, “or, in his absence, by the claustral prior, or finally by the one who performs the greater office at the altar; for he is naturally the prior of all in the office of the altar.”

Alardus Gazaeus likewise understands “prior” in his commentary on Cassian, Book VIII, chapter 8, to mean the weekly priest. But I have understood it more truly, with Bernard of Cassino, to mean the abbot or president of the choir, who asserts that in his own time this practice had fallen into disuse in the monastery of Cassino.

Because of the thorns of scandals that commonly arise.] Smaragdus explains what the thorns of scandals are in these words:

“The thorns of scandals are understood here to be anger, quarrels, dissensions, detractions, rivalries, or certain disputes and disturbances that commonly arise among the brothers. The monks ought to cleanse themselves from these morning and evening, maintaining peace among themselves and preserving continual charity.”

[Col. 0449C] So that those who have been summoned.] “That is, persuaded or drawn,” says Smaragdus; or, as Hildemar says: “Summoned, that is, conquered, broken, overcome, compelled.” Or finally, as Menardus says: “Summoned, that is, addressed—namely, through the pact and pledge of the prayer; for *convenire* means ‘to address,’” which he proves by the authority of Nonius Marcellus, chapter 4.

Through the pledge of that prayer, etc.] That is, the pact which God is said to have made with us, and we with God, as it were: that he will forgive us if we forgive, and will not forgive if we do not forgive.

Here Saint Benedict seems to have had in mind those who, as Abbot Isaac said just above in Cassian, when the Lord’s Prayer was sung by the whole people, silently omitted this passage, lest by their profession they seem to bind rather than excuse themselves.

Concerning this petition of the Lord’s Prayer, it should further be noted that the Pelagians, who considered themselves righteous, did recite the Lord’s Prayer; but they said this petition, “Forgive us our debts,” not for themselves but for others—or, if they said it for themselves, only as an act of humility. For this reason the Council of Milevis, or rather the Council of Carthage, condemned them in canons 7 and 8, and rightly so. For who will be justified in the sight of the Lord while living?

“We sin every day either in thought or in word,” say the Fathers of the Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 9; “every day we ought to pour forth this prayer in the sight of God. Therefore, whoever among the priests or subordinate clergy omits this Lord’s Prayer every day, whether in public or private office, shall be judged guilty of pride and deprived of his rank of honor.”

See Saint Augustine, letters 157, 176, and 178 of the new edition.

[Purge themselves of such a vice.] Namely, resentment, anger, dissension, and contention, just as Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, explains this passage when writing to Rotrude as follows (in Flodoard, *History of Rheims*, book III, chapter 27): “You know that the Rule which you have professed commands that, because of the thorns of scandals which customarily arise in a monastery, the Lord’s Prayer be recited by the prior at the morning and evening offices, so that all may hear it, in order that, fearing the agreement expressed in our saying, ‘Forgive us our debts, as we also forgive our debtors,’ we may drive all resentment from our heart.” Moreover, after Hildemar, Durandus teaches (*Rationale*, book III, chapter 3) that Saint Benedict wished the Lord’s Prayer to be sung aloud for two reasons: namely, on account of the simple and the crafty. On account of the simple, so that, hearing the Lord’s Prayer, they might retain it in memory; but Haeften rightly refutes this reason (*book VII, treatise 8, discussion 3*). On account of the crafty, who, if they recited the Lord’s Prayer silently, would omit the petition concerning the forgiveness of sins, lest they perhaps bind themselves with a double bond.

[For the other things to be done.] That is, at the canonical hours.

Let the final part of that prayer be said, so that all may respond, “But deliver us from evil.”] He wished the Lord’s Prayer to be pronounced aloud only at the morning and evening hours because he did not wish the sun either to rise or to set upon our anger.

## CHAPTER XIV. How vigils are to be celebrated on the birthdays of the saints

[Col. 0449]

[Col. 0449C] On the festivals of the saints, or on all solemnities, let everything be done as we have said it is to be done on Sunday, except that the psalms, antiphons, or lessons belonging to that particular day are to be said. But the procedure written above is to be observed.

## COMMENTARY

295

[Col. 0449]

[Col. 0449D] Here Saint Benedict calls the festivals of the saints their “birthdays”; and we celebrate these in the Church chiefly for three reasons. Saint Augustine—or whoever else may have been the author—assigns the first in these words (*Sermon 220, in the Appendix*): “Whenever we celebrate the martyrdoms of the saints, we proclaim the praises of the Savior; and whenever we affirm their sufferings, we preach the glory of Christ,” thus fulfilling the prophetic wish: “Praise the Lord in his saints.” Saint Caesarius indicates the second reason when he says (*Sermon 225, in the Appendix to the Sermons of Saint Augustine*): “The solemnities of the martyrs are exhortations to martyrdoms, so that one may not be reluctant to imitate what one takes delight in celebrating.” The third reason is to implore their patronage with God. Saint Bernard seems to have noted these three reasons when he teaches that at the festivals of the saints three things are to be considered (*Sermon on the Vigil of Saints Peter and Paul*): namely, the saint’s assistance, his example, and our own shame.

Why, moreover, the deaths of the saints are called their birthdays is known to everyone: namely, because “then they began to be born into life, when they laid down their life for Life,” as Peter Damian puts it (*Sermon 23*).

[Col. 0450D] On the festivals of the saints, or on all solemnities.] Although “festival” and “solemnity” have almost the same meaning and are customarily used interchangeably, Hildemar nevertheless thinks that this distinction can be made between them: that “festival” refers to the birthdays of the saints, while “solemnity” refers to the mysteries of Christ. He also observes here that it is not without significance that Saint Benedict prefixed the universal term “all” to solemnities but omitted it before festivals: “On the festivals of the saints, or on all solemnities.” For not all festivals of the saints, but only the principal ones, are celebrated; whereas all the solemnities of Christ ought to be celebrated by the Church.

“Now the solemnities of Christ,” according to the same authority, “are the Nativity, Circumcision, Epiphany, Presentation in the Temple, the Lord’s Supper, Good Friday, Holy Saturday, Easter, Ascension, and Pentecost. The festivals of the saints regarded as principal are those of the Twelve Apostles, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Lawrence, Saint Mary in mid-August, Saint Martin, Saint Cecilia, Saint Agatha and Saint Agnes, and Saint Benedict during the days of Lent; and on the kalends of November the festival of All Saints is celebrated. All these are principal because they are celebrated throughout the whole world. In addition, the festivals of all the saints who rest in that city where their bodies have been buried are principal.” Thus far Hildemar.

Bernard seems to distinguish festivals from solemnities differently, in such a way that solemnities refer to the principal feasts of Christ or of the saints, while festivals seem to refer to other, less important occasions for which an office of twelve lessons is celebrated. But I would prefer Hildemar’s opinion, which is followed by Boherius and Menardus and is also indicated by Amalarius in the *Supplement*.

296

As we have said it is to be done on Sunday, so let it be done.] Boherius comments on this passage: “This adverb *as* indicates identity in the beginnings and endings of the vigils, but similarity in the middle, as follows, because it refers to the number and manner of recitation.” It is as though he said: the beginning of the vigils should be the same as on Sunday, namely, “God, [come] to [our] assistance”; “Lord, you will open my lips”; Psalms 3 and 94; and the ending should likewise be the same, namely, *Te Deum*, “Praise is fitting for you.” But the psalms, antiphons, lessons, and responsories are to be said not for Sunday but for the particular day itself; nevertheless, just as on Sunday twelve psalms and an equal number of lessons are said, so also the same number are to be said on all festivals of the saints and on all solemnities.

Except that the psalms, antiphons, or lessons belonging to that particular day are to be said.] The words “belonging to that particular day” can receive a double interpretation: either they mean the feast-day itself that is being celebrated and honored, or the weekday on which such a feast falls. According to Bernard of Cassino, some monks formerly defended the latter interpretation with great force of conviction, relying chiefly on the consideration that Saint Benedict commands the entire Psalter to be recited within a week. But Bernard of Cassino opposes two arguments to this opinion: first, the contrary custom, which is the best interpreter of laws; second, that Saint Benedict does not precisely command the entire Psalter to be recited within a week, but rather one hundred and fifty psalms, as he himself explains it. He could have added that, when Saint Benedict commanded the Psalter to be completed every week, he did not speak absolutely but hypothetically—that is, on the assumption that feasts would not occur, since they were rarer in those times.

Moreover, Bernard’s opinion, which is the common opinion and that of nearly everyone, can be strengthened by the following arguments as well.

1. The weekday psalms should no more be said than the weekday lessons and antiphons; for Saint Benedict speaks of all these in precisely the same way. Now it can easily be demonstrated that neither weekday lessons nor weekday antiphons ought to be said at the vigils of the saints. As for the lessons, the holy legislator prescribes twelve on feast days, so that the last four are always from the New Testament; but on winter weekdays only three are prescribed, and on summer weekdays only one, and that from the Old Testament. I therefore ask where the four lessons from the New Testament are to be obtained on those weekdays on which it is customary to read the Old Testament.

Likewise, as regards the antiphons, Saint Benedict assigns them to the first and second nocturns on Sundays, but only to the first on weekdays. Therefore, if weekday antiphons are said at the vigils of the saints, I do not see which antiphons are to be said in the second nocturn, as on Sunday, although the holy Father establishes that the entire procedure be observed. “But the procedure written above is to be observed.”

2. The Cistercians, who undertook to observe the Rule of Saint Benedict literally, retained the weekday psalms at all the daytime hours on the feasts of the saints, but, compelled by the authority of this chapter, changed them at the nocturns. Hence Cardinal Bona says: “At Vespers we never change the weekday psalms, in accordance with the intention of the Rule, which permits a change of psalms at the festivals only for the nocturnal vigils.”

3. When the Council of Aachen, wishing to restrain the excessive freedom of certain abbots to alter the order established by Saint Benedict for the office, decreed that monks should celebrate the office contained in the Rule of Saint Benedict, it nevertheless did not retain the weekday psalms, as can easily be gathered from Amalarius’s *Supplement*, written shortly after that council.

4. Although the popes did not wish to alter the order of psalmody established by Saint Benedict, as Walafrid Strabo teaches (*On Ecclesiastical Affairs*, chapter 23), there is no example or evidence by which it can be proved that weekday psalms were ever sung at the nocturnal vigils of the saints in any monastery of the Benedictine order. I say “at the vigils,” since this chapter concerns only the vigils, not the daytime hours, at which the Cistercians sing the weekday psalms.

These arguments seem to me to possess some weight; nevertheless, I readily leave them to each person’s free judgment.

[Col. 0452D] But the procedure written above is to be observed.] Namely, in the number of things to be said. From this it is clear that, according to the intention of the Rule, no festivals of saints with three lessons ought to be celebrated, but only festivals with twelve. Boherius therefore rightly wrote in his second commentary:

“Some celebrate three lessons for certain saints, and although lessons and responsories are recited concerning the saints, weekday psalms are nevertheless said; but such a mixture does not accord with this Rule. Nor is a festival of the saints approved unless twelve lessons are said, as on Sunday, to which this master expressly refers. Those who also wish to observe this Rule literally must correct this practice in every way.”

Perhaps for this reason we read in the Cassinese Declarations written in 1520: “Concerning the saints, nothing is to be done otherwise than with twelve lessons or a commemoration, except during octaves, at which time only three lessons are to be said.” When festivals with three lessons began among our communities, however, is unknown to us.

## CHAPTER XV. At what times the Alleluia is to be said

[Col. 0451]

[Col. 0451D] From holy Easter until Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0451D] Another reading: *Pentecosten*, with *ad* omitted], let the Alleluia be said without interruption, both in the psalms and in the responsories. But from Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0451D] Several manuscripts: *a Pentecosten*] until the beginning [Note: [Col. 0452D] Other readings: *in caput*; another: *caput*] of Lent [Col. 0452D], let it be said on all nights only with the six final psalms at the nocturnal offices. But on every Sunday outside the period before Lent, let the canticles, the morning office [Note: [Col. 0453A] Oxford manuscript: *a matutinis*; Florence manuscript: *matutinos*. Hildemar also notes that certain manuscripts read *ad matutinos*, which he rejects. *Compendium*: *matutina*; another: *matutinae*], Prime, Terce, Sext, and None be said with the Alleluia; but at Vespers with an antiphon [Note: [Col. 0454A] Oxford manuscript: *ante fana*]. [Col. 0454A] Responsories, however, are never to be said with the Alleluia except from Easter until Pentecost [Note: [Col. 0454A] Another reading: *usque Pentecosten*].

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0453]

[Col. 0453A] Saint Benedict established a special chapter concerning the Alleluia, as a divine and truly angelic utterance, to be sung only by angels—or certainly by human beings who imitate the angelic spirits in the purity of their life. By this utterance those heavenly spirits continually praise God in heaven, as the evangelist John testifies, having heard them do so (*Apocalypse* 19). The prophet Haggai is said to have been the first to sing it among human beings. As Epiphanius writes (*On the Life and Death of the Prophets*), Haggai sang “Alleluia” 517 years before Christ, when he saw the new structure of the Temple, so that what the venerable Tobias had foretold in prophetic spirit might be fulfilled: “All the streets of Jerusalem shall be paved with white and pure stone, and Alleluia shall be sung through the lanes” (*Tobit* 13).

Under the New Law, not only clerics or monks celebrated it, but also the other faithful of Christ, as Saint Jerome testifies (*Letter 17*): “Wherever you may turn, the farmer holding his plow sings Alleluia.” By this sign the nuns were summoned to the collect, as the same Saint Jerome writes (*Letter 27*). Even infants were taught to loosen their tongues first with this utterance, as may be gathered from the same author (*Letter 7*).

What the Alleluia is, and what it signifies, Saint Augustine—or whoever else may have been the author—briefly explains (*Sermon 243, in the Appendix*): “What is Alleluia? It is a Hebrew word. Alleluia: Praise the Lord; Alleluia: Praise God.” The Church nevertheless retained the Hebrew word, “because of its more sacred authority, although it could have been translated,” as the same holy teacher says (*On Christian Doctrine*, book II, chapter 11).

Although this word became so celebrated among Christians and was so greatly commended by the holy Fathers, it did not escape the attacks of the perverse, and it had its adversaries—especially Vigilantius, who, as Saint Jerome writes (*Against Vigilantius*), maintained that the Alleluia ought to be sung only during Eastertide. Perhaps in opposition to his error Saint Benedict wished the Alleluia to be sung throughout almost the entire year when he issued this chapter.

[Col. 0453C] From holy Easter until Pentecost.] As though he were saying, from the beginning of Easter until the end of Easter. For, as Hildemar writes, the entire Paschal season was called “Easter.”

Until Pentecost.] And its octave, as the same Hildemar interprets it.

299 Without interruption let the Alleluia be said, both in the psalms.] That is, at the end of the psalms, says Boherius.

[Col. 0453D] And in the responsories.] And also in the antiphons and verses, for the same principle applies, as practice confirms. As regards the antiphons, the Alleluia was sometimes placed at the end and sometimes at the beginning; for example: “Alleluia. Your saints, O Lord, etc.”; “Alleluia. In the shelter, etc.”

It was customary throughout this entire period for the Alleluia to be sung throughout the universal Church in honor of Christ’s resurrection, as is evident from these words of Saint Augustine (*Letter 55*): “That the Alleluia should be sung only during these fifty days is not observed everywhere; for on other days it is sung differently in different places, but during those days it is sung everywhere.”

But from Pentecost until the beginning of Lent.] That is, until the first Sunday of Lent, on which the Lenten observance began, at least in the West. For they did not yet observe the fast during those four preceding days; it is thought to have originated with the institution of Pope Gregory.

[Col. 0454A] Let it be said on all nights only with the six final psalms at the nocturnal offices.] Namely, on ordinary weekdays, as is prescribed in chapter 9. For on Sundays the six final psalms are to be said with an antiphon, according to chapter 11; only the canticles are to be sung with the Alleluia.

But on every Sunday outside Lent let the canticles, the morning office, Prime, Terce, Sext, and None be said with the Alleluia.] Hildemar comments on this passage:

“There are some who understand *matutini* as a genitive case, so that the meaning is ‘the canticles at the morning office,’ because they understand *cantica* to have been used for psalms, and say so. Those canticles which he commanded to be said at the vigils on Sunday do not create any difficulty, since he had already spoken of them above. But it is better for *cantica* to be nominative; likewise, *matutini* should also be nominative.”

It should be noted that Saint Benedict says “outside Lent,” because the custom always prevailed that the Alleluia was not sung during Lent—“a practice confirmed by the agreement of the universal Church in every part of the world,” as the Fourth Council of Toledo says (canon 10).

Outside Lent, however, the customs of the Churches varied. In Africa, according to Saint Isidore (*On the Ecclesiastical Offices*, book I, chapter 13), the Alleluia was sung only on Sundays and during the fifty days after the Resurrection, as a sign of the future resurrection and joy. He adds: “But among us, according to the ancient tradition of the Spaniards, except on fast days and during Lent, the Alleluia is sung at all times.”

Saint Benedict, however, does not even except the fast days. At present the general custom of the Church is to lay aside the Alleluia at Septuagesima. Hildemar believes that this happened because formerly the Lenten fast began at Septuagesima; when the custom of beginning the fast on that Sunday ceased, the ancient practice of laying aside the Alleluia at Septuagesima nevertheless remained.

Bernard of Cassino makes the same assertion, and says that some in his own time still observed the Lenten fast from Septuagesima. The following words of his show, however, that this must be understood of abstinence from flesh alone: “At other times it is permitted to eat meat, and from that point they begin to abstain.” Indeed, that the Lenten fast began at Septuagesima is clear from Alcuin’s letter to Charlemagne.

Commonly, however, Gregory the Great is made the author of this custom. According to the Roman *Breviary*, he “established that the Alleluia should be said outside the period contained between Septuagesima and Easter.” The Synod of Aachen also decreed (canon 30) that “the Alleluia should be laid aside at Septuagesima” by monks. This was not always accepted everywhere, however, so that everyone laid it aside at Septuagesima.

It is certain that the Cistercians retained it, as is clear from the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapters 10 and 13, and from Peter Abelard’s reproach (*Letter 5*): “You do not interrupt the Alleluia at Septuagesima according to the custom of the common Church, but retain it until Lent.” They certainly retained it until 1601, when, as John Craesbeeck writes, they began to lay it aside by decree of the general chapter. The Cistercians of the Reformed Congregation in Spain, however, had already laid it aside in the general chapter of 1557, as Angelus Manrique teaches in his series of abbots of the monastery of Palazuelos, under abbot 54.

Other Benedictine monks also retained it in the time of Radulph of Tongeren, a comparatively recent author, as he himself testifies in these words: “The Benedictines and Ambrosians retain the Alleluia until the Sunday of Lent.” The monks of Bursfeld retained it as well, according to their *Ordinary*, chapter 15.

Nor should this seem surprising among monks who were striving after stricter observance, since the Ambrosians and certain Churches in the time of Pope Gregory VII, as our Menardus observes, continued to sing the Alleluia until Lent. Indeed, in the most recent Ambrosian breviary issued by Saint Charles, it is stated that the Alleluia is to be laid aside on the Saturday before the first Sunday of Lent, and that in its place *Laus tibi, Domine*—“Praise to you, O Lord”—is to be taken up.

Amalarius writes in the *Supplement* (*Analecta*, volume II) that Saint Benedict derived this custom from the Ambrosian office.

Why the Alleluia is laid aside during Lent is explained by the Fourth Council of Toledo in these words (canon 11): “We have learned that certain priests of Spain sing the Alleluia during the days of Lent. We henceforth forbid this, decreeing that throughout all the aforesaid days of Lent the Alleluia is not to be sung, since this is a time not of joy but of mourning.”

But someone may ask why, after laying aside the Alleluia, we sing *Laus tibi, Domine*, which means the same thing. I reply that the Lord must be blessed at all times; but we retain the Latin expression because, as Amalarius says, the Latin language is humbler than the Hebrew and therefore more suitable to times of mourning and penance.

Indeed, the word *Alleluia* is an expression of joy and exultation; nothing but gladness is redolent in it. Hence it is reported in book IV of Saint Gertrude’s *Revelations*, chapter 27, that all the vowels are found in this word except the single vowel O, which signifies grief.

On this word, see Menardus, Haeften (*book VII, treatise 8, discussion 1*), and John Bona (*On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 16).

But at Vespers with an antiphon. Responsories, however, are never to be said with the Alleluia except from Easter until Pentecost.] Whether it is the feast of a saint or any other solemnity, the word “never” permits it at no time. Therefore neither on the Lord’s Nativity nor on his Epiphany.

“Thus,” says Hildemar, “we have omitted the very responsory, because it is sung with the Alleluia at Epiphany, since the Rule commands that responsories never be said with the Alleluia, and so forth.”

The Rule of the Master nevertheless prescribes (*chapter 45*) that “from the Nativity of the Lord until Epiphany all antiphons and responsories are to be sung day and night with the Alleluia.”

## CHAPTER XVI. How the divine offices are to be celebrated throughout the day

[Col. 0455]

[Col. 0455B] As the prophet says, “Seven times a day I have praised you” (*Psalm* 118). We shall fulfill this sacred number seven if we perform the offices of our service at the times of the morning office [Note: [Col. 0455B] Another reading: *si matutino*], Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline, because he said of these daytime hours: “Seven times a day I have praised you” [Note: [Col. 0455B] *Daytime* is absent in the Oxford manuscript and certain others]. For concerning the nocturnal vigils the same prophet says: “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you” (in the same place). Therefore, at these times let us offer praises to our Creator concerning the judgments of his justice—that is, at the morning office, Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and Compline [Note: [Col. 0456B] Narbonne manuscript: *completoria*]; and at night let us rise to give thanks to him.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0455]
