[Col. 0455C] Saint Benedict deals especially in this chapter with the number of the canonical hours. Before examining the text of the Rule, several preliminary points must be made.

Certainly, the custom of offering daily praises to God at fixed and appointed hours has always prevailed in the Church, although different times and places have had different customs. According to Cassian (*book II, chapter 2*), the Egyptian monks assembled only twice a day: for the nocturnal vigils and for Vespers; they spent the rest of the day in their cells working with their hands, though they did not interrupt the singing of psalms. The same practice prevailed in the monastery of Saint Julian, surnamed Sabbas, according to Theodoret’s *Philotheus*, chapter 2. In the monastery of Saint Publius of Zeugma, they sang the morning office at the beginning of the day and the evening office at its close.

The monks of Tabennisi celebrated three canonical hours daily: the nocturnal vigils, None, and Vespers, as Palladius teaches in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 38. The Egyptian monks celebrated the same number on Saturday and Sunday. On those days, besides the nocturnal vigils and Vespers, they assembled at the third hour for the sake of Holy Communion, as Cassian writes (*book III, chapter 2*).

In the life of Saint Eupraxia, who flourished in the fourth century (*Bollandists, 13 March*), mention is made of the nocturnal psalmody, Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers. The Africans also celebrated these same hours, as Saint Cyprian testifies (*On the Lord’s Prayer*, near the end), although they later became more lax in observing them, so that the Donatists reproached them for their negligence in this matter, as Saint Augustine observes (*Letter 55*). It is also clear from Cassian (*book III, chapter 3*) that the apostles celebrated these same hours.

In the *Apostolic Constitutions* six canonical hours are listed: the morning office, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, and cockcrow. Saint Jerome lists the same number in the *Epitaph of Paula*: “In the morning, at the third hour, sixth, ninth, in the evening, and at midnight, they sang the Psalter in order.” By “morning” he understands dawn, as is clear from these words to Eustochium: “There is no one who does not know the third, sixth, and ninth hours, dawn also and evening.”

He establishes the same number in his letter to Laeta on the education of her daughter: “Let her become accustomed, by example, to rise at night for prayers and psalms, to sing hymns in the morning, and at the third, sixth, and ninth hours to stand in battle array like a soldier of Christ; then, with the lamp lit, let her offer the evening sacrifice.”

Finally, the *Rule for Certain Monks* decrees (*chapter 30*) that “three assemblies during the day and an equal number during the night” are to be held in the church.

Saint Aurelian, at the end of his Rule, wrote down the order of psalmody to be observed by his monks. In it he notes seven canonical hours and mentions Terce, Sext, None, the lighting of the lamps, the twelfth hour, the nocturnal offices, and the morning offices.

Cassian teaches that the same number of hours, although celebrated at different times, was observed in his monastery (*book III, chapters 3–5*). They celebrated the nocturnal vigils; the morning office said at dawn; another morning office corresponding to our Prime, which, he testifies, had been instituted in his own time; Terce, Sext, None, and Vespers.

Cassiodorus likewise recognized a similar number among the monks of his time. Writing on Psalm 118 and explaining the verse “Seven times a day I have praised you,” he says: “If we wish to consider this number literally, it signifies the seven occasions by which the devotion of the monks consoles itself: namely, the morning offices, Terce, Sext, None, the lighting of the lamps, Compline, and the nocturnal offices.”

303 The Rule of Saint Isidore likewise established similar hours, chapter 7.

Finally, Saint Basil also lists seven hours in sermon 1, *On the Institution of Monks*, where he proceeds as follows:

“That arrangement of the hours is to be observed above all which has been prescribed by holy men for prayer. For that outstanding David says: ‘At midnight I rose to give thanks to you for the judgments of your justice.’ Paul and Silas are also found to have followed him, for, being in prison, they both praised God at about midnight.

“The same prophet then adds: ‘In the evening, morning, and at noon.’ Moreover, the Holy Spirit came at about the third hour of the day, as we learn in Acts . . . Furthermore, the ninth hour recalls the Lord’s Passion . . .

“But since we also find this in the same David: ‘Seven times a day I have praised you for the judgments of your justice,’ and since the times of prayer which we have mentioned do not make up the number seven, the midday prayer must be divided in two, so that one part precedes the meal and the other follows it. In this way we may have a perpetual rule for celebrating God with praises seven times during each day’s course.”

Thus far Saint Basil. Although he seems to admit seven hours, in reality he recognizes only six, for he divides the sixth hour, which he calls midday, into two and makes no mention of Prime or Compline.

Elsewhere (*Longer Rules*, chapter 37) he assigns five hours by day and three by night. By day: the morning office or dawn, Terce, Sext, None, and the Eucharist when the day is complete; by night: a prayer at the beginning of the night, midnight, and the hour before dawn. These perhaps correspond to our three nocturnal vigils.

He makes no mention of Prime or Compline, unless someone, with Menardus, should say that the prayer of which Saint Basil speaks here is Compline. Yet this was said when the day had already ended and night had begun; and Saint Basil does not mention it in the sermon on the institution of monks cited above, nor, so far as I know, does anyone in the East before him.

Whatever the case may be, it is certainly clear from what has been said that before Saint Benedict no one celebrated all seven of the canonical hours now observed by the Church together. Although all had by then been instituted, they were not all said in the same place, some omitting Prime and others Compline.

Some celebrated seven hours in the natural day, of which ordinarily six were in the artificial day and the seventh at night. Saint Benedict, however, following the example of the prophet, established seven hours in the artificial day and wished the brothers to rise at night to give thanks to God.

The legislators who came after him increased this number still further. Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, established eleven hours in his first Rule (*chapters 2 and 3*): Prime, Second, Terce, Sext, None, the twelfth hour, Vespers, the beginning of the night, the synaxis at midnight, the synaxis after midnight, and the morning office.

In his second Rule (*chapter 10*) he established fifteen: Prime, Second, Terce, Fourth, Fifth, Sext, Seventh, Eighth, None, Tenth, Eleventh, Vespers, midnight, and cockcrow. He did not expressly state the fifteenth, but it is evident from the text that he instituted that many.

I cannot omit here what an anonymous author writes concerning the established manner of singing psalms instituted by Alexander the Sleepless in the monastery built beside the Euphrates (*Bollandists, 15 January*):

“First, in the Rule of holy institution, he adopted the apostolic norm and established Terce, Sext, None, and the nocturnal office together. Then he considered what God demands and found that the number seven is proclaimed everywhere, as it is said: ‘Seven times a day I have praised you’; and he determined to carry this out. He accomplished it by reciting prayers seven times during the day and conceiving them seven times during the night, following this pattern for seven years.”

Afterward, not content even with this, he instituted perpetual psalmody. Our own Mabillon proves that this also prevailed in several monasteries of our order (*Preface to the fourth century, part II*).

[Col. 0458A] What has been said thus far sufficiently refutes the rashness of the clergy of the Church of Neocaesarea, who dared at one time to reproach Basil the Great because he offered praises to God at fixed and appointed hours, saying that this had not been the custom of the great Gregory called the Wonderworker. Basil refutes them in letter 63.

It also refutes the impiety of the heretic Lampetius, who arose from the filth of the Messalians and asserted that those who celebrated the divine offices at appointed hours were still serving the Law, as can be seen in the Library of Photius, number 52, concerning the Synod of Side.

But let us come to the text of the Rule.

As the prophet says: “Seven times a day I have praised you.”] As though, in the title of this chapter, Saint Benedict had asked himself or someone else: “How are the divine offices to be celebrated throughout the day?”—that is, “How many times?” Then, as though answering, Hildemar, followed by Bernard of Cassino, says that he replies: “As the prophet says: ‘Seven times a day I have praised you.’”

According to these authors, the prophetic words are not adapted to Saint Benedict’s purpose in their meaning. The prophet assigns a definite number for an indefinite one, so that “seven times” means “always,” whereas Saint Benedict understands it as a definite number.

That sacred number seven, and so forth.] He calls the number seven sacred because it contains within itself innumerable mysteries. Saint Bruno, bishop of Segni, reveals some of these in these words (*Sentences*, book IV, chapter 13, sermon 2):

“It is established, not only among us but also among the wise men of the world, that the number seven is most sacred and perfect, because it contains all times and all numbers. For it is composed of the even number four and the first odd number, three; every number, moreover, is either even or odd. Therefore every number is constituted from the parts of seven, and through this the other numbers are contained in this single number.

“Hence the Jews eat unleavened bread for seven days; hence they celebrate festivals for seven days; hence the hands of priests, when they are ordained, are anointed and consecrated for seven days; hence the high priest, touching the blood with his finger, sprinkles it seven times toward the mercy seat and the doors of the tabernacle; hence the leper is shut away for seven days; hence Mary, the sister of Moses, remained outside the camp for seven days; hence the walls of Jericho are circled seven times and fall; hence we praise the Lord seven times a day; hence we are commanded to forgive our debtors not only seven times but seventy times seven; hence Solomon’s Temple is built in seven years and dedicated in seven days.

“This seems to signify the seven churches, seven lampstands, seven lamps, seven seals, seven angels sounding trumpets, and the seven loaves that fed the great multitude in the desert, as well as the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit.”

See Menardus on this passage and John Bona, *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 2, section 5.

Because he said concerning these daytime hours, “Seven times a day I have praised you.”] Saint Benedict understands this verse of the prophet as referring broadly to the artificial day, bounded by dawn and twilight. Saint Basil, in sermon 1 *On the Institution of Monks*, Cassian, and others explain it of the natural day, which includes both light and darkness.

For concerning the nocturnal vigils the same prophet says, “At midnight I rose to give thanks to you.”] He confirms the nocturnal vigils by divine authority, adducing the example of the prophet, who rose at midnight to give thanks to God.

The holy Father does not present this as though he wished us to rise precisely at midnight, since he permits us to rise somewhat later than midnight; rather, he presents it only to show that monks ought to rise at night, as Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino explain. See *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, book I, chapter 1.

Therefore, at these times let us offer praises to our Creator.] Not only with the mouth but also with the heart—indeed, more with the heart. For, as Hildemar says:

“He offers praises to God who thinks in his heart about what he says with his mouth. Therefore Saint Benedict wisely added, when he says, ‘At these times let us offer praises,’ and immediately added, ‘to our Creator,’ as though he were saying: Let us offer praises in such a way that our Creator may be recognized. For there are many who seem to offer praises but do not offer them to God, because they do not direct their hearts to what they say with their mouths.”

### On the judgments of his justice

“On the judgments of his justice.” *Super*, that is, “because of,” says Hildemarus. For by these words he makes clear why we ought to render praises to God both by day and by night—namely, because of God’s judgments. What those judgments are, however, he does not explain; he merely says that they are incomprehensible, yet just: for they are “the judgments of his justice.” Since these did not seem clear and evident to Boherius, he asserts that the judgments of God’s justice are the judgments of the Son of God, who is the justice of the Father.

And indeed, the judgments that Christ suffered at the hands of the Jews the Church intends to honor at the seven canonical hours, as is evident from these verses, which Boherius reports:

> At matins Christ is condemned;
>
> When he rose, the faithful order sings the first hour;
>
> When terce is sung, then he suffered the agonies;
>
> At sext darkness was made throughout the regions of the world;
>
> At the hour of none the divine spirit was sent forth;
>
> At evening Christ’s sacred limbs are enclosed in the tomb;
>
> At the twelfth hour a guard is stationed over Christ.

Cardinal Bona, however, does not entirely approve these verses as less conformable to historical truth (*On the Divine Psalms*, ch. 2, §3), since the resurrection took place before the first hour, and what they say about the twelfth hour is not found in the Gospel. Those very common verses from the gloss on chapter 1, *On the Celebration of Masses*, are therefore to be preferred:

> These are the reasons for which we sing at the seven hours:
>
> Matins binds Christ, who cleanses sins;
>
> Prime fills him with spittle; terce gives the cause of death;
>
> Sext fastens him to the cross; none cleaves his side in two;
>
> Vespers takes him down; compline lays him in the tomb.

The authors who have published treatises on ecclesiastical offices adduce many other pious reasons for the institution of the seven canonical hours; it is not the present occasion to report them all. I shall offer only one, by way of conclusion to this chapter, from Peter Damian (*Opusc.* 10, chapter 1):

> “There are seven light and very small sins,” he says, “into which not only the sinner but also every just person falls daily, even if he already seems to stand upon the lofty summit of perfection. They are these: thought, ignorance, inconstancy, necessity, weakness, forgetfulness, and stealthy transgression . . . . . Because of these seven light and small sins, then, which through human frailty we cannot avoid, this has been instituted by the teaching of the Holy Spirit through the devout teachers of the Church: that we should perform our vows seven times each day. These offices of the seven canonical hours have been established in the bosom of the holy Church as though they were seven baths of baptism, so that we may strive to expiate, with an equal number of streams of daily prayer, the stains of the seven offenses that we contract through the daily conduct of this life; so that the breath of satisfaction may shake off the continual dust of corruptible life, and the frequent wave of abundant prayer may wash away the mud of worldly conduct.”

## CHAPTER XVII. How many psalms are to be sung at those same hours

[Note: [Col. 0459C] Another reading: “said.”]

[Col. 0459]

[Col. 0459C] We have now set out the order of psalmody for the nocturnal offices and for matins; let us now consider the following hours. At the first hour, let three psalms be said separately, and not under a single *Gloria*. The hymn of that hour is to follow the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” before the psalms are begun.

[Note: [Col. 0459C] Another reading: “the hymn.”]

[Note: [Col. 0459C] In Oxford, Cassinese, and Florentine manuscripts *intende* is lacking.]

After the completion of the three psalms, one reading, a verse, and the *Kyrie eleison* are to be recited, and “the masses” are to be said.

[Note: [Col. 0459C] Oxford, Narbonne, and Florence: *missas*. Victor, Paris manuscript: *et missa est*.]

At terce, sext, and none, the prayer is to be celebrated in the same order: that is, the verse, the hymn of those hours, three psalms, the reading and the verse, the *Kyrie eleison*, and “the masses” are to be said.

[Note: [Col. 0459D] Oxford: “the verse, the hymn.” Narbonne: “three psalms, the reading, the *Kyrie eleison*, and the masses.” Florence: “and the masses are said.”]

If the congregation is larger, with antiphons; but if it is smaller, let them sing in direct recitation.

[Note: [Col. 0460C] Narbonne: *psalletur*, “let it be sung.” Hildemarus and Conch: *psallatur*, “let it be sung.” Victor manuscript: *canantur*, “let them be sung.”]

The evening assembly, however, is to end with four psalms with antiphons. After those psalms a reading is to be recited, then a responsory, the Ambrosian hymn,

[Note: [Col. 0460C] Florence: “the Ambrosian hymn.”]

the verse, the canticle from the Gospel, the litany,

[Note: [Col. 0460C] Oxford: “the litanies.” Cassinese: “the litanies.” Florence, together with certain others: “the litany.”]

the Lord’s Prayer, and the *missae* are to be made.

Compline, however, is to end with the saying of three psalms.

[Note: [Col. 0460C] Narbonne: “the compline office.” Florence: “the complines.”]

These psalms are to be said directly, without an antiphon. After them come the hymn of that hour,

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Narbonne: “the hymn . . . one reading, the verse, the *Kyrie eleison*, the blessing.” Florence likewise reads “the hymn . . . one reading.”]

one reading, the verse, the *Kyrie eleison*, and the blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0460D] Another reading: “the blessings.”]

Then the *missae* are to be made.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0459]

“We have now set out the order of psalmody for the nocturnal offices and for matins; let us now consider the following hours. At the first hour, let three psalms be said separately, and not under a single glory.”

But under a threefold glory, so that the Trinity may be glorified with each psalm. The holy Father assigns the same number of psalms to terce, sext, none, and compline—five hours in all:

> “So that we may be admonished that the five senses of our body should excel through the three virtues of the soul, and that we should love God with our whole heart, our whole soul, and our whole mind,”

says Amalarius in the *Supplement* (*Tom.* II of the *Analecta*).

[Col. 0460D] “The hymn of that hour, etc., the *Kyrie eleison*, and the masses are to be said.”

All this is clear and evident and contains no difficulty, except perhaps the two final words, *missae sint*, concerning the interpretation of which not everyone agrees. To shed some light upon a doubtful and obscure matter, it should first be noted that the word *missa* is highly ambiguous and is used to signify many things.

First, *missa* is commonly understood as the unbloody sacrifice of Christ, which priests offer upon the altar. It is used in this sense below, chapter 35: “On solemn days let them wait until the masses”; and chapter 38: “After the masses and Communion, let the reader enter to read.”

Second, *missa* is used for the feast of a saint. Thus the statutes of Saint Adalard say:

> “These are the days on which they are to be spared from labor for the Lord . . . the Nativity of the Lord . . . the Mass of Lady Balthildis.”

The ancient customs of Germany, manuscript no. 30, say:

> “On Sundays and feast days, from the calends of October until the Mass of Saint Martin.”

And below:

> “From the Mass of Saint Martin until the Purification of Saint Mary, etc.”

See the life of Saint Guthlac, no. 32, century III, part I.

Third, *missa* is used for a canonical hour, or for the course of the divine office. Thus in Cassian (*Book* II, chapter 13):

> “Why one ought not to sleep after the nocturnal office.”

And elsewhere (*Book* III, chapter 5):

> “After the canonical office has been celebrated, they extend the vigils thereafter until daylight.”

The Council of Agde likewise says (canon 30):

> “Let morning or evening hymns be sung every day, and at the conclusion of the morning or evening offices, after the hymns, let brief passages from the psalms be said.”

[Col. 0461B]

Fourth, *missa* is used for a reading. Saint Aurelian, in the *Order of Psalmody*, says:

> “On the Nativity of the Lord and on Epiphany, rise at the third hour of the night: say one nocturn, and make six readings from the prophet Isaiah; then say the second nocturn, and let another six be read from the Gospel. On Epiphany likewise: at the first, one nocturn; then make those six readings from the prophet Daniel . . . . On the feasts of martyrs, three or four readings are made: read the first reading from the Gospel, the remaining ones from the passions of the martyrs, etc.”

The Master, in the *Rule* (chapter 46), says:

> “In the order in which readings are celebrated by clerics—that is, when the junior cleric has read the Apostle, the senior deacon follows to read the holy Gospels.”

Fifth, among the ancients *missa* is found used for a prayer or collect, because it is sent to God. Thus the Council of Milevis (canon 12) says:

> “It was also resolved that the prayers, or orations, or masses that have been approved in the council—whether prefaces, commendations, or impositions of hands—are to be celebrated by all.”

The Fourth Council of Toledo, canon 13, says:

> “Thus hymns are composed, just as masses, or prayers and orations, are composed.”

And Cassian (*Book* II, chapter 7) says:

> “We hasten to prostrate ourselves in prayer before the psalm has yet been properly completed, hurrying as quickly as possible to the celebration of the mass.”

Sixth and finally, *missa* is used for dismissal, just as among Cicero’s works, book V *On Oratory*, *collecta* is used for “collection,” and among Tertullian’s works, book III *Against Marcion*, *proba* for “proof”; among Cyprian’s writings, *remissa* for “remission.”

Of these six meanings of *missa*, the controversy here can concern only the last two. For:

1. It is certain that *missa* is not used here for the Eucharistic sacrifice, as a certain learned man once held, whom Menardus rightly refutes at this passage; for, at least according to customary practice, a mass was not said after compline.

2. It is likewise certain that it does not mean a feast, since feast days occur neither every day nor at every hour.

3. Nor does it mean an entire canonical hour; otherwise, once the divine office had been completed, Saint Benedict would be ordering something already celebrated to be celebrated again.

4. Nor does it mean a reading, since in chapter 48 he establishes that after prime and after none one is to devote oneself not to reading but to manual labor.

309 The entire difficulty, therefore, concerns the two last meanings of *missa*: namely, whether Saint Benedict by these words prescribed that prayers should be said, or that an absolution or dismissal should be made. Each opinion has had its supporters, as we learn from Hildemarus:

> “The learned understand *missae sint* in two ways,” he says. “Let dismissals be made. Or, in another way, *missae* is said to mean sendings, so that it refers to that prayer, because through the office of the priest the prayers of the people are directed to God; hence the priest says: ‘Hear, O Lord, the voice of your people,’ and the rest.”

Of these two opinions, Hildemarus supports the second. In commenting on the final words of this chapter, *et missae fiant*, he adds:

> “That is, the prayers or supplications of the monks are sent to God.”

Nearly all the more distinguished commentators on the Rule follow Hildemarus.

Smaragdus says:

> “What he says in other places, ‘and it is completed,’ he says in this conclusion, ‘and the masses are said.’ He repeats, ‘and the masses are said,’ for the prayers of the office, which have been completed by us, are sent to God because they have been celebrated in his honor. Alternatively, prayers—that is, collects—which are said by the priest at the end of the course are called masses, that is, sent to God.”

Bernard of Cassino says:

> “When he says *missae sint*, understand it in this way: when we pray to God, we send prayers to God, and from this sending it is called a mass. Thus when he says *missae sint*, it is the same as if he had said: ‘After the *Kyrie eleison*, let a prayer be said which is sent to God.’ Hence, when he treats of vespers in this chapter, he says that two prayers are to be made, namely when he says in the text, ‘the Lord’s Prayer,’ that is, the *Pater noster*, ‘and the masses are to be said.’”

Nicholas of Fractura says:

> “And the masses are to be said”—supply, “the prayers”; and let the psalmody be sent to the Lord.

Boherius, in his first commentary, says:

> “Whenever we pray to God, we send our prayers to God, and from such sending the prayers that we say at the end of the hours—such as the petitions, the Lord’s Prayer, the following verse, the special prayer of the hour or day, with its proper conclusion—are called masses, as here. Therefore, when he says, ‘And let the masses be said,’ it is the same as if he had said: ‘After the *Kyrie eleison*, let prayers be made which are sent to God.’”

And in his second commentary:

> “Masses—that is, prayers that are sent to the Lord, such as the *Pater noster* and the prayer of that hour.”

John of Turrecremata says:

> “And let the masses be said—that is, let the prayers be said which Saint Benedict here calls masses, because in them we expressly send petitions to God, saying: ‘Let us pray. Almighty and eternal God’; or ‘O God who’; or something of this kind.”

Theobaldus Artaldus Coelestinus, in his French exposition of the Benedictine Rule, renders these words, *et missae sint*, as follows:

> “And let masses be said, that is, the Lord’s Prayer, the Creed, the prayers, and the collect proper to that hour, which through their special efficacy are sent to God the Supreme, etc.”

John Craesbeeck says:

> “Let the masses be said—that is, let prayers be made and sent to God, both by each person privately and quietly saying the *Pater noster*, etc., and communally by one priest reciting the collect aloud; for our prayers are called masses,” etc.

Hugh Menardus says:

> “In this passage, masses are collects or prayers which, according to Cassian, were said by the priest at the end of each psalm. Saint Benedict mentions them only at the end of the hours, for the sake of brevity, as something familiar and well known to his monks, just as he later treats briefly and incidentally of the short prayer, as of something known to the monks and requiring no fuller explanation. Or certainly it must be said that Saint Benedict, following the custom of others which we explained above, relegated such collects to the end of each hour, so that several, rather than one, were to be said; and for that reason he said *missae sint*, not *missa sit*.”

Joannes Caramuel says:

> “The masses are those prayers which we say at the end, before ‘Let us bless the Lord.’”

And below:

> “The masses are those final collects of the office, namely the prayer corresponding to the day, and any commemorations of confessors or martyrs that were then made.”

He has the same in his *Nomenclator*. Finally, Charles Cointius, in volume I of the *Annals of the Church of the Franks* (year 514, no. 32), says:

> “The hours of prime, terce, sext, and none are therefore concluded in this way: after the *Kyrie eleison*, the Lord’s Prayer is said in the manner explained above, then the masses, or collects.”

The practice and usage of the word *missa* to signify collects or prayers confirms the opinion of so many eminent authors. This can be seen in the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers, chapter 6, where, treating of the divine offices, it says:

> “Each of the brothers shall take care that, at the time when masses are made, whether by day or by night, when one must stand longer at prayer, they do not grow faint.”

Another text from the Rule of Saint Macarius, chapter 15, explains this passage:

> “Each shall give attention to God at the time when masses are made during the observance of the vigils, when all assemble, so that they do not grow faint.”

Cassian likewise says (*Book* II, chapter 7):

> “Before the psalm has been properly completed, we hasten to prostrate ourselves in prayer, hurrying as quickly as possible to the celebration of the mass.”

Thus Saint Caesarius (in the Bollandists, 12 January) had prescribed in the Rule for Virgins that from the calends of October until Easter two nocturns be made and “after the nocturns three prayers be read.” In the Rule for Monks, chapter 20, he expresses it this way:

> “In October let them make two nocturns and three masses. At one mass let a brother read three pages, and pray; let him read another three, and pray; let him read another three, and rise.”

It is as though he were saying: “Let them make two nocturns and three prayers: after the first prayer, let him read three pages, and let a second prayer be made; let him read another three pages, and let a third prayer be made; let him read another three, and rise.”

Gregory of Tours also appears to have understood *missa* in this sense (*History of the Franks*, Book VI, chapter 46), when he said that King Chilperic had composed certain “little works, or hymns, or masses, which cannot be accepted for any reason.”

Since it is therefore established that among ancient writers, especially the authors of monastic rules, the word *missa* was used to signify prayers, there is nothing to prevent Saint Benedict from having understood it here in that sense. In particular, it is certain that he admitted prayers into the Work of God, as is clear from chapter 57, where he prescribes that at the final prayer of the Work of God a commemoration of all the absent is always to be made. These words prove not only that he admitted prayers, but also several of them. Hence here too he does not simply say that “a mass” is to be made, but that “masses” are to be made: *missae sint* and *missae fiant*.

For this reason I cannot agree with those who wish *missa* in this chapter to have been used by Saint Benedict for dismissal. If that were true, he would not have said *missae sint* or *missae fiant*, but *missa sit* or *missa fiat*. For we do not see the word *missa* used in the plural by any author to signify dismissal; it is always used in the singular.

I can approve even less the opinion of Saint Hildegard, Antonius Perez, and Benedict Haeften, who say that Saint Benedict admitted no prayer other than the Lord’s Prayer. For, apart from the fact that he always commanded a commemoration of all the absent at the final prayer of the Work of God, he wished the vigils on Sundays and feast days with twelve readings to end with a blessing. According to Saint Hildegard, Perez, and Haeften, that blessing was a collect.

Moreover, Amalarius writes in the *Supplement* (*Tom.* II of the *Analecta*) that:

> “In all offices, when both clerics and monks have completed them, they rightly offer a final prayer to the Lord, which is commended to God the Father through our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The practice of this can be seen among our people of Autun, to whom Saint Leodegarius had commended observance of the Benedictine Rule with such zeal at the Council of Autun. Thus in the life of Saint Medericus, abbot, who flourished in the seventh century, an anonymous author says in no. 7 of a certain monk:

> “As soon as the assembly was to be concluded with the customary prayer, and before he bent his knees, he left the church.”

Certainly it is not credible that Saint Benedict departed from the common practice of the ancient monks, all of whom employed prayers in the divine office. This is clear concerning the Egyptians from Cassian, book II, chapter 7; concerning the Pachomians from Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 38 (see the life of Saint Pachomius, chapter 22, and the Rule, chapters 121 and 126). An angel “appointed that throughout the whole day they should make twelve prayers; when they came to the evening light, and during the nocturnal vigils twelve, and at the ninth hour three”—as many, that is, as there were psalms.

Saint Caesarius also prescribes prayers in the *Rule for Monks*, chapter 20; Saint Aurelian in the *Order of Psalmody*; Saint Isidore in the *Rule*, chapter 7; Saint Fructuosus in chapter 3; the Master in the *Rule*, chapters 33, 35, 36, and 37; Saint Columbanus in the *Penitential*; and Saint Macarius in the *Rule*, chapter 15. See also the Council of Milevis, chapter 12; the Second Council of Carthage, chapter 25; and the Council of Agde, canon 30, where the collects are discussed and where, consequently, they were already in use in the Church before the time of Saint Benedict.

I could confirm this further from the reading found in the oldest manuscript codices of Saint Benedict’s Rule: the Oxford manuscript, written a thousand years ago; the Narbonne manuscript, written nine hundred years ago; and the Florentine manuscript, written eight hundred years ago. In these one does not read *et missae sint*, but only *et missas*, as though Saint Benedict had said: “After the three psalms, let one reading be recited, the verse, the *Kyrie eleison*, and the prayers or masses.”

Nor can anyone object that *missas* is there expressed in the accusative case, while the other words are written in the nominative. For this occurs frequently in those codices, especially in the Narbonne and Florentine manuscripts, where we often read *hymnum* for *hymnus* and *lectionem* for *lectio*.

[Col. 0464B] Nor does Saint Hildegard’s statement move me greatly, that no collect was designated by Saint Benedict “so that weariness might be removed from those praying, and so that the Lord’s Prayer already said might not be neglected.” Experience proves the contrary, and the briefest collect cannot produce weariness except in someone who is tired of the entire office.

If, therefore, some other argument of the opposing opinion presses more strongly, it must be examined. It has only one foundation, drawn from chapters 9 and 12. In the first, when Saint Benedict establishes the order of the nocturnal vigils, after discussing the psalms and readings, he finally concludes:

> “The verse, and the supplication of the litany—that is, the *Kyrie eleison*—and thus let the nocturnal vigils be ended.”

In the other, where he treats of matins, after the Gospel canticle it is added:

> “The litany, and it is completed.”

From these passages they infer:

> “In the same way, in this chapter *et missae sint* has the same meaning as in chapter 9, ‘and thus let the nocturnal vigils be ended,’ and in chapter 12, ‘and it is completed.’”

Moreover, these expressions prescribe no prayers or collects; therefore neither does the phrase “and let the masses be said.”

To satisfy this objection, I answer first that it is quite probable that Saint Benedict followed the custom of the Egyptian monks, who inserted prayers after each psalm, as is clear from Cassian. Although the holy Father did not prescribe this custom explicitly, he prescribed it implicitly, as Boherius teaches, in that he ordered twelve psalms with an *Alleluia* at the end to be sung at the vigils in their manner. By this decree he approved their rite, and he appears to approve it again in chapter 20, where he treats of reverence in prayer—and this with regard to the vigils.

“On the other hand,” Boherius says again, “that an insertion of prayers should be made among the matins themselves, or at the end of that solemnity, he found, I think, to have been ordered by the Fathers; and thus he did not undertake to institute it himself.”

It is therefore quite probable that Saint Benedict inserted prayers among the psalms at the nocturns and at the praises, but relegated them to the end of the office at the other hours of the day. For that reason, when he makes no mention of prayers at the vigils, he says, “Thus let the nocturnal vigils be ended”; at matins or the praises, “and it is completed”; but at the other hours, “and let the masses be said” and “and let the masses be made.”

The Rule of the Master strengthens this opinion to some extent. That Rule consists largely of Saint Benedict’s Rule and Benedictine customs. In chapter 33 it forbids two psalms to be said under a single glory,

[Note: [Col. 0463D] I would prefer to read “under one . . . Glory.” EDITOR.]

lest the prayers that ought to be said among them should be omitted:

> “Care must be taken,” it says, “that psalms should never be joined together, which is not permitted; rather, each must be completed separately with the *Gloria*, so that the prayers which ought to be made among them are not lost.”

Saint Isidore prescribed the same thing when in chapter 7 of his Rule he established:

> “When the monks have completed each psalm, they shall all prostrate themselves upon the ground and adore together.”

I answer secondly that Saint Benedict passed over many things in silence as sufficiently known to the brothers through daily use. For example, in chapters 9 and 10, where he treats of the nocturnal vigils, he makes no mention of the Lord’s Prayer; nor does he do so in chapter 12, where he establishes the order of Sunday matins.

In this chapter likewise he makes no mention of a commemoration to be made for the absent at prime, terce, sext, and so forth. If someone should say that these things are prescribed elsewhere—namely, in chapter 13, where the Lord’s Prayer is to be said aloud at matins and vespers, but quietly at the other offices, and in chapter 57, where the absent are to be commemorated—I reply that I too find Saint Benedict prescribing several prayers there, when he says:

> “At the final prayer of the Work of God, a commemoration of all the absent is always to be made.”

Certainly, if we deny that Saint Benedict admitted prayers or collects because he seems not to have mentioned them when arranging the order of the divine office, then it will likewise have to be said that he omitted the first six petitions of the Lord’s Prayer at all the hours except the praises and vespers, since the holy Father does not explicitly prescribe them.

I answer thirdly that these expressions, “Let the nocturnal vigils be ended” and “It is completed,” can be understood in two ways. Something may be commanded to end either so that nothing further is added, or so that only a few things are added to what has been said or done. Thus, every day, when someone is speaking at excessive length, we tell him to stop—not as though we wished him to say no further words, since that is often neither expedient nor something we would desire.

Finally, it is clear that Saint Benedict’s words, “and thus let the nocturnal vigils be ended,” must be understood in this sense, since the Lord’s Prayer is to be added to what he has assigned above. The same must be said concerning the other expression, “and it is completed.”

Certainly those who prepared the new edition of Saint Augustine understood both expressions in these two ways, in the preliminary notice to the Second Rule of Saint Augustine, which they placed in the appendix to the first volume:

> “‘It is completed,’ they say, means that the office will thus be performed, or that a final prayer will be added, such as the prayer which in the ancient missals is called ‘for completion.’”

All this, however, as far as our ability permits, we submit to the sounder judgment of others, since it has been arranged rather poorly.

“At terce, sext, and none, let the prayer be celebrated in the same order.”

Here *oratio* means a canonical hour, as Boherius observed. The sense is: “Let the third, sixth, and ninth hours be celebrated in the same order as the first,” whose sequence he has just laid out. This is expressed more clearly in the old Venetian edition, which reads:

> “Let the third, sixth, and ninth hours be celebrated in the same order.”

Saint Benedict further explains this by adding:

“That is, the verse.”

Namely, “O God, come to my assistance,” etc.

“The hymns of those same hours, three psalms, etc.”

All this is clear from what has already been said.

“If the congregation is larger.”

What “congregation” means Hildemarus explains in these words:

> “A congregation is where there are twelve brothers. It is rightly a congregation of twelve brothers, because they are able to fulfill their rule; yet this is so in the desert. For near a city it is not good to have only twelve monks under one abbot, because if you send them to the several offices, they are not fully sufficient for the dignity required by the various people who come to the monastery.”

Bernard of Cassino likewise defines a congregation as an assembly of twelve brothers:

> “Because,” he says, “ten according to the laws constitute a people; over ten a dean is appointed, and over the dean a provost is set,”

with an abbot over both.

Boherius asserts the same and says that this was the first congregation of monks, namely the apostles,

> “in which our Savior was abbot, Simon Peter provost, and Judas Iscariot dean.”

We must now inquire what constitutes a larger congregation and what a smaller one.

“If there are more than twelve,” says Bernard of Cassino, “that is, thirteen, fourteen, or more, it is a larger congregation; but if they are below the number twelve, it ought to be called a smaller congregation.”

Nicholas of Fractura says similarly, commenting on the words “if the congregation is larger”:

> “For example, thirteen, fourteen, or more, because twelve constitute a congregation, although sometimes, with respect to the right of election, only two constitute a congregation.”

Boherius, however, distinguishes three kinds of congregation: a simple congregation, which consists of twelve monks; a larger congregation, which is above twelve; and a smaller congregation, which descends below that number as far as two, not counting the superior.

Theobaldus Artaldus and John Craesbeeck likewise recognize as a larger congregation one that exceeds the number of twelve monks.

Cardinal de Turrecremata, however, says:

> “Some call it a larger congregation when there are thirty or more; a smaller congregation when there are fewer than thirty brothers, descending as far as twelve, since fewer than twelve does not seem to constitute a regular congregation.”

This opinion is more pleasing. For Saint Benedict, in chapter 21 of the Rule, establishes deans only in a larger congregation; yet above twelve or fifteen monks, approximately, an abbot and a provost are sufficient. A larger congregation therefore cannot exist unless there are at least two deans, each set over more than ten monks, with an abbot and provost over both—that is, twenty-four monks.

Hildemarus has the same view in chapter 21, where he writes; he adds that according to custom a congregation is larger when it contains thirty or forty monks.

“With antiphons; but if it is smaller, let them sing in direct recitation.”

What it means to sing with an antiphon and what it means to sing in direct recitation Haeften explains in these words (*Book* VII, treatise 4, discussion 3):

> “Saint Benedict intended by psalmody with an antiphon to designate that part of the divine office which is performed with musical notation and melodic singing. He himself indicates this sufficiently: for after saying, as we explained above, ‘with musical modulation,’ of six psalms, he expresses the same thing a little later by saying, ‘After these readings let six other psalms with antiphons follow in order, as the preceding ones.’ Hence it is clear that for Saint Benedict to sing with an antiphon is the same as to sing psalms melodically . . . .
>
> “It will not now be difficult to explain what it means to sing in direct recitation, or *directanee*. The holy Father himself explains it as ‘without an antiphon,’ that is, without notation, melody, or tone, so that everything is pronounced at an even pitch of voice, without rising or falling.”

Certainly Saint Benedict here contrasts psalmody with an antiphon and psalmody in direct recitation. Unless, perhaps, someone should say that singing with an antiphon means inserting antiphons after each psalm, and even after each verse of the psalms, whereas singing in direct recitation means omitting them and singing the psalms in one continuous tone.

Boherius distinguishes these two ways of speaking in his commentary on this passage:

> “So that he might not oppress the few with excessive labor in singing, he relieves them here in two respects: first through brevity, because it is without antiphons; second by dispensing with the proclamation of song, because the psalms are sung in direct recitation.”

At the same time he indicates the reason why the smaller congregation is exempted from antiphons and singing: so that the few may not be burdened by excessive labor, since what is done by many is more easily completed.

In a smaller congregation, where there is usually less material support, it is necessary for some to go outside to gather crops and attend to other needs of the monastery, leaving only a few in the choir. It would be burdensome for them to perform these hours with solemn singing. They may nevertheless do so if God has given them that desire. For Saint Benedict’s decree concerning the minor hours being said in direct recitation is not a precept, as Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata noted with Hildemarus; it is merely permissive.

This applies only to the minor hours of the day. Accordingly, the smaller congregation must perform the nocturnal vigils, matins, and vespers with singing just as the larger congregation does, because at those times all are assembled and free from external duties, and can easily complete them.

“The evening assembly.”

That is, the evening office, which is known to have been called by the ancient monks by the name *synaxis*, as is clear from Cassian, book II, chapter 11.

[Col. 0467A] “Let it end with four psalms with antiphons.”

Five, as at matins, are used by clerics, in accordance with the decision of the Council of Braga:

> “It was resolved by common agreement that one and the same order of singing be maintained in the morning and evening offices, and that diverse and private customs, or the customs of monasteries, should not be mingled with those of the Church.”

Why five psalms are used by clerics, but four by monks, Peter Damian explains in these words (*On Consecration*, distinction 5, chapter “It is fitting,” *Opusc.* 10, chapter 4):

> “Vespers does not have the same number of psalms among the various orders. Among clerics it embraces five psalms; among monks it is completed with only four. Yet neither practice is without reason, if it is investigated with suitably careful examination.
>
> “For the five psalms of vespers admit of the same explanation as that already given above concerning matins. We know from the Lord’s own teaching that the judge of the human race will come by night; but at what hour of the night—whether at midnight, at the cockcrow, or in the morning—we do not know, since, as he himself testifies, he will come like a thief. Thus rightly, in the office of evening praise just as in that of morning praise, the holy Church of the elect awaits her bridegroom. She is fittingly represented by the number of the five prudent virgins. When she sings joyfully with him, adorned with good works and with five psalms, as though with an equal number of lamps burning, she hastens joyfully to meet him.
>
> “But the one who instituted four psalms should, unless I am mistaken, be thought to have had this in view: just as there are four military watches, so likewise there are known to be four principal virtues—justice, fortitude, temperance, and prudence. In these virtues we must continually keep watch through the nocturnal darkness of this mortal life; and, standing in readiness for spiritual warfare, we must patiently stand guard for our camp and fight without weariness. In this office of evening praise, therefore, we are instructed by the four psalms that we sing to keep constant watch over the guardianship of the four virtues.”

John Beleth gives another explanation (*Explanation of the Divine Office*, chapter 52):

> “At vespers we sing five psalms, we who are imperfect, so that what has been committed through the five bodily senses may be entirely forgiven through the singing of the five psalms . . . . . But monks, by whom they show themselves to be more perfect, say only four. For whatever is square, whichever way it is turned, always remains the same, firm and solid. In the same way, the perfect person remains always the same and unmoved, wherever or whenever he may be.”

“After those psalms a reading is to be recited.”

From memory, that is, as at the praises. Otherwise he would have said that it was to be read, not recited.

### “A Canticle from the Gospel”

Namely, the *Magnificat*, as is probable. Concerning it Peter Damian writes as follows (*Opusculum* 10, chapter 4):

> “The canticle of the Blessed Mother is not inappropriately joined to the office of Vespers. For she, as though the long day of the former age had already passed, at the very setting of the world’s evening, as soon as she conceived the light of the eternal Word in the flower of her blessed womb, immediately burst into a voice of divine praise, saying: ‘My soul magnifies the Lord.’ Therefore, in the likeness of her who is the Lord’s mother, the whole universal Church too, which is certainly the mother of Christians and which carries in her mind the same light that she once bore in her womb, now that the day is growing toward evening magnifies God with worthy praise; and, giving thanks for the benefits bestowed, rejoices exultantly in God her Savior.”

“But Compline” — thus Saint Benedict calls the final canonical hour of the day, in which we complete all the offices of the day. Saint Isidore likewise calls it this in *Rule*, chapter 7. But in Book I *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 21, he calls it *completes*; some Fathers call it *completa*. Saint Columbanus, in the beginning of chapter 7 of his Rule, calls it the beginning of the night; Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, calls it the first hour of the night, perhaps because it was said at evening twilight, as can be seen in Eddius’s *Life of Saint Wilfrid*, chapter 64 (*Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part 1), or because the point of night was approaching, as in the *History of the Translation of Saint Genulfus* (*Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part 2), no. 25. This perhaps is the hour that Saint Basil calls the “petition.”

“Let it be concluded with the recitation of three psalms.” Saint Ambrose aptly comments on this passage (*Book V on the Hexameron*, chapter 12):

> “Who, possessing human understanding, would not blush to close the day without the solemn celebration of psalms, when even the smallest birds, with customary devotion and sweet song, accompany the rising of days and nights?”

Peter Damian explains why it is concluded with the recitation of three psalms as follows (*Opusculum* 10, chapter 5):

> “By rendering the account that is owed concerning the three psalms, the Holy Trinity delivers us from obligation; under whose sign, certainly, Compline closes the completed day. For just as the office of the first hour, as was stated above, is dedicated to faith in the Most Holy Trinity, so Compline concludes with the affirmation of that same Most Holy Trinity, so that the final closing of the completed light may end in him for whom the whole course of the day is recognized as having served.”

“These psalms are to be recited directly, without an antiphon.” That is, without singing, or without the insertion of antiphons between the psalms or between the verses of the psalms, or without both at once, as we said above. This may be either because insufficient time remains for celebrating Compline solemnly before they go to bed, or because that time is a time of weeping and sorrow, in accordance with the verse, “At evening there shall be weeping,” to which the joy of song is not suited.

“After them, the hymn of the same hour and one reading.” Is the reading to be recited from memory, or read from a book?

“A verse, Kyrie eleison, a blessing, and so forth.” On these matters see Book I *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, the final chapter.

## CHAPTER XVIII  
### The Order in Which the Psalms Are to Be Recited

In the first place, at all the daytime hours [Note: Cassian and certain others omit the words “at all the daytime hours.”] the verse “O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me,” and the Gloria are to be said. Then comes the hymn for each hour [Note: Florentine manuscript: “the hymn.”]. Next, at the first hour on Sunday, four sections of Psalm 118 are to be said [Note: Oxford manuscript: “four sections are to be said.”]. At the remaining hours—that is, at the third, sixth, and ninth—three sections of the aforementioned Psalm 118 are to be said.

At the first hour of Monday, three psalms are to be said, namely the first, second, and sixth. And so, on each successive day at the first hour, up to Sunday, three psalms are to be said in order, continuing through Psalm 19 [Note: Some manuscripts: “up to Sunday”; others: “until Sunday.”] [Note: Some manuscripts: “through Psalm 19.”]. In such a way, however, that Psalms 9 and 17 are divided into two Glorias [Note: Florentine manuscript: “divided into two”; others: “divided into two Glorias.”]. Thus it is arranged [Note: Some manuscripts: “Thus it is arranged”; others: “and thus it is done.”] that at the Sunday vigils one always begins with Psalm 20 [Note: Oxford, first Cassinese, and Paris manuscripts: “on Sundays.”].

At the third, sixth, and ninth hours of Monday, the nine sections remaining from Psalm 118 are to be said, three at each of those hours. After Psalm 118 has therefore been completed over two days, namely Sunday and Monday, then on Tuesday, at the third, sixth, and ninth hours, three psalms are to be sung, beginning with Psalm 119 and continuing through Psalm 127—that is, nine psalms. These same psalms are likewise to be repeated at the same hours each day through Sunday [Note: Some manuscripts: “until Sunday”; others: “up to Sunday.”] [Note: Narbonne manuscript: “the same.”], while a uniform arrangement of hymns, readings, and verses is maintained on all days [Note: Florentine manuscript: “maintaining a uniform arrangement.”]. Thus, Sunday is always to begin with Psalm 118 [Note: Oxford, Cassinese, and Conch manuscript: “Sunday always.”] [Note: Oxford manuscript: “it will begin.”].

Every day Vespers is to be sung with the modulation of four psalms. These psalms are to begin with Psalm 109 and continue through Psalm 147, except for those taken from this sequence and assigned to different hours: Psalms 117 through 127, Psalm 133, and Psalm 142. All the others are to be said at Vespers. Since three psalms are lacking, those among the number listed above that are found to be longer [Note: Some manuscripts: “from the number.”] [Note: Oxford manuscript: “more important.”] are to be divided: namely Psalms 138, 143, and 144.

Since Psalm 116 is short, it is to be joined to Psalm 115. Once the order of the Vesper psalms has been arranged, the remaining elements—readings, responsories [Note: Florentine manuscript: “the response, the hymn, the verse, or the canticle.”], hymns, verses, or canticles—are to be completed as we have prescribed above. At Compline [Note: Florentine manuscript: “the Compline psalms”; the older Cassinese manuscripts: “the Complines.”], the same psalms are to be repeated every day, namely Psalms 4, 90, and 133.

Once the order of the daytime psalmody has been arranged, all the remaining psalms are to be divided equally among the vigils of seven nights, dividing, that is, those psalms that are longer among them, and assigning twelve to each night [Note: Oxford and Florentine manuscripts: “assigning.”]. We particularly admonish this: if anyone should perhaps dislike this distribution of the psalms, let him arrange it differently if he judges that another arrangement is better, provided that every effort is made to ensure that the Psalter, consisting of the full number of 150 psalms, is sung completely each week.

On Sunday the sequence is always to be begun again from the beginning at the vigils [Note: Hildemar: “they are to be begun again”; Florentine manuscript: “it is to be begun again.”], because monks show themselves to be exceedingly negligent in the service of their devotion if, over the course of a week, they sing fewer psalms from the Psalter together with the customary canticles. For we read [Note: Some manuscripts: “while we read”; others: “because we read”; others: “whenever we read”; others: “while we read that.”] that our holy Fathers energetically completed in one day what we, lukewarm as we are, might that we could complete in an entire week [Note: Hildemar omits “our”; Oxford omits “what we, lukewarm as we are.”].

## COMMENTARY

### “In the first place, at all the daytime hours the verse ‘O God, come to my assistance,’ and so forth”

With this verse Saint Benedict begins all the hours, whether daytime or nighttime. Yet, as Boherius observes, clerics customarily begin their hours in three ways, so as to guard against the threefold sin that is commonly committed: they begin the night vigils with the verse “O Lord, open my lips,” against sins of the mouth; Compline with the verse “Restore us,” against sins of the heart; and the remaining hours with the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” against sins of action.

### “At the first hour on Sunday, four sections of Psalm 118 are to be said”

Saint Benedict calls the groups of eight verses in Psalm 118 “sections”; Cassian calls them “interruptions” (*Book II*, chapter 11); Amalarius calls them “repetitions” (*Book IV on Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 2); Peter Damian calls them “incisions” (*Opusculum* 1, chapter 3).

At the first hour on Sunday we add to this psalm the Creed commonly called the Creed of Saint Athanasius, which some attribute to Eusebius of Vercelli. The Carthusian monks recite it every day, according to the new collection of their Statutes, part I, chapter 13, no. 12. Formerly it was sung each day in certain churches, as is stated by Honorius of Autun (*Book II of the Gem of the Soul*, chapter 59). On this Creed see what we said in Book I *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 4.

### “At the first hour of Monday, three psalms are to be said, namely the first, second, and sixth”

Peter Damian writes (*Opusculum* 10, chapter 3):

> “The first hour of the monks, except on Sunday, appropriately seems to begin from the beginning of the Psalter, so that the origin of the dawning day may correspond suitably with the beginning of the book.”

### “And so, on each successive day at the first hour, up to Sunday, three psalms are to be said in order, and so forth”

Amalarius has set out a fuller treatment of the entire institution described in this chapter by Saint Benedict in his *Supplement*, in volume II of the *Analecta*. Consult it if you wish.

As for why the Holy Father did not command that the highly celebrated Psalm 118 be sung daily at the first hour, Haeftenus offers the following reasons or conjectures (*Book VII*, treatise 7, discussion 3):

> “First, he may have been unwilling for the most beautiful psalm to be repeated every day, so that it might be held in greater esteem, just as more precious ornaments are not worn every day. Second, he may have wished to avoid the tedium that could arise from repetition, and to introduce some variation here. Third, in this way he may have made the psalmody shorter.”

Nevertheless, this psalm too was celebrated by monks, as can be seen in the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*. It was also commended among other things by an angel to the monk Wetinus, according to his vision, no. 4 (*Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, part 1).

### “These psalms are likewise to be repeated at the same hours through Sunday, while a uniform arrangement of hymns, readings, and verses is maintained on all days”

Boherius says:

> “As regards the number—for as regards the quality, such things are sometimes changed.”

Hildemar adds:

> “As if he were saying: however many psalms, however many hymns, however many verses, and however many readings I say on one day, I say the same number on another.”

From this, and especially from Boherius’s testimony, it is evident that hymns assigned formerly to the lesser canonical hours of the day were changed according to the variety of seasons and feasts. The Cistercians still observe this at Terce and Compline, as Cardinal Bona testifies (*On the Divine Psalms*, chapter 18, section 4).

### “Every day Vespers is to be sung with the modulation of four psalms”

That is, with sweet singing, as Boherius says; for *modulation* means the sweetness of song. This modulation should be performed according to the tone appropriate to the antiphon with which the singing began.

### “Since three psalms are lacking, those that are found to be longer in the number listed above are to be divided”

That is, longer, more extended, or greater, says Boherius. Saint Benedict received this custom of dividing the psalms from the Egyptian monks. Cassian reports (*Book II*, chapter 11) that they completed their psalms distinctly and in separate portions, dividing them according to the number of verses by two or three interruptions, with prayers inserted between them. The Council of Narbonne in 589 likewise prescribed such divisions (canon 2).

### “At Compline the same psalms are to be repeated every day, namely Psalms 4, 90, and 133”

These psalms are especially suited to the nighttime.

### “Once the order of the daytime psalmody has been arranged, all the remaining psalms are to be divided equally … and twelve are to be assigned to each night”

Peter Damian gives the following reason for this institution (*Opusculum* 10, chapter 6):

> “Because the evangelical trumpet rouses us to perseverance in continual prayer, saying, ‘We ought always to pray and never lose heart,’ and the Apostle says, ‘Pray without ceasing,’ great care has been taken that, so that the evangelical discipline might fulfill this command not only by day but also by night, the nocturnal vigils should be completed with twelve psalms. For it would have been difficult for the sick, pregnant women, and people of every age and sex to rise during the intervals of the nighttime hours and hurry to church just as they did during the day. Therefore, so that prudent discipline, the teacher of the Church, might temper the labor, it was established by a carefully devised and higher counsel that, corresponding to the number of the nighttime hours, the order of twelve psalms should nevertheless be assigned to the vigils. In this way the whole night might somehow seem to have been spent in prayer, since as many psalms were completed in prayer as there were hours in the night.”

Hildemar notes that formerly some people, on account of this passage—“Twelve psalms are to be assigned to each night”—wished, when prevented by some obstacle, for example while traveling, to substitute shorter psalms for the vigils in which longer psalms occurred. They would say, for example, that they dared to use the gradual psalms in this way, claiming that they did so according to the precept of the Rule, which says: “Twelve psalms are to be assigned to each night.”

But Hildemar says:

> “Such men are convicted on this point: after the order of the daytime psalmody has been arranged, all the remaining psalms are to be divided equally among the vigils of seven nights, dividing those psalms that are longer among them. When they substitute other psalms, they do not divide them; and when they do not divide them, they transgress this precept.”

### “We particularly admonish this: if anyone should perhaps dislike this distribution of the psalms, let him arrange it differently if he judges that another arrangement is better”

This is certainly an outstanding example of humility: a man filled with the spirit of all the righteous submits an order instituted by himself, and arranged with such care and discretion, to another’s judgment.

But Bernard of Cassino says:

> “Whether our master said this out of humility or as a concession, it is safer that no abbot or monk should assume the presumption of arranging the order of psalmody otherwise than he himself arranged it here, since he was filled with the Spirit of God.”

Certainly, if it is a great sign of humility in Saint Benedict that he permits the order instituted by himself to be arranged otherwise, it is no less a sign of pride to presume to do so. For this reason even the supreme pontiffs never wished to change it, as Walafrid observes in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 23.

Since some lovers of novelty had occasionally presumed to do this, it was decreed at the Council of Aachen in 802 that “in monasteries observing the Rule of Saint Benedict, the monks should perform the office of Saint Benedict as the Rule teaches.” At the second council, held in 817, it was decreed that “the monks should celebrate the office contained in the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

The *Chronicle of Moissac* mentions this decree in these words:

> “In the third year of Louis, a great council was held at Aachen in the month of August, and it was commanded that all monks should sing the course of Saint Benedict according to the regular order.”

Pope Paul V, too, who in our own age established a breviary for all who serve under the Rule of the Holy Father Benedict, wished this same arrangement of the Psalter to remain inviolate. Hildemar therefore rightly reproves those who had presumed to change the arrangement of the psalms established by the Holy Father. Walafrid also complains about this in *On Ecclesiastical Matters*, chapter 25, although only a few monks, and not all of them, had adopted the Roman office, as is clear from the *Supplement* of Amalarius, a writer of the same period, who testifies that the offices of monks were then different from those of the clergy.

See Benedict Haeftenus, Book VII, treatises 5, discussions 4 and 5.

For the rest, I observe here, with Hildemar and certain others, that the words of Saint Benedict concern only the arrangement of the psalms, not that of hymns, verses, readings, and so forth.

### “Provided that every effort is made to ensure that the Psalter, consisting of the full number of 150 psalms, is sung completely each week”

Bernard of Cassino, followed by Boherius, notes that the Holy Father Benedict did not prescribe absolutely that the entire Psalter should be sung—meaning that every psalm should be sung every week—but added the words “consisting of the full number of 150 psalms.” This is because, on account of festivals that occur during the week, certain psalms cannot be sung, although one must never depart from the number of psalms.

That is how they explain the passage for their own purpose. But they could have said more briefly and clearly that Saint Benedict’s decree concerning the weekly recitation of the Psalter is to be understood hypothetically: namely, on the assumption that the feasts—which occurred less frequently in his time—do not intervene. What he added, “consisting of the full number of 150 psalms,” seems to refer to something else: he deliberately specified the number of psalms so that no one might insert spurious, foreign, or apocryphal psalms, in accordance with canon 59 of the Council of Laodicea: “Private psalms are not to be recited in church.”

There were formerly psalms under the name of Solomon and of certain others, as Theodore Balsamon says. The council calls them “private” because they had not been received with the authority of the Church. Saint Athanasius lists the psalms and odes of Solomon among the apocryphal writings in his *Synopsis of Sacred Scripture*. Nicephorus, patriarch of Constantinople, also discusses them in his canon and places them among the writings that are disputed.

Athanasius himself, in the *Synopsis*, mentions among the Davidic psalms a Psalm 151, which is also found in ancient manuscript Psalters and has been published in the Polyglot Bible. Many heretics also composed psalms, among them Hierax, as Saint Epiphanius teaches in Book II of the *Panarion*, heresy 67, and Valentinus, as can be seen in Tertullian’s *On the Flesh of Christ*. Finally, the Donatists sang in their churches psalms composed by human ingenuity, as Saint Augustine teaches in letter 55 of the new edition.

From this passage of Saint Benedict, Hildemar accuses as violators of the Rule those who presume to change the Benedictine office into the Roman office, because they do not complete the whole Psalter every week—for example, during the weeks of Easter and Pentecost, when the Romans sing the office more briefly than usual.

### “For monks show themselves to be exceedingly negligent in the service of their devotion”

Rather, in the service of their obligation. What was a matter of devotion before entering the cloister became an obligation and a debt after monastic profession, as Boherius observes.

### “If they sing fewer psalms from the Psalter together with the customary canticles over the course of a week, although we read that the holy Fathers completed this energetically in one day”

The words “in one day” should not be understood as though they recited the Psalter only once and on one day. When Hildemar says “in one day,” he means, as though he were saying “on each day,” or at least “frequently.”

We find that many imitated the fervor of these holy Fathers. Saint Winwaloeus sang fifty psalms three times each day, sometimes in the form of a cross and sometimes kneeling. Saint Neot, abbot in England, immersed in a spring, was accustomed, to increase his austerity, to complete the entire Psalter. The same is reported of Saint Aldhelm in his *Life*, no. 4 (*Acta Sanctorum*, fourth century, Benedictine part 2).

Abbot Ceolfrid, even while traveling to Rome, took care to sing the Psalter in order twice each day, apart from the canonical hours of prayer, as Bede writes in *The Life of Saint Benedict Biscop*, Book II, no. 21. The same is reported of Saint Sequanus, abbot, in his *Life*, no. 2, and of Saint Austrudis, abbess of Laon, likewise in her *Life*, no. 18. They would not taste any food or drink before reciting the entire Psalter. Gervinus, abbot of Centula, is also praised for this in the *Chronicle of Centula*, Book IV, chapter 26 (*Spicilegium*, volume IV).

Finally, Saint Maurus, according to Faustus in his *Life*, and Saint Alberic, abbot of Cîteaux, according to Henriquez in his *Life*, no. 3 (*Acta Sanctorum*, January 26), often went through the Psalter before the night vigils.

Why should I mention entire congregations for whom it was customary to sing the Psalter every day? We read this of the nuns of Saint Odilia at Hohenburg in her *Life*, no. 21:

> “It also happened that one day, as was the custom in that monastery, namely, that each day, according to their strength, they fasted and sang the Psalter in order…”

We learn from Jerome, a Camaldolese monk, in his sermon on Saint Romuald, no. 67 (*Acta Sanctorum*, February 7), that the same discipline prevailed among all the hermits of Saint Romuald:

> “The holy Father Romuald summoned all the hermits, one by one, and taught them that throughout the entire year they were to fast three days a week on bread and water alone, recite the Psalter daily together with the canticles, observe silence inviolably, and practice discipline with whips in their cells.”

Peter Damian writes similarly concerning the hermits of Fonte Avellana (*Opusculum*, chapter 14):

> “It is customary that when two brothers live together in a cell, they complete two Psalters in a day, one for the living and the other for the dead. The Psalter for the living is recited together with the additions that Blessed Romuald established. The one for the dead is recited with nine readings, namely three groups of fifty psalms. Whoever lives alone completes the Psalter for the living in its entirety each day; as for that of the dead, he completes either half or the whole, according to what his strength permits. The psalmody of the canonical hours, moreover, is completed here entirely and in order, just as it is done in the monastery.”

But what the same Peter Damian reports concerning Saint Dominic Loricatus surpasses almost all credibility:

> “There is among us one who sometimes, in a single day continued through the night, goes through nine Psalters in meditation, while almost continually striking his naked body with scourges held in both hands. [lacuna] This brother once complained to me, in fraternal familiarity, that although he often completed nine Psalters in this way by singing them, he had never been able to reach the tenth.”

Finally, it was formerly a general custom throughout the Benedictine Order to recite the entire Psalter on Good Friday, as we showed in Book III *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 14.

### “What we, lukewarm as we are, might complete in an entire week”

With these final words and this fatherly rebuke Saint Benedict adds spurs to his disciples, so that they may add something to the customary service of their devotion. I therefore cannot sufficiently marvel at certain monks who complain when they are occasionally required to recite the Little Office of the Blessed Mary, as though they were burdened by excessively long psalmody. For scarcely any monastic congregation formerly existed that did not undertake to complete it every day, and such devotion formerly grew among our people for increasing the office that, as Boherius writes, “in certain monasteries they added more than three Psalters in quantity” to the course of the divine work instituted by the Holy Father. This is certainly clear from what we reported in Book I *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapters 2, 3, 4, 9, and 11.

I know that some did not approve such prolixity in psalmody, including William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, in his letter to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, and Peter of Blois, who dissuades a certain Carthusian monk contemplating a transfer to the Cluniacs. He writes as follows (*Letter 86*):

> “What sweetness or devotion, I ask, will you find among those for whom the numerous and confused repetition and stuffing-together of psalms has become nauseating? Paul says: ‘I will sing with the spirit; I will sing also with the mind.’ If devotion is not present in those who sing, even if they repeat the same psalm a thousand times, it is not a joyful and beautiful song of praise.”

Later, however, he moderated the fervor of his zeal somewhat, writing to M., abbot of Evesham, as follows (*Letter 97*):

> “I confess that the length of psalmody, if it proceeds from devotion, is most beneficial; if it has weariness as its companion, it is nevertheless an honorable occupation; if it does not entirely suppress the mind’s wandering excursions, through it the mind at least grows accustomed to more honorable pursuits.”

Peter Damian, however, held a very different view. A single testimony of his is sufficient to silence his opponents. Writing to the Cluniac monks, he explains himself as follows (*Book VI, Letter 5*):

> “When I recall the strict and fervent order of your holy way of life, I perceive in it not the work of human invention but the instruction of the Holy Spirit. For so great is the length of the continual perseverance with which the order is observed, and so great especially is the persistence in the ecclesiastical offices, that during the very heat of Cancer or Leo, when the days are longer, scarcely half an hour of the entire day remained in which the brothers were permitted to exchange conversation in the cloister.
>
> “This exercise of such continual labor has, I think, been provided by a sufficiently careful and prudent art of instruction for the purpose of restraining the frailty of weak and infirm brothers and almost removing the opportunity for sin, so that, even if they wish to sin, they can scarcely do so beyond the realm of thought. Thus provision is made for the weakness of the frail when, in completing the appointed order without interruption, the whole span not only of the daytime but also of the nighttime is consumed.”

Before I finish this chapter, I shall observe, with Boherius in his second commentary, that certain people formerly thought that the Holy Father Benedict had used the Gallican Psalter. They inferred this from those passages in which the Holy Father cites the Psalter in the Rule, where various readings are found that do not exist in the Roman Psalter but do occur in the Gallican.

## CHAPTER XIX  
### On the Discipline of Singing Psalms

## [Col. 0475]

We believe that the divine presence is everywhere, and that in every place the eyes of the Lord behold the good and the wicked [Note: “In every place” is absent in the Oxford and Hildemar manuscripts]. Yet we should believe this above all without any doubt when we are present for the divine work.

Therefore, let us always remember what the prophet says: “Serve the Lord in fear”; and again, “Sing wisely”; and, “In the sight of the angels I will sing to you.” Let us therefore consider how it is fitting for us to be in the presence of the divinity and his angels, and let us stand for the singing of psalms in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice [Note: “Always” is absent in Hildemar] [Note: Some manuscripts omit “us.”].

## COMMENTARY

### [Col. 0475A]

Thus far Saint Benedict has treated the divine offices at considerable length, assigning each of their hours, distributing the parts of each hour, and arranging the order of the psalms. One thing seemed to remain, something that would be, as it were, the soul of all these matters and without which scarcely, or perhaps not at all, would the whole be beneficial: namely, the discipline with which the psalms should be sung. He explains this in the present chapter.

This discipline of singing psalms consists chiefly in two things. One concerns the external composure of the person; the other directs the inward affections of the soul. This chapter deals especially with the second. We have already touched extensively on the first both in what has been said above and in Book I *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 2.

I add here only the decree of Pope Benedict XII, that in the churches, monasteries, or places of monks:
