> “All the monks, individually and collectively, are to assemble at the appointed hours for the divine offices with seriousness and modesty, humbly and devoutly; and they are to celebrate these offices with sincere devotion, slowly, distinctly, suitably, and properly, not rushing or syncopating, and observing silence in whatever other matters might impede them; indeed, they are to attend to the divine offices with their hearts intent. Those who transgress the foregoing are to be subject to the appropriate discipline.”

(*Constitution for the Benedictines*, chapter 27.)

The excellent admonition of Saint Bernard may also be referred to here (*Sermon 47 on the Song of Songs*):

> “I exhort you, dearly beloved, always to take part in the divine praises purely and energetically. Energetically, so that, just as you attend the Lord reverently, you may also attend him cheerfully—not sluggish, not sleepy, not yawning, not sparing your voices, not cutting off half the words, not skipping complete ones, not uttering with broken and slackened voices something effeminate and stammering through the nose; rather, with a manly sound and feeling, bringing forth the voices of the Holy Spirit as is fitting.”

Elsewhere he writes (*Letter 312*):

> “If there is singing, let it be full of gravity; let it echo neither wantonness nor rusticity. Let it be sweet without being frivolous; let it charm the ears in such a way that it moves the hearts. Let it relieve sadness and moderate anger. Let it not empty the meaning of the text but make it fruitful. It is no small loss of spiritual grace to be led away from the usefulness of understanding by the frivolity of song, and to devote oneself more to the shaping of sounds than to the communication of meaning.”

Entirely rightly. For all figured singing, the voices—or rather the shouts—of musicians, and all musical instruments are wholly foreign to the humble and simple discipline with which monks should sing psalms. All monks who have ever devoted themselves to solid piety and religious simplicity have abhorred such things. Hence our monks of Casale rightly expelled organs from their churches, issuing the following statute (*Manuscript Constitutions of Casale Benigno*, chapter 66):

> “We also prohibit organs in our congregation, forbidding our brothers to play either organs or other instruments. We likewise prohibit them from learning or teaching their use. Similarly, every kind of figured singing is to be avoided.”

They seem to have received this decree from the Cassinese congregation, since its ancient declarations prohibit the construction of new organs without the permission of the general chapter and permit them to be played only on the principal days—and then by persons other than monks. They forbid monks to play organs or other musical instruments and prohibit them from learning or teaching their use.

The Constitutions of the monks of Fuliens likewise state (chapter 19):

> “In no part of the divine office or of the Mass is it permitted to use figured, symphonic, or musical song, nor organs or any other kind of instrument. Let all these things be kept as far as possible from our monasteries, and let no dispensation be granted in this matter.”

Certainly, one rarely finds the use of organs among ancient monks. Elfegus is said to have constructed some in the new monastery at Winchester, according to the metrical *Life of Saint Æthelwold* (*Acta Sanctorum*, fifth century, Benedictine volume, p. 630); but this was in the cathedral church, which had formerly been entrusted to Benedictine monks at Winchester.

Likewise, the count Aldermannus gave the basilica at Ramsey thirty pounds to manufacture copper organ pipes. These pipes, placed in dense order in their wind chest over a set of channels pierced with holes, were blown on feast days by the stronger breath of bellows and produced a very sweet melody and a sound of trumpet-like resonance (*Chronicle of Ramsey*, part II, chapter 28, fifth-century volume, p. 756). But this was done through the generosity of the count, not at the monks’ expense.

Finally, in the manuscript chronicle of the monastery of Cava I found mention of organs at the dedication of the church performed by Urban II (*Acta Sanctorum*, under the life of Saint Peter, abbot of Cava, March 4). But this occurred at a very solemn celebration and in the presence of the supreme pontiff.

For the rest, in our Gaul I doubt that organs were seen in monks’ churches before three hundred, or at most four hundred, years ago. Navarrus was therefore mistaken when he asserted that the use of organs had not yet been received in the time of Saint Thomas Aquinas. For, in addition to what we have said, in the year 757 “organs were brought from Greece, sent by the emperor together with certain gifts to Lord King Pippin,” as recorded in the *Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon*.

But enough of these incidental remarks; I return to the text of the Rule.

### “We believe that the divine presence is everywhere”

Although the fact that God is present everywhere is self-evident, so that we scarcely conceive of God without understanding him to be present everywhere, there have nevertheless been people who, deprived even of the light of nature, attempted to confine the divine immensity within limits.

Concerning the Platonists and Stoics, Tertullian writes (*Apology*):

> “The Stoics placed God outside the world, so that, like a potter, he might twist this mass from the outside; the Platonists placed him within the world, so that, like a pilot, he might remain within the world that he governs.”

The Jews too—or at least the more uneducated among them—confined God in the temple at Jerusalem, according to Saint Jerome (*Commentary on Isaiah*, chapter 66).

Many heretics likewise attacked the divine immensity: the Valentinians, Gnostics, Manichaeans, and others, as reported by Irenaeus, Tertullian, Epiphanius, and Augustine. In our own time the Calvinist Vorstius struck the same rock, wishing God to exist substantially only in heaven, and elsewhere only by virtue and power.

Erasmus is even reported to have doubted whether God exists in the beetle’s cave and in other more obscene places, although this is nowhere actually found in the works of Erasmus.

Against all these views God cries out: “I fill heaven and earth.”

How, then, we are to understand God as present everywhere, St. Gregory explains admirably in the following words, cited here by Hildemar:

> “God is said to be everywhere because he himself remains within all things, himself outside all things, himself above all things, himself beneath all things. He is above by his power and below by his sustaining; outside by his greatness and within by his subtlety. Above, he rules; below, he contains; outside, he surrounds; within, he penetrates. He is not superior in one respect and inferior in another, nor exterior in one respect and interior in another; rather, one and the same, wholly present everywhere, he sustains by presiding, penetrates by surrounding, and surrounds by penetrating. Thus, from the place where he presides above, he sustains below; and from the place where he encompasses externally, he fills internally. He rules above without disturbance, sustains below without labor, penetrates within without diminution, and surrounds without extension. He is therefore below and above without location; immense without breadth; subtle without attenuation.” [Col. 0477B]

### 328. “And the eyes of the Lord.”

“Hildemar says that ‘the eye of God’ is that divine power by which he sees all things, just as ‘the ear’ is that divine power by which he hears all things.” Or, as Bernard of Cassino says, “The observation of his eyes is infallible, and it is the perception of his knowledge, which is utterly complete.”

“Watching the good and the wicked.”

The good, Hildemar again says, “so that they may be corrected,” as he looked upon Peter; the wicked, “so that they may be punished and condemned,” as he is said to have looked upon the camp of the Egyptians. He is like the sun, which both melts wax and hardens clay.

“Yet let us believe this above all without any doubt.”

What he says by “above all” must not be understood as though God were more in one place than in another. It must be referred to us, not to God himself, as Bernard of Cassino teaches after Hildemar. Certainly, “although we are always seen, at that time we also present and show ourselves as though speaking face to face with God,” says the other Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux.

[Col. 0477C] “When we attend the divine work.”

By “the divine work,” he says, “St. Benedict deliberately wished to designate the solemn praises that are offered to God daily in the oratory, as St. Bernard again explains (Sermon 47 on the Song of Songs), so that he might make still clearer how intent he wishes us to be upon that work.”

“Therefore, let us always remember what the Prophet says: ‘Serve the Lord in fear’; and again: ‘Sing psalms wisely.’”

What it means to sing psalms wisely is explained in various ways by various writers. First, St. Basil says (On the Rules, in Rufinus, chapter 57):

> “If someone applies his soul to each word of the psalms in the way that the sense of taste is applied to distinguishing the flavor of foods, he is the one who fulfills what is said: ‘Sing wisely.’”

Hildemar appears to agree with Basil in these words:

> “He sings wisely who thinks in his heart about what he says with his mouth.”

Bernard of Cassino says:

> “‘Sing wisely,’ that is, tastefully—that is, with the savor of devotion—so that what is held in the mouth while singing may be contemplated with all one’s strength. For some sing, but foolishly, because, while the heart wanders, there is in them only the sound of the lips. He also sings foolishly who seeks only to please his listeners by the modulation of his voice.”

Boherius says the same. The following words of St. Bernard also apply here (Sermon 7 on the Song of Songs):

> “Therefore, singing praise together with the choirs of heaven, as citizens of the saints and members of God’s household, sing wisely. Food tastes in the mouth; the psalm tastes in the heart. Let the faithful and prudent soul not neglect to grind it with the teeth of its understanding, lest, if it swallows it whole and unchewed, it lose the flavor that is desirable and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb.”

Certainly, according to the same Bernard (Sermon 85 on the Song of Songs), if the wise person is one to whom God is sweet, then the person who finds God sweet while singing must be said to sing wisely. The Master in the Rule, chapter 47, appears to follow the same explanation.

Alternatively, the Rule of the Fathers, cited here by St. Benedict of Aniane and Smaragdus, says:

> “He sings wisely who does not contradict with harmful deeds the voice that praises, and who diligently and earnestly pursues how he ought to serve the divine power.” [Col. 0478A]

This agrees with the seventy-second sentence of Prosper of Aquitaine:

> “He rightly sings praise to God whose works agree with his voice. For when the song is finished, the voice falls silent; but a life remaining in good deeds never ceases to proclaim the glory of him whom it rejoices to have working within it.”

Finally, Nicholas of Fractura says:

> “No one acts wisely in what he does not understand. Therefore, when we sing psalms, let us sing wisely—that is, with complete purity of soul and with understanding of the things that are above.”

“And: ‘In the presence of the angels I will sing to you.’”

Hildemar explains this passage in two ways:

> “In one way, it is understood that when we sing to God, we sing in the presence of the angels, because God is not without his messengers and ministers. In another way, it is understood that, if we apply our heart to what we say with our mouth, our intention is joined to the intention of the angels.”

“Therefore, let us consider how we ought to conduct ourselves in the presence of the Divinity and his angels.” [Col. 0478B]

Otherwise, that terrible reproach of St. Bernard might fall upon us (Sermon 7 on the Song of Songs; see Letter 78 to Suger, abbot):

> “I grieve that some of you are overcome by deep sleep during the sacred vigils and do not reverence the citizens of heaven, but appear as though dead in the presence of princes, although they delight to attend your solemnities, moved by your own liveliness. I fear that one day, abhorring your laziness, they may depart in indignation, and that each of you may too late begin to say to God with groaning: ‘You have put my acquaintances far from me; they have made me an abomination to themselves.’ Therefore, pay attention to your princes when you stand to pray or sing psalms, and stand with reverence and discipline . . . . Let us take up the office of those whose fellowship we share, so that praise may be perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children. Let us say to them: ‘Sing to our God, sing’; and let us hear them answer in turn: ‘Sing to our King, sing.’”

“And thus let us stand for singing.”

Bernard of Cassino comments on this passage:

> “He did not say, ‘Let us sit for singing,’ but he said, ‘Let us stand,’ to indicate that the body ought to be upright and thereby also to signify an upright mind. Hence, to this day, when the psalms are sung, the brothers at Monte Cassino do not sit, and so forth.”

But we have spoken of these matters above, at chapter 9.

“So that our mind may agree with our voice.”

This is precisely what St. Benedict intended throughout this entire chapter. For this reason he first mentioned the divine presence when we attend the divine work; that we sing in the presence of the angels; that God must be served with fear; and that we must sing wisely. Finally, he concluded: “Let us stand for singing in such a way that our mind agrees with our voice.”

St. Basil gives the same admonition (Admonition in the Rule, chapter 9):

> “Let your understanding not be discordant with the sound of your voice, but let it attend vigilantly to the words of your tongue.”

St. Augustine says (Rule, chapter 7):

> “When you pray to God with psalms and hymns, let what is uttered in the voice also be present in the heart.”

St. Isidore says:

> “When the spiritual mysteries of the psalms are celebrated, let the monk flee laughter and idle stories; let him meditate in his heart upon what is sung with his mouth.”

The Rule of the Master says (chapter 47):

> “What sounds in the voice of the one singing should itself be in the mind.” [330]

St. Bernard says:

> “While you sing psalms, think of nothing other than what you are singing.”

Such was St. Adalard, abbot of Corbie. Paschasius Radbertus, in his Life of Adalard, section 27 (Fourth Century of Benedictine Writers, part I), reports:

> “Whenever he entered the divine office, as he himself was accustomed to say with joyful spirit, he immediately set all thoughts and concerns about temporal matters outside the door, and entered wholly with himself, so that he might be wholly present to God and to himself.”

Such were our people of Meaux, of St. Faro. Their proven attentiveness to God brought about the complete conversion of the soldier Otger, as is related in his Life, section 19 (same volume). Such were the monks of Saint Gall, whose devotion at the divine work the emperors Otto and Conrad are said to have learned by experience, according to Ekkehard, in his book On the Misfortunes of Saint Gall.

Finally, such was Benedict, a monk at Cluny (Peter the Venerable, Book I of Miracles, chapter 20):

> “He always carried about with him a glossed psalter, because he sang the psalms not casually, as is the custom of some, but with the greatest concentration and devotion. Whenever he encountered something he did not understand, he immediately turned his eyes to the glosses.” [Col. 0479A; Col. 0480A]

## CHAPTER XX. On Reverence in Prayer.

[Col. 0479]

[Col. 0479A] If we wish to make some request of powerful men, we do not presume to do so except with humility and reverence. How much more, then, must we beseech the Lord God of all things with complete humility [Note: [Col. 0479A] Some copies: “with all humility”; others: “with humility of heart.”] and devout purity [Note: [Col. 0480A] Hildemar and Hadrensis: “and with purity of devotion.”]! Let us know that we are heard not through an abundance of words, but in purity of heart and compunction of tears. Therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure, unless it is extended by the fervor of the inspiration of divine grace [Note: [Col. 0480A] In some copies, “of grace” is absent.]. In the assembly, however, prayer must be shortened completely; and when the prior gives the signal, let all rise together.

## COMMENTARY.

[Col. 0479]

[Col. 0479B] “If we wish to make some request of powerful men,” and so forth.

This is certainly a familiar comparison, but all the more effective for persuasion because it is familiar and well known. Tertullian uses the same comparison in his book On Prayer; St. Basil, in the Shorter Rules, question 201; Cassian, Conference 23, chapter 7; Evagrius, in his Monastic Writings, section 11, volume III of the Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments; St. Eligius, homily 9; Haymo of Halberstadt, Book I On Variety, chapter 20; the Master, in the Rule, chapter 48; and Grimlaicus, in the Rule for Solitaries, chapter 31, where he also transcribes almost this entire chapter.

“How much more must we beseech the Lord God of all things with complete humility and devout purity.”

“With complete humility,” he says, that is, of body and soul, according to Hildemar. Bernard of Cassino adds, “and of the mouth.” Both are necessary, and St. Benedict praises both in chapter 7.

The Holy Father rightly commends the virtue of humility to anyone wishing to pray, because God regards the prayer of the humble and does not despise their petitions. Hence St. John Climacus (Step 7; see St. Bernard, Sermon 25 on Various Subjects):

> “When you devote yourself to prayers, stand trembling before the judge, like a guilty person, so that by the humble posture of your body outwardly and of your spirit inwardly you may extinguish the anger of the just judge. For he cannot despise a soul standing sorrowfully before him like a widow and persistently wearying him with prayers, although he himself is never weary.”

St. Benedict adds “with devout purity,” which Bernard of Cassino locates in simplicity of heart, according to the saying: “Seek him in simplicity of heart.” Certainly, “there ought to be no duplicity in prayer; one person should not be found in the mouth and another in the heart,” says the Master in the Rule (chapter 48). Rather, there should be pure intention toward God, “so that the one who prays may seem to hold the feet of the present Christ,” as the same Master says.

“And not through an abundance of words.”

St. Basil teaches the same:

> “Do not prolong the length of your words before him, for God is appeased not through an abundance of words but in the purest mind.”

When the brothers asked Abbot Macarius how one ought to pray, he replied (Rufinus, Admonitions, Book III of the Lives of the Fathers, section 207):

> “Superfluous words are not necessary for us. We need only stretch out our hands and say: ‘God, as you will, and as it pleases you, so let it be.’ But if temptation or assault comes upon us, we should say: ‘God, help us’; for he himself knows what is beneficial for us.”

Indeed, Christ himself says in the Gospel:

> “When you pray, do not speak at length as the Gentiles do; for they think that they will be heard because of their many words. Therefore, do not imitate them.”

St. Augustine explains very learnedly what it means to pray through an abundance of words, and how this differs from prolonged prayer (Letter 130):

> “For, contrary to what some think, praying for a longer time is not the same as praying through an abundance of words. Prolix speech is one thing, prolonged affection another. For it is written even of the Lord himself that he spent the night in prayer and that he prayed at greater length. What else was he doing there except offering us an example, in due season, of the one who prays, while the eternal Hearer is the Father?”

A little later he says:

> “Let much speaking be absent from our prayer, but let much prayer not be absent if fervor persists. For to speak much is to add superfluous words to a necessary matter in prayer; but to pray much is to knock upon the one whom we beseech with prolonged and devout stirring of the heart. Often this business is conducted more by groans than by words, more by tears than by feeling.”

And, as Hugh of St. Victor teaches splendidly (On the Manner of Praying, chapter 4):

> “A person who is being asked is instructed by our account, so that he may know what we want; by entreaty he is urged to grant what we request. But in prayer directed to God, an account is not necessary, unless perhaps a person gives an account so that he himself may understand his petition better—so that, admonished by his own prayer, he may consider what he is asking, and, exercised by consideration of his petition, may pray more devoutly.” [332]

“But in purity of heart.”

Because only the pure in heart will see God. Cassian says (Conference 9, chapter 3):

> “For prayer to be offered with the fervor and purity it ought to have, the following things must be observed in every respect. First, concern for bodily matters must generally be cut away. Next, not only care for any business or matter, but even its memory, must be wholly excluded. Slander, empty talk, or excessive speech, and likewise jokes must be cut off; above all, the disturbance of anger or sadness must be completely uprooted; the harmful tinder of desire and love of money must be torn out by the roots. Once these and similar vices have been entirely expelled and cut away—vices that can also be exposed to human sight—and once the cleansing correction we have described has preceded, a correction accomplished through purity of simplicity and innocence, the unshakable foundations of profound humility must first be laid, foundations capable of supporting the tower that is to enter the heavens. Then the structure of spiritual virtues must be built upon them. The mind must be restrained from every wandering and slippery distraction, so that little by little it may begin to be raised toward the contemplation of God and spiritual vision. For whatever our soul has conceived before the hour of prayer must necessarily confront us in prayer through the intrusion of memory. Therefore, if we wish to be found as people who pray in a particular way, we must prepare ourselves beforehand in that same way for the time of prayer, and so forth.”

“And with compunction of tears.”

St. Augustine explains what compunction is in these words (On the Spirit and the Soul, chapter 50):

> “Compunction is what occurs when, through consideration of one’s sins, the heart is touched by inward sorrow.”

The book On the Manner of Living, among the works of St. Bernard, gives another definition (chapter 10):

> “Compunction of heart is humility of mind, arising from remembrance of sin and fear of judgment. That compunction is perfect which drives from itself every pleasure in bodily things and fixes the mind’s intention, with all its effort, upon the contemplation of God.”

These words distinguish, as it were, two kinds of compunction: one consisting in sorrow for our offenses, the other in exultation over divine gifts, as St. Bernard says (Sermon 66 on the Song of Songs). Grimlaicus, in the Rule for Solitaries (chapter 30), calls them the upper irrigation and the lower irrigation.

According to St. Gregory (Moralia, Book XXIII, chapter 13), there are four conditions through which the soul of a just person is deeply moved by compunction:

> “When he remembers his sins and considers where he was; when, fearing the sentence of God’s judgments, he asks himself and considers where he will be; when, carefully attending to the evils of the present life, he sorrowfully considers where he is; or when he contemplates the good things of the heavenly homeland and, because he has not yet attained them, mournfully perceives where he is not.” [Col. 0481B]

The same may be seen in the aforementioned book On the Manner of Living, chapter 10, and in the Rule for Solitaries, chapter 29. Cassian recounts other causes of compunction in Conference 9, chapter 26. See Peter Damian, Opusculum 15, chapter 26. [333]

“And therefore prayer ought to be brief and pure.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius say that this applies both to duration and to words. The widely circulated Summary of the Teaching of St. Athanasius for Monks gives the same advice:

> “Pray frequently and continually throughout the day; nevertheless, do so without extending the prayer at length, without shouting, and without empty verbosity.”

This is also shown by the example of the Egyptian monks, who, as Cassian says (Book II, chapter 10), considered it more beneficial for prayers to be brief but very frequent. St. Augustine also speaks of them in his letter to Proba (Letter 130):

> “The brothers in Egypt are said to have frequent prayers, but nevertheless very brief ones, thrown out, as it were, in haste, lest that attentive and uplifted intention—which is especially necessary to one who prays—should fade and grow dull through excessive delay. Thus they themselves sufficiently show that, just as this intention must not be blunted if it cannot endure, so, if it endures, it must not be broken too quickly.” [Col. 0481C]

Besides the reason just given by St. Augustine, Cassian adds another explanation for their preference for such brief prayers (Book II, chapter 10):

> “So that we may avoid, through concise brevity, the darts of the ambushing devil, which he especially strives to inflict upon us when we pray.”

In the same work, Abbot Isaac says (Conference IX, chapter 36):

> “We must pray frequently but briefly, lest, while we linger, the enemy lying in wait may manage to insert something into our heart.”

The Master gives two reasons for this brevity, which Smaragdus transcribes here without naming him (chapter 48):

> “For this reason we said that prayer should be brief: lest someone fall asleep under the pretext of a prolonged prayer, or lest, while they lie there for a long time, the devil place various things before their eyes or suggest something else in their heart.”

St. Hildegard adds:

> “Lest, when they later devote themselves to psalmody, they attend less to the psalmody itself because they have been wearied by the preceding and prolonged prayer.” [Col. 0481D]

According to St. Benedict, prayer must therefore be not only brief but also pure. Pure prayer is prayer that asks for God himself, or for something on account of God. St. Bernard lists examples of this in Sentence 17. See also his Sermon 107 on Various Subjects.

“Unless it is extended by the fervor of the inspiration of divine grace.”

Just as the mind’s intention must not be blunted if it cannot persist, so, if it has persisted, it must not be broken too quickly, as St. Augustine said above. Therefore, Hildemar says:

> “We ought to lie prostrate in prayer until, with the Lord’s help, we have suppressed our vain thoughts. But if we see that we are overcome by agitations, and no longer take pleasure in remaining in prayer, we should rise; then we should read, sing psalms, or work.” [Col. 0482A]

Aelred agrees with St. Benedict on this point in his Rule, chapter 14.

“Nevertheless, in the assembly prayer must be shortened completely; and when the prior gives the signal, all must rise together.”

This passage is difficult and obscure, and the authors do not agree in explaining it. I shall therefore report their differing opinions, so that the one that seems preferable may be chosen.

First, Smaragdus appears to understand St. Benedict as referring to the rite of the Egyptian monks, who inserted prayers between the psalms. This is especially clear from the fact that, in explaining this text of the Rule, he says nothing other than the very words of Cassian in which that rite is described.

Hildemar, the ancient commentator on the Rule, explains his view as follows:

> “In the assembly prayer must be shortened completely. For he is not speaking of the prayer said by the priest or by the chapter, but of the prayer of each individual, by which each monk prays in the assembly. For it has been established how many chapters the priest must say, or how much prayer must be offered in the assembly.”

Then, in explaining the following words, “and when the prior gives the signal, all must rise together,” he reports two interpretations:

> “Some understand that signal to be the one given when the priest says, ‘world without end,’ so that you may rise and answer ‘Amen,’ whether there is in you a divine inspiration by which you are able to pray longer or not . . . . Others again understand the signal at which the Rule commands them to rise to be the final signal sounded for the vigils, matins, prime, terce, sext, none, vespers, and compline. When it has sounded, the monk is to be ready, standing in the choir, to answer after the words, ‘O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.’”

It was formerly the custom in our order for the brothers to go around the altars praying between the signals of the divine office; they did this especially during the nocturnal vigils, as we have shown in Book I of On the Ancient Rites of Monks, chapter 1. They understood the text of the Holy Rule to refer to this prayer. Bernard of Cassino and Richard of St. Angelo also seem to have understood it in this way, as did St. Hildegard, who writes concerning this passage:

> “Since he admonished that a prayer be said before each canonical hour, and since he commands in what follows that the kiss of peace not be offered to a guest until prayer has first been said, much more must prayer precede the greeting of almighty God. It must be brief, lest, having been wearied by the preceding and prolonged prayer, they attend less to the psalmody.”

Theobald Artaldus Coelestinus also agrees. In his French exposition of the Rule he renders the passage as follows:

> “The Prayer that is made in the assembly—that is, from the time when, after the ringing of the bell, the brothers have gathered in the church to perform the divine service—must be entirely shortened, without regard to the devout affection of particular individuals, which ought to become common in the presence of the religious community.”

The monk Paulus Augustinus of Genoa, of Cassino, appears to have followed the first interpretation. After citing the text of the Rule, “And when the prior gives the signal, all must rise together,” he concludes:

> “Therefore, in the final part of the office they knelt.”

Cardinal Turrecremata does not depart far from this view. He explains St. Benedict as referring “to the prayer of each individual, which each one prays privately with the whole assembly, just as at the end of the religious office they customarily pray, prostrate or bowed, until the signal given by the superior.” Matthias Lambertus supports this interpretation in his French commentary, and it pleased Hildemar more than the alternative.

Nicholas Bravus combines the two interpretations into one, so that the Rule refers both to the beginning and to the end of the hours—that is, both to the prayer customarily said before the office and to the prayer that follows it. It is certainly plausible that prayer was offered beforehand and repeated after the office had been completed. But whether St. Benedict is speaking here of that prayer is not equally clear.

[Col. 0483A] The other Nicholas, called Nicholas of Fractura, does not explain his opinion sufficiently when he says that the Rule is not to be understood of psalmody or of the other things arranged for the divine offices, “but of the prayer by which each person prays in the assembly.”

Peter Boherius, after reporting the various opinions in his first commentary, inclines toward the view that St. Benedict is referring to the brief and secret prayer that used to precede the canonical hours. In his second commentary, however, expressing his mind more clearly, he argues as follows:

> “I understand this text as referring to the common prayer that was inserted between the psalms according to the custom of the Fathers of Egypt, the Thebaid, and Palestine. They begin and complete these prayers in the following way. When a psalm has ended, they do not immediately fall down to bend their knees; rather, before kneeling, they pray for a short while, and they spend most of the time standing in supplication. Then, after this very brief interval, they throw themselves upon the ground as though merely adoring the divine clemency, and with great speed they rise again. Once more standing upright with hands extended, they linger in prayer in the same manner as before. For, they say, if they remain prostrate on the ground longer, they are attacked not only by thoughts but also more heavily by sleep. I understand this text to refer to that prayer, which is offered during the daytime hours—not indeed between the psalms, but after the Kyrie eleison, which prayers are now called Masses.”

Thus far Boherius. According to his view, St. Benedict inserted prayers among the psalms at the nocturnal vigils and lauds, after the custom of the Egyptian monks; during the daytime hours he placed them at the end of the office, as we have already seen above. He thinks that it is this prayer to which the Holy Father Benedict refers here.

Our own Menardus adopts the same opinion and supports it with two arguments.

First, St. Benedict generally followed the institutions of the ancient monks, especially those described by Cassian. Some of these he either omitted entirely or touched upon only briefly, as though they were already familiar to everyone. Such was the rite of the Egyptian monks, which St. Athanasius commends in his book On Virginity:

> “To every psalm let prayers and the bending of the knees with tears be added.”

St. Pachomius likewise says in his Rule, article 126:

> “In each house, complete six prayers and psalms in the evening.”

Second, the same rite was common among other monks as well, since it is prescribed by St. Isidore in chapter 7 of his Rule, St. Fructuosus in chapter 3 of his Rule, and the Master in chapter 33 of his Rule. These Rules were themselves composed in large part from the Benedictine Rule. To this may be added the Penitential of St. Columbanus, which prescribes, among other things:

> “In common, all the brothers ought every night, at the times of prayer, at the end of every psalm, to bend their knees in prayer with equanimity, unless illness prevents it, saying in silence: ‘O God, come to my assistance; O Lord, make haste to help me.’ After they have sung this verse three times in prayer, they should rise together from kneeling.”

[Col. 0483D] He could have added a third argument: in ancient manuscript psalters, prayers are also written at the end of each individual psalm. A psalter of this kind exists in our monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris. There was also one of the kind that St. Robert brought from Molesme to Cîteaux, and it is still preserved in the Cistercian monastery.

[Col. 0484A] Fourth, there is the account given by Pope Gregory (Dialogues, Book II, chapter 4) of the negligent monk whom St. Benedict corrected. Every day, when the appointed hour had ended and the brothers had given themselves to prayer, this monk would leave the divine work and wander outside. This passage cannot be understood as referring to the entire divine work, as Haeften wishes, for after the divine work has ended all are ordered to leave the oratory in complete silence, below, in chapter 52. It must refer either to the individual psalms to which prayer was appended, as at the nocturnal offices and lauds, or to all the psalms, at whose end St. Benedict may have placed prayers that brought the entire office to a close, at which time the negligent brother used to leave.

Certainly, some monks in former times appear to have been subject to this vice, which the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers wished to remedy by decreeing (chapter 6):

> “During the time when Masses are being celebrated, whether by day or by night, when one must stand longer for prayer, they must not grow faint or withdraw outside unnecessarily.”

The Rule of St. Macarius, chapter 15, says the same, as does the Rule of St. Pachomius (article 11 in the collection of Rules):

> “When the brothers are praying in the assembly, no one may leave without the permission of his superiors.”

But the negligent monk, a disciple of Abbot Medericus (Life of Medericus, section 7, Third Century of Benedictine Writers, part I), paid little attention to laws of this kind. He “would leave the church as soon as the customary prayer of the assembly was about to end and before he bent his knees.” St. Medericus cured his illness with blessed bread.

Finally, Benedict Haeften (Monastic Catechism, part I, dissertation 6, section 2) understands this passage as referring to mental and secret prayer that was offered in the assembly after the divine work had been completed. He relies chiefly upon the testimony of St. Gregory that we have just cited and explained. In his commentary on the Life of St. Benedict, chapter 4, he thinks that this prayer lasted for one entire hour. Whether that should be called shortening the prayer, anyone may judge.

His opinion may be supported by the argument that St. Benedict seems in the preceding chapter to have dealt with the whole divine office, whereas here he deals with prayer that is performed not through an abundance of words but in compunction of tears.

Nevertheless, elsewhere Haeften appears to have held a different opinion. For, when listing the various names of the divine office, he says (Book I, treatise 2, dissertation 1):

> “It is called the divine office of the assembly because the brothers gather for it . . . . And I believe that St. Benedict should be understood in this way when he says: ‘Nevertheless, in the assembly prayer must be shortened completely.’”

The objections he brings against Menardus’s opinion, which Smaragdus supports, do not appear to be of great weight and can easily be resolved.

[337] Moreover, we must not pass over Hildemar’s observation: in the words “In the assembly, however, prayer must be shortened completely,” it is sufficiently shown that at other times the monks were to pray according to each one’s devotion, more briefly or at greater length, as God granted. When the monks neglected this, times were established in each congregation during which all the brothers would devote themselves to prayer. Hence Boherius says:

> “I think that, to clarify the understanding of our master, the threefold prayer was introduced from this practice. In certain monasteries of France it is celebrated with the knees placed upon the ground in the choir before the beginning of the nocturnal hour, before prime, and after the end of compline; it generally concludes with the interval of three Our Fathers.”

It is clear that this practice arose from the institution of Benedict of Aniane, as is shown by his Life, section 52.

## CHAPTER XXI. On the Deans of the Monastery.

[Col. 0483]

[Col. 0483D] If the congregation is large [Note: [Col. 0483D] Some copies: “is large.”], brothers of good reputation and holy conduct are to be chosen from among them [Note: [Col. 0483D] Oxford, Conc., and Hildemar: “from among the brothers.”] and appointed as deans. They are to care for their deaneries in all matters, according to the commandments of God [Col. 0485A] and the instructions of their abbot. Such deans are to be chosen that the abbot may safely share his burdens with them [Note: [Col. 0485A] Conc., Flor., Lyr., Comp.: “may share his burdens.”]. They are not to be chosen in order, but according to the merit of their life and the teaching of wisdom. If one of these deans should perhaps be found puffed up with pride and blameworthy in some respect, then, after being corrected once, twice, and three times, if he refuses to amend, he is to be deposed; and another who is worthy is to be substituted in his place [Note: [Col. 0486A] Oxford, Sabina, and six other manuscripts: “shall succeed him.”]. And concerning the provost we establish the same rule.

## COMMENTARY.

[Col. 0485]

[Col. 0485A] It is the practice of the wisest men, when faced with difficult and arduous matters, to distrust their own strength and to place at least part of the burden they must carry upon the shoulders of others. Since the governance of souls is therefore the art of arts, and nothing is so arduous and difficult as to serve the character of many people, St. Benedict arranged that the provost in the monastery, and, where the number of brothers was larger, the deans as well, should be chosen together with the abbot. The abbot could safely share his burdens with them and, assisted by them, fulfill with equanimity the office entrusted to him.

We shall first discuss the name of these men and then, in explaining the text of the Rule, their duties.

The word “dean” is a military term transferred from the camp to the cloister. Vegetius says (On Military Matters, chapter 8):

> “There were deans appointed over ten soldiers; today they are called the head of a squad.”

Hence St. Isidore says (Etymologies, Book III, chapter 3):

> “They are called deans because they are placed in charge of ten soldiers.”

In monasteries, however, a dean was said to be one who, as the tenth, presided over nine monks, as St. Jerome teaches (Letter 22); or rather, one who was placed over ten, as St. Augustine says (Book I On the Morals of the Catholic Church, chapter 31), especially over the younger monks, as may be gathered from this passage of Cassian:

> “Another is entrusted to an elder who presides over ten juniors; the elder both instructs and governs those entrusted to him by the abbot, according to what we read was ordained through Moses in Exodus.”

Perhaps for this reason Guido Juvenalis, in his French translation of the Rule of St. Benedict, rendered the title of this chapter as follows: “Of the masters of novices or masters of morals.”

The same word was also transferred to judicial offices, for a dean is a judge, as Menardus demonstrates from Book II of the Visigothic Law, title I, law 26. Deans in the Church were also said to be those who buried the bodies of the dead, as the same Menardus proves from Justinian’s Novels 43 and 59.

Among the dignities of canons, the title “dean” is also famous: the dean is the head of the entire chapter. Among the Cluniacs, deans were likewise called the suffragans of the major prior in temporal matters; they were the administrators of the villages, of whom Udalricus speaks in Book III, chapter 5.

Whether the office of the deans, as it was instituted here by Saint Benedict and continued among the ancients, long remained in our Order is altogether unknown to us. There is indeed an article about them in petition 11 of the Fulda monks to the Emperor Charles, and likewise in the Council of Aachen, canons 55 and 56; but there is no mention of them in the Concordia of Dunstan, the Statutes of Lanfranc, or the Customs of the Monastery of Cluny, which deal only with the abbot, the major prior, the village deans who served as administrators [Col. 0485D], the cloister prior, the circuitors, and the masters of the boys. In the Cistercian Order, too, the name “dean” was unknown, says John Craesbeeck; yet the office which appears to reside in the conventual prior was not unfamiliar. Among the Cassinese, formerly there was only one dean after the abbot, and after him a vice-dean, as Nicholas of Fractura writes. But when Pope Celestine V introduced his own men into the Cassinese monastery, “he changed the name of dean, who after their arrival was called prior,” says Richard, cited by Augustine of Genoa in his commentary on chapter 55 of the Rule. And certainly in the monastery of Saint Maurus at Fosses the priors were also called deans, as is clear from the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Babolene*, abbot, chapter 5 (*Benedictine Centuries*, vol. II, p. 595), where Robert of that same monastery is called at one time prior and at another dean [Col. 0486A]. Yet these were not properly deans of the kind instituted by Saint Benedict, whom the Cassinese eventually restored by issuing this statute 339 (*Cassinese Declaration* on chapter 21): “In each monastery only one dean shall be appointed for every ten monks, so that their number may properly correspond to the name.”

In the new Declarations, however, they appoint one dean not for every ten but for every five professed monks living, though in such a way that the deans themselves do not exceed three hundred, as prescribed in the brief of Paul V dated 21 March 1608 [Col. 0486B]. Haeften further notes that other substituted terms have been introduced in place of the name “dean” (*Book III, treatise 6, disputation 4*): “Among others it has become customary for the priors of the Order to be called deans. The first is called simply prior, the second subprior, and the others successively priors—third prior, fourth prior.” And certainly in the old French translation of Saint Benedict’s Rule, which belongs to the monastery of Saint Peter of Conques, the beginning of this chapter is rendered as follows:

> If there is in a monastery a large congregation of monks, let some of them be chosen who are of good conscience and holy conduct, and let them be appointed deans—that is, priors.

The *Rule of the Master*, chapter 11, calls them *praepositi*; Saint Benedict, in the following chapter, chapter 22, calls them *seniors*.

## If the congregation is larger

What constitutes a larger congregation has been explained in chapter 17.

## Let them be chosen

By the abbot together with the convent, says Boherius; for since all the welfare of the monastery is ordered through the deans, their election is among the principal matters which arise, and the abbot should therefore be understood to summon the entire congregation. Or rather, by the abbot alone, to whom belongs the whole ordering of his monastery: if he may choose a provost by himself, much more may he choose a dean. Clearly, if in the election of deans he had to seek the brothers’ consent, men might sometimes be chosen in whom he had no confidence and to whom he could not safely entrust his burdens.

Deans, like provosts, were not appointed for life but only for a time, as is evident from the *Life of Saint Lioba*, chapter 3, concerning the monastery of Saint Tetta (*Benedictine Centuries*, vol. III, part II):

> In that monastery of virgins there was a certain nun who, because of her zeal for discipline and her observance of a stricter life, appeared to preside over the others. She was often appointed provost, but frequently, according to custom, she was established as dean, etc.

Later, however, the Council of Aachen decreed (canon 56) “that a provost, dean, or cellarer should not be removed from his ministry except for a reason of usefulness or necessity.” By these words, I believe, permanence in office was not so much established as excessively easy mobility was prevented. See Innocent III, *Constitutions*, chapter *Cum ad monasterium*.

## Of the brothers themselves

That is, of the brothers; in this, says Hildemar, “he makes clear that the man should not come from elsewhere.” Richard of Saint Angelo nevertheless considers that an election from another monastery would be valid, although not expedient.

## Brothers of good reputation

This, says the aforementioned Richard, “applies when those are to be chosen who are not from within the community, since they should not be chosen unless a praiseworthy reputation makes them known.”

## 340 And of holy conduct

“This applies,” the same Richard adds, “when those from within the community are chosen, because from their past life we can judge what may be expected of their subsequent conduct.” Whether they come from within the community or elsewhere, then, they must be both of good reputation and of holy conduct. Nicholas of Fractura understands “of good reputation” with respect to actions, and “of holy conduct” with respect to character.

## And let them be appointed deans

That is, let them be ordained. The formula of ordination is described by the *Rule of the Master* in these words (chapter 11):

> After the same ten brothers have been summoned by the abbot, with the entire congregation present in the oratory, let them be placed over those ten by the abbot’s word, through the receiving of the staff, in testimony to the Scripture that says: “Rule them with a rod,” that is, with the rigor of fear. Likewise the Apostle says: “What do you want? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in charity?” For Moses too, by the divine staff of power entrusted to him, showed the people committed to him the way of salvation through the depth of the sea.

Here one may observe the ancient custom of appointing deans by handing over a staff. In the same manner abbots, provosts, and all prelates were also appointed, as Menardus observes in his commentary on the *Council of Rules*, chapter 28, section 2.

[Col. 0487B] **Who shall exercise care over their deaneries.**

That is, over the ten brothers placed under them. According to custom, however, one dean could also be placed over fifteen brothers, according to Hildemar; indeed, even over fewer than ten, as the Cassinese still observe. The *Master* places two men over ten brothers in chapter 11 of his Rule.

**In all things.**

Not only in things that please them, but also in things contrary to their own inclinations.

**According to the commandments of God and the precepts of their abbot.**

Lest they suppose themselves free from the authority of the man from whom they derive whatever authority they possess; they are always subject to him, must consult him in difficult matters, and must render him an account of their care. Thus, just as above he imposed a restraint upon the abbot, so that he would not choose just anyone according to his pleasure but brothers of good reputation, so here he restrains the deans, so that they may not do whatever they please, but what God commands and the abbot orders. “In new matters,” says Boherius, “he ought to request the abbot’s command; in other daily or common matters, however, the assignment of the office is regarded as the abbot’s command, without the need for permission.” But it is useful here to derive the care of the deans from other rules and from the institutions and writings of the holy Fathers.

First, according to Smaragdus:

> The dean’s care and instruction toward each person entrusted to him by the abbot shall be this: first to teach him to overcome his own wishes. Exercising him carefully in this, he should deliberately command him always to do what he perceives to be contrary to his spirit, because experience has taught that a monk can never restrain his desires unless he has first learned through obedience to put his own will to death.

Smaragdus writes this while copying Cassian (*chapter 12*). Similarly Saint Fructuosus says:

> The deans who have been appointed over the deaneries shall exercise such care over the brothers assigned to them that they do not carry out any private wishes, do not speak unless questioned, do nothing on their own authority except by command, and do not go elsewhere without being directed, etc.

Second, “since they receive ten brothers under their care,” says the *Master* (chapter 11), “they ought to exercise this care over them, whether by day or by night or in any work: they should first be present with them and work with them in every task, so that when they sit, walk, or stand, they may, through careful observance and watchful attention, restrain the devil’s acts from them.”

Third, the *Master* adds (in the same place):

> Because they are present with the brothers at every hour, let them guard their mouths and gestures from sin and restrain the various vices or wrongs in them. That is, if the provost hears a brother speaking without having been questioned, let him admonish him, saying: “What are you doing, brother? The Rule forbids it. Keep silence until you are questioned.”

Fourth, it was the duty of the deans to visit, console, and instruct brothers who were wavering, as Saint Jerome teaches (*Letter 22*):

> They remained separated, but with their cells adjoining, until the ninth hour. As had been established, no one went to another except those deans whom we have mentioned, so that if someone happened to be wavering in his thoughts, he might be consoled by their conversation.

Hence Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 12):

> Let the brothers conceal from their deans nothing that they have thought about during each day; and let the deans be to them as directors and guardians, as though they would have to render an account to the Lord on their behalf.

Fifth, they brought the incorrigible before the abbot, or before the provost, who himself then brought them before the abbot. “The office of the deans,” says Hildemar, “is simply to guard their subjects; and if they cannot correct them by their admonition, they must then report them to the abbot.” Saint Fructuosus likewise says (chapter 12):

> Let them foresee the negligences of all, and have the power to correct them; and whatever they have not been able to correct, let them not delay accusing before the provost. Let the provosts themselves act in this matter distinctly and reasonably, so that they do not presume in any way to trouble their abbots, except in cases which neither of them has been able to correct.

[Col. 0488B] Sixth, they presided over the tables of the brothers who were eating. Thus the *Master* decrees (chapter 11):

> Let them be present at their tables, so that they may eat silently and moderately with them.

And Cassian, concerning the Egyptians and the Tabennesiots (*Book IV, chapter 17*):

> Such silence is maintained by all that, when so great a number of brothers have sat down together for the sake of refreshment, no one dares even to murmur, except the man who presides over his deanery.

On this passage Alardus Gazaeus writes:

> Hence it appears that in one refectory there were distinct and separate groups of ten brothers, or deaneries, and that each deanery had its own dean or decurion seated and presiding over it. Saint Jerome also indicates this when he writes to Eustochium: “Each group of ten goes to the table with its own superior, and they minister in turn from week to week.”

Seventh, they supplied clothing for the brothers. “Let the provosts keep the brothers’ wardrobe under their care,” says the *Master*. And Cassian (*Book IV, chapter 10*):

> Each provost supplies clothing in turn to his own deanery whenever he sees that the garments in which they are dressed have become dirty.

Here he calls *vicaria* “alternating clothing,” because it was changed in turn.

Eighth, they presided over the work of their own men, as is clear from Saint Jerome (*Letter 22*):

> The appointed work of the day is brought to the dean and then delivered to the steward.

And from Saint Augustine (*Book I, On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31):

> They work with their hands at things by which the body can be nourished and the mind not hindered from God; and they hand over their work to those whom they call deans.

Ninth, they slept at night among their own men. “Let the provosts have their beds near the beds of those men,” says the *Master* (chapter 11), “so that they may correct in them some fault of vice, as we have said, and so that they may sleep more reverently in the presence of their superior.” Saint Benedict’s following chapter, chapter 22, should be understood in this way: “Let groups of ten or twenty rest with their seniors, who are to be solicitous for them.”

Finally, the Cassinese declare (*Cassinese Declaration* on chapter 21) that it belongs to the office of the deans:

> To be solicitous that regular observance be maintained in the monastery; to hear the confessions of the brothers assigned to them by the prelate; to visit the monastery’s workshops at suitable times; to correct the excesses of those brothers, unless they find them serious enough to be reserved for the prelate; to grant them particular permissions according to the authority given to them by the prelate; and, moreover, to take diligent care that the ceremonies of the congregation and the arrangements established by the chapter or the prelate are observed. Let them watch over the devout performance of the divine office, and strive to attend the common exercises of the brothers or the chapter of faults.

## Let such deans be chosen that the abbot may safely share his burdens with them

Three points are noteworthy here.

First, in order that men may be chosen with whom the abbot can safely share his burdens, Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius require six qualities in them:

> 1. Good reputation, specifically with respect to friendliness and sociability;  
> 2. Good conduct, specifically with respect to cleanliness, purity, and holiness of life;  
> 3. Zeal for the progress of souls;  
> 4. Discernment in governing the brothers;  
> 5. Obedience to the commandments of God, and obedience and reverence toward the precepts of their abbot;  
> 6. That, on account of obedience to the abbot, they in no way disregard the commandments of God.

To these add merit of life and instruction in wisdom, which, as Hildemar teaches, are contained in the six qualities mentioned above. If anything is lacking in the dean, the abbot will no longer be able to share his burdens with him securely. Add humility as well; for if he is found to be proud, he is ordered to be deposed. Nicholas of Fractura reduces the six qualities mentioned above to three: maturity of age, gravity of character, and knowledge of letters.

Second, Saint Benedict permits the abbot to share his burdens, but not to lay them down. “This does not make the abbot secure and free from labor,” says Gerard the Belgian monk, “but commands him to choose such men that he may be secure in those who work with him. He commands him to share his burdens with them—that is, what he himself necessarily bears in its entirety, he may entrust to others, whether individual tasks or several at once, so that the welfare of each may be more successfully provided for. Meanwhile, in every matter he threatens the abbot with a dread Judge and tribunal, lest he think it sufficient merely to appoint a good dean or a diligent provost, etc.”

Third, Saint Benedict says, “let him share his burdens,” not his honors; for, as Bernard says, they are burdened more than they are honored. To preside over others is a weight of burden, not of honor, as I may say with Hildemar.

## And let them not be chosen in order

That is, in the order in which they entered the monastery. Formerly this was also prohibited by civil law in the election of an abbot, *Code*, law 46, *On Bishops and Clerics*, etc. Therefore, even if they are the last of all, they may be chosen provided they are worthy; for they may also become abbots. Nevertheless, they must have completed their twenty-fifth year and have received the priesthood, according to the Constitution of Benedict XII, chapter 29.

## But according to merit of life and instruction in wisdom

[Col. 0489C] The dean must therefore be instructed in knowledge of letters [Col. 0490A], perhaps no less than the abbot, whose burden he bears in almost the same measure. It may be for this reason that the *Master* exempts deans from part of the work in chapter 11 of his Rule.

## And if any of these deans should be found swollen with pride and blameworthy

But if such men are chosen as we have described and as Saint Benedict requires, how can any one of them be found swollen with pride? Hildemar answers that this can happen in two ways.

First, some are hypocrites who, while private persons, display an appearance of holiness; afterward, when they are raised to dignities or offices, they lay aside the mask and openly reveal what they were within.

Second, some really were, before attaining the honor, what Saint Benedict requires, but do not remain in their original humility and holiness. It is difficult to be raised up without becoming elated, and honors change character.

## Reproved once, twice, and three times

One should not judge a man to be swollen with pride if he is corrected after three admonitions, say Bernard of Cassino [Col. 0490B] and Boherius. The threefold correction should proceed as follows: according to Hildemar, he is to be admonished twice privately and the third time publicly; according to Boherius, three times publicly, with an interval between the admonitions—long or short according to the seriousness of the offense and the judgment of the superior.

## If he is unwilling to amend, let him be deposed, etc.

This applies if he is blameworthy in matters belonging to his office, according to Hildemar. If, however, he is found blameworthy in other matters specifically concerning himself, Hildemar believes that the correction prescribed by regular discipline should be applied, followed by the brothers’ prayer for him, and finally by his deposition. Boherius, however, believes that even a man who has not offended in his obedience but sins against the Rule in another respect should be expelled, just as the holy legislator decrees concerning the provost.

## And concerning the provost we establish the same things

With due proportion, however: the provost is to be warned four times, then subjected to regular discipline, and finally expelled from his ministry.

# CHAPTER XXII. How the Monks Should Sleep

[Col. 0489]

[Col. 0489C] Let them sleep singly, each in a separate bed. Let them receive bedding [Note: [Col. 0489C] Oxford manuscript: “each in a separate small bed”; later manuscripts: “separate beds.”] according to the manner of their life, in accordance with the provision of their abbot. If it can be done, let them all sleep in one place [Note: [Col. 0489C] Hildemar: “in one”; Narbonne manuscript, with several manuscripts: “in one place.”]; but if their number does not permit it [Note: [Col. 0489C] Another manuscript: “but if it does not permit it.”], let groups of ten or twenty rest with seniors who are solicitous for them. Let a lamp burn continually in the same room until morning.

Let them sleep clothed and girded with belts [Note: [Col. 0489D] Oxford manuscript and the Rule of Donatus: “with small belts.”] or cords. Let them not have their knives at their sides while they sleep, lest the sleepers perhaps be wounded in a dream [Note: [Col. 0489D] Oxford manuscript: “lest he wound those sleeping”; Narbonne manuscript: “lest they wound the sleeper”; [Col. 0490C] Florence manuscript: “lest they are wounded, the sleeper.”]. And [Note: [Col. 0490C] Hildemar says that the particle “and” is superfluous in sense.] so that the monks may always be ready: once the signal has been given, let them rise without delay and hasten to anticipate one another for the work of God, yet with all gravity and restraint. Let the younger brothers not have their beds beside one another [Note: [Col. 0490C] Another manuscript: “beds.”], but let them be mixed with the seniors [Note: [Col. 0490D] Other manuscripts: “mixed,” “in mixed fashion,” or “intermingled.”] [Note: [Col. 0490D] The Narbonne manuscript adds “let them lie there.”]. When they rise for the work of God, let them moderately encourage one another, on account of the excuses of those who are sleepy.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0489]

[Col. 0489D] Since the adversary keeps watch while we sleep and employs almost innumerable arts to harm faithful monks when they are weary and resting, Saint Benedict applies seven safeguards against his snares in this chapter, as Bernard of Cassino has noted. The first [Col. 0490D] is the separation of the beds; the second, the proximity of brothers of good conduct; the third, the presence of many brothers sleeping in the same place; the fourth, the care and vigilance of the seniors; the fifth, the lighting of a burning lamp; the sixth, that they lie clothed and not naked; the seventh [Col. 0491A], the separation of the younger brothers and their intermingling with the seniors. All these points must be explained in order.

## 345 Let them sleep singly, each in a separate bed

This is the first safeguard. Along with Saint Benedict, Saint Athanasius applies it:

> While they sleep, let each one lie down separately, and let each have his own *sticharion*—that is, a hidden pouch—so that when prayers must be offered during the night they may be ready and prepared.

Abba Isaiah says:

> Do not lie down with another beneath the same covering.

Saint Aurelian says:

> Let all remain in separate beds.

Saint Ferreolus says:

> Let two who are near and friendly nevertheless be separated, for the sake of secret prayer, which is more suitably directed to the Lord when there is no witness, so that they may not be held by one mind and one bed. Each person shall himself be the sole possessor of his own bedding, as we have said above, having with him, in the better exchange for the brothers’ dormitory, the Lord who keeps watch.

Saint Isidore says:

> It is not permitted for two to lie in one bed.

Saint Fructuosus says:

> Let two not lie in one bed, nor should anyone have permission to sleep outside his own cell. Let an interval of one cubit separate each bed, lest, when bodies draw near one another, they nourish the sparks of lust.

The *Master* says (chapter 11):

> We command that individuals, not pairs, sleep in each bed.

To these may be added the Council of Tours (canon 14):

> To cut off every opening for an evil suspicion, let no priest or monk presume to take another into his own bed.

From this one is prompted to wonder why the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* prescribes (chapter 14):

> Let two and two sleep in small beds, except the sick and the seniors.

Yet it appears to have guarded against the dangers of this regulation by adding:

> Let them nevertheless not speak to one another, nor look at one another face to face; rather, let one sleep behind the other, so that one of them is always a senior whose religious character is beyond doubt. We absolutely forbid young women to rest together.

Bernard of Cassino further notes that in Saint Benedict’s words, “Let them sleep singly, each in a separate bed,” the words “or let them rest” should be understood as supplied. For the perfect monk does not always sleep lying in bed, but sometimes waters his bedding with tears. Saint Ferreolus urges us to do this, after the example of the Prophet, in chapter 33 of his Rule.

Certainly the saints used to anticipate the night watches with prayers and supplications. Thus Faustus reports in the Life of Saint Maurus that sometimes he recited fifty psalms, sometimes a hundred, and sometimes the entire Psalter before the nocturnal prayer assembly. Likewise Gervinus, the most devout abbot of Centula (*Chronicle of Centula*, book IV, chapter 26), whenever he had obtained little sleep, shook himself from his pallet, entered the house of prayer, and went around all the altars praying, groaning, and bending his knees. When he sensed that the hour of the vigils had arrived, he returned to his bed without making any noise, so that he would not be observed by the sacristans or doorkeepers.

## Bedding

The commentators on the Rule do not agree about what *lectisternia* means. Hildemar says:

> “Bedding” is used in two ways: that is, the house where beds are spread, or also the place where a single bed has been made.

Smaragdus similarly says:

> Bedding means the places where people customarily lie and sit.

Nicholas of Fractura likewise says:

> Bedding means the places in which monks customarily lie.

And Cardinal Turrecremata says:

> Bedding means the places or little spaces in which beds are to be spread.

Bernard of Cassino agrees, writing:

> Concerning this word, *lectisternia*, some say that it means the same as a made bed—that is, a bed with its bedding. Others say that *lectisternium* is the house in which beds are spread. But the truth of the matter is that *lectisternia* are the places in which we customarily sit and lie. For according to the Rule a monk ought to have both a bed in which he may rest and a small place in which he may read while sitting.

Boherius copies Bernard in his first commentary; in his second he says:

> Bedding means the bedding of the beds,

and refers for this to chapter 55: “The bedding of the beds: a mat, a cloak, a woolen covering, and a pillow.”

Finally, Richard of Saint Angelo says:

> Bedding means the rows or arrangements of beds.

Theobald Artaldus agrees with him, rendering this passage into French:

> They must have and keep the places and arrangements of their beds.

Of all these opinions, two appear altogether probable.

The first is the opinion reported by Bernard of Cassino, according to which *lectisternia* means made beds, or beds with their bedding. Menardus follows this interpretation, writing:

> Bedding means beds. Sidonius, *Letter 15, book IV*: “Prepare a varied feast and very spacious beds.” The *Acts of Saint Findanus*, chapter 4: “In place of bedding, he secretly placed beneath the resting body, among the brothers, stones wrapped in cloth.”

The old French translation of Saint Benedict’s Rule agrees:

> Let the beds be prepared as is suitable to their manner of life.

Guido’s version says:

> And let them have beds furnished with what is necessary according to the manner of their life.

Several other French expositions agree.

The second probable interpretation is that given by Boherius in his second commentary, where he interprets *lectisternia* as the bedding of the beds. Saint Gregory sometimes uses the word in this sense:

> I have decided to buy bedding for the servants of God whom you call in Greek *monastriai*, because in their beds they are suffering from severe nakedness in the intense cold of this winter.

And elsewhere, writing to John, abbot of Mount Sinai (*Book XII, Letter 16*):

> We have learned that beds or bedding are lacking in the hospice which Isaurus built there. Therefore we have sent fifteen woolen coverings, thirty blankets, and fifteen beds.

John de Précis, abbot of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, thus rendered this passage of the Rule into French:

> And they must receive such sheets and such coverings as the abbot shall establish.

Both explanations are sound and should be accepted. But the interpretations of Hildemar, Smaragdus, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas, and Cardinal Turrecremata ought both to be rejected. Saint Benedict neither grants each monk a house in which many beds are spread, nor allows each one a separate house in which a single bed may be set up; rather, he wants them all to sleep in one dormitory.

## According to the manner of their life

This is an obscure expression, which the commentators render in different ways. Hildemar understands “according to the manner of their life” to mean “according to the quality of each person’s life.” Bernard of Cassino explains it more clearly:

> According to the manner in which they conduct themselves in the monastery—well or badly, lukewarmly or fervently.

In this he finds a second safeguard against the enemy’s snares: namely, that the good sleep near the bad, and the more fervent near the lukewarm, so that the latter may be instructed by their example and turn toward better conduct. Nicholas of Fractura adopts the same view. Boherius adds another in his first commentary: “According to the manner of their life” may mean according to the quality of the place in which they live, since in cold regions more bedding is genuinely needed, and in warm regions less.

Turrecremata explains “according to the manner of their life” as according to the manner of life, age, weakness, necessity, or some other cause. All these explanations appear good and legitimate. Yet they do not yield to the interpretation offered by John Craesbeeck, who understands *lectisternia according to the manner of their life* to mean bedding suited to the monks’ way of life and institution. One French version renders this “in the monastic manner,” and another “in accordance with their profession.” Since the monastic institution renounces all enticements of the flesh and commends austerity of life, he says:

> The bedding of monks ought not to be soft or costly—things that flatter the senses, delight the flesh, entice it, and invite long and repeated sleep—but hard and inexpensive, sufficient for nature and necessity, subduing the flesh and preventing wantonness.

Certainly, anyone who has acquired even the slightest knowledge of ascetic matters knows that the beds of the ancient monks were of this kind. Gazaeus notes (*Commentary on Cassian*, Conference I, chapter 23) that formerly religious men were accustomed either:

1. To lie on the ground;
2. To lie on beds of reeds;
3. To lie on haircloth.

These three ways of sleeping can be seen in one Life of Saint Antony. Saint Athanasius writes that, when giving his limbs rest, Antony used a mat woven of reeds and haircloth, and sometimes lay upon the bare ground [Col. 0493A]. Saint Jerome likewise reports of Saint Hilarion (*Life of Hilarion*) that he lay upon the bare ground and a mat of reeds until his death. And the holy Doctor writes of himself (*Letter 22*):

> Whenever impending sleep overcame me despite my resistance, I would strike my bones, scarcely held together, against the bare ground.

Finally Saint Paulinus sings of Saint Martin (*Book IV*):

> But if at any time his eyes yielded to brief sleep,  
> Bare earth beneath him was enough for thin slumber.

You will find very many examples of this kind in the acts of the saints, especially our own: in the Life of Saint Maurus by Faustus, no. 8; of Saint Placid by Gordian, no. 5; of Saint Marculf, no. 13; of Saint Paternus; of Saint Samson; of Saint Radegund by Fortunatus, no. 22; of Saint Severus, no. 13; and of Saint Fidoli, no. 10, in the first Benedictine century; of Saint Bavo, no. 11; of Saint Wandrille, no. 8; of Saint Tillo, no. 8, in the second Benedictine century; and of countless others.

The *Compendium of the Teaching of Saint Athanasius to Monks and Clerics* gives similar advice:

> I exhort you, monk and priest, to sleep on the ground if you are able.

See below, chapter 55.

## If it can be done, let them all sleep in one place

This accords with the custom of the ancient monks, which can be observed in almost all their rules. Thus the Rule delivered by an angel to Saint Posthumius, reported in his Life, chapter 8 (*Book I, On the Lives of the Fathers*):

> When you withdraw to sleep, spread woven vines far from one another; let an interval of one cubit be maintained, lest, when bodies draw near one another, the sparks of lust be nourished.

Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles (*Rule for Virgins*, chapter 7), says:

> No one may choose a secluded dwelling, nor shall she have a room, a little cabinet, or anything of this kind that could be locked separately. Rather, let all remain in one cell with their beds separated. As for those who are elderly or infirm, they should be accommodated and arranged in such a way that they do not each have a separate cell, but all are received in one, where they also remain.

Saint Aurelian (*Rule for Monks*, chapter 8; *Rule for Virgins*, chapter 6) says:

> No one may have a cell, a little cabinet, or anything of this kind that could be locked separately.

Saint Ferreolus (chapter 16) says:

> Let one dwelling and one house contain the entire congregation.

Saint Isidore (chapter 14) says:

> If possible, all the brothers ought to remain in one room. If this is difficult, then at least ten should remain together, with one placed over them as dean, almost as their director and guardian.

Saint Fructuosus (chapter 17) says:

> Let an interval of one cubit separate each small bed, lest, when bodies draw near one another, they nourish the sparks of lust.

The *Master* (chapter 29) says:

> In one courtyard or dining hall let the beds be arranged in an orderly circuit. In the middle of this circuit let the abbot have his bed, so that, observing all silence and reverence throughout the circle, he may attend to the flock of all his sheep, gathered within one sheepfold, like a diligent and solicitous shepherd.

The *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* (chapter 14) says:

> If possible, let one house accommodate them all for sleeping, except when illness, old age, a disciplinary sentence, or an untested newcomer requires that they be separated in a cell.

The same is established by the Second Council of Tours (canon 14):

> Monks may not have common little cells in which two may remain or private belongings may be stored separately. Rather, let a common building be constructed through common labor, where all may lie down under the governance either of the abbot or of the provost.

And by Novel 5 of the Emperor Justinian:

> We do not wish monks in any monastery under our authority—whether it contains many or few persons—to be separated from one another and to use private dwellings. Rather, we decree that they eat together and all sleep in common, each lying in his own place, but housed in one building. If one house is not sufficient because of the number of monks, let them be placed in two or perhaps more, yet not separately and by themselves; instead, let them be witnesses to one another’s honesty and chastity in common.

And by Novel 133, monks are not to “live secretly, without witnesses,” but are to “take their food together, lie down in a common place, and pursue a life well ordered in every respect, being mutually witnesses of one another’s honesty.”

The same appears in the Life of Saint Eugendus, abbot of the Jura (no. 21, first Benedictine century, p. 575), who, “after destroying the little dwelling-houses, made all sleep with him in one hospice.”

This was later renewed in 1222 by the Council of Oxford, which issued the following decree (*In Spelman, vol. II of the Councils of England*):

> After careful deliberation, we decree that monks, regular canons, and nuns alike shall sleep and rest together in one dormitory, with a separate bed assigned to each person.

And Pope Benedict XII:

> Let all the monks sleep and lie in one house—or, if their number does not permit it, at least let the greater number of them do so whenever this can conveniently be arranged—in accordance with regular and canonical institutions, not in separate rooms or cells, except those to whom rooms and cells in the infirmary are permitted because of old age, bodily illness, or other reasonable causes.

Nor was this peculiar to monks alone. We read that the same was formerly prescribed for canons in the Council of Tours (canon 23):

> We have determined that the canons and clerics of the cities who live in the bishoprics, residing in the cloisters, should all sleep together in one dormitory and likewise eat together in one refectory.

At the Council of Meaux under Sergius II (canon 52):

> Canons in the city or in monasteries shall sleep in the dormitory and eat in the refectory, as has been established.

And in Chrodegang’s *Rule of Canons*, chapter 13 (*Spicilegium*, vol. I):

> Let all sleep in one dormitory, except those to whom the bishop has granted permission.

From what has been said thus far, we establish:
