1. That formerly monks slept together in one place, which for that reason they called a dormitory.

2. Yet they did so in such a way that they did not touch one another, as is clear from the Rules of Saint Posthumius and Saint Fructuosus. Certainly, they slept in separate beds.

3. No one, except perhaps on account of illness or necessity, spent the night outside the common dormitory; for one who says “all” excludes no one.

4. Therefore not even the abbot did so, since in the Rule of the Master he is ordered to sleep in the midst of the brothers, like a shepherd among his flock. In the ancient customs of the monastery of Cluny, preserved by Udalricus (Book III, chapter 1), we read: “In the middle of the dormitory is his bed near the wall; he himself makes a sound by which the brothers are awakened at dawn to rise.” In the Rule of Saint Aurelian it is likewise decreed (chapter 33) that “the holy abbot shall not remain outside the congregation.” In the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 14): “The abbot ought to dwell together with the brothers in the congregation.” The Council of Frankfurt also states (canon 13): “The abbot shall sleep with his monks, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.” And the Council of London in 1102 says: “He shall eat or sleep in the same house with his monks.” Indeed, it is certain from Book II, chapter 35, of the *Dialogues* of Pope Saint Gregory that Saint Benedict rested in the tower adjoining the brothers’ dormitory. Saint Mummolus, abbot of Fleury, is said to have lain down in the common dormitory of the brothers, according to Adrevald in his *History of the Translation of Saint Benedict*, no. 15, second century of the Benedictine era. Bede writes the same about Easterwine, abbot of Wearmouth, in the *Life of Saint Benedict Biscop*, no. 8.

Three reasons may be assigned for this institution. The first is drawn from the nature of coenobitic life, which permits nothing individual but wishes everything to be held in common. Hence the emperor Justinian says (*Novella* 133): “Let no one possess anything at all as his own, but let him live in common by day and night, and let the nights among them observe the same discipline as the days.” The second reason is that they may be witnesses to one another’s honesty and chastity, as the same emperor says (*Novella* 5). The third is the furious assaults of demons, especially hostile to monks at night and sometimes appearing in dreadful form. A solitary person, deprived of the companionship and prayers of his brothers, could scarcely endure their sight. Perhaps for these reasons Saint Eugendus, abbot of the Jura, destroyed the monks’ little dwellings, and the emperor Justinian ordered them destroyed in *Novella* 133. Most recently Benedict XII did the same in his Constitution for Benedictine monks, chapter 26; the English monks obeyed him by a statute of their chapter in 1341, the monks of Bursfeld according to the *Ceremonial*, distinction 3, chapter 22, and the Cluniacs in the chapter held under John of Bourbon in 1458.

Nowadays, however, the practice has become established in nearly all monastic congregations of dividing the dormitories into several cells and assigning one to each monk. This is done to avoid the curiosity of secular persons, who sometimes wander through our dormitories; so that the brothers may devote themselves more freely to prayer and spiritual reading; so that they may exercise themselves in various works of penance, which shun human eyes; and also for the sake of greater propriety and a stricter observance of silence and solitude. It is also done so that monasteries may represent, in some measure, an image of the heavenly dwelling, as Peter of Blois aptly said of the Carthusians (Letter 86):

“After the pattern of that house of which it is written, ‘In my Father’s house are many dwelling places,’ each person has his own cell and little dwelling, so that he may devote himself more freely to contemplation and prayer.”

Nor is this institution so recent or new that it was unknown among ancient monks. For, according to Saint Jerome (Letter 22), the Egyptians “dwelt separately, but with their cells joined together.” Hence Cassian (Book II, chapter 12): “When,” he says, “the duties of the canonical prayers have been completed according to custom, each person returns to his own cell, which he is permitted to inhabit either alone or with only one other person, and so forth.” The monks of Lérins in Gaul imitated the same institution, as we learn from Eucherius’s letter to Hilary, *On the Praise of the Solitary Life*. Among the other praises of the island of Lérins, he writes:

“This island now possesses those holy old men who, in separate cells, brought the Egyptian Fathers into our Gaul.”

That the monks of Agaunum adopted the same discipline is evident from the very ancient writer of the *Life of Saint Romanus*, abbot of the Jura, preserved by Bollandus (28 February). In the preface, which he addresses to John and Armentarius, monks of Agaunum, after comparing the aforementioned John with John the Baptist and the Evangelist, he adds the following about Armentarius:

“But the other, like a swimming ark, while there in the coenobium, content with the enclosure of a private cell, mocks the storms of the world as they strike him.”

Concerning the monastery of the Jura, we have the testimony of the *Life of Saint Eugendus*, abbot of that place (first century of the Benedictine era), who “rejecting the custom of the archimandrites, more profitably united everyone in one place; for, after destroying the little buildings of the separate dwellings, he made them rest with him in one hospice.” Therefore, previously there had been little buildings of separate dwellings in which each person lived, and he destroyed them.

But we infer that they were later rebuilt from the monk of Fontenelle in the *Life of Saint Wandregisilus*. While living in that monastery, he “one night devoted himself most attentively in a cell assigned to him to prayers offered to the divine ears.” Similarly, in the monastery he had built at Elisangium, he is said to have been “one night, according to custom, wrapped in a hair shirt in his cell, while he had given his limbs over to rest for refreshment, suddenly carried away into an ecstasy of mind.”

As for the disciples of Saint Martin, Gallus must be heard in the third dialogue of Sulpicius Severus (Book III, *On the Life of Saint Martin*): “We had dwellings adjoining the river.” Sulpicius gives a clearer account in Book I:

“Then he”—Saint Martin—“summoned the brothers and reported what the devil had disclosed; and he ordered them to make inquiry through each individual’s cell as to who had been affected by this occurrence.”

In the Rule of the monastery of Tarnat I likewise read (chapter 7):

“It is unlawful to enter another’s cell, except for the abbot and the provost, unless a signal has been given; for only they are permitted to learn the brothers’ secrets and to inquire, by secret inspection, how each person conducts himself.”

Saint Gall is said to have built an oratory (Walafrid, *Life of Saint Gall*, chapter 26) “with little dwellings arranged around it for the brothers to live in.” Saint Willibrord “came to his monastery in order to visit it; and after prayers, brotherly greetings, and peaceful admonitions, he wished, as a kindly shepherd, to go around each of the brothers’ dwellings and investigate whether anything in them needed correction,” as Alcuin says in his *Life* (no. 18).

Finally, concerning the first foundation of the monastery of Hirsau, made in the year 830, Trithemius writes about the cells (*Chronicle of Hirsau*):

“The monks’ dwellings,” he says, “arranged around the cloister, were, as far as the custom of that period was concerned, quite beautiful and orderly; although if our monks were confined in similar cells, they would loudly complain that they had been enslaved by chains and darkness. This was done in imitation of the ancients.”

The Carthusian monks of our own age have cells of this kind. Perhaps the ancients used them not so much for sleeping as for reading. See Menard’s notes on the *Concordance of the Rule*, chapter 55, section 1.

I say nothing about the monks of Sinai, concerning whom Saint Nilus writes (*History of the Massacre of the Holy Fathers on Sinai*, chapter 5):

“They make their dwellings not close to one another, but sufficiently far apart, so that they are twenty or more stades distant from one another.”

For these men were properly hermits. Of the Pachomians, however, the Rule delivered by the angel decrees only this (in Bollandus, 14 May):

“You shall make separate cells and arrange for three persons to live in each cell.”

As for the various inconveniences and dangers that can arise from the separation of cells, the monastic congregations that introduced them in recent times have sufficiently provided against them. On this, see Haeften, Book XII, treatise 3, discussions 3, 4, and 5.

“But if the number does not permit it, ten or twenty.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 14, and Justinian’s *Novella* 5 contain the same provision. Yet considerably more monks were accommodated in the dormitories of the monastery of Jumièges under Saint Philibert, its abbot (*Life of Saint Philibert*, no. 7, second century of the Benedictine era). There, “a double house facing south, two hundred and ninety feet in length and fifty in width, rose for the purpose of providing a place of rest.”

“With the elders.”

“That is, the deans,” says Richard of Saint Angelo; and Nicolaus Bravus confirms this from the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 14.

“Who shall be watchful over them.”

They are to guard the night watches, as Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius explain. For, as Hildemar says:

“When he says ‘let them be watchful,’ he orders them to keep watch in the dormitory; for no one can be watchful at night unless he has stayed awake. When we wish to be watchful for some matter, we keep vigil.”

The emperor Justinian agrees with this (*Novella* 133):

“For not everyone is always asleep; rather, it is clear that while some are occupied with sleeping, others keep watch, and some in fact inspect those who are sleeping.”

But Nicolaus of Fractura (see Book I, *On the Ancient Rites of Monasteries*, chapter 1) places this watchfulness in the duty “of rising during the night to see whether the brothers are sleeping dressed, girded with belts and cords, or otherwise according to the Rule.”

“Let a candle burn continually in the same cell until morning.”

Saint Eugendus had formerly established something very similar (in his *Life*, no. 21): “Let the light of God burn without interruption in the dormitory, as in the oratory.” Saint Isidore likewise says (chapter 14):

“Let a light illuminate the place of those sleeping at night, so that, when the darkness has been driven away, the evidence of undisturbed rest may be visible.”

And the Rule of a Certain Author addressed to Virgins says (chapter 14):

“In the school where they sleep, let a lamp burn throughout the whole night.”

The Rule of the Master also prescribes the same thing in chapter 29.

By the term “candle” here, however, is meant “either a lamp lit with oil, or a wax candle with wax and a wick, or even tallow fitted into a certain vessel,” says Bernard of Cassino; Nicolaus of Fractura agrees with him.

Although Saint Benedict seems to mention only one candle, two or more must nevertheless be lit when one is insufficient to illuminate the entire dormitory, so that the brothers may be clearly visible in their individual beds, says Bernard of Cassino. Indeed, Boherius reports that in the monastery of Cassino, where one hundred monks ordinarily resided, seven lamps customarily burned throughout the night in the dormitory. Nicolaus of Fractura likewise asserts this—not only in the dormitory, but also in the cell called the necessary, to which the brothers go to relieve themselves, and in every place through which the brothers must pass at night, so that they may avoid obstacles both to body and soul.

Boherius testifies that he saw this observed in many monasteries of Gaul:

“For in the cloister,” he says, “at the entrance to the dormitory and the oratory after Compline, and at the first ringing of the nocturnal vigils, certain candles are lit.”

Certainly, in the monastery of Saint-Germain of Paris, according to Jacobus Brolus in his additions to the manuscript history of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, “there were formerly five lamps in the dormitory, to serve all the brothers who lacked cells, besides four other lamps arranged in different places: one of these was in the cell of the grand prior, another in the cell of the subprior, the third in the infirmary, and the fourth in the parlour.” This was confirmed in the year 1377 by the court of the Parliament of Paris.

In the monastery of Crowland there was also one light in the chapter house, three in the cloister, and four in the dormitory, according to the statute of Ingulf cited shortly below.

It was likewise a custom of the Benedictine order that boys, novices, and other younger monks were not permitted to walk at night without lit lamps and without accompanying masters, as Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius write here; this is also evident from the various customary books of monasteries.

According to the Eastern Rule, chapter 28, and the Rule of the Master, chapter 29, it was the duty of the weekly servers to light the candle. By “weekly servers” I understand the kitchen servers. Thus Udalricus, speaking of the boys, says (Book III, chapter 8):

“When they serve in the kitchen, their masters are accustomed to see to it that they light at the proper time the lights of the dormitory, the necessary, and the place for the night offices.”

Ingulf assigns the time for lighting them in these words (chapter 29):

“In that courtyard let a lamp hang, made daily by the cellarer, and let it be lit by the weekly servers late, before Compline, so that they may see how the various persons settle themselves.”

Taking the seasons into account, Hildemar wishes it to be lit in summer, when the days are longer, after chapter—that is, after the reading of the conference—but in winter, when chapter ends as night is beginning, while they are still sitting there. Smaragdus says every day before Compline; Bernard of Cassino, when, because of sunset, the dormitory begins to grow dark.

It is useful here to quote the decree of Ingulf, abbot of Crowland, on this matter:

“As winter approaches, from the feast of Saint Bartholomew to the feast of Saint Michael, immediately after the bell of the conference has ended, the church servants shall light three lights in the cloister and four in the dormitory—namely, two in the dormitory and the other two in the house of the necessary. But the light in the chapter house must be lit before the bell of the conference begins to ring, and must continue burning until, after Matins have ended, all the monks have gone up to the dormitory.

“When winter recedes, from the feast of the Purification of Blessed Mary until the feast of Saint Guthlac, the same manner of illuminating all the aforesaid lights shall be observed in every respect.

“From the feast of Saint Michael until the feast of the Purification, all the aforesaid lights shall be lit before the monks enter the refectory for their regular drink; and they shall remain lit throughout the whole year until sunrise, except for the lamp hanging in the chapter house, which is to be extinguished after the convent has gone up to the dormitory, once Matins in the church have been completed.

“From the feast of Saint Guthlac until the feast of Saint Bartholomew, throughout the whole summer, the sacristan or sub-sacristan shall light the aforesaid lights in the dormitory at sunset, so that no secular person may have occasion to enter the dormitory during the night; and they shall continue burning until daylight becomes bright.

“If, through the negligence of the sacristan, any of the aforesaid lights should remain unlit at the appointed times, the sacristan himself shall on the following day be given bread and water in the refectory, without mercy.

“If, through disregard of this most just ordinance of ours, he should fail in the lighting or continued burning of any of the aforesaid lights, he shall eat in the refectory for a full fortnight, on Fridays in those same weeks, content with bread and water alone.

“If a defect in the aforesaid lights should occur a third time, he shall be removed from office and for the following two years remain ineligible to perform any office.

“If this should happen through the negligence of the servants, they shall lose their allowances for a week for each occurrence.

“If it should happen twice or three times, a more severe correction shall follow, or the previously stated penance shall be doubled.”

Thus far Ingulf, whose entire statute I have wished to report so that everyone might see how highly our ancestors valued even the smallest matters.

The candle ought to burn until morning—that is, until the whole house can be seen in daylight—as Bernard of Cassino and Nicolaus of Fractura explain. Yet the Master in his Rule decrees “that, after all have settled themselves, the brothers be protected from the aforesaid requirement if the monastery should happen to experience a shortage of oil.”

Peter the Venerable, however, took a very different view when he decreed (Statute 49):

“Let none of our brothers sleep at night without a light, at least in his own place. If anyone is so poor that he cannot provide his own lamp in his dormitory, let him take the one that is in the church and transfer it to the dormitory.”

Richard of Saint Angelo gives three reasons for this institution. First, “so that when the dean comes to see whether the monks are sleeping or lying honorably, as is customary, he may be able to inspect this openly. Second, so that the monks may freely go to attend to bodily necessities whenever they require it. Third, so that under this image of temporal light there may be shown that light of which we read in John, chapter 1: ‘He was the true light, which enlightens every person coming into this world.’”

“Let them sleep dressed.”

It is certain that monks formerly slept dressed, not only from the Rule of Saint Benedict, but also from the Rule of Saint Pachomius delivered by the angel, the Rule of the Master, chapter 2, the Rule of a Certain Author addressed to Virgins, chapter 14, and the Rule of the Solitaries, chapter 50. Gregory IX and Benedict XII renewed Saint Benedict’s statute in their constitutions for Benedictine monks.

Someone may perhaps ask what clothing they wore while sleeping. There was no single custom among all in this matter. In the aforementioned Rule of Saint Pachomius it is decreed that “at night they shall put on linen *lebitones*, girding their loins, and each shall have a *melote*—that is, a prepared white goatskin—without which they shall neither eat nor sleep.”

Saint Paternus, first a monk and later a bishop, “was content throughout the night with the garment that he had worn during the day,” as the bishop Fortunatus writes in his *Life*, no. 9. Similarly, Saint Fulgentius, while retaining the life of a monk in his episcopate, “did not seek sleep without retaining even his belt; ... and in the tunic in which he slept, in that same tunic he celebrated the sacrifice. He used to say that at the time of sacrifice it was hearts rather than garments that ought to be changed.”

Saint Benedict defines nothing in this chapter. But from chapter 55 we at least infer that Benedictine monks ought to rest clothed in a tunic and a cowl. For he says that a monk should have two tunics and two cowls on account of the nights and in order to wash those garments.

Although Turrecremata writes in that place:

“Although at first sight the matter may appear to us thus, nevertheless, since this is burdensome and severe, we advise that in this respect the ancient custom of the order, which must be regarded as the interpreter of the law, be followed.”

But apart from the fact that Saint Benedict does not decree this, and apart from its being burdensome, it is certain that the order did not have only one custom.

Saint Hildegard, explaining this chapter, says:

“Let them sleep dressed—that is, in the simple and single garment which is next to the human skin, so that they do not lie naked. It was a woolen garment, and not a double garment, because they could not endure that; girded with belts or cords, so that the garment in which they sleep does not fall away from them, and so that they do not appear naked.”

This explanation seems too lenient. According to the Book of the Customs of the Cistercians (chapter 82), “they must not lie down without a cowl, tunic, and leggings.”

The Bursfeld monks decree as follows (*Ceremonial*, distinction 3, chapter 23):

“They shall observe everything that chapter 22 of the Rule prescribes for observance—namely, that they sleep dressed—yet in such a way that this clothing may be adjusted according to the nature of the place or season: in cold places and seasons they shall use more clothing, but in warm places fewer or lighter garments. As an outer habit they shall use the regular cowl, closed and without sleeves, unless they are traveling; in that case they are permitted to use scapulars at sleeping time. Nevertheless, all who are resting shall wear a tunic and leggings beneath the regular habit.”

The Cassinese monks declare (chapter 22) that “the brothers are to sleep dressed in this manner: wearing a scapular with a hood, as during the day, over a tunic for cleanliness; this garment has almost the form of a cowl, according to the Clementine legislation.”

The Constitutions of Monte Oliveto state:

“At night the abbot shall inspect whether the monks sleep dressed in woolen caps, tunic, scapular, and belt; and he shall arrange for a night scapular to be made for them. If anyone sleeps otherwise, he shall first order him to fast on bread and water; secondly, he shall arrange for him to make amends by a stricter penalty.”

The Constitutions of the Celestines are somewhat more lenient. They require only (chapter 10, section 13) that “the monks themselves not sleep naked, but dressed and girded with a belt, and without a knife, according to the provision of the Rule; and, to avoid uncleanness and the heat of summer, let them be clothed at least in a woolen undergarment and a small scapular.”

The Constitutions of the Feuillants require (chapter 22) that “no one sleep without a cowl and hood—for these constitute the monk’s clothing—or ungirded.”

The Carthusians must not be omitted (Part II, chapter 23, no. 34). According to the New Collection of Statutes, they sleep “dressed in a hair shirt, tunic, leggings, belt, and small cowl”—that is, the smallest scapular.

Concerning coverings for the feet, Hildemar must be heard (on chapter 55):

“It should be known that, if there is a need on account of heat, a monk may lie down without foot-coverings; nevertheless, as soon as he rises for Matins, he must put them on, and with them he must go to the church. ... If it can be done, he should lie down without breeches before lying down without foot-coverings.”

Here one is reminded of what Guigo writes about Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, in his *Life*, no. 31 (Bollandus, 1 April):

“He grieved that some, to the dishonor of holiness, slept with their legs exposed in religious dress.”

“And girded with belts or cords.”

Hildemar explains what a belt and a cord are in these words:

“A cord is made from hemp or linen, twisted round; but a belt is a strap of wool or linen, not round like a cord, but flat and broad like a braid.”

Indeed, Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, used a woolen belt, as is recorded in Book II of his *Life*, no. 34 (Volume IV of Baluze’s *Miscellany*).

“And they shall not have knives at their side while they sleep, lest perhaps they be injured in their sleep.”

Therefore, monks formerly carried knives or short swords at their sides during the day; before going to bed at night they laid them aside, and when they rose in the morning they took them up again. This can be seen in the ancient Customs of the monastery of Cluny (Book II, chapter 10):

“At the sound that is customarily made in the dormitory at dawn to awaken the brothers, the novice does the same thing as at the signal for the night offices: he rises as quickly as possible ... and takes care not to forget to carry his knife with him.”

And later:

“Whenever supper is eaten after Vespers, once supper has been completed, he goes up to the dormitory, lays down his knife, removes his daytime shoes, and puts on his nighttime ones, and so forth.”

This is to be understood of small knives for bread and other edible things, or for cutting something of that sort. For, as Boherius says:

“We are not permitted to have large swords; indeed, those found holding them within the bounds of the monastery are thereby excommunicated, unless they have received explicit permission from their prelates.”

This is from Clement V’s decretal *Ne in agro dominico*. The Master refers to this passage of Saint Benedict when he says (chapter 11):

“For this reason we forbid a brother to use a sheath at night, lest, as he turns over, the blade of the knife should come out in his sleep through the sheath and pierce his flesh.”

“And so that the monks may always be ready.”

That is, for the work of God. This sentence refers back to the preceding words, “Let them sleep dressed and girded.” The order of the words has been transposed: Saint Benedict is giving the reason why he wishes monks to sleep dressed, namely, so that they may always be ready to hasten to the work of God.

Although he gives only this one reason, interpreters believe that he had another purpose in view as well. The Master gives three reasons (chapter 11):

“First,” he says, “we have said that the brothers should sleep dressed and girded so that, when the hour of the work of God arrives and the signal of the oratory sounds, they may immediately rise at night. ...

“Second, the brothers ought to sleep dressed and girded because a brother is not permitted to cover his naked limbs; for from this the uncleanness of lust is introduced into the soul. When the nakedness of the limbs is encountered by touch, the desires of women immediately tickle the heart, and thus the limbs are defiled in sleep by filth.

“Third, and especially for this reason, the brothers ought to sleep dressed and girded, so that, while searching in the darkness for their belongings or belts, they do not lose some prayers or psalms because those who are alert and ready to enter the oratory are still, through negligence, turning over and scattering their beds in the darkness.”

“And when the signal has been given, let them rise without delay.”

As the Rule of Saint Pachomius prescribes (article 73):

“Having heard the signal that awakens them, or the voice of one singing psalms, let all rise and run to prayer.”

“Let them hasten to anticipate one another for the work of God, yet with gravity and modesty.”

This, says Bernard of Cassino, “restrains conspicuous haste of step and lightness of walking.”

“The younger brothers shall not have their beds beside one another, but shall be mixed among the elders.”

So that they may learn gravity and propriety from them. Saint Basil decrees something similar (*Sermon on the Renunciation of Worldly Goods*):

“Whenever you must lie down in order to sleep, take care that your garments do not bring you close together with one another; rather, let an elder always be placed in the middle between you.”

And rightly so. For, as the most devout monk Gerard the Belgian says:

“As coal passes its heat to coal, so the stirrings of passion pass among young men. Therefore old men must be mixed among them—provided that they are themselves cool, not men who are themselves like oil to fires. I consider those temperately cool whom we know to be truly bloodless and truly mortified.”

“When they rise for the work of God, let them moderately encourage one another, because of those who are sleepy.”

Yet they are to utter no word with the mouth, because this is forbidden in chapter 42:

“But either by the sound of the mouth, or of the foot upon the ground, or by touching the bed, without touching the sleeper,” says Turrecremata.

The Rule of Abbot Isaiah is particularly apt at this point (chapter 57):

“If your body is sluggish when it is time to rise for prayer, say to it: ‘Do you wish to take rest for this brief time and then depart for everlasting punishment? Is it not better that you labor a little here and then rest there forever with the saints?’ Then sluggishness departs from you, and divine assistance will come to you.”

Saint Basil teaches in *Brief Rules* 43 and 44 how kindly we ought to receive those who awaken us for the vigils.

## CHAPTER XXIII. On excommunication for faults.

[Col. 0501]

[Col. 0501A] If any brother is stubborn, or disobedient, or proud, or murmuring, or is found to be in any respect [Note: Hild.: *in aliqua causa*, “in any matter,” instead of *in aliquo*, “in any respect.”] opposed [Note: Oxon.: *contrario consistens*, “standing in opposition,” instead of *contrarius exsistens*, “being opposed.”] to the holy Rule and contemptuous of the commands of his elders, he shall, in accordance with the command of our Lord, be admonished once and [Col. 0502A] a second time privately [Note: Other copies: *secreto* instead of *secrete*, both “privately/secretly,” different adverbial forms.] by his elders [Note: Other copies: *a majoribus*, “by his superiors,” instead of *a senioribus*, “by his elders.”]. If he does not amend, let him be rebuked publicly before all. But if he does not correct himself even then, provided that he understands the nature of the penalty, let him be subject to excommunication. If, however, he is incorrigible, let him undergo corporal punishment.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0501]

[Col. 0501A] If any brother is stubborn, or disobedient, etc.] According to the varying punctuation of the readings, six or five causes or cases are assigned in which the penalty of excommunication ought to be imposed. The first is if a brother is stubborn. The authorities explain what “stubborn” means as follows. Hildemar: “A stubborn man is one who scorns to do immediately what is commanded: for example, when he is told, ‘Do this,’ and the stubborn man says, ‘I will not do it.’” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius: “Contumacy is called that by which a person summoned to appear does not appear; or, if he has appeared, does not proceed in court. But here contumacy is understood differently: namely, when someone rebuked for some kind of evil answers proudly and resists his corrector to his face.” Nicolaus of Fractura: “It should be known [Col. 0501B] that contumacy is manifold, and that a person is called stubborn in several ways: when commanded to restore something, he does not restore it; likewise, if summoned to judgment by three edicts, or by one peremptory edict serving for all three, he does not come; or, if he comes, departs without permission. Likewise, if commanded to answer, he does not answer; or, if he answers obscurely, which is the same as though he did not answer. Likewise, if he comes to court but does not appear, or hides behind columns, he is regarded as though he had not come. Here, however, contumacy is understood differently: namely, when someone, having been privately rebuked, tries to resist his corrector.” Richard of Saint Angelo: “A person is called stubborn in three ways: first, if summoned, he does not come; second, if he comes and is unwilling to obey; third, if he departs without permission.” Thus they speak according to the laws. Finally, Benedict Haeften (Book VIII, treatise 4, discussion 3): “They hold that *contumax* is derived either from *contemnere*, ‘to scorn,’ or, as others prefer, from swelling, that is, pride. In legal writers, a stubborn person is one who, after three edicts have been issued, or one in place of three, commonly called a peremptory edict, and after being summoned by the judge’s letters, scorns to present himself. Among monks, however, he is one who not only does not appear, but does not obey.”

The second cause is, “or disobedient.” Hildemar distinguishes this man from the stubborn man in that every stubborn man is disobedient, but not conversely every disobedient man is stubborn; for although he does not carry out an order or command, he does not answer proudly or resist to his superior’s face. This disobedience of which Saint Benedict speaks here, “is,” say Bernard of [Col. 0501D] Cassino, Nicolaus of Fractura, and Boherius, “that by which someone is unwilling to make the satisfaction privately imposed upon him.” It is not, Boherius adds, that disobedience which is opposed by contradiction to the profession of obedience, since by it one wholly withdraws from God. Saint Benedict therefore commands that a disobedient man, after two private admonitions and a third public rebuke, be excommunicated. By contrast, Saint Pachomius (article 89) orders that, if he is of mature age, he be admonished ten times to desist from his faults; afterwards, if he refuses to listen, that he be rebuked according to the laws of the monastery. Saint Basil (*Longer Rules*, chapter 47) orders one unwilling to give an account of his disobedience to be expelled from the fellowship of the brothers. Something similar occurs in Cassian (Book IV, chapter 6). And indeed, the Apostle says: “If anyone does not obey our word by this letter, mark that man, and do not associate with him” [Col. 0502A] (2 Thessalonians 3). Saint Columbanus, however, decrees only in his *Penitential* that “if any brother is disobedient, he shall receive only one *paximatium* and water for two days.”

The third cause is, “or proud,” in whatever kind of pride.

The fourth is, “or murmuring,” that is, one who “is not merely silently disobedient with a proud and unyielding spirit, but by open murmuring spreads his poison among others and stirs their minds to contradiction,” says Haeften. But Bernard of Cassino and Boherius understand Saint Benedict here to mean slight and almost habitual murmuring, not that which draws others into the sin of sedition. We have spoken at chapters 4 and 5 of the murmuring which Saint Benedict punishes by excommunication, and after him the Rule of the Master, chapter 12, and the Rule of a Certain Author addressed to Virgins, chapter 18, where we reported the various penalties by which it was punished among the ancient monks.

359 “Or is found to be in any respect opposed to the holy Rule and contemptuous of the commands of his elders.”] Here Bernard of Cassino finds a fifth and a sixth case in which the remedy of excommunication is to be applied: the fifth, if someone is in any respect opposed to the holy Rule; the sixth, if he is found contemptuous of the commands of his elders. He writes the text of the Rule with this punctuation: [Col. 0502C] “Or, being in any respect opposed to the holy Rule, and found contemptuous of the commands of his elders.” Some manuscripts and the old French translation favour this, rendering the passage: “or that he be contrary in anything to the holy Rule, and that he be found despising the commands of his elders.” But if this punctuation were valid, one should read not *praeceptis* (“commands,” dative), but *praeceptorum seniorum suorum contemptor*, “a despiser of the commands of his elders,” with *praeceptorum* in the genitive. Similarly, Turrecremata places the fifth case in being opposed to the Rule and the commands, and the sixth in contempt of the elders, writing the text with this punctuation: “Or, being opposed to the holy Rule and the commands, he is found contemptuous of his elders.” The French translation of Guido Juvenalis agrees. But this is less correct. Better are those who, with Menard and Haeften, read: “Or, being in any respect opposed to the holy Rule, and found contemptuous of the commands of his elders.” In these words they establish one, the fifth, cause of excommunication. Thus Saint Columbanus says in his *Penitential*: “But whoever blasphemes his superior or the Rule is to be driven out, unless he himself says, ‘I repent of what I said.’ But if he does not humble himself, let him do penance for forty days, because he is held by the disease of pride.” And again: “If anyone contradicts a command or breaks the Rule, let him have one *paximatium* for two days.” The Rule of Saint Pachomius says (article 91): “Those who despise the commands of their superiors and the rules of the monastery, which have been established by God’s command, and who make light of the counsels of the elders, shall be corrected according to the established order until they amend.” The same is read in chapter 19 of the Eastern Rule.

“He shall, in accordance with the command of our Lord, be admonished once and a second time privately by his elders.”] Provided, however, that he is of sound and understanding mind; for those who are hard of heart must be restrained more severely at the very beginning of their sin, as Hildemar observes here from chapter 2 of the Rule.

If he does not amend, let him be rebuked publicly before everyone.] That is, by the superior, who alone has the authority to correct offenders publicly; or also by the seniors acting with his authority. The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins prescribes (ch. 18) that “she should be rebuked privately once or twice by the seniors. If she does not amend, then let her be rebuked by the whole community together.”

If he understands what sort of punishment it is.] Or, as the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins puts it: “If her understanding was previously sound, let her be subjected to excommunication.” Thus Saint Benedict, after three admonitions, subjects the incorrigible person to excommunication. Saint Basil established the same discipline in the *Shorter Rules*, question 3; in the *Monastic Constitutions*, ch. 30; the Eastern Rule, ch. 32; the Rule of the Master, ch. 12; and the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, ch. 18.

What Saint Benedict understands here by the name “excommunication,” the commentators explain as follows. [Col. 0503B] Hildemar: “When he says ‘to excommunication,’ one must understand simple excommunication only; that is, he is to undergo that excommunication which separates the monk from the table.” Bernard of Cassino similarly says: “This excommunication is not called the greater excommunication, nor separation from the sacraments, but separation from participation at table, which will be discussed in the following chapter; for these faults are not counted among the more serious ones.” Boherius says: “Note that this excommunication is not anathema, which is imposed by the bishop alone with a definite solemnity; nor is it the greater excommunication, which separates one from the body of Christ and the Church—that is, from the communion of the faithful—for that ought not to be imposed for the lesser faults discussed here; nor is it the lesser excommunication, which separates one from the sacraments of the Church. Rather, this excommunication is separation from the brothers’ table and from common participation in the church choir, of which the following chapter speaks.”

Menard, on the contrary, says: “This is proper excommunication, which theologians call the greater excommunication; for on the part of the person excommunicated there is first obstinacy, contempt, and the seriousness of the fault; on the part of the person excommunicating, there is a threefold admonition.” Joannes Craesbeeck agrees with him.

The old French version renders the text as follows: “Let him be excommunicated, that is, let him be put outside the community of the others.” But in my opinion Saint Benedict speaks in this chapter of excommunication in general, intending to discuss the same matter specifically in the following two chapters. Whether he wished to inflict upon his brothers, for more serious faults, an excommunication that is properly an ecclesiastical censure will have to be examined at chapter 25.

Meanwhile, consider the ancient formula of excommunication from the Rule of the Master (ch. 13):

“When the abbot has been informed of the deserts of the disobedient man, he is no longer to be called a brother, but a heretic against the law; no longer a son of God, but a worker of the devil, who, by scattering the deeds of the saints, has become like a kind of scab in the flock. Let the abbot summon him in the presence of his superiors, or with the rest of the community standing around; and when the abbot asks his superiors what he has done wrong, or how many times he has been admonished concerning that fault without amending, let them state what they accuse him of.

“After hearing the fault, let him hear the abbot’s voice speaking against him in this manner: ‘O wretched soul, what answer will you give to God, whom you daily provoke by your disobedience when you approach to worship him? Why, while serving under God’s dominion, do you serve Mammon instead? Why do you lie to God, another Judas? That Judas sold justice for the price of wickedness; you tear apart the Christian name by your evil deeds. That Judas generated scandal against the Lord by a false peace; you, under the name of holy service, are even more rebellious against God. That Judas, though a disciple, falsely betrayed the Master; you, a Christian under the holy name, follow the devil even more by your deeds.

“‘For our admonition—or your own spirit, which you resist, together with the flesh, by your own will—will stand before God at the tribunal of the fearful judgment and say: “Lord, he was unwilling to understand in order to do good; he devised wickedness, stood upon every evil path, and did not reject malice, but rather gloried in it; he was powerful in wickedness.”

“‘When you have been accused of these things in judgment, then, together with our voice and that of the fearful Judge himself, you will hear him say to you: “You are the one who hated discipline and cast my words behind you. If you saw a thief, you ran with him, and with adulterers you placed your share. Your mouth abounded in wickedness, and your tongue fashioned deceit. Sitting, you slandered your brother and laid a stumbling block. All day long your tongue devised injustice; like a sharp razor you practiced deceit. You loved wickedness more than kindness, and injustice more than speaking what is right. You loved every word of rashness with a deceitful tongue. You did these things, and I kept silent; you thought that I was like you. I will rebuke you and set it before your face, so that God may destroy you forever; he will tear you away and remove you from your tent, and your root from the land of the living.”

“‘Then all the righteous will see you in judgment, in their glory, when you have been separated from them to the left among the goats; and they will laugh at you, saying: “Behold the man who did not set God as his helper, but prevailed in his vanity, and the fear of God was not before his eyes; for he acted deceitfully in his presence and said, like a fool in his heart: ‘God will not seek it out; he has turned his face away so as not to see to the end.’” And he did not know that the enemies who lie to the Lord will have their time in eternal punishment.

“‘What will you say to God in answer to these things? What excuses for your sins, wretched man, will you be able to bring him, when your own evils will first have attacked you and Gehenna will have waited to consume you?’

“After this voice of rebuke before the community, let the abbot immediately order him to be driven from the oratory and the common table, and let him be counted as an outsider. Since he is designated an enemy of God, from that hour he ought no longer to be a friend to the brothers.”

But if he is shameless.] For Bernard of Cassino, *improbus* means “brazen, or persevering in wickedness”; for Boherius, “one who acts against the law, or is troublesome, or perseveres in evil”; for Joannes Craesbeeck, one whom neither reproaches nor dangers to the soul move.

Joannes de Précis, abbot of Saint-Germain in Paris, renders this passage in French as follows: “If he does not understand it and is rebellious.” The manuscript version of Saint Peter of Conques has: “If he is obstinate.” The version of Guido Juvenalis has: “If he is shameless and pays no attention to this.” More recent versions have: “If he is hardened.”

Let him be subjected to bodily punishment.] “This is understood in two ways: namely, by excessive fasts, or certainly by scourging,” say Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius. But the name “fasting” is to be taken for every bodily punishment, according to Saint Hildegard, who explains the passage as follows: “Let him be subjected to bodily punishment—that is, let him be punished with blows or other bodily chastisements.”

And rightly so; for, as Joannes Craesbeeck says: “The shameless, whom neither reproaches nor dangers to the soul move, must be compelled not by excommunication but by the severity of blows, after the manner of irrational animals, which are guided by no judgment of reason but driven by the whip. Thus those who, blinded and hardened by their wickedness, yield to no reasoning may be moved and brought back to their senses by the affliction and torment of their bodies.”

The Rule of the Master agrees: “But if excommunicated brothers should become so proud that, persisting in the pride of their hearts, they refuse on the third day, at the ninth hour, to make satisfaction to the abbot, let them be guarded and beaten with rods until death; and, if the abbot wishes, let them be expelled from the monastery, and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. What the Measure of Excommunication Should Be

[Col. 0505]

[Col. 0505A] The measure of excommunication or discipline ought to be extended according to the measure of the fault; and the determination of the faults should depend upon the judgment of the abbot [Note: [Col. 0505A] Conc. Comp., “depends upon judgment.” Sabin. Conch., “depends upon discretion.”]. Nevertheless, if a brother is found guilty of lesser faults, let him be deprived of participation at table. When he has been deprived [Note: [Col. 0505A] Narb., *privato*; others, *privatis*; others, *privatus*.] of the company of the table, this shall be the arrangement: that in the oratory he is not to intone a psalm or antiphon [Col. 0506A] nor recite a reading [Note: [Col. 0505A] Narb., “he is not to intone or say a responsory, nor recite a reading.”], until satisfaction has been made. He is to receive his food [Note: [Col. 0505A] Others, “for himself.”] alone after the brothers’ meal [Note: [Col. 0506A] Hild. omits “after the brothers’ meal.”] [Note: [Col. 0506A] Hild. Conc., “let him receive alone.” The printed editions add: “at the measure or hour which the abbot has judged appropriate for him”; these words are absent from all manuscripts.]. Thus, for example, if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, that brother is to eat at the ninth; if the brothers eat at the ninth, he is to eat in the evening [Note: [Col. 0506A] Oxon., *vespertina* (“evening,” adjectival form).], until he obtains pardon through suitable satisfaction.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0505]

[Col. 0505B] The measure of excommunication or discipline ought to be extended according to the measure of the fault.] In the preceding chapter Saint Benedict the Holy Father spoke of excommunication almost in general; in this and the following chapter he speaks of it as it were specifically, dealing with lesser and greater faults. For he does not wish the same punishment to apply to every fault, as the Stoics once maintained. They asserted that all human sins were equal and therefore judged that all should be punished with an equal penalty. Saint Jerome, in Book II *Against Jovinianus*, and Saint Augustine, in Letter 167, refuted this error, which was later revived by the heretic Jovinianus.

Following this teaching, Saint Benedict says: “According to the measure of the fault,” that is, according to the quantity or quality of the fault. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Richard of Saint Angelo, and Boherius teach that the measure of the punishment must be derived from this. “The measure of excommunication or discipline ought to be extended”: that is, the quantity or quality of the punishment, so that he remains excommunicated for as long as he has been at fault, under a greater or lesser excommunication according to the seriousness of the offense.

And Saint Benedict the Holy Father rightly says “of excommunication or discipline.” Although Richard maintains that these are the same thing, Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius distinguish discipline from excommunication. By the name “discipline,” Hildemar understands the rod; Bernard and Boherius understand fasting and the rod together.

The determination of the faults should depend upon the judgment of the abbot.] These words are not to be understood as though it depended upon the abbot’s judgment whether a fault were light or serious, or serious or light; faults are such in themselves, independently of his judgment, from the moment they are committed. Rather, it is his prudence and judgment to discern and assess whether a given fault, affected by such or such a circumstance, is serious or light.

Nor are the words to be understood as though it depended upon the abbot’s will to impose whatever punishments he pleased for faults. Rather, it is his task to recognize and judge what kind of fault it is, serious or light; and once this has been established, he is to impose the punishment prescribed by Saint Benedict, and no other. [Col. 0505D] Hildemar appears to explain Saint Benedict the Holy Father in this way.

Moreover, what Saint Basil also establishes may be referred to here (*Sermon 1, On the Institution of Monastic Life*): “The punishment of one who has been caught in some offense should be according to the measure of the sin: namely, that he either be forbidden to join the others in psalmody, or not be admitted to the communion of prayer, or be excluded from participation at table; and in this matter the one who governs the common discipline will also determine the punishment.”

Nevertheless, if a brother is found guilty of lesser faults, let him be deprived of participation at table.] Saint Benedict did not leave even the lightest faults unpunished, lest, if neglected, they should eventually become serious. For he knew what Saint Chrysostom says (*Sermon 8 on 1 Corinthians*): “He who falls short a little will fall short greatly in the course of progress. For if a body receives a wound from a sword, it is corrupted; if a building opens even slightly, it collapses; if a root is cut a little, it becomes useless. Therefore this ‘little’ is not little, but nearly the whole. When, therefore, we have offended or grown sluggish in a small matter, let us not despise that small matter, because what is neglected becomes great. A garment that begins to tear and is neglected is eventually ripped apart; and when a few roof tiles have fallen, a neglected roof ruins the entire house. Considering these things, let us never despise small matters, lest we fall into great ones.”

To grasp Saint Benedict’s mind more fully, we must inquire which faults ought to be considered light; for we shall investigate the more serious faults in the following chapter. Thus, “he is guilty of a lesser fault,” says Saint Isidore (ch. 16), “who has loved to be idle; who has come late to the office, or to the conference, or to the table; who has laughed in the choir or occupied himself with stories; who, leaving the office or work, has gone outside without necessity; who has loved sluggishness or sleep; who has sworn frequently; who has been excessively talkative; who has undertaken a task assigned to him without a blessing [Col. 0506C] and, once the work was completed, has not asked for a blessing; who has completed an assigned task carelessly and late; who has broken some vessel by accident; who has caused damage to a small object; who has used a book carelessly; who has withdrawn somewhere for a moment; who has secretly received letters from someone or some gift, or, upon receiving a letter, has concealed it; who has written back without the abbot’s consent; who has either seen or spoken with a parent or secular person without the order of a senior; who has been disobedient to a senior; who has answered a senior insolently; who has not restrained his tongue toward the seniors; who has been wanton in speech; who has walked indecently; who has joked; who has laughed excessively; who has spoken, prayed, or eaten with an excommunicated person; who has not disclosed a nocturnal emission to the Father. These and similar faults are to be corrected by a three-day excommunication.” Cassian reports things very similar in Book IV, chapter 16.

[Col. 0506D] Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino, however, count spiritual sins among the lesser faults and carnal sins among the greater. They call spiritual sins those that Saint Benedict listed in the preceding chapter: obstinacy, disobedience, pride, murmuring, and so forth; carnal sins include fornication, adultery, and similar offenses.

For Boherius, lesser faults are venial sins. For Turrecremata they are “transgressions of the Rule or constitutions concerning matters that are not of the essence of religious life and do not pertain to acts of the virtues, but concern ceremonies, such as breaking silence, coming late to choir and refectory, and similar matters; or they are among those things that are by their nature light sins, such as an idle word, empty talk, immoderate laughter, and the like.”

Certainly, concerning Saint Benedict of Aniane, the abbot, they report (Ardo, *Life of Saint Benedict*, no. 32, fourth century, part I) that “his vigilance was so great that if even small grains of legumes, or tiny pieces of leek, or leaves of cabbages were found neglected by him, the offense of which he was judged guilty was immediately marked by a sentence worthy of excommunication.” What that sentence of excommunication was for lesser faults, the Holy Father explains: the offender was to be deprived of participation at table, but not of the oratory; for while the brothers ate in the refectory, he was to be in the church, according to the statutes of Lanfranc, chapter 17. Saint Basil mentions the same punishment in *Sermon 1, On the Institution of Monastic Life*; Saint Caesarius in the *Rule for Virgins*, chapter 11; the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, chapter 19; and the Rule of the Master, chapter 13.

When he has been deprived of the company of the table, this shall be the arrangement.] That is, the procedure will reasonably be carried out in this way, says Bernard of Cassino; or, as Hildemar says, “This is the reasonable arrangement.”

That in the oratory he is not to intone a psalm or antiphon.] Nor anything similar, such as responsories, hymns, and so forth, because the same judgment applies to these, says Boherius.

Nor recite a reading.] Nor celebrate Mass, if he is a priest; nor offer at it, if he is merely a monk, as Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius teach after Hildemar. “For,” they say, “he who is forbidden the lesser is also forbidden the greater.” Their opinion is confirmed by the Statutes of Lanfranc in these words:

“A brother assigned to make satisfaction for a light fault is separated from the common table … In church he is not to celebrate Mass, read the Epistle, reading, or Gospel, sing the responsory, intone the antiphon over the psalms, or do anything of this kind with the others; he is not to vest for the candlestick or thurible, nor approach for the offering or the kiss of peace.”

And the *Ceremonial of the Bursfeld Congregation* (Distinction 1, ch. 8) says:

“One sent to do penance for a lighter fault ought to conduct himself as the Rule itself prescribes. No one, however, is to be assigned to it unless he has committed something that, on account of its enormity, appears to require stricter punishment. Thus, while undergoing this penance, he is not to intone an antiphon or psalm, recite a reading, or perform the office of the invitatory; he is not to kiss the Gospel book, communicate, celebrate, or minister publicly in the community, although he is not forbidden to do these things privately.”

The ancient Customs of the Monastery of Cluny, cited by Ulrich, Book II, chapter 18, and the manuscript of Saint Benignus of Dijon, chapter 32, have only this: “He does not offer; he does not kiss the Gospel book; he does not approach for the kiss of peace.”

But they abstained from this penance on feasts with twelve readings, according to the statutes of Lanfranc, the Customs of Cluny, and Saint Benignus, until the ordinary days returned. On those ordinary days they could also celebrate Masses privately, as the *Ceremonial of the Bursfeld Congregation* states and Peter Boherius teaches in his first commentary.

Until satisfaction has been made.] That is, until he is released from excommunication; how this release was to take place will be explained later, at chapter 44.

He is to receive his food alone after the brothers’ meal.] That is, without a servant ministering to him, without the company of a brother eating with him, in some lodging separate from the common refectory of the brothers, or in the common refectory after the brothers’ meal, as Bernard of Cassino explains.

The ancient Cistercian definitions likewise say (Distinction 7, chapter 5): “They are to eat outside the refectory, wherever it has seemed good to the abbot, according to the Rule. Nor, after the meal, are they to go with the others to drink.”

Nevertheless, Hildemar maintains that Saint Benedict does not take away his place in the order. I think this is not to be understood of the refectory, but of the choir. Hildemar says that he must remain in his place there until the brothers kneel for the supplication of the litany. At that time he goes to the place assigned by the abbot and lies prostrate there until the Work of God is completed, as we shall say below at chapter 44. The Statutes of Lanfranc, however, prescribe (chapter 17) that “in the monastery and in the chapter house, he is to be in the place where he usually is, either last of all or between the two, according to the nature of the fault and the abbot’s command.”

Almost all printed editions add: “At the measure or hour which the abbot has judged appropriate for him.” For if he is shameless, he is to be punished not only with rods but also afflicted with excessive fasts; otherwise, if he is truly repentant for his offense, he ought to be refreshed with the same food and drink as the others. For Saint Benedict does not, says Hildemar, “take away his place in the order, or his food or drink, unless he has not amended through this excommunication.”

Hence the Statutes of Lanfranc also say (chapter 17): “A brother assigned to make satisfaction for a light fault is separated from the common table, but is to use the food and drink that the other brothers use, unless it has been expressly forbidden to him.”

Boherius, in his first commentary, maintains that such a person is not to be deprived of wine; but in his second commentary, writing on chapter 25, he says: “In a lighter fault the measure of food is not changed, but the hour is delayed.”

Thus, for example, if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, that brother is to eat at the ninth; if the brothers eat at the ninth, he is to eat in the evening.] The Rule of the Master says similarly (chapter 13):

“If, perhaps, because of the lightness of the fault, the abbot does not wish to double his fasts, then, if the brothers eat at the sixth hour, he is to receive at the ninth hour a single dish, a fragment of bread for food, and water, offered to him mercifully by his superior. If the blameless brothers eat at the ninth hour, let the meal mentioned above for him be delayed until evening, so that he may perceive what evils his fault has brought upon him and what good things he has lost through negligence.”

Until he obtains pardon through suitable satisfaction.] According to Hildemar and Smaragdus, satisfaction is suitable when penance has been completed according to the measure of the fault. In this matter one must always consider with what intention, or in what manner, he committed the offense, and with what disposition he repents. He is to be absolved sooner if he makes satisfaction humbly and shamefacedly; later if he does so carelessly and lukewarmly.

## CHAPTER XXV. On More Serious Faults

[Col. 0507]

[Col. 0507D] That brother who is burdened with the guilt of a more serious fault is to be suspended both from the table and from the oratory. None of the brothers is to associate with him in any way or converse with him. He is to be alone at the work assigned to him, persisting in the sorrow of penance, knowing that fearful sentence of the Apostle, who says that such a man is to be handed over [Note: [Col. 0507D] Hild., “hand him over.”] [Col. 0508D] to Satan [Note: [Col. 0507D] Oxon. and Lyr. omit “to Satan.”] for the destruction [Note: [Col. 0508D] Others, “in destruction.”] of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord [Note: [Col. 0508D] Others, “for the day of the Lord.” Hild., “on the day of judgment.”]. He is to receive his food alone, in the measure or at the hour which the abbot has judged appropriate for him [Note: [Col. 0508D] Others, “which he has judged”; others, “which he has prescribed.”]. Nor is he to receive a blessing from anyone who passes by, nor is the food given to him to be blessed.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0509]

[Col. 0509A] Before speaking of the punishments by which those excommunicated for more serious faults are to be chastised, it seems necessary to inquire which punishments should be considered more serious. I think that, first of all, we can place among them those faults which the ancient monks corrected with blows or purged by expulsion, and which Cassian reports in these words (Book IV, chapter 16):

“The remaining faults, which among us are admitted without distinction but are also endured by us in a more blameworthy manner, are open insults, manifest contempt, arrogant contradictions, free and unrestrained wandering about, familiarity with women, anger, quarrels, hostilities, and disputes; presumption in undertaking private work; the contagion of love of money; attachment to and possession of superfluous things that the other brothers do not have; unusual and secret consumption of food; and similar offenses. These are corrected not by the spiritual rebuke that we have mentioned, but either by blows or by expulsion.”

Second are the faults that Saint Isidore enumerates in the Rule, writing as follows (chapter 16):

“He is subject to a more serious fault if he is drunk; if quarrelsome; if foul-mouthed; if familiar with women; if sowing discord; if angry; if stiff-necked and haughty; if swollen with pride in mind or immoderate in his boastful bearing; if a detractor, whisperer, or envious person; if presumptuous in acquiring private property; if entangled in the contagion of money; if he possesses anything superfluous beyond the regular dispensation; if he is a defrauder of property entrusted or committed to him, or of property not fully entrusted to him.

“Among these faults are also the following: if he has boasted about things brought with him, or murmured about them through disobedience; if he has caused damage to a greater object; if he has stolen; if he has committed perjury; if he has told a lie; if he has loved disputes and quarrels; if he has openly insulted a brother; if he has stained an innocent person with a false accusation; if he has despised a senior with an obstinate disposition; if he has harbored resentment against a brother; if he has refused forgiveness to one who sinned against him and afterward begged pardon; if he has played with children; if he has lain in one bed with another; if he has taken something privately or secretly outside the common table; if, going out somewhere without consulting his superior or abbot, he has remained away at midday or longer; if, in order to be idle, he has pretended to be ill.

“These and similar faults are to be purged, according to the Father’s judgment, by prolonged excommunication, so that those known to have sinned seriously may be restrained with harsher severity.”

Third, if we consult the commentators on the Rule, Hildemar teaches in chapters 22 and 24 that the more serious faults are carnal sins, such as fornication, homicide, theft, and similar offenses; and in chapter 25 he calls them mortal offenses and criminal sins. Likewise, Smaragdus, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Turrecremata, and Guido Juvenalis understand “more serious faults” to mean mortal sins, because according to the canons no one is to be struck with the greater excommunication unless he is guilty of mortal sin. They add nothing more specific, except that Bernard of Cassino says:

“I nevertheless hold that the Father speaks here without distinction of those mortal sins which are recognized through action and commission, and which the abbot judges to be not lesser but more serious faults.”

Finally, according to Joannes Craesbeeck, “more serious faults are violations of the three monastic vows, and other more serious sins that make a person liable to eternal death. The Apostle lists many such sins (Galatians 5): ‘The works of the flesh are manifest,’ he says, ‘which are fornication, impurity, indecency, licentiousness, the worship of idols,’ and so forth.”

How such faults, then, are to be corrected, the Holy Father explains in this chapter in the following words:

That brother who is burdened with the guilt of a more serious fault is to be suspended.] That is, he is to be excommunicated.

Both from the table and from the oratory.] That is, from the sacraments and equally from the company of men, says Boherius in his second commentary. From his view it would follow that Saint Benedict the Holy Father intended to strike those guilty of more serious faults not with merely regular and monastic excommunication, [Col. 0510A] but with genuinely ecclesiastical excommunication. This opinion could be confirmed by the following arguments.

First, Saint Benedict proceeds in exactly the manner in which the Church proceeds against those to be excommunicated. On the part of the person to be excommunicated, he requires obstinacy, contempt, and seriousness of fault; on the part of the excommunicator, he requires three prior admonitions, as is clear from chapter 23 of the Rule. Although, as some commentators note, a threefold admonition need not always precede; for there are certain crimes in which a person is excommunicated by the very fact of falling into them.

Second, in this chapter above all, Saint Benedict deprives the excommunicated person of precisely those things of which persons bound by ecclesiastical excommunication are deprived. Perhaps for this reason Hildemar asserted that the sacred canons separating a person from the Church were derived from this chapter.

Certainly, he denies the excommunicated person the common table, entry into the oratory, conversation with the brothers, the blessing of those passing by, and any association or cohabitation. The Church forbids those bound by excommunication from these things, as is clear from these two verses cited by Saint Thomas:

“If, for offenses, a person is made anathema,

let mouth, prayer, greeting, communion, and table be denied.”

And although “communion,” insofar as it involves participation in the sacraments, is not expressly named in this chapter, he is nevertheless understood to be sufficiently deprived of it, since he is suspended from the oratory, where it is ordinarily received. Clearly, if those excommunicated for lesser faults could neither celebrate nor communicate publicly, as we saw in the preceding chapter from Hildemar, the Statutes of Lanfranc, Bernard of Cassino, and others, then, all the more, one struck by the greater excommunication will be unable to celebrate or communicate either publicly or privately.

Third, Saint Benedict appears to speak of excommunication as the greatest of all punishments when he says (chapter 23): “If he understands how great the punishment is, let him be subjected to excommunication.”

Fourth, he says that such a person is handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. Saint Augustine explains what it means to be handed over to Satan in these words:

“Every Christian who is excommunicated by priests is handed over to Satan. How so? Because outside the Church there is the devil, just as Christ is in the Church. Accordingly, the person removed from ecclesiastical communion is, as it were, handed over to Satan. Therefore, when the Apostle then proclaims that those people were handed over to Satan, he demonstrates that they had been excommunicated by him.”

Fifth, Saint Benedict wished the person who associates with an excommunicated man to receive a similar punishment of excommunication; and this is known to be a precaution required only in the case of one bound by the greater excommunication.

Sixth, there is the common opinion of the commentators and others, who judge that Saint Benedict speaks in this chapter especially of ecclesiastical excommunication. Such are Hildemar; Bernard of Cassino; Boherius in both commentaries; Turrecremata; Guido Juvenalis; Matthias Lambertus on chapter 25; Joannes Craesbeeck on chapter 23; Alardus Gazaeus in his commentary on Cassian, Book II, chapter 16; Antonius Perezius on chapter 25; Theophilus Raynaudus, *On Ecclesiastical Admonitions*, part II, chapter 1, no. 6; Hugo Menard on the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 30, section 1, chapter 32, section 1, and chapter 34, section 1; and Benedict Haeften, Book VIII, treatise 4, disputation 1. We could also have added Saint Bernard, Sermon 44 on the *Song of Songs*, but I would be excessive in citing all their testimonies. One representative of them all will suffice, namely Hildemar, since he is the most ancient and by no means the least important among the commentators on the Rule.

Writing on this chapter, he says:

“This chapter produced that sentence of the Apostle Paul in which he says: ‘Hand such a man over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh.’ From this, too, the sacred canons that separate a person from the Church were derived.”

And again:

“It must be known that this chapter was drawn from canonical authority. For in the Old Testament it is prescribed that, if someone is a leper, he is to remain outside the camp; but if he is not, he is to remain in the camp. That leprosy signifies the sins for which a person ought to be made an outsider to the Church. Likewise, the impurity of greater sins bears the same figure as leprosy; by the camp, however, the Church is understood.”

And on chapter 27:

“The abbot ought to show great concern for the excommunicated person, lest he happen to die before being reconciled. For if, God forbid, he should die first, then, according to canonical authority, a sacrifice ought not to be offered for him, and so forth.”

This could also be confirmed by the example of nuns whom Saint Benedict the Holy Father excommunicated.

On the other hand, Saint Hildegard, Columbanus Uranx in a manuscript commentary, Silvanus Razzi, a Camaldolese monk, Julianus Parisius in *On the First Manner of Life of the Cistercians*, part II, chapter 6, section 1; Nicholas Bravus; and Cardinal Joannes Bona in *On Divine Psalmody*, chapter 3, section 4, no. 1, judge that Saint Benedict spoke not of ecclesiastical but only of regular excommunication. They rely chiefly upon the following arguments.

First, although Saint Benedict was not a priest, he is said to have excommunicated someone in Book II of the *Dialogues* of Pope Saint Gregory. But this is not conclusive, since a simple abbot, even if not a priest or blessed, can excommunicate provided that he has been lawfully instituted and confirmed. Moreover, the simple monk Theodosius is said to have excommunicated the emperor Theodosius the Younger (Cassiodorus, *Tripartite Ecclesiastical History*, Book X, chapter 27). Certainly the emperor did not disregard his excommunication, although Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny, entirely disapproves of it in Book I of his *Collations*.

Second, the Rule of Saint Benedict was not approved by the Church from the beginning, although the Church is the one that grants this power of excommunicating. Haeften answers this argument by saying that Saint Benedict’s Rule was tacitly approved by the Church, and that at that time an express diploma of the Apostolic See was unnecessary, since the Church had not yet reserved this power to itself; it was sufficient that the bishop in whose diocese the monasteries were being built approve it. Certainly, the discipline of the Church today is very different from the discipline of those times.

Third, the condition of monks would be more severe if they were excommunicated for every more serious fault—that is, for every mortal sin. But a person was not struck with excommunication merely by falling into a more serious fault, except perhaps because of the seriousness of the matter; for a threefold admonition must precede on the part of the excommunicator, and obstinacy and contempt on the part of the person to be excommunicated.

Moreover, by this statute the Holy Father did not impose a command upon the abbot, but gave him authority, which he must use with the greatest discretion and prudence. He is not to excommunicate immediately for every mortal sin, especially since formerly a person who had been excommunicated by that very fact became ineligible for the priesthood.

Therefore Hildemar warns the abbot to consider prudently whether the offender is a priest, or whether he might eventually be raised to the priesthood and render some service to the Church. In that case, unless his fault were of such a kind as to make him unfit for holy orders, he ought to refrain from excommunication. “For,” he says, “if he has been excommunicated for a greater fault, then, if he is a priest, he must not sing Mass; but if he is not a priest, neither ought he to become one.” He teaches the same thing in chapter 23.

Fourth. Saint Benedict wrote the Rule both for nuns and for monks; yet their abbesses cannot excommunicate. But not everything prescribed by the holy Rule is applicable to nuns, such as what is read concerning priests and excommunication. This nevertheless does not prevent their abbesses from imposing upon offenders those penalties appropriate to their state, such as excluding them from the table, from the company of the sisters, and other things of this kind. Saint Jerome records that Paula did this in the Bethlehem monastery in these words (*Epitaphium Paulae*):

> “When she had observed that a woman was talkative, garrulous, shameless, fond of quarrels, and unwilling to amend despite frequent admonition, she would make her pray among the last and outside the assembly of the sisters at the dining-room door, and take her food separately, so that shame might correct her whom reproof had not corrected.”

In the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* it is decreed (ch. 6) that “those sisters who are detained in penance for serious faults are not to stand in the church with the others who communicate, but are to sing the office secretly in another church.” But enough concerning these matters. We present the arguments for both opinions, so that each person may freely embrace whichever opinion he wishes. I return to the text of the Rule.

### “No one of the brothers is to join him in any association or conversation.”

For, “when someone is designated an enemy of God, from that hour he ought no longer to be a friend to the brothers,” as the Master says (ch. 13). Saint Aurelian likewise says (ch. 36): “No one may speak with one who has been excommunicated, except the person whom the holy abbot has appointed as his guardian.” Saint Isidore says (ch. 17): “No one may enter to visit an excommunicated person without the superior’s command; no one may pray or speak with the excommunicated person.” Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga, says in his First Rule (ch. 14): “No one is to speak with the excommunicated person, nor support him by any compassion or pity.” And in his Second Rule (ch. 14): “Without any comfort or conversation with the brothers, he is to lie there, except that the authority of the abbot or provost may command someone to speak with him.”

### “He is to be alone at the work enjoined upon him.”

“Alone,” he says, and indeed imprisoned. For it is clear from Novel 133 of the emperor Justinian that among the other severe punishments of offenders was confinement in prison:

> “If anyone commits an offense, then, if it is a moderate offense, both admonish him and shut him up separately, assigning him a time for penance, so that, having learned a better course, he may return to himself and not lose the labors already expended and exhausted. But if the fall has been greater, according to the measure of the sin let diligence in correction also be applied, and a more vehement admonition and stronger penance be required.”

Saint John Climacus describes the prison of a certain monastery in this way (*Ladder*, step 4):

> “There was a place separated from the monastery by only one stone’s throw, or a mile, called the prison, deprived of every consolation. No smoke from the kitchen was seen there; neither wine nor oil was used for food; nothing was provided except bread and a few small vegetables. Those who, after their religious profession, had fallen into sin, the abbot confined there so that they could never set foot outside. He did not put several together, but kept them separately, or at most two together; and they remained there until the superior was divinely informed concerning each one.”

The same is clear from the Rule of Saint Caesarius for monks (ch. 23): “Whoever has been excommunicated for some fault is to be shut up in a cell and read there with an elder until he is ordered to come for pardon”; from the common monastic Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop (ch. 14): “When someone is excommunicated for a fault, he is to be sent alone into a dark cell, on bread and water only”; from the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* (ch. 19): “But an excommunicated sister, when the faults are more serious, is either shut up in a little cell or separated from the company of the congregation”; from the Council of Aachen (canon 40), in which it is decreed that for those who commit serious offenses in any manner, “a separate house [lacuna] is to be provided, in which a fire may be lit in winter, and a courtyard is to be nearby where they may perform what is enjoined upon them”; from the Statutes of Lanfranc (ch. 17), which prescribe that the culprit of a serious offense, after receiving discipline and laying aside his knife, with his head covered by his hood, is to go to the place appointed for this purpose, preceded by the brother who keeps the key to that place; and from Peter the Venerable, who writes concerning Matthew, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and afterward bishop of Albano (*Book II of the Miracles*, ch. 9):
