> “In the Cluniac manner, he restrained offenders, as seemed just, with bloody beatings, iron, fetters, and chains of various kinds; he confined most of them in a dark prison and crushed the pride of flesh and spirit with intense hunger and thirst. Sometimes, too—he is said to have done this only once, because it was necessary—he restrained one by perpetual burial. He did this when, for a certain man spiritually dead, he prepared an underground pit like a tomb; having shut him inside it, etc.”

Bernard of Cassino writes at the end of this chapter:

> “In some monasteries, a brother who is excommunicated in this manner for more serious faults is confined in some place, and no access is open to anyone wishing to go to him; and they call such a place a prison, appointed for persons excommunicated in this way.”

Boherius writes the same in his first commentary and adds:

> “Among us, however, we do not imprison all who are thus excommunicated, nor release from prison all who are not excommunicated. But when such culprits appear to be incorrigible or fugitive, we sometimes imprison them—either permanently, or for a long, or for a short time.”

[Col. 0513B] Nevertheless, so that those confined would not remain idle in the meantime, some work was assigned to them, as the Council of Aachen, canon 40, decrees; and this is evident from the passage of Saint John Climacus cited above, who adds (*Ladder*, step 4):

> “He placed over them a certain outstanding man named Isaac, who required from those entrusted to him the daily portion of continual prayers and scarcely ever permitted them to cease from their vows. He supplied them with a great quantity of palm leaves, from which they wove baskets to avoid idleness.”

And from the Rule of the Master (ch. 13):

> “From the hour of this excommunication, once he has been placed alone and separated, let some work be assigned to him by his provost on account of his idleness … Whatever he does individually or voluntarily beyond the work assigned is to be scattered or destroyed.”

Thus the monk Hugo of Dervy, because of his flight, was ordered, after being separated from the others, to arrange beautifully the form of the Lord’s cross [lacuna], as recorded in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Bercharius*, no. 22. This is what Saint Benedict means when he says: “Let him be alone at the work enjoined upon him.”

### “Continuing in the sorrow of penance.”

Saint Benedict joins sorrow to penance so that, as Bernard of Cassino says, it may be understood that penance is fruitful when a person washes away his sins with tears and groans.

### “Knowing that terrible sentence of the Apostle, who says that such a man has been delivered to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit may be saved on the day of the Lord.”

Hildemar offers three interpretations of this sentence. The first belongs to those who understand “delivered to Satan” as meaning thrust into prison, because “Satan” is interpreted as “adversary,” and prison is recognized as wholly opposed to the flesh. The second belongs to those who say that the Apostle delivered such a man into the power of the devil, so that the devil would have power to torment him. The third belongs to those who hold that Paul ordered that man to be killed. Of these, only the second seems to accord with the Apostle’s meaning. For “the destruction of the flesh” here signifies not death but affliction and punishment, as Bernard of Cassino teaches.

### “Let him alone receive his portion of food, in the measure or at the hour which the abbot judges suitable for him.”

“Measure” here is to be understood not only as the quantity but also as the quality of the food. For it was customary, in the case of serious offenders and excommunicated persons, not only to subtract something from their ordinary ration but also to give them food inferior to that of the common meal of the brothers, such as bread and water.

Thus Saint Pachomius (article 84) separates from the brothers’ assembly a person easy to anger who does not correct himself after a second admonition, for seven days, with bread and water. Saint Isidore decrees (ch. 17) that “if the suspension of excommunication imposed has lasted two or three days, his evening meal is to consist only of bread and water.” Saint Fructuosus says in his First Rule (ch. 16):

> “For a period of three months, receiving the punishment of excommunication, he is to be shut up alone in a cell under the strictness of penance, sustained from evening to evening by six ounces of barley bread and a small measure of water.”

And in his Second Rule (ch. 14):

> “When someone is excommunicated for a fault, he is to be sent alone into a dark cell on bread and water only, so that in the evening, after the brothers’ supper, he may receive half a *paximatium* [a small loaf or biscuit], and water, but not enough for satiety.”

The Rule of the Master (ch. 13) says:

> “If, perhaps because of the lightness of the fault, the abbot does not wish to double his fasts, while the brothers eat at the sixth hour, he is to be given at the ninth hour, by his provost’s mercy, a single cooked dish, a fragment of ordinary bread, and water.”

The First Council of Tarragona (canon 1) says:

> “But if a religious or monk, shut up in a monastery cell, is occupied with the laments of penance, he is to receive, in solitary affliction and according to the abbot’s arrangement, bread and water as his food.”

From all these passages it follows that the customary food of the excommunicated consisted solely of bread and water: bread alone, I say, and that coarse, ordinary, barley bread; and very little water, given only in the evening.

### “Nor is he to be blessed by anyone passing by.”

Likewise the Rule of the Master (ch. 13):

> “Let everyone pass by without looking at him in silence; to one asking for a blessing, no one is to answer, ‘God [bless you].’”

### “Nor is the food given to him.”

The Master likewise says (in the same place): “Whatever is handed to him is not to be signed by anyone.” And Saint Fructuosus, in the common monastic Rule (ch. 14), says: “He is to receive half a *paximatium* and water, not enough for satiety; and this is to be blown upon by the abbot, not blessed.”

These are the principal punishments that Saint Benedict wished to be inflicted upon offenders. Many other punishments were also in use among monks, such as flogging and expulsion from the monastery, which will be discussed later; shaving the crown, or shaving the head; and spitting in the face, as in chapter 16 of the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop of Braga. Indeed, our Mabillon notes (*Preface to the Fourth Century of the Benedictine Era*, part I, no. 139) that there were certain abbots who, although in their judgment the Rule considered the remedies and punishments for faults sufficient, punished the errors of their monks by putting out their eyes and mutilating their limbs. Therefore Charles the Great, in the capitulary issued for monks in the year 789, chapter 16, ordered “that regular discipline, not secular discipline, be imposed upon monks; that is, they are not to be blinded or suffer other mutilations, except by the authority of the Rule.” And the Council of Frankfurt in 794, chapter 18, says: “We by no means permit abbots, for any fault committed by monks, to blind them or inflict bodily mutilation, unless they are subject to regular discipline.”

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning those who join the excommunicated without the abbot’s command

[Note: In Florentius, the Compendium, and Lyra, “abbatis” is lacking.]

[Note: Others: “join themselves.”]

[Col. 0513] [Col. 0513D] If any brother presumes, without the abbot’s command, to join an excommunicated brother in any way, or to speak with him, or to send him a message [Note: In the Council, “ei” is lacking], let him receive the same punishment of excommunication.

### COMMENTARY

Among the other punishments of the excommunicated that he had described in the preceding chapter, Saint Benedict had said that no one of the brothers should join him in any association or conversation. Therefore, lest anyone, moved by false pity or indiscreet compassion, presume to do the contrary, he wisely added:

### “If any brother presumes, without the abbot’s command, to join an excommunicated brother in any way, or to speak with him, or to send him a message, let him receive the same punishment of excommunication.”

This he took from the ancient discipline of the former monks, among whom, as Cassian says (*Book II*, ch. 16):

> “If anyone has been suspended from prayer for any offense committed, no one at all has permission to pray with him before his reconciliation and pardon for the offense have been publicly granted by the abbot before all the brothers, while he performs his penance prostrate upon the ground. For this reason they separate and segregate themselves from sharing his prayer with such observance, because they believe that he who is suspended from prayer is, according to the Apostle’s sentence, delivered to Satan. And if anyone, moved by inconsiderate pity, presumes to join his prayer before he has been received by the superior, he makes himself a partner in his condemnation—voluntarily delivering himself to Satan, to whom the other had been consigned for the correction of his guilt—and incurs an especially grave crime by mingling with him in conversation or common prayer, thereby providing him with greater fuel for insolence and nourishing the offender’s stubbornness for the worse.”

The Master later established the same rule in chapter 13 of his Rule. The Church likewise maintained this severity toward those who associate with excommunicated persons, as is clear from the Apostolic Canons; from Pope Callixtus’s second letter to the bishops of Gaul; from the Council of Antioch in 341, canon 2; from the Fourth Council of Carthage, canon 74; and from the Lateran Council under Innocent II, canon 3. See Gratian, Part II, question 8.

Hildemar notes that there are five ways in which someone may associate with an excommunicated person:

1. By not knowing that he is excommunicated.
2. By not knowing the law prohibiting association with an excommunicated person.
3. By associating with him in order to provoke him to the satisfaction of humility.
4. By associating with him in order to confirm him in wickedness.
5. By associating with him in order to give him advice about fleeing and provide him with the means to carry out his flight.

Of those who associate in the first and second ways, those who are free from guilt ought also to be free from punishment—except that the master of novices, who failed to teach his disciples the law during their period of probation, should undergo the punishment imposed here on their behalf.

But the person who associated with an excommunicated man in the third way, if he is a priest or could become one, should be judged to have committed a lesser fault. For if he incurred the greater excommunication, he would be rendered incapable of receiving or exercising holy orders. Otherwise, he ought to receive the same punishment of excommunication, but in such a way that he remains excommunicated only for a few days—for example, two or three.

Those who associate in the fourth and fifth ways are to endure the same punishment of excommunication in every respect; that is, they are to be excommunicated for as long as the person with whom they associated was, and ought to be, excommunicated, so that when his bond of excommunication is loosed, the other remains bound.

Thus Hildemar represents the discipline of his own time. Bernard of Cassino and Boherius likewise distinguish three ways in which someone may associate with an excommunicated person:

1. Simply by speaking, drinking, eating, sitting, or working with him.
2. By associating with him through cooperation and counsel.
3. By associating with him through authority or defense.

Those who associate with an excommunicated person in either of the last two ways receive the same punishment of excommunication; but one who associates only in the first way incurs merely a lesser excommunication. Yet in this they speak according to more recent laws. For in the time of Saint Benedict the only recognized excommunication was the greater excommunication; in later centuries the Church relaxed this somewhat, imposing in the stated case only a lesser excommunication. This does not exclude a person from suffrages, from the fellowship of the faithful, or from conferring the sacraments upon another, but only from participation in the sacraments.

Indeed, another moderation was added by the Council of Constance: even the lesser excommunication is not incurred through association with an excommunicated person unless he has been publicly and by name denounced.

Nor should it seem surprising that the Church or the monks imposed such severity upon those associating with excommunicated persons. The right order of discipline required this, both to instill fear of excommunication in others and to cover the excommunicated with shame, thereby provoking them through this confusion to the satisfaction of humility. Otherwise, if they could enjoy the company of others, they would grow increasingly hardened and despise the punishment of excommunication; indeed, they might corrupt others who associated with them. Cassian says (*Book II*, ch. 16):

> “For by providing pernicious comfort, it will make his heart grow harder and harder and will not allow him to be humbled, which was the reason he had been separated; and by this he will either think little of the superior’s rebuke or deceitfully consider satisfaction and pardon.”

Boherius nevertheless notes in his second commentary that this law was not enacted by Saint Benedict as though he wished the person who joined an excommunicated man to incur the punishment of excommunication automatically:

> “Rather,” he says, “the text shows the punishment of which the guilty person is worthy and with which he may deservedly be punished.”

Richard of Saint Angelo says similarly:

> “I do not believe that he incurs this stated punishment of excommunication automatically, since the verb *sortiatur* [‘let him receive’] indicates a future time. Therefore I say that he ought to be excommunicated by the abbot.”

He nevertheless adds:

> “Or you may say that he incurs the punishment automatically, so that what is said here may be feared all the more.”

There are also certain cases in which a person may lawfully associate with an excommunicated man. These are included in the following verse:

> “Utility, law, humility, an unknown matter, necessity.”

Its explanation may be found in the authors who have treated this subject.

## CHAPTER XXVII. How the abbot ought to be concerned for the excommunicated

[Col. 0515D] Let the abbot take the utmost care of delinquent brothers, because “it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill” (Matthew 9) [Note: Narbonne reads *mala* (“evil things”)]. And therefore he ought to employ every means, like a wise physician, sending in, as it were, secret comforters—*sympectas* [Note: Others read *sempetas*, *senpectas*, *sempectas*, *sepectas*, *sinpectas*, and *sempaectas*. More recent editions read *senipetas*. Some older printed editions read *senipectas*.]—that is, wise elder brothers, who may secretly console the wavering brother [Note: The Oxford and Cassinese manuscripts omit “him”] and urge him to the satisfaction of humility. And let them console him [Note: Hildemar omits “and let them console him”], lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow; but, as the same Apostle says, let charity be confirmed in him, and let all pray for him (2 Corinthians 2).

For the abbot ought to be greatly concerned and, with every shrewdness and diligence, take care [Note: Oxford, Florentius, Hildemar, and Boherius read *currere*, “run”] that he lose none of the sheep entrusted to him [Note: Others, “subjected to him”]. For he must know that he has undertaken the care of weak souls, not tyranny over the healthy; and he must fear the prophet’s threat through whom God says [Note: Others, “the Lord”]: “What was fat you took for yourselves, and what was weak you cast away” (Ezekiel 34). Let him also imitate the pious example of the Good Shepherd [Note: Sabinus: “And the Good Shepherd sent a pious example—what?”], who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the mountains, went to seek the one sheep that had gone astray (Luke 19); and he had such compassion for its weakness that he deigned to place it upon his sacred shoulders [Note: Hildemar: “would place it”] and so carry it back to the flock.

### COMMENTARY

### “Let the abbot take the utmost care of delinquent brothers.”

That is, of those excommunicated for an offense, as Richard of Saint Angelo aptly supplies. Let abbots observe with what great care Saint Benedict wishes them to attend to the salvation of an excommunicated brother. He does not simply command them to show care or concern for him, but, as Boherius observes after Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino, to show every possible concern:

> “By himself and through others; by words, examples, admonitions, threats, kindnesses, afflictions, consolations, and spiritual and temporal remissions, lest, if treated too leniently, he have an opportunity to commit similar or worse offenses again, or, if afflicted too cruelly, he happen to despair of mercy.”

So says Bernard of Cassino.

### “Because it is not the healthy who need a physician, but those who are ill.”

Here Saint Benedict shows that abbots and other prelates are superiors not so much for the sake of good monks as for the sake of perverse and imperfect monks—indeed, almost exclusively for such persons—and that their principal burden consists in having been placed over them. Saint Bernard teaches this admirably when writing to Rainald, an abbot excessively anxious about the office of prelate, in these words (*Letter 73*):

> “This is the burden of souls, and of weak ones; for those who are healthy do not need to be carried, and therefore are not a burden. Therefore, whenever you find among your people those who are sad, fainthearted, or murmuring, know that you are their father and their abbot. By consoling, exhorting, and rebuking, you perform your work; you carry your burden, and by carrying it you heal those whom you carry for the purpose of healing. But if someone is so healthy that he helps you more than he is helped by you, recognize yourself as his equal rather than his father, his companion rather than his abbot. Why, then, do you complain that the company of some who are with you burdens you more than it gives you comfort, when you alone of all have been appointed as a comfort to all, as healthier than all and stronger than all, so that by God’s grace you are sufficient to comfort everyone and need strengthening from no one? Finally, to the extent that you are burdened, to that extent you gain; to the extent that you are helped, to that extent you diminish your rewards for yourself, etc.”

### “And therefore he ought to employ every means, like a wise physician.”

Saint Basil makes the same comparison in his *Short Rules*, question 23. A wise physician, says Boherius, is considered to be one

> “who knows how to foresee diseases, who does not drive such a patient into despair because of repeated relapses, and who knows how to administer different medicines according to the diversity of persons and times, because new remedies ought to be prepared for new diseases.”

### “Sending in, as it were, secret comforters, *sympectas*.”

The word *sympecta* is obscure and difficult to explain, and commentators differ in interpreting it. Some, retaining the common reading, understand *senipetas* as “those who seek an old man,” just as Callixtus the pope calls those traveling to Rome *Romipetae*—“seekers of Rome”—in question 24, chapter 3; and demons are called *noctipetae*, “seekers of the night,” in the *Life of Saint Posthumius*. This interpretation seems to be confirmed by Saint Benedict when he adds: “that is, wise elder brothers.”

Yet all the ancient manuscript codices oppose this reading. They read not *senipetas* but *senpectas*, *sempectas*, or *simpectas*. Moreover, the most distinguished commentators on the Rule—Smaragdus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius in both his commentaries—assert that the word is not Latin but Greek. It is therefore clear that the text of the Rule has been corrupted in more recent printed editions, through the ignorance or carelessness of copyists. Not knowing what *sympaecta*, or, as it is read in the manuscripts, *sempecta*, meant, they supposed that the two letters *ni* had been written by the scribes as a single *m*. This could easily be believed from certain manuscripts in which *m* is scarcely distinguishable from *ni*. And since they did not know what *senipectas* meant, they supposed that the letter *c* had been added and read the word as *senipetas*. But *senipeta* is not a Greek word; rather, the word is *sympaecta*.

What Saint Benedict understands by *sympaectas*, “I have not been able to find placed or explained elsewhere,” says Boherius. Nevertheless, the Greek word σύμπαικτης (*sympaiktēs*) is interpreted as “playmate” or “fellow-player.” It is mentioned by Palladius in the *Life of Serapion the Sindonite*:

> “The Fathers relate that, taking a certain monk who was a *sympaectes*—σύμπαικτης ἀσκητής, ‘a fellow-playmate ascetic’—he sold himself in a certain city to pagan actors.”

From this passage Benedict Haeften infers (*Book VIII*, treatise 4, discussion 5) that Saint Benedict intended

> “that some companions and intimates be sent in—men with whom the excommunicated brother had perhaps formerly been accustomed to play and who had shared in his actions—so that, as agreeable friends, they might offer him more effective consolation.”

But this seems to fit poorly with Saint Benedict’s following explanation: “that is, wise elder brothers.” Perhaps, more correctly, one might understand by *sympaectes* an elder brother who would conspire with the abbot to play a trick on the excommunicated man, capture him by a good and salutary deception, and restore him to his proper duty. This is how Paul Augustine of Janua understands it. Moreover, according to Ingulf’s *History*, a quinquagenarian in the order is called a *sempecta*.

### “That is, wise elder brothers.”

This is how Saint Benedict interprets the word, considering the character of the persons rather than the etymology of the word. For, as Menardus says, however this name is read, it cannot signify these three names. Let him therefore send wise elder brothers, so that there may be maturity in the elder, love in the brother, and appropriate caution—or discretion—in the wise man, as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius say.

### “Who may secretly console the wavering brother.”

Julian Paris states in his *Book on the First Way of Life of the Cistercians* (part II, ch. 6, section 3) that it was the custom, when someone was punished for a more serious fault, for the abbot to order everyone to pray for him and designate one or two persons to visit and console him and urge him to the satisfaction of humility.

But the ancient commentators on the Rule—Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius—oppose this custom, which belonged to the Cistercians. They explain “secretly” as meaning that the visitors were not sent by the abbot:

> “As though they spoke to that excommunicated brother not as sent by the abbot, but as having come of their own accord,” says Hildemar.

Bernard of Cassino says:

> “Here ‘secretly’ means that they should not appear to have been specially sent by the abbot, lest, perhaps, presuming too much upon his mercy, he persist in his hardness.”

Boherius says nearly the same in the same words.

Since it is well known, however, that no one may speak with an excommunicated person without the abbot’s permission, lest he presume upon the abbot’s clemency, it will be the task of such *sympaectae* to deceive the unwary man piously and wisely.

Bernard of Cassino says:

> “He may say this: ‘Brother, I have great compassion for you, and I greatly desire the salvation of your soul, and I love you in Christ Jesus. Therefore, out of compassion for you, I obtained from our lord abbot permission to speak with you. But what I am about to say I say on my own, and I ask you that, if you ever speak with the abbot after being reconciled, you not tell him that I said these words to you.’ Then he may begin his consolations and other words suited to winning the soul.”

Hildemar asserts that this duty could be entrusted to the cellarer, if he were prudent, since in his monastery the cellarer was responsible for supplying food to the excommunicated.

### “And let them console him, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow.”

Lest, despairing in this way, he perish forever.

### “But, as the Apostle says, let charity be confirmed in him.”

Bernard of Cassino explains this as meaning that he should be strengthened by charity. Haeften likewise says (*Book VIII*, treatise 4, discussion 5):

> “Let him be confirmed in charity, so that he does not waver concerning the alteration of his condition or fall away from his good purpose and become obstinately rebellious—things that may arise from a lack of consolation.”

But this interpretation assumes that the excommunicated person is already in charity, which would have to be proved.

Hildemar is more correct:

> “‘Let charity be confirmed in him,’ that is, let charity be held and maintained toward him, so that it does not break.”

Or, as Richard of Saint Angelo says, let charity be confirmed in him

> “by loving the brother and not his vices.”

And Boherius, in his second commentary:

> “Let charity be confirmed in him, namely, fraternal charity, so that he may be worthy of the company of others.”

We shall demonstrate that we possess this charity toward him if we carry out what follows.

### “And let all pray for him.”

So that he may be converted to the Lord. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius assert that this prayer is distinct from that which Saint Benedict mentions in the following chapter. Haeften likewise says (*Book VIII*, treatise 4, discussion 5):

> “This is to be understood not of public prayer but of private prayer; or he wishes everyone to intercede with the prelate for the excommunicated person, so that he may be absolved from excommunication.”

Just as elder brothers were sent at times to console the excommunicated person, so they were sometimes sent to rebuke him and test whether his penance was genuine, as is evident from chapter 14 of the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop.

### “For the abbot ought to be greatly concerned for delinquent brothers.”

So that abbots may recognize how highly they ought to value souls redeemed by the precious blood of Christ, he repeats what he said at the beginning of this chapter: “Let the abbot take the utmost care of delinquent brothers.”

### “And with every shrewdness and diligence take care that he lose none of the sheep entrusted to him.”

Consequently, if he fears that someone may flee, he should put him in prison and bind him with chains, fetters, or bonds, as Hildemar infers from this passage.

Bernard of Cassino notes that some manuscripts write not *curare* (“take care”) but *currere* (“run”). Indeed, the English manuscript, Smaragdus of Fleury, Hildemar, and Boherius read it this way, and correctly so. For it is proper to a shepherd to run after the wandering sheep. Yet he ought to “run not with bodily steps but with the steps of the mind and understanding, lest he lose one of his sheep through his negligence, slowness, or laziness,” as Smaragdus says.

### “For he must know that he has undertaken the care of weak souls, not tyranny over the healthy.”

Saint Augustine says the same concerning the prelates of the Church (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, ch. 32):

> “For they preside not more over those who have been healed than over those who must be healed.”

He adds:

> “The vices of the multitude must be endured so that they may be cured, and the pestilence must first be tolerated before it is brought to an end.”

Saint Bernard, describing good prelates, says (*Sermon 25 on the Song of Songs*):

> “Recognizing themselves as physicians, not masters, they immediately prepare not vengeance but healing against the frenzy of the soul.”

### “And let him fear the prophet’s threat, etc.”

These words require no explanation.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning those who, after frequent correction, do not amend

[Note: Others: “do not wish to amend.”]

[Col. 0519C] If any brother, frequently corrected for any fault and even excommunicated, does not amend, let sharper correction be applied to him—that is, let the punishment of blows proceed against him. But if he is not corrected even in this way, or if perhaps—God forbid—he is lifted up in pride [Note: Others: “in his pride”] and wishes also to defend his actions, then let the abbot act as a wise physician.

If he has applied fomentations, if ointments [Note: Hildemar: “or ointments”] of exhortations, if medicines from the divine Scriptures, and finally the cautery of excommunication, or blows [Col. 0520C] with rods [Note: Oxford and Florentius: “or blows of a rod”; Cassinese: “blows with rods”; Council: “blows of a rod”], and has seen that none of his skill is effective, let him also apply—which is greater—his own prayer and that of all the brothers for him, so that the Lord, who can do all things [Note: Oxford and Cassinese: “who is almighty”], may work salvation for the sick brother.

But if he is not healed even in this way, then let the abbot now use the knife of amputation, as the Apostle says: “Remove the evil one from among you” (1 Corinthians 5). And again: “If the unbelieving person departs, let him depart,” lest one diseased sheep contaminate the whole flock (1 Corinthians 7) [Note: Florentius: “infect”; Hildemar: “infect, that is, contaminate”].

### COMMENTARY

### “If any brother is frequently corrected.”

That is, admonished privately twice and rebuked publicly a third time, as Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius explain. According to Nicholas of Fractura, however, “frequently” appears to consist of two occasions.

### “For any fault.”

That is, lesser or greater, as Bernard of Cassino, Richard of Saint Angelo, and Boherius say. For, as Bernard says, a light fault becomes serious through contempt.

### “And even excommunicated.”

With a lesser or greater sentence, says Boherius in his fourth commentary; and the words “for any fault” seem to indicate this.

### “Let sharper correction be applied to him.”

Here the interpreters ask how sharper correction can be applied to an excommunicated person, since excommunication is the greatest of all punishments. We can resolve this difficulty in two ways.

First, by saying that the punishment of blows together with excommunication is a harsher punishment than excommunication alone. This is what Bernard of Cassino intended when he said:

> “Whatever is added is judged harsher—not because it is more dangerous or greater, but because different punishments are feared more than one punishment.”

Second, because “the punishment of blows is harsher and more perceptible to the body,” says Boherius; or, as Richard of Saint Angelo says:

> “You may say that Saint Benedict turned to the conditions of offenders, who suffer more if they are struck externally—that is, in the body—than if they are struck internally, that is, in the soul through excommunication.”

That is, so that punishment by scourging may be inflicted upon him.] We have discussed scourging, or, as it is now called, discipline, in Book II of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 11.

But if he does not amend even in this way, etc., then let the abbot act as a wise physician.] Here Hildemar observes that it is characteristic of a wise and prudent physician not immediately and rashly to change or multiply remedies, but always to use the same ones until they prove useless, and necessity compels him to proceed to others. From this he infers that the abbot, as a wise physician of souls, should not hasten to pass from one degree to another; for example, as soon as he has privately admonished someone, he should not rebuke him publicly, nor, after publicly rebuking him, immediately excommunicate him. Rather, he should wait for some time, in case his patience may lead the offender to repentance.

If he has applied fomentations, if he has applied the ointments of exhortation, etc.] [Col. 0521C] Here he describes, as it were, certain stages by which the spiritual physician should finally proceed to the cutting of the iron, that is, to expulsion from the monastery. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius count six principal stages (see *Consilia Benedictina*, vol. IV of the *Analecta*): namely, 1) a twofold private admonition, 2) public rebuke, 3) excommunication, 4) fasting, 5) punishment by scourging, and 6) prayer. They assert that all of them are designated here.

They say that the first stage is contained in these words: “If he has applied fomentations, if he has applied the ointments of exhortation.” Fomentations are mild medicines, often made with oil; ointments likewise restore fragrance. Thus the terms are used here for private admonitions, which contain nothing harsh, nothing severe, but only what is gentle. “Corrections accompanied by piety and gentleness are rightly called fomentations; exhortations accompanied by the sweetness of mildness are called ointments,” says Smaragdus.

Richard of Saint Angelo, however, understands by “fomentations” the remedy which Saint Benedict prescribes for more serious faults in chapter 25, and by “the ointments of exhortation” the consolations supplied by means of those who provoke the offender to make humble satisfaction; that is, gentleness combined with severity. [Col. 0521D]

If the medicines of the divine Scriptures.] Since these inspire fear, they appropriately signify public rebuke and represent the second stage.

383 If at last the cauterization of excommunication.] Here is the third stage, which the holy Father calls “the cauterization of excommunication,” since it truly burns the soul. “Yet this cauterization cleanses the humble soul from the rust of sin, while it turns the proud soul into the nature of lead,” says Smaragdus.

Saint Bernard discusses these three stages as follows (*Sermon* 44 on the *Song of Songs*):

“The spiritual physician also needs wine of fervent zeal together with the oil of gentleness. This is rightly suited not only to console the fainthearted but also to correct the unruly. For if he sees that the wounded man—that is, the sinner—has not been corrected by the gentle and mild exhortations that have been applied to him, but rather abuses the physician’s gentleness and becomes more negligent through his patience, falling asleep more securely in his sin; when the oil of such pleasant admonitions has been poured out in vain, it will certainly be necessary to use more biting medicines and to pour in the wine of compunction, dealing with him through hard rebukes; and, if the case requires it and his hardness is so great, even to strike the contemptuous man with the staff of ecclesiastical censure.” [Col. 0522A]

They teach that the fourth stage—namely, fasting—is contained in the third stage, and certainly it is usually joined with excommunication. For Saint Benedict commands that the excommunicated receive food at the measure or hour which the abbot judges appropriate for them.

Or blows with rods.] Here is the fifth stage, concerning which we have spoken in Book II of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*.

Let him also employ what is greater: his own prayer and that of all the brothers for him.] As the sixth stage, he prescribes prayer by all the brothers as the most effective remedy of all. For, as Saint Leo says (*Sermon* 3 on the Fast of the Seventh Month):

“The fullest abolition of sins is obtained when the whole Church has one prayer and one confession. For if the Lord promises that everything requested by the devout agreement of two or three saints will be granted, what will be denied to a multitude of many thousands carrying out one observance together and supplicating in harmony through one Spirit?” [Col. 0522B]

You will find nearly the same stages of correction in the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins*, chapter 20. See the *Eastern Rule*, chapter 32 and those that follow.

But if he is not healed even in this way, then let the abbot now use the iron of amputation.] Saint Basil likewise says (*Long Rule*, chapter 28):

“He who is sluggishly disposed toward obeying the commands of God should at first be pitied by everyone as a sick member, and the superior should try whether he can restore him from that sickness by praise. But if he persists in that disobedience and rejects correction, he must be rebuked more severely before all the brothers, and induced by every exhortation to accept healing. If, after much correction, he neither acquires shame nor takes care of himself, then, as the proverb says, being his own destroyer, and as a corrupted and wholly useless member, he must be cut off from the common body with many tears and lamentations, after the example of physicians. For when they find a member corrupted by an incurable disease, they customarily remove it by incisions and cauterizations, lest its sickness spread farther and corrupt everything near it because of its proximity. This is necessarily what we must do with those who, being of a hostile mind, obstruct the commands of the Lord, in accordance with the Lord’s command: ‘If your right eye causes you to stumble, pluck it out and cast it away from you.’” [Col. 0522C]

As the Apostle says, “Remove the evil from among you.”] He confirms by apostolic testimony what he has established here and adapts the Apostle’s words to his purpose: “Remove the evil from among you,” namely, by expelling him from the monastery. For the ancient Fathers of the monastic life had approved the expulsion from the monastery of those who could not be corrected by any means, as is evident from the passage of Saint Basil just cited, from the *Short Rules*, question 44, and from Cassian, Book IV, chapter 16.

The *Eastern Rule* likewise decrees (chapter 35): “If anyone is so hard and so alien to the fear of God that he is not corrected by so many chastisements and so many remissions, let him be cast out of the monastery.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 8): “If they do not allow themselves to be corrected, let them be cast out.”

And again (chapter 14): “But if one who persists in evil continues in it, and refuses of his own will to do penance, and repeatedly remains openly obstinate and a murmurer before the elder or the brothers, and prefers to take revenge with the aid of his relatives, let him be brought before the assembly, stripped of the monastery’s clothing, dressed in the secular garments that he formerly brought with him, and expelled from the monastery with the mark of shame.”

And likewise (chapter 15): “After being scourged, let him again be committed to prison; or, if he refuses to repent, let him be cast out.” [Col. 0523A]

The third Rule attributed to Saint Augustine says (chapter 23): “The convicted man must submit to corrective punishment. If he refuses to bear it, let him be expelled from your fellowship, even if he has not himself departed. For this is not done cruelly but mercifully, lest through a pestilential contagion he destroy many.”

The Emperor Justinian likewise says (*Novella* 133): “If the offense is more atrocious than can be repaired by treatment, then expel him altogether from the monastery.”

Finally, Pope Gregory IV, in his letter to the bishops of Gaul concerning the privileges of the monastery of Fleury (*Miscellanea* of Baluze, vol. II), says: “We also permit that, if the conduct of any one of those brothers is burdensome, he should depart at his own loss rather than pollute the others.”

The practice of this may be seen in the *Life of Saint Sabas*, nos. 41 and 44, vol. III of the *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*; in the *Life of Saint Aigulf, Abbot and Martyr*, no. 13, second century of the Benedictine collection; and elsewhere throughout the works of various authors. Indeed, according to the Sixth Synod, chapter 12, a vicious abbot could be expelled from the monastery.

[Col. 0523B] Two points concerning such expulsion should be observed. First, it was not always perpetual, but sometimes only temporary, as our Menard notes in his commentary on the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 31, section 5. Second, a monk expelled in this way remained under the care of the bishop, as prescribed by the Council of Meaux, canon 59:

“A monk is not to be expelled from a monastery without the counsel and prior knowledge of the bishop or his vicar, once the matter has been regularly brought to this point. By the disposition and authority of the bishop, the subsequent life and conduct of the expelled monk must be ordered and determined, so that he may not be lost forever if he can in any way be saved.” 385

Nowadays, however, a different custom prevails in monasteries: rebellious and incorrigible monks are not expelled but merely imprisoned. Saint Isidore had formerly prescribed this in the following words (chapter 15):

“Although someone may be immersed in the abyss of frequent and most serious vices, he must nevertheless not be expelled from the monastery; rather, he must be restrained according to the nature of his offense, lest one who could perhaps have been corrected through prolonged penitence, when expelled, be devoured by the devil’s mouth.” [Col. 0523C]

The *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* likewise says (chapter 20):

“If she refuses to be corrected even in this way, she is to be segregated from everyone except the custodians within the monastery enclosure under the discipline of penance, and chastised by various corrections for as long as necessary, until her humility becomes evident to everyone with genuine conviction; for salvation is often granted even to the unwilling.” [Col. 0524A]

Saint Gregory, or whoever else wrote the *Books of Kings*, seems to have approved the same principle (Book IV, chapter 9), writing:

“Those who are lukewarm in monasteries should be treated like the sick, not expelled like the dead.”

The new statutes of the Carthusians also support this (Part II, chapter 9, no. 5):

“No one is to be expelled from the order for any crime whatsoever; rather, according to the measure of the crime and offense, he is to be confined in prison either perpetually or for a time.”

Thus, in the eleventh century, Paul, abbot of Saint Alban’s in England, “ordered a foul and strong prison to be prepared for the contumacious,” as Matthew Paris writes in his *Book on the Lives of the Twenty-Three Abbots of Saint Alban’s*.

The same law was established for nuns. When one of them had been expelled from the monastery of Saint Peter at Metz after her veil had been removed, the Synod of Metz in the year 888, canon 9, ordered that she be received again and placed in confinement within the monastery.

Even today, however, incorrigible persons may, with the proper safeguards observed, be expelled from monasteries under the bull of Urban VIII.

And again, if the unbelieving spouse departs, let him depart.] The Apostle says this concerning an unbelieving spouse joined in marriage to a believing spouse; if the unbeliever leaves on account of the faith, he permits the believer to let him depart. Saint Benedict adapts the Apostle’s words to his own purpose: “If the unbelieving spouse departs,” that is, if someone voluntarily leaves the monastery or is expelled against his will, as Hildemar explains, “let him depart.”

So that one diseased sheep may not infect the whole flock.] Or, as the Emperor Justinian says (*Novella* 133):

“So that, when he has turned from better things to worse, he alone may receive the fruit of his wickedness, and may not infect the others with any of his vices, just as flocks afflicted by plague and incurably ill commonly do.” [Col. 0524C]

## CHAPTER XXIX. Whether brothers who leave the monastery should be received again

[Col. 0523]

[Col. 0523C] 386 A brother who leaves the monastery through his own fault, or is expelled from it, if he wishes to return, must first promise complete amendment of the fault for which he left; and then he is to be received in the lowest rank, so that his humility may thereby be proved. If he leaves again, he is to be received in this way up to the third time. After that, he must know that every avenue of return is denied him.

## COMMENTARY

A brother who leaves the monastery through his own fault, or is expelled from it.] Since there is no one so wicked, nor so great a sinner, whom victorious grace cannot finally call back to a better way of life, and since it would be not merely harsh but impious entirely to reject one who truly returns to God, Saint Benedict, having prescribed in the preceding chapter that the incorrigible be expelled from the monastery, immediately teaches whether, how often, and in what manner those who leave or are expelled through their own fault should be received.

To leave through one’s own fault means to Richard of Saint Angelo the same as to leave of one’s own will. Boherius, in his second commentary, understands it as meaning: “Through his own vicious will, because of the spirit of possessiveness perhaps boiling in his heart.” This seems less precise, and the better and more accurate explanation is found in his first commentary:

“Know,” he says, “that he says ‘through his own fault’ in order to exclude the virtuous departure that takes place when a brother, having requested permission though not obtained it, is led by the Spirit of God to enter a stricter religious life; and in order to exclude the transfer from a monastery into the wilderness. Rather, he is speaking of the case in which a brother, through fear of discipline, instability of mind, frivolity, or worldly pleasures, leaves the monastery without permission and returns to the world, concealing himself from the abbot; such a person is called a fugitive.” [Col. 0524C]

Hildemar explains “one’s own fault” differently: it is proper to the fugitive or expelled person in such a way that it is not shared with anyone else:

“‘Proper,’ he says, ‘is the fault in which, when it is committed, no other person is involved, but one person alone carries out the evil.’”

For if he has even one other person sharing knowledge of the fault with him, it is no longer his own fault but a common one. For this reason Bernard of Cassino calls it contagious, concerning which Saint Benedict, following the same Bernard and Hildemar, is silent in this chapter.

Here he distinguishes five causes for which someone may leave a monastery:

1. Some leave because the discipline of regular life has been relaxed in their own monastery, intending to transfer to another of stricter observance.

2. Others seek the wilderness out of a desire for greater perfection or contemplation.

3. Others leave through frivolity and instability or through fear of discipline.

4. Others are expelled because of pride, contumacy, or another fault, or leave through their own rashness.

5. Finally, some are expelled because of a contagious—that is, common—fault, on account of which they are expelled together with another person.

[Col. 0525A] The first and second groups, if they return, should not merely be received but embraced with honor and love, so that others may be edified by their example. The third and fourth are to be received in the manner Saint Benedict describes here.

Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino teach that Saint Benedict is entirely silent about the contagious persons. The same judgment should be applied to them, even though the holy Father does not write it explicitly, as to those who leave or are expelled for the third kind of fault. That is, even after their first departure or expulsion, those who return should not be received; or, if the abbot, moved by mercy, judges that they should be received, he should receive them on the condition that they live in such a place—that is, on a mountain or in locations where they cannot draw others into sin and stain them.

“If they wish to act in this way,” he says, “let them be received for as long as it takes the abbot to know them and trust them without difficulty. Otherwise, if they are unwilling to do this, let them not be received.”

Hildemar nevertheless admits that most of the monasteries of France understood this passage differently. They did not distinguish between a personal and a common fault, but simply received those who had left for any kind of fault up to the third time. Nor did they keep those whom they received after a second or third flight in the penance that they had deserved before their flight.

“Nevertheless,” he adds, “those who act according to the earlier interpretation act better, because those who understand and act in this way are wiser and more discerning. I myself do this in our monastery, and I encourage the others to do the same, just as the wiser men understand and practice it.” [Col. 0525B]

The capital crimes for which a monk deserves to be expelled from the monastery if he does not amend, according to Nicholas of La Fracture, are “sacrilege, homicide, adultery, fornication, false testimony, robbery, theft, pride, avarice, lust; and if anger persists for a long time; and drunkenness, if it is habitual, is also counted among them.”

In their ancient statutes, the Carthusians also make anyone confessed before witnesses or convicted of “unchastity, violent assault, theft, personal property, rebellion, disobedience, the spreading of a charge that one makes against another but cannot prove, conspiratorial leadership, and the frequent sowing of discord” an outsider to the entire order, even if he has been professed.

Let him indeed promise complete amendment of the fault for which he left.] “Complete amendment,” says Bernard of Cassino, “is specifically comprised in two things: that due satisfaction be made and that the fault not be repeated.” Hildemar says the same.

Saint Benedict therefore requires not merely a simple promise that the returning brother will henceforth reform his life, but also a sincere willingness to make satisfaction for the offenses committed before and after his flight or expulsion. Thus, in explaining this passage—“Let him promise complete amendment of the fault for which he left”—Hildemar asserts that it means:

“Let him be received in the very penance that he deserved to undergo when he was expelled or left,” and so forth.

Indeed, he should undergo still greater penance because of the flight and the offenses that ordinarily accompany it. 388

And so let him be received in the lowest rank, so that his humility may thereby be proved.] The Rule of Saint Pachomius likewise says (article 79):

“He who has departed without the brothers’ admonition and afterward comes in repentance shall not be in his rank without the command of the superior.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 20):

“If those apostates have truly been expelled by everyone, and, wandering here and there, unstable and wavering in various places, have been compelled by necessity to ask to return to their monastery, let them be tested in the furnace; and when they have been tested, let them be restored to their monastery. Let them be received not in the first but in the last seat.”

The *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* says (chapter 21):

“Once received in the lowest place among the penitents, let her be examined for as long as necessary, until her life is found to be worthy of approval.”

The Statutes of Guigo say (chapter 77):

“If any inhabitant of this place either flees or is expelled and, led by repentance, returns, promising the amendment of his perverse ways and of the particular fault for which he was expelled or fled, the prior shall consider his case in common counsel and shall act as the number of the brothers, the needs of the house, and his own salvation appear to require. If the decision is made to receive him, he shall be placed in the lowest position as a test of his humility.”

The ancient statutes of the Carthusians say (Part II, chapter 32, no. 26):

“All criminal clerics or laymen, once they have been reconciled, shall always be last among all whom they find, without hope of restoration to their former rank.”

The New Collection of Statutes is somewhat more lenient (Part II, chapter 25, no. 31):

“Once they have been reconciled,” it says, “they shall lose, with respect to rank, the years they spent outside our order; only those years which they spent in the order shall be restored to them. But if they have been reconciled twice, they shall always be last among all whom they find.”

The Institutes of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order say (chapter 64):

“If a fugitive returns within eleven days, he may be restored to the rank that he previously held. But if he returns after eleven days, he may indeed be received, but he shall always remain in the rank in which the last person is received.” [Col. 0526B]

The Institutions of the General Chapter of the same order increase this penalty somewhat. I read the following (Distinction 10, chapter 5):

“All fugitives who are now outside the order or who from now on leave it, unless they return within seven days after their departure, shall always be last among all whom they find; and monks who have left twice shall never be promoted to abbacy. Fugitives who return within seven days shall be last for at least one year.”

Since this passage concerns the reception of fugitives who return voluntarily, it may perhaps be agreeable to readers if I report here the ancient procedure for receiving them in the monastery, which I shall draw both from manuscript books and from printed works.

From the manuscript Customs of the Roman monastery of Saint Paul and of the monastery of Farfa.

[Col. 0526C] 389 When a brother fleeing from the monastery wishes to return, let him come to the chapter naked and barefoot, carrying his cowl in his arms and a rod in his hand. After receiving the judgment [Note: [Col. 0525D] That is, after receiving the discipline of the whip], let him go outside to some place, dress himself, and put on his shoes. Returning to the chapter, let him ask pardon before the abbot; and at the abbot’s command, let him go and sit as the Rule prescribes.

If the abbot is absent, the judgment is to be reserved for him. When the abbot has come, let the brother withdraw from his sight until he reaches a place where he can ask pardon by making satisfaction; and let him do whatever the abbot has commanded him. Let him lie one night in the guesthouse before he is received.

If he fled from some cell and returned there, let him be received as described above; and when he comes to the head of the monastery, let him do the same. If he fled from some cell, did not return there, and came to the head of the monastery, let him be received as noted above until the prior of the cell is summoned and the complaints of both parties are heard. Wherever the fault is found, let it be corrected. After this, if it seems good to the prior, let the brother return to that cell.

From the manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon, chapter 32.

When fugitives from the monastery return, they must make satisfaction in the following manner. If they arrive after chapter, the almoner must receive them until the brothers are in chapter on the following day. Once the brothers have assembled and spoken for a little while about their order, the almoner is sent to bring them.

They, having been stripped and unshod in the auditorium, with the folded cowl in their left hand and a bundle of rods in their right, must come into the middle of the chapter in this manner. They place the cowls on their left and the rods on their right, and humbly ask pardon in the midst of everyone before the lord abbot or prior.

Then, after being told to rise, they sit on the ground, taking up only their cowls and placing them over their knees. [Col. 0527A] If the lord abbot is present, whatever judgment he wishes is given to them. If he is absent, no judgment is given to them, but the person presiding over chapter says to them:

“This judgment belongs to the lord abbot; he must be awaited. Go, put on your clothing, and return.”

Having done this, they ask pardon again and are ordered to go and sit last of all. Thus they are always last in the choir, in chapter, and everywhere else—last of everyone, even the novices—until the lord abbot shows them mercy.

Those who have cast off the habit are received in the same way, except that they do not bring the habit with them into chapter; rather, it is placed before the feet of the person presiding over chapter. After they have made satisfaction naked, as stated above, the presiding officer tells them that, if they wish, they may voluntarily take up the habit which they abandoned of their own will.

When the lord abbot arrives, if they were received in his absence as described, neither group may come into his presence until he himself commands it. They must remain either in the infirmary or in another place until he sends for them. Then they are neither stripped nor unshod, but they prepare their undergarments [*staminea*; sic] so that, if the lord abbot wishes to receive their judgments while naked, they may be found ready.

When they enter chapter, they do not go to their own seats but proceed directly before the lord abbot and do not delay in asking pardon. [Col. 0527B]

Nearly the same provisions are found in the manuscript Customs of Cluny.

From the manuscript *Book of the Uses of Bec*.

When a brother who had left through his own fault or had been expelled from the monastery returns repentant, if the abbot and the community wish to receive him, while he remains outside he shall stay in the almoner’s guesthouse and receive food from the cellarer. If he has no clothing, the chamberlain shall provide it.

When he is to be received, he shall come into chapter naked and barefoot, wearing only his undergarment, carrying the folded cowl over his left arm and rods in his hands. Having received pardon while prostrate, he shall place the rods on one side and the cowl on the other. At the abbot’s command he shall rise, and immediately return to receive discipline, pulling the cowl over his knees.

After the judgment, he shall put on his undergarment and cowl and be led to the place where he is to put on his remaining clothing. Once clothed again, he shall return to chapter to the place where he had previously been and, prostrate with his whole body, receive several pardons, saying after each one, “My fault,” until the abbot says, “It is enough.”

Then he shall receive the sentence for grave fault and leave with his head covered by the hood. A brother shall be assigned to him to lead him to the place designated for this purpose, where he shall remain as long as the abbot judges according to the measure of his fault.

Whenever he is summoned to chapter, he shall say nothing to anyone, nor anyone to him. He shall receive pardon and rise without being ordered to do so; then he shall immediately prepare himself to receive judgment and be led back to his former place.

On the day when he comes to chapter, he shall have all the foods that the community has. If he does not come, he shall have nothing except bread and water, unless the abbot orders otherwise.

At every hour, by night and by day, he shall sit outside the door of the oratory. At the end of the hour he shall lie on the ground, as Saint Benedict commands, with his head covered and face down before the feet of all who leave. He shall do the same at dinner and supper, when the community returns from the refectory, and when, after the verse, it leaves the oratory. When everyone has gone out, he shall return to his place.

He shall not make satisfaction at chapter or at the collation, nor at the entrance or exit, but shall remain in his place until the next hour.

When the abbot releases him from so severe a penance, he shall come to chapter, receive pardon, and ask for judgment. After the abbot has said that he is releasing him from grave fault, the brother shall approach, uncover his head, and fall at the abbot’s feet. Once absolved, he shall sit last in chapter and choir and shall be under the discipline of lesser fault.

He shall not impose an antiphon, sing a responsory, read a lesson, or eat with the brothers. At all canonical hours he shall prostrate himself in the choir before the steps where the blessing is received, beginning when “Kyrie eleison” is begun, and rise when the priest says at the end of the collect, “Through the Lord.”

On feasts with twelve lessons, if the abbot grants permission, he shall not make this satisfaction.

When the lord abbot releases him from lesser fault in chapter, he shall prostrate himself at the abbot’s feet; once again absolved, he shall sit wherever the abbot orders. If he is last among the professed brothers, and among those who have not yet been professed, if there are any, he shall sit as long as the abbot orders.

All of this shall be done for either kind of fault by a brother who, in the monastery or outside it, has committed an act that must be corrected by such penalties.

But if the abbot is so far away from the province that his return cannot presently be awaited, and a brother of this kind returns, the prior may receive him, with the advice of the brothers, in the order described above. For otherwise he must not presume, without the abbot’s knowledge and command, to impose on anyone the penalty of grave or lesser fault. No other person may attempt this in any way, nor may anyone order a brother to be scourged by two men, unless it is the abbot alone, and then only in his presence.

From the Statutes of Lanfranc, chapter 17.

[Col. 0528B]

If the abbot judges that a monk who fled from the monastery and returned should be received into the monastery, he shall be received in the following manner.

He shall first remain for several days in the guesthouse. He shall not approach the cloister, the cloister workshops, or the monastery unless ordered to do so, so that in the meantime he may offer some evidence of his repentance, humility, and patience. No brother shall associate with him, join him in any companionship, or converse with him, unless he is ordered to do so by the abbot, the prior, or the person responsible for maintaining order.

On the day when he is to enter chapter, he shall remove his clothing in the parlor. If he has not abandoned the habit, he shall put on his belt over his undergarment, take the folded cowl on his left arm and rods in his right hand, and, barefoot and naked above the waist, be led into chapter by the brother appointed for this purpose.

Having entered, he shall immediately prostrate himself in the place where this is customarily done. When questioned in the usual manner, he shall state his fault. Then, sitting down, he shall receive corporal discipline at the abbot’s command. After receiving it, wearing only the cowl there, as he came but without carrying the rods, he shall return to the parlor, put on his shoes, and dress according to the Rule. Returning to chapter, he shall remain prostrate until the abbot says to him, “It is enough.”

A satisfaction for grave fault shall be imposed on him, and during that satisfaction he shall conduct himself as described above when grave fault was discussed.

If he returns to the monastery in secular clothing after abandoning the monk’s garments, then, with the other provisions stated above observed, he shall enter chapter wearing the secular clothing in which he returned, belted in the same way as was stated above concerning the undergarment and not carrying the cowl. After receiving discipline, he shall receive the cowl, which the chamberlain places before him, and immediately put it on there.

From the Constitution of Pope Benedict XII, chapter 24.

[Col. 0528D] 392 Those returning to churches, monasteries, or similar places are in no way to be admitted to communion with the other monks or brothers until they have made the required satisfaction. This satisfaction is to be as follows: from the regular gate, the parlor, or another customary place, they shall come through the cloister to chapter with the master of novices or another person assigned to this task, wearing their undergarment or naked, according to the custom of certain churches, monasteries, and religious houses, wearing only breeches and stockings without feet, carrying the cowl, scapular, or floccus on their arms and a rod in their hands. After first receiving pardon there and acknowledging their fault, they shall be publicly scourged before everyone with these implements.

Finally, the abbot or another principal prelate, if present, or the prior, or another person immediately below the abbot or principal prelate, shall impose on them, according to the nature of their offense, the penance or punishment for lesser or grave fault, in accordance with the laudable custom observed by each church, monastery, or place. It must be carefully ensured that the manner of correction does not in any way exceed the measure of the sin. [Col. 0529A]

From the ancient Statutes of the Carthusians, Part II, chapter 31, no. 30.

In the reconciliation of fugitives who are not criminals, the following form is to be observed. When they return, they must first cry out their fault in the presence of the community, asking for mercy and promising amendment. Monks and lay brothers alike, if they return within five days, are immediately reconciled to the order and community; they receive fifteen disciplines in chapter, eat for fifteen days on the ground in the refectory upon a bare board, subject to the exceptions stated above, and are treated as novices. Their own prior, however, with the advice of the community, may restore them to their former rank whenever he judges it appropriate.

[Note: [Col. 0529D] In the New Collection of Statutes, Part II, chapter 25, the provision reads as follows:

“Those who delay returning for more than five days are thereafter, whenever they return, not to be received except into prison. If they are not criminals and have not already fled a second time, their priors, with the advice of the community, may bring them out whenever it seems expedient. Once brought out, they shall receive twenty disciplines in chapter, eat on the ground for twenty days, and undergo the general discipline of the order for one year, unless for some reasonable cause the prior judges that these penalties should be moderated. . . . [Col. 0530D]

Criminal fugitives, however, whether they fled after committing a crime or committed a crime during their flight, are never, whenever they return, to be received except into prison. They may be brought out only by the general chapter or by the Reverend Father. Once brought out, they shall undergo the punishment for criminals described above.”]

But if they delay returning for more than five days, they shall be maintained for at least a week outside the cell and outside the community. Once this period is completed, the prior, with the advice of the community, may fully reconcile them to the community whenever he wishes.

From the first day of their maintenance, these men shall undergo discipline in food for forty days. After they have been joined to the community, they shall be disciplined for twenty days: the monks after vespers, and the lay brothers on weekdays after matins and on feast days after vespers, as was stated concerning criminals. They shall eat on the ground in the refectory for twenty days, like criminals, and undergo the general discipline of the order for one year. They shall have neither an obedience nor a voice in the community, nor may they act against anyone, as was stated above concerning criminals, until permission is granted by the general chapter.

Once they have been reconciled, they shall lose, with respect to rank, the years they spent outside our order; only those years which they spent in the order shall be restored to them. If they have been reconciled twice, they shall always be last among all whom they find. After the third reconciliation, all of them, both clerics and laymen, must know that every avenue of reconciliation is denied them, according to the words of Blessed Benedict.

From the manuscript Statutes of Saint Stephen of Grandmont and of other shepherds who succeeded him, collected by William Pellicier, the first abbot of Grandmont, chapter 11.

Whoever of our order has been outside the order for more than three days shall never again be received into the order except by the general chapter. And novices who have left our order within the year of their probation shall thereafter not be admitted into our order at all except with the consent of the general chapter. Fugitives from the order shall be flogged in chapter for a year, on every Sunday; every Friday they shall receive bread and water; they shall sit on the seat (*solium*) of the refectory at mealtime [variant: *solo*, “on the ground”], in the church at the Hours, and in chapter while chapter is being held; and for a year they shall stand in the lower seats.

From the manuscript Constitution of Pope Clement V for the Order of Grandmont.

[Col. 0529D]

But fugitives from the said order, if they return to that order, shall not be permitted for three years to hold any administration or office in the same order; nor shall the prior or definers be able to dispense them from this rule during the said three years.

From the Constitutions of the Fulien­sians, chapter 29.

[Col. 0530A]

But if they wish to return, they shall be received as follows: confined in prison for as long as the superior of the congregation shall have judged appropriate, they shall fast on bread and water for three days each week and shall be beaten with rods once every week. Once released from prison, they shall be cast down to the lowest place: if clerics, among the clerics; if lay brothers, among the lay brothers; with all hope of restoration to their former place cut off, and at the same time they shall be deprived of the right of suffrage for five years. The superior of the congregation may increase or lessen these penalties according to the circumstances and the person, etc.

From what has been said thus far concerning the manner of receiving expelled or fugitive monks, it is clear: first, that they spent some period beforehand in the almonry or guesthouse before being admitted to the monastery; second, that after admission they received naked the blows of rods in chapter; third, that afterward they endured the penalties of a grave fault and consequently remained either in prison or at least in a cell separated from the common fellowship of the brothers. The practice may be seen in the *Life of Saint Sabas*, who had expelled from the laura a certain James, whom he had expelled as his own murderer because he had cut off his own testicles in order to overcome temptation; nevertheless, afterward “he gave the penitent the order that he should keep quiet and silent in his own cell, should never go out, should receive no one and associate with no one except the one who was to minister to him”; in the book of the *Miracles of Saint Bercharius*, abbot of Dervium, in which, after Hugh, a monk who had escaped from the monastery by flight, had returned, the abbot and the brothers “decided that he should remain in a distant lodging with the necessities for himself, supplying him, as he wished, with everything, even with superfluities—which is grievous to say—and ordering him to arrange, as they knew he could, the form of the Lord’s cross beautifully”; and in Book I of the *Miracles of Saint Bertinus*, chapter 3, where it is related of a certain monk named Benjamin (*Benedictine Century* II) that, after his flight, moved by repentance, he humbly approached the church door every day: “But the Father of the monastery, seeing his humility, understood from the Lord that his heart had been visited, and placed him at the door, providing him with his daily food.” Later, when his sincere repentance and virtue had been proved by a miracle of Saint Bertinus, the brothers “immediately and without delay restored him to his former place.”

Although it appears that, as soon as they returned, they were immediately reclothed in the monastic habit, it was nevertheless denied to some, at least in certain places, as is clear from the aforementioned book of the *Miracles of Saint Bercharius*. There the aforesaid Hugh, a monk of Dervium, eventually seized by illness, “began at once to call back the help of the brothers, so that they might renew him as quickly as possible in the monastic habit.” The ancient statutes of the Carthusians likewise decree (Part II, chapter 31, no. 41) that “the habit should conveniently be taken away from all expelled persons and fugitives, if this can be done; or at least it should be cut short, except in the case of fugitives who receive letters for another order stating that they will not be reclaimed: the cleric, therefore, shall lay aside his cowl, and the layman his hood and beard.” But according to the third compilation of the statutes (chapter 10, no. 6), “apostates are first of all compelled to reassume the habit of the order.” [Col. 0530D] In the synodical canons of Nicephorus the Patriarch it is likewise stated (vol. III of *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*): “A monk who has laid aside his habit and afterward been converted must again put on the monastic garment which he removed, without the prescribed prayers.”

Someone may ask what should be done with the possessions acquired by such men in the world. Justinian defines the matter as belonging to the monastery; but we prefer to offer the example of Peter, abbot of Cava. As the abbot of Venosa writes in his *Life*, no. 24, he received a returning apostate monk with great joy; but he despised everything that the man brought, ordered a huge pit to be made, and burned in the fire everything that had been brought. But enough of this; I return to the text of the Rule.

“But if he should leave again, let him be received as far as the third time; but afterward let him know that every avenue of return is denied him.” The same is found in the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins*, chapter 21. This law binds the fugitive, not the abbot: thus the former cannot demand a fourth reception, although the latter may mercifully grant it. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius in his second commentary, Turrecremata, Theobald Artaldus, Matthias Lambertus, John Craesbeeck, and Nicholas Bravus teach and explain this in that way. To them must be added Peter the Venerable, who, writing to Saint Bernard, treats the same argument fully and elegantly, and finally, after quoting the text of the Rule—“Let him know that every avenue of return is denied him”—concludes as follows (Book I, letter 28):

“Not, he says, ‘it is denied,’ but ‘let him know that it is denied him.’ Since no command is found in this sentence, it is understood that he has not placed an obstacle in the way of mercy, but has attempted to inspire fear in the reckless. Therefore cease speaking in this way, and apply not the Scriptures to your own understanding, but your understanding to the Scriptures; and receive those who truly desire conversion, without any hesitation, even a thousand times. Otherwise you will be found opposed to God and adversaries of the Rule.”

Menardus, however, considers these interpretations too subtle and holds that Saint Benedict’s meaning is simpler: that entrance should be entirely denied to one who has left the monastery a third time and wishes to return. He confirms this from the *Rule of the Master*, which, explaining Saint Benedict’s intention, says:

“If a brother frequently leaves the monastery, let him be received again up to the third time; no more thereafter, because such a man is recognized before the Lord as having the kind of faithfulness in divine service that, among men, has been shown to be instability of foot. And why should one whom God does not possess any longer be needed in the monastery? Therefore, after the third correction, let him justly be treated by the monastery as a pagan and a publican.”

He also confirms it from Peter of Blois, who asserts in letter 88 that Saint Benedict restricted mercy to the number three. Benedict Haeften follows the same opinion, Book VIII, treatise 4, discussion 8. The Carthusians also observe this today, for their statutes read as follows (New Collection of Statutes, Part II, chapter 25, no. 28):

“We decree and declare that criminal apostates, after the third apostasy, are no longer to be sought out and are not to be received into the order.”

The Hermits of Saint Augustine say the same in their Constitutions, Part VI, chapter 14; and the Discalced Carmelites in their Constitutions, Part III, chapter 35, no. 9. Yet the door of mercy is not entirely closed to such a returning person, since, Menardus says, the abbot may, after pardoning the expelled brother three times, show him the offices of charity outside the monastery; and the expelled man may remain under the care of the bishop, who ought to attend to his salvation.

The Cistercians, however, did receive such persons, but not into the habit:

“Fugitives,” say the Institutions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order (Distinction 10, chapter 4), “who according to the Rule are received up to the third time, if they have left more than three times, shall in no way be admitted in the order to the habit of monk or lay brother. An abbot who transgresses this decision shall be on bread and water every Friday until the general chapter, and there he shall ask pardon.”

The ancient Definitions of the same order likewise state (Distinction 11, chapter 3):

“Fugitives who, according to the Rule, are received up to the third time, if they have apostatized more than three times and, repenting, wish to return and make satisfaction for their offense, shall be received without fail either in their own houses or in certain places belonging to them, provided that no other canonical impediment stands in the way—once only for food, and not for the regular habit. They may receive another habit, however, as the abbot shall judge expedient. If they refuse to receive or wear that habit, temporal necessities shall be denied them. But if, after receiving that habit, they again return to the world or commit something for which a monk must be expelled, no one from the order shall be obliged thereafter to provide for them. While they remain in the habit assigned or given to them, they must come to the church at the hours of vigils, outside the choir, and must observe the convent’s fasts. Lay brothers, reduced to the habit of household servants, shall be held to the observances of lay brothers.”

Boherius likewise asserts that they should be received:

“Understand,” he says, “that what is said here about not receiving a fugitive after the third time means not receiving him into the common fellowship of the brothers; he may, however, be received in the workhouse.”

Thus far concerning monks who return of their own accord after fleeing or being expelled. But what of the obstinate, who persevere in sin and do not even contemplate returning? Saint Benedict, the Holy Father, said nothing here about them.
