It therefore appears that he wished the law sanctioned in the preceding chapter to be retained for them: “If the faithless one departs, let him depart.” Certainly, if putrid flesh must be cut away with the knife of amputation, it seems much less appropriate to seek it again.

[Col. 0532B]

Nevertheless, it is clear that from nearly the time of Saint Benedict himself—not to mention earlier times—fugitives were sought out and brought back to their own monastery. Saint Ferreolus says (*Rule*, chapter 20): “It was deemed fitting to recall the fugitive monk who abandoned discipline and was destroying himself, as a despiser.” And Saint Fructuosus (*Rule*, chapter 20): “When anyone has escaped from the monastery through vice, he shall not be received into another cenobium, neither as an act of human kindness nor with the kiss of peace; but immediately, with his hands bound behind his back, he shall be brought back to his own monastery.”

The emperor Justinian likewise decrees (*Novel* 123):

“If any monk leaves his monastery and passes over to secular life, he shall first be stripped of his military service and honor, if he has any, and shall be sent back to the monastery by the bishop of the place and the governor of the province; and whatever possessions he is subsequently shown to have shall belong to the monastery into which he is sent. If he leaves the monastery again, then the governor of the province in which he is found shall detain him and enroll him among the troop subject to him.”

The councils make the same decrees. The Second Council of Orléans states:

“Those monks who have wandered about shall, wherever they are found, be brought back under guard with the assistance of the bishop, like fugitives; and let the abbot know that he will be held guilty who has not restrained such persons with regular correction, or who has received another’s monk.”

The Seventh Council of Toledo states:

“Whoever among the priests or ministers finds wandering monks shall either, if possible, restore them in their own places to their monastery and their superiors, or, if this is difficult, bend them by the force of his authority to be corrected, for the sake of propriety alone.”

The Second Council of Constantinople states:

“If anyone who presides over a monastery does not seek out with great diligence the monks subject to him, or, when he finds them, does not receive them, the synod decrees that he be subjected to separation.”

Balsamon understands this canon to concern fugitives. See the Council of Lambeth of the year 1281, in Spelman. Add also the constitution of Pope Gregory IX for Benedictine monks:

“We decree that those presiding over chapters, according to the statute of the general council, whether abbots or priors, shall diligently seek out every year fugitives and expelled persons from their order. If these can be received in their monastery, the abbots or priors shall, after due admonition, be compelled by ecclesiastical censure to receive them, without prejudice to the discipline of the order. But if the regular order does not permit this, provision shall be made by our authority so that, in the same monastery, they may be supplied with the necessities of life in suitable places, if this can be done without grave scandal; otherwise, they shall be supplied with the necessities of life in other religious houses of the same order, there to perform penance. But if they find such fugitives disobedient, they shall excommunicate them and shall cause them to be publicly denounced to the prelates of the churches as excommunicated until they humbly return at their command.”

Finally, the Constitutions of Richard, bishop of Salisbury, issued in 1217 (*In Spelman, volume II of the English Councils*) state:

“Since certain apostates, forgetful of their salvation, having cast aside the fear of God, do not fear to leave their order without the permission of their superiors and to live in the world as worldly people, having cast aside the habit of religion, we command the archdeacons and also the deans, after suitable admonition, to compel such persons to return to the cloister by ecclesiastical censure. If they cannot by this means be induced to reassume religious life, we order them to be arrested and confined in prison for penance.”

Finally, the synodical canons of Nicephorus the Patriarch, no. 25 (*Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, volume III), state:

“If a monk, having laid aside the holy habit, eats meat and takes a wife, he must be converted; if unwilling, he must be subjected to anathema, and against his will be clothed in monastic garments and confined in a monastery.”

For the ancient practice in this matter, see John the Deacon, Book I of *The Life of Pope Saint Gregory*, chapter 14, and Ardo, *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, no. 24.

CHAPTER XXX. How boys of lesser age are to be corrected.

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533A]

Every age or understanding ought to have its own measures. Therefore, whenever boys, or those in earlier adolescence, or those who cannot understand how great a punishment excommunication is, commit an offense, let such persons either be afflicted with excessive fasts [Note: [Col. 0533A] Florence, together with certain ancient manuscripts: *nimis* (“excessively”).] or be restrained with sharp [Note: [Col. 0533A] Councils, Cassino, Florence, Hildemar, Conches, Compilation: *acris* (“sharp”); [Col. 0534A] Ebrul, Lyra: *acrius* (“more sharply”).] blows, so that they may be healed [Note: [Col. 0534A] Narbonne: *salventur* (“be saved”).].

COMMENTARY

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533B]

“Every age or understanding.” Menardus notes here that age is distinguished from understanding or the capacity to understand. For although the minds of boys are less mature, there are nevertheless some older persons, or those stiff-necked or weak in understanding, whom the rod rather than reason usually governs, and whom the force of excommunication does not affect.

“Each ought to have its own measures.” “That is, the discipline of judgment is not to be applied uniformly to everyone, but according to each person’s age or understanding, and it must be imposed with great moderation. For little ones are to be judged in one way, adolescents and young men in another, old men in another, and those placed in decrepit age in yet another,” says Smaragdus.

“Therefore, whenever boys.” Childhood begins at the seventh year and ends on completion of the fourteenth.

“Or those in earlier adolescence.” Adolescence extends from the fourteenth year to the twenty-eighth. Bernard of Cassino perceptively notes here that the Holy Father Benedict has included two ages: one complete, namely childhood, and the other begun, namely adolescence. He did not simply say “adolescents,” but “those more advanced,” because an age close to childhood departs less from the childish lightness of childhood.

“Or those who cannot understand how great a punishment excommunication is.” “He does not understand,” says Hildemar, “who is not ashamed and does not regard disgrace as excommunication.” Here the Holy Father “includes every age,” as Bernard of Cassino observes, “and he called such persons wicked above, in chapter 23, declaring that they were to be subjected to bodily punishment.”

“Such persons, when they commit an offense.” And the offense requires it.

“Let them be afflicted with excessive fasts.” According to Hildemar, this can be done in two ways: either by taking something away from food and drink while they eat at the same hour as the others, or by postponing until evening or the following day the same meal that the others take. He adds that some understand excessive fasting to mean “only half a pound of bread and one *stauppon* of water in winter, and two in summer; others, however, a quarter of a pound of bread and water as above. But those,” he says, “who prescribe a quarter of a pound of bread do not distinguish correctly.” I think, however, that “excessive” should not be taken strictly as exceeding proper limits in fasting, but broadly, as if he had said “severe fasts,” while nevertheless preserving discretion.

“Or let them be restrained with sharp blows.” Saint Pachomius likewise says (*Art.*, 97):

“All boys who are not afraid to be put to shame for sin and who are not corrected by verbal admonition shall be beaten until they accept discipline and fear.”

Saint Isidore says (chapter 17):

“Those of lesser age are not to be restrained by the sentence of excommunication, but according to the quality of their negligence they are to be corrected with suitable blows, so that those whom the weakness of age does not turn away from that fault may be restrained by the discipline of the scourge.”

The Master says (chapter 14):

“We command that a little child up to fifteen years of age not be excommunicated, but be beaten for his faults.”

Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 6):

“If they are found guilty in anything of what we have said, they shall immediately be corrected with the rod by their own dean.”

But Saint Basil prescribes that boys be punished as follows (*Longer Rules*, chapter 15):

“Has he taken food at an unsuitable time? Let him remain fasting for the greater part of the day. Has he eaten immoderately and disgracefully? Let him be forbidden food at the time of the meal and be compelled to watch the others eating properly, so that he may both be punished by abstinence and learn seriousness. Has he spoken idly? Has he insulted his neighbor? Has he lied? Or has he said something about others that was forbidden? Let him be chastised by fasting and silence.”

“So that they may be healed.” For, as Scripture says, “Folly is bound up in the heart of a child, and the rod of discipline will drive it out” (Proverbs 22).

CHAPTER XXXI. What the monastery’s cellarer should be like [Note: [Col. 0533D] Oxford, Narbonne: “what he ought to be like.”]

[Col. 0533]

[Col. 0533D]

Let a wise man of mature character, sober, not very voracious [Note: [Col. 0534D] Another reading: “not bold.”], not arrogant, not turbulent, not abusive [Note: [Col. 0534D] Another reading: “not quarrelsome.”], not slow, not wasteful, but fearing God, be chosen from the congregation as cellarer of the monastery [Note: [Col. 0533D] Another reading spells it *Cellararius*.]; let him be like a father to the whole congregation. Let him care for everything and do nothing without the abbot’s command. Let him safeguard what is ordered. Let him not distress the brothers. If any brother perhaps asks something unreasonable of him, let him not distress the man by scorning him, but let him refuse the unreasonable request reasonably and with humility [Note: [Col. 0535B] Hildemar omits *cum humilitate* (“with humility”).].

Let him guard his soul, always remembering [Note: [Col. 0535B] Narbonne: *memoret* (“let him remember”); another reading: *memorans* (“remembering”)] the apostolic saying: “He who serves well acquires a good standing for himself” (1 Timothy 4). Let him care with all diligence for the sick, the infants, the guests, and the poor, knowing without doubt that on the day of judgment he will have to render an account for all these persons [Note: [Col. 0535B] Cassino, Narbonne, Florence: *in diem* (“for the day”)]. Let him regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its property as if he were looking upon sacred vessels of the altar. Let him consider nothing negligible; let him neither pursue avarice nor be wasteful or a destroyer [Note: [Col. 0535B] Florence, Hildemar: *et stirpator* (“and a destroyer”); Conches, Compilation, Lyra, and certain others: *aut stirpator* (“or a destroyer”).] of the monastery’s property. Rather, let him do everything in due measure and according to the abbot’s command.

Above all, let him possess humility. To one to whom there is no property to be given, let him offer a good word of reply [Note: [Col. 0535B] Another reading: *et cum substantia* (“and with property”); Hildemar: *tribuatur* (“let it be given”); Paris edition: *dirigatur* (“let it be directed”)], as it is written: “A good word is better than the best gift” (Ecclesiasticus 18). Let him have under his care everything that the abbot has entrusted to him; let him not presume to act in matters from which the abbot has prohibited him. Let him offer the brothers their appointed allowance without any haughtiness [Note: [Col. 0536B] Oxford, Hildemar, Haeften: *sine aliquo typho*; Councils: *sine aliqua typho*; another reading: *sine aliquo verbo* (“without any word”).] or delay, so that they may not be scandalized, remembering the divine saying concerning what he deserves who scandalizes one of the little ones [Note: [Col. 0536B] Cassino adds: “It is better for him that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea.”] (Matthew 18). If the congregation is larger, assistants should be given to him, so that, helped by them, he too may carry out with equanimity the office entrusted to him. At the proper times let what is to be given be given [Note: [Col. 0536B] Another reading: “and let it be given.”], and let what is to be requested be requested, so that no one may be disturbed or distressed in the house of God.

COMMENTARY

[Col. 0535]

[Col. 0535B]

“The monastery’s cellarer.” Thus the Holy Father calls the man to whom he entrusts the care and administration of temporal goods. The name derives from *cella*, or storeroom, in which things necessary for sustaining life are kept and concealed. Some call him the keeper of the storeroom, others the steward, some the provider, and others the procurator. The last term is mentioned in the *Tripartite Book of the Miracles of Saint Robert, Abbot of La Chaise-Dieu*, by Bertrand, distinction 1, no. 3.

[Col. 0535C]

“Let him be chosen.” He does not say, “Let him be appointed at the abbot’s pleasure,” but “let him be chosen,” that is, let the one who has been found better than all the others be appointed. Otherwise there would be acceptance of persons, not election. “For what is election,” says Hildemar, “if not the separation of the best from the better, or the better from the good, or the good from the bad?”

“From the congregation.” Since, as Hildemar says, he should not be chosen from elsewhere. Here “he excludes laymen and those who are ignorant of the customs and practices of religion and of the brothers,” says Bernard of Cassino; and, as Nicholas of Fractura adds, such men “are exceedingly hostile to clerics and religious.” Nothing, however, prevents the occasional use of devout laymen who fear God to carry out the affairs of God’s servants outside the monastery, so that cellarers do not have to go out so frequently and associate with secular people, since this is not altogether beneficial for their souls. See the *Life of Saint John, Abbot of Gorze*, nos. 85 and 86, Benedictine Century V.

Someone may ask by whom, when, and how such a cellarer should be elected. Boherius answers:

“By the abbot together with the convent, since this office concerns important matters.”

So too the Rule of Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 6):

“Let a cellarer of proven patience be chosen, whom the common assembly shall have elected.”

Bernard of Cassino, however, asserts that this election should not be made “according to the order of law, but according to the abbot’s discretion, after some council of elders has been summoned.” Nicholas of Fractura, Turrecremata, Matthias Lambert, and John Craesbeeck likewise say that the abbot should choose him with the mature judgment and at least the counsel of the elders. The Cassinese observe this practice, explaining “let him be chosen” as follows (Cassinese Declaration, chapter 31):

“He is to be proposed by the superior, with the counsel of the elders; he should be a dean and altogether serious in character.”

But the Constitutions of Monte Oliveto prescribe (Part II, chapter 31) that the cellarers of the monasteries be chosen at the *banchetto* by secret votes, with the consent of the greater part of the community. The general abbot shall nominate two suitable men for each monastery for this office, and the one who has received more votes shall be considered elected.

In former times this election was celebrated annually among our people, as Mabillon teaches us in these words (*Preface to Benedictine Century IV*, Part I, no. 126):

“It is an ancient custom, customary in our order, that this office—which the ancients called an obedience—be assigned for one year.”

An anonymous writer confirms this opinion in the *Life of Saint Salaberga* (Benedictine Century II):

“And to the handmaid of Christ, in that same year, the lot of obedience fell, according to the tenor of the Rule, to guard the storeroom and minister to the sisters.”

The same may be gathered from the *Life of Saint John of Gorze*, no. 73. Hildemar, however, maintains that deans and cellarers should continue in office for several years:

“The cellarer,” he says (on chapter 32), “and the dean are not said to succeed one another by turns, but each should remain in his deanery or in his storeroom until a better man cannot be found; even if for ten years he cannot find a better man, he alone should perform that ministry.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius likewise teach that cellarers, deans, and provosts do not succeed one another by turns. But according to the Constitutions of the Congregation of Monte Oliveto, a cellarer “shall serve for four years only; when these have elapsed, he may not exercise the same office in the same monastery for another four years.” We shall speak of the other obediences in the following chapter.

The manner of election was altogether solemn. The cellarer was released from office and blessed with the same blessing by which the prior was ordained, as is clear from Udalricus, Book III, chapter 18, and from the manuscript *Customary of Saint Benignus*, chapter 38.

402 “Wise.” So that the house of God may be wisely administered by wise men. According to Bernard of Cassino, “wise” implies prudence, knowledge, and understanding. He should not merely be wise in arranging human affairs, but above all a philosopher—that is, a lover of wisdom—in divine matters. Hildemar explains what it means to be a philosopher in divine matters as follows:

“Heavenly philosophy is to distinguish between vices and virtues; then to love virtues and hate vices; and thereafter to strive to exercise in works the virtues he has recognized. For it is of no value to know and recognize the good without loving it, or to love it without practicing it. Such a person knows the good and performs it without loving it, just as one who carries bread and wine but neither eats nor drinks from them.”

Richard of Saint Angelo nevertheless says:

“I do not think that knowledge of the divine Scriptures is required in this man, but only natural knowledge, so that he may be mature in character and sober, as follows here.”

“Of mature character.” “In character,” he says, “not in age,” because, as Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura note here, since the cellarer must frequently hurry through the monastery and inspect each of its workshops, he would have difficulty fulfilling the office entrusted to him if he were heavily burdened by age. According to the Constitutions of Monte Oliveto (Part II, chapter 31), he must be “at least twenty-eight years old and professed in religion for ten years.”

“Sober.” Smaragdus understands sober as “cautious or considerate, frugal and sparing in food and drink, temperate in word and deed”; Boherius understands it as “temperate in food and in other matters”; Menardus as “not intoxicated.” Hildemar understands it differently:

“He is called sober who is temperate—that is, who does neither more nor less than he ought.”

Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura interpret Saint Benedict in the same way. Indeed, it is clear from the words that follow—“not very voracious”—that the Holy Father does not here mean merely frugality in food and drink. Let the cellarer therefore be wise, mature in character, and sober, “so that by wisdom he may arrange everything, by maturity of character avoid undue levity, and by sobriety govern himself in actions and words,” says Bernard of Cassino.

“Not very voracious.” The ancient monks particularly wished this vice to be avoided in a cellarer. Thus the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius says (chapter 12):

“The abbot must determine what sort of man should hold the brothers’ storeroom. Only one should be chosen who can master all the suggestions of his appetite and provide food for his brothers according to the evangelical order.”

And the *Rule of the Master* says (chapter 16):

“The cellarer is to be appointed from among the brothers who has been proved by the abbot to be faithful and abstinent, whom the appetite of any desire has never conquered, and who does not greatly love eating or drinking.”

He should avoid this especially when he eats outside the monastery with secular people. On this matter, see the example of John of Gorze.

403 “Not arrogant.” “Arrogant is one who is raised up in pride, bold, boastful, and presumptuous,” says Smaragdus. Hildemar nevertheless distinguishes pride from exaltation in this way: exaltation occurs in spiritual matters, whereas pride occurs in spiritual and temporal matters alike.

“Not turbulent.” According to Hildemar, turbulent “means obscure, insincere, not cheerful, furious, just as the air is called turbulent when it is not calm—that is, bright—or water is called turbulent when it is not clear and bright. So a man is called turbulent when his face is obscure, that is, neither cheerful nor pleasant.” Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Turrecremata explain it in nearly the same way.

“Not abusive.” Ready to inflict injuries and insults.

“Not slow.” “In obeying the superior’s command, that is, and also in distributing the appointed allowance to the brothers,” says Boherius.

“Not wasteful.” That is, not excessively generous or lavish, consuming and squandering the monastery’s goods, lest the ruin of the whole monastery arise from his extravagance. He should conduct himself so that the monastery’s annual expenses do not exceed its income; indeed, he should not spend all of it, so that something may always remain to be distributed to the poor and so that unexpected circumstances may be met in due season.

“But fearing God.” This is, as it were, the conclusion of what has preceded, to which all those qualities must be referred. For whoever fears God will easily observe all the foregoing things.

[Col. 0538A]

“Let him be like a father to the whole congregation.” So that he may administer everything with charity, love all the brothers as sons, and supply them abundantly with what they need, neglecting no one and scorning no one. And because it is a father’s role to undertake care for everything that concerns his household, the Rule appropriately adds:

“Let him care for everything and do nothing without the abbot’s command.” These two instructions may seem to conflict with each other, since a man cannot care for everything if he is permitted to do nothing without the abbot’s command. They can nevertheless easily be reconciled by what follows.

“Let him safeguard what is ordered.” “This is the same,” says Smaragdus, “as if he had said: ‘I have said above that he is to care for everything; let him care for those things that he has been ordered to safeguard, but let him do nothing concerning the remaining matters without the abbot’s command.’” Boherius reasons in the same way in his second commentary.

What are the matters whose care the abbot ought to entrust to the cellarer may be gathered from the Rule of Saint Isidore, in which the following is written (chapter 19):

“To the man placed over the storeroom belongs responsibility for the things in the supply room. He shall provide the weekly servers with whatever is necessary for the food of the monks, guests, and sick. In his presence the things to be brought to the tables shall be distributed. He shall also reserve whatever remains from the expenditure for the use of the poor. At the end of the week, the weekly server shall display to him the vessels entrusted to him, so that it may be inspected whether they have been negligently handled; and they shall again be handed over to the succeeding weekly server in his presence. The granaries also belong to him, as do the flocks of sheep and cattle, wool and linen, and aviaries; he is responsible for administering food to the bakers, beasts of burden, oxen, and birds; and for the provision of shoes, and the care of shepherds and fishermen.”

The Eastern Rule likewise decrees (chapter 25) that the cellarer

“shall guard all the utensils that are in the monastery—that is, clothing, vessels, tools, and whatever is necessary for daily use—and, bringing out each item when it is needed, shall receive it back from the person to whom he entrusted it for use, in order to put it away again. For the food of the brothers he shall bring out and hand things over to the weekly servers; for seasoning the food he shall provide what is necessary according to the custom of daily expenditure, neither lavishly nor stingily, lest through his fault the monastery’s property be burdened and the brothers suffer injury. Considering also the needs and labor of sick brothers, he shall deny the sick nothing that he possesses, insofar as they require it. For visiting brothers he shall prepare food. This shall be the care of the keeper of the storeroom: always having recourse to the counsel of the elders, making inquiries about everything, and especially about those matters that he could not accomplish by his own understanding.”

These final words illuminate this passage of the Holy Rule: in doubtful matters, when he cannot act by his own understanding—or, as Lanfranc puts it (*Statutes*, chapter 9), in matters of greater importance—he should do nothing without the abbot’s command. It will also be most useful, as Bernard of Cassino says, for the abbot to give him a written document setting out distinctly the matters whose care he entrusts to him; or, as Hildemar puts it, the matters he is to oversee:

“The abbot ought to assign them to him in this manner, for example: ‘Under your care shall be the infants, guests, sick, and poor; also the servants assigned to the use of the garden or kitchen, the phlebotomist, and the general body of the monks.’ Then he ought to assign to him the care of guests in this manner, for example: ‘If bishops, abbots, or counts come, strive to serve them in this way; but if clerics or canons come, offer them service in this way. If monks should come, receive them in this way.’ Finally, he ought to say to him: ‘If you encounter uncertainty in these matters, ask me,’ and so forth.”

He adds that if the cellarer is such as Saint Benedict describes him here, the abbot may entrust everything to his discretion.

So that the abbot may ascertain whether the cellarer faithfully keeps what is entrusted to him, he must at specified [Col. 0539A] times require from him an account of what has been done and of the substance administered. Saint Fructuosus prescribes that this be done every month:

> “Whatever has been expended during each month, the provost, who had received the monastery’s substance for distribution, must render an account to his abbot at the beginning of every month, and do so with trembling, simplicity, and true humility of heart, as one who will have to render an account to the Lord.”

The Constitutions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order likewise state (Chapter 78):

> “The senior cellarer shall render an account once a month—or more often, if the abbot wishes—of everything he receives, to the abbot or to those whom he appoints.”

Their Institutions, however, determine only generally, 405 that:

> “The senior cellarer shall, whenever the abbot wishes, render an account to the abbot or to those whom he appoints of everything he receives and expends.”

The Cassinese monks, for their part, require each cellarer to present to the prelate and superiors four times a year—that is, every three months—the monastery’s accounts, reckonings, debts, and credits; all of them are to sign with their own hands. [Col. 0539B] This is in accordance with the constitution of Pope Gregory IX, in which I read:

> “So that the condition of the houses may be known with greater certainty, every three months, before the abbot or, if there is no abbot there, the prior and the seniors, the officials shall render a reasonable account of all expenditures pertaining to their offices. The abbots and priors, acting faithfully, shall twice a year—that is, on the Kalends of October, after the annual fruits have been gathered, and on the Kalends of April—fully disclose the condition of their house in chapter, or before the seniors, and also before the visitors when they come. But any abbot, prior, or provost who fraudulently conceals serious debts in the aforesaid accounts shall be entirely removed from the administration he holds.”

According to a constitution of Pope Benedict XII, chapter 3, abbots, priors, or administrators must render an account each year in the general chapter, while cellarers and other officials must do so three times a year before the abbot and the convent. Something similar is found in the Statutes of the Black Monks, issued at London in 1238. See the Constitutions of Ottobono, the legate in England, [Col. 0539C] in Spelmann, under the year 1248. I return to the text of the Rule.

**“Let him not sadden the brothers.”** Hildemar explains this as follows:

> “He must not give anyone a harsh answer, but must offer them good speech in everything.”

Or, as Bernard says:

> “Let him do or say nothing by which they could reasonably be saddened,”

for example, “by refusing what he ought to give, or by giving it later than he ought,” as Boherius puts it.

**“But if some brother should perhaps ask something of him unreasonably, let him not sadden him by despising him,” etc.****—**Thus Saint Benedict of Aniane, who was cellarer in the monastery of Saint-Seine and later its abbot, strove, “in accordance with the precept of the Rule, to compose himself with all his strength, to grant without delay what was lawfully requested, to refuse gently what was wrongly requested, and to excuse graciously those asking for impossible things” (*Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, no. 9, fourth century).

Before him, Saint Leobinus, after becoming cellarer (first century of the Benedictine era), “made himself so provident that he neither gave anything excessive to one who asked for more than was due, nor withheld suitable nourishment from one in need.” [Col. 0539D]

What ought to be observed both in asking and in distributing is taught by the following verses from Boherius’s first commentary:

> In the one who asks, mark nine things; in the giver, six:
>
> The cause, faith, manner, place, and want, the time,
>
> The age, nobility, together with the petitioner’s condition,
>
> A cheerful mind, a ready hand, and the means to give,
>
> A gracious manner of speech, the giver’s discretion, and order.

**“Let him guard his own soul.”** Smaragdus explains these words as follows:

> “Let him not offend in giving what ought not to be given, or in replying to what ought not to be answered.”

Bernard of Cassino appears to agree in these words:

> “This pertains especially to faithfulness, namely, that he be a faithful keeper and giver; otherwise he would guard his soul badly.”

He adds:

> “Moreover, he guards his soul well when he himself does not sin in the office entrusted to him, nor permit others to sin. This statement can be extended broadly to everything that must be avoided as contrary to God and to everything that must be done with God.”

Accordingly, the Cassinese monks say in their declarations concerning these words:

> “Let cellarers not so immerse themselves in temporal affairs that they have no time for spiritual matters; rather, let them pass through temporal goods in such a way that they do not lose eternal ones.”

The Bursfeld monks likewise state (Distinct. 2, chapter 5):

> “Although the cellarer, following the example of Martha, whose office he has assumed, must necessarily be anxious and troubled about many things, he must not completely withdraw from the conventual observances, nor entirely abandon or shun the silence and quiet of his cell. Rather, as opportunity permits, once the necessary tasks for the service of God and the convent have been completed, let him return to his cell as to a most peaceful and secure harbor, so that by reading, praying, and meditating he may calm the turbulent movements of his soul arising from the management and arrangement of external affairs, and may be refreshed by spiritual consolations.”

Similarly, the Constitutions of the Feuillants state (Chapter 31): [Col. 0540B]

> “Let the cellarer not allow himself to be so overwhelmed by care for temporal things that he grows weak in spiritual matters, since temporal affairs ought to serve spiritual ones as handmaids. Therefore, let him take care to be absent as rarely as possible from choir and the divine office, from meditation and the other regular exercises, provided that these do not hinder his office.”

For the same reason, the Rule of the Master prescribes (Chapter 16) that:

> “Every day the cellarer, together with the weekly servers, shall receive communion before the abbot in the oratory with the congregation,”

lest, under the pretext of conducting business, he abstain from receiving the heavenly bread. He needs it all the more, so that, strengthened by that food, he may travel happily through the trackless and waterless regions of temporal affairs, and so that his heart may not waste away within him if he forgets to eat his bread.

**“Mindful of the apostolic saying, ‘For the one who has served well acquires for himself a good standing.’”** The Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius likewise says:

> “The one appointed to this office must strive to hear that the one who has served well acquires for himself a good standing and gains profit for his soul.” [Col. 0540C]

**“Let him care diligently for the sick, the children, the guests, and the poor.”** Saint Benedict here chiefly entrusts four objects to the cellarer’s care and solicitude.

First, the sick, whose care he wished to be undertaken before and above all else, so that they might be served as Christ truly is served. He also orders the abbot to ensure that they are not neglected by the cellarers or servants.

With the same intention, the Eastern Rule prescribes (Chapter 25) that the cellarer “refuse the sick nothing of what he possesses, insofar as necessity requires.”

The ancient customs of the monastery of Cluny, as recorded by Udalricus (Book III, chapter 18), state:

> “If any brother is so ill that he cannot rise from bed, the cellarer comes to him every day at first light, together with the infirmarian, and asks him about everything that he can have and what he thinks should be prepared for his refreshment.”

And again (Book III, chapter 11):

> “If someone gives us ten solidi, or fewer, these are always assigned to the cellarer for the sole purpose that he may show some charity to the weaker or somewhat delicate brothers, beyond what is generally given to everyone.”

It is astonishing how diligently Blessed Raingardis, formerly a nun and cellarer in the monastery of Marcigny, observed this part of the Rule. Her venerable son, Peter, abbot of Cluny, writes of her (Book II, Letter 17):

> “She had written in her mind what bodily ailment each one suffered from, and had carefully recorded their illnesses and their character [i.e. condition], so that she could assist each one without error, since nothing of this kind escaped her knowledge. She knew them as noble and delicate, as fragile and weak, and understood that, according to their sex, their place, and their customary way of life, they required many things. Therefore she troubled her mind with great anxiety lest anything should be lacking to them.
>
> “The care of servile duties occupied her, and she rejoiced to be the handmaid of God’s handmaids, attending to every humble service. In her heart she varied the preparation of different foods, and, inexperienced in such matters, was compelled to learn the discipline of the kitchen. For one she provided roasted food, for another boiled; salted food for this one, unsalted for another. Concerned with her frequent service, she herself prepared, cooked, and carried in the food. And so that none of her reward might be lost, she allowed nothing to be diminished from her labor. She had gathered the dispositions of each woman into her own heart, and, recognizing what each most desired, she made the effect of her work correspond to the desires of all.” [Col. 0541A]

Second, the children, “so that, considering the frailty of their age and the tenderness of their bodies, he may provide what is necessary with paternal affection,” as Smaragdus says.

Third, the guests, for whom he is to prepare food when they arrive, according to chapter 25 of the Eastern Rule. Or, as Saint Isidore prescribes (Chapter 19):

> “He himself shall provide the weekly servers with whatever is necessary for the nourishment of the monk-guests and the sick.”

Hildemar also observes that among the ancient monks it had been customary for the cellarer to care for guests; but later, because of their excessive number, others were appointed to this office. What the Rule of Saint Benedict enjoins upon the cellarer concerning the care of guests, he says, is to be understood as referring to guests when they are said to be going to eat in the refectory. The Statutes of Saint Adelard, Book II, chapter 3, seem to confirm his view.

Fourth, the poor, for whom he is to reserve whatever remains, according to the Rule of Saint Isidore. Likewise, according to the Rule of the Master (Chapter 19):

> “The cellarer shall give alms when commanded by the abbot and in his presence. In the abbot’s absence, however, he may give alms to a poor person who asks, because of the Lord’s command, which says: ‘Give to everyone who asks you’; and again: ‘Give, lest the one to whom you do not give should himself be Christ.’”

Blessed Raingardis showed truly admirable solicitude for both guests and poor people (Peter the Venerable, Book II, Letter 17):

> “She received the former honorably and provided for the latter diligently, so that neither what was appropriate for those guests nor what was necessary for these poor was lacking. Yet her care was more ardent toward the poor, whose need weighed more heavily in the heart of the holy woman, so that those whom greater want oppressed received greater diligence from her than the others.
>
> “For this reason, if anything could remain from the obedience entrusted to her, she devotedly spent it for their use. Frequent alms were distributed; clothing was prepared as far as possible, either newly purchased or old garments secretly taken from the sisters and given to the poor. To all who asked according to the Gospel she gave, without question, whatever food or clothing she could gather from every source. Some she playfully called her children and refreshed with daily food and expenses.
>
> “Her mind, devoted to God, rested in them and, as though released from the ancient labors of the world, at last believed that she had found a place for the Lord, a tabernacle for the God of Jacob. Whatever she scattered among the poor, she rejoiced to see gathered entirely for herself, knowing that what others considered a loss of property was her own true gain.” [Col. 0541D]

This is plainly an outstanding example of the holy woman’s charity toward the poor—one that cellarers would do well to imitate.

**“Let him regard all the vessels of the monastery and all its substance as though they were sacred vessels of the altar.”** The ancient commentators on the Rule—Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius—teach that these words are not to be understood according to an absolute likeness, but relatively: such things are to be treated according to their value, just as sacred vessels are treated according to their dignity.

Yet, in my judgment, this does not properly accord with the mind of Saint Benedict and the ancient monks, who regarded the monastery’s possessions not as indifferent things but as sanctified and truly consecrated to God. This is evident from the Rule of the Holy Fathers Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius:

> “The brothers must also know that whatever is handled in the monastery—whether vessels, tools, or anything else—is sanctified. If one of the brothers handles anything carelessly, let him know that he shares in the guilt of that king who drank with his concubines from the sanctified vessels of the house of God, and what punishment he deserved.”

Saint Basil likewise, answering the question (Shorter Rules, question 143), “How should those who perform work care for the tools entrusted to them?” replies:

> “As things dedicated and consecrated to God.”

And, answering the question (ibid., question 144), “What if someone loses something through carelessness or abuses it through contempt?” he replies:

> “The one who abuses it must be judged as a sacrilegious person; the one who loses it must be judged as the author of sacrilege, since everything has been dedicated to the Lord and consecrated to God.”

The same was entirely the mind of the other Egyptian monks who, as Cassian reports (Book IV, chapter 20),

> “believe not only that they themselves do not belong to themselves, but also that everything they possess is consecrated to the Lord. Therefore, if anything has once been brought into the monastery, they decree that it must be treated with every reverence as something most holy.”

Likewise, they received and guarded kitchen utensils and vessels “with such solicitude and care, lest anything be diminished or perish, that they believed they would have to render an account for the smallest vessels—not only to the present steward, but also to the Lord—if anything were diminished through their negligence.” [Col. 0542B]

All this is confirmed by the Council of Orléans, canon 7 (in Burchard, Book III, chapter 129):

> “Everything offered to God is held to be consecrated: vineyards, lands, forests, utensils, garments, animals, and other possessions; and whatever is offered to churches is undoubtedly offered to Christ, who is their bridegroom.”

From this doctrine, what follows may rightly be inferred.

**“Let him consider nothing negligible.”** That is, let him not regard anything among the vessels and substance of the monastery as small or without importance.

It is scarcely possible to imagine how religiously the ancient monks treated the smallest things. One example reported by Cassian will astonish anyone. He relates (Book IV, chapter 20) that when a brother assigned to kitchen service allowed three lentils to fall to the ground, he was reported to the abbot by the steward and “judged to be a squanderer and negligent guardian of sacred property, and was suspended from prayer.” [Col. 0542C]

No less striking is what Ardo, the disciple of Benedict of Aniane, writes about that abbot (in his *Life*, no. 32, fourth century of the Benedictine era):

> “His solicitude was so great that if even a few grains of vegetables, or a small strand of leek, or leaves of cabbages were found to have been neglected by him, a sentence worthy of excommunication was immediately pronounced, and he was judged to be guilty. But if someone brought him water for washing and, as often happens, poured out more than was proper, he admitted that he had incurred sin because he had not followed the path of discretion.”

We read something similar about Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, in his *Life*, Book II, no. 53 (Volume IV of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*):

> “If, while walking through the portico or in any other place, he saw vegetables or legumes that had fallen through carelessness and been scattered on the ground, he immediately bent down and gathered them grain by grain, however few they might be. Then, summoning those through whose fault they had fallen, he rebuked them severely for their negligence.”

[Col. 0542D] **“Nor let him be devoted to greed.”** This applies to the decree of the Council of Frankfurt under Charlemagne (canon 4):

> “Let avaricious men not be chosen as cellarers in monasteries, but let such men be chosen as the Rule of Saint Benedict teaches.”

It may also be applied to what the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius prescribes:

> “The cellarer must be chosen as one who can master all the suggestions of his appetite and govern food for his brothers according to the evangelical order; one who fears the sentence pronounced against Judas, who from the beginning was a thief.”

**“Nor let him be extravagant or a squanderer of the monastery’s substance.”** That is, by giving what he ought not to give.

**“But let him do everything in due measure.”** Let him walk the middle path between greed and extravagance, as the Eastern Rule also prescribes (Chapter 25):

> “For the brothers’ food, let him bring forth and hand over to the weekly servers what is needed for seasoning the dishes. Let him give what is necessary according to the custom of daily expenditure, neither lavishly nor greedily, lest through his fault either the monastery’s substance be burdened or the brothers suffer injury.” [Col. 0543A]

The Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins states (Chapter 4):

> “Let her entirely flee the plague of greed and covetousness. Just as she must not be greedy, so also let her not be extravagant—that is, just as she must not conceal and withhold under the vice of greed what she ought to distribute as a gift of almighty God, so also she must not, without proper administration, squander the common substance by lending too freely. Rather, let her temper everything through discretion.”

Finally, Peter Damian says (Opusculum 13, chapter 19):

> “The cellarer must perform the office entrusted to him with such skill in administration that, by opening his hand, he also restrains it, and by restraining it, he opens it prudently, so that in him generosity is frugal and frugality generous. Great care must be taken lest stinginess disguise itself as smallness and extravagance as generosity; for vice often conceals itself under the appearance of virtue. The more what is evil appears to be good, the more difficult it is corrected.
>
> “A good administrator distributes what is necessary for the body in such a way that he also promotes the salvation of souls, because by sparing he nourishes sobriety, and by giving he prevents the vice of murmuring from arising.” [Col. 0543B]

**“Above all, let him have humility.”** To provide an example of this to everyone, it was an ancient custom of our order that whenever this chapter of the Rule was read in chapter, the cellarer would prostrate himself before all and ask forgiveness for every excess committed in the obedience entrusted to him.

Lanfrancus says (in the *Statutes*, chapter 9):

> “When the aforesaid sentence has been read and explained in chapter, and the prior has said, ‘Let us speak of our order,’ he shall immediately prostrate himself in the customary place and say:
>
> “‘I handle this obedience that has been enjoined upon me negligently and lukewarmly through my fault, and in many ways otherwise than I ought; and in it I offend God and our seniors in many things, through my fault. For this I ask your absolution and that of the seniors.’
>
> “When he has said this, the one presiding over the chapter shall absolve him from the offenses he has enumerated there and from all the rest that are included in it. At the end of the absolution, after all have responded ‘Amen’ with the full devotion customary, he shall go to his feet and shall then be ordered to sit, and so forth.” [Col. 0543C]

The Cluniacs did the same in the following chapter, as Udalricus shows:

> “In the next chapter he again asks forgiveness and confesses himself guilty of many negligences arising from the occasion of his obedience. The prior absolves him and orders the fiftieth psalm, with the collect, to be sung for him by everyone together at Saint Mary’s.”

The manuscript Customs of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon speak in nearly the same way (chapter 38).

**“And if he has no substance to give, let him offer a good word in response.”** The Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins, chapter 4, and Saint Dorotheus, *Teaching* 4, no. 46, prescribe the same, and rightly so:

> “For proud and evil speech turns even good men toward evil, whereas humble and good speech changes even evil men for the better,”

as Abbot Macarius said (in Rufinus, Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 127).

The cellarer must therefore be gentle and mild, so that everyone may have free access to him. Many, especially the younger brothers, are timid and would scarcely dare approach a surly and irritable man; consequently, they would be forced to endure great want of necessary things.

Blessed Raingardis offered an outstanding example of this gentleness (Peter the Venerable, Book II, Letter 17):

> “Often, when the poverty of her resources did not answer to the riches of her charity, she was saddened and grieved; and because she could not satisfy everyone according to her desire, she was tormented by great anguish. Yet when much was demanded from one who had nothing, she preserved patience in her heart according to the Rule and displayed gentleness in her speech. No one could leave her unsatisfied whom she had not filled with the cheerfulness of her mind and the pleasantness of her words.
>
> “She excelled so greatly in this virtue that after her death all the sisters testified that during the nearly twenty years she had lived among them, they had never heard even a slightly harsh word from her mouth. Thus always cheerful and always pleasant, she not only displayed nothing gloomy, but whenever she encountered clouds of sadness in troubled minds, she drove them away with the clear light of her words.” [Col. 0544A]

See also the *Life of Saint Antoninus*, abbot of Sorrento, no. 8, fourth century.

Furthermore, the Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins prescribes (Chapter 4) that:

> “Although there may be nothing from which what is requested can be given, she must never reply that she does not have it, but should say in a faithful voice: ‘The Lord will provide.’”

**“A good word is better than a gift.”** This means when the gift is given with ill will, sadness, or anger.

**“The allowance established for the brothers.”** Smaragdus explains what *annona* means here in these words:

> “He calls *annona* the nourishment of food and the entire sustenance of the monks. For the ancients were accustomed to eat at the ninth hour; therefore, from the very time of the ninth hour, when they took their food, the entire sustenance of a person appropriately acquired the name *annona*. Many names are derived from an action or a time.”

Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Peter the Deacon, cited by Augustine of Janua, Richard, and others speak in nearly the same way. [Col. 0544B]

**“Let him offer it without affectation and delay.”** *Typus*, or, as Hildemar reads it, *typhus*, is said to mean “down, that is, green vegetation or whatever floats upon water, which has nothing either in its roots or in its growth, but is recognized or displayed merely as something visible”; and, as Smaragdus says, it “inflates itself from the water,” whence the swelling of ambitious and self-satisfied people is also called *typus*.

If we consider the force of the word, *typus* also means the same as “figure”:

> “For *typos* [τύπος] is a Greek word that we call *figura*, or form,”

says Smaragdus.

Hildemar says:

> “It is interpreted as swelling or figure.”

From these explanations Bernard of Cassino infers:

> “Three things may be considered: first, that one must not give with swelling or inflation of pride; second, that one must not give under any unbecoming form of words; and third, that one must avoid harmful, offensive, or scandalous delay in giving. This is to give without *typus* and delay.”

The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen likewise decrees that:

> “Those to whom the custody of particular things has been entrusted must, with suitable devotion and the most charitable humility, provide what is necessary without delay or annoyance when the senior commands it. They must not, through proud inflation, create occasions for complaint by delaying, whereby murmuring against the labor of those who serve us charitably in the matters assigned to them ought not to be aroused.”

*Typi* are also called cold fevers. The French version prefixed to the Constitutions of the nuns of Val-de-Grâce perhaps had this in mind when it rendered this passage:

> “without acting with sorrowful and disdainful coldness” (*sans agir avec froideur chagrine et dédaigneuse*);

Guido Juvenalis translated it, “without annoyance” (*sans fascherie*); another version, “without sorrow” (*sans chagrin*); and another, “without arrogance” (*sans arrogance*).

Some also interpret *typus* here as an excuse; others think that *typus* and delay mean the same thing.

**“Mindful of the divine saying concerning what is deserved by one who causes one of the little ones to stumble.”** Namely, it is better for such a person that a millstone be hung around his neck and that he be plunged into the depths of the sea. A truly dreadful judgment!

Yet no less terrifying should be what Saint Basil answers in his Shorter Rules to the question, “What if, through negligence, he does not give a brother the things he needs?” He replies:

> “It is clear that this judgment follows from the Lord’s words when he said: ‘Depart from me, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels; for I was hungry and you did not give me food; I was thirsty and you did not give me drink,’ and what follows; and also because ‘accursed is the one who does the work of God negligently.’”

**“If the congregation is larger, let assistants be given to him.”** The Rule of Tarnant also says:

> “Whenever usefulness requires it, assistance must not be refused.”

Here “assistance” means brother-assistants, one or more, from whom the cellarer may receive some relief. In the statutes of Saint Adelard, Book II, chapter 3, such a person is called the junior cellarer.

Among the Cluniacs, the cellarer had three or four assistants, as Udalricus shows:

> “These are the assistants whom the cellarer has. The first takes his place in everything when he is absent and answers for everything for which he himself usually answers. The second is the one who receives the grain, whom we also call the granary keeper.” [Col. 0545A]

In the following chapter:

> “The third is the assistant of that same cellarer who receives and guards the wine.”

And in the next chapter:

> “The gardener must also be subject to the cellarer.”

The manuscript Customs of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon speak in nearly the same way (chapter 38):

> “These are the assistants he has: the granary keeper, the keeper of bread and wine, and the gardener. There is also a first among them, a certain brother who is assigned to him as an assistant and takes his place in everything when he is absent; he answers for everything for which he himself usually answers. The brother who purchases fish is also under him. He may leave the monastery after vespers and go to the obedience assigned to this business. None of these must resist the cellarer’s command and will, unless he orders something that would harm the church.”

Their offices are described both in the aforesaid Customs and in Udalricus. [Col. 0545B]

**“At suitable hours,” etc.** Smaragdus calls suitable hours “appropriate and fitting hours, when both things are permitted to both parties—that is, when it is permitted both for the petitioner to ask and for the giver to give. For when they ought to devote themselves to reading or prayer and maintain silence, neither one may ask nor the other give, except in a case of necessity.”

Bernard of Cassino similarly calls suitable hours those “when the brothers are not heavily occupied with other necessary matters. The night is not a suitable time for asking for necessities, nor are the hours when the brothers are occupied with psalmody or reading; therefore, unless necessity presses, the cellarer or other officials must not be disturbed at those times.”

He adds:

> “Our ancient Fathers say that the cellarer ought to have a fixed seat, and that his subofficials should find him there, so that he is not sought throughout the monastery.”

He seems to have in mind Hildemar’s words:

> “It is reported that among the ancients it was customary for the cellarer to sit in a chair in a known place, and to have disciples whom he directed to give each person what was needed. He sat in one place so that everyone who needed to ask him for something would always find him present.” [Col. 0546A]

Among the Cluniacs, those were called suitable hours during which, for the sake of relaxation, the brothers were to refresh themselves through mutual conversation. We learn this from Udalricus, whose words are as follows (Book III, chapter 11):

> “Whenever they speak in the cloister, the chamberlain, or his junior who carries the key of the chamber, must never be absent. For then he is to hear from each one what this or that person needs; and he does not neglect to go to the boys themselves, to ask whether there is anything they require. On that occasion, therefore, he gives whatever must be given, lest brothers who ask him at another hour, when silence is observed, be unable to keep silence.”

Elsewhere, speaking of things that may be done only during the hour of conversation, he says (Book II, chapter 20):

> “If he needs to ask the chamberlain for anything, he asks especially then.”

The Customs of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon prescribe the same (chapter 43). Hildemar and the aforementioned Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino also clearly imply this when they say that suitable hours are those when the brothers are not required to keep silence, read, or devote themselves to prayer. The same judgment applies to the times of work and meals, when strict silence is imposed upon the brothers.

**“Let what ought to be given be given, and let what ought to be asked be asked.”** Here Saint Benedict silently removes everything superfluous and contrary to the monastic state, binding the cellarer to distribute only necessary things: let what ought to be given be given; and let the brothers ask for what ought to be asked, and for nothing else.

**“So that no one may be troubled or saddened in the house of God.”** That is, in the monastery.

“For truly the monastery is the house of God,” says Richard of Saint-Angelus, “because prayer is always offered there.” Nicholas of Fractura adds: “In it we serve God.” Or, as Smaragdus says, it is “the most holy hearts of good monks and their purest dwelling places, in which they provide the purest dwelling for their Lord.”

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the Tools and Other Things of the Monastery

[Col. 0545]

[Col. 0545C] 414 **[Note: Oxford, Conc., Florence, Cassinese: *substantia* (“property”).]** Let the abbot appoint brothers, whose life and conduct he can trust **[Note: Oxford and Lyc.: *praevideat* (“let him provide/foresee”).]**, to care for the monastery’s property in tools, garments, or any other things; and let him assign individual items to them, as he judges useful, to be guarded **[Note: Hildemar omits *sit* (“is”).]** and collected again **[Note: Oxford: *constituenda* (“to be established/assigned”).]**. Let the abbot keep a brief inventory of these things **[Note: Another reading: *breve* (“a brief one”).]**, so that, when the brothers assigned to them succeed one another in turn **[Note: Oxford, Cassinese, Conc., Conch. Hadr.: *vicibus* (“in turns”).]**, he may know what he gives and what he receives. If anyone handles the monastery’s property basely or negligently, let him be corrected; if he does not amend, let him be subject to regular discipline.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0545]

[Col. 0545D] **“The monastery’s substance.”** Bernard of Cassino explains what is understood here by the word “substance”:

> “Substance is understood as those things by which we live and subsist, or which contribute to our substance.”

Explaining this almost further, Richard of Saint-Angelus says:

> “For example, wheat, millet, barley, and similar things.”

In my judgment, however, Boherius more correctly interprets “substance” in his second commentary as the monastery’s movable goods. Bernard himself acknowledges this in what follows, and Saint Benedict clearly indicates it when he adds:

**“Its tools.”** “That is, things useful for working,” says Richard of Saint-Angelus. By the word “tools” he understands all the instruments the brothers use while working, “whether they are made of iron, bronze, or even wood,” says Bernard of Cassino.

Hildemar says:

> “Tools include the spade, the axe or carpenter’s tools, and other things of this kind.”

**“Or garments.”** Hildemar does not seem to have understood this passage correctly when he says:

> “Garments refer to those clothes that they ought to have for work when they perform something enjoined upon them by the prior.”

Saint Benedict here, however, is speaking of garments of every kind.

[Col. 0547A] **“Or any other things.”** “Such as privileges and other documents of protection, 415, silver vessels, books, ecclesiastical ornaments, grain, wine, and other valuable things that ought not to be placed outside the monasteries,” says Boherius. Correctly.

**“Let the abbot appoint brothers whose life and conduct he can trust.”** The Master wishes such men “to be bound by divine faith, so that through fear of God or testimony before God they may faithfully fulfill what has been entrusted to them.” According to the Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins (Chapter 17), they must also possess “active solicitude of mind and proven firmness of conscience.”

Certainly, the fact that Saint Benedict treats these men immediately after dealing with the cellarer clearly implies (Chapter 13) “that they should be appointed with precisely the same qualities as he,” as Gerard the Belgian monk says—that is, “that they be wise, mature in conduct,” and so forth.

**“And let him entrust the individual things to them, as he judges useful.”** Useful, Boherius says, “for the monastery, not for himself.” He explains that this is to be done “after consultation with all the brothers, or at least with the seniors,” in accordance with the custom of his own time.

[Col. 0547B] **“He shall hand them over for safekeeping and collection.”**] That is, when the manual labor has been completed. Saint Benedict therefore wishes this chapter first of all to establish by the abbot a keeper of the tools; and this according to the custom of the ancient monks, as may be seen in the Rule of Saint Pachomius (Art. 66 in the *Codex Regularum*), which entrusts this duty to the one who is second after the superior:

“When they have reached their houses, they shall hand over the tools with which they have worked, and the sickles, to the one who is second after the superior of the house; and he shall bring them in the evening to a separate cell and lock them there.”

In the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chap. 35):

“When they go to any kind of work, the one who goes first among them shall receive the necessary tools in the morning, counted out by the keeper of the tools, and shall assign them for safekeeping to one of the younger brothers among those who are to go with him, whom he judges suitable for this purpose. When the work has been completed, he himself shall carefully receive them back from that man and hand them over to the keeper, so that nothing may be lost through the usual forgetfulness or the negligence of many.”

[Col. 0547C] In the Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 19):

“The custody of the instruments and tools shall belong to one man whom the Father of the monks has chosen; he shall distribute them to those working and, having received them back, shall keep them.”

In the Rule of Saint Ferreolus (chap. 7):

“All tools and utensils of craftsmen shall be stored in one room, under the custody of one diligent and provident brother. He shall place them separately in a suitable location and, as circumstances require, distribute them to the brothers who request them for work; then, toward evening, gathering them into their proper places, he shall take care that none of them is lost, rusts through negligence, or deteriorates in any way.”

Finally, in the Rule of the Master (chap. 17):

“The tools of the monastery shall be kept in one room, and the abbot shall entrust their preservation to one brother whose diligence he has recognized. Every day he shall issue them to the brothers for their work, counted out, and likewise receive them back from those who return them, clean them, and put them away.”

Saint Basil, too, determined the following concerning the care of tools and utensils (*Long Rules*, chap. 41):

“The care of instruments and, especially, of the utensils belonging to each craft concerns the craftsman of that trade, so that he may preserve what has been assigned to his craft. If, however, it should happen at some time that any of these things is neglected, they shall be collected as a common possession by those who first happen to see them. For although their use is separate and they have been assigned particularly to certain persons, their usefulness is nevertheless common: if someone, as though tools belonging to other crafts were no concern of his, should disregard them, he will bear the mark of an alienated mind. Yet it is not right for craftsmen to claim ownership of their tools for themselves, so that they refuse to allow their superior of the brothers to use them for whatever purpose he wishes; nor may they arrogate to themselves the power to sell or exchange them, discard them in any other way, or acquire other tools in addition to those they possess.”

[Col. 0548A] Next Saint Benedict wishes a second brother to be appointed by the abbot to care for the clothing. Following his example, Saint Fructuosus established the following (chap. 4):

“Whatever belongs to the clothing or apparel of the monks is not to be kept privately by each individual, but is to be stored under the care of one spiritual brother in a single cell; and whenever necessity requires, he shall give each petitioner clothing suitable to his stature.”

Among our people this officer was called the chamberlain (*camerarius*). His office is described in the old manuscript Customs of the monastery of Farfa as follows:

“The chamberlain himself, together with another brother, is to procure all the clothing of the brothers, purchase and find it, and distribute it to each one as is fitting and as has been established in the place; namely, he shall give all the brothers two woolen garments each, likewise breeches, two tunics, and two cucullas with wide sleeves, two little fur garments with tight sleeves, and a third with wide sleeves. He shall distribute night and day leggings, and foot-coverings to ward off the cold. Two pairs shall be given for the night and two for the day; and each man shall have a sheath with a knife, except the scribes, who shall have two, as well as a belt for girding. Writing tablets, needles, a comb with its case, and a cap for the head, which is otherwise called a head-covering. On each bed there shall be assigned a cloak with a fur lining, a woolen blanket, and a pillow.

“When clothing or footwear is torn or unstitched [Note: [Col. 0547D] Sense and syntax require that we read *rumpuntur* and *dissuuntur*—‘are torn’ and ‘are unstitched.’ EDITOR], each brother shall first wash it; then he shall bring it before the door of the auditorium, and the chamberlain shall receive it and carry it to the tailors to be repaired. No brother is to go to them or make any alteration to the clothing according to his own will, except what is customary in the monastery and what the chamberlain has ordered. Whoever does otherwise shall be strictly judged by all the brothers, so that the others may fear; and the brother himself must always be attentive, so that whenever he sees a garment belonging to any brother that has something requiring correction, it may be repaired or removed, since the responsibility rests upon him if he has neglected it.

“He shall frequently make provision with the prior that nothing befall anyone. He shall arrange with the tailors to have straw or hay placed in each bed eight days before the feast of the Prince of the Apostles. He himself shall provide linen suitable for the hands and feet; likewise tablecloths for the refectory. He shall see that he always observes the abbot’s orders; likewise those of the prior, the dean, or the one who holds the office when the abbot is absent. Neither he nor the secretaries or cellarers shall have hidden possessions under their care that are not known beforehand to the prior or dean.

“The same applies to all obediences, because if the matter should come to judgment and something is found among any of these brothers, it will be counted as his personal property, and he will be plunged into punishment, as happened in the monastery of blessed Pope Gregory to the monk Justus, and as we have already learned from many other monasteries. In the kitchen, whether the regular or the domestic kitchen, he himself shall prepare all utensils, including the cooking pots, except the benches and bowls, which are to be supplied by the cellarer and the superior.”

His office is also described in the manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus, chap. 43; in Lanfranc’s Statutes, chap. 7; and in Udalricus, book III, chap. 11. From these sources we also learn that he was responsible for safeguarding the monastery’s money. Hildemar confirms this when, explaining Saint Benedict’s words, “not neglecting or treating lightly the salvation of souls,” he writes as follows (*Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chap. 2):

“The abbot has a wardrobe full of riches, and he sees a brother in need. Such a man, fearing that his wardrobe may be diminished, does not assist the brother suffering need, or he does not restore the cells of the sick because of avarice. Such a man shows that he is more concerned with earthly things than with the salvation of his brother.”

John the Deacon, in book I of his *Life of Saint Gregory the Pope*, chap. 10, where he recounts the holy Father’s remarkable charity toward a poor shipwreck victim, says the following (*Saeculum I Benedictinum*):

“Then the most generous Father summoned the keeper of the wardrobe and ordered six other coins to be given; he discovered that no coins remained in the wardrobe with which the shipwrecked man could be comforted.”

The same may be seen in the Rule of Saint Isidore, chap. 19.

Besides the keepers of the tools and clothing, another man was entrusted with the care of preserving the monastery’s charters, privileges, and documents. He kept them all properly arranged and enclosed in the safest possible place: among the monks of Fleury, in a little tower, according to Tortarius, *On the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chap. 27; in the monastery of Crowland, in a document-house entirely covered by a stone arch, according to Ingulf’s *History of Crowland* (under the year 1091). Copies of these documents were sometimes deposited in several places, as may be seen in the second part of the *Chronicle of Ramsey*, chap. 7. In the *Typikon*, or Rule, of Irene Augusta, chap. 19, this care is entrusted to the keeper of the sacred vessels.

Others were also given charge of keeping the books. Saint Isidore assigns this obedience to the keeper of the sacristy (*On the Rule*, chap. 9), prescribing that “the keeper of the sacristy shall have all the books assigned to him; individual brothers shall receive them from him, and, having read or used them prudently, shall always return them after vespers.”

Among our people this office was ordinarily entrusted to the precentor. For this reason they called him the *armarius*, after the *armarium* in which the books were stored. Gerhohus the priest once held this office in the monastery of Fulda, as appears from Rhabanus’s poem 16; in the monastery of Saint Mary of Toulouse it was held by Blessed Gerald, later bishop of Braga (*Miscellanea* of Baluze, vol. III). Bernard says in his Life of Gerald, no. 1:

“Because he greatly desired to be nourished by the food of divine Scripture, he became keeper of the *armarium* in which the divine books were stored, and he remained in the obedience of this office for many years.”

But according to the Rule of the Master, chap. 17, the keeper of the tools also had the books and documents under his care.

What Bernard writes about Saint Gerald—that he remained for many years in the obedience of the *armarium*—must not be understood as though offices were assigned to monks for life, since it is a constant tradition that they were rather renewed each year. This may be gathered from Saint Jerome, who reports concerning the Tabennesiots (*Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius*, no. 8) that every year, in the month called Mesore, that is, August, “the heads of the monasteries, stewards, superiors, and ministers are appointed as necessity requires”; from Leo of Ostia, who teaches that it was the custom among the Cassinese (*Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book I, chap. 31) for a gathering of all the monks in the surrounding area to take place on the day before the Kalends of September, at which “on the following day they were appointed, recorded, and assigned to the obediences in the various provinces, according to what was appropriate”; from the Life of Saint John of Gorze (*Saeculum V Benedictinum*, no. 73), whom Abbot Einoldus never ceased transferring among different duties; and whose various offices John, abbot of Metz, describes in these words:

“Ordered to be superior, he obeys immediately. Having laid down the superiorship, let him be dean; he accepts the yoke calmly. Going away from there, he takes charge of the cellar; at once he extends his hand. When another succeeds him there, he keeps the brothers’ clothing; he resists no more than before. Thus he served the guests, thus, if it happened, the sick, and thus all others who were entrusted to him, with the greatest eagerness and knowing no delay.”

The same is evident from the Life of Saint Guido, abbot of Pomposa (*Bollandists*, 31 March), whom Abbot William “appointed to all the offices of the monastery in successive periods,” as the anonymous author writes in his second Life, no. 5 (*Spicilegium*, vol. VI); from Fulcuin, *Deeds of the Abbots of Lobbes*, chap. 19, where he asserts that the annual exchange of obediences was a regular practice; from Ekkehard, *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*, chap. 15, where he writes: “Every year, according to Roman custom, offices among us are usually changed”; and finally from Hildemar, who maintains that the brothers ought to succeed one another in the lower ministries by turns.

Nevertheless, if the abbot approved, some could remain for several years in the same office, especially cellarers, deans, and superiors, as the same Hildemar teaches. This is also decreed in the Reforming Statutes for Benedictine Monks of the Province of Narbonne, approved by Gregory IX, chap. 1, in these words (*Spicilegium*, vol. VI):

“And let them surrender their administrations absolutely, without any excuse, delay, or opposition, even without being asked—that is, each year after rendering an account of their administration—into the hands of the abbot, retaining absolutely nothing with themselves or anyone else. Let the abbots, however, restore those whom they find to have served faithfully, so that devoted humility may thus be preserved among subjects and useful prudence among superiors.”

It appears, moreover, that this appointment of officials was celebrated by the ancient monks in the oratory. They received the keys of their obediences from above the altar, as Saint Aurelian prescribes in his Rule for Monks. In chapter 21 I read:

“Those to whom the keys of the cellar, the storeroom, the granary, the gate, and the oratory are to be handed over must be persons who have been tested; and from above the altar or the Gospel they shall receive the vessel, knowing that they will have to render an account to God for the ministry entrusted to them.”

These words appear to have been taken from the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins, chap. 30, where we read:

“Those who are placed over the cellar, the storeroom, clothing, books, the gate, or the wool-work shall receive the keys over the Gospel and serve the rest without murmuring.”

Saint Donatus likewise inserted the same words into chapter 62 of his Rule for Virgins. To this may be added the *Typikon*, or Rule, of Irene Augusta for nuns, which, describing the rite of instituting officials, states:

“Whenever it is necessary to appoint someone to any office, the keys shall be placed before the sacred sanctuary, together with the words of that office copied from the present imperial *Typikon*. After the Trisagion has been said, the woman designated for that office shall approach; having made three genuflections and received the keys, she shall then bow her head to the superior, first proceeding to her feet and afterward rising. The superior shall institute her by saying these words: ‘The immaculate and grace-filled Mother of God designates you for this office.’

“Where there are no keys, the words of the institution itself, spoken by the superior, shall suffice for the appointment, together with the acceptance of the written regulations for each office from the place situated before the sacred sanctuary, as stated above. Each official must receive the particular regulations of the office entrusted to her from the place before the sacred sanctuary, so that she may consider both from where she receives the office and to whom she promises that she will administer it.”

They usually carried the keys of their obediences hanging from their belts, as we gather from the Life of Saint Maximinus, abbot of Micy (*Saeculum I Benedictinum*, no. 25, p. 587):

“When, therefore, as has already been mentioned, the holy man had opened the doors after loosening the keys from his belt, etc.”

But enough on this subject; I return to the text of the Rule.

**“From these he shall keep a brief.”**] Here *brief* is said to mean “a written memorandum which the abbot ought to keep in his archive,” according to Bernard of Monte Cassino.

Among the ancients this word had various meanings. Baronius is worth hearing on the subject:

“That word,” he says (*under the year 142*, no. 10), “is found among the ancients with different meanings. For in Optatus of Milevis, *brevis* denotes the document in which ecclesiastical possessions were recorded, which we more commonly call an inventory; Optatus calls the same thing by another name, *commentarius*. Saint Augustine, in his work against Cresconius, and Pope Gregory likewise use the same word in the same sense.
