Cassiodorus, however, uses it for royal commands; for when Theodoric writes to Gemellus, he says: ‘Our admonition will not be lacking, so that you may be made more fully instructed when you have received what has been defined in the briefs written below.’ But in Lampridius the same word is used for a register or catalogue in which names were written, as also in the Justinianic Code and in the other passages cited above.”

Thus far Baronius. The letters of the Roman pontiffs, issued with apostolic authority, are also called *breves*, or *brevia*. Moreover, in monasteries a *brevis* was the document in which the ministers of the altar and other choir officials were recorded. It is used in this sense in chapter 3 of the *Directory for the Monks of Reichenau*: “so that each day six brothers assigned by the brief may offer the sacred oblation,” and so forth.

Finally, *brevis* was the small document sent to various monasteries to announce the death of deceased brothers. It is commonly understood in this sense in Udalricus and in ancient manuscript ordinals and ritual books.

But here *brevis*, or, as Saint Benedict calls it, *breve*, signifies a written memorandum of the monastery’s possessions. The Cassinese explain it as follows (*Cassinese Declaration on chap. 32*):

“Each official shall, within a month from the day of his appointment, make an inventory of the monastery’s possessions belonging to his office. The prelate shall keep with him a general inventory of all the monastery’s movable and immovable goods, lest they be lost; this inventory shall also be shown to visitors.”

Pope Benedict XII, in his constitution for Benedictine monks, prescribes (chap. 13) that all superiors make inventories and registers “in which it shall be written how many monks may and ought to reside in each place of those administrations, according to the resources of that place; in what condition each person receives the church, monastery, priory, or administration; and, among other things, what animals are present or lacking, and what kinds and quantities of grain, wine, and other foodstuffs, money, gold or silver vessels; and what things, how many, and from whom the church, monastery, priory, administration, or such place owes; and what things, how many, and by whom they are owed to the same, and under what obligations they owe and are owed; and what and how many other movable goods, vessels, ornaments, furnishings, and similar objects are present there.”

**“So that, while the brothers successively take turns in the assignment made to him.”**] These words confirm the annual change of obediences mentioned above, which is made even clearer by chapter 53, where it is prescribed that two brothers enter the guest kitchen for a year. According to Bernard of Monte Cassino, however, “cellarers, deans, and superiors do not succeed one another by turns.” He says this with reference to the practice of his own time.

**“If anyone handles the monastery’s goods in a sordid or negligent manner, he shall be corrected; if he does not amend, he shall undergo regular discipline.”**] That is, he shall be led through the six stages mentioned above, according to Hildemar on chapter 3, and according to Bernard of Monte Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura here.

In the Eastern Rule, however, it is decreed (chap. 13) that “in absolutely any craft practiced by the brothers, if something is lost and dissipated through negligence, the minister of the works shall rebuke the offender; and he in turn shall rebuke the one who lost the work, but only according to the will and foreknowledge of the superior, without whom no one shall have authority to rebuke a brother.”

In the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins:

“If any women are judged to have expended or guarded clothing, footwear, or utensils negligently, they shall be corrected more severely as embezzlers of the monastery’s goods.”

Finally, in the Rule of the Master:

“If a brother does not bring back a clean tool from the ground in the field, and is accused at table by the keeper of the tools, he shall receive at the meal, as a penalty, one quarter less in his portion of bread until the promised satisfaction or correction; for the tool rusts as a result, when it has not been put away clean.”

# CHAPTER XXXIII. Whether monks ought to have anything of their own.

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551C] “Above all, this vice of personal ownership must be cut out from the monastery by the roots, lest anyone presume to give or receive anything without the abbot’s order, or to possess anything as his own—not any object at all, neither a book, nor writing tablets, nor a stylus, but absolutely nothing [Note: [Col. 0551C] Oxford lacks *omnino* (‘at all’).]. For they are not permitted to have even their bodies [Note: [Col. 0551C] Hildemar reads ‘their own bodies.’] or their wills in their own power [Note: [Col. 0552C] Oxford, Hildemar, Ebrulphus, Farfa, and both Victor manuscripts read ‘will’ in the singular.]. Rather, they are to hope for everything necessary from the Father of the monastery; nor is anyone permitted to possess anything that the abbot has not given or allowed.

“And let everything be common to all, as it is written: nor may anyone call or presume anything to be his own (Acts IV). But if anyone is found to take pleasure in this most wicked vice, after being admonished once and again, if he does not amend, he shall submit to correction.”

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0551]

[Col. 0551D] Since the nature of money and other temporal things is such that, like pitch, they can scarcely be touched without sticking to one’s hands, Saint Benedict most appropriately, after dealing with the cellarer and the other administrators of the monastery’s possessions, proceeds to discuss the removal of personal ownership from monks, lest under the pretext of the administration and obedience entrusted to them they presume to claim anything for themselves. In this chapter he attempts to expel ownership first from the heart, then from conduct, and finally from speech. For, proposing the question to himself in the title—whether monks ought to have anything of their own—he answers:

**“Above all, let this vice be cut out from the monastery by the roots.”**] “By the roots,” that is, from the heart, which is the fountain, root, and origin of every evil and every covetousness, “so that nothing of ownership may remain either in intention or in the will, through which it might sprout into some action,” says Bernard of Monte Cassino.

And entirely rightly. For, as Cassian says:

“Not only the possession of money must be avoided, but the will itself must be completely expelled from the mind. For it is not so much the effect of avarice that must be avoided as its inclination must be cut out by the roots. It will be of no benefit not to have money if the will to possess remains in us.”

Yet not only the will and desire to possess, but even the slightest attachment to those things granted to us for use must be cut away. Who would not laugh at monks who, after rejecting the great riches of the world, allow themselves to be held by trifles and cling to them with as much attachment as a miser clings to his treasures—or, if possible, with even more? Nevertheless, Cassian already lamented this in certain monks of his own age in these words (*Conferences* I, chap. 6):

“We have seen some who despised the greatest wealth of this world—not only many talents of gold and silver, but even the magnificence of estates—afterward become agitated over a small knife, a stylus, a needle, or a pen [lacuna]. For often some guard a book with such jealousy that they will not allow anyone even lightly to touch it, and thereby incur occasions of impatience and death. Thus they are warned to acquire the rewards of charity and patience; and although they have scattered all their wealth for the love of Christ, by retaining their former attachment to the smallest things and sometimes becoming violently angry on their account, they are found unprofitable and barren in everything, as those who do not possess apostolic charity.”

**“Let no one presume to give or receive anything without the abbot’s order, or to possess anything as his own.”**] Here the holy legislator prohibits three things.

First, giving anything to anyone without the abbot’s order. Saint Isidore teaches that this must also be understood with regard to the poor, lest false piety deceive anyone (chap. 5):

“One must not presume, without the abbot’s knowledge, to give to the needy or to anyone else from what the monk is known to possess under the regular administration.”

Indeed, one may not even distribute what the abbot has determined should be given to the poor, according to the Rule of Saint Basil (*Short Rules*, question 87):

“To give or receive, even according to an order, is not the responsibility of just anyone, but of the one to whom the task of dispensing has been entrusted with approval. Therefore he shall be the one who, with due regard for the season, gives and receives either an old or a new garment.”

Elsewhere, when asked how those who come to the door and ask are to be dismissed, and whether each person ought to offer bread or anything else, or whether this belongs to the one in charge, he replies (*Question* 100):

“The one to whom the administration has been entrusted must do this with discernment. But if anyone presumes to do it contrary to his will, he shall be confounded as restless and undisciplined until he learns to observe the order of his place, according to what the Apostle said: ‘Let each one remain in the calling in which he was called.’”

Moreover, by this term the holy Father forbids not only giving anything, but also exchanging it or lending it; and this according to the discipline of the ancient monks, as may be seen in the Rule of Saint Pachomius:

“No one shall dare to exchange with another anything that he has received from the superior; nor shall he receive something better and give something worse, or, conversely, give something better and receive something worse.”

In the *Penitential Rules* of an unknown author preserved by Saint Basil (Art. 58; the same appears in the Eastern Rule, chap. 9):

“If anyone exchanges anything with another, or gives anything without the will of the archimandrite, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

In the Rule of Tarnat:

“Let no one be permitted to exchange anything that he has received, neither inferior things for more worthless ones, nor better things for the sake of convenience; whatever has been assigned to him, he shall claim solely for his own use with thanksgiving.”

In the Rule of Saint Isidore:

“No one may exchange anything with another brother unless the abbot or superior has ordered it.”

And in the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins (chap. 17):

“Whatever has been entrusted to her by the abbess—that is, whatever concerns her present need, whether in clothing or in any other matter—let her presume neither to give nor to lend anything from it to anyone, unless the abbess has specifically ordered it.”

In matters of lesser importance, however, the brothers may lend things to one another—for example, a needle, a knife, writing tablets, and similar objects—as Hildemar teaches.

[Col. 0553D] Second, the holy Father prohibits receiving anything without the abbot’s order. Saint Pachomius likewise says:

“No one shall receive anything from another unless the superior has ordered it.”

The Eastern Rule (Art. 58):

“Without the word and authority of the elders, none of the brothers shall do anything, receive anything, or give anything.”

The *Penitentials* of an unknown author preserved by Saint Basil (chap. 31; the same appears in the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers, chap. 1):

“If anyone gives anything outside or receives anything contrary to the will of the archimandrite, let him be excommunicated.”

Saint Fructuosus likewise says:

“No monk shall receive any gift or letters.”

By the same provision Saint Benedict also forbids borrowing anything from another without the permission of the superior. The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen similarly prohibits this in these words (chap. 27):

“Nor shall the brothers be permitted among themselves, out of some private affection, to lend to another brother what one of them has received from the common supply without the prior’s permission, lest illicit affection arise on this occasion.”

[Col. 0554A] Third, Saint Benedict prohibits anyone from having or possessing anything as his own. This is so closely attached to the monastic profession that a person cannot be a monk without rejecting ownership, as Saint Fulgentius once held. For “he frequently said that a monk could neither properly be judged nor be one, if his will persuaded him to have private property.”

Saint Isaac likewise says in Saint Gregory (*Dialogues* III, chap. 14):

“A monk who seeks possession on earth is not a monk.”

With the same outlook Saint Basil said to a certain senator who, renouncing the world, had retained some part of his own possessions:

“You have lost the senator and have not made a monk” (in Cassian, book VII, chap. 19).

And indeed, all who have ever been true practitioners of the monastic life, and all founders of Rules, have either enacted or observed laws concerning the renunciation and banishment of ownership. We have a splendid example in the disciples of Saint Gerasimus, who, as Cyril writes in the Life of Saint Euthymius, “they took as much care to possess nothing as they did about anything else [lacuna]. They were so far removed from every anxiety and so separated from human business that they had nothing except what they wore, so much so that they did not have a second garment [lacuna].”

This law was excellently handed down by Gerasimus (*Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, vol. II): those leaving their cells were to leave them open, so that anyone who wished might enter and take whatever he wanted from the poor things necessary for use, with ownership being forbidden by name.

The same is evident in the disciples of Saint Martin, concerning whom Sulpicius Severus says (*Life of Saint Martin*, chap. 7):

“No one there had anything of his own. Everything was held in common. No one was permitted to buy or sell, as is customary among many monks.”

Finally, among the Tabennesiot monks, concerning whom the Life of Saint Pachomius says (no. 38, in the Bollandists, 14 May):

“Among them no one used gold or silver. Indeed, some were found who, when they came to the end of their lives, did not know at all what gold or silver was. Only those who had been assigned the office of administering necessities knew the accounts of money; and even these, after returning to the monastery, retained nothing in their hands—not even for a single day. Rather, the steward kept the money entrusted to him until they again happened to go out.”

The decrees of this institution may be seen in the Rule of Saint Pachomius itself, where it is prescribed (Art. 47):

“No one shall have in his cell anything except what is prescribed by the monastery’s law—not even a few coins, nor anything of his own apart from his habit. If you find anything, you shall take it away without objection.”

And again (Art. 63):

“No one shall store anything in his cell without the superior’s order—not even apples.”

Likewise, to remove every occasion of personal ownership (Art. 46):

“If anyone is transferred from one house to another, he may not take with him anything except what is necessary for daily use and clothing.”

Similar statutes may be observed in other Rules of monks. Although it may seem lengthy to report them individually here, it will perhaps not be unwelcome to readers. Thus the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius decrees (chap. 7):

“If he is rich and possesses many riches in the world and wishes to convert, he must first fulfill the will of God and attain that chief commandment which is spoken to the rich young man: ‘Sell all your goods and give to the poor; take up your cross and follow me.’ Then he must be instructed by the father who presides that he leave himself nothing except the cross of Christ which he bears.”

The Second Rule of the Holy Fathers (chap. 1):

“Above all, possessing charity, humility, patience, gentleness, and the other virtues taught by the holy Apostle, let no one claim anything for himself, but, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles, let them have everything in common.”

The Third Rule of the Holy Fathers (chap. 2):

“Let no abbot claim anything as his own—much less the monks—since, by God’s favor, everything remains under his authority. But if anyone presumes to retain for himself anything that is forbidden to the younger brothers by the Rule, whether from an inheritance from his parents or from any gift, and does not place everything in common, he shall be reproved by the brothers. If he persists in the vice, the matter shall be reported to the bishop. If, after being corrected by the bishop, he still does not amend, he shall be deposed.”

425 **Rule of Saint Macarius (chap. 24):** A novice “if he wishes to bring any property into his cell, shall have it placed on the table before all the brothers, as the Rule prescribes. If he is then received, from that hour he shall have no authority not only over the property he brought in, but even over himself. For if he had previously distributed something to the poor, or, upon entering the cell, brought something in for the brothers, he is nevertheless not permitted to have anything in his own power.”

**Eastern Rule (chap. 3):**

“No one shall claim anything as his own, nor shall anyone appropriate anything privately; rather, let them have everything in common.”

Saint Basil, when asked (*Short Rules*, question 85) “whether one ought to possess anything as one’s own within the common fellowship of the brothers,” replies:

“This is contrary to those testimonies found in the Acts concerning the believers, in which it is written: ‘No one said that any of the things he possessed was his own.’ Therefore whoever says that something is his own makes himself alien to the Church of God and to the love of the Lord, who taught by word and deed that one should lay down one’s life for one’s enemies, much less external possessions.”

See also his *Monastic Constitutions*, chap. 35.

**Teaching of Saint Orsiesius, abbot, on the institution of monks (chap. 22):**

“To whom some ministry or administration of the monastery has been entrusted: if he makes a profit from it, let it be considered a crime and sacrilege for anything to come from it and be turned to his own use, as though he despised those who have nothing and who are rich in fortunate poverty. Thus not only will he himself perish, but he will also provoke others to perish.”

And below:

“Those who have lived in a coenobium and have diverted anything from the common property to their own uses—woe to them when they leave the body! It will be said to them: ‘Remember that you received good things during your life.’”

**Consensus of the Monks (chap. 8):**

“He cannot retain as his own what by agreement belongs to all and has certainly been consecrated to God.”

**Rule of an Unknown Author (chap. 2):**

“Let no one claim anything as his own, whether in clothing or in any other matter; for we desire to live the apostolic life.”

**Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins (chap. 15):**

“Let no one regard anything as his own, whether in clothing or in any other matter.”

**Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks (chap. 5):**

“Receive nothing secretly. But if a relative or friend gives or sends anything in clothing, gold, or any other matter, it shall be under the abbot’s authority; and if the one to whom it is sent has need of it, let it be given to him. But if he has no need, let it be returned to the common store and given to whoever needs it.”

[Col. 0555D] Rule of Saint Ferreolus (Chapter 10): “We have also determined that this must be established: no monk may dare to claim anything as his own, apart from the fellowship of the brothers, so that even in things that belong to him he should believe himself to have no greater right than the others; for when he has subjected himself to another’s authority, he has transferred everything belonging to him into another’s power. Whatever property, therefore, he has brought with him, once he has sought the fellowship of the monks and, having become a member of the body of the community, has attached himself to it, let him immediately recognize that everything has passed into common ownership; and let him judge this alone to be his own: whatever he possesses indivisibly with the brothers, etc.”

Rule of Saint Columbanus (Chapter 4): “Nakedness and contempt for possessions are the first perfection of monks.”

Rule of Tarnat (Chapter 2): “Let no one be permitted to choose a separate dwelling, nor to have a small cupboard, or anything similar that can be locked more privately, as his own.” And again (Chapter 14): “Nor should you consider anything to be your own.”

Rule of Saint Isidore (Chapter 5): “Monks living in common must dare to make nothing peculiar to themselves, nor presume to have or possess in their cells anything pertaining to food or to any other matter without regular dispensation. On Pentecost, however, which is the day of remission, all the brothers shall bind themselves under their divine profession not to have anything peculiar in their own conscience.”

Rule of Saint Fructuosus (Chapter 8): “Peculiarity, whether in utensils, clothing, or any things whatsoever, however cheap and worthless, must be avoided altogether; for it is an abomination for monks to possess or keep in reserve as private or hidden anything superfluous or dishonorable, which is not far removed from the example of Ananias and Sapphira.”

Rule of a Certain Author for Monks (Chapter 17): “Nothing is to be possessed as one’s own or privately among monks; rather, everything must be common to them.”

[Col. 0556B] Rule of the Master (Chapter 82): “If, therefore, anything peculiar is found in anyone’s possession, let the abbot condemn him to a great and prolonged excommunication, so that, by the example of that punishment, no one may dare to imitate this. For this reason, the superiors should frequently search everyone, lest this exist in anyone; and if a brother is seen to take great pleasure or delight in any object, let it be taken from him and given to another, and let him be given something belonging to another, so that his own will may not be exalted in it.”

Rule of Solitaries (Chapter 6; see also Chapter 41): “Those, therefore, who completely abandon the world ought to possess nothing except the Lord, etc.”

Typikon of Irene Augusta for the Nuns of the Monastery of the Most Holy Theotokos Full of Grace (Chapter 50, in the Greek *Analecta*): “Devote yourselves to the utmost poverty, not only in money, down to the last obol, but also in food and drink, down to the least quantity whatsoever. Therefore, so that this instruction of ours may not be violated, we urge the superior, whenever and as often as she wishes, to inspect you, and to allow no one to have anything more than the cenobitic rule permits.”

To these may be added the decrees of the supreme pontiffs—Innocent III, Gregory IX, Nicholas IV, and Benedict XII—from which it will be sufficient here to cite one passage from Innocent (Chapter *Cum ad monasterium*): “We strictly prohibit, under the obligation of obedience and under the testimony of divine judgment, that any monk possess anything as his own in any manner whatsoever; but if anyone has anything privately, let him immediately surrender it all. If, however, after this he is found to possess any private property, let him be expelled from the monastery in the aforesaid regular manner and not received again, unless he repents according to monastic discipline.” And toward the end: “Nor should the abbot suppose that he can dispense with any monk concerning the possession of private property, because renunciation of property, like the observance of chastity, is so closely joined to the monastic rule that not even the supreme pontiff can grant permission contrary to it.”

The same may be seen throughout the councils, especially in the First Council of Orléans, canon 21; the Council of Auxerre, canon 23; the Lateran Council under Alexander III; and many others. But enough of this. I return to the text.

“Absolutely nothing—not a book, not writing tablets, not a stylus, but nothing at all.”] “Absolutely nothing,” as though he were saying: “Provided it is a thing, I exclude it from you; and ‘absolutely,’ that is, in every way—namely, you are to have it in no manner whatsoever,” says Bernard of Cassino.

“For they are not even permitted to have their own bodies or wills under their own control.”] He gives in these words the reason why a monk ought not to possess anything privately: for if he is not permitted to control either his own will or his own body, much less may he control temporal possessions. That our will and our bodies are not under our own authority is especially clear from the fact that, through flight from the world and love of God, we have sold ourselves, as Saint John Climacus says (*Step* 3). Therefore, just as a thing sold no longer belongs to the one who sold it, so we no longer belong to ourselves but to God, to whom we have been sold through our monastic profession. For the same reason Saint Ferreolus judged that private ownership must be cut away from monks: “because, when he has subjected himself to another’s authority, he has transferred everything belonging to him into another’s power.” And the Master says: “For this reason he is forbidden to have anything peculiar, because no one serving God entangles himself in secular affairs in order to please the one to whom he has proved himself devoted; and when he has subjected himself, together with all his possessions, to another’s authority, there should be nothing in him in which his own will may be exalted.”

Haeften shrewdly observes here that Saint Benedict prescribed in this chapter a threefold renunciation corresponding to the three vows: renunciation of temporal goods, which we reject through poverty; renunciation of the body, which we consecrate to God through chastity; and renunciation of our own will, which we sacrifice to God through obedience. This last renunciation the Venerable Wala, abbot of Corbie, demanded above all from his brothers. Paschasius writes in his *Life*, book I, chapter 21 (*Benedictine Centuries*, century 4, part I), that Wala:

“very often admonished everyone generally, and many individually, with no less skill, concerning the will of free choice and the power over one’s own body, in accordance with the profession of monastic discipline, so that none of us would follow his own will. Otherwise,” he said, “how shall I be able to render an account for anyone unless he leaves to me both the power over his body and the will of his free choice? But if he has retained himself under his own power or will, let him know that he will have to render an account—not only for his own deeds, words, thoughts, or actions, but also because, contrary to the profession of monastic law, he has retained himself under the power or will of his own heart. Indeed,” he said, “I shall be free in proportion as no power owed to me remains granted to me, nor is the will of his own choice released to him.”

“But to hope for everything necessary from the Father of the monastery.”] Several observations arise here.

First, by “the Father of the monastery” God himself may be understood, for he is the common Father of all, upon whom the eyes of all hope, who gives them their food in due season, opens his hand, and fills every living creature with blessing. Or the abbot may be understood, since he acts in the monastery in God’s place and is called by God’s own title, as the Apostle says: “You have received the spirit of adoption, in which we cry, Abba, Father.” Richard of Saint Angelo understood “the Father of the monastery” here in this sense. Or the cellarer may be understood, who, according to chapter 31 of the Rule, is to be like a father to the whole community.

Second, by “everything necessary” one must understand not merely food or clothing, if the words are taken strictly, but everything required for a decent and suitable monastic life. The holy Father appears to have explained this when he says in chapter 55: “And so that this vice of private ownership may be eradicated from the roots, the abbot shall provide everything necessary, namely, a cowl, tunic, foot-cloths, leggings, undergarment, knife, stylus, needle, handkerchief, and writing tablets, so that every excuse of necessity may be removed.”

Third, the abbot and cellarer ought to be very diligent in administering necessities, because “just as it has been decreed that they are to have nothing of their own, so it is just that they should all receive from the holy abbot whatever is necessary,” says Saint Caesarius in his *Rule for Monks* (Chapter 16). Gregory, cited here by Hildemar, likewise says: “If a shepherd wishes to benefit his disciples, he ought to take great care to provide for their temporal needs.” In distributing these things, he should also observe what Trithemius says (*On the Property of Monks*, chapter 9): “What he can grant without guilt, he ought not to deny at the risk of guilt; for he has undertaken the care of the sick, not of the strong.”

Fourth, just as everything necessary must be expected from the Father of the monastery, so superfluity must be cut away: “Necessities, therefore, are to be expected from the abbot,” says Trithemius (*ibid.*, chapter 5), “not superfluities; for where necessity is permitted for the monks’ use, superfluity is condemned as a crime. And just as the abbot is gravely reproved by God if he denies necessities to the brothers, so, if he grants superfluities, he is condemned as a violator of the holy order.” Hence the Council of Trent (Session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 2): “Superiors shall permit the use of movable goods in such a way that their furnishings conform to the state of poverty they have professed, with nothing superfluous in them, and with nothing necessary denied them.” But if you ask what is superfluous, John of Fano answers (*Discourse on the Observance of Poverty among the Friars Minor*): “That is superfluous which, once removed, leaves enough remaining. Of two things, one is superfluous when one of them is sufficient; much is superfluous when little is enough; an expensive thing is excessive if a cheap one satisfies.”

Fifth, Hildemar observes that the holy Father Benedict did not say that everything necessary was to be expected from parents or friends, but from the Father of the monastery. Certainly it is unworthy for a monk who has cast off secular concerns and abandoned secular affections to have recourse, as though disdaining monastic poverty, to the treasures of parents or friends—treasures which he ought to distribute to the poor and store up in the heavenly treasuries.

“Nor may he have anything that the abbot has not given or permitted.”] This should not be understood as though the abbot could permit the brothers to possess private property, since not even the supreme pontiff can do so, as Innocent III said above.

“And let everything be common to all.”] Since “God is common to them, the commerce of common piety, common salvation, common struggles, common labors, and also common crowns,” as Saint Basil says (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 19).

“Nor may anyone say or presume that anything is his own.”] Up to this point Saint Benedict has undertaken to eliminate the vice of private ownership from the monk’s heart and actions. Now he also appears to condemn it in the monk’s speech, saying, “Nor may anyone say that anything is his own.” To illuminate this passage, John Trithemius writes (*On the Property of Monks*, chapter 6):

“Let the abbot not say ‘something of mine,’ ‘my book,’ ‘my field,’ ‘my estate,’ or ‘my income’; but if it is necessary to say such a thing before people, let him say ‘ours,’ not ‘mine.’ For since the monastery’s goods belong to the community, and community presupposes many persons, no one should think it ridiculous if a monk or abbot, as an individual person, says ‘ours.’ The intention of the speech refers to the community; nor are these childish matters, which the most ancient holy Fathers are known to have observed so diligently that they prescribed penance for transgressors.”

As for the holy Fathers, their ancient institutions and rules show with what care they avoided that cold word “my” in common speech. Cassian must be heard concerning the Egyptians and the monks of Tabennesis (*Book IV*, chapter 13):

“In other monasteries also, in which some matters are indulged more leniently, we see this rule still observed with the utmost strictness: no one may dare to say even in a word that anything is his own. It is considered a great crime for ‘my book,’ ‘my tablets,’ ‘my stylus,’ ‘my tunic,’ or ‘my leggings’ to have come from a monk’s mouth; and if such a word should by some chance escape his mouth through inadvertence or ignorance, he must make satisfaction by a penance worthy of it.”

Saint Basil likewise says (*Longer Rules*, chapter 32): “The teaching of truth absolutely forbids the words ‘my’ and ‘your’ to be spoken among the brothers.” The same may be seen throughout the other monastic rules. In the Rule of Saint Augustine (Chapter 1): “Do not call anything your own.” In the Rule of Saint Aurelian (Chapter 25): “Let no one presume to call anything his own.” In the Penitential of Saint Columbanus: “For saying ‘my’ and ‘your,’ six blows.” In the Rule given by Saint David to monks (in Bollandus, March 1): “Everything was common to all, and they said neither ‘mine’ nor ‘yours’; for whoever said, ‘This is mine’ or ‘that is mine’ was subjected to severe penance.”

[Col. 0559A] In the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (Chapter 4): “Nor may any monk, asserting that something is his own, say ‘my book,’ ‘my tablets,’ or the like. If this word escapes his mouth, he shall be subject to penance, lest he appear to have anything private in the monastery.” In the Rule of a Certain Author (Chapter 17): “But whoever says, ‘This or that is mine,’ has sinned before God, unless it was merely a slip of the tongue; nevertheless, for this very thing let him ask God’s forgiveness, take care thereafter, and not dare to repeat it.” In the *Order of Monastic Conduct* (Chapter 10): “Let no brother call anything his own, whether a possession or a member of the body, but always say ‘ours.’ The only thing he ought to call his own is ‘my fault.’” In Udalricus (Book II, chapter 20): “He calls nothing individually his own, but calls everything ‘ours,’ except his father and mother; only of these is it customarily permitted to say ‘my’ and ‘mine.’” The Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon, chapter 31, state: “He calls everything ‘ours,’ except his father, mother, or sin.”

“But if anyone is found to delight in this most wicked vice, let him be admonished once and again; if he does not amend, let him be subjected to correction.”] The holy Father expresses the same elsewhere in these words (Chapter 55): “And if anyone is found to have something which he did not receive from the abbot, let him be subject to the strictest discipline.” What it means to be subjected to the strictest discipline is explained by the commentators on the Rule. Hildemar says:

“If he had that object by theft, then, if it is large—worth four denarii, as we have already said—he is to be judged according to that degree of lesser guilt. But if it is larger, then the object must be burned, and he himself is to be judged as guilty of the more serious offense.”

Bernard of Cassino says: “Since the steps have not been observed, I understand ‘the strictest discipline’ to mean the most severe excommunication, so that he is punished as it was said concerning a notorious possessor of private property.”

Boherius, on the other hand, says in his first commentary: “Say that the possessor of private property must first be admonished privately once and again, then subjected to a more serious correction, that is, public correction, and afterward led through the remaining stages.” Yet shortly afterward he says: “Say that ‘let him be subjected to the strictest discipline’ means corporal punishment, which will be discretionary.” In his second commentary, on the words “let him be subjected to the strictest discipline,” he adds, from Cassian’s Book IV, chapter 16, that this means blows or expulsion. Nicolaus de Fractura appears to follow Bernard’s opinion. Thus they explain Saint Benedict.

For the conclusion of this chapter, it will not be out of place to discuss somewhat more fully the punishments of those who possess private property. We believe that this should be done after we have presented the ancient statutes of monastic rules, the decrees of councils and Roman pontiffs, and finally the constitutions of more recent congregations concerning this matter.

Thus, in the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers it is decreed that an abbot who possesses private property “is to be rebuked by the brothers; if he persists in the vice, the matter is to be reported to the bishop; and if, after being corrected by the bishop, he still does not amend, he is to be deposed.”

The penalties of an anonymous author preserved by Saint Basil state: “If anyone possesses something in the monastery or outside the monastery, let him be excommunicated.” And again: “If anyone gives or receives anything outside the will of the archimandrite, let him be excommunicated.”

Saint Columbanus says in his Penitential: “Presumption in undertaking private work: one hundred blows. Possession of any object which necessity has not generally granted to the brothers is to be punished by the loss of that object and one hundred blows. To make, give, or receive something necessary and permitted without an order is to be punished by twelve blows, unless some justification excuses it, so that humble satisfaction may remit the punishment.”

Saint Donatus (*Rule*, chapter 8): “If any woman is found to delight in this most wicked vice, let her do penance with three prostrations.”

The Rule of a Certain Author for Monks (Chapter 17): “If anyone is incurable in this vice, he must be expelled by all the brothers, because the vice of avarice is the most serious of all vices.”

The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, as though explaining Saint Benedict’s meaning (Chapter 17): “If any sister is found to delight in this vice and, after the first, second, or third correction, refuses to amend, let her be subjected to regular discipline.”

Finally, the Rule of the Master (Chapter 82): “If anything peculiar is found in anyone’s possession, let the abbot condemn him to a great and prolonged excommunication, so that no one may dare to imitate him because of the example of that punishment.”

So much for the rules of the ancient monks; I now turn to the decrees of the supreme pontiffs.

First of all, Saint Gregory refused to ordain a certain Constantius, elected abbot of a monastery, because he was devoted to private possessions and had presumed to travel alone, as Gregory himself testifies (*Book X*, Letter 22).

In his decretal, Innocent III says (Chapter *Cum ad monasterium*): “If anyone has anything privately, let him immediately surrender it all. If, however, after this he is found to possess any private property, let him be expelled from the monastery in the aforesaid regular manner and not received again, unless he repents according to monastic discipline. But if private property is found with anyone at death, let it be buried with him outside the monastery in a dung heap as a sign of his betrayal, according to what Blessed Gregory relates that he did in the *Dialogue*.”

Gregory’s action may be found in Book IV of the *Dialogues*, chapter 55. A similar case is found in the *Life of Saint Leufredus*, abbot of Madriacum, section 23.

Gregory IX does not appear to differ from Innocent when, in his constitution for Benedictine monks, he decrees that “monks who possess private property shall be excommunicated by their abbots; and if one who possesses private property is found at death, he shall be denied ecclesiastical burial. No one at all may have a chest with a key without the permission of his abbot, except for an office entrusted to him; and whenever the abbot asks for it, it must be handed over to him. If he possesses it otherwise, he is thereby deemed to possess private property. The sentence of excommunication against those who possess private property shall be solemnly published by the abbots once a year, namely on Palm Sunday, in the chapter meeting. And if afterward a monk is found to have private property, he shall lose whatever bailiwick he possesses; nor shall another be entrusted to him within the year, and not even then unless he has restored what was private and completed a suitable penance. An abbot who knowingly grants private property to a monk, or neglects to punish him, shall be suspended for a time according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.”

And in a bull addressed to the Cluniacs: “Let a penalty also be inflicted upon monks who possess private property according to the custom of the Cistercian order, and let a sentence of excommunication be pronounced against those who possess private property, unless the monk who possesses it restores the goods that must be surrendered to his monasteries.”

Nicholas IV appears to have somewhat mitigated this penalty in another bull addressed to the Cluniacs: “Moreover,” he says, “let the following penalty be inflicted upon monks who possess private property: they are to be reduced to the new state for a year, and during that year they are to eat continually in the presence of the community while sitting on the ground. Against depositaries who return to monks possessing private property the goods that must be surrendered to their monasteries, let a sentence of excommunication be pronounced after prior admonition.”

Benedict XII, in his constitution, chapter 16, declares monks who possess private property incapable of obtaining any office or benefice whatsoever.

As for the councils, the Second Council of Auxerre states (Canon 23): “If a monk presumes to have anything peculiar, let him be confined in another monastery to perform penance.”

The Council of London, held under Lanfranc in 1075 (in Spelman and in the *Life of Saint Lanfranc*, chapter 12), states: “If anyone is found at death to have anything private without the aforesaid permission, and has not returned it before death, confessing his sin with penance and sorrow, let no bells be rung for him, let no saving host be offered for his absolution, and let him not be buried in the cemetery.”

Another Council of London, held in 1200 (in the same source), states: “If he has personal property, unless it was permitted to him by the abbot for an assigned administration, let him be removed from communion at the altar; and if he is found with personal property at the point of death, let no offering be made for him, nor let him receive burial among the brothers.”

The Council of Trent, however (Session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 2), decrees that anyone “found or convicted” of possessing private property “shall be deprived of active and passive voice for two years, and shall also be punished according to the constitutions of the Rule and the order.” What those constitutions are must now be explained.

First, among the Cistercians I find the following law in the *Book of Institutions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order* (Distinction 6, chapter 16):

“A monk or lay brother found guilty of theft or private property shall be last of all for at least a year, or for as long beyond that as seems good to the abbot; every Friday for a year he shall live on bread and water, and for forty days eat coarse bread. A lay brother shall eat on the ground, sit in the cloister during those forty days, and work in silence at whatever is ordered for him; he shall speak only with the abbot, or with the one who presides over the community, or with the master of the lay brothers, and concerning confession. He shall attend all the canonical hours and all chapter meetings; at every chapter meeting he attends during the year he shall be beaten. A monk shall be beaten in the monks’ chapter for forty days. If the theft exceeds the value of twenty solidi, both the monk and the lay brother, after their habit has been removed, shall be sent out at the gate. If the lay brother is to be received again, he shall be received only as a servant, so that for a year he eats coarse bread and does not use linen. If, however, while in this condition he commits theft again, he shall either be imprisoned or expelled from the order altogether. If a monk is received again, he shall first perform the penance for the more serious fault and, nevertheless, while enduring the punishment imposed above on the monk, abstain from the altar office for a year, even if the theft or private possession concerns a small or worthless object. The abbot shall have discretion to moderate the punishment for a very trifling object.”

Elsewhere (Distinction 6, chapter 5): “Those who possess private property shall each year on Palm Sunday . . . be excommunicated by the one presiding over the chapter, wearing a stole and holding a lighted candle and a pastoral staff, if he is an abbot, by the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of Blessed Mary, and of all the saints.”

In the ancient Definitions of the same order it is stated (Distinction 7, chapter 6):

“Those who possess private property, whom the general chapter decrees to have fallen into the snare of excommunication at the very moment they become involved in such crimes, shall each year on Palm Sunday, after the sermon has been delivered, be publicly declared excommunicated in all the chapters of the order by the one presiding over the chapter, wearing a stole and holding a lighted candle and a pastoral staff, if he is an abbot, by the authority of God the almighty Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, and of Blessed Mary, and of all the saints, and of the entire order.”

Add to this the statute of the general chapter of 1227: “A lay brother who is suddenly found dead with five denarii in his possession, and who had not confessed but had approached holy Communion at the solemn feast of the Nativity of the Lord without having made confession, shall remain buried outside the cemetery as he is.”

I cannot pass over here the deed of Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, of the Cistercian order (Volume IV of Baluze’s *Miscellanies*). When Peter the prior had hidden some solidi out of simplicity rather than greed, “when this became known to the abbot, he was so greatly moved that he removed him from his office and ordered him to live in a more remote cell. There he spent several years in great affliction; at last, when the Lord called him from earthly things to heavenly, from labor to rest, and from pilgrimage to his homeland, he happily departed.”

So much concerning the Cistercians; see their ancient Definitions, Distinction 7, chapter 7.

The ancient statutes of the Carthusians define the following against those who possess private property (Part II, chapter 22, section 19):

“Every year, from the feast of the Circumcision to Quinquagesima, the lay brothers and returned members; but the monks, from Quinquagesima to Palm Sunday, shall display and submit to the prior’s will whatever they possess. On Palm Sunday itself, all—monks, lay brothers, and returned members—shall gather in the monks’ chapter. There, without any other sermon preceding it, the customs of the order shall be discussed, and the prior and each priest shall excommunicate every person, present or absent, who, with the intention of concealment, has retained anything worth more than twelve denarii, until he displays it and submits it to the prior.

[Note: [Col. 0561D] In the new statutes, Part II, chapter 5, it is stated: “More than the value of three Tours solidi.” Those who retain such things are, by that very fact, excommunicated, and on Palm Sunday they are to be publicly denounced as such in the chapter.]

“Or if, since the previous Palm Sunday, anyone has given away, otherwise alienated, or even lent anything without permission beyond the aforesaid sum, he shall remain excommunicated until he confesses to the prior, with the period granted for confession extending to the day of the Lord’s Supper for those present, and to the eighth day after their return home for those absent. Whoever thereafter retains anything, or burdens the house with things given away, alienated, or lent above the value of three solidi, and has not confessed as stated, shall, if convicted, be judged to have possessed private property and expelled from the order. If he has offended below the aforesaid sum, he shall be punished at the prior’s discretion. Whoever has secret locks shall be outside the cell and outside the community.”

The reform statutes of the abbots of Saint-Mihiel and Maizières of the Cistercian order, and of the priors of Liget and Glandier of the Carthusian order, issued by the authority of Pope Gregory X for the Grandmontine order, decree the following penalty for those who possess private property (Chapter 4):

“We decree that every year on Palm Sunday the abbot, wherever he may be, and each conventual prior, in the cell over which he presides, shall excommunicate in chapter all those who possess private property, with their stoles placed around their necks and their candles extinguished. If anyone is found to possess private property at the end of his life, he shall be buried in a dung heap.”

The reform statutes of the Benedictine monks of the province of Narbonne, approved by Gregory IX in 1226, state (in *Speculum*, volume VI):

“But if, after being admonished, he presumes to retain anything, let him be expelled altogether from his own house and confined in another monastery, and let him not be received in his own monastery for any reason until the general chapter so decides. If private property is found with anyone at death, let him be buried in a dung heap as a sign of his betrayal.”

The reform statutes of the Black Monks promulgated by the legate Otto in 1238 (in Matthew Paris’s *History*) state:

“We decree that the prelates shall, at least once a year, publicly in the community pronounce the sentence of excommunication against all who possess private property; otherwise punishing them, if they do not repent, especially by the disgrace of burial.”

Other statutes issued the following year in the general chapter (in the additions to Matthew Paris, page 412) state:

“Those who possess private property, and all who falsely accuse others of this crime, shall each year, on the Monday of the first week of Lent, be publicly denounced as excommunicated by their prelates in the chapters, with stole and pastoral staff.”

The statutes of the provincial chapter held at Northampton in 1343, chapter 6, likewise decree that those who possess private property are to be excommunicated on the Monday after the First Sunday of Lent; and the Bursfeld statutes decree the same for Thursday in Holy Week.

The constitutions of the Congregation of Monte Oliveto decree (Part I, chapter 33) that “those who possess private property, and abbots and superiors who do not punish those who possess private property, as violators of their vow, shall incur, in addition to excommunication—from which they may be absolved only by the general abbot, or by another in the article of death—the penalty of imprisonment at the discretion of the general abbot, fasting on bread and water twice a week, on Wednesday and Friday, for a year, and disqualification from every office for six years; none of these penalties may be remitted by anyone.”

The Constitutions of the Celestines (*Treatise I*, chapter 20, section 16): “If anyone is found to possess private property—that is, if he is an official, three tarenes in money or six in value; but if he is a subordinate, from one small denarius up to a carol—let him endure the punishment for grave guilt for as many days as there are denarii in which the person possessing private property is found. If the sum exceeds this, let him endure the punishment for grave guilt at the abbot’s discretion within three months, and let him be deprived of every lawful act, lose his own office, and be disqualified from every office for three years, in addition to the penalties imposed by the sacred Council of Trent.”

Finally, the Constitutions of the Fuliensians (Chapter 33): “If a monk is found to have fallen into the crime of private property, then, along with other very severe penalties, let him have the monastery as a prison for a year, so that he does not set foot outside it.”

## CHAPTER XXXIV. 435 Whether all ought equally to receive necessities

[Note: [Col. 0563A] Another reading: “ought to receive.”]

[Col. 0563]

[Col. 0563A] As it is written [Note: [Col. 0563A] Florence: “As it is written.”]: “It was distributed to each according to what each needed”; here we do not mean that there should be respect of persons [Note: [Col. 0563A] Oxford: “that there should be respect of persons.”]—God forbid—but consideration of illnesses. Let the one who needs less give thanks to God and not be saddened; but let the one who needs more humble himself because of his infirmity [Note: [Col. 0564A] Oxford omits “needs more.”] and [Note: [Col. 0564A] Omitted in several manuscripts, etc.] not be elated because of the mercy shown him; [Col. 0564A] and thus all the members will be at peace. Above all, care must be taken that the evil of murmuring does not appear in anyone for any reason, in any word or sign, however slight. If anyone is found guilty of this [Note: [Col. 0564A] Another reading: “If this is found,”] let him be subjected to stricter discipline [Note: [Col. 0564A] Narbonne: “discipline.”]

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0563]

[Col. 0563B] “As it is written: It was distributed to each according to what each needed,” etc.] Saint Basil follows the same Rule as his guide in the *Shorter Rules*, question 135; Saint Augustine in chapter 1 of his Rule; the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 14; and Saint Leander in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 13.

“Here we do not mean that there should be respect of persons, God forbid, but consideration of illnesses.”] Gregory IX had this passage in view in his Constitution for Benedictine monks, prescribing that “the abbot should give to each and every one according to what is needed, so that there may be no respect of persons but consideration of infirmity.” This consideration, as Boherius writes, ought to be observed in every infirmity of nature, youth, old age, life, and character. Quite rightly so. For, as Grimlaicus says (*On the Rule of Solitaries*, chapter 47), “There must be great discrimination between noble and ignoble, healthy and sick, old and young. Those who come from luxury and those who have never lived in luxury cannot maintain an equal rigor of abstinence, nor can the healthy and the sick abstain equally.” [Col. 0563C] See Saint Basil’s Rule, in Rufinus’s translation, chapter 10.

“Let the one who needs less give thanks to God.”] For the strength and power of abstinence granted to him.

436 “And let him not be saddened.”] By murmuring that he receives less of something than others, as though he were not content with the divine gift. Or, as Saint Augustine says in his Rule (Chapter 5):

“Those who are weak because of their former habits, if they are treated differently in food, ought not to trouble the others, nor should this seem unjust to those whom a different habit has made stronger. Nor should they consider the former more fortunate because they receive what the others do not; rather, let them congratulate themselves because they are capable of what the others are not. And if those who have come from refined habits into the monastery are given some food, clothing, bedding, or coverings that are not given to the stronger—and therefore more fortunate—others, they should consider how far those persons have descended from their secular life to this life, even though they have not been able to reach the frugality of the others who are physically stronger. Nor should the latter be disturbed when they see the former receiving more—not because they are honored, but because they are tolerated—lest the detestable perversity arise that, in a monastery where the laboring poor are made as poor as possible, delicate poor persons should be made.”

The Rule of Tarnat speaks in nearly the same way in chapter 16, as do Saint Isidore in chapter 20 of his Rule and Saint Leander in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 8.

“Whoever needs more is to humble himself because of his infirmity.” [Col. 0564B] And “he should not hesitate to prefer both the healthy and the sick to himself,” as Saint Isidore says (ch. 20). In like manner Saint Leander, instructing virgins, says: “Let the woman who, on account of infirmity, deserves something gentler be humble before the others; let her grieve that she cannot do what the others can, and let her not regard an easing of abstinence as a virtue, but as infirmity” (ch. 8). And Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, says (in his Life, in Bollandus, 1 January): “Whenever he provided more for certain persons than for the others, he urged them all the more to preserve humility, saying to them: ‘Whoever receives more than others from the common substance is debtor to all whose substance it is; and the debtor is helped by humility alone.’” Indeed, who would not humble himself when considering and weighing this saying of Hippocrates: “The more someone needs, the farther he is removed from God, who needs nothing”?

“And he is not to become puffed up because of the mercy.” Which is shown to him, as though he had deserved to receive it by his own merit. Bernard of Cassino says entirely correctly: “He is foolish who takes pride in the fact that a sheep’s fleece is necessary for him against the cold.”

“And thus all the members will be at peace.” That is, if the abbot, considering the infirmities of those in need without respect of persons, and not the ill will of the envious, distributes to each whatever is necessary according to his need; if those who need less are content with God’s gift and do not murmur, but rather give thanks; and if those who need more humble themselves because of their infirmity and do not become puffed up because of the mercy: then all the members—that is, both the abbot, who is the head, and the brothers, who are members of the monastic body—will be at peace, and the God of peace will be with them.

“Above all, let the evil of murmuring be avoided, etc.” These words [437] concern both inferiors and superiors, according to Hildemar and the later commentators: inferiors, so that they do not murmur if something is lacking for them, or if they receive less of something than others, but rather bless God, as Saint Benedict says in chapter 40; superiors, so that they regulate and arrange everything in such a way that souls may be saved and the brothers may do what they do without any murmuring. In this passage the Holy Father sufficiently expresses how earnestly he desires the evil of murmuring to be kept away from the cloisters: “Above all,” he says. You should recognize that what follows is of great importance; those two preceding words make this clear: “Let the evil of murmuring be avoided.” He does not simply say, “Let there be no murmuring,” but “Let the evil of murmuring be avoided,” lest anyone think it a small matter. This applies to any cause, whether lesser or greater, and to any kind of word. Notice that he does not say merely “in a word,” but adds “in any”; and not merely “in any word,” but “in any kind of word,” so that the transgression and the extent of the evil of murmuring may be understood all the more clearly through the wording of the prohibition. See the Rule of Saint Ferreolus, chapter 7.

“But if anyone is found guilty, let him be subjected to stricter discipline.” By “stricter discipline” here they understand either aggravating the fault through private or public correction, or passing from one step to another while omitting an intermediate one—for example, after the first private correction, omitting the second and proceeding to public correction. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius explain it in this way. We have discussed the punishment of those who murmur elsewhere.

## CHAPTER 35. Concerning the weekly kitchen servers

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565A] Let the brothers serve one another, so that no one is excused from kitchen duty except because of illness [Note: [Col. 0565B] Flor., “illness.” Others, “unless it be illness.”], or if he is occupied with some matter of serious usefulness [Note: [Col. 0565B] Hild., Dunst., “matter.”] [Note: [Col. 0565B] Others, “great.”]; for by this greater reward and charity are acquired [Note: [Col. 0565B] In some copies, “and charity” is absent]. Let assistance, however, be provided for the weak, so that they do not perform this duty with sadness, but so that all may have assistance according to the size of the community or the situation of the place. If the community is larger, let the cellarer be excused from the kitchen, or anyone else who, as we have said, is occupied with more important duties [Note: [Col. 0565B] Hildemar omits “or anyone else who, as we have said, is occupied with more important duties.”]. [Col. 0565B] Let the rest serve one another in charity. Whoever is leaving the week of service is to clean the utensils on Saturday. Let him wash the linens [Note: [Col. 0565B] Others, “linen cloths.”] with which the brothers wipe their hands or feet [Note: [Col. 0565B] Others, “wipe.” Others, “will have wiped.”]. Let both the one who is leaving and the one who is about to enter wash the feet of everyone. Let him return the clean and undamaged vessels of his service to the cellarer [Note: [Col. 0565B] Cassino, “return.”]. The cellarer, in turn, is to hand them over to the one entering, so that he may know [Col. 0566A] what he gives [Note: [Col. 0565B] Others, “how many he gives and how many he receives.”] and what he receives. The weekly servers are to receive, one hour before the meal, in addition to the appointed ration, individual drinks and bread [Note: [Col. 0566B] Oxford, “each one is to drink and eat bread for himself.” Cassino, Concordia, Florence, “individual drinks and bread.”], so that at the hour of the meal they may serve their brothers without murmuring and arduous labor. On solemn days, however, let them wait until the Masses [Note: [Col. 0566B] Others, “until Mass.”].

But the weekly servers who are entering and leaving are immediately after Matins on Sunday to prostrate themselves on their knees in the oratory before everyone, asking that people pray for them [Note: [Col. 0566B] Florence, “to pray.”]. The one leaving the week is to say this verse: “Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me [Note: [Col. 0566B] Oxford, “helped”] and consoled me.” When he has said this three times, he is to receive the blessing and depart [Note: [Col. 0566B] Faron, “let those leaving receive the blessing.” Concordia, Florence, Cassino, the manuscript of Saint-Germain: “having received the blessing, he departs.”]. The one entering is to follow and say: “O God, come to my assistance; Lord, make haste to help me.” This too is to be repeated three times by all [Note: [Col. 0566B] Others, “after it has been said three times.”]. Having received the blessing, he is to enter.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0565]

[Col. 0565C] “Let the brothers serve one another.” “Brothers,” says Saint Benedict, the Holy Father—not secular persons or laymen. For it is unbecoming for monks devoted to humility and penance to make frequent use of servants’ ministry in serving them. Hence, in former times the monks of Fulda earnestly begged the Emperor Charlemagne, in a petition presented to him, “that the services of the monastery itself be arranged through the brothers—that is, the bakery, garden, brewery, kitchen, agriculture, and the other services—as they had been among our predecessors” (see Saint Boniface’s letter to Pope Zachary); “for every duty will be performed more devoutly and worthily by the brothers than by a layman or an ill-disposed servant.”

What they had so earnestly requested, the abbots assembled at Aachen under Louis the Pious soon afterward attempted to establish in all monasteries of the monastic order by issuing a statute (canon 4), “that the monks should work with their own hands in the kitchen, bakery, and other proper workshops.” Certainly, if all the utensils of the monastery are to be regarded as though they were sacred vessels of the altar, they ought to be handled not by profane hands, but by hands sanctified through the practice of religious life.

Away, then, with all those crowds of lay servants [439] whom in our own time we see in monasteries, not without some shame of spirit. Alas, how far we are removed from those times when laymen were not even permitted to set foot in the kitchen while the brothers were working there. If anything had to be brought in or taken out by their labor, it was passed in or handed back through a window, as the Statutes of Saint Adalard prescribe in these explicit words [Col. 0566C]:

“Concerning laymen, this is the one and definite judgment: as long as food is being prepared there or prepared food is being served, whether the brothers are refreshed there beforehand as a group or afterward, no one is to enter. If there are any things of this kind that must first be prepared or afterward cleaned or tended, and that have been assigned to laymen, a window, door, or place outside the kitchen is to be established where the brothers may receive what is to be prepared or return what is to be cleaned, and where the laymen may either place these things or receive what has been placed there, so that they have no occasion to enter the kitchen.”

The same discipline, under the harshest penalties, was in force among the Cistercians. In their general chapter of 1195 it was decreed (Cistercian Institutes, distinction 6, chapter 13) “that secular persons are not to serve in the conventual kitchen or in the infirmaries; and if this has been done in any house, the prior and cellarers, for as long as it has been done, are to receive only bread and water every Friday. If the abbot knows of this and does not correct it, he is to confess this fault in the general chapter; nor is any secular person to serve at the abbot’s table within the abbey, except perhaps in the guesthouse of one who is eating.”

Later, however, the general chapter of 1237 moderated this constitution, decreeing “that in abbeys in which there were no more than eight lay brothers, secular persons might be admitted to such service.” The Cluniacs likewise barred laymen with equal religious strictness from entering the refectory while the tables were being set. Their ancient customs state as follows (Book III, chapter 24) [Col. 0567A]:

“The refectorary has three other brothers under him . . . . . after the Gospel of High Mass has been read, they bring wine, so that it may be distributed according to the portions. Whatever they bring, whatever such work they perform, they always take care that no servant appears in the refectory at their summons.”

The manuscript Customs of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon have the same provision in chapter 42. The Rule of Saint Isidore likewise decrees that “at the time when the obligation of taking food is fulfilled, the cloisters of the monastery are to be closed, and no outsider is to presume to be present, lest his presence disturb the brothers’ quiet.”

What is more, in the Rule of Saint Aurelian, not only is access to the kitchen or refectory restricted, but even access to the monastery itself is not freely permitted to secular men:

“The stewards of the monastery, if they are in lay clothing, are not themselves to be permitted to enter. For those services which we establish in this Rule (chapter 19), they may enter with masons or carpenters if something needs to be made or repaired, or if for some definite reason something must be done for the abbot. Otherwise they are to have no permission or liberty to enter.”

What Saint Aurelian says—“if they are in lay clothing”—recalls the ancient custom of the monastery of Saint Gall, according to which even the most powerful laymen were not permitted on Sundays to follow the procession in the cloister unless they were dressed in monastic habit. Ekkehard the Younger testifies to this in these words [Col. 0567B]:

“I myself saw, before the times of the schism among monks which we suffer at the hands of the Gauls, counts and other powerful knights of the region, out of love, following the cross with us through the cloister on feast days; young and old men, some bearded to the belt and dressed in monastic cowls, entering and proceeding with us wherever we went.”

Moreover, from the ancient memory of the fathers the cloister “was held in such great veneration that none of the most powerful men of the world, whether canons or laymen, was permitted either to enter or even to look inside.”

Saint Columbanus, too, had established this discipline in his monasteries. Thus, among the other accusations brought against the holy man by King Theuderic was this one (Life of Saint Columbanus, no. 19, second Benedictine century) [Col. 0567C]: “Why is access not open to all Christians within the more secluded enclosures?” To this the holy abbot replied:

“He did not have the custom of opening the dwelling of the servants of God to secular men and those alien to religion; rather, he had suitable and appropriate places prepared for this purpose, where the arrival of all guests might be received.”

We infer that the same institution prevailed in the monastery of Farfa from the Life of Saint Paldon, no. 7. There Thomas, abbot of Farfa, is said to have invited noble youths who were traveling to Gaul for the sake of conversion to his monastery, addressing them as follows:

“Return with me to the monastery which I serve; and because of the ardor of your desire, although contrary to the monastery’s custom I shall receive you inside, so that you may eat with the brothers, sleep with them, devote yourselves to prayer with them, and go out together to manual labor. Thus, having been tested by these exercises, you may learn in what ways you can fulfill the monk’s purpose.”

But I return to the subject. If it is unbecoming for monks to use the service of laymen in the monastery, still less should they use that of clerics or other religious persons. This Benedictine pope Benedict XII expressly forbids in his Constitution for Benedictine monks, in these words (chapter 18):

“Moreover, to block the way to scandals, we expressly forbid secular clerics or laymen, or monks of another monastery, or religious persons of another religion, from henceforth being assigned in the churches, monasteries, or other conventual places of the same order or religion to provide food and service to the monks.”

Therefore, since neither laymen nor clerics may serve, let the brothers serve one another. “One another,” I say—that is, taking turns by succeeding one another each week, as is clear from what follows; and this practice became common everywhere among monks.

This can be seen in the Rule of the Master (chapter 18):

“We said above that a group of ten brothers under its care contains two superiors; these are to complete seven days of kitchen service by pairing the ten brothers in turns. When the service of one group of ten has been completed in these turns, after all the utensils have been handed over by the cellarer, another group of ten is to succeed them in the exercise. When that has been completed, they are to succeed one another individually, week by week.”

In the Rule of Saint Donatus for Virgins (chapter 67):

“The sisters are to serve one another in every bodily service, both in the kitchen and in whatever daily use requires; they are to succeed one another by turns, except for the mother or superior.”

In the Rule of Saint Ferreolus:

“At appointed times and with properly arranged turns, let those responsible for preparing the food serve one another; and let them exercise authority over one another in an equal ministry.”

Saint Basil says (Sermon 1, On the Institution of Monastic Life):

“Let service in the common assembly be performed by turns: two, according to their order, are to complete all the work required for use during one week.”

Saint Jerome says in the preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius:

“Let them succeed one another in the ministry of the weeks, according to order.”

Cassian says (Book IV, chapter 19):

“Throughout Mesopotamia, Palestine, Cappadocia, and the whole East, the brothers take turns each week in carrying out these duties, so that, according to the size of the monastery, a corresponding number of servers is appointed.”

Finally, in the Life of Saint Marianus at Saint Germanus of Auxerre, a fifth-century monk, the monk Olinitius is reported to have said:

“It is my lot to serve the brothers at table and prepare their food.”

The Egyptian monks alone, or almost alone, had adopted the contrary practice:

“For among the Egyptians,” Cassian writes (Book IV, chapter 22), “whose greatest concern is work, there is no mutual weekly succession, lest under the pretext of this duty everyone be prevented from the rule of work. Instead, the care of the cellar or kitchen is entrusted to one especially approved brother, who continuously performs that work as long as his strength and age permit.”

Yet Saint Jerome, speaking of the Egyptian monks, says: “Each group, with its father, goes to the tables, at which they serve by turns each week” (Letter 22). Perhaps Saint Jerome is referring only to service at table, not to kitchen duty.

“Thus no one is excused from kitchen duty.” The Holy Father assigns kitchen duty to all the brothers, whereas the Egyptian monks entrusted it to one person alone, as Cassian has just taught. The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen imposes it only upon the younger brothers, in these words (chapter 22):

“In all obediences and services in which the younger brothers succeed one another, let each one willingly and cheerfully complete the week of his turn in whatever service he has accepted, without murmuring and with the grace of God.”

The Venerable Turketul, abbot of Crowland, established a similar custom in his monastery, contrary to the Rule of Saint Benedict. For, as Ingulf testifies (History of Crowland), “dividing the whole community into three ranks, so that each rank might recognize and maintain its own status, he decreed that the younger brothers, from their entrance into the monastery until their twenty-fourth year in the order, should undertake all the work of the choir, cloister, and refectory—singing, reading, serving, and observing all the regular practices according to the instruction of their master, and so forth.” Ingulf himself later renewed this law after becoming abbot of the same monastery.

“Except because of illness or if he is occupied with a matter of serious usefulness.” What the Holy Father had stated almost generally, he now moderates with his customary discretion, exempting the sick and those occupied with more important duties from kitchen service. Indeed, it would be inhuman to assign the sick to this duty.

But someone may ask what is, and rightly ought to be called, a matter of serious usefulness. Hildemar answers that it is something which the brothers, recognizing its importance, accept without murmuring and in harmony, because a certain brother is excused from the kitchen on its account. Therefore, “this great or serious usefulness,” according to Bernard of Cassino, “must be evident to the abbot and not unknown to the brothers, lest it become a cause of discord—for example, if one person were excused while another was laboring” [Col. 0569A].

Someone might perhaps wonder whether the abbot should be counted among those occupied with such more important duties. To me there seems no room for doubt, if one pays even the slightest attention to Saint Benedict’s intention: who in the monastery is occupied with more serious matters than the one who has undertaken responsibility for everything? Certainly, if the cellarer is excused because he is occupied with temporal concerns alone, why should the abbot not also be excused, since responsibility for both temporal and spiritual matters falls to him?

What Saint Benedict, the Holy Father, left unsaid, Saint Caesarius expressed in clear and explicit words in his Rule for Virgins, where he says (chapter 12):

“In every bodily service, both in the kitchen and in whatever daily use requires, they are to succeed one another by turns, except for the mother or superior.”

Saint Donatus copies Caesarius in his own Rule for Virgins, chapter 67. Likewise Saint Aurelian, in his Rule for Monks (chapter 22):

“In every service, whether in the order of chanting, reading, or working, let them succeed one another by turns, except the holy abbot, the very old, little children, and those who are so infirm that they cannot rise at all. They are not to be compelled to do what they are unable to do.”

Nor will I deny that other Rules contain a different provision, and that a different arrangement prevailed in some monasteries of our order—especially in the Rule of Saint Ferreolus, which says (chapter 38):

“Three times each year the abbot is to enter the kitchen to prepare food for the community: on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, likewise on the first day of Easter, and also on the feast of the monastery’s particular patron, the holy and most blessed ever-venerable martyr Ferreolus, or at least on the feast of whatever saints’ names that place has been consecrated. There, undertaking the service of a junior, he is to serve at the tables and display humility in distributing the dishes, willingly submitting himself to this holy abasement, which makes the greater man equal to the others.”

And the Rule of the Master (chapter 23):

“Whenever the weekly servers carelessly serve at the tables, on another day at the hour of the meal the abbot is to rise and, with one of the superiors—or two, if the community is large—he himself is to serve at all the tables, so that he may teach them how they should do it.”

As for our own people, Saint Salaberga, abbess of Laon, “served in turn during her weeks the kitchen, or the other tasks [Possibly: ‘cares’] that are customarily performed for monastic affairs” (Life, no. 24, second Benedictine century).

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, as his disciple Ardo testifies in his Life, no. 14, “sometimes worked together with the brothers who were laboring; at other times he cooked their food for eating, and, occupied with the kitchen, also took pains to write a book. Because of the shortage of oxen, he often carried firewood on his own shoulders together with his disciples.”

Of Eigil, abbot of Fulda, Candidus writes in his Life, no. 24 (Benedictine fourth century, part I):
