“He likewise, as he had always been accustomed to do, established and decreed with the counsel and consent of his brothers that those brothers who were known to oversee services outside the monastery should, each week of the year, according to the arrangement of the superior or the deans, serve the brothers living within the monastery with food, drink, and every other convenience appropriate to monastic life, beyond the ration assigned to them, as an honorable consolation—not under compulsion, but so that their means might permit them to serve of their own free will. Yet he himself first of all, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, gladly undertook the beginning of this service as an example to the others.”

The abbots of the Cluniac monastery formerly did the same, as Udalricus teaches (Book I, chapter 46), and this was likewise the common practice of our order. Certainly, abbots who, when leisure permits, lead their brothers by example in these exercises of humility are especially worthy of approval and praise. They should not think that their authority is diminished or their dignity compromised by that from which the holiest men—once illustrious in the world and leaders among peoples—sought all their glory: Saint William, once the most powerful duke and later a monk of Gellone; Carloman, once king of Austrasia and later a monk of Cassino; and Saints Radegund and Balthild, queens of France, to mention no others. See the First Life of Saint Walter, abbot of Pontoise, no. 11, in Bollandus, 8 April.

Nor should we pass over what is recorded concerning the monks of Saint Vincent of Volturno in the Life of Saint Thomas, abbot of Farfa (third Benedictine century): namely, that at suitable times they came to the monastery of Farfa “and performed their weeks of kitchen duty there just as the other brothers of that monastery did.”

Furthermore, Saint Benedict does not seem in this chapter to distinguish between the weekly kitchen servers and the servers at table. Yet he distinguishes the two in chapter 38, where, speaking of the weekly reader, he says: “Afterward let him eat with the weekly kitchen servers and the servers.” Boherius, in his first commentary, explains this passage as follows:

“Whether these servers serve by weeks or by days I do not care, because I do not find it in the Rule; nevertheless, they perform this service for one another in turn.”

Here he clearly distinguishes the servers from the weekly kitchen servers, who served throughout the entire week. Among the Cluniacs, however, the monks of Saint-Bénigne of Dijon, and the Cistercians, the kitchen servers performed both duties.

Concerning the Cluniacs, we should hear Udalricus (Book II, chapter 35):

“When the hour after which the brothers are about to eat has ended, they quickly go out to serve the beans. The one who is chief among the cooks, if he knows the task well and is in suitable health, sends them with a spoon made for this purpose into the bowls; the others carry them to the tables, beginning with the principal table. Vegetables, on the other hand, are distributed in the opposite manner: they serve them beginning with the last table.”

The manuscript Customs of Saint-Bénigne say the same in chapter 35, and add:

“And not only they, but all who carry bowls in the refectory, must exercise this care: they must not carry the bowl so low that they can breathe into it; meanwhile they must not mutter any psalmody, so that they may ensure that its bottom is not dirty; they must protect the rim of the bowl from their clothing; and they must take care not to dip a finger inside.”

The general portion and the pittancia, however, were served not by these men as their prescribed duty, but by the cellarer and others to whom he gave the instruction, according to both Udalricus and the customs mentioned above. The general portion, served on Sunday, Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, was what was presented to each person in an individual bowl. The pittancia, served on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, was what was given to two people in a single bowl, according to Udalricus.

Concerning the Cistercians, the Book of Usages says in chapter 108:

“When there are four weekly kitchen servers, two are to serve on one day and two on another, in turn.”

The cellarer was added to these, according to chapter 76, where it says:

“The cellarer and the cooks are to see to it that both dishes are set out on the tables before the bell rings, if he considers that this is expedient” [Col. 0570D].

This custom may perhaps be reflected in a passage from the Life of Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, Book II, no. 19, where the cellarer is said, at his command, to have prepared the refectory and adorned the tables with cloths (Baluze, Miscellanies, vol. IV).

Moreover, among both the Cluniacs and the Cistercians there was a refectorary distinct from the weekly kitchen servers. Assisted by other brothers when necessary, he prepared the refectory each day and set the tables with cloths, spoons, knives, bread, and wine. His duty is described more fully in Udalricus, Book III, chapter 21; in the Customs of Saint-Bénigne, chapter 42; and in the Cistercian Book of Usages, chapter 118.

“For by this greater reward and charity are acquired.” This may mean that greater reward is acquired from the foregoing—that is, from illness or from a matter of serious usefulness—if the former is patiently endured and the latter discharged with due devotion. Or it may mean that, because all serve one another, greater reward and charity are acquired, and therefore no one should be excused from this duty, lest he also be deprived of the reward.

Saint Basil expresses the nature and greatness of that reward in these words:

“To serve is a great work, procuring the kingdom of heaven. For it is a net of virtues, comprehending within itself all the commandments of God; first, humility, which contains within itself every virtue and brings an infinite multitude of good things; then also this: ‘I was hungry, and you gave me food; I was thirsty, and you gave me drink.’ Shortly before, he advises the one who has renounced the world not to allow another to perform his duties, lest, being deprived of the reward, he receive it while another is enriched by its abundance.”

In order that both a definite reward in the future and charity in the present world may be acquired, this service must not be performed carelessly or lukewarmly. The Apostle does not promise a good standing simply to the one who serves, but to the one who serves well. To ensure that service is performed well and properly, Saint Adalard requires three things above all from the weekly kitchen servers in his Statutes [445]:

1. That they preserve continual silence while working.

2. That the servers speak only about matters that are necessary.

3. “That all of them may preserve this silence profitably for another reward; the psalms,” he says, “are to be sung without interruption.”

He then teaches what manner they should observe in singing the psalms. This discipline prevailed among the Cluniacs, as Udalricus testifies in Book II, chapter 35, where he assigns psalmody to be recited in the kitchen. I also read the following in the manuscript Customs of Saint-Bénigne, chapter 35:

“There is the strictest silence in the kitchen, no voice and few signals, except for the psalmody that is sung.”

Moreover, it will be useful to season silence and psalmody with some pious and inward disposition of the soul, after the example of that remarkable cook of the monastery of Alexandria, concerning whom Saint John Climacus says (Ladder, step 4):

“I cannot refrain from explaining to you the exceedingly rare and wholly singular virtue of that cook of the place. For when I saw him perpetually occupied in kitchen service, yet always present to himself and flooded by an unceasing fountain of tears, I asked him not to begrudge me an explanation of how he had obtained such grace from God. Compelled by my persistence, he replied: ‘I have never appeared to serve a human being, but God. I have considered myself unworthy of all rest, and by contemplating the fire that is present I have accustomed myself to awaken the constant remembrance of the future fire of hell.’”

Saint Basil required a similar disposition of mind in one who serves (Shorter Rules, question 160). When asked “with what feeling of soul one ought to serve the brothers,” he replied:

“As though the Lord himself were being served, who said: ‘Whatever you have done for one of these least of my brothers, you have done for me.’”

No less edifying is his response to the following question, “with what humility should someone receive what is served to him by a brother?” He answered that it should be received “with the humility with which a servant would receive what was served to him by his lord, and with that which the apostle Peter displayed when the Lord served him.” In this he also teaches us about the danger of those who refuse to be served.

This answer brings to mind another which Silvanus, a monk of Saint Pachomius, is said to have given when the brothers asked why he was constantly weeping while eating (Supplement to the Life of Saint Pachomius, in Bollandus, 14 May):

“Do you wish to prevent me from weeping when I see so many holy men serving me, although I am not worthy to wipe the dust from their feet?”

“But let assistance be provided for the weak.” According to Hildemar, the weak are so called in three senses: first, less precisely, those who are delicate and seem by nature unable to perform this kind of duty; second, those who are recovering from illness; third, the lame and those unable to walk without the help of a staff—for *imbecillis* (“weak”) is understood as if it meant “without a staff.” For Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino, the weak are likewise the fragile, delicate, or physically infirm; this amounts to the same or nearly the same thing. Richard of Saint Angelo gives a shorter and perhaps more accurate explanation, calling weak those monks who have little strength.

Assistance is therefore to be provided for such weak persons—that is, one or more companions, as necessity requires. Saint Adalardus seems to have had this passage in mind when he decreed that not all should serve in their regular order, lest it happen that all the old or all the young should at the same time be performing kitchen service.

“But let all have assistance according to the size of the community or the situation of the place.” Smaragdus explains this passage as follows:

“When he says ‘according to the size of the community,’ this is understood according to the number and quantity of the monks. According to the size of the community, a smaller or larger number of servers is to be appointed. When he says ‘and the situation of the place,’ this refers to the building or construction of the monastery. If the monastery is built in a suitable place, where, according to this chapter of the Rule, everything necessary is contained within the cloister, the cook needs less assistance from others. But if it is built in a confined, narrow, or dry location, where they cannot obtain water without labor or have a garden without hardship, more assistance is to be provided for the cooks.”

Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Richard of Saint Angelo, Boherius in both commentaries, Turrecremata, Matthias Lambertus, and Menardus speak in nearly the same way.

“If the community is larger, let the cellarer be excused from the kitchen.” The Holy Father exempts the cellarer from kitchen duty because he is occupied with more important responsibilities. Therefore, if he wishes, of his own initiative or out of devotion, to perform this duty according to the order of his turn, Saint Adalardus nevertheless decides that it should scarcely be permitted to him, in these words (Statutes, Book I, chapter 3):

“The senior cellarer, both within and without—that is, in the refectory, in the kitchen, or in all the dwellings belonging to the kitchen—is to exercise care in everything and for everything, so that no one presumes, by acting or speaking improperly, to handle either himself or what he is doing except in a manner entirely fitting for our religious life. It is neither to be sought nor demanded of that same cellarer that he personally involve himself, as though out of personal devotion, in preparing the dishes and for that reason postpone this care in any respect. Rather, according to the authority of the Rule, he is to seek other assistance if necessary, so that he himself may remain free to provide for the matters of God on every side.

“We do not say this in order to oppose his devotion when it can be done without hindering the care mentioned above; rather, we say it so that, while he immerses himself as though more devoutly in matters that do not belong to him at that time, he may not presume to postpone the definite responsibility imposed upon him to provide oversight.”

Among the Cistercians, however, it belonged to the cellarer “to prepare the dishes for the cooks of both kitchens, to put salt in the general dishes, and to divide these among the bowls, except where the abbot sometimes judged that this could not be done . . . . To prepare bread and wine, or beer, at the proper hour for distribution in the refectory; to add at supper, where it was available, coarser bread for those who ate bread until the third hour at dinner; and to visit the brothers who were eating, both at dinner and at supper, at least once.”

## “When he is leaving the week, on Saturday he shall perform the cleanings.”

447 What St. Benedict understands here by “cleanings” is explained variously by the commentators. Hildemar, almost the earliest of them all, expresses his view as follows:

> “St. Benedict’s intention was that he should do everything during the same week; but now, since the labor is great, because they cannot serve in the kitchen, sweep the cloister, and perform the other cleanings as well, the work is divided in this way: on Saturday the kitchen is swept, and the stone vessels, bowls, and benches are washed. In the following week they sweep the entire cloister—that is, the area before the kitchen and before the refectory. The chapter room and dormitory before the vestiar­y should be swept by the chamberlain, and the area before the basilica by the basilicanus. The refectory, however, the cellarer should sweep; if this is too much labor for him, he should ask the dean for an assistant.”

Hildemar therefore places the “cleanings” in sweeping the monastery and washing the kitchen vessels. Bernard of Cassino, however, defines the cleanings as consisting altogether in three things: first, “the cleaning of vessels”; second, “the sweeping of buildings”; third, “the washing of the cloths with which they wipe their hands and feet.” Boherius and John of Turrecremata hold the same view.

Matthias Lambert, on the other hand, understands St. Benedict to mean only the cleaning of vessels, while St. Hildegard understands him to mean only sweeping. Menardus defends the latter opinion in these words:

> “He shall perform the cleanings—that is, he shall sweep the monastery. Hence the Master says in chapter 19 of the Rule: ‘Let them perform the cleanings of the monastery.’ To perform cleanings is to sweep. Plautus says in *Stichus*: ‘I want to do the cleaning; bring brooms.’ Nor does this passage of St. Benedict include vessels and dishes, since they must be wiped every day.”

In the manuscripts, too, the *Customs of St. Benignus*, chapter 35, says that “to perform the cleanings” means “to wash the cloister lavatory well with brooms and to clean the floor of the latrines. These cleanings are to be done during Lent between None and Sext; at other times, after None, or after dinner if it is a fast day.”

The practical application of this chapter seems to be addressed by what the *Rule of the Master* prescribes in the following words (chapter 19):

> “During that same week they shall themselves complete the service at the tables and perform every duty of the monastery. During that same week all the brothers shall remove their shoes, with brothers from their decade assigned to assist them; with these they shall both remove their shoes and make the footwear, and in the morning, when the brothers are seated in order, they shall hand it back to them. During that same week they shall also perform the cleanings of the monastery, wash the *refrigeria* [washing vessels], chop wood, provide water for the face, and themselves serve water to the brothers entering for Communion to wash their hands. They shall wash the tablecloths, sheets, towels, and dirty articles of the brothers during the hours when they are not cooking. They shall light and tend daily the monastery candles made by the cellarer. For as soon as they have entered the week, as we have said, on the first day after Prime has been said, their first work of service shall be to clean the oratory and spread the mats of the oratory over the floor; throughout all seven days of their week, after Sunday Matins, this shall be the first work of their service that they perform for the oratory.”

See Udalricus, book II, chapter 35; *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 108; *Bursfeld Ceremonial*, distinction 2, chapter 15.

### 448

“Let him wash the linen with which the brothers wipe their hands or feet.” Here the particle *aut* (“or”) is used copulatively, meaning “and.”

“But let both the one who is leaving and the one who is entering wash everyone’s feet.” This is evidently to be understood as follows: the one who is leaving washes the feet, while the one who is entering dries them. This is stated by Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Turrecremata, book II of the *Cluniac Customs*, chapter 35, the *Customs of St. Benignus*, chapter 35, and the *Bursfeld Ceremonial*, distinction 3, chapter 21.

A chapter of the *Directory for the Monks at Reichenau* concerns this practice:

> “On Saturday, when they customarily perform the cleanings, let them wash their feet in silence, so that no opportunity for speaking may be given. Sitting there, let them complete the reading for the collation, and then let them proceed to Compline.”

Likewise, canon 23 of the Council of Aachen says:

> “During Lent, as at other times, let them wash one another’s feet in turn and sing the antiphons appropriate to this service. On the Lord’s Supper, if the abbot is able, let him wash and kiss the brothers’ feet; finally, with his own hand let him offer them the cup.”

Canon 24 adds:

> “If it is the time of the evening meal, let the *mandatum*—the foot-washing—of both the brothers and the guests take place after the meal.”

The *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 108, describes the rite as follows. After the kitchen-week servants have returned the vessels to the cellarer, “let them prepare what is necessary for the *mandatum*. As soon as the signal has sounded, wearing scapulars, let them lay aside their cowls in the chapter house and then come into the cloister. When the abbot—or, in his absence, the cantor—begins the antiphon *Postquam*, the senior of those entering the kitchen shall wash the abbot’s feet and the junior shall dry them; proceeding in this manner, they shall go through the others on the left side. The junior of those leaving shall wash the feet, and the senior shall dry them, proceeding likewise through the others on the right side.

“And so that this order may not be disturbed, if there are two abbots, the lesser abbot shall sit on the right side. Those who finish sooner shall cross to the other side and assist the others; whenever they pass before the one who is leading the collation, they shall bow reverently. The one who washes the feet and the one whose feet are washed shall bow to each other after the washing; likewise, the one who dries and the one whose feet are dried.

“Moreover, no one shall remove his shoes until the abbot has removed his. Once barefoot, they shall take care, as far as possible, that their bare feet do not appear, but remain concealed beneath the cowl. Nor should the sleeves hang down while they are seated; rather, they should arrange them neatly before themselves. Before the reading, all shall have put their shoes on again.”

Three points are to be observed from what has been said.

1. This washing of the feet, which they call the *mandatum*, was performed in some places in silence, as appears from the chapter of the *Directory for the Monks at Reichenau*; in other places it was performed with singing, as can be inferred from the Council of Aachen and the *Book of Cistercian Usages*.

2. It was performed before Compline, according to the chapter of the *Directory for the Monks at Reichenau*, and after supper, according to the Council of Aachen. Boherius nevertheless writes that in the monasteries of Cassino and Subiaco it was customarily performed before Vespers, except during Lent.

3. It was performed in the cloister, according to the *Book of Cistercian Usages* and the statutes of Saint-Germain-des-Prés; and before the chapter-house arch, according to the *Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, chapter 35.

St. Fructuosus copied this rite from our Rule into his own Rule, chapter 9, 449. St. Benedict had received it from the ancient monks. Cassian writes of them (*Institutes*, book IV, chapter 19) that after supper—not on Saturday, as St. Benedict prescribes, but on Sunday—the monks washed the feet of the brothers who had served during the preceding week.

On the principal feast days and their vigils, however, our monks customarily celebrated the *mandatum* not on Saturday but on the preceding Thursday. Among the manuscripts of the customs of Saint Benignus, the following are listed:

> “The Saturday before Pentecost, before the Nativity of the Lord, before the Assumption of Blessed Mary and the Dedication of the Church, and the feast of All Saints; likewise the Purification of Blessed Mary, the solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity, and the Nativity of Saint Maurice, provided that they fall on Saturdays or Sundays.”

In the *Book of Bec Usages* I also find the following statute:

> “If the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord falls on Saturday, the *mandatum* must be performed on the preceding Thursday. The *mandatum* is not moved for any other vigil if it falls on Saturday. But if the feast of the Nativity of the Lord, or any of those feasts that have the first procession, falls on Saturday—since, that is, the invitatory is said with four or three voices—the *mandatum* must likewise be performed on the preceding Thursday. And if the Annunciation falls on Saturday, the *mandatum* shall be performed on Thursday.”

The manuscripts of the statutes of Saint-Germain-des-Prés say:

> “If a double feast falls on Sunday, the *mandatum* shall not be performed in the cloister on the preceding Saturday, but on the preceding Thursday.”

The first person said to have introduced this change is St. Odilo, abbot of Cluny, in an ancient manuscript ordinary of Corbie. According to that source, he decreed that the *mandatum* should be celebrated by the brothers “on the Thursday preceding Pentecost. He also judged that at the Nativity of the Lord, and at the Nativity of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, and at the Assumption of Blessed Mary, if these feasts fall on Saturdays or Sundays, the same should be done on Thursday.”

St. Hugh added to these “the feast of the Chains of Blessed Peter, the feast of All Saints, the passing of Blessed Martin, the Purification of Blessed Mary, and the Dedication of the Church if it occurs outside Lent, as well as the solemnity of the Most Holy Trinity.”

“Let them return the vessels of their service, clean and sound, to the cellarer. The cellarer shall likewise hand them to the one entering, so that he may know what he is giving and what he is receiving.”

St. Isidore, in chapter 19 of his Rule, and the Master, in chapter 16, make the same provision. According to St. Benedict’s intention, says Hildemar, the cellarer should require three things from those who are leaving, with regard to the vessels: “cleanliness, completeness, and number—cleanliness, whether they are clean; completeness, whether they are sound; number, whether they are all present.”

Boherius asks when the cellarer ought to return the kitchen vessels to the weekly servants who are entering. He answers: either immediately after the departing servant has returned them, or at least before Compline, or finally on Sunday after Matins has ended.

Certainly the ancient monks from whom St. Benedict introduced this rule into his Rule handed such utensils over to their successors on Monday, when they began their week, after the Matins hymns (Cassian, *Institutes*, book IV, chapter 19).

According to the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, “immediately after Vespers, if it is a fast day” (chapter 108), “or after the servants’ meal, if it is Lent; or after their supper, if it is a day on which there has been a midday meal, let them return to the cellarer the vessels and everything else they received in the kitchen, and let the cellarer hand them over to the one entering. If any of the things that must be returned are missing, let them make satisfaction in the chapter house and report what is lacking.”

The number and names of these vessels or utensils can be found in Udalricus, book II, chapter 36, and in the manuscripts of the *Customs of Saint Benignus*, chapter 35.

It should be noted in passing that those who had left kitchen service were responsible during the following week for preparing the common fire in winter. We learn this from Hildemar’s words in his commentary on chapter 6:

> “The abbot should have an assigned place where they may warm themselves, and those who have left the kitchen week should make the fire there.”

Udalricus likewise writes (book I, chapter 41):

> “If the severity of winter is so great, there is a workshop in which a large fire is prepared by the brothers who were cooks during the preceding week; and everyone, both greater and lesser, may freely go there, though with the utmost decorum, as is fitting at such an hour.”

Among the Cistercians, however, this duty was assigned to the infirmarian, whose responsibility it was “to make a fire in the warming room during winter after Vigils, or after Matins, or after Prime” (*Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 116).

In the monastery of Corbie, the brothers in turn heated the winter room, according to book I, chapter 11, of the *Life of Abbot Wala* (*Saeculum IV Benedictinum*, part I). In the *Rule of a Certain Community for Virgins*, it is prescribed (chapter 12) that “in the school, if there are penitents, pairs of them shall make the fires week by week.”

Three things are to be observed here concerning the common fire:

1. According to the *Concordia of Dunstan*, chapter 2, the brothers were allowed access to the fire on the Kalends of November.

2. According to the Hildemar passage cited above, the brothers warmed themselves in silence.

3. According to the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 72, they did so decently and not barefoot in the presence of anyone.

### “But the weekly servants shall [take it] one hour before the meal.”

Bernard of Cassino understands the words “one hour before” in this way:

> “If the brothers eat at Sext, these men should receive the *mixtum* after Terce; if the brothers eat at None, they should receive it at Sext; if the brothers eat at Vespers, they should receive it at None.”

Benedict Haeften explains Bernard’s opinion as follows (*Book X, treatise 4, question 9*):

> “To prevent this taking of the *mixtum* from being anticipated too much, I believe that both Bernard of Cassino and the holy legislator should be understood in the passages cited above as referring to the passing or near completion of the last of the three equinoctial hours corresponding to one canonical hour. Thus, the person who is ordered to take the *mixtum* after Terce, when the brothers eat at Sext, should take it toward the end of the fifth hour; the one who is to take it at Sext, when the others eat at None, should take it around the end of the eighth hour, or shortly before None; and similarly in the remaining cases.”

He confirms his view from Smaragdus, who, explaining this passage, writes:

> “When he says ‘one hour before the meal,’ it is understood to mean during that one hour before the brothers eat.”

He also appeals to the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, which prescribes (chapter 73):

> “If it is a day on which there is a midday meal, the signal for the *mixtum* shall be struck in the church with three blows before Sext; but if it is a fast day, with the same number after Sext.”

Here “the sixth hour” is understood as the canonical hour sung in the church before the meal, not as a civil hour of the day.

He further appeals to the *Bursfeld Ceremonial*, where we read (distinction 3, chapter 17):

> “At all times, once that hour has been sung in the church after which the brothers must immediately eat—whether it is Sext or None—if it is a day on which they customarily take the *mixtum*, the reader at table and the servant shall hasten in taking it before the brothers’ meal, lest the meal be delayed on their account.”

Hildemar could also have been added to all these authorities. He explains St. Benedict in this way:

> “When he says ‘one hour before,’ he is not speaking of the end of the hour, but of a suitable interval, so that they may reasonably receive what has been ordered. For elsewhere, speaking of the reader, he says: ‘Let him receive the *mixtum* before he begins to read.’ For example, if it is the time when the brothers eat at None, when Mass is sung at the eighth hour, after Mass all who are to receive the *mixtum*—the kitchen weekly servants, the reader, the guest-master, and those who serve the sick—go together and find a quarter-pound of bread prepared, and one drink for each.”

I would readily agree with this opinion if it did not seem to conflict with what St. Benedict adds: “But on solemn days let them wait until after the Masses.” These words seem to imply that on other days the *mixtum* was to be taken before Mass, or before the hour at which Mass ended on solemn days—for on ordinary days in St. Benedict’s time it probably was not sung publicly—namely, about one hour before the meal.

Indeed, all the French versions of the Rule of St. Benedict that I have seen render this passage: “One hour before the meal.” Charles Cointius, a most learned priest of the Oratory, follows our opinion (*Ecclesiastical Annals of France*, year 544). He confirms it with the chapter of the *Directory for the Five Monks at Reichenau*, which decrees that while the brothers are reading,

> “at the hour judged appropriate by the provost, or by his substitute, namely the senior dean, the bell signal shall be sounded, so that the weekly servants and the other servants, according to the precept of the Rule, may receive the *mixtum* in addition to the prescribed allowance, so that fasting may not be burdensome for them while they serve. The reader, however, shall receive it after Sext, before he goes to read.”

Here the hour at which the weekly servants receive the *mixtum* is distinguished from the hour at which the reader at table receives it.

### “Let them receive it in addition to the prescribed allowance.”

These words can be understood in two ways: either the bread and wine are to be taken from the prescribed pound of bread and hemina of wine; or something is to be added to the prescribed allowance of bread and wine, so that *super* means “in addition to” or “over and above.”

Menardus, Charles Cointius, the French dissertationist on the hemina of wine and the pound of Benedictine bread, and certain French versions of the Rule follow the first interpretation. In a later edition of his dissertation, however, the dissertationist retracted his opinion. In paragraph 32 he argues that *super* is formed from the Greek ὑπέρ (*hyper*), which properly signifies “what is in excess” or “what is over and above.”

Matthias Lambert holds the same view, as does a Cistercian monk in his French exposition of the Rule of St. Benedict. The former translates the Rule into French as “in addition to the prescribed portion,” the latter as “over and above the portion assigned to them.” Theobaldus Artaldus Coelestinus also explains St. Benedict in the same way.

This is confirmed by actual practice, as can be seen in Hildemar and especially in Udalricus:

> “For the *mixtum* they receive only what St. Benedict prescribes: a quarter-pound of bread apart from their own pound, and likewise of wine.”

It is also confirmed by the *Rule of St. Caesarius for Virgins*, which orders that “to those who cook, a measure of unmixed wine shall be added individually as compensation for their labor.” Certainly St. Benedict grants the drinks and bread only because of the greater labor; and when he grants something on account of labor, he usually adds it to the customary allowance, as in chapters 39, 40, and 41.

Moreover, on Menardus’s and the dissertationist’s interpretation—who so greatly reduce the hemina—if the drinks were to be taken from the hemina of wine, scarcely anything would remain for dinner or supper. St. Benedict would then have granted no substantial relief, and it would certainly not have prevented the servants from enduring the burden of their labor.

The Eastern Rule did not grant this indulgence (chapter 6; the *Rule of St. Pachomius*, article 41, says the same). It states that “the one who cooks shall taste nothing before the brothers eat.”

Nor did the *Rule of the Master* (chapter 21), which directs that after Communion, when the weekly servants are leaving the oratory, the abbot should say:

> “Take care, brothers, lest before the common prayer of the table, at the persuasion of the devil, you presume to take anything of food or drink, and so forth.”

### “One drink each.”

According to Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, and Turrecremata, drinks are “small vessels which, when full, suffice for one moderate draught.” The letter of Theodemar to the emperor Charlemagne supports this:

> “We have also sent the measure of one cup, which the brothers who are to serve customarily receive according to the text of the holy Rule.”

### “And bread.”

The weight is not specified. Antonius Perez understands it as a small piece, or, as Smaragdus puts it, a little bread. Boherius explains this “little” portion as not exceeding a quarter of a weighed pound.

Formerly the common practice of our order was that the kitchen weekly servants were granted, with the wine, a quarter-pound of bread as their *mixtum*. This is clear from Hildemar, Udalricus, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and others.

The Camaldolese grant a morsel of bread and a cup of wine. The Cassinese grant as much wine as can be held by the cup from which they drink in the refectory, together with about two ounces of bread. The Fuliensians grant at most four ounces of bread at all times except ecclesiastical fast days, when they allow at most two ounces together with a cup of wine. The Bursfelders grant a quarter of a pound of bread and one third of the daily drink measure appropriate to each person.

Among the Cistercians, the monks’ *mixtum* consisted of a quarter-pound of bread and one third of a hemina of wine; that of the lay brothers consisted of half a pound of their bread, or a larger quantity of coarser bread, together with water (*Ancient Definitions*, distinction 14, chapter 5, and *Institutions*, distinction 14, chapter 14). John Craesbeek did not distinguish this sufficiently; nor did Benedict Haeften when he cited this passage from the ancient Cistercian definitions in book X, treatise 4, question 7.

Boherius also writes that he had seen “in France such servants being given legumes or vegetables, though in a small and modest quantity compared with that given to those eating the meal; I do not disapprove of this,” he says. But this is beyond the Rule of St. Benedict, although the Bursfelders sometimes permit it. In their *Ceremonial* I find the following (distinction 3, chapter 17):

> “On days when the *mixtum* is permitted, the abbot may, when he judges it necessary, grant some cooked dish in place of the *mixtum*.”

Boherius adds:

> “In certain large monasteries I have seen bread given without a fixed measure to those who taste beforehand. But because boys customarily flock there, the master of novices gave a signal of sufficiency, and then all withdrew together at once.”

### “But on solemn days let them wait until the Masses.”

The ancient commentators on the Rule offer various explanations for this exception.

First, Hildemar explains his view as follows:

> “It was customary in that land, as the canons also do today, to begin Sext immediately after Mass. Blessed Benedict therefore wished to abolish this custom. For that reason he said, ‘Let them wait until the Masses,’ so that, because the reader would not dare to eat before Mass, an interval would be created on his account and the custom would be broken.”

Smaragdus gives a different explanation:

> “When he says, ‘Let them wait until the Masses,’ this is understood to mean until the principal Mass, which is solemnly sung by everyone. For there are many monastic servants who hear Mass in the morning, eat, go wherever they wish, and say that they have heard Mass and thus eaten. Foreseeing and prohibiting this fault, Blessed Benedict said: ‘On solemn days let them wait until after the Masses.’”

Boherius, in his first commentary, writes:

> “Perhaps because they must wait for the reader at table to receive this *mixtum*. For at the end of the greater Mass the reader, still fasting, receives permission and a blessing to read; and then understand ‘solemn days’ as Sundays. Or perhaps because on those days each person ought to hear the greater Mass in its entirety and while fasting. Or because on those solemn days all the faithful were required to go to another church and receive a second Communion.”

I believe, however, that there is no other reason for this exception than that they might receive the sacred Eucharist at the solemn Mass while fasting. Boherius teaches this in his second commentary, explaining the words “until the Masses” as follows:

> “So that they may hear those Masses in their entirety while fasting, and in them receive Communion purely and devoutly.”

This is confirmed by chapter 38, which prescribes that the reader at table should enter to read on Sunday after the Masses and Communion.

From these two passages it can be gathered with considerable clarity that the ancient monks of the Benedictine order, at least on Sundays and feast days, as they are called, received the Eucharist as a matter of obligation.

Concerning the monks of Reichenau, the matter is beyond dispute, as appears from chapter 4 of the *Directory for the Monks at Reichenau*:

> “On Sundays let everyone, in the order in which they entered the monastery, approach together to the kiss of peace and to Communion, except those who, because of extreme old age or illness, cannot stand among the others; these shall nevertheless receive Communion separately. If anyone deprives himself of this spiritual gift—that is, of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ—the father of the monastery, who must always be present while they receive Communion, must certainly learn why this has happened to him.”

Concerning the other monks of Germany, the manuscript *German Customs*, no. 21, prescribes:

> “No one shall dare omit Sunday Communion at the time of the twelve lessons, or the kiss of peace, or the offering at its proper time, without the prior’s permission.”

There can be no doubt that St. Benedict imitated the example of the ancient monks. Cassian testifies (*Institutes*, book III, chapter 2) that on Saturdays and Sundays they used to assemble at the third hour for the sake of sacred Communion. St. John Damascene writes (*Life of Saints Barlaam and Josaphat*, book I, *Lives of the Fathers*) that they

> “go on Sundays from their separate little dwellings to one and the same church and receive the divine mysteries—that is, the sacrifice of Christ’s pure body and precious blood, without bloodshed.”

He appears here to be referring to the monks of Sinai, about whom St. Nilus writes in the *History of the Slaughter of the Holy Fathers on Sinai* (*Bollandists*, January 13):

> “On Sundays they come to one church and assemble among themselves after one week . . . . They therefore receive the divine sacraments and welcome one another with a banquet of their ascetic exercises and fitting discourses.”

Cyril relates the same concerning the disciples of St. Gerasimus in the *Life of St. Euthymius*, no. 89 (*Bollandists*, January 20).

Regarding the Pachomians, Palladius—or rather the angel in the *Rule Given to St. Pachomius*—must be heard (*Lausiac History*, chapter 38):

> “When entering for Communion with Christ on Saturday and Sunday, let them loosen their belts, lay aside their sheepskin, and enter wearing only the cowl.”

To this custom should also be referred the answer given by St. Onuphrius to Paphnutius (*Lives of the Fathers*, book I):

> “Kind father, did you receive Communion from someone on Sunday and Saturday?”

He replied:

> “Every Sunday or Saturday I find an angel of the Lord ready, carrying with him the most holy body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ.”

The same is written of St. Severus, abbot of Agde:

> “He took food only on Sundays, after receiving the Eucharist.”

Together with St. Abbot Theonas, they were convinced that it was more just

> “to presume to receive these sacred mysteries every Sunday as a remedy for our illnesses, with the humility of heart with which we believe and confess that we can never receive them according to our merits, than, through a vainly presumptuous heart, to believe ourselves worthy of sharing in them only after a year.”

Here he rebukes certain people who, living in monasteries, thought that they would receive Communion more worthily and devoutly if they postponed it for a year. To them, he could have said with Ambrose—or with anyone else—the following words (*On the Sacraments*):

> “If it is daily bread, why do you take it after a year, as the Greeks in the East are accustomed to do? Receive daily what benefits you daily; live so that you may deserve to receive it every day.”

There were nevertheless some who participated in the divine mysteries even more frequently, indeed daily. Macnus, the monk of the monastery of Peter, received Communion three times each week (*Lives of the Fathers*, book X, chapter 17). St. Simeon Stylites received the divine food every day (*Lives of the Fathers*, book I).

Rufinus writes of Abbot Apollonius (*Lives of the Fathers*, book II, chapter 7):

> “It was his custom that the brothers who lived with him would not take food before receiving Communion at about the ninth hour; afterward they sometimes remained until evening . . . . He also instructed them that, if possible, the monks should receive Communion in the mysteries of Christ every day, lest the one who separates himself far from them should perhaps become far from him.”

The *Rule of the Master* likewise decrees (chapter 16) that every day the cellarer should receive Communion with the weekly servants before the abbot in the oratory and in the presence of the congregation.

In the *Rule for Solitaries* of Grimlaicus (chapter 36) we read:

> “I believe, not by my own opinion but on the testimony of the holy Fathers, that both of these things can be done: celebrating Mass every day and receiving daily, with trembling and fear, the most sacred mysteries of the Lord’s body and blood.”

To mention our own monks as well, St. Dunstan prescribes in his *Concordia* (chapter 1) that

> “after the kiss of peace, every day the brothers—except those who know themselves to be guilty of some crime or of the weakness of the flesh—should not refuse to receive the Eucharist, wholly intent upon the discipline of the Rule, mindful of what Blessed Augustine says in his book *On the Words of the Lord*: namely, that in the Lord’s Prayer we ask not for annual bread but for daily bread.”

In the manuscript *German Customs*, no. 28, we likewise read:

> “Nevertheless, throughout the entire week of Easter, let everyone go daily to the kiss of peace and to Communion.”

Later, however, as the fervor of the monks gradually cooled, the practice first had to be restored. Accordingly, among the statutes of Peter, abbot of La Sauve-Majeure (*Sylva Major*), we find the following (1188):

> “We admonish all and each of our subjects who are not ordained priests to receive the Lord’s body reverently on every Sunday.”

Some years later, in 1198, the same Peter urged

> “that whenever the deacon and subdeacon are vested for any major conventual Mass, they should reverently receive the Lord’s body.”

Later Pope Clement V became more lenient when, at the Council of Vienne, he issued the following decree (chapter *Ne in agro*):

> “Every month, both in monasteries and outside them, with every obstacle removed, all monks individually shall approach confession at least once; and on the first Sunday of every month they shall always receive Communion in the monasteries, unless perhaps there is some reason which they do not delay to make known to the abbot, prior, or the monasteries’ penitentiaries, and by their judgment they either abstain or approach.”

Pope Gregory IX had previously issued the same constitution. Benedict XII later renewed it in his constitutions for Benedictine monks, at least with respect to Communion, which he prescribed to take place at the high altar.

The monks of Grandmont appear to have had this in view. In their manuscript customs, composed by William Pellicer, abbot, we read (chapter 95):

> “The clerical brothers and lay brothers ought to receive Communion at the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, Easter, and Pentecost, according to *De Consecratione*, distinction 2, chapters *Et si non frequentius*, *A quibusdam*, and *Saeculares*. By the institution of the Grandmontine order, the brothers also receive Communion on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, All Saints, and the first Sunday of every month, and on all Sundays when they perform the duties of deacon and subdeacon.”

Bernard of Cassino reports almost the same observance among his Cassinese monks. Explaining the present passage of the Rule, he writes:

> “Religious persons are bound to receive Communion at least on the first day of the month, according to the statute of Pope Gregory IX, and to make a general confession. Our custom, however, is to receive Communion generally on certain feast days, of which there are more than there are months in the year, so that the statute may be observed. In addition, the ministers of the altar receive Communion every Sunday; and whenever the abbot celebrates in the convent, the ministers are customarily bound to receive Communion, as is also done in the Roman Church whenever the supreme pontiff celebrates.”

Today the Cassinese customarily receive Communion every Sunday (*Cassinese Declarations*, published in 1642). Thus, in their explanation of chapter 38 of the Rule, they state:

> “From what Blessed Father Benedict says here—‘after the Masses and Communion’—and below in the same chapter—‘for the sake of holy Communion’—it is shown that the brothers received Communion every Sunday. Therefore we command that this holy and ancient institution of religion be observed in each monastery of our congregation, unless perhaps, out of reverence for some solemn feast, this Communion is postponed or anticipated.”

In the older declarations it was worded as follows:

> “It is shown that the brothers received Communion every Sunday. We exhort that this be done, especially during Lent and Advent of the Lord and on the principal feasts. Nevertheless, we do not impose it except on the first Sunday of each month, in accordance with the Clementine constitution *Ne in agro*, unless perhaps, out of reverence for some solemn feast, this Communion is postponed or anticipated, according to the concession of Pope Eugene IV.”

We discussed the rite and manner of approaching holy Communion in book II of *Ancient Monastic Rites*. I will remark in passing that the ancient monks received Communion not kneeling but standing, out of reverence for Sunday, on which genuflections were not permitted. This is clear from the *Rule of the Master* (chapter 21), which, discussing the manner in which the kitchen weekly servants and the cellarer should receive Communion, says:

> “After a brief prayer, let them receive Communion standing, and let them be strengthened.”

The French dissertationist on the hemina of wine and the pound of bread did not understand this passage correctly when, in the second edition, he interpreted this text of the Master as referring to a communion of charity and prayers. For anyone who reads the whole of chapter 21 of the *Rule of the Master*, no interpretation other than sacramental Communion can reasonably arise. Moreover, the words “let them receive Communion and be strengthened” definitively determine the matter. For among authors of ecclesiastical rites, *confirmare* (“to strengthen”) means nothing other than to receive Christ’s chalice. Thus “let them receive Communion and be strengthened” is equivalent to “let them receive the body and blood of Christ.”

### “The weekly servants entering and leaving shall, immediately after Sunday Matins has ended, prostrate themselves at the knees of all in the oratory.”

Hildemar aptly says:

> “He rightly said ‘at the knees,’ and not ‘on the ground,’ because there is no canonical authority for bending the knees on Sunday.”

Bernard of Cassino says:

> “Do not understand this as genuflection, but as supplication, which must be made before and behind, in every direction. This is a prostration, as it were a rolling in every direction; for on Sunday it is not customarily permitted to bend the knees.”

### “Asking that prayers be said for them.”

After supper, the ancient monks of the East used to gather together to sing, according to custom, the hymns appointed before sleep. Cassian writes of this (*Institutes*, book IV, chapter 19).

### “But those leaving the week shall say this verse: ‘Blessed are you, Lord God, who have helped me and comforted me.’”

They did so at the presbyteral step and while bowed, as we have stated from Udalricus, book II, chapter 35; the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 108; and the *Bursfeld Ceremonial*, distinction 2, chapter 15.

### “When this has been said three times.”

That is, said by the person leaving, and repeated in full three times by the choristers, according to Boherius.

[Col. 0581A] Let the one entering receive the blessing.] By “blessing” Saint Benedict in chapter 11 means the prayer or collect that concludes the nocturnal vigils. Here, therefore, he calls the prayers and petitions recited over the weekly servers a “blessing”; according to Boherius, these are to be pronounced by the abbot, prior, or weekly server, and according to Udalricus, Book II, chapter 35, the Customs of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, Nicolaus de Fractura, and the Ceremonial of Bursfeld, by the weekly priest.

What that blessing was, however, is not clear. Hildemarus gives the following:

> Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that an eternal reward may be given to this servant of yours for the completion of the duty of this week. Through Christ.

Menardus cites another blessing from a manuscript of Saint Victor, containing these words:

> V. Make your mercies wondrous.  
> R. You who save those who hope in you from those who resist your right hand.  
> V. Send him help, Lord, from the sanctuary.  
> R. And from Zion protect him.  
> V. Save your servant,  
> R. O my God, who hopes in you.

Then follows the prayer:

> O God, who said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened”; [Col. 0581B] refresh this servant of yours with an everlasting reward for his services. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you, and so forth.

Smaragdus also records the same blessing in his Commentary, but in the plural. In the Cassinese Breviary, written by hand in the time of Abbot Oderisius, the following is found:

> V. Save your servants.  
> R. O my God.  
> V. Send them help from the sanctuary.  
> R. And from Zion.  
> V. Lord, hear my prayer.  
> R. And let my cry come to you.

**PRAYER:** O God, to whom the vows of humble souls are always acceptable, look upon the services of these servants of yours, our brothers, and bring them to your grace, so that those who have completed this week by serving their brothers with devoted minds may receive from you the fullest forgiveness. Through Christ.

Udalricus and the Customs of Saint-Germain indicate the same blessing. We too use this one.

As for the blessing of those entering, the authors mentioned above describe the following. Hildemarus:

> Grant, we beseech you, almighty God, that this servant of yours may complete with a devoted mind the duty of this week that he has undertaken. Through the Lord.

A manuscript of Saint Victor:

> V. Let your face, Lord, shine upon your servant. [Col. 0582A]  
> R. And teach him your judgments.  
> V. Let your ears be attentive.  
> R. To the work of your servant.  
> V. With the Lord there is mercy.  
> R. And with him abundant redemption.

> Help, we beseech you, almighty God, your servant who is ministering in brotherly service, and mercifully grant him the everlasting reward of his own service, without murmuring. Through our Lord.

Smaragdus pronounces the same prayer in the plural. Finally, the Cassinese Breviary has:

> Save your servants. Send them help.

**PRAYER:** Merciful and most loving God, who everywhere protect and assist your servants, bring to fulfillment the good purpose of these servants of yours, our brothers; increase their desire, so that with upright hearts they may render services to their brothers. Through Christ.

Udalricus and the Customs of Saint-Germain also indicate this same prayer.

The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins prescribes the following to be said by those entering (chapter 12):

> Our help is in the name of the Lord, who made heaven and earth; and: Help us, O God our Savior.

But the Rule of the Master (chapter 19) decrees that those about to enter are to be introduced as follows: [Col. 0582B]

> “Brothers who are about to enter the week, after Prime has been said in the oratory, are to be brought by their superiors before the abbot. A formal request shall be made on their behalf, saying: ‘Command, lord abbot, that the whole community be called together and pray for these brothers who are entering the week of kitchen service, so that, commended to your prayers, they may deserve not to fear the devil’s impediments and may complete everything for the community of God without fault.’
>
> “After these words, those two brothers shall prostrate themselves in prayer before the abbot; the whole community together with the abbot must do the same behind them. After everyone has risen, the two shall say this verse: ‘Guard us, Lord, as the apple of the eye; under the shadow of your wings protect us.’
>
> “When everyone has prayed for them, the two brothers mentioned above shall rise, kiss the abbot’s knees, and give the kiss of peace to their superiors or to the whole community. After the peace has been given, their superiors shall say to them: ‘Go, brothers, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ; enter upon the week. After asking for the blessing, do everything, saying throughout the duties to be performed: “Bless, so that, once it has been blessed, whenever you do it, the accursed devil may have no power there to impede it.”’”

## CHAPTER XXXVI  
## On Sick Brothers

[Col. 0581]

[Col. 0581C] Care of the sick must be provided before everything and above everything, so that they may be served as truly as Christ; for he himself said [Note: [Col. 0581D] Another reading: “will say.”]: “I was sick, and you visited me.” And: “What you did for one of these, the least of mine [Note: [Col. 0581D] Another reading omits “of mine.,”] you did for me.” But let the sick themselves consider that they are being served for the honor of God; and let them not sadden their brothers who serve them by their excesses. Nevertheless, such brothers are to be borne patiently, because from such persons a more abundant reward [Note: [Col. 0581D] Another reading: “reward and charity.”] is acquired. [Col. 0581D] Therefore, let the abbot take the greatest care that they suffer no neglect [Note: [Col. 0581D] Saint Donatus: “that they suffer no negligence.”]. Let a room be assigned specifically to these sick brothers [Note: [Col. 0581D] Another reading: “separately”; another: “above”; another: “over them.”], and let there be a God-fearing, loving, and attentive attendant.

Let the use of baths be offered to the sick whenever it is useful; but to the healthy, and especially to the young, let it be granted more reluctantly. Meat may also be given to the sick [Note: [Col. 0582D] Oxford and Conc.: “to the wholly debilitated sick”; Florence, together with certain manuscripts and printed editions: “to the wholly debilitated and weak.” But our reading is that of the Cassinese witnesses and Hildemarus, and Menardus and Haeftenus approve it.] and to those who are altogether weak, for their restoration. But when they have improved, let everyone abstain from meat in the customary manner. Let the abbot take the greatest care that the sick are not neglected by the cellarers [Note: [Col. 0582D] Florence: “by the cellars.” The ancients customarily read “by the cellarers.”] or attendants [Note: [Col. 0582D] Another reading: “by the attendants.”], because whatever is done wrongly by the disciples is the abbot’s responsibility.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0581]

[Col. 0581D] “Care of the sick must be provided before everything and above everything,” and so forth.] Saint Benedict could prescribe nothing stronger or more explicit for commending care of the sick, and scarcely anything similar can be found in all the rules of the holy Fathers [Col. 0583A], except perhaps in those that copied the text of Saint Benedict, such as the Rule of Donatus for Virgins and that of Grimlaicus for Solitaries.

Indeed, in the Rule of Saint Antony we read (no. 2):

> “When you rise in the morning each day, inquire about the sick who are with you.”

And again (no. 34):

> “Visit the sick and infirm, and fill their measures or vessels with water.”

In the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius:

> “If someone of this kind is afflicted by illness, the one in charge must provide for how the illness is to be supported.”

In the Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 20):

> “Whoever falls ill is to be led by the superior of the house to the dining room of the sick. If a little cloak, tunic, or anything else necessary for covering or eating is needed, the superior himself shall receive it from the ministers and give it to the sick man.”

In the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Monks (chapter 17):

> “Let the sick be treated so that they may recover more quickly.”

In the Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks (chapter 53):

> “Let care and attention be given to them until they recover.”

[Col. 0583B] The Rule of Tarnat prescribes (chapter 21) that a capable person be appointed

> “who will serve the sick with compassion, regularly maintain monastic discipline, and rationally provide what is appropriate for the sick.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore has the same provision in chapter 20. But the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 10) says:

> “The sick are to be supported with every mercy and compassion, and their illnesses are to be relieved by suitable service.”

In another Rule (chapter 7), the sick are to be

> “supported with such service that they neither seek the affection of relatives nor the luxuries of cities; but the cellarer and superior are to provide whatever they need.”

Finally, the Rule of the Master (chapter 70) says:

> “Brothers who wish to show how full they are of charity should visit, console, and serve sick brothers with devoted effort.”

But Saint Benedict surpasses all these. For he does not simply command that the sick be cared for; rather, he says that their care must be provided before everything and above everything, so that they may be served as truly as Christ. In his Rule he prescribes many things to be done or avoided before everything; but, as Hildemarus observes, he wanted only the care of the sick to be provided before everything and above everything:

> “Because,” he says, “nothing is to be done with such zeal as service to the sick; nor is even the church to be attended to with such zeal as the house of the sick.”

Moreover, concerning the words “before everything and above everything,” Hildemarus adds:

> “It must be understood that ‘before everything’ pertains to time, and ‘above everything’ to zeal: before all else, care of the sick is to be undertaken; and above everything—that is, with greater love, diligence, and zeal than the other things.”

Bernard of Cassino explains it in the same way:

> “Understand ‘before everything and above everything’ as follows: before all other works, care is to be given to the sick; and above everything means with greater love, frequency, constancy, and attention than to the other things.”

Boherius has the same interpretation. To commend this care of the sick still further, Benedict adds:

### “So that they may be served as truly as Christ.”

“Truly,” say Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, [Col. 0583D] “because it is a true reality that Christ is served in the sick brother.” Hence Saint Bonaventure devoutly exclaims (Stimulus of Love, part II, chapter 7):

> “Why, soul, are you anxious all day in pursuit of Christ? I will show you, bride, the one whom your soul loves: surely he lies in the infirmary; there he is distressed, there he is tormented by pain. Run, serve him, and have compassion on him in his illness. Let us no longer ask him, nor say to him, ‘Where do you lie? Where do you rest at midday?’ For we already know the place. We know that he lies in the infirmary; nothing remains except to render service.”

### “For he himself said: ‘I was sick, and you visited me; and what you did for one of these, the least of mine, you did for me.’”

Attending to this saying of the Savior, Saint Basil (in Rufinus, chapter 30), when asked “with what affection we ought to minister to sick brothers,” replies:

> “As though we were offering service to the Lord himself, who said: ‘Whatever you do for one of these least of my brothers, you do for me.’”

The Egyptian monks undoubtedly had this in mind. Saint Jerome writes of them (Letter 22):

> “If someone begins to fall ill, he is transferred to a larger room, and is so carefully supported by the service of the elders that he seeks neither the luxuries of cities nor a mother’s affection.”

And of the Tabenna monks the same Jerome writes (Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius):

> “The sick are supported by marvelous services, and food is prepared for them in every abundance.”

### “But let the sick themselves consider that they are being served for the honor of God.”

Let them conduct themselves as those ought to conduct themselves who represent Christ and in whom Christ is being served.

### “And let them not sadden their brothers who serve them by their excesses.”

To understand the mind of Saint Benedict more fully, we must observe that sick people can sadden the brothers who serve them in many different ways and by many kinds of excess—if I may put it so.

First, by an excess of sadness: when, weighed down by the burden of illness, they make themselves excessively troublesome and grieve over their illness more than is reasonable, far removed from that venerable old man who, “when he was frequently ill in body and languishing, happened one year to have no illness at all; and for that reason he wept and bore it heavily, saying: ‘You have abandoned me, Lord, and have not wished to visit me in the present year’” (Rufinus, Book III of the Lives of the Fathers, no. 158).

Such people should be addressed with the salutary advice of another old man. As Rufinus writes (ibid., no. 157), this old man said to his sick disciple:

> “Do not grieve, son, over the illness or wound of your body. For it is the highest religion that in illness one should give thanks to God. If you are iron, you are losing your rust; but if you are gold, tested by fire, you are progressing from great things to greater. Do not be anxious, then, brother. If God wishes you to be tormented in your body, who are you to take it badly? Endure, then, and ask God to grant what he himself wills.”

Nor is it necessary here to propose the example of Saint Theodore of Sykeon (in his Life, no. 93; in the Bollandists, April 22), who, afflicted by a wound in his body, “said that it had been given to him by God so that he might give thanks to him continually.”

Second, they sadden their attendants by an excess of complaints: when, unable to endure their illness, they add murmuring to their sadness, and sometimes even insults.

Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 7):

> “Let such persons be admonished with such care that not even the slightest or lightest word of murmuring may proceed from their mouths; but in their illness let them always give thanks to God with a cheerful mind, without interruption, with [an unclear, printed ‘tulta’] occasion of murmuring, and with true contrition of heart. And let the brother who ministers to them dare in no way to offend. If, however, as we have said, any trace of murmuring proceeds from their mouths, let them be rebuked by the abbot and admonished not to presume to do such things again, so that the one entrusted with this ministry may report them.”

Hugh of Victor, or whoever the author may be, perceptively notes that religious who are ill, both perfect and imperfect, ordinarily complain for four reasons: namely, about the illness, the medicine, the food, and the order of things.

The imperfect complain about the illness “because they bear the burden of illness unwillingly” (Book I of The Cloister of the Soul, chapter 12); about medicine, because, as they say, they are not assisted with brotherly charity; about food, because it is not supplied sufficiently, or in the manner or at the time they wish; and about the order of things, because they attribute the cause of their illness to the severity of the order, and thus lose badly what they had done well.

The more perfect, however, commonly grieve over the illness because they cannot share in the labor of the brothers; over medicine, because the Church suffers expense on account of their illness; over food, because they eat delicate things while doing nothing, and because someone serves them while they serve no one; and over the order of things, because they are separated from the assembly of the brothers and treated more delicately.

But if they hear from their bed the voices of the brothers singing psalms in choir, they meditate on the psalms, praying in the chamber of their heart with the doors closed. Although they have spent the whole night awake, driven by their pains, they nevertheless judge blessed those who labor through part of the night in God’s service. They do not leave the edge of their bed, yet they think happy those who patiently endure the weariness of the cloister. They confess that they fulfill nothing of the order; but, if I am not mistaken, they fulfill it all.

They are confined within the cloister of illness; they are disciplined by the rods and thorns of anxieties and pains. They fast, keep vigil, and labor, because illness denies them food, sleep, and rest. Yet if a more comfortable bed is prepared for them, or if they are compelled to sleep without their leggings, they fear ending their life in such a condition as though they had committed some crime. Such people need consolation, lest they fail through bodily distress or the affliction of the inner person.

The imperfect, however, should consider that they are being served for the honor of God—not by servants or persons inferior to themselves, but by brothers. And why do I say “by brothers,” when Saint Basil asserts that services are to be received from attendants as from God [in the Rule according to Rufinus, chapter 30]? Saint Antony taught the same thing when, reproaching a man with elephantiasis who had inflicted many injuries upon the monk Eulogius, who had served him for fifteen years, he said (Book VII of the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 19):

> “Do you not know that the one who ministers to you is Christ? How have you dared to speak such things against Christ? For this man has subjected himself to service and attendance for Christ’s sake.”

Third, sick brothers sadden those who serve them by an excess of their own demands when they refuse to take the remedies offered to them. Sometimes this proceeds from the sadness, murmuring, and impatience mentioned above; sometimes from a less mortified disposition, which rejects remedies because of their harshness and bitterness; sometimes from lack of judgment; and sometimes from a pious desire for greater penance.

But Saint Basil shows, from the example of the Apostle Peter, what danger such people incur (in the Rule according to Rufinus, chapter 30). For this reason, even unwilling patients must be compelled to accept comforts, according to the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 12, and the Rules of Saint Caesarius for Virgins, chapter 39, and Saint Donatus, chapter 12:

> “And let them be absolutely confident,” Saint Caesarius adds, “that whatever they receive at any hour by the dispensation or command of the elder, they will receive Christ in that repose.” [Note: [Col. 0585] It may perhaps be read: “that whatever they receive, they may receive”; the printed edition.]

Fourth, sick people are excessive toward the brothers serving them when they demand remedies that are difficult or scarcely possible to obtain. Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, addresses such persons in this statute (Statutes of Guigo, chapter 38; Ancient Statutes of the Carthusians, part I, chapter 44):

> “The sick, according to the words of Blessed Benedict, must be carefully admonished not to sadden those who serve them by asking for excessive or impossible things, or perhaps by murmuring. Let them remember the purpose they have undertaken and consider that, just as the healthy must differ from healthy secular people, so the sick must differ from sick secular people; and let them not ask in the wilderness for things scarcely found even in cities.”

Abbot Isaac clearly understood this. Suffering from a dangerous illness, he refused to taste the little porridge offered him by a brother, into which embers had been placed, saying:

> “Indeed, brother, I should like to remain in this illness for thirty years.”

Fifth, they are excessive when they ask for remedies that, because of their cost, conflict with the monastic poverty they have vowed.

To such people Saint Bernard would say what he once wrote to the brothers of Saint Anastasius (Letter 321):

> “Your venerable abbot asked one thing of me, which seems to me not at all good; yet I believe that I too have the Spirit of God and the counsel of God in this matter. I know that you live in an unhealthy region, and that many among you suffer from illnesses. But remember who said: ‘I will gladly glory in my infirmities, so that the power of Christ may dwell in me’; and, ‘When I am weak,’ he says, ‘then I am strong.’
>
> “I certainly sympathize with bodily illness, but the illness of souls is much more to be feared and avoided. Therefore it is not at all fitting for your religious life to seek bodily medicines, nor is it beneficial to your salvation. It is tolerable sometimes to take something made from humble herbs, such as befits the poor; and this is occasionally done. But to buy medicinal substances, seek physicians, and take potions is unbecoming to religious life and contrary to purity—especially to that of our order. It is consistent neither with honor nor with purity. All these things are sought by the pagans.
>
> “But we know that those who live according to the flesh cannot please God. Spiritual things must therefore be compared with spiritual things, and the potion of humility must be sought; and we must cry out with our whole heart: ‘Heal my soul, Lord, because I have sinned against you.’
>
> “To this health, dearest brothers, devote yourselves; pursue it, preserve it. For human salvation is vain.”

Fastredus, third abbot of Clairvaux, writes similarly (among the letters of Saint Bernard, Letter 397):

> “You offer in your defense the pains of your stomach and head, and the fact that ordinary foods harm you. You are entirely mistaken if you think that a monk may follow the medicines of secular people. We came to the monastery to seek discomforts for the body, not comforts and pleasures.
>
> “If weakness gave Saint Paul strength, why do you try to drive from your house the cause of so many blessings? Believe me, my father, I often saw Saint Bernard eat porridge made from flour, with oil and honey added, and do so cautiously in order to warm his stomach. When I reproached him for this austerity, he answered me: ‘My son, if you knew the obligation of a monk, every morsel you eat would have to be moistened with tears. For we enter this monastery to lament our own sins and those of the people; and by eating the bread that they have prepared by their labors, we eat their sins, so that we may mourn them as our own.’
>
> “He also added: ‘It is not enough for a monk to plead illness. For our holy Fathers and elders sought out damp and sloping valleys for building monasteries, so that often sick monks, even with death before their eyes, would not live securely.’”

How many of the ancient monks never administered bodily medicines to themselves, but relying solely on divine hope used this one remedy: to use no remedy at all. And why do I speak of monks, when we read that not a few women—fragile and weak vessels indeed—entirely rejected every kind of medicine?

I would be more lengthy if I attempted to go through them individually. Yet I cannot omit the remarkable virgins of a certain monastery in Egypt, of whom an anonymous author writes in the Life of Saint Eupraxia, no. 6 (Bollandists, March 13):

> “None of them ever washed her feet with water. As for the bath, it is superfluous to speak of it. When they heard it mentioned, they vehemently condemned it, judging even the mention of it to be full of shame and disgrace; and, as though it were an abominable thing, they could not even bear to hear it. And whenever one of them happened to fall ill, no fomentation or medical aid was given to her. If any one of them became sick, she accepted it as a very great blessing from God and endured the illness until the Lord’s visitation overtook her. None of them went outside the doors.”

The example of Jonah, a monk of the Monastery of Monchonsis, is also astonishing. After having lived for eighty-five years under the laws of Saint Pachomius, “all the brothers affirmed about him that no one knew at all what or how the public place of the sick was, or what foods the sick ate” (Supplement to the Life of Saint Pachomius, no. 14, in the Bollandists, May 14; see also ibid., no. 30, and John Moschus, Spiritual Meadow, chapter 18).

We do not relate these things as though we considered it altogether unlawful for a monk to consult physicians and use medicines. We present them only to restrain the excessively anxious care that some devote to preserving their health, and to recommend the use of remedies appropriate to the poor and to men devoted to penance. One must think not so much about one’s constitution as about one’s profession: we are monks, not physicians. It is the physician’s task to preserve life; ours is to diminish it and, insofar as it is lawful, to hasten toward death.

This was formerly Saint Bernard’s judgment, and this was Guigo’s mind and opinion. Hence in his statutes he says:

> “Except for cauterization and bloodletting, we use medicines very rarely.”

See the book On the Duties and Perfection of Monks, chapter 22.

Sixth, the sick are excessive when they seek remedies harmful to themselves. When cold remedies suit them, they desire hot ones, and conversely. Saint Pachomius says of such people (article 20):

> “The sick man may not enter the dining room and eat what he desires unless he is led there to eat by the attendant appointed for this matter.”

Saint Augustine likewise says (Rule, chapter 12):

> “If he wishes something and it perhaps is not expedient, his desire is not to be obeyed. Sometimes, even if what pleases him is harmful, what pleases him is believed to be beneficial.”

Finally, the Constitutions of the Fulda monks say (chapter 36):

> “The sick are to obey their spiritual physicians for the salvation of the soul, and their bodily physicians and the infirmarian for the health of the body.”

[Col. 0587B] Seventh, among the excessive must also be numbered those who seek useless remedies, or at least remedies for minor illnesses that they could cure by patience alone, without any assistance from physicians. Peter of Blois sharply censures such people in these words (Book on Job, chapter 1):

> “If a religious man finds that his pulse is rapid, his urine inflamed, or his appetite dull, he consults physicians, examines medicinal substances, and prepares electuaries. He uses no condiments unless they are seasoned with cinnamon, clove, and nutmeg.
>
> “How hateful it is in a man who ought always to have been speaking about the celestial hierarchy that he learns to discuss hierapicra and hieralogadi [sic]. This religious man is a disciple of Epicurus rather than of Christ.
>
> “‘This,’ he says, ‘harms the head; this the eyes; this the stomach; this the liver. Butter is changeable by nature; beer causes wind; cabbages are melancholic; leeks inflame bile; peas produce gout; beans constipate; lentils blind; cheese is universally the worst thing.’
>
> “‘Standing long for prayer weakens the nerves; fasting disturbs the brain; keeping vigil dries the body.’ Are these distinctions found in the Gospel or in the Prophets? Certainly they are not part of the institution of Blessed Benedict; flesh and blood reveals such things to the miserable.”

Thus far Peter of Blois.

What would he say about those who, affected by no illness, take what they call preventive medicines? Without doubt he would exclaim with Saint Bernard (Bernard, Apology to William, chapter 8):

> “Medicine is excessively delicate when one is bandaged before being wounded; to mourn a limb that has not been struck; to place one’s hand upon it before the blow has even been received; to apply ointment where there is no pain; to put on a plaster where there is no cut.”

Eighth and finally, those must be counted among the excessive who flee to their father’s house for the sake of their health. I will oppose to them nothing other than this decree of the third Rule of the Holy Fathers (chapter 12):

> “We also specially establish, for the preservation of reputation, that no monk who has fallen ill, leaving the monastery, be entrusted to the care of his parents; for we judge that he is more likely to be polluted by the sight or hearing of secular spectacles than to be cleansed of his illness.”

But enough about this. I return to the text.

### “Nevertheless, such brothers are to be borne patiently.”
