If they happen to make themselves somewhat troublesome:

> “It is fitting for the healthy to bear the sick rather than to be borne by the sick; for we must bear the sick patiently, so that in turn we, when sick, may be borne patiently by the healthy,”

says Smaragdus.

Saint Augustine adds (Rule, chapter 12):

> “If pain is hidden in the body of a servant of God, let what she says hurts her be believed without hesitation.”

### “Because from such persons…”

That is, from troublesome, excessive, and all other sick persons.

### “A more abundant reward is acquired.”

“For patience, labor, good intention, and holy devotion,” says Bernard of Cassino. Hence, when a certain brother asked which of two works was greater—one man’s fasting for six days or another’s service to the sick—the old man replied (Book VII of the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 19):

> “If the one who fasts for six days were to hang himself by the nostrils, he would not be like the other in the sight of God.”

Indeed, while caring for others we lift ourselves up; and while striving to cleanse the bodies of others, we ourselves wash away the filth of our souls and make ourselves much more acceptable to God.

What is reported of John the Younger of Thebes, a disciple of Abbot Ammon, is truly remarkable. Rufinus writes (Book III of the Lives of the Fathers, no. 155) that he

> “served the old man during twelve years while he was sick. Yet when the old man saw him laboring, he never addressed him with a gentle word. When he was passing from the body, however, while other old men were sitting nearby, he took John’s hand and said to him three times: ‘May you be saved, may you be saved, may you be saved.’ Then he handed him over to the old men, saying: ‘This is not a man but an angel, who for so many years served me in my illness, although he never heard a kind word from me.’”

See also Saint Dorotheus, Instruction 14.

### “Therefore, let the abbot take the greatest care that they suffer no neglect.”

From what the Holy Father said at the beginning of this chapter, he draws the conclusion: If the sick are to be served as Christ, then let the abbot take the greatest care that they suffer no neglect.

The commentators reduce this care principally to two heads: matters pertaining to the restoration of bodily health, and matters pertaining to the advancement of the soul’s salvation. So Bernard of Cassino, Boherius in both his commentaries, John de Turrecremata, Matthias Lambertus, John Craesbeeck, and Benedict Haeftenus.

Saint Benedict himself explains in what follows the matters that concern bodily care. Here we should merely note in passing what Gregory IX says in his constitution to Benedictine monks:

> “We command that sick brothers be provided with food, beds, attendants, and other necessities according to what their illness requires and what is contained in the Rule. If an infirmarian is found deficient in any of these matters, he is to be punished with a fitting penalty by his own abbot; or, if an abbot or prior is deficient, by the visitor when he comes to the place.”

See the constitution of Otho, legate in England, in the year 1248, in Spelman, volume II of the Councils of England, page 287.

Saint Benedict did not define anything here concerning care of the soul, but seems to have left the whole matter to the abbot’s prudence and discretion. Bernard of Cassino defines it as consisting in this: “that the sick repent of their sins, receive the sacraments, hear the regular Office, and be visited, consoled, and admonished.”

First, therefore, the abbot must be solicitous that, when a sick man begins to be dangerously ill, he fortify his way with the most holy sacraments of penance, extreme unction, and the Eucharist. I say, when he begins to be dangerously ill. For otherwise it was not customary for sick men who ate meat on account of their illness to celebrate Mass or to be refreshed by receiving holy Communion. We have a notable statute concerning this in the ancient manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon:

> “Those who, for the restoration of their flesh, temporarily live in the house of the sick and eat meat are to abstain from receiving holy Communion. But those who entirely and always abstain from meat wherever they live may, on Sundays and on the greater feasts, if they wish, receive Communion at Saint Benedict’s.” [Note: [Col. 0587D] This was the infirmary chapel.]
>
> “Nevertheless, those who eat meat may receive Communion like everyone else if one of those five principal solemnities should occur.”

The same is read in the manuscript Customs of the monastery of Cluny, chapter 51, and the Farfa Customs agree:

> “A brother leaving the house of the sick may sing Mass on that very day, if he wishes, after making satisfaction in the chapter, because as long as he was in the sickroom, [Col. 0589A] we did not permit him to sing Mass.”

This also explains the passage from the Statutes of Lanfranc (chapter 24), where it is prescribed that from the day on which the sick man received the sacred viaticum, “unless he improves, he is not to eat meat,” because he then received Communion every day, as we saw in Book V of On the Ancient Rites of Monks.

Indeed, sick people who ate meat were treated as though excommunicated: they were separated from the common dwelling of the brothers, deprived of the most holy sacraments of the Church, and alienated, as they say, from every communal exercise. They were not permitted to join the assembly of the brothers unless they had first been solemnly reconciled in chapter.

## Secondly

According to Bernard of Cassino, the abbot must take care that the sick hear the regular office; for, as Hildemar says, all the offices must always be sung before the sick. This was formerly the common practice of our order, as could be demonstrated by almost innumerable testimonies and statutes. Pope Victor III supplies us with a notable example in Book II of his *Dialogues*, where he writes:

> “There was a certain brother named John who, oppressed by age and illness, was drawing his last breath. One day, when some of the brothers had come to him, as was customary, to chant the morning praises, he restrained them as best he could, saying: ‘I do not wish you to chant the canonical hours for me any longer, because the lord abbot has just come to me, together with many brothers dressed in white garments, in order to visit me by grace; and while they were chanting the morning office for me, they said that shortly they would come here, take me with them, and so forth.’”

He adds:

> “What I have reported I found written in a certain old little page, in a style sufficiently unskilled.”

The case reported by Bede the Venerable concerning Saint Benedict Biscop is similar. When he was ill, “because he could in no way rise to pray, and could not easily raise his tongue and voice to complete the regular course of psalmody, the prudent man, prompted by religious devotion, learned to call some of the brothers to him at each hour of the daily or nightly prayer. While they recited the customary psalms, sounding them out in two choirs, he himself, singing with them as far as he could, supplied with their help what he had been unable to do alone.”

The same discipline prevailed in other English monasteries. At Crowland, when the monk Clarembald was ill, Abbot Turketul “did not leave him day or night, but, lying beside him, chanted the regular service in the sick man’s ears,” as Ingulf, abbot of that same monastery, writes (*Ingulf, History of Crowland*, year 974). Likewise, at Jumièges, when Hugh the precentor was ill on the vigil of Saint Valentine, the brothers said to him, as reported by Balderic, bishop of Dol, in his *History of the Translation of Saint Valentine* [in the Bollandists, 14 February]:

> “You will not be able to go to church; therefore you must celebrate Vespers here separately. We shall remain here with you and solemnize it as best we can.”

Udalric confirms all this in Book III, chapter 29, where a brother who wishes to keep vigil beside a sick man is permitted to do so, “especially if he is the sort of person who can chant the regular hours for the sick man and, when he is approaching his end, read the Passion to him.” The *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 68, likewise permits the priest who is to sing Matins for the sick to leave the choir after the hymn has been begun.

These services were performed either in the sick man’s own room or in the oratory, which, as Hildemar says, “the infirmary ought to have nearby, so that they may at least hear Mass while lying down and receive Communion.” This applied when they abstained from meat, or when one of the five principal feasts occurred, on which alone, according to what was said above, sick persons who ate meat were permitted to eat the flesh of the spotless Lamb. It applied when the sick man’s weakness was such that he could not rise from his bed. Otherwise, whether by day or by night, they discharged the duty of divine service together in the aforesaid oratory, as may be seen in Udalric, Book III, chapter 25; in the manuscript *Customs of Saint Benignus*, chapter 46; in the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 92; and in the *Bursfeld Ceremonial*, distinction 3, chapter 30.

This is especially clear in the *Customs of the Monastery of Farfa*, which contain the following remarkable provision:

> “When sick brothers have been sent to the infirmary on account of their illness, as soon as the signal sounds for the nocturnal service, they too shall rise and come to the oratory of Saint Mary. There they shall pray as the Lord grants them strength, and then, having taken their seats (sic), remain in their places. When the signal is sounded again, they shall fortify themselves with the sign of the holy cross and begin the Gradual Canticle. Those brothers who are unable to rise shall have the servants who attend them go and bring them into the church, supporting them with their arms, and place them as best they can. No one should regard this as an unwelcome burden, since we have often seen a brother die from this life and pass to Christ on that very day, even breathing out his spirit in the church itself. Who could doubt that such men immediately enter the kingdom of heaven? Divine works are sweet to those who desire them and bitter to those who do not. Thus they must perform the work of God in every respect as those in the monastery do, except that they should say it lightly and quickly, without making an interval; they should entrust it to God’s ears, and, when the work of God is completed, return to the dormitory. Those, however, who are so overwhelmed by the severity of their illness that they cannot rise at all, as soon as the nocturnal service has been celebrated in the monastery, let the official in charge permit two brothers to chant the divine work for them.”

## Thirdly

Bernard of Cassino wishes the sick to be visited and the abbot to console them. We spoke above, in connection with chapter 4, about the visitation of the sick. Here I shall add only one statute from the *Customs of the Monastery of Farfa*:

> “Whenever the lord abbot returns from anywhere, he must come there and inquire of each person what ailments he has, whether of the soul’s character or of bodily health, and whether he suffers any necessity or neglect from the servants or cellarers. He must also see whether any of them has recovered sufficiently, and grant him permission to return to the cloister.”

## Fourthly

They are to be admonished to take care of their own salvation, lest under the pretext of illness they cast aside all observance of the Rule. Under the term “admonition,” reproofs and corrections are also to be understood. Thus Udalric writes:

> “The visitors,” he says (*Book III*, chapter 27), “frequently visit the infirmary and carefully investigate how the sick men are doing. If the infirmarian notices any negligence, especially in talking, he reports it in chapter. The prior then sends someone to them from chapter, and afterward comes to them himself once and a second time to correct them. A sick man may be such that, if he does not amend, he may eventually even experience the rod.”

The *Book of Cistercian Usages* likewise says:

> “If anyone is such as to disturb the others, murmur against this arrangement for the sick, or presume to transgress in any respect, he shall be corrected. If, after being corrected frequently, he does not amend, then, if it seems good to the abbot, his perversity shall be judged in chapter, where, having been summoned, he shall be rebuked before everyone. If he still does not correct himself, then, if his illness permits it, he shall also be subjected to regular discipline.”

The excellent regulations that the sick were formerly required to observe may also be referred to the care of their souls. It may not be unwelcome to set down some of them here.

First, care was taken that the sick should attend the sacrifice of Mass every day. The Farfa *Customs* say:

> “When they have risen from their beds, at the appearance of daylight or when the sun has already risen, they shall wash their hands and faces, assemble in the oratory of Saint Mary, and hear Mass from those priests who gather there early in the morning. When there are fewer of them, let the brother responsible for them come to the cloister and grant permission to whichever brother he wishes to leave; let that brother leave and say Mass, and let whoever wishes to receive Communion do so. For at no time must the sick be allowed to pass a day without hearing Mass. None of them may read or sing Mass while they remain there, except that they may recite the psalms from memory or, if they wish, the Psalter.”

Udalric writes:

> “He comes to the church for both Masses, the morning Mass and the principal Mass; but at the principal Mass he must remain only until after the Gospel.”

The *Book of Cistercian Usages* says:

> “Let them sing the hours of the day together; afterward, whoever wishes may go to the church for the hours. But for Mass, every day, unless they are greatly burdened . . . Whoever wishes to receive Communion shall receive the kiss of peace outside the choir from one of the community who is going to communicate . . . And this only at the morning Mass.”

Moreover, they were required to recite all the canonical hours, both day and night, at their appointed times. Hence the manuscript *Customs of Saint Benignus* prescribe that the infirmarian, “after prayers have been said at Matins, should take a lamp or sconce and go around the beds of all the sick, to learn whether any of them has not yet risen and for what reason he has remained behind.” For the sake of taking nourishment, however, they anticipated Sext or None; for this reason they attended the principal Mass only as far as the Gospel.

At table they observed the same discipline as the community in the refectory. The Farfa *Customs* state:

> “They must say the table verse as the community does in the refectory. At every serving, whenever food has been given to them, they must always say the blessing. As often as their steward enters through the door with bowls, he must always say, ‘Bless,’ while the others respond, ‘The Lord,’ with complete gratitude and charity. There they shall say the verse after the meal.”

The *Customs of Saint Benignus* add:

> “There they eat in the greatest silence, and no one speaks to another while dining. Nevertheless, if something is necessary, after someone has made a sound with a knife upon the table, one of the servants immediately comes, and the sick man discreetly tells him to bring whatever he needs. When this has been done, the servant immediately withdraws; for the servants must not remain there while they are eating. They may speak to the prior or the infirmarian and, as stated above, to the servants; but at that hour they may speak neither to the servants nor to the infirmarian except about their own necessities. They must sit in their proper order, according to seniority. On Friday and on those days when they do not eat meat, the blessing is given to the whole group as in the refectory. It must also be understood that no one should rise from there unless compelled by the greatest necessity, nor fold his napkin while anyone at all, even the least important person, is still eating. At the beginning and end of the meal, one of them—or a boy, if one is present—reads a short passage from memory. When it is finished, the verse is said, together with ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ by all who are able to stand; standing there before the chairs, they sing it.”

“When the meal is finished,” the Benignian *Customs* continue,

> “they may wait only by standing, sitting, or doing something of that sort until they hear the community leaving the refectory. When they hear this, if the midday rest is observed, they immediately go to their beds; if it is not, they sit in silence like the other members of the cloister, unless they speak with the infirmarian, the chamberlain, or others with whom they are permitted to speak about their necessities.”

Udalric has nearly the same account in Book III, chapter 27. Thus they observed almost as strict a silence as the rest of the community.

In this matter the Cistercians were formerly altogether more severe. Their *Book of Usages* says:

> “The sick in the infirmary may speak with the infirmarian, but only in a place specifically designated for this purpose, and silently, and only about necessities. Whoever wishes to enter that place must ask the infirmarian for permission by a sign and, having received it, enter. As long as anyone is with the infirmarian, no other person may have permission to enter. If someone is so ill that he must remain constantly in bed, or is burdened by a sudden illness, such as fever, or some other serious condition that compels him to remain in bed, then, while he is there, he and the infirmarian may speak with one another if necessary. But when he has improved sufficiently to walk about here and there, he must observe silence as usual, unless perhaps the abbot judges it more expedient for him to speak at the bedside with someone still confined by serious illness.”

The *Bursfeld Ceremonial* similarly says:

> “The sick must not think that they have free permission to speak wherever, whenever, with whomever, and about whatever they wish—especially those who are not constantly lying in bed but walk about here and there. In the infirmary they are permitted to speak with the infirmarian only about necessities and matters of consolation. No one else may dare to speak with any of them without obtaining permission, unless perhaps with one who is lying down and suffering from serious illness. Even such conversation must be restrained during the night hours and when the work of God is being performed in the church; with the others it must be entirely avoided, except in a case of necessity. They must speak not loudly but quietly.”

The rule requiring silence while the work of God is being celebrated is an ancient custom. The *Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon* state:

> “While the regular hour is being sung in the monastery, no one there or in any of the monastery’s workshops may speak, except those sick men who are unable to rise and who speak with the abbot or prior about necessary matters. Otherwise neither the prior nor the abbot may speak.”

They add shortly afterward:

> “There is no rule for one who is completely debilitated, either in food or in speech.”

To this law of silence may be referred what the same Benignian *Customs* state:

> “Whenever the chamberlain, sacristan, cellarer, or others, occupied with obediences inside or outside, enter the infirmary, they immediately become subject to every regular law like any cloistered brother, setting aside the excuse of their obediences. They may not in any way concern themselves with their obediences without permission, to such an extent that even the chamberlain must not go to the chamber without permission, nor the sacristan to the sacristy. Nevertheless, the brothers placed under them must make use of their advice in all matters that need to be done.”

Although the sick were not permitted to read, it was not forbidden for them to hear pious readings. When Abbot Agatho was ill together with another old man, “as they lay there, a certain brother recited from a book of Genesis.” Among our own brethren who were able to rise from their beds, at least those who could do so listened to the reading of the Rule in chapter and to the conference before Compline, though they did not join the assembled brothers.

The *Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon* say:

> “Although he does not go to chapter, he remains inside the church of Blessed Benedict near the door and listens to what is read in chapter—that is, a passage from the Rule, or from the Gospel, together with its exposition—and again at the conference. But when the discussion reaches the faults of the brothers, he must not be curious to hear it.”

Yet so that they would not remain idle in the infirmary meanwhile:

> “They may confess their sins to a spiritual man before and while the brothers are in chapter.”

Finally, what is found among the Farfenses deserves great praise:

> “After Compline, the sick themselves shall receive holy water every day, which they shall find prepared there before the door. Their keepers shall sprinkle holy water on each of their beds, carrying lanterns with them. After everyone has gone to rest, they must inspect how each person is conducting himself.”

The same is found in the Benignian *Customs* and in the manuscript *Customs of the Monastery of Cluny*. But enough of this. We must now inquire what Saint Father prescribes for restoring bodily health.

## For which sick brothers a cell is to be assigned separately

That is, separated from the monastery’s other workshops, says Bernard of Cassino, and after him Boherius. Although, by the institution of cenobitic life, all monks ought to live together, eat together in one refectory, and rest together in one dormitory, it was nevertheless proper to provide sick brothers with a separate dwelling. Piety required this both for the healthy, who would suffer considerable disruption from the sick, and for the sick, who could be treated somewhat more freely in a separate place.

This arrangement pleased the ancient Fathers of monastic life, as may be seen in article 20 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius; chapter 30 of Saint Caesarius’ Rule for Virgins; chapter 53 of Saint Aurelian’s Rule for Monks and chapter 37 of his Rule for Virgins; chapter 15 of a certain Rule for Virgins preserved by Jerome in Letter 22; canon 38 of the Council of Agde; and the *Life of Saint Eugendus, Abbot of the Jura*, in the Bollandists, 1 January.

When Saint Benedict says that a cell is to be assigned to the sick, this “must not be understood as one single lodging,” says Hildemar, “but as a cloister—that is, a house containing various lodgings—so that one who is eating will not be disgusted by someone vomiting, sitting at stool, or even dying.” Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, John of Turrecremata, and Matthias Lambertus speak in nearly the same way.

Such a cell may be seen in the ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall. It was situated in the upper part of the monastery and entirely separated from the other workshops, constructed like another monastery with its own cloister. In its eastern part were a heated room—perhaps a *pyrale*—and a dormitory. On the southern side was a church or oratory, extending in a rounded form from the lower and upper sections, with a single altar to the west.

This church corresponded in a straight line with the major basilica adjoining it, so that the sick could hear the divine offices from it. On the western side were a chamber and a refectory with a kitchen for the sick, for those who had been bled, and a bathing house. Finally, on the northern side were the house of the infirmarian and a place for the very sick.

Adjacent to these were two other houses. One was assigned to the phlebotomist and the person who administered medicines; the other contained a room for the very sick, the physicians’ house, a cabinet for medicinal substances, and the physician’s own lodging. Above it was a herb garden, or garden of simples.

Such was the infirmary in the monastery of Saint Gall at the beginning of the ninth century. Hildemar would have wished it to include one dwelling reserved for the abbot alone. Speaking of the cell for the sick, he says:

> “The abbot ought to make this cell such that he himself may lie there during his illness, so that he may speak without disturbing the sick with guests who come to him, if there is sufficient necessity, and may eat with those sick men who are able to rise from their beds.”

In this cell the sick remained until they recovered, and they were not permitted to take part with the community in any regular exercise:

> “After a brother has eaten or drunk in the infirmary, he must remain outside the community that day and night until the following day at Prime or Terce, as circumstances require,”

say the Benignian *Customs*. Indeed, if necessity ever required someone to enter the monastery’s cloister, he passed through it in such a way that he would not be seen by anyone remaining in the community. Besides the *Customs of Saint Benignus*, the *Book of Cistercian Usages* prescribes this in the following words:

> “The sick are not permitted to enter the church except when the work of God is being celebrated there; nor may they remain in the cloister or exchange signs with the monks who maintain the community. As far as they can, they must take care not to be seen by them or by other people.”

The reason for this institution was love of uniformity and hatred of singularity: the sick should not differ from the others, so that while the others stood, these might not appear to be sitting; and so that, through this separation, they would be compelled—or at least warned—to seek the infirmary only from necessity, not from a desire for a less demanding life.

## And a servant who fears God, and is diligent and attentive

“Indeed, several, if circumstances require it,” says Boherius. The same is decreed in chapter 13 of the Rule of Saint Augustine; chapter 30 of Saint Caesarius’ Rule for Virgins; chapter 21 of the Rule of Tarnat; chapter 20 of Saint Isidore’s Rule; and chapter 10 of Saint Fructuosus’ Rule.

In aptly explaining this passage, Hildemar observes:

> “When Saint Benedict says ‘servant,’ he does not say that he should be a canon or a layman, but a monk. For he did not establish this law for laymen or canons, but for monks. Consider how a hand, foot, or eye can serve the body if it is not in the body; so how can a canon or layman, who is not a member of the monastery, serve a monk—that is, a foreign member?”

He nevertheless adds:

> “If necessity arises for the clothing of the sick to be washed because of filth, as commonly happens with a sick person, a layman or canon may wash the dirty clothing. Likewise, if it is necessary to bring meat, a layman or canon ought to bring it.”

Among the Cluniacs and the monks of Dijon, three servants were assigned to these duties. Hildemar’s observation agrees with this statute of Peter the Venerable (*Statutes*, 24):

> “No lay servants, as used to happen, are to serve the sick themselves or anyone eating in the infirmary; only monks or bearded conversi are to do so.”

Thus, in the monastery of Jumièges under Abbot Saint Philibert, “a monk served the sick according to custom.” In some monasteries, especially those of nuns, the sisters served the sick by weekly rotation. Thus at Poitiers, in the monastery of Saint Radegund, Radegund herself “served the sick outside her own week.” Likewise at Troclar, where Saint Segolena “served the sick during her appointed turns.” Saint Eugendus, however, ordered that “those whom the sick themselves had especially chosen should serve them in their necessity,” as his acts relate, paragraph 21.

The duties of the infirmarian are found in Udalric, Book III, chapter 25; in the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 116; and in the *Bursfeld Ceremonial*, distinction 2, chapter 10.

## Let the use of baths be offered to the sick whenever it is expedient

“Let it be offered,” he says, because one should not wait for the sick man to ask; rather, it should be offered to him, says Bernard of Cassino. The sick must be anticipated: it is not fitting for them to request remedies for themselves, but, after making their illness known to the abbot, they should rest with complete confidence in the arms of his charity.

What Saint Father Benedict establishes here concerning permitting baths to the sick must be understood of private and domestic baths, not public ones. It is not expedient for monks to wander outside, and one rarely finds any ancient or modern monks among whom there was some concern for propriety or religion who used such baths.

The Carthusians say:

> “We entirely forbid swimming and the washing of bodies in the sea, rivers, ponds, or similar waters, as practices of little propriety and altogether dangerous for all persons of our order.”

The Cistercians likewise decree:

> “If any nuns go outside the monastery to baths, they shall be deprived of the regular habit without remission. Those who grant permission for them to seek the aforesaid baths shall incur the sentence of excommunication.”

Saint Jerome may perhaps have occasioned this statute when he wrote to Laeta:

> “I entirely disapprove of baths for a grown virgin, who ought to be ashamed of herself and unable to look upon herself naked. If she weakens her body through vigils and fasts and brings it into subjection; if she wishes to extinguish the flames of lust and the incentives of a fervent age through the coldness of continence; if she hastens to disfigure her natural beauty with deliberate uncleanness, why does she, on the contrary, rekindle fires that have been put to sleep by the warmth of baths?”

## But to the healthy, and especially to the young, let it be granted more rarely

This was the constant and sound teaching of the holy Fathers. Saint Athanasius writes in the *Syntagma of Doctrine for Monks*:

> “If illness requires it, use a bath once or twice; but if you are well, you do not need a bath.”

Saint Jerome says:

> “Let him who wishes to extinguish the body’s heat through the coldness of fasts not seek the warm relief of baths.”

Saint Isidore, speaking of monks, writes in Book II of *On Ecclesiastical Offices*, chapter 15:

> “They should use baths never for bodily pleasure, but rarely, because of the necessity of illness.”

And in his Rule, chapter 20:

> “No monk should go to baths for the sake of washing his body, except solely because of the necessity of illness.”

Saint Caesarius, in his Rule for Nuns, chapter 29, says:

> “Baths demanded by anyone’s illness must not be refused . . . but if she is compelled by no illness, her desire must not be indulged.”

Saint Leander writes in *On the Institution of Virgins*, chapter 10:

> “Use the bath not for the care or cleanliness of the body, but only as a remedy for health. Use it, I say, when illness demands it, not when your will suggests it . . . Let not bodily pleasure entice you to bathe more often, but let necessity arising from illness command it.”

Saint Peter Damian says in *Opusculum* 15, chapter 18:

> “When they are healthy, they do not use baths.”

For this reason they praise Saint Tatto in the *Life of Saint Paldon*, paragraph 17; Saint Pardulf in his *Life*, paragraph 5; Saint Opportunus, abbess, in her *Life*, paragraph 8; and Saint Poppo in his *Life*, paragraph 59 [in the Bollandists, 25 January].

Nevertheless, there were ancient monks who sometimes frequented baths. Saint Augustine even permits them to virgins once a month. Saint Benedict does not entirely deny them to the healthy, but says only that they should be granted more rarely. Hildemar explains “more rarely” in this way:

> “Some understand this to mean that it should be prepared three times a year, namely at the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and Pentecost. Others understand it as twice, namely at the Nativity and Easter, which is more correct.”

The same Hildemar gives another interpretation of this passage: baths may be granted to those soiled by some manual labor, although rarely, and to the young still more rarely.

The former interpretation, however, agrees better with the ancient custom of our order. Its practice may be seen in the *Life of Saint Junianus, Abbot*, where Wlsinus Boetius writes that “a bath was scarcely provided for the body once a year”; in the *Life of Saint Amatus, Abbot of Habend*, where it is said that he “used the relief of baths there only twice a year, namely before the holy day of the Lord’s Nativity and before Easter, the feast of his sacred Resurrection”; and in Bede’s account of Saint Æthelthryth, abbess:

> “She wished to wash rarely in hot baths, except before the approaching major solemnities, for example Easter, Pentecost, and Epiphany.”

We described the rite in Book III of *Ancient Monastic Rites*, chapter 2. Moreover, it seems possible to infer from Hildemar’s commentary on the Rule, chapter 22, and from the Rule of Saint Isidore that they used washing because of a nocturnal illusion. That Rule prescribes:

> “He who has been deceived by a nocturnal phantom shall stand in the sacristy during the office and shall not dare to enter the church on that same day before he has been washed with water and tears.”

To these customs must be referred what is found concerning bathing rooms in Cassiodorus, *On Divine Readings*, chapter 29; in Ingulf’s *History of Crowland*; in the ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall; in the ancient *Customs of the Monastery of Farfa*; and elsewhere. See Haeften, Book II, treatise 5, discussion 7.

## But let the eating of meat also be permitted to the sick and wholly debilitated for restoration

The same is prescribed by Saint Athanasius in the *Syntagma of Doctrine for Monks*; Saint Caesarius in both Rules, for monks chapter 24, and for virgins in the recapitulation, chapter 17; Saint Aurelian in both Rules, for monks chapter 51 and for virgins chapter 35; Saint Fructuosus in his Rule, chapter 5; and several others.

Several points must also be observed concerning the eating of meat.

### First

Hildemar states that the custom in France was not to give meat to the sick until they had risen from their illness; thereafter it was served to them until they had recovered their former strength. Once they had regained it and returned to the refectory, the cellarer supplied them with more delicate foods for two or three days.

That this custom was later abolished, at least in some monasteries, is clear from the manuscript *Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, where the following is found:

> “Whenever one of the brothers begins to fall ill so that he cannot remain with the community, unless he is a child, he first asks permission in chapter. Rising, he says these words to the one presiding over chapter: ‘I am ill and cannot follow the community.’ The one presiding over chapter then tells him to rest outside the choir until he sees whether his health improves. When two or three days have passed, if his health has not improved, he asks permission again and says that he is becoming very ill; then he is ordered to go to the infirmary. Sometimes the prior invites him first, before he asks permission a second time. After he has entered there, on the second or third day, if he has not yet recovered somewhat, the prior goes to him at the hour of dinner, has meat brought to him, places it before him himself, and orders him to eat. If it is not appropriate for the prior to come, he sends it through the infirmarian.”

These words show how cautious and religious our predecessors were in granting meat. Udalric, Book III, chapter 27, and Lanfranc in his *Statutes*, chapter 23, have something similar.

### Secondly

The aforesaid *Customs*, Udalric, and Lanfranc add:

> “From that hour onward he never walks without a staff and unless his head is covered with a cap.”

Saint Bernard nevertheless alluded to this custom, which pleased the holy Fathers, in these words (*Apology to William*, chapter 8):

> “To distinguish the healthy from those who are unwell, the sick are ordered to carry staffs in their hands—plainly necessary staffs, so that what pallor in the face and emaciation do not reveal, the supporting staff may falsely proclaim as illness.”

### Thirdly

The Cassinese Declarations prescribe that the sick “must not eat meat twice in one day without the consent of the physicians.” They also say:

> “We believe that eight ounces for each person are sufficient.”

These last words were deleted from the printed Declarations published at Rome in 1642.

### Fourthly

Saint Benedict permits the eating of meat not only to the sick but also to those who are wholly debilitated. Although Smaragdus confuses these categories in his commentary on chapter 39 of the Rule, writing:

> “When he says ‘debilitated sick persons,’ he signifies not two persons, as many think, but only one. Thus a debilitated sick person is one who has been brought wholly to weakness by a long and severe illness,”

others distinguish them not incorrectly. Although all sick people are debilitated, not all debilitated people are sick.

Hildemar teaches that the debilitated can be understood in three ways:

> “First, infants: the younger they are, the more debilitated they are. Second, the elderly: the older they are, the more debilitated they are. Third, even mature young men may be debilitated if, because of some bodily discomfort, excessive heat, a spasm, or some other discomfort, as we have said, they become debilitated in themselves.”

Haeften considers debilitated those who can be called neither healthy nor sick but occupy an intermediate position between the two. Among them are some who, rising from illness, have not yet recovered their former strength; others are so disposed toward illness that, unless they are helped quickly, disease is imminent.

### Fifthly

Saint Father Benedict permits meat to the sick and wholly debilitated not for delicacy but for restoration, as he himself explains. Therefore, if the nature of the illness is such that recovery can easily be achieved without eating meat, the sick person ought to abstain from it.

Hence the *Book of Cistercian Usages* says:

> “If someone has an illness that does not greatly weaken him or disturb his appetite for food—for example, a swelling, an incision of the limbs, or something of this kind—such a person should neither lie upon a mattress nor set aside the customary fasts nor change the food of the refectory.”

Nor should Saint Father’s phrase “for restoration” be taken so strictly that meat would be denied to sick persons whose recovery is hopeless because death is near. Although meat may not restore their strength, it does sustain it to some extent and prolongs life for a little while.

Sixth, that this provision of Saint Benedict is permissive, not preceptive: [477] therefore, “if the sick entirely abstained from meat, they would not on that account violate the Rule; for in the Rule eating meat is not prescribed to monks, but permitted,” says Goffridus of Vendôme. Nor were there lacking many of the ancient monks who abstained from meat even when sick. Concerning the monks of Condat, an anonymous writer must be heard first, in the *Life of Saint Lupicinus the Abbot*, no. 2 (*Boll.*, 21 March):

> “Although no one in Condat, especially in the monastery, has ever to this day dared, in Christ’s name, to taste anything from an animal, except dairy products, or from birds, except eggs—and this only when ill—he nevertheless very often did not even allow a drop of oil, or at least of milk porridge, to be poured into his own.”

The same is reported of the monks of the Order of Grandmont by James of Vitry (*History of the West*, chap. 19):

> “After they have made their profession, they are never again permitted to eat meat, however serious the illness by which they may be weighed down.”

And certainly there exists on this matter a decree contained in the Rule of Saint Stephen, founder of the aforesaid order, in these words (chap. 57):

> “We command you always to abstain from meat and blood, both of birds and of four-footed animals, whether you are healthy or sick.”

Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, had likewise formed his monks in this discipline before subjecting them to the Cistercian Order, [Col. 0597B] as an anonymous author of his *Life* teaches (Book II, no. 14, *Miscellanea* of Baluze, vol. IV):

> “Among the other changes, meat-eating was also introduced for the sick according to the Rule, something that until then had remained unknown to our brothers. The holy man bore this most grievously, so much so that, moved with indignation, he himself said that they had introduced a slaughterhouse into the house of God, when he saw an animal killed on account of the sick. And when the chapter of the Rule concerning the sick was brought forward against him, he remained silent, because he could neither approve of this nor find the authority of the Rule displeasing.”

Among the Cistercians, however, Saint William, archbishop of Bourges, “from the time he abandoned the world, never ate meat, whether compelled by any illness or persuaded by any kind of diet.”

The Carthusian monks retain this institution to the present day with the greatest praise. Although they had observed this abstinence from the beginning of the Order, as Peter the Venerable teaches and Guigo V, prior of the Grande Chartreuse, implies in the *Statutes*, when he writes (chap. 38):

> “For these alone—the sick—if the illness is so severe, we are accustomed to buy fish,”

they nevertheless seem to have first undertaken it with an obligation in the general chapter of 1254. This is attested by letters of that chapter, subscribed by Rodolphus, archbishop of Tarentaise, and the bishop of Grenoble, in which they declared that they had “spontaneously and voluntarily, not under compulsion, both for themselves and for their convents, unanimously and harmoniously, in full and general chapter, perpetually renounced the eating of meat,” adding that “if any one of them, whether prior or monk, should presume—God forbid—to violate such a statute by rash presumption, he should know himself to have been wholly removed and excluded from the fellowship and communion of the entire Order and from the Order itself.”

In the newer Statutes, however, they moderate such penalties (Part II, chap. 4, no. 32), so that a prior, vicar, or procurator who eats meat, or consents to those eating it, “as an immediate consequence, as a slanderer and transgressor of his own profession, shall lose obedience [478] and shall forever lack the proper votes and places, and the other obediences, of the Order. But if he is a simple monk, or any other person of the Order, then, deprived of voice, place, and obediences, he shall be committed to prison perpetually, at the will of the general chapter.”

To all these must be added the Camaldolese hermits. Concerning them I read the following in Book II, chapter 74, of the *History of Camaldoli*:

> “When the hermit Peter Quirinus urged that a dispensation concerning the eating of meat be granted to sick hermits, Peter [Delphinus], the prior general, shuddering at his proposal as contrary to the most ancient institution of the place, informed him by letter that whenever meat had been served or brought into the holy place, it had always, by a great miracle, appeared to swarm with worms.”

But when they have recovered, let all abstain from meat in the customary manner.] On this passage Hildemar writes:

> “He said ‘in the customary manner’ because it was the monks’ custom to abstain from meat, not only from four-footed animals but also from birds, as the primitive Church did, whose practice monks ought altogether to follow. And therefore he did not say specifically ‘from which meats,’ but used the general term ‘meats’; by ‘meats’ it is to be understood that he means not only four-footed animals but also birds.”

We shall discuss birds below; for the present, it is enough to have indicated Hildemar’s opinion in passing.

As for the ancient practice of our Order, I read the following in the Statutes of Saint Lanfranc (chap. 23):

> “On the day when, having recovered his health, he wishes to return to the convent, if he has eaten meat, let him first enter the choir shaved, at the hour before which the Office of the Chapter is sung; and when Mass is said in the convent after that hour, let him not make an offering at it. Having entered the chapter, when it has been announced that the matter of the Order is to be discussed, let him rise first and, in the place where the custom requires, prostrate himself and ask forgiveness. When questioned, and answering as is customary, and ordered to rise, let him say these and similar words: ‘Lord, weighed down by my illness, I remained for a long time in the infirmary. In food, drink, and many other things I offended and acted against our Order; for this I ask your absolution.’ After he has said this, let the abbot absolve him, saying: ‘May the almighty Lord absolve you from these and all your other faults.’ When the convent has answered ‘Amen,’ let that brother present himself at the abbot’s feet. Then, returning to the place where he had prostrated himself, and giving thanks to the abbot and the whole convent because the things necessary for his illness had been provided to him, let him make three customary genuflections. On that day, and thereafter for as long as necessary, let him be ordered to take the *mixtum*. But if he has not eaten meat, it shall be left to the abbot’s decision at what hour he may return to the convent after requesting permission, and how he is thereafter to conduct himself.”

Udalricus, Book III, chapter 27, and the Customs of Saint Benignus contain something similar. They add that those who have eaten meat are to be assigned, as a penitential exercise, the singing of seven psalms, or, if they do not know them, the Lord’s Prayer seven times; the Customs of Saint Benignus add, alternatively, the *Miserere mei, Deus* seven times. The Ceremonial of the Bursfeld Congregation likewise says that the sick should not return to the convent without the abbot’s permission and without having sought pardon in chapter [479] for their negligences; indeed, according to the Book of the Cistercian Customs, they are to remain fasting unless they must be sent on their way.

But let the abbot take the greatest care that the sick are not neglected by the cellarers or servants.] By the term “cellarers,” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius understand all officials whose obedience obliges them to provide something for the sick. Therefore, let the abbot take care that these men do not neglect the sick, to whom, “whatever they ask must be given, even if it must be purchased,” say the Customs of the Monastery of Farfa; “for the Rule commands that, before and above all things, care and solicitude be shown toward the sick.” Here one recalls with what severity Saint Pachomius rebuked a brother who had denied meat to a sick man who requested it (*Life of Saint Pachomius*, no. 34, *Boll.*, 14 May).

Because whatever is done wrongly by the disciples concerns him personally.] In accordance with the saying of Gregory the Great (*Register*, Book III, chap. 23):

> “I know that the fault of subjects weighs down the life of those set over them; and when sin is not corrected in a subject, the sentence is turned back upon the one who presides.”

## CHAPTER XXXVII. On the Elderly and Children

[Col. 0599]

Although human nature itself [Note: [Col. 0599A] In another copy, *humana* is absent.] is drawn toward compassion for persons of these ages—namely, the elderly and children—nevertheless the authority of the Rule should also provide for them. Their weakness must always be taken into consideration, and the strictness of the Rule must in no way be imposed upon them with regard to food. Rather, compassionate consideration should be shown toward them, and they should eat before the canonical hours.

### COMMENTARY

[Col. 0599A] In the proper order, after Saint Benedict has treated the sick brothers, he consequently treats the elderly and children. The tenderness of the latter and the daily decline, so to speak, of the former approach illness very closely; indeed, if Terence is to be believed, old age itself is an illness (*Terence, Phormio*). Hence also the Rule of the Master (chap. 28):

> “By a just judgment, little children, the advanced in age, and the sick ought to be released equally from the regulation of meals.”

In the title of this chapter itself, where the particle *vel* is used coordinately in the sense of “and,” the holy Father names the elderly before the children, “because old age is weaker than childhood,” says Hildemar; “for old age is diminished in strength by decline, whereas childhood acquires strength by growth. Old age is also more fragile than childhood, because a child, if he lacks what is necessary, does not know how to complain. Therefore he properly mentions the elderly first and the children afterward, so that greater care may be taken of the elderly than of the children.” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius reason in nearly the same way.

[Col. 0599B] Before we approach the text of the Rule, it seems necessary to inquire whom the holy Father understands by the names “children” and “elderly.” Hildemar distinguishes six ages of man here. The first is infancy, lasting to the seventh year; the second is childhood, lasting to the fourteenth; the third is adolescence, lasting to the twenty-eighth; the fourth is youth, lasting to the fifty-sixth; the fifth is old age, lasting to the seventy-third; and the sixth is decrepitude.

Boherius, following Saint Isidore, differs somewhat. He makes infancy last to the seventh year, childhood to the fifteenth year exclusive, adolescence to the twenty-fifth, youth to the fiftieth, the senior age—which he also calls “gravity” and distinguishes from both youth and old age—to the seventieth, and old age to the end of life. You may perhaps encounter other divisions of the ages among other authors. But whatever the case may be, if “infancy” is taken here strictly, those who had reached their seventh year would have to be excluded from the law of indulgence that Saint Benedict establishes in this chapter. Yet the holy Father regularly confounds infants with children in the Rule, as in chapter 70, where he says:

> “The ages of children up to fifteen years are to be under the diligent discipline and custody of all.”

It is clear that children are also understood here under the name “infants.” Hence Boherius, in his second commentary, adds to the word “infants”:

> “That is, children; for infants need not a rule but a mother.”

Hildemar says similarly:

> “This must be noted: the Rule speaks not only of those infants who are up to seven years old, but also of those beyond seven; that is, up to seven there should be the greatest care and increase in food, but after seven less, according to the strength he sees to be in them.”

Bernard of Cassino, however, makes children here extend only to twelve years:

> “But of which infants does the Rule speak here? I think not only up to seven years, but also after seven and up to twelve. Yet as they advance more toward strength, their allowance should gradually be reduced, lest the wantonness of the flesh grow excessively proud along with their strength.”

He seems to have taken this from the Rule of the Master (chap. 28), where we read:

> “We permit infants to receive this relaxation if they are under twelve years old; those who are older are to be held to the rule of adults.”

As for the elderly, the men of Valladolid in Spain declare the following in their Constitutions:

> “To avoid any doubt that might arise concerning who are to be regarded as elderly, so that they may be exempted from the austerity of the Rule in food, drink, and manual labor, we declare that those who have completed sixty years are to be considered such.”

But since some are found whose old age is so vigorous and strong that they are even stronger than younger men, Boherius rightly thinks that this should be left to the superior’s judgment; and the Cassinese writers designate as elderly those who “are to be understood not so much by age as by weakness, according to the superior’s consideration.” Or, as John Craesbeeck puts it:

> “Those who are understood here as elderly seem to be people of such advanced and decrepit age that, through old age, they are unable to bear the common burdens of religion; and therefore they are rightly exempted from the common table, the common law of fasting, attending church, working with their hands, and so forth. They may properly be called emeriti.” [Col. 0600B]

Although human nature is drawn toward compassion in these ages, namely those of the elderly and children, nevertheless the authority of the Rule should also provide for them.] That is, it should look upon them favorably, says Boherius.

Their weakness must always be taken into consideration, and the strictness of the Rule must in no way be imposed upon them with regard to food.] This means both in the quality and in the quantity of food, as Turrecremata says. Add also, “in the hour of eating,” according to the saying of Basil the Great:

> “The time, measure, and quality of meals should be suitably distinguished for children” (*Longer Rules*, chap. 15),

and, with still greater reason, for the elderly. Thus they should be fed before the others, take food in greater quantity, be released from the customary fasts, and eat several times a day, since a weak age could hardly endure a single meal; they should also receive more delicate foods. An opportunity to discuss the meal-time of the elderly and children will arise elsewhere. Concerning the relaxation of fasts, the number of meals, and the quality of food, a few things may be added from the statutes and examples of ancient monks.

As to the first matter, Saint Jerome speaks as follows of the Egyptian monks (*Letter 22*):

> “Only the elderly receive wine; and for them, as also for little children, a meal is often provided, so that the wearied age of some may be sustained and the beginning age of others not be broken.”

And concerning the Tabennesiots (*Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius*):

> “At supper likewise a table is set for those who labor, for the elderly, and for children, and during the most intense heat.”

Saint Isidore says similarly in his Rule (chap. 12):

> “Those who are worn out by bodily age, or restrained by the weakness of tender youth, should not be exercised by daily fasts, lest either old age fail before it dies, or growing age fall before it advances, and perish before it learns to do good.”

And the Common Monastic Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chap. 6) says:

> “From Holy Easter until the eighth day before the Kalends of October, children shall eat four times each day; from the eighth day before the Kalends of October until the Kalends of December, three times; from the Kalends of December until Holy Easter, it shall be in the power of the cellarer.”

Finally, the Rule of the Master (chap. 28):

> “Little children shall fast on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday—but only on the shorter days, that is, in winter—and on the other days they shall eat at the sixth hour. In summer, however, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday the little children shall eat at the sixth hour; on the other days they shall be refreshed at the third hour.”

Concerning the quality of food, Saint Fructuosus must again be heard in the Common Monastic Rule (chap. 8):

> “Those elderly men whom we recognize as quiet, simple, humble, obedient, and frequent in prayer, we command to be cherished with compassionate mercy as little children and honored as fathers. Thus they are to be excused from the bakery and kitchen service and allowed to rest from the field and hard labor, except that some lighter tasks may be assigned to them, lest their weary age be broken before its time. Nevertheless, the foods with which they are refreshed are to be deliberately cooked tender and soft by the weekly servers; meat and wine are to be moderately supplied to them because of their weakness; and all are to be joined at one table and refreshed equally with one food and drink.”

The chapter of the monks appointed to direct the monastery of Reichenau also makes no distinction in food between the monks and children. Whether, however, children may be served meat according to Saint Benedict’s intention could be doubtful. Following the custom of his own time, Hildemar explains the matter himself as follows:

> “The abbot should also give them good clothing, and fish to eat, or milk, or butter. He should give them meat from four-footed animals at the proper times—namely, at Christmas, Easter, or Pentecost, or on the solemnities of the saints—or whenever he sees that the child is weak; because of that weakness he should give him meat more frequently. To those children, as we have said, he should provide everything necessary, so that they suffer no want; for if they are nourished in abundance, when they grow older they will not require that abundance. This must be noted: according to the time of their age he should give them meat from four-footed animals, since they need and require more when they are in their third year; then less in the fourth, more or less in the fifth; thereafter, up to the tenth or eleventh year, they should eat less meat from four-footed animals. In illness or weakness, however, he should give them as much meat from four-footed animals as is necessary. Then, up to the fifteenth year, he should give them other food. After the fifteenth year, they should not precede the adults.”

Boherius says similarly in his first commentary:

> “Meat from four-footed animals or birds is to be supplied to them, since it contains more nourishment and consequently more sustenance than other foods.”

Bernard of Cassino has the same view. And before all these authorities, among the selected chapters of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, the following is found (*Spicilegium*, vol. IX):

> “The children of the monastery shall eat meat for fourteen years.”

But the Council of Aachen advises otherwise, decreeing (canon 37) that “oblates shall eat meat only on account of illness.” Then there is the *Life of Saint Angilbert* (no. 10, *Fourth Century of the Benedictines*), where Hariulf reports that one hundred boys being educated in the schools of the monastery of Centula lived under the same habit and diet as the other monks. From this passage and others, our Mabillon asserts in his note on the passage that oblates in monasteries used the same habit and the same foods [Col. 0601D] as the monks. Certainly, in the monastery of Saint Gall, Abbot Solomon permitted boys to eat meat in the school buildings on three days of the year in the tenth century, as Ekkehard the Younger testifies in Book VI, *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*, chapter 1; this indicates that previously they had abstained altogether. Moreover, Udalricus teaches (Book III, chap. 8) that the boys ate in the same refectory as the others; the Customs of Saint Benignus in manuscript form also state this.

To this may be added Boherius in his second commentary, where, retracting what he had said in the first, he writes:

> “It is worth asking what strictness of the Rule is meant by the relaxation ordered for these persons. Are they to eat meat contrary to the rigor of the Rule? I do not think so, because the Master makes no exception for them in the way he does for the sick, the weak, and the infirm. Although these ages may indeed be called weak, the reason for this passage does not apply to them, because meat is eaten for restoration and improvement of nature, whereas childhood is always improving and old age is declining. Their fasts, therefore, will be relaxed; fish and other liquid foods will be served more frequently; and they will also eat before the regular hours.”

He subsequently adduces the authority of the Council of Aachen, which he calls the great council of the Franks.

Furthermore, since the aforesaid Boherius teaches in both commentaries that by the name “food” not only meals but also clothing and lodging are to be understood, these things must be provided for them with compassion. As to clothing, we have already heard Hildemar. Saint Fructuosus, however, prescribes in the Common Monastic Rule (chap. 8) that “clothing and footwear should be provided to the elderly in such a way that, without a fire, the harshness of the cold may be kept away from them.”

That the elderly should also have been granted separate lodging Haeftenus teaches by the following reasoning (Book I, tract 5, disputation 12):

> “Since in Saint Benedict’s time religious persons did not each have separate cells in which they could sleep and devote themselves to reading in the cloister or elsewhere, there was then great reason for assigning particular bedrooms to the elderly: first, because it would be difficult for them to go up and down the dormitory; second, because through their customary coughing they would easily awaken the others, and it would not be appropriate for them to be awakened for the night watches; and third, because, living with the others in the cloister during winter, they would have to endure severe cold.”

[Col. 0602C] But let compassionate consideration be shown toward them, and let them eat before the canonical hours.] That is, before the regular hours at which the brothers customarily eat, as the commentators explain, and as the meaning of the word itself demonstrates. For *kanōn* (κανών) means “rule” in Greek and *kanonikos* (κανονικός) is rendered “regular.” “It is as though he were saying in other words,” says Hildemar, “that before the other brothers eat, the children and elderly should eat first.” Smaragdus puts it more explicitly:

> “If the brothers eat at the sixth hour, let them be refreshed at the third; if the brothers eat at the ninth, let them receive food at the sixth.”

I think this should be understood not of a complete meal but of a small meal, commonly called *jentaculum*, or breakfast, since afterward they were also refreshed with the others, though in a smaller quantity of food. Udalricus speaks of this small meal as follows (Book III, chap. 8). The boys:

> “receive *mixtum* after the principal Mass; or, if it is a fasting day, or winter, or some such day on which people eat only once, then after the third hour. From the Kalends of October until Lent, if, as I said, there is only one meal, their lunch consists not solely of bread; whatever it may be, something is also set before them.”

He adds:

> “Throughout the summer, on Sundays, mercy is shown to them at supper in the form of milk. If one of them is so small that he needs it, bread and wine are brought to him at earliest dawn in the very cloister where he sits.”

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. On the Weekly Reader

[Col. 0601]

[Col. 0601D] A reading must not be absent from the tables of brothers who are eating [Note: [Col. 0601D] Oxford copy: *mensae* (“table”).]; nor should anyone who happens by chance to pick up a book dare to read there [Note: [Col. 0601D] Cassinese copy: “lest by chance.” Florence copy, with some manuscripts and editions: “nor by chance.”] [Note: [Col. 0602D] Oxford and Conc. copies: “who.”] [Note: [Col. 0603A] Oxford omits “dare.”]. Rather, the one who is to read for the entire week should enter on Sunday [Note: [Col. 0603A] Oxford copy: “on the Lord’s Day.”]. Having entered after Masses [Note: [Col. 0603A] Florence and Hildemar: “after Mass.”] and Communion, he should ask everyone to pray for him, that God may drive away from him the spirit of pride. This verse should be said three times in the oratory by all [Note: [Col. 0603A] Oxford copy: “with all.”], with him beginning it: “Lord, you shall open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise.” Having thus received the blessing, he should go to read. And the greatest silence should be kept at table [Note: [Col. 0603A] Cassinese and Florentine copies omit “at table.”; Hadrian’s copy: “there.”], so that no one’s whisper or voice may be heard there except that of the reader alone.

The brothers should serve one another in turn whatever is necessary for those eating and drinking, so that no one needs to ask for anything [Note: [Col. 0603A] Oxford, Victor, German, and Hadrian copies: “in turns.”]. If anything is needed, however, let it be requested by the sound of any signal [Note: [Col. 0603A] Victor’s principal copy: “by the sound of some signal”] rather than by voice. No one should presume to ask for anything there from the reading itself or from elsewhere [Note: [Col. 0604A] Hildemar: “anything.”] [Note: [Col. 0604A] Another copy: “to report.”], lest an occasion be given [Note: [Col. 0604A] Another copy: “nor let an occasion be given”]; unless perhaps the prior wishes to say something briefly for edification. The weekly brother should receive *mixtum* before he begins to read, because of Holy Communion and lest it be difficult for him to endure the fast. Afterwards he should eat with the weekly kitchen servers and servants [Note: [Col. 0604A] Hildemar omits “afterwards he should eat with the weekly kitchen servers and servants.” The Compendium also omits “and servants.”]. The brothers should not read or sing in order [Note: [Col. 0604A] Another copy omits “or sing.”], but those who edify the hearers should do so.

### COMMENTARY

[Col. 0603]

[Col. 0603A] There must not be a reading at the table of the brothers who are eating.] Since man lives not by bread alone but by every word that proceeds from the mouth of God, Saint Benedict the Father, intending to speak about the measure of food and drink, appropriately first said something about reading at table, so that he might provide for the nourishment of both men—the bodily and the spiritual—though first for the spiritual, as much the more worthy. The same institution prevailed among other monks as well, as is evident from Cassian, Book IV, chapter 17; the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, chapter 19; Saint Augustine, chapter 5; Saint Caesarius, for monks, chapter 9, and for virgins, chapter 16; Saint Aurelian, for monks, chapter 49, and for virgins, chapter 32; Saint Isidore, chapter 10; and the Rule of the Master, chapter 24.

Saint Benedict the Father considered this reading at table so necessary that he wished it to be practiced at absolutely every table, as his complete and unrestricted statement indicates: “A reading must not be absent from the tables of brothers who are eating.” Hence the Synod of Aachen (canon 28):

> “The servants should not eat at one table, but, after the brothers’ meal, they should eat in their own places, and the same reading that was recited to the brothers should be recited to them.”

The practice of this statute can be seen among the Cluniacs, among whom “at mealtime reading was never lacking at either table,” as John the Monk says in the *Life of Saint Odo*, Book I, no. 30. Hence Udalricus, speaking of the weekly reader (Book II, chap. 34), says:

> “The one who reads carries into the refectory and carries back the book from which he is to read to the servants.”

The manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon have the same provision, chapter 37. The more recent Congregations also adopted this institution: the Cassinese, where the congregation is larger, the Celestines, the Olivetans, and the Feuillants, as may be seen in their Declarations or Constitutions. Boherius likewise explained Saint Benedict in this way in his second commentary.

The principal commentators on the Rule extend this decree not merely to second tables, but even to the sick themselves. Hildemar says:

> “It must be observed that he does not say ‘at the tables of the healthy,’ or ‘where the generality of the brothers eat.’ Therefore, just as it is understood generally that reading is to be done for the healthy eating together, so it must also be understood of the sick or phlegmatics, of the elderly or children, and of all the other brothers. This must nevertheless be known: if there are six sick men, or phlegmatics, or elderly men with children, or other brothers, when they eat, there should be reading for them while they are eating, but softly. If there are twenty sick men, reading should be done aloud.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius say similarly in the first commentary:

> “This reading at table is useful not only in the refectory for companions who are eating, but also in the infirmary for the sick, phlegmatics, elderly men and children who are eating, and for the ministers.”

Nicholas of Fractura speaks in nearly the same way. Finally, Pope Benedict XII, in his Constitution for Benedictine monks (chap. 26), says:

> “Whenever several persons eat meat together in the infirmary, the verse and prayer are to be said at the beginning of the meal, and after the meal the hymn and verse; continuous silence is to be observed while they recline, and something edifying to the hearers is to be read there continuously, as in the refectory.”

Saint Lanfranc also prescribes that on the two days following bloodletting, when the men who have been bled receive *mixtum*, “the reading should be recited from memory by someone.”

Nor should we omit what Hildemar adds:

> “It must be known that when the abbot is walking outside, there should be reading at his table, but briefly—that is, a short reading—not as in the refectory, continually until the end of the meal; rather, the reading should end beforehand. If the brothers are at work and remain there, the reading should be given to them fully, as in the refectory. But if there is no general gathering and they do not remain, little should be read. Likewise, if only a few remain, little should be read. Similarly, if a guest eats in the refectory before the hour: but if the guests are of such a number and importance—two or three—little should be read, that is, lightly; if there are more, the reading should continue only until the prior signals the reader to finish.”

The practice of this may be seen in part in Hariulfus’s *Chronicle of Centula*, Book IV, chapter 26, where he writes of the most devout Abbot Gervinus that, while traveling (*Spicilegium*, vol. IV),

> “when supper had been prepared, if he had reclined to eat, he tried to occupy himself by listening to a reading or meditating on divine law.”

Udalricus also says this concerning the deans who administer the villages and eat in their deaneries outside the monastery (Book III, chap. 5):

> “Before he eats, after the verse has been said, something from Holy Scripture is read, either by another or by himself; and likewise at the end, before he rises after the meal.”

Nor should anyone who happens by chance to seize a book dare to read there.] “By chance,” that is, “unforeseen, suddenly, or unexpectedly”; the reading should be prepared in advance, because even very skilled and learned men read badly what they have not previewed. A poor reader, pronouncing badly in pauses, accent, short and long syllables, omissions, additions, and faulty pronunciation, not only fails to edify the brothers who hear him but also provides cause or occasion for complaint,” says Bernard of Cassino. He took this interpretation from Smaragdus, and Nicholas of Fractura, Peter Boherius, John of Turrecremata, and Matthias Lambertus follow him.

Hildemar, however, interprets it differently:

> “‘By chance,’ he says, means suddenly or unexpectedly, as though he were saying in other words: no one should read there unless ordered to do so.”

Theobaldus Artaldus says the same. This interpretation seems both more natural and more agreeable, although I would have readers be especially diligent in preparing their readings. We read that a definite time was formerly assigned to them for this duty (chap. 37):

> “For Matins and the principal Mass,” say the manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon, “the reader takes the book from which he is to read, withdraws into the lesser choir, and previews the reading. But if he is still a young man under supervision, he does not withdraw; rather, he previews as much as he can in the greater choir.”

Udalricus has something similar in Book II, chapter 34. The manuscript Ritual of the monastery of Affligem [at Haeftenus, Book X, tract 2, disputation 2] says:

> “This must be known concerning the weekly reader: between the two Masses, namely Matins and the principal Mass, he is to preview his reading, and he should do so while seated in the rear place, where he can be seen by the convent. If he is young or less practiced in reading, one of the elders should be summoned to listen to his reading and teach him how to place the accents according to the custom observed in the monastery.”

Formerly this was done in the sacristy of the monastery of Corbie, as we gather from chapter 6 of Saint Adalard, *On Admonitions in the Congregation*, where it is prescribed (*Fourth Century*, part I, p. 757):

> “On that Sunday itself, or on other days while the Office is being celebrated outside, no one should remain in the sacristy except the person who ought to prepare this, or the person commanded to do so—and especially not the weekly reader.”

Therefore, on other days, when the Office was not being celebrated outside, he remained in the sacristy.

But the one who is to read for the entire week should enter on Sunday.] That is, he should enter to read.

[Col. 0605C] Having entered after Masses and Communion.] By “Communion” he does not mean the Communion received by the celebrating priest, but that “which the brothers receive, or are accustomed to receive, on Sundays before the high altar immediately after Mass,” as Boherius says. He enters entirely correctly after the sacred Communion, so that he may first be filled with the divine word that he is soon to pour forth to others.

He should ask everyone to pray for him.] “This is not requested verbally, but by bodily prostration, which is again performed in many monasteries after the blessing itself, that is, after the prayer,” Boherius says again.

That God may drive away from him the spirit of pride.] Peter Damian aptly applies the following to this passage (*Opusculum* II, chap. 18):

> “The vice of arrogance is familiar to readers, especially when someone possesses a pleasing eloquence; while his unrestrained tongue traverses the open fields of Scripture, and his heart, devoted to popular favor, is invaded by the spirit of pride. While he directs others along the path of righteousness, he himself falls into the byway of confused error. Hence it is also that the customary prayer for readers at table is: ‘May God take the spirit of pride away from you.’ Therefore, so that humility may be opposed to the arrogance that perhaps threatens from the very beginning of the reading, the blessing is rightly requested with such an art of subjection that the one who is to read is blessed not by the priest but by whomever the priest himself commands.”

And this verse should be said three times by all, with him beginning it.] “And finishing the verse,” says Boherius, “because he himself must say the entire verse three times, and the choir likewise must repeat the whole verse three times.” Hildemar says similarly:

> “He does not say that the reader should merely begin that verse and that the others should follow; rather, he must say the whole thing, and the others likewise must repeat the whole thing. Where it says ‘by all,’ one must understand ‘with them repeating,’ just as above he speaks of the kitchen brothers.”

Menardus declares this interpretation worthy of consideration.

“Lord, open my lips, etc.”] The Rule of the Master likewise prescribes that this same verse be said by the reader; but it arranges the rite somewhat differently (chap. 24):

“On Sunday,” he says, “when the weekly kitchen servants enter upon their week, then this brother also, at the meal of the sixth hour, after the table verse and prayer, when the abbot has sat in his chair, before the basket containing the customary loaves descends by the pulley-rope, shall make himself heard with his voice, saying: ‘Give the order, my lords; pray for me, who am entering upon the week of reading at table.’ At once the abbot, rising with the whole congregation, shall pray with him, all kneeling with their knees fixed to the ground. When they have risen, the new weekly servant shall say this verse: ‘Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise,’ with everyone responding together. After the verse has truly been said and the abbot has completed it, he shall give the kiss of peace first to the abbot, then to everyone; next he shall arrange a chair for himself in the midst of all the tables, and after everyone has taken their seats at the tables, having sought a blessing, he too shall sit in the chair with the book.”

“And having thus received the blessing, let him proceed to read.”] Smaragdus comments on this passage:

“When it says, ‘Having received the blessing, let him proceed to read,’ it is understood that, having received prayer from the brothers and the collected blessing from the priest, he should proceed to complete the reading. If it is agreeable, this collect is given to the reader by the priest before the altar after Mass has been completed, and it is said: ‘Turn away, we ask, O Lord, from this servant of yours the spirit of pride, so that, reading humbly, he may receive the sense and understanding of the reading. Through our Lord, etc.’”

Boherius has the same collect, with these verses prefixed: “Save your servant,” and “Send him help from the Sanctuary.”

Hildemarus gives another blessing in these words:

“These, then, are the little chapters that are to be said: ‘Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you.’ Another: ‘Turn, O Lord, for a little while,’ and ‘Have pity upon your servant.’ Likewise a third: ‘May the Lord guard you from every evil; may the Lord guard your soul.’ Then the prayer: ‘May the Lord guard your going in and your coming out, and take away from you the spirit of pride, he who lives and reigns for ever and ever.’ Response: ‘Amen.’”

The same blessing, with the second verse omitted, appears in the Cassinese Breviary copied in the time of Abbot Oderisius.

Menardus gives yet another from the manuscript of Saint Victor:

“Three verses are to be said by the prior after this verse: ‘May the Lord send you help from the Sanctuary.’ Response: ‘And may he protect you from Zion.’ ‘Turn, O Lord, for a little while.’ Response: ‘And be gracious toward your servant.’ ‘May the Lord guard your going in.’ Response: ‘And your going out, from this time forth and for ever.’ Then follows the prayer: ‘Turn away, we ask, almighty God, from this servant of yours the spirit of pride, and instruct his heart in divine readings, so that, with you aiding him, he may be worthy to complete the office.’”

489 The manuscript Customary of Saint Benignus of Dijon, chap. 37, has the following:

“The priest says: ‘Save your servant; send him, O Lord, help from the Sanctuary. May the Lord guard you from every evil.’ Then, without a greeting: ‘May the Lord guard your going in and your going out, and take away from you the spirit of pride.’ Amen.”

This is also found in Udalricus, book II, chap. 34.
