Besides this blessing, another is customarily given in the refectory before the reading begins. Boherius writes concerning it:

“After the verse has been finished in the refectory, he stands in the middle and asks to be blessed again, bowing until the blessing has followed.”

Udalricus, together with the Customary of Saint Benignus (book II, chap. 34), says:

“When the lord abbot or prior has first sat down, the reader asks for a blessing and hastens to begin the reading.”

Perhaps canon 62 of the Council of Aachen should be understood as referring to this blessing: “That the abbot, provost, and dean, even if they are not priests, should give a blessing to readers”; and canon 67: “That the reader, standing, should ask for a blessing.”

“And let the greatest silence be made at table.”] The commentators distinguish two kinds of silence enjoined by Saint Benedict in the Rule. One is simply called “silence,” without qualification. It does not prohibit every kind of speech whatsoever, but only a certain kind of speaking. In this sense someone is said to be silent when he speaks into another person’s ear, just as Martha is reported in the Gospel to have said silently to her sister Mary: “The Teacher is here and is calling you.” Here “silently” means with a subdued voice, as Saint Augustine explains.

The other kind is “the greatest silence,” or silence with some such qualification. It excludes both a loud and a suppressed voice, and absolutely every sound. Such is the silence imposed here at table, after Compline in chapter 42, and in the oratory in chapter 52. The first kind of silence is what monks should strive to observe at all times; the second is to be observed only at particular times and places. This is more or less the view of Smaragdus, Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius.

“So that no muttering or voice except that of the reader alone may be heard.”] The Holy Father added these words to show what kind of silence he prescribed in this chapter: namely, the greatest silence, excluding every voice and every muttering.

Boherius explains what “muttering” is in these words:

“Muttering is some sign of confused voice, such as a feigned cough, or the sound of someone seeming about to clear his throat, or a restrained whistle. Sometimes muttering means speaking softly or cautiously, or speaking under silence. At other times, to mutter means to murmur.”

Hildemarus and Bernard of Cassino speak in nearly the same way.

Hildemarus notes here that some understand this passage of the Holy Rule to mean that neither the prior nor the inferior should speak at table in any way; whatever cannot be expressed by the sound of some sign, when it is necessary to ask for something, should be expressed in writing. Others, however, say that the prior may speak in such a subdued voice that only one listener can understand him; and that Saint Benedict did not prohibit a voice that could be heard by one person, but only one that could be heard by everyone. Hildemarus says that the first interpretation should be preferred, for the greatest silence suppresses a subdued voice no less than a loud one.

[Col. 0607C] It is certain, moreover, that the law which the Holy Father established here concerning the preservation of silence at table was received by him from the ancient monks.

Concerning the Egyptians, Saint Jerome writes (Letter 22): “There is no disturbance during the meal; no one speaks while eating.”

Cassian writes (Book IV, chap. 17):

“Among the Egyptians, and especially among the Tabennesiots, such silence is observed by all that, when so great a multitude of brothers has sat down together for the purpose of eating, no one dares even to mutter, except the one who presides over his decany. Yet if he perceives that something must be brought to or removed from the table, he indicates it by a sound rather than by a voice. Such discipline of silence is observed among them while they eat that, with their cowls lowered beyond their eyelids—for indeed their unobstructed gaze should not have free opportunity to wander curiously—they look at nothing more than the table and the food placed upon it or taken from it. Thus no one observes how, or how much, another is refreshed.”

Rufinus likewise speaks of the Tabennesiots (Book II of the Lives of the Fathers, chap. 3):

“They maintain the greatest silence while taking food, so that one would not think that any human being was present in the place where they sit at table; and their whole manner of life in the midst of a multitude is as though they were in solitude.”

Palladius has nearly the same statement in the *Lausiac History*, chap. 48.

The Second and Third Rules of the Holy Fathers, and the Rule of Saint Macarius, likewise prescribe that “at table no one is to speak specifically, except the one who presides or the one who has been questioned.”

The Rule of Saint Caesarius for monks says (chap. 9): “While they eat at table, no one shall speak.”

The Rule of Saint Aurelian for monks and for virgins says (chap. 49 and chap. 32): “Sitting at table, let them keep silent.”

The Rule of Tarnat says (chap. 8): “Sitting at table, let them hear in silence the reading that is read.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore says (chap. 10):

“At the time when the brothers are eating together, let all maintain the silence of discipline, obeying the Apostle who says: ‘Working in silence, let them eat their own bread.’”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus says (chap. 5): “There shall be no disturbance during food; no one shall speak while eating.”

The Rule of an Unknown Author for monks says (chap. 16):

“Silence is to be pursued in all things, and the discipline of keeping silent is to be practiced in every respect, especially near the Mass and at table.”

Finally, the same rule is found in chapter 2 of the Rule of an Unknown Author, in chapter 33 of the Rule of Donatus, and in chapter 9 of the Rule of an Unknown Author for virgins.

Nor was this distinctive discipline of silence at table practiced only by monks. Saint Aldricus, bishop of Le Mans, also once imposed it upon canons in a privilege reported in his Acts, number 32 (volume I of Baluze’s *Miscellanea*). Indeed, it also flourished among the pagans, especially the Persians, Medes, and Chaldaeans. Origen praises them for this reason (Book III on Job):

“They do not open their mouths to speak over food and drink, neither those who serve nor those who are served; but they give every instruction to the servants by signs. They received this custom from their predecessors as a command, and observe it carefully as though it were a law. Whoever violated it was tortured as one transgressing the greatest laws.”

491 If such severe discipline prevailed among people of this kind, it should not seem doubtful that, among the laws of other monks, we should find penalties inflicted upon those who violated this silence.

The Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 11, and the Eastern Rule, chap. 36) says:

“If anyone speaks or laughs during the time of eating, he shall perform penance; and he shall immediately be rebuked in that same place, and shall stand until the others rise.”

Among the penalties of an Unknown Author preserved by Saint Basil (number 17):

“If anyone jokes while eating at table, he shall be made to rise for prayer.”

The Rule of Saint Ferreolus says (chap. 24):

“I particularly admonish, command, and establish that all must observe the following: whenever a reading suitable for souls devoted to God is publicly recited in the church, in the refectory, or in any place whatsoever, no one shall be moved by laughter or move another to laughter. Likewise, let them understand that stories are to be avoided at that time. If anyone does not observe this, let him, after being admonished by this present warning, be chastised by a penalty of a three-day fast.”

In the Penitential of Saint Columbanus:

“If someone speaks while eating, without another brother’s necessity: six blows.”

And again:

“He who speaks while eating: six strokes; and he whose voice makes itself heard from one table to another: six strokes.”

The Rule of Saint Donatus says (chap. 33):

“Whoever dares to speak at table shall receive either twenty or thirty blows.”

Finally, the Council of Aachen says (chap. 41):

“If anyone carelessly makes a noise or commits any other offense in the refectory, let him immediately ask forgiveness from the prior.”

The ancients nevertheless observed this silence at table in such a way that, according to Cassian, the decan was permitted to speak; according to the Second and Third Rules of the Holy Fathers, chapter 7, and the Rule of Saint Macarius, chapter 18, the one who presided was permitted; according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, the prior was permitted to speak for edification; and according to the Penitential of Saint Columbanus, everyone was permitted to speak when another brother’s necessity required it.

But the Rule of an Unknown Author for virgins says (chap. 9):

“At table, no one whatsoever, except the abbess or the one whom the abbess has appointed for the common necessity of the sisters, should presume to speak.… The portress, however, who has sought an audience with the abbess for necessary reasons, shall be permitted to speak, because perhaps some such necessity has arisen as ought not to be delayed.… On the feast days of the Lord—that is, the Nativity of the Lord, the solemnity of Easter, the Theophany, Pentecost, or any other principal sacred celebrations of the Lord or of the holy martyrs—if permission has been granted by the abbess, we do not forbid speaking at table. It must nevertheless be done in a restrained rather than an uncontrolled voice, lest, breaking out into sound with a talkative voice, they appear to be motivated more by negligence than by joy. The conversation itself should be of such a kind as to arise from discussion of the Scriptures, producing gain for the soul and not loss.”

Two brief difficulties concerning Saint Benedict’s words must finally be resolved. The first is whether it is permissible to speak in the refectory outside the time of the meal; the second, whether those who eat outside the refectory must keep silent while eating.

Regarding the first: although nothing in the words of the Holy Rule, if taken strictly in themselves, appears to establish that continuous silence in the refectory is prescribed outside the time of the meal—and although chapter 5 of the Rule of the Monks of Saint Gall decrees only “that at the hour of the meal no voice except that of the reader be heard in the refectory”—nevertheless the common custom of our order, confirmed by decrees of the Supreme Pontiffs, has been that perpetual silence should be maintained in the refectory, as can be seen from what was said in chapter 6.

Regarding the second, there is a statute of Peter the Venerable (Statute 22):

“Silence at table is to be maintained everywhere and by everyone, just as in the regular refectory. But if someone comes upon a person eating outside the common refectory, he shall rise; and when he invites him, he shall speak, standing for as long as necessary. But after he has sat down again, he shall keep silent as before.”

Giving the reason for this statute, he adds:

“The reason for this institution is that the Apostle also commands laymen: ‘Let each person eat his bread in silence’; and Saint Benedict likewise commands monks, saying: ‘Let the greatest silence be made at table’; and the religious of ancient and modern times, who, wherever they eat, relax the rigor of silence in no way.”

The Institutes of the Cistercian Order say (chap. 79):

“We decree that no monk or lay brother shall speak at table, except perhaps someone who is on a journey, if he has no one who understands his signs. In that case, he may briefly and silently request, by saying each word individually, water, bread, wine, and other things necessary only for eating. Whoever acts otherwise shall abstain from wine during that meal; but if he has no wine, he shall forgo one dish; if he has two dishes, he shall forgo one of them.”

“If anything should nevertheless be needed, let it be requested by the sound of any sign rather than by voice.”] “By striking a jug, a board, or by any other sign,” says Richard of Saint Angelo.

The Rule of Saint Pachomius likewise says (article 13):

“If anything necessary is wanted at table, no one shall dare to speak; rather, he shall make a sound as a sign to those serving.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus says (chap. 5):

“If anything is lacking at table, the one presiding shall, after giving a sign or by silent gestures, ask for it and indicate to the server what needs to be brought to or removed from the table.”

“And let no one there presume to ask anything about the reading itself or about anything else, lest an occasion be given.”] More recent witnesses add “to the evil one,” which all the ancient witnesses omit.

According to Hildemarus, when it says “lest an occasion be given,” “an occasion for speaking” is to be understood.

Smaragdus similarly says that it means “lest an occasion be given either to the wicked devil for tempting, or to the brothers for speaking superfluously.”

Bernard of Cassino and Nicolaus of Fractura speak in nearly the same way.

“Unless perhaps the prior.”] By “prior,” Boherius understands the person who presides over the brothers’ tables, or one to whom the abbot has entrusted that duty; Menardus understands the abbot.

“Should wish to say something briefly for edification.”]

First, he might question someone about the reading itself, as the Rule of the Master prescribes in these words (chap. 24):

“During the meal itself, when the Rule is being read, so that the hearing of all the brothers may be roused to attention, the abbot should ask whichever brothers he wishes at the several tables what has been read. When each brother has recited what he heard, it will be recognized that at that hour he attended more closely to the reading than to his belly.”

Second, he might explain some difficult passage of the reading, as the same Rule says:

“Let him read in an orderly manner, without rushing, so that the hearers may recognize more clearly the things which it is your duty to fulfill by your deeds; and if there are any ambiguous or obscure passages which the brothers do not understand clearly, let the abbot explain them, either when questioned by the brothers or spontaneously.”

Boherius testifies that this was observed in his own time in certain monasteries of France:

“Where there are unlearned brothers, he does well if he briefly explains to them words that are notably edifying. Thus I have seen this practiced—although rarely among us and in certain monasteries of France—and this is how I understand this paragraph. Bernard, however, says that he does not remember this ever having been done in the monastery of Cassino.”

Where the brothers are learned, Boherius says, the abbot can indicate to them by a sound alone that they should attend to the words of edification; and, if expedient, he can direct the reader to repeat those same words, so that they may adhere more firmly to the memory.

Third, he might correct a reader who is making a mistake, either personally or through another person. Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius agree that the abbot should appoint some learned brother to sit facing the reader and correct him silently whenever necessary.

Fourth, he might offer some words of exhortation from another source, as Alcuin writes concerning Albert, abbot of Esternac (in *The Life of Saint Willibrord*, no. 31, century III Benedictina). On the feast of Saint Wilgis:

“After the evening melody, out of reverence for that day, the brothers returned to the refectory, and after the sacred readings the aforesaid abbot addressed them.”

“But let the weekly brother receive the *mixtum*.”] The ancient and recent commentators on the Rule explain what the *mixtum* is.

“What he says, ‘let him receive the *mixtum*,’” says Smaragdus, “means bread together with wine. In many provinces, bread alone and the wine offered upon the altar is called *mixtum*.”

Hildemarus says:

“*Mixtum* means bread and wine, just as he says above, ‘let each receive his drink and bread.’”

Saint Hildegard says:

“Let him receive the *mixtum*, that is, the meal—that is, bread and drink.”

Bernard of Cassino says:

“Paul the Deacon says that to receive the *mixtum* means the same as to take a bite of what can simultaneously be held before one’s hands; and this is to receive one’s drink and bread.”

Richard of Saint Angelo says:

“*Mixtum*, that is, a small amount of food; for bread strengthens the human heart, and wine gladdens the human heart.”

Peter Boherius says:

“It is customary among Italians to call *mixtum* that light meal which precedes dinner.”

John of Turrecremata says:

“Let him receive the *mixtum*, that is, bread with drink, as was said above concerning the servants in chapter 35 of the Rule, that they should take their drink and bread.”

Theobaldus Artaldus Coelestinus, in a French exposition, says:

“The weekly brother who is the reader may take *mixtum*, that is, drink a good draught and eat a corresponding amount of bread.”

Matthias Lambertus, likewise in a French exposition:

“Let the weekly brother take some *mixtion*, that is, bread and a drink.”

An ancient manuscript version from the monastery of Conques says:

“Let him take *mixtum*; it is bread soaked in wine, or in something else.”

John Craesbeeck, commenting on the words “each his drink and bread,” says:

“This is called *mixtum* below, in chapter 38; perhaps because a certain mixture was made when bread was mixed with wine or with another drink.”

An anonymous Cistercian, in his French dialogues on the Rule of Saint Benedict:

“The weekly brother shall take a piece of bread and drink a draught before reading.”

Against this great multitude of authorities stands Guido Juvenalis alone, in his French version, rendering *mixtum* as “a draught of wine mixed with water.” His opinion is defended and supported by a French dissertation on the hemina of wine and the pound of bread, written by a highly learned man; but, as it seems to me, with no sufficiently solid foundation.

For what he says—that Saint Benedict grants the *mixtum* on account of Communion, and that those who received Communion were given not bread with wine but wine diluted with water—is refuted by John Belethus in these words:

“It has been established in certain churches that on that day bread and wine should be present in the church, and that, when the people have received Communion, each person should immediately be given a small loaf before departing, together with a little wine, lest something of the sacrament should perhaps remain in the mouth and easily be expelled by spitting. This laudable custom, which is approved by all, took its origin from the institution of Blessed Benedict. That most holy man instituted it for the same reason: that those who were to serve the other brothers at dinner after Communion should eat something beforehand. This dinner is commonly called *mixtum*.”

A similar institution once existed in the cathedral church of Saint Gervasius at Soissons. In its ancient ritual, written in the time of Bishop Nivelon, the prescription for Holy Easter Day reads:

“Let a certain table be prepared by the custodians at the northern horn of the altar, and let it be covered with a very clean cloth, furnished with vessels of gold and silver. Into some of these vessels let wine be poured, and let several hosts be placed there.”

A little later it says:

“All who have received Communion should come to this table, so that each may cleanse his mouth with the hosts and wine.”

Add to this that the *mixtum* is given not only on account of Communion, but also lest it be difficult to endure the fast.

Nor is the argument stronger because the Rule of the Master is said to allow the reader only pure wine in chapter 24, since in chapter 27 it grants three pieces of bread dipped in pure wine.

Nor can anyone say that the authors we have cited spoke only according to the custom of their own monasteries.

Apart from the fact that no fair-minded judge of affairs should rise against the general custom of all monasteries, preserved for more than nine hundred years, without authority and reason, Smaragdus and Hildemarus certainly wrote not long after the Council of Aachen. At that council it had been decreed (canon 29):

“That nothing except what the Rule commands should be given to the reader.”

It is therefore reasonable to believe that they spoke in accordance with the council’s intention.

The manuscript Customary of Saint Benignus at Dijon later renewed this canon of the Council of Aachen. It says (chap. 37):

“The same weekly reader, before the general meal, should take a preliminary portion with the cooks, according to the prescription of Blessed Benedict, consisting only of bread and wine, just as the cellarer and the custodian of the church also customarily receive *mixtum* after the principal Mass. It must nevertheless be understood that no *pittantia* is to be mixed into the measure of bread and wine established long ago, as was said, by Blessed Benedict. It has sometimes been heard that certain other small gifts of food were presumptuously bestowed by the deans upon those who anticipated the canonical hours of departure in order to eat. This was not only unreasonable, but was also usurped contrary to the institution of the Rule of the aforesaid Father, in which it is prescribed that only their individual drinks and bread should be given to the weekly kitchen servants and the reader, in addition to the established allowance. Hence it is decreed by a general definition that those occupied in these offices, who refresh themselves with the servants after the general dinner has been completed, are to receive absolutely nothing in the *mixtum* except what the Rule prescribes.”

This lengthy statute illustrates the canon of the Council of Aachen and confirms our opinion. See Mabillon’s preface to the fourth century of the Benedictina, part I, no. 167 and following.

Those who took the *mixtum* formerly prefaced it with a blessing and followed it with thanksgiving. The Cistercian Book of Usages says (chap. 73):

“If both are present, the one of lower rank shall say, ‘Give the blessing’; the one of higher rank, blessing, shall say: ‘May the Giver of all good things bless the food and drink of his servants.’ After the *mixtum*, he shall say silently: ‘Deign to repay with eternal life, O Lord, all who do good for the sake of your name.’”

The Bursfeld customs have something similar in the *Ceremonial*, distinction 3, chapter 17.

Nor should we omit what the aforesaid Cistercian Book of Usages adds:

“It must be understood that from the beginning of the fast until Easter—except on Sundays, and on the three days of Rogations, the Ember Days, and the vigils of the Lord and of the saints—the *mixtum* is not taken.”

The Bursfeld customs have something similar in the place cited.

The Camaldolese, who permit “a morsel of bread and a cup of wine, and nothing else” (on chapter 35), explicitly add: “Except, however, on the days of the Church’s fasts; then let them take nothing.”

Nevertheless, the common opinion is that this kind of preliminary tasting does not break the fast, provided that it does not greatly precede the meal and is not taken in excessive quantity.

“Before he begins to read.”] That is, shortly before he reads, not together with the servants, who must receive the *mixtum* one hour before the brothers’ meal.

“On account of Holy Communion, and lest it perhaps be difficult for him to endure the fast.”] This explains why he permits the reader to take the *mixtum*: first, on account of Holy Communion; second, on account of the hardship of fasting.

Recent commentators on the Rule understand the phrase “on account of Holy Communion” in different ways.

Richard of Saint Angelo, provost of Val-le-Luce, who was writing at the beginning of the fourteenth century, offers two interpretations of this passage:

“‘Holy Communion,’ he says, means the holy congregation. It is as though he said: ‘Lest he fail the holy congregation in reading,’ because *communio* can be derived from *commune*; and where there is a community, there is a congregation, which is derived from *coire*, that is, from coming together into one, as in Distinction 15, at the end of the canons of the general councils. Therefore it can rightly be explained in this way. And explain the following ‘lest’ as ‘not,’ supplying something like this: ‘That he may not fail the congregation, as has been said, and that it may not be difficult to endure the fast,’ as follows.

“Or you may say, according to some, that ‘Holy Communion’ means that, after receiving the body and blood of the Lord, he should not expel it in spittle. For, according to what I have heard, the ancients received the body of Christ every day—a practice now discontinued—and we receive it on certain feast days during the year; laypeople, however, once a year, as in *De poenitentia et remissione*, chapter *Omnis*. But this interpretation does not seem good, because once the body of Christ has been received it is immediately incorporated, and cannot be expelled or passed into the privy, as in *De consecratione*, distinction 2, ‘Tribus gradibus.’ Yet, to preserve the opinion of those who say this, let us say that they did it out of reverence for the body of Christ received, or for greater security, lest it be expelled; for it is written: ‘Hold fast to what is certain and dismiss what is uncertain.’”

Turrecremata adds a third interpretation:

“‘On account of Communion,’ that is, the Communion of goodwill and love, which the person who serves his brothers with murmuring does not appear to preserve.”

Likewise, the French dissertation on the hemina of wine and the pound of bread, in the second edition of its book, does not understand Saint Benedict to mean Eucharistic Communion, but the communion of prayers and charity. According to this view, the Holy Father wished the reader to give everyone some sign of that communion before beginning to read.

A splendid sign of charity indeed: privately eating a morsel of bread before the reading! The dissertation’s author admits that he received this interpretation from a most learned man, deeply versed in tradition, whom he could scarcely fail to defer to. Thus, in favor of that most learned man, prejudices already formed—perhaps by a more learned man—have prevailed.

Our own Mabillon has refuted this opinion, so foolish and contrary to the genuine meaning of Saint Benedict, in a special treatise that is now at press. Anyone may consult his arguments; we shall content ourselves with tradition alone, although the dissertation writer boasts of tradition without producing any argument from it confirmed by authority.

Therefore, it is a settled conclusion based on the testimony of all the authors who wrote on this matter from the time of Saint Benedict that the text of Saint Benedict must be understood of Eucharistic Communion.

First of all, the Master, who wrote his Rule a thousand years ago, taking much of it from the Benedictine Rule, clearly expresses the Holy Father’s intention when he decrees (chap. 24) that the reader,

“as soon as the abbot has received pure wine with everyone at table, should likewise receive his own pure wine on account of spitting out the sacrament, and should begin to read.”

Smaragdus says nearly the same:

“‘On account of Holy Communion,’ he says, so that he may not expel something from it by spitting.”

Peter the Deacon copied Smaragdus in his commentary; Bernard of Cassino copied Peter; and Boherius copied them in his first commentary.

To these may be added Nicolaus of Fractura, who discusses the passage as follows:

“This is what the Master wishes to say here: since in former times the faithful, and especially holy monks, received Communion every day, those who had to read to the brothers while they were eating were permitted to take such a *mixtum*, lest—God forbid—by spitting during the reading, as often happens with readers, they should expel with their spittle some portion of the body of Christ, that is, of Holy Communion. This must be avoided in every way.”

Peter Boherius likewise, who had copied Smaragdus and Peter the Deacon in his first commentary, understands Saint Benedict in his second commentary to be speaking of the Communion whereby one who eats and drinks unworthily eats and drinks judgment upon himself.

Hildemarus, an ancient commentator on the Rule, may be counted among all these. He asserts that the words “Mass” and “Communion” in this chapter were used by Saint Benedict in their proper sense, namely, for the Eucharistic sacrifice and Communion, as he himself explains.

I cannot omit the most ancient writer Amalarius, who, in his supplement to the book *On Divine Offices* (in *Analecta*, volume II), understands Saint Benedict in our sense:

“Saint Benedict,” he says, “should not be thought to disagree concerning reverence for the body and blood of the Lord with the writings of Blessed Pope Clement, in which it is commanded that the spiritual food of Communion be distinguished from carnal food. Thus, if someone receives Communion at the third hour, he should not immediately and indiscriminately presume to take earthly food out of reverence for the heavenly table, but should wait until the sixth hour; and whoever receives Communion around the sixth hour should take care to wait until the ninth, lest the taste of heavenly food be cheapened by earthly food. Saint Benedict, however, commands that the reader be fed before the delay of the reading, saying ‘on account of Holy Communion.’ This is not contrary to the apostolic decrees, etc.”

It is unnecessary to repeat the testimony of John Belethus, doctor of Paris, who wrote approximately five hundred years ago; the reader can see it cited above.

Finally, the most ancient French versions can be added to all these authorities.

The ancient version from the manuscript of Conques renders “on account of Holy Communion” as:

“For Holy Communion—that is, for the body of our Lord, which one normally receives at Mass.”

The exposition of Theobaldus Artaldus Coelestinus:

“For Holy Communion, which the reader has recently received at Mass, etc.”

The version of Guido Juvenalis:

“For Holy Communion, which he has received, so that nothing may remain between his teeth or elsewhere that could be expelled while reading because of the phlegms that arise.”

The exposition of Matthias Lambertus:

“Because of Holy Communion, lest, by spitting, some irreverence toward it should occur through the phlegms he might expel while reading.”

To these may be added the most ancient Alemannic version, made nine hundred years ago by Keron, a disciple of Saint Othmar. It translates the word “Communion” as *Kemeinsamii*, and then, for greater clarity, adds that this means the body and blood of Christ.

I pass over the more recent commentators Antonio Perez and John Craesbeeck, who also infer from this passage that the ancient monks received the Eucharist daily; and Nicolaus Bravus, Hugh Menardus, Charles Cointius, and many others.

The opinion of Richard of Saint Angelo, less genuine and, so to speak, excessively convoluted, ought not to outweigh all these authorities. Nor should the opinion of the more recent cardinal Turrecremata, or that of the dissertation writer, which is supported by no ancient authority.

Indeed, we do not believe that the expression “Holy Communion” is used by any authors in another sense than to signify Eucharistic Communion. If *communion* occurs somewhere in another sense, it is always accompanied by some qualification, such as “of charity” or “of prayers.”

Moreover, our interpretation is confirmed by the practice of the ancient monks before Saint Benedict. After Communion they used to receive a small amount of bread with wine, as a highly learned writer, deeply versed in ecclesiastical and monastic tradition, teaches in the *History of Eastern Monasticism* (book I, chap. 8, p. 123).

To this we could add the example of Saint John Chrysostom (Nicephorus, book XIII, chap. 9), who, in order to restrain spitting, used to eat a small cake after celebrating the divine mysteries, when he was removing his sacred vestments.

The second reason for granting the *mixtum* is lest it should perhaps be difficult for the reader to endure the fast. It would be harsh if, while the others were eating, he had to read while fasting until None or Vespers.

But the question arises whether, on other days, when there is neither fasting nor Communion, the reader may lawfully receive the *mixtum*. I think that in this matter the practice and custom of each congregation should be followed. I do not remember having seen anything in the common usage of our order among the ancients that deprived the reader of the *mixtum* on those days.

“But afterward let him refresh himself with the weekly kitchen servants and the servers.”] They are to have the same foods as the other brothers, according to article 15 of the Rule of Saint Pachomius and chapter 38 of the Eastern Rule; and these foods must first be designated by the abbot or by the superiors, according to chapter 24 of the Rule of the Master.

And this is “not at one table, but in their proper places,” according to canon 28 of the Council of Aachen.

The brothers, however, should not read or sing in turn, but whoever edifies those listening.] To this passage may be referred what is read in the *Book of the Uses of Bec*: “At Easter and Pentecost the cantor himself should be reader in the refectory for the entire week, and in the following week at the collation. On all other feasts, however, as stated above, on which they say the invitatory four times, the reader should be in the refectory only on that day. Such feasts occur this many times in the year: the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the Assumption of Saint Mary, the feast of the saint of that place, the Dedication of the church, and the feast of All Saints.”

## CHAPTER XXXIX. On the Measure of Food

[Col. 0613]

[Col. 0613D] 499 We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal, both at the sixth hour and at the ninth, at all tables [Note: [Col. 0613D] Thus Oxford, together with the printed editions generally. But Cassino, the Council of Florence, Hildemar, Victor, Paris, Ebrulf, Farfa, Saint-Germain manuscript, Conches, Lyre, Comp, Dunstable, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, Guido Juvenalis, and Haeften, together with all the manuscripts he examined, the Cologne and Paris editions, those of Baldwin, and Moreau together with all the manuscripts he collated, read “in all months.” Saint-Germain reads “on all days.”], on account of the different infirmities of the brothers: so that if someone should be unable to eat from one, he may be restored by the other. Therefore two cooked dishes should be sufficient for all the brothers; and if there is anything available—fruit or growing vegetables—let a third also be added [Note: [Col. 0614D] Oxford, together with the more recent copies, reads “if there are things available.” Hildemar reads “a third,” and “as a third.”]. One pound of bread, weighed out, should be sufficient for the day, whether there is one meal or both luncheon and supper [Col. 0614D]. But if they are going to have supper, a third part of that pound should be kept back by the cellarer [Note: [Col. 0614D] Oxford, Cassino, and Comp read “preserved.”] to be given to those who will have supper [Note: [Col. 0614D] Oxford and Florence read “those who are to eat supper.”].

But if the labor should perhaps have been greater, it will be within the abbot’s discretion and authority, if he thinks it expedient, to increase the amount somewhat [Note: [Col. 0614D] Some manuscripts read “to be increased.”], above all avoiding overindulgence, so that indigestion may never steal upon the monk; for nothing is so contrary to every [Note: [Col. 0614D] Oxford reads “every human being.”] Christian as overindulgence, as our Lord says: “See that your hearts are not weighed down with overindulgence” (Luke 21) [Note: [Col. 0615A] Oxford, Hildemar, and Haeften read “with overindulgence.”]. For boys of lesser age, the same quantity should not be maintained, but less than for the older ones, [Col. 0616A] with moderation preserved in everything. The eating of the flesh of four-footed animals, however, should be entirely abstained from by all, except the very weak and sick.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0615]

[Col. 0615A] *We believe that it is sufficient for the daily meal.*] Saint Benedict does not say “for each meal,” but “for the daily meal,” “that is, of each day,” as Boherius says, 500 “according to the saying, ‘he was fed with daily nourishment’”; whether there are two meals, at the sixth hour and at evening, or only one at the ninth hour; so that for the two meals on days when luncheon is eaten, no more should be given than for a single supper during a time of fasting. The manuscript Rule of an uncertain author, which our Mabillon extracted at Rome from a very ancient [Col. 0615B] codex of the library of the Queen of Sweden, seems to have explained Saint Benedict’s meaning in this chapter in agreement with Boherius. For in its sixth chapter we read:

“Saint Benedict says: ‘We believe that at the daily meal, whether there is one meal or both luncheon and supper, one pound of bread and two cooked dishes are sufficient; and if there are fruit or growing vegetables, a third should be added.’ Bernard of Cassino, perhaps explaining these words more clearly, ‘and a third should be added,’ speaks as follows: ‘He does not mean that more than two cooked dishes ought to be given, but that the third should be raw. And the commentators say that this should be done at the time when the community eats only once; for when it eats twice, the third, which is raw, according to the commentators, is reserved for supper.’”

This testimony of Bernard of Cassino, which Boherius likewise transcribes in his commentary, should not be passed over casually. From it, in fact, it is clear that this was not their own isolated opinion, but the settled view of other commentators. The same was the position of Nicholas of Fracture, who wrote his commentary shortly after Bernard. [Col. 0615C] Explaining these words, “and a third should be added,” he says:

“By this it is not said that more than two cooked dishes ought to be given; but the third, if there is one, should be added raw, especially at the time when the community eats once a day; for if it ate twice a day, the third, which is raw, would be reserved for supper.”

Hildemar had likewise hinted at this long before, though not obscurely, when commenting on this passage as follows:

“‘Daily meal’ is understood in various ways. There are some who understand it to mean that, just as on ordinary days, so also on solemn days and at Easter there should be two cooked dishes on solemn days as on ordinary days, because our fathers on ordinary days ate at the ninth hour and on solemn days at the sixth; and thus they ate at the sixth and evening only so much that they did not eat more than on ordinary days at the ninth. For they ate at the sixth and evening only that food which they ate at the ninth.”

Thus Hildemar, whose words agree sufficiently with the opinion mentioned above. Yet, not concealing anything, he adds:

“But the better ones [understand it as] somewhat more, namely three cooked dishes; for they increased the number.”

But whatever may be the case regarding that addition of dishes, which was beyond the Rule, as is clear from Theodemar, whom we shall cite shortly, from this passage at least we learn that the ancient monks did not eat more together at the sixth and evening on solemn days than at a single meal at the ninth during a time of fasting. They considered the principal difference in the breaking of the fast to consist in taking better foods at the two meals of the sixth and evening, although not in greater quantity. From their example it may be inferred that Saint Benedict allowed no more food for the combined meals of the sixth and evening than for the single meal at the ninth; but that what he granted at the ninth during fasting—two cooked dishes and a third consisting of fruit and vegetables—he permitted on other days at the two meals of the sixth and evening: that is, two cooked dishes at luncheon and a third consisting of fruit at supper.

[Col. 0616A] And certainly the same argument seems entirely applicable to the other foods as to the bread. Saint Benedict grants as much bread for one meal at the ninth as for two meals at the sixth and evening. Therefore, just as he wished a third part of the pound of bread to be kept back for those who would have supper, so it is reasonable to think that he also wished one of the three dishes to be reserved for supper.

This opinion is confirmed by the Rule of the Master, which almost transcribes the Benedictine Rule and, as it were, explains it, especially in this chapter. Thus it sets out the measure of food (chapter 26):

“For we believe that for the daily meal, both at the sixth and at the ninth, in all months, two cooked dishes and a third, whatever it may be, raw with fruit are sufficient. Half a loaf weighing a pound shall be sufficient for each brother per day. . . . Therefore, when they eat at the sixth hour in summer, or at other times, a third quarter of that loaf of the Lord, deducted by the cellarer from each one’s daily ration in the cellar, shall be placed on the tables in the evening before that raw dish is brought in . . . so that those portions alone, together with whatever raw dish mixed with fruit there may be, or if anything from the brothers’ luncheon dishes remains, may be sufficient for their supper.”

The practice of the first Cistercians likewise confirms the same opinion. They had proposed to observe Saint Benedict’s Rule literally, and only a double cooked dish was served at luncheon, while a single dish of raw fruit or herbs was served at supper, as can easily be gathered from the *Book of the Uses of the Cistercians*. In its chapter 76, “On Luncheon,” we read:

“Moreover, the cellarer and cooks should take care that both dishes, before the bell rings—if the abbot should nevertheless see this to be expedient—are set out on the tables.”

There is no mention of a third dish. But in chapter 83, “On Supper”:

“After vespers, when the office for the dead has been completed and the signal has been sounded, as we said above, they should go to supper. If fruit, or raw herbs, or anything of that kind is to be distributed generally to the brothers, the cellarer may carry it around the tables before the verse, whenever he has the opportunity.”

It is clear from chapter 84 that in summer, at harvest time, when they were working, they had one cooked dish at luncheon and another cooked dish at supper: “and consequently,” says Julian of Paris, abbot of Foulcard’s Mount (*Notes on chapter 76 of the Book of the Cistercian Uses*), “on other days, whenever they had supper, they received nothing but fruit, vegetables, or growing legumes, and these raw.” The same can also be gathered from chapter 79 of the *Book of the Statutes of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order*, which decrees that “those who speak at table [Col. 0616D] should be deprived of wine, or, if they have no wine, of one dish, if they had two.” Therefore they did not always have two dishes at a meal.

Against the opinion we have proposed so far, it could be objected, first, that Saint Benedict grants two cooked dishes and a third of fruit and vegetables, if there is anything available, on account of the different infirmities, so that whoever cannot eat from one may be restored by another. It would therefore be poorly arranged for the different infirmities if, while two dishes were allowed at luncheon, only a third, and that raw, were allowed at supper. For it could happen that someone could not taste that third dish and would consequently have supper on bread alone. Moreover, the holy Father does not grant the third dish absolutely, but only if fruit or growing vegetables are available. If they are not available, everyone will have supper on bread alone. It would therefore be much fairer, and more consistent with the spirit of discretion with which he was abundantly endowed, to affirm that the holy Father granted two cooked dishes together with one raw dish at luncheon, and as many again at supper.

I reply that Saint Benedict provided sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, for different infirmities by granting two cooked dishes at luncheon and a third at supper, consisting of raw fruit or herbs, which scarcely fail in monasteries built according to his intention—that is, monasteries in which nothing ought to be lacking and in which spacious gardens, cultivated by the hands of the monks, ought to be found. And if these were lacking, it was sufficient for monks committed to penance to have supper on bread alone. Nor should Saint Benedict’s intention be judged from the practice and relaxation of our own times, but from the strictness and austerity of the ancient monks, for whom adding anything to bread counted as great luxury.

Certainly it can be gathered from Udalricus (book I, chapter 49) that the Cluniacs supped on bread alone throughout the entire year, except on the Sunday of Quinquagesima, or at most added raw fruit to the bread:

“At Quinquagesima,” he says, “because during the rest of the year we eat neither cheese nor eggs, after vespers we have a general supper of those eggs cooked with pepper; for nothing more occurs during the whole year, so that on that occasion we have anything besides bread alone. And if raw fruit happens to be available, or those things made very thin on an iron marked with a pattern from a mixture of flour, which people of the Roman tongue call *nebulae* and our own people call *oblatae*.”

The same is contained in chapter 55 of the manuscripts of the Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon, and even more clearly in the Ordinary of the monastery of Corbie. For what Udalricus expressed in ambiguous language is there stated in clear words:

“Throughout the year it does not happen that we have anything generally cooked for supper, apart from bread alone, unless it is raw fruit or those things made on a marked iron, and so forth.”

Second, chapter 16 of the monks of Saint Gall could be brought forward, establishing “that the brothers, when they come to be refreshed, should find before them one dish with drink and a garden-produce dish or fruit, if there are any; after these, let other things be given which the Rule [Col. 0617C] commands.” Those “other things,” however, can be nothing except a second cooked dish. Therefore Saint Benedict grants three dishes at each meal.

I reply that this chapter is to be understood of the meal which is taken only once, at the ninth hour, on days of fasting; for this Saint Benedict certainly allows three dishes. Or at least those monks were speaking according to the custom of their own monastery.

Third, the testimony of Hildemar could be brought forward. Writing on these words, “and a third should be added,” he says:

“But this must be noted: on ordinary days, if there is no heat or exceptionally hard labor, there should be two cooked dishes at the sixth hour and one raw dish, and at evening a third cooked dish, if they are going to have supper, corresponding to the measure of bread. That is, just as he himself says that the monk ought to eat two parts of the pound of bread at the sixth hour and a third at evening, if he is going to have supper, so the same is understood of the dishes: the monk should have two cooked dishes at the sixth hour and a third raw dish; and at evening one cooked dish, which is now the third cooked dish, just as there is a third part of the pound of bread. But if it is time to eat at the ninth hour, he ordered two cooked dishes and one raw dish to be given.”

I reply that Hildemar may have been speaking according to the custom of his own monastery, and that from this testimony at least it follows not that three dishes were to be given at supper, but that only one was to be granted. Nor is it difficult to believe that our predecessors added something to the measure of food prescribed by Saint Benedict, since we have a clear testimony concerning the monastery of Cassino in Theodemar’s letter to Emperor Charles. Its words are these:

“Our blessed Father established that two cooked dishes should be prepared for the brothers in the daily meal, and a third of raw vegetables soaked in water. But, following the institution of our elders, we prepare three cooked dishes on other days; on Wednesday and Friday we prepare only two for the brothers’ meal, except that many of our brothers eat only bread on those days, [Col. 0618A] together with garden herbs; and many of them do not even drink wine. On Sunday, however, and on the principal festivals, we add a fourth dish, except on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.”

Where it is said that four dishes were served on festive days, this is to be understood as applying to both luncheon and supper, so that two were provided at luncheon and two at supper for each person. For it is not credible that in those prosperous times eight dishes were granted on a single festive day.

Moreover, this opinion is confirmed by the practice of the ancient monks, who ate no more in order to break the fast than while keeping it. They were content either to anticipate the time of the meal to the sixth hour or to distribute their usual foods into two small meals.

Some understand “daily meal” here as opposed to the meal of solemn days. On the latter days, they say, better and more numerous dishes should be served than on the other ordinary days:

“There are some,” says Hildemar, “who understand ‘daily meal’ to mean ordinary days, and [understand that] on solemn days there should be more, because Saint Benedict himself elsewhere distinguishes between ordinary days and Sunday. Just as there he divided the days into ordinary days and Sunday when he spoke of the offices, so here too he is understood to have made a distinction when he says ‘for the daily meal.’ Accordingly, by saying ‘for the daily meal,’ he indicates that at the meal of solemn days something more and better ought to be provided.”

Thus the *Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins*, which is largely taken from the Benedictine Rule:

“On ordinary days,” it says (chapter 10), “we decree that two dishes are sufficient, apart from gifts of fruit, made from legumes or vegetables, or from any kind of flour mixture. . . . But on feast days, out of reverence for the sacred solemnity, the bodies are to be refreshed with more foods, that is, with three or four dishes; yet in such a way that, if there are more foods in number, they should be smaller, so that the bodies may be refreshed with necessary food and not condemned through excessive satiety.”

Certainly it was the custom of the ancient monks to be treated somewhat more generously on feast days and Sundays. Saint Caesarius, in his *Rule for Virgins* (in the Recapitulation, chapter 16), says:

“On the greater feasts, dishes should be added at luncheon and supper; and when they depart from it, sweet things should be added.”

Saint Aurelian, in both his Rule for monks and his Rule for virgins (chapters 51 and 35), says:

“Fish should be procured on certain feasts, or whenever the holy abbot wishes to grant an indulgence.”

And in the order of the meal which he appended to both Rules:

“But on feast days, and whenever the abbot wishes to grant indulgences, whatever foods and whatever quantity he wishes may be added, including fresh foods.”

Saint Isidore says (chapter 10):

“Throughout the whole week let the brothers use humble foods of vegetables and pale legumes; but on holy days, from time to time, let them have with vegetables the nourishment of very light meats.”

Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 5):

“Let them live on vegetables and legumes alone, and rarely on little river or sea fish; and let this too occur whenever the brothers’ opportunity or the festivity of some solemnity permits it, with discretion observed in these and similar circumstances.”

Finally, the Master says (chapter 26):

“On Sunday or other feast days, and also because of visiting strangers, the abbot is permitted to add on any day whatever he wishes to the food, as befits a greater occasion; or some sweeter foods, according to the testimony read in the *Lives of the Fathers*, where, on feast days, they asked the Lord for a delicate food, and an angel appeared to them with a honeycomb. Let him only consider equality and avoid corrupting excess.”

But these indulgences, which may to some extent be tolerated among monks who eat nothing but legumes throughout the entire week, must be used with extreme restraint. For Saint Benedict does not oppose feast days to ordinary days either in this chapter or anywhere in the Rule. Indeed, we must always remember what the *Rule of a Certain Author for Monks* says (chapter 11): “A monk has no holidays on earth”; and what another manuscript Rule by an uncertain author says (chapter 7):

“Do not say, ‘Today is a feast, and I shall drink wine; and tomorrow is Pentecost, and I shall eat meat,’ because for monks there is no feast on earth.”

These words are taken from the sayings of the monk Evagrius addressed to brothers living in monasteries and hospices.

*Both at the sixth and at the ninth hour.*] But what of the evening meal taken during Lent? Perhaps he is silent about it here because he will say later that during this period something must especially be subtracted from food and drink, as Boherius notes. He either left the measure of food at these times to the abbot’s provision, or wished his monks to be content with the single pound of bread which he grants per day. For Saint Richmir, abbot (in his Life, no. 15, third century of the Benedictines), when the days of Holy Lent arrived, had as his dry food only barley bread, which he also ground by hand.

Thus Saint Isidore decrees in his Rule (chapter 10):

“During the observance of Lent, as is customary, after the fast has been completed, all shall be content with bread alone and water, while they abstain from wine and oil.”

And indeed, “we call those people fasting,” Peter Damian once said (*Opuscula* 14 and 15, chapter 6), “who take bread with salt and water; but when anything besides these is added, it is not called a perfect fast.”

*For all months.*] This reading, which the commonly printed editions retain, and which Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius report as being found in certain codices, is rejected by Hildemar himself and by the commentators mentioned above. In its place they substitute “in all months,” as it appears in the Rule of the Master, chapter 26.

This reading is followed by the ancient French versions, among them the old version from the Conches manuscript, which renders the passage: “in all the months of the year”; the version of Jean de Précis, together with another old version of the monastery of Saint-Remi at Rheims: “at all times”; Guido Juvenalis: “throughout the whole year”; Matthias Lambert: “all the months of the year”; and another, by a more recent author: “in all the months of the year.”

Menardus prefers this reading, and says that Saint Benedict is here confronting the bad practice of certain people who wanted more dishes to be served every day in summer than in winter because of the heat. Saint Isidore also guarded against this by the following statute (chapter 10):

“In both seasons the meal shall consist of three dishes.”

Nevertheless, the common reading does not seem wholly to be rejected. For if we read “for all tables,” it is clear that the holy legislator was equally confronting the bad practice of certain people who wanted more or better dishes placed on the tables of the abbot and others holding positions of authority than on those of the brothers. Saint Isidore expressly prohibits this in the same chapter:

“Except when sickness requires it, let the abbot take his food in the presence of the brothers together with them; let him not ask that anything be prepared for him other than what the others have, or more elegantly than what is provided in common. . . . For the dishes on all the tables shall be equal, and all the brothers shall be refreshed with similar foods.”

The common monastic Rule of Saint Fructuosus likewise says (chapter 11):

“Except on the arrival of brothers and in cases of sickness, abbots should not dare to eat more delicate foods unless they are such as the brothers also have.”

The Council of Aachen (canon 25) says:

“Let abbots be content in eating, drinking, sleeping, dressing, and working with the measure which their monks have, unless they are occupied with other useful duties.”

And the Council of Oxford in 1222 (in Spelman, volume II, *English Councils*) says:

“Let all eat together in one refectory, and let provisions be prepared not separately for each person but commonly for all.”

Here the excellent institution of the monastery of Cluny may also be mentioned, as Udalricus reports it in these words (book III, chapter 18):

“Whenever fish is provided generally, immediately after the sixth hour—or, if the fast continues that long, after the ninth—everything should be laid out and arranged in bowls on the table in the vestibule of the cellar, so that the prior, coming before he sits down at the signal, may see what is in each of the bowls, whether it is equal, and whether it has been divided so that larger and better portions do not come to the priors. In this matter favoritism toward persons is greatly avoided.”

Now, if it is not permissible for the abbot to have better and more food than the brothers, much less is it permissible for him to hold lavish banquets. Pope Benedict XII prohibits these in his constitution for Benedictine monks, in these words:

“Moreover, we forbid superiors, abbots, priors, and all other persons of that order or religious community from occupying themselves with lavish banquets and feasting; nor are they to incur immoderate or otherwise excessive expenditures on these.”

*Or, “for all tables”*—that is, both the second and the first, as Theobaldus Artaldus explains—lest perhaps servants, readers, and others detained by the monastery’s duties, who could not recline at the first table with the brothers, should think that on account of their greater labor they might indulge themselves in something more than the others.

Thus the Rule of Saint Pachomius says:

“Servants, apart from what has been prepared in common for the brothers, shall eat nothing else, nor dare to prepare altered foods for themselves.”

And chapter 20 of the monks of Saint Gall says:

“All servants, whether inside or outside, shall be content in drink and food, clothing, and all other necessities with the measure by which the other brothers live.”

There is someone who translates it into French as *à chaque repas*—“at every meal.” If this version is accepted, it must be understood of luncheon, not supper:

“For if it is said ‘for all tables,’” says Bernard of Cassino, “the word ‘luncheon’ must be supplied; for so many dishes are not to be given at supper.”

Or one may say that the universal term “for all tables” includes both supper and luncheon.

*Two cooked dishes.*] The Rule of the Master grants the same number, chapter 26; the Rule for Solitaries, chapter 43; and the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, chapter 10. But Saint Caesarius, in his Rule for Virgins, in the Recapitulation, chapter 16, says:

“On all fasting days three foods are to be prepared, but at luncheon only two.”

And Saint Aurelian, in the Order of the Meal, says:

“Every day, three foods are to be provided for the meal, two at luncheon, and two at supper.”

Saint Fructuosus, however, does not make his meaning sufficiently clear when he decrees that “on the principal solemnities three dishes and as many drinks be provided for the brothers.”

What, then, is to be understood by the term *dishes* in the Rule of Saint Benedict must be investigated briefly. “*Pulmentum*,” says Saint Isidore (*Etymologies*, book II, chapter 2), “is called from *puls*, porridge; whether only porridge or something else mixed with it is eaten, it is properly called *pulmentum*.” In this sense, according to Saint Hildegard, Saint Benedict “by *pulmentaria* indicates those foods which, placed on the fire, are moved this way and that with a small piece of wood, lest they burn.” Theobaldus Artaldus, Coelestinus, and several other men distinguished both for piety and learning explain *pulmentum* here in the same way, taking account of the word’s etymology.

Others, no less distinguished for learning, understand by *pulmentum* or *pulmentarium* anything that is added to bread so that it may be eaten more pleasantly. This is also how the word is ordinarily used in speech, as could be demonstrated by almost countless examples. Hildemar’s text alone will suffice:

“*Pulmentaria* are spoken of in many ways. They are used of meat, as Isaac is said in the book of Genesis to have said to his son when he had gone hunting and had made him a dish from his game. They are also used of fish, as you have in the Gospel, where after his resurrection the Lord appeared to the disciples who were fishing and asked them whether they had anything to eat; and when the disciples came to land, they saw a fire of coals, and a fish placed upon it. *Pulmentum* is also used of legumes, as you have in the aforementioned book of Genesis, where it says: ‘Jacob cooked a dish,’ which was made of lentils. For, as the teachers relate, *pulmentum* is whatever is added to bread so that the bread itself may be eaten more easily, such as cheese, leek leaves, eggs, and other similar things. If you eat cheese uncooked with bread, it is not called a cooked dish; but if it has been cooked, it is called a cooked dish. In this passage a cooked dish means something made from vegetables, cheese, eggs, and flour.”

Four considerations persuade me that the word *pulmentum* should be taken in this second sense in this chapter.

First, words in laws must be understood in the sense that belongs to them through common and accepted usage, not according to their etymologies. Otherwise subjects of laws—who are not obliged to know the etymologies of words and frequently cannot know them, since they are forbidden to study—would be made liable to almost countless transgressions.

Second, *pulmentum* in the first sense does not include fish; yet I have never read that anyone asserted that fish were forbidden by Saint Benedict. Certainly the Cistercians themselves, who had proposed to observe Saint Benedict’s Rule literally, although they customarily lived on legumes alone, and those very badly prepared, nevertheless sometimes used fish. This is clear from Saint Bernard (*Sermon 30 on the Song of Songs*), who, criticizing the complaints of certain monks about their food, among other things rebukes them for complaining:

“Fish from a pond or muddy water is altogether unsuitable to my constitution.”

It is also clear from the *Life of Blessed Roger, Abbot of Ellant*, numbers 5 and 10 (in the Bollandists, 4 January). He died in 1175; when “a fairly large fish was once offered to him, he asked whether each of the brothers might receive his ordinary portion from it,” and ordered it to be put into the community’s common vegetable dish. On another occasion, while traveling, he is said to have been refreshed by a fish of extraordinary size.

Third, because the ancients used porridge in place of bread, as is clear from Pliny (book XVIII):

“It is evident that for a long time the Romans lived on porridge, not bread, and from this such foods are today called *pulmentaria*.”

But Saint Benedict here adds bread to the dishes. This is the argument of Nicholas Bravo.

Fourth, because according to the Rule the third dish must specifically consist of legumes. From this it can rightly be inferred that the other two need not consist absolutely of legumes, but may be prepared from any other side dish. Otherwise the holy Father would have said without qualification: “Let three dishes be sufficient for the monks.”

Since, then, in common usage *pulmentum* means whatever is added to bread so that it may be eaten more easily, and since Saint Benedict forbids only the flesh of four-footed animals, all kinds of food that are suitable to the monastic way of life, or that do not conflict with it by reason of their cost or excessive deliciousness, are to be understood here under the name *pulmentaria*. What foods are suitable for monks must be learned from the deeds, sayings, and Rules of the holy Fathers.

Thus Saint Jerome, speaking of the Egyptian coenobites (Letter 22), says:

“They live on bread, legumes, and vegetables, seasoned only with salt; only the old men receive wine.”

Of the anchorites he says:

“Except for salt and bread, they carry nothing else into the desert.”

Similarly, when discussing the Egyptian monks, Cassian says (book IV, chapter 22):

“Nor is much care spent among them on preparing or cooking food, since they make especially great use of dry foods and raw foods, and among them it is a great pleasure, once a month, to have leek leaves, *lapsana*, roasted salt, olives, salted little fish—which they call *maenidia*.”

[Col. 0621D] Palladius speaks as follows of the Pachomians (*Lausiac History*, chapter 39):

“Some are occupied with preparing the tables, placing upon the table loaves, wild vegetables, olives, cheeses, the extremities of meat, and chopped vegetables.”

And it is clear from the *Life of Saint Pachomius* that their customary foods were vegetables, legumes, olives, garlic, and chopped herbs seasoned with oil and vinegar. Thus, rebuking a negligent cook, he says:

“How do you do this, when the established rules of life and the holy Fathers command that on every Saturday and Sunday vegetables be cooked for the brothers who wish to eat them?”

Of the holy Fathers in Sinai we should hear Saint Nilus (*History of the Massacre of the Holy Fathers on Sinai*, chapter 5):

“Few indeed know food made from grain. . . . Many eat raw vegetables and berries, embracing a table that is entirely unelaborate and equipped with no condiments, and considering the ingenuity of those who season dishes and make bread to be of great importance; lest, if they devoted much time to caring for the body, they should become negligent in that which ought rather to be their perseverance.”

The monks living beside the Jordan likewise spent no greater care in preparing their food. Of them we read in the *Life of Saint Mary of Egypt*, number 5 (Bollandists, 2 April):

“Their unfailing food was the divine words; for the body they allowed only what was necessary: bread and water.”

For five days of the week, the disciples of Saint Gerasimus tasted nothing “that was edible except bread and water and dates.” On Saturday and Sunday “they used cooked food in the monastery and drank a little wine.”

Nor was this peculiar only to monks living in the East. The common food of the disciples of Saint Fintan, an abbot in Ireland in the sixth century, was nothing other than wild vegetables, according to his Life, number 2 (Bollandists, 17 February). Of the monastery of Saint Comgall, the second author of his Life says (number 26; Bollandists, 10 May):

“Bread, water, and vegetables alone were already present at that supper; for milk and other foods had previously been unknown to the monastery of Saint Comgall both in sight and taste. . . . Later, at the urging of the bishop, Saint Finbar, and other saints, milk was received, out of consideration for charity, for the old and the sick.”

Later they also admitted fish, as is recorded in the same Life, number 34. According to the Rule of life prescribed for monks by Saint David (Bollandists, 1 March), “they took food more for necessity than for satiety; there too they were content with vegetables and salt, and regarded more luxurious foods as distasteful. Nevertheless, for the sick, the elderly, and those exhausted by a long journey, they sometimes provided the delights of more luxurious food.”

Now, if we consult the sayings of the saints, Saint Basil says (*Long Rules*, chapter 19):

“It is necessary, he says, by every means to use those foods that can be obtained more easily and cheaply, lest under the pretext of abstinence we seek more costly things and compose more expensive foods from costly seasonings. But if there is something in each province that can be obtained more easily and cheaply, and that is commonly used among people, this ought to be adopted for our purposes; and only those things should be sought that are entirely necessary for life, namely oil and similar items, or anything else that is used to relieve the sick.”

And shortly before this:

“If, then, there is anything that can satisfy this bodily need through food more briefly or more easily, that should rather be chosen. The Lord too, as I believe, showed this when he fed the hungry in the desert. Although he could certainly have provided them with more abundant foods by a greater miracle, he did none of these things, but supplied them with simple nourishment; and according to John he set before them five barley loaves and two small fish. As for drink, there was no mention at all. From this it is undoubtedly indicated that the use of water can be sufficient and entirely necessary for everyone.”

Similarly Cassian says (book V, chapter 23):

“Therefore food should be chosen not only that may moderate the burning heat of desire and kindle it less, but also food that is easy to prepare, whose lower price makes it more convenient to eat, and which is common to the way of life and use of the brothers.”

St. Jerome instructs the monk Paulinus concerning the ordering of his life as follows (Epistle 13):

> “Let your food be cheap and taken in the evening: vegetables and legumes, and occasionally regard little fish as the greatest delicacies. Whoever desires Christ and feeds on that bread does not greatly concern himself with what costly foods he may use to produce dung.”

These words agree with what Severus Sulpicius writes when sending to that same Paulinus a cook suitable for preparing the monks’ food (Spicilegium, vol. V):

> “After I learned that all your cooks had resigned from your kitchen, I suppose because they disdained to provide a service involving cheap dishes, we have sent you from our workshop a young man sufficiently skilled in cooking pale beans, seasoning humble beets with vinegar and broth [Col. 0623A], and thrusting cheap porridge into the throats of hungry monks—a man ignorant of pepper, unacquainted with laserwort, familiar with cumin, and especially adept at forcing the mortar to resound with sweet-smelling herbs. He has one fault: he is the sworn enemy of every garden, so that if he is admitted, he will cut down everything nearby with his sword and will never be satisfied with the slaughter of mallows.”

**510** Finally, Evagrius says in *Monastic Precepts*, no. 3 (Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments, vol. III):

> “Take a small meal of no value, not a large one requiring much care. If, under the pretext of hospitality, the thought of expensive food should occur to you, reject that thought and do not cling to it; for through it the adversary lies in wait for you, in order to turn you away from tranquility.”

I come now to the institutions of the ancient monks. The Rule of St. Abbot Isaiah says (chapter 31):

> “If you live with a brother and he says to you, ‘Cook,’ say, ‘What do you want?’ And if he leaves the choice to you, cook whatever comes to your hands.”

The Rule of St. Aurelian for monks [Col. 0623B] says (chapter 51):

> “Meat is never to be taken as food; chickens and all poultry are not to be served in the community. They are to be provided only for the sick, who may receive them. Fish, however, may be procured on certain feast days, whenever the holy abbot wishes to grant permission.”

The Rule of St. Columban says (chapter 3):

> “The food should be cheap and taken in the evening, avoiding the monks’ satiety; and the drink should avoid drunkenness, so that it may sustain without harming: vegetables, legumes, flour mixed with water, with a small quantity of bread-paximatia, lest the belly be burdened and the mind suffocated.”

Nevertheless, it is clear from chapter 6 of the *Life of St. Gall* that St. Columban’s disciples sometimes also ate fish (Benedictine Century II).

The Rule of St. Isidore says (chapter 10):

> “Throughout the whole week the brothers shall eat cheap vegetable foods and pale legumes. On holy days, however, they may sometimes have, together with vegetables, nourishment consisting of very light meats.”

Elsewhere, describing the life of monks, the same St. Isidore says (*On Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II, chapter 15):

> “They abstain not only from meat and wine, as sufficient for subduing lust, but also from everything that provokes the appetite of the belly and throat.”

The Rule of St. Fructuosus says (chapter 5):

> “Let them live on vegetables and legumes alone, and rarely on little river or sea fish; and even this only whenever the brothers’ convenience or the solemnity of some feast provides the opportunity, with the superior’s discretion preserved in these and similar matters.”

Finally, the Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins says (chapter 10):

> “For ordinary days we decree that two dishes shall suffice, apart from the gifts of fruits: dishes filled with legumes or vegetables, or with any preparation of flour.”

To add some examples from our own communities, the disciples of St. Amarinus the abbot “scarcely took, by measure, bread-paximatia with a drink of water.”

Ardo likewise relates of the first disciples of St. Benedict, abbot of Aniane, in his *Life*, no. 12 (Benedictine Century IV, part I) [Col. 0623D]:

> “Their hunger was sometimes driven away by milk brought by neighboring women, because their bodies had wasted away from dryness, as they lived on bread and water alone.”

St. Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, in his constitution concerning the food and clothing of his monks, assigns beans, peas, honey, cheese, eggs, and fattened pigs for fat and bacon; in addition, at Christmas and Easter, bird dishes (*aucipastae*), chicken dishes (*pullipastae*), and chickens. For drink, wine and cider. For the care of the sick, honey and spices.

The Cluniacs prepared their dishes every day, one from beans and another from vegetables; to these they added a *pittantia* or *generale* consisting of cheese and eggs—only on Sunday and Thursday of fish, and then only if these could be found at a reasonable price. Udalricus explains what *pittantia* and *generale* are in these words (book II, chapter 35, and book III, chapter 18):

> “We call *generale* what is given to each person in an individual bowl. *Pittantia* is what is given to two people in one bowl. For example, sometimes, as a *pittantia*, without a bowl, one large piece of cheese or four eggs; as a *generale*, five eggs—cheese never, unless cooked.”

On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday they served *pittantia*; on the other days, *generale*.

The monks of Tegernsee in Bavaria also rarely ate fish, as Gozpertus, abbot of that place in the tenth century, testifies (vol. IV of the *Analecta*):

> “Living, as you know, in the southern region, and abstaining from meat according to the monastic custom, we rarely feed on the catch of fish, because we have scarcely any fish-bearing waters.”

But what shall we say of the Cistercians? Certainly William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, must be heard when speaking of the monks of Clairvaux (*Life of St. Bernard*, book I, chapter 5):

> “They very often prepared their dishes from beech leaves. Their bread, like that prophetic bread, was made from barley, millet, and vetch, so that once a certain religious man, weeping profusely, secretly carried away what had been set before him at the guesthouse, as though it were something to be displayed to everyone as a miracle: that human beings, and such human beings, lived on it.”

And Fastredus, the third abbot of Clairvaux, rebukes a certain abbot who lived more luxuriously (among the letters of St. Bernard):

> “This is not the life that our father and predecessor Bernard, of blessed memory, taught you and me; nor is it the manner followed by the abbots and monks of our holy order, who nourished us on bread made from oats, herbs cooked without oil or fat, and beans and peas even on the feast of Easter itself. This austerity, or something similar in every respect, is observed in all the houses of the order.”

And lest domestic witnesses perhaps seem suspect, we produce outsiders: Stephen of Tournai and James of Vitry. The former, writing to Robert, prior of Pontigny, speaks as follows:

> “In the sweat of their faces they eat their bread, and leisure and foreign food do not make them grow wanton or quarrelsome. Such is their frugality that they use only two dishes, supplied either by the field with legumes or by the garden with vegetables. They use fish so much more rarely that among them it is more often heard of than seen.”

The latter says in *History of the West*, chapter 14:

> “They do not ordinarily eat fish, eggs, milk, or cheese; sometimes, though rarely, out of regard for piety, they use these as *pittantiae* and as the greatest delicacies.”

What Peter the Venerable writes about the Carthusians is remarkable (*Book of Miracles*, book II, chapter 28):

> “They always use bran bread and wine so diluted with water that it is more properly called *villum* than wine. Both the healthy and the sick perpetually abstain from eating every kind of meat. They never buy fish, but may happen to accept fish given out of charity. Only on Sunday and Thursday do they admit cheese or eggs for eating. On Tuesday and Saturday they use either cooked legumes or vegetables. On every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday they are content with bread and water alone.”

Abbot Guibert likewise says (*Life*, book I, chapter 10):

> “On Sunday they receive food from the steward, namely bread and legumes, which is the sole kind of dish cooked by each of them for himself … They use fish and cheese on Sundays and very solemn feast days; I say fish, not fish that they themselves have bought, but fish that they have received through the generosity of certain good men.”

These statements agree with what is prescribed in Guigo’s *Statutes*, chapter 33, and in the *Ancient Carthusian Statutes*, part II, chapters 13 and 14.

From what has been said thus far it is clear what the foods of perfect monks ought to be: cheap, very easy to find and prepare, such as beans, peas, roots, vegetables, legumes, and the fruits of the earth. St. Ambrose once said (*Hexameron*, book III, chapter 7):

> “The example of frugality and the school of moderation is to be content with the nourishment of simple herbs, cheap vegetables, or fruit—what nature has offered and God’s generosity first bestowed. That food is healthful and useful which drives away diseases and cuts off indigestion, produced by no human labor but poured forth as a divine gift, sweet and pleasing without sowing grain or planting seed, so that it is both a pleasure and a benefit even to those who are full; finally, given at the first tables, it remained for the second.”
