That is what he says to everyone; but what should be said to monks? Fish, however, monks ought to eat only rarely, and fish of little value, treating it as a great delicacy.

I cannot pass over here the remarkable deed of St. Lupicinus the abbot, who, as Gregory of Tours relates (*Book on the Lives of the Holy Fathers*, chapter 1), entered a house where food was being cooked for refreshment and saw a large display of various dishes and a great quantity of fish gathered together. He said in his heart:

> “It is not fitting that monks, whose life is solitary, should use such foolish expenditures.”

He immediately ordered a large bronze vessel to be prepared. When it had been placed over the fire and had begun to boil, he put into it all the foods they had prepared at once—fish as well as vegetables and legumes, or whatever had been intended for the monks to eat—and said:

> “Let the brothers now refresh themselves with this porridge; let them not devote themselves to delicacies that hinder them from the work of God.”

And St. Ambrose’s saying has always rightly pleased me (*Commentary on Luke*, book VII):

> “It is unbecoming for people who are fighting for the kingdom to concern themselves with food.”

If these words do not please some, let them hear not me but St. Bernard (*Sermon 30 on the Song of Songs*):

> “‘Whoever wishes to save his soul will lose it.’ What do you say to this, you observers of foods and neglecters of morals? Hippocrates and his followers teach how to save souls in this world; Christ and his disciples teach how to lose them. Which master of the two do you choose to follow? But the one who argues in this way makes himself evident: ‘This harms the eyes, this the head, that the chest or the stomach.’ Surely each person brings forward what he has learned from his own master. Have you read these distinctions in the Gospel, or in the prophets, or in the writings of the apostles? Flesh and blood has certainly revealed this wisdom to you, not the Spirit of the Father. For this is the wisdom of the flesh. But hear what our physicians say about it: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is death.’ Again: ‘The wisdom of the flesh is hostile to God.’ Was I supposed to put before you the opinion of Hippocrates or Galen, or at least something from the school of Epicurus? I am Christ’s disciple, and I speak to Christ’s disciples.”

And further on:

> “What good does it do to abstain from pleasures while spending daily care investigating the differences of constitutions and seeking out varieties of foods? ‘Legumes cause wind; cheese burdens the stomach; milk harms the head; drinking water does not agree with the chest; cabbages nourish melancholy; leeks inflame choler; fish from a pond or muddy water is wholly unsuited to my constitution.’ What is this, that among so many rivers, gardens, fields, and storerooms scarcely anything can be found for you to eat? Consider, I beg you, that you are a monk, not a physician; and that judgment should be based not on constitution but on profession. Spare, I beg you, first your own tranquility; then spare the labor of those who serve; spare the burden of the household; spare conscience—conscience, I say, not your own but another’s, and so forth.”

Finally, concerning seasonings for food:

> “Let sugar, to use the words of the monks of Fuli, be far away, as well as cinnamon, clove, pepper, and other aromatic spices. None of these may be permitted to anyone except perhaps someone who needs them because of illness” (*Fuliensian Constitutions*, chapter 39).

And rightly so. For, as William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, said (*On the Solitary Life, to the Brother of Mont-Dieu*):

> “Concerning seasonings, I beg that our foods be made edible, but not objects of desire or delight. Lust’s own evil is sufficient; and since it can scarcely or in no way reach the fulfillment of its need except by way of some degree of pleasure, if it begins to receive provocations from those who have undertaken perpetual war against its attractions, two are made against one, and thus continence is endangered.”

Certainly St. Father Benedict wants no other seasonings for food than those that can easily be prepared even by people less capable. For he prescribes that the foods be cooked by the brothers and excuses no one from kitchen duty.

This is because of the various infirmities of the brothers, so that perhaps one who cannot eat one dish may be restored by another, and so that no one might be forced to live on bread alone by finding the one prepared dish distasteful.

But what follows if the holy Father permits two dishes only for the various infirmities of the brothers, so that someone who cannot eat from one may be restored by the other? Must the monk be content with one, or may he be restored by both?

Peter Boherius replies:

> “Although he does well if he abstains from the second and gives thanks to God for such possible abstinence, I nevertheless do not believe that a brother sins if he reasonably takes from both, since neither the Master has tacitly prohibited this here nor has he expressly done so.”

Hildemarus likewise says:

> “This must be understood: he may be restored by both, if he is able, since the intention is not that, if he can eat from both dishes, he should eat from only one. That this is so is shown where he says, ‘Let a third be added’; for he certainly would not have said, ‘Let a third be added,’ if he had wished him to eat only from one.”

Menardus also holds this view. Indeed, as he says:

> “It would be badly advised with respect to unnecessary expenses if, when dishes were doubled, portions sufficient for fifty monks had to be set out for a hundred—for each individual dish ought to contain what would suffice to satisfy one monk, since he would be permitted to eat from only one.”

These words completely refute the utterly ridiculous and unworthy opinion of a monk held by certain people, who think that each dish ought to suffice for the proper refreshment of any monk.

**Therefore, two cooked dishes shall suffice for all the brothers.**

Richard of St. Angelo rightly infers from this passage that “the subdeans and the other priors ought not to have more than two dishes, because whoever says ‘all’ excludes or excepts nothing.”

**And if there should be fruit.**

By the word “fruit” he understands every kind of produce that ordinarily grows from trees or herbs. For Bernard of Cassino says:

> “What grows from trees or herbs is called fruit.”

**Or leguminous shoots.**

Gazaeus says that “whatever grows from the sowing of the earth and from pods” is called a legume (*On Cassian*, book V, chapter 5). He proves this from Varro, *On Agriculture*, book I:

> “Legumes are pulled from the earth, not cut down like grain; because they are gathered in this way, they are called legumes.”

He also proves it from St. Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVII, chapter 4:

> “Legumes are so called from gathering; for the ancients gathered the better things by hand, or because they are gathered by hand and require no cutting. There are very many kinds of legumes, among which beans, lentils, peas, chickpeas, lupins, and *phaselus* seem more agreeable in human use.”

What St. Father Benedict means here by “fresh legumes” is explained by the commentators.

Smaragdus says:

> “By ‘fresh legumes’ are understood the sprouts of those same legumes, which, combined with vinegar or other fruits, are suitable for eating.”

Hildemarus says:

> “‘Fresh legumes’ means germinating legumes, because it is the custom of that land, and of Rome and other provinces, to put legumes in water; and when they have sprouted, they eat them.”

Bernard of Cassino explains Hildemarus:

> “Fresh legumes, according to the commentators, are called legumes that are growing or germinating—when they are placed in water and become, as it were, tender, like those that are beginning to sprout and are eaten in the Roman regions, either in that sprouted state or with vinegar.”

Boherius, after reporting the opinions of Smaragdus and Bernard, adds:

> “Or say that here they call ‘fresh legumes’ those things that are born from legumes—that is, from seeds or grains—and are suitable for eating, rather than the legumes or grains themselves, as is evident in pumpkins, cucumbers, radishes, melons, watermelons, parsnips, lettuces, purslane, and similar things.”

I think that “fresh legumes” here properly means recently grown vegetables, which are customarily eaten with salt, vinegar, and oil, such as lettuces and other herbs of this kind, which, when dressed in this way, we commonly call salad. Turrecremata understands the passage in this way.

St. Hildegard’s explanation is somewhat broader:

> “He indicates beans, peas, and other legumes of this kind, which are gathered fresh from the field, just as fruits are taken from trees; and he orders these, not cooked but removed from their husks, to be served to the brothers as the third food. Fish, cheese, or eggs are also to be understood as the third food.”

This does not fit very well with the meaning of *pulmentum* that she had given shortly before.

**Let a third be added.**

That is, a dish; and this one, according to the ancient monastic order, was raw. This is supported by chapter 11 of the *Conversations of Monks*, by Theodemar’s letter to Charlemagne, and by Hildemarus, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, Turrecremata, and Matthias Lambertus. The Rule of the Master agrees, granting “two cooked dishes and a third, whatever it may be, raw with fruit.” Menardus, however, thinks that the third dish may be served either cooked or raw.

As Hildemarus observes here, St. Benedict did not allow fruit at the ninth hour in summer or at the late hour in winter; otherwise there would be three meals when he permits only two in summer, and two when he allows only one in winter. From this we may infer that, at least in some monasteries, the custom of eating fruit at the late hour, even on fast days, and at the ninth hour in summer, had already begun to enter.

Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, gives testimony concerning eating fruit at the ninth hour in his letter to Charlemagne:

> “In addition to these things, in summer, after the ninth hour, if there is any fruit, we also provide our brothers with individual bowls.”

The Council of Aachen seems to have prohibited this, decreeing:

> “Fruit and lettuces are not to be eaten unless some other food is being taken.”

**One *propensa* pound of bread shall suffice for the day.**

The authors do not agree among themselves about the weight of this pound. There are two kinds of pound: the Roman pound of twelve ounces and the mercantile pound of sixteen; each also has a smaller Neapolitan form. It is not known whether St. Father Benedict adopted either of them.

The common opinion is that he established a special pound-weight for his disciples. This is suggested, first, because the holy Father, when sending his disciple Blessed Maurus to Gaul, gave him, together with the sacred text of the Rule, the weight of bread that he was to take with him (Faustus, *Life of St. Maurus*, no. 29). If it had not been a special weight, there would have been no need to send it, since an equivalent could have been found in Gaul.

Second, when the monastery was destroyed by the Lombards and the monks of Cassino fled to Rome, they carried with them the text of the holy Rule and the pound of bread left to them by St. Benedict. After the monastery had later been restored, Pope Zacharias restored its weight there (Leo of Ostia, *Cassinese Chronicle*, book I, chapter 2). Such care would surely have been useless if the holy Father had adopted the Roman pound.

Third, when Charlemagne wished to restore regular discipline, which had everywhere collapsed in the monasteries of Gaul, he sent men to Cassino to bring back to him the weight of the bread-pound established by St. Benedict and the measure of the *hemina* of wine. The emperor would have sent to Rome rather than Cassino if St. Benedict had adopted the Roman pound or *hemina*.

The Council of Aachen unquestionably arranged for the pound sent by Abbot Theodemar to the emperor to be received in all monasteries immediately after Theodemar’s death. It decreed that a pound of bread should be measured by thirty solidi of twelve denarii each—and indeed before it was baked, as the title of the canon indicates.

These words, entirely clear in those times but very obscure in ours, have given many people an opportunity for guesswork. Gazaeus, in his notes on Cassian, book V, chapter 5, understood this canon as referring to the price of thirty solidi, and Dadinus Alteserra supports him (*Asceticism*, book V).

Haeftenus, relying on—or rather misled by—Theodemar’s words to the emperor, understood it as the weight of four pounds, that is, forty-eight ounces. Theodemar wrote:

> “We have also sent the weight of four pounds, according to which the bread ought more properly to be made, so that, in accordance with the sacred text of the Rule, it can be divided into four equal squares of one pound each, since the weight instituted by the Father himself has been found here.”

The decree of the Council of Aachen in 816 also assigned four pounds of bread to each canon and three to the nuns, from which he infers that the monks were not granted a smaller quantity of bread.

Others, interpreting *solidi* as ounces, have asserted that the pound prescribed by the council consisted of thirty ounces. Nicholas Bravus admits that he has been unable to grasp the council’s meaning; meanwhile, however, he accepts as legitimate a Cassinese pound of thirty and a half ounces.

James Brolius, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in the *Supplement to the Antiquities of Paris*, p. 88, and Andreas Quercetanus in his notes to the *Cluniac Library* likewise seem to recognize the same pound as Benedictine.

The learned Antonius Yepezius touched upon the point of difficulty, though by conjecture. He thought that the law concerning the weight of the pound had been issued according to the Frankish custom, by which they usually reckon a pound numerically as twenty solidi, and a solidus as twelve denarii; and that they once used the same method of reckoning for weights.

From this observation he concluded that the pound of unbaked bread assigned by the synod amounted to one and a half pounds, so that the baked bread would amount to one pound according to the Parisian custom. That pound [Note: [Col. 0627D] The reading *qui* seems preferable, so that it refers to *more*. EDIT.] requires twenty-five solidi for one pound, and this, finally, is the pound that St. Benedict calls *propensa*.

But a French dissertation on the *hemina* of wine and the Benedictine bread-pound not only touched upon the knot of the difficulty but solved it. In that little book, printed at Paris in 1667 and reprinted in 1688, the author observes from ancient Frankish laws that a denarius is one twentieth of an ounce, while twelve denarii make a solidus; thus three ounces make five solidi, and twelve ounces constitute a pound of twenty solidi.

Our own Mabillon confirms the same conclusion by other arguments and authorities in his preface to Benedictine Century IV. Thus a pound of thirty solidi contains one and a half Roman pounds, that is, eighteen ounces; after the bread has been baked, this yields approximately fourteen ounces if it is first-quality bread, and sixteen if it is second-quality bread.

Many considerations persuade me that this is the Benedictine pound, which the holy Father calls *propensa* because it exceeds the Roman pound by several ounces.

**517** First, St. Father Benedict followed the ancient monks as guides in many matters and, in this respect also, probably imitated them. Abbot Moses accordingly speaks of them in Cassian (*Conferences*, 2, chapter 19):

> “When they examined the practices of abstinence of various people—those who lived continually on legumes alone, or only on vegetables, or on fruits—they placed before all these the refreshment of bread alone, fixing its most equitable measure at two *paximatia*, which were certainly scarcely the weight of one pound, being small loaves.”

That this pound consisted of twelve ounces is inferred from the weight of the *paximatia*, which clearly amounted to six ounces, as is evident from Palladius, who, speaking of Paul the Simple, says:

> “Antony brings and places on the table four *paxamidia* of six ounces, and he himself soaked one.”

Second, St. Benedict permits something to be added to the measure he established when the labor is greater. But if St. Father had given such a quantity of bread as the authors mentioned above wish—enough to satisfy two or three people abundantly—then certainly nothing would have needed to be added even for the most voracious person, however hungry, exhausted by heat, or worn down by labor.

Third, St. Benedict allows no more bread for two meals than for one when there is a fast. But whoever denies that fifteen or sixteen ounces of bread, with two or three dishes, are enough for one meal for a penitential man desires not so much to appease hunger as, I will not say to fill the belly, but to empty it out.

Fourth, Peter Damian says (*Opusculum* 10, chapter 7):

> “In Gaul, as we learned from the report of a distinguished man, the religious fathers of monasteries, seeing that many of the brothers exceeded the measure of refreshment handed down by Blessed Benedict and could not restrain themselves within the prescribed limit of the regular daily allowance, wisely resolved that, after establishing certain hours for the offices, they would add further psalms, so that they might compensate by an increase of psalmody for the excess of their more relaxed diet.”

If this refers to bread, the Benedictine pound was not so large that it could not suffice for each person’s daily meal.

Fifth, St. Odo, abbot of Cluny, is praised for eating only half a pound of bread per day. That would hardly be great praise if the Benedictine pound were enough to refresh two or three people.

Finally, Peter Damian describes the monks’ pound of bread (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 8) as weighing on balanced scales “as much as nine quail eggs, or three goose eggs.” Nine quail’s or hen’s eggs weigh only a little more than sixteen ounces. All these arguments persuade a fair-minded judge of facts that the Benedictine bread-pound did not exceed fifteen ounces by much.

Someone may oppose this assertion with the various weights of the bread-pound distributed to monks. The Cassinese monks say in their *Declarations*:

> “The weight of the pound, as we received it from our monastery of Cassino, was thirty-three ounces.”

Peter Boherius and James Brolius testify that a similar or nearly similar weight was once preserved in the monastery of Saint Maur at Fosses. Another, of thirty-two ounces, was preserved at Saint-Médard of Soissons and was also used by the neighboring Celestines of Soissons. There was also one at Saint-Croix in Bordeaux, made of Cypriot bronze, weighing twenty-eight ounces. Finally, there was the weight of four pounds sent by Abbot Theodemar to Charles Augustus.

We accept all these weights as genuine and legitimate, although someone might suspect them of being false and spurious. The weight of the Cassinese, Fosses, Soissons, and Bordeaux communities was the weight of two pounds, divided between two monks. The pound of the Cassinese, Fosses, and Soissons communities was sixteen ounces, or somewhat more, before baking; that of the Bordeaux community was fourteen ounces after baking.

No one should object that these weights were not equal. A small difference counts for nothing, and fair-minded men ought not to linger over such trifles, about which critics may quarrel—people who will never approve anything unless they themselves have proved it.

Nor should anyone stumble over the fractional number of thirty-three and a half ounces. This may have resulted from a difference between the ounces now in use and those current in St. Benedict’s time. Indeed, the bronze weight preserved in the Cassinese sacristy, bearing the inscription “Weight of the bread-pound of Blessed Benedict,” is thirty-nine ounces of the Neapolitan kingdom.

Examples of this division are not lacking among the ancients. The Rule of the Master decrees (chapter 26):

> “Let half a loaf weighing one pound suffice for each person per day.”

Thus a whole loaf weighing two pounds was baked; its half, weighing one pound, belonged to one brother.

In the same way, the weight of four pounds sent by Abbot Theodemar to Charles Augustus was divided among four monks, as is clear from Theodemar’s own letter:

> “We have also sent the weight of four pounds, according to which the bread ought to be made, so that, in accordance with the sacred text of the Rule, it may be divided into four equal portions of one pound each. This weight, instituted by the Father himself, has been found here.”

It was therefore divided into four portions of one pound each, and this was done according to the text of the sacred Rule.

By this explanation various difficulties can be resolved which someone might raise on account of the different weights, without resorting to the utterly ridiculous genealogies of weights by which someone might attempt to make monks hateful to secular people.

Certainly all these weights display some antiquity. Our predecessors therefore used them, and we see that they were content with so small a pound that for some it scarcely sufficed.

Now, however, the Cassinese, Camaldolese, Fuliensians, and other monastic congregations generally set before each person as much bread as is sufficient for him.

The Cistercians also seem to have served each person a pound and a half in the refectory, as can be inferred from book II of the *Life of St. Stephen*, abbot of Obazine, no. 27 (vol. IV of the *Miscellany of Baluze*):

> “After terce they entered the bakehouse again and found such a quantity of loaves that the whole community, which then numbered more than one hundred and twenty, would each have had, according to custom, a pound and a half of bread.”

So much for the quantity of bread; now for its quality.

**519** The ancient monks commonly ate *paximatia*. The Rule of St. Columban also mentions *paximatium* bread, chapter 3. For some, *paximatium* is bread baked under ashes; for others, twice-baked bread. Hence the frequent mention in the *Lives of the Fathers* of dry bread.

What kind of bread did St. Benedict want the monks to have? Without doubt, bread for ordinary use and of a coarser kind, such as suits the poor, and bread that the brothers themselves would make with their own hands.

There is a Cistercian statute prohibiting first-quality bread, commonly called white bread, even on the principal feasts (*Cistercian Institutes*, chapter 14):

> “Lest the brothers, overcome by the weakness of flesh and spirit, begin to reject coarser bread and desire more luxurious bread, we therefore establish that white bread shall not be made in our monasteries, not even on the principal feasts; but coarse bread, that is, bread made with the sieve. Where wheat is lacking, it may be made with *seatio*. This rule does not apply to the sick; and to guests, whenever it seems appropriate, we serve white bread, and to those being bled at their bloodletting (*minutio*), as is described in their sentence. This bread—namely, the white bread served to the little ones—as well as the daily dough placed on the balance, must not weigh more, but must be weighed on an equal scale.”

Julian of Paris notes (*On the First Manner of Life of the Cistercians*, part III, chapter 3, section 1) that the Cistercians formerly had three kinds of bread:

1. white bread, for the sick;
2. ordinary bread, made from sifted wheat or from barley, rye, oats, *utilio*, but made with *seatio*;
3. coarser bread made from barley flour, oat flour, and so forth, which they did not sift through the *seatio*.

This bread was given: first, at supper to those who had eaten a third of a pound at dinner; second, as a form of penance; and third, as alms.

The earliest Cistercian institution, however, seems to have been more austere. For, as we read in the *Life of St. Bernard* (book I, chapter 5), their bread

> “was like that prophetic bread, made from barley, millet, and vetch, so that once a certain religious man, weeping profusely, secretly carried away what had been set before him at the guesthouse, as though it were something to be displayed to everyone as a miracle: that human beings, and such human beings, lived on it.”

The bread of the monks of Ellant, in the diocese of Rheims, was undoubtedly of this sort—“not only made of bran, but so bitter that the poor scarcely deigned to receive fragments of it” (*Life of Blessed Roger, Abbot*, in Bollandus, January 4).

Louis of Saint-Malachy writes something similar about the bread of the first Fuliensians. Their constitutions, however, published in 1631, say only:

> “The bread shall be ordinary and common; nevertheless, better bread may be given to guests and the sick.”

Concerning the Carthusians, Guigo must be heard in the *Statutes* (chapter 34):

> “Although the bread is made from wheat, it is a flat loaf; for we do not make white bread.”

The ancient Carthusian Statutes add (part II, chapter 14, §16):

> “Except for the sick.”

Yet lower down they say (chapter 32, §9):

> “It is an ancient custom that we make two kinds of bread, one of which is the finer, for the monks, and the other for the lay brothers; when the prior wishes this to be done, no one may dare to oppose him.”

The *Customs of the Cluniac Monastery* in manuscripts, and the Benignian customs, chapter 40, likewise mention two kinds of bread, of which the best was served to the brothers. Yet even better bread was to be assigned to the sick.

### 520

Before leaving this subject, it should be observed that the Benedictine pound is to be *propensa*, which some explain as “weighed out in excess,” or “weighed beforehand.” So Smaragdus, Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, and others interpret it, in accordance with the custom of the ancient monks, who weighed the bread before placing it on the table. Theodoret provides an example of this in the case of a certain father of monks, Publius (Book IX of *The Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 9): when he approached the scales, he carefully weighed the prescribed measure of bread; and if he ever found it to exceed the stipulated amount, he was greatly displeased and called those who did this gluttons. That this was the custom of our order is also demonstrated by the various weights of pounds that still survive.

[Col. 0631B] In truth, *propensa* is not a Latin word in this sense. For that reason others interpret *libram propensam* as a pound that is “weighed out in excess,” “lavish,” and “generous.” Thus Gazaeus on Cassian, Book V, chapter 5; Menardus in his commentary on this passage; and Mabillon in the Preface to the fourth century, part I. They are supported by certain French translations, which render the passage as follows: “A pound of bread by good weight.”

Nicholas Bravus makes two words out of the single word *propensa*, reading *pro pensa*, as though the meaning were “for the daily allowance.” Manuscripts and all who have hitherto dealt with this matter oppose this division.

“If they are going to dine, a third part of the same pound is to be reserved by the cellarer for those who are going to dine.” This can be done in two ways: either by dividing a third part from the same loaf after baking, or by making two loaves from the same pound of dough. The first method seems to be indicated by the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 26, and was customary among the Cassinese down to the time of Abbot Bernard, who later introduced the other practice, as he himself testifies in these words:

[Col. 0631C] “Until my time this had been observed: a certain restriction was imposed on the third part of the bread, so that there were not two or three loaves, but one. But when I saw that this was not very seemly, I divided a pound of flour-dough into three parts, so that a third of the pound could be reserved not as broken bread but as a whole piece.”

Nicholas of Fractura mentions this institution of Bernard, and it was still in force in his time. Richard of Saint-Angelo, however, thinks that Saint Benedict should not be understood so strictly here, and writes:

“It should not be understood so strictly that a third part is reserved for supper; rather, everything that remains is to be kept, because many perhaps could not eat in the morning owing to natural weakness, and eat in the evening.”

The Cistercians seem to have served a whole pound at dinner and, in the evening at supper, whatever remained from dinner. Thus the *Book of Usages* (chapter 117) says that it belongs to the cellarer “to add at supper, from the coarser bread where it is available, to those who eat up to a third part of their bread at dinner.”

“If the work should perhaps have been greater, it will be in the abbot’s judgment and power, if it is expedient, to increase something.” Bernard of Cassino says that this “increase, I think, should not be extended to bread alone, but also to the dishes.” Boherius and Turrecremata hold the same opinion, and ancient usage of the order confirms their view, although Nicholas of Fractura seems to restrict the increase to the pound of bread alone.

And Saint Benedict rightly says that the matter will be in the abbot’s judgment and power, not in the will and judgment of the brethren. For although the abbot ought to be pious and merciful in relieving the monks’ labors, the brethren cannot demand this consolation as something owed to them, since they ought above all to have resolved, through punishments and labors, to make a way for themselves to the eternal rest of blessedness.

Accordingly, when Saint Basil was asked “whether one does well who, laboring intensely, himself demands something beyond the customary allowance,” he replied (Shorter Rules, question 135):

“Certainly, if he has undertaken the labor in order to receive a reward from God, he ought not to seek relief from it on this account, but should strive to prepare himself fitly to receive the Lord’s recompense, knowing that, just as he will find a reward for his labors, so also he will find consolation in his distress through God’s goodness. Nevertheless, the one entrusted with fulfilling the saying, ‘It was distributed to each according as each had need,’ must necessarily know those who labor individually and provide, as is fitting, for their needs.”

The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, chapter 17, speaks in nearly the same way.

But what is to be understood by “greater labor”? John Bertelius, abbot of Luxemburg, calls it “a greater labor by which bodies are so exhausted that weakness follows, making perseverance in spiritual matters difficult, and which prudent administrators of affairs, according to the quality of the circumstance and condition, recognize as beyond the ordinary.” For example, this may occur in summer, when the monks undertake hard labor in the fields.

Thus Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, says in his letter to Charlemagne:

[Col. 0632B] “When it is the season for cutting hay, we also give the fathers who are laboring a drink made with honey at the fourth hour.”

Likewise the Cistercian *Book of Usages* (chapter 84) states that during harvest “each person may be given a pound and a half of ordinary bread per day, where necessary, and it is to be distributed to each according as the time and place require. At this season, except on the days when the brethren are occupied with reading, they are to have one cooked dish at dinner and another at supper, if possible”—that is, more than usual.

Bernard of Cassino, however, interprets “greater labor” as meaning “not only work in the fields or other occupations, but also duties, such as on solemn days, when the brethren customarily labor more extensively in the performance of solemn offices.” Boherius and Turrecremata say the same, and before them all Hildemar wrote on this passage:

“On solemn days, or whenever the labor has been greater, he ought to give at the sixth hour three cooked dishes and a fourth uncooked one, according as the labor has been; in the evening, however, one cooked dish, as he himself said: ‘If the labor should perhaps have been greater, it will be in the abbot’s judgment and power, if it is expedient, to increase something.’”

That it was indeed an ancient custom of the order to add something to the ordinary allowance on solemn days can be confirmed by many testimonies. The letter of Abbot Theodemar to Charlemagne supplies an excellent example:

“Our blessed father,” he says, “instituted that two cooked dishes should be prepared for the brethren at the daily meal, and a third consisting of raw legumes soaked in water. But, following the institution of our elders, on other days we prepare three cooked dishes for the brethren who are to be refreshed; on Wednesdays and Fridays we prepare only two. On Sunday, however, and on the principal feasts, we also add a fourth dish, except on Mondays, Wednesdays, and Fridays.”

Similarly, in the monastery of Fulda, as the Venerable Eigil is reported by his disciple Candidus to have done (in his Life, fourth century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*), on the anniversary of Abbot Sturm:

[Col. 0632D] “Out of reverence for so great a solemnity, and in keeping with monastic life, he ordered that something more elegant and more agreeable than usual should be prepared for the brothers’ food.”

The ancient customs of the monastery of Fleury likewise state for Easter:

“At dinner we ought to have three courses: first, stuffed eggs; second, fish; third, cuttlefish and leeks from the gardener, and from the baker little rolls; and a portion of the best wine from the wine-keeper; in the evening, little cakes.”

Finally, in the manuscripts of the Customs of the Roman monastery of Saint Paul, at the Easter meal three servings of drink beyond the usual are prescribed: the first to be served by the lay brothers, the second by the deacons, and the third by the priests, “not so much to satisfy gluttony and drunkenness as to preserve charity and for the love of Christ.” They think that this can be justified by the authority of Hildemar in his exposition of the Rule.

“Above all, gluttony having been removed, etc.” Gluttony (*crapula*) is an excess or superfluity of food. It is called *crapula*, as though from *cruda epula* (“raw food”), because its rawness weighs down the heart and renders the stomach unable to digest.

“For boys of younger age the same quantity is not to be observed, but less than for adults.” Boherius explains:

“First, because a boy cannot eat as much as an adolescent or young man; and also because they do not come fasting to dinner, since they must anticipate the canonical hours.”

The Master agrees with Saint Benedict in his Rule, prescribing that “for those under twelve years of age less than a pound of bread per day is sufficient.”

It certainly seems possible to infer that the boys’ pound of bread was somewhat lighter from Hildemar on chapter 30. Speaking of fasts to be imposed on delinquent boys, he says:

[Col. 0633B] “A pound contains twenty-two solidi when the bread is raw, so that when it has been baked it contains only twenty”—that is, twelve ounces—whereas the pound of others, according to the Council of Aachen, consisted of thirty solidi before the bread was baked.

The following passage in Hildebert of Le Mans’s Life of Saint Hugh is also relevant (in his Life, no. 12, in the *Acta Sanctorum*, 29 April):

“How great his discretion and mercy were is shown by the kindness he extended to the younger monks. Although, according to custom, a smaller pound of bread and drink was given to them, he nevertheless decided that an equal amount should be given them, judging it fair that those whom the same burden and heat of the day afflicted should be paid the same denarius, as it were.”

“As for the flesh of quadrupeds, all must entirely abstain from eating it, except those who are altogether weak and sick.” Yet according to the manuscripts of the Customs of Saint-Bénigne, even the healthy abstained from it during Lent; indeed, also during Advent and from Septuagesima until the beginning of the fast, unless the illness was extremely serious.

Here the ingenuity of the authors is greatly exercised. Their opinions can be divided chiefly into three classes:

1. Those who think that Saint Benedict prohibited only the flesh of quadrupeds, while permitting birds.
2. Those who say that the flesh of birds was forbidden to both the healthy and the sick, while the flesh of quadrupeds alone was granted to the sick for restoration.
3. Those who maintain that both birds and quadrupeds were prohibited to the healthy, but that both were permitted to the sick.

I do not intend to settle the matter here with certainty. It is enough, I think, to set out the force of the three opinions, so that each person may freely follow whichever seems preferable.

The first opinion rests on a threefold foundation: authority, reason, and practice. First, Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, understood the text of the Rule in this way when writing to the Emperor Charlemagne:

“Concerning birds, our most prudent Father inserted such a cautious provision in his Rule that, if the monks wish to eat them when appropriate, they do not incur guilt; but if their abbot does not provide such food for them, they cannot demand it as though it were owed.”

Rabanus Maurus supports Theodemar (Book II of *On the Training of Clerics*, chapter 27):

“I believe that the eating of birds was permitted by the Fathers from the beginning because they were created from the same element as the fish. For in the Rule of the monks no other flesh is found to have been forbidden to them except that of quadrupeds.”

[Col. 0633D] The word “I believe” does not qualify the permission itself, as though Rabanus were doubtful about it, but the reason for the permission—namely, that birds were created from the same element as fish.

Rabanus’s testimony is particularly significant because he himself had been a monk of the monastery of Fulda, which Saint Boniface had founded under a stricter and more rigorous observance of Saint Benedict’s Rule. Saint Boniface had sent Saint Sturm to Italy so that, after arranging the monasteries more effectively, he might add a purer and truer understanding of the Rule, which was later to be restored to practice by the monks of Fulda. Consequently, Rabanus could hardly have spoken contrary to the understanding that prevailed in his own monastery.

The same was the opinion of Dietrich, bishop of Metz, who once spoke of the discipline he had seen as a student in the monastery of Saint Gall (Ekkehard, *On the Fortunes of Saint Gall*, chapter 11):

“There were others who lawfully used only birds, because they are creatures of the same kind as fish.”

To this may be added Saint Hildegard, whose words are as follows:

“The eating of flesh is to be granted altogether to the sick and weak for restoration.” She intends flesh both of quadrupeds and of birds, and excludes none of the kinds of flesh that human beings customarily eat. “But when they have improved, they are to abstain from flesh as usual”—that is, from the flesh of quadrupeds, because the healthy did not customarily eat those, or their juices, but the sick did. “The healthy, however, ate the flesh of birds, because it is clean and does not produce burning lust in those who eat it.”

And below she adds:

“He is silent about birds because he does not prohibit their consumption to the healthy, etc.”

### 524

Second, they argue, not without reason, that Saint Benedict used the word “quadrupeds.” For if he had wished to prohibit birds, he would either have said simply, “Let all abstain from flesh,” or would have named both kinds together, as Saint Caesarius does (Rule for Monks, chapter 24):

“Let the healthy never receive chickens or flesh.”

And Saint Aurelian (chapter 51):

“Let flesh never be taken as food. Let chickens or any poultry not be served in the community.”

But since Saint Benedict names only the flesh of quadrupeds, this is a sign that he permitted birds; for when one thing is denied, another is granted.

Richard of Saint-Angelo replies that this is indeed so “unless the reason for the prohibition is the same in the thing granted and in the thing prohibited; for then, when one is denied, the other is denied as well.” The reason is the same for birds and quadrupeds—namely, penance and the restraint of desire. Indeed, it is stronger in the case of birds, since they are more pleasurable and more delicious, and therefore the monk, who renounces every pleasure and delicacy, ought with even greater reason to abstain from them.

If someone asks why Saint Benedict expressly mentioned quadrupeds rather than birds, Richard answers:

“Because people make more frequent use of this flesh than of the other; and laws are also adapted to things that occur more frequently, as in the Digest, *On Laws*, and the senatusconsultum, book … concerning this matter. And that other flesh is understood under the name ‘quadrupeds’ is clear from the law in the Digest, *Si quandiu*, *On the Poor*, final book, where it is said that when quadrupeds are named, bipeds are understood as well.”

Hildemar explains it differently:

“Now, lest the monks be able to say, ‘We know that we cannot and ought not to eat the flesh of birds because it has greater sweetness and pleasantness than the flesh of quadrupeds; nevertheless, we can and ought to eat the flesh of quadrupeds because it has less sweetness and pleasantness to the taste’—Saint Benedict confronts such people by saying expressly that monks ought not to eat the flesh of quadrupeds at all, except because of illness or weakness. For just as the flesh of birds, because of the sweetness and pleasantness of its taste, is accustomed to provoke the impulses of the flesh, so also the flesh of quadrupeds, because of the strength it possesses, contributes the power necessary for those impulses of the flesh to reach completion.”

They repeat another argument from the nature of birds themselves: since their flesh is cleaner and contains less nourishment, it does not produce burning lust. This is Saint Hildegard’s reasoning.

Hildemar would reply to this argument:

“Saint Benedict himself understood that birds have sweeter flesh than quadrupeds, as the doctors say and experience confirms, since kings and princes, because of the greater sweetness and pleasantness of the taste, order the flesh of birds to be prepared for them at their banquets after the flesh of quadrupeds. Therefore those who abstain and do penance are known to abstain from all flesh because of the pleasantness of its taste, not because of the number of feet.”

He adds below:

“The flesh of birds, because of the sweetness and pleasantness of its taste, is accustomed to provoke the impulses of the flesh.”

Indeed:

“The impulses of the flesh more readily rise up where there is greater sweetness and where greater pleasantness of taste is perceived in the food.”

Moreover, there are some birds in which one finds no less juice than in the flesh of quadrupeds.

They derive a third argument from the very origin of birds, which were created from the same element as fish. Rabanus, cited above, touched on this reason. It may perhaps have been why, in former times, some people ate birds together with fish during Lent, as Socrates and Nicephorus testify (Socrates, Book V of the *Ecclesiastical History*, chapter 21; Nicephorus, *Ecclesiastical History*, Book XII, chapter 34), and why some formerly valued abstinence from quadrupeds more highly than abstinence from birds.

But against this argument they set the words of Saint Jerome to Salvina (Letter 9):

“Let pheasants, fat turtledoves, Ionian partridges, and all the birds by which the greatest estates fly away from your banquets be far from them. Nor should you think that you do not eat flesh if you reject the delicacies of wild boars, hares, deer, and other quadruped animals; for these are approved not by the number of their feet but by their pleasantness and taste.”

They also cite Julianus Pomerius (*On the Contempt of the World*, Book II, chapter 23):

“If, while abstaining from quadrupeds, they gorge themselves with poultry such as pheasants or with other costly birds, they do not seem to me to cut away the pleasures of their bodies but to change them. They reject those delicate, less common, and expensive kinds of flesh not as an act of abstinence, but as if because of some uncleanness—or, more truly, because of the tenderness of a nauseated stomach—in order that they may satisfy their pleasures with other flesh, and not merely with flesh, but with more delicate and more expensive flesh.”

Third, from these testimonies of Saint Jerome and Julianus Pomerius they infer that, even before the time of Saint Benedict, it had become customary among monks to take the flesh of birds as food. And lest someone say that they were condemning the abuse and lack of self-restraint of certain depraved monks rather than approving it, the example of Saint Hilarion, a most holy man, is available (Book V of *The Lives of the Fathers*, booklet 4, no. 15; and volume I of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, p. 428). Once, at dinner, Saint Epiphanius set a bird before him. Hilarion refused it, saying:

“Forgive me, father, because from the time I received this habit I have eaten nothing that has been killed.”

He did not say, “Because this is forbidden to monks.” Certainly Saint Epiphanius was not ignorant of the laws governing monastic life, as though he would have wished them to be violated by a most holy man.

After Saint Benedict, they produce countless examples of well-ordered monasteries in which the eating of birds was customary. Thus, if practice is the best interpreter of laws, they conclude that Saint Benedict permitted the flesh of birds.

Examples of this sort are found in the Life of Saint Bertulf, abbot of Bobbio, by his monk and disciple Jonas, no. 21 (second century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*), where the superior of the monastery is said to have distributed a duck among thirty brothers who were guarding the vineyard; in the Life of Saint Judoc (second century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*), who, as the anonymous author writes in his Life, no. 10, was accustomed to raise chickens for himself; and in Bede’s Life of Saint Cuthbert (second century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*, chapter 36), where he is said on one occasion to have served a goose to visiting monks.

Arnulf, a monk of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, writes of the earliest monks of Regensburg that they had a common and poor allowance, yet ate birds (Book II of the *Dialogue*). And that this was not the isolated practice of certain monasteries but the common custom of nearly all is demonstrated from the *Rule of the Master*, which was written not long after the death of Saint Maurus—that is, in the seventh century—and consists largely of material from the Benedictine Rule.

Speaking of wandering monks, and explaining why throughout their entire lives they stayed for three or four days at the cells and monasteries of different communities, it says (chapter 1):

“They wish, because of the arrival of guests, to be received each day anew by different people, and, for the joy of those arriving, they take care that carefully prepared dishes be set before them, and that living creatures, chickens, be killed daily with a knife by their various hosts for their arrival.”

That matters stood thus down to the time of the Emperor Louis the Pious is demonstrated by the addition to chapter 27 of Book II of Rabanus’s *On the Training of Clerics*, where we read:

“Only quadrupeds, not birds, were forbidden to monks. But it is said that in the time of Louis the Pious this was changed, so that they were permitted to use blood in every dish, because of the excessive consumption of birds which they practiced, to the detriment of others as well.”

This change was made at the Council of Aachen, where it was decreed (canon 8) that they should eat birds neither inside nor outside the monastery at any time except on account of illness. Yet it was also stipulated (canon 78):

“They may eat birds at Christmas and at Easter only, for four days, if there is any means to do so; but if there is not, they are not to demand them as a debt. If the abbot or the monks wish to abstain, it is to be left to their discretion.”

Thus the synod restricted a general permission to certain days—not as though it were granting something beyond the Rule. The same practice had been followed by the Cassinese, of whom Abbot Theodemar wrote to Charlemagne:

“We never eat birds except on Christmas Day, if there is any means to do so, and then for eight days. Likewise on the days of the Easter feast.”

This custom also prevailed in the monastery of Saint-Germain at Paris, as is clear from the charter of the Emperors Louis and Lothar reported by Aimoinus (*On the Deeds of the Franks*, Book V, chapter 10). They decree that the monks are to be given “each year birds with eggs from the two feasts, namely Easter and Christmas.” At Fontenelle, too, the Constitution of Abbot Saint Ansegisus concerning the food and clothing of the monks assigns for Christmas and Easter “bird pastries, chicken pastries, and chickens.”

To all these examples and to the decree of the Council of Aachen, Boherius replies:

“If this Rule had not preceded that council, I would have thought that this paragraph had supplied the council with its reason; but I believe the opposite: namely, that the council itself, through a mistaken understanding of the end of this chapter, gave rise to the edict. For let it be far from us to think that the Master granted monks the flesh of bipeds by considering the number of their feet rather than the sweetness of birds.”

These are the principal arguments of the first opinion. I now turn to the second.

The second opinion is altogether opposed to the first, but agrees with the third in asserting that birds were forbidden to the healthy. It differs from the third in also taking them away from the sick.

That birds were forbidden to the healthy is proved, they say, by the authority of all the authors who have written on the Benedictine Rule for approximately nine hundred years, with the sole exception of Saint Hildegard. Smaragdus, above all, clearly explains his view. After citing the present text of the Rule, he produces the decree of Saints Aurelian and Fructuosus, by which poultry is prohibited to the healthy; through their testimony he makes Saint Benedict’s obscure statement clear and intelligible.

Similarly, although Hildemar sometimes appears to have hesitated over whether Saint Benedict permitted birds, he praises those who abstain and elsewhere, with complete constancy and without any remaining doubt, denies that the flesh of birds was permitted. This can be seen in the passages cited above, both in this chapter and in chapter 36.

The same is taught by Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Richard of Saint-Angelo, Peter Boherius, John of Turrecremata, Theobald Artaldus, John Craesbeeck, Matthias Lambertus, Nicholas Bravus, Hugh Menardus, Benedict Haeftenus, and others.

The reason is an argument from the stronger case. If Saint Benedict prohibited the coarser flesh of quadrupeds, then all the more he prohibited the more pleasant and sweeter flesh of birds. The intention of the holy doctors is to include the greater under the lesser. Since use and experience teach that the flesh of quadrupeds is less delicate than that of birds, there can be no doubt that, in forbidding quadrupeds, he also forbade poultry. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Richard, and others argue more or less in this way.

Furthermore, Menardus says:

“It is least of all to be believed that Saint Benedict instituted monks who would judge delicacies of food by the number of feet, when in chapter 36 of the Rule he excludes monks from eating flesh, except the sick. Nor can it be inferred from the prohibition of quadrupeds that the eating of birds was permitted. When one thing is prohibited, it does not immediately follow that the other is permitted, as in Leviticus 19, where it says, ‘You shall not curse the deaf, nor place a stumbling-block before the blind.’ Someone would reason falsely from such laws that it is permitted to curse those who are not deaf and to place stumbling-blocks before those who can see. For a particular reason may be involved in such a prohibition, even if the other matter is not expressly prohibited.”

But to the inference drawn from chapter 36, where flesh is absolutely prohibited, others reply that the ancients did not include birds under the name “flesh”; indeed, they distinguished the two, as is clear in the Rule of Saint Caesarius (chapter 24):

“Let the healthy never receive chickens or flesh.”

The same appears in the Life of Saint Pardulf (third century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*), where he is said “never to have used either the eating of flesh or of birds.”

[Col. 0637B] Finally, these arguments and authorities are supported by the practice of nearly all the congregations in which an unbroken observance of the Rule flourished. Nothing is said about eating birds in the ancient Customs of the monastery of Cluny collected by Udalricus; indeed, in the Life of Saint Odo a monk is once recorded as having been punished for it. Nothing is said in the Statutes of Lanfranc, Dunstan’s *Concordia*, the Cistercian *Book of Usages*, the Declarations of the Cassinese, the Camaldolese, or of other monks.

There are also several ancient Rules in which birds are expressly prohibited, such as the Rules of Saint Caesarius, Saint Aurelian, Saint Fructuosus, and the Solitaries.

Now they think that Saint Benedict also took birds away from the sick, and they believe they can prove this as follows. Saint Benedict granted flesh to the sick only for restoration, not to satisfy desire. But for restoration the flesh of quadrupeds alone is sufficient; therefore he granted only that flesh.

Moreover, since in chapter 36 he prohibited all flesh to the healthy but permitted some to the sick, here, when he shows what he granted, he names only quadrupeds—as though he had said: “Everyone must abstain from flesh except the sick, to whom I grant quadrupeds.” Julianus Parisius reasons nearly in this way in part III, chapter 2, section 2 of *On the First Way of Life of the Cistercians*.

But the third opinion opposes them. It holds that all flesh, both of birds and of quadrupeds, was forbidden to the healthy, while both were permitted to the sick.

That the flesh of birds was forbidden to the healthy is proved by the arguments given above. That sick persons could lawfully eat birds is demonstrated by the common consensus of all the ancients. There were certainly some who thought that poultry was permitted to the healthy; but before Julianus Parisius I know of no one who denied it to the sick. It is scarcely conceivable that monks ever persuaded themselves that birds were permitted to the healthy if the sick had ever resorted to eating them.

For some trace of the ancient tradition would have remained, by which they would have been recalled from such an attempt—namely, the recognition that if Saint Benedict had prohibited the sick from eating birds, he would much more have prohibited the healthy. They would then have begun by violating abstinence from quadrupeds, as the less serious matter; for no one suddenly becomes completely wicked, but begins with the smallest thing. Yet, as we saw above, in well-ordered monasteries the eating of birds existed alongside abstinence from quadrupeds.

Nor was it unusual among the ancient monks to permit birds to the sick. There is a decree to this effect in the Rule of Saint Caesarius for monks, chapter 24; in the Rule of Saint Aurelian for monks, chapter 51, and for virgins, chapters 34 and 35, cited above by us; and in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 5. The latter prohibits the eating of all flesh, “while nevertheless preserving the measure of compassion toward the needs of the sick and the circumstances of those traveling far away, so that the sick may be sustained by eating birds, and those assigned to a long journey, if they are expected by a prince or bishop, may not hesitate to taste them as a blessing and in obedience, while preserving their usual abstinence in other matters.”

Add to this chapter 43 of the Rule of the Solitaries and canon 9 of the Council of Aachen.

The matter is confirmed by practice—not by the practice of later times, but by examples very close to Saint Benedict. We have an illustrious example in the Life of Saint Junianus, abbot of Mariac, who had received the Rule of Saint Benedict from Blessed Maurus and is believed to have survived him by only three years. Ulfinus Boetius writes of him (first century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*):

“For the use of the monks, and especially of the poor, he began to raise animals by which human weakness could be relieved. He gathered a great many chickens, whose flesh could support the needs of the sick, while their eggs could serve those in want.”

Another example is supplied by the Life of Saint Agnellus, abbot (first century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*), who is said, in chapter 2, to have provided chickens for the sick in the hospice he had built.

Ardo writes of Saint Benedict of Aniane, abbot (fourth century of the Benedictine *Acta Sanctorum*) that “from the day of his conversion until the end of his life he refused to eat the flesh of quadrupeds; he took broth made from a chicken if some weakness had arisen.”

Finally, in his Constitution concerning the monks’ food, Saint Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, grants to the infirmary itself wethers, sheep, chickens, and eggs.

Of these three opinions concerning Saint Benedict’s intention, we leave each person free to follow whichever he prefers. In the meantime, however, we approve those who entirely take birds away from the healthy. For even if it were true that they were not forbidden by Saint Benedict, it would not follow that monks, by virtue of their profession, could freely eat them. If they are not prohibited by the literal force of the Rule’s words, they are no less prohibited by the force of the monastic profession, which has left the delicacies of birds to royal banquets.

Boherius gives a fourth opinion in his first commentary, where he argues as follows:

“Note, if you wish to grasp the true meaning. The Master sets out three classes of persons in this Rule. The first are the healthy, and these ought to eat no flesh at all. The second are the weak and sick, to whom, for the support of nature, the eating of quadruped flesh alone is granted, as here; by ‘weak’ I understand the feeble, the decrepit, or those weakened by previous illnesses, while ‘sick’ refers to those who suffer, but not continuously—for example, in the head, stomach, or kidneys. Thus explain ‘altogether’ here as meaning ‘in truth,’ or ‘not fictitiously.’

“The third condition is that of the infirm, to whom the eating of flesh is simply granted for the restoration of nature. Therefore they may eat not only quadrupeds but also the flesh of bipeds, which is more restorative and nourishing.”

Guido Juvenalis seems to have taught the same in his French translation. Yet from the same Guido—or from his corrector, a monk of Clairvaux—Haeftenus derives a fifth opinion. He holds (Book X, treatise 6, disputation 2):

“All eating of flesh is forbidden to the vigorous and healthy, but only the flesh of quadrupeds is forbidden to the sick, so that in illness it is lawful to eat birds alone.”

The flesh of quadrupeds is not granted unless it suits the health of the sick, which rarely happens. This opinion requires no refutation.

Nor does Saint Benedict simply say that one must abstain from the flesh of quadrupeds. He says *omnino*, “altogether,” or, as some manuscripts read, *omnimodo*, “in every way,” “the eating is to be abstained from.”

“Because,” says Bernard of Cassino, “according to this Rule, flesh cut into pieces is not to be eaten, and this is what *omnino* means.”

Boherius adds:

“And this is directed against those who eat chopped meat in the refectory, which they call *mortarolium*. They perhaps assert that after such crushing no appearance of flesh remains, because, as is said in the first book of the *Physics*, in the division of flesh one can arrive at the smallest particle of flesh; if it is divided further, the species of flesh will no longer remain.”

Here one may observe in passing how far blind eagerness to eat flesh has carried people: they did not even think that they were violating abstinence if they ate flesh after it had been minced—as though flesh could be eaten by the ministry of the teeth in any form other than minced.

But Pope Gregory IX attempted to remedy this disorder by issuing the following statute (*Constitutions for Benedictine Monks*):

“And just as we forbid the eating of flesh, so we also deny forcemeats made from particular kinds of flesh.”

What is said here about minced flesh must likewise be said about fat:

“We know,” says Hildemar, “that fat is the flesh of quadrupeds; it is clear that it is not to be eaten.”

Nevertheless, the Council of Aachen granted monks its use, allowing (in chapter 36) “the brothers to have some fat in their daily food,” except on Friday, during the eight days before Christmas, and from Quinquagesima until Easter.

The Cluniacs later restricted this provision somewhat, burying the fat with the Alleluia at Septuagesima. This custom was generally received in all monasteries, as can be seen in Dunstan’s *Concordia*, the Statutes of Lanfranc, the manuscript Customs of Germany, and the *Book of Usages* of Bec.

Indeed, Dunstan, Lanfranc, and Peter the Venerable remove fat throughout Advent. But although the Fathers of Aachen exempted Friday from the eating of fat, the Cluniacs do not seem to have observed this. Later Peter the Venerable ordered them (Statute 10):

“That all the Cluniac brothers abstain from fat every Friday, except when the Nativity of the Lord falls on that day.”

The reason for this indulgence may be given in two ways. The first was as a compensation for fowl, the use of which he had entirely abolished except at the Nativity and Resurrection of the Lord. Thus the addition to chapter 27 of book II of Rabanus’s *On the Instruction of Clerics* teaches, where we read: “Only quadrupeds, not fowl, were forbidden to monks. But at the time of Louis the Pious this is said to have been changed, so that it became permissible to use blood in all their dishes, on account of the excessive consumption of fowl, which was harmful to others, that they practiced.” The second reason was the lack of oil, as we learn from Rupert (*Book IV, on the Rule of Saint Benedict*). Responding to regular clerics who, on this account, preferred themselves to monks because they had voluntarily renounced the use of fat, he says:

> This neither increases their merit nor diminishes that of these men. For the Lord entrusted the keys of the kingdom of heaven to the Church in blessed Peter. Yet the Church, possessing such authority, granted monks fat—which is akin to meat, though not meat itself—because they did not have an adequate supply of oil.

Grimlaicus seems to have had this in mind when, in his *Rule for Solitaries* (chapter 45), he prescribed that “in those regions where oil is lacking, if necessity demands it, they may sometimes use fat.”

The same judgment that is made concerning minced meat and fat must also be made concerning eggs, which are derived from the very substance of the hen, by those who deny that Saint Benedict granted permission to eat fowl. Thus Saint Junianus, in his monastery (*Life of Saint Junianus*), “gathered a very large number of provisions for chickens, whose … eggs were to serve the needs of the poor,” not those of the monks. Nevertheless, Abbot Leo of Cava is said to have served hen’s eggs to guests in book III, chapter 8, of the *Dialogues of Pope Saint Victor*.

On milk, butter, and cheese, concerning which there is greater difficulty, Boherius should be heard:

> Although I may be called excessively strict in this matter, and although my own mouth may condemn me, I plainly think that cenobites who possess sound bodies cannot, with due regularity, use fat, milk, eggs, and cheese. For, as Gregory’s canon says, it is fitting that those who abstain from the flesh of animals should fast from everything that derives its origin from the seed of flesh.

Nevertheless, it is certain that the monks of old, including the Cistercians themselves, frequently used milk and cheese. Indeed, as Hildemarus observes:

> Milk and cheese are not meat, although they come from meat, because it is not meat that is changed into milk; rather, by God’s dispensation, food itself is changed into milk for the nourishment of Christ’s children.

In the same way, wine that comes from the vine is not the vine, nor is oil that comes from wood itself wood; rather, it is the juice of the earth, which is changed both into wine and into oil.

What, then, should be judged concerning those who violate abstinence from meat? Peter the Venerable calls them “crow-like and beastly monks” (*Book VI, Letter 15*), who continually crave bloodstained dishes. Saint Odo unhesitatingly calls them apostates (*Book III of the *Collations*, no. 17):

> Is it not apostasy, he says, to despise the traditions of the Fathers in habit and food, when God has forbidden the transgression of the Fathers’ boundaries, and, scorning the quality or quantity of food prescribed by blessed Benedict, to desire bloodstained dishes with the children of Israel?

Certainly, abstinence from meat has always been regarded among the principal institutions of monastic life. Thus Saint Vitalis, abbot of the Order of Saint Basil (*Life of Saint Vitalis*, no. 18, in the Bollandists), while instructing his successor, among other commands orders him “not to permit meat to be eaten in the monastery.” Saint Theodore of Sykeon extended this rule even to smiths and other secular laborers working within the monastery’s boundaries (*Life of Saint Theodore*, no. 63, Bollandists, 22 April); for this reason he sent them back to the town. Indeed, among the objections that the Greeks, in the time of Michael Cerularius, brought against the Latins (*Humbert, Book Against the Calumnies of the Greeks*), they reproached them because Saint Benedict allowed the sick to eat meat. And among the complaints that they renewed against the Latins in the time of Innocent III was this, their fifty-third: “Their monks eat meat.”

What is more, when monks were promoted to ecclesiastical dignities, it was entirely unlawful for them to eat meat except in cases of illness. We have an illustrious example of this in Hincmar, an archbishop of Rheims who had been a monk of Saint-Denis. Having recently recovered from an illness, he was advised by Pardulus, bishop of Laon, “not to abstain from bacon or quadrupeds until his health was restored, and then to return to the dry, wretched, and more austere monastic foods.”

For this reason it should by no means seem surprising if Saint Fructuosus decreed that a monk who “violated abstinence and, contrary to the rule’s ordinance and ancient custom, presumed to eat meat” should be subjected to confinement and penance for six months (chapter 5). The same words are found in excerpts from book II of the *Penitential of Bishop Egbert of York* (in Spelman, volume I of the *Councils of England*).

Gregory IX likewise says in his constitution for Benedictine monks:

> If anyone presumes to eat meat contrary to the foregoing prescriptions, whether once or even twice, let him undergo regular discipline. If a third time, let him fast on bread and water on the next Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. If he makes a habit of it, let him be subject to grave fault. If an abbot commits this offense, let him be content with bread and water on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday. If he makes a habit of it and, when admonished by the diocesan bishop or visitors, is unwilling to correct himself, let him be deprived of his administration.

In nearly the same way Benedict XII orders in a bull addressed to Cistercian monks that a monk or lay brother who violates abstinence “shall be required to fast on bread and water for three days for each eating of meat or of the aforesaid dishes; and, nevertheless, on each of those days he shall receive regular discipline in chapter.” The abbot, however, if he violates the prohibition, is to be subject not to that discipline but to such fasts. “If he knowingly omits these things or negligently fails to have them observed, he too shall be subject, on account of such negligence, to the aforesaid fasts. These penalties may not be remitted to anyone, nor may anyone dispense with them, wholly or in part. If some are repeatedly found offending in the eating of meat or the aforesaid dishes, or frequently practicing such eating contrary to this ordinance, and, after being canonically admonished by their abbots to abstain from such things, do not desist, then, after that admonition, they shall by that fact be incapable for two years of obtaining any offices or administrations in the same order. Those who already hold such offices shall be removed from them if their abbots deem it appropriate.”

Moreover, in the *Book of the Ancient Definitions of the Cistercian Order* I read the following (Distinction 13, chapter 2):

> Concerning the eating or serving of meat, this shall be held without dispute: what is contained in the Rule of Saint Benedict. Therefore, outside our infirmary, no person belonging to the order may eat meat, except those traveling across the great sea, for as long as they remain at sea. Whoever acts contrary to this shall fall under the sentence of excommunication by that very act. If he is an official, he shall be removed from office and thereafter shall not be promoted to any office without the permission of the general chapter. A monk or lay brother who is not an official shall, for each occurrence, remain deprived of the regular habit for one month. Nuns, lay sisters, and their chaplains shall be subject to the same penalty, even though their habit differs from ours.

Those who classify transgression of abstinence from meat among lesser faults—whether they would really wish such a violation to be punished in this way as light and venial, I do not know. Certainly the Casalists order those who violate abstinence or serve meat to guests in the monastery to fast on bread and water for as many days as prescribed, while reserving absolution from such a sin to the abbot, according to the manuscript *Constitutions*, chapter 56.

I say nothing of the divine punishments with which the supreme Ruler of all things has more than once avenged those who violated this statute. You will find some examples of such vengeance in John the Monk’s *Life of Saint Odo*. Yet I cannot omit what the monk Hermann wrote about the monastery of Saint John of Laon (*Book III of the *Miracles of Saint Mary of Laon*), namely:

> No quadruped animal could enter within the wall or gate of the abbey without immediately being turned into a rabid and insane creature. Therefore, whenever a king, bishop, or other princes came to that abbey, all their horses had to be left outside the gate, and they themselves proceeded on foot to the church.

But the question is whether at least the abbot can dispense the brothers from abstinence from meat. Peter the Venerable resolves the question by issuing a statute (statute 12): “Except for the sick and those who are altogether weak, no one shall eat meat.” Explaining the reason for this statute, he says:

> The reason for this institution was the authority of the Rule itself, in which the same thing is prescribed, and the healthy monk in full strength is forbidden to eat meat. Moreover, no reasonable cause for changing this chapter could be found, as our Fathers found such causes in the case of certain other chapters of the same Rule that were formerly changed.

Writing to the priors and custodians of his order (*Book VI, Letter 15*), he adds:

> And do not imagine that you may have recourse to what you are accustomed to say: that this chapter—namely, chapter 39 of the Rule—was changed, like certain others, by some holy Fathers for a definite reason. I answer that the case is different. If matters concerning the admission of novices, manual labor, clothing, and certain other similar things were changed after Saint Benedict by good Fathers, this was done for a certain and reasonable cause, not a doubtful one. I have carefully described that cause or reason twice in letters sent to the lord abbot of Clairvaux; I consider it superfluous to repeat it here. If you are sufficiently diligent, you will find it fully explained there. But how can the transgression of this chapter be excused? For what reason can a monk in good health and full strength who uses meat be shown not to be guilty? Tell me, I ask, if you have anything to say—if there is any true or plausible reason. Defend meat for yourself, if you can. You have none, none, I say, as I judge, to offer; you plainly have nothing with which to cleanse the stain, not to say the guilt, of perjury. The Rule stands in the way; justice contradicts you.

Since, therefore, no reasonable cause can be offered for breaking abstinence from meat, it is clear that even the abbot cannot dispense monks from eating meat, except perhaps in certain extraordinary circumstances that would scarcely occur once in a thousand years. For the rest, we have not yet been able to find bulls of the supreme pontiffs granting Benedictine monks permission to eat meat three times a week. If any such bulls exist, they were perhaps granted to particular monasteries for a reasonable cause and for a limited time, not to all monasteries and forever. Indeed, there are quite a few decrees of councils by which abstinence from meat, once interrupted in monasteries, was restored.

# CHAPTER XL  
## On the Measure of Drink

[Col. 0641]

[Col. 0641C] “Everyone has his own gift from God: one person in one way, another in another. Therefore the measure of food for others is established by us with some hesitation. Nevertheless, taking into consideration the weakness of the sick [Note: Hild., ‘considering’; Oxford, ‘thinking of continence’], we believe that half a pint of wine is sufficient for each person per day. Those to whom God grants the endurance of abstinence should know that they will receive their own reward.

“But if the needs of the place, labor, or the heat of summer should demand more [Note: Conches lacks ‘more’], let the matter rest with the prior, who must consider [Note: [Col. 0642C] Other copies, ‘of one considering’] everything, lest satiety or drunkenness creep in. Although we read that wine is altogether unsuitable for monks, since this cannot be persuaded upon monks in our times, let us at least agree to this: that we should not drink to satiety, but more sparingly, because wine makes even the wise apostatize. Where the needs of the place require that not even the measure written above can be found, but much less [Note: Conc., ‘but less’; Hild., ‘but much less’], or none at all, let those who live there bless God and not murmur. Above all, we admonish them to be without murmuring [Note: [Col. 0642C] Other copies add ‘brothers’].”

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0641D] “Everyone has his own gift from God: one person in one way, another in another.” From this saying of the Apostle Saint Benedict took the rule governing the food of others: namely, that each person should be given food according to the gift received from God. Saint Pachomius likewise followed this norm in the Rule delivered to him by the angel (*Life of Saint Pachomius*), permitting each person to eat and drink according to his strength, requiring him to labor according to the measure of his eating, and neither forbidding moderate eating nor fasting.

“And therefore the measure of food for others is established by us with some hesitation.” Cassian once experienced the same difficulty, as he himself testifies in book V, chapter 5.

“Nevertheless, taking into consideration the weakness of the sick.” “Here,” says Smaragdus, “he speaks of the weakness of the sick not with reference to bodily illness but to weakness of spirit. For the body cannot practice external abstinence unless the mind within agrees to abstain. Many could abstain because health had been granted to them, but they are unable to do so because of weakness of spirit.” Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, Richard of Saint Angelo, Boherius, and others speak in the same way.

Accordingly, Antonius Perez may rightly be rebuked, since he thinks that Saint Benedict granted half a pint of wine only to the weak. Indeed, when the holy Father orders a latecomer to the table to refresh himself alone, after his portion of wine has been taken away, he is not speaking of the sick and weak but chiefly of the healthy. On this point see Haeften, book X, treatise 4, question 3.

“We believe that half a pint of wine is sufficient for each person per day.” Learned men agree about the name *hemina*, but they dispute considerably about the measure itself. Jacobus Brolius, a monk of the monastery of Saint-Germain in Paris, a learned and religious man, reports various opinions without attaching himself firmly to any of them.

The first is that of Peter Masius, abbot of Casale Benedicti, who defines the measure of the *hemina* in the constitutions of his congregation (*Manuscript Constitutions of Casale Benedicti*, chapter 57) as follows:

> The *hemina*, as we have received from certain interpreters of the Rule, is a measure containing one pound and a quarter of some liquid; it is approximately one-third of a Parisian quart of wine.

The second is Smaragdus’s opinion. Expounding Saint Isidore, he says (*Isidore, *Etymologies*, book XVI, chapter 25):

> A *hemina* of wine weighs one pound, and when doubled makes a *sextarius*.

Julius Rhodiginus follows this opinion in book XXVIII of his *Ancient Readings*.

The third is the opinion of the monks of Fossat, who formerly displayed two leaden weights: one weighing thirty-three and a half ounces of bread, the other thirty-five ounces of wine.

The fourth is that of the Cassinese monks, who assert in their *Explanations of the Rule* that the *hemina* is “much more than would suffice for the ordinary needs of one monk.”

The fifth is that of those who equate the Benedictine *hemina* with the Parisian pint of Saint-Denis.

Finally, Brolius concludes:

> Whether the bronze vessel displayed by the monks of Fossat is the one given by Saint Benedict to blessed Maurus is not sufficiently certain.

From these final words it is clear that Brolius did not recognize the Fossat measure as the Benedictine *hemina*, nor did he adhere to any of the opinions mentioned above. The French disputant on the Benedictine *hemina* of wine and pound of bread therefore failed to understand Brolius’s position when he attacked him with a criticism as biting as it was undeserved. Brolius was an excellent and learned man; if he ever erred, his error should either be excused or at least not exaggerated in this manner.
