Indeed, since he adopted none of the opinions, if, while reporting the Fossat measure, he added, “And this could have been sufficient for a sober monk concerned to preserve the integrity of his lungs, if one *cheopina* (a small measure) were taken at dinner and another at supper or collation,” he should rather be thought to have spoken jokingly and ironically.

It is also reasonable to doubt whether the disputant ever read Brolius. For when discussing the difference between the measures shown to Boherius and to Brolius in the monastery of Fossat, he states categorically that the measure shown to Boherius was a measure of capacity, whereas the object shown to Brolius was a weight. He then says that the *hemina* given by blessed Benedict to Saint Maurus was made of bronze, while the object shown to Brolius was a leaden weight. Let fair-minded men judge whether these claims agree with Brolius’s text.

“Whether the bronze vessel,” says Brolius, “which the monks of Fossat display is the one given by Saint Benedict to blessed Maurus is not sufficiently certain.” Here certainly is a vessel, and it is bronze; yet this does not prevent weights from having been preserved in the monastery of Fossat along with the vessel. These remarks are incidental, not an endorsement of those generous measures of wine, which I reject outright.

Our Menard followed a view wholly opposed to the authors mentioned above. Examining the matter more carefully, he observed that the *hemina* is half a *sextarius*, consisting of six *cyathi*, and that a *cyathus* contains ten drachmas. Consequently, the *hemina* contains sixty drachmas. Since eight drachmas make an ounce, he concluded that the *hemina* weighs no more than seven and a half ounces. The French disputant, however, thought that Menard’s calculation had to be understood as referring to the Greek *hemina*, not the Roman one.

Nicolaus Bravus, a Spanish author, was somewhat more generous, assigning the *hemina* a full ten ounces. The French disputant already cited by us taught that the *hemina* had the same measure. In the treatise on the Benedictine *hemina* of wine that he published in Paris in 1667, he proves that the *hemina* is half a *sextarius*, that the *sextarius* is one-sixth of a *congius*, and that the *congius* contains precisely 120 ounces. He claims to have tested this against the ancient *congius* preserved at Rome in the Farnese palace. From this he concluded that the *hemina* could not contain more than ten ounces.

Whatever may be the case with the Farnese *congius*—which, when compared proportionately with the ancient Roman ounces, has nevertheless not been found to correspond entirely—the disputant’s entire argument concerns the Roman *hemina*, not the Benedictine one. Yet it was precisely the latter that he was obliged to demonstrate.

Our Mabillon took a middle course, and, as it seems to me, a safer one, assigning eighteen ounces to the daily Benedictine *hemina*. On an occasion that arose ten years after the French dissertation had been published, in the first preface to the fourth Benedictine century, he praised the disputant’s learning but conceded that the ancient Roman *hemina* consisted of only ten ounces. He denied, however, that this could be said of every *hemina*, maintaining that measures and weights varied according to different regions and different times.

He proves this both from the ordinance of Charles the Bald concerning the stipends of the clerics of Saint Peter who were subject to the convent of the Blessed Mary of Soissons, by which he granted each priest a *hemina*—that is, three pounds of wine—every day, and from a very ancient author whom the monk Bertigarius transcribed in the ninth century at the archmonastery of Saint Remigius at Rheims. In his treatise *On Weights and Measures*, this ancient author speaks of the *hemina* as follows:

> Among some people, nine *cyathi* seem to make a *hemina*, which amounts to ninety drachmas. Among others, four *acetabula* make it, which amounts to forty-eight drachmas. According to some, the *hemina* weighs one pound; according to others, a pound and a half.

After adding certain further remarks about the *sextarius*, the *choenix*, and the *congius*, he says:

> But we have discovered that these measures are established according to the will of princes or judges.

This is confirmed by the Council of Aachen of 816, chapter 122.

From these considerations he concludes:

1. It is uncertain whether the standard of the ancient measure remained in use at Rome until the time of Saint Benedict.

2. Even if it remained at Rome, it is doubtful whether it was current throughout Italy, since different measures were commonly used in different places and cities.

3. Even if it had been current throughout Italy, Saint Benedict could have established—and in fact did establish—a new *hemina* of wine.

Certainly, the arguments that we presented in the preceding chapter concerning the pound of bread prove this, and they apply equally to the *hemina* of wine.

Investigating how much the *hemina* established by Saint Benedict could contain, Mabillon assumes that it was preserved in the monastery of Cassino until the time of Charlemagne. This can readily be proved. He further assumes that Charlemagne sent messengers to Cassino, who brought him the aforesaid measure of the *hemina*, together with the pound of bread, so that it might be promulgated in the monasteries of Gaul; that he actually received it from Abbot Theodemar; and that, by decree of the Council of Aachen, it was adopted in all the monasteries of Gaul in the time of the Emperor Louis the Pious.

He proves this from Hildemarus, a contemporary author, who, explaining this passage of Saint Benedict’s Rule, writes:

> Hence King Charles, wishing to understand and know what the *hemina* itself meant, sent to Benevento, namely to the monastery of Saint Benedict. There he found the ancient *hemina*, and according to that *hemina* wine is given to the monks. In the same way, we too have one according to that *hemina*.

Since Hildemarus had an entirely accurate knowledge of Saint Benedict’s *hemina*, he demonstrates from another passage of the same chapter that it was somewhat more generous than the Roman measure. Explaining Saint Benedict’s intention of removing the occasion of drunkenness from the monks, Hildemarus says that the measure should be reduced for one “who experiences drunkenness from the measure of the *hemina* alone—that is, who staggers either in speech or in walking.”

This could happen to no head, however weak, if a person used only one Parisian half-*sextarius* per day. I do not see what answer the disputant could give to this argument; and therefore, in his responses, he passed over it in silence as too inconvenient.

The same point also seems capable of being demonstrated from chapter 5 of Saint Fructuosus’s Rule, which orders that a *sextarius* be divided among four brothers—that is, grants each one half a *hemina*. For if the measure of the *hemina* had been so small, it would plainly have been preferable to remove wine from the monks altogether rather than grant them so little per day.

Continuing his investigation of the capacity of the *hemina*, Mabillon maintains that the matter must be demonstrated by facts. First he brings forward an example from the *Rule of the Master* (chapter 27), from which he demonstrates that three cups were contained in a *hemina*.

The *Rule of the Master* does not assign each brother his own *hemina* or wine vessel. Rather, it orders that wine be poured for everyone from the same vessel. In summer, each person was first given a pure portion— that is, a cup of unmixed wine—then four cups of warm wine in addition to that pure wine; and, when they were refreshed at the sixth hour, three late drinks. In winter, at the refreshment of the sixth or ninth hour, they received only three cups of warm wine.

To prevent abuse from entering such an arrangement, the Rule determined the size of the cup from which each person was to drink, lest anyone consume more wine than was appropriate. “The cup,” it says, “or little vessel, by which it is to be served at different times, shall be such that it fills one-third of a mixed *hemina*.” Thus the *hemina* contained three cups; when someone had served these, the mixed wine—that is, the *hemina* already poured—had been distributed.

He confirms this from the Rules of Saint Fructuosus and Saint Isidore, who had the Benedictine Rule before their eyes and expressed its practice when they composed their own. According to the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 10), each brother’s thirst is to be refreshed with three cups. Saint Fructuosus (chapter 5), who grants half a *hemina* on ordinary days, allows the brothers three drinks on the principal solemnities—that is, a full *hemina*.

He further confirms the same opinion from the Statutes of Saint Adalard, abbot of Corbie, who had spent a long time in the monastery of Cassino and composed his Statutes in 822, five years after the synod of Aachen. In book I, chapter 4 (in *Spicilegium*, volume IV), he prescribes that four *sextarii* be divided among twelve canons, so that each receives two cups. From this passage it is clear that in the monastery of Corbie a *sextarius* consisted of six cups and, consequently, a *hemina* of three cups—and these were cups of beer, undiluted with water.

From all this he infers that, since it is scarcely possible to consume less than six ounces of wine in a moderate draught, the *hemina* contained approximately eighteen ounces by weight. Finally, he concludes the whole matter as follows:

> I do not want what I have said thus far about the Benedictine *hemina* to be understood as though I thought I had reached the truth of the matter itself, or as though I wished to enlarge the measure of monastic temperance.

Certainly, there is no danger of excess or abuse if ten or twelve ounces of wine are allowed at dinner and six or eight at supper.

Nevertheless, the French disputant feared precisely this. Accordingly, in the previous year, 1688, he published a second edition of his treatise on the Benedictine *hemina* of wine and pound of bread. Although he changed certain things, he restated his original opinion without new proofs, while adding several responses to the preface of Mabillon. He himself testifies that he did so solely out of regard for the truth, not from a desire for contention or victory—although he more than once flatters himself with the prospect of victory, and does so so confidently that, in responding to the objections, he persuades himself that no opportunity for further opposition will remain.

When the author of the preface had read this second work and was asked what he thought of it, he replied humbly, with his natural modesty, that he possessed arguments and authorities from ancient writers by which the disputant’s entire argument, together with his replies, could be overturned. Yet he did not wish to present himself as a patron of the *hemina* and of drinking.

I would gladly follow his example and pass over the disputant’s arguments in silence, allowing the matter of the *hemina* to rest, in view of the good faith in which he has pursued it, while bidding him farewell over the question of the *hemina*, in the good faith in which he pursues it, and recalling Ambrose’s words: “It is unbecoming for people who fight for the kingdom to concern themselves with food” (*Book VII on Luke*). But the subject before us compels me to examine his responses. Although I am far inferior in ability, and look up with admiration to the profound learning of this most learned man, I shall undertake the task—not from a desire for contention or from a wish to enlarge the measure of wine, but solely out of regard for clarifying the truth. Meanwhile, I praise in the disputant his love of abstinence, which I would greatly desire to inspire in the minds of all monks, so that I might persuade them all to abstain from wine.

Since he proposes no new argument anywhere in the dissertation—or, if he has proposed anything new, since it consists entirely in his responses to objections—I have decided, leaving the dissertation itself aside, to attack those responses, in which I have admired a great deal of intellectual sharpness and subtlety.

In them the disputant assumes the authenticity of the Farnese *congius* and the conclusion he drew from it, namely, that the ancient Roman *hemina* consisted of only ten ounces and that Saint Benedict assigned his brothers no other than the Italian *hemina*. His entire effort is devoted to proving:

1. That the ancient Roman *hemina* remained in use until the time of Saint Benedict;

2. That it was in use throughout Italy;

3. That changes in measures did not occur until a much later period.

Let us see, however, by what arguments he demonstrates these claims.

First, to prove that the ancient Roman measures continued in common commercial use until the time of Saint Benedict, he cites Fannius’s poem *On Weights and Measures*. Fannius wrote it in the time of the Emperor Constantine, that is, two hundred years before Saint Benedict; later Priscian polished it at Constantinople while the holy lawgiver was still alive, without making any change in the substance of the matters treated. Since the poem of Fannius, polished by Priscian while Saint Benedict was still alive, assigns only ten ounces to the *hemina*, this, he says, is evidence that the Roman *hemina* remained in accepted use until that time.

This argument, which the disputant considers so strong, seems to me to have no weight. First, nothing can be inferred from the authority of Fannius, who wrote two hundred years before Saint Benedict. Even if the Roman *hemina* was still current in his time, it could have changed during those two hundred years—and in fact it did change—without remaining in use until Saint Benedict.

Nor does Priscian’s testimony carry any greater force. He did not compose a new poem but polished one composed by Fannius, changing the wording so that the reader might go through it with greater pleasure, but making no change in the substance of the subject, as the disputant himself admits. What relevance, then, does Priscian’s polishing have? If someone today undertook to polish Fannius’s poem, changing its words while preserving the substance, could it rightly be concluded from this that Roman measures had remained in use until our own times? The same judgment must be made concerning Priscian’s revision. In correcting Fannius, he spoke with reference to Fannius’s times; he did not compose a new work. If he had composed a new work, then, writing at Constantinople, he would have described not Roman or Attic measures but Constantinopolitan ones.

Indeed, Priscian is so far from supporting the disputant that, if we examine his poem, we shall rather see that the ancient Roman measures had already been changed and that different measures existed among different places and peoples. This can be proved from the very prologue of the poem, which begins:

> It is useful to know  
> the weights celebrated in the books  
> of the ancients.

Priscian is therefore not describing the weights of his own time but those of the ancients. Other measures, then, were in use in his own day. Soon afterward he says:

> But if weight were generally inherent in these things,  
> different nations would preserve the same weights.  
> Now they vary; for all things do not possess their value  
> by a fixed agreement of nature, but by human law.

Nor does the authority of Cassiodorus, which the disputant cites with such high praise, prove more than this: that King Theodoric, for whom Cassiodorus served as secretary, did not change the measures.

First he cites a passage from a letter written in Theodoric’s name to Duke Ida (*Book IV of the *Variae*, letter 17), in which Theodoric orders him to ensure that the possessions of the church of Narbonne, seized by unjust usurpers, be restored, because he does not wish to unsettle matters reasonably decreed by an earlier king:

> Why, he says (*ibid.*, letter 42), should we disturb what came before, when there is nothing that we ought to correct?

He then cites another passage from a letter to Argolicus, prefect of the City, in which he orders the tower of the circus and the site of the amphitheater to be restored to Marcianus and Maximus, the sons of Volusianus. They complained that these had been taken from them while they were attending to the mournful death of their father. The reason given is:

> We, who preserve the rules of the ancients and observe the measures of piety, decree by a salutary ordinance that, if the patrician and magnificent man Volusianus, father of the petitioners, possessed the aforesaid properties by common right, they ought not to perish for his sons.

But what does this have to do with the Roman *hemina*? From these passages we learn that Theodoric loved justice and did not wish anyone to suffer fraud. Yet no one will conclude from them that Roman measures were not changed either by Theodoric himself or by someone else before him.

[Col. 0647C] A passage from a letter to the patrician Boethius (*Book I, letter 10*) offers greater plausibility. Cassiodorus writes that the household guards, cavalrymen and infantrymen who were continually stationed on guard in the royal palace, complained that the prefects’ treasurer did not pay them solidi of full weight as their customary emoluments, and that they suffered serious losses in the number of coins. Cassiodorus orders that this be corrected.

He then adds several remarks in praise of arithmetic, saying that by the prudent invention of the ancients it had come about that the ounce was found twelve times in the pound according to a mystical number. Finally, he concludes:

> To violate such secrets, and in this way to confuse things so certain—is this not a cruel and shameful tearing apart of truth itself? Let merchants exercise themselves in merchandise: let them buy broadly what they sell more narrowly; let a trustworthy weight and measure be established for the peoples. Everything is thrown into confusion when integrity is mixed with fraud. What is given to laborers certainly ought not to be diminished; rather, the person from whom faithful service is required should receive undiminished compensation.

[Col. 0647D] This letter demonstrates that in Cassiodorus’s time, as now, the Roman pound consisted of twelve ounces. It also shows that King Theodoric wished the weights and measures established by himself or by others to be maintained, that no fraud should be committed—especially by public prefects—and that “the person from whom faithful service is required should receive undiminished compensation.”

But the disputant draws an entirely erroneous conclusion from this passage when he infers that the ancient Roman *hemina* therefore continued to exist in the time of blessed Benedict, and that neither Theodoric himself nor anyone before him had changed the ancient measures.

Finally, Cassiodore wrote as follows in a letter to the Ligurians (Book XI, Letter 16), whom he addresses in these words:

> “You report that you are burdened in matters of weights and measures, and therefore our care will ensure that injustice can no longer harass you in this respect; for we judge it a grave offense either for measures to exceed their proper amount or for a pound not to possess the justice of the fairest weight.”

He shows that exactions must be avoided above all, and that nothing beyond the established measures should be demanded—something that can occur with measures both small and large. But this does not help the dissertation-writer; indeed, it would rather show that the measures had already been altered and enlarged in certain places. Whether the man wished to correct this, or actually corrected it, is not established. Thus this passage seems to oppose the dissertation-writer.

In all these passages, however, Cassiodore is chiefly concerned to prevent exactions and frauds, since he could not tolerate the public miseries and burdens imposed upon his subjects. He recommends the same elsewhere, writing to the *canonicarius* (Book XII, Letter 16), instructing him to admonish his subjects to pay the customary taxes and, above all, that “no one exceed the quantity of a just weighing, and that the pound be perfectly just. There will be no limit to plundering if it is permissible to exceed the weights.”

Therefore Cassiodore—or Theodoric, in whose name he wrote the first five books of letters—wanted nothing else than to abolish fraudulent weights and measures, by which the tax collectors, whom he himself orders to use public weights and measures, were perhaps oppressing their subjects to no small degree. But from this no one can conclude that the ancient Roman measures had not been altered, whether by him or by someone else before him. [Col. 0648A]

Nor does the dissertation-writer make any greater progress when he tries to demonstrate that authors later than Priscian and, consequently, Saint Benedict made the hemina only ten ounces; to prove this he adduces Saint Isidore (Dissertation, no. 17). What judgment should be formed concerning Saint Isidore’s intention in this matter is taught us by the dissertation-writer himself, when he asserts that Saint Isidore wrote down matters reported by other, earlier authors, collecting them without any examination. Certainly, as our Menardus shows, Saint Isidore contradicts himself. Yet even if he did not contradict himself, he would not support the dissertation-writer, who assigns precisely ten ounces to the Roman hemina. For Saint Isidore makes the hemina consist of twelve ounces, and indeed of weight-ounces:

> “The hemina,” he says (Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25), “weighs one pound; doubled, it makes a sextarius.”

[Col. 0648B] It is therefore astonishing that an educated man should put forward so weak an argument—one that a more inexperienced schoolman would certainly have found embarrassing. But what can one say? In defending a bad cause, everything is usually employed, to use the dissertation-writer’s own words (*Response to the Objections*, no. 7).

I think it has now been sufficiently demonstrated that the dissertation-writer did not prove in his responses that the ancient Roman measures remained unchanged down to the time of Saint Benedict. He proves still less that they were in common use throughout Italy at that time. The witness he adduces for this purpose is Nicolaus de Fractura, who wrote seven hundred and fifty-two years after Saint Benedict’s death; indeed, if the printer has not made an error, the dissertation-writer makes him an entire century older than he actually was. Nicolaus is too remote a witness to establish the point, since he wrote that in his own time—that is, in the year 1299—the peoples of southern Italy “generally follow Roman usage concerning a measure of this kind.” For during so long an interval the laws of those peoples could have been changed more than once. If someone were to produce for the dissertation-writer a witness so remote, good heavens, how far away he would order him to be sent!

But let us see whether Nicolaus really taught what the dissertation-writer claims that he asserted:

> “The hemina,” he says, “is a suitable measure for drinking at a single meal; it is preserved to this day in the Cassinese monastery. Upon examination, as I myself have discovered in practice, it can hold a little more or a little less than the amount required, which is a certain measure among the Romans. It is highly probable that the Master understood such a measure, because in the province of Nursia, from which he originated, such a measure is in use; and the people of that province, in buying and selling, generally follow Roman usage concerning a measure of this kind.”

From this passage it may properly be inferred that Roman measures were in use at Nursia in Nicolaus’s time. But when Nursia encompasses Subiaco, Cassino, and the whole of lower Italy, then the dissertation-writer may produce Nicolaus, though a most remote witness, in support of the truth [Col. 0648C] that he intended to prove. For the present, however, he accomplishes nothing. Thus he has demonstrated none of the proofs by which he claims that Roman measures continued down to Saint Benedict and beyond throughout all Italy.

Let us now examine what he brings forward concerning the alteration of those measures by the monks.

“The nature of things,” he says, “is such that disturbances in kingdoms are always followed in monasteries by decline and the collapse of regular discipline.” He says that this occurred especially in the eighth century, when monasteries were surrendered to the greed of clerics, their abbots exulted, the monks lacked necessary goods, and the entire discipline of regular observance was ruined. Then, once the reins had been loosened, the monks rushed headlong into every kind of excess.

Thus, he argues more or less as follows in numbers 6 and 7 of his *Response*: it is not surprising if certain ninth-century authors, ignorant of the facts and inclined to enlarge measures, failed to examine the Roman and Italian measures of Saint Benedict’s time and reckoned as Roman, Italian, and Benedictine measures those that had been altered in the eighth or ninth century in foreign kingdoms and that lay before their eyes.

Then, as though reproaching the author of the preface, he says:

> “Let the author of the preface examine, together with his Reims manuscript, whether Bertigarius the monk, who was writing in that century—that is, the ninth—was one of those men; for of the two opinions he reports, he always favors the more lax.”

But let the dissertation-writer himself see whether he has read carefully and critically what he asserts, or whether he merely skimmed the preface with a hasty eye.

Whether the monks departed from exact observance of the Rule in the eighth century is immaterial to me. I grant that Bertigarius the monk lived in the monastery of Saint Remigius at Reims in the ninth century. But the author who composed the treatise on weights and measures was much older than Bertigarius; Bertigarius was writing it in the monastery of Remigius under Ebo, bishop of Reims, as though it were someone else’s offspring, not his own.

Even if Bertigarius the monk were the true author of that treatise, the dissertation-writer would still not obtain what he desires. For when the author inclines to the opinion that three pounds make a sextarius and one and a half pounds make a hemina, he would undoubtedly have been speaking according to the usage of his monastery—that is, according to the usage established in all the monasteries of Gaul by the Council of Aachen, whose decree established the Benedictine hemina in all monasteries. Bertigarius the monk lived not long after that council.

The same judgment seems applicable to the author of a brief work on weights, which our Mabillon found without an author’s name at the end of Saint Benedict’s Rule in an ancient manuscript codex in the library of Saint Ulrich at Augsburg. It contains these words (Volume IV of the *Analecta*):

> “Twelve ounces make a pound … One and a half pounds make a hemina. Two heminas make a sextarius, etc.”

Nicolaus de Fractura likewise seems to be understood in this way when he says:

> “The hemina is a suitable measure for drinking at a single meal.”

For, in explaining in chapter 35 what the *biberes* are that the holy Father Benedict grants to the servants, he says that *biberes* are “vessels sufficient for one moderate draught”; shortly afterward he adds:

> “Three *biberes* ought to be sufficient for each monk at table.”

If you assign six ounces to each *biber*, as they really ought to contain, you will find that the hemina weighs one and a half pounds. Therefore, when Nicolaus explains the hemina in this chapter and says that its measure is preserved in the Cassinese monastery and, upon actual testing, holds a little more or less than the amount required, which is a certain Roman measure, either a textual error has entered into the name of the measure, or there were two Roman measures called *petitum*, one larger and one smaller—as often happens with measures of the same name—and Nicolaus was speaking of the smaller. For he was far from choosing large measures, as he says shortly afterward:

> “Because wine is granted to the monk more for strengthening the stomach than for pleasing the palate or gratifying nature.”

If the dissertation-writer had read these passages, he perhaps would not have called Nicolaus “a notorious drinker” (*Response*, no. 12).

But what would the dissertation-writer gain even if we granted that the ancient Roman measures had been preserved down to the time of Saint Benedict, and throughout all Italy? He himself admits that the holy Father instituted a special hemina in his monastery, as he in fact did. Yet whether he truly admits this may reasonably be doubted: he both admits and denies it. He admits it when he assigns twelve weight-ounces to the Benedictine hemina and only ten to the Roman; he denies it when he makes both consist equally of six *cyathi*—unless perhaps he wishes to fabricate *cyathi* unknown to antiquity.

But how does he prove that the Benedictine hemina contained only twelve ounces and no more? “If Saint Benedict,” he says, “had made the hemina larger, he would have called it a sextarius rather than a hemina, since it would have approached more closely the measure of a sextarius than that of a hemina.” [Col. 0648D] Hence Saint Isidore, who wrote not long after Saint Benedict, spoke of the hemina as a measure of twelve ounces, assigning it a single pound by weight (Book XVI of the *Etymologies*, chapter 25).

We have already learned from the dissertation-writer what should be thought of Saint Isidore. It is enough to say here that in the books of the *Etymologies* he was speaking not of a monastic hemina but of the common hemina.

As for the argument he presses from the name *hemina*: first, it assumes that the ancient Roman measures had been altered; second, it assumes that Saint Benedict had no other reason for giving this name to the measure he instituted; third, it is merely a conjecture, which might have some weight if no certain arguments to the contrary arose elsewhere.

But it was demonstrated above that the Benedictine hemina consisted of three cups, as is clear from the *Rule of the Master*, Saint Isidore, Saint Fructuosus, the statutes of Saint Adalard, and Nicolaus de Fractura, and also from the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 73, among whom the monks’ mixed drink consisted of one-third of a hemina of wine. For the *mixtum*, or *biber*, held one moderate cup; consequently, it contained no less than one and a half pounds, as the Reims and Augsburg codices state, and as can also be demonstrated from other sources. [Col. 0649A]

“But,” he says, “a hemina of twelve ounces is sufficient to provide those three cups. Since it is established that the hemina contains six *cyathi*, if it is divided in half, we shall have three *cyathi* at dinner and the same number at supper.”

For, according to the constant tradition of all the ancients, both secular and monastic, those three cups were nothing other than three *cyathi*. This is clear from Pliny (Book XXVIII, chapter 62), who proves the point by the authority of Democritus. Pliny says that Democritus composed a book to show that a fourth *cyathus* should not be drunk at a meal. It is also clear from Saint Augustine, who, contrasting a sober man with the affected sobriety of the Manichaeans (Book II on the *Morals of the Manichaeans*, chapter 13), describes the former as drinking three *cyathi* of wine for the sake of preserving his health; and from the third discourse of Abbot Isaiah, in which he permits a younger brother to drink as many as three *cyathi* if concern for his health requires it.

Thus, if in our hemina we have six *cyathi* of wine—three at dinner and, he says, the same number at supper—then, if we mix an equal amount of water with the wine, we serve twelve ounces of liquid at each meal, so that four ounces are consumed in each draught. This ought to be more than sufficient for a sober person’s daily drink.

I pass over here the fact that the dissertation-writer assigns two weight-ounces to a *cyathus*, although the consistent authority of the ancient writers establishes no more than ten drachmas—that is, one ounce and one quarter of an ounce, since an ounce contains eight drachmas—or at most two measuring-ounces, which are somewhat lighter than weight-ounces.

As for his assertion that twelve ounces of drink at a meal are sufficient for a sober person, I leave it to others to judge whether this accords with the laws of discretion. It might occasionally suffice for a young child, or even for certain people endowed by God with an extraordinary gift of abstinence; but the laws of discretion and prudence do not permit an entire community to be bound by such regulations. [Col. 0649B]

Nor should we suppose that those ancient authors who assert that three *cyathi* suffice for a sober person at a meal are to be understood so rigidly and literally that they allowed a sober person only thirty drachmas of wine. By the term *cyathus* they unquestionably mean a full cup, just as we commonly understand it today.

This is clear from the Rule of Saint Abbot Isaiah, whose authority the dissertation-writer boasts of. What the cited discourse calls a *cyathus*, the Rule expresses by the word *scyphus*:

> “If you are compelled to drink wine, do not drink more than three moderate cups” (chapter 2).

But nothing more effective can be brought forward to demonstrate this than the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, cited by the dissertation-writer himself (chapter 5). Although it grants the brothers half a hemina each day, it nevertheless requires that on the principal solemnities three dishes and the same number of drinks be provided.

For if *calix*, *poculum*, and *potio*, according to the constant tradition of the ancients, both secular and monastic, mean the same as *cyathus*, Saint Fructuosus would have granted nothing more on solemn days than on ordinary days. Since he granted half a hemina daily, and half a hemina consists of six *cyathi*, it must consequently be admitted that he granted three *cyathi*, and therefore three drinks, on ordinary days just as on solemn ones.

Moreover, if three *cyathi* strictly understood suffice for a sober person at one meal, and if to exceed that number is to pass beyond the boundaries of sobriety, then the holy Father Benedict—filled with the spirit of all the righteous and writing a Rule distinguished above all by discretion—must unquestionably be said to have been ignorant of the laws of temperance, since he grants an entire hemina to the meal at the end of a fast: that is, six *cyathi*, which the hemina contains.

What we have said is confirmed by the letter of Theodemar, abbot of Cassino, to Charlemagne. In it I read the following, which is directly relevant to our subject:

> “We have also sent a measure of drink, one to be given to the brothers at dinner and another at supper. Our predecessors judged these two measures together to be the measure of a hemina.”

From these words we learn: first, that among the Cassinese the hemina was divided into two measures, one serving dinner and the other supper; second, that these two measures were unequal, since otherwise it would have been enough to send one; third, that the smaller, which was assigned at supper, contained at least six or eight ounces, since the dissertation-writer himself grants six ounces of wine at supper; fourth, that the larger, which was assigned at dinner, was twice as large.

The same judgment seems applicable to a hemina of wine as to a pound of bread, one-third of which Saint Benedict wished to be reserved for supper. Thus, with twelve ounces of wine at dinner and six at supper, we find in Theodemar’s letter a hemina of eighteen ounces.

Therefore the Council of Aachen, which restored this measure of the hemina in all monasteries, decreed as follows (Canon 22):

> “Where there is no wine from which a hemina may be supplied, the monks shall have a double measure of good beer.”

These two measures of beer, which does not admit the addition of water, must have contained at least three cups, and indeed very large ones. For beer is customarily served much more generously and abundantly than wine, so that it is necessary to allow twelve ounces of beer in each cup, since many people drain fifteen ounces or more in a single draught.

Thus, in two heminas of beer we find thirty-six ounces—that is, eighteen in each. This seems to be how the author understood the canon of the Council of Aachen who restored the stricter observance of the Cistercian Order in his monastery in our own times (the abbot of B. M. de la Trappe). Since wine does not grow in that region, he arranged for his brothers to receive a double hemina of *sicera*—that is, approximately eighteen or twenty ounces at dinner and the same amount at supper.

The dissertation-writer brought forward this example rather inappropriately, since it offers him no support. [Col. 0651A]

“But,” he will object (*Response*, no. 5), “among all who cultivate monastic sobriety, the hemina has been regarded as a vessel, and a very small one at that.” He proves this by a passage from the *Life of Saint Hermeland the Abbot* (*Acta Sanctorum*, volume III of the Benedictine series), where it is called smaller than even a very small vessel.

The dissertation-writer could also have added that among the Cluniacs the hemina was contained in a single cup, for in Udalricus (Book II, chapter 4) we find a sign for a cup that holds the daily measure of wine.

Against these examples, however, we set the testimony of Hildemar, which is far more effective for persuasion, since he had a completely accurate knowledge of Saint Benedict’s genuine hemina. Explaining the passage of the Rule that warns lest drunkenness overtake a monk, Hildemar says that the measure should be reduced for one “who experiences drunkenness from the hemina alone—that is, who staggers either in speech or in walking.”

This plainly cannot happen to someone who is content for an entire day with so very small a vessel.

Moreover, the measure of the hemina that we propose does not so greatly exceed the limits of sobriety that it cannot be regarded as a very small vessel in comparison with a larger and more capacious vessel—for example, a *modius*, which might be necessary for supplying drink to a numerous congregation.

The passage cited from Udalricus should be understood of some exceptionally large cup, of the sort occasionally found designated for particular uses, not of the ordinary cup.

We believe that these arguments are sufficient to answer the dissertation-writer. If he should again rise up against us by bringing forward examples of certain saints who drank wine so diluted with water that it seemed to have lost the appearance of wine, we shall reply that all these exceptional examples of the saints work against him and for us. For if you grant each person only six ounces at dinner, they will certainly all be forced to dilute the wine so greatly that it loses the appearance of wine. Thus what is praised as exceptional in certain saints will become common to all monks.

But enough concerning the hemina.

“Those to whom God grants the endurance of abstinence should know that they will have their own reward.”

Peter Damian explains this passage as follows (*Opusculum* 13, chapter 7):

> “It is as though the promulgator of the holy Rule were saying to his hearers: Those who accept what I permit do not sin; but those who do not accept it have a reward; for when mercy has been admitted, you do not incur punishment; but because you have given it up for God, you attain a crown. He adds: ‘And this applies to those who are not weighed down by a particular offense. Otherwise, whoever remembers that he has committed unlawful acts ought now, in turn, to abstain from what is lawful; and whoever arrogantly committed what was forbidden ought now humbly to renounce what has been permitted.’

> “Many people who live softly and pleasantly, if they are ever urged to undertake even a little of the stricter path, immediately put forward a defensive argument. One of them says: ‘I live as I am commanded; by using what is permitted, I preserve the commands of my law.’ Then, as though he wished to appear victorious in the dispute, he proceeds audaciously: ‘Does the Rule take away permission for these and similar things? Does it not grant me these things?’ But whoever argues in this way has not yet learned to distinguish between the writer’s will and his necessity, nor has he understood that some things are permitted by indulgence and others commanded by authority.”

But the question arises whether someone to whom God grants the endurance of abstinence may abstain from wine without any further permission from the abbot. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Richard of Saint Angelo, and Boherius hold the affirmative, extending the endurance of abstinence also to food and clothing.

Although Hildemar considers it good to abstain from wine without the abbot’s consent, he nevertheless adds:

> “A monk acts better if he drinks a little wine, in order to avoid human praise, than if he fasts completely.”

I too think that anyone may licitly and laudably abstain from wine without any additional permission from the abbot when God grants him the endurance of abstinence, because Saint Benedict grants wine to the monk only on account of hardness of heart. The monk, if able, would be very eager to abstain from it, almost in the manner, says Peter Damian (*Opusculum* 13, chapter 7), in which the Apostle speaks concerning the common embrace of married people:

> “I say this by way of permission, not by way of command.”

He immediately adds:

> “I wish that all people were as I myself am; but each person has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that.”

Thus Saint Isidore writes in his Rule (chapter 10):

> “Whoever, sitting at table, wishes to abstain from meat or wine is not to be prohibited. Abstinence is not forbidden but rather praised.”

“But if the necessity of the place, labor, or the heat of summer should require more.”

Here he explains three causes for which something may be added to the hemina granted: the necessity of the place—or, as Boherius explains it, the character of the place—labor, and the heat of summer.

Bernard of Cassino discusses them as follows:

> “The necessity of the place also includes the necessity of the person, because one person may need more quickly and another less. Thus in a very dry and exceedingly arid place, made hot by the continual assault of the sun, greater hydration through drink may be needed, as may be evident on certain islands of the sea, especially the island of Lérins. During bodily labor, moist fluid is dried up, consumed by exertion and sweat, or the natural heat is more strongly stimulated and acts with greater force. For in summer yellow bile predominates, and the heat of the external fire grows stronger.”

Two other causes may be added to these three: the solemnities of the saints and the arrival of guests. Concerning these, the *Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins* says (chapter 10):

> “As for drink, if the customary measure of *sicera*, that is, beer, is supplied, then, if the abbess wishes, or if labor, a feast day, or a pious request occasioned by the arrival of a guest should demand it, the serving of wine is to be increased.”

“Let it depend upon the prior’s judgment.”

That is, the abbot’s. For, says Boherius:

> “The prior, provost, and dean, or even the cellarer, cannot dispense with the Rule in anything or do anything else except insofar as the abbot grants them permission.”

From this passage it is clear that the hemina was not so large a measure as some have maintained. If it had been so large, there would never have been any need to add anything to it.

“Considering in all things lest satiety or drunkenness should creep in.”

Conversely, this shows that the hemina was not so small as others teach; otherwise there would have been no reason to fear satiety and drunkenness. Moreover, Saint Ferreolus suspended a drunken monk from drinking wine for thirty days.

“Although we read that wine is altogether not for monks.”

The commentators ask where Saint Benedict could have read this. Smaragdus, Peter the Deacon, and Turrecremata think that it was uttered by one of the ancient Fathers, and report his statement as follows:

> “Flesh and wine, or drink in which there is drunkenness, must be rejected and not accepted by monks, for whom the world has been crucified for Christ’s sake, and they to the world” (chapter 11).

But they do not explain which ancient Father this was.

The same statement is expressly contained in the *Rule of a Certain Author for Monks*. Yet the author of that Rule seems to have been later than Saint Benedict.

Boherius writes in his first commentary:

> “I read in the *Lives of the Fathers* that certain men related to Abbot Pastor concerning a monk who did not drink wine. He replied to them that wine is altogether not for monks.”

Likewise, in his second commentary he attributes this statement to Abbot Pastor. He also refers, at least implicitly, to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, the Rule of Saint Basil, and Saint Jerome’s letter to Eustochium, where, speaking of the abstinence of monks, Jerome says (Letter 22):

> “Of food and drink I say nothing, since there even sick monks use cold water, and to have received anything cooked is considered luxury.”

Menardus also attributes the statement to Abbot Pastor, as it is related in Book IV of *The Lives of the Fathers*, no. 31, in the translation of Pelagius.

Some have nevertheless doubted whether the matter truly stands in this way, because it does not seem likely that this book was translated by Pelagius before the year 537, when he was serving as a legate in Palestine and the East—at which time Saint Benedict had already written his Rule. But Saint Benedict could have read it after it had been translated by someone else.

In the recently published sayings of the holy Fathers by John Cotelerius, I find that Abbot Xoios once said to a certain brother:

> “Wine does not belong to monks who live according to God” (Volume I of the *Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, p. 580).

Whatever the truth may be, certainly, even if Saint Benedict did not read it, he could at least have seen the statement quoted above in other writings of the holy Fathers. In those writings, at least implicitly, we read that wine does not belong to monks.

Thus Saint Antony says in his Rule (chapter 14):

> “Do not remain in a place where wine is pressed, nor eat meat at all.”

Saint Pachomius says:

> “No one may touch wine or a seasoned liquid, except in the place of the sick.”

Saint Athanasius says in the commonly circulated *Summary of Doctrine for Monks* (article 22):

> “Abstain wholly and entirely from wine, or merely taste it and give thanks to the Creator. But if, like Timothy, you fall ill because of many labors, take a little wine.”

Saint Basil says (*Longer Rules*, chapter 19):

> “The drinking of water, as natural and sufficient for necessity, is set before everyone.”

And elsewhere (*Discourse on Asceticism*):

> “Above all, a monk must abstain from association with women, and likewise from the use of wine, because wine and women make the wise apostatize.”

Saint Dorotheus says (*Teaching* 19):

> “Do not drink wine without necessity or outside the common allowance.”

These statements agree with what some authors write concerning the manner of life of the monks of old.

Saint Athanasius says (*Life of Saint Antony*):

> “As for meat and wine, I think it better to remain silent than to say anything, since even among very many monks nothing of this kind is found.”

Saint Augustine says (*On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, chapter 31):

> “They abstain not only from meat and wine as a sufficient means of subduing lusts, but also from those things that provoke the appetite of the belly and throat with such great intensity.”

Sulpicius Severus says of the disciples of Saint Martin (Book I of *The Life of Saint Martin*):

> “No one knew wine except one whom illness had compelled.”

See also the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, no. 50, in the Bollandists, 14 May.

The monks of Nitria, however, were more indulgent in this matter; according to Palladius, they used wine. Saint Ferreolus, Saint Fructuosus, and the Master in their Rules also permit wine to monks. Saint Caesarius permits it to nuns in his Rule, chapter 28 (Laus., chapter 7). Saint Leander permits it only to the sick, in *On the Instruction of Virgins*, chapter 9.

In the Rule of an unknown author, wine is granted only twice a week (chapter 2), namely:

> “On Saturday and Sunday, as is customary, those who wish may receive wine.”

The first disciples of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, likewise “drank wine only on Sundays and solemn feast days” (*His Life*, no. 12).

The monks of Menat also received a single drink of wine only on Sundays.

There were also some among our own monks who drank no wine at all. Such formerly were the monks of Fulda. As Venerable Eigil writes in the *Life of Saint Sturm*, no. 14 (*Acta Sanctorum*, volume III, part II), when Saint Boniface “had expounded the sacred Scriptures, and had found nowhere that wine was for monks, it was decreed by common consent that among them no strong drink capable of causing drunkenness should be drunk, but only weak beer. After many years, however, when the community had grown, this was changed by synodal decree, in the time of King Pippin, on account of the sick and weak.”

Such also were the monks of Lindisfarne down to the time of King Ceolwulf, who died in the year 760.

> “For when this king had become a monk and brought it about,” says Simon of Durham (*History of the Kings of England*, under the year 854), “permission was given to the monks of the Church of Lindisfarne to drink wine or beer. Before that time they were accustomed to drink nothing but milk or water, according to the ancient tradition of Saint Aidan, the first bishop and monk of that Church.”

Such were the monks of Landevenec in Armorica, who, until the time of Louis the Pious, when they accepted the Rule of Saint Benedict, “did not know the use of wine at all,” as the author of the third *Life of Saint Winwaloe* writes, no. 9 (Bollandists, 3 March).

Such were the monks living in the Bohemian forest, concerning whom the *Life of Saint Gotthard* says (no. 14, Bollandists, May):

> “As for drink, as is known to everyone, there was absolutely nothing there except water; even to guests it was supplied in sufficient quantity, but to the brothers by measure.”

Such were the monks of Sitria, among whom, as Peter Damian testifies in the *Life of Saint Romuald* (chapter 64), “no one there knew wine, even if someone were suffering from the most serious illness.”

Finally, Saint Wunebald wished to be such a man. He even refused to build a monastery at Mainz because wine was used more frequently there, fearing that regular observance might thereby be relaxed (*History of the Gallican Order of Saint Benedict*, Book IV, chapter 18).

Nor should these things seem so astonishing among religious people, since similar examples have occasionally appeared among pagans. The Germans, as Julius Caesar writes, even prohibited wine by law within their territory because they believed it generated unwarlike dispositions. Aristotle removes wine from slaves because it makes them rebellious, and from free men because it makes them insolent (Aristotle, *Economics*, Book I, chapter 1):

> “Therefore among many nations even freeborn men abstain from it, as among the Carthaginians while they are on military service.”

We ought therefore to be covered with much greater shame by what Saint Benedict adds.

“But because in our times this cannot be persuaded to monks.”

As Saint Ferreolus says, they cannot fail to know what the Apostle writes to Timothy:

> “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”

This is the sole refuge of those to whom drinking water is less pleasing.

Yet, as Saint Bernard says (*Rule*, chapter 39; Sermon 30 on the *Song of Songs*):

> “Some people vainly flatter themselves by appealing to Paul’s example, when he urged his disciple not to drink water but to use a little wine because of his stomach and his frequent illnesses. They should observe, first, that the Apostle was not at all recommending such a thing for himself; nor was the disciple, for his part, asking it for himself. Second, this was not being said to a monk but to a bishop, whose life was entirely necessary to the tender and newly emerging Church. This was Timothy: give me another Timothy, and I will feed him—if you wish, even with gold—and give him balm to drink.”

Peter Damian likewise writes (Book VI, Letter 23):

> “To this our weak man replies: ‘But the Apostle commands his disciple, saying, “Do not continue to drink water, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent illnesses.”’

> “Would that we remembered the other sayings of sacred Scripture that commend fasting as readily as we remember this one, which relaxes the rigor of abstinence through discretion. Why do we not likewise remember what Paul says elsewhere: ‘Do not be drunk with wine, in which there is debauchery’ …?

> “But Paul’s statement that you so willingly bring against me, and others like it, is shown by him elsewhere to be commanded with what measure of discretion, when he says: ‘This I say by way of permission, not by way of command,’ and so forth.”

Earlier, attacking those who plead illness as a reason not to abstain from wine, he says:

> “Perhaps you will say: ‘My head hurts; my stomach is weak.’ These are the poultices of the delicate, this is the disguise of monks living according to the flesh. This excuse is plainly very meager, since water also refreshes the sick, while wine frequently kills them.

> “Did the Lord’s forerunner not at some time become ill, although he never drank wine or *sicera*? Is it recorded that James son of Alphaeus sought physicians, although he is said from his mother’s womb to have known nothing of these liquors? Indeed, if we go back to the beginning of the world, it is known that the world itself remained entirely ignorant of wine until Noah’s six hundred and third year; and throughout all those long ages, although many human beings are recorded to have died, no one is recorded to have fallen ill.”

See also, in the same work, the remarkable prosopopoeia in which he introduces water speaking, rebuking monks who are excessively delicate and recounting its outstanding qualities and benefits.

### “For wine makes even the wise apostatize.”]

Saint Basil speaks in the same way in his sermon *On Asceticism*. Smaragdus explains how this happens in these words:

> “To apostatize means to depart from the way of righteousness, to transgress from the faith, to turn back, or to defect from what is good. But observe carefully how wine makes the wise apostatize: Noah, a wise, holy, and most ancient man, whom such enormous masses of water had not overcome, was overcome by a little wine, and, sleeping in drunkenness, was stripped naked. Wine made the patriarch Lot apostatize when he shamefully had intercourse against nature with his daughters. If, therefore, drunkenness from wine spared neither holy nor illustrious men, how much more will it overcome a small and weak monk?”

Saint Jerome is entirely right (*Epistle* 2):

> “But if, without wine, I burn with youthful passion, am inflamed by the heat of my blood, and possess a full and vigorous body, I shall gladly abstain from the cup in which I suspect poison.”

[Col. 0656C] **“But when the needs of the place require that even the measure prescribed above cannot be obtained.”** The needs of the place can here be understood in two ways: first, if the monastery is situated in regions where wine does not grow; second, if the monastery has no vineyards and is so poor that wine cannot conveniently be purchased. This is more or less Boherius’s interpretation.

**“Or much less, or none at all.”** If the quantity of wine was so tiny as the dissertation author maintains, how could an even smaller quantity be found?

**“Let those who live there bless God and not grumble.”** “For if anyone grumbles on account of food,” says Saint Basil, “he is liable to the judgment of those who grumbled in the desert.” From this passage it is reasonably inferred that Saint Benedict did not write the Rule for the one monastery at Cassino, but foresaw in a prophetic spirit that it should be promulgated for the whole world. See Haeften, book II, treatise 6, disputation 3.

## CHAPTER 41. At what hours the brothers ought to take their meals

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Other manuscripts: *oportet*, “it is necessary.”]

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Oxford, Florence, and some others omit *fratres*, “the brothers.”]

[Col. 0655]

[Col. 0655D] **552** From holy Easter until Pentecost, let the brothers take their meal at the sixth hour and dine late.

[Note: [Col. 0655D] Conc., Flor.: *sera*, “late.”]

But from Pentecost throughout the whole summer—if the monks have no agricultural work, or excessive summer heat does not interfere—let them fast until the ninth hour on Wednesdays and Fridays; on the remaining days, however, let them take their meal at the sixth hour.

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Florence, Hildemar, Conches, Lyre, Paris 1: *a Pentecosten*, “from Pentecost.”]

[Col. 0656D] This sixth-hour time for the meal must be maintained if they have work in the fields or if the heat of summer is less intense,

[Note: [Col. 0656D] Florence: *operas*, “works.”]

it shall be left to the abbot’s discretion; and so let him regulate and arrange everything that the souls of the brothers may be saved and that what they do may be done without justifiable grumbling.

[Col. 0657A]

But from the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, let them always take their meal at the ninth hour.

[Note: [Col. 0657A] Cassino: *usque caput*, “until the beginning.”]

In Lent, however, until Easter, let them take their meal in the evening.

[Note: [Col. 0657A] Oxford: *a Quadragesima*, “from Lent.”]

[Note: [Col. 0657A] Other manuscripts: *in Pascha*, “at Easter.”]

[Col. 0658A] Let the evening meal itself nevertheless be arranged so that those taking it do not need the light of a lamp, but that everything may be finished while it is still daylight.

[Note: [Col. 0658A] Florence, Conches, and some Cassino manuscripts: *lumen*, “light.”]

[Note: [Col. 0658A] Hildemar: *consumantur*, “may be finished.”]

Moreover, at all times, whether the hour of supper or of another meal, let the time be so regulated that everything is done in daylight.

[Note: [Col. 0658A] Cassino: “whether the meal or the supper meal.”]

[Note: [Col. 0658A] Florence: *luce*, “in daylight.”]

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0657]

[Col. 0657B] Thus far Saint Benedict has dealt with the measure of food and drink. But since everything has its proper time, and among the other arrangements necessary for rightly ordering life one of the principal is that appropriate times be assigned to each activity, after speaking about meals the holy Father immediately adds at what hours the brothers ought to eat. He arranges the hours of meals in such a way that he also determines the times of fasting—when fasting is to be observed and when it is to be ended. For this reason, before coming to his text, we have thought it worthwhile first to report what the practice of the ancient monks was, from their Rules and other writings.

**553** First of all, the Rule of Saint Antony contains the following (no. 2):

> “Fast every day until the ninth hour, except on Saturday and Sunday. When the ninth hour arrives, do not go to any brother’s cell; and when you have sat down to eat, pray first, and then eat.”

The Rule of the Holy Fathers Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius (chapter 9) states:

> “This order, brothers, must therefore be maintained: on no day are the brothers in the monastery to eat before the ninth hour, except on Sunday and the fiftieth day, Pentecost.”

The self-restraint of the monks living under Saint Eusebius, abbot of Mount Coryphes in Syria in the fourth century, was somewhat stricter. For, as we read in his *Life*, no. 7 (Bollandists, 23 January):

> “He took food every third and every fourth day. Those who lived with him he commanded to eat on alternate days.”

The monks on Mount Sinai were still more austere. Saint Nilus writes of them (*History of the Slaughter of the Holy Fathers on Sinai*):

> “Some take food on Sunday, remaining fasting for all seven days. Others divide the period in half, taking food twice in the week. Others do so after one day.”

The practice was much more relaxed among the Gauls. The Council of Tours II assigns the following fasts to them throughout the year (canon 18):

> “Let the ancient observances of fasting instituted by the monks be maintained: from Easter until Pentecost, except during the Rogation days, let a meal be prepared for the brothers every day. After Pentecost let them fast strictly throughout the whole week. Thereafter, until the Kalends of August, let them fast three times a week, on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, except those who are constrained by some illness. In August, since the saints’ Masses are celebrated every day, let them have a meal. Throughout September, October, and November, let them fast three times a week, as was said. In December let them fast every day until the Nativity of the Lord. And since every day between the Nativity of the Lord and Epiphany is a feast, let them likewise take a meal. The three-day period is excepted, which our Fathers established, in order to trample upon pagan custom, for private litanies to be held on the Kalends of January, so that psalmody might be sung in the churches and, at the eighth hour on the Kalends of the Circumcision, Mass might be celebrated with God’s favor. After Epiphany, however, let them fast three times a week until Lent.”

A few years before the council mentioned above, Saint Caesarius had enacted this law of fasting for monks in his Rule (chapter 22):

[Col. 0658B]

> “From holy Easter until the month of September, fasting is required only on Wednesday and Friday. From September until the Nativity of the Lord, fasting is required every day. Again, during the two weeks before Lent, fasting is required every day, except Sunday, on which it is not at all permitted to fast because of the Lord’s Resurrection: whoever fasts on Sunday sins. From the Nativity of the Lord until the two weeks before Lent, let them fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday; thereafter until Easter, fasting is required every day except Sunday: whoever fasts on Sunday sins. Let three portions be served during a fast, but at the meal and at supper only two. At the meal and at supper let them take two drinks; during a fast, three.”

And in his Rule for holy women, in the recapitulation:

**554**

> “From Pentecost until the Kalends of September, let the mother of the monastery take care to regulate the fast according to what she sees to be their strength and ability. From the Kalends of September until the Kalends of November, fasting is required on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, except on feast days and Saturday, they ought to fast every day. They must fast for seven days before Epiphany. From Epiphany until the week of Lent, fasting is required on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.”

In the order of meals that Saint Aurelian appended to his Rule, we read:

> “From the Kalends of September until the Kalends of October, fasting is required on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday.”

[Note: [Col. 0657D] Perhaps “November,” as in the Rule for Virgins and in the *Concordia Regularum*, chapter 50, § 6.]

> “From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, fasting is required every day except Saturday and Sunday. From Epiphany until Easter, fasting is required every day except the greater feasts, Saturday, and Sunday. After Easter until Pentecost, fasting is required only on Friday. After Pentecost, during June, July, and August, it shall be left to the abbot’s discretion whether there is to be a fast or a meal; he is to regulate it according to what he sees to be the brothers’ capacity.”

Saint Columbanus states the matter more briefly (chapter 3):

> “One must fast every day, just as one must pray every day.”

The Rule of Tarnat moderates this law as follows (chapter 9):

> “When the harvest and vintage are gathered, let them take food twice a day, namely at the sixth and twelfth hours. On Wednesday and Friday, however, they must regulate their work in such a way that, if possible, they do not omit the prescribed fasts; but everything is to be arranged according to the judgment of the superior, as usefulness or labor requires.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore divides fasts into four classes in the following manner:

> “The ancient Fathers chose these days especially for fasting. The first is the daily fast of Lent, in which the monks observe a greater strictness of abstinence, since they abstain not only from meals but also from wine and oil. The second is the alternate-day fast after Pentecost, begun on one day and continuing until the autumnal equinox—namely, for three days in each week—because of the summer heat of the sun. [Col. 0659A] The third is the daily fast that follows, from the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October until the Nativity of the Lord; during it the daily fasts are never suspended. The fourth is likewise a daily fast beginning after the day of the Circumcision and continuing until the solemnities of Easter.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus, bishop, says the following (chapter 18):

> “These periods of fasting must be observed. From Easter until Pentecost, food is to be taken at the sixth hour, and one meal per day is to be maintained. From Pentecost until the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October, alternate-day fasts are to be kept, except for one Lent preceding the feast of Saints Justus and Pastor, which must be carefully observed. During it they must fast every day until the ninth hour and abstain completely from wine. Nevertheless, the abbot must exercise discretion, so that when he sees them burdened by heavy labor, he may grant each of them portions at the meal.”

[Note: [Col. 0659D] In the *Concordia Regularum*, chapter 50, § 5, *potiones*, “drinks,” is read.]

> “From the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October until Easter, they must fast carefully, and during Lent abstain completely from wine and [Col. 0659B] oil.”

The Rule of a Certain Author for Monks (chapter 11) prescribes a perpetual fast:

> “In abstinence from food, one rule ought to be observed by all the brothers, except the old, the sick, and children; and there should be one measure for everyone: namely, they must abstain from food from the ninth hour until the second hour, and before or after the common table set out for the brothers at supper, nothing may be indulged to the mouth, unless illness, difference of age, or some bodily condition compels it.”

The Rule of the Master, however, states (chapter 28):

> “At all times during the week they ought to eat at the sixth hour on two days, namely Thursday and Sunday; on all the other days of the week they ought to eat at the ninth hour. For let us be ashamed, since we are spiritual men, to flee fasting until the ninth hour, when it is known that ancient custom from of old was unfamiliar with midday meals. For this reason fasts are appointed to be ended at the ninth hour on all days, so that something longer may be added during the days of Lent, namely until evening, that is, after the lamp-lighting. From Sexagesima onward, let them always eat after lamp-lighting on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday; on the other days until Lent, let them eat at the ninth hour, so that what they subtract from the forty fasts of the Sunday Lent on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, they may restore from Sexagesima by continuing the fasts until evening, so that the forty fasts may be completed in number.”

The Rule for Solitaries (chapter 42) says:

> “From the octave of Easter until Pentecost, let them eat twice a day. On these days, therefore, let them fast until the ninth hour on Wednesday and Friday, because just as bridles must be placed upon horses, so our bodies must be restrained by fasts. From Pentecost until the Kalends of September, let them fast until the ninth hour on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday; on the remaining days, however, let them eat at the sixth hour and dine in the evening. From the Kalends of September until the beginning of Lent, let them always eat at the ninth hour, unless someone should wish to extend the fast until evening. In Lent, however, until Easter, let them eat in the evening. [Col. 0659D] Moreover, if anyone should wish to fast at all times, except on Sundays and the days of other feasts, he should not be forbidden, because this is what our holy Fathers Antony and Benedict, as well as Macarius and the others, used to do.”

The Rule of an unknown author also presents examples of saints in the observance of fasts (chapter 5, in a manuscript of the library of Queen Christina of Sweden):

> “From holy Easter until Pentecost, as Saint Benedict says, food is to be taken at the sixth hour and supper eaten late. Concerning these days Saint Isidore says in his book *On Offices*: ‘After Easter until Pentecost, although ecclesiastical tradition has relaxed the strictness of abstinence by means of meals, nevertheless, if any monks or [Col. 0660A] clerics wish to fast, they are not to be forbidden; for Antony, Paul, and the other ancient Fathers are also read to have abstained in the desert during these days, and not to have ended their abstinence except on Sunday alone. From Pentecost until the Kalends of October, if it is Wednesday or Friday, the fast is not to be ended, as Saint Apollonius says. Saturdays too are regarded as consecrated to fasting by the apostles and holy Fathers. On Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday, if it is desired, food is to be taken at the sixth hour; otherwise it is to be postponed until the ninth hour. From the Kalends of October until Easter, except on feast days, the meal is to be prolonged until evening.’”

The Rule of Saint Donatus prescribes these fasts for virgins (chapter 76):

> “From holy Easter until Pentecost, let the sisters eat at the sixth hour and dine late. From Pentecost throughout the summer, if heavy manual labor is absent or excessive summer heat does not interfere, let them fast until the ninth hour on Wednesday and Friday; [Col. 0660B] on the remaining days let them eat at the sixth hour. The measure of this meal shall be left to the abbess’s care and judgment, and she shall regulate and arrange everything so that their souls may be saved and that what the sisters do may be done without any grumbling. From the Kalends of February”

[Note: [Col. 0660D] Read “September.”]

> “until the Kalends of November, fasting is required on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday. From the Kalends of November until the Nativity of the Lord, they ought to fast every day except on feast days. From holy Epiphany until the beginning of Lent, fasting is required on Wednesday and Friday. From Lent until holy Easter, let them eat in the evening. Let that evening meal nevertheless be arranged in such a way that those taking it do not need the light of a lamp, but that everything may be finished while it is still daylight.”

The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins permits a double meal, at the sixth hour and late in the day, throughout the Paschal season:

> “From Pentecost,” it says (chapter 11), “if heavy labor does not require it or the arrival of guests does not compel it, until the beginning of Lent they shall eat at the ninth hour—that is, once a day—except on the occasions of great solemnities or if substantial labor requires them to eat twice. From the beginning of Lent until the most sacred solemnity of Easter, except on Sundays, food is to be taken in the evening, so that before the beginning of night the hour of refreshment may be completed with the station of light.”

In the Rule of Saint Stephen, founder of the order of Grandmont, I also read the following (chapter 57):

> “From holy Easter until the Exaltation of the Holy Cross, we arrange for you to take food twice a day, first after the sixth hour and second after vespers, except during the fasts established within this period. But from the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Easter we command you to fast, except on Sundays and the day of the Nativity of the Lord. Again, from the aforesaid feast of the true Cross until the beginning of Lent, we prescribe that you take food after the ninth hour, and thereafter until the Lord’s Resurrection, after vespers. [Col. 0660D] Likewise, from the feast of All Saints until the Nativity of the Lord, and from Septuagesima until Easter, we command you to use only Lenten food; at other times we permit you sometimes to eat eggs and cheese.”

**557** Finally, Guigo’s Statutes prescribe the following (chapter 33):

> “On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday we are content with bread and water, and salt, if anyone wishes. On Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday we cook legumes or something of that kind for ourselves; from the cook we receive wine, and on Thursday we receive cheese or some more refined food. From the Ides of September until Easter, except on solemnities, we eat only once a day. From Easter until the aforesaid period, however, we eat again on Tuesday and Thursday, as well as Saturday.”

The ancient Carthusian Statutes depart somewhat from this severity. They contain the following (part II, chapter 14):

> “We observe the vigils of the Nativity of the Lord, the Ascension, Pentecost, Saint John, the apostles Peter and Paul, the Assumption of Blessed Mary, and All Saints, according to ancient custom, with bread and water, unless they fall on feasts of twelve lessons. Moreover, when the aforesaid vigils fall on Sunday, the same abstinence is practiced on Saturday. […] On the vigils of the blessed James, Lawrence, Bartholomew, Matthew, Simon and Jude, and Andrew, we eat only once. On Monday, Wednesday, and Friday we are content with bread, water, and salt, if anyone wishes, according to ancient custom. Since this has almost fallen into disuse in our time, we wish all monks who are not excused by illness, old age, weakness, or another cause that seems reasonable to the prior to practice at least one abstinence each week. Nevertheless, we do not thereby cancel the ancient custom concerning the observance of abstinences. […] From the Exaltation of the Holy Cross until Easter we eat only once a day, except for chapter feasts until Quinquagesima, the day on which a new prior is received, and the day of the burial of one of our brothers. This is to be observed inviolably, except by the sick, the infirm, the weak, the old, and the young. If the prior otherwise breaks this rule or causes it to be broken, he shall remain outside his seat in the church for forty days. If the vicar does the same, he shall be a novice for forty days. From Easter until the feast of the Exaltation, we eat again on Tuesday and Thursday, as well as Saturday, except during the principal fasts; during that period, however, the fasts of Monday and Wednesday are not to be entirely omitted.”

Finally, one of the first disciples of Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, says the following (*Life*, book I, no. 15, in Baluze, volume IV of the *Miscellany*):

> “No one dared to end the fast except on Sunday, in summer as in winter, unless he was held back by youth or serious illness.”

I think we should add an ancient fragment concerning the fast of the Greeks, which our Jacob Loppin extracted from a manuscript of the Colbert Library, no. 6041, and translated into Latin as follows:

> “An order extracted from the divine and sacred canons and also from the typika of the holy and God-bearing Fathers, for those who desire to lead a life pleasing to God.
>
> “One must begin with the splendid first Sunday of Easter, eating every kind of food throughout the entire new week. From the second day of Antipascha—that is, the second day of the week after Easter—until All Saints, on Wednesday and Friday laypeople are to eat fish, but monks oil. The same is also to be done on the Wednesday of Mid-Pentecost, that is, the Wednesday of the fourth week after Easter. Throughout the week of the Holy Spirit one must live as in the new week, or the week of Easter.
>
> “But from the second day after All Saints, on which we begin the fast of the holy apostles, we keep fast on Monday, Wednesday, and Friday, and eat dry food at the ninth hour. On the other two days, Tuesday and Thursday, we monks eat oil, while laypeople eat fish; on Saturday and Sunday, we eat prepared food. Thus the rule concerning this kind of fast has been laid down.
>
> “We observe the same rule during the fast of August and of the Nativity of Christ. But during the solemnity of the chief apostles Peter and Paul, if it happens to fall on a Wednesday or Friday, we eat neither cheese, oil, nor prepared food; the same applies to the feast of the twelve apostles if it falls on a Wednesday or Friday. The same must also be observed on the commemorations of distinguished saints.
>
> “We end the fast only on feasts of the Lord, on whatever day they fall; on those days we eat oil and fish. But if the vigils of Christ’s Nativity or of the Lights—that is, Epiphany—fall on a Wednesday or Friday, after the liturgy has been completed we refresh ourselves only with wine and cooked foods, without oil. If they happen to fall on Saturday or Sunday, after Chrysostom’s liturgy we take only the blessed bread and wine, and remain in this state until the end of vespers; then we eat a full meal.
>
> “During the twelve days of Theophany, both monks and laypeople eat oil and prepared food. We do the same during the week preceding Meatfare Sunday and also during what is called Cheese Week. If anyone nevertheless eats cheese, he will not sin.
>
> “During Great Lent we eat dry food on the weekdays of each week, using oil and wine only on Saturdays and Sundays. We eat prepared food only on the day of the Annunciation, if it falls outside Holy Week. But at the end of Great Saturday, after the liturgy, having eaten, we also drink wine and nothing more.
>
> “If any bishop, priest, deacon, subdeacon, reader, or other faithful person eats oil and prepared food on Wednesdays and Fridays throughout the year, except on Sundays and feast days, and does so outside illness, then, if he is a cleric, he is to be deposed; if a layman, he is to be excommunicated, as a transgressor of divine law.
>
> “These things have been written for those who are in sound and firm health. As for those who are ill and tormented by hunger because of scarcity: even if during this Great Lent they eat fish every day throughout Lent, the Lord will forgive them in this present age and in the age to come. Amen.”

But enough about the fasts of others. Now let us turn to our own.

### “From holy Easter until Pentecost.”

That is, until the octave of Pentecost, as Hildemar explains.

### “Let the brothers take their meal at the sixth hour.”
