Whether this means the beginning or the completion of the sixth hour will be considered at chapter 48. For the moment it is enough to note that the Cluniacs arranged the time of the meal so that, when it had ended, midday had only then arrived, according to Udalricus, book I, chapter 18. Dunstan, however, prescribes that at the middle of the fifth hour the sixth-hour office should be sung, after which they should wash their hands and go to table.

**559** Before the sixth hour mentioned above, we do not find that Saint Benedict, or any other master of monks, allowed any food to be tasted by his brothers, at least by all of them. Some indeed postponed the meal until the ninth hour or evening; but we find no one who anticipated the sixth hour.

[Col. 0662C] There is one exception: the *Life of Saint Samson* (*Bollandists*, first century of Benedictine history), in whose no. 16 I read:

> “It was the custom according to the law of this monastery to rub garden herbs suitable for health into a drink and divide them individually among the brothers in their own vessels, in small cups—not large ones—so that when they came to celebrate the third hour, they would find the drink already prepared, mixed with garden herbs.”

Before the third hour, moreover, as I may note in passing, it was regarded as religiously improper among the Britons to taste any food, as is clear from Bede’s *Life of Saint Cuthbert* and from the *Life of Saint Guthlac the Anchorite*, no. 29, in the third century of Benedictine history.

### “And let them dine late.”

That is, in the evening. Saint Benedict therefore prescribes no fast at all throughout the Paschal season, in accordance with the ancient custom of the Church, by which from Easter until Pentecost the fast was ended out of reverence for the Lord’s Resurrection. This can be seen in Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*; Saint Epiphanius, *Compendium of Ecclesiastical Doctrine*; Saint Augustine, letter 55; the Rule of the Master, chapter 28; [Col. 0662D] and Haymo of Halberstadt, book I *On Variations*, chapter 14.

The same custom likewise prevailed generally among monks, as is clear from Cassian, book II *On Nocturnal Prayer*, chapter 18, and *Conferences* 21, chapter 20; Saint Jerome, preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius; and Saint John Climacus, step 14. Nevertheless, there were some who did not hesitate to violate this law without reservation.

Indeed, above we saw Saint Aurelian prescribing a fast on Friday during this period; Saint Caesarius and the Rule for Solitaries prescribing it on Wednesday and Friday; the Rule of the Master prescribing it on every day except Sunday and Thursday; and the Rules of Saint Antony, Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius, Saint Columbanus, the monastery of Tarnat, and a Certain Author for Monks prescribing it every day, perhaps except Sunday alone.

Peter Damian, too, speaking of the order of the hermits of Fonte Avellana, writes as follows (*Opusculum* 14):

> “From the octave of the Lord’s Resurrection until the day of holy Pentecost, you fast four days a week; but out of reverence for Sunday, about which no one has any doubt, you take food twice a day on Tuesday and Thursday. At that time, as you know, monks are not forbidden by the authority of the sacred canons to fast.”

Moreover, it was an ancient custom to fast during the Rogation days, as is clear from the Council of Tours II, canon 18, from Hildemar on this passage, and from what we reported in book III *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 19.

### “From Pentecost throughout the whole summer, if the monks have no agricultural work or excessive summer heat does not interfere, let them fast until the ninth hour on Wednesday and Friday.”

Saint Benedict retained the fast of Wednesday and Friday even in summer, since it had been handed down by the apostles.

**560** Concerning this, the Apostolic Canon 68 states:

> “If any bishop, priest, deacon, reader, or cantor does not fast during the holy Lent of Easter, or on Wednesday, or on the Preparation, let him be deposed, unless he is prevented by bodily weakness. If he is a layman, let him be deprived of communion.”

Clement, in the *Apostolic Constitutions* (book V, final chapter), says:

> “After the week of fasting, we command you to fast every Wednesday and on the Preparation.”

Saint Ignatius (*Epistle 4 to the Philadelphians*) says:

> “Do not neglect to fast on Wednesdays and Fridays, distributing the remnants of food to the poor.”

Tertullian (*On Fasting*) asks:

> “Why do we call Wednesday and Friday of the week stations?”

He calls fasts “stations” according to his customary terminology.

Saint Clement of Alexandria (*Stromata*, book VII) says:

> “The believer knows the riddles of the fast of these days, namely Wednesday and Friday.”

Saint Peter, patriarch of Alexandria, says:

> “No one reproaches us for observing Wednesday and the Preparation, on which fasting has been rationally prescribed to us according to tradition.”

Saint Epiphanius, in the *Synopsis*, says:

> “To remain fasting until the ninth hour on Wednesday and Friday was instituted by the apostles.”

Therefore it should not seem surprising that the ancient monks observed this fast with such religious devotion [Col. 0663C] that they considered it wrong to violate it even when guests arrived, and did not dare to end it except in the case of the greatest necessity.

“Except for the appointed fasts of Wednesday and Friday,” says Cassian (*Book V*, chapter 24), “wherever we went, the daily station was ended.”

Saint Antony (*Rule*, no. 15) says:

> “Do not break the fast on Wednesday or Friday except on account of serious illness.”

Saint Macarius (*Rule*, chapter 29) says:

> “Those who break the fast on Wednesday and Friday are regarded as sharers in the guilt of Judas, who betrayed Christ.”

The commonly attributed Saint Athanasius (*Summary of Doctrine for Monks*) says:

> “Carefully observe the fast of Wednesday and the Preparation, except at Pentecost and Epiphany, unless you are seriously bedridden.”

Rufinus explains the reason for this observance. Speaking of Saint Apollonius, he says (*Book II of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7):

> “He taught that the appointed fasts, namely Wednesday and Friday, should not be ended unless some great necessity arose, because on Wednesday Judas contemplated the betrayal of the Lord, and on Friday the Savior was crucified. Therefore anyone who ends the prescribed fasts on those days without necessity will seem either to betray the Savior along with the betrayer or to crucify him along with those who crucified him.”

Saint Maglorius gives the same explanation (*Life*, first century of Benedictine history):

> “On Wednesday and Friday he abstained from every kind of food. He completed the observance of fasting on Wednesday because on that day the sacrilegious and guilty Jews made a bloody pact in order to hand over their Lord and author to death; on Friday, because they completed in action what they had conceived in their hearts by fastening him to the cross.”

Saint Augustine gives the same explanation in his letter to Casulanus, as does Richard of Saint Angelo in his commentary on this passage. Hildemar, however, traces the origin of this custom even further back:

> “This custom of fasting on Wednesday and Friday arose from the holy Fathers; and there was also a Jewish custom, as the Pharisee says: ‘I fast twice in the Sabbath.’”

**561** This fast was still observed by at least some people toward the end of the seventh century, as is clear from Bede’s *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 5 (*Bollandists*, second century of Benedictine history):

> “For it was Friday, on which many of the faithful customarily prolonged their fast until the ninth hour out of reverence for the Lord’s Passion.”

The same Bede also praises Saint Aidan for this, saying (*Ecclesiastical History*, book III, chapter 5):

> “Strengthened by his example, devout men and women of that time made it their custom throughout the whole year, except during the relaxation of the Paschal Pentecost, to prolong the fast until the ninth hour on Wednesday and Friday.”

Nevertheless, although this fast was held in such high religious regard by the ancients, Saint Benedict permits it to be relaxed because of heavier agricultural labor and excessive summer heat. From this concession its complete abolition later arose among our people.

“This practice,” says Bernard of Cassino, [Col. 0664B] “has nevertheless fallen into disuse among many, although it is known to have originated with the holy Fathers.”

And indeed, in the ancient customs of the monastery of Fleury, I read:

> “On the first Wednesday after the octave of Pentecost we ought to fast according to the command of our Father. […] On the other Wednesdays, instead of fasting, we sometimes perform some manual labor or, at the prior’s command, recite certain prayers.”

Udalricus writes likewise (book I, chapter 29):

> “If our weakness permitted it, it would be fitting, according to the command of our teacher Saint Benedict, that immediately after the octave of Pentecost we should fast every Wednesday and Friday. If we do not do this any longer, nevertheless we do not altogether omit it: in some fashion we observe it on one of the aforesaid days, and on the first of them, after the third hour we remain silent, and after the sixth hour, ascending to the dormitory, pretend to be taking our midday rest rather than actually doing so; for soon the signal is sounded for us to return to the church, where we make a procession barefoot. As has been said, we fast on the first day; afterward, in place of fasting, we more often perform some manual labor.”

The ancient manuscript customs of the Roman monastery of Saint Paul do not define the matter so absolutely. They leave everything to the abbot’s discretion and prudence, so that, if he wishes, “because of the weak-minded, or because of the state of the weather, or if the labor has become heavier,” the brothers may eat twice a day.

But the fast on Wednesday, which our people have neglected, the Greeks have continued to observe with great religious devotion, as Arcudius testifies in book III *On the Sacraments*, chapter 5. Referring to Theophylact’s words that the Jews “began their council against Christ on Wednesday, and therefore we too fast on that day,” he says:

> “This opinion is entirely true, received through tradition and confirmed by the very long practice of the Churches. The Roman Church observed it for many centuries; the Greek Church observes it carefully to the present day. Nor can the Greeks give any other reason why on that day they abstain from meat and dairy products.”

The Roman Church retained the Wednesday fast for a long time, as is stated here; in the course of time, however, it was transferred to Saturday and finally, as charity grew cold, reduced to abstinence from meat alone, which is an imperfect fast.

### 562. “On the other days, however, let them dine at the sixth hour.”

Here Saint Benedict makes no mention of supper, perhaps judging that it was sufficient for the brothers to eat once a day, in accordance with the custom of the ancient monks, who considered the fast broken when they ate only once a day at the sixth hour. This is especially clear from Cassian, where Abbot Theonas says as follows (Conference 21, chapter 23):

> “Therefore, so that the established custom of solemnity may be preserved even on feast days, while the most salutary measure of frugality is in no way exceeded, it is sufficient to allow the indulgence of relaxation to proceed so far that the food which ought to have been taken at the ninth hour of the day may, because of the feast, be taken somewhat earlier, that is, at the sixth hour—provided only that neither the customary quantity nor the quality of the food is changed, and so forth.”

The same is evident from Saint Jerome, who writes to Eustochium about the monks (Letter 22) that

> “from Easter to Pentecost, suppers are changed into dinners, so that both sufficient justice may be done to the tradition of the Church and the stomach may not be burdened with a double quantity of food.”

The same point may also be observed in the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, written after the Rule of Saint Benedict, where I read:

> “From Easter until Pentecost they are to eat at the sixth hour, and monophagy—that is, a single meal—is to be maintained.”

Mabillon likewise reports the same concerning our monks of Fulda (Preface to the third century, part I, no. 25): namely, that

> “they abstained from supper throughout the entire year until the time of Abbot Marcward, that is, until the middle of the twelfth century; nor did they admit women into their church before the fourteenth century.”

The same must be asserted of those monasteries that lived according to the standard of the Fulda monks and in which a purer discipline was established.

Nevertheless, there were also some of the ancient monks who prepared a dinner at the sixth hour and a late supper in summer. Saint Jerome reports this especially of the monks of Tabennisi (Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius):

> “Twice a week, on the fourth and sixth days of the week, everyone fasts, except during Pentecost. On the other days those who wish eat after midday, and likewise a table is set at supper for those who work, the elderly, children, and times of extreme heat. Some eat a little for a second time; others are content with only one dish at dinner or supper; some, after tasting a little bread, go out.”

There are also those who understand Saint Benedict’s text as referring simultaneously to dinner and supper. Yet they should be thought to have had regard to the practice of their own time, especially since no reason can be given why above, from Easter to Pentecost, out of reverence for the holy Resurrection and the coming of the Holy Spirit, he said that they should eat at the sixth hour and sup late, whereas here he says nothing of the latter.

I would not, however, define the matter with certainty, since above we saw from Saint Jerome that some of the ancient monks permitted both dinner and supper. The same is also clear from Cassian, Book III, chapter 12, although that supper was extremely light and granted only for those who worked, the elderly, children, and times of extreme heat. Moreover, this meal was an extraordinary one among the monks, and not all were required to attend it, as Cassian teaches. Certainly, that many more of the ancient monks did not sup at all, in addition to what we have already said, is proved by an anonymous manuscript Rule, chapter 2.

### “Their dinner at the sixth hour is to be continued if they have work in the fields or if the heat of summer is excessive.” 563

This applies on Wednesday and Friday just as on the other days. The Rule of Tarnat contains the following (chapter 9):

> “When the harvests and the grape harvest are being gathered, they are to receive food twice a day, that is, at the sixth and twelfth hours. On Wednesday and Friday, however, their work is to be so regulated that, if possible, the appointed fasts are not omitted; but everything is to be arranged according to the judgment of the superior, as usefulness or labor requires.”

### “And let the abbot make the provision.”

Whether on Wednesday and Friday they should dine at the sixth hour or eat at the ninth hour.

### “And so let him temper and arrange everything in such a way that souls may be saved.”

Here the holy Father grants the abbot supreme authority: for whoever says “everything” reserves absolutely nothing. From this authority, perhaps, arose among our monks the custom of drinking in summer after the ninth hour, especially if they ate only once a day, at the sixth hour. This custom was extremely ancient and continued for many centuries in our monasteries, even those properly ordered.

I first encountered mention of it in the Rule of the Master, where the following is written (chapter 27):

> “During these summer days, when food is taken at the sixth hour, every day after None has been said the abbot is to come out of the oratory and sit in his chair. With everyone standing in order around him, the cellarer is to bring out the wine, and the weekly servers are to mix, in the customary vessel, one drink for each group of ten at each table, according to the number of the community and according to his own measure. The abbot is immediately to rise and pray with everyone. After the prayer, before sitting down, he is to bless the vessel offered to him with the mixture. Then he is to order everyone to go with him to their tables and sit as usual; and, drinking first himself, he is thereafter to have the mixture poured out for everyone individually at each table. When this has been completed, they are to rise again and pray; after the prayer, they are all to return to the work they had left.”

The Chapters of the Monks Directed to Augia likewise state (chapter 8):

> “Throughout the entire summer, while the brothers eat twice a day, after the hour of None they are to stand in the oratory, praying with holy awe, and wait until the superior has struck the signal of the little bell for the refectory. When they hear it, they are all to assemble there. Even if someone is unable to drink, he must nevertheless present himself, lest his place appear empty. If anyone who is present is not there to say ‘Amen’ after the blessing, his portion of the drink is to be taken away. After the brothers have drunk, they are to go to the chapter-house and labor at whatever has been assigned to them, and so forth.”

This custom of drinking after None is also mentioned in the Customs of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane, volume IV of the *Analecta*; in the Chapters of the Monks of Saint Gall, chapter 27; in Udalricus, *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 80; and everywhere throughout our monasteries’ ordinaries and customs.

The monks of Monte Cassino added fruit to the drink, as we learn from a letter of Theodemar:

> “In summer, after None, if there is any fruit, we provide our brothers with one bowl each.”

The Council of Aachen, however, seems to have removed fruit when it decreed (canon 10):

> “Fruit and lettuce are not to be eaten unless some other food is being taken.”

### 564

From the same authority granted to the abbot by Saint Benedict, or also from the custom of drinking in summer after None, there arose another practice: drinking after Vespers on fast days. The Rule of the Master says of this (chapter 27):

> “On those summer days when food is taken at the ninth hour, two drinks for everyone are to be sufficient in the evening before Compline. They are nevertheless first to pray before drinking and, after they have drunk, to pray again.”

And below:

> “On those days when in winter food is taken at the ninth hour, after Vespers they are to receive no more than one hot drink each; nevertheless, they are to pray before drinking and, after they have drunk, to pray again.”

The Council of Aachen also grants this indulgence during Lent, decreeing (canon 12):

> “If necessity should require it because of the labor of their work, they may drink even after the evening meal, and likewise during Lent; and when the Office for the Dead is celebrated, they may drink before the reading of Compline.”

See Udalricus, Book I, chapter 41; *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 80, concerning drinking after Vespers; and Book I of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 2.

### “And whatever the brothers do, let them do it without justified murmuring.”

Smaragdus calls “justified murmuring” the murmuring that the monks make unwillingly, or not without cause, but reluctantly and under compulsion.

### “But from the Ides of September, and so forth.”

Here the ingenuity of the commentators is greatly exercised in reconciling this passage with chapter 48, where Saint Benedict prescribes that from Easter until the Kalends of October, “after rising from the table at the sixth hour, they are to rest in their beds.”

Some, as Hildemar reports, thought that this passage had been written by Saint Benedict for those who did not work in the fields, who were to begin the fast from the Ides of September; whereas chapter 48 applied to those working in the fields, whom the holy Father permitted to continue eating at the sixth hour until the Kalends of October, just as throughout the whole summer.

Thus Smaragdus writes among others:

> “A question arises as to how he can say here that they are to fast every day from the Ides of September, when in chapter 48 he is going to say: ‘From Easter until the Kalends of October, after rising from the table at the sixth hour, they are to rest.’ The matter is resolved as follows: If they have work in the fields or are gathering grapes in the vineyards, where they are occupied by this work, they are to eat at the sixth hour until the Kalends of October. But if they have no such work, the general fast begins from the Ides of September.”

Others judged that during the eighteen days lying between the Ides of September and the Kalends of October, they should proceed in the same way as on the two days of fasting throughout the summer—that is, that after the sixth hour they should sleep; then they should sing Mass in such a way that, once it had ended, the eighth hour having been reached, None would be said; after None had been said, they should eat.

This is Hildemar’s opinion:

> “Those who say that this is the proper meaning of Saint Benedict say that during these eighteen days one should act as on the two summer days. This is how one should act on those days when they eat at the ninth hour: after Sext has been sung, they are to go to sleep. Then the one who is to strike the signal, when he sees the appropriate hour, must strike the signal for Mass. After Mass has been sung at the middle of the eighth hour, they are to sing None; then they are to eat.”

Bernard of Cassino testifies that this had been the practice of the Cassinese in his own time.

Peter Boherius, however, seems to have solved the difficulty by explaining “from the Ides of September” as beginning from 13 September exclusively. In fact, the days before the Kalends of October begin to be counted on the following day, that is, 14 September; for this reason the holy Father calls them “the Kalends of October.”

Boherius must therefore be corrected in his first commentary, where he says:

> “On the very day of the Ides of September the brothers eat at the ninth hour, because then they begin to fast.”

The same correction applies to Lanfranc’s Statutes, which prescribe (chapter 1, § 6) that

> “from the Ides of September, on ordinary days, the fasts prescribed by the Rule are to be observed continuously, and they are to begin fasting on the very day of the Ides,”

and to the Customs of the Roman Monastery of Saint Paul, which similarly read:

> “On the Ides of September they are to say Prime as before; then, on that very day, the fast prescribed by the Rule is to begin.”

See Book IV of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 8. Charles Cointius confirms our explanation in his commentary on chapter 48 of the Rule.

### “Until the beginning of Lent.”

“That is, until the Monday after the First Sunday of Lent,” says Menardus, “so that Lent in this passage is understood as the Lenten fast.”

### “The brothers are always to eat at the ninth hour.”

This was the hour at which the ancient Romans were summoned to take food, as we learn from the Rule of the Master, which therefore says (chapter 28):

> “Let us be ashamed, we who are spiritual, to flee the fast at the ninth hour, when it is known that ancient custom formerly knew nothing of dinners but always appointed the evening—that is, supper—for its meals. Even the grain allowance that was distributed to laborers or soldiers is called *annona* to this day because it was distributed at the ninth hour of the day, when it was also consumed; and for that reason the name *annona* has remained to this day.”

Saint Isidore agrees, teaching (Book XX of the *Etymologies*, chapter 2) that the word *annona* derives from the time when the ancient Romans were summoned to their food.

Saint Benedict exempts no day from the fast from the Ides of September until Easter. Nevertheless, by the common custom and law of the Church—which even monks, despite the highest vows of abstinence, willingly obeyed—the fast must be broken on Sunday out of reverence for the Resurrection of the Lord.

The holy Father omitted this as something known to all and universally accepted. He could not have been unaware of what the Fourth Council of Carthage says (canon 64):

> “Anyone who deliberately fasts on the Lord’s Day is not to be believed a Catholic.”

The Council of Gangra likewise says (canon 18):

> “If anyone fasts on Sunday on account of what is considered spiritual discipline—that is, the monastic life—let him be anathema.”

Tertullian writes similarly (*On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3):

> “We consider it unlawful to fast on Sundays.”

Saint Ambrose says (Letter 83):

> “We cannot fast on Sunday, because we rightly condemn even monks on account of fasting on that day.”

And Saint Athanasius writes (*Summary of Doctrine for Monks*):

> “Do not fast on Saturday or Sunday, except on Holy Saturday of the sacred Pasch. … Take care that no one induce you to fast at all on Sunday or to kneel, nor during Pentecost; for this is not the command of the Church. Beware lest the Marcionites or any other heresy deceive you into fasting on Saturday as well as on Sunday.”

See Cassian, Book III, chapter 11, and Conference 21, chapter 20.

For the same reason, some Fathers of the monastic life judged that fasting should also be suspended on the principal feasts of the saints. An entire chapter on this subject is found in the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 2), expressed in these words:

> “These are the days of the monks on which fasts cease. First of all is the venerable Lord’s Day, dedicated to the name of Christ. Just as it is solemn because of the mystery of his Resurrection, so among all his servants it will preserve the celebration of a feast with the joy of a desired banquet.
>
> “Likewise, from the first day of Easter until Pentecost—that is, for fifty continuous days—the fast has been dissolved by the holy Fathers, on account of the Resurrection of Christ and the coming of the Holy Spirit, so that these days may be celebrated not under the figure of labor, which the season of Lent signifies, but in the repose of joy, with the fasts relaxed.
>
> “The Fathers also decreed that the period from the day of the Lord’s Nativity until the day of the Circumcision should be made solemn, with permission to eat. Likewise, the day of Epiphany received, according to the ancient Rule, the indulgence of taking food. Indeed, whenever one of the brothers is converted and brothers from other monasteries come together to visit him, fasts are interrupted for the fulfillment of charity, provided that they have not been general fasts. Apart from these occasions, other times are freely and willingly devoted to fasting.”

The Council of Aachen likewise decrees (canon 46):

> “On the principal solemnities—that is, Christmas and the octave of the Lord, Epiphany, Easter, and the Ascension of the Lord; on the feasts of the saints, namely Saint Stephen, Blessed John the Evangelist, and the Nativity of the Holy Innocents; on the Purification and Assumption of Saint Mary; likewise on the feasts of the blessed apostles and on the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Martin; and on the birthdays of any saint whose honor is specially celebrated in any parish, let the full Office be performed and let them eat twice.”

As Udalricus teaches (Book I, chapters 39 and 43), the Cluniacs relaxed the fast during the octaves of the Nativity of the Lord, Epiphany, and Saint Martin, and on the principal solemnities of the saints.

Peter the Venerable identifies those principal feasts in his Statutes, decreeing (Statute 14):

> “The regular fasts are to be observed by our monks from the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, by eating once a day, except on the feast of Saint Michael and the dedication of the church; on the feasts of the apostles occurring outside Advent and Septuagesima; on the feasts of the Cluniac abbots; during the eight days of the Nativity of the Lord; on Epiphany, but only on the first day; on the feast of Saint Marcellus the pope; Saint Vincent the martyr; and the Purification of Saint Mary.
>
> “The feast of the Conversion of Saint Paul does not break the fast, since the Church celebrates other feasts of that same apostle at other times of the year. On the feast of the Chair of Saint Peter the fast is relaxed on that day; also, because this feast always occurs during Septuagesima, Sext is sung immediately after the principal Mass, and after an interval None follows.”

Peter the Venerable speaks similarly of the Carthusians (Book II of the *Miracles*, chapter 28):

> “They always eat once a day, except during the eight days of the Nativity of the Lord, the eight days of Easter, the eight days of Pentecost, the Epiphany of the Lord, his Presentation—that is, the Purification of Saint Mary; the Annunciation of the Lord, whenever it falls in the Easter season; the Ascension of the Lord; the Assumption and Nativity of the aforesaid holy Virgin, his mother; and except on the feasts of the twelve apostles, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Michael, Saint Martin, and the feast celebrated on the Kalends of November, All Saints.”

In the Institutes of his congregation (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 6), Peter Damian exempts the following days alone from the fast between the Ides of September and Easter: the feasts “of Saint Martin and Saint Andrew; the week of the Nativity of the Lord; one day of Epiphany; and the Hypapante.”

The Cassinese, however (Cassinese chapter 41), dispense from fasting on the feasts of Saint Matthew; Saint Michael; Saint Justina of Padua; Saint Luke; Saints Simon and Jude; All Saints; Saint Martin; Saint Andrew, when celebrated outside Advent; the Nativity of the Lord with the three following days; the Circumcision; Epiphany; Saint Anthony the Abbot; the Purification of Blessed Mary; Saint Matthias, when it falls outside Lent; and the feast of the dedication of the place.

The New Declarations add the feasts of Saint Placidus; All Holy Monks; Saint Maurus; and Saint Scholastica.

Finally, the monks of Fulda (*Constitutions of the Fulda Monks*, chapter 41) exempt from fasting the feasts of All Saints, the Nativity of the Lord, the Circumcision, Epiphany, the Purification, and the feast of the monastery’s patron.

Certainly, since fasts are more appropriate to affliction than to rejoicing, they are not fitting on days of joy, as Saint Thomas says (*Summa theologiae* II–II, question 147, article 5, reply to objection 3). Thus the ancients were accustomed to break the fast on the solemnities of martyrs. To prevent this from occurring during Lent, the Council of Laodicea decreed in chapter 51 that the feasts of martyrs should not be celebrated during Lent.

Nevertheless, those are more praiseworthy who strive to celebrate the feasts of the saints through spiritual rather than bodily joys, and who labor on these feasts to nourish souls rather than bodies. For this reason Peter the Venerable commends the Cistercians in Book I, Letter 28; and even now certain congregations of monks and nuns practice the same with great praise.

### “But during Lent, until Easter, let them eat in the evening.”

This was not something peculiar to monks but was common to all Christians. The custom still prevailed in the time of Saint Bernard, as he himself testifies when addressing his brothers at the beginning of Lent (Sermon 3, on Lent):

> “Until now we alone have fasted until the ninth hour; from now on, all alike will fast with us until evening—kings and princes, clergy and people, noble and humble, rich and poor together as one.”

See Peter of Blois, sermon 11.

### “Nevertheless, let the evening meal be so arranged that those eating do not need lamplight.”

Haeftenus gives three reasons for this (Book X, treatise 1, discussion 3):

1. So that they would not seem to imitate the Jews, who did not break their fast until after sunset.

2. So that it would not be more burdensome to prolong the fast for those who, rising at the eighth hour of the night, had spent a large part of the day in labor, singing psalms, and other spiritual exercises.

3. So that a considerable part of the night would not be taken away from nocturnal rest.

Menardus adds a fourth reason:

> “Because, since lamplight is somewhat dimmer, an opportunity would be given to the Evil One, especially in a large refectory, to incite the brothers to conversation and certain other illicit activities.”

### “But let everything be finished while it is still daylight.”

Those eating near the final hour of the day will easily accomplish this, for before the tenth hour—until which, according to chapter 48, they must devote themselves to manual labor—and after which they most probably sang Vespers, they must take no food.

Saint Gerasimus did not permit his disciples to read by lamplight, as we learn from the Life of Saint Euthymius, no. 91 (volume II of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*).

### “But at all times, whether it is supper or another meal, let the hour be so arranged that everything takes place in daylight.”

Some labor greatly to explain how everything could take place in daylight during winter, when the fast was broken and relaxed. Menardus thinks that

> “Saint Benedict especially binds those who live in Italy and similar regions to this constitution, where around the winter solstice the days are not as short as in northern regions, such as England, Scotland, Denmark, the farthest parts of Belgium, and similar places, where this institution cannot be observed because of the shortness of the days.”

But, as Haeftenus observes (Book X, treatise 1, discussion 3), and as is clear from the Cassinese Declarations, even in Italy supper cannot be completed while it is still daylight without evident harm to the body. Hence he says:

> “I would believe that almost nowhere is this text of the Rule observed literally. If someone should insist that the Rule must be observed absolutely, one might say that perhaps even Sundays, or any feasts, were not exempt from the regular fast in Saint Benedict’s time. But if we wish to say that, since fasting on Sundays was forbidden, they supped, it must be said that this supper was so modest that they did not fear serious inconvenience from it.”

Thus he leaves the matter undefined.

The difficulty, however, is easily resolved by observing that the fast can be relaxed in three ways:

1. By eating twice a day.

2. By eating something more substantial than usual. Saint Peter Damian even called those people fasting “who take bread with salt and water”; when anything else is added, he says, “it is not called fasting in the desert.”

3. By taking the customary meal earlier—for example, dining at the sixth hour in the case of those who on ordinary days ate at the ninth hour.

Thus the Council of Chalon asserts that those who ate at the ninth hour did not fast during Lent, as may be seen in Gratian, *De consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter *Solent*.

Ancient monks used to break their fast in this last way, as is clear from what has been said, especially from Saint Jerome’s testimony to Eustochium, that among them

> “from Easter to Pentecost, suppers are changed into dinners, so that both sufficient justice may be done to the tradition of the Church and the stomach may not be burdened with a double quantity of food.”

See the Rule of the Master, chapter 53.

In light of these observations, it is not difficult to explain how everything could be completed while it was still daylight, even in winter, when they were not fasting.

First, since the holy Father appears to allow at supper no more than one-third of a pound of bread together with, at most, some fruit, they could consume this without bodily discomfort or danger to their health before the tenth hour—that is, before our fourth hour after midday—even if they had dined at the sixth hour.

Second, they could break the fast at the customary hour of the meal by eating something more substantial than usual—for example, fish, when on other days they would take supper consisting only of vegetables.

Third, those who dined at the sixth hour could sup at the ninth hour on ordinary days.

Finally, it is quite probable that the first disciples of Saint Benedict broke the fast on Sundays in this way: partly in imitation of the ancient monks, whose footsteps he strove to follow in many matters; partly because in summer, when he prescribes no fast, he seems to have granted only dinner without supper; and partly because the Rule of the Master, which is almost entirely derived from the Benedictine Rule, instituted nothing else:

> “On those days,” it says (chapter 27; see chapter 53), “in winter when they eat at the sixth hour, they are to have absolutely no supper in the evening.”

Nicholas of Fractura, expounding Saint Benedict mystically, says:

> “With light—that is, with Christ, who is the true light, as he himself testifies concerning himself in the Gospel: ‘I am the true light,’ and so forth.”

## CHAPTER XLII  
### That no one is to speak after Compline

Textual variants: Flor. reads *completorios* (“after the completories”) in the heading. In the first sentence Cassin., Flor., and three manuscripts read *silentium* (“silence”) for *silentio* (“to silence”). Flor. omits “if it is a time for dining.” Other witnesses read “into one place” or “in one place” for “together”; Narb. reads “or another book,” while other witnesses read “or certainly something else.” Cassin., Conc., Hild., and certain others have the singular “if it is a day of fasting.” Narb. reads “all coming together in one to complete the Psalter.” For “when all have assembled together,” other witnesses read “when all have gathered together.” Lyr. reads “as they leave, the reading is not to be neglected.” Oxon. and Cassin. read “a severe punishment” for “a heavier punishment,” while Lyr. omits “heavier.” Other witnesses omit “and moderation.”

At all times the monks must devote themselves to silence, but especially during the hours of the night. Therefore, at all times, whether it is a day of fasting or a day on which they dine, if it is a time for dining, as soon as they have risen from supper they are all to sit together, and one is to read the Conferences or the Lives of the Fathers, or certainly something else that edifies those listening—not the Heptateuch or the Books of Kings, because at that hour it will not be useful for those of weak understanding to hear this Scripture. They are to be read at other hours. But if it is a day of fasting, after Vespers has been said, they are immediately, after a short interval, to proceed to the reading of the Conferences, as we have said; and after four or five leaves have been read, or as much as the hour permits, all are to assemble together during this period of reading. If anyone happens to be occupied with the task assigned to him, he is to come.

Therefore, when all have assembled together, they are to complete Compline; and when they leave Compline, no one is to have permission to speak again. If anyone is found violating this rule of silence, he is to be subject to a heavier punishment, except when the necessity of receiving guests arises or the abbot happens to command something. Even then, however, it is to be done with the utmost gravity and moderation, and in the most proper manner.

## Commentary

### “At all times the monks must devote themselves to silence, and so forth.”

This statement of Saint Benedict, which we explained above in chapter 6, determines nothing absolutely; it merely prepares and disposes the disciples for the next decree: “When they leave Compline, no one is to have permission to speak again.”

### “Therefore, at all times, whether it is a day of fasting or a day on which they dine.”

That is, whether it is a time of fasting or not, because those who fast do not dine; hence dinner and fasting are set in opposition.

### “If it is a time for dining, as soon as they have risen from supper.”

That is, when they sup—only during the Easter season, namely. For, as we said in the preceding chapter, throughout the whole summer the holy Father does not appear to have permitted supper.

Therefore, “as soon as they have risen from the table.” Hildemar says:

> “The word ‘as soon as’ does not indicate continuation; rather, because Saint Benedict did not want there to be a long interval, but only the very shortest between supper and the reading, he said ‘as soon as,’ as if he had said: ‘As soon as they have risen from supper, after the very briefest interval while the servers are eating, they are immediately to proceed to the reading.’”

Bernard of Cassino likewise says:

> “When he says ‘as soon as they have risen from supper,’ he does not mean that the reading should take place immediately after the first brothers have risen, but after the servers have risen, since everyone must assemble for that reading at Compline.”

John Craesbeeck follows the same opinion, as do the Cassinese, who write as follows in their ancient Declarations on this passage:

> “Understand ‘as soon as’ in a broad sense, because they generally delay for an hour or more, lest such a reading be wearisome after a recent supper.”

Haeftenus adds (Book IX, treatise 5, discussion 5):

> “Moreover, this allows the reader and the minister of the table meanwhile to eat supper and put everything back in its proper place. Finally, it allows some relaxation of mind to the religious, for it might be burdensome for them to proceed immediately from one reading, which they had heard at the table during supper, to another, and thus they might easily neglect both.”

Peter Boherius, however, takes the opposite position. After quoting the words of Bernard of Cassino cited above, he adds:

> “But this explanation does not please me; nor does waiting for the servers support it, even though the contrary practice is followed, at least among us.”

Certainly, if one may judge Saint Benedict’s intention from his following words, this short interval could be nothing other than no interval at all. Shortly afterward he adds:

> “But if it is a day of fasting, after Vespers has been said, they are immediately, after a short interval, to proceed to the reading.”

These words are entirely opposed to the preceding ones, especially since on fast days the short interval was unquestionably occupied by supper, which took place after Vespers when there were two meals.

Nor does the supper of the servers present an obstacle, since they can eat it while the reading of the Conferences is taking place. Indeed, Hildemar wants no interval to be observed when it happens that the brothers dine later than usual:

> “This must also be noted: if, during cloudy weather, Vespers is delayed—that is, if it takes place later than on other days—the abbot ought not to wait for or create an interval between supper and the reading as on other days, when things proceed at a moderate pace; rather, they should immediately proceed to the reading.”

The Cluniacs nevertheless observed some interval, as is clear from Udalricus, Book I, chapter 18. Nowadays, according to their new Declarations, the Cassinese sup after Compline. But this is not correct.

### “They are all to sit together.”

That is, together—or, as others read it, “in one place” or “in a single place.” We have discussed the place where the reading is to take place in Book I of *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 11.

### “And one is to read the Conferences.”

Those written by Cassian.

### “Or the Lives of the Fathers, or certainly something else that edifies those listening.”

Smaragdus explains this as referring

> “to the homilies of the Fathers, in which the edification of the listeners is fully written; or certainly to expositions of the Catholic books, which were composed by orthodox men, in whom holy doctrine sufficiently overflows for holy monks.”

Bernard of Cassino similarly says:

> “The homilies of the holy teachers, and other moral and edifying instructions.”

Nicholas of Fractura says:

> “The homilies of the holy Fathers, other moral works, the Book of the Dialogues of Blessed Gregory, the Lives of the Fathers, and other similar writings.”

Thus Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane, joined together a single book “from the homilies of the holy teachers that had been delivered for the exhortation of monks”; he ordered that it be read at every evening gathering.

At the end of the manuscript of the Rule of Saint Benedict in the codex of the monastery of Conques, the following is written:

> “These are the books that are read at the reading: Ephrem, the *Pastoral Rule*, the book *On the Edification of the Cloister*, the Lives of the Fathers, Gregory’s *Dialogues*, and the *Diadem of Monks*.”

### “But not the Heptateuch or the Books of Kings.”

“The Heptateuch,” says Saint Augustine (*On Christian Doctrine*, Book II, chapter 8),

> “contains the five books of Moses, the Book of Joshua, and Judges; for as regards the Book of Ruth, it seems rather to belong to the beginning of the Books of Kings.”

By saying “the Heptateuch or the Books of Kings,” Hildemar continues, Saint Benedict

> “means those books that are similar to them, that is, those written under allegorical figures.”

### “And after four or five leaves have been read, or as much as the hour permits.”

“Hour” means “a period of time.” The holy Father added this because, Boherius says, everything must be completed while it is still daylight.

How long such a period of time lasted I cannot easily say. The Cassinese spend a quarter of an hour on this reading. Haeftenus likewise judges that it did not formerly exceed this interval:

> “Indeed, more than eight hundred years ago this reading at the gathering seems already to have been shorter, so that it perhaps did not fill a quarter of an hour. This may be inferred from the *Diadem of Monks* of Abbot Smaragdus, whose chapters are not very long; he composed that little book for the purpose of reading one chapter from it at the gathering each day.”

Whether such a short period is sufficient for reading four or five leaves of writing that is neither especially small nor especially large, others may judge.

Moreover, exhortations and explanations were sometimes added to this reading, as we gather from these words of Hildemar:

> “At the time and place of the gathering no one ought to speak except the reader who is reading, the abbot who is explaining, or someone else to whom he has ordered the reading to be handed over.”

This custom originated from the Institutes of Saint Pachomius. For, as we read in his Life (no. 79, in the *Bollandists*, 14 May; see also no. 56):

> “From the beginning it was their custom, toward evening, after the manual work and supper had been completed, to sit down together to examine the Scriptures, free at that time from every other concern except that which related to their salvation.”

Whatever the case may be, the reading had to last at least until the reader, the servers, and the others who had been unable to dine at the first table, being occupied with various duties, could arrive. For the holy Father wanted everyone to be present at Compline; and so he adds:

As all were gathering together during this delay in the reading, if anyone happened to be occupied with an assigned duty, let him come when he could.] From this passage it is clear that, according to Saint Benedict’s intention, no one was to be excused from Compline. For this reason he wished the reading to precede it: meanwhile, those occupied with various duties could arrive, and, once assembled, all could complete it. “All,” he says, making no exception. “He excludes,” says Smaragdus, “neither the abbot, nor the provost, nor the deans, who at this hour are sometimes occupied elsewhere in the church with singing, drinking, stories, or councils; rather, he commands all to come at this hour of the collation, and commands all together to sing Compline.” Lanfrancus, however, derogates from this rule by writing the following in his Statutes [Col. 0673C] (ch. 16):

“While Compline is being sung, it is permitted for the prior and for those who remain from Compline with permission to speak about useful and necessary matters. Likewise, while the brothers are saying the canonical hour in church, no one may eat in the refectory, except at Compline alone. Then those who, being detained by some useful task, cannot finish it before that hour, and brothers who come from outside, may eat in the refectory. If those who begin eating before the collation, around the end of Compline, cannot conveniently finish their supper, they may rise from the table and go into the monastery for the blessing, and afterward return to the refectory to finish their supper.”

Much more observant were those whom I find addressed in chapter 9 of the customs of the monks directed to Augia:

“When they have come to the collation, all come together without exception: even the weak and the sick come if they are able to rise from bed. What, then, should be said of the rest? The reader, however, should continue reading until all, once assembled, have completed it” [Col. 0673D].

It is also found in the manuscripts of the Customs of Saint Benignus (ch. 46) that the sick had to come to the collation, although they were not permitted to enter the chapter-house. Instead, they remained inside the church of Saint Benedict—this was the chapel of the sick—near the door, listening to what was read.

Thus all, once assembled, should complete it.] “That is, they should say Compline, or complete this period of the collation,” says Boherius.

And when they leave Compline, no permission should again be given to anyone to speak.] When he says “when they leave Compline,” this must be understood of the liturgical Compline, not of the Compline of the collation: “No one, however, ought to speak after rising from the chapter,” says Hildemarus, “because another silence constrains him.” Together with Saint Benedict, Saint Pachomius prescribes this law of the nocturnal silence in his Rule, art. 53; Saint Aurelianus, ch. 35; Saint Isidore, ch. 14; Saint Fructuosus, ch. 17; the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, ch. 9 [Col. 0674A]; and finally the Rule of the Master, where it says (ch. 30):

“After Compline has been completed, they say this verse at the end: ‘Set a guard, O Lord, over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips.’ Immediately let them enter into silence, and let them settle in their beds, and let them be reduced to such silence that until Matins it may be thought that none of the brothers is there.”

But if anyone is found transgressing this rule of silence, let him be subject to a stricter punishment.] Saint Benedict does not explain what this punishment should be. In the Penitential Rules of an Unknown Author, preserved by Saint Basil, it is decreed (no. 12) that “if anyone is found privately conversing with someone at night, or changing the place where he sleeps without the permission of the one appointed for this purpose, let him be excommunicated.” Likewise (no. 15): “If anyone is found conversing in the evening after the Lord’s Prayer, let him be excommunicated.” Saint Benedict is also said to have imposed the same punishment on nuns who were excessively indulgent in speech. For other penalties for violating silence, see Haeftenus, book VI, tract. [Col. 0674B] 3, disputation 13.

Someone may ask when the nocturnal silence begins to bind: whether at the beginning or at the end of Compline, and again when it ends. Saint Benedict sufficiently clarifies the first point when he says: “When they leave Compline, no permission should again be given to anyone to speak.” Therefore it does not bind until Compline has been publicly completed and the assembly has been dismissed. “When they leave Compline,” he says. Nevertheless, there were some who extended the laws of nocturnal silence. The Parisians of Saint-Germain began silence with the last psalm of Compline. Saint Dunstan, in his Concordia, prescribes (ch. 6) that “at all times, from the striking of the bell for the evening assembly, silence is to be kept in the cloister until the chapter is finished.” The same is read in the ancient Customs that Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, had observed in the monasteries he founded: “Above all, from Vespers until the chapter which takes place after Prime, the strictest silence is to be kept.” From these last words the answer to the second question is clear, namely, that the obligation of nocturnal silence ceases after Prime [Col. 0674C]. This is further established by William of Malmesbury, who praises a monk named Lanzon. Although he was afflicted by such acute illnesses that he could never be at ease for even a moment, whether sitting, walking, lying down, or standing, “nevertheless he never spoke at night. When the brothers asked him to break silence, he did not consent, asking them not to diminish the chastity of his monastic profession: for never, after he had received the monastic habit, from leaving Compline until Prime of the following day had he spoken.”

Finally, they observed this law of nocturnal silence even outside the monastery, as is clear from the aforementioned Customs of Benedict of Aniane, where it is written (book II): “They must always observe nocturnal silence, whether they are inside or outside, until they say the verse in chapter.” The practice of this can be seen in John the Monk’s Life of Saint Odo, where he commends two disciples of that saint who, after being bound by barbarians and harassed for a long time, never violated the nocturnal silence—not even when the barbarian leader, wishing to test their constancy, attacked them and threatened them with death by brandishing a spear [Col. 0674D].

Except when the necessity of guests arises, or perhaps the abbot has ordered someone to do something.] Bernard of Cassino explains this passage as follows:

“It should be considered that during the nighttime there are three circumstances in which breaking silence may be permitted: imminent harm, pressing necessity, or an ensuing question from a superior. For example, if you suddenly saw a fire burning from which harm might result, you could rightly ask for water and afterward even shout. Necessity may be spiritual or bodily: for example, if you saw a brother suddenly suffering from illness, you could speak to him and assist him in his sickness; or if a sick man wished to confess, he could be heard and penance imposed upon the one confessing. There is also the questioning of a superior together with the addition of some command” [Col. 0675A].

Regarding this questioning by the abbot, Hildemarus perceptively notes that Saint Benedict did not simply say, “or the abbot has ordered someone to do something,” but added “perhaps,” because this must not be turned into a custom; rather, it should happen very rarely and, as it were, by chance. Moreover, as Boherius says, this applies “if the abbot has been moved by some necessary cause; otherwise he ought neither to grant anyone permission to speak at this hour nor speak himself.”

Nevertheless, even this must be done with the greatest gravity and moderation, and in the most becoming manner. Here one may observe with what vigilance and religious care nocturnal silence must be broken even when guests arrive, necessity arises, or the abbot gives an order. For, as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius very properly observe:

“You should not think it pointless that, by saying ‘gravity,’ he placed the highest degree, and by saying ‘honesty,’ he used the superlative degree, and that he placed moderation between the two” [Col. 0676A].

The Rule of the Master prescribes (ch. 30) that in such a case a brother “should speak softly into the ear whatever is necessary, so that another, a third person, may not hear him. Likewise, if a brother is compelled by some necessity to say something after sleep and before Matins, he should first softly say to himself the customary nocturnal verse, namely, ‘O Lord, open my lips, and my mouth shall proclaim your praise’; and he should say what is necessary . . . . But if outsiders arrive at the monastery after Compline has been fully completed, the resident brothers should refresh them by silent service, and answer them softly, because of the provision of the Rule. After washing their feet, they should afterward complete Compline for themselves in a low voice, and the travelers themselves should be assigned to sleep in guest beds.””

## CHAPTER XLIII. On Those Who Arrive Late for the Work of God or for the Table

[Note: [Col. 0675C] Another reading: “who arrive.”]

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675B] As soon as the signal for the hour of divine worship has been heard, let everyone run with the greatest haste, leaving whatever they may have in their hands; yet with gravity, so that frivolity may not find an occasion [Note: [Col. 0675C] Oxford: scurrilitatis (“of frivolity”)]. Therefore nothing is to be preferred to the work of God. But if anyone arrives late for the nocturnal vigils [Note: [Col. 0675C] Oxford and Cassino: “at the nocturnal vigils”; Conc.: “at night”; Florence: “nocturnal vigils”] after the Gloria of Psalm 94 [Note: [Col. 0675C] Oxford and Victor p. add: “Come, let us rejoice.”]—which for this reason we especially wish to be said drawn out and slowly—he is not to stand in his place in the choir, but is to stand last of all [Note: [Col. 0675C] Oxford omits “is to stand”], or in the place which the abbot has set apart for such negligent persons, so that he may be seen by him or by everyone, until, after the work of God has been completed, he performs penance through public satisfaction.

For this reason we have judged that they ought to stand last or apart: so that, being seen by everyone [Note: [Col. 0675C] Hildemarus: “by the people”], they may be corrected by the very shame they experience [Note: [Col. 0675C] Oxford: “may correct themselves”]. For if they remain outside the oratory [Col. 0675C] [Note: [Col. 0675C] Another reading: “if they remain outside the oratory”], there may perhaps be someone who lies down again and sleeps, or at least sits outside by himself, or calls out for conversation; and an opportunity may be given to the evil one [Note: [Col. 0675D] Other readings: “and an opportunity is given”; “and thus an opportunity is given”; “lest an opportunity be given.”] But let him enter inside [Note: [Col. 0675D] Oxford and Florence read “let them enter,” and then: “and thus afterward, let them lose . . . let them be corrected”], so that he may not lose everything and may correct himself for the remainder.

During the daytime hours, whoever does not arrive for the work of God after the verse and Gloria of the first psalm—which is said after the verse [Note: [Col. 0676C] Ebrul, Faron, and Lyra omit “which is said after the verse”]—is likewise to stand last, according to the rule stated above [Col. 0676B]. He must not presume to join the choir of those singing psalms until he has made satisfaction, unless perhaps the abbot grants him permission by his own authorization [Note: [Col. 0676C] Another reading: “remission”]; nevertheless, the culprit must thereby make satisfaction.

But as for one who does not arrive at the table [Note: [Col. 0676C] Another reading: “But at the hour of refreshment”] before the verse, so that all may say the verse and pray together and all may approach the table as one: if he has failed to come through his own negligence or fault [Note: [Col. 0676C] Oxford: “through a fault”], he is to be corrected for this [Note: [Col. 0676C] Other readings: “on account of this”; “for this fault”] up to the second occasion [Note: [Col. 0676C] Florence: “until the second occasion”; Cassino: “up to the second occasion”]. If he does not amend again, he is not to be permitted to participate in the common table [Note: [Col. 0676C] Narbonne: “to participate at the table”]. Separated from the company of all, he is to eat alone, with his portion of wine taken away [Note: [Col. 0676D] Another reading: “of wine”], until satisfaction and amendment [Note: [Col. 0676D] Hildemarus omits “and amendment”]. He is likewise to suffer who is not present for the verse said after the meal. No one is to presume to take any food or drink before the appointed hour or afterward [Note: [Col. 0676D] Another reading: “And let no one presume”]. Moreover, if something is offered to anyone by the prior and he refuses to accept it, at the hour when he desires what he previously refused—or anything else at all—he is to receive nothing [Note: [Col. 0676D] Oxford: sumere (“take”); another reading: accipiat (“receive”)] until suitable amendment.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0675]

[Col. 0675D] As soon as the signal for the hour of divine worship has been heard, let everyone run with the greatest haste, leaving whatever they may have in their hands.] The Rule of the Master elegantly explains this passage of Saint Benedict in these words (ch. 54):

“When the indicator struck in the oratory and showed that the divine hour had arrived, immediately those who were working should abandon their task, the craftsmen should lay down their tools, the scribes should not finish the letter, and every hand of the brothers should leave whatever it was doing [Col. 0676D]. Let the foot immediately hasten with gravity to the oratory, and the mind to God, so that they may arrive at the first prayer at once; and, like bees entering toward honey, let the swarm of brothers boil into the oratory, so that the place of the holy oratory, which had been silent, may immediately be filled with the shouting of psalms, and the silence of the holy place may migrate to the workshops and tasks they have left behind. But whenever the indicator has been struck in the oratory, let everyone who hears it, before running, immediately make the sign of the cross on his forehead, answering: ‘Thanks be to God.’”

This was the practice of all the ancient monks, as can be seen especially in Cassian, who discusses the matter as follows (book IV, ch. 12):

“Sitting in their cells and devoting equal attention to work and meditation, when they heard the sound of someone knocking on the door and striking the various cells—inviting them, that is, either to prayer or to some task—each one burst forth from his cell in eager competition. Thus the one who was carrying out the office of scribe did not dare finish the letter he had begun, but, at the very point when the sound of the knock reached his ears, sprang up with the utmost speed. He did not even allow as much delay as would be required to complete the form of the letter’s initial stroke; leaving the unfinished lines, he did not seek to gain the small advantage of completing his task, but hastened with all zeal and eagerness to fulfill the virtue of obedience. They preferred this not only to manual labor, reading, silence, and the quiet of the cell [Col. 0677B], but to every virtue, judging that everything had to be postponed to it and being content to suffer every loss, provided that they should not appear in any way to have violated this good.”

Rules of this sort, especially concerning obedience to the work of God, can be seen in the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins (ch. 10):

“She who comes late to the work of God or to her tasks after the signal has been given shall be subject to a fitting rebuke; but if, after being admonished a second and third time, she refuses to amend, she is to be separated from Communion or from the meal.”

In the Rule of Saint Aurelianus (ch. 30):

“When the signal has been sounded, let every task be set aside, and, like the wisest bees to the hive, strive to hurry forward with swift haste.”

In the Rule of Saint Isidore (ch. 7):

“When the signal has been given at the proper times for the canonical hours, the brothers shall hasten forward, and all shall come to the choir.”

Finally, in the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins (ch. 8):

“Whenever the signal sounds for the work of God at the daytime or nighttime hours, one must immediately rise with the greatest haste, as though the herald of a king were sounding, setting aside every task that was being held in one’s hands.”

The monks directed to Augia also observed the same discipline, as they themselves attest in their Chapters (ch. 1):

“Leaving everything, whatever may be held in their hands, all run with the greatest haste; no one dares to break this constitution, even if he is advanced in decrepit old age” [Col. 0677C].

Udalricus praises the same observance among the Cluniacs (book II, ch. 22):

“If he hears the signal for the canonical hour, and is in the cloister, he does not finish the very word he has in his mouth; instead he immediately falls silent and hastens to be present at the prayer.”

Finally, the monks of Saint Gall commend it in chapter 2, as does Gregory IX in his bull for Benedictine monks.

Nevertheless, the authors prudently warn that the text of the Holy Rule must be understood to mean that, when the signal is heard, whatever is in one’s hands should be left only if it can be abandoned without danger or serious loss. Thus if someone were serving the sick, ministering to guests, preparing the kitchen, or drawing off wine, he should not abandon his task and come immediately. The case is different with one who is writing a book, mending a shoe, or cultivating a garden. Although there have also been some who, for the sake of obedience, left the aforementioned tasks unfinished, and whose obedience we sometimes read was illuminated by miracles, we believe that God regarded their intention, not their action.

Therefore nothing is to be preferred to the work of God.] Those should take heed who excuse themselves from the work of God for trivial, vain, and empty matters. Although they ought to leave even unfinished tasks in order to hasten properly to the celebration of the work of God, they abandon the unfinished work of God itself, disturbing others as well by their wandering about.

How far removed from such people was Saint Liudgerus, bishop [in his Life, by an anonymous author, ch. 32, saec. IV Ben., p. 46; see ch. 33]. When he was summoned a third time by the emperor Charlemagne, and the messengers arrived while he was attending the divine offices [Col. 0678A], he gave them no other answer than that he would follow them as soon as the office had been completed. When, after the psalmody had ended, he went to the emperor, and the emperor asked why, despite being summoned by so many messengers, he had refused to come immediately, he replied:

“Because I considered that God was to be preferred to you, O king, and to all human beings. You yourself commanded this of me when you entrusted me with the episcopal care. Therefore, when summoned by your messengers, I judged it improper to interrupt the service of the Almighty. But as soon as the divine service was completed, I came more ready to obey the king’s command.”

The excellent emperor revered this answer and said: “Give thanks, bishop, because I now find you to be as I formerly judged you. Some people have maliciously interpreted your good deeds to me; henceforth I shall hold them in less favor.”

The most devout Bernard, abbot of Tiron, had the same mind. As Geoffrey writes in his Life, no. 105 (Bollandists, April 14), “no secular matter, nor any person of the greatest power—even though such matters frequently disturbed him throughout his life—took away from him the canonical hours of either day or night; nor did any bodily hardship make him slower, except for that one by which, blessed, he completed his blessed course” [Col. 0678B].

I do not repeat here what I wrote in book V of Ancient Monastic Rites concerning brothers traveling on a journey: even after mounting a horse, if, on hearing the signal for the work of God, they had not yet carried their foot outside the monastery, they immediately dismounted and hurried with the others to the oratory. Nor do I repeat what concerns the shaving of the brothers, which they left unfinished at the signal for the divine office so that they could assemble in church, although they would by no means join the choir of those singing psalms if anything unsightly appeared on the head that might offend the eyes of those standing nearby.

To this should be referred what is read in the manuscript Rule of an Unknown Author (ch. 8, in the manuscript of the library of the Queen of Sweden):

“For according to the authority of the holy Catholic Fathers, at the time of prayer one must cease from conversation with arriving guests.”

These words recall an ancient and praiseworthy custom of our order: observing the strictest silence in every part of the monastery during the time of the divine office. It is mentioned in the manuscripts of the Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon; in the Rule of the Master [579], ch. 54; in the Statutes of Lanfrancus, ch. 16; and in the book of Cistercian Usages, ch. 120.

But if anyone arrives at the nocturnal vigils, etc., he is not to stand in his place in the choir, but last of all, or in the place which the abbot has set apart for such negligent persons.] Hildemarus explains this passage as follows:

“When he says, ‘he is not to stand in his place in the choir, but last of all, or in the place, etc.,’ this means that if such a brother normally stands in a higher place, he must stand at the end. But if he is already last, or in the middle or farther back, he must stand apart.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius attribute the same meaning to Saint Benedict. Later, however, Hildemarus teaches that this passage can be understood in three ways:

“First, that one who comes late to the work of God, if he is among the first, should stand last of all; but if he is already last, in the place of the negligent. Second, that if the one who comes late can assist the choir, he should stand last; otherwise, apart. Third, that whoever has committed the greater negligence should stand apart, while the one who has committed the lesser should stand in the last place.”

Nevertheless, he adds: “In France, none of them stands at the end, but apart.” And he had earlier stated: “In our monastery, however, all stand apart.”

The question arises: what is the place that Saint Benedict wished the abbot to establish apart? Since he defined nothing in this matter but left everything to the abbot’s discretion, it will be sufficient to report here the various customs of different monasteries.

Thus, in the manuscripts of the monastery of Farfa, the following is written:

“If a brother comes after the Gloria of the first psalm, let him go before the altar to the steps, kneel there, then immediately rise and wait until the prior absolves him. After he has been absolved, let him turn around in front and behind, and come into the choir to his place, and again ask pardon. When he rises, all the brothers should bow. If he has remained outside because of some slight illness and has not arrived by the Gloria of the first psalm, let him enter the choir as stated above. After he has been absolved, however, let him go outside, ask pardon on his knees, and do what his illness permits. Likewise, if a brother comes to the hour after the Gloria of the first psalm, or arrives at any other point, up to the Kyrie eleison he should enter inside in this manner, so that he may not lose everything; and he should go to the appointed place until he is absolved. But if he remains for the entire hour, and the brothers kneel on the benches, let him himself do so on the steps; when the hour has been completed, let him depart without an order.”

The same is read in the manuscripts of the Customs of the monastery of Saint Paul in Rome, and Udalricus explains it more clearly in this way (book II, ch. 6):

“If it should ever happen that he does not arrive before the Gloria of Psalm 94, or before the Gloria of the first psalm at any hour, he enters the choir and comes to the altar step; there he honorably and slowly asks pardon on his hands and knees. He extends the top of his froccus slightly [Col. 0679B], so that he can place his hands upon it; then, rising, he bows more deeply toward the altar. From that point he does not move until the hour has ended. While the others bow, he bows only toward the altar. But if it seems good to the lord abbot, he sends one of the brothers to him so that he may withdraw. At the gesture of the one signaling with his hand, he bows slightly, then, having made a bow forward and backward, withdraws to his station, where, again asking pardon as before, he bows toward the community, and the community bows toward him.”

Among the Cistercians, the place assigned to the negligent was the steps of the presbytery, as Julianus Parisius teaches in his book On the First Way of Life of the Cistercians (part II, ch. 6, section 1), and as is clear from the book of Cistercian Usages, ch. 75.

Bernard of Cassino speaks as follows about the Cassinese:

“Thus he is to stand not with the brothers at their seats, but in the middle of the choir, as has been established for certain negligent persons in the Cassinese choir. There is a porphyry disk of precious stone there, distinguished among various other marbles; the place where he stands is visible to everyone, including the abbot. This is what it means to stand apart, and such satisfaction is called public.”

But now among the Cassinese, one who comes late kneels; after a signal has been given by the abbot, he rises, excuses himself, or, without offering an excuse, asks for the last place.

The Constitutions of the Celestines define the matter as follows:

“When the monks come late to the choir, let them turn toward the altar and kneel; silently and humbly, with bowed head, let them repent of their tardiness. Let them continue in this penitence until it seems to the presiding authority that they have made satisfaction in proportion to their fault.”

So that he may be seen by him or by everyone.] Here the particle “or” is used coordinately, in the sense of “and.” In this Saint Benedict differs from the ancient monks, who did not admit those who arrived late for the work of God into the oratory, as is clear from these words of Cassian (book III, ch. 7):

“But he who does not arrive at prayer in the third, sixth, or ninth hour before the psalm has been completed may no longer dare to enter the oratory or mingle with those singing psalms. Instead, he waits standing outside for the dismissal of the congregation, until everyone has gone out; then, having cast himself to the ground in penitence, he obtains pardon for his negligence or tardiness, knowing that he cannot otherwise expiate the guilt of his laziness. He is not even to be admitted to the solemnity that will follow after three hours unless, for his present negligence, he hastens immediately to make satisfaction with true humility.

“But in the nocturnal assemblies, a delay is granted to the latecomer until the second psalm, provided only that, before that psalm has ended and the brothers prostrate themselves in prayer, he hastens to insert and mingle himself with the congregation. Without doubt he is to be subjected to the rebuke and penance mentioned above if he is even slightly late beyond the appointed period of delay.”

Until the work of God has been completed and he has made satisfaction publicly.] Boherius explains this passage as follows:

“This text seems to imply that, after the work of God has been completed, the guilty brother must perform some public satisfaction in addition to what was stated above. If this is so, I believe that it will be the prostration mentioned below in the next chapter. Bernard, however, seems to think in the preceding gloss that this public satisfaction is the separation from the common choir. Nicholas, nevertheless, says that during the final prayer of this office the guilty brother ought to lie prostrate in the middle of the said pavement until the community has left the oratory. Cassianus says the same, as Smaragdus notes here, and I believe this more likely. In my own monastery, however, senior brothers who arrive late at the oratory, or who commit some fault there, customarily kneel immediately in that place; they are considered to have made satisfaction by this. Others are corrected in chapter by rebukes or lashes.”

Other Fathers of the monks established other penalties for those arriving late for the work of God. In the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers (ch. 6), it is decreed that “when the signal has been given for the hour of prayer, if anyone is not immediately ready, setting aside every task he is doing—for nothing is to be preferred to prayer—he is to be shut out, to his shame.” In the Third Rule (ch. 6), that “he is to be corrected by the abbot or provost, and unless he asks pardon while prostrate, he is to be excommunicated.” In the Rule of Saint Macarius (ch. 14), that “he is to be shut outside, so that he may be ashamed.” In the Rule of Saint Pachomius (ch. 2), that “when the trumpet sounds during the day for the assembly, whoever arrives late by one prayer is to be rebuked according to the order of the superior’s correction, and is to stand in the place of rebuke. At night, because somewhat more allowance is made for bodily weakness, whoever arrives after three prayers is to be corrected in the same order, both at the assembly and at the place of eating.”

The superior order was as follows (ch. 1):

“He shall loosen his belt and, bowing his neck, with his hands lowered toward the ground, shall stand before the altar, and shall be rebuked by the head of the monastery. He shall do the same in the assembly of the brothers when they have gathered together for eating.”

In the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Monks (ch. 11), it is prescribed that “if he comes late, he is immediately to receive the rod on his hands.” In the Rule for Virgins (ch. 10), that, after being admonished a second and third time, she “is to be separated from Communion or from the meal.” In the Tarnatensian Rule (ch. 5), that “having been excluded for the guilt of so great a crime, he is to be put to shame.” In the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (ch. 18), that “whoever does not arrive at the daytime prayers after the first psalm is not to dare to enter the oratory with the others, but is to be assigned to penance. The same punishment is to be borne by one who comes late to the nocturnal prayers until the third psalm, or who attempts to join the choir after the three stated psalms.”

In the Rule of the Master (ch. 73), it is prescribed that:

“A brother who has missed the first prayer or psalm at the nocturnal Matins and at the lamps is to be thrown out of the oratory; the abbot is to warn him outside, sternly and with terror, to correct himself. If he has missed the second prayer or psalm, he is to be severely corrected there in the oratory, in the presence of the congregation, after the psalm has been completed. But if he enters after the third prayer or psalm, he is immediately to be cast out of the oratory excommunicated, together with his provosts [Col. 0680D], and he is not to return to ask pardon until he has carried out an act of humble satisfaction, in equal measure, before the threshold of the oratory. But this, as we said in the preceding title, applies within a distance of fifty paces.
