“At Prime, Terce, Sext, and None, whoever, after the signal has been struck, does not hurry to the first prayer and the first psalm is to be severely corrected in the oratory in the presence of everyone. But whoever arrives after the second prayer or the second psalm is to leave outside at once, already excommunicated, together with his provosts” [582].

Finally, in the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, she is to make satisfaction in the same way prescribed in the Rule of Saint Benedict, and in addition (ch. 8):

“When the others, after completing the office, go outside, she, having been placed in the church because of her tardiness, is to sing twelve psalms beyond the sequence of the course. But if she has entirely missed her course, especially at the nocturnal hours, when no other task is an impediment, she is to be condemned to a superposition, that is, an additional fast.”

[Col. 0681A] Moreover, this rite prescribed by Saint Benedict and the other Holy Fathers passed from the monks to the canons as well. For them, I find the following canon enacted at the Council of Aachen in the year 816 (canon 131):

“Whoever comes sluggishly or late to Matins or to the performance of any other divine office ought not to stand with the others in the choir, but last of all, so that he may learn to be ashamed, in the place appointed by the prelates for such negligent persons. He must not presume to remain outside, lest he devote himself to idleness and conversation and be entirely alienated from the praises of God.”

Boherius writes the following also about the canons of the cathedral church of Paris:

“And know that I saw this observed by the canons of Saint Mary of Paris. If they came late to the hours, they did not dare to ascend into the greater choir, but placed themselves in the lower one.”

What is more, something similar seems to have been observed in the court of the supreme pontiff, as the eyewitness Julius Nigronus affirms (On the Fifteenth Common Rule of the Society of Jesus, [Col. 0681B] no. 27):

“I myself saw in Rome cardinals who had arrived in the choir after the pontifical Mass had begun. Having shown reverence to the cross and to the pope, they stood upright in the middle of the choir until the pontiff granted permission for them to take their seats.”

But during the daytime hours, etc. Unless perhaps the abbot has granted permission by his own authorization; nevertheless, the culprit must thereby make satisfaction.] Boherius comments on this passage:

“This means: although the guilty person has been given permission to ascend into the choir of those singing psalms, nevertheless, after the course of the hour has been completed, he is to prostrate himself before everyone at the feet of the abbot or prior, accusing himself of his negligence. If the abbot judges that he has made satisfaction, he will dismiss him with a blessing. Otherwise, he will order him to ask pardon there or again the next day, or repeatedly, in the manner described, or to fulfill some other penance.

“But where is this satisfaction or prostration to take place according to the Rule? In the choir where he committed the offense, as is clearly evident below concerning those who commit a fault in the oratory, and in the following chapter. Or perhaps before the door of the oratory, as Fructuosus and Cassianus mentioned above hold. But today among us such prostrations and satisfactions take place in chapter” [Col. 0681C].

As for one who does not arrive at the table before the verse, etc. He is not to be permitted to participate in the common table, but, separated from the company of all, he is to eat alone.] Whether outside or inside the common refectory after the brothers’ meal, or in the same refectory while the brothers are also eating, he is to eat in a separate place visible to everyone, so that such a negligent person may be covered with the blush of greater shame. This last interpretation, rejecting the others, is followed by the commentators Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius in both commentaries.

Hildemarus’s words are these:

“When it says that, separated from the company, he is to eat alone, some understand this to mean that he should eat after the brothers’ meal, either with the servers or alone. But this interpretation is not sound. Rather, just as it says concerning the oratory that he is to stand apart for the sake of shame, so that he may amend, it should be understood here for the sake of amendment: he should sit alone at another table, separated from the other tables, while the others are eating. For when it says ‘alone and separated,’ this is not to be understood as meaning that he eats after the others have eaten, but that, while the others are eating, he eats separately and does not drink wine. For in France, in my monastery, I have seen such a negligent brother eating in the middle of the refectory while the brothers were eating” [Col. 0681D].

With his portion of wine taken away.] Or of any other liquid used in regions where the vine does not grow.

Up to satisfaction and correction.] Hildemar explains this as follows: “After they have eaten and the brothers now wish to leave, he ought to ask the abbot for pardon before the brothers. If he has done this at Sext, he ought not to do it again at Vespers.” And Bernard of Cassino: “When he says ‘until satisfaction and correction,’ he means that satisfaction and correction whereby, prostrate, he ought to bend his knees before the brothers—and this according to Paul the Deacon. [Col. 0682A] Nevertheless, it seems to me that this satisfaction ought to be as I mentioned earlier, by asking pardon from the abbot. Correction occurs when he amends himself for this negligence, so that he may truly be presumed corrected.” Thus far Saint Benedict on those who come late to table. But what do the other Fathers of the monks say about the same matter?

Saint Pachomius (Article 12): “If anyone,” he says, “comes late to eat, except by command of the superior, he shall likewise do penance and return fasting to his dwelling.”

When Saint Basil was asked (in Rufinus’s translation, chapter 52), “If it is necessary for everyone to assemble at the hour of dinner, how shall we deal with one who remains behind and comes after dinner?” he replies: “If he remained outside the common order because of necessity, whether of place or of work, the one in charge shall approve and pardon him. But if, although he could have arrived, he failed to do so, let him confess the fault of his negligence [Col. 0682B] and remain without food until the hour at which the community assembles for food on the following day.” And in the Penitentials of an unknown author preserved by the same Basil (no. 23): “If anyone is absent from the tables without stating a reason, let him remain fasting.”

Saint Columbanus (in the Penitential): “If anyone does not come to the prayer over the table and after the meal, let him sing twelve psalms.”

Saint Isidore (chapter 10): “At the time of the meal, when the signal has been given, let all assemble together; but whoever comes late to table shall either do penance or return fasting to his work or bed.”

Likewise Saint Fructuosus (chapter 18): “Whoever comes late to table shall be forbidden food.”

Finally, the Master (chapter 73): “Those who were not present for the antiphon or the preceding verse at table shall eat and drink apart, without being marked with the sign [of the cross], and without receiving or giving the blessing, and without anyone’s speech, until they rise. And rightly should one who did not speak with God before the meal [Col. 0682C] refresh himself without any human speech.”

Likewise, let the one who was not present for the verse that is said after the meal suffer the same punishment.] The Penitentials of an unknown author preserved by Saint Basil prescribe (no. 30) that “if anyone rises from table against the will of the archimandrite, he shall be made to remain at prayer until the time of the lamps.” And the Rule of the Master (chapter 73): “Whoever was not present at the later table to give thanks to God after the meal shall receive in the next meal, in seclusion, the same punishment as one who did not speak with God before the meal.”

I think that by “verse” we should understand all the prayers that we recite after the meal in thanksgiving, although Hildemar understands Saint Benedict to mean only the verse that is said in the refectory after the meal has ended. For, he says, “that verse which is said in church, and the verse ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ are not prescribed by the Rule, since the Rule does not say that they are to be said; they are a custom of the monks.”

From this testimony of Hildemar it is clear that it was an ancient custom of the monks [Col. 0682D] and especially of the Benedictines, to offer thanksgiving to God in church after dinner and supper. This is further confirmed by chapter 5 of the Rule of Saint Fructuosus; chapter 3 of the manuscript Rule of an unknown author; chapter 11 of the *Order of Monastic Conduct*; chapter 22 of the Monks of Saint Gall; Ekkehard, *On the Affairs of Saint Gall*, book I, chapter 11; Tortarius, *Miracles of Saint Benedict*, book, chapter 44; Theodoricus, *Miracles of Saint Celsus*, no. 5, in the Bollandists, 23 February; *Miracles of Saint Trudpert*, no. 3; *Life of Saint Hugh of Autun, the Monk*, no. 25; *Miracles of Saint Dunstan*, no. 12; and chapter 76 of the *Book of Cistercian Usages*.

And let no one presume to take any food or drink before or after the appointed hour.] This was the general practice of all the ancient monks, as can be seen both in Cassian and in all their Rules. Cassian says (book IV, chapter 18): “Before or after they have taken their regular [Col. 0683A] common meal, the strictest care is observed that no one presume to indulge his mouth with any food or drink outside the table. Thus, when they walk through gardens and orchards, and apples hanging everywhere from the trees not only present themselves gently and invitingly to the breasts of those passing by but also, scattered on the ground, offer themselves to be trampled underfoot, and, lying ready to be gathered, can easily entice observers to consent to their desire, while their opportunity and abundance provoke even the strictest and most abstinent to long for them: it is regarded as sacrilege not only to taste any of these things, but even to touch them with the hand, unless they are publicly presented to all who are eating together and are openly distributed for consumption by the steward through the service of the brothers.”

Saint Pachomius likewise (Article 4): “No one shall dare to eat grapes or ears of grain that are still unripe, contrary to the order of discipline; and, in general, no one shall eat separately anything from the [Col. 0683B] field or orchard before the Father has presented it to all the brothers.”

Saint Basil (*Sermon on the Renunciation of Possessions*): “Beware lest you incur the sin of clandestine eating.” And elsewhere (*Long Rules*, chapter 15), he orders anyone “who has taken food at an improper time” to remain fasting for a considerable part of the day.

Saint Augustine (chapter 5): “When someone cannot fast, nevertheless let him not take any food outside the hour of dinner, except when he is ill.”

The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chapter 17): “Let no one presume beyond the established custom, whether in food or drink, except with the permission of the prior, who has the authority to regulate and supervise this.”

Both Rules of Saint Aurelian, for monks and for virgins (chapters 52 and 36): “Outside the common table, no one may taste any food or drink, except the sick and those ages that still require nourishment.”

[Col. 0683C] The Rule of Tarnat (chapter 9): “They shall not presume to drink even water before the regular meal.” And again (chapter 16): “If a brother weakened by abstinence is unable to endure the fasts he has undertaken, he should judge it improper to take anything before the hour of dinner has passed. But those who are detained by illness and cannot observe the appointed hours shall be lawfully permitted to take what they can.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 10): “Let no one be polluted by the furtive contamination of eating, or by an immodest or private appetite outside the common table; for whoever tastes anything secretly or [Col. 0684A] outside the ordinary table shall be subject to the sentence of excommunication. Before the time of the meal no one shall dare to eat, except one who is ill; for whoever anticipates the time of eating shall be subject to the subsequent penalties of abstinence.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 5): “Let no monk presume to break his fast, nor, before he eats in common with the others or after they have eaten, dare to taste or touch anything belonging to food or drink, or presume secretly to hide or possess anything privately.”

Finally, the Rule of a Certain Author for Monks (chapter 11): “Neither before nor after the table that is commonly set for the brothers’ supper may anything be allowed to the mouth, unless illness, difference of age, or some bodily condition has compelled it.”

It is astonishing how religiously Abbot Saint Benedict of Aniane wished this provision of the Benedictine Rule to be observed. For “although that region was scorched by the heat of the sun, and the fiery vapor, issuing as though [Col. 0684B] from a furnace, burned rather than warmed, he scarcely allowed his men, who were suffering from excessive heat, a drink of water before the hour of the meal” (*Life of Saint Benedict*, no. 32, *Benedictine Century* IV). Exhausted by labor and scorched by the heat, they desired cold water rather than wine; nor could anyone murmur against him, since he suffered the same things.

Nor should I cease to wonder at this as well, when I consider these words of Saint Basil (*Sermon on the Renunciation of Possessions*): “I have often observed many people who, although afflicted with vices of every other kind, afterward returned to health; but of those who were possessed by this disease—to take pleasure in eating secretly or to allow themselves to be driven by gluttony—I have never seen one who recovered.”

But if something is offered to someone by the prior and he refuses to accept it, let him receive neither what he first refused nor anything else at all until a fitting correction.] Smaragdus comments on this passage: “This is a hyperbaton, whose meaning is to be understood in a differently arranged order, as follows: If something is offered to someone by the prior [Col. 0684C] and he refuses to accept it, then, at the hour when he wishes to accept it—this is understood—let him receive either what he previously refused or nothing else at all.” Peter the Deacon, whom Bernard cites, understands Saint Benedict in the same way. But certain French versions oppose this interpretation, as does Saint Basil, from whom the holy Father may have taken this provision. When Basil was asked (*Short Rules*, question 134), “If someone, in anger, refuses to take things necessary for use,” he replied: “Such a person is not even worthy to receive them when he asks, until the superior judges that this fault, or rather these faults, have been healed in him.”

## CHAPTER XLIV. How Those Who Are Excommunicated Are to Make Satisfaction

[Col. 0683]

[Col. 0683D] Whoever is excommunicated from the oratory and from the table for more serious offenses [Note: Hildemar, Dunstan, and Boherius in the second commentary read “for a serious offense.”], at the hour when the Work of God is celebrated in the oratory [Note: Another reading: “is solemnly celebrated.”], shall lie prostrate before the doors of the oratory, saying nothing, except that, with his head placed on the ground, he shall lie stretched face downward [Note: Hildemar, with some witnesses, reads “prostrate face downward.” Comp. reads “and stretched face downward.” Faron, Ebrul, Conch, and Lyra read “face downward.”] at the feet of all who leave the oratory. He shall do this until the abbot judges that satisfaction has been made. When he comes at the abbot’s command, let him throw himself at the feet of the abbot and then at the feet of all the brothers, so that they may pray for him.

Then, if the abbot orders it, he shall be received into the choir or into the rank [Note: Another reading: “into the rank,” without “into”] that the abbot determines. But he shall not presume to introduce a psalm, a reading, or anything else in the oratory unless the abbot again orders him to do so. At all the hours, while the Work of God is being completed [Note: Cassino and Florus read “while the Work of God is being fully completed.”], he shall throw himself on the ground in the place where he stands [Note: Another reading: “in the place where he stands”]; and thus he shall make satisfaction [Col. 0685A] until the abbot orders him to cease this satisfaction [Note: Another reading: “until he orders him again.”]. Those who are excommunicated from the table alone for lighter offenses shall make satisfaction in the oratory; they shall carry this out until the abbot’s command [Note: Cassino: “and they shall carry this out for so long”], until he blesses them and says: “It is enough.”

## COMMENTARY

Whoever is excommunicated from the oratory and from the table for a more serious offense shall lie prostrate before the doors of the oratory at the hour when the Work of God is celebrated in the oratory.] “Before the doors,” he says, “of the oratory—not inside the oratory itself; for,” says Bernard of Cassino, “he ought not to enter inside until he has been released from the bond of excommunication.” This confirms the opinion of those who think that in chapter 25 Saint Benedict was speaking of ecclesiastical excommunication.

The ancient monks of Mesopotamia had imposed an almost similar punishment on the negligent and those who came late to the Work of God. For if anyone incurred this fault, then, according to Cassian (book III, chapter 7), “he did not dare to enter the oratory or join himself to those singing psalms; instead, he stood outside the doors and awaited the dismissal of the congregation, until, after everyone had gone out, he obtained pardon for his negligence or lateness by performing penance with his head bowed to the ground.”

Saint Benedict did not receive this form of penance solely from the ancient monks, however, but also from the first Christians, among whom it was customary for penitents to lie or stand before the doors of the church in the grief of penance, according to the differing practice of the churches. [Col. 0685B] On this subject, see Menardus’s notes on the *Concordance of the Rules*, chapter 33, section 1.

Saying nothing.] “Except when questioned by the abbot,” says Boherius. “The abbot sometimes customarily says to such a prostrate man: ‘Brother, what do you say?’ And he replies by accusing himself: ‘Father, my fault is great.’ And if he then intends to question him further, he says to him: ‘Rise, brother.’ Then the brother, standing there at his feet, with his head uncovered and his face lowered toward the ground, answers him humbly.”

Except with his head placed on the ground.] “Because, after the deed of sin, everyone ought to blush, and after confession, for the crimes committed, to lower his shameful forehead prostrate upon the ground, for having perpetrated a deed worthy of disgrace,” Boherius again says.

And, lying stretched face downward, let him throw himself beneath the feet of all who leave the oratory [Col. 0685C].] “So that he who raised himself above others through pride may condemn himself, through humility, to be trampled beneath everyone’s feet,” says Bernard of Cassino. “Those who leave should say to him silently: ‘May God have mercy on you,’” according to the Statutes of Lanfranc, chapter 17.

And let him do this until the abbot judges that satisfaction has been made.] Then, after summoning the brothers to chapter, let him absolve him with their counsel. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius understand the passage in this way.

“After Sext or None,” says Hildemar, “when the abbot leaves with the congregation, he ought to summon the congregation, with that brother absent, and say: ‘It is just and reasonable that this brother should cease his satisfaction.’ [Col. 0685D] If they say, ‘It is just, because it is right that he should cease,’ he ought to summon him before the brothers and spare him.”

Bernard of Cassino says: “After displaying the humility mentioned above, that man ought to be summoned to chapter, and there, after seeking the counsel of the brothers, the abbot shall absolve him and judge that he may be received into the oratory. He himself, however, ought to be excluded from the chapter when the abbot asks for counsel about what should be done; and this is what the Father says: ‘Until the abbot judges that satisfaction has been made.’”

Nicholas of Fractura likewise says: “He is absolved by the abbot in chapter with the counsel of the brothers. He ought, however, to stand outside the chapter while the abbot deliberates with the brothers, so that the brothers may express their will about his satisfaction more freely.” Udalricus confirms the same in book III, chapter 3.

But according to the Statutes of Lanfranc, the consent of the brothers was not required for absolving an excommunicated person. Rather, “on the day when, at the brothers’ prayers, [Col. 0686A] the abbot had decided to extend mercy to him,” he absolved him in the manner we shall now relate.

When he comes at the abbot’s command, let him throw himself at the feet of the abbot, and then at the feet of all the brothers, so that they may pray for him.] “Thus he should make a supplication to the ground before the abbot; then he should make the regular and customary supplication before and behind, and say quietly, ‘Pray for me, brothers’; and each brother should answer in a subdued voice, ‘May God spare you,’” as Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius relate.

Lanfranc beautifully describes this rite in the Statutes (chapter 17), and it is not burdensome to quote his words here:

“On the day when, at the prayers of the brothers, the abbot decides to extend mercy to him, let him come into chapter in the manner stated above, confess his fault prostrate, promise amendment, and ask for mercy. Ordered to rise, let him frequently prostrate himself and say the same or similar words, ceasing when the abbot says to him, ‘It is enough.’ [Col. 0686B] He shall afterward be ordered to strip and undergo the judgment of corporal discipline. When this has been done, the abbot shall say to him: ‘Moved by the prayers of our brothers, by your patience and humility, and by your promise of amendment, I extend this mercy to you: henceforth you shall be with the brothers in the refectory, eating in the place we designate for you, and you shall no longer undergo corporal discipline for this fault. In all other matters, to demonstrate your humility and patience further, conduct yourself like a brother who is ordered to do penance for a light fault, except that, when the Kyrie eleison begins, you shall not prostrate yourself at the step; rather, when the regular hour has been completed, you shall make humble satisfaction in the place where you stand, with your knees bent toward the ground, like one who has made a mistake in a psalm, as blessed Benedict prescribes.’

“Having heard this, let that brother go to the feet of the abbot; then, returning to the place where he stood, let him make three genuflections—with one before him, one to the right, and one to the left—with all devotion, giving thanks to the brothers because they have prayed for him and humbly asking them [Col. 0686C] to continue to pray for him. Afterward, let the abbot designate the place where he is to be, and, at his command, let him go to sit.”

And then, if the abbot orders it, let him be received into the choir or into the rank that the abbot determines.] What Saint Benedict says here, “or into the rank,” Richard of Saint Angelo understands to mean “in the place of the first or second watch, or in the last places, as pleases the abbot, as will be said below; or in the diaconate, subdiaconate, or minor orders.”

I would understand it more correctly, with Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, as referring to the rank that the brothers occupy among themselves: that the brother should stand in the last place, or at most in an intermediate one. Thus Udalricus says (book III, chapter 3): “He is ordered to sit last and to be last of all in every place.”

But he shall not presume to introduce a psalm, antiphon, or anything else in the oratory.] For Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, “to introduce” here has the same meaning as “to begin.” Bernard says: “Such a man should never, except together with the others, read a lesson or sing a responsory or antiphon. [Col. 0686D] I also say that he should not celebrate a private Mass, because he does not say it only in the choir but says it in the oratory.”

Udalricus adds (book III, chapter 3): “Meanwhile, he does not communicate, does not come forward for the kiss of peace, does not kiss the Gospel book in church, is not assigned a reading, and is not assigned a song as the others are.”

Menardus and Charles Cointius, however, think that Saint Benedict used “to introduce” here not in the sense of “to begin,” but in the sense of “to recite,” whether this is done by singing or by reading.

And at all the hours, while the Work of God is being completed, let him throw himself on the ground in the place where he stands.] “While the Work [Col. 0687A] of God is being completed,” he says, that is, toward the end of the hours. For, says Boherius, “after the others have risen, while ‘Let us bless the Lord’ is being said, he ought to throw himself on the ground—that is, to lie face downward.” And Udalricus (book III, chapter 3): “After each hour has ended, he asks pardon on his knees in this way, but without turning toward the altar on that account.”

And thus let him make satisfaction until the abbot orders him to cease this satisfaction.] Thus far Saint Benedict on the satisfaction of those excommunicated for more serious offenses. It may perhaps not be unwelcome to readers, however, to learn the practice of this chapter from the manuscript customs of Saint Benignus.

From the manuscript Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon, chapter 32.

Whoever has committed an offense worthy of a serious fault, if he comes while the lord abbot is absent, shall not come into his presence until the abbot himself orders it. Then he is stripped outside the chapter and comes in the same manner as the one to whom, within chapter, it is ordered [Col. 0687B] to go and strip. For if someone of this kind is in chapter itself, when he hears himself accused by the lord abbot, he rises and asks pardon. After he has asked it, he is ordered: “Go, strip, and remove your shoes, and return as is customary.” The chamberlain is ordered to leave with him.

Then, stripped naked down to the belt, barefoot, holding a bundle of rods in his right hand and his well-folded cowl in his left, he returns to chapter. Immediately he places the cowl on his left and the rods beside him on his right, and asks pardon in the middle. When the abbot says, “What do you say?” and he replies, “My fault,” and the abbot again says, “Rise,” he sits on the ground, having taken up his cowl again and placed it over his knees, with his arms laid upon it.

After this, the lord abbot orders whomever he wishes to rise and beat him with the rods he brought. When the lord abbot has given him whatever judgment seems appropriate, he orders him to rise and put on his cowl, and he is told: “Go, put on your clothes and return.”

After he has dressed and returned, he asks pardon [Col. 0687C] again. When he is told to rise, this word is added: “Brother, go into serious fault.” Having heard this, he bows deeply, immediately puts on his cap, humbly leaves chapter, and goes to the place assigned to this excommunication.

There he remains; there he sleeps; he eats without a tablecloth, at the time and with the food prescribed by the abbot. When he hears the first signal for each hour, he waits for the second, when everyone has entered the monastery. He must then stand outside with his head covered, beside the door on the left of those entering, and likewise at Matins, until the congregation begins the Kyrie. Then, removing his cap but not entirely, he prostrates himself on the ground and remains there until the hour is finished and the customary psalms have been sung; and, if the brothers are to leave, until the brothers have been able to leave, except at the hour after which conversation takes place in the cloister.

When they have entered chapter, he likewise prostrates himself and afterward withdraws to the aforementioned little dwelling. At both Masses he remains in the corner of the chapterhouse adjoining the church; he may nevertheless sit if he wishes.

Meanwhile, while he is in this condition, [Col. 0687D] no one speaks to him—not even the one who serves him—and the food given to him is not blessed. Yet, at the abbot’s direction, he is deliberately comforted by two or three elders, who exhort him to accept gratefully whatever temporal correction has been inflicted upon him, so that he may be reconciled to divine mercy.

Those elders, or others who are among the officials closest to the abbot—for this is their responsibility—when they see that the time is suitable and appropriate, whether on their own initiative or at the abbot’s direction, ask for pardon on his behalf in chapter before the abbot, especially if they have truly observed and can testify that, because of his guilt, he has a contrite spirit and a broken and humbled heart.

If the abbot then wishes to show him mercy, he orders the senior or junior prior to bring him. As soon as he has been brought in the same manner as before, with his cowl and rods placed down, he asks pardon; then, sitting and again taking up his cowl over [Col. 0688A] his knees, he receives whatever judgment the abbot sees fit to impose.

Rising from there at the abbot’s command, he is clothed only in his cowl and prostrates himself first at the abbot’s feet, then at those of the prior and of all who are on that side. He does the same at the feet of those on the other side, and finally at the feet of the boys, though much farther away than from the others, without touching their clothing. Everyone bows to him and raises him up, and they ought to pray for him.

When this has been completed and he has again asked pardon, he is ordered to leave and put on his clothing. After dressing and returning, he still asks pardon; he is ordered to sit last and to be last of all in every place.

Meanwhile, he does not communicate, does not go forward for the kiss of peace, does not kiss the Gospel book, does not introduce a chant or psalm in church, and does not read a lesson. He is not forbidden to serve in the kitchen, and may go there for that purpose; but he shall not go to the *scilla* [perhaps a particular work or place; the reading is uncertain].

After each hour has ended, he asks pardon on his knees at his station, without turning toward the altar on that account. Whenever all the brothers dress in white for a procession, he too is dressed in white; otherwise, not at all. [Col. 0688B]

Finally, if the lord abbot sees that it is expedient and that the man’s humility deserves it, when the brothers have interceded for him, he summons him in chapter to rise and come into the middle. After he asks pardon, the abbot speaks words appropriate to the person and the cause, and restores his former place to him, or, if he wishes, gives him another lower one; for by his own evil merit he lost his place.

He goes to the abbot’s feet, as anyone else does, both in church and in chapter, if the abbot promotes him to a higher seat. It should be noted, however, that when he is restored to his rank, if he is a priest, he does not therefore sing Mass; if a deacon, the Gospel; or if a subdeacon, the Epistle, unless he is expressly told to do so. For that restoration to his rank means nothing more than that he may sing and read in the choir like the others.

It should also be known that the prior imposes no judgment of this kind and never absolves anyone. It should further be known that no one is placed under serious fault unless he has repeatedly fallen into the same crime, nor for a hidden offense, nor for any offense, whatever it may be, [Col. 0688C] that he himself voluntarily confesses.

But if someone has committed something known to only a few which, if public, would be judged worthy of the penalty of serious fault, the abbot or prior leads him to a private place, taking with him two or three of those who know the crime, or others whom he wishes. There he imposes a serious judgment according to the gravity of the offense and assigns a penance.

If someone living in obedience in another place commits a public crime, he is stripped publicly in that same place before all its inhabitants and flogged horribly. Then he is brought back to the congregation and placed under serious fault.

Nor should it be left unmentioned that anyone who speaks to a person under serious fault or gives him a sign without the abbot’s order deserves to be placed under the same fault.

If he has sinned secretly, he is beaten very secretly, according to the gravity of the offense. He is brought back to the greater church and afterward never leaves the cloister, unless his correction should appear so great and so evident that it seems worthy and [Col. 0688D] shows that he does not intend to sin again.

Nevertheless, wherever he is sent, he must never again return to the place where he sinned.

But if his offense is not among the more serious evils—for example, if he has argued dishonorably and irreligiously with someone within the hearing of the people, or something similar—then, for such an offense, when Sunday comes and the people assemble in the church at the beginning of the morning Mass, he stands barefoot near the church doors, holding a fairly large book in his hand. He does not put on his cap, so that he may be recognized by everyone. He speaks to no one entering or leaving. A servant is always beside him to tell those who ask why such a penance has been imposed upon him. He does not leave that place until the Mass has ended.

Thus far the Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon. It has also seemed appropriate to append the Cistercian practice from the book of the Institutions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order.

From the book of the Institutions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order, distinction 6, chapter 6.

[Col. 0689A]

When someone is subjected to serious fault, let him receive discipline in the judgment itself. Then, after a penance for serious fault has been imposed upon him, let him immediately place his hood upon his head and leave the chapter for the place that the abbot has judged suitable for him. Let a discreet elder be assigned to him to comfort him and urge him toward humility, lest he be swallowed up by excessive sorrow. Let prayer be enjoined in chapter on his behalf; and, as the Rule says, let everyone pray for him.

The abbot must also take into account both his bodily health and the degree of his fault, for the fault ought to be lightened or made heavier accordingly. He shall receive food in the measure and at the hour that the abbot judges suitable for him, as the Rule provides. The vessels he uses shall either be broken or distributed to the poor.

He shall lie prostrate on the ground at the doors of the oratory while the Work of God is being completed, without his hood on his head, although he must wear it while walking. Whenever [Col. 0689B] Mass or the Office for the Dead immediately follows a canonical hour, he shall not prostrate himself until the congregation has left the church.

When he is to be received into chapter at the abbot’s command, he shall have his hood on his head at the entrance to chapter. After removing it, he shall come before the abbot and prostrate himself before his feet on his knees and on the joints of his hands; then before the prior. Passing through the prior’s choir, if there is a prior, or the abbot in the prior’s place, and then through the abbot’s choir, he shall likewise prostrate himself before the feet of each person. They shall neither bow to him nor assist him, but remain seated quietly.

Whenever he passes before the abbot, he shall bow. Then, coming before the lectern, he shall stand there, not asking pardon until ordered by the abbot to go and sit. He shall not be placed in his rank on that day, nor perform any office until the abbot orders it. But whenever the Work of God is completed, both in church and at work, he shall prostrate himself on the ground in the place where he stands until the abbot orders him to cease this [Col. 0689C] satisfaction.

Those who are excommunicated from the table alone for lighter offenses shall make satisfaction in the oratory.] The manuscript Customs of the monastery of Farfa and those of Saint Paul at Rome prescribe the following concerning the satisfaction of one excommunicated for a light offense:

“Brothers who, according to the Rule, are separated from the table for a light offense shall make satisfaction in the oratory as follows. After the psalmody, when the others bow or bend their knees for the prayers, they shall come before the altar and prostrate themselves at the steps until the prayers and prayer-service are finished. Then, rising and bowing before and behind, they shall do this at all the hours.

“But if a feast occurs before they are absolved, from Vespers until the following Vespers they shall join the brothers in all communion, including Masses if they are priests, and they may celebrate everything belonging to the divine service.”

Lanfrancus likewise says in the Statutes (chapter 17):

“A brother assigned to make satisfaction for a light offense is separated from the common table. He shall use the food and drink of the other brothers unless these have been expressly [Col. 0689D] forbidden to him. He shall eat at None if the brothers eat at Sext, or at Vespers if the brothers eat at None.

“In the monastery and in chapter, he shall be in the place where he is accustomed to be, either last of all or in between, according to the nature of the fault and the abbot’s command.

“In church he shall not celebrate Mass, read the Epistle, lesson, or Gospel, sing a responsory, introduce an antiphon over the psalms, or perform anything of this kind unless he does it together with the others. He shall not vest for service at the candlestick or thurible, and shall not approach for the offering or the kiss of peace.

“Toward the end of the Work of God established by the Rule, both at night and during the day, when they begin the Kyrie eleison, he shall prostrate himself before the step where the blessings are received. There he shall lie prostrate until ‘Who lives and reigns with you’ is said.

“If a feast of twelve lessons occurs, he shall cease this satisfaction until ordinary days return. While the brothers are eating in the refectory, he shall be in the church.”

Finally, the Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon [Col. 0690A] (chapter 32) state:

“The custom for a lighter fault is as follows. In the oratory, when the Kyrie begins at all the regular hours, the offender prostrates himself before the step of the sanctuary and lies there until the hour is completed. When the hour has ended, he rises, bows deeply toward the altar, and returns to his station.

“While he is under this fault, he does not begin an antiphon or psalm in the choir, sing a responsory, or read a lesson; he does not offer, kiss the Gospel book, or go forward for the kiss of peace, unless there has been a feast of twelve lessons, and so forth.”

See Udalricus, book II, chapter 18.

They shall carry this out until the abbot’s command, until he blesses them and says, “It is enough.”] Lanfrancus describes the rite of this absolution as follows (chapter 17):

“When it pleases the abbot to absolve him from this satisfaction, if he is in the monastery with the congregation, the abbot shall send to him, while he is prostrate, one of the priors who are near him. That prior shall give a sign from the abbot to the prostrate man and tell him to rise. Immediately rising, he shall bow humbly to the abbot and go to his place.

“But if [Col. 0690B] the abbot is seated in chapter, then, at the brothers’ request, he shall say to him: ‘This satisfaction for a light fault is remitted to you,’ or something similar. The brother shall immediately rise, go to the abbot’s feet, and afterward return to his place.”

The Customs of Saint Benignus and Udalricus likewise say: “He is absolved especially when he is lying prostrate at the step and a brother is sent to him, by whom he is given a sign that he has been absolved.”

Concerning the absolution of an excommunicated person, the Customs of the monasteries of Farfa and Saint Paul at Rome prescribe several things. It may not be irrelevant to record them here:

“No prior,” they say, “ought to impose such a judgment on a brother while the lord abbot is in the monastery. But even if the abbot should arrive, the prior may meanwhile absolve them himself before knowledge of the case comes before the lord abbot. If he does not do so, and the brother has asked pardon once before the abbot, the prior may afterward no longer absolve him.

“Nor should the master or anyone else, while the abbot himself is [Col. 0690C] inside, send into the judgment of fasting a boy who has stood before him. Any boys whom the master has sent into judgment the prior may absolve without the master’s permission.

“No one else may order anything—not a sign or anything else—but only the one who holds the office. If he thinks that they should be absolved, he shall give the master a sign that they are to be absolved.

“If the lord abbot sends a brother into judgment and then goes somewhere, forgetting to absolve him, the prior is not able to absolve him. And when the prior has sent someone into judgment, the dean cannot absolve him without the prior’s permission.”

Thus far, Saint Benedict and his disciples have dealt with the satisfaction of the excommunicated. But what of others? Saint Isidore (Chapter 18) says:

> “This is the satisfaction of offenders: Once the period of penance has been completed, brothers who have been stationed in the church shall immediately remove their belt and, prostrate on the ground outside the choir, remain there until the service has been completed. When the abbot has ordered it, he shall rise from the ground, enter the choir, and pray. After the abbot has offered a prayer for him, and all have answered ‘Amen,’ he shall rise and ask everyone’s pardon for his negligence, so as to obtain forgiveness after undergoing the discipline of this corrective satisfaction.”

Saint Fructuosus (Chapter 14):

> “When someone is excommunicated or rebuked for his negligence, he shall practice humility until he receives the prayer, nor shall he dare to mix with the others or secretly join himself to anyone. Rather, while everyone is assembling for the exercises of prayer, he shall prostrate himself on the ground, with belt and outer garment removed, and ask pardon for his negligence. He shall also do this when the others leave the office. Likewise, at mealtime he shall stand before the refectory, with lowered face and clothing, until, released through the compassion of the brothers, he receives the pardon he asks for, with downcast countenance and demeanour.”

### 595 Rule of the Master (Chapter 13)

> “But if a brother has committed a grave fault, he shall be excommunicated from both places, that is, from the oratory and from the table; and he shall not attain the superior’s pardon unless, first prostrate before the threshold of the oratory, with a tearful voice, during the interval when the hours’ psalms have ceased, he has satisfied God and all by promising amendment.”

Finally, the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins (Chapter 6):

> “Sisters who are being held in penance for grave faults shall not stand in the church with the others who are receiving Communion; instead, they shall sing the office privately in another church. When the office has been completed, they shall be ordered to go out and stand before the doors of the church in which those receiving Communion complete the office. When the congregation has gone out, they shall prostrate themselves on the ground and ask that the Lord be entreated for them.

## CHAPTER XLV. Concerning those who make mistakes in the oratory

[Note: [Col. 0691B] Alternatively, ‘who cause mistakes.’]

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691A] If anyone makes a mistake while reciting a psalm, responsory, antiphon, or lesson [Note: [Col. 0691B] Oxford, Florence: “has made a mistake.” Cassino: “and has gone wrong”; Sabina: “makes a mistake.”], unless he has humbled himself there before everyone with satisfaction [Note: [Col. 0691B] Narbonne, Sabina, Lyon, Complutum, Haeften: “through satisfaction.”]—[Note: [Col. 0692B] Hildemar omits “there.”]—let him be subjected to a greater punishment [Note: [Col. 0692B] Conc: “correction”], since he was unwilling, through humility, to correct what he had done wrong through negligence [Note: [Col. 0692B] Alternatively, “through negligence”; another reading: “does wrong.”]. But let children be beaten for such a fault.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0691]

[Col. 0691B] “If anyone makes a mistake while reciting a psalm, responsory, antiphon, or lesson; unless he has humbled himself there before everyone with satisfaction, etc.”] What kind of satisfaction of humility is required by this chapter, the Holy Father does not sufficiently explain. Certainly, the ancient Egyptian and Tabennesian monks punished with severe discipline anyone who stumbled even slightly while singing a psalm. For Cassian writes (Book IV, chapter 16):

> “He washed away his negligence only through public penance; and when all the brothers had assembled in the synaxis, he remained prostrate on the ground and asked pardon until the solemnity of the prayers had been completed, obtaining it when he had been ordered by the abbot’s judgment to rise from the ground.”

Saint Columbanus (in the Penitential) requires that “one who has not sung well at the beginning of a psalm because of coughing shall be ordered to make amends with six blows.” In Lanfranc’s Statutes, genuflection is indicated as the satisfaction. Nicholas of Fractura requires the one who makes a mistake to humble himself “by bending his knees and placing his head on the ground.” The Book of Cistercian Usages decrees that “all shall make satisfaction on the joints of their hands in the place where they are, whenever they commit a mistake in the oratory, without turning either to the right or to the left.” It adds: “For merely a musical error we are not accustomed to make satisfaction.”

Finally, concerning the first disciples of Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, we read the following in his Life (Book I, no. 16, volume IV of Baluze’s Miscellany):

> “If anyone in church raised his eyes slightly, or smiled a little, or dozed lightly, or, while holding a book, negligently allowed it to fall, or made some sound through negligence, or sang too far ahead or too impetuously, or displayed some disorderly movement, he immediately received either a rod on the head or a slap on the face, so that the sound of the blow resounded in everyone’s ears. This was inflicted especially on the younger boys, both so that they themselves might be corrected and so that the others might be frightened.”

It should be observed, however, that someone may offend while singing in the oratory in three ways: first, by leading the entire choir into error with him; second, by disturbing only some; third, by making a mistake alone.

“In the first case,” says Bernard of Cassino, “the Cassinese custom requires him to kneel in such a way that he places his head on the ground. In the second case, it is enough for him to kneel without placing his head on the ground. In the third case, it is enough for him to kneel when ‘Glory be to the Father’ is said.”

Hildemar likewise, undoubtedly according to the practice of his own time, says that one who disturbs everyone must humble himself to the ground—that is, kneel on the ground. But one who makes a mistake alone, he says, need not humble himself in the same way as the former; he need only bend his body. In the recitation of lessons, whoever makes a mistake while reading from a correct book should go to the appointed place and ask pardon there; but whoever reads incorrectly out of habit should be corrected for this in chapter.

Now among the Cassinese (Cassinese Declaration, chapter 45), one who makes a slight mistake merely touches the ground with a finger; one who makes a serious mistake kneels before the superior until a signal is given him to rise. Among the Celestines (Celestine Constitutions, chapter 1, § 7):

> “Those who fail slightly in the choir kneel on the benches with their heads uncovered; but those who fail more seriously make satisfaction, prostrate in the middle of the choir, at the signal and nod of the president. When the divine office has ended, before leaving the church, they pray while kneeling, recite verses, prayers, and antiphons according to the breviary, and at the president’s signal all rise together.”

Finally, among the Fulienses (Fuliensian Constitutions, chapter 45), one who sins slightly while singing repeatedly touches the ground with his hand; but whoever, singing alone with the choir listening, makes a mistake, kisses the ground.

“Let him be subjected to a greater punishment.”] Supply: “than if he had humbled himself.” Hildemar explains what this greater punishment should be in these words:

> “What he says—‘Let him be subjected to a greater punishment’—is understood in various ways. Some understand it to mean that he must ask pardon twice or three times in the oratory. Others understand it to mean that he must be rebuked in chapter. But the latter interpretation, that he be rebuked in chapter, is sounder, and he can be led through stages; for once he refuses to fulfill what Saint Benedict says, he must then be led through six stages so that he may be corrected, since, if he emerges from one discipline, another discipline will then receive him.”

“But let children be beaten for such a fault.”] Hildemar accurately observes here that the chapter indicates two faults: one by which someone makes a mistake while singing, and another by which, after the fault, he neglects to make satisfaction. Smaragdus, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Matthias Lambert explain this passage of the latter fault:

> “When he says, ‘But let children be beaten for such a fault,’ Smaragdus says, ‘it is understood that this means unless they have humbled themselves there before everyone.’”

Our Menard, however, more correctly judges that the text of the Rule should be understood of the former fault, so that these words constitute the second part of the chapter, dealing specifically with children who make a mistake in recitation—especially since children are guided more by sense and fear than by shame and humiliation. The same is taught by Theobaldus Artaldus and is confirmed by the practice of the Cluniacs, which Udalric describes in these words (Book III, chapter 8):

> “At nocturns, indeed at all the hours, if the boys themselves should make any mistake in psalmody or in another chant, or by dozing, or by committing any similar fault in any way, the matter is not postponed at all but is judged without delay. They are stripped of frock and cowl and beaten in their shirts, either by the prior or by their aforesaid master, with light, smooth, rounded wicker rods prepared for this purpose.”

From these words someone might perhaps conclude that boys were beaten in the oratory among the Cluniacs. Yet Hildemar says: “A child must not be flogged in the oratory; when he is to be flogged, they must flog him not in chapter but in the school of his masters.”

[Col. 0694A] Concerning the manner in which the boys were beaten, Udalric writes (Book III, chapter 10):

> “If the boys themselves offend in any way, especially by singing or reading negligently, or if they learn a chant less carefully than they should, they receive suitable discipline from him [the precentor]. Above all, however, both he and the others take care, when he beats them, not only that they do not touch their flesh with the hand, but also that his garment does not touch their clothing. Their cheeks are never struck with the palm; but, if necessary, the master alone who leads them may shake their hair; otherwise, never.”

## CHAPTER XLVI. Concerning those who offend in any other matters

[Note: [Col. 0693B] Complutum: “in some minor matters”; Conches: “in some minor faults”; Sabina, Haeften: “in minor matters.”]

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693A] 598 If anyone, while engaged in any work—in the kitchen, storeroom, service, bakery [Note: [Col. 0693B] Oxford, Paris 1: “in the monastery”; the Victorine manuscript omits “in the bakery”], garden, or any craft—or while working in any place, commits some fault, or breaks or loses something, or exceeds in some other way [Note: [Col. 0693B] Oxford: “there”; Hildemar, Florence, Ebrulfo, Lyon: “where and where”; Kero, Conches: “where or where”], and, without coming immediately before the abbot or the congregation, does not voluntarily make satisfaction and disclose his fault, then, once it has become known through another person, he shall be subjected to a greater correction. But if the cause of the sin is hidden within the soul [Note: [Col. 0694B] Hildemar omits “of the sin”; Menard does not require it], let him disclose it only to the abbot or to spiritual elders [Note: [Col. 0694B] Another reading: “to spiritual brothers or elders”; Lyon omits “elders”], who know how to heal their own wounds [Note: [Col. 0694B] Conc, Florence, Dionysius: “and their own”] and not uncover and publish those of others.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0693]

[Col. 0693B] “If anyone, while engaged in any work, in the kitchen, storeroom, etc.”] A storeroom is a pantry or repository, so called “because table equipment is collected there, or whatever necessities for food remain,” as Saint Isidore says (Book XV of the Etymologies, chapter 5).

“In service.”] “That is, in the house of any craft,” says Boherius. Paul Augustine of Janua, Theobaldus Artaldus, and certain French translations, however, understand this text of service at table.

[Col. 0693C] “In the bakery.”] For Boherius, a bakery “is the place where flour is deposited and bread is made. Preparing these things,” he says, “is the monks’ task.” Indeed, formerly, at least in certain monasteries, the brothers performed this task in rotation, as is clear from the Life of Saint Samson (no. 16, Benedictine Century I):

> “The brother of that same priest, after succeeding the other monks in turn, became the baker of this monastery.”

And in the Life of Saint Austreberta (Benedictine Century III):

> “It was customary for the sisters to bake the bread in turn.”

599 “Or breaks something.”] Cassian shows with what severity the ancient monks punished those who had broken something, in these words (Book IV, chapter 16):

> “If anyone by some accident breaks an earthenware jar, which they now call a water vessel, he shall wash away his negligence only through public penance; and when all the brothers have assembled in the synaxis, he shall remain prostrate on the ground and ask pardon until the solemnity of the prayers has been completed, obtaining it when he has been ordered by the abbot’s judgment to rise from the ground.”

In the Rule of Saint Pachomius (Article 70), however, it is decreed only that “if anyone breaks an earthen vessel or some useful object intended for the monastery’s use, he shall do penance.” But the Rule of the Master (Chapter 16) says:

> “If the monastery’s vessels are broken through someone’s negligence, the one who broke them shall not approach the table before, having bent his knees, he has satisfied the abbot through humility as a penitent.”

“Or loses something.”] They punished no less strictly those who had lost the monastery’s property, as can be seen frequently in the Rule of Saint Pachomius (Article 75):

> “If anyone loses something, he shall be publicly rebuked before the altar. But if what was lost belonged to his own clothing, he shall not receive it for three weeks; in the fourth week, after performing penance, what he lost shall be given to him.”

And below (Article 116):

> “The person responsible for a task must take care that no work be lost in the monastery, in any craft whatsoever practiced by the brothers. But if something is lost and has been dissipated through negligence, the Father of the individual works shall rebuke him; and he shall rebuke the one who lost the work, solely according to the will and judgment of the superior, without which no one shall have authority to rebuke a brother.”

And likewise (Article 120):

> “Whoever loses a skin, leggings, a belt, or anything else shall be rebuked.”

Finally:

> “The house superior shall be subject to rebuke for his fault if he has not reported to the Father within three days that something has been lost, whether on the road, in the field, or in the monastery, and he shall do penance according to the established order.”

In the Penances of an uncertain author preserved with Saint Basil (no. 24):

> “If anyone loses something and, having failed to find it, does not report it to the archimandrite, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

And in Saint Basil himself (Brief Rules, question 144):

> “One who has misused something shall be judged as a sacrilegious person; but one who has lost something shall be judged as the author of sacrilege, since everything has been dedicated to the Lord and consecrated to God.”

“Or exceeds in some other way.”] Such are the matters Cassian also describes in these words (Book IV, chapter 16):

> “Anyone who, having been summoned to some task or to the customary assembly, arrives late; or who, while singing a psalm, stumbles even slightly; likewise, anyone who answers excessively, harshly, or insolently; who carries out assigned duties negligently; who murmurs even lightly; who, preferring a reading to work or obedience, performs the prescribed duties sluggishly; who, once the synaxis has been dismissed, does not hasten quickly back to his cell; who stops with someone even briefly or withdraws somewhere for a moment; who holds another’s hand; who ventures to converse, however briefly, with one who is not his cellmate; who prays with one who has been suspended from prayer; who sees one of his parents or secular friends, or speaks with them without his elder; who attempts to receive or write a letter without his abbot.”

All these offenses were punished with the same penance imposed on one who had broken the water vessel.

“And without coming immediately before the abbot.”] The commentators do not wish the word “immediately” to be understood as though the offender should abandon unfinished work, run straight to the abbot, confess his sin, ask pardon, and make satisfaction. Rather, they understand it to mean immediately at the hour when he has been separated from the work; or, as Boherius puts it, “as soon as he conveniently can, or at least when the regular chapter is held afterward, for everyone must hasten to it.” Hildemar appears to suggest the latter when he says: “If he has committed the offense today, let him ask pardon tomorrow.”

Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, Turrecremata, and Matthias Lambert hold this view. In my judgment, however, Richard of Saint Angelo more correctly interprets “immediately” as “at once, without delay.” Practice confirms this interpretation, as can be seen in the case of the Goth whom the holy Father Benedict had received into his monastery for conversion. While he was clearing a place of thorn bushes, the iron flew from the handle of his tool and fell into a lake; “having lost the iron, he ran trembling to the monk Maurus, reported the damage he had caused, and performed penance for his offense” (Saint Gregory, Book II of the Dialogues, chapter 6).

In the Life of Saint Lioba, chapter 5 (Benedictine Century III), a sister who was keeper of the oratory lost the church keys during the night. She “went to the abbess, who, while the sisters were still resting, was as usual occupied with vigils and anticipating the time of nocturnal prayer; trembling and struck with fear, she fell at her feet and, with humble satisfaction, disclosed to her the fault of her negligence.”

And in the Life of Saint Guido, abbot of Pomposa, concerning a certain Sergius, who was also custodian of the church: while he was cleaning the lamps, one fell and broke. “Terrified, he gathered up the fragments, placed them before the altar step, and hurried to Father Guido so that he might inflict on him a severe penalty for the damage caused. When this had been done, he immediately returned to the altar and found the lamp sound and whole.”

Certainly, Hildemar appears to suggest that the fault should be reported first to the abbot rather than to the congregation.

“Before the abbot or the congregation.”] According to Boherius, the particle “or” is used here coordinately, in the sense of “and.” But when the Holy Father says “before the abbot or the congregation,” Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius understand him to mean that, for lesser and lighter faults, the offender should confess before the abbot; for more serious faults, by which the brothers might be scandalized, he should confess before the congregation. Hildemar largely agrees with them, asserting that all faults should first be reported to the abbot and then, if he judges it appropriate, to the congregation.

Subject to better judgment, however, I would think that both lesser and greater faults should be disclosed before the abbot and the congregation. No trace of this distinction appears in the Rule. This should not be understood to mean that, as soon as anyone has broken or lost something, the congregation must immediately be summoned; rather, the matter should be revealed immediately to the abbot and then, at the next chapter, to the congregation.

Thus the Cassinese declare (Cassinese Declaration on chapter 46) that “this is to be observed when the abbot is present there or in a nearby place, and the offender knows this; otherwise, let him make satisfaction before the congregation at the following chapter.”

“Once it has become known through another person, he shall be subjected to a greater correction.”] The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins expresses nearly the same thing (Chapter 16):

> “If a sister who has fallen into one of these cases immediately gives a pure confession to the abbess or superior, and it is discovered that what happened by accident was not her intention, this alone shall suffice: if possible, she must not deny what she has done and committed, but must correct it with a satisfaction of pardon. But if it becomes known not through her own confession but through another person’s disclosure, she shall undergo penance according to the magnitude of the fault, because she did not reveal the fault through a pure confession.”

From this passage it can be gathered quite clearly that there was an ancient practice of public denunciations, by which those who neglected to accuse themselves were brought forward openly and publicly. Saint Isidore appears to refer to these when he says (Chapter 18):

> “The other excesses of the monks shall be reported in the assembly to the abbot or superior, so that the one known to have committed the fault may be restrained with appropriate security.”

See Book I, On the Ancient Rites of the Monks, chapter 5.

“But if the cause of the sin is hidden within the soul, etc.”] These words moderate the severity of the ancient monks, who publicly revealed not only external offenses but also hidden thoughts of the soul, as can be seen in Saint Basil, Sermon 1, On the Institution of Monks.

Saint Hildegard, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Richard of Saint Angelo, Peter Boherius, John of Turrecremata, Theobaldus Artaldus, John Craesbeeck, and Antonius Perezius rightly interpret this passage of the Holy Rule as referring to sacramental confession. Hence the Holy Father wished it to be made not only to the abbot but also to a spiritual elder—for by this name the ancient Greeks and more recent Latins called confessors—because formerly not all abbots were priests and therefore able to absolve. He requires in them the utmost prudence and the utmost secrecy, which properly belong to sacramental confession. This subject should be investigated briefly under four headings: first, how frequently it was practiced by the ancient monks; second, where; third, by what rite; fourth, to whom it was made.

As to the first point, Jonas, bishop of Orléans, perhaps indicates that the ancient monks made daily confessions, at least of venial sins, in Book I of On the Institution of the Laity, chapter 16 (Spicilegium, volume I), where he says:

> “It is the custom of the Church to confess more serious sins to priests, through whom people are reconciled to God; but, concerning daily and lesser matters, there are very few who confess to one another, except monks, who do this daily.”

Certainly, Rotgarius, a monk of the monastery of Saint Faro at Meaux (Benedictine Century II), is said in the Life of Saint Faro, chapter 119, to have been “daily intent on renewing the penances of confessions.”

Crodegandus, however, in the Rule of Canons, chapter 32, prescribes only that “the monks make confession every Saturday, willingly, to the bishop or their prior.”

Saint Dunstan agrees with Crodegandus, decreeing:

> “On Sundays, each of the brothers shall humbly reveal the guilt of his conscience to the spiritual Father, or, if he is absent, to his vicar. But if the crowd is so great that all cannot come to confession on that day, they shall fulfill the same duty on the following day, namely Monday. The school, however, shall in no way omit this, although it consists of boys, but shall perform it customarily like the elders, even though it has not yet been attacked by temptations. Whoever on other days has need of this, being stirred by some temptation of soul or body, should not for that reason delay coming devotedly to the healthful remedy of confession.”

The Carthusians observed the same practice from the very beginning of their order, as Guigo testifies (Statutes, chapter 7):

> “Every Saturday, since we maintain silence in our cells throughout the week, we confess our sins to the prior or to those whom he has appointed.”

The ancient Statutes of the Carthusians explain this as follows (Part II, chapter 11):

> “Every Saturday, unless a chapter feast occurs, we confess our sins to the prior or to those whom he has appointed. If a chapter feast occurs on Saturday, we confess on the preceding day, which occurs without such a feast.”

They add:

> “We always confess on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, unless that vigil falls on Sunday or Monday; in that case, we confess on the following Saturday. Care must be taken that we always make a common confession in each week.”

We also learn that the same institution was in force among the Cistercians from the Book of Institutions of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order (Distinctio 6, chapter 4), where we read:

> “Let abbots and monks confess at least once a week, if they have access to a confessor. The lay brothers who reside in abbeys shall do the same; those who live in granges shall confess whenever chapter is held for them. Nevertheless, all alike, monks and lay brothers, must not fail to confess to their abbots at least once a year, unless perhaps they cannot have access to them.”

Nearly the same is found in the Book of Ancient Definitions, distinctio 7, chapter 4. Clement VIII later abolished this command to confess to the abbot once a year.

In the statutes of the abbots of Samnbyacum and Macerias of the Cistercian order, and of the priors of Liget and Glandières of the Carthusians, made for the Grandmont order by the authority of Pope Gregory X, I read the following statute (Chapter 9):

> “Every brother, cleric or layman, shall confess at least once a week; otherwise, as a transgressor, he shall immediately be content with drinking water until he has spoken of his confession. Any prior who is found neglecting so necessary a statute, so that he does not ensure with all diligence that the constitution is observed in himself and in others, shall be punished most severely by the abbot or visitors without a general chapter.”

And in the Grandmont manuscript Book on the Instruction of Novices (Chapter 3):

> “Let your confession be considered beforehand, brief, frequent, open, complete, modest, tearful, with contrition and without excuse. If you can confess daily, that is good; otherwise, strive to confess every third day, or at least once each week, in a salutary manner according to the statutes of the order you have entered. Always strive to make a general confession once each year, according to the ordinance of the general council of Innocent III.”

Finally, the Bursfeld Congregation defines the following (Ceremonial, distinctio 3, chapter 6):

> “Priests who are to celebrate shall confess in the morning, after morning Lauds have ended, so that during the day they may be more ready for the duty of their order and for the work of God. Let this be regularly observed: no one should ever presume to celebrate on any day unless he has first been prepared, according to his individual condition and disposition, by the antidote of devout confession and meditation. The others may confess at suitable times, provided that they do not exceed the times for confession and Communion established in the Constitutions of Clement V and Benedict XII.”

In the Constitution of Clement V it is decreed that “every month, both in monasteries and outside them, with every excuse removed, each and every monk shall approach confession at least once.”

Gregory IX had previously decreed the same in his constitution for Benedictines, where he says:

> “Each month a general confession of all the brothers shall be made, to which each and every one shall come without any excuse.”

The same is also found in the manuscript Statutes of Peter, abbot of Silva Major, issued around 1198.

Pope Benedict XII decreed (Chapter 27) that monks “who are not priests shall confess, if not more often, at least every week.” By this decree, however, he did not intend to derogate from the customs of monasteries in which they were accustomed to confess more frequently. Here Benedict restored the ancient customs of earlier monks who confessed every week, as we have seen among the Cistercians, Grandmontensians, and Carthusians.

Now the Carthusians, according to the new collection of their Statutes (Part II, chapter 7), may confess more frequently. They say:

> “Every Sunday, or on the preceding Saturday, or at least once a week, and on the principal feasts, monks who are not celebrating Mass, both novices and professed members, shall confess to the prior or to those appointed by him. For this reason, however, we do not forbid them to confess at other times during the week in chapter, or in their cells with the prior’s permission. We strongly exhort those who celebrate Mass to frequent sacramental confession; for this reason we ring the bell every day after Prime for confessions to be made, etc.”

The Celestines prescribe (Celestine Constitutions, chapter 3, § 1) that priests confess once a week, while the other monks and oblates confess at least twice each month.

Finally, among the Fulienses (Fuliensian Constitutions, chapter 38), “all who are not priests are required to confess once a week and to receive Communion, namely on Sunday. Clerics and lay brothers are urged to confess more frequently, and at least once in addition to Sunday. Priests are to confess three times a week, or more frequently; certainly, they must not omit it twice.”

The place assigned for hearing confessions in monasteries was generally the chapter house, as is clear from the manuscript Customs of the monastery of Farfa, from the Benignian customs, from Udalric, and from the Book of Cistercian Usages.

604 The Carthusians confess in chapter and, with the prior’s permission, in their cells. The only distinction is that “whenever we confess in chapter,” they say in the ancient Statutes (Part II, chapter 11), “we should avoid prolixity; in the cell, however, we may confess at greater length.”

[Col. 0698B] Udalric describes the procedure for approaching confession in these words (Book II, chapter 12):

> “If someone needs to come to confession for some offense, he approaches the priest whom he especially wishes to choose. Standing before him, he draws his right hand out of his sleeve and places it on his chest, which is the sign of confession. The priest rises, and the offender follows him into chapter. First, he asks pardon before him, prostrate with his whole body. Ordered by him to rise, he sits down and tells him what he has to say. If something has happened to him during the night which we modestly call weakness, he should say the seven penitential psalms before confession; or, if he does not know the psalms, the Lord’s Prayer seven times. After he has confessed, he should do whatever the priest orders him. On that day he does not kiss the Gospel book, go to the kiss of peace, or approach the offering.”

The same words are contained in the Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon, chapter 31.

Of the Cistercians, the Book of Usages says (Chapter 70):

> “While anyone is confessing, no one should remain there—in chapter—unless he is occupied in a similar task. For they may confess there during the whole time of reading, though only before dinner, and also during the interval before Prime. When they have sat down, let the prior say ‘Benedicite,’ and, when ‘The Lord’ has been answered, let the prior continue, ‘God be with us’; when ‘Amen’ has been answered, let the penitent briefly confess the faults for which he has asked pardon. After these words, let him immediately continue: ‘For these and all other sins I confess myself guilty, and I ask pardon.’ Then the prior, having given absolution over him, shall impose a penance. Afterwards he may comfort, admonish, or rebuke him, as he sees fit, though briefly.”

From this it is clear that among the Cistercians, Cluniacs, and Benignians, confession was made while sitting. Children, however, followed a different practice. In the Benignian Customs it is said: “They confess while standing, and come to confession twice a week.”

This is also clear from the Customs of the monastery of Farfa, which prescribe the following concerning the confession of children:

> “When the children are brought to confession, if the Lord Abbot is present, the master shall lead them all the way to him. When he rises, the master must sit before the entrance to the chapter house. In the place where the children customarily have their chapter, they must also make confession there. Let the first child approach first and make his confession standing; let the other sit in the southern part on one of their seats. After the confession, let the master receive them again. When they wish to confess to the prior and the dean of the cloister, once the master has brought them to him, he shall immediately withdraw. The prior shall lead them into chapter and, after the confession, return them to school. When some children are to leave the school, the Lord Abbot must come to the children’s chapter and make the other children leave. He himself and the master shall remain with those who are to leave and shall hear their confession. After the confession, the master shall return them to the others until they come to the consecration; afterward, he himself must see to it that the others do what is ordered [the Latin is corrupt].”

[Col. 0699A] The Carthusian monks, however, display a greater lowering both of body and of spirit (Ancient Statutes, Part II, chapter 11), among whom “everyone must be prostrate and bareheaded when he confesses.”

And in the Grandmont manuscript Book on the Instruction of Novices (Chapter 3), I read:

> “When you have recalled each sin to memory, go to the priest, remove your hood, kneel humbly, and, with hands joined, say: ‘I confess to God, to Blessed Mary, to the angels of God, to Blessed Stephen the confessor, to all the saints, and to you, Father.’ Then begin to state those sins which you considered above. When these have been stated, add at the end: ‘For these and all my other mortal and venial sins, confessed and forgotten, by which I have offended my Creator, through my fault, etc. Therefore I ask, etc.’”

On the person to whom confession should be made, Saint Benedict prescribes that it be made only to the abbot or to spiritual elders. Hence it always seems to have been left to the abbot, or to those appointed by him, to hear confessions, as may be gathered both from the provisions of Peter, abbot of Silva Major, issued in 1198, and from other manuscript Statutes of the general chapter of the monks of the province of Rheims, held at the archmonastery of Saint Remigius in 1348—although it is clear from the aforementioned Statutes of Peter, abbot of Silva Major, that certain sins were reserved to the abbot.

Among the Carthusians also (Ancient Statutes, Part II, chapter 11) we read: “Those who, by order of the prior, hear confessions impose no satisfaction for a criminal offense on anyone, but send him to the prior, because such matters are reserved to his judgment. In danger, however, even such men may absolve, on the condition that, if they live and are able, they confess to the prior” (Part II, chapter 4). In the new Statutes they seem to understand a “criminal sin” as a certainly mortal sin. But in the third compilation of the Statutes they distinguish between a criminal sin and a mortal sin in this way (chapter 6): although every criminal sin is mortal, not every mortal sin is criminal. They draw up an immense catalogue of criminal sins, from which, as we have said, no one can be absolved except by the prior, and the prior except by the vicar. Moreover, certain sins were reserved to the Apostolic See; from these only the prior of Chartreuse and fifty priors appointed by him could absolve—not, however, by letters, because, they say, such absolution is sacramental, not judicial.

The ancient Statutes further add (Part II, chapter 11): “None of our brothers may confess to Preachers or Minors unless permission has first been obtained from the priors, or unless those Preachers or Minors themselves produce a privilege from the lord pope expressly naming the Carthusian Order.” In the Rule of Saint Stephen of Grandmont I likewise read (chapter 50): “If any one of you should, God forbid, fall into some sin, let him take the utmost care not to confess it to any outsider, however great his holiness may be.”
