“Who know how to care for their own wounds and those of others.”] Saint Antony says nearly the same (Rule, no. 25): “Do not disclose your thoughts to everyone, but only to those who can save your soul.” And Saint Basil says (Shorter Rules, question 229): “In the confession of sins the principle is altogether the same as in the opening of bodily diseases. Thus, just as people do not rashly disclose bodily diseases to everyone, but only to those who know how they should be treated, so confession of sins among you should be made to those who can cure them.”

“Not to disclose or make public.”] “Whoever presumes to do this,” says Boherius, “must not only be deposed from the priestly office, but must also be confined in a strict monastery and prison to perform perpetual penance” (On Penance and Reconciliation, chapter *Omnis*, at the end). “Formerly, the deposed man wandered as a pilgrim all the days of his life” (On Penance, distinction 6, chapter *Sacerdos*). Nicolaus de Fractura agrees, at least regarding deposition and confinement in a strict monastery.

## CHAPTER XLVII. On Announcing the Hour of the Work of God

[Col. 0699]

[Col. 0699C] Let the announcing of the hour of the Work of God, day and night [Note: [Col. 0699C] Another reading: “of the hour to be announced.” Narbonne: “days and nights.” Florence: “days and nights.”], be the abbot’s concern [Note: [Col. 0699C] Another reading: “the abbot’s.”], or let him himself announce it [Note: [Col. 0699C] Compostela: “or let him himself announce it.” Another reading: “or let him announce it himself.”], or let him entrust this responsibility to some attentive brother [Note: [Col. 0700C] Hildemar: “or to another.”], so that everything may be completed at the proper times. Let those who have been ordered to do so impose the psalms or antiphons after the abbot, in their proper order. Let no one presume to sing or read [Note: [Col. 0700C] Cassinese, Florence, Haeften: “and read.”] unless he is able to perform the office itself [Note: [Col. 0700C] The Council manuscript omits “itself.”] in such a way that the hearers may be edified. Let this be done with humility, seriousness, and trembling, and by whomever the abbot has ordered.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0699]

[Col. 0699C] “Let the announcing of the hour of the Work of God be the abbot’s concern, day and night, or let him himself announce it.”] One is at first surprised that Saint Benedict should appoint an abbot, burdened with various cares, to announce the hours of the Work of God. Yet, so that the dignity of the person inviting the brethren to the divine work might correspond to the dignity of that work, it was fitting that the office be assigned to one who held the first place in the monastery. Moreover, since clocks did not exist in those times and it was not so easy to distinguish all the hours, the abbot was prudently and carefully assigned this office in order to prevent every occasion for murmuring among the brethren if they should happen to be summoned too early or too late. Everyone ought to depend upon his direction and will.

I am not unaware that Peter Boherius understood this text of the Rule differently. He does not wish the abbot appointed by Saint Benedict to be the one who strikes the bells, but only “that this kind of announcement be under his care, just as it is by right under the care of the archdeacon, although the sacristan is obliged to strike the bell.” But, apart from the fact that all the offices of the monastery are in this sense under the abbot’s care, the text of the Rule is so clear that it leaves no ambiguity: for it prescribes that he himself announce it, and not a few most holy abbots diligently fulfilled this duty. Yet I would not have this understood as though the abbot were absolutely bound by the precept of the Rule to announce the hours of the divine work, since the Holy Father adds:

“Or let him entrust this responsibility to some attentive brother.”] Not indiscriminately to anyone, but to an attentive brother, from whom Hildemar chiefly demands three qualities: “Understanding, so that he may understand the hours of the night; ability, so that he may be healthy and able to carry out the ministry; and diligence, so that he may not be lazy or sleepy.”

In the laura of Saint Sabbas this responsibility belonged to the steward, as is clear from his Life, no. 59 (*Third Benedictine Century*). Among our own monks it belonged to the sacristan, or, as others call him, the guardian of the oratory. We have an example of this in the Life of Saint Lioba, chapter 5. Whoever he may be, he must above all heed this admonition of Peter Damian (Opusculum 13, chapter 17):

“Let the announcer of the hours know that no one in the monastery must avoid forgetfulness more carefully than he himself. For if he does not keep the appointed time of any synaxis, whether it has been anticipated or delayed, he will unquestionably disturb the entire order of the succeeding hours. Therefore let him not devote himself to stories, let him not mingle lengthy conversations with anyone, and finally let him not inquire what is being done by secular people. Rather, let him always be intent, always watchful, and always attentive to the care entrusted to him; let him continually contemplate the necessity of the revolving sphere, which knows no rest, the passage of the stars, and the constant course of time as it slips away. Moreover, if he wishes to have daily knowledge for distinguishing the hours, let him make a practice of psalmody, so that whenever the brightness of the sun or the variety of the stars cannot be seen because of the density of the clouds, he may measure out for himself, in the quantity of psalmody he has maintained, something like a clock.”

Boherius observes that this text of the Rule can be understood in two ways: “Either the abbot entrusts to a brother the responsibility of striking the bell and discerning when it ought to be struck, or merely that of discerning when it ought to be struck. Hence,” he says, “I have seen in some monasteries that this responsibility belonged to the first cantor; in others, to the cloister prior or subprior. When it was time, according to his judgment, to strike the canonical hours, such a man would signal the sacristan that it was time to strike Prime, Terce, or another hour. Or he would pull a small bell, which among us is called a *mostata*. By means of this same little bell a signal is also given to the sacristan or to the one striking the bell that he should stop ringing, because it is not customary for the sacristan to cease from the first ringing of the hours until the signal has been given to him.”

Someone may ask what signals the ancient monks used to summon the brethren to the Work of God. I answer that they did this chiefly in four ways.

First, by a trumpet—more probably a horn than a bronze instrument, since they were entirely without metal. This may be seen in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 2, and in Saint John Climacus, Step 19.

Second, by a wooden board, as is clear from the Life of Saint Theodosius the Coenobiarch, nos. 73 and 77, in the Bollandists under 11 January; from the *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 11; from the fourth act of the Second Council of Nicaea; and from the Life of Saint Nicholas the Studite, who flourished in the ninth century, no. 50, in the Bollandists under 4 February.

Third, by a voice raised in song, for example, “Alleluia.” Thus Saint Jerome, speaking of the monastery of Saint Paula, says (Letter 27): “After the Alleluia had been sung—the signal by which they were summoned to the assembly—no one was permitted to remain seated.”

Fourth, by a bell, as may be gathered from Cumineus Albus in the Life of Saint Columba, no. 22 (*First Benedictine Century*): “At midnight, when the bell sounded, he rose quickly and went to the church.” And no. 25: “One day the holy man suddenly ordered his servant to strike the bell. At its sound the brethren were roused and immediately entered the church.”

If Saint Benedict wished bells to be used, as is probable, they were certainly not large ones, but entirely small ones, since he often wished them to be struck by the abbot alone, who was frequently an old man. Hence the Cistercians are to be praised, for their Institutions say (Distinct. 1, chapter 12): “The bells of our Order are to be made in such a way that only one person strikes them, and never two together.” Nevertheless, a contrary practice prevailed in our Order, so that monasteries had many large bells, as is evident from the Life of Abbot Sturm and from the Life of Saint Angilbert.

Someone may further ask how many signals should be struck for each of the canonical hours. Among the ancient commentators on the Rule, Hildemar declares that three signals should be struck for Vigils: one for Matins and Prime; two for Terce, Sext, and None; three for Vespers; and one for Compline. Regarding Terce, Sext, and None, there is a canon of the Council of Aachen: “Only two signals are to be struck for Terce, Sext, and None.” For Vespers we have an example in Book I of the Miracles of Saint Bertin, chapter 5 (Bollandists, third century, part I): “When the signal of the evening synaxis had sounded for the third time, etc.”

The customs of Einsiedeln—or rather, the manuscript customs of all Germany—define the matter somewhat differently (no. 2):

“At all times, when the brethren must rise for Vigils, the smallest signal is struck until the boys assemble for the first prayer, or indeed until all the brethren have assembled. After the prayer has been completed three times before the three altars, with everyone seated in the choir, the next signal is struck; after an interval another is struck; after another interval yet another is sounded; and after a further interval, if the feast is one of twelve readings, all the signals are struck at the end; if it is not, the two signals that have not yet been struck are sounded, if there are that many.

“This distinction is observed among the signals of the nocturnal divine office: when they are to be sounded for the office, they begin with the lesser and proceed in order to the greater, leaving a rather long interval between each one, in the same order [lacuna]

“For the day hours there are two signals. The first is struck until the boys come to prayer or complete it; the second, until the prior gives the sign to stop, or until he is first asked by the guardian, if he is able to be present. In summer, on ordinary days, this is done at Terce and Sext—the prior announces Prime—by the principal signal. None is also announced by a smaller signal for washing, and then by the larger one [lacuna]

“Vespers is handled in the same way as the nocturnal office, with one signal or interval fewer, as stated above. Compline is sounded with the same signal as Chapter, and that same signal is struck three times.

“In winter, after Matins, on ordinary days, if there is daylight, Prime is struck with the smallest signal. The same signal is used for the second hour, for putting on shoes, washing, and the three prayers; then the principal signal, and afterward the medium signal for Terce.”

See the Bursfeld Ordinance, chapter 26.

[Col. 0702C] “Let those who have been ordered to do so impose the psalms or antiphons after the abbot, in their proper order.”] What Saint Benedict says—“after the abbot, in their proper order”—can be understood in two ways.

First, that, with the abbot omitted, those who stand after him should each impose the psalms and antiphons in his own order. Bernard of Cassino understands Saint Benedict in this sense, asserting that the obligation of singing is not imposed on the abbot, since it may happen that he does not know the chant or does not possess an instrument suitable for accompanying it, although he may be fully capable of much more important duties, both spiritual and temporal, in the governance of the monastery.

Second, that the abbot should impose the first one, and afterward those who have been ordered to do so should follow him in their proper order. Thus says the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius (chapter 6):

“When they are standing for prayer, no one should presume, without the command of the father who presides, to utter a hymn of praise. This order must be observed, so that no one in the monastery presumes to take precedence in standing or singing.”

And the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen says (chapter 5):

“The priors who stand in the choir are to begin the opening verses of those who sing; or, if illness prevents them, those are to begin whom the Father has ordered, etc.”

The Cistercians also seem to have understood Saint Benedict in this way. Their Book of Usages says (chapter 68): “The abbot begins the first antiphon, or the Alleluia, at the first nocturn.” Yet it also says (chapter 78): “At Vespers the weekly cantor begins the first antiphon.”

“Let no one presume to sing or read unless he can perform the office itself, so that the hearers may be edified; let this be done with humility, seriousness, and trembling, and by whomever the abbot has ordered.”] On this passage Bernard of Cassino comments:

“Humility excludes presumption, seriousness excludes levity, and trembling excludes irreverence in the singer or reader, so that humility may be present in the mind, seriousness in outward bearing, trembling in devotion, and the abbot’s command may be made known in obedience to God and human beings.”

Nicolaus de Fractura nearly agrees with him.

## CHAPTER XLVIII. On Daily Manual Labor

[Note: [Col. 0703C] Florence: “On daily work of the hands.” Lyra: “How works of the hands are to be performed daily.”]

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703A] Idleness is the enemy of the soul. Therefore, at fixed times the brethren ought to be occupied in manual labor, and at other fixed hours in sacred reading. We believe that these two periods should be arranged in the following way: from Easter until the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0703C] Oxford: “until the Kalends of October.” Cassinese: “the Kalends of October.”], when they go out in the morning [Note: [Col. 0703C] Another reading: “from morning.”], they should work at whatever is necessary from Prime until nearly the fourth hour [Note: [Col. 0703C] Another reading: “until the fourth hour.”]. From the fourth hour until approximately the sixth hour they should devote themselves to reading [Note: [Col. 0703C] Oxford, Florence: “they should engage in reading.”].

After Sext, when they rise from the table, they should rest on their beds [Note: [Col. 0703C] Narbonne: “on their little beds.” Florence: “on their bed.”] in complete silence. Or, if anyone wishes to read, let him read for himself [Note: [Col. 0703C] Another reading omits “for himself.”] in such a way that he does not disturb another. Let None be celebrated somewhat earlier [Note: [Col. 0703C] Florence: “at the proper time.” Ebrul, Florence, Bern, Cassino: “earlier.”], at the midpoint of the eighth hour. Then let them again work at whatever has to be done until Vespers.

But if the needs of the place or poverty require that they occupy themselves personally with gathering the crops [Note: [Col. 0703C] Cassino, Florence: “gathering the crops again.”], let them not be distressed, because they are truly monks when they live by the labor of their hands, as did our fathers and the apostles [Note: [Col. 0703C] Narbonne: “as did the apostles, our fathers.”]. Let everything nevertheless be done in moderation for the sake of the fainthearted.

From the Kalends of October [Note: [Col. 0703C] Narbonne: “From the eighteenth day before the Kalends of October.” Cassinese: “the Kalends of October.”] until the beginning [Note: [Col. 0703C] Another reading: “the beginning, with the addition of ‘until.’” Another: “at the beginning.”] of Lent, let them devote themselves fully to reading until the second hour; at the second hour let Terce be celebrated; and until None let everyone work at his assigned task. When the first signal of the ninth hour has been made, let each one leave his work [Note: [Col. 0704C] Florence: “leave her work.” Oxford, Cassino, Boherius: “leave the work.”]; and let them be ready when the second signal has sounded. [Note: [Col. 0704C] Oxford adds: “As soon as the signal has been heard, leaving everything, let everyone run with the utmost haste.”] After the meal, let them devote themselves to their reading or to the psalms.

[Col. 0704A] During the days of Lent, from morning until the full third hour [Note: [Col. 0704C] Another reading: “until Terce”; and immediately afterward, “until the tenth hour.”] let them devote themselves to their reading, and until the full tenth hour [Note: [Col. 0704C] Council manuscript: “the eleventh hour.”] let them work at whatever has been assigned to them.

During these days of Lent, let everyone receive a book from the library, which he should read through in its entirety and in order. These books are to be distributed at the beginning of Lent. Above all, one or two elders should be appointed to go around the monastery during the hours when the brethren are occupied with reading, and see whether perhaps an idle brother may be found who is giving himself to idleness [Note: [Col. 0704C] Another reading: “who is idle.”] or conversation [Note: [Col. 0704C] Hildemar omits “or conversation”], and is not attentive to his reading. Such a brother is not only useless to himself, but also leads others astray [Note: [Col. 0704C] Oxford: “may exalt.” Florence: *distullit*; another reading: *distollit*]. If such a one should be found—God forbid—let him be admonished once and a second time; if he does not amend, let him undergo regular correction in such a way that the others may fear. [Col. 0704B] Nor should brother associate with brother at unsuitable hours.

Likewise, on Sunday let everyone devote himself to reading, except those who have been assigned various duties [Note: [Col. 0704C] Florence: “except the one who has been assigned.”]. But if anyone is so negligent and lazy that he neither wishes nor is able to meditate [Note: [Col. 0704C] Florence: “to meditate.”] or read, let him be assigned some work to do, so that he will not be idle [Note: [Col. 0704C] The Council manuscript omits “some work to do, so that he will not be idle.”]. For sick or delicate brothers, such work [Note: [Col. 0704C] Oxford: “such a work.”] or craft should be assigned as will neither leave them idle nor overwhelm them with the violence of labor, so that they may escape. Their weakness is to be considered by the abbot.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0703]

[Col. 0703D] “Idleness is the enemy of the soul.”] Because every idle person is ruled by desires, and the one who pursues idleness will be filled with poverty (Proverbs 21 and 28); and because idleness has taught many evils (Ecclesiasticus 33). Hence among the Egyptian monks, and as a fixed judgment sanctioned by the ancient Fathers, this saying was established: a working monk is attacked by one demon, but an idle monk is ravaged by countless spirits (Cassian, Book X, chapter 23).

Against this pestilential poison, whose various harms Cardinal de Turrecremata reports in his commentary on this passage, and Haeften in Book IX, treatise 1, discussion 1, our Fathers employed three principal remedies: prayer, reading, and labor. This may be seen in the Life of Abbot Marculf, no. 11; in the Life of Saint Wallaric; and in the Rule of Solitaries, chapter 32. Saint Benedict likewise employs these same remedies in this chapter, and therefore adds:

[Col. 0704D] “Therefore, at fixed times the brethren ought to be occupied in manual labor, and at other fixed hours in sacred reading.”] “They ought to be occupied,” he says. If they ought, then they are not legitimately excused from daily manual labor. So Peter Boherius judges in his second commentary, writing as follows:

“‘They ought,’ that is, they are obliged, since this imposes a necessity on monks, as will be said below. But surely those who live under the Rule of Pachomius, Basil, Augustine, and Francis ought also to work with their own hands? Yes, I say, since each of their Rules expressly mentions manual labor. It is fitting and proper for all religious to provide their food by their own labor, as will be said below; and Augustine proves this even more clearly in his book *On the Work of Monks*, where he answers those who say that they have, or wish to have, their exertions devoted to literary studies or preaching.”

Further on he cites the judgment of Basil, bishop of Caesarea, addressed to a certain Syncletius (Cassian, Book V, chapter 19):

“When he said that he had renounced this world, he had nevertheless kept back for himself certain possessions from his own resources, unwilling to support himself by the exercise of his hands and to seek true humility through nakedness, the hardship of work, and submission to the monastery: ‘You have lost a senator,’ he says, ‘and you have not made a monk.’”

And Saint Jerome says to Rusticus:

“If the apostles, although they had the power to live from the Gospel, worked with their own hands so as not to burden anyone, and gave relief to others for whose spiritual benefit they ought to reap material things, why do you not prepare what will later serve your own needs? Weave a little basket from rushes, or plait a basket from supple branches.”

Richard of Saint Angelo, by contrast, explains this passage of the Rule and asks himself: “When in our own time Cassinese monks and certain others do not practice manual labor, contrary to the provision of this chapter, can they be called transgressors of the Rule?” He answers:

“It must be said that they cannot, for three reasons. First, because it belongs to the abbot to command this, as it says below: ‘Let them work at whatever has been assigned to them.’ Since the abbot does not assign it, they are excused; they are not bound to do it on their own, for that would be counted as presumption, as is said in the next chapter. Second, because at the time when this arrangement was established, monasteries did not abound in riches, and therefore necessity compelled the brethren to work. Since they now abound, it is fitting that, when the cause ceases, the effect should cease as well. The cause was necessity, as I have said; the effect was manual labor. Third, because the divine offices are now celebrated with such solemnity that, once those offices have been performed, scarcely any suitable hour remains for manual labor. Perhaps this was not so then, and the greater good is to be preferred to the lesser.”

We shall examine both opinions below.

“Therefore we believe that these two periods should be arranged in this way.”] “These two periods,” he says, that is, both the periods of labor and of reading—or the periods of summer, winter, and Lent.

[Col. 0705C] “From Easter until the Kalends of October, when they go out in the morning, they should work from Prime until nearly the fourth hour.”] Bernard of Cassino interprets this passage so that, in the morning, at the beginning of daylight, the brethren begin to work until Terce is complete:

“You will note,” he says, “that according to this Rule the brethren are to devote themselves to labor from morning—that is, from the beginning of sunrise—until full Terce. For the brethren to work at the third hour, when the sun is rising, would be difficult, especially in summer. Therefore he assigns the entire period until None to reading, eating, and rest, for at that hour, when the sun is declining, one can better devote oneself to manual labor.”

Boherius copies Bernard in his customary manner, but, as it seems to me, less correctly. For on this interpretation, when would Prime be sung? Hildemar therefore understands “when they go out in the morning, from Prime” more appropriately: after Prime has been sung, followed by Chapter, in which each person’s labor is assigned, they begin to work—that is, when the first hour is nearly finished. He explains this view in the following figure:

[Col. 0705D] “When he says ‘from morning, Prime,’ he does not say that Prime should be kept at its canonical time. Rather, when he says ‘from morning, Prime,’ it is as though he were saying: ‘Let Prime be sung in the morning.’ Then, between Prime being sung and Chapter being held, the first hour is already nearly complete, as the dot in the upper part of this diagram teaches you; and the cross is the light, when Prime ought to be sung, while the dot marks when one may leave Chapter.

“Next, the expressions ‘nearly the fourth’ and ‘approximately the sixth’ are understood in various ways. Spiritual abbots observe ‘nearly the fourth,’ that is, before the fourth begins, as the dot in the third field, or space, of the clock shows. Thus, while Terce is being sung, the fourth hour begins.

“Then there is ‘approximately the sixth.’ This means before the sixth begins, as the dot in the fifth space of the clock indicates: once Sext has been sung, the sixth hour then begins.

“Secular abbots, who wish to work, understand it differently. They take ‘nearly the fourth’ to mean that some part of the fourth hour has passed, as the dot in the fourth space of the clock shows. They likewise understand ‘approximately the sixth’ to mean that some portion of the sixth hour has passed, as the dot in the sixth space indicates. [Col. 0706B] But the earlier interpretation is better, as spiritual abbots understand it.

“There is no doubt about the eighth hour. When they leave the refectory, the sixth hour is complete; then they sleep during the seventh hour and the first half of the eighth; afterward they must rise at the middle of the eighth. Vespers, however, ought to be sung at the beginning of the eleventh hour, as the cross in the tenth division teaches. Hence, if you have worked according to the canonical times, a monk ought to work four hours at every season.”

“From the fourth hour until approximately the sixth hour they should devote themselves to reading.”] Richard of Saint Angelo asks what kind of reading is intended by this passage of the holy Rule. He answers that it seems to him to mean “that the monastery—especially one that can suitably do so—should have two teachers, so that one may teach grammar and the other theology.” Haeften (Book IX, treatise 4, discussion 1), however, interprets Saint Benedict as referring: first, to pious or, as it is called, spiritual reading; second, to theological reading; and third, to the reading of the psalms.

“After Sext, when they rise from the table, they should rest on their beds.”] Sleep at midday was plainly familiar to the ancient monks, as is clear both from this passage of the Benedictine Rule and from the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, which decrees (chapter 11):

“In summer no one may sleep at midday except in his own little bed, unless, by order of the prior, he should sleep outside his own bed beneath the clouds to guard the threshing floor.”

The Rule of Tarnat says (chapter 9): “From the sixth hour until the ninth let them devote themselves to rest or reading.” The Rule of Saint Isidore says (chapter 6): “In summer one ought to work from morning until the third hour; from the third until the sixth hour one should devote oneself to reading; thereafter one should rest until the ninth.” The Rule of Saint Fructuosus prescribes (chapter 6) that “when the office of Sext has been completed, they should go from prayer to the tables; after they have eaten, let them again pray and rest, so that silence may be maintained until the ninth hour.” Finally, an anonymous manuscript Rule says (chapter 2): “After the meal, at the sixth hour, as Blessed Benedict and the other Fathers teach, one must either rest or read.”

The practice of this may be seen in Book I of the Dialogues of Saint Gregory and in the Life of Saint Maglorius, no. 24, Bollandists, first Benedictine century. Saint John Climacus also testifies (Step 27) that it is difficult to ward off sleep in the afternoon hours.

Several observations must be made concerning this midday sleep.

First, Saint Benedict did not grant it throughout the entire year, but only from Easter until the Kalends of October—that is, until 14 September, when the Kalends of October begin to be counted. Hence the Statutes of Lanfranc say (chapter 1, § 1): “At the Kalends of October the midday rest which the monks customarily take in summer is to cease.” Udalric likewise says: “From the Kalends of October . . . the midday rest is entirely discontinued.” It is clear from chapter 11 of the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen and from the ancient Statutes of the Carthusians that this was also adopted as a practice by others. There is a special reason why this midday rest is granted in summer rather than at other times: namely, because of the excessive heat of summer and the shortness of the nights. The Master in chapter 50 of his Rule and Peter Damian in *Opusculum* 15, chapter 17, indicate this reason.

Second, some extended this indulgence of Saint Benedict to other times as well. Among these could be counted the Roman monks of the monastery of Saint Andrew, of whom Saint Gregory writes (Book IX, Letter 38) that “on the feast day of that same apostle the brethren were already resting at midday,” and therefore in the month of November—unless someone should say that this was peculiar to them on that day because of the work of the solemnity, which they had endured in anticipating the vigils and celebrating the other offices.

Third, most people anticipated the time prescribed by the Holy Father. For according to the widespread common practice of our Order, the midday rest began on Palm Sunday. At present, however, the Cassinese begin it on the feast of Saint Benedict, when Easter falls in April.

Fourth, when the need of the place or poverty required that they occupy themselves personally with gathering the crops, the midday sleep was entirely omitted, according to the canon of the Council of Aachen (canon 17):

“If necessity should require the brethren to be occupied in gathering the crops, the appointed time for reading and resting at midday is to be omitted.”

The Cistercian monks, however, did not obey this statute even when sleeping in the fields, as we gather from the Book of Usages, where we read the following concerning the time of mowing and harvest (chapter 84):

“At these times the community usually works until Sext and, if necessary, goes out before Prime; they eat lunch outside the monastery and, if necessary, sleep there. The cook and the reader are to take their mixed portion.”

The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen likewise permits this in these words (chapter 11):

“In the field, when the harvest is being gathered, if it is permitted to sleep at midday, they should not sleep separately, but in one place or in two places.”

Fifth, since Saint Benedict says that, after Sext, they should rise from the table and rest on their beds, he seems to have granted no further rest on Wednesdays and Fridays, when the brethren eat at the ninth hour. Certainly the Statutes of Lanfranc appear to exclude fast days from the midday rest. Nevertheless, the common practice of our Order prevailed, so that on these days the monks still slept at the sixth hour, in accordance with the prescription of the Council of Aachen (canon 71): “When the brethren fast in summer, let them sleep after Sext.”

Peter the Venerable testifies (Statute 25) that “it was an ancient custom of monks, on fast days, to compensate by suitable sleep before the meal for the loss of their customary sleep; hence Jerome says: ‘One must often sleep on an empty stomach.’”

The Rule of the Master likewise says (chapter 50): “Immediately after Sext, both after the meal and during a fast, everyone should take a moderate midday rest in his own bed.”

The Cistercians accordingly decree in their Book of Usages (chapter 84):

“If it is a fast day, after all the prescribed observances have been completed, the lay brothers leading the way, they are to enter the dormitory after Sext and rest in their beds until the eighth hour, etc.”

The Cluniacs on these days simulated rather than actually took their midday rest. This was the reason that Peter the Venerable issued the decree (Statute 25):

“Let the momentary and sham midday rests of fast days, which are customarily taken after Sext in summer, be discontinued; and in place of the time that was uselessly spent, let the brethren sit in the cloister and read, or sing Masses, or perform some necessary work.”

Others adopted another arrangement, sleeping between Lauds and Prime, as we read in the Customs of the monastery of Fleury (chapter 2):

“On all the fasts that occur from Easter until the Ides of September, we go to sleep after Matins until Prime in place of the midday rest, and we eat after None.”

Formerly the Cluniacs also observed the same arrangement during the Rogation season, according to Udalric, Book I, chapter 21.

Sixth, because midday sleep is commonly considered harmful, Haeften (Book XII, treatise 2, discussion 6) requires five conditions so that it may not harm one’s health: first, that it be habitual; second, that it not take place immediately after food has been eaten; third, that the head be raised rather than lowered; fourth, that it not be excessive; fifth, that awakening be gentle and moderate, not tumultuous and sudden.

The second and third conditions, however, conflict with the Rule, which wishes them, when they rise from the table, to rest on their beds. Nevertheless, Abbot Saint Wolphelm of Bruviller, at midday, slept not lying down but sitting, as Conrad writes in his Life, no. 40 (Bollandists, 22 April).

“With complete silence.”] Saint Adalard elegantly describes how great that silence ought to be in his Statutes (Book II, chapter 6, *Spicilegium*, vol. IV):

“When the time for sleeping has arrived, whether by day or by night, just as there must be complete silence in the mouth, so also there must be the utmost care in one’s walking, so that no one suffers injury. No one should shake out his clothing; no one should carelessly climb into or descend from bed; no one should carelessly do anything else of the same kind that might produce a sound through noise or inconvenience to anyone. At all times, as was said above, every precaution must be observed there, both for the sake of propriety and for the rest of the sick, lest, if someone should happen to wish to rest there because necessity compels him, he be disturbed by another’s misconduct.”

See Udalric, Book II, chapter 24.

“Or certainly, whoever wishes to read should read in such a way as not to disturb another.” Concerning this reading we have a canon of the Council of Aachen (canon 38): “When the brothers sleep after Sext, if any one of them wishes to read, let him read in the church or in his own bed.” The customs of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, agree with this canon (*Analecta*, vol. IV):

> “After the meal they return quickly to their beds, especially the young or negligent, whose conduct is being observed. If there are some of whom a good opinion is held, and they wish it, let them be permitted to devote a little time—but briefly—to prayer in the church. But no one is to be found in the cloister or in a forbidden place, lest, God forbid, anyone should devote himself to conversation or idleness.”

The monks of Saint Benignus at Dijon do not even allow a brief sitting in the church. Rather, they say (chapter 43):

> “No one may ever leave the dormitory after entering it for the midday rest or for Compline, except those who are needed outside on account of guests, such as the guest-master, almoner, granary-keeper, and similar officials, if the cellarer has summoned them. If this has happened, it must be corrected with extraordinary severity, unless it happens to someone of much-experienced and mature character whose nose bleeds or whose arm bleeds profusely; such a person may leave the dormitory at midday and go to the washroom. For at night the door of the dormitory is locked, and one must go to the necessary places.”

Nevertheless, the Cluniacs were permitted to sing or read in the cloister, as Udalricus teaches (*Book II, chapter 24*). It is also recorded that Saint Anselm, prior of Bec, devoted himself at midday to correcting books in the cloister (*Life of Anselm*, no. 21, Bollandists, 21 April). The ancient statutes of the Carthusians, however, do not permit this. There it is written (Part II, chapter 18):

> “In summer, when some are working or correcting books, they must not work during the time of sleep without special permission.”

### “And let None be Celebrated Too Early, in the Middle of the Eighth Hour”

That is, in the middle of the time after the seventh hour has elapsed and before the ninth has begun, as Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fracture, Peter Boherius, and John of Turrecremata explain. Thus they devoted an entire hour and a half to sleep: the whole seventh hour and half of the eighth.

The Rules of Tarnat, Saint Isidore, and Saint Fructuosus grant three hours for the midday rest. From Easter onward, the Cassinese (*Cassinese Declaration*, chapter 48)—that is, from the feast of Saint Benedict until mid-April—sleep and keep silence for one hour; from mid-April until mid-August, for two hours; and from then until the Ides of September, for one hour.

As for silence, Hildemar writes that it ought to begin at Terce, although the Rule does not say this; undoubtedly he is speaking according to the custom of his monastery.

### “[Col. 0709A] But if the Necessity of the Place or Poverty should Require Them to Occupy Themselves Personally with Gathering the Crops”

This was done even with the reading omitted, as prescribed by the previously cited canon 17 of the Council of Aachen, and earlier by the Second and Third Rules of the Holy Fathers, chapter 5, and the Rule of Saint Macarius, chapter 10. Faustus also records that Saint Maurus did this (*Life of Saint Maurus*, no. 15): he writes that Maurus went out with the brothers to gather crops at some distance from the monastery and returned with those same brothers at the sixth hour, the hour of the meal, although according to the Rule they ought to have been reading from the fourth to the sixth hour. See the Rule of Saint Donatus for Virgins, chapter 20.

### “For They Are Truly Monks When They Live by the Labor of Their Hands”

This should not be understood as though those who omit rural work and, having other means by which to live religiously, devote themselves to reading and prayer were not true monks. He said this for the consolation of those whom poverty compels to obtain their livelihood by the labor of their hands, as Hildemar explains.

Or else, as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius say:

> “Because poverty and occupation in labor contribute greatly to the monastic state.”

Thus Saint Basil, instructing monks, says (*Sermon 1, On the Institution of Monks*):

> “The means of seeking a livelihood that should be judged most suitable for those who live in this kind of life is precisely that prescribed by the Apostle: namely, that while laboring with their hands each one should eat his own bread honestly . . . so that his command may be fulfilled who orders us to acquire our livelihood in sweat and labor, and to preserve the dignity of honesty free from reproach and stigma, since no necessity of daily sustenance compels them to appear in public.”

### “Just as Our Fathers and the Apostles Did”

The commentators Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata interpret “our fathers” as the ancient monks Paul, Anthony, Hilarion, and others, or as the Fathers of the Old Testament—Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. “But the former meaning is better,” says Hildemar.

Their imitators in Ireland were the first disciples of Saint Finan the abbot (*Life of Saint Finan*, no. 6, Bollandists, 17 February):

> “Working with their hands, after the manner of hermits, they plowed the earth with a hoe, and, rejecting animals, possessed not even one cow. Whenever anyone offered them something of milk or butter, they no longer accepted it.”

Such were the monks of Bangor (*Life of Saint Augustine, Bishop of Canterbury*, first century), “whose number was reckoned at more than two thousand,” and yet “all lived by the labor of their hands.”

Among our own, such were the monks of Fulda, whom Saint Boniface, writing to Pope Zacharias, declared to be men “of strict abstinence, without meat and wine, without beer and servants, content with the labor of their own hands.”

Such also were the monks of Ohrdruf, founded by Boniface (*Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 8, third century of the Benedictines), who, according to Saint Willibald,

> “laboriously acquired food and clothing for themselves with their own hands, after the apostolic manner.”

Such were the Vallombrosans, of whom it is written in the *Life of Saint Aibert* (Surius, 7 April):

> “The institution and canon of Saint Benedict are strictly and inviolably observed, and they live by the labor of their hands.”

Finally, such were the first disciples of Robert of Arbrissel, as Baldric, bishop of Dol, teaches in his *Life* (no. 17, Bollandists, 25 February).

Yet there were serious men who condemned such work in the fields as contrary and harmful to monastic observance. When the abbot wished to send the brothers outside to gather olives, Saint Nonnosus, provost of the monastery of Soracte, “forbade it with great humility, lest, while the brothers went out seeking the profits of oil, they should suffer loss of their souls” (Saint Gregory, *Dialogues*, book I, chapter 7).

John Trithemius, addressing his own monks, says (*Homily 7*):

> “There is another consideration that stirs my mind, so that I may not easily occupy you with external manual works without reasonable cause and evident necessity. For I find that labors of this kind do not suit your regular observance; rather, they destroy the integrity of monastic discipline among you more than they advance it. I am ashamed to say it, yet I am compelled to speak: your labors outside the monastery and cell bring more destruction to the purity of your souls than salvation. For what are your labors? Is it not wandering and running about, indulging in feasts and drinking, and occupying the remaining time with vain and useless conversations? You do not possess within yourselves that holy fervor of the Spirit of God with which we read that the monks of our original institution were once inflamed . . .

> “During the time of the regular fast, they either carefully observed the measure of abstinence prescribed for themselves or, if they rested because of the magnitude of their labors, they ate only enough to make themselves fit and capable for work. But you do not eat in order to work; rather, you work in order to eat, at the time when, according to the Rule, you ought to be fasting. You take the fast as an occasion for breaking the fast.

> “Moreover, what lover devoted to regular discipline could calmly endure the filthy and disgraceful way in which some of you treat your garments? Whose are the things you wastefully consume, my brothers? Everything that belongs to the monasteries of the servants of God is Christ’s patrimony . . . Your labors outside the monastery have therefore been reduced, lest by working badly you sin more grievously.”

The mind of William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, seems to have been similar when, writing to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, he said (chapter 22):

> “Outdoor exercises and works, just as they distract the senses, so they often also exhaust the spirit”; yet they sometimes benefit devout men for the salvation of the soul, “since with the heavier labor of rural works there is greater bodily contrition, even unto contrition and humility of heart; and under the pressure of their fatigue they often express a more intense feeling of devotion. This is likewise clearly seen in the labor of fasts, vigils, and all practices in which the body is afflicted.”

Nor does Saint Benedict prescribe this absolutely (chapter 66), especially since he does not want it to be necessary for monks to wander outside, because this is wholly unprofitable for their souls. For, as Rupert says (*Book III on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 5):

> “From these words it is clear that he does not wish monks to be occupied in those manual works that can be carried out only outside; he permits this only when necessity requires it.”

### “During the Days of Lent, Let Them Devote Themselves to Their Reading from Morning until the Full Third Hour, and Let Them Work Fully until the Tenth Hour at Whatever Is Enjoined upon Them”

Explaining this passage, Hildemar says:

> “When he says, ‘In Lent let them work until the full tenth hour,’ he says ‘full’ because at that time Mass was not sung in his monastery. Now, however, since Mass is sung, the brothers cannot work until the full tenth hour, sing Mass, and do everything while there is still daylight. Rather, the abbot must see to it that they work until such a time that they can sing Mass and Vespers, eat, and do everything in daylight. Therefore the tenth hour should not be full; when the tenth hour begins, they should sing None. Then, after None has been sung, Mass should immediately be sung. After a short interval, Vespers should be sung.”

Here he had in view that canon of the Council of Aachen:

> “In Lent the brothers are to work until None, so that after Mass has been celebrated they may be refreshed at the proper time.”

But no trace of this discipline now appears. Indeed, in Boherius’s time, after the sixth hour had passed, Mass had already been sung, and they refreshed themselves after None, as he himself testifies in his first commentary on this passage:

> “Today among us, and in the Roman Curia, the hours do not run so late; indeed, Mass is generally finished at the sixth hour, and when Vespers has ended and the brothers enter the refectory, the tenth hour begins. Although this is contrary to chapter 41 at the end, and to *De Consecratione*, distinction 1, chapter ‘Solent,’ it nevertheless does not seem very far removed from the Rule.”

Thus far we have heard Saint Benedict assigning hours to reading and manual labor. Now the nature of our office requires us to report what the founders of other monastic rules prescribed on this subject.

### [Col. 0711A]

Saint Anthony speaks only generally (no. 36):

> “Compel yourself to the work of your hands, and the fear of the Lord will dwell in you.”

And below (no. 40):

> “When you sit in your cell, be continually attentive to these three things: the work of your hands, meditation on your psalms, and your prayer.”

The same is read in the Rule of Abbot Isaiah, numbers 7 and 11.

The Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius says (chapter 10):

> “The brothers must keep this order: from the first hour until the third hour let them devote themselves to God. From the third hour until the ninth, let them do without any murmuring whatever has been enjoined by the Father.”

The Second Rule of the Holy Fathers says (chapter 5):

> “Let the brothers have such meditation that they read until the second hour, provided no circumstance arises that makes it necessary, even with meditation omitted, to do something for the community. After the second hour, let each one complete without murmuring or hesitation whatever has been enjoined, until the ninth hour.”

The same is found in the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers, chapter 5, and in the Rule of Saint Macarius, chapters 10 and 11.

The Rule of an uncertain author says (chapter 2):

> “Let them work from morning until Sext; from Sext until None let them devote themselves to reading; at None let them return the books; and after they have refreshed themselves, whether in the garden or wherever necessary, let them work until the lighting hour.”

The Rule of Saint Caesarius for Monks says (chapter 14):

> “At all times let them read until Terce; after Terce, let each one do the work assigned to him.”

His Rule for Virgins likewise says (chapters 17 and 18):

> “At all times let them devote two hours to reading, that is, from morning until the second hour; during the remaining part of the day let them do their work and not occupy themselves with conversations.”

The Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks says (chapter 24):

> “Throughout the day, while they work with their hands, let holy meditation not cease from the heart,”

that is, from the third hour. For later he establishes (chapter 28):

> “When Matins has been completed, let Prime immediately be said; then until the third hour let everyone devote himself to reading.”

The same is found in his Rule for Virgins, chapter 20.

The Rule of Saint Ferreolus says (chapter 26):

> “At every season the monk, both the oldest and the youngest, should make every effort to devote himself to reading until the third hour of the day; only then should care for the work assigned to him follow during the remainder of the day, except for the sick, upon whom the common infirmity does not permit this to be imposed against their own will, or rather their strength.”

The Rule of Saint Columbanus says (chapter 3):

> “One must fast daily, just as one must pray daily; one must work daily and read daily.”

The Rule of Tarnat says (chapter 9):

> “At every season they shall devote two hours a day to spiritual meditation. In summer, after Matins has been completed according to custom and Prime has been said, let all undertake the works that are commanded. Then, after Terce has been celebrated, let them return to completing what they had undertaken . . . From the sixth hour until None let them devote themselves to rest or even to reading. After None, whether in the garden or wherever usefulness requires, let them all provide mutual assistance until the lighting hour. In winter, after Matins or Prime has passed, permission is granted for all to devote themselves to reading until Terce. When it has ended, let them hasten gladly to fulfill what has been enjoined upon them, as already stated, until the lighting hour.”

### [Col. 0711D]

The Rule of Saint Isidore says (chapter 6):

> “In summer one ought to work from morning until the third hour. From Terce until Sext one should devote oneself to reading; thereafter one should rest until None. After None one should work again until the evening hour. At other times—that is, in autumn, winter, or spring—one should read from morning until Terce; after the celebration of Terce one should work until None. After the meal at None, one ought either to work, to read, or to meditate aloud on something.”

### [Col. 0712A]

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 6), after Prime has been said, prescribes work until the third hour of the day; after Terce has been said, reading or prayer; after the meal, rest and silence until None. Then, if necessary, they are to return to work until they assemble for the office of the twelfth hour.

The Rule of a Certain Author writes generally for monks (chapter 12):

> “Monks ought always to work and pass their lives without anxiety. Everything they produce by labor, except—as we have said above—a little bread and clothing, they should distribute to the poor.”

The Rule of the Master says (chapter 50) that in winter, from the winter solstice—which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October—until Easter, because it is cold and the brothers cannot work in the morning, they are to read “from Prime until Terce.” After Terce has been said, they are to work until Sext. After Sext has been sung, they are to work again until None; after None has likewise been completed, they are to work until the lighting hour.

“In summer, however, that is, from Easter until the winter solstice, which is the eighth day before the Kalends of October, because it is cooler in the morning, let them work from Prime until Terce, so that they may not be deprived of the fresh and pleasant—or oppressive—sleep of the short nights. Likewise, after Terce has been said, let them work until Sext.”

After Sext and the brief rest that followed it, let them devote themselves again to work until None; thereafter, from the lighting hour begun somewhat early, to reading.

The Rule of Solitaries prescribes (chapter 40):

> “At every season let them devote themselves to reading from morning until almost the third hour; from the third hour until approximately the ninth, let them work at whatever is necessary, unless perhaps they wish to rest briefly on their beds in summer; and let prayer always be interwoven with work. From the ninth hour until evening let them devote themselves again to prayer and reading.”

The manuscript Rule of an uncertain author (chapter 2, in a codex of the Royal Library of Sweden) says:

> “From Holy Easter until the Kalends of October, after the office of Matins, let Prime immediately follow, and until Terce they are to work with their hands together with divine meditation. After Terce, the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated. When this has been completed, they are to devote themselves to sacred reading until Sext. After Sext, unless it is the fourth, sixth, or seventh feria, they are to refresh themselves. After the meal, as Blessed Benedict and the other Fathers teach, they are either to rest or to read until None. After None they ought to work and sing psalms until Vespers. After the evening office, permission to eat has been granted by certain holy Fathers to those who need it. After this, as much as the hour allows, they are to devote themselves to reading; and while it is still daylight they are to celebrate Compline.”

In the following chapter it says that from the Kalends of October until Easter:

> “The solemn office is to be performed at midnight; when it has been completed, the entire remainder of the night is to be spent in divine prayers until morning. The solemnity of Matins is to be celebrated as daylight begins . . . After the office of Matins has been completed, [Note: Here and below, wherever we have placed asterisks, the syntax requires an ablative absolute. Editor.] one must devote oneself more secretly and most earnestly to God alone in prayers until the second hour of the day . . . After the aforesaid office of Prime has been completed*, let holy reading not leave your hands until the third hour of the day . . . After the third hour has been completed*, one ought to work with one’s own hands, together with divine songs, until the sixth hour . . . When the office of the sixth hour has been completed, hasten again, as above, with divine meditation, to undertake some work with your own hands until the ninth hour . . . After None, the solemnities of Mass are to be celebrated. After this, sacred reading is to be embraced in one’s hands with compunction of heart until the evening office . . . After the meal, let holy reading again rise into one’s hands until the end of daylight.”

The Rule of Saint Donatus for Virgins says (chapter 20):

> “From the second hour until the third, if there is no necessity requiring them to work, let them devote themselves to reading; during the remaining part of the day let them do their work and not occupy themselves with conversations, because of the Apostle’s saying: ‘Working in silence.’”

### [Col. 0713A]

Another Rule for Virgins by a Certain Author says (chapter 12):

> “Manual labor is to begin at the second hour and come to an end at the ninth. From the ninth hour reading is to be practiced. If at any time some particular work must be done, such as sewing or washing a garment, or any other task, she may do it with the permission of the abbess or superior, and so forth.”

The Rule of Blessed Aelred, abbot, for Virgins (chapter 14) prescribes that from the Kalends of November until Lent, after the nocturnal vigils, they devote themselves until dawn to reading, prayer, or some manual work. As dawn whitens, they are to perform the morning praises with the hymns of Prime, and thus, alternating reading, prayers, and psalms, await Terce:

> “When it has been said,” he writes, “let them be occupied in manual labor until the ninth hour.”

From Easter until the aforementioned Kalends (chapter 15):

> “After Prime has been said, let her begin the sacrifice of the day’s work until the third hour. Let her occupy her spirit with reading and prayer until Sext. After Sext, having taken food, let her rest on her little bed until None; and thus let her work with her hands until Vespers.”

In Lent (chapter 18):

> “After Prime has been said following Matins, let her devote herself to psalms and readings until the full third hour. When the praise of the third hour has been completed, let her diligently apply herself to manual labor until the ninth hour, inserting brief prayers at intervals. After this, when Vespers has been said, let her refresh her body; and thus, singing psalms, let her await the time of Compline.”

Finally, the Statutes of Guigo, prior of the Carthusian monastery, say (chapter 29):

> “The period from Terce until Sext in winter, and from Prime until Terce in summer, is assigned to manual works; nevertheless, we wish these works to be interrupted by brief prayers . . . and the time separating None and Vespers is occupied with manual works.”

The ancient statutes of the Carthusians say the same, but add (Part I, chapter 41, no. 20):

> “Moreover, by the periods assigned to manual works we do not intend to exclude the benefit of reading.”

Finally, concerning Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, and his first disciples, we read in his *Life*, book I, no. 15 (*Miscellanea*, vol. IV of Baluze):

> “Manual labor was constant and more burdensome than usual both for him and for the brothers. The entire span of the day was not sufficient for it, and for this reason they very often postponed the meal itself until Vespers, lest anything be diminished from the day’s work on its account.”

From all this it is clear how highly manual labor was valued among the ancient monks, who devoted so many hours of the day to it. Some may now wish to know by what particular kinds of work they occupied such a large amount of time.

Concerning the Pachomians, who were the first of all to follow the coenobitic life, Palladius writes (*Lausiac History*, chapter 39):

> “They practice every craft, and from what remains they even build monasteries and lodgings for women. Thus, rising in the morning, those to whom this duty falls in turn are occupied: some in the kitchen, others in preparing the tables, placing upon them bread, wild vegetables, olives, cheeses, the less desirable parts of meat, and chopped vegetables. The less robust enter and eat at the seventh hour, since they are weaker; others at the ninth, others at the tenth, others late in the evening, others after two days, others after three days, others after four days, and others after five days, so that each element indicates its own hour.

> “Their works were likewise arranged as follows: one worked at cultivating the field, another in the garden, another in the bakery, another in the bronze workshop, another at construction, another in the fuller’s trade, another in preparing leather, another in sewing shoes, another in beautiful writing, another wove large baskets, and another smaller baskets and panniers. Yet all of them could recite the Scriptures from memory.”

Concerning the Basilians, Saint Basil himself must be heard (*Longer Rules*, chapter 38):

> “It is not easy to prescribe particular crafts one by one, because different things are required in different places according to the convenience of each locality’s occupations. Their choice can be determined in general terms: those crafts are suitable for us that preserve the peaceful and tranquil state of our life, that require neither much business to obtain suitable material nor much trouble to distribute what has been made, and that do not bring us into unbecoming association with men or women.

> “We must particularly observe frugality and lowliness, taking care not to serve the foolish and harmful desires of the world by making the things they desire. Thus, in weaving, we should admit into our work whatever serves ordinary commerce according to the custom of life, not what is devised for the plunder and entanglement of young men by the impure and wanton. Likewise, in shoemaking, we should serve by that craft those who require necessary articles for use.

> “The crafts of architects, smiths, bronze-workers, and agriculture, although necessary in themselves for human life and greatly useful, and although they should not be rejected by us on account of their nature, must nevertheless be avoided if they are found at times to generate disturbances among us or to disrupt the gathering of the brothers. We should prefer those crafts that preserve for us a life undivided and devoted to God, and that do not draw us away from the opportunity for singing psalms and praying, or from any other aspect of the discipline of piety.

> “Otherwise, if they cause no harm to the primary purpose of our life, they are to be preferred to many others, especially agriculture, which supplies from itself the necessities of life and frees farmers from the trouble of performing many tasks and running back and forth—provided, as we have said, that it produces no disturbance or tumult either among our neighbors or within the household.”

Elsewhere he says (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 6):

> “It is fitting for a religious person to work at those things that suit him, namely, whatever is free from commerce, remote occupations, and dishonorable profit, and whatever can be completed while we remain under the roof, as many things can. Thus the work is completed and tranquility preserved. If, however, because of some necessity, work must be completed outdoors, this too will not impede philosophy, and so forth.”

Saint Jerome, instructing the monk Rusticus on the ordering of his life (*Letter 4*), recommends these works:

> “Either weave a little basket from rushes, or plait a basket from supple twigs. Let the ground be hoed, and let the garden beds be divided by an even boundary. When seeds of vegetables have been sown in them and plants set out in orderly rows, let irrigation channels be led to them . . . Graft unproductive trees with buds or shoots, so that shortly afterward you may gather the sweet fruits of your labor. Make beehives for the bees to which the proverbs of Solomon send you, and learn in their small bodies the order of monasteries and royal discipline. Let linen threads also be woven for catching fish. Let books be written, so that the hand may produce food and the mind be nourished by reading.”

[Note: Read “they send,” which requires no subjunctive. Editor.]

Finally, in the Rule of Saint Ferreolus (chapter 28) we read:

> “Therefore, let no one think that, if he is unable to perform some work, he has offered a reason for a just excuse. For he who, as we said above, cannot practice agriculture can read and write—which is the principal work—provide for the catching of fish, weave nets, prepare footwear for the brothers, or perform and complete other similar tasks.”

And in the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 6):

> “The brothers should cultivate vegetable gardens and prepare food with their own hands; but the construction of buildings and the cultivation of fields should belong to the work of servants.”

See the *Life of Saint Sequanius*, no. 12; the *Life of Saint Gall*, chapter 6; and the *Life of Saint Stephen of Obazine*, book I, no. 15.

As for our own monks, there is no doubt that their various labors differed according to the circumstances of times, places, and persons. At the very beginning of the nascent order, when they had little income and sought places for living far from the crowds of men, as soon as they had chosen a place in which to settle, they immediately considered building a monastery there. They built it with their own hands, both because necessity required it and because of their love of penance, as Saint Gregory testifies that Saint Benedict did at Cassino (*Dialogues*, book II, chapters 9 and 11).

We have an outstanding example of this in William, abbot of Hirsau (Trithemius, *Chronicle of Hirsau*, year 1082). He had resolved “to build a monastery” and completed it over nine years through his monks. Since there were nearly two hundred of them, there were among them stonecutters, smiths, carpenters, ironworkers, and architects highly skilled in every art and science of architecture; they completed the entire work without the assistance of secular craftsmen, with an excellent timber structure, as the church is seen today.

Indeed, as another William says (William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, chapter 12):

> “It is not fitting that the tabernacle of God with men should be made by men of the world. Those to whom the model of the true beauty of God’s house is shown in the heights of the mind should build it for themselves. Those whom inward concern for themselves commands to despise and neglect all outward things should build for themselves the form of poverty, the appearance of holy simplicity, and the features of ancestral frugality. No craftsmanship will fit it so well as their own negligence.”

Then, since at that time they possessed no property—neither vineyards nor livestock—as Ardo writes concerning the first disciples of Benedict of Aniane, they procured food for themselves with their own hands by cultivating the fields. Saint Gregory attributes this labor to Saint Benedict; Faustus to Saint Maurus; an anonymous author in the *Life of Saint Philibert* to the monks of Jumièges; Bede, in the *Life of Saint Benedict Biscop*, to the monks of Wearmouth; and book II of the *Deeds of the Saints of Redon* to the monks of Redon.

Saint Junianus seems to have preferred such labors above others. According to Wulfinus Boetius, when he complained to the king about the poverty of his monastery (*First Century of the Benedictines*), he declared:

> “Nor do I have a place where the exercise of work can be carried out according to the Rule of the aforementioned Father Benedict.”

Moreover, since some lacked servants, they performed all the monastery’s services with their own hands—the mill, bakery, garden, and other tasks of this kind. The monks of Fulda earnestly requested this in a petition presented to Charlemagne, asking (no. 16):

> “That the services of the monastery itself be organized by the brothers—that is, the bakery, garden, brewery, kitchen, agriculture, and the other services—as they were among our predecessors.”

Furthermore, since some animals appeared necessary for cultivating the fields, bringing wood and other necessities of life into the monastery, and carrying out all the monastery’s services, someone was also entrusted with caring for them while they grazed in the fields. This is clear from the *Life of Saint Benedict, Abbot of Aniane*, where I read (no. 38, fourth century of the Benedictines):

> “In the mountains where the brothers were accustomed to live while caring for the sheep, they built for themselves a small oratory in which to pray.”

Finally, since the Rule of Saint Benedict permits various crafts to be practiced in monasteries, those who were skilled in a particular craft were assigned especially to it. The Camaldolese, as Peter Damian teaches (*Life of Saint Romuald*, chapter 26),

> “all performed manual works: some made spoons, others spun, others tied nets, and others made hair shirts.”

After the monasteries had been enriched with sufficient income through the pious generosity of kings and princes, they devoted themselves to such hard and laborious works no longer because necessity compelled them, but solely from love of penance—and sometimes even to drive away idleness through lighter tasks.

Concerning the Cluniacs, Udalricus must be heard (*Book I, chapter 30*). When asked “what manual work is and how it is done,” he replies:

> “Certainly, not to lie, what I saw most often was nothing other than removing fresh beans, not yet fully ripe, from their pods; pulling weeds and useless plants from the garden, especially those that choked the good plants; and sometimes shaping loaves in the bakery.”

Concerning this last work and others, I read the following in the German manuscripts of customs (no. 33):

> “Sometimes, if necessary, during the time of work they wash their garments. The weekly servers go to the kitchen, and the brothers sometimes enter the bakery as a group, prepare the dough with their own hands, and knead it for making bread.”

For others, writing books seemed especially suitable for driving away idleness and fostering piety. Cassiodorus strongly commends this labor, writing to his monks (*On Divine and Human Readings*, chapter 30):

> “I confess my desire among you: whatever can be completed by bodily labor, I perhaps rightly prefer the work of copyists—provided that they write accurately—because by rereading the divine Scriptures they beneficially instruct their own minds, and by writing they spread the Lord’s commands far and wide. Such an aim is praiseworthy diligence: to preach to men with the hand, to open tongues with the fingers, to give silent salvation to mortals, and to fight against the illicit incursions of the devil with pen and ink. Satan receives as many wounds as the copyist transcribes words of the Lord.

> “Thus, situated in one place, he travels through various provinces by the dissemination of his work. His labor is read in holy places; peoples hear from it how they may turn from an evil will and serve the Lord with a pure mind. Though absent in body, he works through his writing, and so forth.”

Peter the Venerable likewise writes to the hermit Gislebertus (*Book I, letter 20*):

> “Saplings cannot be planted, seeds cannot be watered, nor can any rural work be carried out, because perpetual enclosure prevents it. But let the hand, for the plow, be turned to the pen; let pages be furrowed with divine writings instead of fields. Let the seedbed of God’s word be sown on paper, so that when the crops have ripened—that is, when the books have been completed—it may fill hungry readers with abundant fruits; and thus let heavenly bread drive away the soul’s deadly hunger. In this way, certainly, in this way you can become a silent preacher of the Lord’s word, and while your tongue is silent, your hand will resound with loud voices in the ears of many peoples.”

John Trithemius praised the same labor in a special little work, inviting his brothers to it even after the invention of printing. See the same author's *Book I, On the Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 6.

Finally, Mabillon notes another kind of labor practiced by our monks (Preface to Benedictine Century I, p. 60): namely, that those who, because of bodily infirmity, could not perform arduous tasks with their hands were permitted, by the indulgence of the Rule, to compensate for this by more extended studies. He proves this by the example of Lanfranc, who, as William of Malmesbury says (Book I, *De Gestis Pontificum Anglorum*): “Having become a monk, a man who did not know how to seek a livelihood by agricultural labor, he taught public schools of dialectic, so that by the liberality of the schools he might alleviate the poverty of the monastery”—whereas Abbot Herluin was occupied with baking bread and handling manure—and by the example of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, to whom, in place of manual labor, the care of teaching and preaching the divine word was entrusted, as he himself testifies in a certain sermon (Sermon 10 on Psalm 90) in these words:

“What we sometimes say to you contrary to the custom of our order, we do not do from our own presumption, but at the request of our venerable brothers and fellow abbots, who even impose upon us what they absolutely do not wish to be freely permitted to themselves. For they know that I have a different situation and a particular necessity; indeed, I would not speak to you now if I were able to work alongside you. That would perhaps be a more effective word for you, and also more acceptable to my conscience. But since, because of my sins, and because of this burdensome and, as you yourselves know, manifold bodily infirmity, and also because of the necessity of the present time, this is denied me, would that, by speaking and not doing, I might deserve to be found at least the least in the kingdom of God!”

This is a particularly suitable place to investigate whether monks may be dispensed from daily manual labor and applied to literary studies. For although, from the very beginning of coenobitic life, the study of sacred literature flourished among monks, there have nevertheless been men in our own age who wished them to be so occupied with daily manual labor that they should have absolutely no permission to study. They defend this position with such intense feeling that one might say they consider it necessary to fight for it as for altar and hearth. As soon as the books of these men—although filled with piety and considerable learning—were published, almost all the most learned men disapproved of them on this point. Recalling how much benefit had accrued to the Church from the learning of monks, and especially of Benedictines, they considered it a sacrilege to forbid them so necessary an occupation.

For my part, although I am convinced that Saint Benedict established schools of learning in his monasteries, and that studies cannot be expelled from the cloisters of monks without simultaneously departing both from the mind of the holy Father and from his Rule, I shall nevertheless handle this question in this work without definitively settling the dispute. Since each position has its reasons, patrons, and defenders, and since I can hardly fail to defer to the religion and virtue of either side, I shall be content here to set forth the arguments of both, leaving it to fair-minded readers to embrace whichever of the two opinions they prefer. [Col. 0717B]

Accordingly, those who deny that monks may be dispensed from manual labor and applied to literary studies argue as follows.

First, from the example of the ancient monks, for whom, they say, literary studies were unknown, although they devoted several hours each day to manual labor.

Second, from the example of Christ and the holy Apostles. We read that they sometimes labored with their hands, but never that they studied. It is therefore remarkable that those who have proposed to reproduce in themselves the apostolic life and the actions of Christ should abandon manual labor and devote themselves to the barren study of letters—especially since no legitimate ecclesiastical authority has ever approved a dispensation from labor and the pursuit of studies by monks.

[628] Third, because everyone has been given the command to avoid idleness. Those who wish to apply monks to studies after setting aside labor certainly cannot fulfill this command, since a considerable part of them—indeed, I might say the greater part—are incapable of such mental exertion; and therefore, deprived of manual labor, they must necessarily waste away in deadly idleness. [Col. 0717C]

Fourth, because, for monks destined to penance, bodily labors that wear down the body are more fitting than literary studies, by which the mind is refreshed and the body is deprived of the glory of mortification.

Fifth, because study is hostile to piety: it extinguishes devotion, dries up the tears of compunction, and suppresses the pious movements of the soul. Heavy manual labors, on the other hand, often awaken inward affections of the heart through the contrition of the body.

Sixth, because, as the Apostle says, “knowledge puffs up.” We cannot see learned men without some pain when they are ignorant of themselves, despise the humble condition of their profession, aspire to honors, seek the chairs of preachers, and go beyond the limits of their own station. Would that we did not find this so frequently! Manual labor, however, makes one forget the pride of one’s former life and pleasures and acquires humility of heart through the contrition of the body, as Cassian teaches among others. [Col. 0717D]

Seventh, because studies bring many disadvantages in their train, which certainly ought not to be preferred to the good of manual labor. Through them, all the discipline of regular observance has been thrown into ruin. This became especially apparent in the eighth and ninth centuries, when literary pursuits began to flourish among monks. Since in those centuries monks departed from the correct manner of life, it is not unreasonable to attribute the collapse of regular discipline to the study of letters. The Fathers of the Council of Verneuil complain of this in these words (Canon 3, A.D. 844): “In holy places, that is, in monasteries, we have discovered that some through study and others through idleness . . . have deviated from their profession.”

Finally, eighth, they say that it is sufficient for monks to read the simple text of sacred Scripture, the works written by the holy Fathers for the direction of morals, and the histories of devout monks. But what have investigating the tradition of the Church, learning the decrees of councils and supreme pontiffs, searching through ecclesiastical histories, and disputing about theological dogmas to do with men who are dead to the world? This is more or less how those who consider manual labor preferable to study argue. [Col. 0718A]

Others, on the contrary, maintain, first, that working with the hands is not essential to the monastic order, since among the ancient monks there were serious men, distinguished both by piety and by the merits of their virtues, who abstained altogether from every kind of exterior labor. Such, above all, was Saint Abbot Paul at Ferme, a mountain in Scetis, who lived there with no fewer than five hundred monks. Sozomen writes of him (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VI, chapter 29): “He did no work, nor accepted anything from anyone except what he was going to eat; he devoted himself only to prayer, offering God three hundred prayers every day as a kind of tribute.” Besides Sozomen, Palladius also relates this in chapter 23 of the *Lausiac History*. In chapter 52 he likewise reports of Saint Apollonius, “who was the father of five hundred monks, very renowned and celebrated in the Thebaid, because his work was to offer prayers throughout the entire day: at night, one hundred times, and during the day, just as many, kneeling.” [Col. 0718B]

Julianus Sabas had formed his monks according to precisely the same discipline. For Theodoret writes (*Philotheus*, chapter 2): “He taught them to offer a common hymn to God within the monastery; after sunrise, two were to go out into the desert: one, kneeling, was to offer the adoration owed to the Lord, while the other, standing, was to sing fifteen psalms of David. Then, after exchanging their tasks, one was to rise and sing, while the other, prostrate on the ground, was to adore; and they did this continually from morning until twilight.”

It seems that Abbot Athanasius taught that this was not merely the custom of a few but of many (John Moschus, *Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 130), reproaching his monks because “in the time of our fathers it was the practice to avoid distractions of the mind; but in our times the pot and manual labor have prevailed.” From this it may reasonably be inferred that in the time of his fathers manual labor had not prevailed. [Col. 0718C]

Nor did this observance flourish only in the East.
