Saint Martin introduced it into the West together with monastic life, as Sulpicius Severus testifies (*Life of Saint Martin*, Book I): “There no craft was practiced except by the scribes; younger men were assigned to this work, while the older devoted themselves to prayer.”

Saint Eparchius, abbot of Enculisma, followed the same institution. An anonymous writer says in his *Life*, no. 17 (Benedictine Century I): “He never permitted his monks either to work or even to bake bread, but only to devote themselves to prayer.”

Moreover, we read that “Saint Maurus, the blessed disciple of Saint Benedict, sent to these regions of Gaul to construct monasteries according to his master’s teaching, maintained this custom in the monastery he had built in the diocese of Angers: since all necessities were supplied to them without their own labor, they omitted manual work and, occupied with spiritual exercises, as we have said, were not idle; and thus they preserved most faithfully, by always doing good works, the Rule recently handed down to them by the saint.” So writes Peter the Venerable to Saint Bernard (*Book I, Letter 28*); Rupert, abbot of Tuitius, agrees with him in Book III of his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 7. [Col. 0718D]

If someone should say that these men were few in comparison with the great number who labored with their hands, they reply that although they may seem few to some, they were so eminent in the merit of their virtues and in authority that they easily outweighed the multitude. Indeed, even if only Martin were available, he would be not inferior in authority to all the monks of the East, even if he should not be preferred to them. As for the mind of Saint Benedict, the single judgment of Saint Maurus ought to outweigh all the others that could be produced. For, as Rupert says very well (*Book III on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, chapter 7): “We ought not to doubt, given the testimony of so great a disciple, that his master and the father of monks, the blessed Benedict, did not write about manual labor in such a way as to wish to disturb the leisure of holy contemplation, when the generosity of wealthy faithful provides for their needs.” [Col. 0719A]

The Council of Aachen, assembled under Louis the Pious, confirmed their judgment; it consisted of almost all the Eastern prelates and all the Western ones. In it, the bishops, “with the lord pope in agreement, decreed that monks should cease from arduous work and labor for the honor of the priesthood, and that in place of labor they should sing at the hours certain prescribed psalms, with appointed prayers, for the living and deceased faithful” (*Historical Fragment of the Council of Aachen*, volume I of *Analecta*).

Second, they say that literary studies are not so foreign to the ancient rules of monks as though no commands concerning them were found there. For in the Rule of Saint Pachomius we read (Article 80): “There shall be absolutely no one in the monastery who does not learn letters and retain something from the Scriptures, at least as far as the New Testament and the Psalter.”

In the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chapter 15): “Those who are learning letters and psalms shall be assigned to those who are appointed to receive them; and those responsible for them are either to be reproved for negligence or approved for their instruction and study, etc.”

In the Rule of Saint Aurelian (chapter 32): “Let everyone learn letters.”

In the Rule of Saint Ferreolus (chapter 11): “Anyone who wishes to claim the name of monk must not be permitted to be ignorant of letters; indeed, he must know the entire Psalter by heart, nor may he defend himself with any excuse from being seized by this holy study.”

In the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 19): “The care of rearing the children shall belong to a man whom the Father has chosen, a holy, wise, and mature man, who shall train the children not only in literary studies but also by the instruction and teaching of the virtues.” [Col. 0719C] Earlier, too (chapter 7), he wishes the brothers “to dispute about certain questions of divine reading” before Compline.

In the Rule of the Master (chapter 50): “Let some read, let others listen, and let others learn and teach letters.”

Finally, in the Short Rules of Saint Basil (Question 235): “I certainly think that the one entrusted with the care and governance of others ought to possess and learn the knowledge of everything that has been written, so that he may teach everyone the manifold will of God, showing each person his duty. As for the rest . . . let each person diligently learn and pursue, according to the measure God has assigned, what belongs to his own office, and let him not inquisitively investigate anything further.”

Elsewhere, when asked (Question 292) “whether it is fitting that among the brothers there should be a teacher of secular boys,” he answers affirmatively: “If those who bring them bring them with this intention, and those who receive them are people who have complete confidence that they can educate those brought to them in discipline and correction.” If they taught secular children, how much more did they teach monks, who by their own institution were bound to instruct others in letters? Otherwise, how could they have done so? [Col. 0719D]

To these must be added the Rule of Solitaries, in whose chapter 20 we read:

“Therefore the solitary ought to be a teacher, not one who needs to be taught; he ought also to be wise and learned in divine law, so that he may know how to bring forth new things and old. It is necessary in many ways for solitaries to be instructed in the divine utterances. First, because of the tricks and deceptions of the devil, through which he is accustomed often to plunge himself into the hearts of the ignorant. Then, so that he may be able to irrigate with the flowing streams of doctrine the arid hearts of certain newcomers. For if he has any disciples, he should be able to instruct them abundantly. Finally, in these matters and in all others, knowledge of the Scriptures is greatly necessary for the solitary; for if he possesses only a holy life, he can benefit only himself by living holily. But if he is also learned in doctrine, he can instruct everyone else and repel or refute heretics, Jews, or any other adversaries whom he encounters. Unless they are refuted and convicted, they can easily corrupt the hearts of the simple. His speech ought to be pure, simple, and clear, full of gravity and propriety, full of gentleness, grace, and modesty. For his special office is to treat of the mystery of the law, the doctrine of faith, and the discipline of justice; to read the divine Scriptures, to traverse the canons, to imitate the examples of the saints, etc.”

There can be no doubt concerning the mind of Saint Benedict: he wished his brothers to apply themselves to literary studies. Among the other qualifications required for an abbot to be chosen from the congregation, he requires (chapter 64) that he be learned and know how to bring forth new things and old. He also wishes the deans to be appointed not according to rank but according to the teaching of wisdom (chapter 21).

Moreover, he commands that boys offered to the monastery (chapter 59)—sometimes five years old, sometimes seven, or not much older—be received; and thus he assumed responsibility for their instruction in letters. The same reasoning applies to the Pachomians, Basilian monks, [Col. 0720B] and others who admitted children into their monasteries. Furthermore, he says in this chapter that sickly and delicate brothers should be assigned such work or craft that they may neither be idle nor be overwhelmed by the violence of labor.

Explaining this passage, Hildemar, the most ancient commentator on the Rule, says: “A craft is this: if he knows how to sing, let him teach another a song; or if he knows grammar, let him teach it to others; or other crafts that are useful in the monastery. If he is knowledgeable, let him teach others.”

Finally, in chapter 73, the Rule refers his brothers to the teaching of the holy Fathers.

The reason that both Saint Benedict himself and the other ancient monks appear to have commended labor over literary studies was chiefly threefold.

First, books were scarce. In those times, when books existed only in handwritten form, their scarcity was so great that the number of monks in monasteries sometimes exceeded the number of volumes. The monastery of Centula may serve as an example: three hundred monks once lived there, together with one hundred boys, although there were not three hundred codices there, as is clear from the catalogue of that monastery’s books, compiled in the time of Louis the Pious and reported by Hariulf in his *Chronicle of Centula* (Book III, chapter 3). Thus, even during the hours assigned by the Rule to reading, while one person read, the others were often forced to listen; and Saint Benedict had this in mind when he says (chapter 4) that holy readings should be heard willingly.

Second, there was a scarcity of priests. At the very beginnings of monastic life, not many monks were admitted to the clergy, and they were scarcely distinguished from laymen. Although they regarded learning as highly useful, they did not consider it entirely necessary. Consequently, when the necessity of obtaining food for themselves pressed upon them, far more monks devoted hours to manual labor. On the other hand, they took the greatest care to educate in the sciences those whom they destined for the sacred altars, fearing the Lord’s warning through the prophet: “Because you have rejected knowledge, I will reject you, so that you shall not serve as priest for me”; and also: “The ignorant shall be unknown.”

[Col. 0720D] Third, there was the perverse teaching of the Messalians and of certain wandering monks, who, under the pretext either of prayer or of preaching, condemned labor among the servants of God not only as useless but also as evil and contrary to the words of the Gospel. Saint Epiphanius refuted their impious doctrine in Book III of *Against Heresies*, heresy 80, and Saint Augustine did so in the work he composed at the urging of Aurelius, bishop of Carthage, *On the Work of Monks* (chapter 30), “so that good brothers, obeying the apostolic commands, would not be called transgressors even by the lazy and disobedient; and so that those who do not work would at least not hesitate to acknowledge that those who do work ought to be preferred to them,” as the holy Doctor himself says.

He does not say this, however, as though he judged those who labor absolutely better than those who do not. For those who withdraw into seclusion for the sake of perfection he not only does not place below those who labor, but even says (chapter 23): “As for their exercise in such wondrous continence, since they have leisure in which to practice these things and to offer themselves as examples to be imitated, not in proud exaltation but in merciful holiness, I not only do not criticize it, but cannot praise it as much as it deserves.”

He also asserts of others (chapter 21), “if they are ministers of the altar, if they are stewards of the sacraments,” that they may claim for themselves the freedom not to work.

But he contends that those who labor are better than those perverse, long-haired, wandering monks who reproved labor in others as an evil. Saint Augustine wants nothing else throughout this entire little book, *On the Work of Monks*. If he were alive now, and a new Wycliffe were to arise and say: “All the monks of Saint Benedict who do not wish to seek their livelihood by manual labor have apostatized not only from the order of Saint Benedict but, what is more true, from the discipleship of Christ,” the holy Doctor would tell this new Pharaoh—who, in order to subject God’s chosen people to his service and turn them away from offering the true and supreme God the sacrifice of praise in the desert, attempted to enslave them to brickmaking and manual labor—to go far away from him. He would praise monks who, in order to devote themselves more freely to God or to serve the public good, abstained altogether from manual labor; and still less would he recall those who for that reason devoted themselves to literary studies. [Col. 0721B]

Third, they assert that the flourishing of literary studies among monks can be demonstrated not only from the ancient rules but also from the constant tradition of every age.

Indeed, in the fourth century, when the monastic institution especially began to flourish, the ancient *Life* of Saint Pachomius preserved by Bollandus under 14 May teaches, on the testimony of Saint Antony, that Pachomius was exceedingly well versed in the divine writings. Indeed, the author of the same *Life* reports that Pachomius himself took pains to learn to speak Greek, so that he might more often console a Greek brother by nation whom he had admitted into his congregation.

Moreover, Bishop Ammonius, writing to Theophilus, archbishop of Alexandria (Ammonius, Letter to Theophilus, no. 4, in Bollandus, 14 May), testifies that when he was seventeen years old he had been received into the monastery by Theodore, a disciple of Pachomius, and entrusted by that same man to teachers and superiors—namely to Theodore of Alexandria and to a certain Ausonius, who held the second place under him—so that he might be thoroughly instructed by them in understanding the divine Scriptures. This must certainly be understood not of a simple knowledge of sacred Scripture, which he could have acquired from reading alone without teachers, but of a complete and perfect knowledge, which he could by no means have attained without the assistance of other teachers.

At the same time lived another Ammonius, a disciple of Abbot Pambo, a remarkably learned man (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 12). He “recited the Old and New Testaments from memory, and was so well versed in the writings of the learned men Origen, Didymus, Pierius, and Stephen that he had read six million lines.”

This man was given as a companion to the great Athanasius when he was traveling to Rome. According to Socrates (*History*, Book IV, chapter 18), he was “so little curious that, when he happened to be staying at Rome together with Athanasius, he had no desire whatsoever to see any of the city’s magnificent works except the church dedicated to Peter and Paul.” Thus it is indeed true, as some say, that learning in monks gives birth to curiosity and causes them to devote themselves excessively to external concerns.

To the same category belongs what Rufinus (*Book II on the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 6) and Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 50) report about Abbot Theon, who spent thirty years shut away alone in a little house practicing silence: namely, that he “was a learned man in the threefold grace of languages, in Roman, Greek, and Egyptian writings.”

Besides Basil the Great, Gregory the Theologian, John Chrysostom, and Ephrem the Deacon, who illumined the desert by their learning no less than by the holiness of their lives, we could also add the distinguished and remarkable Or, abbot of Mount Nitria (*ibid.*, chapter 9), who, when visited by the brothers, “immediately turned to teaching, for he was exceedingly skilled in letters”; and the famous Deacon Evagrius (*ibid.*, chapter 86), who composed three sacred books for monks.

But above all we must consider the illustrious virgin Silvania, who, as Palladius writes (*ibid.*, chapter 143), “was exceedingly learned, having embraced learning through love. She turned nights, illuminated by abundant oil, into days, reading through all the writings of the ancients who had published commentaries: three million lines of Origen, and two hundred and fifty thousand of Gregory, Stephen, Pierius, Basil, and certain other men of outstanding virtue. She did not read these slightly or carelessly, but carefully read each book seven or eight times, etc.”

Above all, however, Saint Jerome must be considered, not only an ornament of the monastic order but also of the entire Christian world. When he withdrew into the solitude of Syria, he brought with him that notable library which he had prepared for himself at Rome with the greatest care and expense and had caused to be transported from there to Jerusalem.

He himself tells us what studies occupied him in the desert in these words (Letter 4):

“When I was young,” he says, “and the deserts of solitude surrounded me, I could not bear the goads of vice and the heat of nature. Although I broke these by frequent fasts, my mind nevertheless seethed with thoughts. To subdue it, I placed myself under the instruction of a certain brother who had believed as a Hebrew, so that after the subtleties of Quintilian, the eloquence of Cicero, the gravity of Fronto, and the gentleness of Pliny, I might learn the alphabet and meditate upon harsh, breathy words. What labor I expended there, what difficulty I endured, how often I despaired, how often I stopped, and how often I began again with renewed determination to learn—my conscience bears witness, both mine, which suffered, and that of those who shared my life. And I give thanks to the Lord that from the bitter seed of letters I am harvesting sweet fruits.”

It would take too long to range over all those distinguished and most learned monks whose company Saint Jerome himself enjoyed, or over the other celebrated men whose learning caused solitude to flourish in every branch of knowledge during the fourth century and produced abundant fruits for the common good of the Catholic Church. [Col. 0722C]

In the following, fifth century, letters were also cultivated in the laura of Saint Euthymius, as is clear from the *Life of Saint Euthymius* (*Greek Analecta*, volume I), not only from the great number of his disciples who were raised to episcopal dignity, but especially from the famous Gabrielius. From adolescence entrusted to his instruction, he “was so devoted to letters that he learned to speak and write Latin, Greek, and Syriac correctly,” as Cyril of Scythopolis, a contemporary author, reports.

In that same fifth century, literary studies also seem to have flourished in the monasteries of Africa. This may be inferred from Saint Augustine, who, in order for a good monk to become a good cleric, requires that he possess “necessary instruction and the integrity of a regular person.” Since at that time monks were commonly chosen for the clergy, it may reasonably be inferred that they were adorned both with the necessary instruction and with regular integrity. [Col. 0722D]

The holy Doctor also indicates this quite clearly elsewhere when he says (*On the Work of Monks*, chapter 29): “I would much rather work with my hands each day at fixed hours, as has been established in well-ordered monasteries, and have the remaining hours free for reading and prayer, or for doing something from the divine writings, than endure the most tumultuous perplexities of other people’s lawsuits, etc.”

From this passage it is clearly and plainly inferred that in well-ordered monasteries, besides the common reading, there were free hours for disputation or for doing something from the divine writings. This plainly cannot occur without special study.

That the same custom also prevailed in Gaul is proved by the example of Claudianus Mamertus, abbot of Vienne (Book IV, Letter 11; see also Letter 3). In his epitaph Sidonius Apollinaris sings:

The glory and grief of his brother Mamertus,

The one splendid boast of admiring bishops,

Claudianus gives these limbs beneath this turf.

Under whose teaching a threefold library

Shone forth—Roman, Attic, Christian—

Which, in the green season of life, the monk

Drank in through secluded instruction.

An orator, dialectician, poet,

A commentator, geometer, and musician,

Learned to unravel the bonds of questions,

And with the sword of the word to cut down sects,

If any should assail the Catholic faith.

Around the same time, Bishop Lupus built a monastery in sight of the city of Troyes. There, according to the *Chronicle of Hugh of Flavigny*, the blessed Polichronius, later to become bishop of Verdun, was handed over by his parents to be educated. In that place, together with Polichronius, the following were instructed in the sciences of learning: Severus of Trier, Albinus of Châlons, Aventinus, bishop of Troyes, and Saint Aemilianus—all distinguished by the merit and holiness of their lives.

The same must clearly be asserted of the monks of Britain, both from the life of Saint Gildas, abbot of Rhuys (Benedictine Century I), who near the end of the fifth century “is said to have been entrusted for instruction to Abbot Hildutus. Having received the holy boy, he began to train him in sacred letters; and when he saw him radiant in the beauty of his appearance and intensely devoted to liberal studies, he loved him with kindly affection, etc.” [Col. 0723B]

Samson and Paul also advanced under the same teacher; the former became bishop of Dol and the latter bishop of Oximus, according to no. 3 of the same *Life*.

Of Saint Samson it is indeed established from his *Life*, no. 7, written by a near-contemporary author, who speaks as follows about his teacher Hildutus or Eltutus: “That Eltutus was the most learned of all the Britons in the whole of the Scriptures of the Old and New Testaments and in every branch of philosophy, namely geometry, rhetoric, grammar, arithmetic, and all the philosophical arts.” He adds: “I was in his monastery.”

Saint Maglorius must also be added to these men. As is stated in his *Life*, no. 1, he was taught by Eltutus “the knowledge both of the liberal arts and of the divine utterances.” [Col. 0723C]

Nor was this a unique achievement of Eltutus, since around the same time the boy Saint Maclovius was entrusted to Abbot Brendan, “at that time a man most famous for holiness and learning,” to be instructed in literary discipline (*Life of Saint Maclovius*, no. 1, Benedictine Century I).

I have no doubt that Britain was formerly instructed by monks both in the mysteries of the faith and in the sciences of letters, through the activity of Saint Patrick and his disciples, who first spread the seeds of the divine word in Ireland.

I come now to the sixth century, in which the Benedictine order arose and received its growth—an order in which one might believe that the treasures of wisdom and learning, hitherto hidden away, were stored. We can learn something of the practice of the first disciples of Saint Benedict from what Cassiodorus writes to his monks at Vivarium, who, living not far from Monte Cassino, unquestionably followed Benedictine institutions.

Above all, he commends to them the study of sacred Scripture, the reading of ecclesiastical history, and the writings of the holy Fathers, especially Hilary, Cyprian, Ambrose, Jerome, and Augustine. He then urges them to read constantly the ecclesiastical canons of Dionysius Exiguus, “so that you may not appear culpably ignorant of rules so salutary for the Church.” A little later he adds (*Divine Institutions*, chapter 23):

“And so that no deception may harm you in the rules of faith, read the Council of Ephesus and that of Chalcedon, which you have readily at hand, as well as the *Encyclical Letters*, that is, the letters of confirmation of the aforesaid council.”

After explaining with what diligence sacred Scripture is to be read together with its commentators, he adds (chapter 25):

“We reasonably urge you also to examine the knowledge of cosmography, so that you may clearly recognize in what part of the world each of the places that you read about in the sacred books is situated.”

Among other works he praises the little book on cosmography by Julius the Orator, Marcellinus’ description of Constantinople and Jerusalem, and Ptolemy’s *Cosmography*. Then, in the following chapter (chapter 27), he says:

“We have also thought it necessary to remind you that in both the sacred writings and the most learned commentators we can understand many things through schemata, many through definitions, many through the art of grammar, many through the art of rhetoric, many through dialectic, many through arithmetic, many through music, many through geometry, and many through astronomy.”

After consoling certain simple brothers who could not rise to so demanding a study, he adds (chapter 28):

“Nevertheless, the holy Fathers did not decree that the study of secular literature should be rejected, because through it our understanding is instructed in no small degree for the comprehension of sacred Scripture—provided that, with the assistance of divine grace, knowledge of these matters is sought soberly and rationally, not so that we place our hope of advancement in them, but so that, passing through them, we may desire that the Father of lights grant us profitable and saving wisdom . . . . Many of our Fathers, likewise, educated in such literature and remaining in the law of the Lord, attained true wisdom, as the blessed Augustine recalls in his book *On Christian Doctrine*, saying: ‘We do not consider with how much gold and silver and clothing Cyprian, the most gracious teacher and most blessed martyr, came out of Egypt, nor how much Lactantius, Victorinus, Optatus, and Hilary possessed.’ We add Ambrose, Augustine himself, Jerome, and many other innumerable Greeks. The faithful servant of God Moses also did this, of whom it is written that he was learned in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. Let us, imitating them, hasten to read both kinds of learning, if we can, with the greatest caution and without hesitation. For who would dare to doubt where the manifold example of such men goes before us?”

This final passage of Cassiodorus is sufficient to refute those who boldly assert that the first Fathers of the Church read no books other than those of sacred Scripture.

Finally, he concludes as follows: “But if one of the brothers cannot be perfectly instructed either in human or in divine letters, let him at least, supported by some moderate degree of knowledge, choose what follows:

‘Let me love the countryside and the streams flowing through the watered valleys.’

For it is not foreign to monks themselves to cultivate gardens, work the fields, and rejoice in the abundance of fruit.”

This is nevertheless to be done in such a way that they read the books relevant to their craft.

From what Cassiodorus has said up to this point, it follows without hesitation what studies the first disciples of the holy Father Benedict especially pursued: sacred Scripture, ecclesiastical history, the teaching of the holy Fathers, ecclesiastical discipline, dialectic, rhetoric, grammar, cosmography, and the other liberal disciplines. For it is impossible to believe that so great a man, who knew the laws of monks extremely well and who is himself believed to have professed the monastic life, would have urged them toward studies foreign to their religion.

Dionysius the monk, surnamed Exiguus but truly great in learning, may serve as an example; Cassiodorus composed his eulogy. And certainly, if literary studies had not flourished in the Roman monastery of Saint Andrew during this century, how could Gregory the Great have drawn from it so many preachers of the divine word to send to Britain? For some also had to remain for the common benefit of the monastery itself and of the Catholic Church, which in those times the monks chiefly served.

The doctrine which the Benedictine monks had imbibed in Italy they carried forth and poured out in Britain. We have just shown that the study of letters was already flourishing in Ireland from the Lives of Saints Gildas, Samson, and Maglorius, who learned the liberal arts from Abbot Eltutus; and from the Life of Saint Maclovius, who advanced in the same studies in the monastery of Abbot Brendan. This could be demonstrated still further from the Life of Saint Constantine, no. 1, who, having become a monk from being a king, was taught letters in the cloister in the sixth century and ordained a priest [Col. 0725A] (Bolland, 11 March); from the Life of Saint Columbanus, no. 9, who, submitting himself to the discipline of Abbot Silenus (Second Benedictine Century), “imbued him with the study of all the divine Scriptures”; and from the Life of Saint Gall, abbot, chapter 1, who in the monastery of Bangor (Second Benedictine Century), “with heavenly grace preceding him, drank in the divine Scriptures with such devotion that he could bring forth new things from his treasury and old things; and, with an intellect capable of grasping them, he also attained the rules of grammar and the subtleties of meter,” as Walafrid writes.

The discipline which Saint Columbanus had found in the monasteries of Ireland he carried with him into Gaul, especially into the monastery of Luxeuil (Second Benedictine Century). There, toward the end of the sixth century, “the praiseworthy Agilus, entering upon the age of boyhood, was entrusted to Eustasius, a man of approved religion, to be instructed in the sacred letters, together with the sons of other noblemen who afterward became bishops of churches,” as the anonymous author states in the Life of Saint Agilus, no. [Col. 0725B] 1. Among these are listed Agnoaldus of Laon, Achaarius of Noyon, Audomarus of Thérouanne, and Ragnacharius of Augsburg, bishops whom Jonas also mentions in the Life of Saint Eustasius, no. 5. Under this teacher Agilus advanced so far that he “was more thoroughly imbued with the liberal arts, instructed many by his eloquence, illumined very many by the purity of the Catholic faith, and rendered some suitable, through the most lucid teachings, for the profession of sacred religion, after setting aside the pomp of worldly greatness.”

Nor did the study of letters flourish at Luxeuil only in the sixth century under Columbanus; it flourished also in the seventh under Walbert, Columbanus’s successor after Eustasius (Second Benedictine Century). Under that abbot, “in both the height of religious observance and the perfection of learning,” the monastery of Luxeuil shone above all the monasteries of Gaul, so that monks were sent there from other monasteries for the sake of instruction, as we learn from the Life of Saint Frodobert, abbot of Celle, no. 6.

In this century learning flourished in the principal, if not in all, the monasteries of Gaul [Col. 0725C]. At Longoretum, Francardus, later abbot of that place, “was the nourisher and teacher of the sons of noblemen,” according to the Vision of Barontus, no. 11. At the monastery of Saint Hilary at Poitiers, Aicadrus, later abbot of Jumièges, was entrusted as a boy to the monk Ansfridus, most famous for wisdom, to be educated, according to his Life, chapter 1. At Solignac, “Saint Eligius entrusted the blessed Tillo, whom he had received, to Saint Remaclus, abbot of his monastery of Solignac, to be nourished and instructed in letters . . . and ordered him to remain constantly in his sight, so that he might be instructed both in secular and divine disciplines,” according to the Life of Saint Tillo, no. 4. At Stavelot, secular men entrusted “their children to be instructed in liberal, indeed monastic, disciplines,” according to the Life of Saint Hadelin, no. 5. At Jumièges, “it was the custom of Saint Philibert to send brothers from the monastery throughout the surrounding region to exhort souls,” according to the Life of Saint Philibert, no. 20. Finally, Saints Botulph and Adulph, monks in Gaul, “were not only taught, but by the grace of God attained the authority to teach among the more perfect,” according to the Life of Saint Botulph, no. 2 [Col. 0725D] (Third Benedictine Century).

What we assert here about the monasteries of Gaul can be confirmed by many examples from the English monasteries as well. In the seventh century, Theodore, formerly a monk and later archbishop of Canterbury, and Adrian, the abbot (Second Benedictine Century), “because both were abundantly instructed in sacred and secular letters, gathered a crowd of disciples, and daily poured forth streams of saving knowledge to water their hearts, so that they imparted to their hearers, amid the volumes of sacred writings, instruction in the art of meter, astronomy, arithmetic, and ecclesiastical discipline,” according to the Life of Saint Theodore, no. 5.

Abbot Huetbert also (ibid.; Second Benedictine Century), in the monastery of Wearmouth, “from the earliest years of his boyhood had been trained not only in the discipline of regular observance, but also with no small diligence in writing, singing, reading, and teaching,” according to Book II of the Life of Saint Benedict Biscop, no. 18 [Col. 0726A]. To these must be added Bede the Venerable, whom his disciple Cuthbert, writing his Life, no. 2 (Third Benedictine Century), says was “as a little boy of good promise carefully imbued with both divine and secular learning” in the monastery of Jarrow. “And while he was being educated in the Latin language, he also acquired no ordinary proficiency in Greek.” Nor did he advance only in knowledge of the Latin and Greek languages, but also in every discipline of the liberal arts, as is proved by the various monuments of every kind of learning which he left behind and which have endured to the present day. Moreover, the learning he had received as a little boy he afterward, having become a teacher in the same monastery, handed on to his brothers.

We also infer from the Life of Saint Judoc (Second Benedictine Century), no. 3, that the sciences of letters flourished in the monasteries of the monks of Lesser Britain, called Armorica.

639 If from there we proceed to Spain, we shall find that the same institution prevailed there as well. Since Saint Hildefonsus, bishop of Toledo (in his Life, no. 2, ibid.) [Col. 0726B], while “still living under the rudiments of childhood, touched by the divine Spirit and delighted by the life of monks, having despised his parents’ affections and worldly possessions, sought the monastery of Agalius and conducted himself becomingly as a monk there for many years,” as Bishop Julian relates—and since Julian elsewhere wrote of him (no. 3) that he “wrote very many foremost books in a more brilliant style”—it is necessary to conclude that he had imbibed such learning in the monastery of Agalius.

Nor should we leave the East untouched in this century, for Saint Theodore of Sykeon died there in the year 613. Concerning him, his disciple George, writing his Life, speaks as follows (Bolland, 22 April): “I was brought to him as an infant, and, having been raised in his holy monastery, I learned letters from a most religious superior.”

At about the same time John Moschus, priest and monk in the monastery of Saint Theodosius, abbot and archimandrite of all the monasteries that were in Jerusalem, traveled through various places and visited monasteries [Col. 0726C]. During this journey he also visited very learned men and philosophers for the sake of discipline and study, as he himself testifies in the work he composed, *The Spiritual Meadow*, chapters 171 and 172. These examples should suffice for the seventh century.

In the eighth century, Saint Boniface, having moved to the monastery of Nursling, advanced under the most devout Abbot Wimbert in virtues and letters to such a degree that shortly afterward he himself undertook the office of teaching. Later, when he had gone to Germany and brought that people to the true worship of Christ, he took particular care to establish public schools, “in which,” as our Mabillon says (Preface to the third century of the Benedictines, no. 38), “that uncultivated and savage people might gradually lay aside its harsh customs and, refined by gentler and holier disciplines, acquire a more humane wisdom. Saint Boniface was not unaware how important this was for the newly planted faith. He directed his efforts to this end and first opened public schools at the monastery of Fritzlar, afterward at Fulda, then at Utrecht on the Rhine [Col. 0726D], and in other places. And, lest this kind of exercise should thereafter be maintained after his death, he wrote a letter to Fulrad, then a man of great authority in the kingdom of the Franks, in these words:

> “I beseech the majesty of our king, for the name of Christ the Son of God, to deign, while I am still alive, to inform and command me what reward he may later wish to bestow upon my disciples. For almost all of them are foreigners; some are priests, appointed in many places for the ministry of the Church and of the peoples. Some are monks in our cells, and children appointed to learn their letters [perhaps: ‘children appointed to learn reading’]. There are also some elders who, having lived with me for a long time, have labored and helped me. I am concerned about all of them, lest after my death they be scattered.”

When Wigbert, abbot of the monastery of Fritzlar, had died, Boniface therefore ordered that Wigbert the priest and Megingod the deacon should expound the Rule, be teachers of the children, and preach the word of God to the brothers [Col. 0727A]. 640 Afterward the study of letters flourished in the monasteries, as far as those rusty times allowed, so that the monasteries were not more places of virtue than of learning.” Thus far Mabillon.

Later Charlemagne commended the same cause in the Capitularies of Aachen, decreeing (chapter 72) that schools for boys learning to read should be established, where throughout the individual monasteries and bishoprics they might learn psalms, musical notation, chant, computation, and grammar. It would take too long, and is not the leisure of the present occasion, to survey all the monasteries in detail. Yet I cannot pass over the ardent zeal of Benedictine women in cultivating letters during this century:

> “This praise,” Mabillon says again (Preface to the third century, no. 47), “must also be attributed to Boniface as its author. For while he was living in Britain, he instructed not only men in the disciplines, but also nuns, who, as Willibald writes, sought such a man of wisdom as their teacher. Under this teacher, while passing through the sequence of the pages, they clung earnestly to heavenly scrutiny and continually meditated upon the secrets of the sacraments and the hidden things of the mysteries [Col. 0727B]. Having gone to Germany, he himself summoned religious women there from Britain. Among them, Cunihilt and her daughter Berathgit, highly learned in liberal knowledge, were appointed teachers in the region of the Thuringians, according to Othlo, Book I, chapter 25.

> “Besides these, Lioba, placed by Boniface over the convent at Bischofsheim, devoted herself to reading with such diligence that, unless she was occupied in prayer, the divine page never left her hands. Since she had been trained from the earliest rudiments of childhood in grammar and the other studies of the liberal arts, she strove with such persistent meditation to attain perfection in spiritual knowledge that, as reading cooperated with her intellect, she became extremely learned through the doubled advantage of nature and industry. And, so that you may know more clearly the studies by which she chiefly formed her mind, hear how Rudolph, the author of her Life, continues:

> “ ‘She also added to the fullness of perfection the sayings of the holy Fathers, the decrees of the canons, and the laws of the entire ecclesiastical order. A considerable number of servants of God gathered in that convent, and they were trained according to the example of their blessed teacher in the studies of heavenly discipline. They advanced so far in her teaching that many of them afterward became teachers of others, so that there were scarcely any, or only rarely any, women’s monasteries in those regions that did not desire the instruction of her disciples, and so forth.’ ”

In the ninth century, Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane—called by the ancients “the second Benedict” because of his ardent zeal in promoting the holy Rule—conceived the plan of restoring regular observance and soon also labored to revive the study of letters (Fourth Benedictine Century). “He learned,” says Ardo in his Life, no. 27, “a useful standard and the wholesome customs of monasteries, and handed them on to his monks for observance. He established singers, taught readers, gathered grammarians and those skilled in the knowledge of Scripture, some of whom afterward became bishops.”

Through his efforts, the council assembled at Aachen in 817 decreed (canon 63) that learned brothers should be chosen to speak with monks who arrived from elsewhere [Col. 0727D]; and (canon 45) that “schools should be maintained in the monastery for those who have been offered.” In the Customs which he arranged to be adopted in the monasteries he founded (vol. IV of the *Analecta*), he orders that during the time of reading “the prior should command some more learned brother to give instruction in reading to the less learned brothers or to those who need instruction.”

641 How deeply the science of letters put down roots in our monasteries during this century would take a long time to relate. Anyone who wishes to learn more about this subject should consult Mabillon’s preface to the fourth century of the Benedictines, part I, no. 173, where he treats the subject at length and with his customary learning.

In the tenth century, Bishops Dunstan and Æthelwold, wisely undertaking to repair the collapsed monastic discipline in England, also endeavored for this reason to restore the sciences that had fallen asleep in the monasteries. For, as Ælfric testifies in Spelman (vol. I of the *English Councils*, p. 618), the study of letters in England had declined so far “that no English priest knew how either to compose a letter in Latin or to translate it from Latin, until Dunstan, archbishop of Canterbury, and Æthelwold, bishop, revived it in the monasteries” [Col. 0728A].

For this reason Grimbald, later abbot of Winchester, was summoned from Gaul to England by King Alfred, “so that by his industry he might revive the study of literature, which had fallen asleep in England and was almost dead,” says William of Malmesbury (*Deeds of the English Kings*, Book II, chapter 4). For the same reason, “Saint Oswald, having promptly sent a messenger” (Second Life of Saint Oswald, no. 20, Fifth Benedictine Century), “summoned from the monastery of Fleury a certain highly renowned man, Abbo, who had drunk in the knowledge of the liberal arts to the innermost marrow of his being, and appointed him to direct the schools at Ramsey and to water with the dew of his teaching the young grafts of his newly planted garden.”

In the same century Fulco, archbishop of Reims, who had been educated in the monastery of Sithiu, or Saint Bertin, restored a double school in his church. Over one he placed Remigius of Auxerre, from Saint Germanus; over the other [Col. 0728B], Hucbald of Elnone, or Saint-Amand in Belgium.

In the eleventh century, the sciences of letters flourished everywhere in the monasteries. This fact is so evident that it is unnecessary to linger over its proof.

At the beginning of the twelfth century, the Cistercians renewed the ancient fervor of the earlier monks. From the very cradle of their order they began to devote themselves to the study of letters, certainly while Saint Bernard was alive, as is clear from the book of the statutes of the general chapter of Cîteaux. That book contains the various definitions issued in general chapters from the beginning of the order up to the year 1134, when it was published—approximately twenty years before Saint Bernard’s death.

It contains an entire chapter on boys learning letters (chapter 76), in which it is prescribed that “none of the boys shall be taught letters within the monastery or in the places belonging to the monastery unless he is a monk or has been received as a novice on probation; such persons may study during the time of reading. And it must be noted [Col. 0728C] that no one may be placed on probation before his fifteenth year of age.”

The practice of this statute can be seen in the Life of Saint Hildegund, virgin, no. 21, written by a contemporary author (Bolland, 20 April). She entered the men’s monastery of Schönau, of the Cistercian order, under male clothing and having changed her own name to Joseph. After she had been admitted to probation with the other novices, the lord abbot Gottfried, who was then in charge of the monastery of Schönau [642]—as the author of the Life and her fellow novice relates—“heard Joseph reading and chanting among the brothers and understood that he had been considerably neglected in the pursuit of learning. Therefore, I do not know by what arrangement or for what merit, when I had recently come from the world as a young man to be educated and trained, he entrusted him to me, so that within the probationary house I might educate, govern, and instruct him as far as I could. I did what I could, and so forth.”

And certainly, if the Cistercians had not studied, how could they have supplied the Church with so many highly learned men for episcopal sees and for the overthrow of heretics, especially the Albigensians?

[Col. 0728D] It is unnecessary to speak of the later centuries. The decrees of councils and supreme pontiffs are sufficient to refute those who claim that no ecclesiastical sanctions exist by which studies are permitted or commanded to monks. We do not retract the statutes of the Council of Aachen cited above.

A decretal of Clement V, issued in the Council of Vienne, is famous. Among other things, it reads as follows concerning our subject:

> “So that the monks themselves may not lack a more convenient means of advancing in knowledge, in each of their monasteries, wherever their resources permit it, a suitable teacher shall be maintained to instruct them diligently in the elementary sciences.”

The decree of the Council of Vienne is explained more fully by Pope Benedict XII in his constitution concerning Benedictine monks. He says as follows (chapter 6):

> “Since the pearl of knowledge is acquired through the exercise of reading, and through the study of sacred Scripture one more familiarly reaches knowledge of divine excellence, while through knowledge of human law the mind becomes more rational and is more certainly formed for justice; therefore, desiring that the men of this order or religious institute who labor in the Lord’s field be instructed first in the elementary sciences and afterward in the sciences of divine and human law, namely canon law, [Col. 0729A] and adhering to the constitution of Pope Clement V and of our predecessor concerning the instruction of monks in the elementary sciences within the monasteries where they live, we wish and firmly command that constitution to be observed.

> “Moreover, adding to it, we establish and ordain that in all cathedral churches, monasteries, priories, and other conventual and solemn places belonging to this order or religious institute, wherever their resources suffice for this purpose, there shall henceforth be a teacher who instructs their monks in these elementary sciences—namely, grammar, logic, and philosophy—provided most carefully that secular persons to be instructed are in no way admitted together with the monks being taught.

> “We further command, by virtue of obedience, all visitors appointed in provincial chapters [Col. 0729B] to ensure, by apostolic authority, ecclesiastical censure, and other suitable remedies, with appeal excluded, that each and every provision made above concerning teaching masters, the persons to be instructed, and other related matters be firmly observed. They shall also report to the presidents of the provincial chapter everything they have done and discovered concerning these matters. The presidents, likewise by the aforesaid apostolic authority, if it seems appropriate to them or to the greater part of them, shall not delay proceeding more severely against the negligent or rebellious in these matters, and so forth” (*Spicilegium*, vol. V).

This salutary statute of Pope Benedict was later renewed by Archbishop Tristandus in the Council of Sens in 1485, article 3, chapter 1. Most recently, the Council of Trent decreed (Session 5, decree on reform, chapter 1) that “in monasteries of monks, wherever it can conveniently be done, there shall also be a reading of sacred Scripture; and if abbots have been negligent in this matter, the bishops of the places, as delegates of the Apostolic See, shall compel them to it by suitable remedies.”

[Col. 0729C] This must plainly be understood not merely of the simple reading of sacred Scripture, which can be conveniently practiced everywhere, but of careful study by which the more obscure and difficult questions are diligently elucidated.

### Fourth

They say that the example of Christ and the holy apostles, who are never said to have studied and are sometimes said to have worked with their hands, offers no obstacle to the studies of monks, since the apostles possessed knowledge infused from heaven; once monks have received knowledge in the same way, they too will gladly abstain from study.

As for what is said about the labor of the apostles, it concerns only Paul and Barnabas, for the other apostles are not recorded to have performed manual labor after the coming of the Holy Spirit, as Rupert teaches (*Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, Book III, chapter 5), and before him Saint Augustine (*On the Work of Monks*).

Indeed, Paul labored not from necessity but, as he himself says, so as not to place an obstacle in the way of the Gospel: “He did this,” says Saint Augustine, “out of concern for the weak, lest, agitated by false suspicions, they should hate the Gospel as though it were being sold; as though shaken with paternal and maternal compassion [Col. 0729D].”

For the same reason the holy Doctor exhorts monks to labor:

> “Therefore, have mercy and compassion, and show people that you do not seek an easy livelihood in idleness, but the kingdom of God through the narrow way of this calling. You have the same reason as the Apostle, namely, to cut off the opportunity sought by those who seek an opportunity, so that those who are suffocated by the stench of their own corruption may be refreshed by the fragrance of your goodness.”

### Fifth

Since it is not so much bodily idleness as idleness of the mind that must be feared, they say that the command to flee idleness is fulfilled far more beneficially by studies, which engage the whole mind, than by manual labor, which indeed occupies the body but leaves the mind complete freedom to wander.

If someone continues to object that not everyone is capable of study, they reply: first, that not everyone is capable of labor either; second, that two classes of religious must be distinguished in monasteries: monks, who are destined for the divine altars, and lay brothers, who are destined only for external works [Col. 0730A]. In places that are properly and rightly organized, no one should be admitted among the monks who has not already been imbued with the best studies, or who is not at least capable of studying.

Those who are wholly destitute of learning should instead be assigned to the second class of religious. They are not merely permitted no studies; they are forbidden them in every way. If someone from the first class should perhaps be unable to become perfectly learned in either divine or human letters, Saint Benedict’s precept is available: in such a case, he should be assigned such work or craft that he does not remain idle.

### Sixth

They say that the body is no less worn down by study than by labor, which many undertake for the sake of preserving their health; nor is there only one form of mortifying the flesh among monks. The flesh is mortified by fasts, by vigils, by scourging, by harsh clothing, and so forth.

### Seventh

644 They say that study confers upon monks a devotion [Col. 0730B] far superior to that conferred by manual labor, and that piety is shown to be much more solid in the learned than in the uneducated. Through study the mind is illumined by divine knowledge, the heart is inflamed with heavenly desire, and devout movements of the soul are stirred up. Bodily exercise, by contrast, is useful only to a small degree, whereas piety is useful for all things.

Everyone knows the celebrated saying of Abbot William (*To the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*, chapter 22):

> “Subordinate exercises and works distract the senses, and thus often also exhaust the spirit.”

Abbot Rupert of Deutz had tested the truth of this himself, as he testifies in these words (*Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*, Book III, chapter 12):

> “In well-ordered monasteries, the summer days scarcely suffice to complete the course of the order, especially if the community is large or numerous. And if they sometimes undertake something of manual labor, going out together to work—something which, because of the shortness of the time spent, I would call not so much work as a semblance of work—the entire daily exercise of spiritual work is rendered almost tasteless, obstructed, and mutilated in some portion of itself [Col. 0730C], and so forth.”

Hence the widely circulated account of Abbot Irenaeus concerning an old man living in Scetis (*The Spiritual Meadow* of John Moschus, chapter 55), namely, that “he saw the devil at night offering hoes, rakes, and baskets to the brothers.” When the old man asked him what these things were, he replied:

> “I am preparing distraction for the brothers, so that, occupied with these things, they may become more negligent in praying and glorifying God.”

### Eighth

Since humility is the virtue by which a person becomes contemptible in his own eyes through knowledge of himself, and since he cannot perfectly acquire that knowledge from any other source than the benefit of study or a singular gift of God, they say that the sciences produce far greater humility than ignorance can attain.

Indeed, those whom I found to be the humblest in the monasteries I discovered to be the most learned of all, or favorable to study and the sciences. Of them it could rightly be said what Cassiodorus praised in Dionysius Exiguus, the most learned man of his time (*On the Institutions of Divine Literature*, chapter 23):

> “In him there was great simplicity with wisdom [Col. 0730D], humility with learning, and restraint in speech with eloquence.”

Moreover, the Apostle’s familiar statement, “Knowledge puffs up,” must be understood of knowledge deprived of charity, such as monks not only do not desire but reject by every means.

Manual labor, for its part, also has its puffed-up people—not only “in the splendor and pomp of bodily things,” as Saint Augustine says (*Sermon on the Lord’s Sermon on the Mount*, Book II, chapter 12), “but even in mournful squalor there is boastfulness, and it is more dangerous because it deceives under the name of service to God.” This could certainly not have escaped Saint Benedict, who therefore, speaking of the artisans of the monastery, commands (chapter 57):

> “If any one of them becomes proud because of his skill, on the grounds that he seems to contribute something to the monastery, such a person is to be removed from that craft, and he is not to pass through it again.”

### Ninth

From the agreement of almost all authors it is clear [Col. 0731A] that ignorance utterly weakened the force of the Rule in the monasteries. It is therefore astonishing that some attribute the collapse of regular observance to the study of letters. In doing so they inflict no small injury upon very holy men who, in order to restore the discipline overturned among monks, believed that no more salutary remedy could be applied than to train monks in sacred studies of letters.

This was successfully carried out in Gaul by Benedict, abbot of Aniane, and in England by the most holy bishops Dunstan, Æthelwold, and Oswald, who for this purpose summoned highly learned monks from foreign kingdoms and provinces.

Those who assert that the sciences began to flourish in monasteries only in the eighth and ninth centuries, and make them causes of the collapse of regular observance that occurred around the middle of the ninth century, are far from the truth. First, it has already been demonstrated with the greatest clarity that letters flourished in monasteries long before the eighth century.

Second, it is not true that the collapse of observance arose from the study of letters [Col. 0731B]. If those who teach this had read the histories, they would have attributed the cause not to study but to civil wars and the incursions of the Normans, who, after plundering and burning the monasteries, drove all the monks into scattered exile, so that scarcely any monastery in the entire kingdom of the Franks escaped their fury.

Adso, abbot of Der, recognized this as the true and only cause. In the tenth century he wrote a little book on the miracles and translation of Saint Basolus, in which he plainly teaches that in the monastery of Saint Basolus “partly because of barbarian incursions, and partly because of the frequent and continual dissensions among the rulers of the kingdom, the entire tradition of the institutions of the ancient Fathers perished” (chapter 1, Bolland, century IV of the Benedictines). He adds:

> “At that time other monasteries also were deprived of their honor, the churches were stripped of their possessions, and very many were overthrown.”

Nor does the truncated canon of the Council of Ver appear to favor them; for, to understand it fully, it must be cited here in its complete and entire form:

> “In holy places, that is, in monasteries, we have found that some deviate from their profession through deliberate purpose, others through negligence, and many through the necessity of food and clothing [Col. 0731C]” (chapter 12).

In this canon, deliberate purpose is opposed to necessity; necessity, however, is opposed only to spontaneous will. Therefore, in this passage “deliberate purpose” does not mean literary study, but a corrupt inclination of the soul toward evil.

A highly learned man who recently published a dissertation on the Benedictine measure of wine rendered the canon of the Council of Ver into French in precisely this sense. He says (Response to the Objections, no. 6):

> “The Council of Ver, held under Charles the Bald, testifies that even in his time many monks had departed from their way: some by a formed intention, others through sheer negligence, and most because they had nothing with which to live and clothe themselves.”

Nor do those seem any more deserving of a hearing who attribute to the study of letters the fall of those monks who followed the errors of Origen, embraced the heresies of Eutyches, defended the false novelties of Adelphius and the Euchites, championed the impious doctrines of Nestorius and Severus, or adhered to the Anthropomorphites.

Those who assert this plainly contradict themselves [Col. 0731D], since they teach that the studies in question were unknown to the ancient monks. They would have spoken more accurately and more consistently with the truth if they had attributed the downfall of those monks who stirred up so many disturbances and scandals in the East not to study but to their ignorance.

Certainly, if they had studied, they would not have followed such foolish errors with such blind fury. Hence the disciples of the great Euthymius, who, as was demonstrated above, devoted themselves to study, were also almost the only ones among all the monks of Palestine who adhered to the true faith.

Far be it from us, then—far be it from us—to blame the disorders of monasteries on the sciences, or to say that the inclination toward sacred letters, which supreme pontiffs and councils commend to monks, was left in monasteries by the devil for the overthrow of regular observance.

Adalbero, bishop of the Church of Augsburg, thought and saw quite otherwise. Returning from the monastery of Saint Gall, where all the sciences were then flourishing [Col. 0732A], and which he had visited for the sake of devotion, he was once asked by his people, among other things, whether, as rumor had it, “religion existed with learning and severity with discipline among us.” “I do not know,” he replied, “what the others think; I will state what is in my heart. I sought one holy man, and that one was dead; but the living, I confess as true brothers, I found most holy. Their learning and discipline can be seen in their works of virtue. I delight in remembering such men, whom I scarcely await the opportunity to see again,” and so forth. Thus relates Ekkehard of Saint Gall, a monk, in the Life of Notker the Stammerer (Bolland, 6 April).

Therefore, if some monks who devoted themselves to the sciences occasionally fell, the fault should not be attributed to the sciences, by which they could have been deterred from crime, but to the perverse disposition of their hearts.

Nor should it be thought that their lot would have been better had they not studied [Col. 0732B]. Even if they had not committed the crimes through which they perished by abusing study, they might perhaps have committed greater ones without studying. The object of their sinful will would have changed, but not the evil disposition of their hearts.

### Tenth

Since all monks now receive priestly orders according to the prescription of the Church, and since the principal study both of priests and of monks ought to concern itself with Sacred Scripture in order to attain a perfect understanding of it, they assert and prove that knowledge of the other disciplines is also necessary, especially on the authority of St. Augustine, who is wholly occupied with this matter in his books *On Christian Doctrine*. For the holy Doctor assumes that Scripture is ordinarily not understood for two reasons (*Book II, ch. 10*): “if it is covered either by unknown or by ambiguous signs,” that is, by words. Then, distinguishing between proper and transferred, or metaphorical, signs (*ch. 11*), he says:

> “Against unknown proper signs, the great remedy is knowledge of languages. The speakers of the Latin language whom we have now undertaken to instruct need two other languages for knowledge of the divine Scriptures, namely Hebrew and Greek, so that one may have recourse to the earlier exemplars if the infinite variety of Latin translators should introduce any doubt.”

And afterward (*ch. 16*):

> “With transferred signs, if any unknown ones should happen to compel the reader to pause, they must be investigated partly through knowledge of languages and partly through knowledge of things.”

Therefore, besides knowledge of languages, Augustine holds that knowledge of things is also necessary for understanding Scripture:

> “For ignorance of things makes figurative expressions obscure, when we are ignorant either of the natures of animals, stones, and plants, or of other things that are often placed in Scripture for the sake of some comparison.”

The holy Doctor adds:

> “Ignorance of numbers also causes many things placed figuratively and mystically in Scripture not to be understood.” [647]

And shortly afterward:

> “Ignorance of certain musical matters also closes and conceals no small number of things.”

Then, after saying something about those sciences which a Christian ought to avoid, he adds the following concerning what is useful and necessary for understanding Scripture (*ch. 28*):

> “Whatever, therefore, the account of past times called history indicates greatly assists us in understanding the holy books, even if it is learned outside the Church through childish instruction. For many things are investigated by means of Olympiads and the names of consuls, and ignorance of the consulship in which the Lord was born and that in which he suffered has compelled some to fall into error, etc.”

And after recounting several matters in praise and defense of history, he says:

> “There is also a narrative resembling demonstration, by which not past things but present things are indicated to those who are ignorant. This kind includes whatever has been written concerning the situation of places and the natures of animals, trees, plants, stones, and other bodies. We discussed this kind above, and said that such knowledge is useful for solving the riddles of Scripture.”

In the following chapter he also praises knowledge of the mechanical arts. Then, turning to the liberal arts, or sciences that concern the reasoning faculty of the mind, he praises dialectic above all:

> “The discipline of disputation is of very great value for penetrating and resolving all kinds of questions found in the sacred writings. Only the desire to quarrel and a certain childish display of deceiving one’s opponent must be avoided there.”

After praising dialectic at greater length, he also commends (*ch. 36 and following*) rhetoric and arithmetic, that is, the science of numbers. Finally, near the end of the second book, he says (*ch. 40*):

> “As for those who are called philosophers, if they have happened to say anything true and suited to our faith, especially the Platonists, they are not only not to be feared, but their statements are to be claimed for our use from them, as from unjust possessors.”

What we have said thus far from St. Augustine agrees with what we related above from Cassiodorus. We could also have added the testimony of St. Epiphanius, who asserts that anyone wishing to understand many passages of Sacred Scripture must know the little book that he himself composed concerning weights and measures. But we believe that these things suffice for the benefit of studies.

We now leave it to each person’s freedom to embrace whichever of the two opinions he prefers, provided that those who have resolved to devote themselves to study do not despise others as ignorant and uneducated, because “the humble peasant is better than the proud philosopher who, neglecting himself, considers the course of the heavens” (*Book I of the Imitation of Christ, ch. 2*). Conversely, those who have judged labor preferable to study should not look down upon students as conceited, proud, and corrupt in mind and heart, because “if anyone is to become a perfect monk, he needs both instruction in the divine utterances and integrity of life, so that he may be made worthy of so great a transformation,” as the emperor Justinian once said (*Novella 5*); and because it is certain that “no sharper poison kills the souls and bodies of religious persons than ignorance of letters and sciences,” as the Camaldolese monks say (*Camaldolese History*, Book III, ch. 5). Otherwise, let them hear that saying addressed to themselves by Gilbert of Hoyland, the most renowned abbot of the Cistercian order (*Treatise 7, Part I, no. 6*):

> “Paul says: ‘Bearing fruit and increasing in the knowledge of God.’ These men, on the contrary, not content with their own ignorance, despise the knowledge of others; and, judging enviously, interpret the pursuit of wisdom as stupidity, while they denigrate sober subtlety as madness and vanity, themselves working for food that perishes, not for food that endures unto eternal life.”

### “During these days of Lent let all receive individual books from the library, etc.”

What the procedure was, we must learn from Hildemar:

> “It must be known that books are distributed in this manner at the beginning of Lent. The librarian of the monastery brings all the books, with the assistance of the brothers, into the chapter house. Then carpets are spread, and the books are placed upon the carpets. When the chapter meeting is finished, the librarian reads from the register which brother has the book until that hour. Then that brother places the book he had on the carpet, and the prior, or whoever has been appointed by him, takes the book and wisely questions the brother about it, in order to determine whether he has read the book diligently. If that brother answers concerning the book, then he asks which book would be useful to him, and gives him whichever he requests. But if the abbot realizes that it is not suitable for him, he says: ‘This book is not suitable for you, but such-and-such a book is suitable for you’; and then he does not give him the one he requested, but the one he recognizes as suitable for him. If, however, the brother is unable to give an account of the book in response to the questioning, and the abbot sees that he read the book negligently, he does not give him another, but returns the same one to him, and he keeps it afterward until he has read it diligently. He says to him: ‘Because you did not read it well, you ought to have informed us beforehand, so that we might have given you time to be questioned.’ But if the abbot recognizes that the brother was diligent in reading and nevertheless could not understand, he gives him another book. After all the brothers have left the chapter house, the abbot examines and checks whether all the books listed in the register are present. If he does not find as many books as the register contains, he searches carefully until he finds them.”

You will find almost the same procedure in Udalricus (*Book I, ch. 52*), in Lanfranc’s *Statutes* (*ch. 1, § 3*), in the *Customs of the Monastery of Fleury*, and in the *Book of Cistercian Usages* (*ch. 15*).

They differ in almost one respect only: Lanfranc, Udalricus, and the Customs of Fleury distribute the books on the Monday after the First Sunday of Lent. This custom prevailed among the Cassinese monks in the time of Abbot Bernard. The Cistercian Usages distribute them on the Sunday itself. But Boherius asserts that they should be given on Ash Wednesday, and Bernard of Cassino does not reject this; he says that it was observed in this way in certain monasteries in his own time. Once books had been received, moreover, no one was permitted to exchange them for others, as the Council of Aachen decreed (*canon 19*):

> “During Lent, having received books from the library according to the prior’s arrangement, they shall not receive others unless the prior has determined that it is expedient.”

### “Before all things, indeed.”

Richard of St. Angelo explains this as meaning “before the books are assigned.” And yet the Cistercians, immediately after the distribution of the aforementioned books, designate in the chapter house brothers who are to go around the monastery according to the Rule (*Cistercian Usages*, ch. 15).

### “Let one or two elders be appointed.”

Not so much in age as in virtue and wisdom.

### “Who shall go around.”

Hence, in Dunstan’s *Concordia* (*ch. 7*), they are called *circae*; in Lanfranc’s *Statutes* (*ch. 4*), *circumitores* and *circae*; in the *Customs of St. Benedict of Aniane* (*vol. IV of the *Analecta*), and in Udalricus (*Book III, ch. 7*), *circatores*; in Peter the Venerable (*Book I of the *Miracles*, ch. 20*), *circuitores*; and finally, in the *Statutes of St. Adalard* (*Book II, ch. 6*), *circinnatores*.

### “The monastery.”

That is, the monastery’s departments:

> “They shall inspect the departments,” says the *Book of Cistercian Usages* (*ch. 15*), “the cloister, the oratory, the chapter house, the dormitory, the warming room, the refectory, the kitchen, and the auditoriums, lest anyone be found behaving improperly; and for this purpose they may enter the departments mentioned above, except the auditoriums.”

Yet according to Lanfranc’s *Statutes* (*ch. 4*):

> “They shall never enter the monastery’s departments for this purpose, but shall watch their doors, in case any brothers should wander through the courtyard, or stand or sit there conversing.”

### “At the hours when the brothers are free for reading.”

Indeed, at other times also. Udalricus says (*Book III, ch. 7*):

> “They shall go around the entire cloister not once but many times a day, so that there may be neither place nor hour in which any brother who has committed such a thing can feel secure that he will not be reproved and exposed.”

The manuscripts of the *Customs of St. Benignus of Dijon* list these hours especially (*ch. 4*):

> “They go after the offering of the major Mass and of the minor Mass on every day; and after supper when they eat twice, and, when they eat once, after dinner. They also go to the office for the dead. They likewise rise repeatedly from dinner or supper—not all of them, but some—when they suspect that they will find some negligence in the cellar or almonry, or somewhere near the refectory, so that, if necessary, they may immediately hurry with the others to the verse after the end of dinner. They also customarily go during the interval between the ringing of the bell and dinner.”

Lanfranc’s *Statutes* add two times (*ch. 4*): before Matins and toward the end of Matins, or Lauds.

### “But he also exalts others.”

That is, he distracts them from reading, as Peter the Deacon, cited by Bernard of Cassino, explains it. Or, as Hildemar has it, “he exalts others,” that is, he gives others an occasion for boasting: when they see him devoting himself to idleness and conversation while they are attentive to reading, they consider themselves better than he is, saying with the Pharisee, “I am not like the rest of mankind.” You find both meanings in Nicholas of Fractura.

### “If such a man should be found—God forbid.”

He is to be entered in the records and proclaimed in the following chapter meeting, as can be seen in the *Customs of St. Benedict of Aniane* (*vol. IV of the *Analecta*). The *Concordia of Dunstan* agrees in these words (*ch. 7*):

> “If he finds such a man, he must in no way conceal it in the chapter meeting of the following day.”

Lanfranc’s *Statutes* likewise say (*ch. 4*):

> “While they are going around, they shall make no sign and speak to no one on any pretext; they shall diligently inspect only negligences and offenses, and, passing by silently, shall afterward bring accusations concerning them in the chapter meeting.”

The Customs of St. Benignus of Dijon say the same (*ch. 4*).

From Hildemar, however, the *circatores* appear to have had some authority to correct offenders:

> “These elders,” he says, “must have the power to correct deans and provosts, even the abbot himself, though not all in the same manner: admonishing, entreating, and rebuking subordinates; entreating priors.”

Concerning the priors, however, Udalricus writes as follows (*Book III, ch. 7*):

> “The *circatores* show such deference to the lord abbot and the prior that they never go where they know them to be, because it is written: ‘The disciple is not above his master.’”

When the *circatores* approached, those who were speaking by permission about necessary matters did not delay informing them of this, as Udalricus testifies (*ibid.*):

> “The obedientiaries, who cannot refrain from speaking at times about their duties while the others are silent, if they see one of the *circatores* approaching, immediately rise and briefly indicate what necessity requires them to speak.”

Lanfranc’s *Statutes* say likewise (*ch. 4*):

> “When they find some brothers speaking outside the cloister, the speakers themselves should rise together before them, and one of them should say, if that is the case, that they are speaking there with permission.”

The Customs of St. Benignus of Dijon say the same.

### “Nor should brother join himself to brother at unsuitable hours.”

What the suitable hours are, we have shown in the commentary on chapters 6 and 31: they are called the hours during which, on certain days and at certain times, it is permitted to refresh the spirit through mutual conversation. Boherius confirms this interpretation when he writes concerning this passage:

> “Almost all hours are unsuitable for this, unless these gatherings take place communally or are permitted by the Rule.”

He nevertheless adds:

> “Or perhaps he is speaking here of the laborers, who are not permitted to join together, or even to enter other crafts or the workshops of crafts.”

He proves this from the Rule of St. Basil. To this passage also belongs what is read in the *Penalties* of an uncertain author, preserved by the same St. Basil (*no. 25*):

> “If two are found conversing together, and, when admonished, do not separate, let them be excommunicated until they are corrected.”

### “On Sunday let all devote themselves to reading.”

And to other exercises of piety, which are here included under the name of reading, as though he were saying: “Let them not perform bodily works, but works of the soul,” says Boherius. Thus the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius (*ch. 9*) says:

> “On Sunday they shall do nothing else except devote themselves to God, lest on any pretext they wish to excuse themselves or others. Yet I testify, brothers, that no work is to be found on that holy day except that the day be spent in hymns, psalms, and spiritual songs.”

The petition that the monks of Fulda addressed to Charlemagne should be referred to this passage (*no. 3*), asking:

> “On those festivals that deserve greater veneration, may the brothers be permitted to abstain from work and devote themselves to reading and psalmody, as was permitted among our predecessors—that is, on the feast of Saint Mary and of the twelve Apostles.”

### “Except those who have been assigned to various duties.”

Such as the servants of the kitchen, the sick, and the guests, and the cellarer. The Cistercians, however, abstained from baking bread, as we gather from the *Life of St. Stephen, Abbot of Obazine*, where we read (*Book II, no. 27, vol. IV of Baluze’s *Miscellany*):

> “One Saturday, when we had used so many loaves in almsgiving that scarcely anything remained for the next day, it was decided that on Sunday we should bake contrary to our usual custom.”

### “But if anyone is so negligent and lazy that he neither wishes nor is able to meditate or read, let him be assigned some work to do, so that he may not be idle.”

These words do not refer to the immediately preceding sentence, since one is not to work on Sunday, but must be referred to everything said in this chapter. St. Benedict here identifies two classes of persons: those who can meditate or read but do not wish to, and those who wish to but cannot. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius think that the first group should be led through the six stages and finally assigned work to perform as a means of expulsion. I would assign the work first and afterward lead him through the six stages.

### “Let work or a craft of this kind be assigned to sick or delicate brothers.”

Hildemar draws this distinction between a craft and work: “Every craft is work, but not every work is a craft. A craft is something performed only by a master; work is without craft, such as cleaning beans or grain, and so forth.” Bernard of Cassino speaks in nearly the same way. Hildemar explains what sort of craft St. Benedict is discussing:

> “If he knows how to sing, let him teach another a song; or, if he knows grammar, let him pass it on to others; or, if he knows other crafts that are useful in the monastery, let him teach them to others.”

### “So that they may be neither idle nor crushed by the violence of labor, and so that they may escape.”

“This means,” says Bernard of Cassino, “so that they may not be given a cause for flight, departure, or rebellion.” A similar statute is found in the Rule of St. Ferreolus:

> “Let anyone who is unable to persist in work devote himself more readily to reading.
