Whoever does not cultivate the field should honor God doubly, and among other things should also seek this craft: to paint a page with the finger that does not mark the earth with a plow. Therefore, if anyone does less work, let him not think that he is offering a reason for a legitimate excuse, since the man who, as we said above, cannot practice agriculture can read and write—which is the principal work—provide a catch of fish, weave a net, prepare shoes for the brothers, and perform and complete other similar tasks.”

See also the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius (*ch. 11*), and that of St. Isidore (*ch. 6*).

## CHAPTER XLIX. On the observance of Lent

[Col. 0735]

[Col. 0735D] Although the monk’s life ought to observe Lent at all times [Note: [Col. 0735D] Another reading: *debet* (“ought to observe Lent”).], nevertheless, because this virtue belongs to few, we therefore urge that during these days of Lent they guard their life with complete purity and together wash away during these holy days all the negligences of other times [Note: [Col. 0735D] Another reading: *omnes pariter et negligentias* (“all alike, and the negligences”).] [Note: [Col. 0735D] Oxford omits “of other times.”] [Col. 0736D] [Note: [Col. 0735D] The Conciliar text omits “holy.”] This is done worthily if we restrain ourselves from all vices [Note: [Col. 0735D] Cassinese, Narbonne, Fleury, Conciliar, Afflighem, Hadrianic: “we abstain”; Ebrul: “we abstain inwardly”]: let us devote ourselves to prayer with tears [Note: [Col. 0736D] The Conciliar text omits “with tears”], to reading, to compunction of heart [Note: [Col. 0736D] Hildemar omits “of heart”], and to abstinence [Note: [Col. 0736D] Fleury: *damus* (“we devote ourselves”).]

Therefore, during these days let us add something to our accustomed measure [Note: [Col. 0737A] Narbonne and Fleury: *solito penso* (“to the accustomed measure”); Cassinese: *a solito pensu* (“from the accustomed measure”); Boherius: *a solito penso* (“from the accustomed measure”).] of our service: special prayers, abstinence from food and drink, so that each person may offer God, with the joy of the Holy Spirit, something of his own will beyond the measure imposed upon him—that is, let him withdraw from his body some food, drink, sleep, talkativeness, and frivolity; and with the joy of spiritual desire let him await holy Easter [Note: [Col. 0737A] Oxford: “let him look toward it”]. Nevertheless, let each person report to his abbot what he offers, and let it be done with the abbot’s prayer and consent, because anything done without the permission [Note: [Col. 0737A] Oxford, Dijon, Hadrianic: “consent”] of the spiritual Father will be counted as presumption and vainglory [Note: [Col. 0738A] The Conciliar text omits “and vainglory”], not as a reward [Note: [Col. 0738A] Hildemar: “not as the desire for a reward”]. Therefore everything must be done with the abbot’s consent [Note: [Col. 0738A] Another reading: “let everything be done”].

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0737]

The sacred season of Lent, consecrated by the fast of Christ the Lord, instituted by the Apostles and, as they say, confirmed by a decree of Pope Telesphorus, was observed by monks in the Church with such solemnity and with such constant special devotion and penitence that they strove to withdraw during this period especially from all human company, to penetrate the most remote retreats of solitude, to pass many days without food or drink, and to mortify the body through other exercises of self-denial. It is therefore no wonder that St. Benedict devoted a separate chapter to the observance of Lent. But since the greatness of the penitence is judged from the length of Lent, and since we wish to show more fully what the monks’ fervor was during these days, we think it worthwhile briefly to discuss how many days Lent lasted before St. Benedict.

Although the word *Lent* appears to indicate a period of forty days, the common practice of both the Eastern and Western Churches was that the faithful fasted for only thirty-six days. There was nevertheless this difference: the Easterners celebrated Lent for seven weeks, while the Westerners celebrated it for only six. The former broke their fast on Sunday and Saturday, except for one Holy Saturday; the latter did so only on Sunday. The matter is clear from Cassian, *Conferences* 21, chapters 24 and 27. Later, four days were added in order to complete the number forty. At what time this happened is not established. Certainly it was not before the pontificate of Gregory the Great, since in his homily 16 on the Gospel—which Amalarius cites in support of this point (*Book I on the Offices*, ch. 7)—he counts only thirty-six days in Lent. Whether Gregory established toward the end of his life that the Lenten fast should begin on the Wednesday after Quinquagesima, some may suspect, since in his book of Sacraments that day is designated “Wednesday, Beginning of the Fast,” unless, with Menard, we wish to suppose that a fragment was sewn into the book of Sacraments. See his notes on that book, p. 52. I now turn to the text of the Rule.

### “Although the monk’s life ought to observe Lent at all times.”

Here St. Benedict seems to allude to that famous statement of St. Augustine:

> “Throughout this life, which is lived amid temptations, the Christian ought continually to hang upon the cross; for in this life there is no time for removing the nails.... This cross, I say, is not a cross of forty days, but of the whole of this life, which is signified by the mystical number of those forty days.... Live here always in this manner, Christian, if you do not wish to immerse your steps in earthly mire: do not descend from this cross. But if this must be done throughout the whole of life, how much more during these days of Lent, in which this life is not only lived but also signified.”

### “Therefore during these days of Lent let us guard our life with complete purity and together wash away during these holy days all the negligences of other times.”

Something very similar is said by St. Augustine—or by whoever the author may be:

> “During these days we ought to rest from the sea and waves of this world, as though in the harbor of Lent, and receive the divine readings in the receptacle of our heart with silence and peace, so that, by God’s favor, while devoting ourselves to the love of eternal life, we may strive during these days with every care to repair and set right whatever in the little ship of our soul has been broken, loosened, corrupted, or lost throughout the year amid many storms—that is, amid the waves of sins.”

### “This is done worthily if we restrain ourselves from all vices.”

For what good is abstinence from food if abstinence from vices is absent?

> “Let that member which alone has sinned,” says St. Bernard (*Sermon 3 on Lent*), “alone fast, and that is enough. But if the other members have also sinned, why should they not fast as well? Let the eye, therefore, fast, which has plundered the soul; let the ear fast, let the tongue fast, let the hand fast, and let the soul itself also fast. Let the eye fast from curious glances and every kind of wantonness, so that the eye which wandered freely into guilt may be properly humbled and restrained in penitence. Let the wickedly itching ear fast from tales and rumors, and from everything idle and wholly unrelated to salvation. Let the tongue fast from detraction and murmuring, from useless, vain, and frivolous words; sometimes, because of the gravity of silence, even from things that might appear necessary. Let the hand fast from idle gestures and from all works that have not been commanded. But above all, let the soul itself fast from vices and from its own will.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius observe here that St. Benedict did not say absolutely, “Let us abstain from vices,” but “Let us moderate them,” because there are certain vices which, owing to the concupiscence that remains in us, we cannot completely eradicate, but which we can at least cut back to the root and thus moderate.

### “Let us devote ourselves to prayer with tears, to reading, to compunction of heart, and to abstinence.”

Here the holy legislator prescribes five things. In order to devote themselves to these more freely, the monks of old lived separated from all human company, either shut up in their cells or withdrawing into solitude. The practice can be seen in the *Life of St. Marius, Abbot of Bodan* (no. 4); the *Life of St. Marculf, Abbot of Nantua* (no. 12); the *Life of St. Samson* (Book II, no. 12); the *Life of St. Emiliano* (no. 10); and elsewhere, but especially in the *Life of St. Mary of Egypt*, in which Sophronius speaks as follows of the monks living near the Jordan (*in Rosweyde’s Book I of the Lives of the Fathers*):

> “On Sunday, which customarily is called the first week of the fasts, the divine mysteries were celebrated as usual, and each person became a participant in the life-giving and undefiled body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ. After taking a little food, as was customary, they all gathered in the oratory, and, bending their knees and making humble prayer, the monks greeted one another. Each one, kneeling, publicly embraced the abbot, asking for his prayer, so that they might have him as a fellow-worker and companion in the contest they had begun. When this had been done, the monastery gates were opened. Singing with one voice, ‘The Lord is my light and my salvation; whom shall I fear? The Lord is the defender of my life; of whom shall I be afraid?’ and so forth, they went out, leaving one or sometimes two guardians of the monastery—not to guard what had been placed inside, for they had nothing there suitable for thieves, but lest the oratory be left without the divine solemnities.

> “Each person took for himself as much as he could or wished. One carried enough for his body according to measure; another carried *carycae* [dried figs]; another carried dates, the fruit of the palm; another legumes soaked in water; another nothing except his own body and the garment he wore. When nature required it, they were nourished by the plants that grew in the wilderness. Each person was his own rule and law without transgression: no one was to know how his companion fasted or how he lived. For immediately after crossing the Jordan they separated themselves far from one another, and no one joined himself to his companion, regarding the wilderness as a city.

> “If one of them saw someone approaching from a distance, he immediately turned aside from the road and went in another direction. He lived for himself and for God, frequently singing psalms and eating food at the appointed time. Having kept all these fasts, they returned to the monastery before the life-giving day of the Resurrection of our Lord and Savior Jesus Christ, the holy Church having received the custom of celebrating that Sunday with palm branches.

> “Each returned with his own conscience as the witness of his own labor, knowing how he had worked and what seeds of labor he had sown. No one in any way asked another how or in what manner he had completed the struggles of his labor.”

This custom of withdrawing into solitude during Lent was pleasing not only to monks but also to bishops, as can be seen in the *Life of St. Walaric* (ch. 13) and the *Life of St. Kentigern* (ch. 3, *Second Age of the Benedictine Acta Sanctorum*, Bollandists, January 13). William of Malmesbury also relates this concerning St. Aethelwold (*Book IV of the English Bishops*, at the end).

### “Therefore during these days let us add something to our accustomed measure of our service.”

The phrase “to our accustomed measure” can be understood in two ways.

1. It may refer to the customary manner of life of other times. “For above,” says Hildemar, “he had defined how much bread, how much pottage, and how much sleep there should be. Now, by saying ‘let us add to this measure,’ he urges that something be added to that amount.” The preceding words can support this explanation, since he urges them to wash away the negligences of other times during these holy days.

2. It may refer to the accustomed measure, that is, to the measure prescribed by the Rule even during Lent. This meaning seems more natural, for the things that the Rule prescribes for Lent must be observed equally by everyone; but the things that he here urges to be added are not imposed in the same way, but depend upon each person’s will and the abbot’s blessing. The following words explain what these things are.

### “Special prayers.”

For Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino, special prayers are private prayers, “as distinct from the common and regular prayers that are performed by everyone in the assembly at the appointed times,” says Bernard of Cassino. He adds:

> “Those prayers may also be called special which are added and performed beyond those that a person performed or neglected to perform outside Lent.”

In order to fulfill this ordinance of the holy Rule more freely, the other Bernard, the abbot of Clairvaux, even abstained from writing books. Thus, when his friend William, the abbot, urged him to oppose Peter Abelard and refute his errors, he replied as follows (*Letter 392*):

> “I think it worthwhile, especially given the opportunity, for me and for them alike to meet somewhere and discuss everything. Nevertheless, I do not think that this can be done before Easter, lest the study of prayer imposed by the present season be hindered.”

See *Book III of Ancient Monastic Rites*, ch. 10.

### “Abstinence from food and drink.”

And especially this, since the holy legislator commends it three times in this chapter, as Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius observed. First he said, “Let us devote ourselves to abstinence”; then, “abstinence from food and drink”; and finally, “let him withdraw from his body some food and drink,” and this beyond the measure imposed upon him.

The measure imposed during Lent seems to have been nothing other than bread, and perhaps water alone. For the passages cited above in the commentary on chapter 39 imply that only bread was permitted. What we add concerning water can be gathered clearly enough from the *Life of St. Placidus*, in which it is written that, living a Lenten life throughout the whole year, he never drank wine. This is confirmed by the Rule of St. Isidore (*ch. 10*):

> “In the observance of Lent, as is customary, after the fast has been completed, all shall be content with bread alone and water, while all shall abstain from wine and oil.”

And by the Rule of St. Fructuosus (*ch. 18*):

> “During Lent one must abstain completely from wine and oil.”

Indeed, it was fitting that monks should practice greater abstinence than secular people. It is established from canon 50 of the Council of Laodicea and from Tertullian’s *Book I Against the Psychics* that secular people used only dry foods during Lent. Tertullian speaks as follows:

> “We observe *xerophagy*, drying our food, abstaining from all meat and broth, and from every kind of juicy fruit, so that we neither eat nor drink anything vinous.”

That secular men also abstained from wine in the time of St. Augustine is taught us by the holy Doctor (*Sermon 206*), when he warns the people not to seek unusual beverages, because he does not drink wine. What is more, the Greeks even now observe *xerophagy* during their fasts, and Balsamon testifies that abstinence from fish is practiced among them. The Armenian Christians, although Eutychians and schismatics, abstain not only from the flesh of land animals, dairy products, and eggs, but also from fish, wine, and oil, as various travelers who visited these nations in our own age have written. Furthermore, Balsamon teaches in his commentary on Apostolic Canon 69 that the Greeks also observe *xerophagy* throughout the year on Wednesdays and Fridays, to such an extent that neither on those days nor during Lent is any dispensation ever made, even for the seriously ill and even at the point of death—except with regard to fish.

To this burden of service, then—that is, if we conjecture correctly—to the evening refection consisting solely of bread and water, St. Benedict wishes something to be added: namely, that those to whom a full pound of bread is granted each day should subtract some portion of it from themselves; indeed, if God should grant it, that they should pass entire days without food or drink [Col. 0740C]. St. Benedict himself and his first disciples, Maurus and Placidus, are said to have done this in their Lives. An anonymous author also relates of St. Austreberta in her Life (second Benedictine century) that “throughout all the Lents, except Sundays, she ate only three times during the week.” And Gervinus, the most devout abbot of Centula, according to Hariulf, during Lent in 657, “by very rarely taking bread made from wheat, with a small quantity of water allotted for drink and using such nourishment as his food, was meanwhile refreshed after three days” (*Chronicle of Centula*, book IV, chapter 26, *Spicilegium*, vol. IV).

But what Fortunatus writes of St. Radegund (in her Life, no. 22, first Benedictine century) is altogether worthy of admiration. This woman, formerly the most powerful queen of France but made a humble religious at the monastery of Poitiers, once, during Lent, shut herself away and “took no bread as food except on Sunday, but only roots of plants or greens made from mallows, prepared without a drop of oil and without salt; moreover, throughout the whole fast she took not even two sextarii of water.”

St. Fidolus, abbot (in his Life, no. 10, first Benedictine century), also “during the time of the holy Lent always imposed upon himself, as a persecutor of his own body, such severity of abstinence that he generally got through it by eating only three loaves; often one of those very loaves would remain; as drink, however, at such a refection he took nothing other than lye-water” [Col. 0740D]. See the *Life of St. Macarius of Alexandria*, chapters 3 and 5, in the Bollandists, January 2.

Afterward, however, when charity grew cold, such fervor of abstinence also cooled among the monks. For the Master, in his Rule (chapter 53), already grants for the whole of Lent one cooked pottage and another uncooked one; during the first week, two drinks, namely one unmixed and one hot. During the second week he grants each person one unmixed drink, and thereafter, until Easter, withdraws wine, allowing hot water mixed with salt, cumin, and celery seed, and on Good Friday taking away all food altogether.

The more lenient manuscript *Customs of Germany* prescribe only the following (no. 30) [Col. 0741A]:

“In Septuagesima, fat is to be left for eating; in Quinquagesima, eggs and cheese; in Lent, on the second, fourth, and sixth days of the week, one must abstain from fish. And throughout the entire year, except for the fifty days after Easter, on Wednesday and Friday they must always abstain from fish and fat and follow the crosses, unless a feast of twelve lessons intervenes or the prior has decided otherwise.”

[Textual note: The supplied *pinguedo ad edendum dimittatur* literally says “let fat be left for eating.” The sense of *dimittatur*, “be left,” is uncertain in this fasting instruction: it can be understood as allowance to eat or as relinquishment of the food. The translation preserves the wording rather than silently deciding between these opposed readings.]

The customs of the monks of Fleury likewise arrange their food during Lent as follows (chapter 7):

“The pound of bread ought to be larger and more delicate than usual, and the wine better than at other times [lacuna]. On Sunday, Tuesday, and Thursday the cellarer gives fish or the equivalent value in fish; on the other days, dried vegetables and millet throughout Lent, which the provost must distribute. On Wednesdays and Fridays we ought to receive raw herbs from the gardener, and likewise during the Ember fasts throughout the year.”

Finally, the Cistercians, more austere than all the rest, defined only the following, as far as I know, in the general chapter of 1293 (*Book of Institutes*, distinction 13, chapter 6) [Col. 0741B]:

“Friday abstinence during Lent is to be observed as follows: on three Fridays we shall use bread and water in the convent; on the other three we shall be content with one pottage and the customary drink.”

### On Sleep

Thus, “he who was accustomed to sleep from the end of Compline until he was summoned for the vigils, or after Compline, or before he was summoned to the vigils, shall devote himself to prayer or meditation, or certainly to the silent recitation of psalms,” as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius put it.

Likewise, in the monastery of Piscaria (*Chronicle of Piscaria*, book III, *Spicilegium*, vol. V), “two brothers, following a pious Lenten custom, were accustomed to rise from their beds before Matins and, kneeling before the bones of the most holy martyr, pour forth prayers and sobs, sing psalms, and invoke the saints of God with litanies for the assistance of the Christian people” [Col. 0741C].

### On Talkativeness

Therefore they spoke at other times, since during Lent they are ordered to reduce something of their talkativeness. For carrying out this command, the Statutes of Lanfranc decree (chapter 1, §3) that during Lent “on three days, namely Monday, Wednesday, and Friday until Easter, the board is not to be struck after chapter, nor are they to speak in the cloister.” This was not peculiar to Lanfranc, but was common everywhere among the Benedictines, as is shown by what was said in book III of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 10.

Indeed, Peter the Venerable imposed continuous silence upon the Cluniacs during Lent in statute 20. The Cassinese still allow no recreations during Advent and Lent (*Cassinese Declaration* on chapter 6, no. 5); they say that it is sacrilegious for monks even to think of such things, much less to permit them.

### On Buffoonery

Buffoonery is forbidden to monks at all times.

### “Nevertheless, let each one suggest to his abbot what he offers”

The Rule of the Master explains this custom in the following manner (chapter 53) [Col. 0741D]:

“On the very day of Lent, when they receive Communion at the first fast, before they communicate, such permission is to be given by the abbot in the oratory. The abbot shall say to all the brothers: ‘Brothers, whoever wishes to labor spiritually for his soul and to abstain from something, we grant him free choice for this good work; whoever does not wish to do so shall receive what the Rule has established under this heading and shall be content with the Lenten measure.’ Then those of the brothers who wish to abstain from something shall go there in the oratory and humble themselves at the abbot’s knees, giving thanks for the permission granted them to undertake a good deed; and after performing this act of humility, they shall inform the abbot together and with their own mouths what each wishes to abstain from.”

Our order, however, had adopted the common practice that this permission to fast should be granted after the distribution of the books.

### “And when it has been done with his prayer and will”

“With his prayer”—that is, by which he implores God’s help, so that for those to whom he has given the vow of adding something to their customary burden, he may supply the assistance needed to accomplish what they requested under divine inspiration [Col. 0742A].

The commentators observe here that the abbot must not presume too much upon his own prayer; rather, he should enlist the prayers of the other brothers along with his own. He may do this generally, asking for the prayers of everyone in chapter that God may graciously receive the offerings of the congregation; or specifically, commending certain brothers who burn with an exceptional zeal for penance, for example in these words:

“There are some in this congregation of ours who, with our permission, have bound themselves to a great mortification of the body; I commend them especially to your prayers.”

Likewise, if he finds some so negligent that they do not wish to fast according to the Rule, he ought to commend them to the prayers of the others.

I consider this to be St. Benedict’s genuine meaning. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata follow it, and it is confirmed by a certain French translation, which renders this passage as follows: “May their mortifications be assisted by his prayers.” Nicholas of Fractura, however, interprets “prayer” here as a blessing [Col. 0742B]:

“‘With prayer,’ he says, that is, with a blessing, so that the abbot may say to the brother proposing abstinence: ‘May you do this in the blessing of God.’”

### “And will”

He does not use the simple word for permission, but “will,” so that the abbot’s will may intervene both for the one who wishes to exceed the limits of discretion and mortify his body beyond measure, and conversely for the one who has no intention of doing anything at all: restraining the former and impelling the latter toward greater things, as Hildemar teaches. He does not, however, advise that the abbot absolutely compel someone unwilling to add anything to his customary burden.

“When someone offers something, the abbot ought to consider whether the person is discreet, whether volatile or stable, constant and firm; whether his nature is capable of enduring it; whether he is healthy or infirm, fervent or lukewarm; and according to these considerations, he should grant either everything he asks, or part, or nothing at all,” says Bernard of Cassino.

### “Because what is done without the permission of a spiritual father will be reckoned presumption and vainglory, not reward”

Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata rightly observe here that one who undertakes some good thing without the abbot’s permission incurs, according to St. Benedict (*Sermon on Renunciation of Possessions*), three losses [Col. 0742C]:

“For he incurs the sin of presumption, falls into the snare of vainglory, and does not obtain a reward for his labors or abstinences.”

Indeed, if we believe Basil the Great (*Book IV, Letter 28*), he even commits theft and sacrilege.

Thus Abbot Goffridus of Vendôme rightly reproved the monk Robert because, by his own choice and without any permission from a superior, he refreshed himself on only three days of the week. St. Basil said (*Sermon 2, On the Institution of Monks*):

“The true and perfect obedience of subjects is shown not only by abstaining, on the advice of the superior, from disgraceful things, but also by doing praiseworthy things only according to his judgment. For abstinence and every mortification of the body are useful for some purpose; but if someone follows his own will and, disregarding the superior’s advice, does whatever pleases him, the evil he does will be greater than the good. For whoever resists authority resists God’s ordinance, and the reward of obedience is greater than continence” [Col. 0742D].

For this reason St. Teresa (*Additions to her Life*), when she once saw a certain nun mortifying herself with great works of penance and wondered whether she too would do better by setting aside her confessor’s advice and giving herself to more severe penitential exercises, heard the Lord answer her:

“Far be it from you, daughter. You cannot err if you hold to the path you are following; walk in it cautiously and securely. The mortifications of that religious woman are great, but I value your obedience more.”

See Haeften, book X, treatise 8, discussion 6.

### “Therefore everything is to be done with the abbot’s will”

Thus “no will at all is to live within us apart from the abbot’s command,” as Cassian says (book XII, chapter 32). For this is the safe and only path for monks striving toward perfection, and it has been followed by all who have ever excelled in monasteries [Col. 0743A].

Hence also the Rule of St. Posthumus, delivered by an angel:

“If on the road you tread upon a thorn,” it says, “you are not to pull it out until the abbot has ordered it.”

See the shorter rules of St. Basil, question 137, and St. Dorotheus, *Teaching* 7.

## CHAPTER L

### On Brothers Who Labor Far from the Oratory or Are on the Road

Brothers who are entirely far away [Note: Oxford and Hadrian manuscripts read “are far away,” omitting “at work”; Affligem reads “are far away from the oratory”; others read “are far away from the oratory or on the road”] at work and cannot arrive at the appointed hour at the oratory, when the abbot recognizes that this is indeed the case, shall perform the Work of God there where they are working, with divine fear, bending their knees.

Likewise, those who have been sent on a journey must not let the appointed hours pass them by; but as they are able, they shall perform them for themselves [Note: Others read *agant ibi*, “let them perform it there”] and must not neglect to render the burden of service [Col. 0743].

### COMMENTARY

#### “Brothers who are entirely far away at work”

That is, those who labor very far from the oratory and monastery [Col. 0743B].

#### “And cannot arrive at the appointed hour at the oratory”

Namely, before the Gloria of the first psalm, as Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius explain.

#### “And the abbot recognizes this”

This recognition is knowledge and permission granted to the working brother either by the authority of the Rule or by the abbot’s spoken instruction. For the abbot may say in general:

“The brother who is so many paces or stadia away from the oratory, or as far as such-and-such boundaries, is not bound to come to the oratory at those hours,” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius again state.

#### “They shall perform the Work of God there”

It was not unusual for ancient monks to celebrate the divine offices outside the oratory, even in the middle of the fields, as is evident both from this testimony of St. Benedict and from other rules of holy monks: especially from the Rule of St. Pachomius, article 142; the Rule of St. Basil translated by Rufinus, chapter 56; the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, chapter 12; that of St. Ferreolus, chapter 11; that of St. Fructuosus, chapter 6; and finally the Rule of the Master, in which it is decreed that when brothers are working fifty paces from the monastery, they are to perform the Work of God there [Col. 0743C]. Nor should it certainly seem surprising that they performed the Work of God in the fields, since they also refreshed their bodies there with midday sleep, as we noted above.

As for our own monks, however, it should be noted that they did not always perform the divine office under the open sky. Rather, so that they might complete it more decently and easily, they built oratories for themselves where they were accustomed to work.

Thus the disciples of Blessed Benedict of Aniane, in the mountains where the brothers habitually lived while caring for the sheep, “built for themselves a small oratory in which to pray” (*Life of St. Benedict of Aniane*, no. 38, fourth Benedictine century).

Likewise, Leonas, abbot of Piscaria, “having received a plot of land from the royal court, built an oratory at the corner of the city near the gate called Maranesca, so that the brothers who were sent out on business and to guard and preserve those possessions might have a place where they could sing the psalms and occupy themselves there more frequently and freely in the service of the offices” (*Chronicle of Piscaria*, book III, *Spicilegium*, vol. V) [Col. 0743D].

#### “With divine fear”

Or, as the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen has it (chapter 12):

“With discipline and fear of God, in harmonious voice, not muffled as each person might wish under the pretext or occupation of his work.”

They were to do this not individually but all together, divided into two choirs, according to the constitution of Pope Benedict XII, whose words are as follows (chapter 27):

“Those who cannot come to the choir or church, being occupied elsewhere with preaching, reading, study, administrative duties, their offices, or pious and lawful works, with the permission of the person to whom the matter belongs, shall, insofar as possible, several together meet in another suitable and decent place at the proper hours and duly recite the divine office and render their daily burden of service” [Col. 0744B].

Those who were on a journey likewise observed this, as appears from Faustus in the *Life of St. Maurus*, no. 30 (first Benedictine century), where the holy man is said to have celebrated “the morning hymns with other men of the same habit”—that is, with brothers who had been sent with him into Gaul—in the basilica of the place where they had stopped (*Life of St. Maurus*, no. 30, first Benedictine century).

#### “Bending their knees”

That is, for prayers and supplication; and this, as Bernard of Cassino and Boherius say, on the days when the brothers in the convent bend their knees. Here one sees the ancient custom of kneeling for the prayers of the divine course. Yet both all the faithful and the monks refrained from it on Sundays and from Easter to Pentecost, as is evident from Tertullian, *On the Crown of the Soldier*, chapter 3; St. Ambrose, sermon 61, *On Pentecost*; St. Jerome, *Dialogue against the Luciferians*, and the preface to his *Letter to the Ephesians*; Cassian, book II, chapter 18; and Alexander III in his decretal, book II of the *Decretals*, chapter “Quoniam.” Rabanus Maurus gives the reason for this institution in book II of *On the Institution of the Clergy*, chapter 4 [Col. 0744C].

#### “Likewise, those who have been sent on a journey must not let the appointed hours pass them by”

This passage was a source of many disputes among monks, especially between the Cluniacs and Cistercians. Some, referring the word “likewise” to the preceding words “bending their knees with divine fear,” wished travelers reciting the canonical hours to bend their knees. Others, on the contrary, referred it to the following words, “they must not let the appointed hours pass them by,” and denied that kneeling was intended.

Although the latter opinion seems more probable from the immediately following words, the former is confirmed by the common practice of monasteries, at least with respect to the genuflections customarily made at the beginning of the hours for the three prayers.

Lanfranc writes (Statutes, chapter 15):

“Brothers sent on a journey, when they recite the regular hour, or say a prayer, or say ‘O God, come to my assistance’ with the Gloria Patri, shall bend their knees as in the monastery if it is such a day. But they shall never do so before or afterward, nor ask pardon when they make a mistake, unless they are in church. On days when they pray upon the forms, if they are about to recite an hour while riding, let them dismount; and once the hour has begun and pardon has been requested, let them remove their gloves from their hands and their hoods from their heads, and, having remounted, let them finish the hour” [Col. 0744D].

The manuscript customs of the monasteries of Farfa and St. Paul of Rome likewise state:

“Brothers sent on a journey, when they perceive that the time of the hour has arrived, if there is a suitable place where they have stopped or through which they are passing, shall bend their knees, dismounting from their horses. If in the monasteries they bend their knees upon the forms, they too shall do so where they are staying. When the prayer has been completed, let them impress the sign of the holy cross upon their foreheads and not turn around; but let them merely ask pardon and begin the hour while mounting their horses, proceeding and singing the hour, and let them keep their gloves off their hands until they finish the divine office.”

Udalricus, speaking of the provosts of village districts, says (book III, chapter 5):

“When he is on the road, if it is an ordinary day, and one on which pardon must be sought at each hour, whenever he has sung any hour he too dismounts to the ground, removes his cap from his head and his gloves from his hands, asks pardon, and says the Lord’s Prayer. Then, rising, making the sign of the cross, he asks pardon again, and, once the hour has been imposed, continues on his way” [Col. 0745A].

Peter the Venerable teaches the same in writing to Bernard (book I, letter 28):

“Whatever the Rule commands concerning the genuflections of the regular hours, we observe in every respect; and before we begin to sing the hour, wherever we may be, we bend our knees with divine fear. Sometimes excessive rain, deep snow, muddy ground, or similar conditions prohibit this; then, instead of the *metanoia*, we sing the psalm ‘Have mercy on me, O God,’ and by such an exchange we compensate for the command that we cannot fulfill.”

Finally, the Cistercian *Book of Usages*, speaking of those sent on a journey, says (chapter 88):

“When he is about to recite the hours during the day, if it is a day for prostration, let him devote himself to prayer upon the ground; saying the Gloria Patri, let him bend his knees again and remain silent until he has settled himself and continues the hour he began. By day and by night, when he is not riding, let him recite the hours standing, if he is not greatly burdened” [Col. 0745B].

Thus those who abstained from such genuflections did not abstain from something lawful but uncommanded; they did so by dispensation, reciting the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God” in place of the *metanoia* or genuflection, as is clear from the passage of Peter the Venerable cited above.

Hence Boherius, copying Bernard of Cassino in his first commentary, says:

“Because of this word, namely ‘likewise,’ some say that even those who are riding ought to dismount at every hour and bend their knees; this is what the Cistercians do to this day when they are on a journey. Nevertheless, the abbots and brothers of our time do not do this. They admit, however, that in place of the genuflection they say the psalm ‘Have mercy on me, O God’ at each hour. For, because their garments ought to be ankle-length, because of their weight, the frequent rains, and the muddy roads, they consider it difficult to do on the road what they do likewise while working in the fields” [Col. 0745C].

Hildemar, older than all these authorities, also inclines to this interpretation:

“Although we do not know St. Benedict’s precise intention, nevertheless it is better that, if they can, those who are riding should dismount to the ground and perform their office with bent knees.”

The Master likewise prescribes in his Rule (chapter 56) that brothers traveling on the road should turn aside from it a little, bend their knees, and, after the prayer has been imposed, break into a psalm while walking. When it has been completed, they should stand briefly and pray a little with bowed head; then, after the prayer, continue along the road with a psalm. When that has been completed, they should again stand and pray. Then, while proceeding, they should similarly sing a psalm; when it has been completed, they should again pray while bent over.

Finally, in the common monastic Rule of St. Fructuosus I read (chapter 10):

“When the need to hurry arises for them and they recognize that the times of the hours have arrived, they shall immediately prostrate themselves upon the ground and humbly ask pardon from the Lord, and so forth.”

What St. Benedict says—that travelers must not let the appointed hours pass them by—the commentators interpret as follows [Col. 0745D]: “They are to say Terce at the hour of Terce, Sext at the hour of Sext, and so at each hour they are to say its proper hour.” Thus Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius. Hildemar adds, however: “If they can; for if necessity compels them, let them do what they can.”

This was the practice of the ancient monks:

“Observe also the hours of prayer,” says St. Antony (*Rule*, no. 4), “and omit none of them, lest you have to give an account for it.”

And the Eastern Rule says (chapter 12):

“Let no one invent excuses for the gathering or for psalmody by which he may say that he is occupied, as though he could not go. Whether he is in the monastery, in the field, on a journey, or engaged in any service, let him not omit the time for prayer and psalmody.”

These words are taken from the Rule of St. Pachomius, article 81.

Thus Abba Sosimas, as Sophronius testifies (*Life of St. Mary of Egypt*, chapter 7, book I of *The Lives of the Fathers*), “while spending twenty days on a journey, when the hour of Sext arrived, stopped briefly on the road, turned toward the east, and performed his customary prayer. For he was accustomed, at the appointed time of day, to halt his journey, stand and sing psalms, and pray on bended knee.”

Likewise St. Maurus, sent into Gaul, performed the nocturnal office during the night while traveling, as his companion Faustus testifies in the *Life of St. Maurus*: “That night, while we were celebrating the nocturnal office, two more of our brothers arrived there” [Col. 0746B].

Likewise St. Bertulfus, returning from Rome to Bobbio, when black night had already fallen, summoned his companion Jonas and asked him about the nocturnal vigils, as the same Jonas writes in his Life, no. 8.

Likewise St. Fructuosus, later bishop of Braga, while on a journey, is said to have celebrated “the sacred office with his brothers” on a ship (*Life of St. Fructuosus*, no. 13, second Benedictine century; Bollandists, March 1).

Finally, the monk Germanus, at an inn, “according to his custom, after resting for a while, rose at the dead of night and performed the nocturnal psalmody,” as we read in the *Life of St. Eudocia*, no. 3.

#### “As they are able, let them perform them for themselves”

Bernard of Cassino understands “as they are able” to mean that “in this place they cannot perform prayers of equal length, nor the office slowly and deliberately; but as they can—that is, at least complete words, the number of psalms, and the number of readings.”

As for “let them perform them for themselves,” that means “within themselves, privately, without singing; for themselves alone if they are alone; and, if they are two or more, saying the verses of the psalms and hours to one another” [Col. 0746C].

Some manuscripts read *agant ibi*, “let them perform them there,” that is, on the journey. Menardus approves this reading.

#### “And let them not neglect to render the burden of service”

Therefore, “they ought to obtain from the library a book in which the office is arranged,” says Bernard of Cassino. This accords with the constitution of Pope Gregory IX for Benedictines, which prescribes that “they are to say the hours on the road, and books are to be provided for them.”

Benedict XII likewise agrees in his constitution for Benedictine monks, where I read as follows (chapter 24):

“No monk who is to spend the night outside the church, the monastery, or his own place is to be permitted to depart without a closed regular cowl and also a breviary in which he can render the burden of service to his Creator” [Col. 0746D].

## CHAPTER LI

### On Brothers Who Do Not Travel Very Far

[Note: The Council manuscripts read “travel far enough”; others, “do not travel far.”]

A brother who is sent out on any business and is expected [Note: The Council manuscripts read “are expected”; more recent manuscripts, “hope”; Dunstan, “hope for themselves”] to return to the monastery that same day must not presume to eat outside, even if anyone should invite him [Note: Others read “absolutely anyone”], unless perhaps his abbot [Note: Lyre and Ebrul add “or prior”] orders him to do so. If he acts otherwise, he shall be excommunicated [Col. 0745D–0746D].

### COMMENTARY

#### “A brother who is sent out on any business”

“Business,” as Menardus proves from book II, *Dialogues* of Pope Gregory the Great, chapter 12, and book II, letter 47, is a matter that someone handles outside; hence those sent to conduct business were called *responsales* [Col. 0747A].

#### “And is expected to return to the monastery that same day, must not presume to eat outside”

This accords with the discipline of the ancient monks, which did not permit brothers to eat outside the monastery.

“Monks were by no means accustomed to take food in a secular house,” says the ancient author of the *Life of St. Pachomius*, no. 42.

And the Rule of uncertain authorship says:

“No one shall eat or drink outside the monastery without an order, for this does not belong to the discipline of the monastery.”

Almost the same words occur in the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 9. Cassian praises, in this connection, the religious discipline of two young men (book V, chapter 40), whom hunger consumed in the desert even while they were carrying figs.

This may also be referred to what happened when St. Cuthbert set out with two companions for the land of the Picts: “they took no provisions with them, as though they would return more quickly,” writes the Venerable Bede (*Life of St. Cuthbert*, chapter 11, second Benedictine century) [Col. 0747B].

Such an institution may perhaps seem harsh, especially to those who leave very early in the morning and return only late in the day. Yet it did not seem harsh to Peter Damian, who even made it stricter when, speaking of the institutions of his congregation, he said (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 11):

“It is a rule for monasteries that those who are sent on a journey are not to eat outside if they hope to return that day. To this observance we add among us that, whether someone went out that day or on another day, except on principal feasts, he must always return to the hermitage fasting; otherwise penance will not be lacking.”

He says the same in *Opusculum* 14, speaking of the order of the hermits of Fonte Avellana.

And certainly, when one considers how dangerous it is for monks to eat together with secular people and take part in their banquets, and how necessary it is that, stimulated by hunger, they return more quickly to the monastery, St. Benedict’s decree will appear entirely reasonable. Hence Gregory IX, in his constitution for Benedictines, says [Col. 0747C]:

“No abbot or monk shall eat or spend the night in a secular house near his monastery or his monastery cell, within one league.”

#### “Even if anyone should invite him”

Even if it is a bishop, abbot, magnate, or any nobleman, to whom, as Bernard of Cassino says, “a brother without permission must reply that he is not allowed to eat” [Col. 0748A].

#### “Unless perhaps his own abbot orders him to do so”

Because, as the commentators warn, the abbot must always act with the greatest discretion. Taking into account the person who is being sent, the person to whom he is being sent, and the labor of the journey, he ought to grant permission to eat if the brother happens to be invited by a bishop or prince, or if he must return only late.

Otherwise the condition of such a brother sent on a journey would be worse than that of an excommunicated monk, who would refresh himself sooner in the monastery. See the Rule of the Master, chapters 59–62.

#### “But if he acts otherwise, he shall be excommunicated”

Peter, abbot of Silva Major, renewed this decree in 1198 in the following words (the manuscript statutes of Peter, abbot of Silva Major) [Col. 0748B]:

“We command and order, by the authority of holy obedience and under penalty of excommunication, that no monk of our order eat, drink, or sleep in the village of Silva Major or in other villages where we have priories.”

Whether the Rule means major or minor excommunication, St. Benedict does not make sufficiently clear; but, considering the nature of the offense, he seems to have left the matter to the abbot’s judgment. Nicholas of Fractura, however, interprets St. Benedict as referring to excommunication by which the offender is separated both from the table and from the oratory.

In the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers we read (chapter 9):

“If anyone, without the knowledge of the abbot or superior, leaves any place and joins himself to gluttony or drunkenness, or, if he has been sent nearby, does not return immediately to his cell once his business has been completed, when he is discovered in this offense, he shall either, as the canons prescribe, be separated from Communion for thirty days, or be beaten with rods as correction.”

St. Benedict himself acted far more mildly with two brothers who had been sent on some business and, having been forced to delay until a later hour, took food at the home of a devout woman [Col. 0748C]. When they confessed their offense, he immediately absolved them from guilt (St. Gregory, book II of the *Dialogues*, chapter 12).

From this it is clear that the excommunication mentioned in this chapter is not imposed as a command but as a threat.

## CHAPTER LII

### On the Oratory of the Monastery

Let the oratory of the monastery [Note: Hildemar adds “of the monastery”] be what it is called, and let nothing else be done or stored there [Note: The Council manuscripts read “or contended over.” Gratian, Burchard, and Ivo, from whom Menardus thinks this passage should be restored, add: “except what is appropriate to the divine services.”]

When the Work of God has been completed, let everyone leave in the deepest silence, and let reverence be shown [Note: Others read “let reverence be maintained”] to God, so that a brother who perhaps wishes to pray privately may not be hindered by another’s misconduct [Col. 0747C–0748C].

But if another perhaps wishes to pray more privately, let him simply enter and pray—not in a loud voice, but with tears and concentration of heart.

Therefore, one who does not perform such a work must not be permitted to remain [Note: The Council and Compendium manuscripts read “after it has been completed”; Oxford omits “in the oratory,” and Narbonne reads “there”] in the oratory after the Work of God has been completed, as has been said, lest he cause another to be hindered.

### COMMENTARY

#### “Let the oratory be what it is called”

Menardus in this passage and Haeften, book VII, treatise 1, discussion 1, discuss the oratory itself and its name at greater length; the reader may consult them [Col. 0747D].

#### “And let nothing else be done or stored there”

This passage seems to have been referred to by the Council of Tours cited by Ivo, chapter 3, when he said (*Ivo*, part III, chapter 75):

“For if the house of God is called a house of prayer, it ought to be what it is called, and nothing else ought to be done or stored there” [Col. 0748D].

St. Augustine speaks in almost the same way in his Rule, chapter 4, as does the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 15.

I omit a fuller account of what may or may not be done in the oratory, since Haeften, book VII, treatise 1, discussions 2 and 3, is more than sufficient for that purpose.

I will observe only this: according to the interpretation of Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius, St. Benedict here had in mind the ecclesiastical canons forbidding banquets in churches [Col. 0749A].

“Blessed Benedict teaches propriety,” says Hildemar, “following canonical authority; for the canons prescribe, in the Council of Laodicea, chapter 24, whose title is: ‘Meals must not be held in churches.’”

Nevertheless, long after the Council of Laodicea, the custom of eating in churches continued, even among monks. See the *History of Eastern Monasticism*, written in French, book II, chapter 2, no. 9.

Having completed the Work of God, let all go out in the utmost silence.] For this was the practice of the monks of old: always to maintain the greatest silence in the oratory, especially while celebrating the divine praises:

“If it should happen that, during the time of psalmody or prayer, or in the middle of a reading, someone speaks or laughs,” says the Rule of Saint Pachomius (Art. 1), “he shall loosen his belt and, bowing his neck, with his hands lowered toward the ground, shall stand before the altar and be rebuked by the head of the monastery.” And below (Art. 68): “Whoever comes late to one prayer, or mutters, or speaks to another, [Col. 0749B] or laughs, shall do penance during the remaining prayers, according to the established order.”

The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chap. 9): “No one may, while the Work of God is being sung, for any reason address speech against another brother, except only to an elder.” The Rule of Saint Caesarius for Monks (chap. 8): “While psalmody is being sung, no one should presume to speak.” The Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks (chap. 29): “While psalmody is being sung, they should presume neither to work nor to speak.” The Rule of Tarnat (chap. 6): “Whoever presumes to chatter while others are praying or singing psalms should not doubt that he is guilty not only before the brotherhood but also before the Divinity.” The Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 7): “When the spiritual mysteries of the psalms are being celebrated, let the monk shun laughter and chatter.”

Hence Saint John Climacus, discussing the Alexandrian monks (Step 4), says: “And when we had frequently been present at their prayers, their holy superior noticed certain men speaking among themselves. He ordered them to stand before the doors of the church for the entire week and to ask pardon of all who entered and all who departed.” And, as concerns our own monks, I read in the ancient Customs of Saint Benedict of Aniane (vol. IV of the *Analecta*): “In the oratory, the greatest silence and the greatest reverence in singing psalms; . . . in the sacristy, profound silence and the most orderly administration.” And below: “We also saw another observance worthy of note, for anyone who wished to attain perfection in silence: none of the brothers presumed to speak anything in any place, except the two appointed for this purpose. In the church no one spoke except for the divine office and the words of prayer. If anyone had necessity to speak to another, he touched the abbot’s garment, or that of any brother, and signaled toward those places; after they had exchanged a very few words, and those reasonable ones, they immediately withdrew, fearing that through necessary words they might fall into harmful and useless speech.”

And let reverence be shown to God.] Either by greeting the altar, according to Hildemar and Boherius, or through the utmost silence, according to Bernard of Cassino.

But if someone perhaps wishes to pray more privately, let him simply enter and pray.] Where “what he says by ‘simply,’” says Bernard of Cassino, “is as though he said: plainly, not loudly, not with a great stamping of the feet, not coughing or clearing the throat loudly, but modestly, plainly, silently.”

Yet since Saint Benedict the Holy Father keeps the monks continually occupied—apart from the times of rest and refreshment—in manual labor, reading, and the divine offices, how will those who wish to pray be able to enter the oratory? Hildemar replies that those to whom the Lord has granted the grace of compunction and contemplation should not be deprived of their tears; they may lawfully leave their work or book and enter the oratory, although this virtue belongs to few. I would add: with the abbot’s blessing.

Not in a loud voice.] Because, as Abbot Isaac says in Cassian (Conference 9, chap. 35), “we must pray in the greatest silence—not only lest we distract the brothers standing nearby with our whispers or cries and disturb the minds of those praying, but also so that our enemies themselves, who especially lie in wait for us when we pray, may remain unaware of the intention of our petition.”

But with tears and concentration of heart.] See what we said above on chapter 20.

Therefore whoever does not perform a similar work must not be permitted to linger in the oratory after the Work of God has been completed.] Our forefathers observed this with the greatest religious strictness, expelling laypeople after each course of the Work of God had ended, as could be demonstrated by many examples and practices. One example will suffice here: Udalricus, speaking of the sacristan’s office, writes as follows (Book III, chap. 12):

“He also closes or opens the doors of the church in various ways at different times. For although he always opens them for Matins, both in winter and in summer, in winter he nevertheless always closes them after the office sung during the night; they then remain closed until the bell sounds for Terce. When the morning Mass has ended, he closes them, and they remain closed until the bell is rung for Sext. Then they are opened, and after Mass has ended they are closed until Vespers. After Vespers the regular doors are closed and remain so until Matins.

“In summer, however, since they are closed immediately after regular Matins, they are opened at Prime and remain open until the morning Mass has ended. They are then closed and opened again for Mass; after that they are shut until Vespers. When Vespers has ended, they are completely closed until Matins. During Lent, on weekdays, they are closed after the morning Mass and reopened after Sext as soon as the bell has sounded; they are not closed again until Vespers has ended. At the Twelve Lessons, both in winter and summer, they are opened at the bell that is rung after the chapter.”

This custom is also reflected in the *Book of Miracles of Saint Walter, Abbot of Pontoise*, where we read: “On the following day, which was Sunday, the sacristan compelled everyone to leave after Masses,” and so forth.

# CHAPTER LIII. On Receiving Guests

[Col. 0749]

[Col. 0749D] All guests who arrive are to be received as Christ, because he himself will say: “I was a guest, and you received me” (Matthew XXIII). And suitable honor is to be shown to all, especially to members of the household of faith and to pilgrims. Therefore, as soon as a guest has been announced, the prior or the brothers are to go out to meet him with every expression of charitable service; and first of all they are to pray together, and thus join one another in peace. The kiss of peace is not to be offered before prayer has been said, because of demonic illusions. In the greeting itself [Note: [Col. 0749D] Florence: *ipsa* (“itself”), omitting *in*.] every form of humility is to be shown. For all guests, whether arriving or departing, with head bowed or with the entire body prostrate upon the ground [Note: [Col. 0750D] Oxford and Conc.: “on the ground” is absent. Others: “onto the ground.”], Christ is to be adored in them, since he is the one being received.

Guests who have been received are then to be led to prayer; [Col. 0751A] afterward the prior is to sit with them, or the person whom he himself has ordered to do so [Note: [Col. 0751B] Oxford: “the person whom he has ordered.”]. Let the divine law be read before the guest, so that he may be edified; and after this let every act of kindness be shown. The prior is to break his fast for the sake of the guest, unless it happens to be a principal day of fasting that cannot be violated. The brothers, however, are to continue according to the customary fasts [Note: [Col. 0751B] Others: “the customary fast.”].

The abbot is to give water to the guests for their hands; the abbot and the entire community are to wash the feet of all the guests [Note: [Col. 0751B] Conc.: “of all” is absent.]. When they have been washed, they are to say this verse: “We have received your mercy, O God, in the midst of your temple” (Psalm XLVII). Special care is to be diligently shown in receiving the poor and pilgrims, because Christ is received more particularly in them. For the fear inspired by the rich itself demands honor for them.

[Col. 0751B] The abbot’s and the guests’ kitchen is to be separate, so that guests arriving at uncertain hours, who are never absent from the monastery, may not disturb the brothers [Col. 0752A]. [Note: [Col. 0751B] Narbonne, Cassino, and Florence: *non inquietentur* (“may not be disturbed”). Oxford and Florence: *in qua coquina* (“in which kitchen”) for *in quam coquinam* (“into that kitchen”).] Two brothers who can properly fulfill this office are to enter that kitchen for a year; they are to be provided with assistance as they need it, so that they may serve without murmuring [Note: [Col. 0751B] Oxford: “may be.”]. When they have less work, they are again to leave and go to the work commanded to them [Note: [Col. 0752B] Others: “the work that is commanded”; another: “when it has been commanded to them”; another: “the work commanded to them.”; another: *in opere* (“at work”) for *in opera* (“to work”).]. And not only in their case, but in all the offices of the monastery, this consideration is to be maintained: when they need assistance, help is to be supplied to them; and when they are free, they are to obey what is commanded. [Note: Others read *ipsis, sed et omnibus*, omitting *in* twice.]

Likewise, a brother whose soul is possessed by the fear of God is to be assigned to the guesthouse. There are to be enough beds made up [Note: [Col. 0752B] Others: “beds and bedding.”], and the house of God is to be wisely administered by the wise [Note: [Col. 0752B] Florence and Cassino: “and wisely”; Sabina: “built.”]. No brother who has not been ordered to do so is in any way to associate or converse with guests; [Col. 0752B] but if he encounters or sees one, he is to greet him humbly, as has been said [Note: [Col. 0752B] Others: “as we said.”], ask his blessing, and pass on, saying that he is not permitted to converse with a guest.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0751]

[Col. 0751B] We pass from the oratory to the guesthouse; for the affinity between the two places is so great that they ought not to be separated from one another. In both places Christ is adored, in both he is received: in the oratory at the altar, but in the guesthouse in the guest and pilgrim.

Nor do I think it necessary here to commend the virtue of hospitality at greater length, since so many and such eminent holy Fathers have celebrated it with praises. Peter of Blois praises it sufficiently in Letter 29, which may be consulted if desired. For the present, let the example of the patriarchs, the command of the apostles, and the promise of Christ the Lord suffice—he promised a heavenly kingdom to those who received him in a guest—so that Gregory IX rightly decreed in a constitution for Benedictine monks:

“In every monastery or priory, the abbot or prior—or, if they are absent, the visitors who hold office at the time—are to arrange, according to the possibilities of the places, for hospitality to be provided for giving alms, with a designated guesthouse for receiving the poor and other guests, and with a suitable servant appointed to attend them. If hospitality is denied to any religious person, the one assigned to the guesthouse is to fast for three days on bread and water.”

671 All guests who arrive are to be received as Christ.] All guests who arrive, “because,” says Bernard of Cassino, “it is unknown in whom Christ may more truly be received. Sometimes a poor and needy person is received who at first sight is thought to be prosperous and wealthy; sometimes, too, one who is received humbly is edified by the charity of those receiving him, assumes gentleness of spirit, is freed from harshness of mind, and consequently becomes a dwelling-place of Christ. Thus it happens that Christ is received in him. Therefore no one is to be passed over, no one rejected, no one excluded; everyone who arrives is to be received.” Peter Boherius says the same.

Yet when Hildemar explains this passage, he says: “What he says—‘all’—seems arduous and almost difficult, since there are many guests who come to the monastery. But it may be understood in this way: either he said ‘all guests’ because few came at that time, as Cassian says in the *Conference* and as is read in the *Life of the Fathers*, although Saint Benedict says that guests are never absent from the monastery. It may also be understood that one or two came, for perhaps there were not then as many as now; and Theodulf understood it in this sense. By God, if Saint Benedict were present now, he would have the door closed against them. Or ‘all’ may be understood in another way, with the words ‘whom the monastery is able to receive’ understood: they are to be received as Christ, because the Rule says nothing impossible. Or the matter is resolved by considering the intention: in intention, all are to be received as guests just as Christ, although it is not possible to serve everyone as Christ, but only a few.”

Although the monastery ought to receive without distinction all guests whom it is able to receive, both sound reason teaches and ancient custom warns that hospitality must nevertheless be denied to some. First among these we must count heretics, against whom our forefathers closed their cloisters:

“Hospitality is dear to us in the monastery,” says Saint Jerome (*Apology against Rufinus*), “and we receive all who come to us with a cheerful face of kindness; for we fear that Mary with Joseph might find no place in the inn, and that Jesus might say to us, when excluded: ‘I was a guest, and you did not receive me.’ Heretics alone we do not receive.”

And Saint Basil (*Shorter Rules*, question 124): “Concerning the taking of food with heretics, we have the Apostle’s command regarding those from whom it is fitting to abstain,” and so forth.

Second, by the same law, malicious men, prepared for every crime, must be excluded from the guesthouse. This is what the monks of Fulda earnestly requested in their petition to Charlemagne, in these words (chap. 17):

“Men of malicious and frenzied mind, most ready to perpetrate every outrage, are not to be gathered within the monastery, as happened in the case of that murderous cleric who killed a monk and who was installed in the monastery against the will and consent of all the brothers.”

Nevertheless, to speak with Saint Augustine (Letter 38): “In receiving unknown guests, we are accustomed to say that it is much better to suffer a bad man than perhaps, through ignorance, to exclude a good one while taking precautions against receiving the bad.”

Third, women must also be included under this rule. Not only access to the monastery but sometimes even access to the oratory was denied them, as we demonstrated above in chapter 4:

“Do not allow a woman to approach you,” says Saint Antony in the Rule (no. 7), “nor permit her to enter your dwelling; for anger walks behind her.”

And Saint Ephrem (*Various Teachings*, vol. II): “It is not fitting for a monk to have any association with a woman. Do not approach one who professes virginity at all, if any carnal feeling remains alive in you; for a monk to mingle with women at table is the same as throwing himself into fire. Whoever flees their company should flee it like a deer from nets and like a bird from a snare.”

Here belongs what Godehard, abbot of Tegernsee, writes to a certain abbess (vol. IV of the *Analecta*):

“This sister of ours came to us before Christmas, complaining to us of the misery of her manifold needs. We would most willingly permit her to remain with us and would order that we provide her with whatever necessities we could, if the nature of her sex allowed women to live with the monastery of the brothers. For, as holy men have proved, straw, chaff, and fire never make peace with one another unless one quickly consumes the other to its detriment.”

The strictness of the Cistercians in this matter was experienced by a woman who traveled out of devotion to the tomb of Saint Robert (Bollandists, 29 April). For “as day was declining [the printed *dam* is materially uncertain, apparently corrupt] she came to the monastery of Quincy, begging hospitality from the monks. But because their tradition does not admit the female sex within their boundaries, the wretched woman was compelled, after leaving, to spend the night in the forest,” as the author of the *Life of Saint Robert, Abbot of Molesme*, writes (no. 17).

Gregory IX later confirmed the same in a bull to the Cistercians, in which I read: “By the authority of this present document we forbid anyone in your houses to presume to use meat, or any woman to presume to enter them, contrary to the statutes of the order.”

[Col. 0753C] Nevertheless, there were those who showed the kindness of hospitality to women outside the monastery cloister, especially the Pachomians, whose Rule contains the following (Art. 29):

“If secular people, or the infirm, or weaker vessels—that is, women—come to the door, the one receiving them shall take each person to separate places according to the order of the superior and according to his or her sex. Women in particular are to be cared for with greater honor and diligence, with complete fear of God, and a place separated from all proximity to men is to be assigned to them, so that there may be no occasion for blasphemy. If they come at Vespers, it is wrong to turn them away; but they are to be received, as we have said, into a separate place, shut in with every discipline and precaution, so that the flock of brothers may freely perform its office and no one be given an occasion for slander.”

The Cluniacs did the same, as Peter the Venerable testifies in writing to Saint Bernard (Book I, Letter 28), and so did the monks of Farfa, according to the manuscript Customs of that monastery. The Cistercians themselves, although they did not receive women for lodging, nevertheless provided them with food outside, according to the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 120.

Fourth, “what Saint Benedict says by ‘those who arrive’ seems to exclude neighboring or nearby inhabitants, who may more properly be called members of the household or fellow citizens than guests,” as Boherius says with Bernard of Cassino. He adds: “But discretion must be exercised concerning whether such people are to be admitted indiscriminately or excluded altogether. Nevertheless, I urge that the poor be admitted, whether they are distant or nearby.”

There were also those who thought that hospitality, as contrary to monastic peace and solitude, should be entirely kept away from monks’ monasteries. For this reason Saint Augustine did not wish guests to be received in the monastery at Hippo where he lived as a priest. In the statutes of Guigo, prior of the Carthusian order, I also read (chap. 19): “We care only for the persons of the guests, not for their horses.”

[Col. 0754A] They are to be received as Christ, because he himself will say: “I was a guest, and you received me.” It is above all on this point that the holy Fathers commend hospitality, especially Saint Augustine (Sermon 136):

“Learn,” he says, “to receive guests, in whom Christ is recognized. Do you not know that if you receive any Christian, you receive Christ himself? Did he not say, ‘I was a guest, and you received me’? And when it is said to him, ‘Lord, when did we see you as a guest?’ he replies, ‘When you did it to one of the least of mine, you did it to me.’ Therefore, when a Christian receives a Christian, members serve members, the head rejoices, and he counts as given to himself what has been bestowed upon his member. Let Christ, then, who is hungry, be fed here; let him who thirsts receive drink; let the naked be clothed; let the pilgrim be received; let the sick be visited.”

Indeed, he who says that he is received in a guest once wished to be received in his own person, as Saint Gregory testifies concerning an unknown man in these words (Homily 23 on the Gospels):

“A certain head of a household, with his entire household, served with great devotion to hospitality. Since every day he received pilgrims at his table, one day a certain pilgrim arrived among the others and was led to the table. As the head of the household, following his customary humility, wished to pour water over his hands, he turned and took up the pitcher; but suddenly he did not find the man into whose hands he had wished to pour the water. While he wondered at this within himself, the Lord said to him in a vision that same night: ‘On other days you received me in my members; yesterday you received me in my own person.’”

What the holy pontiff relates of one unknown man, John the Deacon relates of another in Book II of the *Life of Saint Gregory*, chapter 22 (Second Century of the Bollandist *Acta Sanctorum*); and in the following chapter he also reports that on another occasion an angel was received by him. Something similar is read concerning Saint Agilo, abbot of Rebais, in his *Life*, chapter 20, and concerning Saint Cuthbert, in Bede’s *Life* of him, chapter 7.

And suitable honor is to be shown to all.] On this passage Bernard of Cassino and Boherius write:

“For a bishop and an abbot must be honored in one way, a cleric or monk in another; a superior in one way, a subject in another; a brother arriving with a reputation for great holiness in one way, a Sarabait or gyrovague in another; noble and powerful persons in one way, the ignoble and poor in another. Therefore he says ‘suitable,’ so that, according to the quality of the person received, there may be appropriate condescension in the display of honor, in the preparation of food, in going out to meet him, and in accompanying him. There ought to be one charity toward all according to the inner person; [Col. 0754C] but there ought to be diversity in the display of outward honor. For the poor, coarse bread, vegetables, and beans are sufficient; for the rich, scarcely a pig, or beef, or delicate fowl is sufficient. The poor lie anywhere; for the rich, even an expensive bed scarcely gives satisfaction.”

And Smaragdus says:

“Although one charity embraces everyone inwardly, it is fitting to serve the poor in one way and the powerful outwardly in another. A seat is not to be prepared equally for everyone, nor is an equal preparation of food suitable for everyone; rather, each person must be provided, with charitable discretion, a suitable place, suitable food, and a suitable bed. Suitable honor must be shown to all.”

From these words the solution is clear to the difficulty that Hildemar raises and resolves concerning the care and solicitude that the holy legislator commands to be shown more abundantly toward the poor and pilgrims. For “this statement,” he says, “in which he says that suitable honor is to be shown to all, concerns the outward person; but the statement in which he speaks of the poor and pilgrims concerns the inner person. That is, it is as though he said: in preparing service, each guest is to be received according to his station; nevertheless, in the mind the poor man is to be preferred to the rich.”

Especially to members of the household of faith and to pilgrims.] Smaragdus explains this passage as follows:

“A member of the household is called a friend, familiar, or companion. We must understand this in two ways: either generally, as all Christians who share with us one faith and one baptism; or specifically, as monks who, together with us, render to God the service of faith and religion in a special way. A pilgrim is one situated in the territory of a distant homeland.”

Bernard of Cassino speaks in almost the same way. Likewise the Rule of Saint Pachomius (Art. 28): “When certain people come to the door of the monastery, if they are clerics or monks, they are to be received with greater honor.” The Eastern Rule has the same provision in chapter 40. And the Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 21): “Although the good of hospitality must graciously be rendered to all, a more abundant honor of hospitality is nevertheless to be offered to clerics and monks.” Finally, the Rule of Saint Stephen, founder of the order of Grandmont (chap. 36): “Take care to show religious persons more honor and reverence than the others.”

Therefore, as soon as a guest has been announced, the prior or the brothers are to go out to meet him with every expression of charitable service.] Here Saint Benedict begins to describe the rite of receiving a guest. First of all, he wishes the newcomer to be met, according to the custom of the ancient monks, which may be seen in Rufinus, Book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapters 1 and 7, and also chapter 21. Speaking there of the monks of Nitria, Rufinus writes:

“When we were approaching this place, as soon as they sensed that pilgrim brothers were arriving, each one immediately rushed out of his cell, like a swarm of bees, and hastened toward us with joyful running and eager alacrity. Many of them carried pitchers of water and bread, in accordance with the prophet’s rebuke of certain men: ‘You did not go out to meet the children of Israel with bread and water.’”

See Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 52, and the *Life of Saint Martin, Abbot of Vertavium*, First Century of the Bollandists, p. 378.

675 But the care that each of the Nitrian monks assumed for going out to meet guests, and which the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius entrusts to the one assigned responsibility for hospitality, Saint Benedict enjoins here with a distinction between the prior and the brothers: the prior is to go out to meet persons of higher rank, and the brothers persons of lower rank, as Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino explain.

“Since,” says Smaragdus, “two kinds of persons usually come to the monastery, he reasonably orders two kinds of persons to go out to meet them. The prior must go out to meet persons of higher rank; a brother must go out to meet a brother. If a king, bishop, or some powerful person of the highest rank comes, the abbot is to go out to meet him; if someone else comes, another person is to go out to meet him.”

What Saint Benedict says, “or by the brothers,” is not to be understood as meaning all of them, but those whom the abbot has appointed for this office, as is clear from the *Book of Cistercian Usages*, chapter 87.

And first of all let them pray together, and thus join one another in peace.] Secondly, Saint Benedict prescribes that they should first pray together. Richard of Saint Angelo understands this as “one greeting the other, or each saying ‘Bless,’ as I have seen,” he says.

Saint Hildegard more correctly explains “let them first pray together” to mean that “all, whoever they may be, are to be led to the church to adore, so that the brothers may pray to God not to violate their regular order because of these guests, while the guests, seeing their way of life, may become better.”

The rite by which this was done is explained in the *Book of Cistercian Usages* (chap. 87):

“Those going out to meet the guests are to remove their hoods from their heads, if they are wearing them at that time, and then, kneeling, lead them to prayer. Once they have entered the church, the person charged with that duty is to sprinkle them with holy water. Afterward they are to pray, either bent over or prostrate, as the time requires. But if the guest is a bishop or abbot, the one receiving him is to offer him the sprinkler, kissing his hand, and, after leading him to the place where he is to pray, withdraw a little with his companion behind the one praying, and pray as stated above. When the prayer is completed, they are to make the sign of the cross and leave.”

The monks of Bursfeld have nearly the same provisions in their *Ceremonial*, distinction 3, chapter 26. The Cluniacs led guests to pray at several altars, as Udalricus testifies, Book III, chapter 22. The monks of Sithiu of Saint Bertin led them to the altar of Saint Denis, according to John, a monk of Bertin, in the *Miracles of Blessed Bernard the Penitent*, no. 31.
