The Cassinese prescribe (*Cassinese Declaration*, chapter 53, no. 2) that “there should be, as far as circumstances permit, a chapel near the monastery gate, into which such guests may be brought for prayer.”

This should certainly not seem so new or recent, since Hildemar writes in chapter 66: “In our province there is a gallery over the gate, and an oratory there as well.” The monks of Valladolid require (*Constitutions of Valladolid*, chapter 74) that the superior receive guests in an assigned place, or send someone to receive them; afterward they are to be led to the church, or to some place in the guesthouse where they may decently offer prayers before an image.

Finally, in the manuscript Constitutions of Casale Benedicti I read (chap. 32):

“It will suffice to pray mentally and to say something pertaining to prayer or the praise of God, such as ‘Thanks be to God,’ or ‘Blessed is he who comes in the name of the Lord,’ or ‘Let God be praised,’ or something similar. Otherwise, after the kiss of peace, the guest is to be led to the oratory, and prayer is to be offered there.”

This rite came down from the ancient monks, as Rufinus teaches in these words (Book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chap. 1):

“For this is the custom in Egypt: whenever they arrive, they immediately join themselves to one another through prayer.”

And speaking of Saint Apollonius (ibid., chap. 7):

“When we entered the monastery, after prayer had first been offered, as is customary, he washed our feet with his own hands.”

And concerning the Nitrian monks:

“Then, after receiving us, they first led us with psalms to the church.”

The same is evident from the *Life of Saint Pachomius*, no. 44, in Rosweyde.

The kiss of peace is not to be offered before prayer has been said, because of demonic illusions.] Third, after the guests have been led to prayer, the holy legislator commands that the kiss of peace be offered: as a sign of reconciliation, as a sign of love and affection, as a sign of peace, and as a sign of catholic unity. For the author of the book *On Friendship*, preserved by Saint Augustine, distinguishes four kinds of such a kiss, although he says in chapter 6 that the last is offered especially to guests.

He wished it to be offered only after prayer had first been said, because of demonic illusions. He had learned this also from the ancient monks, as Rufinus testifies (Book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chap. 1):

“For this is the custom in Egypt: whenever the brothers arrive, they immediately join themselves to one another through prayer . . . For this reason such a form is observed among the monks: if anyone comes to them, whether man or woman, old or young, unknown or known, first of all prayer is offered and the Lord’s name invoked, because if there has been any transformation of a demon, it will immediately flee once prayer has been made.”

Some of the ancient monks, however, also offered a kiss to a guest before prayer, as is clear from the same Rufinus (ibid., chap. 9), where he writes concerning Copres:

“When he saw us and had greeted us with a kiss, and, according to custom, had also washed our feet after prayer, he asked what was happening in the world.”

And concerning the monks living under the discipline of Saint Apollonius (chap. 7):

“They came out to meet us with psalms. For it is their custom to remain silent at the arrival of all monks, and, adoring with their faces to the ground, they kissed us . . . Some of the brothers went before us, others followed us; but both groups were singing psalms. When we had already begun to draw near, having heard the sound of the psalm, Apollonius himself also came out to meet us. As soon as he saw us, he first adored us to the ground; then, rising, he received us with a kiss. When we entered the monastery, after prayer had first been offered, as is customary, he washed our feet with his own hands.”

Even now the Cassinese, after a mental prayer alone has first been offered, give the kiss before leading the guests to prayer (*Cassinese Declaration*, chap. 53). On the kiss itself, see Haeftenus, Book XI, treatise 2, dissertation 1.

Concerning the manner of giving it, Peter the Deacon, cited by Bernard of Cassino, writes:

“When the ancients received people who came to them, they stood in the doorway of their house, placed the guest’s feet upon their own feet, and gave them peace; thus they received them into their house.”

The Cistercians, however, prescribe (*Book of Cistercian Usages*, chap. 87) that after prayer, when they have left the church, “the one who is to read the lesson should say, ‘Bless’; then they should kneel once before everyone, and, rising, kiss them; afterward they should sit down.”

In the greeting itself every form of humility is to be shown.] Every form, that is, both of mind and of body, as the commentators say.

According to Boherius, a greeting “is commonly made by word, hand, and kiss; sometimes it is made by word alone. Thus the greeting of the Spaniards is ‘We humble ourselves’ (*Humiliamus nos*), to which corresponds the French expression ‘God save you’ (*Deus vos salvet*); that of the Lombards, ‘Good day’ (*Benevehau*); that of the Saracens, ‘There is no god but God’ (*Ey ylla Melaac*). Many today, however, greet by bowing the head and removing the cap or hood from the head, either entirely or in part.”

For all guests, whether arriving or departing, with head bowed or with the entire body prostrate upon the ground, Christ is to be adored in them, since he is the one being received.] On this passage Hildemar writes:

“We ought to greet kings, bishops, and abbots prostrate upon the ground, following the example of the prophet Nathan, who greeted King David prostrate. But when a monk sees a queen, he ought not to greet her while prostrate; he should place one knee on the ground, or humble himself by bowing his head. If we see our abbot only rarely, we ought to greet him upon the ground. Others—that is, counts, priests, monks, and the rest—we ought to greet with bowed heads.”

Here he distinguishes three forms of greeting: the first, in which kings, bishops, and one’s own abbot are greeted with the entire body prostrate; the second, in which a queen is greeted with one knee bent; the third, in which the others are greeted by bowing the head.

In my judgment, however, Smaragdus is more correct. Saint Benedict, he says, “here, as above, introduces two kinds of arriving persons: one of ordinary rank, before whom the brother merely bows his head; the other of the highest rank, before whom he adores with his entire body prostrate upon the ground. Nevertheless, in both cases the Lord Jesus Christ is adored in them, since he is the one being received.”

Bernard of Cassino speaks similarly:

“For kings and bishops are to be honored by bending the knees; others of ordinary rank—counts, abbots, and the rest—by bowing the head. Therefore he says ‘or.’”

And Nicholas of Fractura:

“With head bowed, if they are persons of ordinary rank, or even counts, barons, abbots, and the rest, they are to be honored by bowing the head. Or with the entire body prostrate upon the ground: this applies if they are kings, princes, marquises, or persons superior to them, whether spiritual or temporal, who are to be adored with the body prostrate. Thus the prophet Nathan is read to have acted: when he saw the king, he adored him.”

Indeed, monks did not approach a king except with their bodies prostrate upon the ground. Thus Wulfinus Boethius, in the *Life of Saint Junianus*, no. 9 (First Century of the Bollandists), writes: “When he approached the king’s throne, he adored the king face downward, as is the custom of monks.”

By the time of Peter Boherius, however, this had already become obsolete:

“I have neither seen it observed,” he says, “nor read a clear explanation of how it ought to be understood. Therefore I believe that this paragraph should be understood of the inclination of the head or body that takes place in the oratory while the guest is praying. Nor does it establish a distinction between persons, but between times: when the brother who accompanies the guest prays together with him, as he is required to do above, he should bend his knees and body at the time when the brothers do so in the assembly; or he should bow his head if the brothers do not prostrate themselves upon the ground during the Hours. In this way Christ is adored in them—that is, together with them—since he is the one being received.”

### “The guests who have been received, however, shall be led to prayer.”

“That is, to the church before the altar,” says Richard of Saint Angelo. Above he had said, “let them pray together”; now he again says, “let them be led to prayer.” Whether this should be understood as referring to two prayers or only one, the commentators do not explain sufficiently. Nicholas of Fractura understands it of a single prayer; Menard interprets the first passage as referring to the prayer made at the very entrance of the monastery because of demonic illusions, and the second as referring to the prayer made in the oratory, when the guest who has been received is led there to give thanks to God for his safe arrival and to ask forgiveness for the errors committed on the journey.

[Col. 0758A] Perhaps Saint Benedict also had in mind the following provision of the Rule of Saint Pachomius (Art. 28):

> “If they [the guests] wish to come to the assembly of the brothers at the time of prayer and the gathering, and if they are of the same faith, the doorkeeper or the steward of the guesthouse shall announce it to the Father of the monastery, and thus they shall be led to pray.”

And in fact guests formerly used to take part with the brothers, both by day and by night, in the divine praises. Thus Saint Hidulfus, “putting all things within the cloister in religious order, decided to build the guesthouse at the gate of the monastery, so that the brothers might not be troubled by those arriving; and beside it, a chapel in which the guests might gather to hear the divine offices,” as Richerus writes in his Life, chapter 19 (Appendix to the third Benedictine century). Hence Saint Benedict of Aniane, according to Ardo in his Life, no. 52 (fourth Benedictine century), wished that at night “with the doors of the church thrown open, entry should be available to the guests.” Hence also, in the ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall, opposite the basilica is depicted the reception of arriving brothers, together with their dormitory.

[Col. 0758B] Finally, Ingelramnus, abbot of Centula (second Benedictine century), while a guest at the monastery of Corbie, is said to have attended Matins in book I of the *Miracles of Saint Adalard*, chapter 2. And when Pope Urban II came to the monastery of Cava (Manuscript Chronicle of the Monastery of Cava, in Bollandus, 4 March):

> “Having entered the building, the pontiff first rendered worship to the most holy Eucharist, then withdrew to the cave . . . . and that very night, while the brothers were solemnly celebrating Matins, he devoutly took part with them.”

Let these remarks be understood as incidental, not as though I absolutely wished to assert that this was Saint Benedict’s meaning, but to demonstrate the ancient custom by which the guests themselves also took part by night in the divine offices.

### “And afterward the prior shall sit with them, or whomever he himself shall have ordered.”

Since the prior—that is, the abbot—may be “otherwise occupied; or he may be someone for whom an interpreter is necessary; or the guest may be a person of lesser rank, for whom another companion than the prior should suffice; nor could the abbot or prior fulfill this duty in monasteries where guests frequently arrive,” as Boherius says.

[Col. 0758C] The man whom the abbot orders for this duty ought to be learned and literate, according to the Council of Aachen, which decreed (Canon 63) “that learned brothers be chosen to speak with those who arrive.”

### “Let the divine law be read before the guest, for his edification.”

Much deserves consideration here concerning this reading.

First, by the name “divine law” are understood not only the Decalogue or the five books of Moses, but both the Old and the New Testament—indeed, “every word taken from the divine law that edifies,” says Bernard of Cassino. What, however, should be read specifically, scarcely anyone determines. Formerly, in the Cassinese monastery, “certain exhortations excerpted from the books of Saint Gregory the Pope were read before the guests,” as Paul Augustine of Genoa attests. Our Mabillon saw these exhortations, or sermons, in the Cassinese library.

Rodulfus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Theoderic near Rheims, ordered the *Life of Saint Theoderic* to be read before Robert, Count of Flanders, and the Danish [Col. 0758D] queen, as Adalgisus writes in the *Book of His Miracles*, chapter 15 (first Benedictine century).

Finally, the Fathers of the English Congregation decree (on chapter 53):

> “Let him be led to the guesthouse, where the brother entrusted with the care of guests shall read to him a lesson from the First Epistle of Saint John, chapter IV: ‘Beloved, let us love one another,’ and so on to the end; and let him say, ‘But you, O Lord’; and immediately let him prostrate himself before the guest, kissing the ground, so that Christ may be adored in him according to the Rule.”

Second, immediately after the prayer had been made in the church and the kiss of peace had been given, before the guest was led to the guesthouse, a reading of this kind took place, as can be seen in the *Book of Cistercian Usages* (chapter 87):

> “Let them kiss them, and afterward sit down; and when the passage has been read, if the guest requires an explanation, let it be explained to him; then let him be led to the guesthouse, or presented to the hospitaller; but let the brothers return to the cloister.”

[Col. 0759A] Richard of Saint Angelo likewise says, in connection with the words, “After this let every kindness be shown to him”:

> “After this—that is, after he has been led to prayer and the divine law has been read before him.”

The Bursfeld Congregation, however, after the guest has been led to the guesthouse, recites something from the divine Scriptures before him. The Cassinese explain this passage as follows (*Cassinese Declaration*, chapter 53):

> “We especially approve of this being done if it can conveniently be done and the time permits: while the meal is being prepared, something should be read to the guest, or spiritual matters should be discussed, from which he may be edified, with due regard to the person’s character and needs. At the very least, it should not be omitted that something be read to the guest at table, according to his condition, for his edification.”

Similarly, I read the following in the manuscript *Constitutions of the Casalines* (chapter 32): after the kiss of peace,

> “let him be led to the guesthouse, and let the divine law be read before him while the meal is awaited, if time permits; or let spiritual matters be spoken for his edification. At the very least, it should not be omitted that something be read to the guest at the beginning and at the end of the meal, according to the person’s condition.”

[Col. 0759B] Third, this reading was formerly held in the auditorium, as is clear from the *Life of Saint William*, duke and monk of Gellone (fourth Benedictine century), where the manner of his reception into the monastery is described. First, in no. 21, the brothers go out to meet him from a distance, he is led to prayer, and he presents gifts to the church. Then, in no. 22:

> “When the prayer had been completed, and due veneration had been offered to each of all the altars . . . . they go to the auditorium; after the brothers have been kissed, and the customary reading has been given, together with a brief sermon appropriate to the occasion on the edification of the soul, the man of God immediately adds and openly declares the reason for which he has come.”

The same may be seen in Ekkehard, in the *Book of the Accidents of Saint Gall*, chapter 11. He relates how the bishops and abbots whom Emperor Otto had sent to visit the monastery of Saint Gall were received:

> “They all arrive,” he says, “and are received ceremoniously; the response ‘Citizens of the Apostles’ is sung. The abbot, sitting infirm in the auditorium, rises when they are brought in. While they are seated, a reading is given on charity and its handmaid, discretion. When it is finished, all rise [Col. 0759C] for the kisses of the abbot and the brothers. Then the abbot says: ‘Blessed are you by the Lord.’ And the brothers: ‘Who made heaven and earth.’”

Perhaps the passage in the *Life of Saint Alcadri*, abbot of Jumièges, no. 11 (second Benedictine century), is to be understood in the same way:

> “Having received the monks, he led them to the auditorium.”

The auditorium is a place near the chapter house; it is commonly called the parlour. Our Mabillon, however, understands the chapter house here by the term *auditorium*.

[Col. 0759D] Fourth, the reading that had been recited was explained to the guest, as Hildemar teaches:

> “If the guest is of such a kind, the reading should also be explained.”

This is evident from the *Book of Cistercian Usages* cited above, chapter 87, and from the monk Adalgisus in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Theoderic*, chapter 15. He relates that Abbot Rodulfus received Count Robert of Flanders and the queen in his monastery and provided them with a reading from the *Life of Saint Theoderic* at table:

> “He placed before them, as a most health-giving dish for the soul, the Life of the most blessed Theoderic, illustrious for its virtues, read and explained before them by the brothers; and each of them valued it more highly [Col. 0759D] than all other expenditures and expenses.”

Fifth, when an unknown monk arrived, the entire community assembled for the reading, as is evident from the *Chapters for Monks Sent to Augia* (chapter 12):

> “They receive all arriving guests with a reading from the divine law; but when unknown monks arrive, the whole community gathers together for the reading, so that Christ may be adored in them, since he is also received.”

Sixth, Hildemar says:

> “It should be known that there are many who, after reading the lesson to a guest the first time, never afterward read to that same guest again, even if he should come after one, two, or ten years. Such men do not act according to the Rule, since the Rule says that a reading is to be given to the guest. If kindness is to be shown to him, why should a reading not also be given him, which is the better course? How can this be called discretion? For if the guest frequently comes to the monastery, so that he returns after fifteen or twenty days, every time he comes [Col. 0760A] a reading should be given him, and every kindness should be offered.”

Finally, Saint Benedict was by no means the first to prescribe a reading for guests. In the *Rule of Abbot Isaiah* I read the following (chapter 33):

> “Receive the stranger cheerfully and greet him, lest your departure from one another be harmful; and take care, when he comes to you, not to ask him useless questions. Rather, ask him to pray; and when he has sat down, say to him: ‘How are you, my brother?’ and offer him some book to read.”

### “And after this, let every kindness be shown to him.”

Smaragdus explains “every kindness” as “every compassionate affection, and the full and perfect service of love that ought to be shown to guests in the administration of food, drink, and everything appropriate to them.” Hildemar understands it as “every affection . . . . every sufficient courtesy . . . in temporal things—that is, bread and wine, food, a bed, and so forth.” Similarly, Nicholas of Fractura understands kindness as referring “to food, drink, a bed, and the other [Col. 0760B] qualities of the things to be supplied.” Saint Hildegard understands it as including “both friendly and sociable conversation and every necessary bodily provision.” Finally, according to Richard of Saint Angelo, “let every kindness be shown” means, as it were, “let goodwill be displayed toward them, by leading him through the monastery, asking about his province, and saying similar things.”

Kindness also includes every outward demonstration of honor. Thus Saint Sabas, as related by Cyril in his *Life* (*Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, vol. III), “when he had received a certain guest who arrived, and who had priestly ordination, made him perform the holy offering in the oratory.”

Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata believe that the eating of meat is also included in every kindness:

> “A king, bishop, or prince would be badly served,” says Bernard, “if they were compelled to abstain from meat. Let whoever wishes think otherwise; nevertheless, in this universal expression I believe that all such provision is [Col. 0760C] included, with due consideration of discretion toward healthy religious guests, who are not permitted to eat meat.”

And Turrecremata says:

> “If meat were indiscriminately denied to guests, it could not be judged that every kindness had been shown them.”

This opinion, however, is contrary to the excellent practice of the monasteries of our order and was expressly condemned by Pope Innocent III in a brief to the abbot and convent of Great Selve, who had ventured upon something of the kind. It may rightly be opposed by the saying of Saint Ambrose (*Book V on the Hexaemeron*, chapter 8):

> “Hospitality with vegetables and gratitude is better than the preparation of fattened calves with discord.”

And by the saying of Evagrius in the *Monastics*, no. 2 (*Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, vol. III):

> “If, under the pretext of hospitality, the thought of costly food should come into your mind, cast that thought away and do not cling to it; for through it the adversary lies in wait for you . . . . Even if you have only bread, or salt, or water, you can through these obtain the reward of hospitality. And if you have not even these, [Col. 0760D] but have received the stranger only with a good disposition and have honored him with kindly speech, you can in the same way obtain the reward of hospitality.”

Also relevant is the whole of chapter 20 of Saint Basil’s *Longer Rules*, where he forbids the customary foods to be changed on account of whatever dignity or authority the guests may possess:

> “Unless perhaps we shall also change our garments whenever we must associate with more distinguished persons. But if that would be more shameful, it is much more shameful to change the frugality of our table for the sake of certain delicate persons.”

A little later, rebuking an excessive and overly luxurious provision of food, he adds:

> “When you prepare a table for a brother beyond the customary measure, with an abundance and luxury of foods, for pleasure, you accuse him of luxury and dishonor him with reproaches for gluttony through the things you set out, while you blame him because he delights in such luxury and pleasure.”

The ancient custom of our order supports this position. Formerly, when popes, kings, and other great men were received in the monasteries, fish, [Col. 0761A] vegetables, legumes, and similar monastic foods were served to them. Saint John Gualbert, founder of the Congregation of Vallombrosa, received Pope Leo with the whole Roman Curia as guests and served them fish, as is recorded in the acts of his life.

More sparingly, Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, served Pope Innocent II a small fish, while the cardinals scarcely had legumes, as can be seen in his Life. The king of the English sometimes came to the monastery of Lindisfarne under Saint Colman and ate with the brothers in the refectory of their ordinary food, as the Venerable Bede writes in Book III of the *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, chapter 26. King Ferdinand of Castile, when he came to the monastery of Sahagún, used only the ordinary food of the brothers, as Roderic reports in Book VI of *On the Affairs of Spain*, chapter 14. King Conrad of the Romans ate with two bishops in the refectory of the monastery of Saint Gall on the Feast of the Holy Innocents, together with the monks, content with their humble food; the following day he did the same, satisfied with bread and raw beans, [Col. 0761B] as is related in the *Life of Saint Notker*, chapter 16.

Certainly, it can scarcely be said how religiously the Cistercians guarded this observance, or by how many decrees and statutes they forbade meat to be served to guests in any way. In the *Book of Institutions* (Distinction 13, chapter 3) they say:

> “To bishops and other persons who are not of our order, within the precincts of the abbey and in the adjoining houses, meat shall in no way be served or permitted to be eaten, unless they are seriously ill.”

And in the general chapter of 1192:

> “Abbots who serve cheese and eggs to guests on Friday shall spend three days in light guilt, one of them on bread and water.”

In the *Book of Ancient Definitions*, where the decree mentioned in the *Book of Institutions* is renewed, they add (Distinction 13, chapter 2):

> “Likewise, secular persons or members of another religion shall in no way be permitted to live near our cemeteries or to eat meat. Any abbot who, within the precincts of the abbey or in the adjoining houses, serves or causes meat to be served to such persons—[Col. 0761C] except to poor sick persons or to persons who habitually reside in the abbeys, in a place specially assigned for this purpose—shall ask pardon for it in the general chapter and shall be severely punished. The officials, monks, and lay brothers who arrange or carry this out shall be on bread and water every Friday until the following general chapter.”

And below (Distinction 15, chapter 2):

> “In monasteries of nuns also we strictly forbid meat henceforth to be served to any regular or secular persons, except in extreme necessity; but, if necessary, conventual foods may be served on one day. Wherever anything else has been attempted, both those who serve and those who arrange for it to be served shall be punished by removal of the habit.”

To these must be added the decrees of the supreme pontiffs, who forbade even bishops visiting monasteries of the Cistercian order in their official capacity to demand meat from them, as can be seen in the *Clementines*, Book III, title 13, chapter 2. They also forbade nobles, under the pretext of patronage, to introduce their wives into monasteries and presume to eat meat, [Col. 0761D] as is evident from the bull of Pope Gregory IX cited above by us.

Therefore, let all fat meat and every excessive and costly provision of food be far removed from our guesthouses. Such things belong in the houses of kings, not of monks. “When a brother knocks at your cell,” says Peter Damian (*Opusculum* 15, chapter 10), “let the gloomy wrinkles immediately depart; let the contracted face relax; let a cheerful countenance meet him; let the eager brow display joy.”

This is all the kindness that we ought to show guests. Let no one invoke the authority, nobility, or power of guests to excuse more sumptuous provisions of food. Whatever might be brought forward for this purpose, Saint Jerome refuted long ago, and with great force, when he wrote to Nepotianus (Epistle 2):

> “You must avoid the banquets of secular persons, and especially of those who swell with honors. It is shameful that before the doors of a priest of the crucified and poor Christ, [Col. 0762A] who even ate another’s food, the lictors of consuls and soldiers should keep watch, and that the governor of a province should dine better with you than in the palace. If you reply that you do these things in order to ask on behalf of the wretched and the subjected, the secular judge will show greater respect to a self-controlled cleric than to a rich man, and will revere your holiness more than your wealth. Or, if he is such a man as will not hear clerics on behalf of those in distress unless he is among goblets, I shall gladly do without such a benefit and shall pray to Christ for the judge, who can help more and more quickly than the judge. For it is better to trust in the Lord than to trust in man; better to hope in the Lord than to hope in princes.”

This is an excellent and salutary admonition. I beg that those monks take heed who sometimes spend at a single banquet what would suffice to feed one monk for an entire year.

### “Let the prior break the fast on account of the guest.”

For, as Abbot Theonas says in Cassian (*Conference* 21, chapter 14):

> “If anyone, at the arrival of a brother in whom he ought to refresh Christ through kindness and embrace him with a most gracious welcome, [Col. 0762B] wishes to maintain the austerity of the fast, does he not incur the charge of inhumanity rather than gain praise or the merit of religion?”

And Abbot Moses says (*Conference* 2, chapter 26):

> “It is exceedingly absurd that, when offering a table to a brother—or rather, to Christ—you should not take food together with him and should make yourself a stranger to his refreshment.”

See the same Cassian, Book V, chapter 24.

### “Unless perhaps it is a principal fast-day which cannot be violated.”

Such, says Hildemar, are “an appointed fast, and the days of Lent, or of the Litanies, and the other fasting days observed by the Church.” And Smaragdus says:

> “The fasting days that cannot be violated are understood to be the days of the holy paschal Lent, of the Litanies, and of the four Ember seasons, or when the vigil of a feast day is to be observed, at which time not only canonical clerics but also Catholic laypeople fast.”

Nicholas of Fractura and Richard of Saint Angelo speak in nearly the same way.

[Col. 0762C] Among these principal fasting days, which cannot be violated, the ancient monks also counted Wednesday and Friday:

> “Break the fast if some brother has come to you from abroad,” says Saint Athanasius (*Doctrinal Collection for Monks*, and so forth), “but by no means break the fixed fast of Wednesday, Friday, Lent, or the Passion. The reference is to the fast for which you yourself are responsible—namely, that of Monday, Tuesday, and Thursday.”

And Cassian, speaking of the Egyptian monks (Book V, chapter 24):

> “Except on the appointed Wednesdays and Fridays, wherever we went the daily fast was broken.”

See Rufinus, Book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 7, and Palladius, in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 52.

### “But the brothers shall continue the customary fasts.”

This is so that, under the pretext of kindness, the strictness of the fast and discipline should not be entirely relaxed, especially since guests are never absent from a monastery. Indeed, the Carthusian Statutes rightly decree (*New Collection of Statutes*, part II, chapter 3, no. 31):

> “The prior in his house ought not to eat indiscriminately [Col. 0762D] and without distinction with arriving guests, but only with respectable persons and those to whom he cannot conveniently refuse this; and even then, the less frequently, the better.”

### “Let the abbot give the guests water for their hands.”

Formerly even bishops performed this same service as an act of hospitality, as is evident from Baudemundus in the *Life of Saint Amandus*, chapter 20. When the saint arrived in a certain city, “the bishop, according to the custom of hospitality, poured water over his hands.” Indeed, secular men themselves did so, as is clear from Bede in the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 29.

### “But both the abbot and the whole community shall wash the feet of all the guests.”

[Col. 0763A] This sentence can be understood in two ways:

1. That the abbot and the entire community together wash the feet of each guest; or
2. That each monk of the community, each in his appointed order, beginning with the abbot, washes the feet of each guest.

Thus the entire community is said to wash the guests’ feet in the same way that all the brothers are said to perform the kitchen duty, because each carries it out in his turn.

In the first sense, I would scarcely ever have believed that this chapter of the Rule was observed, except perhaps in the case of unknown monks, for whom the entire community gathered for the reading of the divine law prescribed by the holy legislator, as we saw above.

In this way, shortly afterward, the abbot is said to have washed the hands and feet of the bishop of Verdun together with the brothers of the monastery of Thérouanne (in his Life, no. 3, second Benedictine century). Saint Thomas, abbot of Farfa (third Benedictine century), “having received as guests the most holy men Paldon, Taso, and Tato, performed with the brothers, as was his custom, the washing of their feet according to the Lord’s command, as is proper to monks and good Christians,” writes Autpertus in the *Life of Saint Paldon*, no. 5.

Otherwise, if the whole community had been required to wash the feet of all guests indiscriminately and simultaneously, the brothers occupied with this work of hospitality would not have been able to fulfill the other duties of the Rule. This is the strong argument advanced by Peter the Venerable in a letter to Saint Bernard.

[Col. 0763B] Saint Hildegard seems to have understood Saint Benedict in the second sense with regard to the words “the whole community shall wash,” for she writes:

> “Namely, those to whom the abbot assigns that work.”

Richard of Saint Angelo says:

> “That is, some members of the community.”

Hildemar explains it more clearly:

> “When he says that the whole community shall wash the feet of the guests, a rotation should be arranged by days.”

And below:

> “We do the same in washing the feet of the poor: those who offer at Mass during the day also go after Vespers to wash the feet of the poor; they wash the feet while singing, and after the feet have been washed they mix [the object is unspecified]. After mixing, they say the chapters and the prayer, ‘Be present to the service of our ministry,’ and so forth.”

Here he seems to have had in mind the chapter for monks sent to Augia (chapter 3):

> “Let six brothers be assigned each day by rota to offer the sacred oblation, beginning with the abbot, all in order, just as we ourselves once did; [Col. 0763C] and let these also wash the feet of pilgrims on each weekday.”

Of the Cluniacs Peter the Venerable writes to Saint Bernard (Book I, Letter 28):

> “Nevertheless, we do what we can, and throughout the entire year, every day, we wash the hands and feet of three pilgrim guests, offer them bread with wine, and have the abbot do this in his appointed order, excluding only the sick, who are unable to fulfill these duties.”

Bernard of Cassino implies that the same practice was observed in his time at the monastery of Cassino. At present, however, the Cassinese chiefly wash the feet of those who come for conversion (*Cassinese Declaration*, chapter 53).

In the *Regularis Concordia* of Saint Dunstan I find the following provision on this matter (chapter 10):

> “Every day without interruption, three poor men are to be chosen from among those who are continually fed in the monastery, and the service of the same commandment is to be performed for them; they are to be fed with the same provisions that the brothers use. The order of going there shall be carried out in this way: on Saturday, the boys of the right choir, with their custodian, shall perform it; [Col. 0763D] on the following Sunday, the remaining boys of the left choir, with the other custodian; thereafter, on each day of the week and for each weekday, as many brothers shall be appointed for this duty as are required, so that no one except the abbot may be excused from this obligation of service. The abbot, however, is not to perform it on only one weekday, but more often, whenever he has leisure and opportunity allows.

> “As for poor pilgrims who arrive, the abbot, with the brothers whom he chooses, shall perform the service of the commandment according to the precept of the Rule.”

Something similar is found in the manuscript *Customs of the monastery of Farfa*. To these we may add the decree issued by Abbot Ingulfus for his monastery of Croyland. Although it may seem lengthy, it contains much worthy of edification—things which pious readers might rightly wish to see among us (*History of the Monastery of Croyland*, year 1091):

> “For the honor of God and the edification of his people, remembering that in the monasteries overseas [Col. 0764A]—namely, Fontenelle, Fécamp, Jumièges, Molesme, Cluny, and also Fleury, as well as in all the other more ancient monasteries—the service for the poor is performed daily after the high Mass, and that the people of God are greatly edified by it, while in all the English monasteries such service for the poor is either omitted or entirely unknown, I have decided, with the counsel of my whole community, that henceforth it shall be performed daily in our monastery for our benefactors.

> “I grant our almoner, whoever he may be at the time, permission to leave the choir immediately after the consecration of the Lord’s sacrament at the high Mass. I wish the almoner then to proceed directly to the monastery gate and to bring three pilgrims into the large parlour before the end of the high Mass. If there are no pilgrims, three poor old men shall be brought in. If there are not even such old men, then three respectable boys shall be brought into the parlour in place of three paralytics lying in beds throughout the town, both women [Col. 0764B] and men. Their feet shall be washed as those of the other pilgrims or old men, but the provisions shall be sent in full to the paralytics in whose place they have sat.

> “The feet of the pilgrims and old men shall be washed, and they may eat their provisions there if they wish; they may also carry away with them the remains of the food and drink. If they do not wish to eat there, they may freely take all the provisions with them into the town.

> “Each day, for the performance of this service, the almoner shall receive three monastic loaves, three jugs of conventual beer, and three kitchen dishes. He shall ensure that all these are prepared there before the arrival of the monks, who, when the high Mass is finished, shall immediately come from the choir to wash the feet of the poor mentioned above; and he shall arrange for both the persons and the provisions as honorably as he can.

> “If, persuaded by the devil through the evil of avarice or hatred of obedience, the said almoner should at any time bring in not three poor persons but two or one, [Col. 0764C] he shall spend that day on bread and water, without any mercy being shown him in this matter. And unless he makes up on another day the number he withheld on that day, the same number of portions shall be withheld on the following day as the number of persons he withheld—while he nevertheless remains in his penance for his disobedience, unless a Sunday or the feast of some saint intervenes.

> “If he is unwilling to correct himself even by such penance, he shall be removed from his office, and another almoner shall be appointed who is more willing to manage the affairs of the poor according to the form prescribed above.

> “For when we had maintained this custom for some time, some of our fellow-professors from other monasteries came to us. Having been greatly edified, when they returned to their own houses they introduced the same practice among their brethren.”

Before we leave this subject, someone may perhaps ask at what particular time the ancient monks washed the feet of guests; for Saint Benedict does not say. The Rule of Saint Pachomius seems to require this immediately after the guests’ arrival, even before they are led to the guesthouse (Art. 28). In the Rule of Saint Fructuosus, however, I read (chapter 10):

> “The services of reverence, charity, and ministry are to be provided to guests and pilgrim brothers with the greatest respect; their feet are to be washed in the evening; and if they are exhausted from the journey, they are to be anointed with oil.”

Thus Saint Barnard, abbot of Ambronay and afterward bishop of Vienne (fourth Benedictine century), “washed the feet every evening of all the pilgrims received as guests,” as is recorded in his Life, no. 5.

[Col. 0764D] “But blessed Father Benedict himself,” writes Saint Hildegard, “when the guests whom he had received were about to eat, offered them water for their hands; and when they had risen from the table, he washed their feet. He did this because of the example of the Son of God, which he displayed at supper for the disciples, except in the case of women, whose feet he did not touch; but he showed them contempt for the world both in his clothing and in his holy manner of life.”

Finally, in the Council of Aachen there is a [Col. 0765A] canon (Canon 22):

> “If it is the time of supper, the service of the commandment for both brothers and pilgrims is to be performed after supper.”

Nevertheless, when the bishop of Verdun later stayed at the monastery of Thérouanne, his feet were washed immediately after prayer, as his acts relate, no. 3. Nicholas Bravus writes that among Easterners it was customary to wash guests’ feet before food was taken, but among Westerners after supper and before going to bed (Distinction II, chapter 12). The Bursfeld Congregation likewise prescribes the washing of guests’ feet after Compline in its *Ceremonial*.

### “Let careful attention be devoted especially to the reception of the poor and pilgrims.”

Formerly, in our monasteries, a particular brother was placed in charge of receiving the poor; he received them in the monastery’s guesthouse, situated near the monastic buildings. Examples of this are found in the *Life of Saint Agilus, abbot of Rebais*, no. 20, second Benedictine century; in Adrevaldus, in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Benedict*; in Walafridus, in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Gall*, chapter 43; in the *Life of Saint Poppo*, no. 13; and in Bollandus, 25 January.

Formerly the monks of Fulda also [Col. 0765B] earnestly requested this in a petition to Charlemagne, asking (no. 13):

> “That the reception of pilgrims and the washing of their feet not be neglected, but that whenever they come they be mercifully received according to the Rule and according to the custom of our predecessors, and that the washing of their feet be performed for them by all the brothers.”

### “The abbot’s and the guests’ kitchen shall be separate,” and so forth.

On this passage Smaragdus writes:

> “Many believe that, just as the kitchen other than that of the brothers was established in another place, so the abbot’s table was not then placed in the common refectory with the other tables, but was set apart in another room, which the frequently arriving guests would often find prepared with food. But now, by the salutary decision of the great council of bishops, abbots, and other Franks, it has been determined that, for the safety of himself and the brothers, he should have a table in the common refectory, where he may dine with the guests when they are present; when they are absent, he may dine with whomever [Col. 0765C] he wishes before the brothers.”

This great council of the Franks was none other than the Council of Aachen, in which it was decreed (Canon 27):

> “The abbot, or any of the brothers, shall not dine at the monastery gate. In the refectory he shall show them every kindness in eating and drinking. He himself, however, shall be content with the measure of food and drink that the other brothers receive. If, on account of a guest, he wishes to increase something beyond the customary measure for the brothers and for himself, this shall remain within his discretion.”

More will be said on these matters below, at chapter 56. For the present, it is enough to note from Hildemar that the guests’ kitchen should be placed next to the monks’ kitchen in such a way that there is a small window between them, through which food may be served on one side to the brothers and on the other to the guests eating in the refectory.

### “Two brothers shall enter that kitchen for a year, and they shall perform the office properly.”

For, says Saint Fructuosus (chapter 10):

> “Such ministers are to be assigned to them as will prepare the dishes diligently, serve them with devoted ministry, and neither defraud them of what remains, [Col. 0765D] nor pollute themselves there by secret and illicit eating.”

According to the Eastern Rule (chapter 25), the cellarer “shall prepare food for the various brothers who arrive.”

### “Let the assistance they require be provided,” and so forth.

Relevant here is what is read in the manuscript *Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon* (chapter 44):

> “So that there may never be a lack of persons who can serve the guests honorably, it has been established that the servants of the lord abbot and the prior, who are accustomed to ride with them, shall all receive their daily provision from the hand of the hospitaller and shall be in his presence every day, so that they may do whatever he orders. If any of them goes anywhere without his permission, he shall be deprived of his ration that day.

> “Moreover, he has his own servants, his own cook, and two asses assigned to the guesthouse, which are to bring wood every day, so that when guests arrive there may be an ample supply of wood ready.”

[Col. 0766A] Likewise, let a brother have an assigned guest-house, etc.] Haeften describes its duties in book II, treatise 2, discussion 3. By “cell” Saint Benedict understands an entire guest-house divided into several cells. It is especially noteworthy that formerly in our monasteries the monks’ guest-house was separate from that of rich and poor guests, as is evident from the Customs of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane (Analecta, vol. IV), where we read: “In the guest-house of the monks there is the most honorable reception of guests, the house of reception for other guests being separated.” Hildemar writes on this passage as follows:

“It must be noted that, if it can be done, the enclosure for noble guests ought to be like that of the monks, with its own arrangement. The enclosure for the poor should likewise be like that for the sick. The enclosure for monastic guests should also be like that for the sick, where everything necessary can be prepared. But if it cannot be as I have said, let the places for bishops be separate from those of the rich, yet together separate from the poor, abbots, and monks, since a count and a bishop cannot meet together with poor people and with foreign abbots.”

And elsewhere (on chapter 67):

“But because the Rule says concerning the reception of guests, ‘And let the house of God be wisely administered by the wise,’ they understand this to mean that the dormitory where monks are to be received is separate from the room of the laymen—that is, where laymen sleep—because laymen may remain awake until midnight, and talk and play, whereas monks ought not to do so, but should rather keep silence and pray. Therefore, beside the oratory of those monastic guests is their dormitory, where they may sleep alone and reverently, and may rise at night at whatever hour they wish and go into the church . . . But if the dormitory of the monastic guests is not beside the oratory for the sake of prayer, but is together with the laymen, then the house of God is not wisely administered by the wise.”

The dormitory of the monastic guests was therefore beside the oratory; and perhaps it was the same as the brothers’ dormitory, or at least was not far from it, as is evident from book II of Saint Gregory’s Dialogues, chapter 35, where Saint Benedict is described as resting in a tower together with the deacon Servandus: “Before that same tower there was a more spacious dwelling, in which the disciples of both rested”—namely, those of Benedict and of Servandus. Hence the decree of the Council of Aachen (canon 58): “Let a dormitory be established beside the oratory, where visiting monks may sleep.”

In the ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall, however, the dormitory of the monastic guests was far removed from the brothers’ dormitory, although it too was opposite the oratory: the brothers’ dormitory was adjoining the church on the southern side, while the dormitory of the monastic guests was on the northern side. What we have said about the separation of the monks’ guest-house from the guest-house of the rich and the poor is confirmed by the same plan, by Bernard of Cassino, and by Boherius.

Where there are beds sufficiently furnished.] Here Smaragdus says: “They are called strati, ‘spread out,’ from sternere, ‘to spread’; strati is as if one said storiati, for storia is what we call a mat or mattress. In ancient times the monks used to sleep only on these, and only with these did they make their little beds.” Peter the Deacon speaks in the same way, but Bernard of Cassino and Boherius understand strati lecti to mean beds “arranged with their bedding—that is, prepared with everything necessary for resting.” Richard of Saint Angelo similarly understands them as arranged beds, which Saint Fructuosus also wishes to be soft, chapter 10. See the Rule of the Master, chapter 79.

And let the house of God be wisely administered by the wise.] Saint Pachomius “entrusted the care of the entire administration concerning the brothers and strangers to those who followed him in rank,” as we read in his Life, chapter 25 (in Rosweyde, book I, On the Lives of the Fathers).

But let no one to whom it has not been commanded associate or converse with guests.] This was the common practice of the ancient monks, as can be seen in nearly all the old Rules. The Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius (chapter 8) says:

“Nor shall it be permitted for a brother to converse with him when he arrives; he is not to concern himself with asking where he came from, why he came, or when he will depart, except only the Father who presides, or those whom he himself has ordered to do so.”

The Second Rule of the Holy Fathers (chapter 3) says:

“To a visiting stranger he shall offer nothing more than peace; he shall not concern himself with where he came from, for what purpose he came, or when he will depart, nor shall he join him in conversation.”

The Penances of an uncertain author, in Saint Basil (no. 39), say:

“If anyone meets and converses with visiting strangers, except in giving them peace, unless he has been designated for this purpose, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

The Rule of Tarnat (chapter 7) says:

“To those who arrive, the junior brother shall offer nothing except the disposition of humility and the service that is due; he shall not presume to concern himself with the reason for which the visitor came or with when he will return, since this should be investigated by the diligence of the elders, not by the presumption of juniors.”

Finally, the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 22) says:

“No one shall dare to see a guest, whether a relative or a stranger, or a monk, family member, or kinsman, without the command of the elder.”

Saint Isidore appears to have had in mind the following passage of Saint Pachomius (article 30):

“If anyone stands before the monastery gate, saying that he wishes to see his brother or kinsman, the gatekeeper shall announce it to the Father of the monastery. He shall summon the superior of the house and ask whether the man is under his charge; and, with the superior’s permission, he shall take as his companion for the departure someone whose fidelity has been tested. Thus he shall be sent to see his brother or relative.”

But if he meets him or sees him, let him greet him humbly, as has been said, and, having asked for a blessing, pass by, etc.] What that blessing was, and how it was requested, Boherius explains in these words:

“According to the manner of religious life, when greeting one’s elders the religious say, ‘Benedicite’—‘Give your blessing.’ I think this is what the blessing consists in; or the brother should say, ‘My lord, or Reverend Father, I am not permitted to speak with you; therefore, with your blessing, I depart.’ The guest, however, should answer both: ‘Go, Father,’ or ‘Brother, in the blessing of God.’”

And in his second commentary:

“Having asked for the blessing—that is, having said ‘Benedicite.’ But what, I ask, is the proper answer to him? ‘Go, Father,’ or ‘Brother, in the blessing of God.’”

Nicholas of Fractura likewise says that the blessing is requested by the words “Benedicite.”

Moreover, it was the custom among the ancient monks not only to ask blessings from the guests themselves, but also to ask the guests to receive a blessing from them, as is clear from Rufinus (book II, On the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 1):

“When we had greeted him . . . we asked him to give us prayer and blessing together.”

When they departed, they again received it:

“But when,” the same Rufinus adds, “we began to wish to depart from him, after he had given us his blessings, he said, ‘Go forward, sons.’”

And speaking of Saint Apollonius (chapter 7):

“Thus he dismissed us with a blessing, and gave the blessing in these words: ‘May the Lord bless you from Zion, and may you see the good things of Jerusalem all the days of your life.’”

So too the monk Marculfus (Benedictine Century II), who had visited Saint Columbanus, “having received his blessing, returned by the road by which he had come,” as Jonas writes in his Life, no. 14.

## CHAPTER LIV. Whether a monk ought to receive letters or anything else

[Col. 0767]

[Col. 0767B] Let it in no way be permitted for a monk to receive or give letters, eulogiae, or any little gifts, either from his parents, or from any human being, or to one another, without the command of the abbot. [Note: [Col. 0767C] Lyr., omits “or from his parents.”] And if something is sent to him even by his parents, let him not presume to receive it unless it has first been reported to the abbot. If he orders it to be received, it shall be in the abbot’s power to whom he orders it to be given [Note: [Col. 0767C] Al., “to give.”]; and let not the brother to whom it had perhaps been sent be saddened [Note: [Col. 0768C] Al., “had been sent”], so that an occasion may not be given to the devil [Note: [Col. 0768C] Al., “the evil one.”]. Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall be subject to regular discipline.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0767]

Let it in no way be permitted for a monk to receive or give letters, eulogiae, or any little gifts, either from his parents, or from any human being, or to one another, without the command of his abbot.] Bernard of Cassino observes aptly:

“Saint Benedict names three classes of persons in this prohibition, and three classes of things. The persons are parents, any other people, and also the brothers among themselves. The things are letters, eulogiae, and little gifts. A monk may not receive these from his parents, lest he appear to retain something from the affection of his parents by means of a gift; nor from other people, because a monk has nothing in common with the world; nor may brothers give or receive them among themselves, because this would indicate an exclusive affection or an unlawful bond.”

First, therefore, the holy Father forbids letters to be sent or received without the abbot’s permission. This follows the discipline of the ancient monks, as can be seen in Cassian, book IV, chapter 16; in Saint Basil, cited here by Smaragdus; in the Penances of an uncertain author preserved by the same Basil; in the Rule of Saint Augustine, chapter 9; in Saint Caesarius, To Monks, chapter 15, To Virgins, chapter 23, and in the Recapitulation, chapter 6; in the Rule of Saint Aurelian, To Monks, chapter 6, and To Virgins, chapter 4; in the Penitential of Saint Columbanus; in the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 19; of Saint Isidore, chapter 22; of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 8; and of Saint Donatus, chapter 53.

The principal reason for this institution was that the mind devoted to divine contemplation should not be drawn away from God. The tongue can scarcely express, nor the understanding grasp, how many disturbances excessive and disordered letter-writing stirs up in the soul. “What a tumult there is in the mind of those dictating,” Saint Bernard says (Letter 89), “when a multitude of words clamors; when a variety of expressions and diversity of meanings converge; when what first occurs is often rejected and what has slipped away is sought; when one attends with the utmost care to what is more beautiful according to the wording, what is more coherent according to the meaning, what is clearer for understanding, what is more useful for the conscience, and finally what ought to be placed before, after, or in relation to what; and many other matters that learned men observe with excessive care in such things!”

How many movements of the soul are struck by the recollection of the past, of dear ones and relatives, and by the sweet memory of one’s abandoned homeland! When a certain monk seriously considered these things (Cassian, book V, chapter 32), and “after fifteen years several letters had been brought to him from his father and mother and from many friends in the province of Pontus, he took up the large bundle of letters and, turning the matter over in his mind for a long time, said:

‘How many thoughts will this reading cause me! It will drive me either toward empty joy or toward fruitless sadness. For how many days will the remembrance of those who wrote them recall my mind from its appointed contemplation! After how long a time will this confusion conceived in my mind be digested, and with how much labor must this state of tranquility be restored, if my soul, once disturbed by affection for the letters and by reviewing the words and faces of those whom it abandoned so long ago, begins again to revisit them, to dwell with them, and to attend to them in heart and mind? It will have been of no benefit to have abandoned them bodily if it begins to behold them in the heart, and if it revives and once again admits the memory which each person, when renouncing this world, rejected as though dead.’

“Turning these things over in his heart, he resolved not only not to open any letter, but not even to untie the bundle, lest, by reading the names of those who had written or recalling their faces, he should cease from the concentration of his spirit. Thus, just as he had received it bound, he handed it over to the fire to be burned, saying: ‘Go, thoughts of my homeland; burn together, and do not try any longer to recall me to the things from which I fled.’”

A truly noble deed, and worthy of a true monk!

With precisely the same frame of mind, Gerard, the devout Belgian monk, “never read letters sent to him except in the afternoon, unless they concerned a very serious matter and he was obliged to answer immediately, lest he deprive the most important part of the day, as he called it, and the time more sacred to God, by profane reading, or open a door to distraction. If he seemed to be affected in any way by them, he was also accustomed often to set them aside for a long time before reading them. When carefully reading letters sent to his relatives, if they brought any rumor from the world, he would delete or cut out such passages; if they appeared likely to bring disturbance or empty glory, he burned them entirely. Whatever seemed useful in them, he himself reported” (Bucelinus, additions to Gerard’s Commentary, chapter 54).

[Col. 0769C] Second, Saint Benedict forbids giving or receiving eulogiae without the abbot’s command. What eulogiae are must now be investigated.

Eulogiae does not derive from the Greek εὖ, “good,” and the Latin lego, “I choose,” as though it meant “something good that has been chosen,” as Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius hold. Rather, it derives from the Greek εὖ, “well,” and the Greek λέγω, “I say,” or λόγος, “speech”; in Latin it means “blessing.” By this name is understood:

First, any gift given out of charity. This is a formula of speech derived from the Hebrews, who called little gifts “blessings,” as in 1 Samuel 25: “Accept this blessing which your handmaid has brought”; the Septuagint reads εὐλογία, eulogia, in this passage. Saint Bernard is to be understood in this sense when writing to the bishop of Laon (Letter 272):

“Since you began to be a bishop, we have not yet received any blessing from you—not a purse, not a bag, not even shoes for our feet.”

And to Guido, cardinal deacon (Letter 335):

“I was concerned for our brothers . . . and also for the blessing which you had intended to provide.”

Second, more specifically, eulogiae were gifts sent from the relics of the saints. Thus Saint Gregory, writing to Eulogius, bishop of Alexandria (Register, book XI, chapter 47), says:

“We have received the eulogiae of Saint Mark sent by your blessed fraternity with the same love with which they were sent, according to our knowledge of them.”

And again in the same letter:

“Furthermore, we have sent a small cross in which a blessing has been inserted from the chain of your beloved ones.”

Third, eulogiae means the bread intended for the consecration of the Eucharist, as can be seen in John Moschus (book X of On the Lives of the Fathers, chapter 25):

“The deacons placed those same blessings upon the holy altar; and when John the priest offered them, etc.”

Fourth, it means the Eucharist itself, as in Maximus the Martyr (On Ecclesiastical Hierarchy, chapter 3):

“Lifting up the sacred bread, the priest displayed the eulogia, saying, ‘Holy things for the holy.’”

Fifth, among our own people the blessed hosts were called eulogiae. These were offered in the refectory each day before the common food to monks who had not received Communion. See book I, On Ancient Monastic Rites, chapter 9.

Eulogiae were also called the loaves blessed in church and formerly distributed to those who, because of some impediment, did not receive the Eucharist on feast days and Sundays. Some have thought that this practice arose from a decree of Pope Pius, although the letter from which they derive it is spurious. See the Council of Nantes, canon 9, and the capitularies of Hincmar, bishop of Reims, chapter 7. These loaves were also sent to the faithful as a sign of participation in the same faith. Hence the Council of Laodicea, canon 32, decrees “that it is not lawful to receive the eulogiae of heretics.”

Sixth, any blessed object was called a eulogia. In this sense Fortunatus, in the Life of Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, no. 11, calls blessed liquid a eulogia, and in the Life of Saint Medericus blessed bread is called a eulogia.

Seventh, they also called eulogiae ordinary bread which people sent to one another as a sign of love and goodwill. Thus Paulinus, Letter 1 to Severus:

“We have sent you Campanian bread from our little cell as a eulogia.”

And the priest Florentius sent poisoned bread to Saint Benedict as though it were a blessing, as Saint Gregory testifies in the Dialogues, book II, chapter 8.

Eighth: “In law,” says Richard of Saint Angelo, “eulogium, that is, a testament, is explained in the title On Testaments, chapter ‘Vos quidem,’ and in the Code, book II, chapter ‘Jubemus.’”

[Page 694] Ninth: “Or you may say,” the same Richard adds, “that they are good speeches made about someone. This is how it is explained in *pe. san.*, *Extra de do. et cantu*, ‘Cum olim,’ above the first gloss.”

It is now asked in what sense Saint Benedict takes eulogia here. Some, as Bernard of Cassino reports, have said that eulogiae is an adjective modifying letters. Menardus understands Saint Benedict to mean the eulogiae of bread, which the ancient Fathers forbade to be given without the superior’s permission, as can be seen in the Rule of Saint Caesarius, chapter 23, and of Saint Donatus, chapter 53. For Hildemar, “eulogiae are larger gifts, such as a silk cloak or something else of greater value.” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius hold the same view. Richard of Saint Angelo says that they are *gaudeolas* (“little delights”). I, however, think that by eulogiae every kind of gift is forbidden. Benedict Haeften likewise says:

“It seems that it must be maintained that he forbade eulogiae of every kind, whether they were loaves, food, or any other gifts, so that the phrase ‘or any little gifts’ may be taken as an explanation of the preceding expression.”

Third and finally, the holy Father forbids any little gifts. I do not understand this as an explanation of the preceding expression, as though Saint Benedict had understood by eulogiae only little gifts, for he also prohibited larger gifts. Rather, he added “any little gifts” so that no one might presume on his own authority to give or receive them on the grounds that they were of lesser value.

Moreover, in sending and receiving letters or eulogiae, we must pay particular attention to the words of Saint Jerome (Letter 2):

“Frequent little gifts, handkerchiefs, little bands, offered and tasted foods, and flattering and sweet little letters do not belong to holy love.”

Above all, we must beware of gifts from parents, according to the words of Saint Orsiesius (no. 39):

“If anyone lives in the monastery under a superior, lacking nothing that he is permitted to have in the monastery, and has a father, brother, or dearest friend, let him receive absolutely nothing from them—not a tunic, not a little cloak, nor any other thing.”

Yet, so that the brothers may have no occasion for complaint, he wisely adds:

“But if it is established that he lacks something of what has been prescribed, all blame and correction shall fall upon the superior.”

And if something is sent to him even by his parents, etc.] The Rule of Saint Aurelian, chapter 5; the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 19; and that of Saint Isidore say nearly the same.

And let not the brother to whom it had perhaps been sent be saddened, so that an occasion may not be given to the devil.] That is, through sadness, envy, or murmuring, as Smaragdus explains.

Whoever presumes to act otherwise shall be subject to regular discipline.] These words may refer either to the preceding sentence—“and let not the brother be saddened,” etc.—or to everything contained in this chapter. Smaragdus follows the former interpretation; Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Richard of Saint Angelo, and Boherius in both commentaries follow the latter:

“That statement,” says Hildemar, “that he shall be subject to regular discipline refers to everything forbidden above: if he has given or received letters, eulogiae—that is, larger gifts—or little gifts—that is, small ones—or if he has murmured or become saddened, and so forth, he shall be subject to regular discipline.”

How highly Saint Gregory regarded this chapter of the Benedictine Rule is clear from the fact that, when the monk Catellus had sinned against it and the abbot Urbicus later asked that he be made superior of the monastery of Lucus under Abbot Bonus, the holy pontiff refused. He said (Book IX, Letter 42):

“We have recognized that he is not a monk; for, over a small eulogia which the monk Bonus had received, he did not hesitate to make a contentious claim while on a journey, asking for a share. From how great a bitterness of heart this arose, your Love could discover if you had wished to know the Rule of the monks.”

The more ancient monks likewise ordered those who wrote or received letters without permission to gather with the brothers in the synaxis, prostrate themselves on the ground, and ask pardon until the abbot had forgiven the fault (Cassian, book IV, chapter 16). The Penances of an uncertain author, preserved by Saint Basil, no. 49, excommunicate them; Saint Columbanus condemns them to a superposition (a prescribed fast) in his Penitential; the Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 16, decrees that they are to be corrected by a three-day excommunication. Finally, in manuscript codex 47 of the Cassinese library, among cases reserved to the prior for nearly three hundred years, the third is:

“That no one send a letter or embassy outside the monastery, nor receive one from anyone, without permission.”

[Col. 0772B] If they punished those who sent or received letters in this way, how much more severely would they punish eulogiae or any other little gifts, which, according to the Rule of the monastery of Tarnat (chapter 19), “shall be assigned to strangers and unknown persons, or at least burned in the fire.” Those who received or sent them were to be flogged at least in chapter, according to the book of the Institutes of the General Chapter of the Cistercian Order, distinction 6, chapter 9.

## CHAPTER LV. On the clothing and footwear of the brothers

[Note: [Col. 0771D] Flor., “On the clothing and footwear.” Cassin., together with certain others, “On the clothing and footwear.”]

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771B] Let clothing be given to the brothers according to the character of the places where they live and the temperature of the air, since more is needed in cold regions and less in warm ones. This consideration belongs to the abbot. Nevertheless, for temperate places we believe that one cuculla and one tunic per monk are sufficient [Note: [Col. 0771D] Al. omits “for the monks.”]: a woolly cuculla in winter [Note: [Col. 0771D] Sabin., “woolen”], and in summer a plain or old one; and a scapular for work; garments for the feet, socks and shoes. Concerning the color or thickness of all these things, let the monks not quarrel, but accept what can be found in the province where they live [Note: [Col. 0771D] Al., “where they dwell”; Al., “in which they dwell”], or what can be bought more cheaply.

Let the abbot provide clothing of such a measure that it is not too short for those who use it, but properly fitted. When receiving new clothing, they shall always immediately return the old, to be stored in the wardrobe for the poor. It is sufficient for a monk to have two tunics and two cucullae, for the nights and for washing these garments; anything beyond that is superfluous [Note: [Col. 0771D] Cassin. omits “is”] and must be cut off. They shall also return their socks and whatever is old when they receive something new.

Those who are sent on a journey shall receive trousers from the wardrobe; when they return, they shall return them washed there [Note: [Col. 0772D] Oxon., Flor., and certain manuscripts, “those who return”]. Their cucullae and tunics for traveling shall be somewhat better than those they ordinarily have; when they go out on a journey they shall receive them from the wardrobe, and when they return they shall give them back.

[Col. 0772C] Let the bedding of the beds be sufficient: a mat, blanket, woollen coverlet [Note: [Col. 0772D] Oxon., “linen”], and pillow. Nevertheless, the beds must frequently be inspected by the abbot, lest private property be found there. If anyone is found to have something which he did not receive from the abbot, let him be subject to the strictest discipline.

And, so that this vice of private property may be eradicated from the roots [Note: [Col. 0772D] Conc., Hild., Flor., Sabin., Dunst., Guido, Paris edition, “private”], let the abbot provide everything necessary: that is, a cuculla, tunic, socks, shoes, breeches, a knife [Note: [Col. 0772D] Al., “a knife”], a stylus, a needle, a napkin, and tablets, so that every excuse of necessity may be removed. Yet the abbot must always bear in mind the statement in the Acts of the Apostles: “Distribution was made to each according to his need” (Acts 2). Thus the abbot should consider the weaknesses of those in need, not the ill will [Note: [Col. 0772D] Oxon., “with ill will”] of those who are envious. In all his judgments, however, let him think of God’s recompense.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0771]

[Col. 0771D] Let clothing be given to the brothers according to the character of the places and the temperature of the air, etc.] What the holy Father Benedict says here—“according to the character of the places”—is understood in two ways, according to Hildemar:

“First, it may mean according to the character of the places, insofar as the abbot can find clothing in the place where they live. Secondly, it may mean according to the character of the place and the temperature of the air, which signifies one thing; as if he had said ‘according to the character of the places,’ and, explaining what the character of the places is, added ‘that is, the temperature of the air.’ This second interpretation, however, is the more accurate.”

Smaragdus and Peter the Deacon explain “the character of the places” according to whether the place is more or less laborious, or according to whether the monastery is situated in a harsher or more pleasant location, or according to whether they must work more or less because of poverty; for the more they work, and the harsher the place, the more they consume footwear and clothing. Bernard of Cassino, Richard of Saint Angelo, and Peter Boherius accept both explanations. Saint Benedict himself explains what he means by the temperature of the air when he adds that more is needed in cold regions and less in warm ones.

Nevertheless, for temperate places we believe that one cuculla and one tunic per monk are sufficient, etc.] What a cuculla, tunic, scapular, foot-cloths, and leggings are must be briefly investigated.

Among the ancients, cuculla was a kind of garment surrounding the head and shoulders. Cassian teaches this especially (book I, chapter 4), speaking of the cucullae of the Egyptians as follows:

“They continually use very small cucullae by day and night, extending down to the boundary of the neck and shoulders, so that they cover only the head; namely, so that they may be continually moved, even by the imitation of this covering, to preserve the innocence and simplicity of little children.”

The learned Floridus gives us the same understanding of cuculla in the book he composed in the French language On Christian Customs, where he writes as follows (p. 367):

“The cuculle was a hood worn by peasants and the poor. This head-covering became common to everyone in later centuries; and, being convenient against the cold, it remained in use in our Europe until about two hundred years ago. Not only clerics and men of letters, but even nobles and courtiers wore hoods and caps of various kinds.”

The monks, however, wore it not so much for convenience and usefulness as as a sign of innocence and simplicity. This is evident both from the Cassian passage cited above and from these words of Evagrius (vol. III of the Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments, p. 68):

“The cucullus is indeed a sign of the grace of God our Savior, which covers the principal part of them—the head—and fosters infancy in Christ.”

It is also evident from Sozomen, who speaks of the monks as follows (Ecclesiastical History, book III, chapter 13):

“They covered their heads with a covering which they usually call a cucullus, thereby showing that they led a life as simple and sincere as that of children nourished on milk, whose heads they wrap in such a tiara so that they may at once be covered and protected.”

Finally, it is evident from Saint Dorotheus, Teaching I. Nuns also wore such cucullae, as is clear from Palladius (Lausiac History, chapter 41). The Pachomians sewed the figure of a purple cross onto their cucullae, and clothed only in these they approached Communion of the Body of Christ on Saturdays and Sundays, as the same Palladius testifies (ibid., chapter 28). From this one may infer that those cucullae covered not only the head and shoulders but the entire body as well. For who would believe that they approached Communion almost entirely naked?

Theodemarus suggests another meaning of cuculla in his letter to Charlemagne:

“But since you have asked what garment should be understood by cuculla, we say that cuculla is what we call casula by another name. Hence the blessed Father established that it should be woolly in winter and plain or old in summer, since this kind of garment is ordinarily woven with shaggy pile.”

Saint Isidore agrees with this meaning (Etymologies, book XIX, chapter 24):

“Casula,” he says, “is a hooded garment, derived by diminution from casa, because it covers the whole person.”

And Smaragdus says:

“Cuculla is said by diminution from casula, casulla from casa, and cuculla from casulla.”

That the casula was certainly a garment of monks is clear from the Life of Saint Severinus, abbot of Agaunum, in Bollandus, February 11; from the Life of Saint Caesarius, bishop of Arles, book II; from the Acts of Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe; and from the Life of Saint Philibert, abbot of Jumièges, Benedictine Century II.

Saint Isidore explains what a casula is: a garment that covers the entire person. It is called casula, as though “a little house,” because it contains the whole body within itself, without sleeves. Perhaps the Pachomians approached Holy Communion in cucullae of this sort—a sufficiently inconvenient type of garment. If there is room for conjecture, Saint Benedict may have permitted the scapular in its place for work, since it is open on both sides, allowing the arms to be exercised more easily and giving workers freer use of them.

Casula is also sometimes used for a tunic reaching to the feet, and sometimes for another kind of garment, as our Mabillon teaches in the preface to Benedictine Century I, p. 55.

Smaragdus explains cuculla in yet another way:

“He”—Saint Benedict—“calls cuculla what we now call a cappa.”

Hildemar, whom we shall cite below, says the same. What a cappa is, however, I can scarcely determine. Theodemarus explains himself in the aforementioned letter to Charlemagne:

“That garment which the Gallican monks call coculla, and which we call cappa, which properly designates the habit of monks, we ought to call melotes, just as it is still called by some in the province. Concerning this, as blessed Gregory wrote in the book of the Dialogues, the boy Placidus, rescued from the water by the monk Maurus, said: ‘When I was being drawn out of the water, I saw the abbot’s melotes above me, and I observed him pulling me out of the waters.’”

From Isidore we learn what melotes is (Etymologies, book XIX, chapter 34):

“Melotes, which is also called a *pera* (‘bag’), is a goatskin hanging from the neck and girded down to the loins, etc.”

Alardus Gazaeus believes that penula should be read instead of pera in this passage, in his commentary on Cassian, book I, chapter 8. But whether Saint Benedict ever wore a garment of this kind I would rightly doubt.

Haeften believes that in Saint Benedict’s time the melotes was called cuculla by another name. This could be supported by the capitulary of Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, in which it is prescribed that, in the ordination of monks, the abbot should veil the monk’s head with a cuculla for seven days. For, when Hildemar mentions this rite in his commentary on chapter 58 of the Rule, he calls the garment a melote, whereas Theodore calls it a cuculla.

Yet, writing on this passage, Hildemar himself says that the melotes resembled the scapular, which some nevertheless also called cuculla. He distinguishes the cuculla—which he teaches to be the same as the cappa—from the melote:

“For the cuculla is one thing and the melota another, since Saint Benedict calls cuculla what we call cappa.”

The Bursfeld monks describe the cappa differently in their Ceremonial, in these words:
