“When traveling, they may, if they wish, use a round cappa instead of the floccus. It should be shorter than the floccus, so that on each side it has an opening through which the arms may be extended, and above it a hood sewn on, like the regular hood. Underneath the cappa they should wear a scapular, and on the outside a black felt cap, not shaggy but smooth.”

[Col. 0774D] More recent writers provide a clearer account of the cuculla. Saint Hildegard says that the cuculla is a garment “ample and descending to the ankles, with short sleeves extending slightly beyond the hands, and with two gores on each side flowing downward from beneath the armpit; a hood was attached above it, which is the distinctive sign of a monk, signifying that he should not look out this way or that toward the world when he has it over his head.”

The cuculla of the kind just described differs little from that once worn by the monks of Fulda. Our Mabillon displays its form from the Fulda panel, which depicts before the eyes the embassy sent to Emperor Louis to obtain a new abbot, in his preface to the fifth Benedictine century. In it, he says, one sees “a cuculla not especially ample, with fairly tight sleeves, a hood ending in a point and more open at the chest; otherwise it surrounded the whole body down to the ankles.” An ancient image confirms this description of the cuculla: “Desiderius, the hooded abbot—that is, in an ankle-length garment closed all around and not especially loose, with sleeves not large.” Angelus de Nuce says that this image was preserved in the Cassinese archive, in his notes on Theodemar’s letter to Charlemagne.

Bernard of Cassino also writes as follows on this passage:

> Peter the Deacon says that the cuculla is a cape, because of its diminutive relation to the *casula*; *cuculla* is its diminutive. Paul the Deacon, however, says that the cuculla is a woolen tunic. Here on Mount Cassino we call a garment with a hood, closed on every side and furnished with long sleeves, a cuculla; and the Cistercians follow Cassino in both the word and the form.

Nicolaus de Fractura agrees with Bernard; from their testimony it may be inferred that, from the time of Desiderius onward, the sleeves of the Cassinese cucullas were enlarged. As for the Cistercians, whom Bernard mentions here, see the work that Julian Varnerius composed in French on the ancient practice of the Benedictine Rule, chapter 29.

According to Boherius, however, “the cuculla is a long and ample garment, but without sleeves; the *flocus*, which is not mentioned in the Rule or in the ancient law, is a garment with long sleeves.” Boherius thus assigns some distinction between the cuculla and the frock, which some confuse with it. Bernard of Cassino, whom we shall cite below, also recognized this distinction when he wrote that the Cluniac and transalpine monks call the scapular a cuculla and wear over it a sleeved garment without a hood, which they commonly call a frock.

The writer of the *Apologia of the Emperor Henry IV* confirms and explains this difference. He writes:

> A cuculla is so called because it is a hooded garment, on account of the hood, which is a covering for the head . . . . . Therefore the cuculla is an ankle-length, hooded, sleeved tunic, having the appearance of a cross extended in four directions, so that this four-horse chariot may enclose on every side the person who has been crucified to the world.

And after much else:

> But because idleness is hostile to the soul, Saint Benedict therefore established another cuculla specifically for work. It is called the scapular because such a garment is suitable for covering only the head and shoulders.

Thus this author distinguishes two cucullas: one small, which, as he writes below, descended only to the loins and which Saint Benedict called the scapular; the Cluniacs and other transalpine monks simply called it a cuculla, and the Cluniacs still call it so. The other was larger, surrounding the whole body and having sleeves and a hood; they called it the *flocus* or frock, of the kind described above, with this difference: the frock of the Cluniacs lacked a hood, whereas the larger cuculla did not.

The holy legislator granted both garments, and both with a hood: one for work and the other for use outside work. Boherius therefore must be corrected when he writes that the frock is not contained in the Rule, since the frock, if a hood is sewn onto it, does not differ from the larger cuculla.

Saint Benedict wished this garment to be shaggy in winter and plain in summer. The Cluniacs, however, as Nicolaus de Fractura writes, wore it shaggy both in summer and winter. According to Bernard of Cassino, some understand “shaggy” to mean that it should be made of shaggy cloth—that is, that the sheep’s fleece should be used to provide warmth. Others say that a sheepskin with its fleece should be attached to the cuculla. “But whatever the cuculla may be,” he says, “it ought to be with fleece, so that it may repel the cold.”

Indeed, it could be demonstrated by countless examples that monks and nuns formerly used fur garments. Saint Austrudis, abbess of Laon, certainly used them in the seventh century, as is evident from her Life, no. 24, in the second Benedictine century. But enough about the cuculla; now let us turn to the tunic.

The tunic, which they also called by another name the *colobium*, was a linen garment with sleeves so very short that they did not extend beyond the elbows. Hence it was commonly called a sleeveless garment. Cassian writes about it when discussing the monk’s habit (*Book* I, chapter 5):

> Clad in linen colobia, which scarcely reach the lower part of the elbows, they leave their hands bare for the rest of their length.

It also seems possible to infer that sleeves were not formerly sewn onto monks’ tunics from Book I of the *Miracles of Saint Bertin*, chapter 2; and from the Life of Saint Austreberta, abbess, no. 10. The point is clear from the Life of Saint Guthlac, no. 26, in the third Benedictine century. Evagrius gives the following reason for this (*Tome IV of the Monuments of the Greek Church*): “That they have bare hands signifies a life without hypocrisy and pretence; for vainglory is able to cover and obscure the virtues, since it always seeks praise from men and drives out faith.”

Cassian testifies that they wore tunics of linen. But according to Hildemarus, “the tunic is to be understood as woolen; for a tunic may also be linen or silk, but in this passage he seems to mean that the tunic ought to be woolen.” The Master, in chapter 81 of the Rule, orders that tunics for those entering the kitchen should be made of sackcloth and cucullas of coarse fabric.

Our Fulda monks wore hoods sewn onto their tunics, as Haeftenus notes from Browerus (*Book* V, treatise 3, dissertation 7). The Cistercians did the same, as is clear from the *Book of Usages*, chapter 70. Julian Varnerius testifies that in 1612 he saw in the monastery of Clairvaux a tunic with a square hood sewn onto it, sleeves reaching to the length of the arm and so broad that they could contain two fists. They asserted that it had been made after the model of Saint Bernard’s tunic.

The statutes of Lanfranc likewise prescribe that a novice be dressed in a tunic with a sewn-on hood. Yet Saint Hildegard describes the tunic as woolen, “somewhat tighter than the cuculla, but somewhat wider around the legs and reaching to the feet, with sleeves neither very broad nor very tight, extending to the hands; and also with a gore on each side, descending from beneath the armpit, which lacked a hood above.”

Bernard of Cassino writes:

> We call a tunic the garment that we wear beneath the cuculla, covering our body on both sides but lacking a hood, with sleeves of moderate and measured length.

Boherius says similarly:

> A tunic is the garment that we wear beneath the habit, covering the body on both sides but lacking a hood, with sleeves of moderate length and proportion. Among us it is called a *cotardia*. It ought also to be round all around and not slit, and it should not be marked by excessive length or shortness. It has broad sleeves extending to the fist, not sewn together.

The scapular, also called the *analabus*, is a monastic garment that the ancients represent to us in the form of a cross, as may be seen in Evagrius, *Tome III of the Monuments of the Greek Church*, p. 69. Menardus proves this in his notes on the *Concordance of the Rule*, chapter 62, § 1: it hung down in front and behind and was broader at the shoulders. He therefore understands as referring to the scapular the passage from the Life of Saint William, duke and monk of Gellone, in the fourth Benedictine century:

> He is clothed in an apostolic garment in the likeness of a cross.

Our Mabillon also approves this interpretation.

Hildemarus writes of this garment:

> The scapular is that which the Greeks call *schema*, with which they cover their heads and bind it around themselves; the garment that we call the *melota* seems to resemble it.

Bernard of Cassino writes:

> I think that the scapular is named from the shoulders, because it covers the shoulders. To this day both the Cassinese and the Cistercians call a hooded habit hanging from the shoulders on both sides a scapular. But the Cassinese habitually close this same scapular beneath the arms around the middle of the body, as though at the place of a belt, sewing it together to a measure of about half a palm. When they work, they gird the scapular above so that it will not impede their work. Without this scapular, or without the sleeved cuculla, they may not put on the sacred garments for performing the divine offices. Moreover, this scapular is blessed by the abbot when a monk makes his profession. The Cluniac and transalpine monks, however, call that scapular a cuculla and wear over it a sleeved garment without a hood, which they commonly call a frock. I think that the Cistercians went back to the source—to the Cassinese [Editorial note: Read “Cassinese,” or “of the Cassinese.”]—and derived from them both the name and the form of each garment, the scapular and the cuculla.

Nicolaus de Fractura says something similar. For the Cistercians, see Julian Varnerius at the place cited above.

The Bursfeld monks describe their scapular as follows (*Distinctio* 3, chapter 21):

> For manual work, and, by apostolic indult, even in the divine ministry under the sacred vestments, we also use a scapular. Its hood, sewn onto it, shall extend one palm behind and on each side, and shall be less broad when spread out than the cuculla. The part of the scapular hanging down in front and behind shall be about half an ell in width; its length shall extend to the ankles.

The Cassinese, however, prescribe (*Cassinese Declaration*, chapter 55) that “the monks’ scapulars should be long over the tunic by half a quarter, and as wide as the width of the *rascia*.” The scapulars of novices should be narrow and short, extending to the knees.

[Col. 0777B] Saint Benedict, the holy Father, granted the scapular for work in place of the cuculla, which they then removed. Hence it was given the name cuculla, either because it took the place of the cuculla or because of its hood. Accordingly, the following passage from the Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane, in the fourth Benedictine century, may rightly be understood of the scapular:

> The custom had made them different in their clothing; for on some the cucullas hung down to the ankles. Therefore the man of God established one uniform measure to be observed by all monks, so that it should not exceed two cubits in length or be able to reach to the knees.

Smaragdus confirms this interpretation, writing on the passage:

> What he calls the scapular on account of work, we now call the cuculla.

Later, however, the practice became established that the scapular should be worn not only for work but at all times, while the cuculla was worn more rarely and only for the divine offices and similar exercises.

Saint Benedict makes no mention here of a belt, although above, in chapter 22, he prescribed its use, decreeing that monks should sleep clothed and girded with belts or cords. It is clear from Bede’s Life of Saint Cuthbert, chapter 23, that Saint Cuthbert used a linen belt. But Saint Fulgentius, bishop of Ruspe, “used a leather belt like a monk,” as we read in his Life. On the use and significance of the belt, see Haeftenus, Book V, treatise 4, dissertation 1, and treatise 10, dissertation 7.

Nor does Saint Benedict say anything about shirts or undershirts. Saint Robert, abbot of Molesme, is said to have rejected them, as we read in Orderic Vitalis, *History*, Book V, and consequently the Cistercians did so as well. Their Institutes, chapter 4, decree: “Their clothing shall be simple and poor, without furs, shirts, or woolen undergarments—in short, such as the Rule describes.”

Haeftenus argues that, in place of these garments, Saint Benedict and his first disciples wore a hair shirt next to the flesh (*Book* V, treatise 3, dissertation 7). An example may be found in Saint Tillo, a monk of Solignac, in the second Benedictine century. His acts state that “his clothing was exceedingly poor, namely only a tunic and cuculla, and next to his flesh a hair shirt, which he wore until, through excessive age, it was worn out and fit for no use.”

Guigo also grants two hair shirts to the Carthusians in his Statutes, chapter 28. Arnulf, a monk of the monastery of Saint Emmeram at Regensburg, writes of its first monks (*Book* II of the *Dialogues*) that “the elders who were able to have them used linen shirts; the rest used woolen ones, because of the scarcity of hair garments.”

Later, however, woolen shirts or woolen undergarments took the place of the hair shirt, as is clear from the Life of Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, in the fourth Benedictine century. His disciple Ardo testifies that “for the sake of necessity, on account of which the Rule gives command, he allowed two woolen undergarments, and so forth.” Saint Fructuosus had previously allowed the same number to his monks in chapter 4 of his Rule, as did the Council of Aachen in canon 22 and the *Rule of Solitaries*, chapter 49.

Ansegisus, abbot of Fontenelle, also assigned to his Fontenelle monks “twenty white pieces of cloth, from which twenty shirts could be made,” in his constitution concerning the food and clothing of monks.

Finally, Saint Odilo, abbot of Cluny, “one day found two boys on the road, dead from hunger. Immediately dismounting from his horse, he drew from his body the woolen undershirt that he was wearing next to his flesh, and, wrapping each corpse in it as far as the quantity of cloth allowed, gave burial to the dead,” as Peter Damian writes in his Life.

For our monks, however, the use of linen shirts was never permitted, except perhaps for the sick. Pope Zacharias writes in his letter to Pepin and to all the bishops and abbots of France (*Baronius, year 744*):

> Monks should continually use woolen clothing, according to the norm and rule of monastic discipline and the tradition of the holy and approved Fathers, because monks must abstain from all unlawful things. The apostles, however, were given the divine command not to have two tunics. By “tunics,” therefore, he meant woolen ones, not linen.

Earlier, Saint Ferreolus had prescribed in his Rule, chapter 31, “that a monk, however delicate his body may be, should not use linen next to his naked body.” Saint Isidore likewise says: “A monk ought not to be clothed in linen.”

In a letter from G., abbot of Mouzon, and A., abbot of Marchiennes, to the abbots of Saint-Thierry (*Manuscript History of Saint-Thierry*, under the year 1279), in which they appoint them visitors of their province, I read:

> You must strictly prohibit in those same chapters that abbots or monks use linen outside the monastery when they ride, since this causes scandal among secular people and brings ridicule upon our entire order; nor may they use it inside the monastery, unless evident illness and bodily weakness require it.

In their constitutions for Benedictine monks, Innocent III, Gregory IX, Nicholas IV in his bull to the Cluniacs, and Benedict XII decree the same. The Cluniacs nevertheless permitted linen shirts for boys, according to Udalricus, Book III, chapter 8. Aelred, however, allowed his virgins two shirts of tow (*stupacium*) or woolen shirts, in chapter 20 of his Rule.

For covering the feet, Saint Benedict permitted foot-cloths and leggings. What precisely foot-cloths and leggings are, however, I cannot easily explain. Smaragdus says:

> He calls foot-cloths what we now call shoes; leggings he calls what we call socks or ankle-coverings. Leggings are so called from the callus of the feet, or because they are tied, for they are also called footwear.

Hildemarus says:

> Foot-cloths are garments made in the form of a tube, but they cover the feet. Since they are put onto the feet, they are called foot-cloths. There are many monks who, because of sweating feet, divide what they put on their feet so that it will not be burdensome for them to wash. Leggings, as Isidore says, are so called from the callus of the feet or because they are tied; for socks are not tied but inserted.

Bernard of Cassino writes:

> Although commentators explain these two foot-garments in different ways, whatever is put onto the feet, whether made of leather or wool, may properly be called a foot-cloth. Foot-cloths are so called from the foot, whereas leggings are named from the footwear of the legs: from *calceo*, *calceas*, *calciare*, hence *caliga*, *caligae*. Or a *caliga* may be said to derive from *colligo*, *colligas*, as though tied around the neck, because leggings are tied . . . . But note that the transalpine monks have woolen foot-cloths distinct from the garment made in the form of a boot, and they cover the shin for ease of washing and sometimes to avoid sweating of the feet. At night they remove these foot-cloths and, with their feet now bare, keep the boot-shaped garments in bed while they rest, lest the foot-cloth retain within it the fumes emitted through the pores and thereby harm the head as they rise to the brain.

Nicolaus de Fractura understands “foot-cloths” as leather garments and “leggings” as woolen ones.

Richard of Saint Angelo, on the contrary, says that leggings are “boots, or footwear, or another kind of garment. They are so called,” he says, “from the callus of the feet or as though from binding together, because they are tightly fastened.”

Boherius, in his first commentary, after reporting the opinions of Bernard and Smaragdus, adds:

> I agree with Cato that *pedules* is derived from *pes*, “foot,” and is the part of the leggings that encloses the foot, although perhaps the Master understood the word more broadly here, as stated above. You should know that we use leather socks more conveniently; these are not tied, but the leggings are. They are merely slipped on; this is what both the Germans and we call *botas*.

An ancient French manuscript version renders the two words *pedules* and *caligas* as *chaussons et hautx soullez* (“slippers and high-soled footwear”); the version of John of Précis, *soulers chauçons* (“shoes and stockings”); that of Theobald Artaldus, *les chauces et les chauçons de drap, et les souliers de cuir* (“hose, cloth slippers, and leather shoes”); that of Guido, *des souliers, ou des chaussons, et des chausses* (“shoes, or slippers, and hose”); and the more recent version, *des bas et des souillers* (“stockings and shoes”).

Our Menardus says that the foot-cloths were bandages. Indeed, it is clear that the ancients used bandages from Aimoinus, *Book II of the Miracles of Saint Benedict*, no. 2: “After loosening the bandages from his shins, he tied himself to the two planks of the bridge.”

He understands the leggings as footwear made of skins, rising to the middle of the calf and fastened with many strings or straps. Haeftenus interprets foot-cloths as woolen socks, in French *des chaussons*. He interprets leggings as sandals or simple soles without an upper leather covering, but tied with many straps, almost like the sandals now worn by the Capuchin Fathers.

Yet Saint Radegund, in the first Benedictine century, made two sleeves for herself from her leggings, as is written in Book II of her Life, no. 8. This hardly agrees with leather sandals. Amid such great variety, it is difficult to determine anything with certainty.

As far as I know, I have found nothing about foot-cloths among the earlier monks. They did, however, use leggings to repel the cold in winter and, in summer, whenever the heat of the midday sun required them. Someone might suppose that Saint Benedict permitted leggings in summer and added foot-cloths to them in winter, whatever those foot-garments may ultimately have been.

Saint Isidore, who allows both foot-cloths and leggings, says:

> They shall use foot-cloths in the monastery for as long as the violence of winter requires, or while the brothers are walking on a journey or setting out for the city.

Saint Fructuosus likewise says:

> The following practice should also be observed with footwear: in winter, those who wish may put on foot-cloths, from the first day of November until the first day of May. During the remaining summer months they are to be protected only by the comfort of leggings.

The Master, however, has the following provisions about footwear in his Rule, chapter 81:

> The brothers ought to have iron-studded triple-soled leggings, not for play but for use; they should use them in winter and store them greased during the summer. All should have studded leggings, both in the monastery and on the road, so that the leggings kept in storage may be preserved for a long time and the brother’s foot may be cooled within the legging. For the night office they should use wooden clogs, so that, returning to their beds with soiled feet, they may not soil the bed coverings. In winter, for the night office, they should use fur foot-cloths because of the coldness of the feet.

What is said here about studded leggings may be confirmed by Pope Gregory’s account of Abbot Equitius (*Dialogues*, Book I, chapter 4): “He was shod with studded leggings.”

Saint Eugendus, abbot of Condat, had “strong and rustic footwear in the manner of the ancient Fathers; his legs were confined in boots and the soles of his feet with bandages,” according to his Life, no. 6, in the first Benedictine century. But did he understand by “boots” leggings and by “bandages” foot-cloths?

His predecessor, Saint Lupicinus, used footwear only when he entered the court on some errand, perhaps to intercede for someone. In the monastery, even when he went out for an extended time to work the land, he continually used only wooden soles, commonly called socks in the monasteries of Gaul.

There were also both ancient and more recent monks who walked barefoot. This may be gathered from the Life of Saint Anthony, chapter 23. Saint Fructuosus, according to Valerius in his Life, no. 3, in the second Benedictine century, “entered wooded places barefoot.” Later, in no. 11, he is described as being “in a poor habit, barefoot and with naked feet.” Peter Damian says the same of the monks of Sitri in the Life of Saint Romuald, chapter 64. Finally, it is known from the Life of Saint Robert, no. 8, that the first Molesme brothers sometimes entered the city of Troyes barefoot.

Thus far we have discussed the garments granted by Saint Benedict. Perhaps someone may wish to learn what garments the other Fathers of monks granted and wore. It is useful to clarify the matter from their ancient rules and practices.

Beginning with Saint Pachomius, who was the first Father of the coenobites, his Rule, as printed in the *Codex of Rules*, says as follows (Article 81):

> Apart from those things that will be distributed by the superiors of the houses at the direction of the monastery’s Father—that is, his equipment, two *levitonaria* and a third worn out from use, a longer *sabanum* which wraps around the neck and shoulders, a little skin hanging at the side, *gallicae*, two cucullas, a belt, and a staff—you shall take away without objection whatever else you find.

The teaching of Abbot Orsiesius and his disciple has almost the same provisions (no. 22):

> It is enough for us to have what is sufficient for a man: two *levitonaria*, another worn one, a little linen cloak, two cucullas, a linen belt, *gallicae*, a skin, and a staff.

We learn what the clothing of the Basilian monks was like from the Life of Saint Philaret, written in the eleventh century by his contemporary, the monk Nilus, no. 21. Describing Philaret’s reception into the monastic habit, it lists these garments: a *sticharion*, that is, a tunic; a cloak, which is over the neck and shoulders; a *cucullium*, which we place on the head; a cross to be worn on the forehead; and a belt with its buckle.

Among the clothing of the Egyptian monks, Evagrius of Scetis, in his letter to Anatolius (*Tome III of the Monuments of the Greek Church*), names the cuculla, the *analabum*, the *melota*, the belt, and the staff. Cassian adds others in the book he composed on the monk’s habit, where he explains their garments and their symbols: the cuculla, the *colobium*, arm-coverings, *mafortes*, the *melota* and goatskin, the belt, and leggings.

Abbot Patermuthius advanced a young man who approached him for the sake of conversion, “clothed in a *lebiton*, with a cuculla placed around his head, a *melota* over his shoulders, and girded with linen, according to the monastic institution and discipline,” as may be seen in the *History of Egyptian Monasticism* (*Tome III of the Monuments of the Greek Church*).

In the Rule of Saint Isidore I read (chapter 13):

> The servants of Christ shall be content with three tunics, two cloaks, and one cuculla each. To these shall be added a fur *melota*, a little cloth, sleeves, foot-cloths, and leggings.

In the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 4):

> Their clothing should not be plentiful or excessive: only two cucullas, one shaggy and one plain, one little cloak, three tunics, and two woolen undergarments should suffice for every necessary complaint. The following practice should also be observed with footwear: in winter, those who wish may put on foot-cloths, from the first day of November until the first day of May. During the remaining summer months they are to be protected only by the comfort of leggings. The use of breeches is to be permitted to no one, especially to those occupied in the ministry of the altar.

Finally, in the Rule of the Master (chapter 81):

> In winter the brothers ought to have a thick daily outfit of wool, and another nighttime tunic, which after the night office they *puduclent* [sic; meaning uncertain], since during the day they are occupied with various labors. In winter they should also have a woolen cloak, woolen breeches, and bandages or foot-cloths. In summer they should have a linen outfit, not too thick because of work and sweat; and they should have light, fine linen cloaks, not too thick because of the heat and sweat, and linen breeches. We forbid the men of God to use linen bandages, so that the monk may differ in some respect from the cleric. They should also have individual, finer linen outfits, which they shall use only on feast days in processions. In summer they should have one linen towel each because of perspiration, and one towel each per week [lacuna] The tunics of those entering the kitchen for their weekly service should be of sackcloth, and their cucullas of coarse fabric.

From what has been said thus far, the opinion of those who confidently assert that the ancient monks were not distinguished in dress from secular men, except that they wore simple and rustic garments, has been sufficiently refuted.

Certainly, it is written in the ancient Life of Saint Pachomius, no. 4, that Saint Palaemon, after admitting the young Pachomius into his cell following many prayers, clothed him in the habit of the monks. Among the instructions delivered to him by an angel, the Rule given to him contained this statement:

> If a stranger from another monastery should come, wearing a different habit, no one shall eat with him, except one who is traveling and cannot observe this rule.

Among the precepts of Saint Pachomius that the continuator of Bollandus published after his Life, the sixteenth prescribes that anyone wishing to become a monk should be stripped of secular clothing and dressed in the habit of novices.

Saint Benedict himself, when fleeing the world, sought the habit of holy conduct, as Saint Gregory writes in Book II of the *Dialogues*. And, as Saint Basil argues most convincingly (*Long Rules*, chapter 22):

> According to each person’s profession, a suitable garment ought to belong to him. Just as the habit of a soldier differs from that of a senator, from which it is understood that this man is a senator and that one a soldier, so a monk ought to have his own clothing, by which, even at a glance, he may be recognized as a monk.

As for the color or thickness of all these things, monks should not complain.] Hildemarus explains this as follows:

> Monks should not complain if the foot-cloths are white and the tunics dark—that is, if the foot-cloths are of one color, the tunics of another, and the cucullas of another, or if the garments are thick.

Bernard of Cassino, however, says:

> If it is not splendid or beautiful, or if it is not very poor, humble, and contemptible, they should not complain.

Authors disagree among themselves about the color of the Benedictine habit. Commentators generally defend black: Bernard of Cassino, Nicolaus de Fractura, Richard of Saint Angelo, Peter Boherius, and others. Their principal arguments are these.

First, they assert that Saint Benedict used black clothing. “It is handed down in the writings of certain ancient Cassinese doctors,” Bernard says, “that blessed Benedict used black and poor garments.” Nicolaus writes:

> In the ancient Chronicle of Peter the Deacon, we and our forefathers find it written how, in the monastery of Fleury, the hood of the cuculla of blessed Benedict was discovered, woven from black fleece.

And further:

> We read in the Life of Charlemagne, by a monk of the Cassinese monastery, that when Charlemagne had built a monastery in honor of blessed Martin in the territory of Vitry, at a place called Macyatus, and had subjected it to the Cassinese monastery, he placed there the hood of Our Holy Father Benedict, woven from black fleece and three inches long.

Richard of Saint Angelo writes the same. Peter Boherius says:

> Nevertheless, some ancient holy Cassinese doctors hand down that blessed Benedict used black garments. Some of them say that on Mount Cassino the monastic *schema* used by blessed Benedict has continued to the present day.

Finally, when Peter the Deacon was asked by a Cistercian monk in the presence of Emperor Lothair why they always wore black garments, he replied:

> Because Father Benedict used such garments, so that he might appear to have renounced the world by his habit as well.

But let these authors bear responsibility for the truth of their claim.

The second reason is that they assert that not only Saint Benedict but also all his first disciples wore black garments. Antonius Yepezius says that this continued at least until the year 1000 in his *Chronicle* under the year 525. Hence they were given the name “Black Monks,” by which they are known to have been called for nearly a thousand years, as is evident from a charter issued by King Ethelbald in the year 716. It reads as follows, according to Ingulf in his *History of Crowland*:

> I give and grant to almighty God, blessed Mary, and Saint Bartholomew, from my dominions, for the foundation of the Black Monks serving under the rule of Saint Benedict, the whole island of Crowland.

Later, in the year 755, King Offa of Mercia is said by Ingulf to have founded “a monastery of Black Monks in the city of Verulam, in honor of God and Saint Alban, the protomartyr of the English.”

Thomas, a monk of Ely, confirms this in the Life of Saint Ethildritha, queen, in the second Benedictine century. Concerning her, he says in no. 24:

> In place of the royal diadem she is humbly shaded by a veil; in place of fine linen and purple she is surrounded by a black and rough garment.

An anonymous writer of Trier, in his Book on the Relics of Saint Matthias, no. 11, records:

> Meanwhile certain wicked men, having formed a plan, wanted to carry Matthias away from there, asserting that monks who were black in their clothing and likewise black in their morals were unworthy of Matthias.

Hence arose such obstinacy among our monks in retaining the black habit that, when Pope Celestine V wished to unite the Cassinese monastery to his congregation and induce its monks to change their habit, many preferred to withdraw from Cassino rather than abandon the black garment. This is taught in their commentaries by Nicolaus de Fractura here and by Richard in chapter 21, cited by Augustine of Genoa.

The third reason is drawn from the example of the monks who lived before Saint Benedict and whom they say wore black garments. Peter the Venerable develops this argument at length and elegantly in a letter to Saint Bernard (*Book* I, letter 28, and Book IV, letter 17). Among others, he cites Saint Martin, whom Sulpicius describes as wrapped in a black and hanging cloak; Saint Jerome, writing to Nepotianus, “Avoid dark garments just as you avoid white ones”; and Saint Paulinus, who writes in his letter to Sulpicius Severus about a certain noblewoman recently converted to the religious life:

> We saw a thing worthy of God: the confusion of this world, with purple silk and gilded furnishings serving in old and black rags.

He could also have added the statement in chapter 3 of the third Rule of the Holy Fathers:

> The abbot ought to arrange the clothing necessary for the brothers in such a way that it suits monks and is not dyed in different colors, except for the cucullas. If they are black, we judge that they ought to be used.

Likewise, the Rule of Saint Aurelian for monks says in chapter 26:

> You shall not wear clothing of any other color except gray, white, and black.

Finally, the Rule of Saint Ferreolus says in chapter 32:

> A monk should take care not to have fragrant garments or excessive brilliance, on account of pride; but, following the Apostle more closely, let him say: “We are the good fragrance of Jesus Christ.” Let him also avoid white or excessively red color in these garments, by which the appearance of the body is often commended to those who see it, to the body’s own destruction; and let him not desire to possess such garments.

See Saint Augustine’s letter 269, no. 9, in the new edition.

Boherius suggests the fourth reason in these words:

> We hold that, when the Lord was crucified and dead, certain apostles made black coverings for themselves. To this day widows and dear friends make such coverings after the death of their husbands and loved ones, and they are called mourning garments. In these regions of Italy, they are said to have preserved this color in their habit in memory of Christ’s death. The Greek monks also use the color black.

There is no doubt that he derived this from Nicolaus de Fractura.

Peter the Venerable explains the fifth reason as follows (*Book* IV, letter 17):

> To confess what I think: it seemed to me, and appears so to me, that the black color in question was more fitting for those great Fathers—more fitting for humility, more fitting for penitence, and more fitting for mourning. Since a monk must devote his entire life to these pursuits, they decreed that the color should be joined to their morals and the garments to their virtues by whatever affinity they could have, and so forth.

Richard of Saint Angelo writes:

> The color black suits a monk more than any other color. For it signifies sadness, just as ordinarily, when a father dies in this world, all his relatives put on black garments to signify their grief.

Nicolaus de Fractura develops the same point at length. Finally, Saint John Climacus writes (*Ladder*, step 7):

> Let the very appearance of your body and your religious garment stir you to mourning; for all who mourn the dead walk about in dark clothing.

At length Richard of Saint Angelo says: “I believe that black was chosen for this reason: because it is uglier and baser than the other colors, as is evident from the nature of the thing, or so that we might always remember the ugliness of the devil, who is said to be of this color, although at times he transforms himself into an angel of light.”

Nevertheless, despite these arguments, our Mabillon stands for the white color in his preface to the fifth Benedictine century, where he argues as follows (p. 40):

“There are three garments proper to our institute: the tunic, the cowl, and the scapular. The tunic falls to the ankles; eight hundred years ago it was generally white, as we have observed in various images of Rabanus and others, and also in the Anian Ritual. Reason itself certainly demanded this, since the tunic, which clung to the skin—for woolen undershirts were permitted only later, contrary to the authority of the Rule—had to be washed frequently for cleanliness, and therefore it was more fitting for it to be made of white rather than black wool. The scapular is so called because it chiefly covers the shoulders and head; it was granted by the most holy legislator for work performed with the body. The cowl is the outermost garment, together with its head covering; it wraps the body and arms on every side. Both were always black in color, whence monks were called Black Monks; but the Cistercians were called White, because they wore a cowl of white rather than black color.”

[Note: I do not see to what the word “black” could refer; it appears redundant. EDIT.]

That the cowl, too, was white is proved by what Wlfinus Boetius writes about Saint Junianus, who lived at the same time as Saint Maurus, in his *Life*, no. 7 (*Benedictine Annals*, vol. 1): “His garment was a haircloth made of goats’ hair, which, in the form of the caracalla that we now call a cape, remains among us to this day. It has remained so intact that it gives off no scent of antiquity, being suffused with a white color.”

Odo, abbot of Glanfeuil, also wrote in the year 869, in his *History of the Translation of Saint Maurus*, no. 9 (fourth Benedictine century, part 2), that Saint Maurus appeared to James, abbot of the monastery of Cormery, wearing the brightest white monastic habit. Ansegisus, in his *Life* of Saint Maurus (*Benedictine Annals*, vol. 4, part 1), in the provision concerning the food and clothing of the monks of Fontenelle, assigns “fifteen gray, coarse sacks, from which capes are to be made.” Now, as has been established from the foregoing, the word *capes* means cowls; and everyone knows that gray is closer to white than to black. Thus there were also white cowls, at least in some monasteries—for who would assert this of all of them?

Otherwise, Mabillon’s opinion is confirmed by what he writes elsewhere: that he saw in the Vatican Library a manuscript (*Italian Journey*, p. 122) “which contains the Dialogues of Gregory and Victor III concerning Saint Benedict, and everything pertaining to the Holy Father, with various figures of monks and abbots, in which the cowl is black and the tunic white.” In the Barberini Library, too, he saw an autograph manuscript of the *Chronicle of Saint Vincent of Vulturno* (ibid., p. 133), in which various figures are depicted, among them “a monk with a white tunic and a nearly black scapular fastened on each side with three cords.” There is also in the Cassinese Library, manuscript no. 370, before the beginning of the litany of Saint Gregory for the plague, an image of a deceased monk whose tunic is white, while his small cowl or scapular is of a darkish violet color.

Certainly, countless testimonies could demonstrate that the garments of the ancient monks were generally white. Bollandus proves that Saint Antony’s habit was of this kind in the preliminary commentary on his *Life*, §15 (*Bollandists*, 17 January); this is also evident from chapter 23 of his *Life*, where he is said to have provoked his judge’s attention by appearing girded in a shining garment.

Likewise, in the Rule given by an angel to Saint Pachomius, as it is found in his *Life* and in Palladius’ *Lausiac History*, chapter 38, it is prescribed “that each should have a *melote*, that is, a goatskin, made white, without which they should neither eat nor sleep.” The five hundred disciples of Saint Apollonius were clothed entirely in white, according to Palladius in the same *Lausiac History*, chapter 52. Hence Saint John Chrysostom, speaking of monks in homily 70 on Matthew, says: “Why do we not walk toward those angels? Why do we not put on white garments, and so forth?”

Saint Patrick in Ireland, too, was wrapped in a white cowl, as Jocelin relates in his *Life*, chapter 185. Bishop MacCaille, as Cogitosus records in the *Life of Saint Brigid the Virgin*, no. 5 (*Bollandists*, 1 February), “placed a white mantle and a white garment upon her venerable head.” Finally, in the *Life of Saint Columba, Abbot of Iona*, written by Cummene the White, no. 26 (first Benedictine century), I read: “They lifted into the air the white tunic of the blessed man, in which he had been clothed at the hour of his death.”

Now, if we consult the ancient rules, apart from the Pachomian Rule just cited, the Rule of Saint Caesarius for virgins states as follows (chapter 40): “Let all their garments have only a simple and respectable color, never black, nor shining, but only gray or cream-colored, made within the monastery through the diligence of the superior or the care of the wool-worker.”

The Rule of Saint Aurelian, likewise for virgins (chapter 22), says: “Do not wear garments of any other color except gray and cream-colored.”

The Rule of Saint Donatus (chapter 63) says: “I especially admonish you never to use shining garments, or garments with purple or beaver fur, except only gray and cream-colored ones.”

Finally, the Tarnatensis Rule (chapter 19) states: “The garments are to be procured in such a simple and natural color that variation in clothing may not nourish the vice of arrogance.” Now the natural color of sheep is ordinarily white.

From all this it is clear how unjustly the Cistercians were once reproached for preferring white clothing to black, since they ought rather to have been praised for returning in the color of their garments, as in many other matters, to the primitive source.

The Camaldolese, Carthusians, Celestines, and Olivetans wear white along with the Cistercians, although the Celestines use a black scapular and cowl. The hermits of Fonte Avellana, too, wore white garments with a blue mantle. We read in the *Monasticum Anglicanum*, p. 704, and in Mabillon’s *Italian Journey*, p. 197, that the monks of Tiron wore a gray habit. Hence Gaufredus writes of them in the *Life of Bernard, Abbot of Tiron*, no. 71 (*Bollandists*, April):

“They had the habit of monks, but it was mean, unadorned, shaggy, and very unlike the habit of the other monks, closely resembling the sheep themselves from which it had been taken.”

In the statutes of Gauderic, abbot of Rougemont, dating from about the year 1280, it is also decreed that each year a cowl and a frock of russet cloth be given to each monk. Finally, Antonius Yepezius writes that the principal habit of his congregation was chestnut-colored or deer-colored.

To avoid every diversity in habit, Clement V decreed at the Council of Vienne “that their outer garment, corresponding to their habit, should be black, brown, or white.”

But why discuss the color of garments at greater length, since Saint Benedict forbade monks to quarrel about it? Peter the Venerable says (Book IV, letter 17):

“Do not, I beg you, brother, if you wish to be a sheep of Christ, quarrel over the varied color of the fleece, because that Shepherd casts none from his fold except the one whom not variety of color but injury to faith or charity separates from the flock of his sheep. I repeat: he separates no one from his fold because of color—he who gathered into one sheepfold of Christian faith both Jew and Gentile from such distant and diverse regions.”

And the other Peter, namely Peter of Blois (Letter 97), says:

“Whether in white clothing or in dark clothing, in every profession and order, among every people, whoever does the will of the Lord is acceptable to him. He does not distinguish between white and black habit, with whom there is no distinction between Jew and Greek. The Lord considers the mind, not the garment; merits, not color. On Monte Cassino, the monastic habit used by blessed Benedict is said to remain to this day. Who would dare to blaspheme the habit of so great a father in his sons? For if the first portion is holy, so is the whole mass; if the root is holy, so are the branches. Whether someone is whiter than snow with the Nazarites, or whether his skin has been blackened upon the coal with blessed Job, each works out salvation in the house of the Lord.

“Indeed, in Jacob’s sheepfold there are white and black lambs; in the vineyard of Sorek there are white and black grapes. The bride, too, who gleams whiter than the lilies of the valleys, says of herself: ‘I am black, but beautiful.’ Among the bride of Christ such variety is not absurd, since she herself is described as surrounded with varieties. That variety itself is the cause of uniformity, for on a lyre uniform harmony is produced by the diversity of its strings.”

Nor does the holy legislator forbid monks to quarrel only about color; he also forbids them to quarrel about thickness, wishing them to be content solely with garments that can be found in the province where they live, or that can be purchased more cheaply. Nothing is more unworthy of a monk than a costly and shining garment.

“Let the monk’s garment,” says Cassian (Book V, chapter 3), “cover the body only, ward off the shame of nakedness, and blunt the assault of cold—not nourish the seeds of vanity and self-exaltation, and so forth.”

Saint Odo, abbot of Cluny (Book III of the *Collations*, no. 17), says:

“Is it not apostasy to despise humble clothing and seek the beauty of garments, since the apostate angel, exalting himself in perfect beauty, fell into Tartarus?”

And elsewhere:

“As blessed Jerome declares in his letter to the daughter of Mauricius (Book II, no. 7), preference for worldly and secular adornment is a great insult to divine grace; and after the sanctification of chrism it is a crime to adorn with any earthly beauty the head or body of one who already shines with heavenly splendor.”

Below, he introduces Saint Cyprian speaking in his book *On Virgins*:

“Those dressed in silk and purple cannot put on Christ; those adorned with gold, pearls, and necklaces have lost the ornaments of the heart.”

See also the monastic Constitutions of Saint Basil, chapter 31; Saint Dorotheus, *Doctrines*, chapter 19, and *Rule for Solitaries*, chapter 49; and Saint Bernard, homily 4, *On the Annunciation*.

Here Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, and Nicholas of Fractura astutely observe that Saint Benedict did not prescribe simply cheap garments, nor garments that were altogether the cheapest. For if he had prescribed cheap garments, he might seem to incline toward costly ones; if he had prescribed the very cheapest, toward filth and an excessively affected abasement or uncleanness. Saint Jerome, letters 2 and 22; Saint Isidore, chapter 13 of his Rule; and the Council of Aachen, canon 20, all teach that monks must avoid both with equal care.

Thus Saint Cuthbert, as Bede testifies in his *Life*, chapter 16 (*Benedictine Annals*, vol. 2), “used ordinary garments, conducting himself with such moderation that he was conspicuous neither for their cleanliness nor for their filth. Hence,” he says, “to this day his example is observed in the same monastery: no one is to have clothing of varied or costly color, but they are to be content especially with the kind of garment that the natural wool of sheep provides.”

They also tell of Saint Maglorius (*Life*, *Benedictine Annals*, vol. 1) that “his body was continually covered with a haircloth; his outer garments were neither excessively various and cheap nor costly, but of moderate quality, lest he should be flattered by the soothing encouragement of human praise, which is a snare of eternal damnation.” And of Saint Bernard (*Life*, Book III, chapter 2): “He always favored poverty in clothing, never filth; for he used to say that these were surely signs of the soul, either of one who is negligent or of one who outwardly seeks human glory.” See also the *Life of Wala, Abbot of Corbie*, Book I, chapter 22 (*Benedictine Annals*, vol. 4).

“But let the abbot provide for the proper measure, so that the garments themselves are not short for those who use them, but are made to measure.”

That is, they should be neither too long nor too short: the former suggests vanity, the latter insufficient modesty. For Bernard of Cassino, a garment is too short “if, when extended, it does not reach the ankle”; it is too long “if it trails along the ground and stirs up dust or gathers mud.”

The Roman customs of Saint Paul and those of the monastery of Farfa, written down approximately seven hundred years ago, say the following concerning the measurement of garments:

“Saint Benedict entrusts the clothing of the brothers to the prudence of the abbot, so that it may be made to measure. What that measure is, according to the definition of the Fathers, we shall investigate as far as we can.

“The cowl, which belongs especially to our order and which in ancient times was called a *colobium*, that is, a tunic without sleeves, should have only so much width that it may suitably fit both elbows. Its length in front should reach as far as the ankle, and it should fit the body so that it is round on every side.

“Its hood, apart from the complete hem, should contain on every side the square measure of one man’s foot. The upper opening should extend one cubit to the top of the thumb; the lower opening should be a full cubit, and the width of the cowl at the head-opening should appear in front as three fingers.

“Likewise, the tunic below, around the feet, should be round and proportionately measured. It should have gores or gussets only so large that, when walking, they do not impede the traveler either through excess or through scantness. Its sleeves should extend on both sides as far as the second joints of the fingers.

“The woolen undergarment should have such a measure that, when girded, it can reach to the instep. Likewise, like the cowl, its lower opening should end at the finger. Its hood should be one full foot; its sleeve likewise at the broader part, while toward the hand, where it usually remains, it should be narrower, extending from the root of the thumb to the end of the index finger.

“The strap by which the woolen garment is girded, once fully extended, should have a width of one thumb. The knife, between blade and handle, should have half a foot plus three fingers in length. The breeches that Saint Benedict granted to travelers, since it is now uncertain when or at what times they are sent outside, are granted to everyone. They should be measured so that their length fits the body suitably; in width, each side, doubled as is customary, should have one cubit up to the thumb once sewn.

“The stockings, once sewn, should have a full foot above; they should also be made long enough to fit the legs suitably according to the man’s stature, which must be taken into account in all garments. From the top to the foot they should be tightened in such a way that, when they have the foot above, they have half a foot below.

“The ankle-piece of the stocking, once sewn, should be long enough to be gathered within the fist. The shoe, apart from the hem that is sewn on, should have a height of half a foot. At the front it should have a width of the joints of the fingers. The foot-wraps should likewise be measured so that they fit the feet sufficiently.”

The manuscript customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon define the measurements of garments as follows (chapter 43):

“But to touch briefly on the measurement of these garments: the frock should be long enough to reach the strap, so that it can be seen whether the brother is shod. It should contain three gores on the right and three on the left; nevertheless, the central one should be as wide as the other two, and the edge of each should join the sleeve.

“The sleeves should be one foot and three fingers wide. According to ancient custom they ought to reach to the middle of the index finger, but nowadays they are made longer. The opening should be one foot.

“The cowl should reach as far as the top of the straps, like the frock; in width it should cover the elbows, and it should be hemmed on every side. The upper opening should extend from the elbow to the little finger; it should then be sewn for half a foot, open for a full foot, then joined, and afterward opened in the same way.

“The hood should have one full foot and three fingers on every side, doubled. The hem, when sewn, should be three fingers wide, with at least one finger between the inner seam.

“When worn and girded, the woolen garment should be shorter than the cowl, hemmed on both sides, and open for one full ell. The outer hem should be sewn double and be two fingers wide. One sleeve should be an ell beside the armpit, and at the top it should be doubled in width from the root of the thumb to the tip of the index finger. The opening for the head should be one foot.

“The breeches should be three ells, with one [ell] between the two seat portions and the saddles. The seat portions should be twelve [in number]. The *naslerius* should measure four shaved ells; once sewn with two folds, it should be a full thumb in width.

“The girdle for fastening should be one thumb wide when fully stretched. The knife, between handle and blade, should be half a foot and three fingers; the sheath should be somewhat longer than the hood. The strap from which it hangs, without the hanging wraparound, should be half a foot.

“The shoe should have one foot, and at the front three fingers, and should be hemmed all around. The strap should be long enough to go around the foot three times. The foot-wraps should likewise be long and cut straight. The night footwear should likewise be long, not fastened, but closed.”

“Whenever they receive new garments, they should always return the old ones to be stored in the wardrobe for the poor.”

Thus there was a wardrobe in the monastery, that is, a place where garments were kept under the care of some diligent brother. Concerning this, the Rule of Saint Augustine says (chapter 10):

“Keep your garments in one place, under one custodian, or two, or as many as may be sufficient to shake them out, lest they be damaged by moths; and just as you are fed from one storeroom, so let yourselves be clothed from one wardrobe.”

Saint Isidore appointed as custodian of the wardrobe the same man whom he appointed custodian of the sacristy. We described his office above from the customs of the monastery of Farfa, at chapter 32. His principal duty was to provide each person with the garments he needed. In distributing them, he did not wait until they had been completely consumed by use and wear, but supplied each person with his garments at fixed times.

In the monastery of Crowland, Egelric, who died in the year 992, “clothed the whole convent every year with its set of tunics, every other year with cowls, and every third year with frocks,” as Ingulf records in his *History of Crowland*.

Concerning the Cluniacs, we should hear Udalric (Book III, chapter 11):

“Each brother is given a new frock and a new cowl every year, so that both are ready and sewn before the Nativity of the Lord. A new fur garment is given in the second year, on the feast of Saint Michael; meanwhile, while the community is in the refectory for dinner, it is placed on his bed. Again, on the feast of Saint Martin, foot-wraps are given. I have said elsewhere how shoes are given on Maundy Thursday. Concerning woolen undergarments and breeches, or any other things of this kind, nothing else has been established except that, when they have become old and no longer useful, they are to be washed and returned by the brothers to the chamber, and other garments are to be given.”

Concerning the distribution of shoes on Maundy Thursday, on which day “all garments that are to be given to those in need” must also be supplied, according to the manuscript customs of Germany, we spoke in Book III of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*.

The customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon say the following concerning the distribution of garments (chapter 43):

“A new fur garment is given in the third year, on the feast of Saint Michael; while the community is in the refectory for dinner, it is placed on his bed. Shoes are given on Maundy Thursday. Every year, on the feast of Saint Martin, foot-wraps are given. Concerning frocks and cowls, woolen undergarments and breeches, or any other things of this kind, nothing else has been established except that, when they have become old and no longer suitable for use, other garments are to be given after they have been returned to the chamberlain—though the woolen undergarments and breeches must first be washed—and the old ones are to be handed over to the almoner for distribution to the poor.”

Pope Alexander, confirming the statutes made by Hugh, cardinal-priest of the title of Saint Sabina, for the reform of the monastery of Athanacum, first grants as many cowls, frocks, and shoes as are necessary, and each year, at the beginning of Lent, three woolen undergarments and three pairs of breeches to each monk. He also grants two pairs of stockings: one thick pair on the feast of Saint Luke, and another made of corded cloth on Maundy Thursday. On the feast of Saint Luke, one year a tunic and the next year a fur garment are to be given; and every three years, night footwear.

The Constitution of Pope Benedict XII likewise decrees (chapter 17) that “where no other fixed term has been established for this matter, garments are to be supplied each year, namely on the first day of October.”

The Constitutions of the Celestines state (chapter 10, §5):

“Each monk is to be provided at one and the same time with the aforesaid garments every three years, in the manner written below. In the first year of the three-year cycle, the superiors of the monasteries must provide each monk with a tunic, scapular, and hood, according to the arrangement given above. In the second year, with three woolen undershirts and a scapular with hood, as above. In the third year, with a tunic, scapular with hood, and cowl, as above.

“All the aforesaid articles are to be handed over at one and the same time, namely on the feast of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ, complete and without any delay or postponement. Every year, on the feast of All Saints, they are to be provided with breeches, stockings, and sandals. Shoes are to be supplied according to need and want.

“Professed oblates are to be provided in the first year with a tunic, scapular, and cap. In the second year, with three undershirts, a scapular, and a cap. In the third year, with a tunic, scapular, cap, and mantle, at the time specified above. They are likewise to be provided every year, on the feast of All Saints, with breeches and stockings. Shoes are to be supplied according to their need.”

The Council of Aachen preferred the following provision (canon 53): without regard to any fixed time, “whenever necessity demands, garments, shoes, and all necessities are to be given to the brothers.”

The Cistercians follow this law in Book I of the *Institutes*, distinction 8, chapter 9; the Bursfeld Congregation in the *Ceremonial*, distinction 2, chapter 9; and the Cassinese in their *Declarations* on chapter 53.

To ensure that nothing should be lacking to the brothers, the Cassinese decree that “each year, after the superior has returned from the chapter, all are to draw up an inventory of every garment they possess, noting its condition—whether old, new, or of middling quality—and there they are to record which garments they need. They are to hand this written inventory to the superior, who, having considered each person’s need, will provide reasonably for all, so that superfluities may be cut away and necessities abundantly supplied with the charity that is fitting.”

When they received new garments—which, according to Hildemarus, the wardrobe-keeper had to give publicly in chapter—Saint Benedict instituted that the old ones should always be returned, and this for the sake of the poor. Gregory IX renewed this law in his Constitution to the Benedictine monks in these words:

“No one, when receiving new garments or shoes, is to defraud almsgiving of the old ones; rather, all these things are to come into the hands of the almoner, who shall distribute them to the poor. Nor are new things to be given to one who does not surrender the old.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus likewise decrees (chapter 4) that “whatever has become old among the garments, shoes, or bedding of the monks, when they receive new articles, is to be given entirely by the abbot to the poor.”

The Rule of Saint Caesarius for virgins (chapter 41), however, says only that “when they receive new garments, if they have no need of the old ones, the abbess is to return the garments themselves to the poor, or distribute them among beginners or younger members.” Almost the same words are found in the Rule of Saint Aurelian for monks, chapter 45.

Hildemarus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius understand “old garments” to mean those that can no longer be worn; for they think that garments which can still be worn ought to be reserved for summer. I do not think, however, that this should be understood as though they were to be worn until they had been entirely consumed by wear and were afterward suitable for no use at all; otherwise, what would be given to the poor? The Holy Father adds another reason why the old garments should be returned, namely, so that all superfluity may be cut away from the brothers. Hence he adds:

“For it is enough for a monk to have two tunics and two cowls, and so forth.”

Saint Isidore allows three tunics with one cowl (Rule of Saint Isidore, chapter 13); Saint Fructuosus, three tunics and two wool-lined cowls (Fructuosus, chapter 4). It is no objection that Christ says in the Gospel, “Do not have two tunics,” for, as Saint Ferreolus rightly explains, “we must understand ‘two tunics’ not numerically, if they should appear necessary because of winter, but as more than use requires, if they have been kept in reserve.”

“For the nights.”

Bernard of Cassino teaches that this can be understood in two ways: “Either because the air is usually colder at night, and therefore we need more garments; or because those who lie down clothed commonly discharge certain natural excretions that were not deliberately produced, and therefore the garment must be washed, nor is it fitting for the monk to remain naked.”

Nicholas of Fractura and Boherius say the same. But the true reason seems to be that, when sleeping clothed, they removed their daytime garments and put on night garments, in which they both slept and celebrated the night offices. When they rose from bed, they did not remove them, as Menard observes here. Hence Sidonius, Book VII, letter 16, sent to Chariobaudus, abbot, “a night cowl in which he might fittingly cover his limbs, worn out by fasts, while praying and sleeping.”

“And for washing the garments themselves.”

They therefore washed their garments, undoubtedly with their own hands, as the Synod of Aachen declares when it decrees (canon 4) “that monks should work with their own hands and wash their garments at a suitable time.” Certainly this was the practice of the ancient monks, as may be seen throughout their rules.

Thus the Rule of Saint Pachomius (article 37) says:

“If anyone wishes to wash a garment, he shall inform his superior, and the superior shall send another man with him. When the garment has been washed, they shall return home, and the one to whom the task was assigned shall put it away once it is dry.”

The penalties of an uncertain author preserved by Saint Basil (no. 22) state:

“If anyone washes another’s garment or his own without the permission of the archimandrite, let him be deprived of the blessing.”

The Rule of Saint Augustine (chapter 11) says:

“Let your garments be washed at the discretion of the superior, either by yourselves or by fullers.”

The Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chapter 28) says:

“Let no one dare to wash his own garments or bedding without the prayer and permission of the superior.”

Finally, the Tarnatensis Rule (chapter 19) says:

“It must also be observed that the garment not contract the filth of the inner soul through an excessive desire for cleanliness. Therefore the garments are to be washed according to the superior’s arrangement.”

To these may be added the acts of Saint Salaberga, abbess of Laon, no. 20 (*Benedictine Annals*, vol. 2): “A certain sister, washing the dirt from the garments, came, as was customary, to the cell where such work was usually performed, and so forth.”

Concerning the discipline and procedure they observed in this work, we should again hear Saint Pachomius in the Rule, as it is printed in the *Book of Rules*:

“No one is to wash a *levitonarium* or anything else belonging to the monks’ clothing on Sunday, except sailors and bakers. Nor are they to go to wash until the signal has sounded for all. They shall follow their superior and wash silently and with discipline. No one is to wash with his garments drawn up higher than has been prescribed. When all have washed, they shall return together. If anyone remains behind at the time when they go to wash, or is not present at that time, he shall inform his superior, who shall send another man with him; and, when the garment has been washed, they shall return home.

“In the evening they shall take up the dry *levitonaria* and give them to the second man, that is, the one next after the superior, and he shall put them away in the cell. If they are not dry, they shall be spread out in the sun the next day until they dry; they are not to be left in the heat of the sun beyond the third hour. When they have been gathered up, they shall be gently softened. No one shall keep them with himself; rather, they shall give them over to be put away in the cell until Saturday.”

Hildemarus writes as follows concerning our own practice (on chapter 6):

“They must not wash cloths except in this way. Those brothers who have completed their week in the kitchen must heat the water, and on the fifteenth day they must heat that water. For example, if the brothers are shaved on Saturday, the water must be prepared on the following Tuesday, Monday, or Wednesday. Then, on the day when the water is prepared, the abbot must say to the brothers: ‘Let each one wash his garments today . . .’ And this must be understood: everything must be prepared—that is, the place, basin, water, soap, and the other necessities.”

Udalric also writes concerning the Cluniacs (Book II, chapter 15), in his account of the instruction of novices:

“If he wishes to wash anything among his garments, he finds in the regular kitchen a bronze vessel intended for this alone, in which the water is heated and the lye is mixed. In the cloister there is a very large hollowed-out trough with numerous compartments, so that the woolen garment can be washed in one place and the breeches separately in another. He puts them into hot water beforehand so that they may soften; after the striking of the board he washes them, and no longer, except for as long as permission to speak lasts. If it is a fast day, he is not forbidden to wash after the third hour; or if it is Lent or an ordinary day, he washes not only after the third hour but also after the sixth, even though they do not speak in the cloister. Whatever he washes, however it has been washed, he removes and dries after the washing hour, so that it does not lie there dirty and hideous, especially where the whole community will see it while leaving the refectory.”

“Whatever is now superfluous must be cut away.”

Nevertheless, Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, “granted and allowed, for the sake of necessity, which is why the Rule commands two woolen undergarments, breeches, fur garments, their coverings, two capes, and whatever other necessities he foresaw, in order to remove every pretext for evasion,” as Ardo writes in his *Life*, no. 52.

The Council of Aachen also decreed (canon 22) that the abbot “should provide entirely that each monk have two shirts, two tunics, two cowls, and two capes; for those who need them, a third is to be added; four pairs of foot-wraps, two pairs of breeches, one frock, two fur garments reaching to the ankles, and two bandages. For those who need additional garments for travel, two more [garments are to be supplied], gloves in summer, woolen mittens in winter, two pairs of daytime shoes, two low shoes for summer nights, and wooden shoes in winter.”

The garments of the Cluniacs were “two frocks and two cowls, two woolen undergarments, two pairs of breeches, two pairs of shoes with straps, one pair of lined shoes for winter nights and another without lining for summer nights, two pairs of stockings, three fur garments—or one *gunella* in place of the third—one fur hood, and five pairs of foot-wraps.”

[Col. 0790C] **“Those who are sent on a journey are to receive breeches from the wardrobe, etc.”**] Those remaining in the monastery did not wear breeches; and we infer that the disciples of Saint Martin likewise abstained from them, from Sulpicius Severus (*Book III of the Life of Saint Martin*). Saint Robert also took breeches away from the monks of Molesme, as Orderic Vitalis writes (*Ecclesiastical History*, Book VIII). Bernard of Cassino gives the same account of the Cistercians and Cassinese monks of his own time. Indeed, concerning the Cassinese monks in our own age, Paulus Augustinus of Genoa writes:

> “In our Cassinese congregation, down to our own time, we have seen old men who did not use breeches inside the monastery, but tied their undergarment, which fell below the knees, around the knees themselves.”

Hildemar likewise disapproves of their use, speaking as follows on this passage:

> “It must be noted that there are monasteries where, whenever necessity arises, they receive breeches from the wardrobe: these monasteries are entirely good. Again, there are other monasteries where everyone without exception receives breeches, but not everyone without exception always wears them, except when necessity demands it; although everyone receives them, these monasteries are good, because the greater part of the monks never wears them. Again, there are other monasteries where everyone receives them and everyone wears them: these monasteries are not praiseworthy.”

Here he seems to be referring to monasteries beyond the Alps, in which, at least in Bernard of Cassino’s time, the brothers indiscriminately used breeches. The Rule of the Master (chap. 81) also allows woolen breeches in winter and linen ones in summer. Likewise, the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chap. 4) says:

> “The use of breeches is to be permitted to anyone, especially to those engaged in the ministry of the altar; but anyone who does not wish to make a practice of this is not to be reproved, since even to this day it is established that many monasteries, including those in these regions, do not have this practice.”

What is said there about ministers of the altar recalls what Udalric writes about the monks of Cluny (Book III, [Col. 0791A] chap. 11):

> “The priest and deacon ordinarily have three pairs of breeches, so that, if anything happens to them during the night, they may readily change them.”

Peter the Venerable proves the justice of this regulation by the following argument (Book I, letter 28):

> “We defend breeches on the grounds of necessity, cleanliness, and propriety, recalling, moreover, that God commanded that the high priest should not presume to approach his altar without linen breeches, lest, if he did so, he incur the penalty of death . . . . And although chastity was enjoined upon the ministers of God by means of linen breeches, the propriety of covering the body was not excluded; rather, it was carefully commanded. Hence the Apostle says: ‘The dishonorable parts of our body we treat with greater honor.’”

Why, however, Saint Father Benedict forbade breeches to those remaining in the monastery, Saint Hildegard explains in these words:

> “Because at that time the multitude of men did not use breeches, that same Father, on account of human custom and as a sign of childish simplicity and humility while they remained in their cells, did not grant breeches to his disciples. [Col. 0791B] But when they went out, whether on horseback or on foot, he allowed them breeches for the sake of an example of chastity and of manly propriety and respect for other people.”

Besides the breeches which the holy Father granted to travelers, Saint Philibert, abbot of Jumièges, also carried mittens, or gloves, on a journey, as we learn from the anonymous author of his *Life*, no. 11 (*Second Century of Benedictine Authors*).

**“And let the cowls and tunics be somewhat better than those which they ordinarily have.”**] That is, in those regions “where they are accustomed to use very cheap garments,” says Smaragdus; “but where the garments are better, they are not to be changed on account of journeys.” Hence Hildemar says:

> “Those who wear good garments inside ought not to wear other garments.”

And indeed, since there are some “who wear better garments in the monastery than those which Saint Benedict said were to be kept in the monastery for wearing outside,” as Hildemar puts it, it would be wholly contrary to the purpose of monastic poverty to wear still more costly garments outside the monastery.

Bernard of Cassino perceptively observes on this passage:

> “Note three qualifications: he says *somewhat*, *moderately*, and *better*. By saying *somewhat*, he indicates something greater in price. But so that this *somewhat* should not be understood as much, he says *moderately*. And so that excessive shabbiness should not be implied and reproved as conspicuous, he added *better*.”

**“Which, when they go out on a journey, they are to receive from the wardrobe.”**] Hildemar explains what is meant here by a journey: it is not a journey “when they go nearby to people they know and who know them, but when they have to go farther away.” A little later he says:

> “It is not a journey if he goes on an obedience, such as to a cell; but it is a journey when he goes to an unknown bishop, or to noble and powerful men. And not only ought we to wear other garments when we are traveling; if such a person, who is noble, comes to the monastery, then the brother who has to wait upon him ought to have better garments, on account of the distaste which the rustic monastic garment might cause.”

**“The bedding is to suffice as a mat.”**] *Matta* in Greek is *psiathion* (ψιάθιον), a covering woven from reeds, as is clear from Gregory of Tours’ account of Saint Monegunda (*Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, chap. 19):

> “She had no bed with the softness of hay or straw, except only that which is customarily made from woven reeds, which people commonly call mats. This she placed upon a small frame; upon this alone she spread herself; this was her daily bench, her mattress, her little cushion, her blanket, and all the comfort of her bed.”

Hence Peter the Venerable, writing to the hermit Gislebert (Book I, letter 20), says:

> “If marshy places are nearby, make mats, the ancient work of monks, upon which you may sleep either always or frequently.”

Haeften distinguishes four uses of the mat among the monks of old (Book XII, treatise 1): first, they slept upon the mat—indeed, at times lying upon one part of it and covering their bodies with another part; second, they sat upon mats, using them as seats; third, when they wished to pray, they knelt upon the mat, or *psiathion*; fourth, they spread a mat beneath those who were on the point of dying.

Bernard of Cassino, however, explains *matta* differently in this passage:

> “A mat is either a felt covering, according to the Cluniacs, or that which is used in place of a mattress. Hence, even to this day, what is placed upon straw is commonly called a *mattaratium*. I do not, however, understand it to be something delicate in softness; for a monk ought rather to sleep exhausted by labor and vigil than enticed by the softness of a bed.”

Nicholas of Fractura says similarly:

> “A mat—that is, a cloth or felt covering used in place of a mattress. Or, according to our usage, you may say *matta*, that is, *mattaratium*, not very soft, but such as almost mortifies and macerates the flesh, or wearies it by mortifying it. In Pavia, however, *macta* means a cell; hence *mactilla* means a mattress.”

The ancient Gallican versions of John de Précis and Guido Juvenalis confirm this interpretation, rendering *matta* as *un matteras*. The former explanation, however, seems preferable, for the mat was a hard bed, suitable for mortification, as is clear from Saint Augustine (*Against Faustus the Manichaean*, Book V, chap. 5).

**“A quilt.”**] Saint Hildegard describes this as follows (*Book XIX of the Origins*, chap. 24):

> “Made either of coarse linen or of hemp, almost shaped like a sack, and filled with a certain kind of bedding; it was placed upon the mat, and the monks used it as their bed covering.”

Bernard of Cassino’s understanding of the word agrees with this:

> “I think that, according to modern usage, this *sagum* is what contains straw or hay, and this agrees with the common speech of this kingdom.”

Nicholas of Fractura says the same; and the word is used in this sense in the ancient *Life of Saint Eugendus, Abbot of the Jura*, where I read:

> “Having lain for a long time in the wilderness upon a bed of straw, bound together with a very humble little quilt and covered with a skin, he rested.”

Here it should also be observed incidentally that, according to Lanfranc’s statutes, the hay in all the beds was to be renewed every year, between the feast of Saint John and that of the Holy Apostles Peter and Paul, as prescribed by the *Customs of Saint Benignus*, chap. 43.

Haeften nevertheless thinks that the *sagum* was the covering of the monastic bed, since the monks slept upon the mat itself. Guido Juvenalis agrees, translating *sagum* into French as *une grosse sarge velue à mettre sur le matteras* (“a thick, shaggy cloth to place upon the mattress”).

**“A woolen covering.”**] Hildemar calls this “a double cloak, or royal garment”; Smaragdus calls it “a kind of shaggy garment, which we call a *toxa*; others call it a *galnapa*.” A *galnapis*, or *galbanis*, is a shaggy blanket capable of resisting the cold.
