Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Richard of Saint Angelo, Boherius, Turrecremata, Menardus, and Haeften all think that Saint Benedict uses the word here in this sense. An anonymous writer of Durham, however, seems to confuse *laenae* with *saga* in Book I of *The Translation and Miracles of Saint Cuthbert*, chap. 1 (*Fourth Century of Benedictine Authors*, part II).

**“A pillow.”**] This word derives from *caput* (“head”), because it is placed beneath the head; it is a cushion filled with wool, straw, or feathers. Hence Smaragdus says:

> “By *capitale* he means what we call a feather cushion.”

These, then, are the bedding materials which Saint Benedict allowed the brothers. What did others allow?

The Rule of Saint Pachomius, delivered by an angel (chap. 41), prescribes that the monks “sleep not lying down, but sitting upon seats built for themselves somewhat inclined backward, and there, with their coverings placed upon them, let them sleep while seated.”

The Rule of Saint Caesarius for virgins says:

> “Let the bedding itself be simple; for it is most unbecoming if secular blankets or decorated carpets shine in a religious bed.”

The Rule of Saint Donatus, chap. 63, says the same.

Likewise, the Rule of Saint Aurelian for monks (chap. 27) says:

> “You shall not use secular bedding made in various colors.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 14) likewise states:

> “A monk may not possess attractive or varied furnishings. His bedding shall be a mat and a blanket, two woolen skins, a shaggy covering, a cloth for wiping, and two small pillows for the head.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chap. 4) says:

> “Proper discipline is to be observed in bedding, and no one is to demand anything more than one blanket, a shaggy hemp covering, a small cloth, and two woolen ram skins. [Note: [Col. 0793D] The syntax is entirely disturbed. The word *praeter* should be read in place of *quam*, with all the complements that follow put in the accusative; alternatively, the conjunction *quam* should be construed with a nominative. EDIT.]”

Finally, the Rule of the Master (chap. 81) says:

> “In winter let them have in their beds one mat apiece, one quilted *sagum* apiece, and wool. In summer, instead of wool, let them use rushes because of the heat; and before each bed let them have one skin on which they may wipe the dirt from their feet before climbing into their beds.”

**“These beds, however, are frequently to be inspected by the abbot, etc.”**] He says “frequently” without specifying an interval. The Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 14), however, prescribes that “each month the abbot or the provost is to inspect everyone’s little beds, lest the brothers lack anything or have anything superfluous.” The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins (chap. 2) says:

> “Every Saturday, after the ninth hour of prayer, both the senior and the junior superiors are to visit the beds of all the sisters and do so in order to investigate their negligence, or to see whether anything illicit has been found there and retained without permission.”

Finally, the Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chap. 17) says:

> “The abbot or provost is to turn over and search the bed of each person twice a week, to see whether anyone has anything superfluous or concealed there.”

Hildemar describes the procedure for searching the beds among our monks as follows:

> “In the morning, when everyone had assembled in the chapter, the abbot warned the brothers that the beds were to be searched. Then, while everyone else remained in the chapter, he sent four or five brothers of good conduct to the dormitory, and they inspected each person’s bed. If they found any private possession anywhere, they returned to the chapter and placed it before the feet of the person whose bed had contained it. When ordered by the abbot to give an account, that person was punished according to the seriousness of the offense.”

**“And if anything is found belonging to someone which he did not receive from the abbot, let him undergo the severest discipline.”**] Hildemar understands this to mean that, if someone is found to possess an item acquired by theft, and the item is worth four denarii, he is judged to be guilty of a lesser offense. But if its value is greater, “then the item ought to be burned,” he says, “and the man himself is to be judged guilty of a more serious offense.”

Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura understand “the severest discipline” here to mean the greater excommunication, but in such a way that “the quality and quantity of the thing which was taken must be considered, since these matters are to be prudently weighed in the penance imposed,” as Bernard says.

The Rule of Saint Donatus prescribes that:

> “Any sister who presumes to hide anything belonging to her bed, or anything pertaining to eating or drinking, is to be rebuked publicly before everyone; and then, having been openly reproved before all present, she is to be compelled to endure the *superposition*.”

**“And so that this particular vice may be eradicated from the roots, let everything necessary be given by the abbot—that is, a cowl, tunic, stockings, shoes, breeches, a knife, etc.”**] We have already explained some of these terms; something must now be added concerning the remainder.

Some think that *bracile* is a garment for the arms, believing that the word derives from *brachium* (“arm”). Thus Guido Juvenalis renders *bracile* in his French version as *manche*, and another version as *manchon*, but without the testimony of any established authority. Haeften derives *bracile* from *bracca* (“breeches”) and maintains that it is a shorter garment suitable for covering the private parts; but this too is unsupported by any ancient authority.

Menardus more correctly asserts that *bracile* is a belt or girdle, and proves this by the authority of Papias:

> “*Brachile* is what we call a *succinctory* or tie, which now serves not as a belt for the arms but for the loins.”

He also cites the Rule of the Master, chap. 11:

> “During the day, he is to gird himself with *bracilia*.”

This is further confirmed by the monk Bobolenus in the *Life of Saint Germanus, Abbot of Grandval*, no. 15 (*Second Century of Benedictine Authors*):

> “One of the brothers, on the very day of his killing, found among the ranks of the enemy, in the hands of those who were dragging him, a belt which is commonly called a *bracile*.”

The ancient and more recent versions likewise support this interpretation, rendering *bracile* in French as *sainture* or *ceinture* (“belt”). For Boherius, *bracile* is “a belt from which hang the breeches and the straps by which the leggings are fastened.”

A *graphium* was a stylus with which people wrote on wax. At first the Greeks, Etruscans, and Romans used an iron one; later they used one of bone, as Saint Isidore explains in these words (*Etymologies*, Book VI, chap. 8):

> “For the Greeks and Etruscans first wrote on wax with iron. Afterwards the Romans ordered that no one should possess an iron stylus; hence among scribes it is said: ‘Do not cut the wax with iron.’ Later it was established that they should write on wax with bones, as Atta indicates in his satire when he says: ‘Let us turn the plowshare into wax, and plow with a bone point.’”

It is nevertheless clear from Martial, Book XIV, epigram 21, that the Romans later returned to the iron stylus. The *graphium* was pointed at the end used for writing and blunt, or broad, at the other end, so that the characters written in wax could be erased or scraped away. Hence among the Latins *vertere stilum* (“to turn the stylus”) meant the same as to correct, revise, or change one’s opinion.

Concerning the needle, see Haeften, Book V, treatise 2, dissertation 6.

A *mappula* is a small sweat-cloth, or linen cloth suitable for wiping away mucus. The Vulgate version of Alcuin’s *On the Offices of the Church*, chap. 39, says:

> “The *mappula*, which is carried on the left side, with which we wipe the discharge from the eyes and nose.”

Honorius of Autun says:

> “Finally, the priest places the *fanon* on his left arm; it is also called a *mappula* and a *sudarium*, by means of which sweat and the filth of the nose were formerly wiped away.”

Hildemar (*Book I of the Jewel of the Soul*, chap. 108) says:

> “He commanded that a *mappula* be given for wiping away sweat during labor or on a journey. For in France, when Saint Benedict said that a brother should have a *mappula*, he is understood to have meant it for sweat and travel. And although Saint Benedict’s intention may perhaps have been that a *mappula* should also be kept in the monastery as a face-cloth, nevertheless in France nowadays cloths are commonly provided with which the brothers wipe their faces.”

Saint Hildegard says:

> “A *mappula* is formed like a linen *sudarium*, with which they wiped away the sweat flowing from them while they labored at their work.”

Nicholas of Fractura says:

> “A *mappula*, that is, a small towel, which some people customarily carry at their side in summer for wiping away sweat.”

Paulus Augustinus of Genoa adds:

> “Our old men retain this custom to the present day. Formerly, since they did not use breeches, they carried a *mappula*, a key, and a knife hanging at their sides.”

All this sufficiently refutes the opinion of Antonius Perez, who, removing the punctuation and joining this word to the following one, reads *mappulas tabulae* and says that this means “table napkins.” But neither is *tabulae* used here for a table, nor *mappulae* for linen spread upon a table; for what need would a single monk have of such furnishings? Certainly the French versions commonly interpret *mappulas* as *des mouchoirs* (“handkerchiefs”). Hildemar writes as follows concerning their size:

> “For the dimensions of a *mappula*, it ought to be two cubits long, apart from the border, and one foot wide.”

**“Tablets.”**] These are writing tablets on which one writes, or in which writing is impressed and then erased, as Nicholas of Fractura explains. See Haeften, Book IX, treatise 2, dissertation 5.

Moreover, concerning the things which Saint Father Benedict prescribes in this chapter to be given to each brother, Hildemar states that it was an ancient custom to give everyone soap for wiping the face and hands, and grease for anointing the shoes, in one and the same vessel, which they kept beside the bed. They received the vessel from the abbot and the soap from the chamberlain, equally distributed in the chapter.

## CHAPTER LVI. The Abbot’s Table

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795A] **725** “Let the abbot’s table always be with the guests and pilgrims. Whenever there are fewer guests than he wishes to invite from among the brothers, it shall be in his power to do so. Nevertheless, let him arrange that one or two of the seniors always be left with the brothers, for the sake of discipline.”

[Note: [Col. 0795A] Hildemar reads *Seniorem* (“one senior”).]

[Note: [Col. 0795A] The Council omits *cum fratribus* (“with the brothers”).]

[Note: [Col. 0795A] Another reading is *dimittendos* (“are to be left”). But in the Oxford manuscript this sentence is read as follows: “Nevertheless, one or two seniors are always to be left with the brothers.” The same reading appears in the Concordia of Vendôme, apart from the first word, *seniores*. [Col. 0796A]]

### COMMENTARY

[Col. 0795]

[Col. 0795A] **“Let the abbot’s table always be with the guests and pilgrims, etc.”**] The commentators distinguish here between guests and pilgrims. Hildemar says:

> “Guests are those who come from the same nearby region. Pilgrims are those who come from another region; for *peregrinus* is so called, as Cassiodorus says, as though from *pergens longius*—‘going farther away.’”

Bernard of Cassino says the same. After Boherius had quoted his words in his first commentary, he adds:

> “Or pilgrims are those who turn aside to a monastery or some place for the sake of devotion; guests, however, are those who approach those places for another reason.”

Nicholas of Fractura gives both distinctions. Richard of Saint Angelo writes:

> “By guests we understand the poor and the non-poor; by pilgrims we understand those who go through oratories to obtain indulgences.”

He nevertheless adds:

> “Or you may say that they are one and the same.”

Those who reside in the same city or town where the monastery is situated, and who either voluntarily solicit a meal or are invited by the abbot, are not to be called guests but rather fellow diners, as Menardus notes.

Menardus perceptively observes that this passage mentions neither the abbot’s cell, chamber, nor palace, where he might dine separately from his congregation with guests and pilgrims, but only the table. From this he infers that the abbot is to dine with the guests and pilgrims in the assembly of the brothers.

This opinion is not peculiar to Menardus. For many centuries the matter had already been disputed, as is clear from Smaragdus, from Hildemar, who will be cited below, and from Bernard of Cassino. Smaragdus, writing on the words of chapter 53, “The abbot’s and guests’ kitchen is to be separate,” says:

> “It is thought by many that, just as the kitchen was different from that of the brothers and was located in another place, so the abbot’s table was not then placed in the common refectory with the other tables, but was set apart in another room, which the frequently arriving guests would often find prepared with food.”

From this passage one may argue as follows: if it was thought by many, then it was not thought by all; therefore some thought that the abbot’s table ought to be in the common refectory of the brothers, with the other tables of the brothers.

Bernard of Cassino states the matter more clearly:

> “Some say here that the abbot ought always to eat in the refectory with the brothers, and they have also declared this in a statute made concerning the matter, saying that the abbot’s table ought to be in a higher place, and that there, with the guests seated, he ought to take his meal.”

Udalric seems to indicate that this was the discipline of the Cluniacs in the following words (Book III, chap. 3):

> “For clerics and pilgrim monks who travel on foot without a mount and are to eat with us in the refectory, he [the abbot] provides water for their hands; and such men sit at the principal table.”

I shall therefore follow and defend Menardus’s opinion, while not concealing any contrary arguments or authorities that may exist.

Accordingly, the ancient and established practice of the monks of old proves that the abbot ought to dine with the guests in the common assembly of the brothers. It is not easy to believe that Saint Father Benedict departed from this practice in a matter of such importance. This practice can be seen everywhere in their rules and records.

The Third Rule of the Holy Fathers states:

> “We also decree that abbots dine with the brothers at all times, because at the time when they ought either to correct the brothers for negligence or to instruct them with spiritual speech, they ought not to withdraw without clear necessity.”

Saint Caesarius, in his letter to the abbess Oratoria (chap. 11), writes:

> “In the daily nourishment of the body and in the common meal, be equal to those with whom you share an equal seat at table; finally, delight in the same flavors of dishes as the sisters, and let the servers and cupbearers provide you with equal foods and common drinks, etc.”

Saint Aurelian’s Rule for Monks (chap. 50) says:

> “The holy abbot shall not dine outside the congregation unless inequality makes it necessary.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 10) says:

> “Except when illness requires it, the abbot is to take his food in the presence of the brothers, equally with them; he is not to request anything different from what the others have, nor anything more elegantly prepared than what is provided in common.”

The common monastic Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chap. 10) says:

> “Abbots, together with the brothers and with guests and pilgrims who arrive, are to live communally at one table.”

The Rule of Saint Donatus for Virgins (chap. 59) says:

> “Unless compelled by some inequality, illness, or occupation, the abbess is not to dine outside her congregation.”

He took this from the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins, chap. 38. Finally, the Rule of the Master repeatedly indicates that the abbot ought to dine in the refectory.

Practice confirms the same. Concerning Saint Eugendus the abbot, the author of his *Life* says:

> “That abbot never reserved his own little table or his food apart from the brothers, as I recently heard some people do.”

Saint Easterwin, according to Bede in Book I of *The Life of Saint Benedict Biscop*, “always ate in the same house and the same food as the other brothers.”

Saint Hermeland, showing the grace of hospitality to Count Agatheus in the monastery at Antrum, “led him with him into the refectory and ordered a cup of unmixed wine to be given to him,” as the anonymous author of his *Life* writes, chap. 13. Further on, in chap. 15, he lists among the corrupt customs of Adalfred, the abbot who succeeded Hermeland, that he “began to build a hall for himself.”

Caramuel even states that almost all the Spaniards believe that Saint Benedict treated pilgrims and outsiders in the regular refectory, and frequently at the common hour.

To this may be added the decree of the Council of Aachen, which states (*Disputation 132 on the Rule of Saint Benedict*):

> “The abbot, or any one of the brothers, is not to dine with the guests at the monastery gate. In the refectory, however, he is to show them every courtesy in eating and drinking. He himself is nevertheless to be content with the measure of food and drink which the other brothers receive. If, because of a guest, he wishes to add something to the customary measure for the brothers and for himself, it shall remain in his power.”

This statute is confirmed by the ordinance of Charles the Bald concerning the division of the estates of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, in which he assigns vineyards for the use of the brothers and guests who eat in the refectory.

Furthermore, when Saint Benedict treats in chapter 38 of the Rule of the reader at table, he decrees that no one there is to presume to ask for anything from the reading or from elsewhere, lest an opportunity be given to the Evil One, unless perhaps the prior wishes to say something briefly for the sake of edification. Here “prior” is used for the abbot.

But if the abbot never dines in the assembly of the brothers—for he ought to dine with the guests, who are never absent from the monastery, and if they are absent it remains in his power whom he wishes to invite from among the brothers to dine with him—then it is pointless to allow him to say something about the reading in the refectory, since he will never be eating there with the brothers.

To evade the force of this argument, Haeften replies that the word “prior” here means any superior, whether abbot, prior, or subprior, who presides over the conventual table. But our Menardus rightly maintains that, in every passage of the Rule where the word *prior* is used singly and absolutely rather than relatively, it signifies the abbot (Menardus, *Commentary on the Concordance of the Rule*, chap. 47, § 1). Haeften himself admits elsewhere that the word *prior* is often used in the Rule for the abbot, as in chapters 6, 7, 13, 40, and 53 (Haeften, Book III, treatise 6, dissertation 2). Why should it not have that meaning in this passage as well?

Certainly the monks of old were especially unwilling for the abbot to be absent from the common table of the brothers so that he could speak words of edification to them after the meal and instruct them with spiritual discourse, as the Rule of the Holy Fathers cited above says. For when the meal was over, a spiritual conference was held among them, as the same Haeften proves (Book X, treatise 5, dissertation 4). No one can reasonably believe that Saint Benedict neglected this practice, still less that he wished or allowed the abbot to entrust his role in giving exhortations to another, since exhortations are nowhere more effective than from the mouth of the abbot and superior.

Moreover, the Rule of the Master (chap. 24), from which Saint Benedict borrowed this statute, clearly and distinctly prescribes that the abbot should ask each table of brothers whatever he wishes concerning what has been read—not the provost or any other prior.

Furthermore, as Hildemar argues most effectively, Saint Benedict wanted the abbot to fulfill the title of “greater” by his deeds, and to show all good and holy things more by deeds than by words. But if he has a separate table apart from the brothers, he no longer teaches his disciples by his actions; for they do not see with what moderation, with what silence, and with what gravity he eats with the guests.

In addition, the holy legislator decrees that everyone is to be present for the verse said before the meal, and that all are to come to the table together. Here “he did not exempt the abbot,” says Hildemar, “saying, ‘except the abbot, who is going to eat with the guests’; he simply said, ‘Let all say the verse.’ Nor was it enough for him to say ‘all’ once; he said it twice when he added, ‘and all together let them come to the table.’ Accordingly, this must be understood to mean that the abbot’s table ought to be in the refectory with the tables of the brothers.”

Finally, no reason can be produced by which Saint Father Benedict could have been induced to separate the abbot’s table from the brothers. For what Bernard of Cassino says cannot be tolerated:

> “The most blessed Benedict wished the abbot’s table to be separate for the sake of charity. Those who issued a contrary statute either pursued greed or wished to remain unknown as to how they lived.”

What kind of charity is it that destroys all charity, segregates the shepherd from the flock, opens a free path to the wolf, and provides access to every vice? Who could express how many evils arise from this, both spiritual and temporal, while the abbot’s pot boils and the congregation’s kettle grows cold? How much license is permitted to the abbot when he is given the opportunity to feast daily with secular people, to squander, gorge himself, and dissipate the monastery’s goods! What corruption of monastic life results from this; how many murmurs among the brothers against the abbot, how many slanders, how many curses—not to mention anything worse! O extraordinary charity!

It is a splendid argument indeed which some make (cited in Haeften, Book XI, treatise 3, dissertation 4): that Saint Benedict, foreseeing what would happen—namely, the separation of the abbot’s table from the monks’ table—issued this chapter not in the form of a command but in the form of a prophecy of what he saw would occur. As though the holy Father, foreseeing what would happen, would not have confronted so serious a disease and fortified his monks against it.

Nor are the arguments which Haeften gives of greater weight (in the same work, dissertation 1):

> “There were just reasons for a separate table: first, so that the brothers would not be disturbed; second, so that the guests might be received more generously than the brothers; third, so that they might perhaps not be offended by the conduct of less perfect brothers; fourth, so that there might be no occasion for the guests to speak to the brothers without permission.”

For he himself later refutes these same reasons. Certainly they did not move the Fathers of Aachen, who decreed (canon 27):

> “The abbot, or any one of the brothers, is not to dine with the guests at the monastery gate; but in the refectory he is to show them every courtesy in eating.”

Nor did they move the Second Council of London, which decreed “that abbots should not make knights, and that they should sleep and eat in the same house with their monks, unless some necessity prevented it.”

Nor did they move the Cluniacs or the other monastic congregations that strove to order their lives according to the purer standard of the Rule. All of them send the abbot to the common refectory of the brothers, and allow the guests to be brought there and to eat.

Experience shows that there is not much reason to fear that the brothers will be disturbed by this. Moreover, what prevents the guests from being received more generously in the refectory? As for the fear that the guests might be scandalized by the conduct of less perfect brothers, one would rather have had good reason to hope “that when the guests see both the abbot and the monks eating with the fear of God, reverence, moderation, and even gravity, they will glorify the Lord, as the Lord says: ‘Seeing your good works, they glorify your Father who is in heaven’; and at some point, by the Lord’s mercy, those guests themselves, despising the things of the world, will hasten to enter the service of God,” as I put it with Hildemar.

Finally, experience, which is the teacher, shows that there is no danger that the brothers, who have not been commanded to do so, will speak to the guests.

[Col. 0798C] There is one matter which seems to present greater difficulty. Since Saint Benedict wishes the abbot to break his fast because of a guest, and since guests are never absent from the monastery, if the abbot is to dine with the guests in the refectory, it will follow that the abbot must break his fast every day before the whole community while the others continue fasting. Who could believe this?

This objection, which at first sight seems to possess some force, in truth contains none. For what is better: to break the fast outside the community or before it? What is more perfect? Moreover, the objection applies only when the abbot is compelled to anticipate the customary hours of the meal because of a guest. For when the guests dine together with the community, the abbot neither ought to break his fast nor, at least ordinarily, use food different from that of the brothers.

It is not, however, so frequent for the abbot to anticipate the customary hours of the meal, since guests do not arrive every day and often readily wait for the hour of the community. Moreover, Saint Father Benedict prescribes that whenever there are fewer guests, it is to be in the abbot’s power to invite whichever brothers he wishes—namely, those who will dine in his place with the guests—provided that he leaves two seniors with the brothers for the sake of discipline, so that he himself may take his meal in the common assembly of the brothers. To explain the text of the Rule in this way involves no difficulty.

The major difficulty arises from two passages in the Rule that seem to favor the separation of the abbot’s table. The first occurs in chapter 53: “The kitchen for the abbot and the guests shall be separate.” Explaining this passage, Smaragdus says:

> “Many think that, just as there was a kitchen different from that of the brothers and situated in another place, so also the abbot’s table was not then placed in the common refectory with the other tables, but was separated in another chamber, which the frequently arriving guests would often find prepared with food.”

But what many held as an opinion was maintained contrariwise by others, as we saw above. Certainly, in former times the abbot’s and the guests’ kitchen was built [Col. 0799A] 730 near the monks’ kitchen, and between the two there was a window through which, on one side, the monks’ pottages and, on the other, the guests’ dishes were served, as Hildemar teaches in his commentary on chapter 53.

Saint Benedict therefore wished the guests’ kitchen to be separate, not so that they might dine with the abbot separately in another place, but so that guests arriving at uncertain hours would not disturb the brothers. For since he wished guests to be received somewhat more generously, and since he excused no one from the kitchen service, if brothers who were otherwise sufficiently unfit to cook the monks’ food were compelled to prepare dishes for guests, they would certainly be considerably disturbed—especially since guests arrive at uncertain hours and everything must be prepared in a short time. For this reason Saint Benedict separated the abbot’s and the guests’ kitchen; not, however, so that the abbot might feast apart with them and squander all the monastery’s goods in banquets.

The other passage is contained in the following words of this chapter:

> “Nevertheless, when there are fewer guests, it shall be in his power to call from the brothers whom he wishes. But he shall always arrange for one or two of the seniors to remain with the brothers, for the sake of discipline.” [Col. 0799B]

Here the carnal abbots triumph—for why should we not call them so, with Hildemar? He says:

> “The carnal abbots indeed say that the abbot’s table ought to be with the guests outside the refectory. They take as support for their error what Saint Benedict says: ‘Nevertheless, when there are fewer guests, it shall be in his power to call from the brothers whom he wishes; but he shall always arrange for one or two of the seniors to remain with the brothers, for the sake of discipline.’ For what need would Saint Benedict have had to say, ‘He shall arrange for one or two to remain with the brothers, for the sake of discipline,’ if the abbot were supposed to eat in the refectory? For if the abbot eats there, he himself can maintain discipline, so that no one does or says anything dishonorable. And in his saying ‘to remain,’ it is apparent that the abbot himself is in one place and those over whom he leaves the seniors for the sake of discipline are in another place, and not together, etc.” [Col. 0799C]

We have already offered one solution to this difficulty: namely, that when there are fewer guests, it is in the abbot’s power to call from the brothers whom he wishes, so that they may perform his duty of eating with the guests, not so that they may dine with him outside the common refectory.

Accept another solution from Hildemar:

> “It is asked in this passage where the abbot ought to eat: in the refectory or outside? There are some who say that he ought to eat in the refectory. How, then, ought he to leave his brothers with the brothers in the refectory, if he himself is supposed to eat there? Those who answer say that blessed Benedict therefore said that the seniors should be left, because there are refectories in which the brothers sit in such a way, on account of the multitude of the brothers, that they cannot be seen by the abbot, as is the case at Saint Gall.”

This answer is confirmed by the Rule of the Master, which, although it sometimes departs from the Benedictine Rule, may nevertheless in many matters be regarded as its interpretation and commentary (chapter 84):

> “At the abbot’s table,” it says, “let the seniors, newly arriving outsiders, or brothers who sing the psalter by turns, whom the abbot wishes, sit, except the provosts, who are ordered to be present at their own tables in their decads for this reason: that they may preserve the cause of God—that is, silence and gravity—in those entrusted to them.” [Col. 0799D]

Perhaps the passage in the Life of Saint Philibert the abbot, no. 3 (Second Century of Benedictine Sources), should likewise be understood in this way: “Accordingly, he was ordered to sit at the first table, etc.”

If anyone does not wish Saint Benedict to have had in mind those spacious refectories, it is nevertheless highly plausible that he mixed the seniors among the juniors at the tables, so that they might watch over them—just as he did not wish the younger brothers to have beds beside one another in the dormitory, but ordered them to sleep intermixed with the seniors.

Certainly the deans, whom Saint Benedict calls seniors in chapter 22, according to the ancient discipline of the monks, sat at table in their deaneries, as we said above in discussing chapter 21. Saint Benedict the legislator did not wish to depart from this discipline. Thus, since he did not wish the abbot to remain alone at his table when there were few or no guests, he allowed him to call some of the seniors, but in such a way that he left one or two of the brothers intermingled with the others, lest he seem entirely to abandon this discipline received among monks. And indeed, what kind of discipline would it be if, after leaving one or two seniors with the brothers, the abbot indulged himself separately with the rest?

Hildemar also gives another answer: this passage should be understood of those days on which, for the sake of hospitality, the abbot is compelled to anticipate the customary hour of the meal. For then, when there are few guests, he may call from the brothers whom he wishes, so that they may dine with him and the guests in the refectory.

Haeftenus will reply that this restricts Saint Benedict’s words to a particular case which he nowhere indicates. But what prevents us from restricting Saint Benedict’s text to a particular case when sound reason demands it, and when the most ancient commentators on the Rule, who best understood the mind of the holy Father, interpreted the words of the Rule in this way?

As for what Haeftenus presses concerning the word “always”—for Saint Benedict says, “Let him always leave the seniors with the brothers”—this certainly does not carry the force he assigns it. For, as Hildemar says very well, that word is not always used universally in the divine Scriptures; nor is it so used in the Rule of Saint Benedict, as I could easily demonstrate. Therefore, when the holy Father says, “Let him always leave the seniors with the brothers,” this should not be understood as though he ought to take brothers with him every day. Saint Benedict does not permit that every day, but only when there are fewer guests and the abbot, for the sake of hospitality, anticipates the canonical hours of eating.

One might also object by citing the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and another Macarius, which prescribes as follows:

> “When the brothers come at the hour of the meal, a visiting brother shall not be permitted to eat with the brothers except with the one who presides, the Father, so that he may be edified.”

But this passage is understood not of every kind of guest, but of visiting brothers—that is, those arriving from far away—whom it is not always expedient to admit [Col. 0800C] with the brothers. Nor does it concern every visiting brother, but one who arrives at the hour of the meal and consequently finds nothing prepared for him, at least nothing by which he might be received with somewhat greater humanity.

For those to whom these arguments are not sufficient, what Peter the Venerable writes to Saint Bernard ought certainly to suffice. He says (Book I, Letter 28):

> “Does not the abbot, by feeding all whom he feeds from the monastery’s substance, make them participants in his own table? But if, according to you, the Rule can in no way be fulfilled by us in this manner, and it is asserted that this is the command—that they eat with the abbot—this sometimes happens in the case of respectable persons. For we believe it indecent that, in the presence of the assembly, an incongruity displeasing to everyone should be introduced indiscriminately among persons of every kind; and perhaps scandal might thereby arise even among good people.
>
> “If you object that guests ought to be joined to the abbot’s table not in the assembly but outside the assembly, we reply that on this pretext abbots have been accustomed to separate themselves from the brothers, to indulge themselves and their intimates in more luxurious banquets under the pretext of receiving guests, and not to care for the feeding of their sheep. According to the Prophet—as we say without prejudice to the mystical meaning—they took what was fat and cast away what was weak; and when they drank the clearest water, they disturbed the rest with their feet and gave the Lord’s flock muddy and filthy water to drink. That is, while providing excellently for themselves, they cared nothing for the others.
>
> “Because they abused a good command badly, a new plaster had to be placed upon a new sore, and a command that had once been salutary had to be changed by more salutary counsel. Therefore, so that the vice which had arisen from virtue might again be extinguished by virtue, when the Rule had transferred the common table to a separate one, the rule of reason and charity once more brought it from the separate table to the common table. Hence our abbots, unless illness prevents them, always eat with us: sometimes with the guests, when such guests are present, and sometimes without them, but they never—or only rarely—depart from the common table. They do not allow anything to be lacking to guests and pilgrims.” [Col. 0800D–0801A]

Let them also hear another Peter, Peter Damian (Opusculum 33, chapter 7):

> “Several monasteries in our region have recently imposed upon themselves an excellent rule of discipline: among their other works of piety, the abbot always keeps three poor men beside him at his private table and sets before each of them the same measure of food that any brother receives. For since the regular rule prescribes that the abbot’s table should always be with the guests, in this way both requirements are newly fulfilled: the abbot’s table is joined not to the proud of the world but to holy guests, and he himself does not cease to eat with the brothers.”

# CHAPTER LVII  
## On the Craftsmen of the Monastery

[Col. 0801]

[Col. 0801A] If there are craftsmen in the monastery, let them practice their crafts with all humility, if the abbot permits it. But if any one of them becomes proud [Note: [Col. 0801B] Hildemar: “becomes lifted up.”] because of his skill in his craft, on the ground that he appears to contribute something to the monastery, let such a man be removed [Note: [Col. 0801B] Oxford: “let him depart.” Cassinese, with Floriacensis and certain others: “let him be raised up.” Others: “let him be expelled.”] from that craft; and let him not pass through it again unless, after he has been humbled, the abbot should once more command him to do so.

If anything from the work of the craftsmen is to be sold, let those through whose hands the transaction is to be conducted take care that they presume to commit no fraud against the monastery. Let them always remember Ananias and Sapphira (Acts 5), lest perhaps the death which they suffered in the body be suffered in the soul by these men, or by all who commit any fraud concerning the monastery’s goods. In the prices themselves, however, let the evil of avarice not creep in [Note: [Col. 0802B] Hildemar: “let it not creep in.”]; but let the goods always be sold somewhat more cheaply than they are sold by other secular people [Note: [Col. 0802B] Some copies: “than they may be sold.” Other copies omit the phrase], so that God may be glorified in all things.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0801]

[Col. 0801B] “If there are craftsmen in the monastery, let them practice their crafts with all humility and reverence, provided that the abbot has ordered it.”

Since everything in monasteries is subject to obedience, Saint Benedict did not permit craftsmen even to practice the crafts they knew unless the abbot commanded it. He could derive this from the ancient rules of the monks, for the Pachomian Rule says (Article 123 in the Codex Regularum):

> “No one shall do any work, carry about vessels full of water, or even twist a cord, unless the superior has ordered it.” [Col. 0801C]

And when Saint Basil was asked (Short Rules, Question 142), “Should those who know crafts undertake any work without the knowledge or command of the one who presides and is responsible for the work?” he replied:

> “Such a man will be guilty of theft, or will be like those who join themselves to thieves.”

The same may be seen in the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, chapter 33, and in the Rule of Saint Aurelian for Monks, chapter 23.

Those who were working, however, remained alone, and no one was permitted to enter another’s workshop without the abbot’s authorization:

> “Let no one,” says the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chapter 26), “have the shameless and importunate boldness to enter, without the order of a senior, either the storeroom or any of the individual workshops of the craftsmen; for this presumption greatly impedes the common usefulness and causes resentment in the craftsmen’s hearts through excessive importunity.”

“If any one of them becomes proud because of his skill in his craft, on the ground that he appears to contribute something to the monastery, let such a man be removed from that craft.”

“And deservedly,” says Gerardus Belga the monk, “he is forbidden his craft and workmanship who loses more by them than he gains.” For the man who becomes proud because of his skill loses his soul for the sake of the slight and temporal profit he contributes to the monastery, and nothing is more precious than the soul. He is altogether far removed from the humility of the Egyptian monks, concerning whom Cassian writes (Book IV, chapter 14):

> “Although each of them contributed daily to the monastery from his own work and sweat such proceeds that from them he could support not only his own frugality but also have an abundance for the needs of many, nevertheless he was not puffed up in anything, nor did he flatter himself over the great profit and sweat of his labor. Apart from two *paximatia*, which there were sold for scarcely three denarii, no one presumed to take anything more for himself.”

Those whom Saint Benedict removes from their craft, Saint Basil likewise wished their work to be removed from the work of the brothers (Long Rules, chapter 29):

> “The work of one who is discovered either to murmur or to be proud in spirit while laboring,” he says, “must not be mixed with the labor performed by those humble in heart and contrite in spirit; nor should it at all be consumed for the use of religious persons, because what is exalted among men is an abomination before God . . . . The superiors must carefully ensure that they neither undermine the judgment of the one who said, ‘He who walks in the blameless way served me; he who acts proudly shall not dwell in the midst of my house,’ nor support one who mixes transgression with the commandment and stains his work by the negligence of his labor or by the elevation of his spirit, which exalts him above the rest, allowing him to persist in this perversity. This happens when they approve his work and do not permit him to arrive at a recognition of his own defect.” [Col. 0802B–C]

“And let him not pass through it again unless, after he has been humbled, the abbot should once more command him to do so.”

Here Hildemar notes two things. First, it is not in the abbot’s power to involve again in the same craft a proud craftsman who has been removed from it unless he has been humbled. Second, even after being humbled, he may not return to it unless the abbot permits him.

“If anything from the work of the craftsmen is to be sold.”

The ancient monks sold their work not only to provide themselves with necessities but also to relieve the poverty of others and to have something from which they could give to those suffering need.

“Let them take care.”

“That is, the abbot and the brothers, because such works are common property,” says Boherius. Yet Saint Benedict seems to be speaking of the craftsmen themselves, although they would dispose of their work according to the abbot’s pleasure.

“Through whose hands the transaction is to be conducted.”

“That is, into whose hands the goods are to be placed for sale, so that he may be a lawful or trustworthy seller,” says Richard of Saint Angelo. Thus the monks themselves should not sell them, but should do so through members of the household or other friends, because it is a great danger for monks to leave the cloister even for the shortest distance.

For the same reason Saint Stephen of Grandmont (On the Rule, chapter 15) did not wish his brothers to purchase anything themselves, but said:

> “When you wish to buy something, command one of your friends to bring it to you. If, after you have asked him to purchase it, he does not wish to give it to you, do not accept it in any way. But perhaps you will say to us, ‘We shall trade better if we go to the markets.’ We forbid this to you, for it is much better for you to lose a little property than, by returning to the world, to lose your soul.” [Col. 0802D–0803A]

And indeed, it was formerly decreed that monks should not sell, as may be seen throughout the councils. Yet before the time of Saint Benedict they commonly practiced this, although Saint Basil by no means approves it. Concerning the sale of their work he writes (Long Rules, chapter 39):

> “Care must be taken that the brothers’ work not be exposed for sale somewhere far away, lest they themselves go out into public for the sake of selling. For it is more honorable and also more useful for mutual edification and the careful preservation of daily discipline that they work in one place, so that it is better to deduct something from the just price than to travel beyond the boundaries of the region for the sake of a small profit.
>
> “If experience itself shows that this cannot be done, places and cities of pious men should be chosen, lest we establish a fruitless form of perfection. Care must also be taken that several brothers travel together to the appointed markets, each carrying what he has made. They should avoid the common company of strangers, so that they may complete the journey with psalms and prayers and with the other forms of edification they practice among themselves.
>
> “When they have arrived at the place to which they are to travel, they should choose the same lodgings, so that they may watch over one another and neglect no time of prayer, whether by day or by night. They should also avoid encounters with the avaricious, with whom it is difficult to agree in selling, and with fraudulent men. This can be done with less loss when one is accompanied by many than when one is alone, for even the most unjust men flee the testimony of many.” [Col. 0803A–B]

“Let them remember Ananias and Sapphira, etc.”

Saint Benedict seems here to imply that Ananias and Sapphira suffered only bodily death, not death of the soul. This is also asserted by many highly authoritative Fathers of the Church, especially Origen, *Tractate 8 on Matthew*; Saint Augustine, Book III *Against Parmenianus*, and Sermon 148; Cassian, *Conference 6*, chapter 11; and Peter Damian, *Opusculum 12*, chapter 3. See Haeftenus, Book IX, Treatise 3, Question 4. [Col. 0803C]

“In the prices themselves, however, let the evil of avarice not creep in.”

For this is the servitude of idols, which, as Gerardus Belga says, “does not make a monk filthy, but a monk a devil. For what pride makes out of an angel, avarice makes out of a monk; and just as pride accuses an angel of ingratitude toward God, so avarice makes a monk perjured.” [Col. 0804A]

“But let the goods always be sold somewhat more cheaply than they are sold by secular people.”

Evagrius teaches the same in *Monastics*, no. 8 (Volume III of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*):

> “Whether you sell or buy, defraud yourself a little of the just price, lest, being led into excessively exacting habits or into greed for profit in regard to price, you fall into causes harmful to the soul, etc.”

And the Rule of the Master (chapter 85):

> “When each craft has produced something finished, unnecessary for the monastery’s uses, or in abundance for sending eulogies, and the value of the price has been inquired, however much it can be sold for by secular people, let it always be sold for a lower price by a smaller number of coins, so that in this respect it may be recognized that spiritual men are distinguished and separated from secular practices . . . . This reduction in price ought to be determined by the abbot’s judgment for the craftsmen, so that they may know what sum should be received from the buyers and may not be able to commit fraud in the price received, since the abbot already knows the amount.”

The Rule of Saint Stephen of Grandmont says likewise (chapter 16):

> “If you can sell grain, or anything else purchased by you for your expenses, at a higher price than that for which you bought it, do not do so out of greed; for by this you would become merchants. Rather, we command you to sell what you sell more cheaply and to buy what you buy more dearly, so that you may always turn away from fraud.”

Hildemar gives the practical application of this statute:

> “If others wish to give twenty denarii for that object, you should give one less—that is, nineteen. And although the Rule does not say this specifically, it is understood that, when you buy something for which others are willing to give twenty denarii, you should give twenty-one.”

And Udalricus, describing the customs of the Cluniacs, says (Book III, chapter 11):

> “Whenever the chamberlain has bought or sold something of this kind, after completing the transaction, he voluntarily adds or returns several denarii to the merchant with whom he has dealt, according to the nature of the transaction and the person involved, because of Saint Benedict’s command that our goods should always be sold more cheaply than those of other people.” [Col. 0804B–C]

With what religious scrupulousness Saint Pachomius wished this to be observed may be seen in his Life, in Bollandus, no. 23, and in Surius, chapter 75, May 14. See also the Life of Saint Philibert, abbot of Jumièges, no. 21, Second Century of Benedictine Sources.

# CHAPTER LVIII  
## On the Discipline for Receiving Brothers

[Col. 0803]

[Col. 0803C] When someone newly comes for conversion [Note: [Col. 0803D] Some copies: “for community life”], he is not to be granted an easy entrance. Rather, as the Apostle says: “Test the spirits, whether they are from God” (1 John 4). Therefore, if the newcomer perseveres in knocking, and after four or five days appears to bear patiently the injuries inflicted upon him and the difficulty of entering, and persists in his request [Note: [Col. 0803D] Narbonne: “persists in his request”], let entrance be granted him, and let him remain for a few days in the guesthouse. Afterward let him be in the novices’ cell, where he shall meditate, eat, and sleep.

Let a senior be assigned to him who is suited to winning souls, who shall watch over him with the utmost care and concern to see whether he truly seeks God, whether he is zealous for the Work of God, for obedience, and for reproaches. Let all the hard and difficult things by which one goes to God be proclaimed to him. If he promises perseverance in his stability [Note: [Col. 0803D] Some copies: *de stabilitate sua perseverantiam* (“perseverance in his stability”); Sabinus: *stabilitatis suae perseverantiam* (“perseverance in his stability”) [Col. 0804D]; Narbonne: *Deo stabilitatis suae perseverantiam* (“perseverance in his stability to God”)], after the lapse of two months let this Rule be read through to him in order, and let him be told:

> “Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier. If you can observe it [Note: [Col. 0804D] Some copies: “keep it”], enter; but if you cannot, depart freely.”

If he still remains, let him then be led to the aforementioned novices’ cell, and let him again be tested in all patience.

After the lapse of six months [Note: [Col. 0804D] Some copies: “after six months”], let the Rule be read to him, so that he may know what he is entering. If he still remains, after four months let the same Rule be read to him again. If, after deliberating with himself, he promises to observe everything and to keep all that is commanded him, then let him be received into the community, knowing himself to be bound by the law of the Rule [Note: [Col. 0805B] Oxford: “knowing that he is established under the law of the Rule”; Hildemar, with some copies: “knowing that he is established by the law of the Rule”; Cassinese: “knowing that he is now established under the Rule”; Menardus thinks it should read: “knowing that he is established by the law of the Rule”; Sabinus: “knowing that he is subject to the law of the Rule”; Narbonne: “knowing that he is established into the law of the Rule”], so that from that day onward he is not permitted to leave the monastery or to shake his neck free from the yoke of the Rule, which, after such lengthy deliberation, he was permitted either to excuse himself from or to accept.

The one who is to be received shall promise in the oratory before everyone concerning his stability [Note: [Col. 0805B] Sabinus: “his stability”], his conversion of conduct [Note: [Col. 0806B] Hildemar: “conversion”], and his obedience [Note: [Col. 0806B] Hildemar and Florence: “obedience”] before God and his saints, so that, if he should ever act otherwise, he may know that he is to be condemned by the One whom he mocks [Note: [Col. 0806B] Oxford, with some copies: “by God”]. Concerning this promise of his, let him draw up a petition addressed to the names of the saints whose relics are there and to the present abbot [Note: [Col. 0806B] Oxford: “with the abbot present”]. Let him write this petition with his own hand; or, if he does not know letters, let another write it at his request. Let the novice make his mark and place it with his own hand upon the altar. When he has placed it there, let the novice himself immediately begin this verse:

> “Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my hope” (Psalm 118).

Let the whole community respond to this verse three times [Col. 0806A], adding, “Glory to the Father.” Then let the novice brother prostrate himself at the feet of each person, asking them to pray for him; and from that day [Note: [Col. 0806B] Some copies: “from that hour”] let him be reckoned among the community.

If he has possessions, let him either distribute them first to the poor or, after making a solemn donation, give them to the monastery, reserving nothing for himself, since he is to know that from that day he will no longer have power even over his own body. Immediately, therefore, let him be stripped in the oratory of his own garments in which he is clothed and let him be dressed in the monastery’s garments. The garments of which he was stripped are to be stored in the wardrobe, so that, if at any time—God forbid, through the persuasion of the devil—he should consent to leave the monastery, he may be stripped of the monastery’s clothing and cast out. Yet the petition of his which the abbot took from above the altar [Col. 0806B] is not to be returned to him; rather, it is to be preserved in the monastery.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0805]

[Col. 0805B] “When someone newly comes for conversion, he is not to be granted an easy entrance.”

Since the chief good of the religious life depends upon the reception of novices, Saint Benedict did not wish everyone to be admitted easily and without discrimination into monasteries. Rather, he wished those tested by God’s Spirit to be led, those who lacked the defects and impediments that ordinarily close the entrance to a monastery, and who were endowed with both bodily and spiritual qualities without which it is scarcely, or not at all, possible to live as a monk. What those defects and what those spiritual qualities are must be briefly investigated.

Above all, our predecessors judged that slaves were to be excluded from the monastic life unless they had first been granted freedom by their own masters. Thus Saint Ferreolus says in chapter 5:

> “Let him be asked whether he is free.”

And Saint Fructuosus says in the Common Monastic Rule, chapter 4:

> “If they are slaves, let them not be received unless they bring with them freedom granted by their own master, ready to be presented.”

Later, however, the civil laws of the emperors were somewhat more indulgent toward them. See Menardus’s notes on the *Conciliar Rule*, chapter 65, section 13.

Second, they required a lawful age. Those who had not reached it were not admitted to the monastery. We shall speak of the necessary age below, when we discuss profession.

[Col. 0805D] Third, the emperor Maurice prohibited from the monastic life those who had held public office or had been counted among the soldiers, unless they had completed their military service or had been discharged because of bodily weakness. Saint Gregory the pope complains about this matter when writing to the physician Theodore, in these words (Book II of the *Registrum*, chapter 103):

> “He ordered that no one who had held public office, no one who had been marked by office or by the hand, or who had been counted among the soldiers, might convert in a monastery unless perhaps his military service had been completed. This law, as those who know the ancient laws say, was first promulgated by Julian, of whom we all know how much he was opposed to God.”

He also wrote in response concerning the injustice of this law. Nevertheless, being subject to it, he obeyed it, promulgating it in various places, as he himself testifies in these words (Book II of the *Registrum*, chapter 100):

> “I, indeed, subject to the command, caused this same law to be transmitted through various regions of the earth; and because the law itself is in no way in harmony with almighty God, behold, through the document of my representation I have informed the most serene lords. Thus in both respects I have fulfilled what I owed: I have both offered obedience to the emperor and, for God’s sake, have not kept silent about what I thought.”

Nor was the holy pontiff’s rebuke entirely fruitless. For five years later, writing to several bishops, he said that soldiers coming to the monastery for the sake of conversion were not to be received rashly, but were to be tested for three years in their own habit before being clothed in the monastic dress:

> “In this matter, believe me, even the most serene and Christian emperor is altogether appeased.” [Col. 0806B–C]

Fourth, those joined in marriage, while their wife was alive and had not vowed continence, were by no means received:

> “If anyone wishes to convert while married,” says Saint Isidore (chapter 4), “he is not to be received into the monastery unless he has first been released by his spouse, who has professed chastity.”

The Council of Avranches in 1172, chapter 10 (in Spelman), says:

> “A man shall not enter the religious life while his wife remains in the world, nor a woman while her husband remains there, unless both have passed beyond the time for attending to the works of the flesh.”

And the Constitutions of Richard, bishop of Salisbury (in the same source), say:

> “Let priests frequently teach the people and prohibit under anathema that either spouse should enter the religious life, and let neither be received except by us or by our permission.” [Col. 0806C–D]

Hence Saint Gregory the pope, writing to Abbot Urbicus concerning the reception of Agatho, says (Book V of the *Registrum*, chapter 149):

> “Know that he is to be received only if his wife likewise wishes to convert. For since the two have become one body through the bond of marriage, it is unfitting that one part should convert and the other remain in the world.”

Elsewhere (Book IX, chapter 44), he orders a husband who had converted against his wife’s will—even though he had already been tonsured and made a monk—to be restored to his own wife.

I also read the following in the Book of Cistercian Usages (chapter 102):

> “If it should happen that someone bound by the bond of marriage is received by the monks in ignorance of the fact, let him be expelled as soon as it becomes known. But if afterward he produces the seal of his bishop or a reliable witness showing that his wife, by vowing chastity, has released him, he may be received, provided that he again completes a full year of probation. If he has already received the monastic habit, let him likewise depart; but if he dies in the cell, let what is done for him be done as for a monk.” [Col. 0806D–0807A]

Nevertheless, Saint Basil wished married persons to be admitted even against the reluctance of their spouse. For he says (Long Rules, chapter 12):

> “If some who are married wish to approach this life, it must be examined whether they do so with consent, according to the Apostle’s command. For, he says, the one who is such does not have authority over his own body. They are then to be received after several witnesses have been brought forward; for nothing owed to God in obedience is to be preferred to anything else.
>
> “But if the other party dissents and resists, understanding less clearly what pleases God, one must remember the Apostle’s saying: ‘God has called us to peace’; and the Lord’s command: ‘If anyone comes to me and does not hate father and mother and wife, etc., he cannot be my disciple.’ Nothing, therefore, is to be preferred to obedience to God.” [Col. 0807A–B]

Human laws also favor Basil, as we learn from Saint Gregory (Book IX of the *Registrum*, chapter 44), although Gregory does not approve them:

> “For although worldly law orders that, for the sake of conversion, a marriage may be dissolved even against the will of either party, divine law nevertheless does not permit this to be done.”

See Cassian, *Conference 21*, chapter 9.

Fifth, those who are received ought to be healthy and robust in body, so that they may bear the yoke of the monastic life more easily, and especially they ought to be free from contagious and incurable diseases. For although the monks of Fulda once petitioned Charlemagne in a supplication (no. 6):

> “That suitable compassion be shown to all who come to the monastery out of love for this life; that neither the sick, nor the elderly, nor the delicate be driven away by hardship, but that all be received with mercy and that the assistance they request be honorably granted to their infirmity,”

nevertheless experience, that great teacher, showed that from receiving such people the vigor of regular observance was relaxed to no small degree, although nothing ought to be more important to monks than that observance.

Hence Saint Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont, says:

> “We command” (On the Rule, chapter 44) “that no one under twenty years of age, nor any sick man unless he is able to come either riding or walking, be received into this religious life. We also prohibit anyone clearly known to be a leper from being received into our religious life.” [Col. 0807B–C]

And the Cistercian Institutions (Distinction 10, chapter 2) say:

> “Novices who contract leprosy during their probation are to be dismissed by right, but provision may be made for them out of mercy. The same is established concerning epileptics.”

Sixth, the greatest care must be taken that the person to be received does not convert unwillingly or become a monk because his parents compel him. Thus the monks of Fulda petition in their supplication (no. 9):

> “That no one be compelled by force to become a monk or to be tonsured for the clergy, whether he is free or a slave; for such persons, once received into a monastery, are the authors of crimes and the executors of vices.”

Seventh, the Cistercians prescribe (Ancient Book of Definitions, dist. 11, chap. 1) that “in receiving clerical novices, such diligence must be exercised regarding competent learning, lawful age, and the testing of spirits, whether they are from God, that they may redound to the usefulness and honor of the order. [Col. 0807C] Therefore it is most strictly forbidden that anyone henceforth be received into the order unless it is established that he was born of a lawful marriage, or unless he produces letters of the Apostolic See concerning his dispensation. But if anyone suffering from an irregularity of birth should be received through the recipient’s deceitful concealment, he is to be expelled by the visitor as soon as this becomes known to him; and an abbot delinquent in this matter is to be summoned by the father abbot or the visitor before the general chapter. The same penalty is to apply to anyone who presumes to associate with our order a member of one of the mendicant orders, or an apostate, 741 or fugitive, or anyone from another order.”

In the ancient statutes of the Carthusians I also read the following (part II, chap. 23, no. 3): “If someone wishing to become a monk, lay brother, or a *redditus* (one given over to the house) pleases us enough to be received for probation, he is first to be asked before witnesses whether he has left any order, whether he is free, whether he has been absolved, whether he is free from an incurable disease, and whether he has made satisfaction for any complaints against him. [Col. 0808A] He who wishes to become a monk is additionally to be asked whether he is capable of advancing to sacred orders. He is also to be examined as to whether he knows and is able to read and sing. Whoever he may be, cleric or layman, he should know that if he has concealed what he was questioned about, he may even be expelled after profession.”

The same provisions appear in the New Collection of Statutes, part II, chap. 17, no. 11. Nearly the same provisions are also found in the Bursfeld Ceremonial, dist. 3, chap. 1.

Among more recent regulations, the Olivetans establish the following concerning the reception of novices (Constitutions, part II, chap. 58): “In those to be received as novices, it must first be considered whether they are moved by the Spirit of God; whether, being born of a lawful marriage, they are of good character; whether, having completed their fifteenth year, they have entered their sixteenth; whether they have led a good life in the past; and whether they have at least learned grammar. Care must be taken that no one be received through favor or goodwill unless these qualities shine forth in him. Bastards and those afflicted with incurable diseases are not to be admitted. Criminals, evil-doers, [Col. 0808B] infamous persons, and men of bad life, who dare to flee to religion as to an asylum in order to avoid secular justice, are to be excluded unless they have for a long period displayed the most certain signs of repentance, contrition, and devotion. Those who have fathers engaged in infamous occupations are not to be accepted unless they are tested by a stricter examination than others and unless as many qualities are found in them as suffice to erase the stain of their father. Those expelled from another religious order, or those who have abandoned one, are not to be accepted, even if they remained in it for only a very few days.”

The Constitutions of the Celestines likewise state (chap. 5, § 2): “Those to be received must be sound in body, born of a lawful marriage, free in status, and of lawful age, having completed at least their fourteenth year; instructed in the rudiments of grammar; not excommunicated, not schismatic, and not professed in another religion, unless the supreme pontiff has expressly ordered that they be received. They must not be stained by any common infamy, suspected of any error, criminal, [Col. 0808C] burdened with debt, or liable to render an account of any administration; they must be sound in mind, fearing God, and must have observed and maintained the faith and obedience of the holy Roman Church in all things and in every respect. They must also have suitable limbs and no notable defect in them, nor scars on the face; finally, they must be such as can lawfully and canonically be promoted to sacred orders. If they are over twenty years of age, they are not to be admitted except by the definitorial chapter.”

Finally, the Fulienses declare (Constitutions, chap. 58) ten impediments by which those knocking at the door of religious life are to be excluded:

1. An age below seventeen years, or above forty-five for clerics; for lay brothers or *donati*, below twenty or above forty;

2. if anyone has been a heretic, or is probably suspected of heresy, or is even descended from Jews;

3. if he has been a schismatic;

4. if he is bound by an irregularity admitting no dispensation, or only a difficult one;

5. if he was not born of a lawful marriage;

6. if he is bound by debt, [Col. 0808C] or is obliged to assist the poverty of certain persons;

7. if, as a future cleric, he is ignorant of the Latin language;

8. if he is marked by any disgrace, especially in the very place where he seeks the habit;

9. if he is stained by shameful acts or crimes;

10. if he suffers from such a bodily infirmity that he appears unable to endure the austerity of discipline for long.

Nevertheless, except in the case of impediments 2, 6, 9, and 10, a dispensation may be granted for just reasons by the superior of the congregation with the counsel of the assisting elders.

Besides such impediments, by which entry into religion is delayed or entirely prevented, William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, writing to the brothers of Mont-Dieu, also requires simplicity and humble prudence in the person being received, in these words (chap. 12): “The inhabitants of the cells must be recruited from two kinds of men: either from the simple, [Col. 0809A] who appear fervent and humble both in understanding and in will for attaining religious prudence; or from the prudent, who are shown to be devoted imitators of religious and sound simplicity. But foolish pride, or proud folly, must always remain far from the tabernacle of the righteous. Every pride is foolish, although not every folly is proud; for folly without pride is sometimes found to be simplicity. If it is ignorant, perhaps it can be taught; and if it cannot be taught, perhaps it can be guided. The habitation of religion is a proper city of refuge for simplicity, unless that simplicity is unwilling to be humbled or is so brutish that it cannot be governed and guided. A good will, however, even if very brutish, is not to be abandoned, but is to be directed by salutary counsel toward a laborious and active life. But the proud person, however prudent he may seem to himself, must be left to himself and driven away; for if a proud man is admitted, on the first day he enters to live there he begins giving laws, while the excessively foolish cannot learn the laws he finds. Therefore it must be carefully [Col. 0809B] and prudently weighed who is admitted to live with him; for whoever lives with himself has with him only himself, such as he is. A bad man, however, never lives safely with himself, because he lives with a bad man; and no one is more troublesome to him than he himself.”

“But as the Apostle says: Test the spirits to see whether they are from God.” For there are four kinds of spirits, as Saint Bernard teaches (Sermon 23, On Various Matters): the spirit of the flesh, which persuades to softness; the spirit of the world, which persuades to vanity; the evil spirit of the devil, which persuades to bitterness, such as quarrels, scandals, and the like. Sometimes our own spirit joins itself to these; and finally there is the Spirit of God, which persuades to chastisement of the body, humiliation of the heart, and preservation. It is chiefly this spirit that Saint Benedict requires here. Saint Pachomius had the same spirit in view in his Rule, art. 26; Saint Basil in the Rule translated by Rufinus, chap. 7; Saint Ferreolus in his Rule, chap. 5; and the Rule of Tarnat, chap. 1.

[Col. 0809C] “Therefore, if the one who comes perseveres in knocking, and after four or five days appears to bear patiently the insults inflicted upon him and the difficulty of entry, etc.” The Holy Father extends the probation of those coming for conversion only to the fourth or fifth day, imitating the great Antony, who, according to Palladius (Lausiac History, chap. 28), received Paul the Simple into his cell after the fourth day. In the monastery of Abbot Timothy, too, those who knocked were tested for five days, as is clear from the Life of Saint Simeon Stylites, chap. 2.

Saint Pachomius lengthened this number of days somewhat. Palladius writes (Lausiac History, chap. 20) that he admitted Macarius, after rejecting and rebuking him, after seven days. This period of probation is also established by the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius, chap. 7, where they say: “Those who are such, when they wish to free themselves from the allurements of the world, should, upon approaching the monastery, lie before the doors for a week. None of the brothers is to associate with them, and hard and laborious tasks are always to be assigned to them. [Col. 0809D] If, however, they persevere in knocking, entry is not to be denied them.”

Others preferred to establish ten days of probation. Cassian writes: “Anyone seeking to be received into the discipline of the coenobium is not admitted at all until, keeping watch before the doors for ten days or more, he has demonstrated the judgment of his perseverance and desire, as well as of his humility and patience.”

Likewise, in the Rule of Life prescribed for monks by Saint David (in his Life, in Bollandus, 1 March): “Whoever, turning from the world through a holy purpose, desired to enter the company of the brothers first remained for ten days before the doors of the monastery, as though rejected and reviled with insulting words. If, however, making good use of patience, he persevered until the tenth day, he was accepted and placed under an elder who was in charge at the time, and served him. There, laboring for a long time and broken by many hardships, he finally earned [Col. 0810A] the fellowship of the brothers.”

Hence Saint Fructuosus, bishop, also states in his First Rule (chap. 21): “The decrees of the Fathers teach that one converted from the world is not to be received into the monastery unless he has first given proof of himself through work and want, through insults and abuse; and unless, persisting for ten days at the gate of the coenobium, he has devoted himself to prayer and fasting, to patience and humility.” But in his Second Rule (chap. 4) he shortened this number of days so that “monks who seek to enter the monastery for the sake of religion must first keep watch before the doors for three days and nights, and must deliberately be continually reproached by the weekly officers.”

What the probation of those knocking was like in the meantime is suggested by Saint Benedict when he says that, after enduring insults and the difficulty of entry, the one who perseveres should be granted admission. Here he seems to have had in view the passage of Cassian (Book IV, chap. 3): “When, [Col. 0810B] having fallen at the knees of all the passing brothers, and having been deliberately rejected and despised by everyone, as though he desired to enter the monastery not for the sake of religion but under pressure of necessity, and when he had also undergone many insults and reproaches and thereby given proof of his steadfastness, and when his future character had been revealed by his endurance of reproaches in temptations, and he had thus been received after the ardor of his mind had been tested, the greatest care is taken to determine whether any contamination from his former possessions clings to him, even to the extent of a single coin.”

In the Rule of the Master it is prescribed (chap. 90) that “when some newcomer has fled from the world to the monastery for the service of God and has declared that he wishes to convert, he is not to be believed so easily. For, as a pretense, the abbot is to deny him residence in the monastery by words alone and not by deeds; grave matters are to be proposed for his probation; things contrary to his wishes and bitter to him are to be announced in order to discover his obedience; and daily fasts are to be promised him. From the reading of the Rule and the abbot’s statement he should recognize this also: that in the monastery no one is permitted to say, ‘This I want, and this I do not want; this I love, and this I hate,’ so that his own will may not be chosen. Let him know that whoever has converted in the monastery is not permitted to have whatever he wants according to his own will.” [Col. 0810C]

[Col. 0810D] In much the same way Saint Stephen, founder of the order of Grandmont, would approach those whom he received into his discipline: “When someone came to him and asked him for charity so that he might come to him,” says a manuscript book on his teaching, “before granting it he would answer him in this manner: ‘Brother, how will you be able to bear the burden that you wish to impose upon yourself? Look at the cross: it is very difficult to remain there. If you come here, you will be fastened to it, and you will lose the dominion that you possess over yourself, over your eyes, your mouth, and your other limbs. You will abandon your own will in eating, fasting, sleeping, and keeping vigil, and in many other matters; and what you love in the world will come to be hateful to you. From then on you will not return to the house of your relatives; and if they come to you, you must never show them your poverty. Will you be able, brother, to be a digger, to carry wood and dung, and to serve all the brothers? All this would be easy; but, seized in such a prison, you will remain where there is no opening through which you may return to the world unless you yourself make one. I will not take care of you, nor will I allow you to take care of yourself: for I have cut off my feet from the world, and if I do not return for my own sake, I will not return for yours. There is still something else: perhaps I might send you into some forest, and I would take the food that you acquired by laboring with your own hands and a wooden spade and give it to those who guard me here. But something even more horrible remains: it is a hundred times better for you to be damned in the world than here. For whoever falls from a higher place is more seriously injured; and if you fell from here into hell, you would be lower than all the others who are lost. You can instead go to any monastery where you will find large buildings and delicacies appointed for their proper times; there you will find animals and wide lands, whereas here there is only the cross and poverty.’ [Col. 0811A] By such words the good man tested whether the other possessed a heart firmly resolved to abandon the world.”

[Col. 0811A] Hildemar, also explaining this passage of the Rule, says: “When someone comes to the monastery, he ought to say insults to him in this manner: ‘Brother, perhaps you have committed theft, or adultery, 745 or some other crime; and now you have come to the monastery both to deceive yourself and to deceive another.’ But the first time he ought to speak these insults harshly; the second time, more gently, whether by deed or word. If for four or five days he patiently bears this delay or these insults, then he ought to receive him into the guesthouse.”

Again: the abbot “ought to say to him: ‘Brother, you cannot observe what you are asking for. It is better for you to remain in the world than to come here and promise things that you cannot observe. Perhaps you did evil in the world; now you come here to destroy others.’” He adds: “One of the brothers ought, however, to say to him privately: ‘Brother, our Rule says that our abbot should not receive you quickly; but if you persevere in knocking, he will do for you as you ask, because the Rule says: “Let entry not be granted easily.” Therefore our abbot did not tell you to come.
