But come to the gate of the monastery, and let us offer you some help and relief [Col. 0811B] until you speak with him again.’”

Bernard of Cassino writes likewise: “For the sake of probation, the doorkeeper may say certain words to him that usually quickly call impatient people back to their senses, such as: ‘Brother, how do we know whether you have committed theft or adultery, or whether you are of servile condition and fleeing from your master?’—and similar things. Or he may perhaps impose upon him some extremely menial task, which may seem to be offered as an insult, such as cleaning some filthy place, and other things of the same kind.”

See the probation of Drogo, monk of Fleury, in Aimoinus, Book I of the Miracles of Saint Benedict, no. 13, and the Council of Clovesho, chap. 24, in Spelman, vol. I.

“And let him remain in the guest cell for a few days.” What he is to do there, and how long he is to remain, Richard of Saint Angelo and Boherius consider to be left to discretion. But [Col. 0811C] the matter can be learned both from the ancient founders of Rules and from commentators on the Benedictine Rule:

“When, therefore,” says Cassian (Book IV, chap. 7), “someone has been received and approved by this perseverance of which we have spoken, and, having put aside his own clothing, has been girded with the monastic habit, he is not immediately permitted to mix with the congregation of the brothers. Rather, he is assigned to an elder who, living apart not far from the entrance of the monastery, has charge of the care of pilgrims and newcomers, and devotes every attention to their reception and kindness. When he has served there for a full year, displaying his service toward the pilgrims without any complaint, and has thereby been imbued with the first training in humility and patience and recognized through long practice in it, he is then to be admitted to the congregation of the brothers.”

Similarly, the Rule of Tarnat (chap. 1): “Assigned to one of the elders, he is to be ordered to serve the newcomers until his devotion has been demonstrated by the witness of his patience.”

The Rule of Saint Isidore (chap. 4): “He who has renounced [Col. 0811D] the world and come to the monastery is not immediately to be assigned to the company of monks; for each person’s life ought to be examined in the service of the guesthouse for three months.”

The Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chap. 21): “He shall carry straw for guests or pilgrims, warm water for their feet, and humbly perform all services; carrying a bundle of wood daily upon his back, he shall bring it to the weekly officers.”

The Rule of the Master (chap. 87): “During these two months, under the care of the brothers who guard the pilgrims, they themselves are likewise to be guarded unexpectedly; and they are to sleep in the pilgrims’ cell, so that their entrance into or departure from the monastery may be observed in the presence of the guards.”

Saint Basil may also have had this in view (in Rufinus, chap. 6), when he wrote: “Before he is inserted into the body of the fraternity, certain laborious tasks ought to be imposed upon him, tasks that secular people regard as disgraceful. It must be observed whether he willingly, freely, [Col. 0812A] and faithfully performs them, and whether he does not bear their humiliation heavily, and whether he is found tireless and ready in labor.”

Finally, Hildemar says: “Then he is to be received into the guest cell while still a layman. The brother who is in charge of the guesthouse ought to receive him and order him to remove the guests’ shoes, make a fire, and perform whatever services the guests require. That guest-brother should admonish him to strive to be obedient and mortified. If the guest-brother has come to know him over two months, then he should have the Rule read to him.”

Finally, the Council of Aachen states (canon 34): “Let entry into the monastery not be granted easily to a novice, and, for the sake of probation, let him serve the guests in the guest cell for a few days.”

But these practices had long since fallen into disuse. The Cluniacs kept novices in the guesthouse for only one day, according to Udalricus, Book II, chap. 1; the Cistercians for only three days, according to the Book of Usages, chap. 102; the Camaldolese for three or four days, according to their Constitutions, chap. 58; and the Vallisoletans [Col. 0812B] until they had read the Rule from beginning to end and had spent several days preparing for a general confession of sins, according to their Constitutions, chap. 58.

“Afterward let him be in the novice cell.” This cell was separated from the common dwelling of the brothers like another monastery, possessing its own cloister, refectory, kitchen, dormitory, infirmary, and washroom, as is clear from the ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall. This was entirely in keeping with the intention of the ancient monks, who did not permit novices to be mixed with the body of the congregation, as can be seen in Cassian, Book IV, chap. 7, already cited; in the Life of Saint Sabbas, vol. III of the Monuments of the Greek Church; in the Rules of Saint Ferreolus, chap. 5, and Saint Fructuosus, chap. 22; in Bede, Book IV of the Ecclesiastical History of the English People, chap. 23; and in the Life of Saint Austrudis, abbess of Laon, no. 34.

The same cell is mentioned in the Life of Saint Hermeland, in the Life of Saint William, duke and monk of Gellone, and in the Chronicle of Regino; in Leo of Ostia, [Col. 0812C] Cassinese Chronicle, Book III, chap. 31; in Udalricus, Book II, chap. 2; in the Statutes of Peter the Venerable, no. 19; and frequently elsewhere.

The Customs of the monastery of Farfa say concerning it: “Let a novice cell be constructed, and let it be arranged in four corners: namely, the first where they meditate, the second where they eat, the third where they sleep, and the fourth where the latrine is at the side.”

Later, with the passage of time, novices began to be mixed with professed monks. Udalricus, speaking of the Cluniacs, says: “When they are fewer in number, they do not sleep separately.”

The Statutes of Lanfranc, chap. 18, state: “Let him sleep in the novice cell, or in the dormitory. If the monastery does not have such a cell, let him sit separately in the cloister with his master, in the place assigned to the novices.”

Finally, Pope Clement VIII attempted to restore the ancient arrangement, decreeing that in all orders there should be a common novitiate in which novices would be educated in a place separate from the professed.

“Where he may meditate.” In saying that he should meditate, [Col. 0812D] Bernard of Cassino says, he understands reading, meditation, prayer, psalmody, and everything included among spiritual activities, so that meditation here serves as the genus. Boherius and Turrecremata agree; and Smaragdus says: “Let him meditate on canticles, psalms, and hymns, or on the precepts of the Rule that are to be handed down to him and observed.”

“Let him eat.” He is to follow precisely the same discipline as the professed monks, so that “when he eats, he should listen to a reading and remain silent,” as Hildemar says.

Udalricus is relevant here (Book II, chap. 2): “When the novices are about to dine, before the community they leave the church and, having washed their hands, proceed to the regular kitchen, so that each may bring his own beans. For the general dish or the pottage, as many rise from the table as are needed and as the person serving them in the place of the cellarer wishes; for they also have [Col. 0813A] readings and a bell, and in other ways imitate the same discipline that we have in the refectory.”

The Cassinese commentator explains this passage to mean “that the novices eat in the refectory together with the monks, but at a table separate from theirs, where they can conveniently be seen by the Fathers.”

“And let him sleep.” The master of the novices is to sleep with him; since he must be able to devote all care to them, he should not be separated from them. Hence Hildemar says: “That master of the novices ought to eat and sleep with him, and ought to be attentive in every respect, and must in no way leave him. He is to be admonished, corrected, excommunicated, and scourged just as a monk.”

“And let an elder be assigned to him who is suited to winning souls.” Since Saint Benedict had separated the novices from all fellowship with the brothers, and it would be no small danger for them to remain alone, he places over them a wise elder, suited to winning souls, who will instruct them in the religious life.

Haeftenus [Col. 0813B] understands this (Book IV, treatise 4, question 1) to mean that a separate elder should be assigned to each novice; but the arguments he offers in support of this scarcely establish it. Certainly, if separate masters were appointed over each novice, the novices would live not separately but mixed with the professed, and it would not be necessary to assign a separate cell to them, since the number of novices may at times approach the number of the professed. Moreover, it would be difficult to find so many masters in a congregation. For although you may easily find people who can be governed, you will scarcely find those who can govern—especially according to Haeftenus’s view, which requires the elder to be advanced not only in character but also in age.

He notes that three things are required in such an elder. 748 First, he must be old in age and character; for, he says, Cassian’s judgment is most true, that others cannot be profitably instructed by one “who has not in reality experienced the arduous struggles of the virtues. For the understanding of these matters can in no way be either handed down, understood, or retained in memory through idle meditation and verbal teaching; [Col. 0813C] everything rests solely upon experience and practice.”

Second, he must be suited to winning souls. Saint Basil describes such a man in these words (Sermon on the Renunciation of Worldly Goods): “In all the pursuits of the life you have chosen, follow as your most trustworthy guide a man of this kind: one who knows how to point out the sure path to God to those wishing to journey toward him; who is adorned with virtues; whose actions throughout his entire life testify that he possesses love for God; who has knowledge of the divine Scriptures; an upright man who recoils from greed, is not at all eager to involve himself in business, is tranquil, loves God, is devoted to the needy, is not irascible, and is forgetful of injuries; naturally inclined to teach those who approach him; not inflated by empty glory, not exalted by pride, not broken by flattery; stern and steadfast; finally, a man for whom nothing is preferable to God.”

Third, he must be solicitously attentive to the novices. [Col. 0813D] Saint Benedict explains how far this attentiveness should extend in the following words:

“And let him be solicitous as to whether he truly seeks God.” What it means to seek God truly and “in simplicity of heart,” as they say, Saint Bernard teaches: “not something else as though it were him, not something else besides him, not something else after him.” Further on he says: “If we do not wish to seek God in vain, let us seek him truly, seek him frequently, seek him perseveringly, so that we turn neither to something else before him, nor to something else with him, nor from him to something else. For it is easier for heaven and earth to pass away than for one who seeks in this manner not to find, one who asks in this manner not to receive, and one who knocks in this manner not to have the door opened.”

If someone now asks by what signs a novice may be recognized as seeking God in this way, Adam, abbot of Persenne, answers in a letter to the monk Osmund (vol. I of Baluze’s Miscellanies): “Certainly, if the master finds him ready for those three things; if he recognizes him as fervent in the work of God; if he sees him offering the good and cheerful service of obedience to superiors, equals, and inferiors; [Col. 0814A] if he can understand him to be patient in bearing reproaches; and if, with fortunate perseverance, he does not fail to bring a happy beginning to its conclusion.”

“To the work of God.” That is, to the divine office, so that he may see “whether, as soon as the signal for the hour of the divine office is heard, he immediately leaves whatever he may have in his hands and hastens there with the greatest speed; whether at night he hastens to arrive before the others for the work of God; whether he frequently arrives late, and for what reason; whether he anticipates the office; and whether he is diligent in learning the things that concern it,” as Haeftenus says (Book IV, treatise 3, question 5).

Smaragdus understands and extends “the work of God” here somewhat more broadly, namely “to those things that properly pertain to God: prayer, sacred reading, the nightly vigils, the daytime offices, fasting, and every divine service.” Similarly, Nicholas of Fractura understands it as “those things by which one goes to God, such as the canonical hours, the Lord’s Prayer, reading, psalmody, and the like.”

“To obedience.” This is the proper aim of [Col. 0814B] coenobitic life, in which the novice must above all be trained; if he departs from it even in the smallest degree, he must be driven far from the congregation. For, as William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, rightly said (On the Contemplative Life, to the Brothers of Mont-Dieu): “It is impossible for a discerning natural man, a prudent novice, or a wise beginner to remain long in a cell and endure in a congregation. Let him become foolish so that he may be wise, and let all his discernment consist in this: that in this matter there be no discernment.”

Hence Severus Sulpicius, speaking of monks (Dialogue 1, chap. 11), says: “The chief and first virtue there is obedience; nor is anyone coming to the monastery received by the abbot except one who has first been tested and approved and who will never refuse any command of the abbot, however arduous, difficult, or unworthy of being endured.”

Cassian likewise says (Book IV, chap. 8): “This will be his principal concern and instruction: to teach the younger man first to overcome his own wills. Exercising him carefully and diligently in these matters, he will [Col. 0814C] deliberately make a point of always commanding him to do those things that he perceives to be contrary to his mind. For, taught by many experiences, they hand down that a monk, and especially a younger one, cannot restrain even the pleasure of his desire unless he has first learned through obedience to mortify his own wills.”

“To reproaches.” By this he means insults, humiliations, mockery, abasement, and other mortifications both of mind and body. This is because, as Abbot Isaiah said (Monuments of the Greek Church, p. 445), “nothing is so useful to a novice monk as abuse; for just as a tree is irrigated each day, so is a novice when subjected to and enduring abuse.”

Hence Saint Basil writes (Longer Rule, chap. 10): “The manner of testing anyone should be whether he is prepared for every kind of humility without shame, so that he allows the most menial tasks to be imposed upon him, by which it may be established with certainty whether his zeal will be useful. Especially if anyone has abandoned a more distinguished life and aspired to that humility of life which is modeled on our Lord Jesus Christ, such tasks are to be assigned and imposed upon him as secular people regard as disgraceful. It must be observed whether, with complete diligence, he shows himself to be an unashamed laborer for the Lord.”

[Col. 0814D] “Let all hard and difficult things be announced to him.” First, at the monastery gate before he is admitted; second, in the guest cell after he has been admitted; third, in the novice cell where he is to be tested.

Adam, abbot of Persenne, explains what it means to announce hard and difficult things in the aforementioned letter (vol. I of Baluze’s Miscellanies): “To announce this to him means nothing other than to show from the Scriptures or from personal examples that the way leading to life is narrow and difficult. He certainly does not walk along that way who does not strive, according to the Lord’s command, to enter through the narrow gate.”

“Although ‘hard and difficult’ seem almost to mean the same thing,” says Bernard of Cassino, “those things are properly called hard which can be endured through perseverance. [Col. 0815A] Someone might perhaps bear the yoke of the Order lightly for two or three days, but it would be extremely difficult for one who does not love it to persevere to the end. Difficult things are the regular food, the abstinence of the Order, the hard bed, continual silence, the lengthy office, long vigils, self-abasement, the harsh commands of the superior, patience in adversity, total renunciation of the world and of affection for relatives and all kinsmen, living without possessions and without one’s own will, and similar things.”

“And if he promises perseverance in his stability.” That is, if he says that he will promise it, since his promise, which pertains to profession, is not yet to be received, say Bernard of Cassino, Richard, and Boherius.

“After the completion of two months.” Hildemar wishes these months to be spent in the guesthouse, with the remaining ten being spent in the novice cell. Yet the more equitable interpretation of the Rule [Col. 0815B] seems to indicate that the entire year of probation is to be completed in the novice cell, as Smaragdus, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius also teach with little ambiguity. In explaining the following words—“Let him be led into the aforementioned novice cell”—they assume that he has left it in order to hear the reading of the Rule.

“And let this Rule be read to him in order.” In accordance with the institutions of the ancient monks, who command that the Rule be read to those coming for conversion so that they may know why they are entering, as can be seen in the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers, chap. 1; in the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins, in the Recapitulation, chap. 8; in the Rule of Saint Aurelian, chap. 1; of Saint Ferreolus, chap. 5; of the monastery of Tarnat, chap. 1; and in the Rule of the Master.

Saint Benedict differs from these—if Saint Caesarius is excepted—in this one respect: they decree that the Rule be read only once to the person entering or admitted, whereas Saint Benedict prescribes it three times during the very year of probation. Pope Gregory IX renewed this provision in a constitution for Benedictine monks, decreeing that “hard and difficult things be announced to novices; and that, once admitted, the Rule be read and explained to them three times a year, at the periods of probation established by Blessed Benedict.”

The Holy Father instituted that this reading be carried out in order. Bernard of Cassino explains this to mean that it should not be “superficial, but careful, explanatory, and intelligible. And this,” he says, “is what it means to read in order.” Hence Hildemar says: “He rightly said, ‘Let the Rule be read to him in order,’ so that he may know what he must observe; and the entire meaning of the Rule must be made clear to him.”

The place assigned for this reading was the chapter house or auditorium, as is clear from Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino. The former, explaining the passage of the Rule, “Let him be led into the aforementioned novice cell,” says: “It is understood that he has left the novice cell itself and come to the auditorium, or to the place chosen by the abbot, and there hears the precept of the Rule; then he returns again to the novice cell.” [Col. 0815D]

The latter says concerning the same passage: “Because he had left it in order to hear the abbot’s admonition and to state for himself whether he would remain or depart; for he had gone to some auditorium, or to the chapter house itself.”

Hildemar, however, designates the guesthouse: “Within two or three days he may read the Rule to him and make its meaning clear . . . then, after he has read the Rule in the guesthouse,” and so forth.

Besides this reading of the Rule, the Council of Aachen decrees “that all monks who are able learn the Rule by heart.” The Constitutions of Otho, legate in England in the year 1248, prescribe the same, in Spelman, volume II of the Councils of England, p. 285.

“And let it be said to him.” Namely, in the chapter house, before everyone, according to the Cistercian Book of Usages.

“Behold the law.” He calls his Rule a law. On this usage, see Haeftenus, Book II, treatise 2, question 1.

[Col. 0816A] “Under which you wish to serve as a soldier.” Smaragdus aptly applies the following to this passage: “He does not say, ‘Behold the law under which you may rest, or, free from work, live quietly at leisure’; but he says, ‘under which you wish to serve as a soldier,’ so that you may understand that human life upon earth is a military service, and that his days are like those of a hired laborer.”

“Then let him be led to the aforesaid cell of the novices.” After he has been commended to the brothers’ prayers, according to Udalricus, book II, chapter 26: “And sometimes,” he says, “if it seems appropriate, let the abbot order one psalm to be sung after each of the canonical hours on that day.”

“And let him again be tested in all patience.” For, as William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, says (*To the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*, no. 17): “Pious simplicity, both in the profession of religion and in solitude, is the new man who possesses neither a reasoning faculty that leads him, nor one that draws him, nor discretion that moderates him. Rather, he uses a certain force against himself, as a figure fashioned by a potter; by a kind of law of God’s commandments, he must be made and formed as though by another’s hands, fashioned in all patience, upon the revolving wheel of obedience, and subjected to the will and judgment of his maker and former in the fire of his testing,” etc.

Thus Saint Plato, when admitted to the monastery of the Symbola, “doing everything correctly, was reproved in the presence of guests; and, as though he had been praised, he remained unmoved. A man most worthy of praise read aloud in the hearing of the brotherhood, as was fitting; and, as though he had read offensively and badly, he was corrected and, being most wise, blushed with shame,” etc., as Theodore the Studite writes in his *Life*, no. 12 (Bollandists, 4 April). See Peter of Blois, letter 13.

“Let him be received into the congregation.” That is, after the completion of a year—the period of time which the monks of old had prescribed for testing novices, as is clear from this testimony of Cassian (*Book IV*, chapter 7): “And when, having served for an entire year without any complaint, he has displayed his service toward the guests . . . he is to be admitted into the congregation of the brothers and handed over to another elder who presides over ten young men.”

From the Rule of Saint Caesarius for virgins (chapter 3): “Therefore, she who, inspired by God, is converted may not immediately assume the religious habit unless her will has first been approved through many tests. Rather, once she has been entrusted to one of the elders, let her remain for a full year in the habit in which she came.”

From the Rule of Saint Ferreolus (chapter 5): “If anyone comes seeking religion and intending to enter the monastery, he shall not be joined to the company of the monks until a full year has first elapsed—or, certainly, if it should seem good to the abbot to shorten the period somewhat, until the number of six months’ days has been completed.”

From the Rule of Tarnat (chapter 1): “And no one shall be permitted to change his habit until the year has been completed.”

From the First Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 21): “And so, after having been entrusted for that entire year to one spiritual elder, he shall not immediately be mixed into the congregation.”

From the Second Rule (chapter 18): “For an entire year he is deliberately tested by insults from all the brothers.”

Finally, from the Rule of the Master (chapter 90): “When, therefore, from that day he has completed everything in the monastery together with the other brothers without blame for an entire year, only then shall he be tonsured without any hesitation, or the garments of his holy purpose shall be changed for him.”

Nevertheless, Saint Caesarius, Saint Ferreolus, Saint Fructuosus, and the Rule of Tarnat sometimes permit the annual testing to be shortened for legitimate reasons; Saint Ferreolus, indeed, permits it to be reduced to six months. Saint Isidore likewise reduces it to a period of three months in chapter 4 of his Rule.

But in the monastery of the Acoemetae, a probation of forty days was sufficient, as is clear from the *Life of Saint John Calybita*, who flourished in the fourth century. When he requested admission to the congregation, the abbot is said to have replied to him (Bollandists, 15 January): “It is our custom that whoever wishes to profess the monastic life remain at the monastery for forty days; and when he has observed the rule of the discipline, let him then be tonsured.” Although, impatient with the delay, he obtained from the abbot that on the same day he “both came to the monastery and was made a monk.”

Therefore it should by no means seem surprising that Peter the Venerable, writing to Saint Bernard, says (*Book I*, letter 28): “When we see that it is expedient, we wait for a full year before receiving a novice; sometimes, after half a year, we join him to the other brothers; very often we do not wait not only a month or a week, but even not two days. Nevertheless, we never delay doing what we judge to be more useful for souls; thus, while following charity, we follow the Rule.”

And in the *Statutes* (statute 37): “It has been decreed that, in place of an annual and regular probation, at least a monthly probation—that is, a probation of one month—be observed with regard to novices before they are bound by the vow of obedience they have promised.”

Although this practice is not explicitly contained in the Rule, he nevertheless endeavors to defend it by the following arguments.

First, because neither the Lord nor the apostles drove those approaching the faith away for a year; Christ merely did not permit the man who wished to depart in order to bury his father.

Second: “We are not contrary to the Rule,” he says, “because we keep the eye of charity open toward the salvation of our neighbor. For we consider that, if we were to deter him from our Order so harshly, after turning back to the world he would turn back to Satan, and the one who had come for salvation would fall into destruction . . . . . We also consider this: good things are often bestowed even upon the unwilling. We say what we often observe happening among us: some, having submitted their necks to this yoke, after a certain time, overcome by various temptations or afflictions, would return to the filth of the world which they had abandoned unless they considered that what they had once done could not be violated without eternal damnation. If they sometimes venture to do so, afterward, compelled by this fear, they return to the fold; and because they know that they cannot otherwise be saved, willingly or unwillingly, they keep what they vowed.”

Third, he responds to his opponents and adapts to his purpose that saying of the Rule: “Thus let the abbot temper and arrange everything so that souls may be saved.”

Fourth, he argues that, out of regard for charity, it is often permissible to depart from the institutions of the Fathers, and to moderate the precepts of the Rules for the benefit of souls. He proves this with many examples and treats it at great length.

To these considerations is added the testimony of Peter Damian (*Opusculum* 16, chapter 9). After citing the text of the Rule, “Let one newly coming to conversion not be granted admission too readily, but, as the Apostle says, ‘Test the spirit to see whether it is from God,’” he draws the following conclusion: “From these words it is plainly understood that whoever approaches conversion, prompted by the divine Spirit, will not at all need such an extended interval of testing.”

But these arguments are opposed by this pronouncement of Pope Alexander II: “The Rule of Saint Benedict, and especially the canonical institution of our father and predecessor Saint Gregory, forbids a monk to be made before a year of probation has been completed.”

Whatever the case may be—whether someone professes before completing the year of probation lawfully or unlawfully—Innocent III declared that the profession is valid if it is made with the consent of both parties. He states (*Third Decretal concerning Rules*, etc., chapter *Ad apostolicam*): “The time of probation was granted by the Holy Fathers not only for the benefit of the convert but also for that of the monastery, so that he might test the austerities of the monastery and the monastery might test his character. If, however, before the time of probation regularly prescribed, the person who wishes to be converted receives the habit and makes profession, and the abbot, either personally or through another, receives the profession and grants him the monastic and monk’s habit, each appears to renounce what is known to have been introduced for his own benefit. Therefore, by the profession made and likewise accepted, he is bound to regular observance, and he must truly be considered a monk, because many things are forbidden which, once done, nevertheless obtain validity.”

Now, by decree of the Council of Trent (Session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 19), a profession made before the completion of the year of probation is considered invalid. And not without reason. For, as the Cistercians once objected to the Cluniacs: “It has happened that, because people are received carelessly, those received carelessly conduct themselves even more carelessly; and because those who come do not understand what they are coming to, once they have been joined to the others they do not know what they ought to do. While they are not trained in the arena, like athletes before a contest, when they come to the conflict, they flee when they ought to fight; and when they ought to win by fighting bravely, they are defeated, being inexperienced in such matters.”

For this reason the monks of Fulda, in a humble petition to Charlemagne, formerly requested (no. 7) “that no one be received before probation, nor joined to the body of the monastery, lest someone perhaps wish to join himself to the monastery more for earthly advantages than for love of eternal life, and, once received, disturb the brothers by his disgraceful behavior.”

And the Council of Clovesho (in Spelman, volume I, *Councils of England*), held in the year 747, decrees in canon 24: “If any layman desires to undertake the service of the holy profession, let him not receive the habit of the tonsure until his conduct, his morals, and the quality of his morals have been more clearly tested according to the definition of the monastic Rule, in accordance with the apostolic command: ‘Test the spirits to see whether they are from God,’ unless some reasonable cause persuades that he should be received into the congregation earlier.”

But the question arises: when should the year of probation be considered to begin? If Smaragdus is to be believed, “this course of the year is completed by the novice from the time when, having knocked, he comes to the monastery; during this year, while he is still staying in the cell of the novices, the Rule is read to him three times in due order.”

Hildemar begins the year of probation from the time when the novice enters the guesthouse to serve there. He wants the novice to remain two months in the guesthouse and only ten months in the cell of the novices. The Cistercians count it from the day on which he inhabits the cell of the novices, according to the *Book of Usages*, chapter 102. Boherius also seems to hold the same view, when he requires novices to remain two months in the cell of the novices before the Rule is first read to them. The monks of Bursfeld count it from the day on which the novice is clothed in the novice’s habit.

[Col. 0818C] But while the annual period may have seemed too long to some for testing the character of novices, it was judged excessively short by others. Consequently, Pope Saint Gregory thought that another year ought to be added. He writes to Fortunatus, bishop of Naples (*Book VIII*, letter 23): “Let your fraternity forbid all monasteries to tonsure those whom they have received for conversion before they have completed two years in conversion. Rather, during this period let their life and character be carefully tested, lest any of them be dissatisfied with what he has chosen or fail to approve what he has selected. For if it is serious to associate untested people with the service of men, who could say how much more serious it is to attach the unapproved to the service of God?”

Yet some were not satisfied even with this period. The Rule said to have been delivered by an angel to Saint Pachomius prescribes three years. For, as it appears in Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 38), I read the following: “If one enters once and cannot endure the contest with them for three years, you shall not admit him; but after he has performed more difficult works, let him depart after three years.”

John of Antioch seems to refer to this in his discourse on monasteries and donations to laymen, no. 14 (volume I of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*), where he writes: “The sacred law of the monks commands that the one who has already renounced the world and the things of the world be received by the superior of the monastery and the brothers, but be tested for a full three years to see whether he can become a monk. If he appears suitable, let him be tonsured and enrolled in the company of the monks; if not, let him return whence he came.”

We also find this rule of a three-year probation confirmed by both civil and ecclesiastical laws. The emperor Justinian says in Novel 5: “We decree, following the sacred Rules, that those who profess the solitary life not immediately and readily receive the monastic habit from the most reverend superiors of the venerable monasteries; rather, for a full three years, whether they happen to be free or slaves, let them endure without yet earning the monastic habit, but using the tonsure and clothing of those who are called laymen, and remaining so.”

And shortly afterward: “When they have remained in that life for a full three years, demonstrating themselves to be excellent, tolerable both to themselves and to the other monks and to the superior, let them earn the garment and tonsure.”

Nevertheless, the same emperor elsewhere states as follows (Novel 123): “If anyone wishes to come to the monastic life, we command that, if it is established concerning him that he is subject to no servile condition, the superior of the monastery give him the habit whenever he sees fit. If it is not established to what condition he is subject, let him not assume the monastic habit within three years; rather, within the aforesaid period, let the superior of the monastery test whether he wishes to turn back.”

The First and Second Councils of Constantinople likewise decree, in canon 5, “that no one be considered worthy of the monastic habit before the period of three years, left to test them, has shown that they are approved and worthy of such a life.”

Similarly, the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19, decrees a three-year probation before the reception of the habit for nuns who are not bound to perpetual enclosure. Saint Gregory also wished this to be observed with regard to soldiers whom he forbade to be clothed in the monastic habit (*Book VII*, letter 11), “unless their life has been carefully examined. According to the regular norm,” he says, “they ought to be tested in their own habit for three years, and then, with God as author, receive the monastic habit.” See Mabillon, volume II of the *Analecta*, p. 207.

The discipline of certain monks was much stricter: they tested their novices for many years. Thus a certain Isidore, a leading citizen of Alexandria, came to the monastery; according to Saint John Climacus (*Ladder*, step 4), “when he had completed seven years and had attained the deepest humility and compunction, the Father, after the incomparable man’s endurance—of which he had earlier given a suitable demonstration—wished to number him among the brothers.”

Still more astonishing is what the same author reports concerning another brother named Abbacyrus. When asked why he was expelled from the table every day and ordered to sleep without supper, he replied: “Believe me, Father, my fathers are testing whether I wish to be a monk; but they are not doing this in earnest. Knowing the intention of the Father and the others, I endure everything very lightly and without any distress. And behold, I have now been thinking this for fifteen years, just as they themselves told me when I entered the monastery that those who renounced the world were accustomed to be tested until the thirtieth year.”

“Knowing that it has been established by the law of the Rule that from that day he may not leave the monastery.” That is, so that he may return to the world; for, as Pope Saint Leo writes to Bishop Rusticus: “The purpose of a monk, once undertaken by his own judgment or will, cannot be abandoned without sin.”

This is cited in excerpts of Bishop Egbert of York, in Spelman, volume I of the *Councils of England*, under the year 750, and by Gratian, Causa 20, question 3, chapter *Propositum*. Hence the Council of Chalcedon (Act 5, canon 7): “Those who have chosen the life of monks, we decree, shall not enter military service or any worldly dignity. Those who attempt this and do not repent, so that they may return to what they originally chose for the Lord’s sake, are to be anathematized.”

Saint Basil teaches the same in his *Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 22; Saint Caesarius in his *Rule for Monks and Virgins*, chapter 1; and Saint Aurelian in his *Rule for Monks*, chapter 2. See Peter of Blois, letter 13.

“Nor may he shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule, which, after such prolonged deliberation, he was permitted either to refuse or to accept.” Peter of Blois appears to refer to this passage when writing to E., prior of a small monastery, in these words (letter 131): “At one time it was within one’s discretion not to accept the yoke of the Lord; once accepted, however, it may not be cast off. God therefore now demands what has been offered, although he had not demanded that it be offered. The will has been transformed into necessity, and you are constrained by the bond of profession to fulfill the vows which your lips have uttered.”

“But the one who is to be received shall promise in the oratory, before everyone, his stability and the conversion of his conduct, and obedience, before God and his saints.” Here Saint Benedict expresses the form and substance of monastic profession. It may not be out of place to report here the various forms preserved for us from antiquity.

### From the letter of Theodemar, abbot of Monte Cassino, to Charlemagne

“In the name of the Lord. I, N., promise that in the holy monastery of the blessed martyr—or confessor—N., according to the institutions of the blessed Benedict, before God and his holy angels, and also in the presence of our abbot N., I shall persevere all my days, from now and henceforth, in this holy monastery, and that in all obedience I shall obey whatever is commanded me. I, N., have written and confirmed this promise made by me in my own hand before witnesses.”

### From the Bellilocian chartulary

“I, Brother Gerald, promise my stability in this place according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and of the holy apostles Peter and Paul, in the presence of the lord Abbot Gerald and the other brothers; and I transfer some of my possessions to this monastery, which has been built in honor of Saint Peter, where the venerable Abbot Gerald appears to preside.”

### From Smaragdus

“I, N., promise in this monastery of Saint N. my stability, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints.”

### From Udalricus, book II, chapter 27

[Col. 0820C] “I, Brother N., promise the stability of a monk, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery, which has been built in honor of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, in the presence of the lord Abbot N.”

### From a manuscript codex of Saint-Denis in France

“I, Brother N., humble monk of the monastery of Saint-Denis in France, in the diocese of Paris, vow and promise to God, the blessed Mary, [Note: [Col. 0819D] This rite of making vows to God and his saints is ancient, as is clear from the *Miracles of Saint Marius, abbot of Bodon*, first Benedictine century: “Let those who in this church have promised God and Saint Marius stability of conduct see to it.”], the blessed Dionysius, the blessed Benedict, and all the saints, and to you, Father, obedience, chastity, and poverty. Moreover, I promise stability in this place and conversion of conduct, according to the constitution of this place and the tradition of the Fathers, in the presence of these witnesses.”

### From the First Commentary of Boherius

“I, Brother P. B., promise my stability, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, before God and his saints, in this monastery of Saint Aignan, which has been built in his honor.”

The formula of the Bursfeld monks is the same. The formulas of the Cassinese, the Valladolid monks, and the nuns in Belgium may be found in Haeften, book IV, treatise 5, discussion 4.

### Formula of the Cistercians

“I, Brother N., promise my stability, the conversion of my conduct, and obedience according to the Rule of the abbot Saint Benedict, before God and all his saints, whose relics are kept here, in this place called N., of the Cistercian Order, built in honor of the most blessed Mother of God, Mary ever-virgin, in the presence of the lord Abbot N. of this same place.”

### From the Statutes of Guigo, chapter 23

[Col. 0821A]

“I, Brother N., promise stability, obedience, and the conversion of my conduct before God and his saints and the relics of this hermitage, which has been built in honor of God, the blessed ever-virgin Mary, and Saint John the Baptist, in the presence of the lord prior N.”

### From the discourse of John of Antioch on monasteries and donations to laymen, volume I of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*

“I renounce parents, brothers, relatives, friends, household companions, possessions, resources, and empty and vain pleasure and glory alike. And I reject not only these things, but also my own soul, according to the Lord’s command. I endure every austerity of the monastic life, and I preserve myself in purity, virginity, and poverty for the sake of the kingdom of heaven. I remain in the monastery and in the monastic life until my final breath,” etc.

See other formulas in the fourth century of the Benedictine era, volume I, toward the end.

To return to the text of the Holy Rule: “By the strap of our promised stability we are tied like obedient beasts to the heavenly manger; by the conversion of our conduct we are made like the piety of the angels; by the display of obedience we imitate the angelic ministries themselves,” says Adam, abbot of Persenne, writing to the monk Osmund (volume I of Baluze’s *Miscellany*). It is necessary to explain somewhat more fully what is promised to God by these three vows.

Although in some formulas of profession we see stability of place expressly stated, that alone is not sufficient to fulfill all the obligations of the vow of stability. In addition, stability of state is required, that is, perseverance in the purpose of monastic life once undertaken. This is clearly demonstrated by the customary formula of profession among the Cluniacs, in which stability is not simply promised, but “the stability of a monk.” It is also shown by the first formula of petition published at the end of the fourth century of the Benedictine era, in which the novice expresses the stability he is to promise as follows: “With the Lord as witness, we profess with devoted mind that we will preserve the stability of our manner of life in your congregation, together with observance of the Rule, until the end.”

Perhaps the passage in the *Life of Saint Rembert*, no. 12 (fourth century of the Benedictine era, part I), where he is said to have promised stability of his conduct, should be understood in this way.

Nor do the authors who have written on the Rule of Saint Benedict give us any other understanding of stability. The very ancient Hildemar, almost the oldest of them all, must be heard on this matter: “Stability,” he says, “pertains to perseverance . . . . For to stand means to persevere in a good work once begun. Here it must be noted that if he does not persevere in that work or desire once begun, but fails to persevere either in some respect or altogether, such a person may appear to stand in the monastery before men, yet before God he does not stand.”

Therefore stability of place alone is not sufficient unless stability in the good work undertaken and in the desire for perfection is added. Bernard of Cassino states the matter more clearly: “By stability the monk is bound never in any way to abandon monasticism, and not to leave the monastery without necessity and the authority of his superior.”

The same is taught by Nicholas of Fractura, Peter Boherius, John de Turrecremata, Columbanus Uranx, Antonius Perezius, and Benedict Haeften, book IV, treatise 6, discussion 3.

Saint Bernard also suggests this when writing to Adam in these words (letter 7): “But on the day when—which God forbid—I begin to live by other laws, conduct myself according to other customs, serve different observances, invent new practices, and adopt foreign customs, I am confident that I shall no longer be preserving the stability I promised, but shall be a transgressor of my profession.”

Indeed, Saint Benedict himself seems to have explained the vow of stability when, before prescribing the form in which profession was to be made, he prefaced it with these words: “Knowing that it has been established by the law of the Rule that from that day it is not permitted to him to leave the monastery, nor to shake his neck free from beneath the yoke of the Rule, which, after such prolonged deliberation, he was permitted either to refuse or to accept.”

The vow of stability therefore includes two things: perseverance in the monastery until death and observance of the Rule. Saint Benedict explains this more clearly elsewhere when he permits a cleric to be joined to the monastery, provided that he promises either observance of the Rule or his own stability. The conjunction “or” appears to make these two things synonymous.

Above all, however, the holy legislator intended by stability to retain monks permanently in the monastery, in order to avoid those frequent migrations from monastery to monastery and to restrain the restless wanderings of gyrovagues. Hence Saint Bernard (*On the Precept and Dispensation*): “Let the pact of stability henceforth prescribe an end to every slack decline, contentious departure, wandering and inquisitive roaming, and, finally, to every frivolous form of instability.”

The first Council of England, according to Bede, had also decreed (*Ecclesiastical History*, book IV, chapter 5) “that monks should not migrate from place to place—that is, from monastery to monastery—unless released by their own abbot, but should remain in the obedience which they promised at the time of their conversion.”

And rightly so. For, as William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, said (*To the Brothers of Mont-Dieu*): “It is impossible for a man to fix his mind in one place if he has not fixed his body in some place.”

This must not, however, be understood as though monks vowed themselves to eternal enclosure, although Saint Aurelian once prescribed this, and the monks of Valladolid in Spain promise in their profession perpetual stability of enclosure.

There are certain cases and reasons for which someone may lawfully leave. Hildemar lists three: for improvement, for salvation, and for obedience.

For improvement: so that he may live more perfectly in another monastery than in his own, even if observance flourishes in his own monastery.

For salvation: so that he may safeguard his salvation if the monastery in which he vowed stability is endangering it.

For obedience: when the abbot commands it.

Julian of Paris assigns four other reasons in his book *On the First Way of Life of the Cistercians*:

1. To found a new monastery;

2. Because of the poverty of the monastery in which he vowed stability;

3. To perform penance for some offense committed;

4. To reform monasteries that have departed from stricter discipline.

Concerning the second and third cases, there is a decree of Gregory IX in a constitution for Benedictine monks: “If the poverty of the place, or its inadequacy, or the deficiency of the Order, or the punishment for an offense requires that some monks be sent away from their own establishments, the abbots to whom such persons have been sent shall not refuse to receive them for as long as the visitors judge it expedient, unless they are such that their conduct cannot be tolerated without grave scandal. If they refuse to receive them when they are able to do so, let the visitors compel them,” etc. See Haeften, book IV, treatise 6, discussions 3 and 4.

Conversion of conduct is commonly understood in two ways: from evil to good, and from good to better. Hildemar calls it the uprooting of vices and the planting of virtues, by which “the monk binds himself not to live in a worldly manner, but to direct his conduct according to the Rule,” as John de Turrecremata says after Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius.

But according to Boherius in his Second Commentary, “conversion of conduct in this case is the same as renunciation of worldly things, which is threefold. The first,” he says, “is that by which we despise bodily all the riches and resources of the world. The second is that by which we reject our former conduct, vices, and affections of mind and flesh. The third is that by which, drawing our mind away from all present and visible things, we contemplate only future things and desire those that are invisible.” He took this from Cassian, *Conferences*, conference 3, chapter 6.

Richard of Saint Angelo, however, when explaining this passage of the Rule and raising the objection “that he either has good conduct or bad conduct: in the first case it is not necessary for him to be converted, since he is already converted; if his conduct is bad, then he should not be received for such a conversion, lest one diseased sheep infect the whole flock,” expresses his understanding of conversion of conduct as follows:

“It may be said, ‘of his conduct,’ that is, of his worldly actions. Although he had already been converted, as is clear from what was said above, nevertheless he must now promise with the solemnity which follows here; and thus he will be bound in a civil manner, whereas previously he was bound by nature. Or say that he may perhaps have retained certain worldly habits whose conversion he now promises. Or say that the conversion of his conduct is from good to better, so that the meaning is this: if he was good during the aforesaid probation, from now on let him become better, in accordance with the saying, ‘They shall go from strength to strength.’ For by this conversion of conduct, or promise concerning it, he entirely removes the old man, without any hope of returning to the world, and puts on the life of monks forever, as follows below.

“Or say that, if formerly he was converted in body, he now promises conversion of mind. Therefore explain ‘conversion’ as the turning of mind and body. Hence the blessed Bernard says: ‘Conversion of the body, if it is alone, will be nothing.’”

Finally, Haeften (book IV, treatise 6, discussion 5) asserts that by virtue of this vow the monk is bound:

1. To complete renunciation of the world;

2. To exact observance of the Rule;

3. To the good customs of the place that were observed at the time of profession.

The third vow of monastic profession is obedience, which is the first and greatest virtue of monks. Saint Benedict intends and commends it above all in the Rule, and it is, as it were, the Rule’s spirit.

Hildemar defines it in this passage as follows: “Obedience is that which, in prosperity, does not follow its own will, but, in adversity, follows its own will—that is, it proceeds unwillingly toward the honor, pleasure, and prosperity of the world, but willingly toward the world’s sadness, disgrace, and adversity. For if you go willingly toward joys and prosperity, you are not obedient; but if you proceed unwillingly toward sadness and temptations, you are not obedient. Therefore you must consider what sort of obedience you are practicing and observe with what disposition you practice it.”

And Bernard of Cassino says: “By obedience the monk is bound not to live according to his own judgment or his own will, not to go where he wishes, not to do what he wishes, but to remain subject to another’s command and another’s will.”

Since we have already said more about this in chapter 5, these few remarks will suffice. Nevertheless, before proceeding further, several points concerning these three vows of monastic profession should be observed.

The first is how appropriately Saint Benedict wished his monks to be bound by these three vows—stability, conversion of conduct, and obedience. For, as Menard observes, since the human mind is inconstant and subject to change, the vow of stability was entirely appropriately instituted, by which the monk promises that he will persevere in the cenobitic state.

Next, because it is not enough to live in a monastery unless one lives as a monk, the vow of conversion of conduct was added.

Finally, because many difficulties, differing opinions, and rivalries can arise within a congregation, from which no small storms and tempests may be stirred up, the third vow, that of obedience, was added, so that all the monks individually and collectively, subject to one ruler, might live with the greatest security and tranquility.

Furthermore, since in chapter 1 Saint Benedict had chosen the cenobitic type from among the four kinds of monks, setting the others aside, he wished his own monks to be distinguished from the others by particular vows: from the gyrovagues by stability, from the sarabaites by conversion of conduct, and from the anchorites by obedience, as Bernard of Cassino notes here.

The second point is that the three aforesaid vows are not promised simply and absolutely, but according to the Rule. This applies not only to obedience but also to stability and conversion of conduct, so that the monk observes the stability prescribed by the Rule and the constitutions of the place, converts his conduct according to their prescriptions, and obeys the superior in matters consistent with the Rule.

Hence Saint Bernard says: “The will of the superior is prescribed no small limit by the fact that the one who professes indeed promises obedience, but not obedience without restriction; rather, he promises it specifically according to the Rule, and according to no Rule other than that of Saint Benedict. Thus the one who presides must not loosen the reins of his own will over his subjects, but must know the measure assigned to him by the Rule and finally moderate his commands accordingly, concerning only what has been established to be right.

“Therefore, if my abbot, according to that Rule, should attempt to impose upon me something else that is not according to the Rule, or even something that is not according to these institutions—for example, those of Basil, Augustine, or Pachomius—what necessity, I ask, compels me to obey in this matter? For I think that only what I promised can be required of me.

“You see, then, the limits of obedience that you demand, if the mode of obedience is determined by the tenor of the profession, and if the power of the one commanding cannot extend further than the vow of the one professing.”

Third, it makes no mention of poverty or chastity in the formula of profession which it prescribed for us—something we share with the Carthusians, [Col. 0824B] Premonstratensians, Carmelites, and Hermits of St Augustine, as Haeften proves, book IV, treatise 6, discussion 6. Nevertheless, monks are no less bound to chastity and poverty than to obedience; for, as Innocent III says (*Cap. Cum ad monasterium*), “The renunciation of ownership, as also the observance of chastity, is so closely joined to the monastic rule that not even the supreme pontiff can grant permission contrary to it.” Some consider poverty and chastity to be included under conversion of morals, [p. 762] such as Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and others; some under obedience, such as St Thomas, Turrecremata, and others. Certainly they are included under both, indeed also under stability. For these obligations are so connected with monastic profession that they cannot be separated from it, and whoever has promised one is considered to have promised the others as well—just as clerics, when they are initiated into sacred orders, are understood tacitly to profess continence. Nevertheless, there have been, and even now there are, some among our own people who explicitly vow chastity and poverty, such as the Dionysians, whose formula we cited above; the Celestines, according to their Constitutions, chapter 5, § 13; and certain nuns in France and Belgium.

Fourth, that profession is to be made in the oratory, as St Fructuosus, together with St Benedict, decrees in chapter 21 of his Rule, prescribing that “when the year has been completed, and he has been proved in morals and refined by labors, after receiving the blessing in the church, he is to be admitted into the fellowship of the brothers.” And rightly so: a sacred act should be performed in a sacred place, and the one who consecrates himself to God should have present the God who dwells in a special manner in the temple.

Fifth, in order to make the monks more solicitous about making their profession, he wished God and his saints to be called as witnesses: “before God and his saints,” he says.

**“If at any time he should act otherwise.”** — By abandoning stability through apostasy, rejecting the regular way of life and giving himself over to secular living, casting off the bridle of obedience and running through the fields of his own will, as Bernard of Cassino puts it.

**“Let him know that he will be condemned by the one whom he mocks.”** — Let him know that he will be condemned as a sacrilegious person; “for whoever has offered himself to God, if afterward he recoils into another kind of life, becomes sacrilegious, since he steals himself from God and takes away the offering made to God,” says St Basil (*Long Rules*, chapter 14). Hence St Gregory, writing to a certain Venantius who, from being a monk, had become chancellor of Italy (*Book I of the Registers*, chapter 33), attacks him as follows:

“Ananias had vowed his money to God, but, overcome by the devil’s persuasion, he took it away; yet you know by what death he was punished. If, then, the man who took away the coins he had given was worthy of the danger of death, consider how great will be the danger at the divine judgment to which you will be liable, since you have taken away not coins but yourself from almighty God, to whom you had devoted yourself under the monastic habit.”

See Cassian, book IV, chapter 33, and Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 16, chapter 4.

**“Concerning this promise of his, let him make a petition in the name of the saints whose relics are there, and of the abbot who is present.”** — [Col. 0825A] More recent commentators on the Rule confuse this petition with the promise, although from the very text of the Rule they plainly seem to be distinct. This is even clearer from the ancient commentators on the Rule, Smaragdus and Hildemar. Both describe the order for initiating a monk in this way: first, the novice promises stability, conversion of morals, and obedience according to the Rule of St Benedict. “And when he has said this in making his promise,” says Hildemar, “then [p. 763] he ought to make a petition—that is, either he should then write the petition itself, or, if the petition has already been written, he should write something there in the presence of the others, namely his name; or, if he does not know how to write, then in the presence of the brothers he should make the sign of the cross there. Then, when he has done this, he should place the petition itself with his own hand upon the altar.” But Smaragdus is much clearer, for in his commentary he presents the formulas of both the petition and the promise. We have cited the formula of the promise above; it may perhaps be worthwhile to reproduce the petition here.

[Col. 0825B]

“Carefully considering the beginning of my monastic life, I reflect that at first an entrance into the monastery was not readily granted to my petition; rather, after I had knocked for a long time, a lodging was mercifully assigned to me only with difficulty. Having stayed there a very few days, I proceeded to the novices’ house, where the elder carefully proclaimed to me at the outset hard and harsh things, and where the promise of my stability was humbly fulfilled. The elder, threatening me, impressed these terrifying words upon my ears:

‘Know for certain that if, after the promise of regular observance, you turn back and look behind you, you will not be fit for the kingdom of heaven. Moreover, know that you will be cast forth from them [the monastery’s cloisters] in such clothes as those in which the cloisters of the monastery received you. And because the world had ruined you, stripped of your old rags and likewise stripped of vices, it is right that it should receive back its servant clad in both, to be kept forever to the disgrace of all.’

“But strengthened by David’s example, crying out to the Lord, I said: ‘Because of the words of your lips I have kept to difficult ways’; [Col. 0825C] knowing with complete certainty that if I become a sharer in Christ’s passion, I shall also be a sharer in his resurrection. Strengthened by these and similar divine oracles, I declared that I would steadfastly endure everything for eternal life.

“When the Father saw our constancy, he ordered that throughout the year the Rule should be read and handed on to us in due course three times, with an admonishing declaration, saying:

‘Behold the law under which you wish to serve as a soldier: if you can observe it, enter; if you cannot, depart freely.’

“Seeing, therefore, that a very orderly and lengthy period of testing had been allotted to me, and setting aside the opportunity for hesitation, I earnestly beg and implore you to deem me worthy now to be joined to your body.

“Having already wisely undertaken deliberation concerning my salvation, I promise, with the Lord’s help, to observe in all things the institutions of this Rule; willingly to keep the commands of my abbot; and, with the Lord’s favor, to obey all the commands of the senior brothers. For the sake of eternal freedom, I further promise to be faithfully bound from now on by the laws of this Rule, so that from this day it will no longer be permissible for me to leave the monastery or to shake off my neck from beneath the yoke of the Rule—a yoke which, under the yearly option, I was permitted either to excuse myself from or to undertake. But, as I have said, setting aside every excuse, I promise stability in the monastery and conversion of my morals; and, for the service of my profession, the reward of eternal life, and fear of Gehenna, I submit myself to serve under holy obedience before God and his angels.

“And so that this petition of my promise may be firmly kept by you, I hand over this written petition, made in the name of the saints whose relics are contained here and of the abbot who is present, [p. 764] to be kept forever; and, after confirming it with my own hand, I place it upon the altar, to be preserved perpetually in this monastery.”

Mabillon published two other formulas of the petition at the end of the fourth Benedictine century, part I, p. 738. In them, just as in the promise, the novice promises stability, conversion of morals, and obedience, or something of this kind; but by the promise he makes himself bound to God, while by the petition, as though by a contract and agreement, he makes himself bound to the abbot and to the religious community. He used to make the promise first and then the petition, as the natural sense of the Rule requires, and as is clear from Smaragdus and Hildemar. This order, however, did not prevail everywhere; for in the formulas published by Mabillon, the petition precedes the promise, and the petition placed upon the altar is mentioned within the promise itself.

**“Let him write this petition with his own hand; or, certainly, if he does not know letters, let another, asked by him, write it; and let the novice make his mark and place it upon the altar with his own hand.”** — Bernard of Cassino comments on this passage:

“Consider, therefore, that the monk binds himself in almost three ways: first, he binds himself by the spoken word; second, in writing; third, in a manner by oath. First, in the promise of the vow; second, in the acknowledgment or signing of the written document; third, by placing the writing itself upon the altar, in which there is the expression of an oath or the confirmation of a vow.”

Arnulf of Lisieux indicates these three things in letter 13 (volume XII of the *Library of the Fathers*), where he says:

“You must know that in one who has professed religion disobedience is a crime, and that he is bound to the strictest diligence, since he has pledged obedience to his prelate by word of mouth and in writing, and also by a bodily oath, together with the salutary impression of the cross.”

One should also note what Boherius writes in his second commentary, chapter 7. Explaining the words, “You have placed men over our heads,” he says:

“For in many Gallican monasteries, after the profession has been read, the novice places it upon his own head and thus carries it to the altar, although the text nevertheless orders him to do this with his own hand.”

**“When he has placed it, the novice himself is immediately to begin this verse: ‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word,’ etc.”** — Hildemar says that this is the same as if he were saying:

“Lord, your word is the word in which you said, ‘Whoever has left all that he possesses shall receive a hundredfold,’ etc. And behold, because of this word—that is, your command—I have abandoned the world and renounced all that was mine; and now I ask you to receive me. He gives the reason why when he says, ‘And I shall live,’ and, according to the sense, ‘so that I may live’; and I ask that you not put me to shame in my expectation. It is as though he were saying: ‘I ask your mercy, so that, because I delayed converting for so long, you may not for this reason put me to shame—that is, may I not be a source of shame and disgrace before you.’”

**“Let the whole congregation answer this verse a third time, adding ‘Glory be to the Father.’”** — [p. 765] Bernard of Cassino understands this to mean that the whole congregation repeats the entire verse after it has been recited in full by the novice, and, after repeating it a third time, adds “Glory be to the Father”; the novice does not add it.

**“Then the novice brother himself is to prostrate himself at the feet of each person, so that they may pray for him; and from that day he is to be counted among the congregation.”** — Thus, plainly, the Holy Father wished monks to be consecrated to God. We hope it will not be displeasing to readers if we report here the various rites of their consecration.

### From the Rule of the Master, chapter 89: How the new brother ought to confirm his entrance into the monastery

[Col. 0826D]

“When the two months allowed for consideration have been completed, and he has chosen stability under a gentle discipline and is pleased to fulfill the perseverance promised with the firmness of the Rule that has been read to him, the new brother is questioned again by the abbot concerning what he has decided within himself during the granted period of delay. When, in his response, he promises to fulfill obedience in all things, the abbot should reply: ‘Thanks be to God.’

“On another day, after Prime has been said and the Mass has ended, as the abbot leaves the threshold of the oratory with the congregation, the new brother should bend his neck at the abbot’s knees, asking him—or asking the whole congregation—to remain for a short while in the oratory and pray for him. They should then pray for him for a very long time. When everything has been completed and the abbot wishes to leave, the new disciple should humbly seize his garment and retain it in his hand, indicating by his request:

‘There is something I wish to say first to God and to this holy oratory, or to you and the congregation.’

“When the abbot has replied, ‘What is it? Tell me,’ the petitioner should continue:

‘I wish to serve God through the discipline of the Rule read to me in your monastery.’

“When the abbot has replied, ‘And does this please you?’ the future disciple should continue:

‘This pleases God first, and thus also me.’

“Then the abbot should say:

‘See, brother, you promise nothing to me, but to God and to this oratory or holy altar. If you obey the divine commands in everything, or my admonitions, you will receive on the day of judgment the crown of good works, while I shall gain some measure of forgiveness for my sins, since I encouraged you to overcome the devil and the world. But if you refuse to obey me in anything, behold, I call upon the Lord as witness—and this congregation too will bear witness for me on the day of judgment—that, as I have said, if you do not obey me or the congregation in anything, I shall be acquitted at God’s judgment, while you will render an account for your own soul and contention.’

“After these words, if he has entered with his possessions, then the brief document or deed of gift by which his possessions have been given to God or to the monastery is to be placed upon the altar by the donor’s own hand, while the brother himself says:

‘Behold, Lord: together with my soul and my poverty, I return and offer back to you whatever you have given me. And I wish my possessions to be where my heart and soul shall be, yet under the authority of the monastery and of the abbot whom, Lord, you set over me in your place, to be feared, when you say to them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” [p. 766] Therefore, since through him you provide all things necessary for us, we ought to possess nothing privately, because you are sufficient for us in all things and alone fully adequate, so that from now on Christ may be our life and our hope, and death our gain.’

“After this the new brother himself should say this responsory:

‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.’

“After this responsory the abbot should say this verse:

‘Confirm, O God, what you have wrought in us.’

“After this verse has been said, peace is immediately given to him by everyone. The abbot should complete the rite, take the brief document from the altar, and immediately place the new disciple under the superior. Having been entrusted to their hands, he should leave for discipline with the other brothers.

“On that same day, as a sign of humility, he himself should minister water to the brothers entering for Communion; and as he gives it, he should kiss everyone’s hands and ask each person to pray for him.

“As for the briefs of gifts made by the brothers, the abbot should insert into his testament a provision that, at the time of their death, he will restore them for the uses of the monastery, including the names of those known to have made the gifts, so that after his death no one who happens to leave the monastery may have the confidence to reclaim his possessions, break the stability of the monastery and the faith of the deceased, or claim that anything belonging to him remains in the monastery without a deed of gift.”

### From the Capitulary of Theodore, archbishop of Canterbury, no. 2, volume IX of the *Spicilegium*

“In the ordinations of monks the abbot ought to celebrate Mass and complete three prayers over the monk’s head. For seven days he should cover his head with his cuculla, and on the seventh day the abbot should remove the veil from the monk’s head. Just as in baptism the priest removed the infant’s veil on the seventh day, so also the abbot should do this for the monk, because it is a second baptism, according to the judgment of the Fathers, and all sins are forgiven as in baptism.”

### From Hildemar’s Commentary on the Rule of St Benedict, chapter 58

“Here begins the order of what the novice ought to do when he promises the Rule.

“First, when he comes into the oratory, he should promise before the assembled men in these words:

‘I, [lacuna], promise my stability, the conversion of my morals, and obedience according to the Rule of St Benedict, before God and his saints.’

“And when he has said this in making his promise, he should then make a petition—that is, either he should write the petition itself at that time, or, if the petition has been written beforehand, he should write something there in the presence of the others, namely his name; or, if he does not know how to write, then in the presence of the brothers he should make the sign of the cross there. Then, when he has done this, he should place the petition itself with his own hand upon the altar.

“Then, when he has placed it upon the altar, he should immediately say this verse three times, bowing his head:

‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.’

“And when the brothers have [p. 767] said the verse, they should also add: ‘Glory be to the Father,’ etc.

“Then, when they have said these things, the novice should place his knees upon the ground and greet all the brothers, turning around in a circle, so that they may all pray for him. After he has greeted all the brothers, as I have said, the novice should then prostrate himself and lie face down upon the ground before the altar. Thus, kneeling, they should sing for him five psalms appropriate to this rite: ‘I lift up my eyes’; ‘To you I lift up my eyes’; ‘If the Lord had not been with us’; ‘Out of the depths’; and ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy,’ with the doxology (‘Glory be to the Father’). All should sing, and three times say, ‘Lord, have mercy.’

“After these five psalms have been sung, either the abbot or, if the abbot does not wish to do so, a priest should say the ‘Our Father,’ followed by ‘And lead us not into temptation,’ and then say the short passages pertaining to this verse:

‘Save your servant’;  
‘Turn, O Lord, how long?’;  
‘May the Lord guard you from every evil’;  
‘May the Lord guard your going in and your going out, from this time forth and forever’;  
‘The Lord be with you’;

and the prayer appropriate to this rite.

“Then, when all these things have been done, everyone, including the novice, should rise. When the novice has risen, the abbot should cover the novice’s head with the *melota*. After this the novice should kiss all the brothers and keep his head covered until the third day. On the third day he should remove the covering and receive Communion, and the abbot should uncover the novice’s head before the altar.”

What is read here concerning covering the novice’s head for three days is established by canon 35 of the Council of Aachen. [Col. 0828C]

### Also from the same Hildemar, in the same place

“After he has completed a year and has appeared patient, obedient, and approved, he should come into the chapter, and the abbot should say to him:

‘Are you able to observe it?’

“And if he replies:

‘With the Lord’s help, I can and I wish to,’”

then the abbot should say to him:

‘Behold, brother, if you wish to serve almighty God in the monastic habit, and the holy Rule pleases you, go and sell everything, give it to the poor, and come, follow Christ.’

“If he says, ‘I wish to give it to this monastery,’ then the abbot should say to him:

‘Brother, with God’s help your property is not necessary to us, since we have the means by which our own need is supplied. There are people—or even monasteries—poorer than we are; or certainly your parents are poorer than we are. Therefore it is better for you to give it as a reward to those who are in greater need than to us.’

“But if he says, ‘I would rather give it to this monastery for the reward of my soul than give it to another,’ then he should give his property either to the poor or to the monastery.

“When he has done this, he should come into the oratory, be stripped of his own clothing there, and be clothed in the monastery’s garments in one corner of the oratory, the petition having already been made. It should be noted that whether he is clothed in the oratory before he makes his promise or afterward makes no difference, provided that his head is veiled after the promise, and that on the seventh day (in another version, the eighth) it is unveiled, because the [p. 768] *melota* is in place of baptism.

“Then he should come before the altar and say:

‘I promise my stability, the conversion of my morals, and obedience before God and his saints.’

“Then he should place upon the altar, according to the Rule, the petition he has in writing . . . . After he has placed it there, he should say three times:

‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.’

“Then the whole congregation should answer three times, as the Rule says. The novice should then lie prostrate upon the ground, while the whole congregation remains only on its knees. They should sing for him these psalms: ‘Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy’; ‘Out of the depths’; and the other psalms appropriate to this rite.

“After this they should rise and say these short passages:

‘Save your servant, my God, who hopes in you’;  
‘Turn a little and be gracious to your servant’;  
‘May the Lord guard your going in and your going out, from this time forth and forever.’

“Then a prayer should be said for him.”

### From a manuscript of St Benedict of Fleury

“When the novice has already been well tested in the novices’ cell by examination of the Rule, he should leave together with his master and come into the chapter. The novice himself, according to what has been handed down to him, should prostrate himself at the abbot’s feet; while all the brothers are seated, he should ask to be joined to the holy congregation.
