If this is granted him, he should hasten to kiss the abbot’s feet. Then, in the presence of all the brothers and on his knees, [Col. 0829B] he should make his petition.

“The abbot should order him to write his profession; or, if he does not know letters, another who knows how, asked by him, should write it.

“When Terce has been sung, or the litany, in the presence of the abbot and all the brothers standing by, the novice, carrying the document with him, should come before the altar and, raising his voice, say:

‘I, Brother N., promise my stability, the conversion of my morals, and obedience according to the Rule of St Benedict, before God and his saints, and in the presence of the lord abbot N.’

“Immediately he should place his hand upon the altar and say this verse:

‘Receive me, O Lord, according to your word, and I shall live; and do not put me to shame in my expectation.’

“At each verse he should bend his knees. The whole congregation should answer the verse, adding ‘Glory be to the Father.’

“Then he should lie prostrate upon the floor with his whole body, with groaning and compunction of heart.

“Then the ministers should bring the abbot a stole, as well as a book and holy water. He should rise and say:

‘Lord, have mercy. Christ, have mercy. Lord, have mercy.  
Save your servant. Send him help, O Lord. Let the enemy accomplish nothing against him.’

“[Prayers:] ‘God, Father of forgiveness,’ etc.; ‘O God, who through your coeternal Son,’ etc.; ‘Lord Jesus Christ, who are the way without which,’ etc.; ‘Lord Jesus Christ, who are the way, the truth, and the life,’ etc.; ‘Holy Spirit, who are God,’ etc.

“Then the novice should rise from the floor and remain bent over until the [p. 769] abbot has said over the cuculla garment the following prayer:

‘Blessing of the cuculla: God of good virtues,’ etc.; ‘Be present, O Lord, to our supplications,’ etc.

“Then the novice should be stripped of the clothing he was wearing. After holy water has been sprinkled over the cuculla and also over the novice himself, the abbot should clothe him, saying:

‘May the Lord strip you of the old man with his deeds and clothe you with the new, who has been created according to God.’

“Then he should place [lacuna] upon the novice’s head:

‘Lord Jesus Christ, who are the covering,’ etc.; ‘Grant, O Lord, to this servant of yours N.,’ etc.; ‘O God, who [lacuna] your servant,’ etc.

“When these things have been completed, he should receive the kiss of peace from all the brothers, [Col. 0829D] and thus be placed in the last rank. He should keep the hood of the cuculla on his head day and night until the third day; he should also observe complete silence, offer at Mass, and receive Communion.

“On the third day, after the peace of the principal Mass, as soon as the abbot has given him the kiss of peace, the abbot should remove the cap from his head, and from then on he should be counted among the congregation as one who will persevere until death. Amen.”

### From Peter Boherius’s First Commentary on the Rule of the Holy Father Benedict

“When the novice makes solemn profession, the abbot puts on the vestments in order to celebrate Mass. After the offertory the abbot questions him, saying:

‘Brother N., do you wish to renounce the world and all its pomp?’

“He replies: ‘I do.’

“Again the abbot asks:

‘Do you wish to undertake the conversion of your morals?’

“He replies: ‘I do.’

“Again the abbot asks:

‘Do you wish to profess obedience according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict?’

“He replies: ‘I do.’

“And the abbot adds:

‘May God help you.’

“Then the novice reads the profession mentioned above, or another person whom he has asked to do so reads it. When it has been read, he places it upon his head and then upon the altar. After this, kneeling in the four directions in the form of a cross, he says the verse ‘Receive me,’ etc., as above.

“After ‘Glory be to the Father,’ ‘Lord, have mercy,’ the ‘Our Father,’ and the litanies are said, while the novice lies silently prostrate upon the ground before the altar until the end of Mass. While the litanies are being said, however, the brothers ought to remain on their knees in the choir.

“When the litanies have been said, very devout prayers instituted by the Fathers follow. Immediately after Communion, before the prayer is said, the novice’s garments, which have been folded before the altar, are blessed together with their prayers; they are incensed and sprinkled with holy water by the abbot. After ‘Go, the Mass is ended,’ the novice rises from the ground. Once his original, unblessed habit has been removed, he is clothed in the blessed one, the abbot saying:

‘May the Lord strip you,’ etc.

“After the abbot has given him the kiss, all the brothers in turn give him the kiss of peace. With his head covered for three days, he remains in continuous silence, receiving holy Communion during those days. Thus what is said—‘and from that day he is counted among them’—is fulfilled. See book V, *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 4.”

Thus far concerning the ancient rites of monastic profession. It remains for us to say something about the age required for making profession. The Holy Father Benedict does not define the matter absolutely, since, judging no age unfit for serving God, he wished even infants and children to be received [p. 770] into monasteries. Nevertheless, the ancient Fathers rightly thought that some limits should be set to the devotion and zeal of the young, lest a religious profession undertaken carelessly and without sufficiently mature judgment should afterward become a source of weariness and trouble to one unable to shake it off.

For this reason Basil the Great, although he considered every age suitable for serving God, nevertheless did not wish a profession of virginity made before adulthood to be firm and permanent. Thus, in the Rule translated by Rufinus, chapter 7:

“We consider every period from earliest childhood suitable for receiving the fear and instruction of the Lord. Nevertheless, the profession of virginity will be firm only from the time when adulthood has begun, and when the age that is ordinarily judged suitable for marriage has been reached and completed.”

And in his second letter to Amphilochius, canon 18:

“We judge professions to be valid from the time when the age of reason has reached completion. For one ought not to consider childish utterances wholly ratified in these matters. Rather, when a girl is more than sixteen or seventeen years old, has attained the use of reason, has been examined and tested for a long time, has persevered, and strives by her petitions to be admitted, then she ought to be enrolled among the sacred virgins, her profession ought to be approved, and any weakening of it ought to be punished without mercy.”

The Sixth Synod, held at Trullo, does not go quite so far; in canon 40 it requires only ten years in the person making profession, where it says:

“Therefore, whoever is about to take up the monastic yoke must not be less than ten years old. The examination of this matter is left to the discretion of the bishop, who may judge whether it would be more advantageous to extend the period before his introduction and establishment in the monastic life.”

Leo the emperor embraces and reconciles the position and definition of both authorities in this way: those who undertake monastic life in their sixteenth year are to have free disposition of their possessions; those who do so at ten are not to have such disposition until they reach the lawful age.

At least with regard to certain places, St Gregory was somewhat stricter. He forbade adolescents under eighteen to be admitted into monasteries:

“Because,” he says (*Book I, letter 48), “the community of monks on the islands is rigorous, we prohibit children from being received in those monasteries before the age of eighteen. If there are any there now, let your experience remove them and send them to the city of Rome.”

Gregory IX, another pope, requires the same age in his constitution for Benedictine monks:

“No one who has not completed the eighteenth year of his age is to be admitted, nor is any permission to be granted for admitting such persons.”

Similarly, the Council of Oxford in 1222, in Spelman’s collection (*Volume II of the Councils of England*):

“Let monks under eighteen not be received, unless evident utility or necessity dictates otherwise.”

The Cistercian Institutions likewise say (Distinction 10, chapter 1):

“Novices received under the age of eighteen are to be expelled by the visitors. Abbots who knowingly receive such persons are to be placed on bread and water every Friday for as long as they have retained them. Those who inhabit distant regions, such as Phrygia, Hungary, Poland, Bohemia, Livonia, and parts of Germany, [p. 771] and other places in which adults rarely come for conversion, are excepted from this law; they are permitted lawfully to receive those who come for conversion at fifteen years of age and above. If they receive anyone under fifteen, they are to be subject to the penalties stated above.”

Previously, however, novices everywhere were received after completing their fifteenth year, as is clear from the *Book of Institutes*, chapter 76. Gregory IX and Nicholas IV require this same age for those to be admitted to profession in their bulls addressed to the Cluniacs, although we read that Peter the Venerable decreed (*Statute* 36):

“No one, even by concession, who is to become a monk is to be clothed in the regular garments before the age of twenty.”

This age especially pleased Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, whose ancient Statutes say (chapter 27):

“We do not receive boys or adolescents, because we grieve that many things have happened to monasteries through them and fear great spiritual and bodily dangers alike. Rather, we receive men who, according to the Lord’s command through Moses, can proceed to the sacred wars at not less than twenty years of age.”

Likewise Stephen, founder of the order of Grandmont, says in his Rule (chapter 44):

“We prescribe that no one under twenty years of age [lacuna] be received into this religious order.”

In later constitutions for that order, Innocent IV and Clement V renewed his decree. Novices in the monasteries founded by St Patrick also made their vows at the same age.

But in the latest period before the Council of Trent, the age required for monastic profession was exactly the same as that required for contracting marriage—namely twelve years for females and fourteen for males—as is clear from *Significatum* and *Cum virum*, in the section on religious orders. Finally, however, the Council of Trent (Session 25, *On Regulars*, chapter 15) declared every religious profession made before the age of sixteen invalid and null. See Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 16, chapter 6.

“Whatever possessions he has, let him first distribute to the poor, etc.”]

Recognizing how dangerous and harmful the possession of earthly things is for monks, and following in the footsteps of the earlier Fathers, Saint Benedict was unwilling to admit anyone to solemn profession of the religious life before he had renounced absolutely all goods and possessions. Thus, as Cassian says, those ancient monks of Tabennesis and Egypt carefully investigated whether any trace—even that of a single coin—of the novice’s former resources remained attached to him:

> “For they know,” he says (Book IV, chapter 3), “that he cannot remain long under the discipline of the monastery; that he will not even attain the virtue of humility or obedience, nor be content with the poverty and strictness of the coenobium, if even the smallest amount of money lies hidden in his conscience. But as soon as any disturbance arises on any occasion, encouraged by confidence in that small sum, he will immediately flee from the monastery like a stone hurled from a sling.”

Hence the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius, teaching how those who turn from the world are to be examined, says:

> “First, the riches of this world must be cut away from such persons. And if someone appears to be converting as a poor man, he too has riches which he ought to reckon, as the Holy Spirit shows through Solomon when he says: ‘The proud poor man is hateful to the soul, and the lying rich man’; and elsewhere he says: ‘As a wounded proud man.’ Therefore, the one in charge, the Father, must observe this rule with great care: if a poor man converts, he must first lay down the burden of pride, and thus, emptied, be received . . . But if he is rich and possesses many riches in the world, and wishes to convert, he must first fulfill God’s will and obtain that chief commandment which is given to the rich young man: ‘Sell all your goods, give to the poor, take up your cross, and follow me’ . . . But if he wishes to contribute a portion to the monastery, let him know in what manner both he and his offering are to be received.”

And the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers (chapter 1) says:

> “If he wishes to bring any property into his cell, it shall be placed on the table before all the brothers, as the Rule prescribes. But if he is received, from that hour onward he shall have no judgment concerning not only the property he brought in, but even concerning himself.”

The same words are contained in the Rule of Saint Macarius (chapter 4).

Saint Basil teaches the same in the Rule translated by Rufinus, using the example of Jacob and John, who left their father and the boat in which they were; and of Saint Matthew, who abandoned the tax office in order to follow Christ. He develops the matter at length in the Longer Rules, chapter 8.

Saint Caesarius likewise says (Rule for Monks, chapter 1; for Virgins, chapter 4):

> “Let his secular garments not be changed unless he first makes deeds of sale of his property, as the Lord commanded, saying: ‘If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have, give to the poor, and come, follow me.’ Certainly, if he does not wish to sell, let him make deeds of gift either to his relatives or to the monastery, provided that he remains free and possesses nothing as his own.”

Saint Aurelian speaks in the same way in his Rule for Monks, chapter 3, and for Virgins, chapter 2.

In the Rule of Saint Isidore I read (chapter 4):

> “Those who, having left the world, turn with pious and salutary humility to the service of Christ should first distribute all their possessions to the needy or contribute them to the monastery. For then the servants of Christ offer a free spirit to the divine service, when they cut off from themselves all the bonds of worldly hope.”

Saint Fructuosus also wishes those who approach the monastery under the pretext of entering the religious life to be asked (Common Monastic Rule, chapter 4):

> “Whether they have rightly renounced the world or not: whether they have done all that they heard from the voice of truth in the Gospel, which says: ‘Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple.’”

He adds:

> “But if anyone of those whom we have mentioned has, in the manner of false piety, wrongly left even a single coin somewhere, we command that he be immediately expelled, because we see in him not a follower of the apostles but a companion of Ananias and Sapphira.”

Finally, the Master prescribes (chapter 87) that the abbot say to one who comes for conversion:

> “We have established a salutary counsel: hear the voice of the Lord saying to you, ‘Go, sell everything, give to the poor, and come, follow me.’ If, therefore, you wish to follow this voice, go, sell what you have, and bring the entire price here before me, so that, while you are present, it may be distributed by me to the poor, so that no pledge of yours may remain in the world by which you might return to it again.”

See Saint Augustine, Letter 83.

Saint Benedict, however, established that the novices’ goods should either be distributed to the poor or, after a formal donation had been made, transferred to the monastery. The latter practice was strictly avoided by the Tabennensian and Egyptian monks, who, as Cassian writes (Book IV, chapter 4),

> “for this reason do not even consent to accept from him [the novice] money which would be useful for the needs of the coenobium. First, lest, puffed up by confidence in this offering, he should in no way deign to make himself equal to the poorer brothers. Then, lest, through this offering, never descending to Christ’s humility, he should leave when he has been unable to persevere under the discipline of the coenobium and, having grown cold after the spiritual fervor with which he had been inflamed at the beginning of his renunciation, attempt to take back and demand, in a sacrilegious spirit and not without injury to the monastery, what he had brought in. They had often been taught by many experiences that this had to be guarded against in every way: for in monasteries that were less cautious, certain persons were simply received, and afterward, with great blasphemy, attempted to demand the return of what they had brought and what had been spent in God’s work.”

For the same reason the Common Monastic Rule of Saint Fructuosus commands (chapter 18):

> “Let nothing from his former possessions, not even a single coin, be received into the same hearth where he seeks to enter the monastery; rather, let him distribute everything with his own hand to the poor, and afterward, once he has been tested, let him be admitted into the monastery under the Rule.”

Saint Basil seems to agree with this, for, without mentioning the monastery, he asserts only that the novice’s goods are to be distributed to the poor.

Nevertheless, there are—and indeed in greater number—rules of monks that agree with the Benedictine rule: the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius; the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers; those of Saints Caesarius, Aurelian of Tarnatensis, and Isidore; and the Rule of the Master. Indeed, Saint Caesarius permits the goods to be distributed to the parents, and Saint Aurelian permits them to be distributed to whomever the novice wishes. Saint Philibert once refused to do this with great firmness of spirit (in his Life, Benedictine Century II). When he came to Saint Agilus at Resbacum,

> “he distributed whatever he was able to possess as alms, and afterward gave nothing freely to friends or relatives; rather, he carefully and faithfully administered the whole as though royal business had been entrusted to him.”

From all this it is clear how far removed from the ancient discipline of monks are those who refuse to admit novices to profession until, by agreement, a stipulated sum has been paid in full, so that, if even a single coin is lacking, they are forced to return to the world, perhaps to perish there.

Certainly, we find no trace of this corruption in the ancient rules. They either entirely forbid anything to be given to the monastery once the possessions have been distributed to the poor, or, if they permit something to be contributed, they plainly permit it only in such a way that they first advise distributing it to the needy.

Indeed, Hildemar tells us that monasteries reluctantly accepted goods voluntarily offered by novices; this is proved by the rite for admitting profession cited above.

Charlemagne utterly rejected this diabolical invention of Simon Magus when he decreed in his Capitularies (number 15):

> “That no abbot should seek a reward for receiving novices.”

The Second Council of Nicaea likewise rejected it, session 8, chapter 19; so did the Council of Frankfurt in 794, canon 16; Aachen, canon 75; Melfi in 1090, canon 7; Westminster in 1127, chapter 3, and again in 1175; the Third Lateran Council in 1179, chapter 10; London in 1200, chapter 14; the Fourth Lateran Council in 1215; Oxford in 1222; and Sens under Tristan in 1485. All of these attempted to pierce this monstrosity with their decrees and sanctions.

Whether, however, the parents who thrust into a monastery children deprived of their rightful inheritance are thereby to be excused, I do not discuss here. Meanwhile, if you wish, see the letter of Rudolph, abbot of Saint-Trond, to Sibert, prior of Saint-Pantaleon, together with Mabillon’s notes in volume II of the *Veterum Analectorum*.

From this passage of the Rule Peter the Venerable also rightly infers that monks may possess lands and estates. When the Cistercians had objected to the Cluniacs that they differed in no respect from secular people, since they indiscriminately accepted

> “castles, villages, peasants, male and female slaves, and—what is worse—toll revenues and nearly every profit of this sort,”

among other replies he answered:

> “Above all, we appeal to the Rule. For when it treats of receiving novices, it says: ‘If he has possessions, let him first distribute them to the poor, or, after making a formal donation, transfer them to the monastery.’ By saying ‘if he has possessions,’ it excepted no possession; and if it excepted no possession, it excepted neither any estate, nor village, nor peasants, nor male slaves, nor female slaves, nor anything of this kind. But it is clear that nothing was excepted. Therefore it is evident that the things we have listed were not excepted.”

The same author proves this further by the authority and example of Saint Gregory, Saint Maurus, and Saint Columbanus.

Yet although monks may possess lands and estates, we greatly prefer those who, judging the poverty of Christ to be a greater wealth, reject all possessions altogether. Many such men existed among the ancients: Saint Euthymius, for example, who refused the revenues offered by the Empress Eudoxia; and Saint Sabas, who is said to have replied to the emperor in a similar circumstance (volume III of the *Monumenta Ecclesiae Graecae*, p. 343):

> “Those who pray for your piety have no need of such revenues, for their portion and their income is the Lord.”

Likewise Saint Paemen (ibid., volume I, p. 593),

> “who did not wish to accept anything from anyone, evidently to avoid the disturbance of crowds.”

And Saint Lupicinus, abbot, who, according to Gregory of Tours (*Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 1), went to Chilperic, king of Burgundy, to request assistance for the food and clothing of his brothers, who lacked many things because of their great number. When the king offered him fields and vineyards to meet their needs, he replied:

> “We will not accept fields and vineyards. But, if it pleases your authority, assign us something from their produce; for it is not fitting that monks should be lifted up by worldly possessions, but that in humility of heart they should seek God’s kingdom and his righteousness.”

To these may be added Saint Isaac, who, as the other Pope Gregory writes (*Dialogues*, Book III, chapter 14),

> “when his disciples repeatedly and humbly pressed him to accept for the monastery’s use the estates that were offered, firmly held to the strong judgment of his poverty and said: ‘A monk who seeks possessions on earth is not a monk.’ Thus he feared losing the security of his poverty just as greedy rich men are accustomed to guard their perishable riches.”

The monks living under the laws of Saint David likewise

> “rejected possessions and gifts, detested riches, and never brought the neck of an ox among them for plowing.”

Among our own examples is Saint Richmirus, abbot among the people of Le Mans. When he had asked Bishop Gilbert for a place where he could build a cell under the holy Rule and gather brothers, the bishop

> “wished to give him a wealthy place for completing this work. But he refused it and said: ‘I do not seek a wealthy place, nor one raised up by many buildings, but a poor one, in which I, poor, may deserve to follow and imitate poor Christ.’”

Saint Corbinianus likewise (ibid.), enriched by the alms of the faithful, lamented his accumulated wealth just as a miser laments the riches he has lost.

Finally, Saint Vitalis, abbot of the Order of Saint Basil (Bollandists, March 9), when near death, exhorted his followers, saying:

> “Abstain from earthly possessions.”

We have related these matters at greater length for the benefit of those who are bound by the stricter bond of poverty, so that, by the examples of so many illustrious and renowned monks, the zeal for this singular virtue may be more deeply fixed in our hearts. For it is shameful that monks, after renouncing the resources of the world, should cling excessively to earthly things.

We could have added many more examples, but, lest they weary the reader, we shall refrain from recounting them. I cannot, however, pass over those remarkable virgins in Egypt. When the noble matron Eupraxia had offered them gold and silver, the abbess refused to accept the gift, saying (Life of Saint Eupraxia, in the Bollandists, March 13):

> “My lady senator, your servants do not need revenues, nor do they desire money. For they left everything and despise everything in this world for this very reason: that they might deserve to enjoy eternal goods. We wish to possess nothing, lest we be deprived of the heavenly kingdom.”

Again, when the same abbess was near death, she said to the successor whom she had chosen:

> “I adjure you by the undefiled and consubstantial Trinity: do not seek the riches or possessions of this world, nor occupy the sisters with earthly concerns; rather, let them despise temporal goods and deserve to receive eternal ones.”

Most admirably, Saint Stephen, founder of the Order of Grandmont (in his Life, volume II of Labbe’s *Bibliotheca*), when his disciples asked how they would live without temporal goods after his death, replied:

> “I leave you God alone, whose are all things, and for whose love you have left all things together with yourselves. If, by loving poverty, you cling steadfastly to him and do not turn aside from the way of truth, he himself, according to his providence by which he wondrously governs all things, will bestow on you what he knows to be expedient.”

But enough of this. I return to the text of the Rule.

Saint Benedict therefore permits in this passage that a novice, after making a formal donation, may transfer his goods to the monastery. But what is to be understood by a formal donation?

Richard of Saint Angelo replies that a formal donation is one made in writing, before public persons, expressing the donor’s intention and the amount of the donation. Boherius similarly says that it is one made in writing; Smaragdus, that it is one made religiously before witnesses and the entire monastery community.

Smaragdus adduces this passage from the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers (chapter 4):

> “If a novice wishes to bring any property into his cell, let it be placed on the table before all the brothers.”

He also adduces another passage from the Rule of the Master (chapter 87):

> “Together with his soul, let him offer everything to God and to the monastery oratory by donation, with religious witnesses, the bishop, priest, and deacon, or the clergy of that territory, subscribing; and in the deed itself let him stipulate that, if he should ever wish to leave the monastery, he should depart from the monastery without his goods and from God without forgiveness of sins.”

Another passage from the same Rule of the Master may be added (chapter 89):

> “If he has entered with his goods, then the written instrument or donation of his goods made to God or the monastery shall be placed by the donor’s own hand upon the altar, while the brother himself says: ‘Behold, Lord: together with my soul and my poverty, whatever you have given me I return and offer to you. And I wish my possessions to be where my heart and soul shall be. Yet they are under the power of the abbot, whom, Lord, you set over me in your place, to be feared, when you say to them: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me.” Therefore, since through him you consider all necessary things for us, we ought to possess nothing privately, because you are sufficient for us in everything and alone suffice for all things, so that henceforth Christ may be our life and our hope, and death our gain.’”

The bringing of the donation to the altar by the donor’s own hand certainly seems to have belonged to the solemnity of the donation. They did this especially so that the religious scruple against revoking the gift would be greater. Hence the Rule of Tarnatensis, chapter 1:

> “If his vow is such that he desires to contribute what is his to the uses of the monastery, let sincere devotion commend his offering in its entirety, and let him place it upon the altar, so that reclaiming anything from it may be judged sacrilege.”

This rite is mentioned in the Chronicle of Piscaria, Book I (*Spicilegium*, volume V), where:

> “the noble and very wealthy Luto, son of the late aforementioned Aderisus, offered himself, together with all his movable and immovable goods which he possessed at Bectorita, to Lord Romanus, the abbot. Coming before the altar, he made an offering of his goods, and, assuming the monastic life according to the custom of the Rule, was received into the community.”

In the charter of the donation of the estate of Porta, made by Ingelrannus, count of Ponthieu, to the monastery of Centula (*Chronicle of Centula*, Book IV, chapter 21), after the subscriptions we read:

> “This transfer was made upon the altar of Saint Richarius, on the day of the burial of Count Hugh, twelve days before the Kalends of December, by Ingelrannus, his son, together with his nobles.”

In the Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon, it is said that in the year 1017 a certain knight Hugh

> “renewed his donation at the altar of Saint Benignus before a multitude of people”

(*Spicilegium*, volume I). In the year 1052, Hugh, archbishop of the see of Chrysopolis, is said to have

> “placed the donation of a certain church upon the altar of Saint Benignus, while celebrating Masses there on the feast of that martyr.”

In the charter of Wihtred, king of Kent (Spelman, volume I of the English Councils), by which he donated certain land on the Isle of Thanet to Abbess Eabba in the year 696, I read near the end:

> “For the completion and confirmation of this matter, I placed a turf of the aforesaid land upon the holy altar, and with my own hand, because of my ignorance of letters, I marked this charter with the sign of the holy cross, etc.”

Finally, Matthew Paris reports that Offa, king of the Mercians and founder of the monastery of Saint Alban (in the *Lives of the Abbots of Saint Alban),

> “offered the charters of his donation upon the high altar of Saint Alban in the presence of Abbot Willegod, the entire convent, and many distinguished nobles.”

See Menard’s notes on the *Councils of the Rules*, chapter 65, section 17.

“Then, in the oratory, let him be stripped of the things of his own with which he is clothed, and let him be clothed in the things of the monastery.”

Lest he seem to cast pearls before swine, and lest the monastic garment should at some time be defiled by the unworthy; and also lest the novices should become subject to the decrees of the Council of Nicaea, which imposed very severe penance on those who, having been called by grace and having once laid down the belt of military service, returned to the world, Saint Benedict did not wish them to be clothed in monastic garments before they had made profession. Instead, he required them to remain for the entire year of probation in secular dress.

This seems to have been the practice of the ancient monks, especially in the West, as may be seen in the Rule of Tarnatensis, chapter 1; the Common Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 18; the Rule of the Master, chapter 90; and the Rule of Saint Caesarius for Virgins.

There is also a decree concerning virgins of the Fifth Council of Orléans, held in 549, which decrees (canon 19):

> “Whatever girls, whether they seek the monastery by their own will or are offered by their parents, shall remain for one year in the same garment in which they entered. In monasteries where they are not kept enclosed permanently, they shall remain for three years in the garment in which they entered; afterward, according to the statutes of the monastery in which they have chosen to remain, they shall receive the garments of the religious life.”

The same rule is confirmed by civil laws, as is evident from Novel 5 of the Emperor Justinian, whose words are:

> “We decree, following the sacred rules, that those who profess the solitary life should not immediately and readily receive the monastic habit from the most reverend bishops of the venerable monasteries, but should endure a full three years—whether they happen to be free persons or slaves—not yet deserving the monastic habit, but using and remaining in the tonsure and clothing of those who are called laymen, while learning the divine Scriptures.”

Here “laymen” does not mean converse brothers, as Haeften thought, but either slaves or servants assigned to the service of the monks. They generally wore neither monastic clothing nor the monastic tonsure; only the excess of their hair was cut away, they wore modest clothing, and they carried out their secular duties.

Such persons are those assigned to service in our congregation. Their hair is not worn as long as that of other secular people, nor do they wear clothing as costly. Saint Isidore speaks of them in his Rule (chapter 20): “The baking trade shall belong to the laymen.” The Rule of Saint Fructuosus likewise says (chapter 23): “The laymen shall carry out the orders of the abbot or the superior outside.”

Among the Cluniacs they wore the *froccus*, at least those who served the deans responsible for the estates, as is evident from these words of Udalricus (Book III, chapter 5):

> “In the deanery itself, the servant who supplies him with food and drink never serves in only a shirt or only breeches, unless he is also clothed in a *froccus* or fur garment and leggings.”

Alternatively, “laymen” may mean secular clerics, whom he calls laymen in distinction from regular clerics, that is, monks. It was not unusual for the ancients to call them laymen, since the Rule of the Master, chapter 83, even calls priests themselves laymen.

This is clearly proved by Hildemar. Describing the manner in which novices were received in certain monasteries, he says that the candidate for the monastic life first remained for five days at the monastery gate. He was then received into the guesthouse, where, after spending two months in lay clothing, the Rule was read to him over two or three days. If he declared himself capable of observing it, he was then brought into the chapter wearing his own fine garments—that is, cuirass, shield, lance, sword, and belt.

After the abbot’s exhortatory sermon, if he continued to renounce the world, he was granted another period of delay and then came again to chapter according to the same rite. There, before the brothers, he laid aside either his belt and armlets or only his sword.

If he absolutely refused to return to the world, he then discarded all his other clothing in the same place, was shaved, and clothed in other garments—that is, his own CLERICAL garments—and at last was sent to the novices’ cell.

Aigradus appears to confirm this interpretation in the Life of Saint Ansbert, number 8. After leaving the king’s court and fleeing to Fontenelle, Ansbert was received as a guest. He began to ask the servant that he might be permitted to see the holy Father of the monastery. Humbly prostrating himself at his feet, he asked to be made a monk.

When the venerable Father heard this holy and God-worthy request, he said that he wished to take time for the matter. When the period had passed, the illustrious Father, after receiving the counsel of the spiritual brothers, fulfilled his pious wishes as he had requested and made him honorable in the clerical habit.

Others, however, laid aside neither weapons nor secular clothing until the year of probation had been completed. The Council of Aachen favored this practice, decreeing (canon 34) that a novice

> “should neither be tonsured nor change his former clothing before he promises obedience.”

The practice may be seen in the Life of Saint Landelinus, number 3, Benedictine Century II; the Life of Saint Botulphus, number 2, Century III; the Life of Saint Leufredus, number 9, in the same century; the Lives of Saints Harlindis and Reinula, number 11, in the same place; and the Chronicle of Centula, Book IV, chapter 14.

But this custom has long since become obsolete. Benedict, who afterward became abbot of Aniane, came to the monastery of Saint-Seine and, after obtaining permission to enter,

> “immediately cut off his hair and assumed the habit of a true monk.”

The Cluniacs likewise gave novices the tonsure and monastic habit, except for the cowl, as we learn from Udalricus. This later became the common practice. Hence the Statutes of Lanfranc decree (chapter 18):

> “Let the novice, whether layman or cleric, be tonsured and shaved in the manner of monks; then let him be stripped of secular garments and clothed in the regular garments of the monastery, except for the cowl, with its hood sewn to the tunic.”

Among the Cistercians also (Book of Usages, chapter 102), the novice was clothed in the same material as the other professed monks,

> “except for the monastic habit, in place of which he had a cape and mantle, or skins.”

Yet at the very beginning of the newly founded order secular clothing was retained until profession, as Saint Bernard’s Letter 1 to his nephew Robert proves. He writes:

> “By your prayers and many tears you obtained the mercy you had long awaited, and you gained entry to the one whom you had desired sufficiently. Afterward, having been tested for a year according to the Rule, having conducted yourself with complete patience, perseverance, and without complaint, you freely made profession after the year. Then for the first time, rejecting secular clothing, you assumed the habit of the religious life.”

Bernard of Monte Cassino must be heard concerning the Cassinese:

> “We modern men, by custom—would that it were a reasonable one!—at the very entrance into probation both shave and tonsure the novice and clothe him in the habit, though not in the blessed habit. Although this custom is not rejected by usage, it nevertheless seems more prudent to follow the opinion of the aforementioned Paul.”

This is the opinion of Hildemar, which we cited above and whom he usually cites under the name of Paul the Deacon.

Boherius adds:

> “I believe it is well done if, at the beginning of probation, regular clothing, tonsure, and enclosure are given to him, so that he may be tested in them for a year and in the other hard and rigorous observances of the order.”

And below:

> “Nevertheless, this habit ought to have the likeness and severity of a monastic habit, as is found today in the constitution of Pope Benedict, chapter 22. Yet it should be distinguished from the habit of professed monks by its cut, color, or blessing.”

Certainly, since wearing the monastic habit belongs to the austerity of the religious life—for everyone sees that wearing wool next to the skin, sleeping in one’s clothing, and wearing a garment despised by the world are contrary to nature—and since novices ought elsewhere to experience all the austerity of the monastery, later generations did not without reason judge that they should be clothed in monastic garments with some distinction.

There are also examples of this among the ancient monks, especially in the East, where the Egyptian and Tabennensian monks clothed their novices in the monastic habit at the very entrance into the religious life. Cassian testifies to this in these words (Book IV, chapter 5):

> “Thus, when someone has been received, he is stripped of all his former property, so that he is not even permitted thereafter to retain the garment with which he is covered. Instead, he is brought into the midst of the assembly of the brothers, stripped of his own clothing, and clothed by the hands of the abbot in the garments of the monastery. By this he learns that he has been stripped not only of all his former possessions, but also, after laying aside all worldly pride, has descended to the poverty and neediness of Christ. Henceforth he is to be supported not by resources obtained through worldly skill or preserved from his former unbelief, but is to receive the provisions of his service from the holy and pious gifts of the monastery. Knowing that from then on he is to be clothed and fed by it, he learns both to possess nothing and nonetheless not to be anxious about tomorrow, according to the Gospel saying. He is not ashamed to be made equal to the poor—that is, to the body of the brotherhood—with whom Christ is numbered and whose brother he was not ashamed to call himself; rather, he rejoices that he has been made a member of Christ’s household.”

That this was the practice among the Tabennensians, or Pachomians, is clear from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, chapter 26, and even more clearly from his precepts published by the Bollandists after his Life. In number 16 (May 14) it is prescribed:

> “If anyone comes to the monastery wishing to become a novice, they shall give him the Gospel prayer—the Lord’s Prayer—and teach him the psalms. He shall remain at the monastery gate and be tested there; whatever the other brothers know, he too shall learn there. After this, they shall strip him of his secular garments and clothe him in the habit of the novices.”

The practice of this precept can be seen in the letter of Ammonas to Theophilus, number 1, also published there by the Bollandists. Saint Pachomius himself is also said to have been admitted by Palaemon and immediately clothed in the monastic habit.

This would be the place to speak of monks *ad succurrendum* (“for succour”), that is, those who, being at the point of death, requested monastic clothing as an act of penance. Once they had been clothed in it, they were counted among the professed if they afterward recovered. Our Mabillon discusses them in the preface to Benedictine Century IV, part II, p. 99, which anyone may consult.

“But let the clothing from which he has been stripped be placed in the wardrobe for safekeeping.”

The Rule of the Master prescribes the same thing, chapter 90. Cassian likewise reports the same practice among the Egyptians and Tabennensians, Book IV, chapter 6. The matter is clear concerning the Tabennensians from the Rule of Saint Pachomius, article 26, and from the supplementary material to his Life published by Bollandus. There it is said that, because of his diminished fervor after twenty years, the monk Silvanus was ordered

> “to be stripped of his monastic clothing in the assembly of the brothers, dressed in secular clothing, and expelled from the monastery by the brothers.”

John Moschus also relates of a certain robber (*Spiritual Meadow*, chapter 166) that, having become a monk at the monastery of Firminus, he approached the abbot after nine years and said:

> “Give me my secular clothing and take back the monastic clothing.”

After he had received it, the wretched man hanged himself the following day.

“But let him not receive that petition of his which the abbot took from the altar; rather, let it be kept in the monastery.”

So that, even against his will, if the abbot wishes, he may use it to bring him back into the monastery and keep him subject there. Or perhaps, if he says that he is not a monk, overcome by that petition he may be reduced to monastic service,” says Smaragdus.

Or also, as Hildemar says:

> “So that, if at some time he denies the monastic or perhaps clerical habit, it may be produced before the bishop as proof that he must live either in the monastery or, certainly, under canonical discipline, even if compelled by the bishop, after he has left the monastery, according to the authority of the Nicene canon.”

It should also be noted what Boherius relates about preserving such a petition:

> “Among us it is customarily kept in the reliquary cupboard, not in the record office, since obligations concerning persons ought to be preserved more dearly than those concerning property.”

In a manuscript constitution of Clement V for the Order of Grandmont I also read that the novice should

> “offer the profession document upon the altar; the prior receiving it and handing it to the cantor of that monastery, so that it may be placed in the sacristy of that monastery for eternal remembrance of the matter.”

## CHAPTER LIX. Concerning the sons of nobles or poor men who are offered.

[Note: Another reading: “how.”]

[Column 0839]

If someone from among the nobles offers his son to God in a monastery, and the boy is still underage [Florence manuscript: “of the nobles”; Hildemar and Florence, with some others: “younger”], let his parents make the petition mentioned above. With the offering, let them wrap both the petition and the boy’s hand in the altar cloth, and in this manner offer him.

Concerning his property, let them promise in the present petition, under oath, that they will never, through an intermediary person or in any other way, give him anything or provide him with any opportunity to possess anything.

But if they do not wish to do this and wish to offer something to the monastery as alms for their own reward, let them make a donation from the property they wish to give to the monastery, reserving for themselves, if they so wish, the usufruct [Oxford: use of the fruits; Florence: usufruct; another manuscript: use of the usufruct; Narbonne: enjoyment of the fruits].

In this way let everything be closed off [Oxford, Concordia, and Bernard of Cassino: “observed”], so that no suspicion remains for the boy by which, deceived, he might perish—God forbid; for we have learned this by experience.

Let the poorer parents act likewise. But those who possess absolutely nothing should simply make the petition and, together with the offering, offer their son before witnesses [“before witnesses” is absent from the Florence and Hadrumetum manuscripts].

## COMMENTARY

[Column 0839]

### [Col. 0839B]

From the reception of adults Saint Benedict passes to the offering of infants. It is established that infants were formerly admitted and brought up in monasteries not only from this chapter of Saint Benedict, but also from the ancient rules of monks and from numerous other reliable authorities. The holy legislator ordained that these children should be received impartially from both the poor and the rich, because there is no distinction between the two before God; indeed, a humble poor person is usually more acceptable to Him than a proud noble. Hence Saint Augustine, and Saint Isidore after him, speaking of monks, said (Augustine, *On the Work of Monks*; Isidore, *Ecclesiastical Offices*, book II):

> “They also come from rustic life itself, from the practice of crafts, and from plebeian labor—indeed, all the more happily because they have been more strenuously brought up; and if they are not admitted, it is a grave offense. For many great and exemplary men have arisen from that class. For this reason also God chose the weak things of the world, to confound the strong, and so forth.”

Yet this was not the opinion of Leofric, the tenth abbot of Saint Alban’s in England. Matthew Paris writes of him (*Lives of the Twenty-Three Abbots of Saint Alban’s*):

> “He was a respecter of persons: he admitted no one to the monastic state unless illustrious by birth, or at least legitimate, maintaining that men of ignoble and illegitimate birth—especially the unknown and unstable—would be more prone to outrageous conduct.”

Saint Fulgentius, however, thought very differently (*In his Life*, in Bollandus, 1 January). He “freed from temporal hunger, by giving generously, those whom he wisely admonished to renounce the world, and persuaded those who possessed nothing to despise the desire to possess.” So too Saint Gildasius, abbot of Rhuys (*Bollandists, first century of Benedictine hagiography*), who, “so that he might offer more pupils to the Lord, gathered monks with him both from the noble and from the poor, from orphans and from children deprived of their parents,” as his acts relate, no. 12.

Certainly the judgment of Gerard the Belgian monk is true and certain:

> “It is all the more disgraceful not to admit a poor man, as it is shameful for a monk to be proud—provided that those who are poor in Christ are proved to be so not merely by fortune but also in spirit, and that it is evident that they do not come to cast off poverty but to seek it more diligently.”

These remarks may be made in passing on the occasion of the title of this chapter, which is: “Concerning the sons of nobles or of the poor who are offered.” I now come to the text.

### “If someone perhaps from among the nobles…”

By “nobles” Saint Benedict here understands the term not strictly, as meaning persons distinguished from commoners by some rank, title, or dignity, but broadly, as meaning any powerful or wealthy persons. “Whether they are noble or ignoble,” says Hildemar, “that is, he is speaking of those who possess wealth.” Boherius likewise says: “From among the nobles, that is, the rich and powerful.” Indeed, here the holy Father sets the nobles in opposition to the poor.

### “Offers his son to God in the monastery.”

That he may be instructed in the disciplines of the Rule and remain there in God’s perpetual service.

### “If the child himself is of a younger age…”

“That is, if he is under fourteen years of age,” says Richard of Saint Angelo. Boherius says: “For a male, the younger age is fourteen years; for a female, twelve.” Nicholas of Fractura says the same, and this was defined in the Tenth Council of Toledo, canon 16:

> “Parents shall have permission to hand over their sons to religion only until they have reached the fourteenth year of age.”

At least, this is how Gratian read it (*Decretum*, part II, question 2, chapter *Si in qualibet*). Ivo of Chartres, however, in part VII of his *Decree*, chapter 27, has not “fourteenth” but “twelfth”; in the edition of the Councils, “tenth” is read. Perhaps you should correct both readings, since the canon of the Council of Toledo was adapted to the practice of its own time.

Therefore, after this age it was no longer lawful for parents to offer their children to monasteries. Saint Benedict did not explain whether children of every kind should necessarily be received if offered before this age, nor did Saint Basil. The Rule of Saint Aurelian, however, prescribes (chapter 17) that:

> “Those of younger age are not to be received into the monastery except from ten or twelve years onward, when they no longer require to be nursed and know how to avoid faults.”

The Sixth Synod in Trullo likewise decreed (canon 40):

> “He who is about to take upon himself the monastic yoke must not be less than ten years old.”

Unless, perhaps, the council is understood to refer to those who offer themselves voluntarily, rather than to those offered by others.

In most monasteries, children offered by others were not admitted before their seventh year. This may perhaps be the meaning of Saint John’s statement in Rufinus (*History of the Monks*, book II, chapter 1), when he said to a certain military commander concerning his son:

> “Let him be brought up in your house without any pagan contamination for seven years. When these have been completed, hand him over to the monks, to be instructed in holy and heavenly disciplines.”

In the Rule of Saint Caesarius for virgins we read (chapter 5):

> “If it can be done—indeed, with difficulty, or perhaps never—let no little girl be received into the monastery before six or seven years of age, when she is already able both to learn letters and to obey obedience. The daughters of nobles or of ignoble persons are not to be received at all for nursing or instruction.”

The same is found in the Rule of Saint Donatus, chapter 6.

At about this age we find most of those offered in our monasteries: Placidus, Faustus, Gordianus, Bertulfus, and Bede. Many were younger, such as Samson, Boniface, Godefrid, and Peter the Deacon, who were five years old. Some were three years old, and even some only a year old.

Here I cannot omit the pious institution of Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine. As we read in his Life, book II, no. 4 (Baluze, volume IV of the *Miscellany*), he had united two communities, one of men and one of women, and had ordained that children should be admitted into both in such a way that in the monastery of women they would be brought up until they passed the age of five years, after which they would move to the monks’ house.

### “His parents…”

“Hildemar says that by ‘parents’ he means only father and mother, because *parentes* is derived from father and mother, from giving birth.” Smaragdus says the same, reporting Saint Isidore’s testimony, in which Samuel is mentioned as having been offered to God by his mother Hannah:

> “From this it is understood,” he says, “that by parents he means no others than the father or mother who begot him.”

Boherius says the same.

Bernard of Cassino nevertheless maintains that it is possible that, according to the common usage of the region, the child wished to call his closer blood relations “parents.” Nicholas of Fractura also seems to support this. The contrary, however, is proved by the text itself, in which the person to be offered is called a son; this can certainly apply to no one except a father or mother.

The question is then asked: by which of the parents is the child to be offered? Hildemar replies:

> “If the father is alive, the father must pronounce the petition. If he is dead, the mother must pronounce it; for another relative ought not to do so.”

Suárez, however (*On Religion*, volume III, book V, chapter 2), teaches that the power of offering the child resides in both parents, and that when one dies it remains with the survivor. If the father offers the child while the mother objects, he says, the offering is valid and lawful; the reverse is not so if the mother wishes to offer the child while the father objects. Nevertheless, an offering made by the mother without the father’s consent would be lawful and valid, provided that the father does not retract it; even so, he could reclaim his son within a year.

The same right, he says, belongs to a guardian, because in everything concerning the child’s education the guardian succeeds to the place of the parent, and the law made no exception for this case. Indeed, a guardian may offer the child against the mother’s wishes, but the mother may not do so against the guardian’s opposition.

The distinguished Peter of Gussanvilla, on the other hand, writes in his notes on Peter of Blois’s letter 54 that guardians, relatives by marriage, and blood relatives may not permanently devote to a monastery minors orphaned of both father and mother who are unwilling. For this he cites the Fifth Council of Orléans, the Ninth and Tenth Councils of Toledo, Saints Benedict, Lanfranc, and Bernard, who use the word “parents,” which properly signifies father and mother, not relatives by marriage, blood relatives, or guardians.

This is also Mabillon’s opinion in volume III of the *Ancient Analecta* (p. 479), and Charles Coint’s in volume I of the *Annals of the Church of the Franks*, under the year 544.

Parents could nevertheless have their children offered by others, as is clear from Othlonus’s *Life of Saint Boniface*, chapter 2 (*Benedictine century III*, part II). There a five-year-old boy was sent to the monastery by his sick father through suitable agents. The same is clear from the formula of offering used among the Cluniacs, in which a monk offers a boy to God in the monastery in place of his parents.

Peter Boherius seems to have understood the matter in this way when he says that in his monastery boys were offered either by their parents or by their friends. Guardians and blood relatives themselves could also offer children when the children desired it, but not when they resisted.

We also sometimes read of adults being offered by their parents. On these matters see what we said in book V of *The Ancient Rites of the Monks*, chapter 5.

### “Let them make the petition which we mentioned above…”

That is, in the preceding chapter, also promising on behalf of the son stability, conversion of conduct, and obedience, as is evident from Smaragdus, Hildemar, Boherius, and others. From these authorities Bernard of Cassino should be corrected, for he interprets the petition here as the one by which the parents jointly ask the abbot and the community that their children be brought up in the monastery.

Thus, after reporting Hildemar’s opinion under the name of Paul the Deacon, he says:

> “But certainly, as it now seems to me, and as I think, we ought to understand this petition as in the preceding chapter: ‘To persist in his petition for four or five days,’ and so forth. That is, they are to ask that he be received into the monastery, brought up, and instructed in the disciplines of the Rule; and, insofar as it depends on them, they are to offer him to God. For according to the laws, when he reaches the age of discretion he can object and return to the world. Therefore I do not understand this to refer to the words of profession.”

Richard and Nicholas of Fractura agree with Bernard.

The contrary, however, is established by the following text of the Rule, which prescribes that the child’s hand be wrapped in the altar cloth together with the petition itself.

Our Acherius printed several formulas of this petition or offering in his notes on Lanfranc; our Mabillon printed others, and Charles Coint, whom we cited above, printed still others. Smaragdus also gives another, reported by Haeften (*Book IV*, treatise 1, disputation 4). I add here two shorter ones. The first is from an old manuscript codex of Saint Cecilia of Albi, written in the ninth century, and is as follows:

> “I hand over this boy in devotion to our Lord Jesus Christ, before God and His saints, so that he may persevere all the days of his life and become a monk until his death.”

The second is from a manuscript codex of Mont-Majeur, in these words:

> “It has been ordained in the Old and New Testament that children should be offered to God, as Abraham and [a word is missing here] are read to have done; instructed by their example and that of many others, I, so-and-so, for the remedy of my soul and of the souls of my parents, now offer this son of mine, so-and-so, to almighty God and to Saint Mary His Mother, according to the Rule of Blessed Benedict, in the monastery of Mont-Majeur, in the presence of its lord abbot, from this day onward; so that it may not be lawful for him to withdraw his neck from beneath the yoke of the Rule. I promise never, either by myself or through any suspect person, in any way to give him an opportunity to leave, God forbid. And so that this writing may remain firm, I confirm it with my own hand.”

### “And with the offering…”

This offering was the very matter of the unbloody sacrifice: bread and wine. This is clear from Hildemar:

> “He must place in his son’s right hand the offering with the little cloth, and in his left hand the small vessel.”

And below:

> “The offering refers to the bread and wine which are offered in sacrifice.”

The same is evident from Lanfranc’s Statutes (chapter 18):

> “The boy who is to be offered, after his head has first been tonsured, carries in his hands the host and the chalice with wine, as is customary.”

It is also clear from Udalricus:

> “The boy himself receives, with the offertory, the paten and chalice, with the host placed upon it and wine poured into it; and thus the appointed minister wraps the boy’s hand in the altar cloth.”

From these passages Nicholas of Fractura should be corrected, since he understands “offering” perhaps to mean an offering of the child’s possessions to the monastery.

### “Let them wrap [his hand] in the altar cloth…”

It is said that touching the sacred altar cloths was forbidden to women consecrated to God and to nuns by a decree of Pope Soter. The Synod of Auxerre likewise decreed (canon 37):

> “A woman may not place her hand upon the Lord’s cloths.”

It may therefore seem surprising that Saint Benedict permitted boys who were still laymen to touch the cloth, when the same act is recorded as forbidden to women consecrated to God.

This passage of the Rule, however, does not refer to the consecrated altar cloth placed immediately beneath the Lord’s body, which was sometimes also used to cover it and was therefore called the *corporale*. [Note: Col. 0841D: In the testament of Saint Aredius, volume II of the *Analecta*, we read of *pallae corporales* (“corporal cloths”).] Rather, it refers to the linen or covering with which the altar is spread and covered, part of which formerly hung down before the face of the altar. It was easy to wrap the boys’ hands in this part. It was called *palla*, from *palliare*, “to cover,” because it covered the altar.

This explanation of *palla* is confirmed by the book of the Miracles of Saint Remaclus, bishop, no. 14 (*Benedictine century II*):

> “She removed the cloth with which the aforesaid matron had covered the altar.”

It is also confirmed by Lanfranc’s Statutes (chapter 18):

> “After the priest has received the aforesaid offering, let the parents wrap the boy’s hands in the cloth with which the altar is covered and whose front part hangs down.”

And by the *Book of Cistercian Usages* (chapter 114):

> “Washing separately in the vessel appointed for this purpose the altar cloth upon which the corporal is spread.”

For the corporal is not spread except upon the altar cloth.

The French versions support this interpretation, explaining *palla* as “the altar cloth” (*la nappe de l’autel*). Nicholas of Fractura says:

> “In the altar cloth, that is, in the towel or consecrated cloth which is always upon the altar.”

I believe Bernard of Cassino understood it in this way when he said:

> “I think that, according to the literal meaning, it should be understood of the cloth that is upon the altar; and I have also seen this carried out in practice.”

Richard says:

> “I believe that the upper part of the altar is called *palla*, as the term is used in *On Consecration*, distinction 1, chapter *Altaris palla*.”

Boherius, however, explains the practice of his monastery in his first commentary as follows:

> “Among us, after the reception has taken place in the chapter house, the boy is offered at the altar by his parents or friends. While he kneels with bowed head, two brothers place upon him the cloth, or pallium, which hangs before the altar.”

Hildemar disagrees with all these interpretations. He explains *palla* as the little cloth with which the boy presents the offering:

> “For he does not say that he is to be wrapped in that altar cloth which is consecrated, that is, which is placed upon the altar. Rather, he speaks of the cloth with which we make the offering, which we call the little cloth. It is an altar cloth because the altar’s office is performed through it.”

### “And thus let them offer him…”

This also follows from the decree of the Council of Aachen, canon 36:

> “At the time of the offering, let them also make the petition for him before lay witnesses, which the boy himself is to confirm when he reaches an age at which he can understand.”

It is useful here to describe the entire rite of offering from Hildemar:

> “This is how it is to be done. If the father is alive, the father must speak; if he is dead, the mother must speak, for another relative ought not to do so. He must say:
>
> ‘I, so-and-so, promise before God and His saints, on behalf of my son, his stability, the conversion of his conduct, and the obedience he is to maintain.’
>
> He must have the written petition and the promise in his hand on behalf of his son. For example, when the Gospel has been read, at the time when they are to offer him, before they begin the offertory, he must place in his son’s right hand the offering with the little cloth, and in his left hand the small vessel of wine.
>
> Then the father must hold the child before him and wrap his son’s hand in the little cloth with which he makes the offering, for it is this little cloth, not the consecrated altar cloth, that is called the altar cloth. Then he must hold the hand of his son, wrapped in that little cloth, with his own hand, together with the petition by which he confirms his son in that monastery; and witnesses must be present.
>
> Then the abbot must question him in this manner:
>
> ‘What do you ask, brother?’
>
> He must answer:
>
> ‘I wish to hand over my son to almighty God, to serve Him in this monastery, because the Lord commanded in the Law that the children of Israel should offer their sons to God. Therefore I too wish to offer this son of mine to God in the same way.’
>
> Then the abbot must say to the witnesses:
>
> ‘Do you hear, brothers, and do you see what this man says?’
>
> They must answer:
>
> ‘We hear and we see.’
>
> Then the father must lead his son before him to the place where people customarily make offerings. The priest must take the offering and the small vessel from the child’s hand, which the father has been holding, and the abbot must receive the child and take the petition. The father must nevertheless place the petition upon the altar, since the abbot is to take the petition from the altar, as is stated in chapter 58: ‘Let him place it upon the altar’; and elsewhere: ‘Let him not return the petition which he has taken from the altar.’
>
> It is better, however, if it can be done, for the abbot himself to sing the Mass, so that he may also receive the offering and the wine. Blessed Benedict therefore commanded that the child be offered with the offering, so that what is done may be signified by what is shown outwardly: just as the offering becomes a holocaust to the Lord, so too may the child become a holocaust to the Lord, and so forth.”

See Lanfranc’s Statutes, chapter 18; Udalricus, book III, chapter 8; and book V of *The Ancient Rites of the Monks*, chapter 5.

### “Concerning their possessions, either in the present petition let them promise under oath that they will never, either personally or through an intermediary, or in any manner, ever give him anything or furnish him an opportunity to possess anything…”

“As Bernard of Cassino says, someone can find opportunities in many ways—for example, if they were to ask someone to make the offered boy his heir, or if they were to substitute him as an instituted heir, and in many other ways which malicious people know how to devise.”

Hildemar explains precisely how the parents are to make this promise. The father, “when he offers his son, must say”:

> “Saints, I promise by Him who lives forever that I will never give him his inheritance or anything at all. Rather, I disinherit him from all my inheritance, so that he may be an heirless person forever, and so that by no device may he claim my inheritance as his succession.”

Something similar may be seen in the formulas of the petition among Smaragdus and the other authors cited above.

Boherius, however, says in his first commentary:

> “This is not observed among us.”

Perhaps this was because of some privilege of the Apostolic See by which monks were granted power to share in their parents’ inheritance. We read of such a privilege once granted by Innocent IV to the monastery of Saint Thierry near Reims, in a manuscript history of that monastery under the year 1247. The same pope, together with Nicholas, granted a similar privilege to the monks of Saint-Germain-des-Prés in these words:

> “By the authority of this present document we grant you the favor that you may freely receive, claim, and retain possessions and other movable and immovable goods which may have come by right of succession, or by another lawful title while remaining in the world, to persons who, fleeing from the world, assume the religious habit in your monastery and bind themselves there by the bond of profession—excepting feudal property.”

### “Or, if they are unwilling to do this, and so forth…”

“That is,” says Hildemar, “if they are unwilling to disinherit him from his possessions but wish to offer his portion to the monastery, then let them offer his portion together with the child. For it must be done in this way: if they wish to offer his portion to the monastery, then, when he offers his son, he must also say:

> ‘I also offer his portion for the remission of my soul to this monastery, so that, when I have joined his portion to it, I may retain the usufruct; but after my departure, let his inheritance come to this monastery, or at least something greater than his portion.’”

They mentioned this donation in the formula of the petition, near its end, which they wrapped together with the child’s hand in the altar cloth. This accords with the ancient custom by which we sometimes read that offerings made to God were wrapped in the altar cloth or pallium.

Thus, in the Life of Saint Virgil, bishop of Salzburg, no. 16 (*Benedictine century III*, part II), Count Gunther is said to have handed over to Bishop Virgil “through the altar pallium that church itself, together with everything that he had previously donated.”

The passage of the *Rule of the Master*, chapter 91, also concerns this matter. There parents are first advised to distribute their son’s entire portion to the poor, according to the Lord’s command. If they are unwilling to do so, they are at least to divide the same portion into three equal parts: one is to be distributed by the abbot’s hand to the needy, another is to remain with his parents or brothers, and the third is to be applied to the common benefit of the monastery.

### “And thus let everything be secured, so that no suspicion remains in the boy by which, if deceived, he might perish—God forbid—as we have learned by experience.”

Smaragdus comments on this passage:

> “For he had seen young men leave the monastery on such an occasion, abandon the service of God for earthly things, and love the world. Therefore he says, ‘as we have learned by experience.’ If this formerly happened rarely, we now know that it happens very frequently.”

Our Menardus therefore rightly concludes from this passage of the Rule that children offered to monasteries in this manner were bound to the monastic state in such a way that afterward, even when they had reached the years of puberty, it was not open to them to withdraw and return to the world.

For why would parents disinherit their children, and do so with a solemn oath never to give them anything, if it were free for them, once they reached puberty, to cast off the yoke of monastic life? It would be a wholly unjust disinheritance and an irreligious oath.

Moreover, if it had been lawful to return to the world, why would everything have had to be secured in such a way that no suspicion or opportunity remained for the boy by which, if deceived, he might perish? Would he perish because he rejected that way of life, when he had been bound to follow it by no bond whatsoever? He could have returned to the world with a clear conscience.

This inference from the Rule of Saint Benedict is confirmed by the formula of the offering or petition, in which the parents remove from the son every liberty to return to the world. They hand him over “to remain according to the Rule, so that from this day it may not be lawful for him to withdraw his neck from beneath the yoke of the Rule, but rather so that he may understand that he must faithfully observe the institutions of that same Rule and serve the Lord with a grateful heart together with the others,” as is found in the formulas of Smaragdus, Udalricus, and others.

Or else:

> “So that he may persevere all the days of his life and become a monk until his death,”

as is read in the formula of Saint Cecilia of Albi.

For this reason also they promised stability, conversion of conduct, and obedience on behalf of the son, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict.

The same is confirmed by the Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 4), where we read:

> “Whoever has been assigned to a monastery by his own parents must know that he is to remain there.”

This passage is found in the excerpts of Egbert, bishop of York, no. 92 (in Spelman, volume I of the *English Councils*).

### [Page 789]

The same is evident from the councils.

The Fourth Council of Toledo (canon 49) says:

> “Either parental devotion or one’s own profession makes a monk; whichever of these has bound him shall hold him. Therefore we forbid such persons to return to the world and prohibit every entrance into the secular life.”

And below (canon 55):

> “Whoever, having received penance from among the secular, has had his hair tonsured, and then, transgressing again, has become a layman, is to be apprehended by his bishop and recalled to the penance from which he withdrew. If some, through penance, are irrevocable and, after admonition, will not return, they are truly to be condemned before the Church by the sentence of anathema as apostates. The same applies to those who were tonsured by their parents, or who, after losing their parents, voluntarily devoted themselves to religion and afterward assumed secular dress, and so forth.”

The Council of Worms (canon 22) says:

> “If a father or mother, while their son or daughter is still in the years of infancy, has handed him or her over within the enclosure of a monastery to the discipline of the Rule, it is not lawful for them, once they have reached the years of puberty, to leave and marry. This must therefore be avoided by everyone, because it is impious that the reins of pleasure should be loosened for those offered to God by their parents. Therefore, as we have said, it is never lawful for them to lay aside the habit they have received. Rather, once it has been proved that they have at any time worn the tonsure or religious clothing, they must be compelled, willingly or unwillingly, to remain in the observance and habit of religion.”

The Council of Tribur (canon 6) says:

> “He whom his parents have handed over to a monastery, and who has begun to sing and read in the church, may neither marry nor leave the monastery. If he departs, he is to be brought back; if he abandons the tonsure, he is to be tonsured again; if he has taken a wife, he is to be compelled to leave her.”

To this may be added the response of Pope Gregory II to Saint Boniface, apostle of the Germans, who had consulted the supreme pontiff on this matter. The Council of Worms cited above expressed his words.

Hence there is the case of a certain Lambert mentioned by Gratian. His father had unwillingly clothed him in a cowl between his eighth and tenth years, and not long afterward a bishop had also unwillingly given him the monastic habit. Later, when he protested, he was absolved and dispensed by Pope Nicholas I—not because, having received monastic clothing while under age, he later protested, but because his father had clothed him in the cowl against his will, his hand had not been wrapped in the altar cloth, and he had received no blessing from the abbot.

Saint Bernard likewise writes to Robert, his nephew, who offered among other reasons for his transfer from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs the fact that he had been offered to the Cluniac monastery by his parents. Bernard answers as follows (*Letter 1*):

> “Although there is no doubt that he was promised, not given—for his parents did not make the petition prescribed by the Rule on his behalf, nor was his hand wrapped in the altar cloth together with that petition so that he might be offered before witnesses.”

If he had been offered in this way, therefore, his offering would have been entirely valid.

Elsewhere (*Letter 324*) Bernard teaches that Thomas, once offered at the monastery of Saint Bertin, was not to be prevented from transferring from the Bertinians to Clairvaux—not because his offering did not bind him, but because:

> “The parents’ vow remains intact, and their offering has not been emptied but increased.”

### [Page 790]

Aldric is likewise recorded by an ancient author as having been offered by his parents at the monastery of Centula, in book I of the *Miracles of Saint Richarius*, abbot, no. 14 (*Benedictine century II*):

> “On the condition and under the stipulation that afterward he should not wish to turn back from this profession.”

Similarly, at the monastery of Farfa, Aldric the younger was offered by his parents “to serve God perpetually,” as an anonymous author testifies in his Life, no. 4 (*Benedictine century IV*).

Nevertheless, the boy himself had to confirm the offering “at an age of understanding,” according to canon 36 of the Council of Aachen, Lanfranc’s Statutes, and Udalricus. This was not so that he would undertake a new obligation, but so that he might be shown to ratify and accept the obligation already undertaken.

What we have said thus far is so clear and evident that even a blind man could touch it with his finger. Anyone who has failed to notice these things must be entirely deprived of the light of reason. It is therefore astonishing—or rather, astounding—that some people, through repeated attacks of alien and violent glosses, twist these passages into the opposite meaning, although they can establish their opinion upon no foundation either of reason or of authority.

Who can deny that the power to offer children so that they would remain perpetually in a monastery belonged to the parents? Those who can give, sell, or subject them to the yoke of servitude can certainly submit them to Christ’s most gentle yoke and consecrate them to God. Those who could bind them to the Christian religion by baptism of their own will could also bind them to the monastic life.

“But,” they will say, “this practice is the source, cause, and origin of the damnation of many who, detained unwillingly in monasteries, rush into worse things.”

They would have spoken much more fairly if they had said:

> “This practice has been the source, cause, and origin of the salvation of many—and plainly of far more—who, while living in the world and participating in its corruption, would otherwise have incurred the eternal punishment of damnation.”

Moreover, who will believe that those unable to bear the light burden of monastic life would be better and more likely to be saved in the world? Why do they wish to leave the monastery? To become disciples of Christ, or of the world? Plainly, of the world: to serve its empty spectacles, to be consumed by its pleasures, to rejoice in its riches, and to be exalted by its honors.

And who will be saved with these? He who denies that he can be saved in Christ’s school—will he be saved in the school of the devil?

On the other hand, we could assert not without foundation that the ability to return to the world, granted to those who had reached the age of discretion, became the ruin of many. For some, the mere power to return to the world, like fuel for temptations, became the occasion of their turning back and consequently of their perdition.

If they had not possessed this power, they would nowhere have thought of returning to the world. Instead, turning necessity itself into virtue, they would have persevered religiously and humbly in the service of God, knowing the world only by name.
