Some legal texts are brought forward, but they are either false, or at least doubtful, or concern adults alone and not children, or are of later date.

For by a new law, children offered by their parents are permitted, when they reach the age of discretion, either to confirm their parents’ offering or to return to the world. This permission was granted to them by Clement III, chapter *Cum virum*, under *On Regulars*, and by Celestine III, chapter *Cum simus*, under the same title. The reason was the abuse of certain persons who, not so much from devotion as to relieve their families, thrust into monasteries any sons they had who were hunchbacked, deformed, or unfit for the world. This practice worked harm not only to the children themselves but also to the ruin of regular discipline.

For this reason some abbots, even earlier, were entirely unwilling to receive children into monasteries. On this matter Saint Udalricus says in his preface to the *Customs of Cluny*, addressed to William, abbot of Hirsau (*Spicilegium*, volume IV), praising him because he had enacted a law preventing children from being admitted into the monastery:

> “So that,” he says, “the secular persons mentioned above may be obliged to provide another nest for themselves, in which they may place their abortive chicks, as though they had been disinherited.”

A little later he adds:

> “On this matter let each person think as he wishes. I am certain that you have uprooted entirely that root from which alone, above all, all the monasteries that have been destroyed—whether in the Teutonic or in the Roman tongue—were destroyed.”

Guigo, the fifth prior of the Grande Chartreuse, had noticed the same thing, as he himself testifies in the Statutes (chapter 27):

> “We do not receive children or adolescents, because we grieve that many things have happened to monasteries through them, and because we fear great spiritual and bodily dangers at the same time.”

For this reason Peter Damian, writing to the Cassinese monks (*Opusculum* 36, chapter 16), says:

> “Among the other flowers of virtue which I found in that field, full of which the Lord has blessed, I confess that this pleased me greatly: I did not find there schools of boys, who often weaken the rigor of holiness; rather, all were either old men, with whom that noble man indeed sat at the gates of the church, or men rejoicing in the grace of youthful life.””

Saint Anselm, however, was far more kindly disposed toward children. When an abbot complained to him that he had to endure unruly boys, Anselm replied that this arose not so much from the boys’ bad nature as from the poor instruction of their superiors, as Eadmer relates in book I of his Life of Anselm (Baluze, volume IV of the *Miscellany*).

Anselm’s opinion could be confirmed by what is read in the Life of Saint Stephen, abbot of Obazine, book II, concerning the remarkable simplicity, piety, and holiness of children.

In any case, to guard against the dangers that might arise from the bad character of children, monasteries did not admit just anyone indiscriminately, but those who had been tested—at least in some monasteries—for a year, just as adults were. This is proved by the decree of the Fifth Council of Orléans, canon 19:

> “Any girls who either seek the monastery of their own will or are offered by their parents are to remain for one year in the clothing in which they enter.”

There is no doubt that the same law was imposed upon boys, who were clothed in the monastic habit at the very time of their offering.

Furthermore, the abbot did not receive anyone he wished at his own pleasure; he received those whom the brothers had approved. That the brothers’ counsel and consent were required is clear from the Life of Saint Willibald, written by a nun, no. 5 (*Benedictine century III*, part II). There Willibald, aged five, is said to have been offered to Abbot Egbald:

> “Immediately that abbot of the monastery declared the matter to his congregation according to the discipline of regular life, and he requested that this be done with their counsel or permission. At once that assembly of the brothers gave their response or permission, saying that all these things might lawfully be done at their discretion, and so forth.””

### [Page 792]

What has been said thus far concerning the offering of infants reminds me that I should briefly resolve a question once raised concerning widows who have children but nevertheless desire to renounce the world: how should they provide for their children’s education and salvation, a duty which by law rests especially upon the widows?

[Col. 0848B] Because it would be exceedingly dangerous to leave them alone in the world, and because formerly parents retained every legal right over their children, those who, summoned by a special vocation of the Holy Spirit, wished to reject the vanity of the world and pursue Christ’s humility in monasteries offered their children together with themselves, to serve God; in this way they adequately provided for their children’s welfare and education. In support of this interpretation there is the *Life of Saint Rictrudis*, abbess of Marchiennes, chapter 11, in the second Benedictine century of the *Acta Sanctorum*.

“Likewise, the poorer.” That is, the less wealthy. For, as the commentators here observe, Saint Benedict distinguishes three classes of people in this chapter: the wealthy, whom he calls noble; those of moderate means, whom he calls poorer; and the entirely poor, who possess absolutely nothing.

“Let them make the offering.” As was said above concerning the nobles: by disinheriting their son, or by transferring whatever portion belonged to him to the monastery through a solemn donation.

“But those who possess absolutely nothing should simply make the petition.” Without making any donation or disinheritance.

[Col. 0848C] “And with the offering let them offer their son.” “With the offering”—that is, with the unbloody sacrifice of the Mass, or with the bread and wine to be offered for it, according to what was said above. Accordingly, Caramuel deserves criticism: casting darkness over a very clear text, he asserts that the preposition *cum* (“with”) here stands for *pro* (“for”), so that he gives the sense: “Let them simply make the petition, and with the offering and for the offering let them offer their son,” as though the son himself were the offering. “That the text ought to be explained in this way,” he says, “is clear, because what offering could they give to God, when they are supposed not only to be poor but to possess absolutely nothing?” Saint Benedict, however, requires no other offering from them.

“Before witnesses.” “Perhaps two or three,” says Richard of Saint Angelo; and indeed laymen, according to the Council of Aachen, canon 36, lest the testimony of monks in their own affair arouse suspicion. Saint Basil likewise says (*Longer Rules*, chapter 15, and in Rufinus, chapter 7): “Infants, however, who are offered with the will and consent of their parents—or rather, offered by the parents themselves—ought to be received [Col. 0848D] in the presence of many witnesses, so that every opportunity for the slander of wicked men may be removed.” Practice has confirmed that this is to be understood of the noble as well as of the poor.

## CHAPTER XL. Concerning priests who may perhaps wish to dwell in the monastery

[Col. 0847]

[Col. 0847D] 793 If someone from the order of priests asks to be received into the monastery, assent should not be given to him too quickly. Nevertheless, if he persists altogether in this petition, he must know that he will observe the entire discipline of the Rule, and that nothing will be relaxed for him, so that it may be as it is written: “Friend, for what purpose have you come?” (Matthew XXVI). He may nevertheless be permitted to stand after the abbot and to give blessings or celebrate Masses, provided that the abbot orders him to do so. Otherwise, he must presume to do none of these things [Note: [Col. 0849A] “Aliqua” is absent in Hildemar], knowing that he is subject to regular discipline, and that he must give everyone an even greater example of humility.

And if he should happen to be in the monastery because of ordination or for some other reason, he should observe the place he occupied when he entered the monastery, not the place granted him out of reverence for the priesthood. If any cleric wishes to join the monastery with the same desire [Note: [Col. 0849A] Certain manuscripts give the remainder in the plural: “if any,” etc.], he should be placed in an intermediate position. And he himself nevertheless, if he promises observance of the Rule or his own stability [Note: [Col. 0850A] Florentius: “his own stability.”].

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0849]

[Col. 0849A] “If someone from the order of priests.” “The term ‘priest,’” says Hildemar, “applies to a bishop, presbyter, and deacon, as he himself says below.” Rupert, however, interprets this passage only of bishops (*Book III on the Rule of Saint Benedict*); this is confirmed by a manuscript codex of the monastery of Saint Adrian of Mount Gerard, whose present chapter is entitled “Concerning bishops who wish to dwell in the monastery.” Certainly, *sacerdos* properly refers to a bishop.

Saint Hildegard, on the contrary, understands Saint Benedict here not of bishops but only of presbyters. Thus she says: “By ‘priest’ we must understand one who presided over a provostship, an archpresbyterate, or a parish, and who, because of that same position of authority, could scarcely restrain his soul into submission; not a bishop, since it would be unbecoming for the ruler of the souls of the people, who had also been the abbot’s teacher, to be subjected to an abbot. But if such a man should wish to be converted, let him remain alone in penance, without subjection to a teacher’s authority.”

Yet ancient practice in our monasteries teaches and proves that this passage is to be understood both of bishops and of presbyters. For, as Peter the Venerable writes (*Book II, Letter 11*), “Clerics of various orders, canons of different professions, and the very summits of the Church—I mean bishops—used to exchange pontifical dignity for the lowliness of monks, and to humble themselves from the highest degrees of ecclesiastical honors to the lowly order of this vocation.” Examples include Saint Arnulf of Metz, Saint Claudius of Besançon, Saints Wulframnus and Amatus of Sens, Saint Hidulfus of Trier, Leidradus of Lyon, Adalbert the apostle of the Bohemians, Leo of Ravenna, Peter Damian of Ostia, Bruno of Segni, and many others who, having laid aside their episcopal insignia, did not hesitate to wear the humble habit of monks in the cloister.

“If he asks to be received into the monastery.” Haeften aptly observes that Saint Benedict does not say here, as above, “if he wishes to be converted,” but “if he asks to be received,” because clerics are considered already converted from the world when they assume the clerical state. He proves this from the Council of Chalon, canon 5, which prohibits “secular persons who have not yet been converted to the clerical state from being entrusted with the affairs of parishes.”

“Assent should not be given to him too quickly.” On this passage Bernard of Cassino writes: “The word ‘too quickly’ may be comparative with what was said in chapter 58, namely, that an easy entrance should not be granted to him—as though Saint Benedict were saying: assent should not be given to him more readily than to a layman at his entrance; rather, just as the layman is tested, so should this man be tested.” Indeed, more is required. Boherius says the same.

Grimlaicus explains how he should be tested in the *Rule for Solitaries*, chapter 18, in these words:

“But lest someone should attempt to enter this way of life with a feigned mind, he must first be tested severely. This can readily be discerned if he bears with equanimity every bodily labor imposed upon him and willingly inclines toward a harsher life; or if, when questioned, he is in no way ashamed to confess his own offense and gladly accepts the remedy applied to that offense; and if he inclines to every form of humility without embarrassment, and, should reason require it, is not ashamed to submit himself to meaner and more contemptible crafts. When he has been tested by these and other exercises, if he remains steadfast and ready in spirit, then it is fitting that he be received.”

Rufinus translated these words from Saint Basil’s Rule, chapter 6, where they are spoken generally of everyone; Grimlaicus applies them individually to priests.

“Nevertheless, if he persists altogether in this petition, he must know that he will observe the entire discipline of the Rule.” “For it is fitting that those who undertake the same life with others should experience the same discipline in the laws,” as Alexander III says (*Decretals*, chapter *Recolentes*). Hildemar observes here that the word *disciplina* has several meanings; in this passage some take it principally to mean a scourge, while others understand it as observance of the Rule. The latter meaning is to be preferred to all others:

“By ‘the discipline of the Rule,’” says Smaragdus, “he means regular instruction in everything and the precepts of holy teaching. For *disciplina* takes its name from learning; whatever is learned in the holy school of the Rule is appropriately called discipline. Regular instruction consists in the precepts of the same Rule, in corrections and rebukes, and in various judgments; whoever perseveres in these to the end will be saved.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius speak in nearly the same way, and the following words clearly demonstrate that this is the meaning of the Rule.

[Col. 0850C] “Nothing will be relaxed for him.” “Because,” says Hildemar, “he must be tested through every stage like a layman, and even more than a layman. For novices are tested in three stages: first at the monastery gate for four or five days; then in the guesthouse for a few days—that is, two months; and third in the novices’ cell for ten months.”

Bernard of Cassino likewise understands this to mean that nothing is to be relaxed concerning the stages of testing, of which he counts the same number. Turrecremata and Matthew Lambert hold the same view. Our Menardus, however, interprets Saint Benedict as speaking not of the novitiate but of observance of the Rule.

In my judgment Richard of Saint Angelo and Boherius are more correct in their first commentary, since they understand the passage of both: nothing is to be relaxed either in observance of the Rule or in the stages of testing. Thus, “when a cleric came to Saint Pachomius to be enrolled among the monks, respect was indeed shown to his rank, as divine law prescribes for us; but as regards observance of the canon binding the brothers, he fulfilled it equally with the others,” as the *Acts of Saint Pachomius*, no. 18, report.

“So that it may be as it is written: ‘Friend, for what purpose have you come?’” The implied words are “do this,” by which Saint Bernard used to rouse himself. According to William the abbot (*Book I of his Life*, chapter 4), “he always had this in his heart and often also on his lips: ‘Bernard, Bernard, for what purpose have you come?’” Saint Arsenius likewise said: “Arsenius, why have you come?”

Hildemar observes that these words of Christ the Lord to the traitorous disciple can be understood in two ways. “Some say that they are the voice of one grieving, as though the Lord had said sorrowfully: ‘Friend, for what purpose have you come?’—that is, into what crime have you fallen? You have come as a disciple to betray your master, as a servant to betray the Lord, as a creature to betray the Creator; and although you were an apostle, you have become a traitor.

“Others, again, understand ‘Friend, for what purpose have you come?’ with ‘do’ understood: that is, you have not come to give a kiss but to betray, as though he were saying: ‘Do what you have come to do’—that is, betray him and fulfill what you promised. Saint Benedict understands it in this sense here: ‘Friend, for what purpose have you come? Do what you have come to do’; that is, you have not come to command but to be commanded, to serve rather than to be served, to be subject rather than to preside.”

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius likewise adopt this interpretation.

“Nevertheless, he may be permitted to stand after the abbot.” “And therefore before the provost and the deans, if they are not priests,” says Menardus. Bernard of Cassino, however, explains “after the abbot” as standing only “in some higher place with the elders—as at Cassino, he says, during the third watch”—and this on account of the honor due to the priesthood.

This applies only if his life is such as to merit that position of authority. For if he has fled to the monastery as a penitent because of some crime, he should not be placed before the others in this way; rather, he must humbly be content with the place belonging to his order, as Smaragdus says.

Among our monasteries the common practice is that all priestly novices precede even professed non-priest monks until the latter attain the priestly rank. Among the Cassinese and Fuliense, however, priestly novices are placed before only the other non-priest novices. See the passage cited above from the *Life of Saint Pachomius*.

“To give blessings”—namely, to bless food and drink in the refectory, or to give blessings at the readings in church, as the commentators explain.

“Or to celebrate Masses.” We observed above that *Mass* has several meanings. Here, however, it refers to the unbloody sacrifice of Christ. Thus, according to the commentators and the French versions, *missas tenere* means “to celebrate Masses,” and to do so in one’s proper order, as Theobaldus Artaldus explains. One translator renders it in French as *faire dire des messes* (“to have Masses said”).

Moreover, *missas tenere* can mean to attend Masses and hear them, as is clear from the Council of Agde, canon 47: “We specifically command that secular persons attend the whole Mass on Sunday.”

“Provided that the abbot orders him to do so.” Hildemar writes: “By saying ‘if the abbot orders him,’ he shows that the abbot ought to give the order only after testing the man’s life.”

[Col. 0851C] “Otherwise, he must presume to do none of these things.” From what has been said above—namely, standing among the elders after the abbot, giving blessings, and celebrating Masses—“he must abstain from these things and occupy a humbler place,” says Bernard of Cassino.

Certainly this was once the custom among the Cluniacs: priestly novices were not immediately permitted to offer the sacrifice, indeed not even immediately after profession. Udalricus attests to this (*Book II*, chapter 28), where, speaking of the novices’ residence for three days after they had made their vows, he writes among other things:

“The abbot carefully examines those who are priests and deacons concerning the manner of their ordination, the extent of their knowledge, and the state of their conscience; he tests their conduct for a certain period before permitting them the license to exercise this ministry. In particular, anyone who was already a priest before coming is altogether prohibited from the office until, by observing repeatedly, he learns with what manifold care such a sacrament is handled by us.”

The manuscript *Customs of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, chapter 31, say the same. We likewise gather that the same practice prevailed among the Cistercians from the *Book of Ancient Definitions* (Distinction 4, chapter 1), where I read:

“If teachers of theology or other distinguished persons transfer themselves to the Order and are priests, they may, with the counsel of the abbot of that place, celebrate during the time of their probation.”

From this it may rightly be inferred that others who were not teachers did not celebrate at all. The Cassinese likewise prohibit it for a time (*Cassinese Declaration*, chapter 60):

“They generally prohibit the aforementioned priests from celebrating Mass for a period, so that their humility may thereby be tested and so that they may learn the rite more thoroughly. At that time, they say, let them receive Communion with the clerics.”

Nor should this seem strange, since even professed priests did not celebrate Mass daily, as we demonstrated in Book II of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 6. Indeed, Clement, of royal English lineage, first a monk of Fécamp and then of Dijon, “declared himself so humbled and insignificant that, although he held the priestly rank, he did not dare approach this ministry more than once in his entire life,” as the chronicler of Saint Benignus relates.

“Knowing that he is subject to regular discipline.” “Here he removes every occasion for presumption by recalling to his mind the state of his subjection,” says Bernard of Cassino.

“And that he must give everyone an even greater example of humility.” Richard of Saint Angelo explains this passage as follows:

“This sentence can be interpreted in two ways. First, the meaning may be that he is to appear more humble than another monk. Second, it may mean that if the abbot orders him to celebrate or to sit after him, he is to appear still more humble.”

“If he should happen to be in the monastery because of ordination or for some other reason, he should observe the place he occupied when he entered the monastery, etc.” The commentators explain this passage in various ways.

1. Hildemar understands Saint Benedict as follows:

“If he should perhaps be worthy to become a dean, provost, or counselor, or to undertake some useful office, he must give counsel to the abbot, or carry out whatever has been enjoined upon him, with the same humility, reverence, and subjection with which he spoke when he entered the monastery.”

Turrecremata interprets it in the same way.

2. Smaragdus and Peter the Deacon explain it in this manner:

“When he says, ‘If he should perhaps be there because of ordination,’ this may mean because he has been ordained a priest, or because he has received from the abbot authority to exercise the ministry of ordination in the monastery. ‘Or for some other reason’ means that he has been exalted in the monastery. He should observe the place, etc.”

3. Boherius, after reporting both interpretations, adds a third in his first commentary:

“Or he means that, apart from the matters already mentioned, he must always preserve his proper order according to the time of his conversion. Thus, if difficult matters are to be arranged in the monastery and the abbot asks the brothers for counsel, he should not answer first or speak first.”

In his second commentary he writes:

“This also means that, although a priest is honored in seating, blessings, and Masses, in other deliberations and offices he must retain the place he occupied when he entered.”

4. Saint Hildegard explains “if he should perhaps be there because of ordination” in this way:

“If, in obediences, offices of authority, or external affairs, matters must be discussed there through counsel, he should observe the place he occupied when he entered the monastery—that is, the purpose of his way of life: humility and subjection, by which he acquires a good and exalted rank, etc.”

Finally, Theobaldus Artaldus interprets “he should observe that place” to mean that he should carefully consider what place he ought to occupy if the circumstances of his entrance into the monastery were taken into account, so that he may be humbled by it, rather than occupying the place granted him out of reverence for the priesthood, lest he become proud.

“If any of the clergy wishes to join the monastery with the same desire.” Although the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius prescribes that “no cleric is to be permitted to dwell in the monastery except one whom the fall of sin has brought to humility and who is wounded, so that he may be healed in the monastery by the medicine of humility,” Lupus of Ferrières clearly proves from this testimony of the Rule that clerics were to be admitted and were admitted into monasteries. They were not only criminals but also pious and upright men, as is evident from the fact that the Rule permits them the rank of authority and the ministry of the altar—things not rightly permitted to criminals.

The same is clear from the Rule of Saint Pachomius cited above. The Fourth Council of Toledo held the same view when it issued this statute (canon 49):

“Since clerics who desire the monastic vocation wish to follow a better life, the bishop ought to grant them free entry into the monastery.”

A similar decree is found in the Council of Augsburg in the year 952.

Pope Paschal II likewise had this in view when he wrote to John, prior of Valerius, in these words (*Miscellanea of Baluze*, volume II):

“Let no opposition from any bishop or provost prevent you from receiving laymen or clerics living in the world for conversion.”

Innocent IV wrote similarly in letters sent in 1244 to the abbot and monks of the monastery of Saint Theodoricus (*Manuscript History of Saint Theodoricus*):

“You may also receive into conversion, and retain without any opposition, clerics and free laymen who, liberated from the world, flee from it.”

The Council of Aachen likewise decrees (canon 42) “that no commoner or secular cleric be received into a monastery to dwell there unless he wishes to become a monk.”

See Saint Gregory, Book X, Letter 39, to Desiderius, bishop in Gaul. When Desiderius wished to recall Pancratius, formerly his cleric and later made a monk, to the church to which he had been attached, Gregory admonished him not to attempt it.

See also Peter the Venerable, Book II, Letter 50, to Atto, bishop of Troyes, whom he exhorts to fulfill the vow of the monastic life; and Saint Anselm, Book II, Letter 12, and Book III, Letter 13.

“He should be placed in an intermediate position.” “If they know that his life is of an intermediate quality; but if he is such that he ought to stand beside the abbot, he should be placed there. Likewise, if he is such that he should stand at the very end, let him stand there,” says Hildemar.

“This applies only if he promises observance of the Rule or permanent stability of his own accord.” “That is, after they have been tested and have made the vow of profession; before that they are no more than novices and remain under the master of novices,” says Bernard of Cassino.

Such a promise must be made both orally and in writing, as by the others. Thus Saint Ursmarus, in the monastery of Lobbes, receiving the priest Erminon, “according to the custom of those living there, made him promise to observe the Rule and to show obedience to his superiors,” as Anso reports in the *Life of Saint Erminon*, no. 4.

## CHAPTER LXI. Concerning how foreign monks are to be received

[Col. 0853]

[Col. 0853B] If a foreign monk comes from distant provinces and wishes to dwell in the monastery as a guest, and is content with the custom of the place that he finds, and does not perhaps disturb the monastery through his extravagance but is simply content with what he finds, he is to be received for as long as he wishes.

If, however, he reasonably and with the humility of charity criticizes or points out something, the abbot should deal with it prudently, lest perhaps the Lord has directed him there for this very purpose.

If afterward he wishes to confirm his stability, such a desire is not to be rejected, especially because his life could have been examined during the time of his hospitality.

But if he is found to be extravagant or vicious during the time of his hospitality, he should not merely be refused association with the body of the monastery; he should also be courteously told to depart [Note: [Col. 0853C] The words “or vicious” are absent in the Concordance], lest through his misery the others also be corrupted [Note: [Col. 0853C] Narbonne: “lest through the vice of his misery.”].

If he is not such as deserves to be cast out, then, if he asks, he should not merely be received and joined to the community; he should also be encouraged to remain, so that others may be instructed by his example, since in every place one Lord is served and one King is served as soldiers.

If the abbot recognizes that he is such a man, he may place him somewhat higher [Note: [Col. 0853C] Other manuscripts: “somewhat.”]. Moreover, the abbot may establish not only a monk but also one of the aforementioned ranks of priests or clerics in a position higher than that in which he entered, if he finds their life to be of such a character [Note: [Col. 0854C] Other manuscripts: “in which they entered.”].

Let the abbot beware lest he ever receive for residence a monk from another known monastery without the consent of his abbot or letters of recommendation, because it is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit IV) [Note: [Col. 0854C] Other manuscripts: “to someone else.”].

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0853]

[Col. 0853C] 800 “If a foreign monk comes from distant provinces and wishes to dwell in the monastery as a guest, and is content with the custom of the place that he finds.” The ancient monks were accustomed to bring a monastic guest, after two or three days, into the common manner of life of the community.

The monks of Nitria allowed him (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 7) “to remain idle for one week; on the following days they occupied him with tasks, either in the bakery or in the kitchen. If someone came whose status required consideration, they gave him a book to read, not allowing him to converse with anyone until the sixth hour.”

In the Rule given to Saint Pachomius by an angel, however, I read this prescription (*Life of Saint Pachomius*, in Bollandus, 14 May):

“If a guest from another monastery comes wearing a different habit, no one is to eat with him except someone who, while traveling, could not observe this rule.”

“And does not perhaps disturb the monastery through his extravagance.” Hildemar understands extravagance as referring to food, drink, or some task; Bernard of Cassino applies it to food, drink, sleep, bed, and labor.

“For,” he says, “these extravagant men say: ‘I cannot eat these beans, these chickpeas, these lentils, this old oil, this moldy cheese, these rotten eggs, these spoiled fish. This wine has no taste for me; this is bread for dogs, not for human beings.’ Such extravagances disturb the monastery, because the brothers are scandalized by them, and some who are less perfect are corrupted by the example of these words.”

Boherius copies Bernard in his customary manner.

“He is to be received for as long as he wishes.” “That is, for one or two years,” says Hildemar. Thus at Mount Nitria (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 7) “there was a guesthouse near the church in which they received a guest for the entire time he came, even if he wished to remain for two or three years, until he chose to depart of his own accord.”

When Saint Basil was asked the question (in the *Rules* translated by Rufinus), “If someone says, ‘I wish to spend a little time with you, so that I may profit from you,’ ought he to be received?” he replied:

“It is fitting that entry be granted him, because the outcome of affairs is uncertain. Sometimes it can happen that, over time, he profits and delights in the holiness of the life and perseveres in what he has begun, as we know frequently to have happened. It also serves to make the truth of our institutions manifest, since people may perhaps think otherwise about them.

“Nevertheless, one must deal with him more cautiously and diligently, so that whether he truly remains and progresses, or whether the truth of our institutions is being tested, it may be found credible and pure. In this way we shall please God, and he will either progress, if he is sincere, or, if he is pretending, he will be ashamed.”

For this reason the Anonymous writer of the *Life of Saint Philibert* (second Benedictine century of the *Acta Sanctorum*) writes that “other abbots would leave their own monasteries, or send very well-tested monks to him, so that by remaining with him for a long time they might learn his life and conduct, in order that they might rightly benefit their own monasteries.”

The Cassinese monks likewise testify in a letter to the Alemanni (*Analecta*, volume IV):

“Many who desire our custom and our manner of life send here from their own communities one whom they recognize as suitable, so that he may perceive by actual sight, and not merely by hearsay, the reasons for which he was sent. In this way some remain here as one of us for an entire year, and some even longer. When everything has been observed, he returns to his own community, confident and joyful.”

Lest monasteries should thereby be burdened excessively, the letters of G., abbot of Mosomum, and A., abbot of Marchiennes, to the abbots of Saint Theodoricus (*Manuscript History of Saint Theodoricus*) and Saint Crispin of Soissons appoint them visitors of their province. Among the statutes of the general chapter whose observance they particularly commend is this:

“No guest is to be detained for more than a year unless it proceeds with the consent of the abbot and community to whom he was sent, or unless it has seemed appropriate to the visitors” [the final word is uncertain in the supplied text: *ex edire*].

[Col. 0855B] “If he reasonably and with the humility of charity criticizes or points out something.” This may be done by word or example, whether concerning the service of God, observance of the Rule, or the keeping of the Lord’s commandments.

Boherius notes here that there are three kinds of correction: authoritarian correction, which is made by an exercise of power and is granted only to superiors; rash correction, which is made with an evil intention; and fraternal correction, which is permitted to those of lesser rank and must be offered without bitterness, with a devoted and reverent spirit. Saint Benedict is speaking of the last of these here.

“The abbot should deal with it prudently.” “Within himself and with those who know the guest’s conduct and words,” says Bernard of Cassino.

“Lest perhaps the Lord has directed him there for this very purpose.” The following remarks of Hildemar, near the end of chapter 63, should be referred to the practical application of this Rule:

“This is how monastic guests are treated in France. If the monk is a familiar guest, he sleeps in the monks’ dormitory, reads in the cloister with the other monks, eats in the refectory, and comes to the brothers’ chapter in the morning and in the evening. If he sees negligence, he should admonish them so that it may be corrected.

“If, however, he is a new guest, he comes only to the brothers’ chapter, for the sake of edification through the reading that is given, and he is led into the brothers’ refectory to eat. He must sleep outside, in the dormitory for monastic guests.

“When this new guest first arrives, the prior leads him through all the monastery’s *officinae* [Note: [Col. 0855D] It may perhaps be necessary to read *officia*, a word that could signify places assigned to the performance of duties. Thus, in Pliny the Younger, *officium praetoris* means the praetorium. EDIT.] and says: ‘Brother, wherever you may have seen negligence, we ask you, for the love of charity, to tell us, so that we may correct it.’”

“If afterward he wishes to confirm his stability, such a desire is not to be rejected.” On this passage Smaragdus writes:

“How he is to confirm his stability—whether only in his heart or in his heart and also by word—he does not state openly here. But, as may be understood, just as a novice promises his stability before God and his saints, knowing that if he ever acts otherwise he will be condemned by the one whom he mocks, so this man, although he does not make a promise because he already has one, must nevertheless confirm his stability in his heart and likewise by word before God, his saints, and suitable witnesses, lest he deserve condemnation for his excessive and unlawful wandering.”

Hildemar gives the following formula for confirming stability:

“I, N., coming from distant provinces to this monastery, because I have been pleased by the conduct of the brothers of this place and they have been pleased by my conduct, therefore by this document written in my own hand I perpetually confirm my stability in this monastery.”

Hildemar adds:

“If he does not know how to write, he should ask someone else to write, and below he should say: ‘Subscribed by my hand for greater firmness.’ It should be noted, however, that he must not name the monastery from which he came.”

Bernard of Cassino, writing on this passage, says:

“I think that by promising obedience to the abbot of this place, especially if he has been professed in another monastery, his stability can be sufficiently confirmed. We have no custom of confirming stability in any other way.”

Nicholas of Fractura says the same.

“Especially because his life could have been examined during the time of his hospitality.” Saint Benedict prescribes no additional period for testing foreign monks beyond the time of hospitality, although Boherius wishes that period to be one year. It may therefore be understood that as soon as they ask to confirm their stability in the monastery, they are to be joined to the body of the community.

Certainly the Rule of the Master establishes only a period of two months for monks of this sort who have already been converted; when it has ended, it permits them to confirm their stability.

Concerning the Cistercians I find the following in the *Book of Institutions* (Distinction 2, chapter 3):

“A professed monk of another order, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, who is received into one of our monasteries, if he has not been blessed, is to remain for one year in the novices’ cell and is to be blessed according to the same rite as a novice. If he has been blessed, he is immediately to be given the cowl; and after at least four months have been completed, he is then, at the abbot’s discretion, to make a petition in chapter concerning the profession he is to make. Reading his profession in the church, as a novice monk, he is to offer it upon the altar, doing nothing more.”

“He should be courteously told to depart.” Saint Benedict’s indulgence is truly admirable: even a superfluous and vicious man he wishes to have dismissed courteously, rather than disgracefully, as he deserves. Hildemar teaches that this should be done in the following way. He should be told:

“Brother, we had hoped that you would be better, but now, since your conduct does not agree with ours, nor ours with yours, take what will suffice for you on the road and go.”

Otherwise, “if such men were admitted into the community, they would offer their guests the sort of repayment that, according to the common proverb, a mouse in a bag, a serpent in the bosom, and fire in the lap habitually offer,” as Richard of Saint Angelo says.

803 “But he should also be encouraged to remain.” According to Smaragdus, he should be told:

“Stay, brother, steadfast with us in this monastery, so that others may be instructed by your good example. There is no need to seek God in another place, since he is everywhere and wholly present. We serve the same Lord in this place, and we serve as soldiers under the same King. There is one Lord in every place, whom his servants serve daily, and one King of kings, whom his soldiers serve always and everywhere. Therefore you have no need to seek another place in which to serve the Lord better, because by laboring well here and serving the Lord faithfully, you will be able to obtain the kingdom of heaven.”

This is not without precedent among the ancients. When the monk Zosimas, at God’s command, had entered a monastery near the Jordan, the abbot urged him to remain there in these words (*Life of Saint Mary of Egypt*, Book I of the *Lives of the Fathers*):

“Because the love of Christ has invited you to see our poverty, remain with us, if you hastened to join us for this reason. The grace of Christ God, and that same good shepherd who gave his life for our redemption and called his sheep by name, will satisfy us all together.”

When he had finished speaking, Zosimas bowed his face to the ground. After they had prayed together and completed the prayer, they said, “Amen”; and so he remained.

“So that others may be instructed by his example, since in every place one Lord is served, etc.” Saint Benedict gives two reasons why a foreign monk should be retained. One concerns the monastery: others are to be instructed by his example. The other concerns the foreign monk: since the Lord is served in every place and one King is served as soldiers, he should not begin, perhaps from remembering his former monastery and from the remorse of conscience that commonly follows, to make fresh excuses concerning his broken stability.

Saint Bernard says (*On Precepts and Dispensations*, chapter 16): “Regarding such a scruple, he offers a general consoling judgment when he says: ‘For everywhere one God is served, and one King is served as soldiers.’”

If the abbot has recognized that he is such a man, let him be permitted to place him somewhat higher in rank.] Thus St. Majolus promoted William, a monk of Lucca, honorably in the monastery of Cluny, “with the counsel of the brethren,” as Rodulf Glaber testifies in his Life of St. William. Likewise, in the monastery of St. Vannes at Verdun, Abbot Richard promoted St. Poppo “to a higher place than that which he had occupied.” Likewise, after Peter Abelard had established himself firmly at Cluny, Peter the Venerable raised him to a higher rank, as he himself teaches in writing to Heloise. From this passage, however, Haeften rightly infers that, by common law, this monk from elsewhere ought to be placed last in rank. Certainly, in the Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius, I read as follows (chapter 13): “That monk, whatever number of brothers he found in another monastery, should know that he has that same number of seniors; nor should it be considered what he was previously, but what he has begun to be should be tested.”

But let the abbot take care never to receive a monk from another known monastery to dwell with him without the consent of his abbot, etc.] This was the ancient and constant practice of the early monks, confirmed by the decrees of councils, supreme pontiffs, and monastic rules. The Council of Agde, presided over by St. Caesarius, bishop of Arles, states as follows (canon 27): “Unless with the permission or consent of his abbot, no abbot shall presume either to receive or retain a monk migrating to another monastery.” These words are taken from the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers, chapter 14. The Council of Autun, under St. Leodegar (canon 10), states: “We decree that no one shall presume to retain another’s monk without the permission of his abbot.” The English Council convened by Theodore, bishop of Canterbury, in the year 673, states in canon 4: “That monks themselves should not migrate from place to place—that is, from monastery to monastery—unless released by their own abbot, but should remain in the obedience which they promised at the time of their conversion.” This passage is cited in the excerpts of Egbert, bishop of York, chapter 66. It should be noted that in certain copies of Bede one reads: “That bishops who are monks,” etc.; hence, if this was not permitted to bishops who were monks, much less was it permitted to others.

The Seventh Council states: “A monk or nun ought not to leave his or her own monastery and transfer to another. If this should happen, it is necessary to receive that person as a guest; but it is not proper to receive him without the mind—or full consent—of the monastery.” Pope St. Gregory, writing to the subdeacon Anthemius (Book I, Letter 40), says: “Neither should a monk be permitted thereafter to migrate from monastery to monastery, nor should you ever permit them to possess anything privately. But if anyone should presume to do this, let him be returned, with suitable correction, to the monastery in which he first lived as a monk and under the rule of the abbot from which he had fled.” Selected chapters from an ancient collection of canons made in Ireland around the eighth century (Spicilegium, vol. II, p. 28) state: “Those monks whose abbot we do not exclude from the table of the saints on account of infamy, we ought not to receive against his will; how much less those coming from holy abbots and otherwise under no suspicion!” St. Basil says (Monastic Constitutions, chapter 31): “The teachers of spiritual congregations ought to cultivate mutual goodwill among themselves and to care for one another in turn; they ought not to undermine one another’s efforts and pursuits, nor rashly and without judgment receive brothers who have defected from another congregation. For this tends toward the utter confusion, dissolution, and indeed destruction of the spiritual building.”

Nor was this established so piously and beneficially by the Holy Fathers without reason. One of the principal reasons was that peace and harmony should remain safe and undisturbed in the monasteries. Thus St. Benedict says: “For it is written: What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another.” The Rule of Saints Serapion, Macarius, Paphnutius, and the other Macarius gives this reason as follows (chapter 13):

“Nor must we be silent about how monasteries may maintain firm peace among themselves. It shall not be permitted to receive brothers from another monastery without the consent of the Father who presides over it; nor ought this to be disregarded, as the Apostle says, because he who has invalidated his first faith is worse than an unbeliever. But if a brother should ask the father who presides over his monastery that he be allowed to enter another monastery, let him be commended by that father to the one who presides over the monastery where he wishes to remain, and let him then be received. For without the consent of the Father who ought to preside over the monastery, a brother must in no way be received elsewhere. But if anyone should presume to do such a thing, let him know that he will be summoned to appear before a synod of bishops or an assembly of his brothers; and then he shall depart as his junior, until he asks pardon from the one whom he has injured, so that, because of his fault, other Fathers may not be despised.”

The Rule of St. Ferreolus gives the same reason (chapter 6):

“For from this, he says, incurable quarrels often arise not only between abbots but also between monasteries, when one strives to defend the man he has received and the other seeks to recall the man it has lost. In the end, unless the man requested is returned to the one requesting him, and the restoration of the one received satisfies the latter’s injured sense of wrong, it comes about that, contrary to the blessed Apostle, they do not overcome evil with good, but both are overcome by evil through a single evil. Nevertheless, we have not thought this should be passed over: if perchance a monk or cleric from another place, as I said above, brings letters from his abbot or bishop in which it is clearly proved that he is not to be avoided because of vices but has been sent for the love of God, he alone may obtain permission to become a member of the congregation.”

St. Bernard likewise adduces the same reason (On Precept and Dispensation, chapter 16): Blessed Benedict “forbids with regard to a neighboring monastery what he commands with regard to a monk from elsewhere, lest proximity between monasteries become a fuel for scandal and material for quarrel if they agree to receive one another’s monks without mutual consent.”

Finally, for the same reason the Cistercians promulgated this statute in their Book of Institutions (Distinction 10, chapter 3):

“For the sake of peace and charity, we decree that we shall receive no one from the Carthusian Order without their permission, nor shall they receive anyone from our order without our consent. But if any of our members should pass over to the Order of Preachers, the Friars Minor, or any other religious order, let them be regarded as fugitives.”

Although this Cistercian statute seems to be understood only of fugitives or expelled members, who, after doing penance, are later permitted by the Statutes of Guigo (chapter 77) to go to another religious house in which they may save their souls—for it is not credible that, in orders so holy, brothers would have passed at will into other religious communities after abandoning the purpose of their profession, in which everything necessary for their secure attainment of eternal salvation was abundantly provided—still, we would wish to have at least some example of this matter.

St. Basil gives another reason in these words (Monastic Constitutions, chapter 34):

“If a more sluggish man should see that he is free, once he has chosen a congregation, to flee its labors and turn to another dwelling of the brothers, living without any supervision according to the license of his own temperament, he is easily torn away from the fellowship of the brothers; and the one who readily receives him will be guilty of his destruction. If this evil advances, it often even leads those who are walking correctly away from the straight and just path, and thus the destruction of all falls in full measure upon the one who has given occasion for such falls. Therefore, lest this occur, let us either admonish brothers who have defected and lead them back to those from whom they defected; or, if they refuse to obey, let us beware of them and avoid them, and refuse their companionship. Let us also proclaim this to all the brothers, so that, chastised by such avoidance, they may return to their own concern and be fed under the flock into which they were first gathered; or, if they themselves obstinately despise spiritual fellowship, so that at least the others, observing how abominable such men are held, may be warned by their example and refuse to imitate those whose disgrace they detest.”

We may add a third reason: namely, that by letters of release or commendation true monks may be distinguished from fugitive and apostate monks. Concerning the latter, the Common Monastic Rule of St. Fructuosus states (chapter 20): “When anyone has fallen away through vice from a monastery, let him not be received into another coenobium, neither out of human kindness nor as a kiss of peace; but immediately, with his hands bound behind his back, let him be returned to his own abbot.”

Those letters of commendation, which it has also been customary to call letters of release, were of two kinds. Some were special, sent to one particular and individual abbot; others were general, addressed to all abbots or bishops. Receive here the forms of both kinds, which some may wish to have.

From the manuscript Customs of the monasteries of Hildemar, Farfa, and St. Paul of Rome.

[Col. 0859B]

“I, an unworthy abbot. Let your charity know that this brother, named John or Paul, has petitioned us to grant him permission to dwell with you. But because we have learned that you maintain regular discipline, we have granted him permission to dwell with you. Now I commend him to you, so that you may treat him as I do, and render an account to God for him as I do.”

From Bernard of Cassino and Boherius.

“To the venerable Father N., abbot of such-and-such a monastery, the abbot of such-and-such a monastery sends greetings in the holy kiss.

“Since our monastery is burdened by various oppressions and poverty, we ask your fatherhood to receive our brother into your monastery to dwell there. By these letters of commendation or release, we commend him to your jurisdiction and obedience. Or thus: We release him from our obedience, so that he may serve the Lord under your obedience.”

From Richard of St. Angelo.

“To the reverend Father in Christ. Or: To the religious and honorable man. Or: To the venerable man N., abbot, from such-and-such an abbot, greetings in the Lord.

“Let your holy fraternity—or your kindness, or your holiness—know that the religious man, Brother N., has earnestly asked us to deign to write him letters of commendation by which, commended to your fraternity—or holiness, or kindness—and placed under the protection of your governance, he might be able to serve the Lord in your monastery. Consenting to his wish, in accordance with canonical authority, we grant him these letters of commendation, by which we give you permission to receive him into your monastery within the space of one month; otherwise, from that time onward, we decree that these letters shall be invalid. Once he has been received into your monastery, we release him from our obedience and grant Brother N. permission to transfer to your monastery, knowing that he was not expelled from our monastery because of his wickedness, but because he greatly desired to serve the Lord in your monastery. Therefore, for the future remembrance of the matter, etc.”

General letters from Hildemar.

“To all bishops, or to all the orders of the holy Church, and also to all the faithful people.

“Let it be known to you that I have given permission to this brother of ours, named John or Paul, to dwell wherever he finds it convenient, provided that he lead a regular life, for his own benefit and that of the monastery.”

From Bernard of Cassino.

“Since Brother N. desires to remain in another monastery where, as it seems to him, he may save his soul and serve the Lord, know that we have given him permission, by these letters of release, to transfer to another monastery.”

Besides these general and special forms of letters by which monks were permitted to transfer to another monastery, there were also others for abbots or monks sent to found a new monastery. By these, they were released from the obedience of their own abbot and subjected to the abbot of the future monastery to which they were being sent, as is clear from the Life of St. Germanus, abbot of Grandval, no. 10 (Benedictine Century II). You will find the form of these letters in Hildemar, in volume II of the Analecta, p. 81.

Moreover, when St. Benedict requires letters of commendation, he is referring only to those coming from a known monastery, not to monks from elsewhere, who, as the commentators observe, could lawfully establish themselves in another monastery without letters of release.

But since St. Benedict is here discussing a change of monastery, which he also recommends to monks from elsewhere, while permitting a transfer to a neighboring monastery with the abbot’s consent, the famous question arises whether it is advantageous for a monk to transfer from one monastery to another. To resolve it more clearly, I suppose that it can be proposed in three ways.

First, someone may transfer from a disordered monastery in which discipline has utterly collapsed and fallen, with no hope of restoring observance, to another in which it remains whole and unimpaired. Second, someone may transfer from an ordered monastery in which he can live with a safe conscience and without any danger to his salvation to another of stricter observance, with a view to greater perfection. Third, someone may transfer from an ordered and strict monastery to one of looser observance, and do so with the permission of the supreme pontiff.

In the first case, I say that the transfer to another monastery in which one may live religiously and securely is not only lawful but in some manner necessary. For, says St. Bernard (On Precept and Dispensation, chapter 16), “if these things cannot perhaps be obtained there, because of the wickedness and irreligion of those dwelling together in that place, I unhesitatingly advise, under the guidance of the spirit of freedom, that one transfer to another place where a man will not be prevented from rendering to God the vows which his lips have uttered. Indeed, with the holy you will be holy, and with the perverse you will become perverse.”

Elsewhere (Letter 7), explaining why he received those who transferred from other monasteries to his own, he says:

“For this reason, then, we receive them: because we do not think it evil if, wherever they can, they render to God, who is everywhere, the vows of their lips which they were indeed able to promise in their own places but were wholly unable to fulfill; and if they compensate for the losses of stability alone by the complete observance of the remaining regular precepts.”

And below, against those who murmured about their coming to him:

“Why are you troublesome to your brother, since he is striving to ensure that he does not render void what has proceeded from his lips? If a man is seeking where and how he may fulfill what he promised to God, what are you losing? Perhaps, if you held him as a debtor for some amount of money, you would compel him to travel over sea and land until he repaid the entire debt to the last farthing. What, then, has God deserved from you, since you do not wish him also to receive from his debtor what is his?”

Peter the Venerable teaches the same thing, writing to St. Bernard (Book I, Letter 28):

“We know that no one ought to receive another’s monk without his permission, so long as, like a true father toward his son and a good shepherd toward his own sheep, he provides everything necessary both for body and soul—namely, those things without which neither the soul can be saved nor the body sustained. But if any of these things is lacking, it is permitted for a brother, even against the abbot’s will, to leave a place that is useless to him, indeed so harmful and dangerous, and to avoid the destruction of his soul by every means, and to seek another place where he may fulfill what he previously could not. . . . For a monk cannot be called a transgressor of his vow or profession if, after leaving a place that did not allow him to fulfill his vow, he transfers to one where he can fulfill it, so that he may say with the prophet: ‘I will pay my vows to you, which my lips have uttered.’ Rather, he ought to be reproved and judged deserving of death if, treating the loss of so great a matter as insignificant, he should endure his own death through foolish patience.”

Hence the Church of Cluny retains from the Apostolic See a concession to receive in this manner monks coming to it; yet it holds this not as a private or singular privilege, but as something common and lawful to all. For monks who come in this way ought to be received, retained, and supported not only by that church but by all the monasteries of Christ.”

Thus far Peter the Venerable. Regarding his statement that his monastery had received permission from the Apostolic See to receive other monks coming to it, Andreas Quercetanus, in his notes on this letter, cites two papal diplomas: one of Alexander II to St. Hugh, and the other of Urban II. Gregory IV had the same matter in view in his letter to the bishops, etc. (Baluze, Miscellanea, vol. II), concerning the dignity and privileges of the monastery of Fleury, written in the year 834.

To all this may be added the testimony of St. Lanfranc, who writes to Abbot Ralph (Letter 60):

“If I, Lanfranc, had sworn with my own hand that I would not leave a certain monastery, but saw that I could not save my soul there, I would leave, nor would I incur the crime of perjury. For whoever is bound to God for God’s sake is not released from him unless he is released against him. But he is not released from him against him who, for love of God and in order to please him well, migrates from the sons of discord, pride, and distrust—or, to put it more aptly, from the sons of the devil—to the sons of peace, humility, and hope, indeed to the sons of God. For one who transfers in this way, does he not plainly flee from the seat of the devil to the seat of God? Etc.”

The teaching of St. Anselm is the same (Book I, Letter 29).

Second, I say that, with a view to greater perfection, a monk may indeed transfer from an ordered and regular monastery to another of stricter observance; nevertheless, in general it is not advantageous, nor should it be undertaken rashly, since such a desire is almost always a pure temptation of the evil spirit.

This is the sound and constant teaching of the holier Fathers of monastic life, which can be confirmed by their nearly countless and very clear testimonies. Thus St. Euthymius, whose words to his monks Cyril reports in his Life (Bollandists, 20 January), says:

“If someone here perhaps cannot practice virtue, let him not think that, if he transfers elsewhere, he will be able to carry out more easily and correctly what he desires. For good action arises not from the nature of the place but from the free determination of our mind. On the contrary, this is dangerous for monks and can render them weak and deprived of the fruits of virtue. For even a plant cannot bear fruit if it is continually transplanted.”

Thus, in Cassian, Abbot Nesteros says (Conference 14, chapter 5):

“It is useful and suitable for each person to hasten, according to the purpose he has chosen or the grace he has received, with the utmost zeal and diligence toward the perfection of the work he has undertaken; and, while praising and admiring the virtues of others, never to depart from the profession he has chosen.”

St. Anselm, writing to the monk Larzo, who was perhaps considering such matters, discusses this argument at length and elegantly, and answers everything that might be brought forward against this position.

No testimony can be brought more plainly to bear on this matter than that of St. Bernard:

“Certainly, concerning religious and well-ordered monasteries,” he says (On Precept and Dispensation, chapter 26), “no member of a religious profession should, on my advice, leave without the permission of his superior, not even out of a desire for a stricter life. . . . And understand more clearly from examples the reason for this judgment. Perhaps someone wishes to exchange the observances of Cluny for the stricter poverty of the Cistercians, choosing the purity of the Rule over those customs. If he asks my advice, I do not advise him to do so unless he has obtained the consent of his abbot. Why? First, because of the scandal to those whom he abandons. Second, because it is not certain that one should abandon certainties for uncertainties: perhaps he will be able to maintain the one and not the other. Third, I distrust the fickleness by which we often, before testing what we readily desire, no longer want it once we have experienced it—within almost a single moment both desiring and rejecting the same thing, as lightly and irrationally as possible.

“We often encounter many such people who, scarcely remaining an hour in one resolve, driven by the breeze of fickleness, waver like drunkards, wandering and unstable, here and there; they change their judgment according to experience—or rather, they fluctuate and rage without judgment, presuming as many plans for themselves as the places they visit, always desiring what they do not have and finding distasteful what they do have.”

Elsewhere, writing to the abbot of St. Nicaise (Letter 32), he says:

“We admonish Brother Hugh of Lausanne, through your mouth and in our spirit, not to believe every spirit and not to be quick to abandon certainties for uncertainties; knowing that the devil always lies in wait for perseverance alone, which alone he knows to be crowned, and that it is safer simply to persevere in the vocation to which one has been called than, under the appearance of a supposedly better good, to abandon what one has already begun and perhaps not be capable of what one presumes to undertake.”

Again, elsewhere (Letter 86), to William, abbot of St. Thierry, who was burning with an ardent desire to cast off the pastoral burden and lead a private life in the monastery of Clairvaux:

“Therefore, on my advice, hold to what you hold; remain where you are and strive to benefit those over whom you preside. Do not refuse to preside so long as you can benefit them; for woe to you if you preside and do not benefit them, but greater woe if, because you fear presiding, you refuse to benefit them.”

Finally, to the Premonstratensian abbot (Letter 253):

“I found in your cloisters men who, moved and converted by the word of our preaching, had decided to come to us; but behold, when your people solicited them, they withdrew their steps and were received and retained in your order and habit. Later, however, with conscience reproaching them, they wished to leave, and, if I am not mistaken, they would have left had they not been strengthened by our support—not merely by our consent but also by our encouragement.”

Certainly, the holy doctor was accustomed to repel monks who wished to come to him from other monasteries and to send back those who came, as is clear from this letter and from Letters 67 and 293. Thus, if he sometimes admitted certain men, he admitted them either from a monastery that was not known or with the consent of their abbot; or else these few were received contrary to the holy man’s common practice and for particular reasons. No one can adduce their admission as an example.

The judgment of Abbot William was the same, although he himself eventually transferred to the Cistercians by a singular divine vocation. Among other things, he writes to the brothers of Monte Dei (chapter 9):

“It is impossible for a man faithfully to fix his mind in one place if he has not first steadfastly fixed his body somewhere. For he who, through sickness of mind, tries to flee by migrating from place to place is like one who flees from his own body’s shadow: he flees from himself, carries himself about, changes his place but not his mind; everywhere he finds the same self, except that mobility itself makes him worse, just as carrying a sick man about commonly harms him by shaking him.”

Peter of Blois speaks in the same manner in Letter 102. Finally, Peter, abbot of Celle, demonstrates the same point by various comparisons (Book IX, Letter 12):

“If only I could, by a brief admonition, drive away—or rather eradicate—the frogs and flies disturbing the innermost chambers of your hearts! I do not deny that Aristotle holds it not useless to inquire into individual matters. But I retain from Hippocrates that the greatest changes generate diseases. Gregory says that plants which are frequently transplanted do not put down roots. . . . In the parable of the Gospel, too, when the foolish virgins went to buy oil, the door was shut.

“The meaning of these authorities is this: let us not be unstable, let us not fluctuate, let us not be carried about by every wind, let us not say, ‘Behold, here is Christ,’ or, ‘Behold, there.’ Therefore, look to your vocation, and establish your foundations and your plants upon the rock; and say with Job: ‘In this little nest I shall die,’ and, like a palm tree, I shall multiply my days.”

Finally, in the Rule of St. Stephen of Grandmont there is an entire chapter 40, “On Not Receiving Men of Another Religion,” which begins as follows: “We entirely forbid men of another religion to be received into this religion.”

I know that some have transferred with praise to stricter monasteries; but, lest anyone flatter himself on the basis of their example, I also know that many more have attempted this to their own confusion and that of others. St. Bernard once complained about this to Abbot William in these words (Apology to William):

“I know that some have flown from other congregations and institutions to our order, knocked, and entered. By doing this, they left scandals for their own communities and nonetheless brought them to us: they disturbed us as greatly by their miserable conduct as they had disturbed their own communities by their rash departure, because they proudly despised what they held and rashly presumed upon what they were not capable of.”

See Haeften, book IV, treatise 2, discussion 6, and Geoffrey of Vendôme, book IV, letter 2.

Third, concerning those who transfer from a regular and ordered congregation to looser observance with the permission of the supreme pontiff, one might perhaps rightly answer with what St. Bernard wrote to his nephew Robert, who had transferred from the Cistercian family to the Cluniacs (Letter 1):

“O senseless boy! Who has bewitched you so that you do not fulfill the vows which your lips have uttered? Will you not be justified by your mouth, or condemned by your mouth? . . . Why does anyone flatter you in vain about an apostolic absolution, when divine judgment holds your conscience bound? ‘No one,’ it says, ‘who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.’ Remove all occasions, reject flatteries, close your ears to praise, question yourself about yourself, since you know yourself better than another does. Attend to your heart, examine your intention, consult the truth; let your conscience answer you why you left, why you abandoned your order, your brothers, your place, and me, who am your kinsman in the flesh and still closer in spirit.

“If it was so that you might live more strictly, more correctly, more perfectly, be secure: you have not looked back; rather, glory with the Apostle, saying: ‘Forgetting what lies behind and stretching forward to what lies ahead, I pursue the palm of glory.’ But if it was otherwise, do not be high-minded, but fear; for—if I may say so with pardon—whatever greater indulgence you have allowed yourself in excessive food and clothing, in idle words, in licentious and curious wandering, than you promised and maintained among us: this is without doubt to look back, this is to transgress, THIS IS TO APOSTATIZE.”

The same doctor’s words to the monk Adam could also be applied to them (Letter 7):

“Fearing this also, as you rightly do, and not sufficiently confident in your own case, you have tried to soothe your remorseful and reproaching consciences with apostolic permission. A very frivolous remedy! It is nothing other than, after the manner of our first parents, covering consciences that have been seared with loincloths—as a covering, not as a cure, etc.”

Elsewhere he explains his mind by the authority of Pope St. Gregory (Letter 94):

“Whoever has proposed to undertake a greater good,” he says, “has made the lesser good, which he was able to undertake, unlawful for himself.” To prove this, he adds testimony from the Gospel: “No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of heaven.” And he concludes: “Therefore, whoever had applied himself to a stronger effort is shown to be looking back if, after abandoning greater goods, he turns back to lesser ones” (St. Gregory, Pastoral Rule, part III, chapter 28).

Again, in his third homily on Ezekiel:

“There are some who do indeed perform the good works they know; and while performing them, they deliberate about better things. But, on reconsideration, they alter the better things they had planned. They perform the good works they had begun, but fall short of the better things they had planned. These people seem to stand before human judgment in their actions, but before the eyes of almighty God they have fallen in their deliberation.”

Finally, elsewhere (Letter 371), speaking of those who, after transferring from looser to stricter observance, later return to their former manner of life:

“I, Bernard, will say of myself what I feel. If I had passed freely, in vow and deed, from good things to better things or from dangerous things to safer things, and had presumed, with an unlawful will, to return again to what I had changed, I would fear becoming not only an apostate but also unfit for the kingdom of God. Blessed Gregory says the same: ‘Whoever has proposed to undertake a greater good has made the lesser good, which was lawful, unlawful for himself.’ For it is written: ‘No one who puts his hand to the plow and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.’ Therefore, whoever had applied himself to a stronger effort is shown to be looking back if, after abandoning greater goods, he returns to lesser ones.”

## CHAPTER LXII. On the Priests of the Monastery

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863C] If any abbot should request that a priest or deacon be ordained for him [Note: [Col. 0863D] Another reading: “deacon.”], let him choose from his own men one who is worthy to perform the priestly office. Once ordained, however, let him beware of exaltation or pride. Let him presume to do nothing except what is commanded him by the abbot, knowing that he is much more subject to regular discipline [Note: [Col. 0863D] Florence manuscript: “subjected.”]. Let him not, on account of the priesthood, forget obedience to the Rule and discipline, but rather make ever greater progress toward God.

Let him always observe the place in which he entered the monastery [Note: [Col. 0863D] Another reading: “entered into the monastery.”], apart from the ministry of the altar [Note: [Col. 0863D] Narbonne manuscript: “of the priesthood.”], and unless the choice of the congregation and the will of the abbot should wish to promote him on account of the merit of his life. Nevertheless, let him know that he must observe for himself the rule established by the deans or superiors [Note: [Col. 0864D] Another reading: “be observed.” The printed editions read: “which must be observed.”]. If he should presume otherwise, let him be judged not a priest but a rebel [Note: [Col. 0864D] Oxford manuscript, with the printed editions: “rebellious.”]. And if, after being frequently admonished, he does not correct himself, let even the bishop be called in as a witness. But if he does not amend even then, let him be expelled from the monastery when his faults have become manifest—provided that his contumacy is such that he is unwilling to submit to or obey the Rule.

## Commentary

[Col. 0863]

[Col. 0863D] If any abbot should request one for himself.] “For himself,” that is, for his own monastery. Menardus observes here that in former times priests were ordained under two different titles: either for their own monasteries, as is clear from this chapter; or for secular churches or parishes, as is found in Distinction 16, question 1, chapters “If Anyone,” “In Your Parish,” “When It Is for the Benefit of the Church,” “Monks,” and “Lest for Anyone.”

The first group is addressed by the observation of our Mabillon, who teaches (Preface to the Benedictine Century V, p. 83):

“Formerly monks were ordained not—as now—under the title of poverty, but under that of their monastery. This is clear from the Council of London of the year 971, in which King Edgar grants certain laws and prerogatives to the monastery of Glastonbury, and, among other things, decrees: ‘He also ordained that whenever the abbot or monks of the place should decide that some of their own men ought to be initiated into the sacred orders, they should have those whom they judged suitable—both monks and clerics—canonically ordained under the title of St. Mary by any bishop, either at his see or in that same monastery of St. Mary at Glastonbury.’

“This had indeed been decreed in the Council of Chalcedon; but afterward this discipline was changed. The words of the council are found in canon 6: ‘No presbyter or deacon, nor anyone at all in an ecclesiastical order, ought to be ordained absolutely—that is, without a title—unless the person to be ordained has been specifically assigned to a church of a city or district, to a martyr’s shrine, or to a monastery.’

“The contrary custom was introduced, as we conjecture, by the example of the Mendicant orders and by the instability of monks. On this occasion, it should be observed that in the Acts of St. Dunstan, no. 29, we note that he was first ordained bishop without a title, chiefly for the reason that he might continually be present at the royal court on account of his prudent counsels.” See also the Life of St. Dunstan by Osbern, no. 12, in Benedictine Century V.

The second group is addressed by what Pope St. Gregory writes to Marinianus, bishop of Ravenna, for the benefit of the monastery of Saints John and Stephen (Book VII, Letter 18):

“No one from that place is to be advanced to ecclesiastical office unless the abbot of the place, after being admonished, should offer him of his own will. But whoever from the aforesaid monastery proceeds to an ecclesiastical order shall thereafter have neither any authority nor permission to dwell there.”

Conversely, those who were ordained under the title of a monastery were bound to it in such a way that they were compelled to remain there permanently. This is clear from the same St. Gregory, who writes to Victor, bishop of Palermo (Book VII, Letter 92), instructing him to ordain one monk in the monastery of Praecoritana as a priest:

“Let him establish by our authority that he is to be assigned neither to a church nor to any other place, but is to remain there continually, so that, while he is not occupied elsewhere, he may be found both constant and useful in his office; and so that the congregation, which asks that he be ordained for it, may, whenever necessary, be strengthened by his celebrating the solemnity of the sacrifice with due reverence.”

Hence Felix had St. Fulgentius, abbot of his monastery and wishing to remain in hiding, ordained a priest, “so that, adorned with the office of abbot and priest, he could neither leave the monastery nor be ordained by chance in another church.”

Whether the Council of London of the year 1075 has this matter in view when it decrees—“Let no one ordain or retain another’s cleric or monk without letters of commendation”—remains to be considered.

## “Who may be ordained priest or deacon.”

Formerly monks were not accustomed to be initiated into sacred orders except upon request, or at least with the permission of their own abbot, as is clear from the letter of Saint Gregory cited above to Marinianus, and also from the Council of Agde (Canon 27):

> “If it should be necessary for a cleric to be ordained from among the monks, let the bishop presume to do so with the consent and approval of the abbot.”

When presented by the abbot, unless some other obstacle intervened, he was ordained by the bishop, according to the decree of Pope Gelasius, which Gratian reports in these words (Distinction 16, question 1, chapter [Col. 0865D] “If there should be a monk”):

> “If there is a monk who, by the merit of his venerable life, appears worthy of the priesthood, and the abbot under whose authority he serves Christ the King requests that he be made a priest, he ought to be chosen by the bishop and ordained in the place which he [the bishop] shall judge appropriate.”

What, however, bishops required of the man to be ordained we learn from this canon of the Council of Clovesho (in Spelman, *Councils of England*, vol. I):

> “Let bishops ordain no one from among the clerics or monks to the sacred rank of the priesthood unless they first clearly investigate what his life has been like, whether he then possesses probity of conduct, and whether he has knowledge of the faith.”

### “Let him choose from among his own.”

Not from outsiders, so that he may always be available to administer the sacraments to the brothers, and so that it may not be necessary to go outside in search of a foreign priest. For it is by no means expedient for monks to go outside [Col. 0866A].
