Saint Gregory had this in mind when, at the request of Urbicus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Hermes, he wrote to Victor, bishop of Palermo (Book V, letter 41), that the man chosen by the congregation,

> “whose life, character [Note: [Col. 0865D] *Mores* seems to be the reading required for the sense. *Ed.*], and conduct may be suited to so great a ministry,”

should, with the Lord’s assistance, be consecrated without delay, so that he might not be compelled to leave his monastery for this purpose, nor be forced to bring in an outsider to perform the sacred work.

Certainly such an outsider might be unavailable, and in fact sometimes was unavailable, as is clear from Rufinus, *Life of the Fathers*, Book II, chapter 11, where, speaking of Saint Helenus, he writes:

> “At another time, on the Lord’s Day, he came to a certain monastery of brothers. When he saw that they were not observing the solemnity of the day, he asked the reason. When they replied that it was because there was no priest present—the priest lived across the river—etc.”

From this it is evident how far from the truth are those who confidently assert that monks formerly took part in the divine mysteries in parish churches. This may perhaps be true of hermits, and possibly of some women consecrated to God, but it can nowhere be demonstrated of cenobites. Indeed, their first Father, Saint Pachomius, whenever he had no priest-monk among his own people,

> “when it was necessary to perform the sacred mysteries, summoned a priest from one of the neighboring churches, and thus the solemnity was completed for them,”

as we read in his *Life*, no. 18 (Bollandists, 14 May). I said “excepting perhaps women,” because nuns living in the city of Antinoe under the abbess Talida did in fact go out to church on Sundays for the sake of communion, as Palladius testifies in the *Lausiac History*, chapter 138.

“Let him therefore choose from among his own,” not by his own initiative alone, but with the agreement and counsel of the entire congregation. For this appears to have been the practice of monasteries, as may be gathered from Saint Gregory’s letter to Victor, bishop of Palermo, concerning the ordination of a priest in the monastery of Praecoritana. He writes as follows (Book VII, letter 92):

> “Because the congregation of monks residing in the monastery of Praecoritana is evidently in need of the ministry of a priest for the celebration of the sacred solemnities of the Mass, and because they request that one from their own congregation be consecrated to this office, we exhort your Fraternity by this present letter to ordain without delay or any excuse as priest in the aforesaid monastery the man whom they unanimously determine to choose from their own congregation.”

The same is evident from the *Life of Saint Germanus*, abbot of Grandval, no. 7 (*Benedictine Acta*, century II), where, “when Blessed Waldebert saw that he was an industrious man, he ordered him to be made a priest; and the entire choir of brothers cried out in his honor, saying that Germanus was worthy of the priesthood.” Likewise from the *Life of Saint Sivard*, abbot of Anisolus (*Benedictine Acta*, century III), who “was made not only a monk, but also, by the election of the brothers, a priest.” And from the *Life of the Venerable Benedict*, abbot of Clusa, written by William, his disciple (*Benedictine Acta*, century VI), who “with the brothers consenting and the abbot ordering it, was promoted to the priesthood.”

Hence Boherius writes in his first commentary:

> “Although the abbot may be presumed to know the consciences of the monks, and the command in the reception of such orders belongs to him, I nevertheless advise that he make use of the counsel of the seniors; for many things escape the eyes of a superior.”

And in his second commentary:

> “I think this election ought to be made on the testimony of the brothers. In ancient times the priest of the monastery was called the Father of the monastery, and therefore this election should be counted among the principal matters.”

See also the *Life of Saint Hugh*, monk of Autun, no. 6, century V, and the *Life of Saint Gerard*, abbot of Brogne, no. 9, also century V.

Moreover, from this passage it is clear that neither was Saint Benedict’s intention, nor was it the custom, that everyone indiscriminately in monasteries should be initiated into the priesthood, as has now become customary. If everyone had been admitted indiscriminately to sacred orders, election would not have appeared necessary. Indeed, in many monasteries formerly there were either no priests or only a few [Col. 0867A].

Saint Pachomius did not permit anyone of his own monks to rise to the clerical rank, as the author of his *Life* testifies, chapter 24 (in Rosweyde). In many other monasteries, only priests sent by the bishop celebrated the sacred mysteries. In certain others, it was regarded as a great distinction for there to be one or two priests in the monastery. Thus Saint Epiphanius, excusing himself to John of Jerusalem for having ordained Paulinianus, Saint Jerome’s brother, priest in the monastery at Bethlehem, writes as follows (among Saint Jerome’s letters, letter 60):

> “When I saw,” he says, “that a multitude of holy brothers were living in the monastery, and that the holy priests Jerome and Vincent, out of modesty and humility, were unwilling to perform the sacrifices due to their office and to undertake this part of the ministry, which is the chief salvation of Christians; and since you could not find or seize upon a servant of God who, because he was unwilling to undertake the heavy burden of the priesthood, had often fled from you—and no other bishop could easily find him either—etc.” [Col. 0867B]

On Mount Nitria there were indeed eight priests for all the monasteries established there. Yet, as long as the first priest of their church lived, no other priest was to offer, judge, or deliver a sermon. This situation was found not only before Saint Benedict’s time, but also long after his death, as is clear from the letters of Pope Saint Gregory, from which we learn that priests were sometimes lacking in monasteries. Nor is this surprising, since it is also known that priests were sometimes lacking in the parishes themselves, as appears from Book I, letters 45 and 51; Book V, letter 2; and Book VII, letter 77, second indiction.

Finally, Saint Aurelianus decrees in his Rule (chapter 46):

> “Let no one receive the honor of the priesthood or diaconate except the abbot, if he wishes to be ordained priest, and one deacon and one subdeacon, whom he himself wishes and whenever he wishes; he shall have the power to ordain them.”

Afterward, however, gradually and imperceptibly, the number of priests in cenobies increased to such an extent that, at the beginning of the ninth century, many had already been initiated into sacred orders. In the monastery of Centula, under Saint Angilbert, abbot who died in 814, at least thirty-two of the three hundred monks were priests. This is established by a writing of his reported by Hariulf in the *Chronicle of Centula* (*Spicilegium*, vol. IV), where he orders:

> “Let no day pass without the chanting of the sacred Masses; that is, if not more, at least thirty Masses should be celebrated daily by brothers of different choirs at different altars, besides the two celebrated most solemnly in the assembly, in the morning and at midday.”

Not long afterward, under Solomon, abbot of Saint Gall:

> “There were together in our monastery forty-two priests, twenty-four deacons, fifteen subdeacons, and twenty boys,”

says Ekkehard the Younger in his *Book of the Affairs of Saint Gall*, chapter 1 (*Spicilegium*, vol. IV).

In the letter of the monks of Reims, Saint Remigius, by which they entered into fellowship with the Dionysians around the year 838, there is a catalogue of the brothers of the monastery of Saint-Denis in France. Among one hundred and twenty-three monks it lists one bishop, thirty-three priests, seventeen deacons, twenty-four subdeacons, and seven acolytes [Col. 0867D].

Of the thirty monks of the monastery of Crowland whom Ingulf (*History of Crowland*) says fled the fury of the Normans in the year 870, ten were priests. In the *Chronicle of Piscaria* in the year 1047, when Abbot Dominic was elected, nineteen priests, one deacon, and the remaining monks subscribed from among the thirty-two monks (*Spicilegium*, vol. V). Finally, in the subscriptions to a sale of land made by the monks of Laon to the monastery of Saint Theodoric in the year 1184 (*Historical Manuscript of Saint Theodoric*), among fourteen monks there are recorded eight priests, three deacons, and three subdeacons.

At last Clement V, in the Council of Vienne, for the enlargement of divine worship, decreed:

> “That every monk, at the admonition of his abbot, should have himself promoted to all the sacred orders, in the absence of a legitimate excuse.”

## “Who is worthy to exercise the priesthood.”

Alexander III, in the Lateran Council, chapter 3, identifies this dignity and the merit of the priesthood chiefly in three things [Col. 0868A]:

> “In all the sacred orders and ecclesiastical ministries, maturity of age, gravity of conduct, and knowledge of letters must be sought.”

The monks of Fulda urged that this be observed with the greatest care in a petition to Charlemagne, requesting (no. 2):

> “That those should be chosen for sacred orders who are learned in speech, proven in holy conduct, neither thieves nor criminals, and who are entirely ignorant of the law of priesthood.”

As for age, there is a statute of Peter the Venerable (*Statute* 43):

> “That none of our men be promoted to the priesthood until the age of thirty, or at least twenty-five.”

Perhaps someone will wish to learn the ancient procedure by which our forefathers promoted their own men to the rank of the priesthood. It is worthwhile to learn the matter from the most ancient commentator on the Rule.

Whenever an abbot wished to honor one of his own men with the priesthood, he would approach the man to whom that brother was accustomed to confess his sins. He would disclose to him his intention of promoting the monk to the priesthood and ask his advice, since some hidden impediment might exist in the monk of which the abbot himself was unaware. When the abbot had received his answer, he would devise some pretext by which the man to be ordained would not come alone into the chapter.

“And then,” says Hildemar, “the abbot ought to address the brothers on behalf of that brother:

> ‘With God’s help I wish to make this brother a priest. Therefore I ask your charity that, for the love of God, for our salvation, and for the salvation of his soul, whoever knows anything about this brother should say so by our authority. Something has already been reported about him; but I do not wish to state or disclose it myself, but to learn it through you. For in time to come I shall bind you by a more serious oath if you do not disclose it.’

“Having said this, he ought to grant an interval of eight days. Then he ought to come into the chapter, if no one has spoken and reported anything about that brother, and adjure them all in this manner:

> ‘I adjure and solemnly charge you by the communion of the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ, by holy baptism, by the reward of heavenly joy, and by our profession, which we have professed, that whoever knows that he is detained in some sin which prevents him from approaching the offering of the sacrifice must report and disclose it to me, so that I may not become a transgressor of this command.’

“Then, if anyone knows something, he should come and report it. If no one comes, he ought afterward to summon each man individually and question him about that brother’s movements and gait. If he cannot discover that he is unworthy, he should then present him for ordination.”

The monks of Fuliens partly imitate this discipline. In their Constitutions I read the following (chapter 62):

> “Whenever someone is to be ordained in any monastery, the matter should be publicly announced in the chapter of the monastery to which he belongs, so that if anyone knows of any stain or defect in him on account of which he ought not to be ordained, he may report it, not publicly indeed, but privately to the superior or to one of the seniors.”

This concerns the abbot’s part in choosing the man to be ordained. What, then, belongs to the man himself? He should follow the exceedingly salutary counsel of Saint John the Abbot (*Lives of the Fathers*, Book II, chapter 1):

> “Thus, my little sons, we do not say that clerical office or the priesthood must be avoided in every way, nor again that they must be sought in every way. Rather, it must be left to God’s judgment whom he wishes, and if he wishes, to take for himself for ministry or for the priesthood.”

Such seems to have been the disposition of the monk Fromundus of Tegernsee, which he reveals in these words when writing to his abbot Peringer (*Analecta*, vol. IV):

> “I neither reject this rank very much nor desire it very much; but in this I obey you and the other seniors.”

Let the man seeking the honor of the priesthood therefore take particular care not to approach the abbot on his own initiative, extort sacred orders from him, or rise to so great a rank against his will. For, to use the words of Saint Basil (*Monastic Constitutions*, chapter 10):

> “To desire clerical office or the presidency over the brothers is in no way fitting for a religious man. It is a diabolical disease and a vice of ambition, bearing the judgment of the devil’s extreme malice.”

Hence also the saying of a certain emperor:

> “Surely he is unworthy of the priesthood unless he has been ordained unwillingly.”

And Pope Lucius III, writing in reply to the archbishop of Tours, says:

> “It is more honorable and safer for subjects, by rendering due obedience to their superiors, to serve in a lower ministry than, to the scandal of their superiors, to seek the dignity of a higher rank. Nor should the desire of subjects in this matter be encouraged.”

For this reason the Cistercians of old rightly decreed:

> “Those who trouble their abbots, either personally or through others, so that they may be promoted to orders, shall not be ordained for two years from the day on which they have done this, unless they have been promoted as abbots.”

Since Saint Benedict first mentioned priest and deacon together, someone might perhaps be moved to wonder why he afterward mentions only the priesthood [Col. 0869B], saying, “Let him choose from among his own who is worthy to exercise the priesthood.”

But, with Menardus, “it should be noted that the name ‘priesthood’ is sometimes attributed to deacons. For the diaconate is a certain order of the priesthood, which is called the third, while the presbyterate is the second, as is clear from Optatus of Milevis, Book I against Parmenianus:

> ‘Why should I mention the deacons established in the third priesthood, and the presbyters in the second priesthood?’

“Therefore it can rightly be said that a deacon is worthy to exercise the priesthood, because the priesthood is spoken of not only with reference to the episcopate and presbyterate, but also with reference to the diaconate.”

It may also be added, with Bernard of Cassino, that the phrase “to exercise the priesthood” refers to all the sacred orders, of which he names the priesthood as the more eminent.

## “Once ordained, let him beware of exaltation or pride.”

For, as Saint Bernard says:

> “It is difficult, and altogether unusual, for one placed on high not to think highly of himself.”

And, as Saint Gregory says (Letter 42):

> “The ruler commonly swells with inward exaltation by the very fact that he surpasses others.”

Again, he says (*Pastoral Rule*, Part II, chapter 6):

> “The human mind is often lifted up even when supported by no authority; how much more does it raise itself on high when authority is also joined to it!”

The holy legislator therefore wisely deters the ordained man from self-exaltation and pride, saying: “Once ordained, let him beware of exaltation or pride.” Although these two may appear to signify precisely the same thing, “they nevertheless differ,” says Bernard of Cassino, “in that exaltation concerns the inner man, whereas pride concerns those signs by which a man is judged and recognized to be proud of his rank.”

The ordained man must avoid both with the greatest care, because the more he has been set above others, the humbler he ought to be: the height of dignity should be the measure of humility. Basil the Great rightly says (*Sermon on Renunciation of the Worldly*):

> “Let the clerical rank not exalt you, but rather humble you. The soul’s progress ought to produce progress in humility. Conversely, being left among the last and dishonored is born of exaltation. The closer you happen to come to the sacred ranks, the more humble yourself.”

This was precisely the mind of Saint Romanus, abbot of the Jura, who, as the most ancient author writes in his *Life*, no. 6 (Bollandists, 28 February), after being ordained a priest,

> “remembering his former profession, trampled upon the authority of his clerical office with monastic humility. Thus, when the solemnity arrived, he could scarcely be compelled by the brothers to stand above them for the sake of the sacrifice; on all other days, presenting himself as a monk among monks, he displayed nothing of priestly eminence.”

Saint John Damascene likewise, as John of Jerusalem testifies, after being made a priest from a monk and entering the laura of Saint Sabas (*Surius*, 6 May),

> “never allowed that the presbyters were worthy of a double honor to enter his mind. Rather, as though changing the wording of this statement, he revolved this thought within himself: that presbyters must strive after double humility, and that presbyters must claim for themselves an exercise of religious life twice as great as before.”

### “[Col. 0870A] Knowing himself to be much more subject to regular discipline, etc.”

Hildemar comments on this passage:

> “In this place, where it says ‘knowing himself to be much more subject to regular discipline,’ some understand that he ought to be led through the seven degrees—that is, that he should also be scourged. This is confirmed by what it says below: ‘Let him not, on account of the priesthood, forget the obedience and discipline of the Rule.’ Obedience refers to the exercise of the work; discipline to the seven degrees.”

Bernard of Cassino likewise says:

> “This clause refers to the exercise of the work; discipline may be referred to being led through the seven degrees.”

Boherius adds:

> “Or understand discipline as the rigor of the Rule, or as coercion and correction.”

### “But let him make progress more and more in God.”

“For the monk-priest ought to be so much more perfect,” says Gerardus Belga, a monk, “inasmuch as the more perfectly a priest at the altar is bound not merely to imitate Christ, but to represent Christ—Christ obedient unto death, the little Lamb made for us all a holocaust and sacrifice” [Col. 0870B].

### “Let him always bear in mind the place where he entered, the monastery, except for the service of the altar.”

“This means,” says Hildemar, “except when he is performing the service of the altar.”

And Smaragdus says:

> “Always intent upon humility, let him preserve his place in all things according to the Rule, and so let him approach for the kiss of peace, for communion, for the imposition of the psalm, for standing in the choir, and for every place whatsoever, except the service of the altar—that is, when he ministers at the altar. For while assisting at the altar, he stands first, sacrifices, and prays first for all, even if he is found to be last in rank. Therefore no place is assigned to him there, nor is any order observed.”

Bernard of Cassino explains it as though Benedict were saying:

> “The priest shall not sit above his senior acolyte, except when he is performing the service of the altar. For then, when he is vested in the sacred garments, he sits after the abbot, or the provost, or the dean, above all the others; and when he celebrates, he is above all and offers the sacrifice to God for all.”

Indeed, in the catalogue of the monks of Saint-Denis in France cited above (*Spicilegium*, vol. IV), priests and others initiated into sacred orders, even the bishop himself, are enrolled among the other monks.

### “And if perhaps.”

“Explain it as ‘unless perhaps,’” says Richard of Saint Angelo.

### “The election of the congregation.”

For Boherius, in his second commentary, election here means “a vote, or petition, or approval.” According to Bernard of Cassino, however, “election” here is taken to mean approval alone.

### “And the will of the abbot.”

Bernard of Cassino interprets “will” as a command; Boherius as a command or permission.

### “If he wishes to promote him.”

That is, by conferring a higher rank or office upon him.

### “Yet knowing that he must observe the Rule established for him by the deans or provosts.”

That is, “let him observe whatever has been commanded him by the deans and provosts,” says Hildemar. Here “Rule” means “precept,” as Bernard of Cassino teaches. For neither deans nor provosts can issue a Rule, as Boherius writes, although Richard of Saint Angelo infers from this passage “that deans or provosts can order or establish something in the monastery,” and cites the argument in the chapter *Cum accessissent*, outside the section *De constitutionibus*.

### “But if he should presume otherwise, let him be judged not as a priest but as a rebel.”

This can be understood in two ways: either that he should be regarded as a rebel, or that he should be punished as a rebel. Hildemar brings out this double meaning as follows:

> “The phrase ‘let him be judged’ is understood in two ways: in one way as ‘let him be condemned,’ and in the other as ‘let him be regarded.’ Thus learned men understand that passage in different ways. Those who understand it as ‘let him be regarded,’ so that the priest is not scourged or excommunicated but is treated with canonical reverence, take it in this sense because Saint Benedict says: ‘And if, after being frequently admonished, he does not amend, let the bishop be called as witness.’ If he has been deposed, then afterward he may be scourged or excommunicated. . . . Nevertheless, in the monasteries of the Franks a priest is scourged just like another monk.”

Hildemar himself explains the passage below in this way:

> “The sounder sense is that, as we said concerning the monks, if the person is such that the scourge is not appropriate to him, it should in no way be applied; but if he is such that the scourge will help him and not harm him, let the scourge be applied.”

Bernard of Cassino likewise thinks:

> “Although some take this passage otherwise, it seems to me that it should be understood as follows: since he is disobedient and obstinate, he should no longer be judged as a priest—that is, he should not be treated as a priest—but should be judged as a rebel, that is, as an obstinate and rebellious man.”

Richard of Saint Angelo similarly says:

> “It is better to say that he can and ought to be judged, or punished, as one who resists.”

Our Menardus nevertheless follows the former opinion:

> “Because of the dignity and reverence of the priesthood . . . it does not subject them to scourging or excommunication, but decrees that they be judged as rebels. Then, if they do not amend, they are to be admonished repeatedly; if they still do not amend, the bishop is to be called as witness. Finally, when their faults become clear—that is, public and manifest—so that because of the dignity of the presbyterate they become a scandal to others, they are to be expelled.”

### “And after being frequently admonished.”

“As though he were saying,” explains Hildemar, “he is not to be led through the degrees, but admonished.”

Boherius, in his second commentary, explains “frequently” as three times, as above concerning the deans, or four times, as below concerning the provost of the monastery.

### “Let the bishop also be called as witness.”

Different commentators explain this passage in different ways. Hildemar explains his view as follows:

> “It should be noted that, concerning those priests who come into the monastery already priests, the Rule does not say that the bishop is to be called as witness, but only concerning those priests who are consecrated in the monastery. Therefore the bishop need not be called as witness for those who come into the monastery already priests, because they were consecrated under another title. But those priests, because they were consecrated under that title, must therefore have the bishop called as witness.”

Bernard of Cassino does not think that calling the bishop as witness is a matter of necessity, but only of propriety:

> “This statement can have a place in monasteries that are not exempt, concerning the diocesan bishop, because according to some he is to be deposed by the diocesan bishop after being led through the seven degrees. I, however, adhering to the letter, when it says ‘let him be called as witness,’ think that it should be explained simply as exposing the contumacy and disobedience to the bishop, so that he may be, as it were, a witness for justifying the correction and discipline. Therefore I do not think this is necessary, but proper. For it is evident from what follows that the matter still remains in the abbot’s court, to be judged by him, since it follows: ‘If he does not amend even then, when his faults have become clear, etc.’”

Nicolaus of Fractura understands this to refer “to monasteries that are not exempt, where the correction of the excesses of subjects who are not corrected by the abbots belongs to the bishops.”

Boherius likewise thinks that this applies to a monastery that is not exempt, so that, after being led through the seven degrees, the man may be deposed by the diocesan bishop. In former times, certainly, monk-priests were subject no less to the bishop than to the abbot, as Menardus proves. Radulfus Glaber, however, seems to have disapproved of this in the *Life of Saint William*, first a monk of the monastery of Luciacum and afterward abbot of Saint-Bénigne at Dijon, where he writes:

> “The practice of an evil custom had also become established, namely, that none of the brothers of that place—Luciacum—would first receive the rank of the Levitical order before promising under oath that he would preserve fidelity to the bishop.”

### “And if he does not amend even then, etc.”

Hildemar writes:

> “When it says, ‘But if he does not amend even then, etc.,’ it makes clear that this priest must be led through eight degrees, not seven, as another monk or priest. The first degree is private admonition; the second, public correction; the third, simple excommunication; the fourth, excessive fasts; the fifth, scourging if he is worthy of it; the sixth, prayer; the seventh, the bishop; and then expulsion.”

From this passage it may be gathered with some clarity that monk-priests were not formerly expelled from monasteries without consulting the bishop. See the Council of Meaux, canon 59.

# CHAPTER LXIII

## On the Order of the Congregation

[Col. 0871]

[Col. 0871C] Let them preserve their ranks in the monastery in such a way that the time of their conversion and the merit of their life determine them, and as the abbot shall have established. Let the abbot not disturb the flock entrusted to him, nor, as though [Note: [Col. 0871D] Hildemar reads, “nor as though.”] exercising unrestricted power, arrange anything unjustly; but let him always bear in mind that he will have to render an account to God for all his judgments and actions. Therefore, according to the ranks which he has established, or which the brothers themselves possess, let them approach for the kiss of peace, for communion [Note: [Col. 0871D] The words “for communion” are absent in the *Concordia*.], for the imposition of the psalm, and for standing in the choir. And in every place whatsoever, let age not distinguish ranks [Note: [Col. 0871D] Other copies read, “let age not be distinguished in rank.”], nor prejudice them, because Samuel and Daniel, though boys, judged priests.

Therefore, except for those whom, as we have said, the abbot has preferred by higher judgment, or degraded for definite reasons, all the rest take rank according to the time of their conversion. For example, he who came to the monastery at the second hour of the day should know himself to be junior to him who came at the first hour of the day, whatever his age or dignity may be. In every respect let discipline toward boys be preserved by all [Note: [Col. 0872D] Other copies read, “let it be observed,” “let it be maintained,” or “let it be shown.”].

Therefore the juniors should honor their seniors, and the seniors love their juniors. In the very use of names, no one may address another by his bare name; rather, the seniors should address their juniors by the name “brother.” The juniors, however, should call their seniors *nonnos*, that is, “fathers,” which signifies paternal reverence. The abbot, because he is believed to act in Christ’s place [Note: [Col. 0872D] The Oxford copy reads, “because he acted in Christ’s place.”], is to be called “Lord” and “Abbot,” not by his own presumption, but in honor and love of Christ. He himself, however, should reflect and conduct himself in such a way as to be worthy of such honor.

[Col. 0873A] Whenever brothers meet one another, the junior should ask the senior for a blessing. When an older brother passes by, the younger should rise and give him his seat. Nor should a junior presume to sit down unless his senior orders him to do so, so that what is written may be fulfilled: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12). Boys, children, and adolescents should observe their ranks with discipline in the oratory and at table. Outside, or wherever they may be [Note: [Col. 0873A] The *Concordia* and Hildemar read, “or wherever and wherever.” Other copies read “wherever,” omitting “or.” The Narbonne copy reads “everywhere here.”], they should be kept under custody and discipline until they reach the age of understanding.

# COMMENTARY

[Col. 0873]

[Col. 0873A] “Let them preserve their ranks in the monastery in such a way that the time of their conversion and the merit of their life determine them, and as the abbot shall have established.”

He wished three things to be considered in establishing ranks: first, the time of conversion; second, the merit of life; third, what the abbot shall have established. Some, as Hildemar reports, confuse the second with the third, because it belongs to the abbot to discern the merit of life, and no one should presume to request a higher rank on account of the merit of his own life. Anyone who dared to do so would rightly deserve, on account of the merit of his life, to obtain not a higher place but a completely lower one.

Nevertheless, others distinguish the two not without reason. There are some who, on account of the merit of their life, deserve no higher place, yet whom the abbot’s will alone customarily promotes to a higher position for reasons of necessity or usefulness. For example, someone may be no different from the others in holiness of life, but because he sings exceptionally well, he is preferred to the others in the choir by the abbot’s sole decision. Such men, however, ought to take precedence only in those activities in which they excel others: for example, the cantor in the choir, but not in the chapter, not in the refectory, and so forth, as Hildemar rightly observed.

Therefore, although it belongs to the abbot to discern the merits of individuals, and although he can promote each one, as he wishes, to a higher rank than that which he entered, he ought nevertheless to use this power with moderation. Hence Saint Benedict adds:

### “Let the abbot not disturb the flock entrusted to him, etc.”

Here, as Bernard of Cassino writes, he binds the abbot’s consideration with a threefold bridle. First, the abbot must attend to the peace of his subjects by not disturbing the flock. Second, he must arrange everything justly and not abuse the freedom of his power. Third, he must fear the scrutiny of the final judgment, remembering that both his deeds and his judgments are known to God.

### “Let them approach for the kiss of peace.”

That is, the peace given at Mass, as Bernard of Cassino, Nicolaus of Fractura, Richard of Saint Angelo, Boherius in his second commentary, Theobaldus Artaldus, and Nicolaus Bravus teach; or the peace given to arriving guests or at Mass, as Menardus holds; or, finally, the peace given at Mass, to arriving guests, to professed monks after Mass, or, in certain monasteries, at Mass after the Gospel has been read, from the text of the Gospel without the cross, as Boherius explains in his first commentary.

For the manner of giving and receiving the peace at Mass before communion, which is how I interpret this passage, see what we said in Book II of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 3.

### “For communion.”

All the commentators explain this passage as referring to communion of the body and blood of Christ, and, as far as I know, none dissents. All approached it in their respective order, though the ministers of the altar went before the others.

Here it should be observed what Udalricus writes (Book II, chapter 30): if the abbot, for just reasons, wished to elevate someone who had been converted in the chapter or in the refectory, nevertheless he had to approach “for the kiss of peace, for communion, and for holy water according to the order of his conversion.”

Moreover, those who were absent from Mass for just reasons nevertheless hurried to arrive around the time of the Lord’s Prayer if they intended to communicate, as we learn from the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen (chapter 13):

> “At the hour when we are going to receive the holy body and blood, let us hasten to be present to say: ‘Deliver us from evil.’”

From this passage it is clear that not all monks formerly attended the entire sacrifice of the Mass on Sundays, when they communicated especially. This could particularly happen to those serving the weekly turn in the kitchen.

### “For the imposition of the psalm.”

That is, for the imposition of the psalm’s antiphon—that is, the antiphon that precedes the psalm—as Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicolaus of Fractura, Boherius, Turrecremata, and Haeftenus explain.

Bernard of Cassino adds:

> “Here it must be supplied that those who can fulfill the office should read or sing according to their ranks, so that this may agree with chapter 38, where it says: ‘The brothers, however, shall not read or sing in order.’”

### “Because Samuel and Daniel, though boys, judged priests.”

Samuel judged Eli and his sons; Daniel judged the two wicked elders who sought to oppress Susanna. Thus Saint Ignatius admonishes the Magnesians not to despise Bishop Dema on account of his younger age, since Daniel, at twelve years old, convicted the aged calumniators; the young Samuel rebuked ninety-year-old Eli; Solomon, when he had reached his twelfth year, judged the women concerning their children; and Josiah, having assumed power in his eighth year, destroyed altars and temples and cut down the sacred groves.

## “Let all the rest be as they are converted.”

That is, let them observe their proper order according to the time and day of their conversion. Saint Benedict received this discipline from Saint Pachomius and his disciples, concerning whom Saint Jerome says (*Preface to the Rule of Saint Pachomius*):

> “Whoever first enters the monastery sits first, walks first, says the psalm first, first reaches out his hand at table, and communicates first in church; nor is age considered among them, but profession.”

Saint Isidore later decreed the same in his *Rule* (chapter 4):

> “Whoever enters the monastery first shall be first in everything according to rank or order; nor should it be asked whether he is rich or poor, slave or free, young or old, rustic or learned. For among monks neither age nor status is considered, because before God there is no difference between the soul of a slave and that of a free person.”

Saint Fructuosus likewise says (chapter 23):

> “Whoever is first converted in the monastery shall walk first, sit first, receive the blessing-loaf first, communicate first in church, speak first when the brothers are questioned about some matter, say the psalm first, stand first in the choir, perform the weekly service first, and first reach out his hand at table. Nor is age alone to be considered among the brothers, but their manner of life and their purpose of labor and devotion. Hence this distinction of the senior is also to be awaited: he should honor the one whom he sees fervent in love and worship of God. For neither nobility of birth, nor the wealth that anyone possessed in the world, nor advanced age is to be sought, but uprightness of life and the merits of ardent faith must be weighed. The one who is closer to God is to be judged the superior.”

Saint Donatus, in his *Rule for Virgins* (chapter 66), copies Saint Benedict almost word for word; and the *Rule of a Certain Author*, also for virgins (chapter 22), agrees with him.

There is one Master, however, who differs from the others and, taking no account of the time of conversion, wishes the ranks to be confused daily by the abbot, so that no one among the brothers appears first and no one appears last. The abbot says (chapter 92):

> “Let him always confuse their ranks, and make them sit beside him at table by turns; let him order them all to stand beside him in the oratory by turns, and let them all impose the psalms after him by turns, so that no one may become elated over having been assigned the second place of honor, nor may anyone become despondent because of the lowest rank.”

But I return to the text of Saint Benedict.

Since the holy Father established that everyone should be ranked according to the time of his conversion, the question arises whether the time of conversion should be understood as beginning with entry into the monastery or with the profession that was subsequently made. Boherius asserts the latter, Haeftenus the former.

Boherius’s principal basis is that the brothers are not perfectly converted until their monastic profession, through which alone they then first begin to be received and reckoned as members of the congregation. Haeftenus, on the contrary, draws his conclusion (*Book III, treatise 3, question 6*) from the very text of the holy Rule, which Saint Benedict himself, as though explaining it, says: whoever comes to the monastery at the second hour of the day should know himself to be junior to one who came at the first hour of the day. He insists that this passage is to be understood not of profession but of entry into the monastery, since it could scarcely happen that one person professed at the first hour and another at the second. If several must make profession in the same hour, experience teaches that they pronounce their vows in that same hour, not at different times. He confirms this by the authority of Peter Walnen and Walloncapellius, [Col. 0875B] who hold the same opinion.

Indeed, I learned from my predecessors that this was once observed in our own Dionysian houses. I also read the following in the *Institutions of the Cistercian Order* (*Distinction 10, chapter 2*, and *Ancient Definitions*, distinction 11, chapter 2):

> “Of the novices, whoever first enters the chapter house, if he perseveres, shall be considered senior, even if the one who entered later is blessed before him.”

And in the *Statutes of Guigo* (chapter 26):

> “As for order, whether in the refectory or anywhere else, we all maintain the order given to each by his arrival.”

The ancient Statutes of the Carthusians depart from this when they write (*Part II, chapter 24*) that:

> “When two novices come to some house, the one who comes later, if he makes profession first, shall thereafter remain first.”

In all these matters, however, I think the praiseworthy custom of each congregation should be followed. Nor should Saint Benedict’s example be taken so literally that it cannot perhaps have been proposed merely to teach more clearly that the one who was first incorporated into the congregation through monastic profession ought to precede the others.

But since Blessed Benedict permits some to be placed before others for particular reasons, someone may perhaps wish to know who those persons should be. The constitutions of each monastery and congregation make this sufficiently clear.

Hildemarus explains the custom of his own time as follows:

> “It must be understood that the lesser deans or circators, merely because they are deans or circators, ought not to preside over others—that is, they ought not to be placed first in the choir, in the chapter house, or in any other place—unless the abbot, provost, or greater dean is absent. Then one of them should be placed first to occupy the abbot’s position. For I said that they should not be placed first because it is unreasonable that in one year, when they hold the office, they should be placed above others, and in the following year, when they do not hold the office, they should again sit lower, in the place where they entered. The greater dean or provost, however, should be placed first because they occupy the abbot’s position when he is absent. When the abbot is absent, the provost occupies the abbot’s position; when the provost is not present, the greater dean occupies the abbot’s position in excommunicating and in everything else.”

Among the Cluniacs, according to Udalricus (*Book III, chapter 4*), the greater prior sat at the abbot’s right. The cloister prior did not likewise do so, as Udalricus says in chapter 6 of the same book:

> “The cloister prior is in every respect the vicar of the greater prior. He is the one who remains continually in the cloister, wherever the lord abbot or the prior may travel, and who chiefly bears the burden of the entire order. Nevertheless, he is not advanced at all in the choir, except that, when the prior is absent, he offers first, goes first to the kiss of peace, and goes first to the holy water.”

Among the Cistercians, according to the *Book of Usages*, chapter 111, the prior everywhere held the first place after the abbot. But while the abbot was present, the subprior did not change his customary place either in the choir, in the chapter house, or at the conference, according to chapter 112. The same discipline prevailed among the Bursfeld Congregation, according to the *Ceremonial*, distinction 2, chapters 2 and 3.

[Col. 0876A]

Boherius further asks “whether, with respect to places and signatures among abbots assembled in councils, the time of conversion or the time of promotion should be taken into consideration,” and he answers:

> “I say that it is the time of promotion. For it is a general rule that those who attain a dignity earlier are preferred to others, and that rank precedes the others which longer labor and longer service have caused to advance first. I nevertheless think exempt abbots should be preferred to the others; for when the others are competing on equal terms, regard must be had to the reason of the privilege.”

### “But in all things the boys shall be subject to the discipline of everyone.”

Therefore, what Saint Benedict has said thus far concerns only those converted in adulthood, not boys, who were instructed separately from the others together with the *pulsantes*, or novices, as is clear from the most ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall, in which the following verse is written over the novices’ cells:

> “The oblates in this cloister are associated with the novices.”

They therefore had to preserve their respective order among themselves, apart from the others, until they reached their fifteenth year. At that time, or thereabouts, when they left custody, they received the place in which they had entered the monastery, as Hildemarus states in his commentary on chapter 70 of the Rule.

Thus Peter Boherius, explaining this passage, says:

> “He says this so that no one may think that a boy or adolescent should be placed before an aged man or priest who was converted last.”

### “In the very use of names, no one may address another by his bare name.”

Saint Fulgentius is praised in this regard because “he was so gentle toward each one that he never called any of the brothers by his bare name.”

To be called by one’s bare name means to be called by the name alone, as Hildemarus says; or, as Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius put it, without any addition. This could happen in three or four ways: by pronouncing only the baptismal name, for example, “Peter” or “Paul”; only the family name, for example, “Le Blanc,” “Le Noir,” or “La Perche”; only the nationality, such as “German” or “Spaniard”; or the office or dignity, such as “Sacristan,” “Cantor,” “Dean,” or “Provost.” Such forms either savor of the secular world or imply contempt, and sometimes even provide an occasion for pride, when a man is reminded by his thoughts that he is not like other people, since he holds such an office or comes from such a distinguished and illustrious family.

### “But the seniors shall call their junior brothers.”

Here “juniors” does not mean infants, or simply those younger in age, as the term is commonly understood. It means those junior in comparison with the older and senior members in the order of profession, as the pronoun “their” indicates. For he does not say, “Let the seniors call the younger brothers,” but “their juniors”—that is, those inferior to them in the order of profession.

Hence it can happen that one and the same monk is called both “brother” and “father”: “brother” by someone older than him, and “father” by someone junior to him. Certainly, in the twelfth century, a priest and monk named John is called “Brother John” in the *Life of Saint Aibert*, number 7 (*Bollandists, 7 April*).

Another custom, however, prevailed among the Cluniacs. In their ancient *Customaries* I find the following (*Book II, chapter 20*):

> “If he calls someone ‘brother,’ he never calls him by his bare name unless he adds ‘lord’; and he calls boys ‘brothers.’ Likewise, when he says the proper name, he always places ‘brother’ before it.”

Hildemarus explains why Saint Benedict wished juniors to be called brothers:

> “He rightly ordered that they be called brothers, because they have been reborn in one sacred baptismal font, sanctified by one Spirit, professed one profession, desire to attain one reward, and have been born from one mother—that is, holy Church.”

Bernard of Cassino has something similar. See Haeftenus, book III, treatise 4, question 2.

### “But the juniors shall call their seniors *nonnos*, which signifies paternal reverence.”

“Thus *nonnus* signifies the same as ‘reverend father.’ It is an ancient word, customarily used among monks as a term of honor and reverence, as is clear both from this passage and from the Council of Aachen, which decreed (canon 54) that ‘those who are placed in authority should be called *nonni*—that is, with paternal reverence.’”

Papias likewise says:

> “We call our elders *nonnos* out of reverence, for this is understood as paternal reverence.”

Saint Columbanus uses this word of the apostle Peter:

> “He gave the privilege to the keeper of the keys, the common *nonnus* of all.”

Since the Synod of Aachen decreed that superiors should be called *nonni*, someone might suspect that superiors, rejecting the name *nonnus*, had assumed the title *domnus* (“lord”), which belongs only to the abbot, whether out of honor, ambition, or some other reason, and that the synod wished to correct this.

Or perhaps it means by “superiors” all those senior in profession who, according to the Rule, are placed everywhere above their juniors, and who had already changed the name “father” into “lord.” This is suggested by Smaragdus, an author of that period, who, explaining this passage, writes:

> “Just as at that time paternal reverence was displayed among them by calling the seniors *nonni*, so now it is required among us that, out of that same paternal reverence, our seniors be called *domni*.”

This custom also prevailed among the Cluniacs, as Udalricus testifies (*Book II, chapter 20*).

Among our Corbie monks, however, the title *nonnus* survived into the ninth century, as is clear from the *Life of Anscharius of Corbie*, first a monk and later bishop of Bremen (*Benedictine Century IV, part II*), where I read:

> “The venerable abbot found for him, from your brotherhood, a companion, Nonnus Witmar.”

It also survived among the Cistercians, according to the *Book of Usages*, chapter 98, and the *Life of Charles, Abbot of Villers* (*Bollandists, 29 January*), which contains the words:

> “When you see Nonnus Conrad, the novice of Villers.”

And likewise:

> “Together with Nonnus Walter, a simple monk.”

It survived among the Cassinese until the time of Bernard of Cassino, as is clear from the ceremony for announcing officials that he established:

> “The order of the vicar requires that in the coming week Nonnus Amicus sing Mass; Nonnus Remigius perform the kitchen service; Nonnus James serve in the church, and so forth.”

But on this word see Menardus, Haeftenus, and Du Cange’s *Glossary*.

### “But because the abbot is believed to act in Christ’s place, let him be called both ‘lord’ and ‘abbot.’”

Bernard of Cassino writes:

> “The transalpine text does not have *dominus*, as the Cassinese text does, but has *domnus*. Without doubt, *domnus* seems to convey greater reverential maturity, while *dominus* conveys more fearsome authority.”

Nicholas of Fractura follows Bernard. Richard of Saint Angelo also reads *dominus*. The same reading is found in the *Concordance of Rules*, the Victorine manuscripts, the edition of Guido Juvenalis, the Louvain edition, and John Bertelius. Paul Augustine of Genoa attempts to defend this reading at length, asserting that it is found in all the manuscripts of the Cassinese library.

To the ancients, however, there seems to have been only one “Lord,” namely God. Thus Augustus the emperor is said by Orosius (*Book VI, chapter 22*) to have refused the title *dominus*. Later, however, scribes, wishing to use a humbler word, formed *domnus* by contraction from *dominus*. They used this word to address holy men, bishops, kings, and other honorable and noble persons. Hence, in ancient litanies, the supreme pontiff is called “the lord apostolic.”

Thus, in Severus Sulpicius (*Letter 2*), they announce that “Lord Martin” has died; in the *Life of Blessed Alcuin*, number 22 (*Benedictine Century IV*), we read, “Go to the tomb of Lord Martin”; Saint Gregory (*Book I of the Register, chapter 6*) writes, “I ask in my name that Lord Alexander, Lord Theodore, my son Marinus, Lady Eusicia, Lady Eudocia, and Lady Dominica be greeted”; the *Statutes of Saint Adalard* contain “the Mass of Lady Balthild”; and Aimoinus (*Book IV, On the Deeds of the Franks, chapter 68*) says, “Lord King Charles held a general assembly in the city of Worms.”

Hence the familiar little verse:

> “Call the heavenly one *Dominus*, the mortal one *domnus*.”

But whereas the name *domnus* once belonged only to the abbot, it is now applied indiscriminately to almost all monks. This is shown to have become customary already in the time of Abbot Smaragdus, from the passage cited above, and among the Cluniacs also, according to the Udalricus passage already mentioned.

Even if we suppose that there were formerly some who rejected both titles, *dominus* and *domnus*, and were simply called “fathers,” this is what happened with Hilboldus, abbot of Heri, who is called “Father Hilboldus” by Ermentarius in the *Translation of Saint Philibert*, chapter 1. Likewise, Geilo, abbot of Heri, is called “Father Geilo” in the *Chronicle of Tournus*. Usuardus, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés, is called “Father Usuardus” by Aimoinus in the *History of the Translation of Saints George and Aurelius*, number 6. Finally, in the *Life of Saint Anscharius*, the man whom we first read called Nonnus Witmar is later called “Father Witmar.”

Moreover, in signing their names, not only simple monks but even abbots themselves customarily placed “brother” before their proper names. In the *Chronicle of Centula*, book IV, Gervinus begins a charter as follows:

> “I, Brother Gervinus, abbot of the monastery of Saint Richarius.”

In the eleventh century (*Benedictine Century III, part I*), Bovo, abbot of Sithiu, writing to Guido, archbishop of Reims, addresses his letter as follows (*Spicilegium*, volume V):

> “To the most excellent lord Archbishop Guido, Brother Bovo, unworthy abbot of the monastery of Sithiu.”

In the signatures of the monks of Pescaria at the election of Abbot Dominic, everyone—including the provost and the other priests—places “brother” before his proper name.

In 1313, Adam, abbot of Saint-Faron of Meaux, begins a charter as follows (*Benedictine Century II, page 601*):

> “Brother Adam, by divine permission humble abbot of the monastery of Saint-Faron of the Order of Saint Benedict.”

Finally, in 1493, in the *Instrument of the Reform of the Cistercian Order* prefixed to the Parisian articles, all the abbots are styled “brothers” (*Nomasticon Cisterciense*, page 574).

### “Whenever the brothers meet one another, the junior shall ask the senior’s blessing.”

That is, “in those places and at those times where speaking is permitted; but if they meet in other places or at other times, he shall ask for the blessing in his heart, bowing his head,” says Hildemarus.

Bernard of Cassino likewise writes:

> “Where and when speaking is permitted, he may modestly say, ‘Bless.’ Where and when speaking is not permitted, merely bowing the head constitutes the request for a blessing.”

Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, and Turrecremata agree. Peter the Venerable therefore rightly replied to the Cistercians’ objections (*Book I, letter 28*):

> “Whenever the brothers meet one another, the junior asks the senior’s blessing, saying ‘Bless’ if they are outside the regular places and bowing humbly; but if they meet one another inside the regular work areas, he says nothing aloud. If you say that this must always be requested by speaking, let discerning persons consider whether useful silence should be imposed on superfluous speech or be subjected to it. We call it superfluous because the tongue is not necessary for something that can be done equally well in silence, and we therefore consider it superfluous, especially since the Rule contains no mention of pronouncing any words for this greeting. Even if this were granted indiscriminately, as you wish, perhaps some who were not firmly grounded in maturity would utter empty things instead of useful ones, jokes instead of serious words, and curses instead of blessings. To prevent this, we prohibit it by the discipline of silence.”

What Peter the Venerable has said thus far prompts us to ask more fully how, and with what words, this blessing discussed here by the holy Father was requested and given.

The *Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins* decrees (chapter 22):

> “Whenever they meet one another on the road or in any place, they should ask for a blessing from one another with complete humility, bowing to each other; and if one of them is older, the younger should first ask for the blessing, and then the older should respond.”

Chapter 29 of the monks of Saint Gall orders:

> “Whenever the brothers meet one another, the junior, asking for a blessing, should remain bowed in one place until the senior who gives the blessing has passed.”

Saint Hildegard makes this request for a blessing consist simply in “a greeting by which he demonstrates with all humility that he is subject to his senior.”

Boherius, however, wishes the blessing to be requested “by both bowing and speaking, if it is a time when speech is permitted; otherwise by bowing alone. And in the same manner,” he says, “the senior makes the response.”

We learned the actual words by which the blessing was requested from the *Order of Monastic Conduct*:

> “Whenever thereafter the brothers meet one another, the junior, bowing his head to the senior, shall say, ‘Bless.’”

This agrees with what Peter the Venerable and Bernard of Cassino wrote above.

We may add that Boherius writes in his second commentary:

> “In the monasteries of Subiaco and Monte Cassino this is practiced very well. For when they meet, as I myself saw, the junior always says to the senior, ‘Bless me, father.’ But I did not hear the senior reply anything, nor do I understand the Rule to say anything about the senior’s response, except that he might reply, ‘Thanks be to God.’”

What escaped Boherius is made clear by the *Rule of the Master*, which prescribes (chapter 13) that, when an excommunicated person “asks for a blessing, no one should answer, ‘God’ (*Deus*).”

Bernard of Cassino, speaking of the excommunicated person in chapter 25, says:

> “If he should happen to say, ‘Bless’ (*benedicite*), no one ought to answer, ‘God’ (*Deus*) or ‘Lord’ (*Dominus*).”

The Constitutions of Valladolid likewise say:

> “We ask for this blessing by saying ‘Bless’ and bowing toward the one who is passing by. If he is the dean or one who has professed for a long time, he should say, ‘Lord’ (*Dominus*). Or, if he prefers, out of greater humility, he may ask the blessing of his junior, saying, ‘Bless.’”

The Cassinese now understand this request for a blessing to be expressed more by a sign than by a word, and therefore prescribe that it be made by bowing the head alone.

Saint Benedict derived this custom of requesting a blessing not only from the ancient monks, among whom Macarius, meeting Saint Apollinaris, said to him, “Bless me, father” (*Bollandists, 5 January*), but also from the first Christians, who, when conversing and meeting one another, blessed one another in greeting, as is clear from Tertullian (*On the Testimony of the Soul*, chapter 2):

> “That every blessing among us, as a matter of goodness and kindness from God, is the supreme sacrament of discipline and conduct, you pronounce as readily as it is necessary for a Christian to say, ‘God bless you.’”

### “When a senior passes, a junior shall rise, and so forth.”

Saint Basil likewise says (*Sermon on Renouncing Worldly Possessions*):

> “Do not hurry to sit down before an older man. If he orders you to sit, do not sit on the same seat with him; but looking around, hasten to find a lower chair, so that God may honor you for this humility.”

Saint Fructuosus says (chapter 12):

> “Before their seniors, no prior should walk, nor should he sit or speak without being ordered to do so. He should suitably show honor and reverence to his senior brother, as is fitting.”

The *Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins* says (chapter 22):

> “If another sister arrives while the sisters are seated, those who are junior in rank should rise and give the senior her place,”

provided, of course, that she is to remain there. For if she is merely passing through, Hildemarus says:

> “She should rise slightly and bow her head, asking for a blessing.”

Saint Benedict’s statement, “Nor should he presume to sit with him unless his senior orders him to do so,” instructs the senior, as Bernard of Cassino says,

> “that just as the junior rises, asks for a blessing, and reverently indicates a place to sit, so the senior, as though at that same moment, should in a way anticipate him by greeting and blessing him and ordering him to sit beside him or nearby elsewhere. Thus what follows is fulfilled: ‘anticipating one another in honor.’”

Hildemarus therefore says concerning this passage:

> “It must be understood that the abbot should teach in the chapter house that just as the junior ought to rise before his senior, so the senior should immediately indicate to the junior that he should sit. If the senior does not immediately tell his rising junior to sit, he should be admonished according to the discipline of the Rule, as we have said, through the seven stages. If he does not correct himself, the senior should place him in the lowest rank, and he should learn how a senior ought to tell his junior to sit.”

While sitting, one should observe the following saying of Saint Basil:

> “When you sit, do not place one leg over the other, for that is the posture of an elevated and inattentive mind.”

The custom of rising before an elder was sacred not only among monks but also among pagans:

> “Honor is owed to every senior on account of age,” says Aristotle (*Nicomachean Ethics*, book IX, chapter 2), “by rising, yielding one’s seat, and other such gestures.”

Cicero likewise says (*On Old Age*):

> “The Lacedaemonians used to rise for all old men who entered the theater and receive them into their seats.”

Juvenal says of the Romans (*Satire 13*):

> “They believed it a great crime, one to be paid for with death,
>
> if a young man did not rise for an old man, and if a boy did not rise
>
> for any bearded man.”

### “Little boys.”

Saint Benedict rightly adds this expression, “boys, or little ones,” to distinguish them from servants and sons, says Boherius. For, as Saint Jerome teaches (*Commentary on the Letter to Titus*), according to the Greeks the word “boy” can signify both a servant and a son.

### “Let them attain their proper order under discipline.”

“According to the time of their entry into the monastery,” says Menardus, “not only among themselves but also among the other monks, because age should not create a distinction or prejudice the order, as he said above, unless perhaps the abbot, for a reasonable cause, wishes to place someone before them.”

Boherius and Haeftenus, however (*Book IV, treatise 1, question 6*), taught the opposite above. From this passage of the Rule Haeftenus rightly inferred that boys were once instructed separately from the other monks in our order. He says:

> “When he says ‘their proper order,’ he plainly signifies that they are not to be mixed with the ranks of the seniors, but are to have a particular order among themselves. Hence Bernard of Cassino says: ‘Here mention is made of boys who have their own special places and their own special teachers, and who neither sit nor stand with those of greater age.’”

That this was the common custom of the order is proved by what we said in book V of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 5. Saint Benedict may have received it from Saint Basil, who in the *Longer Rules*, chapter 15, established that boys should be separated from the seniors, while nevertheless their prayers should be common to all.

### “Outside, or wherever.”

“That is, in every place,” says Hildemarus. “For when he says ‘wherever,’ he leaves out no place.”

### “Let them be kept in custody and under discipline until they reach the age of understanding.”

Hildemarus—whom Bernard of Cassino and Boherius cite here under the name of Paul the Deacon—understands the age of understanding as extending to fifteen years for well-behaved boys. If they lack the necessary maturity, however, he thinks that some should remain subject to the master’s rod until twenty, or even thirty, years of age.

## CHAPTER LXIV. On Appointing an Abbot

[Col. 0879D]

> In appointing an abbot, this principle must always be observed: the one whom the entire harmonious congregation [Note: Narbonne, with two other manuscripts and four editions, reads “the cohort of the congregation”; Lyra reads “fellow participant.”] has chosen for itself, according to the fear of God, or whom even a very small part of the congregation has chosen with sounder [Note: Narbonne reads “older.”] judgment, shall be appointed. The one to be appointed should be chosen for the merit of his life and the instruction of his wisdom, even if he is last in the order of the congregation.
>
> But if the entire congregation, God forbid, should with equal agreement choose [Note: Some copies read “have chosen.”] a person who consents to its vices, and if those vices have become known to the bishop in whose diocese the place lies, or to the abbots, [Note: Some copies read “to the abbots,” or “to neighboring Christians.”] or to neighboring Christians, they must prevent the wicked consensus from prevailing and appoint a worthy steward over the house of God, knowing that they will receive a good reward for this if they do it chastely and with zeal for God, just as, conversely, they will incur sin if they neglect it.

> Once appointed, the abbot should always consider what a burden he has undertaken and to whom he will have to render an account of his stewardship. He should know that it is more necessary for him to benefit than to rule. He must therefore be learned in divine law, so that he may know and have from where to bring forth new things and old [Note: Some copies read “so that he may know from where.”], be chaste, sober, and merciful, and always exalt mercy above judgment [Note: Some copies read “mercy [above] judgment” or “mercy [exalts] judgment”], so that he himself may obtain the same. Let him hate vices and love the brothers.
>
> In correction itself, let him act prudently, and not go too far, lest, while he wishes too zealously to scrape away the rust, the vessel be broken. Let him always be suspicious of his own frailty and remember that a bruised reed must not be broken. In saying this, we do not mean that he should permit vices to be nourished, but that he should cut them away prudently and charitably, as he sees to be expedient for each person, as we have already said. Let him strive to be loved more than feared. Let him not be turbulent or anxious [Note: Narbonne reads “anxious” in a different form], excessive [Note: Some copies read “a buffoon, nor excessive”], or obstinate; let him not be jealous or excessively suspicious, for he will never rest [Note: Cassinese and Florentine copies, the *Concordance of Rules*, and certain manuscripts read “he does not rest.” Narbonne reads “he would not rest.”].
>
> In his commands let him be prudent and considerate, whether they concern God or the world. Let him distinguish and moderate the tasks he imposes, remembering the discretion of holy Jacob, who said: “If I make my flocks labor more by driving them, they will all die in one day” (Genesis 33). Taking these and other testimonies of discretion, the mother of virtues, let him moderate everything so that there is something the strong may desire and the weak will not avoid [Note: Narbonne reads “so that there may be something for the strong to desire”]. Above all, let him preserve the present Rule in everything [Note: Some copies read “let them preserve”], so that, having administered well, he may hear from the Lord the words concerning the good servant who gave his fellow servants their wheat at the proper time: “Amen, I say to you, he will set him over all his goods” (Matthew 24).

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0881]

### “In appointing an abbot.”

That is, in electing one; for this is how the ancient laws speak, says Boherius. We have discussed this at greater length in book V of *The Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 1.

### “This principle must always be observed: the one whom the entire harmonious congregation chooses for itself,” and so forth.

The election of the abbot therefore belonged to the congregation itself. This was the ancient discipline of the monastic order, confirmed by the rules of the early monks and by ecclesiastical and civil laws. Menardus proves this here, and it is clear from the ancient formula for drawing up a charter when someone builds a monastery on his own property, and from the formula for establishing a benefice, which may be seen in *Benedictine Century IV*, part I, page 743; from the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*, number 27; and from numerous charters of emperors, kings, and princes, some of which are included in volume IV of the *Ancient Analecta*.

The *Rule of the Master*, however, adopted a different procedure for appointing an abbot: namely, that the one whom the dying abbot had chosen before his death should be appointed. If the abbot happened to die an unexpected death, one of the neighboring abbots was to be chosen by the bishop and clergy, and he was to remain in the congregation for thirty days. After those days had elapsed, the person whom he had designated from within the congregation was to become abbot.

Nevertheless, the abbot was to be chosen not only by the congregation but also from within the congregation itself. If no suitable person were found there, another was to be chosen from another monastery, as is clear from the formulas and charters cited above, of which there are countless examples. For secular abbots were unknown to the ancient monks; they appeared especially in the eighth century, with the permission of Charles Martel. On this subject see the preface to *Benedictine Century III*, part I, page 89.

But what St. Benedict says—“Or even if a part, however small, of the community should choose by sounder counsel”—causes no little difficulty to some interpreters. Hildemar does not explain his meaning very clearly, writing as follows on this passage:

> “This must be noted, because in this passage, when he says ‘however small,’ it is understood that if half of the community should choose by sounder counsel, or even if the greater part of the community should choose by sounder counsel, consent must be given to those who choose by sounder—that is, better—counsel. What is a small community? For example, if there are fifty monks who choose a bad abbot, and two good brothers who choose a better abbot, consent must be given to those two, and not to the fifty, and so forth.”

Now, if nothing is missing from his text, he seems first to understand “the smaller part of the community” as half of the brothers; then he teaches the opposite, asserting that the better counsel of two is to be preferred to that of fifty bad men, a view that he confirms with other examples of the same kind.

The opinion of John Caramuel is entirely opposed to this position. In his commentary on the Rule of St. Benedict, no. 1479, he writes on this passage:

> “The words are difficult, and, unless they are carefully examined, they appear genuinely schismatic. If a few choose someone by sounder counsel, let him be abbot. But who will determine which part relies upon sounder counsel? Almost everyone thinks that St. Benedict asserted that the one who was elected by the sounder counsel even of the smaller part ought to be the monastery’s superior. Yet the text must not be explained in this way, unless perhaps one wishes to contradict the legislator’s intention. The holy Father does not compare the smaller part with the greater, but the part with the whole: he says that the one should be declared abbot whom either the whole community has chosen, or at least the part of sounder counsel, even if small—that is, the part to which the larger number have subscribed, although those subscribing are few. The matter will become clearer by an example. Suppose there are twenty active votes: if all favor Peter, there is no room for dispute. If four favor Peter, seven John, six Paul, and the remaining votes Ambrose, the most holy legislator wishes John to be preferred. For although the part of the community that elected him is small, it is nevertheless larger than the others and is therefore presumed to be sounder.”

By contrast, the Cassinese monk Paul Augustine of Genoa—whose interpretation Caramuel says is that of almost everyone and nevertheless rejects—persuades himself that he comes closer to the holy legislator’s intention on the basis of, as he says, the ancient understanding of his monastery and its practice. He proves this from the codex of Abbot John, that is, Hildemar’s commentary, which, as we have seen, reads these words as follows:

> “If there are fifty monks who choose a bad abbot, and two good brothers who choose a better abbot, consent must be given to those two, and not to the fifty. Likewise if there are one hundred, likewise if two hundred, five hundred, and so forth; but the others are three, or four, or five, and so forth.”

And from Richard:

> “The small part in number is preferred to the larger in counsel. And know that it is then preferred to the larger part when the larger part knowingly chooses an unworthy man, according to some authorities; otherwise, if it does so unknowingly, then both elections would be annulled.”

The manuscript of Richard of St. Angelo that we possess, however, reads somewhat differently. At the word “small” it adds:

> “Supply: ‘yet greater in number and sounder in counsel,’ as follows below.”

This is precisely Caramuel’s opinion. Richard nevertheless adds:

> “And know that the smaller is then preferred to the larger when the larger part knowingly chooses an unworthy man; otherwise, if unknowingly, both elections would be annulled, as it is written in *Extra*, *De electione*, *Scriptum est*. They would then hold another election in the same manner, as in *C. t. Victorum*. Some say that if the elections were made in one continuous proceeding, and the smaller part chose a worthy man while the larger part chose an unworthy man, even unknowingly, the election made by the larger part is valid. I heard this from Master Richard of Siena, my teacher, when he was lecturing on the chapter *Congregato*, *Extra*, *De electione*. But if all unknowingly chose an unworthy man, they are not deprived of the power of electing; rather, they ought to elect again, as is read and noted in *C. t. Innotuit*.”

To Caramuel’s question—namely, who will determine which part relies upon sounder counsel—Paul Augustine of Genoa replies, on the basis of the Rule’s meaning, that this belongs to the abbots and neighboring Christians, or to the bishop of the place. Finally, he confirms his opinion with the example of Pope Innocent II, who, after the death of Honorius II, was proclaimed supreme pontiff with the votes of only sixteen cardinals and was preferred to Anacletus, whom twenty-one cardinals elected shortly afterward.

Menard seems to have held the same opinion. He interprets “small part” as “the lesser part” and thinks that the passage contains a Hellenism in which the positive degree is used in place of the comparative; this he proves learnedly, in his customary manner.

**“Let the one who is to be appointed be chosen for the merit of his life and the teaching of wisdom.”** [Col. 0883C]

Here the holy Father explains what sort of person he wishes to be elected abbot: namely, someone distinguished by the merit of his life and by instruction in wisdom. For although, “as Boherius says, the merit of a cenobite’s life is sufficient, it is nevertheless fitting that an abbot possess instruction in wisdom.” Here St. Jerome’s saying may be applied:

> “As holy rusticity builds up the Church of Christ through the merit of life, so it does equal harm if it does not resist those who destroy.”

But he cannot resist unless he has been instructed in the teaching of wisdom. Therefore, insofar as this is possible, the man who is to be appointed abbot should shine both in holiness of life and in knowledge.

If no such man can be found, Hildemar prefers that a holy and devout man lacking learning be appointed rather than a learned man who is otherwise of bad character. Yet if the latter is not very bad but merely more vulnerable, a learned man who possesses zeal for discipline should be chosen in preference to a devout and holy man lacking discernment.

Moreover, as Bernard of Cassino says:

> “The merit of life may suitably be referred to soundness of conscience and to the truth of the saints. The teaching of wisdom, however, may suitably be applied to prudence, sound understanding, eloquent speech, eminent or less adequate knowledge, and prudence concerning temporal matters.”

**“Even if he is the last in the order of the community.”**

These words can bear a twofold interpretation.

1. They may mean that even the brother who is lowest by birth, if he is worthy, should be chosen; for no consideration of family or lineage should be admitted in these matters. Thus St. Benedict Biscop, abbot, repeatedly gave the following admonition to his brothers, according to Bede (*Second Century of Benedictine History*, p. 1007):

> “He was accustomed diligently to repeat this command to them: that no one should think the lineage of a family was to be sought in the election of an abbot, rather than excellence in living and teaching. ‘And truly,’ he would say, ‘I tell you that, in comparison with two evils, it would be far more tolerable for me—if the Lord should so judge—for this entire place in which I founded the monastery to be reduced to perpetual desolation than for my own blood-brother, whom we know does not walk in the way of truth, to succeed me in governing it under the title of abbot,’ and so forth.”

2. It may mean that even the last in profession, if he possesses such maturity and prudence, should succeed the deceased abbot. For neither age nor rank should prejudice the matter, as the emperor Justinian teaches in *Novels* 5 and 123. Accordingly, we read in the *Chronicle of Centula*, book III, chapter 23, that Ingelard of Corbie, while still attending school and being only a subdeacon, was placed in charge of the monastery of Centula around the middle of the tenth century. We also read in the respective Lives of Wulfetrude of Nivelles and Austreude of Laon that they were only twenty years old, and that Rusticula, or Marcia, was appointed to Arles in the eighteenth year of her age. What is more, Eusebia, aged twelve, was substituted for Gertrude, abbess of Hamay, after her death, as is recorded in the *Life of St. Rictrudis*, chapter 16.

We nevertheless wish these examples to be received with caution. For age must not be entirely dishonored in elections, and rank likewise, as Justinian said (*Novella* 5); nor is it at all fitting for beginners and disciples in the spiritual art immediately to become masters. Both monastic and ecclesiastical laws forbid this.

Cassianus, speaking of the ancient monks, says (*Book II, chapter 3*):

> “No one is chosen to preside over a community of brothers before the one who is to be placed in authority has learned, by obeying, what ought to be commanded to those who will obey, and has acquired, through the institutions of his elders, what he ought to hand down to his juniors. For they declare that governing well, or being well governed, belongs to the wise, and they define it as the highest gift and grace of the Holy Spirit. No one can prescribe saving commands to those who obey unless he has first been instructed in every discipline of virtue; nor can anyone obey an elder unless he has been perfected in the fear of God and completed in the virtue of humility.”

And St. Fructuosus says in the *Common Monastic Rule* (chapter 3):

> “First, an abbot must be carefully selected who has been hardened by the discipline of a holy life, not one newly converted, but one who, laboring for a long time in the monastery under an abbot, has been tested among many.”

Likewise Pope St. Gregory says (*Book III of the Register*, chapter 11):

> “We most emphatically forbid young girls to become abbesses.”

The canon law likewise says:
