> “One who has not assumed the form of a disciple ought not to be taken as a master; nor should one who has not learned to be subordinate be placed in authority.”

The same is taught by Pope Zosimus in his letter to Hesychius, chapter 1; likewise by Pope Celestine in his letter to the bishops of Gaul, chapter 3; by Ruricius, book II, letter 25; and finally by the Council of Trent, which decrees (*Session 25, On Regulars*, chapter 7):

> “Let the abbess, prioress, or superior or governess called by any other name be elected only if she is not less than forty years of age and has lived commendably for eight years after her solemn profession. If no one possessing these qualities is found in the same monastery, she may be elected from another monastery of the same order. If this too should seem inconvenient to the superior presiding over the election, let her be elected from among those in the same monastery who have passed their thirtieth year and have lived properly for at least five years after profession, with the consent of the bishop or superior.”

This concerns women. As for men, by current law they must be priests and consequently must have reached twenty-five years of age.

This was first decreed in the year 826 by Eugene II at the Roman Council, in these words (canon 27):

> “Let abbots be appointed from among the monasterials, who are able to govern their subjects well and have also attained the priestly rank.”

Later, at the Council of Poitiers in 1078 (canon 7):

> “Let abbots who are deacons and not priests become priests, or let them lose their prelacies.”

Long before this, however, such a practice had virtually acquired the force of law, as is clear from the *Acts of St. Maximinus, Abbot*, chapter 5 (*First Century of Benedictine History*, under the year 520, p. 585). It is there said that one thing was lacking in him with which, **“according to the regular sanction,”** the one who presides over monks ought to be distinguished—namely, priestly ministry. At the request of St. Euspicius, he received this from Eusebius the bishop, who further added the blessing by which fathers and abbots of monks are customarily confirmed.

The same is clear from the *Acts of St. Leobinus*, first abbot and afterward bishop of Chartres (*First Century of Benedictine History*, year 556, p. 124). When Bishop Aetherius recognized his holiness, advanced him to the office of the diaconate, and placed him over the brothers of the monastery of Braye, he judged it fitting that Leobinus should carry out the office of governor more effectively and accordingly raised him, in due order, to the burden of the presbyterate.

In the West, however, that practice had not yet become so general. We find many abbots who were only deacons, and St. Eugendus, abbot of Condat (*First Century of Benedictine History*, p. 572), said:

> “It is much more useful for an abbot, because of the ambition of the younger men, to preside over the brothers free from the priesthood and not to be bound by a dignity which those who have renounced the world and withdrawn from it are least suited to desire.”

The mind of the Eastern monks was very different (*Monuments of the Greek Church*, vol. III, p. 205). Those who rebelled against St. Sabbas the abbot accused him before Bishop Sallustius, among other things, on the ground that:

> “He himself did not possess holy orders, nor had he allowed another to become a cleric.”

Certainly, before St. Sabbas all abbots commonly exercised the priesthood. This is shown especially by the letter of Martin, Peter, and eighteen other archimandrites to the emperor Marcian against Eutyches, all of whom were priests (*Labbe, Councils*, vol. IV, p. 531); by the record of the deposition of Eutyches, the heresiarch, at the Council of Chalcedon, session 7 (*Labbe, Councils*, vol. IV, p. 230), where eighteen priests among twenty-three abbots subscribe; and finally by the petition of the monks to the Council of Constantinople during the reign of the emperor Justinian for the condemnation of Severus (*Councils*, vol. V, p. 171), in which sixty-four abbots subscribe, all priests except one deacon.

There is also another petition of the monks of Apamea to their own bishops concerning the crimes of Peter (*Councils*, vol. V, p. 250), in which sixteen of eighteen abbots are recorded as priests and two as deacons. Moreover, abbesses themselves were formerly ordained as deaconesses, as Henschenius teaches in his notes on the *Life of St. Eupraxia*, proving it from the *Life of St. Irene* (*Bollandists*, 13 March).

In any case, it is clear from this text of the Holy Rule that abbots are to be chosen from the body of the community itself, and not from elsewhere, especially if those from elsewhere belong to another order. Only through the gravest abuse should secular clerics, as they are called, be placed over monasteries of monks, contrary to the express prohibition of Pope St. Gregory (*Book III of the Register*, chapter 11):

> “Do not permit priests, deacons, or clerics of any other order who serve churches in any way to become abbots in monasteries. Either let those who have assumed the clerical service not be advanced to monastic orders, or, if they decide to remain in the position of abbot, let them in no way be permitted to retain the service of the clergy. For it is very incongruous that, when someone cannot diligently fulfill one of these offices because of its magnitude, he should be judged suitable for both; and that thus, in turn, the ecclesiastical order should impede monastic life, and the rule of monasticism should impede ecclesiastical usefulness.”

The same holy teacher rightly says elsewhere (*Dialogues*, book I, chapter 1):

> “It is the practice of an upright way of life that one who has not learned to be subordinate should not dare to preside, nor should he command obedience from subjects who has not learned to show it to superiors.”

**“But if the whole community also, etc. Let them prevent the consent of the wicked from prevailing.”**

The bishop does this by restraining the wicked through his authority; the abbots by directing the brothers through sound counsel; and the neighboring Christians by assisting, if necessary, with practical execution—to put it in the words of Bernard of Cassino.

**“Knowing that for this they will receive a good reward if they do it chastely and with zeal for God.”**

“Chastely” means without the corruption of vainglory or rewards; and “with zeal for God” means with love for carrying out God’s commands, as Hildemar explains.

**“Just as, conversely, it is sin if they neglect it.”** [Col. 0886A]

From this passage it is clear that formerly abbots and their monasteries were under the jurisdiction of bishops, although later, for the sake of the monasteries’ peace and to restrain the exactions of certain bishops, provision was wisely made to exempt monks from such subjection to bishops.

Richard, archbishop of Canterbury, strongly disapproved of these exemptions, however, writing to Pope Alexander III as follows (in Peter of Blois, letter 68):

> “The monasteries that have obtained this benefit of most damnable liberty, whether by apostolic authority or—as happens more frequently—through forged bulls, have incurred more unrest, more disobedience, and more poverty. Therefore many houses renowned for holiness and religion have either never wished to possess these immunities or have immediately rejected them after possessing them.”

And earlier:

> “What sort of justice is this—or rather, what distortion of law—to forbid disciples to agree with their teacher, sons to obey their father, soldiers to follow their prince, and servants to be subject to their lord? What is it to exempt abbots from the jurisdiction of bishops except to command contumacy and rebellion, and to arm sons against their parents?”

Peter of Blois, who wrote the aforesaid letter in Richard’s name, held the same opinion. Writing to William, his brother and abbot, he dissuaded him from introducing such an exemption in these words (letter 90):

> “If the Roman pontiff has exempted you from the jurisdiction of your bishop, I beg you not to use a privilege that introduces a basis for rebellion.”

But Pope St. Gregory’s mind was very different. He had learned by personal experience that such exemptions were necessary, as he himself testifies in these words:

> “How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries and to take thought for their perpetual security is taught us by the office previously carried out by us when we governed a monastery. And because we know that in many monasteries monks have suffered many wrongs and burdens from their bishops, it is necessary that the provision of our fraternity arrange their future peace by a salutary ordinance, so that those who dwell in them may, with God’s assistance, persevere in God’s service with a free mind.”

St. Theodore of Sykeon, archimandrite of the monasteries in Galatia, had recognized the same necessity. From the emperor Maurice and Cyriacus, patriarch of Constantinople, he obtained the privilege that his monasteries should be:

> “subject to no other episcopate, but only to the most holy and great apostolic royal Church of that city,”

as his disciple George writes in his Life, no. 72.

And Gregory VII says (*Book II*, letter 69):

> “Do you not know that the holy Fathers and religious monasteries have often been separated from the subjection of bishops, and bishoprics from the parish of the metropolitan see, because of the harassment of those presiding over them, and that, by granting them perpetual freedom, they decreed that these members should adhere to the Apostolic See as to their principal head?”

See also the letter of Peter the Venerable to St. Bernard and the notes on Peter of Blois’s letter 68.

[Col. 0886D] **“But once he has been appointed.”**

And indeed by the bishop, as we said in book V, *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*.

**“Let him always consider what a burden he has undertaken.”**

Hildemar writes on this passage:

> “For it must be understood that he does not say ‘honor’ but ‘burden,’ that is, weight. And he rightly says that he has undertaken a weight and not an honor, because whoever undertakes this weight ought not to undertake it in order to be honored, but in order to labor and benefit others.”

**“And let him know that he ought to benefit more than to preside.”**

St. Bernard likewise says (*Sermon 36 on Various Subjects*):

> “Let the superior possess purity of heart, so that he desires to benefit rather than to preside; that is, so that in his prelacy he seeks neither his own advantage, nor worldly honor, nor anything else, except the good pleasure of God alone and the salvation of souls.”

And elsewhere:

> “You seek to preside very wickedly when you do not care to benefit; and you claim subjection for yourself with excessive ambition when you do not zeal for the salvation of those subject to you.”

And again, to Pope Eugene (*On Consideration*, book III, chapter 1):

> “Therefore preside in such a way that you provide, advise, take pains, and preserve; preside so that you may benefit; preside as the faithful and prudent servant whom the Lord appointed over his household. For what purpose? To give them food at the proper time—that is, to distribute, not to command. Do this, and do not desire to lord it over human beings, you who are yourself human, so that no injustice may lord it over you.”

**“Therefore he ought to be learned in divine law.”**

Although, as Cassian says (*Conferences*, 10, chapter 14), “it is clear that no one is entirely excluded from perfection of heart because of ignorance of letters, nor does rusticity hinder the attainment of purity of heart and soul”; indeed, although secular knowledge, as St. Bernard testifies (*Sermon 9 on the Song of Songs*), often “intoxicates with curiosity rather than charity, fills rather than nourishes, puffs up rather than builds, and stuffs rather than strengthens,” no one can rightly doubt that an abbot, and every shepherd of souls, nevertheless needs knowledge—not necessarily secular knowledge, but at least knowledge of divine law. Secular knowledge too is altogether useful if it is rightly employed.

Hildemar interprets knowledge of divine law as knowledge of the Old and New Testaments. I would add to this both ecclesiastical and monastic enactments, and the writings of the holy Fathers.

**“So that he may know how to bring forth things new and old.”**

Richard of St. Angelo explains this as sayings from the New and Old Testaments. Hildemar, however, says:

> “He knows how to bring forth things new and old who knows how to speak of eternal punishment and the joy of the heavenly homeland. For what, he asks, is meant by ‘new’ except joy, and what by ‘old’ except punishment? Because, as Blessed Gregory says, that preacher is learned in the holy Church who knows how to bring forth new things concerning the sweetness of the kingdom and to speak of ancient things concerning the terror of punishment.”

**“Let him be merciful, always setting mercy above judgment.”**

Hildemar aptly says here:

> “It must be noted that he ought to be merciful in food, drink, and clothing. But when the matter comes to vices, and there is doubt whether he should exercise punishment or mercy, it is more tolerable to incline toward mercy than toward punishment.”

Bernard of Cassino speaks in nearly the same way:

> “Let there be justice in an abbot, but not cruel justice; let there be mercy, but not excessive laxity. When there is doubt concerning a judgment, one must never rely solely on the severity of justice. When the judgment is clear, however, punishment should never go beyond what is deserved, but should be exercised around what is deserved. In this way mercy is preferred and exalted above judgment.”

You have an outstanding example of this mercy in Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny (*Book VI*, letter 46), whose witness and account are themselves free from all pretense:

> “I am accustomed to suffer,” he says, “and accustomed also to show indulgence. The schism of Pontius demonstrates this—although innumerable people turned toward it and committed abominable deeds unheard of in the monastic order, they never experienced my sword, my blade, or my weapon; scarcely ever did they hear a harsh word from my mouth. I did this then, and afterward often did the same, even if not concerning offenses so grave, yet concerning serious offenses which, if tolerance had not intervened, would perhaps justly have been punished severely. I still do this frequently and, so to speak, do not cease doing so continually.”

St. Odilo, his predecessor, was similarly criticized on this account and replied that, if he were to be condemned, he would rather be condemned for clemency than for severity.

Such pastors certainly ought to be the kind represented by the supreme and good Shepherd of all, who never punished any offense according to its full deserts. Superiors sometimes do more harm through excessive severity than if they had left the sin wholly unpunished: they exasperate minds rather than correct them, and cause those whom they ought to reform to rush into worse conduct.

For just as someone who places a heavier load upon a weak back either forces the person to throw off the load or makes him collapse under its weight, so abbots who impose too heavy a penance upon offenders cause them either to reject the judgment or, by submitting to it, to offend more seriously.

Thus our own Mabillon (*Preface to the Fourth Century of Benedictine History*, part I), among the causes of the collapse of regular discipline, places first the excessive strictness of certain abbots. Some punished the errors of their monks by putting out their eyes and mutilating their limbs—something forbidden by Charlemagne in the capitulary of 789, chapter 16, and by the Fathers of the Council of Frankfurt in 794, chapter 18.

**“Let him hate vices and love the brothers.”**

St. Gregory likewise teaches this (*Book IX*, letter 8):

> “Know that the order of correction is this: love persons and persecute vices.”

And elsewhere (*Book I*, letter 24):

> “A high position is therefore well governed when the one who presides dominates vices rather than brothers. He governs authority well who knows both how to retain it and how to oppose it; he governs it well who knows how, through it, to rise above offenses and, with it, to bring himself into equality with others.”

The holy pontiff himself observed this rule. Thus, writing to Venantius, chancellor of Italy (*Book I*, letter 33), he says:

> “I pursue your fault in such a way that I love you; I love your person in such a way that I do not embrace the fault’s vice.”

St. Fulgentius followed the same rule (*Bollandists*, 1 January). “Hating vices and loving human beings, he appeared severe for as long as the usefulness of spiritual discipline required it. At other times, however, he was so gentle, approachable, and affable toward each person that he never addressed any brother by his bare name, nor did he command anyone, however insignificant, with the arrogance of secular domination.”

**“And in correction itself let him act prudently.”**

It is useful to hear from another source how correction ought to be carried out. St. Dorotheus, addressing the superiors of monasteries, says (*Doctrine* 17):

> “In the lapses and errors that generally occur, do not become excessively indignant; but without disturbance of mind, show the ugliness and harm of the error or fault. Rebuke, if necessary, while observing the quality and dignity of both persons and the appropriate time. Do not become an excessive exactor and severe investigator in small mistakes and minor faults, as though you yourself were excessively righteous and a perfect interpreter of the law. Do not rebuke and reprimand frequently and continually; for this is exceedingly burdensome and harsh, and through constant repetition loses its force and is scarcely felt. Do not preside and command arrogantly and imperiously, but with humility of mind and gentleness, after taking counsel with your brother.”

From this you can see what is necessary for prudent and useful correction:

1. It must be given without indignation or disturbance of mind.
2. The person’s quality and dignity, and the appropriate time, must be observed.
3. It must not be excessive in the case of minor mistakes.
4. It must not be frequent and continual.
5. It must be carried out with humility and gentleness.

**“And let him do nothing to excess.”**

This is a familiar maxim, much celebrated by the ancients and established as a rule of sound discernment and prudence. Diogenes Laertius, in book I of his *Life of Solon*, makes the wise Solon its author. Boherius rightly thinks that St. Benedict placed it here “because of the two extremes of justice or equity, namely severity and leniency, since each is defective in correcting and punishing vice.”

Hence the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* (chapter 1):

> “In both respects an abbess must beware: lest by excessive kindness she nourish vices in the hearts of her subjects, or lest, through excessive disciplinary authority, those things that ought to have been healed by gentle rebuke be torn apart by harsh correction.”

Pope St. Gregory particularly censured this in Abbot Urbicus (*Book IX*, letter 42):

> “I grieve exceedingly because I find your monastery to be other than I had thought. This could have arisen from no other cause than that your affection is disordered in its government. You are unable to arrange anything with gravity; at one moment you strive gently to flatter those who entreat you, and at another you become excessively angry in a disorderly and immoderate fashion.”

[Col. 0889A] Although the holy legislator had both extremes in view and condemned excessive severity and indiscriminate leniency equally, the following words show that he was especially concerned with the former.

**“While he is too eager to scrape away the rust, let him not break the vessel.”**

St. Gregory uses another comparison when writing to Bononus, abbot of Lérins (*Book IX*, letter 8):

> “You must cut away the wound in such a way that you do not ulcerate what is healthy; lest, if you press the iron farther than the matter requires, you harm the one whom you hasten to benefit.”

See St. Dorotheus’s sixth doctrine.

**“Let him always be wary of his own weakness.”**

St. Gregory speaks excellently to this point (*Morals*, book XXIII, chapter 8):

> “Let us consider whether we are such as those whom we correct, or whether we were once such, although by the working of divine grace we are no longer so, so that we may correct with a humble heart all the more moderately as we recognize ourselves more truly in those whom we reform. But if we are neither now nor formerly what those whom we undertake to correct still are, let us recall their other good qualities before our eyes, lest our heart become proud and fall more grievously because of that very innocence while we correct their evils. If they have no good qualities at all, let us have recourse to the hidden judgments of God. For just as we received the very good that we possess without any merits of our own, so grace from above can also be poured into them, so that, once stirred up, they may later even anticipate the good things that we received earlier.”

**“And let him remember that a bruised reed must not be broken.”**

[844] “That is,” says Smaragdus, “a monk worn down by the stains of sins and shattered by various vices must not be driven into the pit of despair or into the path of flight. For without doubt he breaks the bruised reed who offers a sinner an occasion not for salvation but for destruction. Hence Blessed Jerome says (*On Matthew* XII): ‘Whoever does not reach out to the sinner and carry his brother’s burden breaks the bruised reed.’”

Richard of St. Angelo teaches that this happens in two ways:

> “First, if through excessive leniency or immoderate forgiveness the sin is allowed to continue, and the person thereby falls into the snare of eternal death; second, if he is corrected immoderately and in the same way falls into the snare of death through despair. To avoid this, it is commanded that the bruised reed must not be broken.”

**“In these matters we do not mean that he should allow vices to be nourished, but that he should cut them off prudently and with charity.”**

“For nothing is uglier than a furious teacher,” says St. Jerome, cited here by Boherius in his commentary on the Letter to Titus,

> “who, when he ought to be gentle and learned, instead, with a grim expression, trembling lips, wrinkled brow, unrestrained insults, and a face changing between pallor and redness, shouts noisily and drives those who err not so much back toward the good as toward evil through his savagery.”

**“As we have already said.”**

That is, above, where he said: “Let him hate vices and love the brothers,” and: “In correction itself let him act prudently.” Bernard of Cassino and Boherius explain it in this way in their second commentary, or in chapter 2 of the Rule; Boherius in his first commentary and Richard of St. Angelo, however, refer it to the preceding passage.

**“And let him strive to be loved more than feared.”**

St. Bernard speaks beautifully on this passage (*Sermon 23 on the Song of Songs*):

> “Let superiors who always wish to be objects of fear to those entrusted to them, and rarely of benefit, hear this. Learn, you who judge the earth; learn that you ought to be mothers of your subjects, not lords: strive to be loved rather than feared. And if severity is sometimes necessary, let it be paternal, not tyrannical. Show yourselves as mothers by nurturing and as fathers by correcting. Become gentle; lay aside ferocity; suspend the lashes; bring forth the breasts. Let your breasts grow rich with milk, not swell with arrogance. Why do you make heavier the yoke of those whose breasts you ought rather to carry?”

In all these matters, however, St. Gregory’s rule to Bononus, abbot of Lérins, must be followed. He writes (*Book IX*, letter 8):

> “Let the sweetness in you be cautious, not lax; let correction be diligent, not severe. Let one be seasoned with the other, so that the good may have, through love, something to fear, and the wicked, through fear, something to love.”

**“Let him not be turbulent and anxious.”**

“Smaragdus says that a turbulent man is one disturbed by the agitation of anger, gloomy, troublesome, or fierce. An anxious man is one filled with acedia or anxiety.”

Hildemar says that a turbulent man is one “who does not display cheerfulness in his countenance”; an anxious man is “excessive, as we say. Or an anxious man is one who wants to do different things at the same time without any interval.”

Finally, according to Bernard of Cassino, “a turbulent man is one who always walks as though angry, or disturbed or agitated by anger; an anxious man is one who is agitated.”

[845] **“Let him not be excessive and obstinate.”**

According to Hildemar, “excessive” and “obstinate” mean the same thing. An obstinate man is one “who hastens to do something precipitately and without taking it back.”

Smaragdus, however, distinguishes the two as follows. An excessive man is:

> “Lavish, prodigal, or an excessive and superfluous dispenser of the monastery’s resources.”

An obstinate man is:

> “Unyielding, hardened, stubborn, and obdurate.”

Similarly, according to Bernard of Cassino:

> “Excess belongs to prodigality; obstinacy to the hardening of one’s own judgment: lest by the one he dissipate the monastery’s resources indiscriminately, and by the other, trusting in his own judgment, either fail to seek advice or foolishly disdain to follow advice once sought.”

The monks of Fulda explain all these matters excellently in their petition to Charlemagne (no. 20), asking that the abbot:

> “Be not turbulent in countenance, not anxious in mind, not excessive in judgment, and not obstinate in counsel; but cheerful in face, glad in mind, discerning in action, and consenting in what is useful.”

**“Let him not be jealous or excessively suspicious.”**

Smaragdus explains what “jealous” or “suspicious” means—the significance of the two words is the same—in these terms:

> “A jealous man is said to be full of zealous concern and filled with the appearance of suspicion. He suspects that even things that are not happening are happening in his absence, and fears that things no one is committing are being committed in secret. Therefore his spirit never rests.”

The venerable Eigil, abbot of Fulda, carefully avoided this vice (*Fourth Century of Benedictine History*, part I). Candidus writes in his Life, no. 8:

> “He did not consent to hear the trifles and frivolous babbling of accusers, knowing that he would be more disturbed than pleased by them. As a lover of peace, he absolutely did not permit suspicion to dominate his mind, nor did the simple man take pleasure in the angular intrigues of ambushes.”

In the commands themselves, let him be prudent and considerate.] Both with regard to the persons to whom they are entrusted and with regard to the matters themselves that are commanded to be done, as Bernard says.

Whether they are according to God or according to the world.] “That is, whether they concern temporal or spiritual matters,” says Richard of Saint Angelo. Hildemar refers these words not to the commands but to the works that are enjoined. He places a comma after *consideratus* and reads the remainder accordingly: “And whether it be according to God or according to the world, let him discern and regulate the work that he enjoins.” Bernard of Cassino says that Hildemar did this “[Col. 0890D] because in certain Rules the word *sit* occurs twice. For another reading says: ‘Let him be prudent and considerate, whether it be according to God or according to the world.’ But where,” he says, “there is only one *sit*, this exposition of Paul”—that is, of Hildemar, whom he customarily cites under the name Paul—“is unnecessary. Where, however, there are two *sit*s, the exposition is good; and I think that reading in which the word occurs twice is the better.”

Nevertheless, Menard considers the Vulgate reading, which is also found in the most ancient Oxford manuscript, preferable, so that the substantive verb *sint* refers to the commands. He cites Smaragdus, who explains the passage as follows:

> Commands according to the world are those that concern the body, such as ploughing and reaping; those according to God concern the soul, such as praying and fasting.

But another manuscript of the same Smaragdus of Fleury, copied about eight hundred years ago, reads *sit*, not *sint*, and likewise presents the exposition differently [Col. 0891A]:

> Works according to God are these: vigils, fasts, abstinence, and the like; works according to the world, on the other hand, are works performed for the body alone and not for the soul, namely ploughing, digging, reaping, and all similar bodily works.

Let him discern and regulate the works that he enjoins.] Let him discern, namely, whether they ought to be done or not, as Hildemar says; and if they ought to be done, let him regulate them—that is, he should not command more than is appropriate, but should impose them as in the Rule of Saint Pachomius, delivered by an angel (in his Life, in Rosweyde):

> Let stronger works be assigned to the stronger who eat, but lighter works to the weak and to those who abstain.

Thinking of the discretion of Saint Jacob, who said: “If I make my flocks work harder by walking, they will all die in one day.”] For this reason Ratgar caused such disturbances in the monastery of Fulda that he even compelled his own sheep to seek another shepherd. He assigned the monks harsh labor and did not allow them time on feast days to perform the sacred offices; indeed, on his own authority he abolished feast days, forbade books and study, denied the sick medicines and everyone the clothing they needed, as the monks of Fulda complain in their supplication to Charlemagne [Col. 0891B].

Thus drawing these and other testimonies concerning discretion, the mother of virtues.] Saint Benedict calls discretion the mother of virtues because, as Peter the Venerable says (*Book I, Letter 20*), “unless she nourishes them as a mother does her daughters, the entire offspring of the virtues will immediately perish.” Cassian commends it at length in *Conference 2*. In chapter 4 he says [Col. 0892A]:

> It was determined by the judgment both of blessed Antony and of all the others that discretion is what leads the monk, with a firm and fearless step, to God; continually preserves the aforementioned virtues unharmed; enables him to ascend to the lofty heights of perfection with less fatigue; and without which many, although laboring with greater zeal, have been unable to reach the summit of perfection. For discretion is the begetter, guardian, and governor of all the virtues.

So that there may be something which the strong desire and the weak do not shrink from.] “For,” says Hildemar, “if the work has been properly regulated, the weak do not shrink from it, and the strong desire to perform it, as we said above. For if he restrains the strong, who are able to labor, those strong men will always desire to perform that work more and more, because they wish to do as much as they can but are not permitted to do so; while the weak do not shrink from it. It is like someone leading a horse that is excessively eager to walk and also leading a feeble one: he puts the bridle on the eager horse so that it does not go too far, and he does not distress the feeble one, but leaves it in its freedom to walk as it wishes.”

847 Especially so that he may preserve the present Rule in all things.] On this passage Bernard of Cassino writes [Col. 0892B]:

> Let those who say that the abbot is not bound to observe the Rule hear this statement, for the Rule contradicts them. The Father therefore says in the text, “especially,” because he ought to observe the Rule above all others who has others to form according to the Rule. He also says “present,” so that he may not make another Rule for himself, but preserve this one. He says “in all things,” thereby excepting none of the institutions of the Rule.

Boherius, Turrecremata, and Matthew Lambert speak in much the same way. Hence also the decree of the Council of Aachen (canon 1):

> Abbots, as soon as they have returned to their monasteries, shall read the Rule in full, examining it word by word, and, with God’s help, shall strive effectively to fulfill it with their monks.

For it is just “that he who is first in name should also be first in action; that he should complete by his deeds what he preaches with his mouth; and that, being first, he should carry upon his own shoulders or neck what he commands the brothers to carry, so that by experience he may learn whether the burdens he imposes on the brothers are light or heavy. He should show by his conduct that the primacy which he holds first at table is also first in the frugality of virtue, and by experience learn the abstinence which he preaches with his tongue,” to speak with Smaragdus.

## CHAPTER LXV. On the Provost of the Monastery

[Col. 0891]

[Col. 0891C] It often happens that serious scandals arise in monasteries through the appointment of a provost [Note: [Col. 0891D] Oxford and Fleury: “arose.”], when certain men, puffed up by the evil spirit of pride and considering themselves to be second abbots, assume tyranny for themselves, nourish scandals, and create dissensions in the community—especially in those places where the provost is appointed by the same priest, or by the same abbots, who appoint the abbot.

How absurd this is can easily be understood, because from the very beginning of his appointment an occasion for pride is given to him: his thoughts suggest to him that he has been released from the authority of his abbot, since he has been appointed by the same persons [Note: [Col. 0891D] Cassino, Fleury, Council: “since you too have been appointed by the same persons.”] by whom the abbot was appointed. Hence envy, quarrels, slander, rivalries, dissensions, and disorder arise. And when [Note: [Col. 0891D] Cassino, Hildemar, Conches: “While.”] the abbot and the provost hold opposing views [Note: [Col. 0891D] Another reading omits “each other.”], their own souls must necessarily be endangered amid this dissension [Note: [Col. 0891D] Council, Fleury: “this dissension.”]; and those under them, while flattering the opposing parties, [Col. 0892C] go to perdition. The evil of this danger falls upon the heads of those who made themselves responsible for such an appointment [Note: [Col. 0892D] Cassino: “such disorderly appointments”; another reading: *actores* (“agents”).].

Therefore, for the preservation of peace and charity, we foresee that it is expedient for the ordering of his monastery to depend upon the abbot’s decision [Note: [Col. 0892C] Others: “we foresaw”; “we saw”; “we see.”]. If it can be done, the entire administration of the monastery should be entrusted to deans, as we previously arranged, according to the abbot’s disposition, so that when responsibility is entrusted to several men, one may not become proud.

But if either the place requires it or the community requests it, the abbot, with reason and humility, should appoint for himself as provost whomever he chooses with the counsel of God-fearing brothers. Nevertheless, that provost must carry out with reverence whatever has been entrusted to him by his abbot, doing nothing against the abbot’s will or appointment [Col. 0892D]; for, to the extent that he is superior to the others, he ought to observe the precepts of the Rule with correspondingly greater diligence [Note: [Col. 0892D] Cassino: “to that extent”; Hildemar: “so much”; Oxford, Hildemar, Guido: “diligently.”]

If that provost is found to be vicious, or deceived by the pride of self-exaltation [Note: [Col. 0893A] Another reading: *superbire* (“to be proud”),] or is proved to be a despiser of the holy Rule, he shall be admonished verbally up to four times. If he does not amend, regular disciplinary correction shall be applied to him. If he is not corrected even then, he shall be removed from the office of provost, and another worthy man shall be substituted in his place. If afterward he is not quiet and obedient in the community, he shall also be expelled from the monastery [Note: [Col. 0893A] Oxford, Cassino: *pellatur* (“be driven out”).]. Yet the abbot must consider that he will render an account to God for all his judgments [Note: [Col. 0894A] Oxford: “will have to render an account,”] lest the flame of envy or zeal perhaps burn his soul.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0893]

849 On the provost of the monastery Saint Benedict treats here chiefly of two matters: how he is to be appointed and how he is to be corrected if he is found to be vicious. What the provost is, the reasons for establishing the office, its duties, and its virtues, he either leaves entirely unmentioned or touches so lightly that he seems almost to have passed them over. Therefore, before examining the text of the Rule of Saint Benedict, we have thought it worthwhile to gather these matters from elsewhere [Col. 0893B].

The provost, then, if we attend to the force of the name, signifies the same as a superior. Among the Romans this was the title of the prefect of the royal bodyguard, as is clear from Theophylact Simocatta (*Book IV, chapter 15*): “He sent to Martyropolis the commander of the royal bodyguard, whom the Romans customarily call the provost.” In the Apostle [Hebrews] we read of bishops and pastors: “Remember your superiors, who spoke the word of God to you.” And: “Obey your superiors and be subject to them.” Among monks, the one who stood first after the abbot was called the provost, as is clear throughout their Rules. The superiors of several monasteries were also called provosts when they were subject to a single abbot, as Menard observed; Haeften may likewise be consulted, book III, treatises 6, questions 1 and 2.

Today, although the office and function of the provost remain in monasteries, the name has nearly fallen into disuse, and we generally use the word “prior” in its place. Lanfranc also used this term in his *Statutes*, where he says [Col. 0893C] (chapter 3):

> While preserving reverence for the abbot in all things, the prior, who is also called the provost in the Rule, is more honorable than the other ministers of the house of God.

Ingulf uses the same designation more than once in his *History of Crowland*, especially when he reports that, during the destruction of the monastery, “Lord Asker, the prior, in the vestry, and Lord Letwyn, the subprior, in the refectory,” were killed by the swords of the barbarians. Long before this, Saint Gregory the Great wrote to Bishop Victor in these words (*Book IV, Letter 4*):

> Victoria scattered the monastery’s possessions so that she might reach the position of prioress, and she herself ought meanwhile to have been found after the abbess.

We can enumerate three principal reasons for establishing the office.

The first is that of Saint Basil (*Longer Rules*, chapter 45): when the abbot is absent, someone should always remain to govern the monastery and care for the brothers.

> Since it very often happens, says the holy teacher, whether because of bodily illness, a necessary journey, or some other circumstance, that the superior is absent from the brothers, there should be someone else who has been chosen for this purpose after examination by him and by others competent to judge: namely, that in his absence he may take upon himself the care of the brothers, so that while the brothers are present they may be governed by the exhortation of one man and, in the absence of the superior, may not seize upon some kind of democratic order to the destruction of the Rule and the established discipline, but may carefully preserve what has been decreed for the glory of God, and so forth.

850 The second reason is that even when the abbot is present, he should have someone to assist him, by whose help he can bear the burden imposed upon him more easily. This reason can be seen in the Rule of Saint Ferreolus, chapter 17; in the common monastic Rule of Saint Fructuosus, chapter 11; in the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins, chapter 2; and in Saint Gregory, book IX, letter 42.

Thus Saint Aventinus appointed Fidolus provost of his monastery (Saec. I Ben.), “so that he might devote himself to prayer and divine contemplation with greater security, knowing that Fidolus would neither do nor command anything outside the order of the common Rule,” as the Acts of Saint Fidolus state, number 8.

The third reason is that, if the abbot should happen to be negligent, the discipline of the order may remain safe and intact through the provost’s diligence. Saint Gregory gives this reason in writing to Victor, bishop of Palermo, instructing him to place Gregory, the abbot and priest of the monastery of Saint Theodore, who was afflicted by penance, in his former position [Col. 0894B]:

> Yet in such a way, he says (*Book IV, Letter 4*), that Urbicus, the provost of my monastery, must appoint one of the servants of God to become his provost, so that what is neglected through the negligence of the former may be preserved through the diligence of the latter.

Now someone may ask in what matters the provost ought chiefly to assist the abbot, and what the duties of his office are. Saint Benedict does not sufficiently explain his mind on these matters, being content to say that the provost should carry out with reverence whatever has been entrusted to him by his abbot. The matter must therefore be sought elsewhere.

Accordingly, according to the Rule of Saint Pachomius, articles 152 and 154 (in the *Book of Rules*), it belonged to the provost to report the brothers’ negligences to the abbot; and according to article 152, to give two conferences each week, that is, catechetical instructions.

The Eastern Rule decrees only in general terms (chapter 3) [Col. 0894C]:

> He who, according to the order of discipline and by the appointment of the abbot, with the counsel and will of all the brothers, has been placed over the brothers shall draw to himself all care for the discipline of the brothers and all diligence for the monastery, having the authority, in the abbot’s absence, to do everything that the abbot does when present.

The Rule of Tarnat says (chapter 23):

> It will belong especially to the provost to refer to the abbot, whose authority among you is greater, whatever exceeds his ability and strength [lacuna]. Let him correct the restless, console the fainthearted, receive the sick, and be patient toward all. Let him gladly maintain discipline and inspire fear; and although both are necessary, let him desire to be loved rather than feared.

The Rule of Saint Isidore (chapter 19) says:

> The care of the monks, the conduct of legal affairs, the management of possessions, the sowing of fields, the planting and cultivation of vineyards, the care of flocks, the construction of buildings, and the work of carpenters and smiths belong to the provost.

The First Rule of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 3) says:

> The provost, standing in the middle of the dormitory until everyone is at rest, shall, when all have gone to bed, silently go around and inspect each person’s bed, lest anyone either toss about late or engage in secret murmuring outside the Rule. By examining more fully the conduct and merits of each person, he shall understand whom he should honor and receive, and in what manner [lacuna]. Before midnight the provost is to be awakened by the brothers assigned to the vigils, 851 so that, with his blessing, the signal may be given and he may diligently inspect all their beds before they rise. This is also to be done at every nocturnal prayer: the provost must always rise before the others are summoned to rise, and he himself must see how each person lies, lest anyone, while sleeping, fall into some wantonness through negligence in his rest.

And the common monastic Rule of the same author says (chapter 11):

> The provosts shall have authority over the entire Rule of the monastery [lacuna]. The provosts shall receive all the monastery’s property for administration. If any captive should ask the abbot for food, or if anything is needed for any reason, the provost himself shall provide it; and, so that the abbot may have no labor, except for the matters mentioned above, he shall attend to everything with complete diligence. The provost shall have the authority to excommunicate, just as the abbot does. At the beginning of every month he shall render his abbot an account of what has been spent, and this with fear, simplicity, and true humility of heart, as one who will render an account to the Lord. Whatever he does must always remain subject to the abbot’s judgment.

The Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins (chapter 2) says that the superior:

> ought to be attentive to every bodily and spiritual need, so that she may provide assistance for present necessities and, through constant admonition, rouse and lift up the hearts of her subjects to resound with praise of the Creator. By honoring the humble and those subject for Christ’s sake, she should raise them to a higher state; but those who exalt themselves she should draw back to the steps of humility with the rod of correction. She should care for every matter of the monastery, whether vessels or furnishings, so attentively that she is found in no respect darkened by the shadows of negligence. While applying herself to the whole work of sacred labor, she should receive from the Almighty the fruit of her labor.
>
> Every Saturday, after the ninth hour of prayer, both the older and younger superiors shall visit the beds of all the sisters and make inquiry into their negligences, or whether anything has been found there that was unlawfully retained without permission. Likewise, after Compline they shall visit all the beds with lights, so that they may recognize whether the senses of each are awake or growing lukewarm after prayer. Similarly, this must be done at all the nocturnal offices, so that they may know which sisters rise for the office with fervor and which with lukewarmness; and those whom they find blameworthy through tardiness or sluggishness they shall correct according to their fault or age, either by rebuke or by scourging.

But these are the practices of others; what of ours? The Council of Aachen decrees only this (canon 31) [Col. 0895C]:

> The provost, whether within or outside the monastery, shall have authority after the abbot greater than that of the other persons subject to the abbot.

This appears to be explained by the chapters of the monks of Saint Gall in these words (chapter 50):

> In the abbot’s absence, the provost shall occupy his place in the church, in the chapter, and in the refectory; in his stead he shall interpret the readings at each assembly and give the blessing to those who read. If the provost is not present, the senior dean shall do the same. When the abbot is present, they shall retain their proper places.

Hildemar says:

> It must be understood that when the abbot is not in the monastery, the provost ought to have the same authority that the abbot has: namely, in rebuking, excommunicating, scourging, and in the other places as well. If there is no provost, the dean ought to have this authority; if there is no dean, the man whom he appoints in his place ought to have it.

A little earlier he had said:

> He is called provost because he is the organizer or ruler of those subject to him and of those who serve.

Udalric gives a fuller account (*Book III, chapter 4*) [Col. 0895D]:

> From the hour of his appointment, after the Lord Abbot, he concerns himself with every matter or case belonging to the monastery, both spiritual and temporal. All who hold any obedience look to him; and if they are about to undertake any important matter, they do not act without his counsel and direction. In the choir he stands highest on the left, and in the refectory at the highest table, which is on the right of the Lord Abbot; and if the latter is absent, he sits in his seat, and so forth.

Nearly the same words occur in the manuscript *Customary of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, chapter 2. If desired, see Lanfranc’s *Statutes*, chapter 3; the *Book of the Usages of Cîteaux*, chapter 111; and the *Ceremonial of the Monks of Bursfeld*, distinction 2, chapter 2, where the office of the prior is described at length.

Here it is enough to note that the chief office of the provost was to manage the monastery’s external affairs. This is clear from the Rules of Saint Isidore and Saint Fructuosus cited above, from Udalric, and from Faustus in the *Life of Saint Maurus* (Saec. I Ben.), where he writes in number 15 [Col. 0896A]:

> Blessed Maurus, who, by the command of our Father, was then provost in the monastery and administrator of the entire monastery, exercised the office after him.

Finally, it is clear from what Pope Saint Gregory writes (*Dialogues*, book I, chapter 2) about Libertinus, provost of the monastery of Fundi, whom he repeatedly represents as managing the monastery’s interests outside it and reports scarcely anything else about him.

From what has been said it is clear what virtues provosts ought to possess, and how rightly Saint Fructuosus, chapter 11, requires the same qualities in him as in the abbot, while Saint Ferreolus (chapter 17) wishes the office and title of provost to be assumed by a vigorous person who greatly loves discipline.

It is useful to hear the Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins discussing this matter (chapter 2) [Col. 0896B]:

> The superior of a monastery should be appointed not for her old age but for her character. Length of years often raises a person up, but the disgrace of a sluggish life, through growing lukewarm, brings her back to the immaturity of childhood. The superior should therefore be serious in character, skillful in speech, strong in understanding, watchful in judgment, tireless in activity, compassionate in correction, moderate in discipline, chaste in conduct, temperate in behavior, fair in administration, adorned with humility, patient, gentle, not turbulent, not irascible, not stained by the vice of pride or arrogance, not wasteful, not talkative, but adorned in every action with religious devotion. She must know how to accommodate the dispositions of the weak and to rouse the sluggishness of those growing lukewarm. The abbess should rest upon her, so that she may deviate in nothing from the abbess’s commands; but, being subject in all things and restrained by the orders of her superior, she must neither do nor order anything contrary to the abbess’s will, but must do everything by asking her.

To this should be added what the Rule of Saint Pachomius says in article 128 about the vices that the provost must avoid, and what the Eastern Rule says in chapter 17. See also Peter Damian, *Opusculum* 13, chapter 16.

I now come to the text of the Rule.

It often happens that serious scandals arise in monasteries through the appointment of a provost, and so forth. Here Saint Benedict declares how far he wished scandals to be banished from monasteries, revealing their causes, effects, and remedies.

[Col. 0896C] Especially in those places where it is done by the same priest.] That is, by the bishop, who is properly called a priest; other priests are to be honored only with the title.

Or by the same abbots.] “Supply: assisting the bishop who performs the ordination,” says Bernard of Cassino. Here the particle *or* is used coordinately, in the sense of “and.”

Who appoint the abbot, and by those same persons the provost is also appointed.] For, as Smaragdus says:

> Their custom at that time was that when the abbot was appointed, the provost was also appointed by the same bishop and by the other abbots standing present. But because the vice of pride arose from this, today among us he is no longer appointed by another; rather, obedience to the provost’s office is imposed upon him by his own abbot, so that whenever the abbot sees fit, he may remove him from the office of provost, lest fuel for pride arise in him.

The evil of this danger falls upon the heads of those who made themselves responsible for such an appointment.] “This,” says Smaragdus, “seems to be said of those who appointed the provost just as they appointed the abbot. They ought to have entrusted the appointment of one monastery not to two persons but to one; and, lest dangerous scandals arise between two men, they ought to have entrusted its care solely to the abbot of the community.”

Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius speak in nearly the same way.

Therefore we foresee that, for the preservation of peace and charity, it is expedient for the ordering of his monastery to depend upon the abbot’s decision.] Boherius interprets this as referring to the appointment of places, affairs, and officials; Bernard of Cassino, more correctly, refers it only to the appointment of officials, since the holy Father is speaking of the appointment of the provost.

And, if it can be done, let the entire administration of the monastery be entrusted to deans, as we previously arranged, according to the abbot’s disposition.] Charles Cointius understands this to mean that, with no provost appointed, only deans should be established and appointed to govern the monastery under the abbot. Hildemar agrees, explaining Saint Benedict as if he had said [Col. 0897A]:

> Whatever is to be ordered in the monastery, the deans ought to order; and the deans ought to arrange it according to the abbot’s disposition.

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, however, understand “deans” in both commentaries to mean officials. I understand them to be men placed over ten monks, among whom officials themselves could be found. Hence Hildemar says:

> As I understand it, there was an ancient custom that in every office and obedience of the monastery there was always one dean over ten monks. For example, if there were grammarians who were learning, one dean was over those brothers who had been assigned to that obedience. These deans cared for their bodily needs, and they asked the abbot about those needs. They were also responsible for their negligence, as is read in the *Institutes of the Fathers*, when they sat at table: the deans would give a signal if the brothers needed to ask for something.
>
> Then perhaps, when they were obtaining bread—or perhaps baking it—four or three deans went with the brothers, as necessity required. When they went into the garden, four deans went with their deanery. No one from one deanery dared to go to another deanery or speak there unless ordered to do so. Likewise, in the chapter there was always a dean over his deanery; and wherever the dean went, his deanery went with him. There was great diligence in this, but it is no longer done.

Finally, the Council of Mainz renewed this decree of the Rule under Charlemagne in these words (canon 12):

> We therefore decree, as the holy Rule says, that, where possible, the monastery be organized through deans, because those provosts often fall into pride.

So that, when responsibility is entrusted to several, one may not become proud.] Albricus, bishop and abbot of the monastery of Utrecht, may perhaps have had this passage in mind. Alfric reports the following in the *Life of Saint Liudger, Bishop*, book I, number 15 (Saec. IV Ben., part I) [Col. 0897C]:

> The same Albricus divided the year into four periods, so that in the monastery at Utrecht, above the other provosts, he himself presided over the brothers during the spring for three months in the study of teaching and holy conduct. After him, in summer, the priest Adalger served in his place for three months. After him the priest Liudger served for three months. Then in winter the priest Thiadbraht served for three months.

But if either the place requires it, and so forth.] Here Bernard of Cassino, followed by Boherius, says:

> Four things must concur in the appointment of a provost: the usefulness of the monastery, the humble request of the community, a reasonable cause, and the judgment or will of the abbot.

Richard of Saint Angelo says nearly the same:

> Three things must concur in the appointment of this provost: that the place require it, that the community request it, and that the abbot judge it appropriate.

As for what Saint Benedict adds, “with the counsel of God-fearing brothers,” Hildemar understands this to mean the elders, but in such a way that afterward he asks all the brothers in chapter. The practice may be seen in Udalric, whom we shall cite shortly, and in the manuscript *Customary of Saint Benignus of Dijon*, chapter 2.

According to the Eastern Rule, however, the provost is to be chosen by the counsel and will of all the brothers (chapter 3). In the monastery of virgins at Portus, Saint Austreberta is said to have been appointed superior “with all choosing and the mother consenting, though unwilling,” as we read in her Life, number 9 (Saec. III Ben.). At Cluny, Saint Hugh was appointed prior “with the consent of the brothers,” as Hildebert testifies in the *Life of Saint Hugh*, number 3 (Bollandists, 29 April). At Celle, God, in whose hand are human hearts, “inspired the brothers to choose the man of God Robert as their prior,” as we read in the *Life of Saint Robert, Abbot of Molesme*, number 3. Finally, at Crespin, Saint Aybert is said to have been made “provost and cellarer by the common election of the brothers,” in his Life, number 9 (Bollandists, 7 April).

Unless someone should say that “election” and “consent” are being used broadly here for “counsel,” as when Saint Aventinus, seeing Fidolus ascending to the heights of virtue, “by the unanimous counsel of the brothers assigned him the place of provost,” as the Acts of Saint Fidolus state, number 8 (Saec. I Ben.).

In the book of the Cistercian Institutions I also read the following (distinction 7, chapter 23):

> Priors are under no circumstances to be elected; rather, the abbots shall appoint them with the counsel of God-fearing brothers, whom they may summon for this purpose as they wish and in whatever manner they wish.

This seems more correct and more in keeping with the mind of Saint Benedict.

Moreover, what we said above about the abbot must also be affirmed of the provost: he must be chosen from within the monastery. Thus the Council of Aachen decreed (canon 32):

> A monk, and no one but a monk, shall be appointed provost over monks.

And the capitulary of Charlemagne issued at Thionville in 805 says (number 15):

> Laymen shall not be provosts of monks within a monastery.

Indeed, even a priest is required, according to this decree of the Council of Westminster in 1126 (in Spelman, volume II of the Councils of England):

> No one shall be promoted to dean unless he is a priest; no one to prior unless he is a priest; and no one to archdeacon unless he is a deacon.

We have a formula or rite for instituting a provost both in the manuscript *Customary of the Monastery of Farfa* and in Udalric.

The Farfa custom says [Col. 0898B]:

> When the prior has been elected by all the brothers, after chapter let everyone rise and go to the church. Then the man who is leaving the office shall say three times, with everyone repeating the verse before the altar: “Blessed is the Lord God.” After receiving the blessing that is said when the brothers are released from an office, he shall depart. Let the man who is entering the office approach and say three times, with everyone listening, the verse: “O God, come to my assistance.” After receiving the blessing that is said when the brothers are appointed to an office, let him administer that office.

Udalric gives a somewhat fuller account (*Book III, chapter 4*):

> When a prior is to be appointed, the Lord Abbot first takes counsel with the elders of the community. Then he reports his decision in chapter, and everyone approves what seems good to him. The man whom he chooses, if he has understanding, asks pardon and excuses himself, saying that he is not suitable for such an office. Finally, when obedience has been commanded and imposed upon him, he does nothing but bow. He sits to the left of the Lord Abbot.
>
> When they have risen from chapter, they go with the customary psalmody to the principal church. There the new prior goes before and behind, saying three times: “O God, come to my assistance,” and the entire community likewise responds. The Lord Abbot himself gives him this blessing:
>
> “Most merciful Father, we humbly beseech your omnipotence to deign to pour upon this servant of yours, whom we dedicate to your service and that of your servants, the spirit of wisdom, understanding, and discretion. Grant that in this your house he may act and administer the office entrusted to him in such a way that he may be able to please you and, with your help, fulfill most perfectly the needs of your servants, for which may he receive from you, the most gracious giver, both in this age and in the age to come, the reward of his labors in the company of your saints. Through the Lord, etc.”
>
> When he is to be released from the office, he accompanies him with the verse: “Blessed are you, Lord, who have helped me.” He is released with this blessing:
>
> “Lord Jesus Christ, who are a generous rewarder and merciful giver to those who piously serve you, respond in your accustomed goodness to this servant of yours, who has faithfully labored in this your house until now and, obeying you and your servants, has administered the office entrusted to him with your help. Show yourself a gracious remunerator, and grant that he may remain continually in this house and receive from you, both here and in the recompense of the just, the reward of his labors; and may he not doubt with complete faith that you are the giver of every good thing.”

The manuscript *Customary of Saint Benignus* contains the same material, chapter 2.

Nevertheless, that provost must carry out with reverence whatever has been entrusted to him by his abbot.] Saint Pachomius says likewise (article 128):

> The provost himself shall do nothing except what the Father commands, especially in a new matter; but he shall observe the rules of the monastery in matters that have descended from custom.

These words are to be understood not only when the abbot is present but also when he is absent. Thus, although the provost’s authority in the monastery may be great during the abbot’s absence, the abbot’s will always sets limits to his power.

Hence the *Book of the Cistercian Usages* (chapter 3) forbids the provost, in the abbot’s absence, to do the following [Col. 0899A]:

> He shall not occupy his place—that is, the abbot’s—in the church; he shall not sing solemn Masses in his place; he shall not bless candles, ashes, branches, fire, a crown, or a novice; nor shall he give the blessing at the Gospel. He shall not anoint the sick or bury the dead. He shall promote or degrade no one, nor have anyone ordained. He shall impose no grave disciplinary penalty on anyone, nor absolve anyone from one. He shall not expel a monk from the monastery or receive a novice unless the abbot has ordered it; nor shall he hear a confession concerning serious offenses except from those who are at the point of death. The care of works, flocks, or granges shall not be entrusted to him; his own office is sufficient for him.

[Doing nothing against the abbot’s will or command.] St. Fulgentius (Bollandists, 1 January) “said that those were true monks who, having mortified their own wills, were prepared neither to will nor to refuse anything, but only to observe the counsels or commands of their abbot. Therefore, without his counsel he did not allow that brother who held the office of provost to do anything,” as the author of his Life writes.

Now, concerning the text of St. Benedict, two points are noted by the commentators on the Rule, Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata. The first is that the provost must presume to do nothing contrary to the abbot’s ordinance, whether expressed verbally or in writing. The second is that everything cannot be defined verbally or in writing and reduced to a fixed rule; whatever he knows or believes to be the abbot’s will in such matters, he should carry out diligently. Thus, if that will is not sufficiently known, he should consult the abbot, in accordance with the Eastern Rule (chapter 3): “The senior of the monastery who is set over the brothers shall observe this: referring everything to the abbot, especially those matters which he is unable to explain by himself”; and the Tarnatensis Rule: “It will belong especially to the provost to refer to the abbot, whose authority among us is greater, whatever exceeds his own capacity and strength.”

[The provost, if he is found to be vicious or contemptuous of the holy Rule.] Here Boherius observes in his second commentary that, on this text’s account, some have denied that the Rule we possess was written by St. Benedict, because it calls the Rule “holy,” and consequently have rejected the credibility of what Gregory the Great writes in Book II of the *Dialogues*. But St. Benedict did not call his Rule holy because it had been written by him; rather, he did so because it contains holy and salutary precepts, whose practice leads to the highest summit of perfection.

[Having been proved.] For a mere suspicion ought not to suffice here.

[He shall be admonished verbally up to four times.] This is to be done privately, according to Bernard of Cassino, and by the abbot, according to Boherius. A simple monk should be admonished twice, a dean three times, and a provost four times.

[If he does not amend, regular disciplinary correction shall be applied to him.] As Hildemar says, it is as though he were saying: “If he has been admonished four times and has not amended himself, let him be led through the stages—that is, public correction, excommunication, excessive fasts, and, if he deserves it, the scourge; then prayer; afterward let him be removed from the rank of provost; and finally let him be expelled.” Bernard of Cassino, Boherius, and Turrecremata say the same.

[But if he does not reform even in this way, then he shall be deposed from the rank of provost.] Thus, in the Life of Benedict, abbot of Aniane, written by Ardo, no. 24 (Fourth Century of Benedict, part I), we are told that Benedict once deposed a certain provost who had been lifted up by pride. Pope Gregory IX explains the causes or grounds for such a deposition of a provost in a bull addressed to the Cluniacs, in these words:

“Conventual priors, so long as they administer spiritual and temporal matters well, ought not to be removed except for certain causes: namely, if they have been wasteful, disobedient, rebellious, infamous, or incontinent, or if they are to be advanced to a greater dignity. We wish the same to be observed concerning the greater officials; and no one shall possess letters of confirmation stating that he may not be removed from his priory or obedience.”

Nicholas IV says the same in another bull addressed to the Cluniacs, as does the Council of London in the year 1200, in Spelman, volume II of the *Councils of England*.

[He shall be expelled from the monastery.] Richard of St. Angel understands this to mean that “he shall be placed in another, stricter monastery, so that he may not derive any advantage from his wickedness.”

[But let the abbot consider that he must render an account to God for all his judgments.] Hildemar aptly observes here that whenever St. Benedict speaks of a judgment to be given by the abbot, he places a bridle upon the abbot by reminding him of God’s judgments.

858 [Lest the flame of envy or zeal, etc.] Although zeal and envy signify one and the same thing, as the commentators note here, Hildemar nevertheless observes that zeal concerns past evil, while envy concerns what is future—as though St. Benedict were saying: “Let him not expel him from the monastery because he sees that he is good, or that he will become good.”

## CHAPTER LXVI. Concerning the Porters of the Monastery

[Col. 0899]

[Col. 0899C] At the gate of the monastery let a wise old man be appointed, who knows how to receive an answer and to give one, and whose maturity does not allow him to wander about [Note: [Col. 0899D] Oxford, *vagare*]. The porter ought to have a cell beside the gate, so that those who come may always find him present and receive an answer. And as soon as anyone knocks, or a poor man cries out, let him answer, “Thanks be to God,” or let him give a blessing [Note: [Col. 0899D] Florentine, Conc., and two manuscripts: *benedic*, “bless”], and with all the gentleness of the fear of God let him give an answer promptly, with the fervor of charity. If the porter needs assistance, let him take a younger brother.

The monastery, moreover, if it can be done, ought to be arranged in such a way that all necessities—that is, water, a mill, a garden, a bakery [Note: [Col. 0900D] The bakery is absent from the Cassinese and Florentine manuscripts], or various crafts—are carried on within the monastery, so that the monks have no need to wander outside, since this is wholly disadvantageous to their souls. We have often wished this Rule to be read in the congregation, so that none of the brothers might excuse himself on the ground of ignorance.

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0899]

[Col. 0899D] Since the porters of the monastery are, as it were, the guardians of the congregation, in former times this office was entrusted only to especially distinguished and worthy men. Thus St. Benedict, after treating of the appointment of the abbot and of the provost of the monastery, next discusses the porters, as the most worthy after those officials.

Indeed, in the monastery of the Thebaid belonging to the great Isidore there was a priest serving as gatekeeper, according to Palladius (*Lausiac History*, chapter 71); or, as Rufinus puts it (*Book II of the Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17), a serious older man, chosen from among the foremost. St. Willibald, during the ten years in which he lived as a monk in the monastery of Cassino, is said in his Life, no. 25 (Third Century of Benedict, part II), to have been appointed in his first year as chamberlain of the church, in his second as dean, and for the remaining eight years as porter. St. Veremundus, abbot of Irache, had previously been the gatekeeper of his monastery, as we read in his Life, no. 8 (Bollandists, 8 March). In the monastery of St. Theodoric near Rheims, Eilbert, who later became abbot of Marcilly, served as porter, as Everhelm testifies in the Life of St. Poppo, no. 13 (Bollandists, 25 January). At Tegernsee, Fromundus, the porter of St. Quirinus, appears to have been one of the more distinguished monks of his monastery, as may be inferred from the letter he wrote to Theodulus, bishop (*Analecta*, volume IV), in which he excuses himself for having been unable to attend the synod on account of his office. The same may be said of Ingelbaud, porter at Vendôme (*Miscellanea* of Baluze, volume II), who was sent with Prior Frotmund to Pope Urban II on behalf of his monastery. But, leaving these matters aside, let us come to the text of the Rule.

[At the gate of the monastery.] From the first word of this chapter Haeften (*Book III, treatise 7, disputation 5*) infers that, according to the mind of the holy legislator, not several gates but only one gate should be established in the monastery. The emperor Justinian likewise decreed this in Novel 133: “And first of all, a monastery should not have many entrances, but only one, or perhaps two.”

[Let an old and wise man be appointed.] “It should be noted,” says Smaragdus, “that he did not say: ‘Let an old man in years be appointed at the gate’; rather, he says: ‘Let an old man wise in character be appointed.’ From this it is understood that what is sought in a porter is not bodily age, but wisdom and understanding.”

John Craesbeeck follows Smaragdus, as do the Cassinese commentators (*Cassinese Declarations*, chapter 66), who explain this chapter by declaring that the porter should be appointed not so much for his age as for his character. Yet both the common opinion of the commentators and the ancient practice of the early monks oppose this view. For although in the divine Scriptures “old man” means the same as “wise,” as Hildemar notes here from St. Ambrose and St. Gregory, “nevertheless,” the same author adds, “St. Benedict wishes him to possess two things in this passage: old age by years, and wisdom by life. For why he wishes both is made clear below when he says: ‘That he may know how to receive an answer and give one, whose maturity does not allow him to wander.’ When he says ‘that he may know how to receive and give an answer,’ this pertains to wisdom; when he says ‘whose maturity,’ it pertains to age.”

Bernard of Cassino agrees with Hildemar in these words:

“In this text St. Benedict says three things: that he should be old, wise, and mature. Old in conduct, wise, affable, and discerning; mature, stable and firm . . . . . If this old man in years possessed the following two conditions, he ought to be porter. But if such an aged man cannot be found, let there at least be one who is wise and mature. For wisdom is indicated by what the text says: ‘who knows how to receive an answer and give one’; maturity by: ‘whose maturity does not allow him to wander outside.’”

Boherius copies Bernard in his first commentary. The same opinion is held by Nicholas of Fractura, John of Turrecremata, Matthias Lambert, Hugh Menard, Benedict Haeften, and Nicholas Bravi. All doubt is removed by what St. Benedict subsequently adds: “If the porter needs assistance, let him take a younger brother.” Although younger in age, this brother must unquestionably be older in character; otherwise he would not be appointed at the gate.

This opinion is confirmed by the practice of the ancient monks, who appointed men old not only in character but also in age at the gate, as is clear from the Rufinus cited above and from the Rule of the Master, which commands (chapter 95) that “a cell within the gates of the monastery should be established near the entrance for two brothers decrepit with age, who are assigned there to close the monastery at every hour after those who have gone out, to open it for those entering, and to announce those who arrive to the abbot.”

The *Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins* says (chapter 3): “The female porters or gatekeepers of the monastery should be such as to build up the reward of all alike: women of old age, to whom the world is silent, who no longer desire anything from the spectacles of the present.”

And Justinian’s Novel 133 says: “Let men of grave and chaste age, and also approved by the testimony of all, stand at the gates.”

Gerard the Belgian, a monk, explains why old men should be appointed at the gate in these words:

“It is useful: first, for strengthening the holy humility of the aged in perfection, when an old man is commonly considered worthless and useless in every other respect; second, for edification, since all who come to the gate and courtyards of the house of God observe the holiness of the place and its inhabitants; third, from necessity, because at every entrance there must be a circumspect and vigilant man on watch, who excludes all worldly rumor from the monastery and drives all curiosity away from the gate.”

But this holy and praiseworthy custom has now almost become obsolete among monks. You will scarcely find a single monastery in which not merely a wise old man, but even a monk, is appointed porter. Indeed, it is considered a great thing if this office is entrusted to a lay brother, or, as they call him, a convert. When this practice ceased, I have no idea.

Certainly the Cistercians once reproached the Cluniacs for having departed in this respect from the prescription of the Rule. Peter the Venerable, writing to St. Bernard, replied as follows (*Book I, letter 28):

“Why should we place a porter at the gate, when we do not even have a gate? Our gates are not closed during the day; rather, they remain constantly open and offer entrance to those who arrive, without distinction of persons. Nor is it necessary for anyone to knock, nor for anyone to cry out, since whoever comes finds not only the entrance through the walls but also the entrance to the guesthouse open, and, lying down immediately, finds everything prepared. But lest the brothers be forced to remain outside their own houses, we arrange for a wise and respectable servant to remain and sleep nearby, who at midday, or at those hours when all the monastery doors are customarily closed, responds to those who knock or cry out—not merely by the sound of his voice, but by offering service.”

This is an entirely singular example, and I very much doubt that a similar one can be found. The arrangement was quite different in the monastery situated beside the Jordan. For there, as Sophronius testifies in the Life of St. Mary of Egypt, chapter 5 (*Book I of the Lives of the Fathers*), “the gate was never opened, but was always closed, and the monks completed their course without any disturbance. For it was not permitted to open it at any time, unless perhaps a monk came because of some necessary task.”

861 The same custom seems to have prevailed in the monastery of Abbot Isidore in the Thebaid (Palladius, *Lausiac History*, chapter 72), where “there was a priest as gatekeeper, who allowed no one to go out and no one else to enter, except someone who wished to remain there until death, proceeding nowhere.”

The Cistercians themselves, to whom the aforementioned Peter the Venerable was replying, decreed the following in their general chapter of 1217 (*Book of Institutions*, distinction 7, chapter 10):

“At the doors of the cloister in the larger congregations, two monks, or one monk and one lay brother, shall sit in turn. They shall diligently and courteously endeavor to deter secular persons who wish to enter the cloister, reciting the canonical hours there. They may also speak with those whom they deter from entering the cloister, and so forth. In the smaller congregations, one person of mature character shall be appointed for this purpose, and shall suffice.”

[Who knows how to receive an answer and give one.] “To receive an answer,” says Menard, “is to understand the intention of the person arriving, having inquired of him what he wants.”

[Whose maturity does not allow him to wander.] The *Rule of a Certain Author for Virgins* adds (chapter 3): “They should in no way lend an ear to stories which they hear at the gate either from secular persons or from anyone else; and if they have unwillingly heard or understood them, they should in no way repeat them to their companions.”

[The porter ought to have a cell beside the gate, so that those who come may always find him present.] Thus, according to the mind of St. Benedict, the gatekeeper should never at any time withdraw from the entrance.
