The Rule of the Master, however, prescribes (chapter 95) that “at the hours when it is necessary to read in the monastery, the gates being barred, they should join the congregation so as to hear the readers; and when the bell of the oratory sounds for the divine office, the gates being again barred, they should present themselves at the oratory for the work of God.” This is certainly an excellent institution, so that no one is permitted to be absent from his office.

[So that they may receive an answer.] He did not say “who opens the monastery gates.” For the entrance of the monastery ought not to be open to everyone who comes, and the door should not be opened until an answer has been received from the abbot. At least this was formerly “the custom of the Cassinese monastery: that the arrival of guests from wherever they came should be announced to the abbot, or to his representative, before they entered,” as Nicholas of Fractura writes.

The Cistercian *Book of Usages* likewise prescribes (chapter 120):

“If someone from the neighboring area or someone known comes to the gate, after learning what he wants, let the porter make him wait outside the gate until he learns from the abbot what is to be done with him. But if he is someone whom it would be improper either to announce or to keep there, let him enter and go wherever he wishes.”

Related to this is what I read in the Life of St. Alexander, abbot of the *acoemetae* (Bollandists, 15 January). When he came to the monastery of his brother Peter, “taking one brother with him, he knocked at the door. The porter, however, said: ‘Wait here a little; let me first report to the provost, and then you may enter.’”

There was a small window in the door through which the porter looked at and spoke with those arriving, as is clear both from the Life of St. Agilus, abbot of Rebais, chapter 20 (Second Century of Benedict):

“He heard at the gate of the monastery the thin voice of a man, as though lamenting; and when he opened the window attached to the gate, he saw a poor man lying before the doors, covered with sores.”

The same is clear from the Life of St. Eudocia, no. 29 (Bollandists, 1 March), where a certain Philostratus, “having advanced in the guise of a monk to the closed doors of that convent, knocked at the entrance. A girl serving as gatekeeper, one of the virgins of the place, appeared. She opened the little window of the door only slightly, through a narrow slit barely sufficient for the passage of the voice, and, turning her face away, briefly asked who he was and what he wanted when he knocked at the door. He replied in the customary formula of the monks: ‘I am a sinner, asking for a share in your prayers and for a blessing.’”

[And as soon as anyone knocks, or a poor man cries out, let him answer, “Thanks be to God,” or let him give a blessing.] The commentators unanimously hold that St. Benedict here designates two classes of people, namely, the rich and the poor: the poor man cries out, while the rich man knocks, as Hildemar puts it.

Accordingly, he assigns two responses: the poor man is to be told “Thanks be to God,” while the rich man is to be given a blessing—*benedic*, “bless,” in the imperative, as Hildemar explains—or “May your fatherhood bless me,” as Turrecremata understands it. Turrecremata says that this request for a blessing should be made only to ecclesiastical persons possessing some authority; to secular persons, or to ecclesiastical persons without such authority, one should reply, “Thanks be to God.”

Smaragdus, Hildemar, and others, however, understand the passage differently, asserting with one voice that “Thanks be to God” applies to the poor, and “let him bless” to the rich or powerful. Certainly it was customary among the ancient monks to request a blessing not only from ecclesiastics but especially from other monks.

The Cistercians used both expressions, “Thanks be to God” and “Bless.” The first was used after hearing the voice or signal of one knocking or crying out; the second when they approached him:

“When a guest knocks,” says the *Book of Usages* (chapter 120), “let the porter open the door after answering ‘Thanks be to God’; and after he has said ‘Bless,’ let him humbly ask who he is or what he wants.”

And below:

“If, while an hour is being celebrated in the church, a guest knocks at the gate, let him say, as usual, ‘Thanks be to God’ and ‘Bless.’”

The same was also the custom among the monks of Bursfeld.

The word “let him bless” could also be understood in another way: namely, that the porter bestows a blessing upon the person who arrives. For when the ancient monks came to stay at a monastery, they were accustomed, upon approaching from outside, to ask for a blessing by saying *benedic*, “bless,” or something similar, as is clear from the Life of St. Eudocia cited above and from the Rule of the Master, chapter 1.

The ancient French version by John of Précis favors this interpretation, rendering it *ou dogne beneisson* (“or that he give a blessing”), as does another, more recent version: *ou qu’il donne quelque parole de bénédiction* (“or that he give some word of blessing”). Nevertheless, the former interpretation, which belongs to nearly all the commentators, is preferable: it is more consonant with monastic humility and more in keeping with St. Benedict’s intention. For in chapter 53 he wishes a blessing to be requested from the arriving guest. Accordingly, St. Benedict of Aniane, in his *Concordia of the Rules*, reads *benedic* (“bless”) instead of *benedicat* (“let him bless”).

[Col. 0904B] Another ancient French version gives a different sense of this word, as though the gatekeeper were offering some prayer to God. It translates it *ou benere Dieu* (“or bless God”). Guido Juvenalis likewise has *ou bénisse*, “or let him bless,” as though saying, “Let us bless the Lord.” Another more recent French version has the same.

Boherius interprets it differently again:

“Here *to bless* is used for ‘to say good words,’ so that he may say to the person knocking: ‘You are welcome’; or: ‘Blessed be God who sent you here.’”

As for the expression “Thanks be to God,” Christians formerly used it in greetings and encounters, as our Menard observes from St. Augustine on Psalm 132 and from Optatus of Milevis, Book II *Against Parmenianus*. Haeften also teaches that it was customary among the ancient monks (*Book III, treatise 4, disputation 7*).

Boherius writes in his second commentary on this passage:

“This greeting is always in the mouths of the brothers, as I myself have seen in the monasteries of our Father Benedict—namely, Cassino, Subiaco, and the Sacred Cave. It is perhaps a response to ‘Bless,’ concerning which we read above in the section on the order of the congregation.”

[Col. 0904C] [And with all the gentleness of the fear of God let him give an answer promptly, with the fervor of charity.] The Eastern Rule says similarly (chapter 26):

“Let it be the porter’s care to receive all who arrive within the gates, giving them a courteous answer with humility and reverence, and immediately announcing either to the abbot or to the seniors who has come and what he has requested; and let him allow no outsider to suffer injury.”

St. Benedict does not explain the other duties of the gatekeeper; therefore they must be supplied from elsewhere.

The first duty was care of the guests, including the preparation of food for them, as Hildemar teaches in his commentary on this passage:

“In ancient times those who worked in the abbot’s kitchen were also the porters, because then there was not a multitude of guests coming to the monastery; and therefore they were able to do this.”

The abbot’s kitchen and the guests’ kitchen were the same, according to the Rule. St. Isidore states the matter more clearly (chapter 19): “The care of guests and the guardianship of the outer cloisters belonged to the gatekeeper.”

[Col. 0904D] The second duty was the distribution of alms, as can be seen in the Cistercian *Book of Usages* (chapter 120):

“The porter ought to have loaves in his cell for distribution to passersby.”

And below:

“The porter usually eats with the servants, while one of them meanwhile guards the gate and gives alms to passersby. He also usually takes his vessels to the kitchen to collect the remnants of food, and receives in them the food of the deceased and whatever else the cellarer gives him. After rising from the meal, he ought to distribute it to the poor at the gate. He must not neglect this distribution on account of the subsequent divine office; rather, using few and measured words, he should quickly complete what he has begun.”

The Bursfeld ceremonial likewise says (distinction 2, chapter 11):

“It belongs to the porter’s office to distribute alms to beggars. Therefore he ought to collect the remnants from the meals of the brothers, the guests, and the kitchen, and distribute them to those who ask.”

[Col. 0905A] Hence Hildemar also says in his commentary on this passage: If there is a poor man, “he signals to him that he should go to the hospice.” This hospice had been built near the monastery for the reception of the poor.

Moreover, the Rule of the Master entrusts the care of animals to the porters:

“They shall begin receiving the allowance for the dogs from the cellarer, and provide them with it together with water or the broth remaining from the kitchen. They shall attend to the animals within the monastery, with the assistance of the weekly servers, and shall keep the gates clean.”

Finally, in the monastery of Rebais under Abbot Agilus (Second Century of Benedict), “the custom was that when the signal was sounded for Compline, the porter immediately secured the monastery doors and brought the keys to him.”

[If the porter needs assistance, let him take a younger brother.] Richard of St. Angel writes concerning this passage:

“From this it is clear that the porter ought to be a monk, although the contrary is observed in some monasteries—and wrongly, because our way of life ought to be private and removed from the activities of laymen.”

The duty of this younger brother was to announce arrivals to the abbot, while the wise old man remained with the guest and received the answers of those who arrived. It would be harsh for the old man always to run about; on account of his edification and wisdom, it would be more fitting for him to remain at the gate, so that he might sit with the guest, if the guest’s status required it.

[The monastery, if it can be done, ought to be constructed in such a way that there is water.] That is, a spring, well, or cistern.

[A mill.] For grinding wheat.

[A garden.] Concerning this, the Rule of St. Isidore also says (chapter 1):

“Let a little garden be enclosed within the monastery, so that while the monks work inside, they may not wander outside on any pretext.”

And below (chapter 6):

“Let them cultivate vegetable gardens and preparations for food with their own hands.”

Nevertheless, one person was specially appointed for this work. Concerning him the same Rule says (chapter 19):

“It will belong to the gardener to fortify and guard the gardens, to care for the beehives, to attend to different kinds of seeds, and to announce what ought to be sown or planted in the gardens, and when.”

St. Adalard performed this office commendably in the monastery of Corbie, as Paschasius testifies; Lantredus did so at Laon, according to the Life of St. Salaberga; and Condelucus at Redon, according to the book on the Deeds of the Saints of Redon. See also Udalricus, Book III, chapter 20.

[*Pistrinum* (the baking-place).] Concerning this Hildemar writes:

“*Pistrinum* is almost *pilitrinum*, because formerly they pounded grain with a pestle. Hence in ancient times they were called not millers but bakers, as though *pinsors*, from pounding (*pinsare*) grains of wheat. For the use of the mill did not yet exist; rather, they broke the grain with a pestle. Hence Virgil wrote:

‘Now roast the grain in flame; now crush it with a stone.’

Here he seems to distinguish the bakery from the mill.”

Indeed, “in ancient times the mill itself was called *pistrinum*, because grain was not ground but pounded,” says Paulus Augustine of Genoa, who also writes that *pistrinum* is found in no Cassinese manuscript.

Moreover, St. Isidore distinguishes the baking craft from the preparation of dough and bread in his Rule (chapter 19). He assigns the former to laymen and the latter to the brothers:

“The baking craft shall belong to laymen; they shall clean the wheat and, according to custom, grind it. The monks shall prepare the dough, and make their own bread with their own hands. As for the guests and the sick, the laymen shall make their bread.”

From this someone might perhaps suspect that *pistrinum* was added to the Rule, especially since it is absent from the Cassinese manuscripts. Nevertheless, it is present in the very old Oxford manuscript, in the text of Hildemar, in that of Smaragdus of Fleury, in the *Concordia* of Benedict of Aniane, and in all our manuscripts.

Whatever the case may be, both tasks were certainly customary among our monks: they both ground or pounded the grain and mixed the flour themselves, as is clear from what was said above concerning chapter 48, and also from the German manuscripts of the *Customaries*, in which I read:

“The brothers sometimes all enter the bakery and prepare and knead the dough with their own hands for making bread.”

Indeed, they performed the baker’s office weekly, as we saw above in chapter 46; this is also clear from the Life of St. Stephen, abbot of Obazine, Book II, no. 54. Ordinarily, however, the task was entrusted to one person, an office which St. William, founder and monk of Gellone, performed there with the greatest humility.

[Or let various crafts be carried on within the monastery.] Such was the monastery of Fulda under Abbot Sturm, according to Abbot Eigil in his Life, no. 20; such was Flavigny under St. Geremar, according to his Life, no. 25; such was Solignac, according to the Life of St. Audoin in the Life of St. Eligius; such was Lescy, according to the Life of St. Hiltrude, no. 3; such was Centula, according to Hariulf’s Chronicle, Book II, chapter 7; such was Talipiacum, according to the Deeds of St. Aldric, no. 28; such was St. Gall, according to its ancient description; and finally such was the monastery of St. Benignus at Dijon, according to its Chronicle.

The council held at Mainz under Charlemagne likewise wished monasteries to be constructed in this way, renewing St. Benedict’s precept in these words (canon 20):

“It is fitting and necessary that the envoys sent to the various places, together with the bishop of each diocese, inspect the locations of monasteries of canons, monks, and likewise women, to see whether they have been placed in a suitable and appropriate location where the necessary resources can be obtained for the usefulness of the monastery, as is said in the Holy Rule: ‘The monastery ought to be arranged in such a way that all necessities are carried on within the monastery, so that the monks or clerics have no need to wander outside, since this is wholly disadvantageous to their souls.’”

The Rule of the Master also supports this (chapter 95):

“All necessities ought to be inside, within the gates: namely, the oven, the mill, the cooling place, the garden, and all necessities, so that there may not be frequent occasion for the brothers to go outside, mingle with secular people, and perhaps be seen by the eyes of the religious. To our condemnation, they might then worship us as angels and undeservedly say, ‘Bless us.’”

This was also the practice of the ancient monks, as may be seen in Rufinus, who speaks as follows of the monastery of Abbot Isidore (Book II of the *Lives of the Fathers*, chapter 17):

“We also saw in the Thebaid the very famous monastery of Isidore, surrounded by vast spaces and enclosed by a wall, in which spacious dwellings were provided for the men who lived there. Within were several wells, irrigated gardens, orchards of every kind of fruit tree, and everything necessary for use, provided sufficiently—indeed, abundantly—so that none of the monks living inside would ever have any need to go outside to seek anything.”

St. Benedict, however, does not require all these things absolutely, but conditionally: “if it can be done.” Hildemar explains his meaning in this way (*History of the Gallican Order of St. Benedict*, Book III, chapter 28): if only some of the things mentioned are lacking, the monastery should nevertheless be built. Thus St. Berta built a monastery in the territory of Rheims with everything St. Benedict commanded except a mill, because water was lacking. But if all the things mentioned are lacking, the monastery should not be built.

When someone considers building a monastery, Hildemar says that four matters must be provided for. First, the place where it is built must not be subject to interference from kings, princes, bishops, or other nobles; it should therefore be distant from such a court.

We have an outstanding example of this in the Life of St. Frodobert, abbot of Celle (Second Century of Benedict). Although many nobles of the region were most intimately attached to his holiness, “he nevertheless considered it improper to request from any of them a portion of land or property. He was concerned not only for himself but also for those who would come after him, lest the religious brotherhood which he was beginning to gather in the holy habit should suffer any disturbance or trouble from a secular person on account of the place of its habitation.”

[Col. 0907A] Second, that the monastery be situated far from those places “where women, or clerics, or laymen come to perform some duty”—that is, places where crowds of people gather out of devotion or on pilgrimage, since the monks’ peace is thereby considerably disturbed. Hence, indeed, we sometimes read of miracles of the saints—if it is permissible to speak so—as having become hateful to our predecessors, because they attracted crowds of people to their churches. Thus Gaufredus writes of the monks of Sarlat in Book I of his *Chronicle*, namely that “the body of Saint Pardulf, by inviting crowds of people there through the signs of many miracles, was then causing disgust to the religious monks who lived there.”

Yet what we read concerning Saint Hidulf in the *Chronicle of Senones* seems worthy of the highest admiration. In his church, while divine power was performing frequent miracles through the merits of Saint Spinulus, “Saint Hidulf could not bear the annoyance of the disturbance he suffered from those who came, although it seemed that some profit was being brought to his monastery by that people, on account of the saint’s miracles and the income from the saltworks. The blessed man Hidulf, who had not taken upon himself the burden of poverty in order to acquire the riches of the world, seeing that he and his monks were being led considerably astray from their purpose by the influx of people, thought it necessary to seek divine assistance in the matter. At length he reached the church of Blessed Gregory, supporting his limbs with a staff, for he was already greatly weakened by vigils, prayers, and fasts. Conceiving in his heart the distress caused by the crowds pressing upon him, when he had arrived at the tomb of his beloved Spinulus, he devoted himself to prayer; and, as though he were speaking to a living man, he said:

‘We give thanks to God our Savior, brother Spinulus, because, since the miracles that attest the faith make us most certainly believe that you stand before the divine Majesty, we rejoice that you have also escaped the shipwrecks of the present age and possess heavenly glory. But if we should for some time be oppressed by the crowds of people whom God has caused to flow here through you, you will see that we are deviating not a little from the royal road that leads to life. Therefore, by that obedience which, while you lived, you were accustomed to offer us without weariness, we admonish and exhort you in the Lord to intercede for us with God, who is abundant and the giver of all good things, so that, once the disturbance of the nations has been restrained and the waves of the present life removed, we may be permitted to traverse the course of the heavenly life with unimpeded step.’”

The chronicler adds: “You would have seen the dead man obeying his master’s command as though he were alive, when the signs of the miracles had ceased, and so forth.”

I have wished to report this example at greater length for the edification of morals. Bertrand, in his three-part book of the miracles of Saint Robert, division 2, no. 8, reports similar complaints by the monks of La Chaise-Dieu against Saint Robert. For when the saint shone with many signs, through which the divine offices were being disrupted, “the elders and those more fervent in spirit are said to have approached the blessed man’s tomb and addressed him in words such as these:

‘These deserts, lord, father of the wilderness, we desired under your leadership; and we entered them joyfully so that we might obtain forgiveness of sins and the grace of the Redeemer. But the abundance of the present miracles has brought upon us such a lack of divine offices that we are unable either to mourn our sins or to render divine praises suitably. Therefore, may your merits obtain for us that, once these importunities have been put to sleep for a time, we may serve Christ the Lord in tranquility, so that in the future we may be able to find forgiveness of our sins.’

Accordingly, in the meantime it was decreed that no sick person should approach the tomb, since from then on neither would its doors be opened to him nor would services be rendered.”

Add to this what Fremonus relates about the monks of Grandmont: “Peter, the second abbot of Grandmont, when he saw crowds rushing competitively to the tomb of Saint Stephen, inflamed by a certain holy zeal, is said to have reproached the saint—in words nevertheless full of reverence—that, although he had commanded them to keep quiet, he himself should go troubled. Finally, he asked—or rather, with a certain simple innocence, obtained—that the saint cease performing miracles; otherwise, he would dig up his bones and throw them into the water. [Col. 0908A] The saint obeyed his successor’s command and, so long as Peter lived, performed no further miracle. Later, Peter IV, the prior, hearing that many miracles were taking place elsewhere through the invocation of Saint Stephen, feared that they would again draw a crowd to the church of Grandmont. He secretly removed the saint’s bones from the tomb and hid them in the cloister, as though he believed that prayers not directed to the relics themselves would be less readily heard.”

Something similar is related about Saint Bernard and certain other saints.

Third, the monastery should be built in a place where there is water, woodland, and the other things which Saint Benedict enumerates here—things rarely found in cities, where monasteries are consequently more difficult to establish. Indeed, Saint Benedict is never read to have built monasteries in cities (*Dialogues*, Book II). Saint Gregory the pope writes that he built twelve in the solitude of Subiaco, one on Mount Cassino, and another near the city of Terracina, but none within the walls of any city. When Saint Maurus went to Gaul, he is said to have told Florus, who wished to build a monastery for him (*Life of Saint Maurus*, first century): “The observance of our order demands the utmost quiet and security.”

Similarly, when Ansoald, bishop of Poitiers, “wished to keep Saint Philibert with him in the city,” while Saint Philibert always desired the solitude of the wilderness, “by the Lord’s generosity he established a monastery on the island of Herio in the sea” (*Life of Saint Philibert*, second century). This was generally the practice of our predecessors, who are scarcely ever recorded to have established a monastery in a city. The Cistercians especially seem to have avoided this more than others, for I find the following in their ancient Institutes (chapter 1): “No monasteries of ours are to be built in cities, castles, or villages, but in places removed from human habitation.” They renew the same statute in the *Institutions*, where they add (division 1, chapter 1): “All the churches of our order are to be founded and dedicated in honor of Blessed Mary.”

Fourth, whoever founds a new monastery must endow it with sufficient income for the food and clothing of the monks who live there. For from their lack of resources there commonly arises among the brothers an occasion for murmuring and for wandering outside. Saint Maurus seems to have had this in mind when, by the authority both of himself and of his congregation, he fixed the number of monks in his monastery at Angers at one hundred and forty—a number which it was not permitted either to reduce or to exceed, “because,” says Faustus, “the resources which had already been assigned there were sufficient for so many brothers in the necessities of life; and if the number were larger, it might perhaps give rise to the experience of need.”

Therefore the Cistercians also require in the Book of the Institutes (chapter 12) “that twelve monks, with an abbot as the thirteenth, be sent to new monasteries; yet they are not to be assigned there until the place has been furnished with books, buildings, and other necessities: specifically, with the Missal, Epistolary, Text, Rule, Book of Usages, Psalter, Hymnal, Collectary, Antiphonary, Lectionary, and Gradual; with the buildings, namely the oratory, refectory, guesthouse, and porter’s lodge; and also with temporal necessities, so that they may immediately be able both to live there and to observe the Rule.” They repeat the same provision in the Book of the *Institutions*, division 1, chapter 6. The Carthusians likewise decree the same in the new *Collection of Statutes*, part II, chapter 21, no. 3.

Yet just as care must be taken that a monastery being founded does not lack necessities, so provision must also be made that it does not abound in superfluities. Excellent in this regard are the admonitions which the distinguished abbots Saint Adalard and his brother, the Venerable Wala, gave to their Corbie monks in Saxony when the monastery was first being established (*Book I of the Life of Wala*, chapter 18, fourth century). Paschasius writes:

“They earnestly admonished them in three matters: that they should not rejoice in becoming greatly enriched in possessions, nor desire riches so as to set their hearts upon them; that they should flee delicacies and pleasures as though they were poisons; and, finally, that they should not take delight in honors and the pomp of pride, as though these were granted for the sake of religion, [Col. 0909A] lest perhaps they should be altogether hidden and perish in vain, as we see that many churches formerly well founded in Gaul have perished.”

And below, in chapter 19:

“They admonished us—both us, the Corbie monks of France, and them, the Corbie monks of Saxony—not to accept unnecessary possessions, nor to strive to possess ample resources as though for the sake of God’s religion; but to impose a limit upon the possessions and property of the church, lest they should extend a finger beyond it, as the prophet warns, or join field to field without end through covetousness.”

Moreover, the emperor Justinian decreed (Novella 5):

“Whenever and wherever anyone wishes to build a venerable monastery, he is not to be permitted to do so until he has summoned the bishop of the place, beloved of God. Let the bishop stretch out his hands toward heaven and consecrate the place to God through prayer, fixing there the sign of our salvation—that is, the cross, which is to be adored and truly honored—and thus let him begin the building, laying here a certain good and fitting foundation. Let this, therefore, be the beginning of the pious construction of venerable monasteries.”

In these words two things may be noted: first, that no monastery is to be built without the bishop’s permission; second, that before construction begins, a cross must be placed in the spot where the building is to be erected, especially where the altar is to be located.

Examples of both practices may be found throughout the *Acts of the Saints* (second century). The first appears in the *Life of Saint Humbert the Confessor*, who founded the monastery of Maroilles “after obtaining the permission of the bishop of Cambrai”; and in the *Life of Saint Aicadri*, who is said to have done the same in the diocese of Poitiers with the permission of Bishop Ansoald, since he “was fully instructed and was not ignorant even of the canons: for he had read that no one might build a church or erect an altar in another’s diocese without the permission of his own bishop”; and in the *Life of Rabanus* (fourth century, part II), “who built churches, with the permission of his bishop, both in the cells of the brothers entrusted to him and in many other places belonging to him where previously there had been none; and, gathering holy relics from every quarter, had them consecrated in their name and honor.” See the *Life of Saint Theuderius*, abbot of Vienne, no. 7, first century, p. 680.

Examples of the second practice are found in the ancient *Apophthegmata of the Fathers* (*Greek Ecclesiastical Monuments*, vol. I), where Saint Antony, having found a place for building a monastery, said: “Let us pray, and let us set up a cross here, so that those who wish to build may build in that place”; in the *Life of Saint Botulf*, abbot, where the anonymous author, speaking of the construction of the monastery of Icanho by him, says: “In Christ’s cross the sign of heavenly power is fixed beforehand, and the dwelling of divine inhabitation is built”; and in the *History of the Translation of Saint Vitus to Corbie*, no. 11, concerning the construction of Saxon Corbie (fourth century, part I):

“Therefore, in the year 822 of the Lord’s Incarnation, on the eighth day before the Ides of August, in the eleventh year of the reign of Louis, the most serene Augustus, they came to the place mentioned. Having surveyed it on every side and gone around it in all directions, they prostrated themselves in prayer and chanted the psalms belonging to this office. After completing the litany and prayer, they stretched out a line, drove in pegs, and began to measure first the church, and then the dwelling places of the brothers. . . . First they asked the bishop to come, sanctify the place, and set up the banner of the holy cross at the site of the altar, and they gave the place the name Corbie.”

In the *Life of Saint Stephen*, abbot of Obazine, Book II, no. 9 (*Miscellany of Baluze*, vol. IV), he is said to have acted as follows: “Whenever he was about to build a place, he took a cross and blessed water and went there with a few brothers. Having measured the ground according to what the quality or size of the future building required, he fixed a cross where the altar was to be founded, and so forth.”

The cross itself was either placed by the bishop who had first been summoned, as in the *History of the Translation of Saint Vitus to Corbie*, or at least was first blessed by him, as we infer from the same *Life of Saint Stephen of Obazine*, Book I, no. 7. When two of his disciples had approached the bishop of Limoges, he “blessed and consecrated the cross which they had brought to him; and he handed it over to them together with water blessed by himself, granting them the authority to celebrate Mass and to build a monastery—but only on the condition that they follow in all things the custom handed down by the Fathers.”

We have related all these matters at length so that it might be evident with what religious devotion our predecessors proceeded in founding monasteries. In constructing not only monasteries but every kind of building, they would not lay the first stone until they had solemnly implored divine assistance. This may be seen especially in the aforementioned *Life of Saint Stephen of Obazine*, Book II, no. 18, where the following is said concerning the construction of a new basilica of the monastery of Obazine:

“On the following Friday, which falls before Palm Sunday, everyone proceeds devoutly from the monastery to the building site with a cross and blessed water. After the litanies and psalms pertaining to this rite have been recited, the first stone is placed in the foundation by the bishop, the abbot, and the chosen master of the work, with an invocation of the Trinity’s majesty, and so forth.”

As for the arrangement of the monastery itself, they were accustomed to observe that the church should be placed on the northern side and face east in its upper part, where the principal altar was customarily located; and west in its lower part, where the door was. The brothers’ dormitory, with the chapterhouse beneath it, was to be built toward the east. The guesthouse was to be toward the west, near the monastery door, so that guests would not be permitted to penetrate into the monastery’s inner places. To the south was the refectory; the kitchen was in the lower part of the refectory, as far as possible from the church and especially from the choir; and between all these stood the cloister.

The novices’ quarters and the infirmary were each separated from the regular areas, like a second monastery. At least, this is more or less what can be seen in the ancient plan of the monastery of Saint Gall. The Romans, however, placed the cloister toward the western side, as Candidus teaches in the *Life of the Venerable Eigil*, abbot of Fulda. See the *Life of Ansegisus*, abbot of Fontenelle, no. 9.

I add here one detail concerning the dormitory, from the deeds of Saint Aldric, bishop of Le Mans. In the monastery he had built, he “had a new and suitably arranged dormitory constructed; in that dormitory he magnificently built an apse on the eastern side, and in it he built and erected an altar. On the fourth day before the Ides of September, he solemnly consecrated the apse itself, together with the aforementioned altar and its relics, in honor of Saint Benedict, the eminent confessor.”

[871] So that the monks would not have to wander outside, since this is altogether harmful to their souls.] Rather, it is entirely destructive, as Peter Damian clearly demonstrates in these words (*Opusculum* 12, chapter 11):

“To mention only a few things from among many: a monk on a journey cannot keep the fast, because the kindness of his host does not permit it; he does not chant the psalms wisely, because the talkativeness of the company walking with him distracts him; he does not persist in the nightly vigils, because the privacy required for solitude is absent; he does not devote himself to bending his knees, because the labor of travel does not accord with the zeal of holy devotion; he is in no way restrained by the discipline of silence, because, when causes frequently arise, he is forced, even against his will, into many words; and so forth.”

See also chapters 12, 13, and 14 of the same *Opusculum*, and chapters 3 and 5 of *Opusculum* 27.

Peter of Blois also treats this argument admirably in Letter 134. Everyone knows the saying attributed to Saint Antony by Saint Athanasius in his *Life*, chapter 53, and by Sozomen in Book I of his *History*, chapter 13; Rufinus attributes it to the abbot Moses in Book III of the *Lives of the Fathers*, no. 109: “What water is to fish, the cloister is to monks.” Thus, just as a fish quickly dies outside water, so a monk very easily perishes outside the monastery. It is therefore not surprising that certain Fathers even refused to permit their monks to leave the cloister in order to console their parents.

On this subject we have an excellent testimony from Peter of Blois in the letter mentioned above:

“According to the teaching of Jerome: Be honorable in your house; be rarely seen in public. If one of your parents falls ill or dies, let neither their illness nor their death be an occasion for you to leave. Let the dead bury their dead. The affection of kinship is deceptive and treacherous. Carnal love will quickly seize you outside the love of God, and affection for the world, which had already withered within you, will revive to the ruin of your soul.”

We have already said much about this matter in chapter 4. To that material one may add what Saint Anselm wrote to the nun Mabilia (*Book III, Letter 127*):

“My daughter, why do you need to visit any of your relatives, since they in no way need your counsel and assistance, nor will you receive from them any counsel or assistance concerning your purpose and profession which you cannot find in your cloister? The purpose of your life is divided from their way of life. They will not become monks for your sake, nor will you return to secular life for theirs. . . . If they wish to see you, or in any way need your counsel or assistance, let them come to you. They are permitted to wander and travel through different places; you should not go to them, because you are not permitted to leave the cloister except in a necessity attested by God.”

[Col. 0911B] If, then, it is not fitting for monks to leave the cloister even on account of their parents, much less is it fitting on account of other works of piety. Hence the Rule of Saint Stephen of Grandmont (chapter 35) says:

“You must not leave your cells in order to provide for the poor. No one can provide for the poor better than Martha provided for God, namely by providing for God; yet Jesus Christ did not say to Mary, who was sitting at his feet: ‘Rise and help her.’”

And elsewhere:

“We command you not to leave the solitude in order to preach. For while you remain in the wilderness and guard yourselves from the world, you are a light upon a lampstand—that is, a good life shining upon the faithful people. For, as Blessed Gregory says (chapter 48): ‘The life of the just is a living sermon.’”

And finally (chapter 49):

“Moreover, we command you not to leave the wilderness in order to hear a sermon. For it is certain that John the Baptist remained in the wilderness while Jesus Christ preached on earth; yet the Gospel does not say that John left it in order to hear the Lord’s preaching.”

The same must be said of pilgrimages which some undertake out of devotion or penance. Thus Saint Bernard dissuaded a certain monk from the pilgrimage he had begun with the permission of his abbot and sent him back to his monastery (*Letter 319*):

“Judging more rightly,” he wrote to the monk’s abbot, “that however guilty a monk may be, he should perform penance in his own monastery rather than wander outside through the provinces. For the purpose of monks is to seek not an earthly but a heavenly Jerusalem; and this is achieved not by traveling with the feet, but by advancing in one’s affections.”

And Gaufredus, abbot of Vendôme (*Book IV, Letter 21*):

“Certainly the faith of the monastic profession cannot be preserved by going to Jerusalem; rather, it is violated. For just as going to Jerusalem is permitted to laymen, so it is forbidden to monks by the Apostolic See. I know this myself, as did the man whose ears were near the mouth of Pope Urban, when he both instructed laymen to make pilgrimage by going to Jerusalem and forbade that pilgrimage to monks, and so forth.”

On this matter there is a decree of the Council of York in 1195 (canon 13, in Spelman):

“The profession of religious holiness requires that monks, regular canons, and religious nuns be kept in religious and regular observance. Therefore, in order to remove from them the opportunity for wandering, we prohibit them from holding the revenues called obediences on lease, and from undertaking a journey of pilgrimage.”

Similarly, the Council of London in 1200 forbids monks “to leave the cloister under the pretext of pilgrimage.” See Saint Lanfranc’s Letter 57 and Saint Anselm’s Book III, Letter 130.

What is more, certain men did not even approve of monks going outside to administer the monastery’s temporal affairs. Certainly this seems to have been the mind of Pope Saint Gregory, as we infer from his letter to Peter, subdeacon of Sicily, in which he commands him to entrust the external administration of the monastery to Faustus. He writes (Book I, Letter 67):

“As befits our concern, just as monks must be removed from lawsuits in the secular courts so that they may devote themselves piously and diligently to the divine ministries, so it is necessary that, through our provision, we arrange how their affairs are to be managed, lest the disciplined mind be dissipated through the various cares of litigation and become weakened and sluggish for the celebration of its customary work.”

And below:

“For it is advantageous that the servants of God remain at peace, at the cost of a small inconvenience, away from the tumult of lawsuits, so that the interests of the cell may not perish through negligence and the minds of God’s servants may remain freer for the work of the Lord.”

This was also the mind of Saint Dunstan, who appointed his own brother Wulfinus “as a powerful overseer for him externally in the affairs of his estates, so that neither he himself nor anyone from the monastic profession might wander outside in an unsuitable pursuit of secular business.”

Indeed, there were monks who, in order to remove every opportunity for going about outside, refused to possess estates beyond the monasteries. This is clear concerning the Carthusians from the Statutes of Guigo, chapter 41; from the ancient Statutes, part II, chapter 19; and from the third compilation of the Statutes, chapter 3, no. 7; and concerning the monks of Grandmont from the Rule of Saint Stephen and from his Life, in Labbe, volume II of the *Bibliotheca nova*.

Finally, except in the cause of charity, they judged it altogether unbecoming for monks to go outside. Hence Saint Bernard, comparing monks to the teeth of the bride and assigning to them their particular properties (*Sermon 93 on Various Subjects*), says:

“It is unbecoming for them to appear, except perhaps occasionally for laughter; for nothing is more disgraceful than a monk running through cities and castles, unless he is compelled by that which covers a multitude of sins. For charity is laughter, because it is cheerful—joyful, indeed, but not dissolute.”

But even this must be done with great caution:

“For it commonly happens that one who, not content with his own affairs, goes forth to care for another’s salvation is compelled instead to suffer danger to his own; and when he stretches out his hand to another, as to one struggling amid stormy shipwrecks, the devouring wave itself engulfs him as well.”

See Saint John Climacus, Step 3.

Moreover, what we have said up to this point concerns abbots and other superiors no less than the brothers themselves. Hence Gregory IX, in his constitution for Benedictines, writes:

“Since abbots and priors ought not to run about or wander, we wish them to remain in the cloister with the brothers and to attend the divine offices with them, especially vigils, chapter, and collation, as well as the other divine offices, unless they are prevented by a necessary or honorable cause.”

And the *Rule of a Certain Person for Monks* (chapter 20) says: If an abbot “runs about from place to place in carriages and on horses, he is not only unworthy of authority over the brothers, but must also be judged a murderer of souls, and another must be appointed to govern his monastery. But if the monks cannot endure this, let them leave him, and let him be excommunicated.”

We wish this Rule to be read frequently in the congregation.] These words may be referred to what has just been said in this chapter, so that the monks may learn from them how great a danger it is to go outside; or they may refer to the entire Rule, as Bernard of Cassino understands them.

Certainly the more ancient Fathers of the monks decreed that their Rule should frequently be read in the assembly of the brothers. The Rule of Saint Augustine, according to chapter 24, and the Rule of Tarnat were read each week in the assembly. The Rules of Saint Aurelian and Saint Ferreolus were read once a month, namely on the Kalends. The Master orders his Rule to be read daily in the refectory. Likewise, the *Rule of a Certain Person for Virgins* (chapter 9) says: “Before the meal, one or more chapters of the Rule should always be read, if the abbess so wishes.”

Saint Benedict, however, assigned no definite time for reading the Rule, content merely to say that it should be read frequently in the assembly. Nevertheless, the ancient custom of our order prevailed that something from it should be recited every day, at least once in chapter. This may be seen in the Council of Aachen, canon 69; in the *Supplication of the Monks of Fulda*, no. 1; in the *Life of Saint Benedict of Aniane*; in the *Life of Saint Odo*; in the manuscript Customs of Germany; in the *History of the Translation of Saint Walaric*; and in Bernard of Cassino, who writes concerning this passage:

“It has become customary among us that one chapter of the Rule be read each day. Indeed, it ought to be carefully explained, in order to remove all gross ignorance. Novices, however, ought to repeat it so often in reading that they know the whole Rule perfectly by heart, just as they know the Psalter.”

Boherius likewise says:

“Among us it is customary for the Rule to be read daily in chapter, one chapter of it each day, except on the twelve-reading days and the vigils of festivals, when the Gospel with its homily is recited, as on the vigils of Easter, Pentecost, and similar feasts. The longer portions are nevertheless divided after the manner of longer psalms: the prologue of this Rule, chapters 2, 43, 48, 63, 64, and 65. The papal constitutions, however, ought to be read twice a year and once in the provincial chapter.”

When reading the Rule, the Cistercians divided the individual chapters in such a way that they went through it four times a year. The days on which its reading was to begin are explained in these verses:

[Col. 0913B]

“On the vigil of John the Baptist, you begin with the chapter of Benedict.

On the following day, on Andochius’ feast; finally, on the feast of the boys.”

When the feast of Blessed Benedict was transferred, the beginning of the Rule’s reading was transferred as well, according to the Book of the *Institutes*, division 6, chapter 1.

So that none of the brothers may excuse himself on grounds of ignorance.] From these final words of the chapter Bernard of Cassino rightly infers that the Rule must not merely be read but also explained; otherwise someone could excuse himself on the grounds that he did not know it. Indeed, there are certain passages in the text of the Rule which can bear various meanings and cannot easily be understood unless they are explained.

Hildemarus had already shed light on this matter for Bernard: “That reading is of no value unless its instruction is also supplied.” Hence the synod assembled at Aachen decrees (canon 70) “that the reading be handed on at chapter”—that is, explained. “Likewise at collation, if the time is suitable.”

Alcuin, writing to the brothers of the churches of Wiremuth and Jarrow, says (Letter 49):

“But you, who are fathers and shepherds of the holy congregation, teach with the greatest diligence and fraternal love the household entrusted to you for governance, and display every example of goodness in yourselves. Let the Rule of Saint Benedict also be frequently explained in the brothers’ assembly in the vernacular, so that it may be understood by everyone.”

Similarly Saint Dunstan (*Concord*, chapter 1):

“While they are seated, let the Rule be read; or, if it is a feast day, the Gospel of that day. After the reading, let the prior speak, as the Lord grants.”

And Udalricus, concerning the chapter held on Thursday of Holy Week (*Book I, chapter 12*):

“After the meaning of the Rule has been explained, at the command of the lord abbot the chamberlain rises, and so forth.”

Finally, John Trithemius (*Preface to the Book of the Region of the Cloister*) writes:

“As is customary in the Bursfeld observances—for we belong to that union and observance according to the Rule of Saint Benedict—I am compelled each day to explain to my brothers one paragraph from that Rule, which is customarily read to us in chapter three times a year. Concerning it, I must gather my thoughts and draw from the storehouses of the saints, so that, when speaking, I may have at hand something pleasing to my hearers.”

Add to these the constitutions of the supreme pontiffs. Gregory IX says:

“Because in many monasteries the Rule is understood by only a few when it is read, we order that the reading of the Rule which takes place in chapter be immediately explained in the vernacular, for the sake of the less learned, by the one presiding over the chapter himself or by someone whom he appoints.”

The same is stated by Clement V in his decretal and by Benedict XII in his constitution. Hence the Cistercians of the Reformed Congregation in Spain, in the general chapter of 1557, commissioned Louis de Estrada to write commentaries on the Rule of Saint Benedict, “which the abbots could use in private chapters to explain it,” as Angelus Manrique writes in his *Series of the Abbots of Palazuelos*.

Perhaps this is also how a passage of Bede in chapter 16 of the *Life of Saint Cuthbert* (second Benedictine century) should be understood: “Frequently discussing the Rule in the assembly of the brothers, and so forth.”

## CHAPTER LXVII. Concerning Brothers Sent on a Journey

[Col. 0913]

[Col. 0913C] When brothers are to be sent on a journey, let them commend themselves to the prayer of all the brothers or of the abbot [Note: Another reading: “to the prayers.”]; and at the final prayer of the Work of God, let a commemoration always be made of all who are absent.

When the brothers return from a journey, on the very day of their return, during all the canonical hours, while the Work of God is being completed, let them prostrate themselves on the floor of the oratory [Note: Oxford: “in a place of prayer”; Narbonne: “in the place of the oratory”] and ask the prayers of all, because of their faults [Note: Oxford: “lest anyone …”; Conques and Florence: “lest perhaps some things have stolen upon them”; Cassino: “lest something have stolen upon anyone …”], lest something harmful have perhaps stolen upon them during the journey—whether sight [Note: Lyra: *visu, aut auditu*, “by sight, or by hearing”], or hearing, of some evil thing, or idle speech [Note: Narbonne: *otiosus sermo* (“idle speech”), for *otiosi sermonis* (“of idle speech”)].

Let no one presume to report to another [Note: Hildemarus, *Compendium*, and Haeftenus: *alii* (“to another”); printed editions: *aliis* (“to others”), for *alio* (“to another”)] anything whatsoever he has seen or heard outside the monastery [Note: other readings: *monasterio* and *monasterii*], because this is a very great destruction [Note: Oxford: “discretion.”]. If anyone presumes to do so, let him undergo the regular punishment.

Likewise, whoever presumes to leave the monastery cloister [Note: Florence: *clausa*, “the closed places”], or to go anywhere, or to do anything, however small [Note: several manuscripts: *parum*, “a little”], without the abbot’s command [Note: Narbonne adds: “let him undergo the punishment”].

## COMMENTARY

[Col. 0913]

[Col. 0913D] Sending brothers on a journey.] Peter Boherius, in both of his commentaries, explains this passage perceptively; Haeftenus observes after him that Saint Benedict used the plural here for good reason, thereby at least tacitly indicating that monks should not proceed outside the monastery without a brother as companion.

That this was indeed the discipline of the ancient monks is clear from the Rule of Saint Antony, no. 12; the Third Rule of the Holy Fathers, chapter 8; that of Saint Macarius, chapter 22; Saint Pachomius, article 34; the Eastern Rule, chapter 22; Saint Basil, *Long Rules*, chapter 39; the Rule of an Unknown Author, chapter 3; Saint Augustine, chapter 12; the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 2; Saint Isidore, chapter 22; from the *Life of Saint Benedict*, passim; from the *Lives of Saint Samson*, Saint Eparchius, and Pope Saint Gregory by John the Deacon, Book I, chapter 11; and from the *Life of Saint Cuthbert*, chapter 11. Yet Cuthbert is said on one occasion to have gone out with a single boy as his companion, in chapter 12 of the same *Life*.

The Council of Aachen renewed this discipline in a special canon, decreeing “that no one be sent on a journey alone and without another brother.” Gregory IX likewise says the following in his constitution for Benedictine monks:

“We also strictly forbid that monks be given unrestricted freedom to wander, or that they grant cloistered monks permission to revisit secular affairs, except perhaps very rarely, for a reasonable cause, and for a short time, with a suitable companion assigned to them for their protection.”

Saint Gregory valued this custom of monks so highly (*Book X of the Register*, chapter 22) that he rejected the monk Constantine, whom the brothers had requested as abbot, because he was devoted to singularity and because “he presumed to travel alone, without any of his brothers, to the monastery situated in the province of Picenum. From this action of his,” he says, “we recognize that if he walks without a witness, he does not live rightly.”

The Constitutions of the Celestines prescribe (Treatise 1, chapter 12) that monks who go out without permission, or alone, are to be handed over to prison. The reasons for this institution may be found in Haeftenus, Book XI, treatise 4, question 1.

[Let all the brothers or the abbot commend themselves to prayer.] You find the same provision in the Rule of St. Isidore, chapter 22, and in that of the Master, chapter 66. Hildemar explains the rite in these words:

> “And this should be noted: if they are going on a long journey, such as to the king or to some distant place, then either the abbot or any others who are setting out will come to the chapter house, and there, in the presence of the brothers, the place to which they are going is made known. In that chapter house they first prostrate themselves before the brothers, commend themselves to their prayers, and kiss them all” [Note: Thus, when St. Maurus was sent into Gaul, St. Benedict is said to have given him the kiss, as recorded in the Life of St. Maurus, no. 29; and when St. Placid was departing for Sicily, likewise in his Life, no. 20.]. “Then they prostrate themselves in the oratory, and so depart. But if they are not going very far, let them merely ask for a blessing in the oratory,” and for the prayers of the brothers, “saying: ‘Pray for me, brothers,’” says Richard of St. Angelo.

According to both Smaragdus and Hildemar, and according to the Book of the Cistercian Usages, chapter 88, they were to perform this prostration before the altar if circumstances permitted; otherwise they were merely to bow: 877 although in the monasteries of France they always genuflected, with this distinction: on days when the prescriptions of the Church required kneeling, they also prostrated themselves; on other days they did not, as Hildemar testifies. According to the same author, those who prostrated themselves said:

> “Lord Jesus Christ, you know my frailty; help me on this journey, so that I may be able, through the prayers of the brothers, to complete this journey of my obedience without offense.”

You will find the prayers to be said over them in Smaragdus and Haeften; they occur frequently in the ancient books. Moreover, the Cistercians valued this rule concerning the requesting of a blessing so highly that, unless they were excused by evident necessity or by the usefulness of the order, they punished with a penance of bread and water those who did not ask for it when they were to return on the same day, as stated in the Booklet of Ancient Definitions, distinction 10, chapter 2.

Two points remain to be noted here concerning the text of the Rule. “Let all the brothers or the abbot commend themselves to prayer,” says St. Benedict.

1. The universal term “all” may have moved St. Stephen, abbot of Obazine, to commend himself, “when he was about to set out on a journey, after the general blessing of the brothers, also to the prayers of the lowest-ranking brothers.”

2. The particle *vel* (“or”), which Menard asserts is here copulative, must, according to Bernard of Cassino and Boherius, be understood disjunctively, on account of unforeseen and unexpected circumstances and pressing necessities that do not permit the community to assemble—for example, when one must depart at night while the brothers are still lying in bed, or during the day while they are working outside the monastery. In such a case St. Benedict wished the departing monk to receive only the abbot’s blessing. The practice can be seen in Book I of the Dialogues of Pope St. Gregory, chapter 2, where we read concerning Libertinus:

> “A matter had been arranged for the benefit of the monastery. After the morning hymns had been completed, Libertinus came to the abbot’s bed, and humbly asked for a prayer for himself.”

[Let the commemoration of all who are absent always be made at the final prayer of the Work of God.] Menard and Cointius understand “the final prayer of the Work of God” to mean the collect of Compline, not the final prayer of any canonical hour. Peter Boherius, on the contrary, explaining this passage in connection with the word “always,” says: “That is, at all the canonical hours.” This practice has prevailed not only among us but also among the Camaldolese and among the Cistercians, the most tenacious observers of the Rule according to its letter, as Julian of Paris testifies in his book *On the First Manner of Life of the Cistercians*, part III, chapter 4, § 1. The reason is that, just as the service of the absent benefits all who remain in the cloister, so it was fitting that the prayers of the whole congregation should also benefit the absent. St. Benedict does not explain what form that commemoration should take; hence diverse practices have prevailed everywhere. On this, see Haeften, book II, treatise 4, discussion 3, and Menard here.

[But when the brothers return from the journey, on the very day on which they return, etc.] From this passage commentators rightly infer that travelers must conduct all their business in such a way that, even if they return late in the day, they enter the monastery at least before Compline. Thus Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius in his first commentary. Hildemar’s words are these:

> “St. Benedict did not say ‘on the very night on which they return,’ but ‘on the very day,’ because St. Benedict’s intention was that the monk should arrive during the day, so that, at all the canonical hours preceding the hour at which he arrived, he might be able to wipe away his negligences. Hence, for this reason, it is the custom in our land—and it ought also to be done—that he should arrive at such an hour that he may be ready even for Compline, if he cannot arrive during the other hours, so that he may fulfill this chapter and not prove a transgressor of his profession. Or, if he cannot arrive at such an hour, he should go to a lodging in another one of our places, if we have one. Or, if this too is impossible, let him remain at the monastery gate that night; and there food should be prepared for him according to his need, as for a guest, or as best it can be prepared for him, provided that he cannot go elsewhere to eat. But if he could find another place, it is dishonorable for him to eat at the monastery gate.”

[Let them ask the prayers of all.] According to the Book of the Cistercian Usages, chapter 78, this prayer was made before the commemorations. Boherius, however, in his second commentary, thinks that the abbot’s blessing alone sufficed for those who departed and returned on the same day. You will find the form of the prayer in Menard and Haeften, book II, treatise 4, discussion 3.

[On account of transgressions.] Smaragdus and Bernard of Cassino interpret *excessus* here as a lapse into transgression. For Hildemar, however, *excessus* means especially a fault committed not deliberately but unexpectedly; Boherius inclines toward this interpretation, deriving *excessus* not from *excedo* (“to transgress”) but from *excido* (“to slip or fall away”). The following words show that this is the genuine meaning intended by the holy Father: “lest something should perhaps slip in.” He does not say “lest he should commit something,” but “lest something should slip in,” that is, lest it should escape the notice of one who is not sufficiently attentive.

[Nor should anyone presume to report to others whatever he has seen outside the monastery, etc.] The same rule is prescribed in the Rule of St. Pachomius, articles 34, 48, and 49; in the Oriental Rule, chapter 23; and in the Rule of Tarnat, chapter 2.

[For it is a very great destruction.] Abba Poemen says nearly the same in the *Apophthegmata of the Fathers*, volume I of the *Monuments of the Greek Church*:

> “If you see spectacles and hear conversations, do not relate them to your neighbor; for it is a military overthrow.”

St. Hugh, bishop of Lincoln, plainly understood this, as Surius records in his Life, chapter 22. When peace had been made between the kings of England and France and his Carthusian brothers asked him how it had been concluded, he replied sadly: “It is permitted to bishops to hear and report rumors, but it is not permitted to monks.”

[But if anyone should presume to do so, let him undergo regular punishment.] The Cassinese commentators explain the passage as follows:

> “If anyone has transgressed notably in this matter, let him confess his fault in the chapter house and eat on the ground in the refectory, with bread and water, at the discretion of the superior, as many times as he has transgressed.”

Nevertheless, on their return travelers were required to give the abbot an account of everything, as St. Basil prescribes in these words (*Long Rules*, chapter 44):

> “After his return, the superior should examine the one who has come back from the journey: what sort of transactions he has conducted, with what men he has had dealings, what conversations he has held, what thoughts have occupied his mind, whether he spent both day and night in the fear of God, whether, shaken by fear of external calamities or weakened by his own negligence, he overturned any of the ordinances. If anything was administered properly, let him confirm it by approval; but if any error has crept in, let it be corrected with careful and prudent instruction. In this way those brothers who travel abroad will be more watchful because they must render an account, and we shall appear not to neglect their life even when they are absent.”

[Likewise, whoever should presume to leave the cloister of the monastery, etc.] St. Pachomius in his Rule, article 36; St. Basil in the *Shorter Rules*, question 120; St. Ferreolus in his Rule, chapter 20; and St. Isidore, chapter 22, speak in nearly the same way. In granting this permission, however, the abbot should not show himself too ready to do so, but should consider only the monastery’s necessity or some pious usefulness. Then both those who depart and those who return should receive the abbot’s blessing, according to the custom of the ancient monks, which can be seen in the Sixth Synod, canon 46; in the *Penitentials* of an unknown author preserved by St. Basil, no. 1; in the Rule of St. Fructuosus, chapter 8; in Book II of the Dialogues of Pope St. Gregory, chapters 7 and 12; and in St. John Climacus, Step 4. They gave this blessing to those departing by making the sign of the cross over them, as is clear both from the Penitential of St. Columbanus and from Ardo’s Life of St. Benedict of Aniane, no. 23.

As for St. Benedict’s addition, “or wherever he may go,” Menard understands it to refer “to those who are sent on a journey, so that they go only to the place to which they have been sent and, without turning aside to the right or left, proceed directly there.” But all the Cassinese commentators interpret it as referring to movement within the monastery’s cloister, so that no one may wander about the monastery without the abbot’s command. Certainly such wandering is not expedient and can only be harmful to the brothers. Hence the Rule of St. Pachomius also says (article 47):

> “No one shall have permission either to walk about in the monastery or to go outside the monastery wall, unless he has asked the superior and the superior has granted it.”

And the *Penitentials* of an unknown author, preserved by St. Basil, say (no. 37):

> “If anyone goes out to the doorkeeper or porter, and permission has not been granted him by the appointed superiors, let him be deprived of the blessing. But if he goes out to inspect the fortification, let him be excommunicated.”

See the Rule of Saints Paul and Stephen, chapter 26, and the book *On the Ancient Rites of Monks*, chapter 17.

## CHAPTER LXVIII. If impossible tasks are imposed on a brother

[Col. 0917]

[Col. 0917B] If some burdensome or impossible task should perhaps be imposed on any brother [Note: Hildemar: *injungantur* (“should be imposed”).], let him indeed accept the command of the one giving it with complete gentleness and obedience. But if he sees that the weight of the burden altogether exceeds the measure of his strength [Note: Hildemar, with another manuscript: *operis* (“of the task”). Florence manuscript: *humeris* (“of the shoulders”).], let him patiently and suitably make known to the one who is over him the reasons for his inability [Col. 0918B], without acting proudly, resisting, or contradicting. But if, after he has made his explanation, the superior persists in his decision, let the junior know that this is for his good, and, trusting through charity in God’s help, let him obey.

### Commentary

[Col. 0917]

[Col. 0917C] [If some burdensome or impossible task should perhaps be imposed on any brother.] Here St. Benedict distinguishes two things: burdensome tasks and impossible tasks. The difference is that burdensome tasks are harsh, difficult, or scarcely accomplishable except with the greatest effort, whereas impossible tasks cannot be done in any way. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, Boherius, and Turrecremata generally understand the matter in this way.

With Boherius, we may distinguish three kinds of impossibility:

1. Legal impossibility, as when something contrary to law is commanded.
2. Impossibility of fact, as when one is ordered to move the Alps beyond the sea.
3. Impossibility by nature, as when one is ordered to climb to heaven or touch it with a finger.

Or, with Ambrose (*On the Faith*, book IV, chapter 3), we may distinguish four kinds of impossibility:

1. Something is impossible by nature—for example, for a bird to acquire wisdom or an art.
2. Something is possible by nature but impossible because of weakness; thus it is impossible for a sick man to carry the burdens of a strong man.
3. Something is impossible because of inexperience or incapacity; for example, for an illiterate person to teach letters.
4. Something is impossible because of the definition of an unalterable resolution, the steadfast perseverance of the will, and fidelity to friendship—for example, if someone is ordered to act contrary to the law of God or to vows.

Menard and Caramuel, however, believe that “impossible” must here be understood not physically but morally.

[Let him indeed accept the command of the one giving it.] Without making any distinction at all between burdensome and light tasks, possible and impossible ones. For nothing is harsh, burdensome, or impossible to one who obeys perfectly. As St. Basil says (*Rule translated by Rufinus*, chapter 82):

> “He who faithfully and purely loves God, and is certain of the Lord’s recompense, does not think that what is imposed on him is sufficient for himself; rather, he always seeks an increase in his work and desires and longs for greater things than those imposed, even if what he is doing appears to be beyond his strength.”

Hence Cassian also says (*Institutes*, book IV, chapter 10):

> “True obedience is that which, even when something difficult is commanded, attempts to carry out and complete what has been ordered without examining anything and without any hesitation of heart; and, out of reverence for the elder, does not judge the impossibility or foolishness of the command, but receives in full faith and devotion whatever has been said as commanded to him not by a human being but by God.”

[With complete gentleness and obedience.] This means, says Hildemar:

> “He must not merely say with his mouth that he does not wish or is unable to accept it; he must also not indicate by his expression that he is resisting, so that just as he shows gentleness in his body, he may also show it in his mind.”

[But if he sees that the weight of the burden altogether exceeds the measure of his strength, etc.] Bernard of Cassino rightly says concerning this passage:

> “Observe the meaning of the text. He does not say that any excuse should be offered in the case of burdensome or difficult tasks, but only in the case of impossible ones. And observe that the task must be so impossible that, after weighing both his strength and the burden, he ought truly to judge it impossible for himself. The burden and the strength must be carefully weighed in relation both to the nature of the task imposed and to the weakness of the one undertaking the obedience.”

Boherius says the same in both his commentaries.

St. Benedict also wished five things to be observed in such an explanation:

1. It must be made patiently, that is, with humility, as Hildemar says.
2. It must be made suitably, that is, at the proper time and privately, not publicly.
3. It must not be made proudly, as though rejecting what has been commanded by a superior.
4. It must not be made by resisting, that is, by refusing to carry out openly what has been ordered.
5. It must not be made by contradicting, that is, by shouting aloud that the command ought not to be carried out.

[If the command of the superior persists.] Menard understands “the superior” here to mean the elder, whom he contrasts with the junior when he says, “Let the junior know that this is for his good.” Boherius objects that all the ancient and more recent French versions that he has seen interpret *prior* here as “prelate” or “superior.”

[Let the junior know that this is for his good.] “As though he were saying,” says Hildemar, “let him not abandon obedience on this account; for if he obeys in those most difficult matters, it is beneficial to his salvation.”

[And, trusting through charity in God’s help, let him obey.] Unless perhaps something is commanded that is legally impossible or, as St. Ambrose says (*On the Faith*, book IV, chapter 3), impossible by the definition of an unalterable resolution, the steadfast perseverance of the will, and fidelity to friendship. Since such a command would conflict with God’s law, it cannot be carried out through charity. Everything else that may be commanded, however impossible it may be in whatever way, must be undertaken with firm hope in God’s help, so that, even if the deed cannot be accomplished, the disposition may at least be shown.

Bernard of Cassino exclaims most beautifully on this passage:

> “Wonderful is the perfection of regular obedience, which extends even to impossibilities and leaves the matter to God alone when what is commanded is impossible; and wonderful is the consolation of our holy Father, who says that even this is beneficial and promises confidence in God’s help when he says, ‘Let the junior know that this is for his good,’ and so forth. Since God, according to John, is charity, and nothing is difficult for one who loves, nothing will be impossible to one who possesses God in charity, because, according to the Lord’s word, what is impossible with human beings is possible with God. Charity, as this text explains, makes everything beneficial; confidence produces help through God’s merit and applies it in action.”

## CHAPTER LXIX. That no one should presume to defend another in the monastery

[Col. 0919]

[Col. 0919B] Care must be taken [Note: Oxford manuscript: *recavendum* (“must be guarded against”).] lest, on any occasion, one monk presume to defend another in the monastery [Note: The words “in the monastery” are absent from two manuscripts.] or, as it were, to protect him [Note: In some copies, *quasi* (“as it were”) is absent], even if they are joined by any degree of kinship [Note: Oxford and Conciliar manuscripts: *quavis* (“any”), for *qualevis*; Oxford manuscript: *jungatur* (“is joined”); Boherius: *conjungatur* (“is joined”).] [Col. 0920B]. Monks must not presume to do this in any way, because from it the gravest occasion of scandals may arise. If anyone transgresses this rule, let him be more severely restrained.

### Commentary

[Col. 0919]

[Col. 0919B] [Care must be taken lest, on any occasion, one monk presume to defend another in the monastery or, as it were, to protect him.] The commentators distinguish between *defendere* (“to defend”) and *tueri* (“to protect”) in this way: *defendere* refers to open and manifest defense, whereas *tueri* refers to secret and crafty defense, not apparent but concealed under words:

> “There are some,” says Hildemar, “who defend others openly and manifestly. To prevent this, he said ‘to defend.’ And there are others who do not dare to defend openly; they defend cleverly with pleasing words and by other hidden means, thinking that the abbot does not understand that they are doing this in order to defend the person. Of these he said ‘as it were to protect.’”

Bernard of Cassino, Nicholas of Fractura, and Boherius in both commentaries agree with Hildemar. Smaragdus, however, says that *tueri* means to sustain, assist, or provide protection; and for Menard, *tueri* is more than *defendere*. Nevertheless, many will prefer the first interpretation, because St. Benedict does not simply say *tueri* (“to protect”) but *quasi tueri* (“as it were to protect”), which seems rather to signify crafty defense.

[Even if they are joined by any degree of kinship.] Hildemar reasons here very well: since St. Benedict did not leave his disciples even their own wills in their own power, and wished them to obey in everything even one who commanded impossible things,

> “If this is so—that a monk does not dare to say anything on his own behalf—much less may he speak on behalf of others.”

St. Columbanus agrees with this, as cited by St. Benedict of Aniane in the *Concordia*.

[Monks must not presume to do this in any way.] “Defense is made in many ways,” Hildemar observes: “sometimes on account of kinship; sometimes on account of one’s homeland, because the person is from the same country; sometimes on account of discipleship; sometimes on account of friendship; sometimes on account of gluttony.” But monks must presume to do this in no way.

[Because from it the gravest occasion of scandals may arise.] For, as St. Basil says (*Rule translated by Rufinus*, chapter 26):

> “The delinquent no longer accepts correction for amendment, but defense for the confirmation of his sin. He also provokes others to a similar evil, so that what is said applies to the one who defends sinners: ‘Because if you do not show fruits worthy of repentance, you will be cut down and thrown into the fire.’”

Orsiesius likewise says (*Doctrine*, chapter 24):

> “If the superior of a house corrects one of the brothers subject to him, instructing him in the fear of God and desiring to correct him from error, and another wishes to speak for him and defend him, overthrowing his heart, the one who does this sins against his own soul, because he overthrows the one who could have been corrected, casts to the ground the one who was rising, and deceives by evil persuasion the one striving toward better things. He himself errs and causes others to err. The following saying will suitably apply to him: ‘Woe to him who gives his neighbor a drink as a turbid overthrow, and makes him drunk! Woe to him who causes a blind man to wander on the road, who scandalizes any one of those who believe in God! It would be better for him if a millstone were hung around his neck and he were thrown into the sea.’ For he has overthrown, as we have said, one who was raising himself up; he has turned the obedient toward pride; he has changed into bitterness the one who could have walked in the sweetness of charity; and by evil counsels he has corrupted the one subject to the laws of the monastery, made him hate and resent the one who was teaching him the discipline of the Lord, and sown quarrels and discord among the brothers.”

[But if anyone transgresses this rule, let him be more severely restrained.] Hildemar understands these words in two ways:

> “Either he should be rebuked more harshly in the rank in which he stands, or he should be subjected to a penalty one degree higher.”

Bernard of Cassino, however, says:

> “I think that Blessed Benedict intended the punishment of transgressors to be imposed according to the gravity of the offense, leaving the determination of the punishment to the abbot, so that medicine may be administered according to the illness.”

Boherius, after reporting both interpretations, expresses his own as follows:

> “I say that he should be punished more severely, namely, the one who defends the person who has sinned.”

Certainly, if the one “who defends another’s error is much more culpable than those who err, because he not only errs himself but also prepares and confirms stumbling-blocks of error for others,” then the one who protects others deserves to be punished more severely.

St. Pachomius therefore says aptly (article 99):

> “He who consents to sinners and defends another who is delinquent will be accursed before God and human beings, and will be corrected with the severest rebuke.”

The Oriental Rule likewise says (chapter 33):

> “If anyone consents to his error and, in accordance with his hardness, gives him further counsel so that he may humble himself more slowly, let him know that, when he is found in this error, he is to be judged culpable in the same way.”

Finally, the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers says (chapter 5):

> “But if any of the brothers, or any who dwell in the cells, consents to his error, he will be culpable and altogether worthy of excommunication.”

## CHAPTER LXX. That no one should presume to strike anyone indiscriminately

[Note: Some add: “or excommunicate.”]

[Col. 0921]

[Col. 0921A] Every occasion for presumption must be forbidden in the monastery [Note: Some copies read *vitatur* (“is avoided”); printed editions have *ut vitetur* (“so that it may be avoided”).]. We decree that no one may excommunicate or strike any of his brothers, except one to whom power has been given by the abbot. Sinners, however, are to be rebuked in the presence of all, so that the others may have fear. But those who are children, up to the age of fifteen years [Note: Some copies read *infantibus* (“for children”).], are to be carefully disciplined and guarded by all [Col. 0922A].
