Yet this too must be done with complete measure and reason. For if anyone in the more mature age presumes to do so [Note: Cassinese and Florentine manuscripts: *praesumit* (“presumes”)], in any degree, without the abbot’s command, or if he flares up without discernment even against the children themselves, let him undergo regular discipline [Col. 0922B], because it is written: “What you do not wish to be done to you, do not do to another” (Tobit 4).

### Commentary

[Col. 0921]

[Col. 0921B] There is equal danger on both sides: defending the guilty and persecuting the innocent. Therefore, after St. Benedict had forbidden the former in the preceding chapter, he condemns the latter in the present chapter. As for the word “indiscriminately” in the title, Hildemar interprets it as “lightly, presumptuously, as one wishes, commonly, everywhere”; Smaragdus as “disorderly, incongruously, and without rational measure”; and Boherius as “indiscreetly, indiscriminately, whenever one pleases.” According to Hildemar, this concerns both the abbot and those to whom he has granted the power of excommunicating and striking, as well as anyone else: no one may strike or excommunicate anyone at will, lightly, disorderly, or indiscriminately; rather, everything must be done with weight and measure.

[Every occasion for presumption must be forbidden in the monastery.] This clause, Menard writes, is a general decree establishing what follows.

[We decree that no one may excommunicate any of his brothers.] Whether for greater or lesser faults.

[Or strike him.] Whether directly or through another; whether by striking him physically or by imposing a penance.

[Except one to whom power has been given by the abbot.] Either power granted through the commission of some office to which the correction of the brothers is attached, or by special delegation for a particular act of this kind, as Turrecremata says after Bernard of Cassino and Boherius. This authority is commonly granted to the major prior and subprior, or, as our elders called them, the claustral prior:

> “For among us,” says Boherius, “these men exercise this office especially in the abbot’s absence.”

It is also granted to the deans and seniors.

St. Ferreolus decrees the same with St. Benedict in chapter 21, and rightly so. St. Basil argues very well (*Long Rules*, chapter 53):

> “If rebuke is medicine, it is not the task of just anyone to rebuke a delinquent, just as it is not the task of just anyone to treat a sick person, unless the superior has entrusted this duty to someone with greater authority.”

[But sinners are to be rebuked in the presence of all.] Here Hildemar raises another passage of the Rule, where sinners are ordered to be corrected by two private admonitions, not publicly. He himself resolves the objection by distinguishing between private and public sins: private sins are to be corrected secretly, public sins publicly before all. Hence he writes this sentence with the following punctuation: “Sinners, in the presence of all, are to be rebuked”—supply: “in the presence of all.”

St. Augustine likewise reconciles this passage of the Apostle, “Those who sin are to be rebuked in the presence of all,” with the saying of Matthew, “If your brother sins against you, go and correct him between you and him alone” (Sermon 82, *On Scripture*):

> “Those sins are to be corrected before all which are committed before all. Those sins are to be corrected secretly which are committed more secretly. Distinguish the circumstances, and Scripture is in agreement.”

Smaragdus, Richard of St. Angelo, Boherius, Turrecremata, and Matthias Lambertus likewise interpret this passage of the Rule as referring to public sins. The Rule of Tarnat accordingly decrees (chapter 8):

> “Whatever offenses are committed without witnesses, if they come to the abbot’s knowledge, are to be corrected more secretly; but if they become known to everyone, the accused is to be rebuked before everyone for the crime committed.”

The practice of this can be seen in the ancient Customs of the monastery of Cluny, by the author Udalric, where the following is read:

> “There are still among us other kinds of correction, which are practiced not only by the lord abbot but also, if necessary, by the prior. For I have heard the lord abbot say with complete truth (Book III, chapter 3) that no church of monks is dishonored because such a thing is committed by one brother; rather, what plainly brings disgrace upon us is that, if something wicked is committed, it is left without worthy correction. Therefore, if anyone is reported among the people for some disgraceful act, he is accustomed to be corrected in the presence of the people, so that those who have learned of his transgression may also learn of his correction. In the sight of all who wish to see, and especially in the middle of the street, he is stripped, bound, and flogged. If the fault is not among the more serious offenses but perhaps consists in his having contended dishonorably and irreligiously with someone in the hearing of the people, then, on Sunday, when the people have gathered at the church for the beginning of the morning Mass, he stands barefoot near the church doors, holding a large book in his hand. He does not put on a cap, so that he may be recognized by everyone; he speaks to no one entering or leaving; and one servant always stands beside him to tell those who ask why such a penance has been imposed upon him. He does not leave that place until the Mass is finished.”

See what we said above from the Benignian Customs concerning chapter 44.

Bernard of Cassino, on the other hand, complains here about certain religious who, “when one of the brothers corrupts even secular people by his evil example, punish him secretly or transfer him from one place to another, and, although the sin is public, either deceitfully deny it or shamefully conceal it. Those who had been corrupted by the delinquent’s evil example, because they do not know of the hidden disciplinary punishment, are corrupted still further and take courage to do similar or even worse things.” Against such persons Blessed Benedict inveighs with this authority: “Those who sin are to be rebuked in the presence of all.”

[But those who are children, up to the age of fifteen years, are to be carefully disciplined.] And even beyond that age if they are not well behaved, as Hildemar teaches. Nevertheless, in an excerpt of Bishop Egbert of York there is a canon of the Romans and Franks (Spelman, volume I of the *English Councils*):

> “A child up to the age of fifteen shall be punished for an offense by bodily discipline; after that age, whatever offense he commits, or if he steals, he shall make restitution or pay according to the law.”

[And guarded by all.] By those who do not themselves need discipline and who know it thoroughly:

> “For it does not follow that those who need discipline and do not know discipline should administer it,”

says Hildemar. Hence Menard also says:

> “When it says ‘by all,’ this is understood of the superiors, deans, priests, deacons, seniors, and others who have reached such maturity of age that they are able to discern the time, reason, and manner of measured correction. Or, as St. Ferreolus puts it, those to whom it belongs either to know the manner of correction or to exercise judgment. Nor do I think that it was ever permitted to those who had barely reached the age of seventeen or sixteen, or even twenty, to strike boys indiscriminately.”

[For if anyone in the more mature age should presume, etc.] St. Aurelian accordingly decrees (chapter 13) that “if a brother dares to lay hands on a brother, he shall receive legitimate discipline.” These words are cited as though from the Council of Ilerda, chapter 7, by Ivo of Chartres, part 6 of the *Decree*, chapter 292. But St. Aurelian seems to have taken them from the Rule of St. Caesaria for virgins, where we read (chapter 24):

> “If, as human frailty sometimes permits, any of the sisters should dare, instigated by the devil, to break out into such great wickedness as to commit theft or lay hands upon one another, it is just that they receive legitimate discipline.”

In the Rule of St. Ferreolus it is prescribed (chapter 21):

> “Whoever is found so uncontrolled in his hands that he does not know how to refrain from unlawful acts, let those hands which he raised against his neighbor be wearied for a long time not only by fasting but also by constant labor, so that thereafter they may be raised to God in prayer rather than extended against a brother in anger.”

Moreover, what St. Benedict establishes here concerning the striking of children up to the age of fifteen is confirmed by the practice of the ancient monks, which can be seen in Sulpicius Severus, Book I of the Dialogues, chapter 5. He reports that two boys, one twelve and the other fifteen years old, were beaten by their abbot because they had disclosed to the other brothers a miracle they themselves had performed, lest they perish, swollen with empty glory.

## CHAPTER LXXI. That they should be obedient to one another

[Col. 0923]

[Col. 0923B] The good of obedience must be shown by all not only to the abbot, but the brothers must also obey one another in this way [Note: In some copies *ita* (“in this way”) is absent], knowing that by this way of obedience they will go to God. After the command of the abbot or of the superiors whom he appoints [Note: Conciliar manuscript: *ut praepositorum* (“or of the superiors”)], to whom we do not permit private commands to be preferred [Col. 0923C], all the juniors must thereafter obey their seniors with complete charity and solicitude. If anyone is found to be contentious, let him be corrected.

But if any brother is corrected for any very small reason by the abbot or by any of his superiors, in whatever manner; or if he should lightly perceive that the mind of any superior is angry or agitated against him, even to a small degree [Note: Cassinese, Narbonne, and Florentine manuscripts, together with certain other manuscripts: *animos … iratos vel commotos* (“their minds … angry or agitated”)], let him immediately, without delay, remain prostrate on the ground at the superior’s feet, making satisfaction, until that agitation is healed by a blessing. But if anyone refuses to do this [Note: Some copies: “But whoever refuses to do this”], let him undergo bodily punishment; or, if he is obstinate, let him be expelled from the monastery.

### Commentary

[Col. 0923]

[Col. 0923C] [The good of obedience must be shown by all not only to the abbot, but the brothers must also obey one another.] Abba Isaiah teaches the same doctrine in his Rule in these words (chapter 30):

> “If you live with another brother, be toward him as a stranger; do not command him anything, do not make yourself superior to him, and do not act presumptuously toward him. If he commands you something you do not wish to do, cut off your own will and do not grieve him, lest peace be cut off from you. And know that the obedient person is the greater.”

St. Basil teaches the same in the *Shorter Rules*, question 115; St. Dorotheus, *Doctrine* 19; the *Rule of a Certain Person for Monks*, chapter 3; and St. Bernard, Sermon II on the *Song of Songs*.

Knowing that they will go to God by this path of obedience.] A truly excellent and worthy saying of Saint Benedict, which ought to inspire courage in many, if only we could be stirred by suitable goads. He does not promise merely with some uncertainty that the obedient will go to God, but asserts it firmly and most certainly, saying: “KNOWING that they will go to God by this path of obedience”; because “eternal salvation is owed by hereditary right to the obedient alone,” as Peter Damian says (*Sermon on Saint Benedict*), or whoever else may be the author. Hence Saint Fructuosus likewise says in his *Monastic Rule* (chapter 5): “Those who desire to go through Christ to God . . . must obey the abbot unto death, to such an extent that they do not do anything according to their own will, but according to the Father’s.”

“Having first submitted to the command of the abbot and of the superiors appointed by him.”] By “superiors,” Saint Benedict does not here understand only those who, after the abbot, rank immediately above the deans; he also includes the deans themselves, the inspectors, the officials, and the superiors of every kind of work.

“To whom we do not permit private commands to be preferred.”] The order of obedience requires that we obey first our superiors and then our inferiors, as Saint Augustine also teaches in these words (*Sermon 62, On Scripture*): “Observe the ranks of human affairs. If a curator gives an order, must it not be carried out? Yet if he orders something contrary to the proconsul, you do not thereby despise authority, but choose to serve the greater; nor should the lesser be angry if the greater has been placed above him. Again, if the proconsul himself gives one order and the emperor another, is there any doubt that, disregarding the former, one must obey the latter? Therefore, if the emperor commands one thing and God another, what do you judge?”

“For the rest, let all the younger brothers obey their elders with complete charity and solicitude.”] Since Saint Benedict occupies the brothers at every moment with some task—for the Rule commands them at one time to celebrate the divine praises in church, at another to devote themselves to reading in the cloister, at another to engage in manual labor in the garden or elsewhere, at another to take food in the refectory, and at another to indulge in sleep in the dormitory, leaving absolutely no interval of time, or scarcely any—Hildemar asks here how the brothers ought to obey one another. For if someone shows obedience to his brothers, he consequently denies it to the Rule; and if he observes the Rule, by that very fact he cannot obey his brothers. Hildemar gives three answers to this objection:

1. Everyone obeys who serves everyone, whether by preparing food in the kitchen, serving a newcomer in the guesthouse, caring for the sick in the infirmary, or performing other obediences.

2. Nothing prevents one who cannot obey by his actions from obeying at least in heart and will, which God especially regards.

3. Even those assigned to the same obedience can obey one another. For example, when brothers are sent to wash clothes, one may wash the clothes of a delicate brother who asks him to do so; and one assigned to kitchen duty may obey a companion less skilled in that work who asks him to do something connected with the kitchen service.

Bernard of Cassino and Boherius likewise give the first and third answers.

“But if anyone is found to be contentious, let him be corrected.”] Hildemar comments on this passage: “And rightly, when he had mentioned obedience, he added: ‘If anyone is contentious, let him be corrected,’ because contention is suited to no one more than to the disobedient.” According to Hildemar, a contentious person is “one who, whatever he does, always does it with murmuring or detraction, whether with an evil defense or with cleverness.” According to Bernard of Cassino, however, “contentious” pertains to disobedience; but here it means more—namely, that the person not only scorns obedience but also arrogantly quarrels with the one giving the order. For Boherius, a contentious person is one “who provokes another with harsh and insulting words, and who returns evil for evil when someone speaks evil, or responds badly to someone doing good.”

“But if any brother is corrected for any very minor matter by the abbot or by any of his priors.”] Boherius understands this passage in his second commentary as referring to correction that takes place “in the regular chapter, where, according to custom, the offender must also be publicly accused before everyone and corrected for amendment.” But in his first commentary he had spoken more accurately: “I believe that this refers to private correction, which all priors may exercise toward the younger brothers, not to the public correction that takes place in chapter by words and sometimes by blows; for that correction only the abbot, or the person to whom he has entrusted it, ought to administer.” Certainly, the Holy Father is not speaking here of correction administered by the abbot or by the prior alone, but of that administered by any of one’s priors.

“By any means.”] Whether justly or unjustly.

“Or if he should lightly perceive the spirit of any prior to be angry or agitated against him, even slightly.”] Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius distinguish between “agitated” and “angry” in this way: a person is called angry when inflamed by greater anger, and agitated when affected by lesser anger.

“Immediately, without delay, let him lie prostrate on the ground before his feet for as long as necessary, etc.”] This was a common practice among the ancient monks, as can be seen throughout their Rules. In the Rule of Abbot Isaiah (chapter 24): “If you have sinned in any matter, do not be ashamed to confess it, nor excuse yourself with a lie; instead, bend your knees, confess your offense, and ask pardon, and it will be forgiven you.” In the Second Rule of the Holy Fathers (chapter 7): “This too must be observed: that a brother who is accused or rebuked for any fault should have patience and not answer the one accusing him, but humble himself in everything.” The same is found in chapter 16 of the Rule of Saint Macarius. In the Rule of Saint Aurelian (chapter 38): “If anyone is rebuked for any fault or transgression of the Rule, or receives discipline, let him not presume to answer the one rebuking him.” More clearly, in the Rule of a Certain Man for Monks (chapter 7): “At the first word of rebuke by the senior, the steward, or any brother, pardon must be requested, and he must remain prostrate on the ground until the senior has completed his rebuke. If the senior repeats the rebuke, he too must repeat his request for pardon.” In the Second Life of Saint Comgall (no. 22, Bollandists, 10 May): “It was the custom in the monastery of the Holy Father Comgall that, if anyone rebuked another, even if the latter were guilty or innocent, the one rebuked would immediately bend his knees humbly.” In the *Life of Saint Eupraxia the Virgin* (no. 14, Bollandists, 13 March), when she was reproved by the abbess for having concealed her temptations, she “fell at the abbess’s feet and said: ‘Forgive me, my lady, because I was ashamed to reveal this matter to you.’” Rufinus, reporting the case of a certain Eulalius (*Lives of the Fathers*, book 3, no. 29), says that “when he was accused by the elder brothers, he did not deny it, but prostrated himself on the ground and, worshiping them, said that he had sinned and acted negligently.” The Council of Aachen renewed the same institution, decreeing (canon 13) “that whenever one of them has been rebuked by any of his priors, he should first say, ‘My fault’; then, prostrating himself at the prior’s feet with his cloak, if he has one, he should ask pardon; and then, when ordered by the prior, he should rise and humbly give an account of what he has been questioned about.”

Here Hildemar asks whether an elder ought to prostrate himself at the feet of a younger brother who rebukes him, since Saint Benedict does not say this. He answers affirmatively. The order of monastic conduct says likewise: “If a brother is rebuked, reproved, or corrected by any prior, or by anyone else, or indeed by a younger brother, for any matter whatever, he should immediately fall on his face with the greatest speed and ask pardon; for this same humility is shown to God, not to man; and if it is from the heart, he will quickly merit forgiveness.”

“Until that agitation is healed by a blessing.”] Hildemar asks again what should happen if the angry or agitated brother does not wish to bless the brother who has humbled himself. He answers—and Bernard of Cassino and Boherius agree with him—that such a person must be brought down by stages, and rightly so. For one must have cast off every sense of humaneness who refuses to spare someone asking pardon and humbling himself. Hence Boherius cites Pope Fabian: “If anyone who has been grieved refuses to be reconciled with his brother when the one who caused the grief has made satisfaction, let him be afflicted by the severest fasts until he receives the satisfaction with a joyful heart.”

“But if anyone scorns to do this.”] That is, to humble himself before the one rebuking him.

“Or let him be subjected to bodily punishment.”] Hildemar and Bernard of Cassino understand this as referring to fasts and scourging, in accordance with the words of Saint Fructuosus (chapter 17): “For the insolent person who persists and, through pride or contentiousness, refuses to acknowledge his fault, a greater and stricter correction, and the penalty of scourging, shall be imposed.” Saint Ferreolus agrees, chapter 2.

“Or, if he is obstinate, let him be expelled from the monastery.”] Yet above he had said that an obstinate person should first be corrected by two private admonitions. That earlier passage, chapter 23, must be understood of an obstinacy that is temporary and corrigible; this passage concerns persistent obstinacy, which cannot be broken in any way. Hildemar, Bernard of Cassino, and Boherius thus reconcile Saint Benedict’s statements.

“Nevertheless, in this expulsion,” Hildemar adds, “the person’s condition must be taken into account, as has often already been said. If he came from the world already advanced in age, then he should be expelled; but if he was brought up in the monastery while still young, he should not be expelled but sent to prison, because it is better for him to be in prison than to go back to the world, that is, to a worse way of life.” Thus, when Hugh, formerly offered to the monastery of Dervy, escaped by flight, the abbot and the monks “decided that he should remain with the necessities of life in a remote lodging,” as is related in the *Book of the Miracles of Saint Bercharius*, no. 22 (*Benedictine Century II*). The Rule of a Certain Man for Monks is partly in agreement with this (chapter 7): “If anyone is found slow to ask pardon, or has uttered words contrary to religion, or has spoken in excuse for his offense, he must be sent to prison and do penance according to the judgment of the senior until he is corrected. But if he is found obstinate, he must be separated from the brothers.”

Richard of Saint Angelo understands this expulsion in such a way that the expelled person “is placed in another, stricter monastery; otherwise an opportunity for wandering would be given, which must not happen.” But he is speaking according to more recent laws, not according to the ancient custom of the old monks, who drove obstinate persons out of the monastery lest one diseased sheep infect the entire flock.

## CHAPTER LXXII  
### On the good zeal that monks ought to have

[Column 0927]

“Just as there is an evil zeal of bitterness, which separates from God and leads to hell, so there is a good zeal which separates from vices [Note: The Council: ‘from vice.’] and leads to God and eternal life. Let the monks therefore practice this zeal with the most ardent love; that is, let them anticipate one another in honor [Note: Hildemar: ‘anticipating one another.’]. Let them bear with the greatest patience one another’s infirmities, whether of body or of character. Let them eagerly offer one another obedience. Let no one pursue what he judges useful for himself, but rather what is useful for another. Let them offer the charity of brotherhood with chaste love [Note: Narbonne: ‘Let them offer the charity of brotherhood with chaste love.’]. Let them fear God; let them love their abbot with sincere and humble charity [Note: Oxford, with three manuscripts: ‘let them love him with humility.’]. Let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ, who may bring us all together to eternal life.”

## COMMENTARY

“Just as there is an evil zeal of bitterness, etc.”] Although among the ancients *zeal* properly signifies envy, in the sacred Scriptures and among the Holy Fathers it is used indiscriminately in both a good and a bad sense, as here by Saint Benedict. According to Hildemar, “zeal when understood in a good sense means force, that is, love of the mind; and evil zeal means envy.” The Holy Father distinguishes the two philosophically, as Bernard of Cassino puts it, by setting one against its contrary, “so that one may appear more clearly through the other. For he distinguishes between good and evil zeal by stating the properties and effects of each.” The property of good zeal is that it is good by nature, and of evil zeal that it is evil. “Good zeal is love of virtues and horror of vices; evil zeal is love of vices and horror of virtues,” as Hildemar writes.

Saint Benedict notes three effects of good zeal: first, that it separates from vices; second, that it leads to God; third, that it grants eternal life. He assigns two effects to evil zeal: first, that it separates from God; second, that it leads to hell.

“Let the monks therefore practice this zeal with the most ardent love.”] Observe how ardently he desires zeal to burn in his disciples. Not content with ardent or even more ardent love, he insists that they be moved by the most ardent love of all. He chiefly establishes its practice in eight exercises.

“Namely, let them anticipate one another in honor.”] This is the first exercise of good zeal. I wish those who contend for a standard of conduct contrary to monastic life would pay attention to it, although I do not wish worldly ways of acting to be transferred into the cloister, from which every monk is obliged to separate himself.

“Let them bear with the greatest patience one another’s infirmities, whether of body or of character.”] This is the second exercise of good zeal. Abbot John commends it in Cassian in these words (*Conferences* 19.9): “He is truly, and not merely in part, perfect who bears with equal greatness of soul both the squalor of solitude in the desert and the infirmities of life in a coenobium.” Saint Bernard likewise says (*Sermon 12 on the Song of Songs*): “Whoever among you not only patiently bears the infirmities of his brothers, both of body and of soul, but also, if permitted and able, helps them by his services, strengthens them by his words, and instructs them by his counsels—if he cannot do this because of discipline, at least, concerned for the sick brother, does not cease to console him by his prayers—whoever, I say, does such things among you spreads an entirely good fragrance among the brothers, the fragrance of the finest perfumes. Such a brother is shown by the finger as a balm in the mouth of the congregation, and everyone says of him: ‘This is a lover of the brothers and of the people of Israel; this is the one who prays greatly for the people and for the whole holy city.’” Elsewhere he says (*Sermon 1 on All the Saints*): “With what praises do you think that brother worthy, and with what affection ought he to be embraced, who lives among his brothers without complaint, takes every care that there be nothing in him that others would have to bear, and most patiently bears whatever is burdensome in others?” See also the same Saint Bernard’s *Sermon 36 on Various Subjects*.

“Let them eagerly offer one another obedience.”] Yet with the command of the abbot and the superiors placed first: this is the third exercise of good zeal.

“Let no one do what he judges useful for himself, but rather what is useful for another.”] This is the fourth exercise, concerning which Ardo Smaragdus praises Benedict of Aniane in his *Life*, no. 31.

“Let them offer the charity of brotherhood with chaste love.”] Saint Benedict places the fifth exercise of good zeal here. As Bernard of Cassino and Boherius note, he did not say “chaste” without reason: “namely, in order to restrain and exclude disordered, indiscriminate, carnal, impure, or polluted love.” Thus Saint Macarius also said (chapter 7): “Everyone ought to love the brothers with whom he trusts that he will see the glory of Christ.”

“Let them fear God.”] With filial fear, certainly; and this is the sixth exercise of good zeal.

“Let them love their abbot with sincere and humble charity.”] This is the seventh. Sincere charity is that which is corrupted neither by any carnal love nor by consideration of fear or reward, but is offered solely for the love of God.

“Let them prefer absolutely nothing to Christ.”] Whoever prefers anything to Christ plainly deserves to be put after everything else, since nothing may be preferred to the highest and infinite good. This is the final exercise of good zeal. Although it must be practiced without any thought of reward, it is nevertheless not without its recompense, which the Holy Father indicates when he adds:

“Who may bring us all together to eternal life.”] The commentators unanimously interpret “together” as meaning all at once, excluding no one. Some manuscripts add “amen.” Boherius says of this word in his second commentary: “The Gallican manuscripts rarely have this ‘amen,’ though it fits well, since this is the true end of the Rule; for the following chapter is not properly a rule but the master’s intention. It briefly indicates the effect of the Rule. ‘Amen’ is therefore placed here optatively, to show that this is the conclusion of the same work.” It is nevertheless absent from the oldest Oxford manuscript, from the Cassinese manuscripts, from Hildemar, Smaragdus, Haeften, and many other manuscripts and printed editions.

## CHAPTER LXXIII  
### On the fact that not every observance of righteousness is established in this Rule

[Column 0929]

“We have written this Rule so that, by observing it in monasteries [Note: Oxford: ‘in this monastic observance’], we may show ourselves to possess at least some degree of moral uprightness or the beginning of the monastic way of life [Note: Another reading: ‘the beginning of conversion.’; Oxford: ‘that our beginning of the way of life is shown.’]. But for those who hasten toward perfection of the monastic way of life, there are the teachings of the Holy Fathers, whose observance leads a person to the height of perfection [Note: Another reading: ‘may lead’; another: ‘led.’]. For what page, or what discourse of divine authority in the Old and New Testament, is not a most upright rule of human life? Or what book of the holy Catholic Fathers does not resound with the call that we should reach our Creator by a straight course?

“Likewise, the Conferences of the Fathers, their Institutes [Note: In the Council’s text, ‘and their Institutes and life’ is absent.], and their lives [Note: Other readings: ‘lives’; ‘life’]; and also the Rule of our holy Father Basil—what else are they but instruments of virtue for monks who live well and obey? But for us who are sluggish, live badly, and are negligent, they are a shame and confusion. Whoever, therefore, hastens to the heavenly homeland, complete, with Christ’s help, this little Rule of initiation that has been written down; and then at last, under God’s protection, you will reach the greater heights of teaching and virtue mentioned above [Note: Florence adds: ‘Amen. For those who do these things, life will be eternal.’ The Concordance, with certain manuscripts and commentators, has: ‘For those who do these things, the heavenly or eternal kingdom will be opened’; some also add ‘Amen.’ But this conclusion is absent from the older Cassinese manuscripts, and it is clearly an addition, as appears from Hildemar, who ends his commentary with these words: ‘It ends, thanks be to God. Amen. The exposition that the monk Hildemar explained concerning the Rule of Saint Benedict and handed on to his disciples ends. For those who do these things, the heavenly kingdom will be opened. Amen.’].”

## COMMENTARY

“We have written this Rule so that, by observing it in the monastery, we may show ourselves to possess at least some degree of moral uprightness or the beginning of the monastic way of life.”] The holy Father evidently thought this way about himself and greatly desired his disciples to be founded and strengthened in humility: those who observe this Rule, distinguished by discretion and brilliant in language, which Saint Gregory also lists among his principal miracles (*Dialogues*, book 2), should consider themselves to possess not moral uprightness or the beginning of the monastic way of life absolutely, but only to some extent.

John de Turrecremata teaches that moral uprightness consists in three things:

1. In fleeing vices, according to the words of Saint Ambrose (*On Duties*, book 1, chapter 46): “What else is honorable except that things to be fled are fled?”

2. In fear, love, and worship of the Creator, according to the same Ambrose (*ibid.*, chapter 45): “It is honorable, Lord, that we fear you, love you, implore you, and honor you; for praise is due to you in Zion.”

3. In disciplined external conduct, according to the Rule of Saint Augustine: “In your walking, your posture, your clothing, and all your movements, let nothing be done that would offend anyone’s sight, but only what is fitting for your holiness.”

“But for those who hasten toward perfection . . . there are the teachings of the Holy Fathers, etc.”] Peter Damian aptly discusses monastic perfection in relation to this passage (*Opusculum* 13, chapter 3):

“To this cultivation of the heart, Joshua figuratively urged the sons of Joseph when, as they complained about the smallness of their allotment, he said to them: ‘Since you are a numerous people, go up into the forest and clear a space for yourselves in the land of the Perizzites and Rephaim, because the mountain of Ephraim is too narrow for you.’ To apply this properly to what is nearer at hand, the one who decides to be content with the Rule of Blessed Benedict alone has confined himself within the narrow possession of Mount Ephraim. But hear how the new Joshua urges you toward the mountain and commands you to hasten toward broader possessions. ‘We have written this Rule,’ he says, ‘so that, by observing it, we may show ourselves to possess at least some degree of moral uprightness or the beginning of the monastic way of life.’ Behold Mount Ephraim. But because he recognizes that the possession there is narrow, he immediately leads us to greater and broader heights. ‘For those who hasten toward perfection,’ he says, ‘there are the teachings of the saints, the Conferences and Institutes of the Fathers, etc.; and since we know these are already very familiar to you, we judge it superfluous to set them down here.’”

Moreover, according to Bernard of Cassino and Nicholas of Fractura (in the second commentary), the teachings of the Holy Fathers “are to be understood more through examples of deeds than through written words.” Hence Boherius astutely observes that Saint Benedict did not say *doctrina* in the singular but *doctrinae* in the plural, “because,” he says, “one kind of teaching is verbal, while another is exemplary.”

Richard of Saint Angelo, without distinguishing between these two kinds of teaching, understands the teachings here as those “which are received by the Roman Church.” These are, he says, “first, the works of Blessed Cyprian, martyr and bishop of Carthage; likewise the works of Blessed Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria; likewise the works of Blessed Basil, bishop of Cappadocia; likewise the works of Blessed Gregory, bishop of Nazianzus; likewise the works of Blessed John, bishop of Constantinople; likewise the works of Blessed Hilary, bishop of Poitiers; likewise the works of Blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan; likewise the works of Theophilus, bishop of Alexandria; likewise the works of Jerome, presbyter; likewise the works of Prosper, a religious man; likewise the works of Pope Leo addressed to Flavian, bishop; likewise the works and treatises of all the orthodox Fathers who in no respect deviated from the Holy Roman Church; and likewise the decretal letters that the most blessed popes issued at various times in the city of Rome for the consolation of various Fathers—all these are to be received with reverence.”

Boherius, however, places Saint Jerome first among the Catholic Fathers and Doctors of the Church, especially with regard to coenobitic practices, since Jerome lived a coenobitic life in Rome, an eremitical life in the vast Egyptian desert, and an abbatial life in Bethlehem, and wrote excellently on monasticism, particularly in his letters to Heliodorus, Nepotianus, Paulinus, and Rusticus.

“For what page, or what discourse of divine authority in the Old and New Testament, etc., does not resound with this, that we should reach our Creator by a straight course?”] This was expressed most clearly by Abbot Pynufius in Cassian, when he set forth a short path to perfection and arranged the stages by which one ascends to charity itself, which is God (*Institutes*, book 4, chapter 43):

“Hear in a few words the order by which you can ascend to the highest perfection without any labor or difficulty. According to the Scriptures, the beginning of our salvation and wisdom is the fear of the Lord. From the fear of the Lord arises salutary compunction; from compunction of heart proceeds renunciation, that is, nakedness and contempt of all possessions; from nakedness humility is born; from humility the mortification of the will; through the mortification of the will all vices are uprooted and wither; through the expulsion of vices the virtues bear fruit and grow; through the growth of the virtues purity of heart is acquired; and through purity of heart the perfection of apostolic charity is possessed.”

“Likewise, the Conferences of the Fathers, their Institutes, and their lives.”] Here the commentators understand the Conferences of the Fathers to be those twenty-four books that Cassian wrote. By the Institutes they understand the twelve books he composed on the institutions of those renouncing the world. By the Lives of the Fathers they understand either the books containing the sayings and deeds of the ancient monks, commonly called the *Lives of the Fathers*, or also the written acts of any saints, whose examples greatly stir the sluggish toward a more perfect life, as Saint John Climacus teaches in these words (*Ladder*, step 26): “The lives and virtues of religious Fathers, when heard, recited, or read, stir our minds toward the desire to imitate them. The hearing of their teaching is a lamp that drives away darkness, brings wanderers back to the road, and enlightens the blind.”

Certainly Gregory, bishop of Tours (*Book on the Lives of the Fathers*, final chapter), sent the *Lives of the Fathers* and the *Institutes of the Monks* to the monk Leobard, enclosed in the monastery of Major, in order to fortify him against temptations.

“But also the Rule of our holy Father Basil.”] Namely, Basil of Caesarea, bishop in Cappadocia. We possess his shorter rules, his more fully discussed rules, and a third rule composed from both, which Rufinus, a presbyter of Aquileia, translated from Greek into Latin, together with the Monastic Constitutions. We have cited all these more than once in this commentary. We are therefore surprised that Boherius attributed the Rule of Basil mentioned here by the Holy Father Benedict to a certain monk Basil distinct from the bishop of Caesarea. For the Rule of that monk Basil, which, he says, the Eastern coenobites observe and which he himself frequently cites, is in no way different from the rules written by the bishop of Caesarea.

The fact that Saint Benedict calls him “Father” and “his own” does not imply that he served under the institutions of Saint Basil. He calls him Father either as a mark of honor, as an elder, according to Saint Augustine’s words: “For the sake of honor we call Fathers those who have preceded us either in time or in merits; for it is an honor that we daily address old men as Father”; or because, as Saint Jerome says, “in common speech, especially in the monasteries of Palestine and Egypt, they call one another Fathers.” Thus Cyril, bishop of Alexandria, addressed a letter to the priests and deacons that is found in the acts of the Council of Ephesus to “the monastic Fathers.” Or finally, because the title Father was customarily given to the most distinguished writers of the Church, among whom Saint Basil was certainly not inferior, as Haeften observes (*Book 2, treatise 1, discussion 1*).

Likewise, when Benedict calls him “his own,” adding the pronoun “our,” he did so chiefly either as a mark of honor and respect, or because the title “our holy Father” is customarily prefixed to the books of saints, especially monks, as can be seen in all the works of Saint Basil, Saint John Climacus, and Saint Germanus, patriarch of Constantinople. Indeed, the Greeks themselves announce Saint Benedict’s feast in their *Menologion* on 14 March as follows: “Our holy Father Benedict, Father of many monasteries, renowned for piety and illustrious for the multitude of his miracles.”

“But for us who are sluggish, live badly, and are negligent, they are a shame and confusion.”] Here, as Bernard of Cassino observes, the Holy Father accuses us of three things: sluggishness, by which we omit to do good; an evil life, by which we commit sins; and negligence, by which we despise our faults and do not care to rise from our iniquities. For us, therefore, who are such, these things are a shame and confusion—“namely, to read and attend to the books and deeds of the Fathers; for it is a great shame and confusion for us to bear the name of holy monks and not to do their works,” says Boherius.

Or, as Hildemar says, the Conferences, Institutes, and Lives of the Fathers, together with the Rule of Saint Basil, which are instruments of virtue for monks who obey and live well, are for us who are sluggish a shame and confusion. It is the same as when two men are assigned the same labor, given the same tools, and promised the same reward: what is material for praise to the diligent and industrious becomes an occasion of blame and confusion to the negligent and sluggish.

“Whoever, therefore, hastens to the heavenly homeland.”] You rightly hasten, for it cannot be reached by a slow step.

“Complete, with Christ’s help, this little Rule of initiation that has been written down.”] Here we may properly apply the words of Orsiesius concerning Father Pachomius: “Let us consider the traditions of our Father a ladder extending toward the kingdom of heaven.” Saint Paldo the abbot likewise used to say, in order to strengthen the brothers in the poverty they had embraced (*Life*, no. 3, Benedictine Century III): “Believe me, brothers: the monk who remains in this monastery and perseveres in it until the end will by no means suffer eternal punishments in his soul, but will possess eternal life.”

Saint Benedict calls his Rule “the little Rule of initiation” either out of modesty or humility, or in relation to the anchoritic life, for which it is a prelude, or because it is easy to observe, as Haeften discusses at length (*Book 2, treatise 2, discussion 5*).

The phrase “with Christ’s help,” according to Bernard of Cassino, may be connected either with the preceding word “written” or with the following word “complete.”

“And then at last, under God’s protection, you will reach the greater heights of teaching and virtue mentioned above.”] The greater things mentioned above are those at the beginning of this chapter: the teachings of the Fathers, their Conferences, Institutes, and Lives, and the Rule of Saint Basil. As Bernard of Cassino observes, Saint Benedict calls them “greater” because “they contain within themselves the holiness of teaching, the acquisition of virtues, and the summit of the heavenly homeland.”

Richard of Saint Angelo refers “mentioned above” either to the preceding chapter concerning the good zeal that monks ought to have or to this present final chapter. Boherius refers it to several other passages of the Rule. But our earlier view, which is Hildemar’s, is more persuasive.

[Column 0933]

## WORKS OF THE HOLY FATHER BENEDICT (G, S)*

### SERMON OF THE HOLY FATHER BENEDICT DELIVERED AT THE DEPARTURE OF SAINT MAURUS AND HIS COMPANIONS

[Column 0933A]

“If there were reason to grieve over such a matter, dearest Fathers and sons, I ought to grieve over it more than you, since, as far as the present is concerned, I seem to be deprived of great consolations. But because, as the Apostle says, charity is kind, we must in every way show the kindness of our charity to those whom we know to need it in some way, seeking not so much what is ours as what belongs to others. Therefore, out of the solicitude of paternal love, we ask you to restrain yourselves from tears and grief, because God is able, after this body has been laid aside, to send better men than ourselves into this holy congregation, by whose merits and examples you may be built up far more excellently than by ours.

“But we must also take the greatest care lest the ancient enemy, by his cunning, inflict some harm upon us through the very thing by which salvation is acquired for others—namely, by turning it into the evil of sadness. For those whom concord has once joined in holy charity, no distance of lands, however long, will ever divide. Rather, through the inward vision of the inner man, who is renewed according to the image of the one who created him, we shall look upon one another throughout the time that we live.

“After these words, he addressed Saint Maurus and his companions as follows: ‘But you, dearest brothers, whom we are sending to those regions to build up the work of the Lord, act manfully, and may your heart be strengthened in your holy purpose and religious commitment. Know without doubt that the harsher the things you endure, for the sake of the salvation of others, along the road of this world, the greater will be the heavenly joys of reward that you receive from God. Nor should the wasting away of this little body of ours make you sad in any way, for once I have laid aside the burden of the flesh I shall be more present to you, and by God’s grace I shall remain your constant co-worker.’”

### NOTE

This sermon cannot be confirmed more securely than by the testimony of an eyewitness and ear-witness, namely Blessed Faustus, a disciple of Saint Paul, to whom and to the other three companions the final words of this sermon were addressed. He came to Gaul together with Blessed Maurus. After Maurus’s death, he was summoned to Rome by the brothers and, writing the *Life of Saint Maurus* at the command of the supreme pontiff, attributed these very words to Saint Benedict.

Following Saint Faustus is Adrenaldus of Fleury, a most ancient author—he was flourishing in the year 890—in book 1 of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 6. Saint Faustus, he says, composed the *Life of Blessed Maurus*, “from which work we too have borrowed what we have written.” Immediately afterward he adds this sermon together with the letter sent to Saint Maurus. See Surius, volume 1, and Arnold Uvion, *The Tree of Life*, book 1, chapter 1.

Finally, the truth of this sermon seems strongly confirmed both by the words of Saint Maurus with which he consoles Saint Romanus concerning the death of Saint Benedict, in the work of the ancient author of the *Life of Saint Romanus* preserved in the Library of Fleury, and by these verses of Peter Damian, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church, where he speaks of the praises of Mount Cassino in the following words:

“If Mount Sinai, which once gave the law, has fallen . . .”

I would not wish to believe, nevertheless, that its walls have perished,

For the Rule remains, inscribed by consecrated fingers,

Handed down to the blessed disciples Maurus and Placidus.

If King Antiochus sold the altar for gold,

Maccabeus will rebuild a new altar by law and labor.

The Lawgiver says: “I am more present to you;

After death I am present; this I shall now declare to those who cry out.”

Arnold Uvion cites this in his Martyrology under the day of Saint Maurus.

## LETTER OF SAINT BENEDICT SENT TO SAINT MAURUS

[Col. 0934B]

Receive, most beloved, the final gifts of your teacher. They will both testify to our longstanding love and provide you and your fellow soldiers with an everlasting defense against every obstacle of evil. For after you have completed the entire course of three times twenty years since you undertook monastic perfection, you are to be introduced into the joy of your Lord, as the Lord deigned to show us yesterday, after you had departed from us.

I also foretell that, on your journey, you will endure delay and will find a suitable place only with difficulty, because of those things which will both be accomplished by God’s ordering and be stirred up against you by the enemy of the human race through the contrivance of his cunning. Nevertheless, the kindness of the merciful God will never be lacking to you. Rather, although he may delay, and although he may test your heart’s desire at length, he will deign to grant you a most suitable settlement elsewhere than we had hoped.

And now, may you be happy in your profession, and destined to be happier in your arrival.

## [NOTE]

All the authors cited above in the note to the sermon delivered at the departure of Saint Maurus also include this letter and attribute it to Saint Benedict. It therefore seemed superfluous to cite them again. I add only the testimony of Adrevald of Fleury, in the same book mentioned above, chapter 7, where, speaking of Saints Maurus and his companions, he says:

“Thus, having set out from the monastery of Cassino during the days of Epiphany, on Thursday they arrived that same day at an estate belonging to the monastery, not far away. They were received by two brothers whom the most reverend father had sent there the previous day for this purpose. While they were spending the night there for the sake of rest, two brothers sent by Saint Benedict, bearing pious gifts—namely, a reliquary box and a short letter—came upon them while they were celebrating the nocturnal synaxis,” etc.

That reliquary box, which is made of ivory, is displayed at Saint-Maur-des-Fossés near Paris. Some testify that the letter was buried with Saint Maurus, according to his desire and wish.

# APPENDIX TO THE WORKS OF SAINT FATHER BENEDICT

[Col. 0935]

## SPURIOUS WRITINGS (C, G, S)

## LETTER OF SAINT BENEDICT SENT TO SAINT REMIGIUS, BISHOP OF RHEIMS

[Col. 0935A]

To Remigius, priest of the Lord, Benedict, brother and fellow-servant in Christ Jesus, humble devotee of the monastic life: the gift of eternal blessing.

As a priest of the highest King, I rejoice in your most holy progress, because we are members of the supreme Head. Whatever I feel to be lacking in myself, I believe, praise be to God, that I possess wholly in you. Behold: what my sins have prevented from being accomplished, the priestly merits of your authority possess. Let human rumors about me cease now, since in you the perfection of every virtue is manifest.

I entrust this captive woman, besieged by the ancient enemy, to your high office, so that you may offer a sacred sacrifice to God for her liberation and may gladden me greatly by that victory itself. Farewell, most charming little stone of Christ’s priests.

When he was bidding farewell to the guests by means of these marked letters, he sent his own messenger with them to Gaul, so that he might offer this gift of such humility to blessed Remigius. When they entered the city of Rheims and the holy pontiff of the Lord had beheld the letter of so great a father, he burst into abundant tears and exclaimed:

“Thanks be to you, most merciful Christ the Redeemer, who have raised our times to such glory that throughout the whole world the Church magnifies you in your special servant Benedict.”

At once the glorious archimandrite Remigius rose and clothed himself, as was customary, in his episcopal vestment. Then, intending to offer sacrifice to God, he hurried into the church. When that pitiable girl, the consolation of her parents, had entered the church, that cunning and deceitful spirit unwillingly uttered these words through the girl’s mouth:

“O priest Remigius, do not boast against Benedict, for I am compelled to depart not by your command but by his humility.”

After these words the woman was freed. All who heard it gave glory to God, who is wondrous in his saints and blessed forever.

## [NOTE]

Hincmar, bishop of Rheims, the successor of Saint Remigius and the most ancient writer of his Life—he flourished in the time of Charlemagne, more than eight hundred years ago—reports this letter together with the miracle contained at its end.

Although, in the testament of Saint Remigius preserved by Brissonius in his *Formulas*, Remigius himself attributes to himself the miracle of healing the daughter of a certain nobleman named Benedict, we do not reject the possibility that this miracle may be attributed first and chiefly to the sacrifice of the Mass, secondly to the fervent prayers of Saint Remigius, and thirdly to the humility of Saint Benedict, which this entire letter—and indeed his whole life and teaching—displays to an extraordinary degree.

If you should still suspect that an error has entered this account because of the similarity of the name Benedict, why should the opposite conjecture not be more appealing: namely, that the agreement of these names provided Saint Remigius with a most suitable occasion for acknowledging the holy Benedict, whose reputation for holiness was spreading everywhere, and especially in our Gaul through Saint Romanus? Romanus had given the holy Father the habit of holy conduct. When he was divinely told to spare those places because “another friend” was there, he had come to Gaul, where he was building the monastery called Fons Regis in the territory of Auxerre at the time when Saint Maurus came to Gaul. This is attested by Adrevald of Fleury, who flourished in the year 890, in Book I of *The Miracles of Saint Benedict*, chapter 8.

The same letter is reported by the appendix to the *Chronicle of Cassino*, and by Arnold Uvion in Book I of *The Tree of Life*, who also says that it was printed frequently in various places. I saw it printed together with the Rule and with an exposition of the Rule made by Cardinal Torquemada, in the year 1517.

## SERMON OF SAINT BENEDICT ON THE DEATH OF SAINT PLACIDUS

Just as it belongs to a father to rejoice in the progress of his sons, so it belongs to sons to regard their father’s increase as their own gain. Therefore know that my sweetest and most beloved son Placidus, adorned with the robe of martyrdom, has departed to the Lord.

Already, with my inward eyes, I have led his spotless and God-pleasing sacrifice into the heights of heaven. When I received him from his father, I remembered that he was mortal, and my expectation did not deceive me. Now I have no cause for complaint; I have reason to give thanks to God, because I always desired that a sacrifice from the fruit of my heart should be offered to almighty God.

I had nothing more precious, nothing more beloved, nothing dearer than this sacrifice. For Placidus chose momentary death for Christ and reached him, reigning on the heavenly throne at the right hand of the Father. For this reason Christ died for all, so that we might live not for ourselves but for Christ.

I give thanks on behalf of all to the Redeemer, because I cannot be ungrateful. I ought to rejoice with myself that I possessed such a disciple, not grieve that I have lost him. The former was a gift; the latter is a debt. I performed the service of my disciple Placidus for as long as God willed; afterward, the One who gave him took him back.

What belonged to common nature, Placidus surrendered for Christ; what belongs to singular grace, he merited. Why should I grieve that my son Placidus has been taken from me, when God, not sparing his own Son for the sake of our salvation, handed him over for us all?

Who has ever been exempt from the condition of dying if he was not exempt from the condition of being born? Therefore I shall not mourn Placidus as a son, since I know that he has passed from death to life. In his death there is reason for rejoicing, not mourning, because he tasted death for the sake of truth.

Why should I mourn you, Placidus, dearest son, who were taken from me in such a way that you might belong to everyone? You have not lost the use of nature but exchanged it: previously separable from God in body, now abiding indivisibly with God.

Happy were the words I spent upon you! Happy the labors I endured for you! While you lived with me, not even the love of your father, the patrician Tertullus, could tear you away from me; nor did you ever place your father before me, until you departed into eternal life.

## [NOTE]

You may find this sermon in Surius, volume VII, in the Life of Saint Placidus, which is attributed to Cordianus, a disciple of Saint Benedict. It is also included in the appendix to the *Chronicle of Cassino*, at the end of the letter sent by the Sicilians to Saint Benedict, and it is cited by Arnold Uvion in Book I, chapter 1, of *The Tree of Life*.

Beyond the authorities mentioned above, a probable conjecture that it is by Saint Benedict is supplied by the similarity of its style to that of the preceding sermon delivered at the departure of Saint Maurus, which many ancient authors attribute to Saint Benedict.

# CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING LITTLE WORK

[Col. 0937]

[Col. 0937A]

We do not presume to present the following little work as the genuine offspring of the great Saint Benedict, although Arnold Wion had it printed as an appendix to the Benedictine Rule as early as 1593. The Fathers of the Bursfeld Congregation did the same at Paris in 1610, and the Cistercians inserted it into their statutes. Indeed, the editors at Lyons wished to include it in the *Great Library of the Fathers*.

For the celebrated Mabillon, when speaking of the letters to Saint Remigius, observes a profound silence concerning this little work. Nor does he regard those letters as true and genuine, even though he acknowledges the sermon of Saint Benedict delivered at the departure of Saint Maurus, while expressing it in different words.

For this reason the illustrious Calmet attributed this little work to Saint Benedict of Aniane, whose ardent zeal for monastic observance shone forth especially in the composition of his *Concordia of Monastic Rules*.

Whatever the case may be, it is a very ancient monument of monastic discipline, and therefore worthy of being numbered among the additions to the Holstenian codex, since the testimonies of so many learned men appended at the end of the work prove its antiquity abundantly.

# MONASTIC ORDER ATTRIBUTED TO SAINT FATHER BENEDICT

## How the brothers ought to conduct themselves religiously and diligently in the monastery and serve the Lord

[Col. 0937]

[Col. 0937B]

First of all, during the night hours, when a brother rises from bed for the divine office, he shall first make upon himself the sign of the holy cross through invocation of the holy Trinity. Then he shall say the verse, “Lord, open my lips”; afterward the psalm “O God, come to my assistance,” with “Glory be to the Father.”

Then the brother shall attend to the bodily needs of nature and hasten to the oratory, singing the psalm “To you, O Lord, I have lifted up my soul” to the end. He shall enter with the greatest reverence and caution, lest he disturb others who are praying. Having gone to a suitable place, he shall pour out his prayers in the presence of the Lord, more with the heart than with the mouth, so that his voice may be nearer to God than to himself. Then he shall give thanks to God, saying:

“I give you thanks, almighty God, who have deigned to guard me during this night. I beseech your boundless mercy to grant that I may spend the coming day in your service with humility and discernment, so that I may please you. Amen.”

Then let everyone be ready, standing in his place in the choir in orderly fashion, so that when the final signal has ceased they may offer praises to God in the presence of the angels with the utmost humility and propriety.

If someone is troubled by frequent coughing or phlegm from his chest or nostrils, let him spit behind his back or beside him. Let him take particular care that it does not turn the sick brothers’ stomachs; rather, whatever is spat out should always be trampled underfoot, so that, when they hasten to prayer, their garments may not be soiled. This rule is to be observed everywhere: whether in the church, the refectory, the portico, or any other place and gathering. Whatever is spat out must be trampled underfoot.

After the nocturnal praise has been completed, let there be absolute silence during the interval, both in voice and in walking, and in the sound of anything else, so that each person may confess his sins to the Lord without disturbing another and may ask, with tears, for pardon and remission of them.

When the signal sounds at the beginning of dawn, let everyone hasten with humility of heart, as though crying out to God and making himself acceptable to his mercy. With ready willingness, measured tones, neither excessively prolonged nor excessively hurried, and with the greatest gravity and propriety, let them perform the divine office of morning praise. During this morning praise also, let there be complete and principal silence in praying or speaking.

When the brothers assemble for Prime, after the office itself has been completed and before the fiftieth psalm, let them confess their sins to one another, praying for each other with humble eagerness. When this is finished, let them all come to the chapter-house. Turning toward the east, let them salute the cross and humble themselves on every side before the other brothers; let them do likewise at every gathering.

After the names of the saints whose feasts the following day will celebrate have been recited, let them rise together and say the verse “Precious,” followed by a prayer from the prior; then the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” three times, with “Glory be to the Father.” Rising again, let them say the verse “Look upon your servants, O Lord,” with “Glory be to the Father.” After this verse let the prior say the prayer “Direct and sanctify, O Lord,” etc.

Afterward, the one who is at fault shall ask pardon and receive punishment according to the measure of his fault. In the cloister as well as in any gathering or place, let a brother ask pardon before the lord abbot, provost, dean, or any of the elders. When the elder says, “What is the cause?”, the brother who asks pardon shall reply, “My fault, lord.” If he says anything else, he shall thereby be judged guilty.

Afterward the lord abbot or the others from whom obedience is to be received shall say whatever is necessary and useful for the monastery as a whole. The brother who asks pardon for his fault must be judged by the prior with greater mercy and leniency in proportion to the depth of his humility and the force with which he declares himself guilty. For it is necessary that throughout this present life we judge all our negligences—whether of thought, tongue, or deed—through humble confession and humility, so that they may not make us guilty after death.

Rising from the chapter-house and going out to their work, let all those present together say the verse “O God, come to my assistance,” etc., “Glory be to the Father,” and the Lord’s Prayer, kneeling. After the Lord’s Prayer, let the prior say, “Our help is in the name of the Lord,” and let everyone answer, “Who made heaven and earth.”

Then let them all go together or separately to the work assigned to them. Maintaining silence, let them sing psalms or say the Lord’s Prayer, in pairs or individually, according to what is appropriate, speaking of nothing else except, perhaps, what must necessarily be said about the work itself; and let that be said cautiously.

When the signal for the divine office at the canonical hours is heard, as the Rule prescribes, let them immediately leave whatever they have in their hands, taking care nevertheless that it does not perish. Then let them all assemble at the entrance of the oratory, or at least be ready for obedience, and let them say the verse “Blessed are you, Lord God, because you have heard me and consoled me,” three times, the prior beginning, and adding “Glory be to the Father,” while kneeling. When the prayer has been completed, let them rise, and let the prior say, “May almighty God have mercy on us,” to which all shall answer, “Amen.”

From the Kalends of October until Easter, let them do this at the third hour; from Easter until the Kalends of October, let it be done at the sixth and ninth hours.

At all times, let the strictest silence be maintained in the church, except for what pertains to the ears of God. No brother shall ever dare to call another by his bare name. Rather, as is fitting, let the elders call the younger brothers “brothers,” while the younger shall call their elders “grandfathers,” which expresses paternal reverence. Let everyone call the abbot “lord” and “father.”

[Col. 0939A]

Let no one utter any other oath except “Believe me,” as we read that the Lord affirmed to the Samaritan woman in the Gospel, or else “Certainly” or “Truly.”

If a brother is rebuked by the prior for any reason, or by anyone else, even by a younger brother, let him immediately fall on his face with the greatest speed and ask pardon. For this humility is offered to God, not to man, and, if it is done from the heart, it will merit forgiveness.

Above all, they must be obedient to one another. Obedience itself, if it is offered wholly to God with an upright heart, is what leads to life. For one prayer of an obedient person is heard more quickly than ten thousand prayers of one who despises obedience.

Whenever brothers meet one another, let the younger everywhere say to the elder, “Bless me.” If the younger is sitting and an elder passes by, let him rise; and if the elder wishes to sit, let the younger not sit unless ordered to do so.

If a brother is found to be retaining envy, anger, or sadness in his heart, let him immediately be corrected so that he may amend. For however many days he neglects to confess this, let him do penance for that many days. If he answers humbly and asks for penance, let him be judged with pardon.

When the lord abbot, or any of the elders, commands a brother to perform some task, let the younger receive the command of the one ordering it with the utmost propriety. Let his ear be ready to hear as though the command were spoken by God; let his feet be prepared, his hands ready to perform the work; and, with his head bowed, let him say, “Bless me.”

When they leave a house or a gathering, let them say, “Bless me,” even if they are alone, because the Lord is present everywhere, ready to demand an account from each person who asks.

If a brother has neglected something in the storeroom, refectory, kitchen, or any other place, let him immediately, without any delay, run to ask pardon. If the thing he neglected is one that he can hold in his hand, let him hold it while prostrating himself on the ground and asking pardon for what he has done.

Let them beware of worldly and excessive laughter and of frequent conversation with secular friends, except when necessity requires it. When it cannot be otherwise, no one shall speak alone with a secular person unless other brothers are present and listening, brothers whose faith is known to be trustworthy. Let this be observed especially among the young, for a mind that desires to serve God must despise and abandon the speech and company of worldly people.

Let them not wander about within the monastery wherever they wish unless the obedience assigned to each person requires it or they have obtained permission.

Let them not presume to undertake any work, even if it appears good, without an order. Let them neither give nor receive anything without the abbot’s command. Let no one possess anything as his own except what the abbot has given or permitted. No one shall be given more in food, drink, or clothing than the Rule prescribes. Whoever desires to possess more does not fear to stir up against himself an opportunity for our hidden enemy.

[Col. 0939D]

Let no one reproach another with a past or shameful sin. If an elder sees a younger brother sinning, let him correct him privately, between himself and that brother alone, once, twice, and three times, but only in the case of lighter faults. If a serious offense is committed, let the offender immediately be corrected according to the Rule.

Anyone who wishes to correct another should take care to bind up the wound gently according to the nature of the neglect, because a broken limb is often broken more severely by careless binding.

For impure thoughts and harmful or foolish speech, let the brother always have recourse to confession. Let the brothers answer one another humbly.

When the signal for a canonical hour is heard, let them quickly return to prayer, and let them not quarrel about anything. If a quarrel should occur, let the one who first becomes silent be considered the wiser.

Let them take no food before or after the appointed hour, except for the sick and children, whose weakness the prior must consider.

Let no one slander or consent to a slanderer. Let the brothers sow peace among themselves, not the discord of worldly people. Let stories and idle tales be far from them.

At the appointed hours, let them not neglect manual labor, since it is beneficial to soul and body. During the other hours, let them devote themselves to reading. If possible, let them sit in one place or in the cloister, so that, seeing one another, they may restrain themselves, and let them read in silence. Let no one join himself to another unless necessity requires it; even then, let it be done without disturbing the other.

In summer, let each person go to his own place with the greatest caution and, without disturbing anyone else, read or sleep.

No brother shall call anything his own—whether an object or any part of his body—but always call it “ours.” The only thing that should be called one’s own is “my fault.” Everything that God gives us ought to be held in common, except sin, which comes from our weakness.

The abbot’s command concerning anything must be fulfilled with the greatest care, because this same obedience, if rightly carried out, is rendered not to the one who commands but to God. If it should be neglected—which God forbid—the offender must quickly return to ask forgiveness.

When they stand in the choir to sing psalms, let them sing with one voice and one heart. Let the verse be begun by the one who can do so more usefully than the others, so that the rest may join him by the first or second syllable in their vocal pronunciation.

At the hour of eating, after the office has been completed, let them wait in the church, singing in the choir. When they hear the cymbal, let them enter the refectory in orderly fashion and without any noise, having washed their hands. Let them salute the cross with their faces turned toward the east, and let everyone sit at the table in his proper order, in complete silence.

No one shall presume to take any food or drink before the lord abbot; the abbot himself, however, shall not delay in taking it. When they receive bread, let each brother say to the other, “Bless me,” and let the other answer, “The Lord.” Let them do the same with drink when they first drink. It is not necessary to ask for another blessing over the other dishes on the table.

Before they begin eating, let the reader ask for a blessing and begin reading. Let no voice be heard there except that of the reader, unless something brief is said for edification.

Afterward, whatever dish is served from the kitchen, the server shall begin with the last person and continue serving until he reaches the lord abbot. Then let the cymbal be sounded quietly, and let the brothers say, “Bless me,” with equal and prolonged voice. After the blessing has been given in common, let them wait, as we have already said, for the abbot to take his portion first; afterward, let each say, “Bless me.”

When they bless food, drink, or anything else, let them bless it standing, not sitting. If something is to be mixed with such things, the cellarer shall make a small sign to the server. The young brothers shall immediately rise to mix it, fill the washed cups with a measured quantity of water, and stand in order as they are positioned.

Then the cellarer shall again sound the cymbal quietly, and the brothers shall say together, with one prolonged voice, “Bless me.” After the prior has given the blessing, the younger brother who places the cup in the hand of the seated brother shall humbly bow his head. When the work of mixing has been completed, let him bow around to all the brothers and likewise to their tables.

Apples and every kind of produce of the earth that is eaten raw, whether at the hour of the midday meal or together with other food, shall be divided by the cellarer among the individual brothers before they come to the table or sit down. They shall eat these immediately after the other food has been served.

When this has been completed, let the reading end at once. Rising from the table after the appointed verse has been said, let the left choir leave first in orderly fashion, the right choir afterward, and the lord abbot last. Let them sing the psalm “Have mercy on me, O God,” and so forth, distinctly and without haste.

When they enter the oratory, let them bow while singing until “Glory.” At “Glory,” let them kneel. After the Lord’s Prayer, let them rise and go in silence according to what is suitable for the time.

After Vespers, when the signal has been given at the appropriate hour, let everyone assemble in the chapter-house. Let Scripture that edifies the hearers be read for as long as the hour permits. When the reading is finished, let everyone rise together, and let the lord abbot say, “Our help is in the name of the Lord.” Let everyone answer, “Who made heaven and earth.” Then, in silence and reverence, let them enter Compline, pray with concentrated minds, confess their sins to one another, and thus begin Compline.

When the office has been completed, let them maintain absolute silence. Let prayers be made secretly with mouth and heart, together with recollection of sins, groaning, tears, and weeping, but without sighing in such a way that anyone disturbs another.

Then let each give thanks to God in these words:

“I give you thanks, almighty and eternal God, who through your holy mercy have deigned to guard me on this day. I beseech your boundless mercy to grant that I may pass through this night without any sin or hindrance from Satan, in sweet and chaste rest, so that, when morning comes, I may rise pure and energetic and be able to offer praises to you, my God.”

Then, with great caution, let them go to the dormitory. When a brother has approached his own bed and is settling himself, let him say the psalm “O God, come to my assistance,” in full, with “Glory.” Then let him say the verse, “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth and a door of restraint for my lips.” Thus let him fortify himself with the sign of the holy cross and sleep in the Lord. Amen.

## [NOTE]

This is how it appears in an old Cassinese manuscript, a copy extracted from the original and communicated to me by the Reverend Father James du Breuil, a monk of Saint-Germain-des-Prés. That manuscript attributes these ordinances to Saint Benedict because they were found at the end of the Rule which Saint Benedict wrote with his own hands and handed to Saint Maurus when he sent him to Gaul.

Dom Peter the Venerable, the ninth abbot of the monastery of Cluny, found them in that same Rule at the greater monastery of Tours—the Rule being preserved there as a relic—and asked that they be sent to him. Thus the manuscript records it.

If this is so, these ordinances must be considered very ancient. Even if they are not by Saint Benedict, they were at least the pious and holy constitutions of a most ancient monastery of our Gaul. For this reason Brother Arnold Wion arranged for them to be printed together with the Rule at Venice in 1593, by the Giunti press.

# CERTAIN MONUMENTS TO BE APPENDED TO THE WORKS OF SAINT FATHER BENEDICT

[Col. 0941]

## SERMON OF ALBERIC THE DEACON ON SAINT SCHOLASTICA (S)

### PROLOGUE

[Col. 0941C]

At the time when Justin the Elder governed the laws of the Roman commonwealth, and John, of blessed memory, was regarded as a pontiff most worthy of the supreme see both in life and in teaching, Saint Benedict, a father truly and in every respect apostolic, shone forth in the western regions. East and west, south and north marvel at his incomparable holiness, magnificent virtues, and astonishing signs.

He had a sister named Scholastica, who from infancy, under the instruction of the Holy Spirit, lived in the school of Christ in the habit of a consecrated woman. Through continual fasts, frequent prayers, tireless vigils, the privilege of compunction, and the grace of tears, she appeared entirely unequalled among those whose company she was permitted to share.

To enclose her innumerable virtues in very few words, she was Benedict’s sister not only by blood but also in holiness. Following her brother in conduct and in bodily footsteps, she established herself, with his will and consent, near Mount Cassino. There, as will become clear in what follows, she completed her most holy life by a celebrated death.

When she came there, she earnestly begged her brother to grant her at least one day from the whole year, on which she might visit him at an appointed place and converse with him about faith, hope, love of God, and love of neighbor.

Her holy brother consented to his sister’s pious requests and judged suitable for this purpose a place on the downward slope of the mountain, where later generations built a church in honor of the same virgin. The ascent to it would not be excessively burdensome for the virgin, while the descent from the monastery would not be far for him.

To this place, for as long as her virginal soul governed her body, the virgin ascended every year on the appointed day, and Benedict descended, always accompanied by a choir of disciples. Having spent that day in conversation about spiritual matters and, as the sun declined, refreshed their bodies with thanksgiving, she returned to the cell of the virgins and he to the dwelling of the monks.

## THE SERMON BEGINS

[Col. 0941]

[Col. 0941D]

“At that time Jesus told his disciples this parable:

‘The kingdom of heaven is like ten virgins who took their lamps and went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. Five of them were foolish and five wise.’ And so forth. Matthew 25:1.

You have heard, dearest brothers, that the kingdom of heaven was compared with ten virgins who, having taken their lamps, went out to meet the bridegroom and the bride. You have heard that among those same virgins some were sluggish through the fault of foolishness, while others were skillful through the virtue of prudence.

You have heard that the foolish, having taken their lamps, did not take oil with them, while the prudent had with them both lamps and oil in vessels. When the bridegroom delayed for a long time, both the foolish and the prudent fell asleep together.
