At midnight a cry was made announcing the bridegroom’s arrival, and all rose together to prepare their lamps. When the lamps of the foolish virgins had gone out because the oil was exhausted, the foolish virgins were sent by the prudent to the sellers of oil. While they were going away, those who were ready entered together with the bridegroom into the wedding feast. When the foolish returned, the door was shut, and they repeatedly raised their supplications that the door should be opened to them. The bridegroom immediately answered them in these words: ‘Amen, I say to you, I do not know you.’

When the parable had ended, a concluding admonition was immediately added, the Lord saying: ‘Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.’”

My brothers, I wish to pass briefly before your ears through the profound mysteries of this comparison, as far as I am able without the darkness of obscurity, so that afterward we may freely devote an appropriate interval to the praises of the holy virgin Scholastica, whose departure to the heavenly realms we celebrate today.

You know, beloved brothers, that this is the rule of the Catholic faith: it affirms that the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit are three persons, and it holds each of these persons individually to be perfect God, while teaching that all three together are not three gods but one God, who is to be believed in the heart for salvation and confessed with the mouth for righteousness.

Thus the unity of the Godhead joined to the Trinity of persons produces the number four. The number five is completed when we believe in the emptying of the Word of God, of whom it is written that he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of human beings and found in appearance as a human being, and humbling himself, offering obedience to the Father even unto death, and death upon a cross.

Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name that is above every name, so that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus sits at the right hand of the Majesty on high, from where he will come to judge the living and the dead.

Since this, then, is the orthodox and apostolic faith—that the unity of the Godhead is believed in three persons, and that the Word made flesh is believed to have accomplished the salvation of the human race through the flesh—it is entirely right and fitting that all who hold this faith of the fivefold reckoning should be designated by the number five.

They are also most appropriately called virgins because they could not be divided from the integrity of this faith by any schism or violated by any pollution of heresy.

But because this faith is dead in some people, according to James, when it lacks works of love, while in others, according to Paul, it does not cease to work through love, in both groups faith, divided into five parts, completes the number ten.

The five prudent virgins, therefore, are most suitably understood as those in whom the faith signified by the number five continually watches through the works of righteousness, moved by the affection of love.

Those in whom this same faith perhaps performs works that appear to belong to righteousness, but in whom the works proceed more from the pursuit of some temporal gain than from the intention of a loving affection, are likewise called virgins and five, because of the undefiled faith signified by the fivefold compunction; yet they are called foolish because of the unintelligent and misguided intention of their works.

That people lacking charity and love can nevertheless perform many things that appear to be righteous, while receiving no benefit of salvation from them, the Chosen Vessel makes perfectly clear when he writes:

“And if I distribute all my possessions as food for the poor, and if I hand over my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing.”

This, then, is the oil which the foolish virgins do not have in their vessels—that is, in the inner receptacles of the human person—and therefore they are called foolish. Oil signifies charity because, just as oil always rises above all liquids with which it is mixed, so charity surpasses all virtues. Hence the Teacher of the Gentiles, intending to speak of charity, first says: “I will show you, brothers, a more excellent way.” And after recalling many things in praise of charity, he adds: “Now these three remain: faith, hope, and charity; but the greatest of these is charity.”

This, then, most beloved brothers, is the oil by whose light the holy works of the prudent virgins, as though nourished by it, emit a great brilliance of light. Because the foolish virgins’ lamps—that is, their works—do not possess the nourishment of this oil, although they may by no means seem to be extinguished in the present, they nevertheless shine only to be extinguished in the course of the strict examination. All these virgins prepare themselves to go out to meet the bridegroom and the bride, because the fivefold faith is held by everyone in the hope that, after the span of life has been completed, all may joyfully present themselves before the sight of Christ the Bridegroom and his bride, who is the heavenly Jerusalem.

But while the bridegroom delays, all the virgins grow drowsy and sleep, because while the Judge postpones the examination, everyone begins the course of this life and measures out what has been begun. To grow drowsy is to begin the course of life; to sleep is to pass through it by measuring out what has once been begun. That the name “sleep” can signify the course of this life, we are instructed by the authority of the Psalmist, who says: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands.” All the men of riches sleep their sleep while they continue to walk through the span of this present life. But they are said not to be sleeping, but to have slept, when death has already brought their course of life to an end. Then they find nothing in their hands, because here they have left behind all the riches they gathered in vain.

While this sleep is received by both the foolish and the prudent virgins, so that all may hasten to meet the bridegroom, a cry is heard at midnight. This present age, my brothers, is called night in comparison with the future, because here, according to the Apostle, “we see through a mirror and in an enigma,” but then “face to face”; and here “we know in part,” but then “we shall know even as we are known”—when, namely, the Lord will come, who will both bring to light the hidden things of darkness and reveal the counsels of hearts, and then each person will have praise from God.

At this midnight, then—this night not yet ended, not yet completed—a loud voice is heard, so that all the virgins ought to prepare themselves to meet the bridegroom who is coming. This, most beloved brothers, is the cry enjoined by the Lord’s command upon Isaiah, who says to him: “Climb upon a high mountain, you who evangelize Zion; raise your voice with strength, you who evangelize Jerusalem; raise it, do not fear. Say to the cities of Judah: Behold your God; behold, the Lord God will come in strength, and his arm will rule.” Again he cries to the same man: “Do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet, and announce to my people their crimes, and to the house of Jacob their sins.”

You have heard, brothers, that in the prophet’s cry, though the words are different, the meaning is not different: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming”; “Behold,” he says, “your God”; “Behold,” he says, “the Lord will come in strength.” You have heard that the prophet is also commanded to shout and cry, “Go out to meet him,” when he is ordered by the Lord’s voice to announce to his people their crimes, and to the house of Jacob their sins, together with the many things that follow. In all these things, certainly, nothing else is being done except the admonition that urges the virgins to go out to meet the bridegroom who is coming.

This cry, brothers, while we sleep in the night of this age, is made in our ears through the Law, through the Psalms, through the prophecies, through the Gospels, through the apostolic Epistles, and through the expositions and admonitions of the orthodox Fathers. This is the cry of all; this is the proclamation of all: “Behold, the bridegroom is coming; go out to meet him.” Behold, he is coming; he is near; he will already be present. Go out, meet him, run to meet him. It is already the hour to rise from sleep, for now our salvation is nearer than when we believed. The night has passed; the day has drawn near. Let us cast off the works of darkness and put on the weapons of light; let us walk honorably as in the day.

At this cry the virgins—both prudent and foolish—rise; they prepare their lamps and make themselves ready for their works. The foolish virgins lack oil; they lack the affection of love; they lack the intention of charity; they lack the compassion that would enable them to earn mercy at the strict examination. Oil receives its name from mercy: for ἔλεος in Greek is called misericordia, “mercy,” in Latin, and therefore mercy is suitably signified by oil.

Do not think, dearest brothers, that I am now saying something different from what previously sounded in your ears from my mouth. It may perhaps appear to some that what I previously said—that charity ought to be understood by oil—is different from what I now say, namely, that mercy is signified by oil. Never, my brothers, can charity be separated from the compassion of mercy; never can mercy be without the affection of love. Oil, therefore, cannot be a type of charity without also being equally a type of mercy; nor can it bear the figure of mercy without likewise bearing the figure of charity. When, therefore, charity is said to be signified by oil, mercy too is understood to be signified by oil at the same time. And when mercy is said to be designated by oil, love must necessarily be understood to be designated by oil as well.

The foolish virgins, then, do not have this oil, and often they recognize that they do not have it. They lack compassion; they lack the affection of love; they understand that they are without it. Therefore they flee to the prudent virgins and beg them to give them some of their oil. Sometimes the reprobate understand that their works are either not right or do not proceed from a right intention. They understand and are pierced with compunction; but because they are sown beside the road and are temporary, they believe for a time and, when tribulation comes, fall away.

The foolish virgins come to the prudent, loudly declaring that their lamps are being extinguished and demanding that oil be given them. For sometimes the reprobate, struck with compunction, flee to holy men and openly confess that the good things they seem to do proceed from an evil intention. They commend themselves to their charity; they commend themselves to their love; they commend themselves to their prayers; they commend themselves to the compassion of their hearts. This is to ask them for oil; this is to wish their lamps to burn from the warmth they provide.

But you have heard what the prudent virgins replied: “Perhaps,” they say, “there will not be enough for us and for you. Go instead to those who sell it, and buy some for yourselves.”

Sometimes, brothers, the God-fearing say this; humble souls say this. They answer those who strive to commend themselves to their prayers and supplications: “Hardly do our prayers, hardly do our petitions, hardly do the services we offer to God suffice even for us. Hardly are we such people as may be found worthy to be heard on our own behalf. Our prayers and our service before God are not so important that through them others can obtain salvation. Do not place your hope in our prayers, which are of no account; strive instead to labor for yourselves.”

You yourselves confess that you do not possess oil. You can find many sellers of oil. The sellers of oil, the sellers of mercy, are the poor, because when we show mercy to them, we ourselves earn mercy from the Lord. These are the people who, through the bond of friendship arising from the unrighteous mammon, receive us into eternal dwellings. And with the measure by which we measure to them, it will be measured back to us. Go, then, to these people; make them your friends. Give from your mammon of iniquity—not with the intention of vanity, as you have done until now, but in the hope of obtaining oil, in the hope of attaining divine mercy. Be certain and without doubt, for they will give into your bosom “a good measure, pressed down, shaken together, and running over.”

The foolish virgins hear the counsel of the prudent and go to buy oil. But while they are going, the bridegroom comes; he enters with those who are prepared for the wedding, and the door is shut.

What does “they go” mean? They decide, determine, and arrange. To decide, determine, or arrange something in the mind is to go. They are said to have gone to buy oil, not to have bought it. They go, but they do not buy, because they determine but do not act; they promise but do not fulfill; they make assurances but do not carry them out. They delay, procrastinate, and put things off.

While the foolish are going to buy oil, and the prudent are fitting their lamps with the oil they have in their vessels, the bridegroom comes. For while the reprobate continually delay doing good and the elect persist in doing it without ceasing, the Judge summons both to examination through death. The elect are taken through death into glory, while through death the door is likewise closed to the reprobate, never to be opened to them again forever.

That hour has already come upon them of which Truth speaks elsewhere: “The hour will come when no one can work.” The acceptable time has passed from them, and so has the day of salvation, of which the Lord says through the prophetic voice: “At an acceptable time I have heard you, and on the day of salvation I have helped you.” Therefore they repeat their cries in vain, though the time for being heard has expired; and it is said to them: “Truly I say to you, I do not know you.” He denies them in that life who denied him in this life, if not in words, then nevertheless by their deeds.

That what the Lord has affirmed in words can be denied by deeds is plainly shown by the testimony of the eminent preacher, who spoke these words concerning certain people who taught what was right but did not withdraw from what was wrong: “They profess that they know God, but by their deeds they deny him.” What, then, the whole sequence of the parable is directed toward, the concluding admonition immediately makes clear, when the Lord adds and says: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

Having briefly completed the explanation of the Gospel reading, let the next part of our discourse now turn, as we promised at the very beginning, to the praise of the virgin whose natal day we celebrate. Let it first be our concern to observe that Scholastica lacked none of those things which, according to the Lord’s account, we have learned the prudent virgins to possess.

She shone with complete virginity: in addition to the common virginity of faith, she preserved the chastity of her flesh with an undefiled purity of spirit. She was prudent: fixing her eyes upon the ends of things, she provided herself with lasting goods through untiring constancy. She kindled her lamp to meet the bridegroom: longing for the vision of Christ, she scattered everywhere the light of holy actions, brighter than the rays of the sun. She received oil in her vessels; in the receptacles of her soul she always kept the nourishment of devoted charity.

Through the inward power of this charity Scholastica was able, by the miraculous display of a wonder through which she watered the face of heaven with showers of tears, to resist the will of her most holy brother and prevent him from returning to the brothers as he had planned, while heaven itself fought on her behalf.

Thus prepared, with her lamps lit, she went out today to meet the bridegroom who was coming, and rejoicing she entered with him into the nuptial feast.

What sort of gentleness her soul possessed while governing her bodily members became known to the world when God revealed it, at the moment when she was commanded to leave the prison of the body: for she was shown to the eyes of her brother entering the secrets of heaven in the form of a bird without gall.

Other properties of the dove are also said to exist, most beloved brothers, whose mysteries can most suitably and truly be applied to the most holy virgin. This bird is said willingly and frequently to build its nest in the holes of a rock; it is said to eat nothing living; it is said to defend itself neither with its beak nor with its claws, but by the movement of its wings; it is said to love companionship in flight; it is said to have bleary eyes; and, flying against the rays of the sun, it is unable with clear sight to see the hawk approaching it.

Therefore it is said to be accustomed to perch upon a tree planted beside flowing waters, and, unable to expose its eyes to the sun’s rays, to fix them upon the waters and, observing in the waters the hawk’s reflected image, to avoid its deceits and attacks as it hastens to seize it. Who, then, my brothers, does not know that the song of doves is nothing other than a groan?

If we contemplate all these properties in Scholastica, most beloved brothers, many reasons will become clear why divine Wisdom judged it fitting to reveal to her brother’s eyes the soul of the virgin, departed from the body, in the form of a dove.

Our dove, then, nested in the holes of the rock, for she placed all her confidence for salvation and life in the passion and death of Christ. The Chosen Vessel taught you that Christ is called the Rock. This rock was pierced at the time when his feet and hands were fastened to the cross with iron nails. The opening in this rock was also that place where a soldier opened his side by thrusting in a lance.

In these openings, then, Scholastica established her nest, because through them she placed an undoubted hope for herself of an eternal dwelling in heaven. In these openings she established her nest, because she held with certain faith that they were the causes of her salvation. In these openings, I say, she established her nest, in which she preserved herself most securely from the devil, the hawk of souls.

Nothing living was the food of our dove; for, hearing the Apostle, she strove to put to death her flesh with its vices and desires. She defended herself from no one with claws or beak, but solely with the protection of her wings: knowing nothing of repaying evil with evil, she fortified herself against all adversaries through love of God and neighbor alone.

She loved companionship in flight, for she sought to draw with her toward heaven everyone whom she could. She had bleary eyes, for in this life she saw, with Paul, “through a mirror and in an enigma.” The tree planted beside flowing waters, upon whose summit this dove was accustomed to perch, is Christ the Lord. Upon whose head—which the Apostle testifies to be God—she established for herself a seat most firm and fortified.

According to the psalmist prophet, this tree is planted beside channels of waters because whatever the faithful believe about him is firmly established by the authorities of Scripture. “Deep waters,” says the wisest of men, “are words from the mouth of a man, and a flowing torrent is a fountain of wisdom.” Fixing her gaze upon these waters, she detected the approaching hawk; intent upon the sacred Scriptures, she perceived the ambushes of the treacherous enemy and avoided them.

The song of our dove was a groan. Imitating prophetic action, she labored in her groaning; each night she washed her bed and watered her couch with tears, and from the voice of her groaning “her bones clung to her skin.”

Finally, my brothers, to commend the most holy virgin in the fewest and most sufficient words: she was Benedict’s sister by blood and also by holiness.

Having completed these brief praises of the virgin, let us return, most beloved brothers, to exhorting you. Let us impress again and again upon both your ears and your minds that conclusion of the Gospel reading: “Therefore keep watch, because you do not know the day or the hour.”

Keep watch, brothers, I exhort, urge, and admonish you. Keep watch, because you do not know the day of your departure, and you are ignorant of the hour. Run while you have the light, lest the darkness of death overtake you. Work while there is opportunity, while it is permitted, while the Judge postpones the sentence. For the hour will come when no one will be able to work.

With the Apostle we exhort you not to receive the grace of God in vain. For he says: “At an acceptable time I heard you, and on the day of salvation I helped you.” Behold, now is the acceptable time; behold, now is the day of salvation.

Seek, then, my most beloved brothers, the Lord while he can be found; call upon him while he is near. Let the wicked man abandon his way, and the unjust man his thoughts; let him return to the Lord, and he will have mercy on him, and to our God, for he is abundant in forgiveness.

Is honor lost? It can be recovered. Is rank lost? It can be recovered. Are riches lost? They can be recovered. Countless are the things that can be recovered after being lost. But if the time for working, the time for repentance, and the time for pleasing God are once lost, they can never be recovered again forever.

We know, most beloved brothers, that it is still permitted us to turn to God through repentance; but we do not know whether this permission will remain with us until evening. Knowing, therefore, most beloved, that God’s patience leads us to repentance, let us not, according to our hardness and impenitent heart, store up wrath for ourselves on the day of wrath and of the revelation of God’s just judgment, who will repay each person according to his works.

Therefore keep watch, most beloved brothers; keep watch, because you do not know the day, and you are ignorant of the hour. “Blessed are those servants,” says Truth, “whom the Lord, when he comes, will find watching. Truly I say to you, he will set them over all his goods.”

May Christ Jesus our Lord make us participants in those goods. To him, with the Father and the life-giving Spirit, power, dominion, and authority remain without end, for ever and ever. Amen.

[Column 0949]

THE RULE OF THE HOLY ABBOTS PAUL AND STEPHEN FOR MONKS. (C,S)*

TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING THE RULE OF THE HOLY ABBOTS PAUL AND STEPHEN

[Column 0949B] Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, very frequently cites testimonies from the Rule of Paul and Stephen in the Concordia of Rules, or, as on pages 388 and 619, “From the Rule of the holy Paul and Stephen”; he also sometimes cites it under the name of Stephen alone or of Saint Stephen.

[Column 0950B] Abbot Smaragdus, in his Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 23: “Concerning this chapter the abbots Paul and Stephen wrote as follows: If anyone [does this] to another, etc.,” as in chapter 36.

CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

[Column 0949]

[Column 0949C] Even if we are ignorant of the homeland and status of these two holy men, and cannot ascertain the monks for whom this rule was composed, they nevertheless seem to have lived in some region where grain was threshed in the countryside and in the fields, as is customary among the Italians and Spaniards. The often-mentioned Calmet thinks that these saints wrote their rule around the time of Saint Benedict.

This alone is certain: Saint Augustine is expressly praised there in chapter 14, and Holy Scripture is usually cited according to the Old Vulgate, not according to Saint Jerome’s translation. It will therefore be difficult to assign a definite period to these saints, although they are the true authors of this Rule, which Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, cites under their name in his Concordia of Rules.

[Column 0949]

TABLE OF CONTENTS

[Column 0949D] 1. First, concerning the fear of God, mutual charity from a pure heart, and the unanimity that must be maintained. 2. What the seniors ought to be like toward the juniors. 3. How the juniors ought to conduct themselves toward the seniors. 4. That no one may leave the Work of God without permission. [Column 0950D] 5. That the beginning of a verse in the choir should be begun by one person. 6. That it should continually be pronounced by the choirs. 7. Concerning the manner of psalmody and the judgment of the seniors. 8. That those who sing should not grow drowsy. 9. That no one should occupy those who are singing and praying even with the slightest conversation. [Column 0951A] 10. That after Prime no one should lie back in bed. 11. That at midday each person should sleep in his own bed for a prescribed period. 12. That they should chant the Divine Office with discipline while at work. 13. That at the hour when Communion is to be received, all who are within the same enclosure should strive to be present. 14. That what has been ordered to be sung should be sung. 15. Concerning those who are learning the Psalms: that those assigned to dictate them should observe the rule. 16. That what is received from the juniors according to custom should be returned at table. 17. That no one should presume to exceed the established measure in food or drink. [Column 0951B] 18. That while eating they should listen quietly to what is read. 19. That no one should arrange to eat anything privately at table. 20. That no one should move from the table assigned to him to another. 21. That an overflowing cup should not be mixed. 22. Concerning the turns of the ministers. 23. If someone from the order of juniors is removed from a ministry. 24. That no one should presume upon what has been assigned to another. 25. That those entrusted with custody should serve with devoted charity, and should not themselves, conversely, be vexed improperly. 26. That no one should dare to enter the storeroom or the workshops of the craftsmen importunately and without being ordered. 27. That no one should presume to use another’s possessions, nor should they be permitted to exchange them among themselves. 28. Concerning the preservation of clothing and bedding. 29. That no one should cut his hair except by order of the prior. 30. Concerning what one brother finds when another has lost it. 31. Concerning those who wish to learn any craft. 32. That everyone should promptly attend in the bakery or at any agricultural labor. 33. Concerning work from an earlier time, and that nothing necessary should be withheld even from those who are negligent. [Column 0952B] 34. That at prayer the accustomed laziness should be cast off. 35. Concerning the care of tools during work. 36. That no one should conceal the person who has sinned. 37. That excessive joking and laughter should be avoided. 38. That one person should not involve himself when others are quarreling. 39. That no one should involve himself in extraneous matters. 40. That no one should dare to avenge himself by human strength against the wicked excesses of peasants. 41. That the rules of the Fathers should also be read assiduously.

I. First of all, therefore, we exhort everyone to possess the fear of God, mutual charity, and unanimity in good pursuits.

II. The seniors should show paternal affection toward the juniors. [Column 0951C] When it is necessary to command, they should enjoin what is needed for the common good, not with swelling hostility and loud voices, but confidently, with tranquil simplicity and the authority of a good life.

III. The juniors should obey the seniors with sincere submission. They should not answer with a swelling neck in any matter, nor, with a disdainful mind and an inattentive ear, refuse to obey those who command. Rather, unanimously and harmoniously, in both spiritual work and earthly labor, all should respond with faithful intention.

IV. No one may leave the Work of God without the prior’s permission. Whoever is compelled by an evident cause may leave only after requesting and receiving the prior’s prayer. [Column 0951D] They should not leave in pairs or groups of three, but singly, requesting prayer; those who are healthy should return immediately, while the sick may return to bed with permission.

V. The seniors who stand in the choir should begin the beginnings of the verses being sung. If illness prevents them, those should begin whom the Father has ordered to do so. Once they have begun, all should immediately join in—if possible on the first or second syllable—with one accord and one voice, so that there may be no dissonance among the singers, which usually arises especially from an irregular beginning and from a kind of contentious variation.

VI. The juniors, especially those who are still preparing to learn the Psalms, should dictate them through the choirs in order and without negligence. Thus, from the place where the younger ones still do not know, those juniors who have already completed the Psalter should succeed one another in order in dictating, so that the practice of recitation may never be lacking.

VII. The manner of psalmody, if possible, must always be maintained by us with moderation, so that it is neither drawn out excessively nor shortened beyond measure, but, as has been said, always spoken with measured modulation. Nevertheless, the prior’s will and judgment must be observed. He must always consider and weigh the time, the hour, and the circumstances in every respect; and if, with sound judgment, he orders it to be prolonged or hastened, it should be sung at his command, whether he wishes it to be higher or lower, but still in harmony, as though from one mouth.

No one should presume, without the prior’s permission, either to exceed the measured manner through raised loudness of voice—which often produces in the unwary the boastfulness of self-inflation and the arrogance of pride—or to exceed or alter the measure of moderation through turbulent haste. Nor should the prior dare to abuse in practice the freedom of consideration granted to him, without a definite necessity, knowing that he will render an account to the Lord, who said: “Sing psalms wisely” (Psalm XLVI).

VIII. When the Work of God is being recited, sleep must be driven entirely from us with God’s help, fearing the Prophet’s words: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jeremiah XLVIII). And also: “They have slept their sleep, and all the men of riches found nothing in their hands” (Psalm LXXV).

IX. No one may, at the time when the Work of God is being sung, speak to another brother on any pretext whatsoever, except to the senior. To him, without doubt, causes concerning the ordering or correction of any matter sometimes properly arise.

[Column 0953A] X. In the morning, after Prime has been recited, no one should lie back in bed, except on Sunday or feast days, when those who wish may rest their limbs in their beds for a short while after Prime, having been made more tired by the labor of the vigil and by the usual work of the preceding day. This is not permitted at all times, but only during the summer months. During the rest of the year, each day, immediately after Prime, while what has been received from the juniors is being corrected, everyone should put on his shoes and be ready for the signal customarily given by striking a board, so that all may assemble without delay at the appointed place to learn the work that is to be undertaken during the coming day.

XI. During the summer no one may sleep at midday anywhere except in his own bed, unless perhaps, at the prior’s command, he sleeps outside his bed under the open sky to guard the threshing floor. [Column 0953B] In the fields, however, when the harvest is being gathered, if sleeping at midday is permitted, they should sleep not separately but in one place or in two places. For it is not unknown how much evil the devil has caused on this occasion. We should observe the periods during which, if there is free time, we are to sleep at midday from the day of the Ides of May until the day of the Ides of September.

XII. The Work of God, which the brothers laboring in any place during the day recite at the appointed hours, should be spoken with discipline and the fear of God, in a harmonious voice—not in whatever manner each person might wish to overwhelm it on the pretext of work or occupation.

Nor should a junior, presuming upon himself, spring out ahead of a senior and proceed with premature haste. The Divine Office, which must be performed with fear, should not be sung foolishly and unwisely through disordered boldness. For by such a custom the minds and throats of some brothers have already become so infected that they cannot be restrained into harmony within the oratory except by a great check upon their agitation.

Therefore, so that you may cast this vice of usurpation away from you, we exhort you with the simplicity of charity. For God is the hearer of all such people: “He sent his angel and brought me out from my father’s sheep” (Psalm CLI, according to the Septuagint).

XIII. At the hour when we are about to receive the holy body and blood of the Lord, let us hasten to be present for the recitation of “Deliver us from evil,” except for those whom a definite cause, known to the senior, prevents from being present. Every precaution must be taken lest we receive the holy body and blood unworthily, to our judgment.

XIV. No one should presume, in this congregation, either to practice or recite responsories or antiphons which some people sing with an elaborate melody according to their own pleasure, rather than taking them from canonical Scripture. Nor should anyone dare, without the prior’s command, to practice any such things from a visiting guest, lest they become ensnared by foreign teachings of variation and by the sweet attractions of a kind of delirium, grow weary of the maturity of simplicity and truth, and, shackled by the fetters of frivolity and idleness through the sounds of song, either hasten to fly from the congregation at the devil’s prompting or, puffed up within the monastery as though possessing unique knowledge, despise everyone else.

We ought instead to imitate the one and simple apostolic teaching and that of our Fathers, to be established by grace, and to subject heart and conduct to discipline. [Column 0954A] We ought to sing those things which, as blessed Augustine says, have been written in such a way that they are to be sung; but what has not been written in that way, let us not sing.

Nor should the things manifested to humanity by the Lord himself through his prophets and apostles be spoken by us in his praise in any manner other than that which he himself commanded. Let us not turn what ought to be sung into the manner of prose, as though into a reading; nor, conversely, turn by our presumption into tropes and the art of song what has been written for use in the sequence of readings.

For if we ought to offer God a sacrifice of confession and praise, how he himself commanded it to be offered shows that the Lord seeks from us the sacrifice of obedience more than sacrifices. He delights not so much in the skill of musical artistry as in observance of the commandments and purity of heart.

[Column 0954B] XV. Those learning letters or Psalms should attend, in order to receive dictation, to those to whom they have been assigned; these instructors are to be reproved for negligence or commended for their teaching and diligence. If a departing dictator has neglected to assign someone personally, the one who receives the dictation should return to the Father, so that he may appoint someone in the absent person’s place who is to dictate to him. When the absent dictator returns, the recipient should return to his own dictator.

XVI. At the hour of the meal, whatever is received each day from the Psalms by those who receive them should always be returned according to custom at the first table of the brothers. Whoever has neglected to practice and has not returned it should not eat until the meal hour of the following day.

XVII. No one may presume, without the prior’s permission, to exceed the established custom either in drink or in food; he has the authority to arrange and judge such matters. If, however, something ought to be added beyond the usual measure for brothers fatigued by strenuous work, this may be done only with the prior’s agreement and permission, not at the presumption of just anyone.

XVIII. While eating, let us listen to the readings with thanksgiving and the fear of God. Let us receive God’s gift not with contention, murmuring, indignation, loud voices, the clatter of feet, or the noise of vessels, but with charity, quiet, and the sweetest restraint of discipline. Let us fear the examples of the carnal Israelites (Numbers XI), who, while eating their fill of the bread of angels (Psalm LXXVII) and quail meat to nausea, murmured with full mouths, and against whom the wrath of God was directed for their destruction.

[Column 0954D] XIX. No brother may bring to the table, for eating, an apple, any vegetable for seasoning, or anything else for his own use, as though arranging a private provision, lest through the slightest occasion either resentment among the brothers concerning injustice or a dreadful opening for private attachment be created. Whatever of these things anyone finds, by God’s gift, must instead be faithfully handed over to the storeroom keeper, so that he may distribute them either each month or whenever each person has need.

XX. No one may dare to presume to leave the table at which he is registered to eat and pass to another. Nor may anyone receive another who comes to him from a different table to eat. Each person should eat at the table assigned to him, so that if the greater part of the brothers is absent from a table, the remaining brothers, up to three in number, should sit at their own table. Those remaining below this number should eat at another table, according to the assigned order.

XXI. No one may fill the cup of the cupbearers so that it overflows. Nor may anyone accept it if it is offered to him overflowing by an inexperienced minister. He must fill it moderately and suitably, as the Apostle says: “Let all your things be done honorably and in order” (1 Corinthians XIV).

XXII. In all services and ministries in which the junior brothers succeed one another in turn, each person should gladly and without murmuring, by the grace of God, complete the week of his turn in whatever ministry he has willingly undertaken. If it should happen that the person who has undertaken a service is occupied with another duty, on a journey, or by the necessity of illness, the person who appears next in order after him and is present should fulfill his turn. If that person is absent, the third, or the fourth or fifth after him, whichever is found present and free, should perform his service in his place, so that the established order of the ministry—offered mutually through the love of charity and devotion—may in no way be disturbed.

XXIII. If, within the very order of the juniors who succeed one another by turns in the individual ministries, some person should happen to be included whom the senior judges ought to remove from his turn of service, no one should dare to provoke him or, in jest, inflict upon him the goad of suspicion and shame.

XXIV. No one may presume, on his own authority, to take anything from the storeroom, from any workshop of the craftsmen, or any tool or other object assigned to individual brothers for safekeeping. An exception may be made only if such a serious reason—such as the absence or illness of the person entrusted with care in any capacity—compels it that, at the abbot’s command, or at least with the permission of the person to whom it was assigned, it may be handled by another.

XXV. Those also to whom the care of particular duties has been entrusted shall, with suitable devotion and the most loving humility, provide without delay and without annoyance whatever is necessary, at the senior’s command. Nor, through proud self-importance and delay, shall they create occasions for complaints, [Col. 0955D] by which murmuring ought not to be stirred up against the labor of those who serve us with charity in the matters assigned to them.

XXVI. No one may enter either the storeroom or any of the workshops of the craftsmen with improper and importunate boldness, without the senior’s order; for this presumption greatly obstructs the common good and inflicts resentment upon the craftsmen themselves through excessive interference.

XXVII. No one may, through wrongful presumption, touch for his own use any garment, footwear, boards, or anything at all, however small, whether new or old, that has been given to another brother. Nor may the brothers lend among themselves to another brother, as though out of private affection, anything that one of them has received from the common stock, unless the prior has permitted it: lest illicit affection arise on this account. Rather, let each person willingly and gladly accept whatever is given him through the distribution of charity, and take pleasure in having it for use.

XXVIII. No one may dare wash his own garments or bedding without prayer and the prior’s permission.

XXIX. No brother may dare to be tonsured without the abbot’s prayer; nor may anyone desire to be tonsured with any tonsure other than our customary one—except the sick, whom, at the physician’s direction, it may perhaps be more appropriate to tonsure more closely because of an opposing bodily humor.

XXX. If anyone finds anything whatsoever that another brother has lost, whether inside the cell or outside, [Col. 0956B] he shall not keep it with himself for a day, or, if possible, even for an hour. Rather, he shall place what he has found in the appointed location, and the person who lost it shall look for it there, so that the one who lost something may not suffer the error and labor of searching for it among individuals.

XXXI. No one may presume on his own initiative to learn any craft without the prayer of the senior, or of one to whom he has granted the authority to appoint and arrange such matters—except only those who, by the prior’s judgment, are assigned in their proper order to particular crafts with the grace of prayer. Nor may anyone presume, as though by his own authority, to study letters, psalms, or readings; for this would produce evil pride, the arbitrariness of an undisciplined will, and private ambition, rather than advancing spiritual benefit. But if anyone desires, out of good will, to learn any earthly craft, or in spiritual matters something beyond what is taught to us daily, let him await its being granted to him by the prior with the greatest humility. And if it is granted him, let him begin what he desires after receiving prayer. If it is denied him because perhaps it is not expedient for him, let him remain glad and not sad. Nor may anyone, without the prior’s knowledge and order, secretly and as though by stealth show another person letters or any craft whatsoever. If anyone presumes to do this, he will undoubtedly be subject to a twofold guilt—that is, both theft and pride.

XXXII. Above all, everyone must take care that no brother comes lazily, or not among the first, [Col. 0956D] either to the bakehouse or to any manual labor.

XXXIII. For the exhortation to labor that we have hitherto commended to your charity with such moderation has been weakened and relaxed only in proportion to the difference between persons, when compared with that apostolic insistence of blessed Paul (Ephes. IV). While he commands us to labor with our hands to such an extent that we may have something with which to give to one in need, we have said that we should labor at least enough to provide what suffices for us. He says that he himself labored with his own hands in hunger and thirst, in cold and nakedness, by night and by day, so that necessities would not be lacking for himself and those who were with him (II Cor. XI; I Thess. II; II Thess. III). We, by contrast, having double clothing and footwear for our use, [Col. 0957A] and a fully abundant daily provision of food from the house of God sufficient for our satisfaction, exhort you not to love idleness, but, through sincere agreement in unity, let each person labor according to his strength. He commanded: “Let the one who does not work not eat” (II Thess. III). But, weighing our weakness in you, we have not hitherto taken away necessities from any of you who, through a deceitful and slippery will, have delayed faithfully undertaking labor, patiently enduring this much so that we might not be conquered by evil, but conquer evil with good (Rom. XII).

XXXIV. Knowing this, brothers: a monk who is idle in body can never be idle in mind with respect to sordid thoughts, as Solomon says: “Every idler is occupied with desires” (Eccli. XXXIII). And again: “Idleness devises many evils.” Therefore, let the one who has been such up to now cast this vice away from himself and hasten eagerly to every task; for it is written: “Do not hate laborious work, nor farming, created by the Most High” (Eccli. VII). Thus, by the Lord’s gift, we may abound in the products of our own labor and in daily necessities, and may meet with suitable moderation those whom spiritual love invites to visit us; or, when severe necessity presses others, may serve them from our own labor with the ministry owed to them, since it is certain that the Lord our Redeemer commanded: “It is more blessed to give than to receive” (Acts XX).

XXXV. When going out to any task, the one who is senior among those departing shall receive the necessary tools, counted out in the morning by the keeper of the tools, and shall assign them for safekeeping to one of the younger brothers who are going with him, whom he judges suitable for this. When the work is completed, he shall carefully receive them back from that brother and hand them over to the keeper, so that nothing may be lost through the customary forgetfulness and negligence of many.

XXXVI. If anyone sees another doing something illicit, whether in speech or in action, and delays reporting it to the prior, let him know that he is a nourisher of sin and in every respect equal to the sinner. Since he is the harshest enemy both to his own soul and to the person whom he conceals, he will consequently be regarded as accursed and faithless before God, who hates evil, and before the entire brotherhood. Through an abundance of wickedness he was unwilling to expose the erring person so that he might be corrected; through hatred of discipline he loved wickedness, and “stood in every way that was not good” (Psal. XXXV). [Col. 0957D]

XXXVII. Therefore, all of us must beware of the immoderate indulgence of joking and laughter, through which the bitterest scandals usually arise among the brothers. Nor should an occasion for discord arise from this matter; even if litigation did not result, we must nevertheless beware of speech that does not contribute to edification. And knowing that an account must be rendered to the Lord even for idle speech, who does not know that excessive laughter is the gateway of indiscipline and frivolity, through which the devil subtly supplies harmful food to wretched souls? [Col. 0958A]

XXXVIII. If one person, provoked by another contrary to the prohibition, responds and brings the matter to contention, no one shall involve himself in their dispute—that is, in another person’s case—lest among the brothers the partisanship of litigants, as though divided into factions, be nourished. The exception is the senior who, by moderating the discord between them, may insert words of peace with moderation, discipline, and sincere faith.

XXXIX. No one may presume to involve himself in any cases belonging to others, whether concerning parents, blood relatives, or any worldly circumstances, without the prior’s order. The tears of the poor and oppressed often move him to approach as a petitioner before judges or before anyone else where necessary. Nor may the person directed to do so presume to speak more than he is ordered to say. For it is written that no one serving as a soldier for God should entangle himself in worldly affairs, so that he may please the one to whom he has proved himself (II Tim. II). If we desire to flee and avoid necessary matters—that is, the affairs of the monastery, which are very burdensome to us—how much more ought we to shun and flee matters belonging to others and lying outside the monastery’s welfare?

XL. None of you may dare to resist or defend himself by his own strength or human arm against the fury and wrongful excesses of the peasants, which they often exercise against us when armed by the devil, since God alone is our defender, together with the protection of the blessed apostles and all God’s saints. [Col. 0958C]

XLI. The Rules of the Fathers are also read to us continually so that, applying the inner ear to their holy exhortations, we may conceive the sweetest love of discipline and, with the Lord assisting in all things, follow the examples of their lives. For this reason we must hasten to expel from our minds the sluggishness that has grown there. We have not presumptuously dared to present to you these matters, which we speak to you individually in the present writing, as though disparaging the Rule of the holy and most blessed Fathers; rather, we have taken care to impress upon you in writing only those matters specifically drawn from their constitutions. The fullness of holy conduct and the perfect instruction of the spiritual life are read to us daily in the Rules of those holy Fathers, whose proven life, by God’s gift, has also been granted the authority to teach. [Col. 0958D]

Now may almighty God, who is the author of peace and who alone can cause people of one mind to dwell in a house, prepare you all to do his will, doing in us what is pleasing in his sight through Jesus Christ our Lord. May he plant and nourish in your hearts, through the grace of the Holy Spirit, the seed of this exhortation and admonition, and bring it to the mature perfection of good works. Amen. And, forgiving us our sins, may he keep us with his peace in eternal rest. Amen.

[Col. 0959]

# [Rule of Saint Ferreolus, Bishop of Ucetiensis, for Monks (C)]

## Testimonies of the Ancients concerning Saint Ferreolus the Bishop and his Rule

[Col. 0959A] Gregory of Tours, *History of the Franks*, Book VI, chapter 7: “At that time Ferreolus, bishop of Ucetiensis, a man of great holiness, died, full of wisdom and understanding. He composed several books of letters, following Sidonius, as it were.”

Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, also frequently praises this Rule of Saint Ferreolus the bishop and transferred a very large part of it into the *Harmony of Rules*. [Col. 0960A]

Smaragdus likewise cites much from it in his *Exposition of the Rule of Saint Benedict*.

John Trithemius, *On the Property of Monks*, Book 1, chapter 5: “Finally, in the Rule of the monastery of Saint Ferreolus, bishop and martyr, it is written in the tenth chapter: ‘We also judged that this ought to be established,’ and so forth.”

## Critical Observation on the Following Rule

[Col. 0959]

[Col. 0959A] Saint Ferreolus of Uzetensis, a bishop in Occitania, built a monastery for monks around the year 558; it is still called, after his name, the Ferreolacensian Monastery. This most devout pontiff therefore wrote the present Rule for the monks of that monastery. It consists of thirty-nine chapters, and he dedicated it to Lucretius, bishop of Die, submitting it to his judgment. [Col. 0960A] It contains much that differs from the other ancient rules and makes no mention of them. In particular, this seems distinctive: in chapter 38 it commands that the abbot serve in the kitchen [Col. 0960B] on the monastery’s three more solemn feasts—namely, the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and the feast of Saint Ferreolus the martyr, who was the monastery’s patron.

## Preface to the Rule of Saint Ferreolus the Bishop

[Col. 0959]

[Col. 0959B] To the holy Lord, holiest in comparison with all others, companion of the apostles and disciple of Christ, Pope Lucretius: Ferreolus, bishop.

Once, when God was at work, I was urged on, kindled by a single devotion, in which the divinity itself would establish for itself a dwelling-place for the servants of God. I offered this land, adding another land to it. What I assign to the holy congregation, I believe is given for my salvation, so that a multitude gathered together as one, in the manner of religious bees, [Col. 0959C] may offer the flowers of their prayers fully for my sins and make such sweet honey in intercession.

And since it was necessary that this new people should be placed under the yoke of a new law—not so that I might press down their necks, but rather that I might incline the necks of their minds—we have written a rule to be observed by them as law, with permission both sought and received from you. If, in your judgment, you determine that anything in it is harsh through severity or excessively softened through leniency, the page will more readily receive the judgment of your hand, to its own advantage, in whatever way it is approved. Thus it will bring much greater glory if the rule is found worthy because you have corrected it, fleeing from the face of embarrassment.

If, however, as I believe, the judgment of love should undertake a genuine correction of the writing, whatever ineptness an uncorrected reading may finally produce will be free from the blame of error, since I acknowledge that I have submitted the little book to your [Col. 0960C] judgment. Yet I must pray that what we have written may please first God, then you, and those to whom we entrust its observance. Thus, in the name of the Lord Jesus Christ, may they obey all the divine commandments, and may the eternal rewards and endless glory purchased by the price of a good life be claimed by them, through our Lord and God Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives, rules, and reigns forever and ever. Amen.

# The Rule of Saint Ferreolus, Bishop of Ucetiensis, for Monks

[Col. 0959]

[Col. 0959D] Beginning of the Rule concerning the matters established for observance by the monks of the Ferreolacensian monastery. I pray that, with the Lord’s help, these sons whom I have begotten for the Lord through faith may observe all this with wholehearted and holy intention, and, pursuing the best and most perfect course of life, may, as it is written, seize heaven by force and prepare dwellings prepared for worthy inhabitants. Thus may it come to pass that, by following the Lamb wherever he goes, they may despise the present in order to seize the future.

## Chapter I. On Obedience

First, the monk, whose proper task is to build many virtues within himself, must place obedience as his foundation, so that he may fulfill what the blessed Apostle admonishes us to observe when he commands, saying: “Obey your leaders and submit to them; for they keep watch, as those who will render an account for your souls, so that they may do this with joy and not with groaning; for this is beneficial for you” (Hebr. XIII).

## Chapter II. On How Much Reverence Is to Be Observed

Let reverence toward the abbot be preserved by all in every way with love, so that love may display concord and fear may acknowledge discipline. He is rightly feared as a lord [Col. 0961A] and loved as a father, since, with the flock of the holy congregation entrusted to him, the care of souls is specially committed to him. The responsibility entrusted to him daily either drags him toward punishment or leads him to glory along that path which is unavoidable for those who must die. Scripture says: “To whom more has been entrusted, from him more is certainly required” (Luke XII).

The Gospel likewise opens the truth to us through the likeness of a parable, where it is read that the Lord entrusted five talents to a servant; and because he had gained another five, he deserved to hear from the Lord: “Well done, good and faithful servant. Because you have been faithful over a little, I will set you over much. Enter into the joy of your lord” (Matt. XXV).

## Chapter III. On Charity

Third, and also because of the sacred number of the Trinity, we judged that charity, the mother of all virtues, ought to be inserted [Col. 0961B]. The Apostle praises it above all virtues in these words: “Charity does not act wrongly; charity never fails” (I Cor. XIII). And again: “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (I Pet. IV).

Monks therefore ought to cling to this commandment, so that, according to the blessed Apostle, many may become one body in Christ (I Cor. XII), and so that what the reading of the Acts of the Apostles, set forth as an example for all, places particularly before the eyes of religious persons may be fulfilled in them: “They had one heart and one soul” (Acts IV). And also that which is in the Book of Psalms: “O God, who makes those of one mind dwell in a house” (Psal. LXVII).

A monk must therefore beware in every way lest he harbor any hostility or hatred in his heart, express it in action, or display it when overcome by anger, because of what the Apostle says: “The anger of man does not accomplish the righteousness of God” (James II); and what the most wise Solomon says: “Anger rests in the bosom of a fool” (Eccl. VII); and also what the Apostle says: “Let all bitterness, anger, indignation, clamor, and blasphemy be taken away from you, with all malice” (Ephes. IV).

## Chapter IV. That No Woman May Enter the Monastery

We suitably believe that this must be established: no woman whatsoever may approach the monastery, even if she appears to seek admission out of affection. Likewise, to religious women and girls also we remove permission to approach, so that no possible excuse may be left for those who understand less clearly. For a dwelling cannot remain secure for long when the enemy is near or the adversary close at hand, especially since it becomes doubtful who will be overcome by a public enemy and secret warfare, where now nothing remains but either to conquer or perish.

But if an evident cause compels any brother to converse with women who are at least honorable far from the monastery, he shall, with the abbot’s knowledge or permission and with witnesses present—that is, with two brothers accompanying him—receive permission to converse. Nevertheless, the abbot must not be ignorant of the matter about which the conversation has arisen.

## Chapter V. On How One Who Wishes to Be a Monk Is to Be Received

If anyone comes seeking the religious life and intending to enter the monastery, he shall not be joined to the company of the monks until a full year has first elapsed—or, if it seems good to the abbot to moderate the period somewhat, until the number of six months has been completed [Col. 0962A]. This is so that during such a span he may show those who do not know him what he will be like, and so that prolonged observation may reveal whether he has brought any cruelty with him.

When he first comes to the monastery and asks to be received among the monks, he shall be asked whether he is free. Nor, after he has satisfied the abbot in his initial answer, should a subsequent answer be added: whether he was driven by anything other than devotion to seek the monastery. After this, the monastery’s Rule shall be read to him at the abbot’s command, so that afterward he may recognize anything new or unusual, whether he passes beyond it when he departs or acknowledges it if he remains.

While he observes the appointed period of overnight residence, let him receive a cell near the monastery and await his daily food from the monastery if he works among the others. Above all, let him devote himself to reading and prayer, so that the almighty Searcher and Knower of the hidden things of his household may deem him worthy to number among the merits of the holy congregation, and so that, as it is written, there may be “one flock and one Shepherd” (John X).

## Chapter VI. That No Monk or Cleric Is to Be Received for Retention

We entirely do not wish, forbid, and prohibit that a monk or cleric from another place or monastery be received for any reason. We foresee such matters in the pursuit of charity, lest they perhaps introduce some new scandal as it arises. For Scripture says: “Whatever you do not want done to yourself, do not do to another” (Tob. IV).

From this, lawsuits that cannot be healed often arise, not only between abbots but also between monasteries, while one strives to defend the person he has received and the other to recall the person he has lost. In the end, unless the requested person is returned to the petitioner and restoration of the one received appeases the injury suffered by the other, it can happen that, contrary to the blessed Apostle (Rom. XII), they do not conquer evil with good, but are instead conquered by one evil through another.

Nevertheless, we judged that this also should not be passed over: if, as I said above, a monk or cleric from another place brings letters from his abbot or bishop in which it is clearly proved that he is not to be avoided because of vices but has been sent because of the love of God, he alone may obtain the right to become a companion of the congregation. If, indeed, it can in any way be believed that anyone wishes to be stripped of his own good so that another may be clothed in his nakedness.

## Chapter VII. On the Murmuring or Slander of Monks

Let no one hear in the congregation any murmuring or slander—something monks are especially accustomed to—against the abbot or any other brother. Otherwise, the anger of God, which has often condemned a wretched people for this fault, may likewise be stirred up for the destruction of the crowd of murmurers, and their own murmuring may cause them to lose the promised land, which we rightly understand as the place of future blessedness, owed by divine promise.

The psalm announces that the followers of this vice are condemned: “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor, him I will pursue” (Psal. LX). And again the Apostle reproves them, saying: “Whisperers, slanderers, hateful to God” (Rom. I). And again: “These are grumblers and complainers, walking according to their desires, and their mouth speaks arrogance” (Jude I).

## Chapter VIII. On Avoiding Pride and Arrogance

Let arrogance and pride be entirely avoided by monks, lest one fall through boasting; let exaltation be laid aside for God’s sake. Rejection and great humility are a lofty height. Otherwise, what will it mean to have abandoned the world if one has not cut away its vanity from oneself? What will it mean to have chosen a solitary life if the heart swells inwardly?

What benefit is there in outward humility if the person who wishes to find where he may fall does not quickly cast these evils away from himself, fearing that terrible saying of divine Scripture: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (I Pet. V). And this: “The proud of eye and the insatiable of heart—I did not eat with such a one” (Psal. C). And, not forgetting the Apostle’s words, let him hear him say: “Know this, that in the last days perilous times will come. People will be lovers of themselves, greedy, arrogant, proud, blasphemers” (II Tim. III), and the rest that follows.

## Chapter IX. On Envy

Above all, let a monk exclude envy, which is the greatest vice, from the doors of his mind, and not allow the purity of his soul to be corrupted by hidden resentment, lest an adulterous mixture destroy the good seed scattered in his mind.

Let him always stand like a strong man in battle, resisting the weapons of envy with the shield of charity. Let him overcome envy above all because he is not overcome by envy, not ignorant of the Scripture that says: “Through the envy of the devil death entered the world” (Wis. II). Those who belong to his side imitate him.

## Chapter X. That a Monk May Claim Nothing as His Own

We also judged that this ought to be established: no monk may dare to claim anything as his own apart from the fellowship of the brothers, so that even in those things that are his he may not believe that he has any greater right than the others. For when he has subjected himself to another’s authority, he has transferred everything with himself into another’s authority.

Whatever property he has brought with him, after seeking the fellowship of the monks and once he has joined the body of the congregation as a member, let him immediately understand that everything has passed into common ownership. Let him judge this alone to be his own: whatever he possesses indivisibly with the brothers. For the reading of the Acts of the Apostles also records that, at the time of the rising Church, the faithful of Christ lived in this way: “No one,” it says, “called any of his possessions his own, but everything was common to them” (Acts IV).

## Chapter XI. That No Monk May Be Ignorant of Letters

Everyone who wishes to claim the name of monk must not be permitted to be ignorant of letters. Indeed, let him know the entire Psalter by heart, and let him not defend himself with any excuse so as to avoid being captured by this holy study.

Likewise, those who are sent from the congregation to tend flocks, as is customary, shall take care to devote themselves to the psalms just as the others do, lest the lesser be found in what is greater and that saying be fitted to them as a reproach: “The natural person does not perceive the things that are of the Spirit of God” (I Cor. II).

## Chapter XII. That the Psalms Are to Be Sung in Order on All Days

Let the psalms be sung in order at all times, through to the end of the Psalter, privately for each person’s own reward; except for the public course of psalmody on the Lord’s Day, let each person offer God praises each day through deliberate hidden meditation.

Likewise, let it be fitting to keep vigil at night with frequent psalmody, followed by prayer, so that this may be fulfilled: “By day I cried out, and by night before you” (Psal. LXXXVII); and: “He will meditate on his law day and night” (Psal. I).

## Chapter XIII. On Vigils

Whenever a night vigil is requested out of devotion or is owed because of a feast, for the purpose of entreating God, no monk who is present may presume to be absent except because of certain illness or necessity. He must not become accustomed to labor under excessive inner weariness, so that his spiritual soul dies while the flesh lives. Rather, eager for that promise, let him strive to seek and find it together with the others, as the one who said: “I love those who love me, and those who watch for me early shall find me” (Prov. VIII).

The psalm also says: “Then they sought him, turned toward him, and came to him before dawn” [Col. 0964C] (Psal. LXXVII). We also admonish that all should rise daily for matins, if this is not judged excessive. At the nocturnal offices, however, let everyone rise every day so promptly and together that, when all hasten together, no one is found to have arrived later than the others. Whoever is found to act contrary to this statute shall fast alone for as many days as the hours during which he was unwilling to keep vigil with the brothers.

## Chapter XIV. On the Clothing of Monks

A monk shall not seek clothing beyond what is sufficient. Let him obtain no more than the abbot judges necessary for daily use, according to the Lord’s saying to the disciples: “Do not have two tunics” (Luke VII). We should understand “two tunics” not numerically, if two appear necessary because of winter, but as counting those retained beyond use.

Therefore, whatever exceeds this will be considered another’s property. For whatever an avaricious possessor locks away, the chest uses more than the master does. To avoid this, the blessed Apostle rises as a very great witness for us, saying: “Having food and clothing, with these we shall be content. But those who desire to become rich fall into temptation and a snare of the devil, and into many desires that are useless and harmful, which plunge people into ruin and destruction. Greed is the root of all evils; in coveting it, some have suffered shipwreck of the faith and entangled themselves in many sorrows. But you, man of God, flee these things; pursue righteousness, piety, faith, charity, patience, gentleness. Fight the good fight of faith; take hold of eternal life, to which you were called and for which you made the good confession before many witnesses. I charge you before God, who gives life to all things, and Christ Jesus, who gave testimony under Pontius Pilate to the good confession, to keep the commandment without stain and free from reproach until the appearing of our Lord Jesus Christ” (I Tim. VI).

Therefore, brothers, take care that what is written to one person, namely Timothy, is observed by one congregation.

## Chapter XV. That No One Is to Be Baptized in the Monastery

We have considered that it is unnecessary for infants to be baptized in the monastery, as is observed in the other monasteries. Nor may any monk anywhere receive the children of anyone from the holy font, lest he gradually become joined to their parents by an illicit or shameful familiarity, as commonly happens. [Col. 0965B] If anyone presumes to do this, let him be corrected as a transgressor of the Rule.

## Chapter XVI. That No One Except the Abbot May Have a Separate Cell

No monk may have a private cell, either for dwelling or for any other use, except the abbot. Craftsmen, however, may have one solely for working—those, nevertheless, to whom it has been granted by the abbot’s arrangement. For one dwelling and one house shall contain the entire congregation.

Those whom bodily weakness debilitates, when illness has overtaken them and they have recognized their own infirmity, shall meanwhile be separated from the congregation within the monastery in an assigned and suitable dwelling, until they regain their former strength through the restoration of bodily health. Thus the very separation from the congregation may bring them recovery more quickly.

## Chapter XVII. That the Monks Are to Have a Provost or *Formarius* under the Abbot’s Authority

We have decreed that, under the abbot, a capable person who greatly loves discipline and who will undertake the proper care and title of provost be appointed as the abbot’s support, so that the office may be less burdensome to him while daily responsibility is undertaken by two through a division of labor. Therefore it will be right that reverence and obedience be shown to the provost at the abbot’s command.

After the provost mentioned above, who is to be a model in good things, we also establish a regular *formarius*, so that, with this assistant added, the abbot, whose name is Father, may more easily reap abundant fruits from the perfection of his beloved sons. Nevertheless, both of them, together with and among the others, must recognize that they are under the abbot’s authority.

## Chapter XVIII. On the Passions of the Martyrs That Can Be Found, So That They May Be Read at Their Proper Time Without Being Hindered by Sloth

We decree that the deeds of the martyrs—that is, the passions of the holy faithful, some of which have been assembled with care and arranged in literary form—be read in the oratory before all who are listening when the yearly course brings back the day of their departure according to the laws of its cycle. Thus the day may not pass idly, but may be regarded as equal to the other days, a day which was then made illustrious by the martyr’s steadfastness and is now commended by the memory of his passion.

## Chapter XIX. That Reading Should Frequently Be in the Monk’s Hands

[Col. 0966A]

Because the sluggish minds of some must be aroused—minds in which divine reading often produces weariness, so that they prefer to occupy themselves with idleness rather than drink salvation from the Holy Scriptures—it has seemed entirely appropriate to add that every monk, whether he is doing some work inside the monastery or outside, must not allow a single day to pass without nourishment from divine reading.

Whenever his hands cease from work, let his soul be cultivated by reading, with all listening to the admonitions of blessed Paul to his disciple Timothy: “Attend to reading, exhortation, and doctrine” (I Tim. IV). And again: “Every Scripture inspired by God is useful for teaching, for refuting, for correcting, for instructing in righteousness, so that the man of God may be perfect, prepared for every good thing” (II [Col. 0966B] Thess. III).

## Chapter XX. On Wandering or Fugitive Monks

For a monk to wander through different places is as unfitting as it is improper, lest, captured by some vice, he slip away into the world’s pleasure and return to his vomit. Through a renewed inclination of the soul, the former despiser of the world may rise as a new lover of it and, turned aside from the way of salvation, wander from the path.

Therefore, we have established that the following must be observed: apart from those whom the abbot orders to make journeys here and there for the monastery’s benefit, no one may presume, for any matter or necessity, to leave the monastery to stay in another place without the abbot’s permission. Otherwise, what the Apostle says concerning younger widows may apply to him: “At the same time they learn to go around from house to house—not only idle, but also talkative and inquisitive, saying things they ought not” (I Tim. V).

Therefore, anyone who departs contrary to the decision, through some act of opposition, so that he is found to have been a transgressor of it, shall fast for twice the number of days corresponding to the period of time during which he was absent from the monastery, and shall be punished by condemnation. He shall receive the measure of food that the abbot imposes, with wine denied him each day.

A fugitive monk who abandons discipline and loses himself is to be recalled as a despiser.

## Chapter XXI. That a Brother May Not Lay Hands on a Brother

A monk inflamed with anger against another monk—a most shameful thing—must not presume to lay hands on him, except those to whom it belongs either to know the measure of correction or to exercise judgment concerning it. Otherwise, when one sins, the audacity of the others to presume such acts will increase, and, with the order of discipline confused and the law of life broken, the rights of the sacred religion will be lost by individuals.

Therefore, whoever is found to have acted so uncontrollably with his hands that he does not know how to refrain from what is illicit shall have those hands that he raised against his neighbor wearied for a long time not only by fasting but also by continuous labor, so that thereafter they may be raised to God in prayer and not extended against a brother in fury.

Nevertheless, we decree that pardon be granted to the one who asks for it, according as the abbot wishes to moderate the matter, if, after the prescribed penance, while he begs forgiveness for his guilt, he has also drenched his face with an outpouring of tears.

## Chapter XXII. That Monks Are to Refrain from Abuse and Cursing

[Col. 0967A]

Let no abuse or curse proceed from a monk’s mouth, nor let a tongue loosed by the stirring of impatience utter anything unbridled through the gates of the lips. Rather, when moved by anger, as is human, let him say: “Set, O Lord, a guard over my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Psal. CXL). Let him add also: “I said, I will guard my ways, lest I sin with my tongue” (Psal. XXXVIII), keeping before his eyes the Apostle’s saying: “For neither shall those who curse possess the kingdom of God” (I Cor. VI). Therefore, if anyone, untamed in mind in these matters, bursts forth, let him be kept apart from all intercourse with the brothers for thirty days, until, recognizing that he has incurred solitude while still in the congregation, he chooses to seek pardon.

## Chapter XXIII. That a Monk Both Cease and Refrain from Swearing

[Col. 0967B]

So that the practice of swearing may, if possible, be entirely removed from the conversation of the monks, so that, even if in accordance with human frailty they are perhaps less able to avoid the sin of lying, they may at least avoid the perjury that must be condemned. I ask and at the same time admonish them to make a habit of using sacred words, so that oaths may never be necessary. We have learned from the blessed Apostle’s warning how all must avoid the disgrace of this vice; for he says: “Do not swear, either by heaven or by earth or by any other oath whatever. Let your word be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no,’ so that you may not fall under judgment” (Luke V). Likewise, Scripture says [Col. 0967C]: “A man who swears much will be filled with iniquity, and the scourge will not depart from his house” (Ecclesiasticus XXIII).

With these great and most evident testimonies, the reading of the Gospel—which is the fullest authority—also bears witness in the same way, when the Lord says to the disciples: “You have heard that it was said to the ancients: ‘You shall not commit perjury; but you shall fulfill your oaths to the Lord.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all: neither by heaven, because it is God’s throne; nor by earth, because it is the footstool of his feet; nor by Jerusalem, because it is the city of the great King; nor shall you swear by your head, because you cannot make one hair white or black. Let your speech be ‘Yes, yes,’ ‘No, no’; whatever is more than these is from evil” (Matthew V). Let it therefore suffice that we have taught by these examples the admonitions that must be inserted and the things that must be avoided.

## CHAPTER XXIV. That a monk should laugh rarely

[Col. 0967D]

I also believe it fitting for monks that they abstain from laughter—not constantly, perhaps, but frequently. Therefore, if anyone reading the example should seek a model among the brethren, let this alone suffice for him: we read in the Gospel that our Lord Jesus Christ wept (John XII), but we do not know that he laughed; he was made sorrowful by tears, not carried away by laughter. Yet, lest someone say that apart from this we have no other testimony from Scripture, let him hear Solomon saying: “Laughter will be mixed with sorrow, and mourning takes possession of the end of joy” (Proverbs XIV). And again: “Anger is better than laughter, because through the sadness of the face the mind of the sinner is corrected. The heart of the wise is where there is sadness, and the heart of fools where there is joy” (Ecclesiastes VII). And again: “A fool raises his voice in laughter, but a wise man will scarcely smile quietly” (Ecclesiasticus XXI).

Therefore, whoever in the congregation, whether young in mind or age, does not avoid laughter and jokes—as is customary—what else does he change from a monk but a public entertainer? In the more populous cities such men devote themselves solely to this: being free for jokes, applause, and loud laughter.
