Yet I especially warn, order, and establish this for all to observe: whenever a reading suitable for souls devoted to God is publicly recited in church, in the refectory, or anywhere else, no one is to be moved to laughter or move another to it. Likewise, let them understand that stories must be avoided at that time. If anyone, having been admonished by this present warning, does not observe it, let him be chastised by the penalty of a three-day fast [Col. 0968B]. We do not want anyone to complete these three days under one continuous fast, lest the discipline lack some measure of discretion; rather, we order the three fasts to be separated each day by an evening meal. We establish that this too be observed concerning the other fasts by which the guilty are corrected according to the Rule—provided that the abbot sees in the monk at fault neither pride nor stubbornness.

## CHAPTER XXV. That a monk should entirely avoid obscene speech

[Col. 0968B]

Out of love for chastity, obscene speech must be disgraceful for a monk to utter; he must avoid words of lust, which, just as they arouse the mind, so they inflame the body. For the blessed Apostle says: “Put away from you malice, blasphemy, and obscene speech” (Colossians III). I ask you, brothers [Col. 0968C]: what less does the man do than an adulterer whose tongue shares in the sin? What less practice of lust has the man undertaken who has defiled a chaste mouth by corrupt speech? And so that fear of condemnation may impose on everyone the duty of avoiding this filth, we establish that the person guilty of this fault shall have neither communion from the Lord nor the kiss of the brethren for six months.

## CHAPTER XXVI. That monks should read every day until the third hour

Let a monk, both the senior and the least, strive at all times to devote himself to reading until the third hour of the day, and only then let him undertake the work assigned for the rest of the day. The sick alone are excepted, since common infirmity does not permit this to be imposed on them against their own will—or rather, against their strength [Col. 0968D]. Nor will those to whom the abbot has commanded that, during the season of gathering the crops, they perform some work or labor in the morning hours be bound by this rule; nor will they be judged to have acted contrary to this definition, since they have completed what was commanded for the sake of the community’s benefit.

For it is customary among farmers, when morning has scarcely yet returned, to cut the dry grain only after it has been moistened by the fallen dew, so that they may more easily rescue the less vigorous crop from the following heat, while they preserve the mildness of the gentle air at the beginning of the day. I know that it has often been deliberately arranged that, while the light was still uncertain, before—as we may say—the sun’s heat had drunk up the grain gathered into sheaves, its reaping, together with its fruits, escaped the flames of the fiery rays [Col. 0969A]. If this practice is also observed by the monks who devote themselves to such work, as we said above, they are not to be declared transgressors of the Rule for the sake of expediting the work.

## CHAPTER XXVII. That no monk should eat or drink before the third hour

No monk, except the sick, is to presume to eat or drink before the third hour of the day has been completed, whether by asking or by accepting an invitation, even if the arrival of some neighbor or friend provides a carefully sought opportunity for the appetite—except at the time when the customary fasts are relaxed. After that hour, let him extend the decision to eat until the sixth hour, if either his friend or his stomach permits it. But at this meal let him seek and arrange to have one or two brothers as companions [Col. 0969B], so that, while he appears public in this fellowship and courtesy, he may not seem to have been secretly placed there.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. That a monk should perform some work every day

We decree that a monk who spends the day without work, except on established solemnities or in evident illness, is to be excluded from the meal, in accordance with the blessed Apostle’s command: “If anyone does not work, neither let him eat.” Yet we foresee the excuses that useless men will offer and therefore set a limit for the idle. One of them will say: “I cannot work, because, having lost the strength of youth, I am an old man, weak for everything.” Another will say: “Nor can I, because I am already broken by illness” [Col. 0969C]. A third, if one can be found, will say: “I too cannot, because constant labor has crushed me, the length of journeys has weakened me, assigned responsibilities have taken away my strength, and imposed activity has stripped me of my vigor.”

But a contrary word of reason should meet these men, refuting them and saying: “If someone is unable to apply himself to work, let him devote himself more readily to reading. Whoever does not cultivate the field should honor God doubly; and among other things let him acquire this craft also, that he paint a page with his finger, since he does not mark out the earth with a plow.” Therefore, let no one who is unable to do manual work think that he has a just excuse: for whoever, as we said above, is unable to practice agriculture can read and write—which is the principal work—provide for the catching of fish, weave a net, prepare shoes for the brothers, or perform and complete other similar tasks [Col. 0969D]. Whoever among all these alternatives does not choose some work with which to occupy himself should be content to endure hunger together with reproach.

## CHAPTER XXIX. That a monk should speak sparingly

Let a monk maintain restraint in speaking in every conversation; therefore Scripture says: “In much speaking you will not escape sin” (Proverbs X). And again in the Gospel: “Do not speak much, as the Gentiles do” (Matthew VI). It is also said in the psalm: “The man of many words will not prosper upon the earth” (Psalm CXXXIX). Therefore, whoever that brother may be, let your words be few.

Not only this, but the presence of the abbot or another senior should also impose silence on you, so that, unless questioned by him or ordered to break silence, you do not presume to speak, obeying Scripture, which says: “Before you hear, do not answer; and do not thrust yourself into the midst of elders” (Ecclesiasticus XI). We declare most explicitly that this must also be observed at meals [Col. 0970A].

## CHAPTER XXX. That the abbot should undertake no work against his own will

If the abbot does not work as the others do, no one should dare to criticize him, because it is more fitting for him to devote himself to reading, by which he may teach the others daily, educate those entrusted to him, and continually discipline everyone through holy admonition. Yet he should take care that, whenever he is not holding a book in his hands, he should, according to his strength [Col. 0970B], make himself a common participant in any work of the brothers, so that, even if no one dares call him idle, no one may silently murmur that he is disdainful.

## CHAPTER XXXI. That monks may not use linen tunics

A monk, however delicate his body may be, must not use linen next to his naked body. For it is unfitting that he should pamper the flesh—which always grows proud through the fault of nature—with soft garments, and flatter it as though it were rather weak; for each day it is stirred up as a new and most powerful combatant for the conquest of the soul. It regains strength to fight against the soul whenever it receives anything like a rebellious slave granted relief.

The blessed Apostle speaks of this struggle: “The flesh desires against the spirit” (Galatians V). And again: “I see another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind and taking me captive under the law of sin, which is in my members” (Romans VII) [Col. 0970C]. And again: “A thorn was given to me in my flesh, an angel of Satan to strike me; for this I entreated the Lord three times that it might depart from me, and he said to me: ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for power is perfected in weakness’” (II Corinthians XII). And again: “If you live according to the flesh, you will die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the flesh, you will live” (Romans VIII).

Therefore, whoever loves that life must mortify the flesh that is destined to die. By daily struggle he must afflict it with certain harsh bonds of discipline, like an ever-active conqueror continually battling it, so that it may fight against the soul even over a small indulgence, following the Apostle’s teaching and example, who says: “I chastise my body and bring it into servitude, lest perhaps, after preaching to others, I myself should be rejected” (I Corinthians IX) [Col. 0970D].

## CHAPTER XXXII. That the clothing of monks should not have refined scents

A monk should take care not to have clothing that is fragrant or excessively bright for the sake of ostentation. Rather, following the Apostle, who says more suitably, “We are the good fragrance of Jesus Christ” (II Corinthians II), let him avoid in clothing the color white or excessively red, by which the appearance of the body is often commended to observers to its own destruction, and let him not desire to have such colors. Otherwise, he would carry with him a testimony to his vanity; and while he temporarily labors to adorn the body with garments that are quickly worn out, he may fail to care for the ornaments of the soul, if any could be eternal [Col. 0971A].

For divine Scripture rebukes those who act in this way: “Do not glory in the adornment of clothing, and do not exalt yourself on the day of glory” (Ecclesiasticus XI). As for footwear, we establish that you retain the custom of the other monks. But care must also be taken that the foot be bound by its straps with moderation, so that it is not tightly fastened as a sign of ostentation, but may more holily be loosened by a less restrictive bond. Thus, in all things, simplicity joined with holiness may commend to God the one whom, possessed by love of him, the world has seen to be a proven despiser of worldly things.

## CHAPTER XXXIII. That monks should have separate beds

Two monks, however close or friendly they may be, are not to share a bed or be kept together in one bed, for the sake of private prayer, which is better directed to the Lord without any witness [Col. 0971B]. Let the contrite mind believe that greater freedom for prayer has been granted to it when it need fear neither anyone as a witness to its vigil nor anyone as its judge.

Therefore, by keeping vigil, praying, and singing psalms, let each one take care that only the smallest portion of the night yields to sleep, lest he who is free from a companion be deceived by the enemy; for one cannot completely claim one’s own bed except while awake. What the prophet sings to us as a kind of admonition also seems worthy of imitation: “Every night I will wash my bed; I will water my couch with tears” (Psalm VI). And again: “In the nights lift up your hands to the holy place and bless the Lord” (Psalm CXXXIII). And this: “I remembered your name, O Lord, in the night, and I kept your law” (Psalm CXVIII).

Therefore, so that each devoted monk may more profitably fulfill this during the time granted for rest [Col. 0971C], he alone shall possess his own bed, as we said above, having with him—in a better exchange for a companion in the dormitory—the Lord, who keeps watch.

## CHAPTER XXXIV. That a monk should not hunt

Among the other pleasures of the world, a monk should know that he is forbidden to practice hunting, and that he must not engage in a dangerous and fruitless contest with wild animals. He ought rather to know that vices are the beasts to be slaughtered. Therefore, neither local custom, nor the proximity and convenience of forests, nor an accessible or easy ascent of a mountain, nor hollow valleys, secluded woods, or dense tracts of land should entice him to undertake such useless labor [Col. 0971D].

For, remembering the Apostle’s judgment, he must not bring loss upon his religious commitment; the Apostle warns that “each person should remain with God in the calling in which he was called” (Ephesians IV). Let him judge that the good course of his life must not be lost in empty pursuits, and let him beware of becoming a source of harm, lest, by setting aside the monk, he too be captured by the capture of wild animals and, entangled in worldly desires, become a hunter of savage beasts and himself the quarry of the adversary.

Let him rejoice that he is free for God alone, whom he seeks; let him serve continually the one whom he has chosen, knowing that we are bound by the evangelical command in this way: “You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (Matthew IV). And elsewhere: “One thing I asked of the Lord; this I shall seek: that I may dwell in the house of the Lord all the days of my life” (Psalm XXVI). Therefore, after setting everything else aside, he should strive continually to please him through every service [Col. 0972A], so that he may make a sharer in his kingdom the one whom he sees to be wholly his worshiper.

Nevertheless, we did not think this should be omitted: if perhaps more violent wild animals lie in wait among the crops for someone seeking food by his own labor, let him appropriately drive them away with the ferocity of dogs, but only to avenge the damage to the crops; he should take greater pleasure in driving them off than in pursuing them, so that he may appear to be a lover of crops rather than of hunting.

## CHAPTER XXXV. That a monk should not presume even to touch fruit without permission

If any monk plucks an apple or other fruit of any kind still hanging on its tree without authorization, merely for the sake of eating; or if, when it has fallen to the ground, he dares, through lack of restraint in appetite, to violate the firstfruits of that or of the other fruits, as is customary—like the first man, Adam [Col. 0972B]—let him fittingly repent by a fast corresponding to the chastisement, as though he were judged unworthy of the banquet of paradise.

Unless he first obtains forgiveness from all the brothers, he is not to be permitted to come to the table; for it is just that he should seek the indulgence of everyone, since he has taken away from all what was common to all. Therefore, everyone must take care that whatever is designated as food for human consumption, if it happens to be received or even found by one of the brothers, be kept wholly intact and in complete trust before he brings it to the table or hands it over to the steward. Let him avoid stealing for himself by tasting the common food intended for all; and although no companion may be beside him, let his appetite nevertheless be his companion in destroying innocence or carrying out a theft.

Therefore, the congregation shall always have one common property, so that all things belong to all and everything belongs to everyone [Col. 0972C].

## CHAPTER XXXVI. That the abbot should not presume to manumit a slave belonging to the monastery

The abbot shall not have permission to set free a slave belonging to the monastery without the consent of all the monks, unless he gives all the brothers, from his own resources, a replacement of equal merit or age in the slave’s place. For the slave of many cannot pass into freedom through the release of one, nor can a person become a freedman whom all do not unanimously absolve, since it is clear that he has as many masters as there are monks.

## CHAPTER XXXVII. Concerning how the abbot should conduct himself

Let the abbot be commended to all the monks over whom he presides by energy, but also by gentleness, and above all by his life, so that they fear him as holy rather than as severe, and fear in him more the fact that he is first in merit than that he is chief in rank [Col. 0972D]. Let him maintain moderation in correction and restraint in familiarity. In all his conduct let him be so disciplined that he calls by kindness and chastises by fear, making himself more loved by all because he hates vices.

His entire conduct should be like a foundation laid so that anyone who wishes to draw near to God in merit by imitating him may be built upon it. No one is to be condemned by him through power, but through reason; yet no one should be so familiar with him that he presumes more than the others, nor so offended that, once contrition has been completed, he does not return to seek forgiveness [Col. 0973A].

For it is fitting that he who is feared by all should fear everyone, and should take the greatest care and diligence that no one whom he has undertaken to govern through his own care should, through any adverse circumstance, depart from the number. Therefore, it is necessary for him to assist the illnesses of the monks with many remedies and to apply the treatment of spiritual care to the sicknesses of their minds. If he sees someone proud, let him offer him the potion of humility through continual exhortation; if someone angry, let him offer him the ointment of patience; if someone pursuing falsehood, let him provide the antidote of truth. In this he should be stirred up by the admonitions of the blessed Apostle, who says: “Attend to yourself and to your teaching; persist in them. For by doing this you will save both yourself and those who hear you” (II Timothy IV). And again to Timothy: “Hold to the pattern of sound words that you have heard from me, in faith and love in Christ Jesus” (II Timothy I). And again: “But you, be vigilant, labor in all things, do the work of an evangelist; fulfill your ministry” (II Timothy IV).

The blessed Peter likewise writes: “I exhort the elders who are among you, as a fellow elder and a witness of the sufferings of Christ and a sharer in the glory that is to be revealed: feed the flock of God that is among you” (I Peter V). And he adds: “Not as domineering over the clergy, but becoming examples to the flock, so that when the chief Shepherd appears, you may receive that unfading and flourishing crown of glory.”

The most holy Jeremiah also says in the person of the Lord: “I will give you shepherds according to my heart, and they will feed you with knowledge and teaching” (Jeremiah III). And again: “Thus says Adonai the Lord to the shepherds of Israel: Do shepherds feed themselves?” [Col. 0973C] And he adds: “Therefore, shepherds, hear the word of the Lord. Thus says Adonai the Lord: Behold, I myself am against the shepherds, and I will require my sheep from their hands” (Ezekiel XXXIV).

The Lord himself, questioning Peter, the chief of the apostles, whether he loved him, adds in the Gospel: “Feed my sheep” (John XXI). It is therefore clear, brother, whoever you are whom you see placed over the monks: a great burden has been laid upon you through this honor, so that although you are first in dignity, you labor bent beneath the weight of all.

Therefore, run along the path of the straight road that leads to heaven; show the flock an unobstructed way; precede it also by the steps of holiness. Strive in such a way that whoever follows you as a guide by imitating your steps does not go astray, so that you may appear to have fulfilled the Apostle’s command, which says: “Be an example to the faithful in word, in conduct, in love, in faith, and in chastity” (I Timothy IV) [Col. 0973D]. And again: “Take diligent care to present yourself approved to God, a worker without shame, rightly handling the word of truth” (II Timothy II).

This title, then, abbot, is specifically marked out for you, so that you may not grieve that you were passed over in the discourse of the Rule, and so that you may recognize yourself as one member of the congregation. We admonish you—or rather, we beseech you before God—to observe all these things with fervent zeal and, for the sake of example, to keep also the other things that have been prescribed for the rest.

## CHAPTER XXXVIII. At what times the abbot should attend the kitchen, and likewise wash feet

Three times each year the abbot is to enter the kitchen to prepare food for the congregation: on the day of the Lord’s Nativity, likewise on the first day of Easter, and also on the feast of the monastery’s particular patron, the holy and most blessed ever-venerable martyr Ferreolus—or, in any case, on the feasts of those saints to whose names the same place has been consecrated [Col. 0974A]. There, undertaking the service of a junior, he should serve at the tables and display in the dishes a model of humility, willingly bowing to this holy lowliness, which raises him above the others by making him their equal. His authority gains all the more in every respect the more he descends to the lower duties through equality in service.

He should also frequently strive to wash the feet of the brothers and even of pilgrims, imitating the divine example, fulfilling the Lord’s command, and giving the monks an example through deeds rather than words. For in the Gospel the Lord says to the disciples: “If I, Lord and Master, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet. For I have given you an example, so that, just as I have done for you, you also may do” (John XIII) [Col. 0974B].

Let all the monks imitate the abbot who does these things, with willing hearts and in observing this rule, so that at appointed times and in distinct turns they serve one another attentively in preparing food, and through equal service exercise authority over one another in turn.

## CHAPTER XXXIX. The correction of monks for various offenses

This title has undertaken, through many admonitions, to correct the negligences of monks. It demands not so much the condemnation of persons as of faults. Let love of health, desire for perfection, expectation of truth, the promise of glory, the permanence of life, and that dwelling with the Creator which we believe in render them clean and, as it were, purified from the pollution of every vice. Concerning this the Apostle says: “We shall be caught up in the clouds to meet the Lord, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (I Thessalonians IV) [Col. 0974C].

The following is the word of correction for those who sow quarrels among the brothers: if faith does not draw them back from so perverse a way, let them be struck not only by the abbot’s sentence but also by the hatred of all, until they abandon their customary error. Concerning such people the evangelist Luke recalls that the Lord said: “It is impossible that scandals should not come; but woe to the one through whom they come. It would be better for him if a millstone were placed around his neck and he were thrown into the sea” (Luke XVII).

This sentence concerns those who, after correction, oppose the judgments of their elders and strive to excuse their sin, and who, instead of turning to repentance through remembrance of their fault, have gone too far into the harshness of indignation [Col. 0974D]. Until they are recalled from their proposed intention and lay aside the swelling of their minds through evident amendment, they are to be subjected, according to the abbot’s judgment, to the most rigorous discipline. For they did not say, “I acknowledge my sin” (Psalm L), but said what is read in the prophet Jeremiah concerning the rebellious: “There is no one who repents of his sin, saying, ‘What have I done?’” (Jeremiah VIII).

Those who put themselves before their superiors and, through the fault of arrogance, are not ashamed to seize the places of others, and who contradict the Lord’s commandments by which we are ordered: “Whoever wishes to become greater among you shall be your servant; and whoever wishes to be first among you shall be your slave” (Matthew XX), are to be shamed by the rebuke of the abbot or of the others and recalled to the proper place that they had abandoned [Col. 0975A]. We decree that they be promoted more slowly to a higher rank, lest their rooted presumption grow stronger when dignity is added to it.

We establish this also: when the brothers are gathered at table, no one is to presume to take or snatch another’s portion from what has been set out, lest he too frequently thrust his hand greedily into the dish, in accordance with the Apostle’s saying: “One is hungry, another is drunk” (I Corinthians XI). And again: “Food is for the stomach, and the stomach for food; but God will destroy both the one and the other” (I Corinthians VI) [Col. 0975B]. And again: “The kingdom of God is not food and drink, but righteousness and peace and joy in the Holy Spirit” (Romans IV). And again: “Such people do not serve Christ our Lord, but their own belly” (Romans XVI). And again: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Philippians III).

We also read in the psalm, concerning those who are far from monks: “While their food was still in their mouths, the wrath of God rose against them” (Psalm LXXVII). Whoever violates this statute, it shall remain to the abbot’s judgment by how many fasts the violence done to the table is to be punished.

As for drunkenness, I think it superfluous to admonish a monk about it, since even if he takes a little wine, he departs from the appointed mortification of the body. Yet, because the monks cannot be unaware of what the Apostle writes to Timothy, saying, “Use a little wine for the sake of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (II Timothy III) [Col. 0975C], let them receive, according to the resources of the monastery, whatever wine is offered to them each day by the abbot’s order or discretion, and let them demand absolutely no more. We establish that this also be observed concerning the other allowances.

For we prove from the testimonies of Scripture that drunkenness is forbidden even to those who live in the world, since the Apostle writes to the Ephesians: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Ephesians V). And likewise the Prophet: “Woe to those who are mighty at drinking wine and powerful at mixing strong drink” (Isaiah V). And again: “Woe to those who rise early and pursue strong drink, who wait for evening so that they may burn with wine.”

Therefore, if a monk should at any time be seen drunk—which it is impious even to say—then, burning with righteous anger, I order him to abstain from drinking wine for thirty days [Col. 0975D], so that during this period his soul may be emptied of the accumulation produced by the infusion through its digestion.

Those monks whom even the end of a single day finds at odds with one another, who drag their quarrels until evening and do not exclude hatred before the sun knows its setting, contradicting the Apostle’s command, “Let not the sun go down upon your anger” (Ephesians IV), through disobedience—we decree that they be worn down by abstinence until they voluntarily turn to genuine reconciliation. After a long scandal, they may not reconcile secretly, lest the purity of charity admit something feigned; rather, their reconciliation must be public, since their discord was manifest.

Therefore, in the presence of all the brothers standing by, let them ask forgiveness of one another. Each is marked as guilty by a prolonged quarrel, whether one ceased to seek pardon or the other, desiring to be asked, did not forgive. Thus the one remained impious, the other unrepentant [Col. 0976B]: the former condemned after anger, the latter after fault.

Therefore, let the offended person not retain his anger in contempt of the Gospel, but let him quickly return to that example: “Forgive, and you will be forgiven” (Luke VI). And to the Apostle’s words: “Put on, as God’s chosen and beloved, compassion, kindness, humility, gentleness, and patience, bearing with one another and forgiving one another if anyone has a complaint against another; just as the Lord forgave you, so you also must forgive” (Colossians III).

Let the one who inflicted the injury be quickly frightened by this example: “The Lord executes judgment for those who suffer injury” (Psalm CXLV). And elsewhere: “Whatever a man sows, that he will also reap” (Galatians VI).

We order one guilty of theft—if we may still call him a monk—to be subjected to the same scourging as an adulterer and to be counted among those suffering great affliction [Col. 0976C], assigning him the same sentence as the fornicator, because he too has indulged his lust in stealing. We rightly call them alike, since we find them placed together in sacred reading.

The Lord therefore says through the Prophet: “There is no knowledge of God upon the earth” (Hosea IV). And shortly afterward: “Theft and adultery have overflowed.” And again in the psalm: “When you saw a thief, you ran with him, and you placed your portion with adulterers” (Psalm XLIII). We also read in the Gospel that the Lord said: “Fornications, thefts”—and without delay he added—“these are the things that defile a person” (Matthew XV). From these words, the servants of these crimes can certainly understand that, just as the vices rule them equally, so equal punishment is owed to them.

[Col. 0976D]

And so that you, dearest brothers in Christ, may not through forgetfulness neglect anything of what has been written above, read all these things together once every thirty days—that is, on the kalends.

[Col. 0975]

# THE RULE OF THE TARNATENSIAN MONASTERY

## TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING THE TARNATENSIAN MONASTERY AND ITS RULE

[Col. 0975D]

Josias Simler, *Description of Valais*, Book I: “Below Octodurum, on the left bank of the Rhône, these villages follow one another: Juviana, Servantia, Verosa, and soon the town of Tarnadae. Following Antoninus, we call this town Tarnadae; most of the ancients called it Agaunum. Very ancient inscriptions survive in this place, bearing witness to its antiquity. At this place, under the emperor Maximian, the Theban Legion, whose commander was Maurice, was slain because of its confession of the name of Christ [Col. 0976D]. About 220 years after their martyrdom, when this place was held in great veneration among the Burgundians, who ruled in these regions, King Sigismund of the Burgundians, moved by the exhortation of Maximus of Geneva, Theodore of Sion, and other bishops, built at the same place a celebrated monastery in honor of the martyrs. He enlarged the walls of the nearby little town of Tarnadae and joined it to the monastery. From that time the name Tarnadae gradually fell out of use, and it is now commonly called Saint-Maurice.”

Marius, bishop of Aventicum, *Chronicle*, under the year A.D. 515: “In the consulship of Florentius and Anthemius, the monastery at Acaunum was built by King Sigismund.”

[Col. 0978A]

Saint Benedict of Aniane, abbot, frequently cites the Tarnatensian Rule in his *Concordia of Rules*; so does Smaragdus in his *Commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict*; likewise Trithemius in Book 5 of his work *On the Proper Duties of Monks*.

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

[Col. 0977]

[Col. 0977A]

This present Rule was written for the monks living in the Tarnatensian or Tarnadensian monastery. There is considerable disagreement among scholars concerning its location. Mabillon, in the *Benedictine Annals*, believes that this monastery is identical with the priory of Ternan or Tarnay, situated between Lyon and Vienne, whereas the cited Simler and other historians of great authority establish that it was located beside the Rhône.

For it is undisputed that the town of Tarnadae once existed below Octodurum on the left bank of the Rhône and was sufficiently famous; the ancients called it Agaunum because of the rock of the same name, at whose foot it had been built. Hence the monastery is sometimes called Tarnatensian, sometimes Augian, and more often the Monastery of Saint Maurice, because of the patronage of that holy martyr, to whose sacred name it too had been dedicated. At this very place Saint Maurice, commander of the Theban Legion, suffered martyrdom with his soldiers under the emperor Maximinus. In sacred memory of this event, therefore, and at the urging of certain devout bishops, Sigismund, king of the Burgundians, established this monastery around the year 515, as the testimonies cited above report.

This Rule, then, may perhaps not have been committed to writing until the seventieth year of the sixth century. Calmet believes that the monks of Tarnadae compiled it according to the commendable customs already in use in the monastery, and that its author or compiler lived near the end of the sixth century. Indeed, he thinks that he was the same man who wrote the *Life of Saint Luguendus* at the direction of Saint Marinus, abbot of Lérins [Col. 0978A].

Nor should we be surprised that this monastery was governed at first without any written rule. In the earliest centuries of monastic life this was common: monks were governed by the living voice and example of the abbot and father of the monastery, as is plainly established concerning Lérins in Gaul, Hy in the land of the modern Scots, and Lindisfarne in Northumbria.

Meanwhile, this Tarnatensian discipline—at least with regard to perpetual psalmody in choir—also spread to other Gallic monasteries, especially after Saint Apollinarius, abbot of Toul, assumed responsibility for this monastery around the year [Col. 0978B] 579, as we learn from Fredegar under the twenty-fourth year of Guntram.

Nor does it matter greatly that the eminent Noris, in his *History of the Pelagian Heresy*, believes that certain chapters of this Rule have a close connection with the Rule that Saint Augustine wrote for virgins. In those times there was such unity of monastic life everywhere that written rules differed little in their principal matters; they differed from one another only in certain rites and ceremonies proper to each place and community.

For this reason, distinguished writers—and Noris himself, who has just been mentioned—acknowledge that this Rule of the Tarnatensian monastery, consisting of twenty-three chapters, was never composed for regular canons but was adapted solely for monks; such canons had not yet arisen in the Church.

# THE RULE OF THE TARNATENSIAN MONASTERY

[Col. 0977]

## CHAPTER ONE

[Col. 0977C]

If anyone, kindled by the ardor of faith and renouncing the world, chooses and seeks the monastery with great resolve, he is not immediately to be granted permission to enter on account of his novelty; rather, it must first be diligently investigated whether he has come voluntarily or has been compelled by some necessity, or whether he is bound by any condition of servitude. When this has been reported to the abbot by the superior, one of the elders shall be assigned and ordered to attend to the newcomer until his devotion has been demonstrated by the testimony of his patience. Next, he is to be instructed in the disciplines of the Rule, and is to learn what he ought to do and whom he ought to serve. Thereafter, the entire constitution of the Rule shall be read to him, and, in order to test his obedience, hard and difficult commands shall be imposed upon him. He shall retain no property of the things he brought with him [Col. 0977D].

But if his vow is such that he wishes to contribute his possessions to the uses of the monastery, his offering is to be commended in its entirety by sincere devotion and placed upon the altar; hence, to ask for anything back is judged sacrilege. If he has brought animals of any kind when coming to the monastery, he shall receive their price from the abbot, and he shall not be denied the right to do whatever he wishes with that price. If the abbot does not wish to purchase them, he shall be permitted to sell them to whomever he wishes; or, what is better, he shall entrust them to the superior to sell. The price itself, [Col. 0978C] as has been said, shall be distributed by the person to whom the goods formerly belonged, provided that nothing of it remains in his possession. For it is unlawful that one who seeks to escape the snare of this world should keep anything by which the devil’s assault might entangle him.

If he brings with him a dependent, servant, or relative, and requests that this person be admitted into the religious community, the person should be tested by a similar examination and then joined to the brothers. Whoever was previously subject to him in servitude is to be counted as a brother placed in the service of the Lord, because, as the Apostle teaches, with God there is no partiality [Col. III]. Yet the one who has been received from a lowly condition into the equality of brotherhood must not grow proud through any swelling of arrogance; rather, through humility, let the good qualities in him grow strong. Let him serve not only the one to whom he has become equal, but the entire brotherhood, with devotion and humility, as a true servant of Christ.

For just as the one who seemed greater in the world is called a brother in the Lord through an attitude of humility, so the other, remembering his former condition, must not despise it by seeking higher things, but must exalt it by the testimony of humility, so that he may find grace with God.

No one, however, shall be permitted to change his habit before the completion of a year. But if the petitioner’s compunction is so great that he persistently demands by supplication that this not be denied him, what is granted to one faithful petitioner must not thereby be regarded as generally lawful. The garments also brought with him, which the use of the first year does not wear out, shall be converted into money and given to whomever the abbot orders. For when he has deserved other clothing, his former garments shall no longer be in his possession, so that the change in the outer person may fully correspond to the progress of the inner person [Col. 0979A]. He shall not be permitted to exchange any of the things he has received, neither for cheaper ones on the grounds of rejection nor for better ones for the sake of convenience; whatever has been assigned to him, he shall claim solely for his own use, with thanksgiving.

## CHAPTER II.

No one may choose a dwelling apart from the others, nor may he be permitted to claim as his own a small chest, cupboard, or anything similar that can be locked privately. He shall not undertake a journey alone unless accompanied by a brother as his companion. Those returning shall not dare to report what they have seen being done outside, except only what may edify those who hear it.

When an elder is present, a younger brother must beware of bursting into presumptuous talk. But if, as often happens, the elder is of a simpler nature, then the younger shall carry out whatever instructions have been given to him. No one may seek out a celebrated monk on any feast day unless permission has been granted, since the Lord, as the Gospel confirms, has promised that he will hear the one who prays secretly [Matt. VI].

## CHAPTER III.

If any brother is sent by the elders on any business to the city, a fortified town, or a village, he must not presume to approach any place other than the one to which he has been sent. He must by no means agree to become a spiritual father without the abbot’s command. But if a matter of such necessity arises, or if, overcome by the requests of some faithful person, he cannot escape what has been forbidden, then, out of regard for charity, he must in every way accept what is known to have been imposed upon one who objects [Col. 0979C].

## CHAPTER IV.

Since conversations with an unfamiliar woman are legitimately prohibited by the authority of the canons when there are no witnesses, they must likewise under no circumstances be permitted to mingle secretly in the talk of mothers or sisters, lest such women overthrow those who are still newly established in the service of the religious life through worldly presumption. No one may depart in any direction without permission granted by a superior.

Nor may anyone presume to ferry a boat to the farther bank without the command of an elder; nor cut his hair or beard; nor make a cord or undertake any other such action, unless the elder’s relaxation of the rule permits it. During the evening and night hours [Col. 0979D], when the other brothers are resting, anyone found absent from his dwelling or bed shall be punished by the rebukes of the elders. While resting, no one shall speak to another.

## CHAPTER V.

Whoever comes late, once the signal has been given, either to the work of God or to any other work, shall be excluded and put to shame for the offense of so great a crime. For any fault, however serious the rebuke with which he has been corrected, he must consider it unlawful to answer the one rebuking him; rather, by humbling himself, he must show that correction of the offense will follow, because God has promised that he will give grace to the humble [I Pet. V].

With one who has been removed from participation in prayer or at table because of a committed fault, no one may converse except one who is able to sweeten the bitterness of the expelled brother by mingling instruction with charity [Col. 0980A].

## CHAPTER VI.

At the vigils, while the readings are being read to all who are seated, or while they are engaged in prayer, no one should think that he has been granted the freedom to enter or leave. Whoever is compelled by a matter of common necessity may depart while the others are singing the psalms, without fear of incurring anyone’s guilt, provided that he immediately returns to the work being carried out.

Whoever presumes to chatter while others are praying or singing psalms must not doubt that he has made himself guilty not only before the brotherhood but also before God. Care must also be taken lest idle hands invite sleep. Therefore, the following tasks are to be performed during the vigils: tasks that do not occupy the mind or burden the hearing of the worker, but that can drive away the torpor of drowsiness [Col. 0980B]. Nothing, however, is to be preferred to prayer and the word of God.

On the Lord’s Day night, out of reverence for the Lord’s resurrection, manual labor shall cease. The same observance should also be kept on certain solemn feasts.

## CHAPTER VII.

While the brothers are meditating, no one may involve himself in other affairs, nor may he regard it as permissible to leave the school or the place where the brothers are meditating. Whoever violates this presumption shall rightly be subject to excommunication.

It is unlawful to enter another’s cell without a signal, except for the abbot and the superior, because only they are permitted to learn the brothers’ secrets and to investigate, by hidden inspection, how each one conducts himself. Where craftsmen are working, no one may presume to enter without the persons mentioned above.

To newcomers, the younger brother shall offer nothing beyond the devotion of humility and the service that is owed. He must not presume to concern himself with the reason for which the newcomer has come or when he will return, because this must be investigated by the concern of the elders, not by the presumption of the younger brothers [Col. 0980C].

## CHAPTER VIII.

A younger brother must not dare to rebuke an elder. But if he notices that something is being done, or has been done, contrary to the Rule, he must reserve the matter for the abbot or the superior, so that what is criticized may be corrected through regular discipline.

Whatever is done by anyone without witnesses, if it comes to the abbot’s attention, shall be corrected more privately. If it becomes known to everyone, the person guilty of the offense must be accused before everyone.

One who secretly confesses the assaults of his thoughts for the sake of receiving consolation must not be despised or disclosed to others; rather, as far as possible, he should be encouraged with gentle exhortation. Whoever speaks inappropriately while others are singing psalms in silent meditation shall be rebuked according to the Rule.

Therefore, in whatever work they are engaged, they shall either meditate upon holy things or certainly keep silent. At table, no one may presume to speak, except one who has been questioned. Whatever is necessary for food, the superior ought to recognize, and whatever is lacking according to custom, he shall order to be supplied privately.

Those seated at table shall listen in silence to the reading being read. If there is no reader, they shall ruminate on meditation upon the Holy Scriptures as on food, so that the body may receive not only nourishment, but the hungry soul may also be fed by the word of God.

Devote yourselves to prayer at the appointed hours and times. When the Lord is entreated with psalms and hymns, let what is spoken by the voice be planted in the heart. Let the plowman, holding the plow, sing “Alleluia”; let the sweating reaper refresh himself with psalms; and while the vinedresser trims the curved vine-shoot with his pruning hook, let him sing something from David. Let these be your songs; these, as people commonly say, your love-songs; these the shepherds’ whistle; these the instruments of cultivation.

Let the monks have no concern for what the people of this world do, but let the meditation of their hearts be intent upon the fear of the Lord [Col. 0981A].

## CHAPTER IX.

At all times they shall devote two hours a day to spiritual meditation. In summer, after the morning office has been completed according to custom and Prime has been said, they shall all undertake the tasks that have been commanded. Then, after Terce has been celebrated, they shall return to complete what they had undertaken [Col. 0981B]. They must not occupy themselves with conversations of any worldly kind, unless perhaps the speaker says something that edifies the soul of the listener.

From the sixth hour until the ninth they shall devote themselves to rest or to reading. After the ninth hour, whether in the garden or wherever usefulness requires, until the hour of lighting the lamps, they shall all lend their assistance for a common support.

In winter, after Matins or Prime has been completed, all are permitted to devote themselves to reading until Terce. When it has ended, they shall hasten gladly to fulfill what has been assigned to them, as has been said, until the hour of lighting the lamps.

Those who appear to have been assigned to cultivation cannot be bound by this observance because of the constant demands of their work. Instead, they shall be governed according to the judgment of the superior, as time requires or as their labor shows the assigned work to demand [Col. 0981C]. Nevertheless, they too shall devote two hours to reading.

When the harvests and grape-gathering are being collected, they shall receive food twice a day, namely at the sixth and twelfth hours. On Wednesday or Friday they must so regulate their work that, if possible, they do not omit the prescribed fasts. But everything shall be arranged according to the judgment of the elder, as usefulness or labor requires.

No one, however, may eat or drink outside the monastery. For the discipline of the Rule does not permit even the taking of cheap fruit; nor may they presume to drink water before the regular meal.

## CHAPTER X.

When they make bread, or in any bodily service, they shall relieve one another’s labor. Whatever work they may appear to be engaged in [Col. 0981D], they must not omit the times for praying and singing psalms, so that while they strive to prepare bodily food, they may be spiritually nourished by the word of God and meditation upon a good conscience.

No one ought to be absent from this work except one whom illness keeps away or whom the superior has ordered to be occupied in another matter. The person placed in charge of the storeroom shall be appointed by the judgment of the abbot or the counsel of the elders—not someone who considers the wishes of a few, but someone who considers the needs of all, with fear of the Lord and love of the brothers. In the superior’s absence, harmonious obedience shall nevertheless be rendered to him; and whenever usefulness requires it, assistance must not be denied him.

## CHAPTER XI.

The monastery’s administrators ought to be chosen or appointed as persons who are proven to edify others by the example of their lives and who preserve with the greatest care, for fear of the Lord, the alms assigned to the monastery and the things collected by the brothers [Col. 0982A].

For if anyone neglects to preserve the substance entrusted to him that belongs to the servants of God, as one of the Fathers says, he harms God; and if he scatters it, he will have to render an account to the Lord.

Whatever has been given to them for the love of God, once added to the monastery’s offering, must benefit the entire congregation. If we desire to choose the apostolic life, why should we claim as our own what we know will quickly perish?

## CHAPTER XII.

The gardener should be appointed in such a way that he may be supported by the assistance both of the superior and of the storekeeper. Since the storehouse’s expenses are helped by the produce of the vegetables, they must be both consumed and cultivated according to the storekeeper’s arrangement.

All tools and the remaining utensils should likewise be guarded by both persons [Col. 0982B]. Each one, however, must guard carefully and with the utmost diligence whatever has been entrusted to him. No one may presume to take from another’s storage anything that does not belong to him, without the consent of the one into whose charge it was placed.

Whoever presumes to do this with wicked authority, because he does not fear producing scandals over the smallest matters, must be shown to be guilty before the entire congregation by neglecting the Rule.

No one may choose for himself the work to be done during the day; it must remain within the elder’s discretion, so that he may command whatever he sees to be useful according to his judgment. No one should do anything while murmuring, lest he suffer the outcome of those whose example he follows.

No one may frequently visit his relatives. Nevertheless, access for visits at certain times shall be granted to a person who is proven to be concerned for the salvation of his relatives [Col. 0982C]. Even so, he must take great care to avoid the snare of the world, lest, while he thinks he can gain others, he alienate himself from the Lord.

## CHAPTER XIII.

No one may attend a wedding feast, lest through the frivolity of worldly people he become acquainted with the things of the world and—God forbid—be recalled in spirit, even if not in body, to the life of this world, as the most blessed Cyprian said: “Adultery is committed when it is seen and learned” [Eph. II].

Whoever presumes to say something jocular or suited to laughter in the assembly of the brothers, or whoever wishes to exchange idle words with younger men or to maintain friendships with those of immature age, shall rightly be subject to rebuke.

If anyone finds anything, he must not conceal what he has found or hide it from those who ought to know. If he is proved to have kept it for the space of one day, he must recognize that he has stained himself with the contagion of theft [Col. 0982D].

If anyone learns that a person who cannot endure the strictness of the monastery is contemplating flight, and does not immediately disclose it, he must not doubt that he has become a participant in that person’s destruction. He is to be separated from the assembly of the brothers until the fugitive can be recalled.

If anyone does not strive with every strength to observe these things that please the Lord, and does not improve after being corrected once and twice, the offense must be punished according to the form appropriate to his age.

## CHAPTER XIV.

These are the things that the constitution of the monastery requires to be observed for the love and fear of God [Col. 0983A]. Since you have been gathered together in one place through fear of the Lord, you ought to dwell with one mind in the house of the Lord, and you should have one soul and one heart, ever watchful in the fear of the Lord.

You must not regard anything as your own; rather, let everything be held in common and distributed to you at the abbot’s command—not equally to all, but as the principles of distribution or the cause of illness require. Nevertheless, each person shall receive according to his need, as we read in the Acts of the Apostles: “Everything was common to them, and it was distributed to each according as each had need” [Acts IV].

Those who possessed anything in the world, when they have been deemed worthy to seek the monastery, should gladly hand over what will benefit everyone. Let them strive, when they have relinquished their property, to strip themselves at the same time of the desire to possess it: when possession is relinquished, let attachment also be cast away.

Those who possessed nothing, however, should be ashamed to seek what they do not remember having left behind. Nor should they consider themselves fortunate because they have found in the monastery what they could not find outside it. They must not grow proud because they are associated with people whom, previously, they could not approach on account of abundant wealth or the splendor of their birth. Rather, let them lift up their hearts and not seek things that are perishable or quickly passing away.

Where the rich are humbled, let the poor not be inflated, lest monasteries begin to be more useful to the rich than to the needy. Those who appeared wealthy in the world should not disdainfully receive brothers coming from poverty into the holy fellowship; rather, they should rejoice in the companionship and association of such persons.

Nor should they be lifted up if they contribute any portion of their means toward the expenses of the brotherhood [Col. 0983C], and afterward fall from the place to which they had previously wished to rise. What good does it do to scatter wealth and become poor by giving to the poor, if the wretched soul becomes more proud by despising riches than it had been by possessing them?

Therefore, remaining united in mind, honor God in yourselves, whose temples you have been deemed worthy to become. Above all, let us love God with the whole strength of our soul, and then our neighbor; for these are the commandments specially given to us.

After God, honor must be offered to the abbot and reverence reserved for him. To the superior, as befits servants of God, let full love and harmonious obedience be given.

## CHAPTER XV.

In the oratory, nothing at all may be done apart from the worship of prayer and psalmody, so that the works continually performed may agree with its name. If anyone enters to beseech the Lord outside the appointed hours, let no unrelated activity delay his prayer.

Do not sing anything except what you read is to be sung. Mortify your flesh through abstinence; discipline it with fasts and vigils. Wash your soul, however, with the purity of a good way of life.

## CHAPTER XVI.

If a brother weakened by abstinence is unable to bear the fasts he has undertaken, he must consider it improper to receive anything before the hour of the meal has passed. Those who are detained by illness and cannot observe the appointed hours may be permitted to eat lawfully; let them receive food when they can.

Nor should it cause annoyance to others if a more generous provision of food is made for those who, in their worldly life, were accustomed to more lavish treatment. Nor should those whom either the modesty of their birth or some other habit has made stronger regard themselves as happier for this reason.

Nor should they consider those more fortunate to whom, in illness, what is withheld from the healthy out of strict observance is supplied. If those whose parents raised them more delicately are given more generous food or clothing, the brotherhood ought not to be disturbed because what is denied to the physically stronger by the constitution of the Rule is granted to them out of consideration for charity [Col. 0984A]. Regard must be paid to how much each person has despised out of love for the religious life and to what degree of abasement he has submitted himself through divine inspiration.

Nor should the foregoing indulgence, when granted to a few, be regarded by the whole community as an established rule. For it is not equitable that in a blessed dwelling where the rich are humbled, the poor should be raised up.

Those constrained by inequality must indeed be treated in such a way that generous provision quickly strengthens the powers exhausted by illness; and, for those remaining in sickness, distinctions of persons must not introduce distinctions in food.

Once they have recovered full bodily strength, however, they must be held to the customary restraints of abstinence, because it befits the servants of God not to diminish but to increase their habitual practice of good works.

## CHAPTER XVII.

Let your habit not be conspicuous, nor seek to please by your clothing, but by your conduct. When you go out, walk together. When, with the Lord’s protection, you have reached the desired place, let the entire brotherhood remain together.

In walking, standing, and every movement of the body, let nothing indecent appear that might offend the gaze of an observer. Rather, devote yourselves to what is fitting for your holiness [Col. 0984C].

## CHAPTER XVIII.

If your eyes, directed in any direction, should encounter the faces of women, nevertheless let your mind, devoted to God, not be stained by any mark of lust. Since you are not forbidden to go out and cannot avoid seeing women, yet to desire them or to wish to be desired by them is a crime.

Lust toward women is incurred not only through touch and affection, but also through the gaze. Do not claim to have chaste eyes if you possess immodest minds, because an immodest eye is the messenger of an immodest heart.

Whoever directs his gaze toward a woman with awareness of lust must not think that what his sin-laden mind has conceived remains hidden [Col. 0984D]. But suppose that it is certain to remain hidden, so that no human being sees what he has done: what will he do with the examiner from whom secrets do not escape and from whom hidden things cannot remain concealed?

Therefore, let the holy man fear displeasing God, to whom he wishes to show himself a faithful servant. Let him take care not to introduce into his mind women who may please him wrongly. Let him fear the one to whom no human action can be hidden. Let the fear of the one of whom it is written always be present: “The one who fixes his eye is an abomination to the Lord” [Prov. XVI].

Therefore, whenever you are together in church or in any place where women may be present, let each of you carefully guard your chastity, each taking responsibility for all. For God, who dwells in you, will deign to protect you when this kind of vigilance is exercised [Col. 0985A].

If anyone notices in one of you the wantonness of the eyes of which I speak, let him immediately warn him so that he may be corrected at once. Let him not think himself malicious when he reports this; and therefore the one who behaves in this way must be exposed, lest he grow worse.

If, after being warned, he neglects to correct himself, the matter must be reported to the abbot, so that he may undergo corrective discipline from him. If he still does not improve, let him be cast out from your fellowship like a diseased sheep, lest he destroy others by his example.

Thus must the fault of desire be investigated: when someone is recognized as suffering from this vice, he must be disciplined by many, with love for one’s neighbor and hatred of vices.

## CHAPTER XIX.

Whoever presumes to receive letters or small gifts from anyone, if he does not immediately make public both who gave them and what he received [Col. 0985B], shall be subjected to the strictest discipline.

The things that have been sent shall be assigned to pilgrims and strangers, or else burned in a fire. If anyone has sent something to his sons or to persons related to him in any way, it shall be converted into common property and given to whoever needs it.

If the abbot orders that the thing sent be given to the recipient, he shall receive it with thanksgiving, like the other gifts of the faithful.

Care must also be taken lest an excessive desire for clean clothing produce stains in the inner soul. Therefore, garments are to be washed according to the superior’s arrangement. They should be prepared in a simple manner and in their natural color, so that differences in clothing do not nourish the vice of arrogance. They must be distributed to those in need, lest, if they are held back through the vice of greed, an opportunity be given for individuals to make provision for themselves [Col. 0985C].

If anyone carelessly thinks these things should be sought, it shall be the superior’s responsibility to correct the one who misappropriates the monastery’s goods.

Above all, take care that you have no quarrels. If quarrels arise at the devil’s instigation, let them be healed by swift reconciliation; let remedies be brought forth from the place where the wounds were made. “Let not the sun go down upon your anger.”

Reject the habit of swearing. Let your speech be “yes, yes; no, no” [Eph. IV], because, as the Lord says, “whatever is more than these is from evil” [Matt. V].

## CHAPTER XX.

Women must not frequently visit your dwelling. But when, out of devotion or love for your religious life, they seek the monastery, they must not be permitted to enter the monastery’s inner doors. Rather, honor and kindness should be shown them in the oratory or in the guesthouse [Col. 0985D], not out of expectation, but in accordance with the constitution of the Rule and the discipline of the monastery.

## CHAPTER XXI.

A person who is wholly trustworthy and energetic should be placed in charge of those suffering from illnesses or some other weakness. He must serve the sick with compassion, regularly maintain the monastery’s discipline, and reasonably distribute what is appropriate for the sick.

## CHAPTER XXII.

Those placed in charge of the storeroom or of the books [Col. 0986A] must serve the brothers without murmuring. They must not receive books requested outside the appointed time, and those who have more books in their possession than has been determined must not dare to keep them.

When you do these things in the name of Christ, you know that you are making progress and continuing in the monastery with gentleness and tranquility.

When, however, the necessity of discipline in correcting behavior compels you to use harsh words, even if you perhaps feel that in those words you have exceeded the proper measure of discipline, you are not required to ask forgiveness, lest, among those who ought to be subject, excessive humility weaken the authority of governance.

Nevertheless, forgiveness must be sought from the Lord of all, who knows with how much goodwill you love even those whom you perhaps rebuke more severely than is right.

The charity of which it is written that it “does not seek its own” [I Cor. XIII] is understood to be preserved here as well: while they strive to humble another’s pride, they cannot humble persons as much as they wish. For the love among you must not be carnal but spiritual. Therefore, think more diligently about the salvation of all, because each person will render an account to the Lord for the souls entrusted to him [Col. 0986B].

## CHAPTER XXIII.

Obedience must be given especially to the superior, and much more to the abbot, who cares for all of you, because whoever despises them despises the one who said: “Whoever hears you hears me, and whoever despises you despises me” [Luke XVII].

Therefore, so that all these things may be observed, and so that, if anything has not been observed, it may not be negligently passed over but may be corrected and amended, this will belong chiefly to the superior: he must report to the abbot, whose authority among you is greater, whatever exceeds his own measure or strength [Col. 0986C].

The one who presides over you should consider himself blessed not by ruling with power but by serving with love. Let him be superior in honor before you, but before God let him be subject at your feet. In all things let him present himself as an example of good works.

Let him rebuke the restless, console the fainthearted, receive the weak, and be patient toward all. Let him willingly maintain discipline and impose fear. Although both are necessary, let him desire to be loved more than feared, always thinking that he will render an account to God for you.

Therefore, by obeying more fully, you show mercy not only to yourselves but also to him, who, to the degree that he occupies a higher place among you, is in greater danger [Col. 0986D].

May the Lord grant that you observe all these things with love, as lovers of spiritual beauty and fragrant with the good odor of Christ through a good way of life—not as servants under the law, but as free persons established under grace.

So that you may be able to look upon yourselves in this little book as in a mirror and neglect nothing through forgetfulness, let it be read to you once a week. Whenever you find yourselves doing what is written, give thanks to God, the giver of all good things. Whenever any one of you sees that something is lacking in himself, let him grieve over the past, beware of the future, and pray that his debt may be forgiven and that he may not be led into temptation.

[Col. 0985]

# [THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER]

## TESTIMONIES FROM ANTIQUITY CONCERNING THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER

[Col. 0985D] Saint Benedict, abbot of Aniane, very frequently praises this Rule of a Certain Father, written for monks, in his *Concordia of Rules* [Col. 0986D], as well as another written for virgins. He does not distinguish between them himself, however, but indiscriminately calls both the “Rule of a Certain Father,” or the “Rule of a Certain Father,” as in chapter 8, section 7, and elsewhere.

[Col. 0988A] Smaragdus the monk likewise occasionally cites testimonies from this Rule of a Certain Father in his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict.

## CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

[Col. 0987]

[Col. 0987A] Under this obscure title we possess two Rules, one for men and the other for holy virgins, and we do not know the author of either, although one and the same person wrote both Rules.

Under this same uncertain title, Benedict of Aniane, in his *Concordia of Rules*, and Smaragdus often cite this Rule, as Holstenius has noted here. This Rule, comprising thirty-two chapters, is harsher than the others, especially toward disobedient or murmuring monks; indeed, it prescribes perpetual fasting and imposes other exceedingly severe commands upon its sons.

Hence the often-mentioned Calmet thinks that it was once used by Scottish monks, especially in the monastery of Bangor, where Saint Columbanus was educated, since that holy abbot prescribes the same distribution of the divine office to his monks at Luxeuil.

We recognize, indeed, that this Rule was written for Scottish monks. For it contains the strict discipline of the Scots, which was common to all the monasteries of present-day Scotland and Ireland and therefore was not peculiar to a single one.

Whoever carefully considers the monastic order once used in the monastery of Culross will find that, long before the time of Saint Comgall and Saint Columbanus, this strict discipline was already practiced among Scottish monks. Thus, from the life of Saint Kentigern, once a monk of Culross and later bishop of Glasgow in Scotland, we learn that he nourished nine hundred monks on bread and water alone and did not use dairy products except on Sundays and feast days.

Later, the northern English, instructed by Scottish monks at the monastery of Lindisfarne in Christian doctrine and the monastic life, abstained from eating meat and from drinking wine and beer, contenting themselves with milk mixed with water, until King Ceolwulf of Northumbria, who became a monk there, arranged for his fellow monks to have a moderate use of wine and beer.

The matter of perpetual fasting, likewise practiced everywhere among them, must be considered in the same way, as is entirely clear from the aforementioned monastic order of Culross. It is therefore not surprising that Ratramnus, a monk of Corbie writing against the Greeks in the ninth century, mentions the perpetual fast of the Scottish monks, since Saint Columbanus, in chapter 3 of his Rule, commands: “Let the food of the monks be poor and taken in the evening . . . . Therefore one must fast daily, just as one must pray daily.”

Since it is certain that the strictest manner of life was once cultivated in all the monasteries of the Scottish monks, I would ascribe this present Rule to Saint Columba, patriarch of the Scottish monks, who alone among the many legislators of the monastic life can properly be called an archimandrite: he was the founder of a hundred monasteries and, if not the author, at least the restorer of the entire monastic discipline throughout present-day Scotland and Ireland.

For he is that archimandrite of whom Saint Columbanus says in chapter 7 of his Rule: “Under one archimandrite there are a thousand abbots, for whom the number twelve of the psalms was common at each of the four nightly vigils.”

Nor can it be doubted that among so many Columban monasteries, generally situated among the rugged mountain ranges, some were built in such barren places that scarcely any grain was sufficient for food. Thus the Rule must have permitted the common use of dairy products, just as it also allowed milk mixed with water as the ordinary drink, as is granted in chapter 22 and is still practiced today in the barren regions of the Scottish Highlands.

It is therefore very close to the truth that the author of this Rule was Saint Columba, abbot of the monastery of Iona, the true patriarch and archimandrite of the Scottish monks. The venerable Bede writes about him in his *Ecclesiastical History* and offers many praises of him and of his disciples.

# THE RULE OF A CERTAIN FATHER

[Col. 0987]

## IN THE NAME OF THE FATHER, AND OF THE SON, AND OF THE HOLY SPIRIT

[Col. 0987D]

### I.

Let the good reader beware of subjecting the Scriptures to his own understanding; rather, let him subject his understanding to the Holy Scriptures.

The cup of suffering is bitter, but it heals every disease completely. The cup of suffering is bitter, yet the physician drank first, so that the sick person would not hesitate to drink. For the one who wishes to heal another’s wounds must remain healthy and free from every disease of weakness.

The devil destroys a monk and drags him to death through no other vice than this: when he sees that the monk, neglecting the counsel of the elders, trusts in his own judgment and defense.

### II.

Before all things, God must be feared and loved with all one’s strength [Luke X], and one’s neighbor must be loved greatly, according to the Lord’s command.

### III.

Next, the virtue of obedience must be sought and practiced according to each person’s strength. At the first word of an elder, all the brothers who hear must rise. Whoever does not rise must ask forgiveness and do penance for as long as the elder judges; and he must carry out what he has been ordered to do, even if it appears difficult.

Obedience must be rendered even unto death, according to the example of the Lord, who was obedient to the Father unto death [Phil. II]. Each person must serve his brother as he serves his own abbot or father, as the Apostle says: “Serve one another in the fear of Christ” [Eph. V]. And again: “Let all your things be done with charity” [I Cor. XXXVI].

IV. If any brother is found to be disobedient to the abbot, the steward, or any of the brothers, he is to be sent to prison and do penance for as long as the senior shall determine. But if, after examination in prison, he is found incorrigible—once and twice, again and again—he is to be cut off from the entire body of the brotherhood, according to the Lord’s command: “For it is better for you that one of your members perish than that your whole body go into the gehenna of fire” (Matt. 5); and because “a little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5).

V. One must not obey everyone in the presence of the abbot or steward, since one person cannot attend to everyone. [Col. 0989B] Nevertheless, let each one strive to obey his senior brother as the Lord. Whatever he does for his neighbor, let him not doubt that he does for the Lord.

VI. If any brother is found to be murmuring, he himself is to be sent to prison, and his work is to be rejected. Let him do penance according to the senior’s examination. If he is permitted to do so, let him make satisfaction; but if he does this frequently, he is to be expelled from the monastery.

VII. At the first word of correction from the senior, the steward, or any brother, pardon must be sought, and the offender must remain prostrate on the ground until the senior has completed the correction. If the senior repeats the correction, the offender must likewise repeat his request for pardon. If anyone is found slow to seek pardon, or utters words contrary to religion, or speaks in excuse of his offense, [Col. 0989C] he is to be sent to prison and do penance according to the senior’s judgment until he is corrected. But if he is found obstinate, he is to be separated from the brothers.

VIII. Lying, taking oaths, and idle speech are to be condemned throughout the whole body of the brotherhood. If any brother is found guilty of one of these things, he is to be sent to prison and do penance until he is corrected of the vice, because “the mouth that lies kills the soul” (Wis. 1); and the Lord prohibited oaths in the Gospel, saying: “But I say to you, do not swear at all” (Matt. 5). And again: “For every idle word that people speak, they will give an account for it on the day of judgment” (Matt. 12). The Apostle also says: “Let no evil speech proceed from your mouth, but only what is good for building up the faith, so that it may give grace to those who hear” (Eph. 4). If any brother, after examination in prison, is unable to avoid these vices, he is to be expelled from the brothers and condemned.

IX. If any brother is found to be wrathful, he will be guilty in the council of the gehenna of fire unless he repents, just as putrefying wounds must be burned out by correction—that is, by the medicine of fire—and a swollen wound must be treated by the incision of a spiritual blade. In other words, capital and mortal crimes, which lead to death, must be treated and corrected severely until the person is reformed and becomes healthy, according to the judgment of the abbot or steward.

X. If any brother speaks about another brother [Col. 0990A] when that brother is neither listening nor present, and if what is said does not concern his praise and love, the speaker is to be judged as a blasphemer. He must immediately ask God for pardon and confess to the brother what he has said about him. If he is found to repeat the offense, he is to be sent to prison and do severe penance until he learns what the Apostle said: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt” (Col. 4). An excuse for an offense is not proper before pardon has been granted by all the brothers; after pardon, it is proper.

XI. In abstaining from food, one rule is to be observed by all the brothers, except the elderly, the sick, and children; and there is to be one measure for all: namely, they are to abstain from food from the ninth hour until the second hour. Neither before nor after the common meal served to the brothers for supper may anything be indulged in by the mouth, unless illness or a difference of age or bodily condition has compelled some exception. But one must not eat to satiety. Meat and wine, or any drink that causes drunkenness, are to be rejected by monks and not accepted by those for whom the world has been crucified through Christ, and they themselves to the world. A monk is not to have holidays on earth, except that, on the arrival of brothers, food may be somewhat more plentiful as an expression of charity. Nevertheless, abstinence must be concealed, lest we fall into the fault of boasting, which is the gravest of all vices.

XII. We must seek nothing from the things that belong to the world except our daily bread and a short garment with which to clothe ourselves. These very things are to be sought by us without anxiety, lest we should at some time be found [Col. 0990C] not to be thinking about the kingdom of God, and it be said of us: “The nations seek all these things” (Matt. 6). Nevertheless, monks must always work and pass their lives without anxiety; whatever they have earned through labor, except—as we have said above—a little bread and clothing, they are to distribute to the poor. Care for the poor must always be practiced, and everything we do must be done with charity; without charity our works are fruitless before God.

XIII. It is to be left to the judgment of each senior how he is to provide his monastery with its annual bread: whether by hoeing or with oxen, as is customary for some—as it is with us—or by crafts, commerce, hired labor, or any kind of work.

XIV. It is not especially necessary to consider how each person labors, but how each person lives. One must always work as the resources, circumstances, and location of each place permit, and observe the law of God, which contains both visible and invisible things. Nothing from God’s commandments, whether great or small, is to be neglected, because “whoever transgresses one commandment has become guilty of all” (Jas. 2).

XV. The purpose of the monk that we have promised must be practiced and fulfilled with all our heart and all our love; it consists in three renunciations. First, we must entirely reject all our possessions, and recognize that all the riches of the world are alien to us. Second, all the vices of body and soul must be abandoned and avoided: “Let all anger, indignation, shouting, and blasphemy be removed from you, together with all malice” (Eph. 4). The third renunciation, therefore, is this: in regard to all those things that appear to exist, whether in heaven, on earth, or in the sea, or among all God’s creatures, we must not only refrain from making any of them like the Lord, but must also regard all of them as beneath us, since we extend ourselves beyond them toward the kingdom of heaven and toward knowledge of the Lord himself. Therefore we do not devote ourselves intensely to these things, which are perceived by the senses for our well-being and immediately pass away, according to what the Apostle says: “All the things that are seen are temporal, but the things that are not seen are eternal” (2 Cor. 4).

XVI. Silence is to be pursued in all things, and the discipline of keeping silent is to be practiced everywhere, especially [Col. 0991B] near the Mass and the table. Indeed, nothing is to be said in any circumstance except what necessity requires. If anyone, contrary to this discipline, responds with shouting and excessively harsh speech, he is to be reprimanded until he is corrected. But if this vice cannot be cured, he is to be expelled from the fellowship of the brothers.

XVII. Nothing is to be possessed as one’s own, especially among monks; everything is to be common to them.
