Whoever says, “This is mine,” or, “That is mine,” has sinned before God, unless it happened merely through an inadvertent utterance; even in that case, however, he must ask God for pardon, take care thereafter, and not dare to repeat it. If anyone proves incurable in this vice, he is to be expelled by all the brothers, because the vice of love of money is the gravest of all vices, and “love of money is the root of all evils” (1 Tim. 6).

XVIII. If any brother falls through a grievous lapse—that is, fornication—he is to be expelled from the congregation of the brothers and do penance until the day of his death, whether in another region or elsewhere. Sisters, therefore, are to be seen rarely, and we forbid the desire to speak with them frequently, lest we be found to have given occasion to the weak. Nevertheless, we command that benefits and generosity be shown to them wholeheartedly, because they are members of Christ and mothers of the Lord, and Christ redeemed us through a virgin. Gifts, however, are to be sent to them through men who are wholly faithful and thoroughly approved, so that the opportunity for slander may be avoided, for the sake of wicked people.

XIX. No one is to be permitted to preside over the congregation of the brothers unless he has learned through obedience those things that ought to be commanded to others. Even if he is sufficiently instructed in the Holy Scriptures, he must nevertheless confirm his teaching by the deeds of his life—that is, he must fulfill in practice what he teaches, displaying humility arising from charity, patience, and gentleness, fulfilling the senior’s will, and carrying out all the Lord’s commandments.

XX. If any senior, or one who is called abbot, is found to be pleasure-loving, drunken, and rich, and one who conforms himself to this world—that is, who travels from place to place in carriages and on horses—he is not only unworthy of rule over the brothers but is also to be judged a murderer of souls. Another is to be appointed over his monastery. But if this cannot be done, [Col. 0992A] the monks are to leave him, and he is to be excommunicated. If he repents, let him submit himself under the authority of a senior and subject himself to servitude until the one who presides has tested him.

XXI. We do not permit monks to travel about in carriages or on horses, except the sick, the disabled, and the lame. If they do so, they are to be excluded from the fellowship of the brothers.

XXII. To brothers whose dwelling is in barren land—that is, where there is no bread—but who are in mountainous and fruitful regions, we permit a little milk mixed with water. We do not permit a monk to live with women, that is, with mothers and sisters.

XXIII. How ought we to obey the one who urges us to perform the work commanded? As an infant obeys a nurse, or a woman who invites him to her breasts; indeed, even more promptly and swiftly, because the future life is much more precious than the present. We ought to obey unto death.

XXIV. How ought a senior to conduct himself toward the brothers? As a nurse cherishes her little ones, loving and strengthening each one, opening to them the way of perfection, and himself advancing in complete perfection and holiness of heart and body. Without any distinction of persons, he must love them all equally and with sincere affection, as his own children, with all his heart. But if he sees one of them transgressing the Lord’s commandment, he must not be moved to anger against him, but to pity and compassion, following the one who said: “Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is made to stumble, and I do not burn?” (2 Cor. [Col. 0992C] 11). But if he is negligent in matters concerning the needs of body and soul, he will doubtless be subjected to the sentence that says: “Go, accursed ones, into the eternal fire prepared for the devil and his angels. For I was hungry, and you did not give me food; I was thirsty, and you did not give me drink” (Matt. 25), and what follows. And: “Cursed is the one who does the work of God negligently” (Jer. 48).

XXV. If any senior or abbot is found to be wrathful, he is to be reprimanded until he is corrected. But if he is incurable in this vice, he is to be removed from command of the brothers, since one ought not to become angry, whether justly or unjustly.

XXVI. If anyone slanders his senior, he does not slander the senior but the Lord, for whom the senior performs his work. But if he does this frequently, he is to be cut off from the brotherhood and from the care of the brotherly body. If he repents, his sins are to be forgiven. “The one who secretly slanders his neighbor,” says the Prophet, “him I persecuted” (Ps. 100).

XXVII. If anyone is found to despise his senior in anything, he does not despise a human being but God, and so forth. If anyone does this, let him do penance, and he will be reconciled to his senior. Everything that the senior commands is to be fulfilled according to the Lord’s commandment.

XXVIII. If any brother is found to be negligent toward the monastery’s property, he is to be judged guilty of sacrilege against the sacred treasury. If anyone sees this and fails to assist and correct it on that day, he is to be judged a neglecter and perverter of sacred property. For everyone ought to work and act with greater care toward the monastery’s possessions, as though he himself were lord of all and ruled over everything. Yet again, through excessive humility, he should regard himself as a stranger to them and request from them nothing beyond his daily *paximatia* [bread ration].

XXIX. If anyone does not immediately rise at the voice of the one summoning or inviting him to anything whatsoever, he is guilty of disobedience. Let him ask God for pardon and not presume to repeat the offense. For everyone ought to rise at the first voice of the one inviting him, as though a burning coal had risen upon him. If this obedience, of which we speak, is absent, it is dead [Col. 0993B] and unacceptable before God. “Whatever is not from faith is sin” (Rom. 14). Everything must always be done with joy: “Rejoice in the Lord, you righteous, and praise is always fitting” (Ps. 32). The Apostle likewise says: “Rejoice in the Lord always; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. 4). But if something is offered by us among God’s gifts with sadness, it will not be acceptable before God.

[Col. 0994A] XXX. The community is to assemble in church at three gatherings during the day and an equal number during the night. Three psalms are to be sung at each daytime gathering; twelve, however, are to be sung at the nighttime gatherings, apart from the Mass celebrated at sunrise. Prayers and two readings—one from the Old Testament and the other from the New—are to be given at each nighttime gathering. At these gatherings, namely on Saturday and Sunday, the Mass is to be celebrated until cockcrow; and vigils are to be performed according to what each person’s strength can bear.

XXXI. Whoever does not arrive for the first psalm during the day is not to be admitted to the assembly of the brothers, but afterward he must seek pardon publicly. If he does this frequently, he is to be rebuked until he is corrected. At night, a delay is permitted until the second psalm.

XXXII. On Sundays the Eucharist is always to be received as a remedy for sins. We must approach the body and blood of our Lord Jesus Christ with a pure heart and complete holiness of heart and body. Amen.

---

## RULE AGREED UPON BY THE MONKS (C, S)

### CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

The author of this Rule is uncertain, although the profiteers of sacred antiquity have until now passed it off as the first Rule of Saint Augustine and have even dared to insert it into the older editions of the holy doctor’s works. Today all scholars agree that Saint Augustine wrote no other Rule except one for virgins, which Holstenius presents in the third part of this volume; we shall therefore say more about it in its proper place. Meanwhile, this is a short Rule, containing only nine articles and setting forth certain general precepts concerning the monastic state. It is called the *Rule Agreed Upon by the Monks* for no other reason than that it was promulgated with the common consent of all who were present in that monastery, as we gather from its opening. Its antiquity is sufficiently indicated by the fact that its author habitually cites Holy Scripture according to the ancient Vulgate, not according to Saint Jerome’s version.

## RULE AGREED UPON BY THE MONKS

[Col. 0993]

[Col. 0993C] I. By common decision we have decreed among ourselves what no one thereafter will ever be able to violate.

While we are all residing in the monastery in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, it has pleased us, according to apostolic tradition, to be of one mind and to possess everything in common, as it is written: “Being of one mind in the Lord” (Acts 2). Let no one claim anything as his own; but, as it is written in the Acts of the Apostles: “They held everything in common, and no one said that anything was his own” (ibid.), so it is written for us. Let us therefore hold fast in the Lord to the right of observance and law, and remain in it to the end, because it is written: “Whoever endures to the end will be saved” (Matt. 10).

II. If someone wishes to come to the congregation of the brothers, who appear to be united as one, he must not be ignorant of the Gospel saying: “Let him sell all that he has and distribute it to the needy and the poor” (Matt. 19). And again: “Let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow Christ” (Luke 9). He must not deliberate in his heart about food, clothing, or the other things necessary for the body, since the Lord himself warns and says in the Gospel: “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What will you eat?’ or, ‘What will you wear?’ For the nations think about these things. Your Father knows that you need all of them. Seek the kingdom of God and his righteousness, and all these things will be supplied to you” (Matt. 6).

III. Nevertheless, before he decides to remain in the monastery, he must test the purpose and example of the brothers, and he himself must be tested in his entire way of life by the one who is senior and by the others consenting, in accordance with what the Prophet teaches and admonishes when he says: “Do not quickly approve a friend.”

IV. But if it happens that someone is taken away from the monastery for any necessary reason, he must not even conceive in his mind of taking with him any of all the things that were in the monastery—whether something he had once brought with him or something he acquired with the brothers—because it is written: “A man changeable in speech will fall into evils” (Prov. 13). And again, he must not entice any of the brothers to leave with him, lest he be judged more a destroyer than a builder of the monastery, in accordance with what is written: “Whoever is not with me is against me, and whoever does not gather with me scatters” (Matt. 12). Whoever, enticed by someone, wishes to depart from the monastery must either rebuke the one who entices him or inform the abbot. Nothing of what we have decreed in common is to be withheld from the abbot, because it is written: “Let many be at peace with you, but let one of a thousand be your counselor” (Ecclus. 6).

V. The things that are written here must be observed continually and with the utmost care, by the abbot down to all the brothers. If anyone has heard teaching from someone other than that which he received in the monastery from the person to whom he entrusted himself, he must either not accept it or not conceal it from the teacher, because it is written: “Everything that is revealed is light” (Eph. 5). If the teaching is good, it is to be praised; if it is wrong, it is to be rejected.

VI. Concerning the brothers who remain in unity: if one suddenly quarrels against another once, let him be permitted to plead his case according to the Gospel. But if he refuses to correct himself, the one who has suffered the insult must, after the first or second correction, report the matter to the abbot if he has not recalled the insolent man, lest through silence both he and his brother perish. As the Prophet says: “Whoever conceals hostility devises deceit” (Prov. 26).

VII. But if, as commonly happens, a sudden attack or hostility arises, so that it is impossible for the brothers to flee together because of the pursuit of enemies, [Col. 0995C] and afterward, with God’s favor, they escape and are able to reach the place where they know the abbot to be, they must hasten to him like sons to their father. In no way can those whom divine charity has joined together be separated, because it is established that “perfect love drives out fear” (1 John 4).

VIII. If anyone, for the necessary reason mentioned above, retains what he has carried away from the monastery, he must bring it to the place where his abbot is, because he cannot properly retain what belongs to everyone by agreement and has in any case been consecrated to God. But if he has considered retaining some of these things, he appears to contradict the Apostle, who says: “Owe no one anything except to love one another” (Rom. 13).

IX. Therefore all the brothers are to observe and subscribe to everything contained in this book, because they desire to be one in the Lord. These provisions, however, are made for those who are known to be steadfast in all things.

---

## TO THE READER

[Col. 0996]

To the *Rule Agreed Upon by the Monks*, which the profiteers of sacred antiquity have until now passed off as the Rule of Saint Augustine, I append another fragment of an ancient Rule, which likewise lies hidden under Augustine’s name, but which learned and highly respected men have long since rightly attributed to someone else. For it is certain that Augustine wrote only one Rule, and that for virgins; we present it below in its proper place. The third Rule, *On the Eremitical Life for a Sister*, is clearly much more distant from Augustine’s age and style; indeed, we know with certainty that it belongs to Blessed Aelred of Rievaulx, abbot in England, who lived around the year 1150. May fortune grant that the author or age of this fragment also become known through more certain evidence.

[Col. 0995]

## [ANOTHER RULE BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR (C, S)]

### CRITICAL OBSERVATION ON THE FOLLOWING RULE

What we said concerning the preceding Rule can also be applied to this one, because its author is uncertain and it is wrongly attributed to Saint Augustine as his second Rule. It contains only five articles. The first is concerned for the most part with the arrangement of the divine office, where the author distinguishes Vespers from the lighting service, assigning to the latter one psalm and one responsory, three antiphons, and three readings. This distribution of the divine office appears to have been taken from the Rules of Saint Caesarius and Saint Aurelian. Hence the most reverend Calmet believes, in his *Critical Observations*, that this Rule was written for certain monasteries of Gaul or Spain situated near the Mediterranean Sea. In the meantime, I wish to note that the service called *lucernarium* corresponds in time to our Vespers, and is not to be understood as Compline, which was instituted by Saint Benedict as the completion of the entire divine office. For that reason, after it had been completed, no one in Benedictine monasteries dared to speak or read publicly; yet according to the Rule the monks gathered together after the *lucernarium* and listened to public readings.

## ANOTHER RULE BY AN UNKNOWN AUTHOR

[Col. 0995]

[Col. 0995D] I. Above all, dearest brothers, let God be loved (Deut. 6); then one’s neighbor (Matt. 18), because these commandments have been given to us as the principal ones. We describe how it is proper for us to pray and sing the psalms: namely, at Matins, Psalms 3, 62, 6, and 88 are to be said, with the appropriate antiphons, verses, and responsories. At Prime and Terce, their appointed psalms are to be said, with two antiphons and two readings. Likewise, at Sext and None, their appointed psalms are to be said, with the appropriate responsories and antiphons. The same is to be observed at Vespers and Compline. At the *lucernarium*, one psalm, one responsory, three antiphons, and three readings are to be given. At the proper time after the *lucernarium*, with everyone seated, the readings are to be read. At the night offices, in November, December, January, and February, there are to be twelve antiphons, six psalms, and three readings; in March, April, September, and October, ten antiphons, five psalms, and three readings; in May, [Col. 0997A] June, July, and August, eight antiphons, four psalms, and two readings.

II. Let them work from morning until Sext, and from Sext until None let them devote themselves to reading; at None they are to return the books. After they have refreshed themselves, whether in the garden or wherever necessary, let them work until the hour of the *lucernarium*. Let no one claim anything as his own, whether clothing or anything else, for we desire to live the apostolic life (Acts 2 and 4). Let no one do anything while murmuring, lest he perish under the same judgment as the murmurers. Let them obey faithfully; after God, let them honor their father; let them show deference to their superior, as is fitting for saints. While seated at table, let them keep silent and listen to the reading. If anything is needed, let their superior attend to it. On Saturday and Sunday, as is customary, those who wish may receive wine.

III. If there is need for anyone to be sent on an errand, let two go. Let no one eat or drink outside the monastery without permission, for this does not belong to the discipline of the monastery. If brothers are sent to sell the monastery’s products, let them take careful precautions not to do anything contrary to the commandment, knowing that they provoke the Lord in his holy ones. If they buy anything necessary for the monastery, let them act carefully and faithfully, as servants of God.

IV. There must be no idle word among them. In the morning let them sit down to their work; after the prayer of Terce let them go to their work. Let them not stand about weaving stories, unless perhaps something is said for the benefit of the soul; while seated at their work, let them keep silent, unless the needs of the work should require someone to speak.

V. If anyone, with all his strength and with God’s mercy assisting him, does not strive to fulfill these things but despises them with a rebellious mind, then, after being admonished once and again, if he does not reform, let him know that he is subject to the discipline of the monastery, as is proper. But if his age is such that this is appropriate, he will also be beaten. Faithfully and devoutly observing these things in the name of Christ, you will make progress, and our joy at your salvation will be no small one. These are the things that we command you to observe, having been established in the monastery.

[Col. 0997]

## [THE ANCIENT ROMAN ORDER (C, S)]

### ADMONITION CONCERNING THE FOLLOWING ROMAN ORDER

[Col. 0997]

I wish to append to the exposition of the ancient Roman Calendar and the Gallican Liturgy [Note: [Col. 0997] That is, the minor works prefixed to the Ancient Order printed here in Martène’s *Thesaurus*, from which we reproduced it. In that Order we were obliged to preserve the manuscript’s orthography and syntax. ED.] an ancient Roman Order adapted for the use of monasteries approximately a thousand years ago. Its antiquity is demonstrated not only by the character of the Morbach manuscript, from which we have taken it—a script representing at least nine hundred years—but also by the various rites prescribed in it, which have long since become obsolete both in the Roman Church and in the monasteries of Gaul, where it appears to have been in use.

First among these is the prescription that the feast of the Conception of the Blessed Virgin—by which, when the angel announced it, she received the incarnate Word of God in her womb—be celebrated one week before the Lord’s Nativity. This rite is commended by the Tenth Council of Toledo, held in 656, as already observed in various parts of the world, and it has been retained to the present day by the Churches of Milan and Toledo. The order of the sacred books to be read during the nocturnal vigils likewise breathes great antiquity: it prescribes that the prophets, rather than the Apostles’ epistles, be read after the Epiphany. We found this same practice prescribed in another Morbach manuscript at least a thousand years old. We judge the rite of announcing the coming feasts by the deacon after Communion to reflect the same antiquity; nowhere else have we encountered it prescribed.

Moreover, although many noteworthy things appear in this Order, one deserves particularly careful consideration: it prescribes that the prayers to be said after the oblation be recited secretly, with no one else hearing them. This passage [Col. 0998C] ought by itself to suffice to refute certain lovers of novelties who, contrary to the custom of the universal Roman Church, on their own authority recite the entire Mass, the secret prayers, and the Canon in the same tone of voice—that is, aloud. For although they reply that the ancient authors prescribe that the secrets and the Canon be recited silently, and claim that “silence” in those authors is opposed only to singing, not to speaking aloud, they are wholly proved false, leaving them no further place of escape, since a thousand years ago in the Roman Church and in other churches following its Order these things were said *secretly, with no one else hearing them*.

## THE ANCIENT ROMAN ORDER ADAPTED FOR THE USE OF MONASTERIES APPROXIMATELY A THOUSAND YEARS AGO, FROM THE MORBACH MANUSCRIPT

In the name of the Most High God begins the brief outline of the ecclesiastical order: how, in monasteries, those who faithfully serve the Lord are to celebrate, with the Lord’s help, the solemnities of the Mass, the birthdays of the saints, and the divine offices throughout the yearly cycle, by day and by night, both according to the authority of the Catholic and Apostolic Roman Church and according to the arrangement of the Rule of Saint Benedict, as it was handed down in the holy Roman Church by wise and venerable Fathers.

[Col. 0999A] First, during the Advent of the Lord, they begin to celebrate the entire divine office from the first of December. On that very night they begin to read the prophet Isaiah at the vigils, continuing until the Lord’s Nativity; the readings are always begun again from the beginning of the book. Then, one week before the Lord’s Nativity, they begin to sing concerning the Conception of Saint Mary.

[Note: [Col. 0999D] This passage is to be understood of the active conception of the Blessed Virgin, by which she conceived the divine Word in her womb through the working of the Holy Spirit.]

During that week, on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday, they hold public stations; everyone is to fast; and the solemnities of the Mass, together with the entire divine office belonging to that Order, are celebrated. On that Saturday, priests and the other ministers of the Church are ordained if necessary. But if the vigils of the Lord’s Nativity should also fall on the preceding Saturday, all the celebration and ordination mentioned above are completed on that Saturday.

[Col. 0999B] In the ordination of priests, however, no one is ordained outside the four seasons of the year. The first is spring, which is the first week of the first month, March—provided that this week falls within Lent. Then comes the summer season, in the fourth month, June, which follows the first week after Pentecost. The third is the autumn season, the seventh month, September, observed in the third week of that month. After this comes the fourth season, winter, which is the tenth month, December, as we said above. This is the first week before the Lord’s Nativity, during which, as we said, the celebrations take place on Wednesday, Friday, and Saturday.

The deeds [Note: [Col. 0999D] The Cassinese monks formerly commemorated Saint Eugenia on the third day before the Ides of September, together with Saints Protus and Hyacinth.] of Saint Eugenia, or her commemoration, are celebrated only at the vigils on the day before the Lord’s Nativity. At Matins on that preceding day, her Mass is sung and celebrated at the third hour. On that very day, unless it happens to be a Sunday, everyone is to keep the public fast; at the ninth hour they celebrate the Mass of the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, and the *Alleluia* is not sung. Whenever they fast and celebrate Mass at the ninth hour, neither “Glory to God in the highest” nor the *Alleluia* is sung.

On the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity, when night comes, the monks in the monasteries rest for a little while. Then, rising early, they celebrate as is fitting for the vigil of the Lord: that is, after completing nine psalms with antiphons, or nine readings from homilies of Saint Augustine, Pope Leo, or Saint Gregory, with responsories, they conclude the vigil; then Matins follows with antiphons.

After Matins has been completed, they prepare themselves to celebrate Mass; and [Note: [Col. 0999D] This clearly indicates that the first Mass on the Lord’s Nativity was celebrated at the first crowing of the cock, around midnight. We have found this prescribed in several ancient Sacramentaries and have demonstrated it in our book *On the Ancient Discipline of the Church in the Celebration of the Divine Offices*, p. 88.] as soon as the cock has crowed, they immediately enter the Mass with the entire dignity and order of the priests. When the solemnity of the Mass has been completed, everyone receives Communion, and during that night they sing both “Glory to God in the highest” and the *Alleluia* at the Mass.

Then, as soon as daylight appears, they proceed to another church, and another Mass is celebrated in the same way as the first.

[Note: [Col. 1000D] From this you may infer that the three Masses on the Lord’s Nativity were celebrated not in one church but in different churches, as we have proved elsewhere.]

Likewise, at the appropriate hour of the day, they proceed again to a church and celebrate the Mass of the holy Nativity. One is celebrated after the cock has crowed, another in the morning at Prime, and a third during the day, as is customary, in honor of the Holy Trinity. Saint Gregory speaks of this in his homilies, saying: “Because today we are going to celebrate the solemnities of the Mass three times, so we too ought likewise to celebrate the solemnities of the Lord’s Nativity with the number of Masses belonging to the Trinity.”

[Col. 1000B] The manner or order for carrying out the solemnities of the Mass, both on this day and on all the principal feasts, appears to be as follows. When the hour has approached for entering upon the Masses, the priests and levites enter the sacristy and put on the vestments in which they are to celebrate the Masses. They arrange the offerings reverently in their proper place according to their orders, as is customary, and wash their hands again.

Likewise, in a monastery into which women do not enter, after the priest has first washed his hands, the priests enter the sacristy with the levites and take the offerings. They then go out from the sacristy, and the offerings are placed upon the altar while the brothers sing the offertory. Then the priest approaches the altar, takes his own offerings, raises his eyes and hands with them toward heaven, prays to the Lord, and places them upon the altar. He offers the wine in the same way.

The deacons go behind the priests and take their places in order. The subdeacons walk behind the altar and stand in their proper order. The priests stand in their appointed order before the altar. Then the priest asks the other priests, on his right and left, to pray for him; bowing his face toward the ground, he says the prayer [Col. 1000C] secretly, so that no one else hears him, until he comes to the words “World without end,” at which all say, “Amen.”

[Note: [Col. 1000D] This passage strikingly confirms what we said in book I of Ancient Church Rites, chap. 4, art. 8, no. 5, concerning the secrets and canon of the Mass being pronounced in silence.]

Immediately he says, “The Lord be with you.” Then he says, “Lift up your hearts.” Then: “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God,” and he proceeds into the Preface, so that he may be heard by nearly everyone. When he comes to the words “Let the Dominations adore,” all the priests and [Col. 1000D] levites bow their faces to the ground. When he reaches the words “Confessing with humble devotion, saying: Holy,” the deacons, clergy, and all the people bow again.

[Col. 1001A] While all proclaim “Holy” with great reverence and trembling, the priest begins the Canon softly, in a different voice. The priests, deacons, and subdeacons themselves remain bowed until the place where they say, “We also, sinners”; and as soon as he reaches the words “deign to regard with a favorable and serene countenance,” the priest, with bowed head, humbly supplicates before the altar until he says, “that all who shall partake of this altar.”

When the subdeacons have risen, one of them comes and receives the paten from the acolyte. He returns to the place where he had been standing and holds it before his breast until the priest has said, “All honor and glory.” When the priest reaches the words “through him and with him,” he lifts his own offerings from the altar and puts them into the mouth of the chalice, which the deacon holds, [Col. 1001B] raising it slightly until he has said, “World without end. Amen.”

The priests and deacons remain bowed until this point, except for the deacon who raises the chalice. The subdeacon holding the paten hands it to the deacon at the very words “all honor and glory.” The deacon holds it until the Lord’s Prayer has been completed and then hands it to the priest.

After the Lord’s Prayer and the prayer that follows it, the priest takes the offerings and places them on the paten. He breaks off a small portion of the offering, puts it into the chalice, making the sign of the cross three times, and says, “The peace of the Lord be always with you.” The people then make peace.

After this, if necessary, the priests break the offerings upon the altar. The deacons, near the altar, break the offerings while the subdeacon holds the paten [Col. 1001C] before them, while the brothers sing “Lamb of God.”

[Note: [Col. 1001D] From this you may conclude that, in former times, the offerings consecrated for the communion of the people were not small but very large, and that the deacons broke them into many pieces.]

Then the priests and levites receive communion in their proper order. Afterward the deacon takes the chalice on the right side of the altar, raises it in his hands, and announces the saints’ feasts occurring during the coming week, saying: “On the coming [weekday] is the feast of Saint Mary,” or “of a confessor,” or “of whichever saint’s feast occurs,” according to the martyrology. Everyone responds, “Thanks be to God.”

After this, while the communion antiphon is being sung and everyone is receiving communion, the priest gives the prayer, and the deacon says, “Go, the Mass is ended.” Everyone responds, “Thanks be to God,” and the rite is complete.

Afterward the priest returns to the sacristy with the ministers of the church, or with all the ornaments, just as he had gone out before; he removes the vestments in which he has celebrated the solemnities of the Mass, and everything is concluded.

After the Nativity of the Lord and until the octave, apart from the feasts of the saints, the entire divine office, both by day and by night, is to be sung from the liturgy of the day of the Lord’s Nativity. During the octave of the Lord, the entire divine office, by night and by day, is observed in every respect according to the order followed at the Lord’s Nativity. Thereafter, until the Epiphany, except on Sundays and the feasts of the saints, the offices of ordinary weekdays are sung.

On the eve of the Epiphany they hold a public fast, celebrate Mass at the ninth hour, and enter at midnight for the vigils. They sing psalms, lessons, and responsories for that day, dealing only with the gifts of the Magi and the baptism. The wedding at Cana in Galilee is celebrated on the octave of the Epiphany. Throughout the entire week until the octave of the Epiphany these things are sung. The Mass of the Epiphany follows the order described above for the Nativity of the Lord.

Then, on the second day of the month of February—that is, the fourth day before the Nones of that month—the Purification of Blessed Mary is celebrated with great splendor and many lights burning. This is when she presented the Lord Jesus Christ in the Temple, and blessed Simeon received him in his arms and blessed God.

[Note: [Col. 1001D] That the faithful formerly observed a fast on the vigil of the Epiphany was demonstrated in a separate little book by John Des Lions, dean of the church of Senlis, against the profane superstitions of certain people who spend this day drinking.]

After the Nativity of the Lord, until fifteen [Col. 1002B] days before the beginning of Lent, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, and Daniel, together with the twelve minor prophets and their expositions, are read. The letters of the Apostle Paul are read at all times among the later lessons at the Sunday vigils. The treatises of Saint Jerome, Saint Ambrose, and the other Fathers are read as the order requires.

In the spring season—that is, beginning fifteen days before Lent—the five books of Moses, together with Joshua, Judges, and Ruth, are read until fifteen days before Easter. From that point the book of the prophet Isaiah, the Lamentations of Jeremiah, Hosea, and Zechariah are read, insofar as they are appropriate to the passion of Christ. During the days of Easter, the letters of the apostles, the Acts, and the Apocalypse are read until Pentecost. From Pentecost onward, the books of Kings and Chronicles, [Col. 1002C] then the books of Solomon, Job, Tobit, Judith, Esther, and Maccabees are read until the Kalends of December.

On the vigils of all the apostles and of the other saints whose feasts are celebrated, everyone fasts. At the ninth hour, in anticipation of their feast, the solemnities of Mass are celebrated without “Glory to God in the highest” and without “Alleluia.” That night, at the vigils, their passions or deeds are read.

If their feast falls on a Sunday, whether during Advent or at any other time, the psalms are sung together with their passions or deeds, with responsories or antiphons appropriate to them. If their deeds are too brief to provide nine lessons, they are read only in the final three lessons. Their octave is celebrated with its own responsories or antiphons and with the solemnities of Mass, just as their feast is celebrated on the first day.

If the feast of another saint falls during their octave, their octave is celebrated on the preceding day, by authority of the holy Rule.

At all times, on Sundays, a lesson from the holy Gospel is read according to the season; the hymn “Te Deum laudamus” follows, together with a verse and “Kyrie eleison,” and the Vigils conclude. At the Sunday morning Lauds, except during Lent, the psalms are to be sung with “Alleluia.” One week before the Nativity of the Lord, they begin the celebration of the conception of Blessed Mary.

This, however, which we ought to have written above concerning the seventieth day before Easter, they celebrate when the Sunday of Septuagesima begins. They do this out of reverence for so great a feast, and for the instruction of the people, so that by counting the days they may recognize that the holy day of Easter is approaching. Let each person prepare himself according to his devotion and strength, so that he may reach that holy day with trembling and reverence, his body chastened and his heart pure.

Not only Septuagesima but also Sexagesima, Quinquagesima, Quadragesima, the thirtieth, twentieth, tenth, and octave are always celebrated in this order, so that the more clearly they recognize that [Col. 1003B] the holy day of Easter, our redemption, is approaching, the more earnestly they may abstain from every defilement of the flesh and from impurity, so that they may be worthy to receive the body and blood of the Lord.

Monks and devout Romans, or good Christians, begin at Quinquagesima; country people and the rest of the common folk begin at Quadragesima.

The first fast is publicly observed on the fourth and sixth days after Quinquagesima—that is, one week before Lent. Then, in the first week of Lent, they again hold public stations on the fourth and sixth days and on Saturday, and the fast concludes on that Saturday with twelve lessons. If that Saturday falls in the month of March, they ordain priests.

If it falls in another week, or in the third week, when the bishop has determined it, they again hold the station on the fourth and sixth days and on Saturday, with twelve lessons as before; those who are to be ordained are ordained.

From the beginning of Quinquagesima until the fifteenth day before Easter, as we have already said, the Heptateuch is read at the vigils and responsories are sung from it. If there are too few responsories from it, Lenten responsories are sung.

At Sunday morning Lauds, beginning with Lent, they sing “Have mercy on me, O God.” Then Psalm 117 follows, with antiphons drawn both from the Prophets and from the Gospel. Beginning fifteen days before Easter, they begin to celebrate lessons, responsories, and antiphons with verses concerning the passion of the Lord.

On the fifth feria [Thursday] before Easter—that is, the Lord’s Supper—no introit antiphon is sung at Mass; the Apostle and the Gospel are not read; no responsory is sung; the priest does not give the greeting “The Lord be with you”; and they do not make peace until Holy Saturday. They enter upon the Masses in silence.

That night, during the vigil of Good Friday—that is, on the sixth day—“Glory” and “Kyrie eleison” are not sung, nor is the bell rung, until the vigils of Holy Saturday.

On Good Friday, which is the sixth day and the day of the Lord’s passion, everyone gathers in the church at the ninth hour. Two lessons are read, which are recorded in the capitulary or sacramentary, together with their responses; the passion of the Lord according to John is read; and the priest says the prayers recorded in the sacramentary.

After each prayer the deacon admonishes everyone. He says, “Let us bend our knees,” and everyone prostrates himself on the ground with tears and contrition of heart. When the prayer has been made, the deacon again admonishes them to rise, saying, “Arise.”

After these prayers have been completed, the priest says, “Let us pray,” and says the prayer “Instructed by saving commandments,” together with the Lord’s Prayer. The prayer “Deliver us, we beseech you, O Lord” follows.

The deacon takes the body and blood of the Lord, which had remained from the preceding day, the day of the Lord’s Supper, and had been consecrated, and places them upon the altar. Everyone receives the body and blood of the Lord [Col. 1004B] in silence, singing nothing.

That night no light is lit in the church; it is concealed so that it may not be seen by everyone, until Saturday. When these things have been completed, they enter upon Vespers. That night all the devout monks and venerable religious men abstain from every bodily luxury, taking no food except bread and water mixed with vinegar. Whoever is given the strength by the Lord passes without food until the vigil of Easter on Holy Saturday; at the ninth hour of the day they enter upon the vigils.

[Note: [Col. 1003D] The Council in Trullo supports this vow in canon 89: “The faithful ought to spend the saving day of the Passion in fasting, prayer, and contrition of heart, and to fast until midnight of the Great Sabbath.” The Rule of the Master, [Col. 1004D] chapter 58, likewise decrees that anyone—apart from infants, the sick, and the elderly—who wishes to taste any food on Good Friday is to be deprived of the blessing bestowed upon food.]

First the priests, together with the deacons, put on the vestments in which the vigils are celebrated. The levites alone then come out of the sacristy with the subdeacons, walking two by two closely beside one another, without lights being lit, while the brothers sing the litany.

When they have reached the altar, they stand in their proper order. The person who is to bless the candle stands in the middle, asks them to pray for him, and makes the sign of the cross over the candle. He receives from the subdeacon the light that had been hidden on Good Friday, lights the candle, and says, “The Lord be with you.” Everyone responds, “And with your spirit.”

Then he says, “Let us pray,” and says the first prayer. Then he says, “The Lord be with you.” Everyone responds, “And with your spirit.” Again he says, “Lift up your hearts.” They respond, “We have them with the Lord.” Again he says, “Let us give thanks to the Lord our God.” They respond, “It is worthy and just.” Everything is done as recorded in the sacramentary.

After the candle has been blessed, they return to the sacristy. Then the priests come out of the sacristy with the deacons, in their proper orders, carrying candles lit from that light, together with censers of incense. The litany is sung again. When it has been completed, the priest gives the prayer behind the altar, as is customary, while they stand.

The priests sit in their proper order, and they enter for the reading. After each lesson the priest gives the prayer, as recorded in the sacramentary. When the lessons, their canticles, and their blessings have been completed, all the ministers of the church return to the sacristy with their candles lit, [Col. 1005A] awaiting the hour at which they must enter for the Masses.

When a star appears in the sky, they immediately begin the litany for the third time and come out of the sacristy as before, with lit candles and censers. When the litany has been completed, the abbot or the priest who is celebrating the Mass begins, “Glory to God in the highest.” When this is finished, the lesson from the Apostle is read, and “Alleluia” and “The Lord reigns” are sung. A tract may be sung as desired, and the Gospel lesson is read, either by the bishop or by the priest.

At Communion, “Lamb of God” is sung, and the entire solemnity of the Mass is completed in the same order as on the other Sundays. During these seven days of Easter, and in the entire divine office, everything is done as on the holy day of Easter, except that the psalm appointed for each day is always sung with “Alleluia.”

Until the fiftieth day after Easter, which is Pentecost, all psalms, responsories with their verses, and antiphons are to be sung with “Alleluia.” On the Ascension of the Lord, the entire divine office relating to that day is celebrated as on the other Sundays. Responsories and antiphons concerning the Ascension of the Lord are sung until Pentecost Saturday.

On Pentecost Saturday everyone fasts, and the entire divine office, including both the lessons and the baptism, is celebrated in the order described for Holy Saturday. Beginning at the seventh hour, they enter upon the vigils and the solemnities of the Mass, so that everything may be completed when the ninth hour of the day has ended.

The holy day of Pentecost is celebrated in the same way as the holy day of Easter. During the week immediately following Pentecost, they fast on the fourth and sixth days and on Saturday, and the solemnities of the Mass and the entire office are celebrated as recorded in the sacramentary.

The octave of Pentecost is celebrated in the same way as the preceding Sunday. After these days, throughout the course of the year until Advent, except on the feasts of the saints or the commemorations mentioned above, the psalms, responsories, antiphons, and morning and evening Lauds are sung from the offices of ordinary weekdays.

The office for the dead is sung at the vigils, and psalms and lessons with responsories or antiphons are sung at morning Lauds without “Alleluia.” At their Masses neither “Glory to God in the highest” nor “Alleluia” is sung, and everything is concluded.

# TABLE OF CONTENTS OF THIS VOLUME

## POPE JOHN II

Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*, 9.

### LETTERS, 1

Letter of King Athalaric to John.—Confirmation of the senatorial decree issued against the Simoniacs. Ibid.

Letter of Cassiodorus to John.—After being appointed prefect of the praetorium by the king, he implores the pontiff’s prayers to God for good governance, 13.

Letter of the Emperor Justinian to John, 14.

Letter of John to Justinian.—He praises the outstanding piety of the Catholic emperor and the religious devotion with which he honored the apostolic see. He asks Augustus to recall, with every effort, those whom he knew to be straying from the right path of the Catholic faith, 17.

Letter of John to the senators.—He confirms the faith concerning Christ’s divinity and incarnation and warns that the Acoemete monks are to be avoided, 20.

Letter of John to the bishops of Gaul.—He deprived Contumeliosus, a bishop of Gaul, of his episcopate and sent him back to a monastery for penance; he commends his Church to Caesarius of Arles, 24.

Letter of John to the priests and deacons of Contumeliosus, 24.

Letter of John to Caesarius of Arles, 25.

Letter of the African bishops to John.—They consult the pontiff about certain doubts, ibid.

Letter of John to Bishop Valerius.—He teaches that Christ is equal to the Father according to the nature of his divinity but lower according to his human nature, 27.

Canons attributed to John, 28.

## POPE AGAPETUS I

Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*, 31.

Letter of Justinian to Agapetus.—Following the custom of his ancestors, he presents his profession of faith to the newly elected Roman pontiff, ibid.

### LETTERS OF AGAPETUS, 35

First letter of Agapetus, to Justinian.—He confirms Justinian’s statement of faith, 37.

Formerly Letter IV, to the same.—He thanks Justinian for congratulating him on his election to the pontificate; he exhorts him to defend the Catholic faith; he replies that fallen bishops cannot be received with their honors, 38.

First copy of Justinian’s prayers to Agapetus, 41.

Second confession of faith presented by Justinian to Agapetus, 42.

Formerly Letter II, to the African bishops.—He congratulates them on having escaped from the hands of heretics and replies to the matters on which they had consulted John, 43.

Formerly Letter III, to Reparatus.—Agapetus gives thanks because Reparatus had congratulated him on his election, while also indicating that he had answered his consultations and would provide the same through legates. Meanwhile, he urges him to ensure that what he has written in defense of the Catholic faith is circulated, 45.

Formerly Letter VI, to Caesarius.—Ecclesiastical estates are not to be alienated under any title, ibid.

Formerly Letter VII, to the same.—Concerning Contumeliosus, after he had appealed to the apostolic see, 46.

Interpretation of the synodal letter, 48.

Memorial presented to Agapetus by the monks, 50.

Memorial of the Eastern bishops, 67.

Formerly Letter V, to Anthimus.—Agapetus shows that in Christ there are two perfect natures, 77.

## POPE SILVERIUS

Notice from the *Liber Pontificalis*, 79.

### LETTERS OF SILVERIUS, 85

First letter, to Vigilius the false pope.—Silverius reproaches Vigilius for ambition regarding the apostolic see and for the crime of simony, and anathematizes him, ibid.

Letter of Amator of Autun to Silverius.—To relieve the hardship of his exile, he sends the pontiff small gifts, 86.

Second letter, to Amator.—Silverius praises Amator’s charity and explains what was done against him. False witnesses against a bishop are not to be admitted, ibid.
